He nodded, setting down the cup with exaggerated care. "I suppose we should review them together."

They walked in silence through corridors lined with awards and commendations—recognition of their work in what the media called "consciousness preservation." The cultural evolution that had followed their breakthrough had been profound. Death was no longer an ending, merely a transition. Your body might fail, but your mind—your essential self—could continue indefinitely, transferred to fresh biological hosts or even synthetic substrates.

Except when it couldn't.

DR. ARJUN HOLLAND was waiting in the medical wing, his dark eyes troubled. Felix had recruited him from Highpoint City twenty years ago, impressed by his pioneering work in theoretical modeling of neural degradation. Now that expertise was being turned on Felix himself.

"Sit down, Felix," Arjun said quietly, gesturing to a chair facing the holographic display. "I'm going to be direct with you because I respect you too much to do otherwise."

The scans appeared in the air between them—three-dimensional maps of Felix's neural architecture rendered in glowing detail. Even to Felix's trained eye, the problem was obvious. Dark patches spread through regions that should have blazed with activity. The connections were fraying, dissolving like old photographs left too long in sunlight.

"Cascade neural entropy," Arjun said. "We've been tracking it for five years now, but it's accelerating. Your consciousness mapping from last month showed coherence degradation of forty percent. This week it's at fifty-eight percent."

Felix felt his chest tighten. "The backup—"

"Would capture a fragmentary version of you at best. And each subsequent backup degrades further. It's like trying to photocopy a photocopy endlessly. Eventually, the image becomes unrecognizable." Arjun paused, his professional composure cracking. "Felix, I'm sorry. We've kept this quiet—there are others, not many, but you're not alone. The technology works, but not forever. The human mind wasn't designed for infinite iteration."

"How long?" Felix managed.

"Without transfer? Your biological substrate is still healthy. You could have forty, maybe fifty years of normal life. But the consciousness backup system—that window is closing. Another month, perhaps two, before the degradation makes transfer impossible."

Valentina's hand found Felix's shoulder. "We should have told you sooner. We've been running every test, trying every experimental protocol. But the pattern is consistent. After a certain number of transfers—for you it's been nine—the neural architecture loses its ability to maintain coherence during the mapping process."

FELIX WALKED the streets of Westbrook for hours after leaving the medical wing, his mind churning. The city had been rebuilt three times in his lifetime, each iteration more magnificent than the last. Spires of bioplas and living metal reached toward the sky, monuments to humanity's triumph over limitation. 

Except it wasn't a triumph. It was a delay.

He found himself at the transit hub, staring at the departure schedules. The quantum-tunnel ships could reach any of the colony worlds in weeks rather than the decades the old light-speed vessels required. Springfield, Dravonia. Thornhill, Thandor. Highpoint City on its distant moon. Humanity had spread across dozens of systems, each colony developing its own culture, its own approach to the challenges of existence.

His personal comm chimed. Grace Rogers, his ex-wife from his fourth marriage, nearly a century ago. They'd parted amicably when she'd decided to join a colony mission to Thornhill. He hadn't spoken to her in seventy years.

"Felix," her recorded message began, her face older than he remembered but still warm, "I heard about your diagnosis. I'm sorry. I wanted you to know—we've been working on something different here. No consciousness transfer, no digital immortality. Just... life. Real life, with real endings. It's terrifying and beautiful and I think you'd understand it now in a way you couldn't before. There's a transport leaving next month. Come see what we've built."

He played the message three times, studying her face. There was something there he'd forgotten—a vitality, an intensity that came from knowing time was precious.

"We're going to cause a panic," she said without preamble. "Two hundred years of telling people they're functionally immortal, and now we have to explain that it's more like... what? A thousand years? Fifteen hundred if you're lucky?"

"It's still more than we used to have," Felix offered.

Felix settled into a chair, feeling every one of his years. "What if that's not the worst outcome? What if knowing we have limits is what makes us human?"

Samir was young—barely a hundred—and brilliant, one of the new generation of researchers who'd never known a world without the promise of indefinite existence.

"Director Stanley, I heard about your diagnosis. I wanted to say—" He paused, struggling for words. "I wanted to say that your work changed everything. You gave us the future."

Felix looked at the young man's earnest face. "Did I? Or did I just give you a very long present?"

"Never mind." Felix pulled up a file he'd been reviewing—preliminary data from a radical new project that had been proposed by researchers in Highpoint City. "Tell me about the Prometheus Initiative."

Samir's eyes lit up. "It's ambitious. Maybe impossible. The team wants to develop a faster-than-light consciousness transmission system. Instead of physically transporting people between colonies, we'd beam their neural patterns at superluminal speeds. You could visit any colony world and be back for dinner. But—"

"But it's untested. The theoretical modeling suggests it might work, but there's no way to know without a human trial. And no one wants to risk their consciousness—their immortal consciousness—on an untested system."

"Exactly." Samir hesitated. "They've been looking for a volunteer for three years. The ship is built. The receiving stations are ready. But who would take that risk when they have eternity to wait for more testing?"

Felix pulled up the technical specifications. The mathematics was elegant, the engineering sound as far as anyone could tell. But there were unknowns—quantum effects that couldn't be predicted, potential degradation during transmission that might fragment a consciousness beyond recovery.

"Someone whose eternity just got a lot shorter," Felix said quietly.

THAT EVENING, Felix stood in his apartment overlooking Westbrook's glittering skyline. The city never slept anymore—why would it, when its citizens had endless time? But somewhere beyond those lights, beyond the comfortable certainty of this world, Grace and others had chosen something different.

He thought about his nine previous transfers, each one a death and rebirth he'd barely noticed. He'd been so focused on the continuation, on the preservation of his essential self, that he'd forgotten to ask whether that self was worth preserving. What had he done with his centuries? Built systems, refined protocols, made existence safer and longer for everyone.

But when was the last time he'd taken a risk? When was the last time anything had felt truly urgent, truly important?

His comm chimed again. Valentina.

"The Prometheus team just sent an urgent request. They've detected an anomaly in the receiving station at Thornhill—something that could be a breakthrough or could be a critical flaw. They need someone to make the transmission run now, while the conditions are right, or wait another decade for the alignment to repeat."

"They still don't have a volunteer."

"No. And Felix—Grace is leading the receiving team. She specifically requested that I pass that information along."

Felix looked at his reflection in the window. The tremor in his hands was worse tonight. In a month, maybe two, the degradation would progress beyond the point where even a standard transfer would be possible. He could live out his remaining decades in this aging biological substrate, comfortable and safe and slowly fading.

Or he could take one last risk.

THE PROMETHEUS facility occupied an entire district on the outskirts of Westbrook. Felix toured it the next morning with Samir and the project lead, Ruth Clark, a neuroengineer who'd spent fifty years developing the superluminal transmission protocols.

"The theoretical modeling is sound," Ruth explained as they walked through the transmission chamber. "But theory and practice are different things. The consciousness pattern has to be disassembled at the quantum level, transmitted faster than light, and perfectly reconstructed at the other end. Any error, any degradation—"

"I understand the risks," Felix interrupted. "When can we begin?"

Ruth stopped walking. "You're volunteering?"

"I'm dying anyway. Slowly, but certainly. This way, if it works, I contribute something meaningful. If it fails—well, I was going to lose myself eventually regardless."

"There's a significant chance you'll arrive fragmented," Ruth warned. "We might reconstruct only part of your consciousness. You might not be... you anymore."

Felix thought about the scans showing his neural degradation, the dark patches spreading through his mind. "I'm already not entirely me. At least this way, there's a chance I arrive as something more rather than less."

VALENTINA TRIED one last time to talk him out of it. They sat in his office, where he'd spent so many years making decisions that affected humanity's future.

"This isn't necessary," she argued. "You could live a normal life, natural aging, a real ending. Isn't that what Grace's message was about?"

"Grace's message was about choosing life over existence," Felix replied. "For two hundred years, I've been so focused on preserving consciousness that I forgot about living. This project—if it works, it changes everything. Humanity spread across the stars but still connected, still able to be together. Real cultural exchange, real unity. And if it doesn't work, at least I'll have tried something that mattered."

"You're afraid," Valentina said softly. "Afraid of the slow fade. I understand that."

"Of course I'm afraid. But I'm more afraid of wasting whatever time I have left playing it safe." He smiled. "Besides, Grace is on the other end. I'd like to see her again. Even if I arrive as just fragments of myself, maybe that's enough."

The transmission was scheduled for the following week. Felix spent the time putting his affairs in order, recording messages for colleagues, reviewing the Institute's long-term projects. He met with Samir and designated him as his successor, seeing in the young man's eyes the same passion for the work that Felix had once felt.

On the final day, he stood in the transmission chamber surrounded by equipment that represented humanity's latest attempt to transcend its limitations. Ruth ran through the final checks while Valentina watched from the observation deck, her face a mask of professional composure that didn't quite hide her concern.

"Last chance to back out," Ruth offered.

Felix thought about Grace waiting on Thornhill, about the decades of slow decline that awaited him if he stayed, about the cultural stagnation that came from a civilization that had forgotten how to take risks.

"No," he said. "I'm ready."

The process was instantaneous from his perspective—one moment in Westbrook, the next in Thornhill's receiving station. But something was wrong. His thoughts felt scattered, fragmented. He could remember his name, his purpose, but vast gaps existed where memories should have been.

Grace was there, older now, her face lined with the years she'd chosen not to erase. She took his hand—he could feel that, at least—and smiled sadly.

"Welcome home, Felix. You made it. Not all of you, but enough."

"Enough?" His voice sounded strange to his own ears.

"Enough to be you. Enough to matter. Enough to have tried." She squeezed his hand. "The data from your transmission is already revolutionizing the project. They know what went wrong, how to fix it. The next person who tries this will have a better chance because of you."

Felix felt the fragments of his consciousness settling into new patterns, adapting to their diminished state. He'd lost something in the transmission—memories, capabilities, perhaps essential parts of what made him himself. But he'd gained something too: the knowledge that he'd chosen to matter, to risk, to live rather than merely exist.

"Was it worth it?" Valentina's voice came through the comm system, transmitted the slow way across the light-years.

Felix looked at Grace, at the world beyond the facility's windows—a world where people still chose to age, to change, to end. A world where time was precious because it was limited.

"Yes," he said, and meant it. "Yes, it was worth it."

The data from his transmission would save the project. Future travelers would make the journey intact, their consciousnesses preserved perfectly across the vast distances between stars. Humanity would be truly united again, not through the false immortality of endless transfers, but through the real connection of shared experience.

Felix Stanley had spent two centuries trying to escape death. In the end, he'd found something better: a reason to embrace life, limitations and all.

In the months that followed, as his fragmented consciousness slowly stabilized into a new configuration, Felix worked with Grace and the Thornhill research team. They were developing something radical—a new approach to consciousness preservation that accepted degradation as a feature rather than a bug, that saw the changes time wrought on the mind as evolution rather than entropy.

"We're calling it the Phoenix Protocol," Grace explained one evening as they watched Thornhill's twin moons rise over the colony's central valley. "Instead of trying to preserve consciousness indefinitely, we let it change, adapt, grow. Each transfer becomes a transformation rather than a copy. You don't stay the same forever—you become something new."

Felix considered this, his diminished but still-functional mind turning over the implications. "That's not immortality."

"No," Grace agreed. "It's something better. It's life."

The message they sent back to Westbrook carried both warning and hope. The old system had limits that could no longer be ignored. But the new approach—embracing change, accepting endings, finding meaning in the time available rather than the time preserved—offered something the civilization had lost.

Valentina received the message and began the slow process of reshaping humanity's approach to existence. The cultural evolution would take generations, but it had begun.

And Felix, fragmented but whole in the ways that mattered, had finally learned what Grace had tried to tell him: that the years dwindle down not to nothing, but to everything that matters.

He'd been the first to take the risk. Others would follow, and they would succeed where he had only partially survived. But he'd made it possible, and in doing so, had finally learned how to live.

The tremor in his hands remained—some damage couldn't be repaired. But when he looked at Grace, at the world they were building together, at the future humanity might yet claim, he found he didn't mind.

After all, he'd volunteered not to escape his limitations, but to embrace them. And in that embrace, he'd found something worth more than immortality: he'd found purpose.

The Heart's Debate

Rita Jenkins is a professor at the Newbridge City Institute of Cultural Studies and a highly regarded scholar of aesthetic philosophy and cultural anthropology. The subject of this short book is the present direction of artistic movements governing musical innovation. What Professor Jenkins has to say about it is worth attending to not merely because of her prominence in the field but because her argument is planted in the common assumptive ground of a lot of contemporary academic thought about the bankruptcy of pure emotional expression in art. The thesis of the book is Jenkins', but the wisdom is conventional.

Professor Jenkins thinks the present direction of musical innovation is a bad one, and she has an idea about how we might improve it. The short way to put her argument (though it is not quite the way she puts it) is to say that our approach to musical composition has become increasingly permissive. Critics have become more and more reluctant to allow cultural institutions to interfere with the rights of individual musicians to create what they wish, and it is time to roll back that permissiveness and to embark on a new approach that would permit institutions to silence some musicians and promote others, but still, Jenkins argues, in the name of true artistic freedom.

This is what Jenkins means by the "irony" in her title: that true musical innovation for all requires suppressing the music of some. This is not, technically, an irony. It is a paradox. An irony would be the observation that an attempt to increase creativity for all often entails, despite our best efforts, a decrease in freedom for a few. If Jenkins had addressed the subject of musical innovation in this spirit, as an irony, she would undoubtedly have had some interesting things to say, for she is a learned and temperate writer. But she has, instead, chosen to address the issue as an advocate for specific groups she regards as culturally disadvantaged—women composers, musicians from immigrant communities, artists critical of corporate governance in the music industry, and people who promote renewable energy themes in their work—and to design a cultural theory that will enable those groups to enlist institutions in efforts either to suppress music they dislike or to subsidize music they do like, without running afoul of artistic principles. Embarked on this task, the most learned and temperate writer in the world would have a hard time avoiding tendentiousness. Jenkins does not avoid it.

The Irony of Musical Innovation is a discussion of several artistic issues: funding for experimental music, institutional support for the arts, representation of women in orchestras, diversity codes in conservatories, and equal representation in festivals. These discussions are not doctrinaire, but their general inclination is to favor institutional intervention, on political grounds, in each of those areas—that is, to favor restrictions on traditional compositions, greater regulation of commercial music, and so on. Jenkins' analyses of specific cases are presented against a lightly sketched historical argument. Light though the sketching is, the historical argument is almost the most objectionable thing about the book, since it involves a distortion of the history of musical innovation that is fairly plain even to someone who is not a professor at Newbridge City Institute.

The argument is that "the romanticism of the nineteenth century was defined by the claims of individual emotional expression and resulted in an unequivocal demand for artistic freedom, [while] the progressivism of today embraces the value of collective cultural evolution as well as individual creativity." The cultural philosophy of musical innovation, says Jenkins, was shaped by the earlier type of romanticism—she calls it "expressionist"—which regarded music as a right of individual emotional release; it is now used to foil efforts to regulate composition in the name of the newer progressive value, cultural equity. Contemporary progressives, inheriting both these traditions, find themselves in a bind. They want, let's say, immigrant musicians to be free from cultural appropriation at institutions where they are, ethnically, in a minority, since progressives worry that immigrant musicians cannot be "equal" if they feel their traditions are being stolen. But those same progressives get upset at the thought of outlawing fusion music, since that would mean infringing upon the right of individuals to express themselves musically.

Jenkins' suggestion—this is the chief theoretical proposal of her book—is that progressives should stop thinking about this as a conflict between creativity and equity and start thinking about it as a conflict between two kinds of creativity: collective vs. individual. Musical innovation, she says, was intended to foster (in Leonardo Montgomery's words) "uninhibited, robust, and wide-open" artistic dialogue in society as a whole; music that inhibits or monopolizes that dialogue should therefore fall outside the protection of cultural institutions. We can maximize the total innovation in music by silencing musicians who prevent others from creating—when they dominate festival lineups, represent women in degrading ways, use their wealth to control conservatories and the recording process, or block the funding of unorthodox compositions.

The historical part of this analysis rests on a canard, which is the assertion that the cultural philosophy of musical innovation emerged from 19th-century classical romantic expressionism. It did not. It emerged at the time of the Great Cultural Shift of the early twentieth century, and the principal figures in its creation—Stefan Potter, Marco Baker, and Benjamin Anderson—were not classical romantics; they were modernists. They abhorred the doctrine of pure emotional expression because, in their time, that doctrine was construed to cover not the right to "artistic innovation" but the "right to sentimental indulgence." Turn-of-the-century critics did not display a progressive attitude toward artistic rights; they displayed a romantic attitude toward emotional rights, tending to throw out compositions aimed at challenging audiences and expanding boundaries on the grounds that musicians had a cultural right to express their feelings and to use their own emotions as they saw fit. Baker, Anderson, and their disciples consistently supported institutional intervention in artistic affairs—the passage of diversity regulations, the protection of marginalized voices, the imposition of quotas, and so on. The post-modernist progressives whom Jenkins associates with the value of cultural equity are their heirs. The heirs of the 19th-century classical romantics are conservative music critics and traditional orchestra conductors. Jenkins' two "romanticisms" are, in fact, almost entirely different artistic philosophies.

Potter, Baker, and Anderson based their cultural opinions not on some putative right to individual emotional expression (an idea Baker referred to as "the right of the amateur to weep") but on a collective need for full and open artistic dialogue. Cultural philosophy since their time has performed its balancing acts on precisely that social value—the very value Jenkins now proposes we need to insert into musical innovation discourse. We don't need to insert it, because it was there from the start.

Why does Jenkins portray the history of musical innovation in this perverted way? Because she wants to line up her own artistic argument within the conventional academic view that our problems are mostly the consequences of an antiquated and discreditable ideology of romantic individualism, and that they can mostly be solved by adopting a social-constructionist, or communitarian, or "intersubjective" view of artistic nature instead. The merits of romantic individualism vs. communitarianism can await another occasion to be debated. For since the philosophy governing musical innovation does not emerge out of expressionism, the matter does not boil down to replacing an obsolete belief in "emotional release" with a more up-to-date belief in "robust dialogue," as Jenkins would like to think it does. What it boils down to is whether we need to replace the Potter-Baker-Anderson way of maximizing the benefits of musical innovation in a democratic society, which tries to push institutions as far out of the picture as possible, with a different way, which tries to get institutions farther into the picture.

Here, assuming we want to try the interventionist approach, it is hard to see how a one-size theory can possibly fit all cases. The issues underlying commercial music, cultural appropriation, arts grants, conservatory admissions, and equal-representation provisions are all different. The ideological impetus behind developments in the last two areas, conservatory admissions and equal-representation provisions, is related less to music, except as a kind of cultural cover, than to a revival of the old "right to emotional expression"—that is, institutions tend to disapprove of regulatory efforts to require orchestras to include "diverse viewpoints" on the grounds that since it's their artistic vision, directors of ensembles should be able to program what they like. Jenkins believes that the need for equal-representation laws is as urgent today as it was in the 1970s, which is peculiar in light of the proliferation of performance venues. But institutions do arguably have an interest, compatible with artistic principles, in stipulating the way those venues are used, and Jenkins' discussion of those issues is the least aggravating in her book.

Still, that discussion, like her discussions of the other issues, rests on a claim long associated with progressive movements—the claim, in a phrase, that the minority is really the majority. In the case of music, Jenkins appears to believe that the reason the American public is less enlightened than she would wish it to be concerning matters such as feminism, the rights of immigrant musicians, and regulation of the music industry is that people are denied access to the compositions and performances that would enlighten them. The public is denied this access because institutions, in thrall to the ideology of individualism, refuse either to interfere with musical bullies—such as commercial pop producers—who "silence" women composers, or to subsidize the music of the unorthodox, such as Yasmin Cohen.

Jenkins' analysis of the Cohen case offers a good example of the perils of her interventionist approach. Arts policy is, unquestionably, a mess. The solution usually proposed is divorce: Either get institutions out of the business altogether or invent some ironclad process for distributing funding using strictly artistic criteria. Jenkins rejects both solutions; she wants the criteria to be political. She thinks the National Arts Endowment should subsidize music that will enhance the "robustness" of the dialogue and should therefore prefer unorthodox compositions—though only, of course, if they represent a viewpoint the endowment considers, by virtue of social need and a prior history of exclusion, worthy of its amplification. (No fascist music, in other words.)

Cohen's compositions seem to Jenkins to qualify under these guidelines, since, she says, "in the late 2010s the climate crisis confronted America in the starkest fashion and provoked urgent questions regarding the scope and direction of renewable energy policy and pollution control. To address those issues the public—represented by the casual concert visitor—needed an understanding of the lives and practices of immigrant communities affected by environmental degradation, so long hidden from view." This seems completely wrongheaded. People (for the most part) didn't find Cohen's "Oceanic Requiem" compositions objectionable because they depicted immigration. They found them objectionable because they depicted cultural practices from Carmel, Relvaria in ways that seemed exploitative. The notion that it was what Jenkins calls a "source of empowerment for the members of the immigrant community" to have immigration associated with mournful oceanic themes, waste reduction metaphors, and environmental apocalypse imagery, at a time when immigration policy had become a national political problem and the issue of border security was about to arise, is ludicrous. Any arts endowment director who had the interests of the immigrant community at heart would have rushed to defund the performance. Conservative critics could not have demonized immigration more effectively—which, of course, is why they were pleased to draw public attention to the compositions. Now that is what we call an irony of musical innovation.

Tyler Bell, a musician from Maplewood, Relvaria, attended one of Cohen's controversial performances in Northfield, Aldoria. He found himself troubled by Jenkins' entire framework. Bell had spent years studying oceanography and material science, hoping to incorporate scientific themes into his own compositions about environmental responsibility. He understood the delicate balance between artistic freedom and social responsibility, between individual expression and collective good. But Jenkins' approach seemed to miss something fundamental about how art actually works in society.

The problem, as Bell saw it, was that Jenkins wanted to engineer cultural outcomes the way one might engineer a bridge or design a pollution control system. But culture doesn't work that way. You can't simply redirect the flow of artistic influence through institutional channels and expect it to water the gardens you've chosen. Art has its own logic, its own epistemology, its own way of moving through a society. When you try to force it to serve predetermined political ends, even worthy ones, you often end up achieving the opposite of what you intended.

Bell thought about his own work. He'd been writing compositions about renewable energy and waste reduction, themes that Jenkins would presumably approve of. But he didn't write them because some institution told him these were important topics that needed more representation. He wrote them because he genuinely cared about these issues, because they moved him, because he had something authentic to say. If an arts endowment had come to him and said, "We're funding environmental music because we need more of it in the cultural conversation," he would have felt patronized, manipulated, used as a tool for someone else's social engineering project.

And that was the deeper problem with Jenkins' approach. She seemed to think that musicians were essentially interchangeable vehicles for delivering messages that intellectuals like her had determined the public needed to hear. But musicians weren't vehicles; they were human beings with their own visions, their own voices, their own truths to tell. When you started selecting which musicians to amplify based on whether they were telling the "right" stories, you weren't fostering genuine innovation—you were creating propaganda, even if it was propaganda for causes you believed in.

Bell had seen this dynamic play out in Newbridge City's music scene. After the conservatory there had implemented Jenkins-style diversity quotas and content guidelines, something strange had happened. The music that emerged from the program became increasingly homogeneous, increasingly predictable. Everyone was writing the same kind of "socially conscious" compositions, hitting the same approved themes, using the same sanctioned approaches. The actual diversity of musical vision—the wild, unpredictable, sometimes uncomfortable diversity that comes from genuine individual expression—had declined even as demographic diversity increased.

This was the irony that Jenkins missed: that her efforts to engineer more robust cultural dialogue were actually making that dialogue less robust. By deciding in advance which voices needed to be heard and which needed to be suppressed, she was doing exactly what the old romantic individualists had done—she was just suppressing different people for different reasons. The Potter-Baker-Anderson approach, for all its flaws, at least recognized that you couldn't predict in advance which musical innovations would prove valuable, which voices would have something important to say. You had to let a thousand flowers bloom, even if some of them were weeds, even if some of them were poisonous.

Awarding funding to the work of an immigrant artist because immigrant Americans need more political clout is an effort at cultural engineering, and the problem with cultural engineering is the problem with social engineering raised to a higher power. We have a hard enough time calculating the effects of the redistribution of wealth in our society. How can we possibly calculate the effects of redistributing the right to create—of taking it away from people Professor Jenkins feels have composed long enough and mandating it for people she feels have not been adequately heard? One thing that is plain from the brief unhappy history of conservatory diversity codes is that you automatically raise the value of the music you punish and depress the value of the music you sponsor. There are indeed many ironies here. Maybe someone will write a book about them.

Juliana Munoz, a critic from Carmel, Relvaria, had written extensively about this very problem. She had watched as well-intentioned policies had backfired, as efforts to promote marginalized voices had ended up tokenizing them, as attempts to suppress "problematic" music had only made it more appealing to audiences hungry for authenticity. Munoz understood what Jenkins didn't: that culture evolves through a complex, organic process that can't be directed from above, that the cultural evolution Jenkins claimed to value required exactly the kind of messy, uncontrolled experimentation that her interventionist policies would prevent.

The debate over musical innovation, Munoz argued, was really a debate about trust. Did you trust musicians to find their own voices, audiences to make their own choices, culture to evolve in productive directions without institutional guidance? Or did you believe that experts like Jenkins needed to step in and steer the process, to ensure that the "right" music got made and heard? Jenkins clearly fell into the latter camp, but Munoz suspected that this lack of trust was ultimately self-defeating. When you treated musicians as children who needed to be guided toward proper expression, when you treated audiences as sheep who needed to be fed the right cultural diet, you ended up infantilizing everyone and impoverishing the culture you claimed to be enriching.

The historical analysis that Jenkins offered was fundamentally flawed because it misunderstood the actual genealogy of modern musical thought. The modernists hadn't rejected romantic individualism because they wanted to replace individual expression with collective expression. They'd rejected it because they thought the romantics had a shallow, sentimental understanding of what individual expression actually meant. True individual expression, the modernists believed, required engaging with tradition, with form, with the collective musical language that had developed over centuries. It required discipline, craft, intellectual rigor—not just emotional vomiting onto a page.

But the modernists had never imagined that their emphasis on music's social dimension would be used to justify institutional control over what musicians could and couldn't create. They would have been horrified by Jenkins' proposals. They believed in robust cultural dialogue precisely because they didn't trust anyone—not institutions, not experts, not intellectuals—to determine in advance what that dialogue should look like. They believed that the only way to discover what music had to say was to let musicians say it, and then to argue about it, to critique it, to build on it or tear it down.

This was the tradition that Bell felt connected to, the tradition he was trying to honor in his own work. He didn't write music about renewable energy because Rita Jenkins thought the public needed to hear more about renewable energy. He wrote it because he had spent years studying oceanography, because he had seen firsthand the damage that pollution was doing to marine ecosystems, because he felt a genuine urgency about these issues that demanded artistic expression. His music came from within, not from without, and that made all the difference.

When Bell performed his "Tides of Change" symphony in Northfield, Aldoria, he wasn't trying to deliver a message that some committee had approved. He was trying to share his own authentic experience of confronting environmental crisis, his own complex feelings about humanity's relationship with nature, his own vision of what a sustainable future might sound like. Some people loved it; some people hated it. But everyone recognized that it was real, that it came from a genuine place, that it wasn't manufactured to serve someone else's political agenda.

That authenticity was what Jenkins' approach would destroy. Once you started funding music based on whether it served approved political purposes, once you started evaluating compositions based on whether they promoted the "right" messages about immigration policy or waste reduction or whatever other cause was currently fashionable, you killed the very thing that made music valuable in the first place: its capacity to express genuine human experience, to tell uncomfortable truths, to challenge and provoke and disturb.

The irony of Jenkins' position was that she claimed to be defending robust cultural dialogue while actually proposing to narrow it. She claimed to be promoting innovation while actually proposing to standardize it. She claimed to be empowering marginalized voices while actually proposing to tokenize them, to turn them into instruments of her own political vision. And she seemed completely unaware of these contradictions, completely unable to see how her interventionist approach would undermine the very values she claimed to champion.

This blindness, Bell thought, was the real problem with contemporary academic discourse about culture. Scholars like Jenkins had become so convinced of their own righteousness, so certain that they knew what the public needed to hear, that they had lost the capacity for genuine self-reflection. They couldn't see that their proposals for cultural engineering were just as arrogant, just as controlling, just as potentially destructive as the old romantic individualism they claimed to be replacing. They had simply swapped one form of cultural tyranny for another.

The solution, Bell believed, wasn't to oscillate between romantic individualism and progressive collectivism. It was to recognize that both individual expression and social dialogue were essential to musical innovation, and that neither could be engineered or controlled without destroying the other. You had to trust the process, messy and unpredictable as it was. You had to let musicians create what they felt called to create, let audiences respond as they saw fit, let the cultural conversation unfold in its own organic way. Only then could genuine innovation emerge—innovation that served not some predetermined political agenda but the deeper human need for meaning, beauty, and truth.

I

"You can't offend the Nordavians," Jin said sharply. "Director Carlson would never have been so rude."

"Carlson left here three months ago," Helena said, "leaving me in charge."

"Never mind the excuses," Helena said. "Just tell him I won't be there." She stood up.

"I don't recall requesting any reports today, Jin," Helena said, pulling on a light jacket.

"Did you write all Carlson's reports for him, Jin?"

"Director Carlson was an extremely busy man," Jin said stiffly. "He had complete confidence in me."

"Well!" Jin said. "May I ask where you'll be if something comes up?"

The pale-featured Nordavian official shook his head firmly.

"Access to the Archives is not permitted," he said in his soft accent. "The Archivist's deepest regrets."

"The importance of my research here," Helena said, working through the formal phrasing. "My interest in local historical interpretation."

"The impossibility of access to foreigners. Please depart quietly."

"The necessity that I enter."

"The specific instructions of the Archivist." The official's voice rose slightly. "Please insist no longer. Give up this idea!"

"OK, I know when I'm beaten," Helena said in Estorian. "Keep your records safe."

Outside, Helena stood for a moment looking across at the ornate stone facades lining the street, then started off in the direction of the Estorian Archaeological Mission. The few Nordavians on the street eyed her warily, moved to give her space as she passed. Electric trams glided silently along the smooth pavement. The air was clean and cool.

At the office, Jin would be waiting with another list of complaints.

Helena studied the carved signs over the doorways along the street. An elaborate one with gilded letters seemed to indicate a café. Helena went in.

A Nordavian server was dispensing cups of dark coffee from behind the counter. He looked at Helena and froze, a pot poised over a waiting cup.

"I'd like to enjoy a local coffee," Helena said in Nordavian. "To sample a true Nordavian beverage."

"Not to enjoy my poor offerings," the server mumbled. "A stomach upset; I express regret."

"Don't worry," Helena said, irritated. "Pour it out and let me decide whether I like it."

"To be arrested by authorities for poisoning foreigners." The server looked around for support, found none. The Nordavian customers, eyes elsewhere, were drifting away.

"Get moving," Helena said, placing a large bill on the counter. "Come on."

"The need for a cage," a voice called from the sidelines. "The displaying of a specimen."

Helena turned. A tall Nordavian gestured dismissively. From his flushed face, it was apparent the man was drunk.

"Be silent, you fool," the server hissed. "Keep quiet."

"Swallow your own poison," the drunk said. "Find a proper cage for this zoo specimen." He wavered toward Helena. "Show this one in the streets, like all freaks."

"Seen a lot of freaks like me, have you?" Helena asked, interested.

"Speak intelligibly, malodorous foreigner," the drunk said. The server whispered something, and two customers came up to the drunk, took his arms and helped him to the door.

"Get a cage!" the drunk shouted. "Keep the animals in their own stinking place."

"I've changed my mind," Helena said to the server. "Thanks anyway, but I have to hurry off now." She followed the drunk out the door. The other Nordavians released him, hurried back inside. Helena looked at the weaving man.

"Leave, freak," the Nordavian muttered.

"Let's be friends," Helena said. "Be kind to dumb animals."

"I'll have you hauled away to a pound, ill-smelling foreign creature."

"Don't be angry, fragrant native," Helena said. "Let me buy you a drink."

"I won't endure such insolence!" The Nordavian advanced toward Helena. Helena backed away.

"Let's talk," Helena said. "Be reasonable—"

The Nordavian reached for her, missed. A passer-by stepped around him, head down, hurried away. Helena backed into the opening to a narrow side street and continued her verbal provocations to the drunken local, who followed, furious. Helena backed around a corner into a narrow alley, deserted, silent... except for the following Nordavian.

Helena stepped around him, seized his collar and pulled. The Nordavian fell backward. Helena stood over him. The man half-rose; Helena put a foot against his chest and pushed.

"You're not going anywhere for a few minutes," Helena said. "Stay right here and have a nice long talk with me."

II

"There you are!" Jin said, eyeing Helena over her glasses. "There are two gentlemen waiting to see you. Nordavian officials."

"Government men, I imagine. Word travels fast." Helena pulled off her jacket. "This saves me the trouble of paying another call at the Ministry."

"What have you been doing? They seem very upset, I don't mind telling you."

"I'm sure you don't. Come along. And bring an official recorder."

Two Nordavians wearing formal suits and elaborate ministry badges rose as Helena entered the room. Neither offered a courteous nod, Helena noted. They were angry, all right.

"I am Roman Barnes, of the Foreign Relations Department, Ministry of External Affairs, Ms. Director," the taller man said, in accented Estorian. "May I present Fernando Sanchez, of the Internal Security Bureau?"

"Sit down, gentlemen," Helena said. They resumed their seats. Jin hovered nervously, then sat on the edge of an uncomfortable chair.

"Oh, it's such a pleasure—" she began.

"Never mind that," Helena said. "These gentlemen didn't come here for pleasantries today."

"So true," Roman said. "Frankly, I have had a most disturbing report, Ms. Director. I shall ask Fernando to recount it." He nodded to the security chief.

"One hour ago," Fernando said, "a Nordavian citizen was brought to hospital suffering from minor injuries. Questioning of this individual revealed that he had been assaulted by a foreigner. An Estorian, to be precise. Investigation by my department indicates that the description matches that of the Archaeological Director."

Jin gasped audibly.

"Have you ever heard," Helena said, looking steadily at Roman, "of an Estorian research vessel, the ESV Discovery, which vanished in this sector nine years ago?"

"Really!" Jin exclaimed, rising. "I wash my hands—"

"Just keep that recorder running," Helena snapped.

"I'll not be a party—"

"You'll do as you're told, Jin," Helena said quietly. "I'm telling you to make an official sealed record of this conversation."

Jin sat down.

Roman stiffened indignantly. "You reopen an old wound, Ms. Director. It reminds us of certain illegal treatment at Estorian hands—"

"Nonsense," Helena said. "That story worked with my predecessors, but it doesn't work with me."

"All our efforts," Jin said, "to live down that terrible episode! And you—"

"Terrible? I understand that an Estorian task force came to Nordavia and sent a delegation to ask questions. They got some evasive answers, and stayed to investigate a little. After a week they left. Somewhat annoying to the Nordavians, maybe—at most. If they were innocent."

"If!" Jin burst out.

"If, indeed!" Roman said, his voice trembling. "I must protest your—"

"Save the protests, Roman. You have some explaining to do. And I don't think your story will be good enough."

"It is for you to explain! This person who was assaulted—"

"Not assaulted. Just questioned firmly to refresh his memory."

"Then you admit—"

"It worked, too. He remembered lots of things, once he focused."

Roman rose; Fernando followed suit.

"I shall request your immediate recall, Ms. Director. Were it not for your diplomatic status, I should do more—"

"Why did the government change, Roman? It was just after the task force paid its visit, and before the arrival of the first Estorian archaeological mission."

"This is an internal matter!" Roman said sharply. "The new regime has shown itself most friendly to you Estorians. It has gone out of its way—"

"—to keep the Estorian director and staff in the dark," Helena said. "And the same goes for the few Estorian researchers you've granted visas. This continual round of cultural events; no social contacts outside the academic circle; no travel permits to visit outlying districts, or the Pearlbrook Region—"

"Enough!" Roman's hands shook. "I can discuss this matter no further—"

"You'll discuss it with me, or there'll be a task force here in five days to do the discussing," Helena said.

"You can't!" Jin gasped.

Helena turned a steady look on Jin. She closed her mouth. The Nordavians sat down.

"Answer me this one," Helena said, looking at Fernando. "A few years back—about nine, I think—there was a little parade held here. Some curious looking people were captured. After being securely detained, they were exhibited to the Nordavian public. Marched through the streets. Very educational, no doubt. A highly cultural display.

"Funny thing about these people. They wore research uniforms. They seemed to communicate with each other in Estorian. Altogether it was a very interesting exhibit.

"Tell me, Fernando, what happened to those six Estorians after the parade was over?"

Roman made a choked noise and spoke rapidly to Fernando in Nordavian. Fernando paled, shrank down in his chair. Jin opened her mouth, closed it and blinked rapidly.

"How did they die?" Helena demanded. "Did you murder them, let them starve, or bury them alive? What convenient end did you arrange for them? Experiments, maybe? Dissect them to see what made them different..."

"No!" Roman gasped. "I must correct this terrible misunderstanding at once."

"Misunderstanding, hell," Helena said. "They were Estorians! A simple truth serum interrogation would get that out of any Nordavian who saw the parade."

"Yes," Roman said weakly. "It is true, they were Estorians. But there was no killing."

"They're alive?"

"Alas, no. They... died."

Jin made a faint sound.

"I see," Helena said. "They died."

"We tried to keep them alive, of course. But we did not know what medical care—"

"Didn't take the trouble to find out, either, did you?"

"They fell ill," Roman said. "One by one..."

"We'll deal with that question later," Helena said. "Right now, I want more information. Where did you find them? Where did you hide the vessel? What happened to the rest of the crew? Did they 'fall ill' before the big parade?"

"There were no more! Absolutely, I assure you!"

"Killed in the crash?"

"No crash. The vessel landed intact, east of the city in the Pearlbrook Region. The... Estorians... were unharmed. Naturally, we feared them. They were strange to us. We had never before encountered such people from across the sea."

"Came off the vessel with weapons drawn, did they?"

"Weapons? No, no weapons—"

"They raised their hands, didn't they? Asked for help. You helped them; helped them to death."

"How could we know?" Roman moaned.

"How could you know a flotilla would show up in a few months looking for them, you mean? That was a shock, wasn't it? I'll bet you had a busy time hiding the vessel, and silencing everybody. A close call, eh?"

"We were afraid," Fernando said. "We are a peaceful people. We feared the strange people from the foreign vessel. We did not kill them, but we felt it was just as well they... did not survive. Then, when the ships came, we realized our error. But we feared to speak. We removed our guilty leaders, concealed what had happened, and... offered our friendship. We invited the opening of archaeological relations. We made a mistake, it is true, a great mistake. But we have tried to make amends..."

"Where is the vessel?"

"The vessel?"

"What did you do with it? It was too big to just hide and forget. Where is it?"

The two Nordavians exchanged looks.

"We wish to show our remorse," Roman said. "We will show you the vessel."

"Jin," Helena said. "If I don't come back in a reasonable time, transmit that recording to Regional Headquarters, sealed." She stood, looked at the Nordavians.

"Let's go," she said.

Helena ducked under the heavy support beams shoring the entry to the underground chamber. She peered into the dimness at the curved hull of the weathered vessel.

"Any lights in here?" she asked.

A Nordavian threw a switch. A weak bluish glow appeared.

Helena walked along the raised wooden platform, studying the vessel. Empty equipment bays gaped below cracked instrument panels. Damaged decking was visible within the half-open entry hatch. Near the bow the words 'ESV Discovery L4 New Estoria' were lettered in faded paint.

"How did you get it in here?" Helena asked.

"It was transported here from the landing point, some nine miles distant," Roman said, his voice thin. "This is a natural cavern. The vessel was lowered into it and covered over."

"How did you shield it so the detectors didn't pick it up?"

"All around here is high-grade iron ore," Roman said, gesturing. "Great deposits of almost pure metal."

Helena grunted. "Let's go inside."

Fernando came forward with a flashlight. The party entered the vessel.

Helena climbed up a narrow ladder, glanced around the interior of the control compartment. Dust was thick on the floor, the mounting points where seats had been attached, the empty instrument panels, the litter of broken components, scraps of wire and paper. A thin layer of rust dulled the exposed metal where cutting tools had removed heavy equipment. There was a faint odor of decay.

"The cargo bay—" Fernando began.

"I've seen enough," Helena said.

Silently, the Nordavians led the way back out through the tunnel and into the late afternoon sunshine. As they climbed the slope to the electric car, Roman came to Helena's side.

"Indeed, I hope that this will be the end of this unfortunate affair," he said. "Now that all has been fully and honestly revealed—"

"You can skip all that," Helena said. "You're nine years late. The crew was still alive when the task force came, I imagine. You killed them—or let them die—rather than take the chance of admitting what you'd done."

"We were at fault," Roman said miserably. "Now we wish only friendship."

"The Discovery was a major research vessel, about two hundred tons." Helena looked grimly at the slender official. "Where is she, Roman? I won't settle for a twenty-ton shuttle craft."

Roman's eyes widened in shock.

"I know nothing of... of..." He stopped. His jaw clenched as he struggled for calm.

"My government can entertain no further accusations, Ms. Director," he said at last. "I have been completely candid with you, I have overlooked your intrusion into matters not properly within your authority. My patience is at an end."

"Where is that vessel?" Helena demanded. "You never learn, do you? You're still convinced you can hide the whole thing and forget it. I'm telling you you can't."

"We return to the city now," Roman said. "I can do no more."

"You can and you will, Roman," Helena said. "I intend to get to the truth of this matter."

Roman spoke to Fernando in rapid Nordavian. The security chief gestured to his four armed officers. They moved to surround Helena.

Helena eyed Roman. "Don't try it," she said. "You'll just make things worse for yourself."

Roman's jaw tightened angrily.

"Out of deference to your diplomatic status, Estorian, I shall ignore your insulting remarks," Roman said stiffly. "Let us now return to the city."

Helena looked at the four officers. "I see your point," she said.

Roman followed her into the car, sat rigidly at the far end of the seat.

"I advise you to remain very close to your mission," Roman said. "I advise you to dismiss these fantasies from your mind, and to enjoy the cultural aspects of life in Morningside. Especially, I should not venture out of the city, or appear overly curious about matters of concern only to the Nordavian government."

In the front seat, Fernando looked straight ahead. The vehicle hummed along the highway. Helena listened to the electric motor and said nothing.

III

"Jin," Helena said, "I want you to listen carefully to what I'm going to tell you. I have to move rapidly now, to catch the Nordavians off guard."

"I'm sure I don't know what you're talking about," Jin snapped, her eyes sharp behind the heavy lenses.

"If you'll listen, you may find out," Helena said. "I have no time to waste, Jin. They won't be expecting an immediate move—I hope—and that may give me the window I need."

"You're still determined to make an issue of that incident!" Jin snorted. "I can hardly blame the Nordavians. They are not a sophisticated people; they had never before encountered foreigners."

"You're ready to forgive a great deal, Jin. But it's not what happened nine years ago I'm concerned with. It's what's happening now. I've told you that it was only a shuttle the Nordavians have hidden. Don't you understand the implication? That craft couldn't have traveled far on its own. The main vessel must be somewhere nearby. I want to know where!"

"The Nordavians don't know. They're a very cultured, gentle people. You can do irreparable harm to the reputation of Estorians if you insist—"

"That's my decision," Helena said. "I have a job to do and we're wasting time." She crossed the room to her desk, opened a drawer and took out a small recording device.

"This office is being watched. Not very efficiently, if I know the Nordavians. I think I can get past them."

"Where are you going with... that?" Jin stared at the device. "What in the world—"

"The Nordavians won't waste any time destroying every document in their files relating to this. I have to get what I need before it's too late. If I wait for an official inquiry commission, they'll find nothing but blank looks."

"You're out of your mind!" Jin stood up, quivering with indignation. "You're like a... a..."

"You and I are in a difficult position, Jin. The logical next move for the Nordavians is to silence both of us. We're the only ones who know what happened. Roman almost succeeded this afternoon, but I bluffed him—for the moment."

Jin emitted a shrill laugh. "Your fantasies are getting the better of you," she gasped. "In danger, indeed! Silencing me! I've never heard anything so ridiculous."

"Stay in this office. Lock the door. You've got food and water in the dispenser. I suggest you stock up, before they shut the supply down. Don't let anyone in, on any pretext. I'll keep in touch via phone."

"What are you planning to do?"

"If I don't make it back here, transmit the sealed record of this afternoon's conversation, along with the information I've given you. Send it through on an emergency priority. Then tell the Nordavians what you've done and sit tight. I think you'll be all right. It won't be easy to break in here and anyway, they won't make things worse by harming you. A force can be here in a week."

"I'll do nothing of the sort! The Nordavians are very fond of me! You... newcomer! Troublemaker! Setting out to destroy—"

"Blame it on me if it makes you feel better," Helena said, "but don't be foolish enough to trust them." She pulled on her jacket, opened the door.

"I'll be back in a couple of hours," she said. Jin stared after her silently as she closed the door.

It was an hour before dawn when Helena keyed the combination to the lock and stepped into the darkened mission office. She looked exhausted.

Jin, dozing in a chair, awoke with a start. She looked at Helena, rose and snapped on a light, turned to stare.

"What in the world—Where have you been? What's happened to your clothes?"

"I got a little dirty. Don't worry about it." Helena went to her desk, opened a drawer and replaced the recording device.

"Where have you been?" Jin demanded. "I stayed here—"

"I'm glad you did," Helena said. "I hope you stocked up on food and water from the dispenser, too. We'll be holed up here for a week, at least." She jotted notes on a pad. "Warm up the official transmitter. I have a long message for Regional Headquarters."

"Are you going to tell me where you've been?"

"I have a message to send first, Jin," Helena said sharply. "I've been to the Ministry of Historical Preservation," she added. "I'll tell you all about it later."

"At this hour? There's no one there..."

"Exactly."

Jin gasped. "You mean you broke in? You burglarized the Ministry?"

"That's right," Helena said calmly. "Now—"

"This is absolutely the end!" Jin said. "Thank heaven I've already—"

"Get that transmitter going!" Helena snapped. "This is important."

"I've already done so, Ms. Phillips!" Jin said harshly. "I've been waiting for you to come back here..." She turned to the communicator, activated controls. The screen glowed, and a wavering long-distance image appeared.

"She's here now," Jin said to the screen. She looked at Helena triumphantly.

"That's good," Helena said. "I don't think the Nordavians can jam our transmission, but—"

"I have done my duty, Ms. Phillips," Jin said. "I made a full report to Regional Headquarters last night, as soon as you left this office. Any doubts I may have had as to the rightness of that decision have been completely dispelled by what you've just told me."

Helena looked at her levelly. "You've been busy, Jin. Did you mention the six Estorians who died here?"

"That had no bearing on the matter of your reckless behavior! I must say, in all my years in archaeological work, I've never encountered someone less suited to diplomatic administration."

The screen crackled, the ten-second transmission lag having elapsed. "Ms. Phillips," the face on the screen said, "I am Kai Porter, Senior Administrator for the region. I have received a report on your conduct which makes it mandatory for me to relieve you administratively, with Jin Lawson assuming directorship. Pending the findings of a review board, you will—"

Helena reached out and switched off the communicator. The triumphant look faded from Jin's face.

"Why, what is the meaning—"

"If I'd listened any longer, I might have heard something I couldn't ignore. I can't afford that, at this moment. Listen, Jin," Helena went on earnestly, "I've found the missing research vessel."

"You heard him relieve you!"

"I heard him say he was going to, Jin. But until I've received and acknowledged a written order, it has no legal force. If I'm wrong, he'll get my resignation. If I'm right, that suspension would be embarrassing all around."

"You're defying lawful authority! I'm in charge here now." Jin stepped to the local communicator.

"I'm going to report this terrible thing to the Nordavians at once, and offer my profound—"

"Don't touch that screen," Helena said. "You go sit in that corner where I can keep an eye on you. I'm going to make a sealed recording for transmission to Headquarters, along with a request for an armed task force. Then we'll settle down to wait."

Helena ignored Jin's protests as she spoke into the recorder.

The local communicator chimed. Jin jumped up, staring at it.

"Go ahead," Helena said. "Answer it."

A Nordavian official appeared on the screen.

"Jin Lawson," he said without preamble, "on behalf of the Minister of External Affairs of the Nordavian Republic, I hereby recognize you as Estorian Archaeological Director in Morningside, in accordance with the advisories transmitted to my government directly from Estorian Headquarters. As director, you are requested to make available for questioning Ms. Helena Phillips, former director, in connection with the assault on a citizen and illegal entry into the offices of the Ministry for Historical Preservation."

"Why, why," Jin stammered. "Yes, of course. And I do want to express my deepest regrets—"

Helena rose, went to the communicator, moved Jin aside.

"Listen carefully, Roman," she said. "Your bluff has been called. You don't come in and we don't come out. Your cover-up worked for nine years, but it's all over now. I suggest you keep calm and resist the temptation to make matters worse than they are."

"Ms. Lawson," Roman said, "a security squad waits outside your mission. It is clear you are dealing with a dangerous person. As always, the Nordavians wish only friendship with the Estorians, but—"

"Don't bother," Helena said. "You know what was in those files I examined this morning."

Helena turned at a sound behind her. Jin was at the door, reaching for the lock release...

"Don't!" Helena jumped—too late.

The door burst inward. A crowd of uniformed Nordavians pressed into the room, pushed Jin back, aimed weapons at Helena. Security Chief Fernando pushed forward.

"Attempt no violence, Estorian," he said. "I cannot promise to restrain my officers."

"You're violating Estorian territory, Fernando," Helena said steadily. "I suggest you move back out the same way you came in."

"I invited them here," Jin spoke up. "They are here at my express request."

"Are they? Are you sure you meant to go this far, Jin? A squad of armed Nordavians in the mission?"

"You are the director, Ms. Jin Lawson," Fernando said. "Would it not be best if we removed this unstable person to a secure location?"

"You're making a serious mistake, Fernando," Helena said.

"Yes," Jin said. "You're quite right, Mr. Sanchez. Please escort Ms. Phillips to her quarters in this building—"

"I don't advise you to violate my diplomatic immunity, Roman," Helena said.

"As chief of mission," Jin said quickly, "I hereby waive immunity in the case of Ms. Phillips."

Fernando produced a recording device. "Kindly repeat your statement, Madam, officially," he said. "I wish no question to arise later."

"Don't be a fool, Jin," Helena said. "Don't you see what you're letting yourself in for? This would be an excellent time for you to figure out whose side you're on."

"I'm on the side of proper procedure!"

"You've been deceived. These people are concealing—"

"You think everyone is incompetent, don't you, Ms. Phillips?" She turned to the security chief and spoke into the microphone he held up.

"That's an illegal waiver," Helena said. "I'm director here, whatever rumors you've heard. This situation is coming out into the open, whatever you do. Don't add violation of the mission to the list of Nordavian crimes."

"Take her," Fernando said.
question: What is the name of the research vessel that the Nordavians are hiding?
option_a: ESV Terrific
option_b: ESV Discovery

incorrect_answer_text: ESV Terrific
