As Sophie sat in her tower study, surrounded by glowing manuscripts that floated gently in the air around her, she marveled at what she had discovered. There had been fifty-three Ascension Speeches since the first Queen, Rosa the Wise, had taken the throne in what the common folk called the Year of First Light. Each speech was worth studying—not just the famous ones like Rosa's founding address, the speeches of King Vincent the Unifier during the Great Schism, or Queen Juliana's rallying cry during the Shadow Wars. Reading them gave Sophie a peculiar sensation, as if she were standing in those ancient moments, not as a scholar of the present looking back through centuries, but as an ordinary citizen who shared the hopes, fears, and limited understanding of those distant times.

Among all the past monarchs and their counsel of advisors, there had been only one who possessed what the realm called the Gift of True Speech: King Vincent Hart, who ruled during the Shadow Wars. His second Ascension Speech, delivered after the realm had been nearly torn apart, still brought tears to the eyes of any who read it, even after two hundred years. The magical resonance embedded in the words themselves could make one's blood run cold with its power and beauty. None of the other speeches possessed such raw magical potency, though they were dignified and thoughtful addresses given by capable rulers, each attuned to their era's needs and conscious that their ascension was the most sacred moment of their reign.

Sophie had noticed that the tone and approach of the speeches seemed to fall into three distinct phases. The first, lasting until King Vincent's time, was characterized by what she termed "the humble servant style." The second phase, continuing through Queen Samir Zhang's reign, took on a more administrative character—what Sophie called "the managerial monarch approach." The third phase, which began with King Miguel Ortiz and continued to the present day, embodied what she described as "the visionary leader-prophet style." This classification wasn't perfect, of course. Some rulers seemed to bridge categories, and individual circumstances sometimes demanded departures from the prevailing style. But the overall trend was unmistakable.

When Sophie first examined Rosa the Wise's inaugural speech, she was immediately struck by its modesty. Rosa had been chosen unanimously by the Council of Elders, the first time in recorded history such agreement had been reached. She was more revered than any subsequent monarch at the moment of their ascension. And yet, what did she say?

"The weight and complexity of this sacred duty, to which the voice of our people has called me, being sufficient to cause even the wisest and most experienced among our citizens to question their worthiness, must surely overwhelm one who—possessing only modest gifts from the Source and untrained in the arts of realm governance—ought to be especially aware of her own limitations."

None of her successors expressed such profound humility, though echoes of it appeared in nearly every speech for the next three centuries. The one exception was King Luis Hughes, Rosa's immediate successor, who seemed so envious of Rosa's legacy that he spent much of his speech enumerating his own considerable qualifications and magical abilities.

That era of deep humility ended with King Vincent. Subsequent speeches routinely contained expressions of modesty, but they felt perfunctory, lacking the sincere vulnerability of the earlier monarchs.

Sophie theorized that this early modesty served multiple purposes. It reflected the courtly etiquette of the time, certainly, but it also addressed specific political concerns. In the realm's early centuries, many citizens feared that the monarchy might transform into a tyranny, with the ruler becoming more dictator than servant. Later, perhaps after the Reformation of the Second Age, a new anxiety emerged. The southern provinces, particularly around Cliffside in Fendria, had developed distinct cultural practices and systems of local governance. They worried that central authority might be used to interfere with their autonomy. The monarchs' assurances of limited power may have been intended to comfort these regions.

King Vincent faced an entirely different situation. With the Shadow Wars threatening to tear the realm apart, he could only fulfill his sacred duty to "preserve, protect, and honor the Ancient Covenant" by asserting the full authority of the Crystal Throne and his own power as sovereign. It was no time for self-deprecation. Vincent's successors inherited a monarchy with far greater centralized authority—and more need to exercise it—than had existed before the wars. They had less motivation to minimize themselves and their powers.

In the third phase, the Ascension Speech transformed from describing governmental policy to inspiring the people's behavior and consciousness. Monarchs recognized—or at least believed—that the realm faced challenges they ought to address but could not solve through governmental action alone. This represented a shift in consciousness studies and cultural sociology within the realm.

Thus, in his first speech, King Miguel Ortiz proclaimed: "At last, a vision has been granted to us of our realm in its entirety. We see the corruption alongside the virtue, the decay alongside the vitality. With this vision, we approach our future."

If the realm suffered from moral decay, the cure had to come from elevating the people's consciousness, not merely from royal decrees. Similar diagnoses and prescriptions appeared in later speeches.

Monarchs derived their authority to serve as visionary leader-prophets from an observation made by Queen Samir Zhang, though not in her Ascension Speech. She had remarked that the Crystal Throne was "a sacred platform for teaching," a metaphor that suggested not just written proclamations but direct magical and spiritual connection between ruler and subjects. The development of the Resonance Crystals—and even more so, the Vision Pools—made this possible across the entire realm. A telltale sign of the leader-prophet style was the repeated use of the phrase "Let us..."—meaning, effectively, "Follow my guidance." This expression appeared occasionally throughout the history of speeches, but it became dominant in recent centuries. King Luis Grant used it eighteen times in his Ascension Speech, and Queen Rosa Porter repeated it twenty-four times in her second speech.

The change in literary style from formal classical language to more accessible common speech could be demonstrated statistically. In all speeches from Rosa the Wise through King Thomas the Mediator, the average sentence contained sixty-two words. From King Vincent through Queen Samir, it dropped to forty-five words, and in the modern era it averaged thirty-four words. Sophie didn't consider this a decline in quality—her own scholarly writing averaged about twenty-three words per sentence—but it reflected changes in the audience and communication methods. Early monarchs could reference obscure magical theorems and ancient philosophical texts, expecting their audience to understand. That wouldn't be true today. But those ancient audiences wouldn't have understood references to theoretical modeling in consciousness studies or behavioral economics in trade policy.

Sophie discovered that monarchs and their advisors often borrowed memorable phrases from their predecessors without attribution. King Luis Grant's famous rallying cry, "Ask not what magic the throne can work for you; ask what magic you can work for the realm," had an ironic history. In his speech, King Thomas the Builder—hardly a model for the charismatic Luis—had said, "Our most dangerous tendency is to expect too little of our rulers while doing too little for our realm." And even before his ascension, Thomas had proclaimed in a speech at the Academy, "In our great destiny, we must have citizens less concerned with what the throne can do for them and more devoted to what they can do for the realm."

Many issues had their moment in Ascension Speeches before fading into history. These included the Dragon Accords, the Coastal Shield Barriers, territorial expansion into the Wildlands, the Great Canal project, reform of the Guild system, regulation of necromancy, and prohibition of blood magic. Some subjects that Sophie expected to find were conspicuously absent. King Samuel's speech, delivered just before the Great Economic Collapse, contained no hint of financial vulnerability. Queen Juliana's second speech, given as dark forces gathered in the Shadow Realms, made no reference to the coming war. But what amazed Sophie most, reading from her perspective in the modern era, was the near-total silence regarding the rights of the Fae-touched—those born with mixed human and Fae ancestry.

The word "Fae-touched" didn't appear in any speech until Queen Samir's first address, and even then only as part of the phrase "humans and Fae-touched," never acknowledging their specific concerns or the discrimination they faced. Even King Thomas, the first monarch chosen in an election where Fae-touched citizens could vote throughout the realm, didn't remark on this historic change in his speech.

One subject that received consistent attention was taxation and financial regulation. "Taxes" or equivalent terms appeared in forty-five of the fifty-two speeches. King Marcus said in his speech: "The time approaches when we can reduce the tax burden. I oppose extremely high rates, for they generate little revenue, harm our prosperity, and are fundamentally unjust." Royal taxes then consumed about four percent of the realm's economic output. King Rafael said essentially the same thing three centuries later, when taxes claimed twenty-two percent.

The most troubling aspect of the entire collection of speeches was what was said—and left unsaid—about the treatment of the Shadowborn, those born in the cursed regions of Shadowbrook Town and surrounding territories. The words "Shadowborn," "cursed ones," or "shadow-touched" didn't appear at all until King Jonathan's speech in the Year of Reconciliation. Queen Elizabeth the Prosperous had asked rhetorically in her speech, "Upon whom has injustice fallen in any corner of our realm? Who has been denied their rights or property?" These questions were meant to elicit the answer "No one!"—as if there weren't thousands of Shadowborn living in bondage, denied basic human rights, their very existence considered a stain upon the realm.

Before the Shadow Wars, the word "bondage" appeared only in the speeches of King David the Cautious and King Robert the Reluctant, and then only to argue that, pursuant to ancient law and to preserve realm unity, the system should not be challenged. But although generally unmentionable, the issue was reaching a crisis point, and would explode into the Shadow Wars.

After the wars, it was in the speeches of King Jonathan, Queen Catherine, and King William that Sophie found the most explicit discussion of the need to transform into reality the rights and freedoms granted to the Shadowborn on paper by the Three Great Edicts. Catherine's speech was particularly forceful on this point. She had studied at the Academy in Oakdale during an era when it had been a sanctuary for escaped Shadowborn, and her commitment to human rights ran deep. But then the subject began to fade from the speeches. King Alexander said in his first speech, "The persecution of Shadowborn must not be tolerated in a great and civilized realm such as ours," but he said it without passion or urgency. Queen Victoria raised the subject only to express satisfaction at the progress that had been made. And then it vanished. Queen Juliana never mentioned it in any of her four speeches, despite reigning during a period of renewed discrimination.

After the Restoration, the subject returned to Ascension Speeches, but in vague, abstract terms. This was true even of monarchs Sophie knew had been deeply concerned with Shadowborn rights—like King Marcus, Queen Helena, and the current Queen Lucia. Perhaps each felt they had made a sufficient statement by having a prominent Shadowborn perform at their ceremony—a famous singer, a celebrated mage, or a renowned poet. In Queen Lucia's first speech, the only allusion to Shadowborn rights was this sentence: "From our founding, through the Shadow Wars, the Great Collapse, and the Rights Movement, our people have always found the strength to build from these crises the foundations of our future." Sophie noted this not to suggest their concern wasn't genuine, but to indicate what was considered acceptable to say in a speech intended to appeal to values shared by all citizens.

There was much more to contemplate in these speeches than Sophie had summarized in her analysis. There was much to take pride in—the realm's endurance through countless challenges, the peaceful transfer of power through the Crystal Throne's magic, and the general wisdom of the monarchs the people had chosen. But there was also a lesson in humility to be learned. Sophie looked back with astonishment at the ignorance and moral blindness revealed in what past leaders had said and past citizens had believed. She recognized that fifty or one hundred years hence, scholars would shake their heads at what her own generation was saying and believing.

As Sophie prepared to attend Queen Lucia's second Ascension Speech, she wondered what future scholars would make of this moment. What would they see that she was blind to? What injustices of her own time would seem obvious to them but remained invisible to her?

She gathered her notes, extinguished the floating manuscripts with a wave of her hand, and made her way down from her tower. The ceremony would begin at sunset, and she had been granted the honor of standing among the Memory Scribes to record this historic moment. As she walked through the ancient streets of Oakdale toward the palace, she passed citizens of all kinds—humans and Fae-touched, merchants and mages, even a few Shadowborn who had made their way from the southern territories. They were all heading in the same direction, drawn by the same anticipation.

Whatever Queen Lucia would say from the Luminous Balcony, whatever vision she would cast for the realm's future, it would become part of the great tapestry of Ascension Speeches. And someday, perhaps centuries hence, another scholar would sit in a tower study, surrounded by glowing manuscripts, trying to understand what this moment had meant and what it revealed about the consciousness of the age.

Sophie smiled at the thought. The work of understanding never ended. Each generation had to grapple with the wisdom and folly of those who came before, while remaining humble about their own limitations. It was the scholar's burden and privilege—to preserve the past, illuminate the present, and leave questions for the future.

As she approached the palace gates, the first stars began to appear in the darkening sky, and somewhere in the distance, ceremonial bells began to ring, calling the realm to witness another chapter in its long, complex, and continuing story.

option_b: That the Dragon Accords would fail and that the Great Canal project would not be completed

CARBON HARVESTER
BY FELIX CHANG

I

The woman with the pristine carbon-neutral badge gleaming on her lapel watched the tribunal lead Timothy Lawson out of the hearing room. He recognized her as old Gibson's daughter Isabel, no doubt come to see justice served. She didn't have the sheltered look Timothy would have expected in someone whose father owned the most lucrative environmental remediation franchise in three sectors. She wasn't afraid to meet his eye, the eye of a judicially certified violator. There was, perhaps, a crease of puzzlement in her brow, as if she had thought environmental crimes were committed by callous corporate types, not by young atmospheric engineers who still wore their university pins.

Paul Graham, Gibson's operations director, was her escort. Timothy felt certain, without proof, that Graham was the one who had framed him for the charge of carbon credit fraud by planting falsified atmospheric data in his laboratory systems. The older man stared at Timothy coldly as he was led out of the hearing room and down the corridor back to detention.

Sasha, Timothy's cellmate, took one look at his face as he was returned behind the security field.

"Guilty," Sasha said.

Timothy glared at him.

"I know, I know," Sasha said hastily. "You were framed. But what's the sentence?"

"Five years or one."

"Take the five," Sasha advised. "Learn meditation in a nice climate-controlled rehabilitation center. A year on a biomod contract will seem a lot longer, even if you're lucky enough to survive it."

Timothy took four steps to the far wall of the cell, stood there briefly with his head bent and turned to face Sasha.

"No," Timothy said softly. "I'm going into a conversion tank. I'm going to be a carbon harvester, Sasha. I'm going out to Goldfield on Calderon and collect atmospheric diamonds."

"Smuggling? It won't work."

Timothy didn't answer. The Gibson company had gone after him because he had been working on a method of synthesizing atmospheric diamonds artificially. The Gibson company would be happy to see him mark time for five years of so-called social reorientation. But if he could get out to Calderon, with his physiology adapted to the environment of that brutal world, he could study the diamonds under conditions no laboratory could duplicate. He might even be able to cause trouble for Gibson.

His only problem would be staying alive for a year.

An interview with a doctor from the Biomodification Corps was required for all persons who elected conversion status. The law stated that potential converts must be fully informed of the rights and hazards of altered physiology before they signed a release. The requirement held whether or not the individual, like Timothy, already had experience with the science.

By the time humanity colonized distant worlds, medical biology had made it possible to regenerate and redesign human organs for extreme environments. Regeneration was limited only by advanced age and genetic compatibility. As long as cellular integrity could be maintained, however, any person could have enhanced lungs for toxic atmospheres and reinforced bones for crushing gravity, if they could pay for the treatment.

From regeneration it was a short step to specialized adaptation. The techniques were perfected to allow humans to work on the dozen barely habitable worlds humanity had discovered. Even on the moons of Jupiter, where pressure suits were theoretically adequate, a person could work more efficiently with redesigned physiology than encased in protective gear. On more extreme planets light-years away, the advantages of biomodified bodies were even greater.

Unfortunately for planetary development corporations, hardly anyone wanted to become biomodified. High pay lured few volunteers. So a law was passed permitting a convicted criminal to earn freedom by serving one year as a biomod for every five years they would otherwise spend in rehabilitation.

"What types of biomods do you have contracts for right now, doctor?" Timothy asked the woman assigned to his case. It would look suspicious if he asked for Calderon without preliminary questions.

"Four," answered the doctor.

"Thermal adapts for Richmond on Fendria. Modified for extreme heat tolerance and with enhanced cooling systems. Then we need pressure adapts for Unity on Galdoria. If you want something closer to baseline human, there's Harborview on Quendor, where we'd just enhance your radiation resistance and boost your immune response. Last, of course, there's always a need for carbon harvesters on Calderon."

The doctor shrugged, as if naturally no one could be expected to choose Calderon. Timothy frowned in apparent consideration of the alternatives.

"What's the pay range?" he asked.

"Ten thousand credits per year on Harborview. Fifteen on Richmond or Unity. Twenty-five on Calderon."

Timothy raised his eyebrows.

"Why such a difference? Everyone knows about carbon harvesters living in the acidic atmosphere while they hunt atmospheric diamonds. But don't your conversions make the biomod comfortable in the new environment?"

"Sure they do," said the doctor. "We can make you think sulfuric mist feels better than spring rain and we can have you moving efficiently despite the gravity differential. But we can't make you like the sight of yourself in a mirror. And we can't guarantee that a Screamer won't kill you."

"Still," Timothy mused aloud, "it would mean substantial compensation waiting at the end of the year."

He leaned forward to fill in the necessary form.

Since it was cheaper to transport a baseline human than to rig special life support in a spacecraft, every planet operated its own conversion facilities. On the freight hauler that carried him from Earth, Timothy Lawson was confined to a small cabin that was opened only for an automated system to deliver meals and remove waste. He was still a prisoner.

Sometimes he could hear voices in the passageway outside, and once one of them sounded like a woman's. But since women neither served on freight haulers nor worked in the surface operations on harsher worlds—or so he thought—he decided it was his imagination. He might have been inert cargo for all he learned about space travel.

Nevertheless his time was not wasted. He had as a companion, or cellmate, another convict who had elected conversion to carbon harvester. More important, his companion had served time on Calderon before and had wanted to return.

"It's the atmospheric diamonds," explained Juan, the repeat offender. "The ones you see on Earth are already degrading, but they're still worth a fortune. There's nothing like a fresh one, though. And I'm not the first to become obsessed. When I was reconverted and returned home I had nine thousand credits waiting. That'll buy a six-month-old diamond that still has maybe a quarter of its luminescence. So I stole a fresh one and got caught."

Timothy had held an atmospheric diamond in his hand as he gazed into it. He could understand the obsession. The crystalline structure was transparent as glass, formed from carbon extracted directly from Calderon's dense atmosphere through a process that remained mysterious. Within the lattice played tiny currents of bioluminescence, part of some unexplained metabolic process. Scientific instruments detected electromagnetic signatures from the diamonds, but the phenomenon remained poorly understood.

Hardly anyone who witnessed an atmospheric diamond's beauty bothered to question its workings. For a few breathtaking moments there would be only faint, intermittent glimmers, and then there would be a cascade of light, dancing through the crystalline structure in a symphony of brilliance.

It took about three years for an atmospheric diamond to die after removal from Calderon's environment. Beauty, rarity, and fading value made the diamonds a luxury commodity unlike anything humanity had ever encountered. If Timothy had found a means of preserving them indefinitely, it would have made him wealthy at the expense of the Gibson monopoly.

"You know what I think?" Juan asked. "I think those light pulses are the diamond signaling its parent organism. They glow like captured starlight when you extract one from the acid pools, and immediately a Screamer always comes diving out of the clouds at you."

"I've been meaning to ask you," Timothy said. "How do you handle the Screamers?"

Juan grinned.

"First you try to hit it with a neutralizer blast. If you miss, you start running for the shelter. All this time you're broadcasting for help, understand. When the Screamer catches you, you dodge while it plunges its feeding appendages into the ground where you were standing. You grab onto its carapace and hang on while it thrashes around. Finally, if the transport comes—and if they don't accidentally blast you instead—you live to tell the story."

II

Timothy Lawson kept his normal form on Calderon just long enough to experience the discomfort of the planet's gravity and atmospheric pressure. He was told he needed a final physical assessment and was taken directly to a medical bay. His heart was laboring to maintain circulation in this oppressive environment, but the doctor had apparently learned to make allowances.

"Swallow this," said the doctor after completing a series of scans.

Timothy swallowed the capsule. Two minutes later he felt consciousness beginning to slip away.

"This is it," he thought in alarm.

He felt someone guide him back onto a medical platform. Before consciousness faded completely, he realized that no one received a chance to reconsider biomodification, that he was on his way to the conversion tank immediately.

When he finally awoke, he felt rested and surprisingly comfortable. But for a long time he was afraid to open his eyes.

"Come on, Lawson," said a deep, resonant voice. "Let's test our new capabilities."

It wasn't Juan's voice, but it had to be Juan. Timothy opened his eyes.

Everyone had seen images of carbon harvesters. It was different having one stand beside you. Juan looked somewhat like an enormous salamander except that his head retained mostly human features. He stood on reinforced legs, his lower limbs bent to support massive thighs, and his trunk angled forward so that his arms hung to the ground. The arms were thick as tree trunks. The hands had become efficient tools, with broad fingers tipped with crystalline claws capable of cutting through rock. The skin had turned a mottled gray-green and had developed thick, overlapping scales. Not a single hair remained anywhere on the body.

This, Timothy realized, was what he looked like now.

It would have been more bearable if the head had not retained strong traces of humanity. The nostrils were wide and the jaw structure had changed, but the ears were recognizably human and the eyes, under those protective ridges, were human eyes. Timothy felt certain those eyes could still express human emotions.

He started to walk forward and stumbled. Juan laughed.

"Easy there, newcomer," Juan said, extending his hands. "Try moving with your center of gravity lower. And take it slow."

Timothy adjusted his stance and found nerve and muscle coordination to be perfect. He could move with surprising agility.

"That's better," Juan said approvingly. "Now put this on and we'll go outside."

Timothy fastened a harness that held equipment pouches and protective coverings. He followed as Juan pushed open a pressure door to lead the way out of the recovery room.

They entered a staging area partly enclosed by the Gibson company's atmospheric dome. The far section of the area was open to the yellow-green haze that hung perpetually over Calderon's surface and turned most of it into acid pools and mineral flats. A high barrier enclosed the outer portion of the staging area. Along the barrier were thirty stations for carbon harvesters.

From across the staging area, a carbon harvester bounded over to them in powerful strides. Attached to a harness across his shoulders were a neutralizer weapon and various tools.

"Names?" he growled. He was larger than Timothy and intimidating in every way.

"Juan. I'm back, Talia."

"I'm Lawson."

"Juan again? Just resume where you left off. You, come with me." Talia pointed to Timothy and moved toward the open section of the staging area.

"Do what she says," Juan whispered to Timothy. "She's essentially a supervisor and enforcer combined."

Timothy was put through exercises to acclimate him to his transformed body, to teach him how to move efficiently and how to extract diamonds. He was shown how to operate the communications system he would carry and how to fire the neutralizer weapon. Finally he was told to consume some native vegetation. He did so and immediately experienced severe nausea.

Talia laughed.

"That's to remind you you're still human," Talia said, grinning. "Everything that grows on this planet is toxic to your core biology. So if you have ideas about hiding until your term expires, forget them. This facility is where you eat."

Timothy turned without a word and moved slowly away from Talia. He lifted his head to survey the area and saw two baseline humans watching from an observation platform on the dome.

He jumped for a better view.

Gazing at him with visible distaste, after witnessing the end of his session with Talia, were Isabel Gibson and operations director Paul Graham.

The woman's presence merely puzzled Timothy, but Graham's being here worried him. Graham had tried to eliminate him once and was now in an excellent position to make that elimination permanent.

At the evening meal, crouching beside a low table with the dozen other carbon harvesters operating from the dome, Timothy asked what the two were doing out here.

"The woman will inherit this operation eventually, won't she?" asked one of the others. "She wants to see what kind of workers are generating her wealth."

"Maybe that guy Graham brought her along to demonstrate his authority," said another. "Just hope he doesn't take direct control of operations."

III

Next morning Talia distributed weapons, tools, communicators, and collection pouches to carry any diamonds the harvesters found. She gave each worker a navigation device and assigned the sectors to be worked during the shift. Finally she called Timothy aside.

"In case you're interested in reducing your sentence," Talia said, "you can get a week removed for every diamond you bring in. Now get out there and work."

Talia sent Timothy and Juan out together so the veteran could show Timothy proper procedures. Timothy had already learned that the barrier around the staging area was to keep Screamers out, not harvesters in. He climbed over it and moved along after Juan.

Feet splashing through acidic puddles, they traveled about eight kilometers from the Gibson station, swimming cautiously across pools too wide to traverse otherwise. The acid, while not precisely pleasant, was not uncomfortable to their modified skin, and the dense atmosphere felt natural to their redesigned lungs. Small native organisms skittered out of their path. Finally Juan stopped. His experienced eye had detected a disturbance pattern in the mineral deposits.

"Stay alert," Juan said. "There's been a Screamer in this area recently. If you see something like an armored tank headed our way, start shooting."

At each position along the trail they scanned their surroundings carefully. They saw no Screamers, but this meant little, as the creatures could emerge from underground with little warning.

Juan halted again when they reached a roughly circular area some fifteen meters in diameter where the mineral crust had been disturbed.

"We're fortunate," he said as Timothy stopped beside him. "A diamond was deposited somewhere here within the last few days. These sites are difficult to locate once new growth begins."

Juan surveyed the area thoroughly.

"No immediate threats. We extract."

They started at the center of the disturbed area, breaking through mineral crust with their claws and sifting through the substrate beneath. Usually a harvester worked in a spiral pattern outward from the center, but Timothy and Juan worked in gradually expanding semicircles opposite each other. They had to dig over a meter deep, and progress was slow until they had a pit large enough to work in efficiently. Each handful of material had to be examined carefully before being discarded, to ensure it didn't conceal a diamond. As he worked, Timothy kept thinking what an inefficient system this was from a supply chain management perspective. Everything about the operation violated basic principles of organizational behavior.

"Found it!" Juan shouted. He climbed out of the pit and began cleaning a spherical object about ten centimeters in diameter. Timothy climbed out to observe.

"A large one," Juan said. He held it, still covered with traces of substrate, carefully in his palm, then lifted it to eye level. "Just look at it."

The diamond was pulsing with extraordinary luminescence, like captured lightning dancing through crystal. Static crackled in Timothy's audio pickup and he recalled what Juan had said, that the light display was the diamond's signal to a parent Screamer. Timothy looked around quickly.

"Move!" he shouted.

At the edge of the clearing, a segmented mass of armored plating, some three meters tall and four meters wide, had risen from beneath the surface. The front segment was dominated by feeding appendages already extended. Before Timothy could draw his weapon, the Screamer lowered its bulk and surged forward.

Timothy leaped with all his strength, covering significant distance. While still airborne he activated his communicator.

"Calling transport!" he spoke rapidly. "Juan and Lawson, sector twelve, eight kilometers out. Emergency!"

"Lawson?" asked a voice in his audio pickup. "What's the situation?"

"We have a diamond but a Screamer is attacking."

"En route."

Timothy landed and immediately turned, his weapon ready.

Juan must have been struck by the Screamer's initial charge, as he was attempting to move on one damaged leg. The diamond lay on the ground where Juan had dropped it, still pulsing with light. The Screamer, its multiple legs churning, was repositioning for another attack.

Aiming quickly, Timothy fired a neutralizer blast at the creature's midsection. The energy burst penetrated the armor and caused the Screamer to convulse. It twisted toward Timothy. He dodged to one side, firing from an awkward angle and missing, and saw the Screamer turn toward where he would land. His legs were tensed to move again the moment he touched down, but he realized the Screamer would reach him first. As he landed he thrust his weapon forward almost into the creature's feeding appendages and fired again.

Even as he was knocked aside, Timothy's body was showered with fragments of alien tissue scattered by the neutralizer's discharge. Desperately pushing himself upright, he saw the massive body shudder and become still.

Timothy took a deep breath and looked around.

"Juan!" he called. "Where are you?"

"Over here." Juan stood briefly and collapsed again. Timothy moved over to him.

"Thanks," Juan said. "Harvesters look out for each other. You'll make a good one. I wouldn't have survived. My leg's badly damaged."

"The transport should arrive soon," Timothy said. He looked at the dead Screamer and shook his head. "Tell me, what are the actual survival statistics for this work?"

"Last time I was here, there was approximately one harvester killed for every eight diamonds recovered. Of course you're not supposed to stand there admiring the diamonds like I did while a Screamer approaches."

Timothy moved to the diamond, which continued pulsing with light where it rested on the ground. He excavated a depression in the substrate and buried the diamond.

"Just in case there are more Screamers nearby," he explained.

"Doesn't matter," said Juan, pointing upward. "Here comes the transport, late as usual."

The large vehicle descended, hovered to inspect the dead Screamer, and settled on landing struts. Through the transparent cockpit Timothy could see Paul Graham and Isabel Gibson. The operations director opened the hatch and leaned out.

"I see you neutralized the Screamer," he said. "Hand over the diamond."

"Juan has a damaged leg," Timothy said. "I'll help him aboard and then retrieve the diamond."

While Juan grabbed the hatch frame to pull himself into the transport, Timothy positioned himself under his companion and lifted him by the torso. He hadn't fully appreciated the strength of his new body. Juan, as a carbon harvester, would have weighed close to four hundred pounds on Earth.

Graham made no move to assist, but Isabel reached under Juan's shoulder and strained to help him inside. Once he was aboard, Timothy saw, the cabin was crowded.

"Are you going to have room for me as well?" he asked.

"Not this trip," Graham answered. "Now give me the diamond."

Timothy didn't hesitate. "The diamond stays with me," he said quietly.

"You do what I tell you, harvester," said Graham.

"No. I want to ensure you return." Timothy turned his head to Isabel. "You see, Ms. Gibson, I don't trust your associate. You might ask him to tell you about it."

Graham stared at him with narrowed eyes. Suddenly he smiled in a way that made Timothy uneasy.

"Whatever you say, Lawson," Graham said. He turned to the controls. Within moments the transport was airborne.

IV

A round trip for the transport should have taken no more than thirty minutes, allowing time for Juan to be evacuated at the facility.

After an hour passed, Timothy began to worry. He was certain Graham would return for the diamond. Finally he realized that Graham could locate the diamond approximately by the position of the dead Screamer. Graham could return for the diamond at any time with another harvester to extract it.

Timothy activated his communicator.

"This is Lawson, calling the transport," he said. "When are you returning?"

There was no answer except the hum of the carrier signal.

If he tried to carry the diamond back, Timothy knew, Screamers would attack him throughout the journey. A harvester had virtually no chance of traveling eight kilometers with a diamond alone. He could abandon the diamond here, of course. Even then he would be fortunate to make it back, following an uncertain navigation course from which he and Juan had certainly deviated during their outward journey. There were no landmarks in this wasteland to help him navigate. Workers were supposed to home in on facility signals if they became disoriented, but Graham would deny him that assistance.

What was the night like on Calderon? Perhaps Screamers were less active at night. If he could stay alert, and if he didn't succumb to hunger in this modified body, and if the Screamers left him alone....

A mechanical sound made Timothy react in alarm.

Then he relaxed somewhat, for it was the transport, returning across the mineral flats. But what if it was Graham, returning alone to dispose of him without witnesses? Timothy moved toward the carcass of the dead Screamer and took cover behind it.

No barrage of neutralizer fire came from the transport. The large vehicle descended erratically, tilted awkwardly in an inexpert attempt to land, struck the ground hard and slid forward. As Timothy jumped aside, the landing struts caught against the Screamer's body and the transport tipped forward, one of the stabilizers plunging into the substrate.

Timothy moved forward in alarm. Not only was his means of safe return to the facility compromised, but now he would have the additional burden of assisting the pilot. When he reached the cockpit of the transport, he saw that the pilot, extracting herself from the controls to stand, was Isabel Gibson.

"Are you injured?" Timothy asked her. She reached for his shoulder to steady herself as she climbed out of the vehicle.

"I don't think so," she said. "But taking an impact in this gravity is unpleasant. From the way my face feels I should be developing significant bruising soon."

"What happened?"

"I made an error in judgment." She gestured back toward the facility. "Graham wasn't going to retrieve you. He said anyone who defied his authority should try reasoning with the Screamers."

She looked at the defensive weapon mounted on the transport.

"They feed at night, you know. And they consume their own dead," she said. "The Screamer you killed would attract them inevitably."

Timothy glanced around quickly to ensure no Screamers had already arrived. He regarded the transport with concern at the thought of what an inadequate shelter it would provide.

"Anyway," Isabel said, "I informed him he couldn't simply abandon you here and we began arguing. I lost my composure. He thought he had brought me to Calderon on an inspection tour. I told him the real reason I was here was to evaluate for my father how he was managing operations and there appeared to be significant problems. So he told me very formally that I could manage things as I saw fit and he walked away."

She shrugged, as if to indicate she had mishandled the situation.

"And you took the transport yourself," Timothy said, as if he could hardly believe it.

"On Earth I can pilot a transport expertly. But I wasn't accustomed to this gravity and atmospheric density. I don't suppose you could right this vehicle?"

Timothy pulled at the body of the Screamer until he freed it from the landing struts. He strained with all his strength at the stabilizer embedded in the substrate, but the weight of the transport held it fast and the ground gripped it with considerable resistance. After several minutes he had to concede defeat.

"We defend against the Screamers, then," she said, as matter-of-factly as if that challenge was resolved. "If it helps, I know how to operate the defensive weapon."

"No. In this haze, at night, the Screamers would reach us before we could detect them. We must attempt to return to the facility." He stood in thought while she observed him patiently. "What happened to the other harvesters who went out today?" he asked.

"They were recalled when the transport departed initially. Some of them may not have returned yet."

Timothy considered the implications. This was partly a question of environmental ethics—what responsibility did they have to minimize their impact on the native ecosystem? But more immediately, it was a matter of survival and ethical decision-making under pressure. The organizational behavior principles he'd studied seemed almost laughable in this context, yet the supply chain management concepts were relevant: they needed to optimize their route back, manage their limited resources, and coordinate with any available support.

"Here's what we'll do," Timothy said finally. "We'll use the transport's emergency beacon to mark this location. Then we'll start back toward the facility using the navigation device. If any other harvesters are still out, they might intercept our signal and provide assistance. And we'll bury the diamond here—its signal is what attracts the Screamers most strongly."

Isabel nodded. "That makes sense. But I should mention—I'm not biomodified. I can't survive out here for long."

Timothy looked at her, suddenly understanding the full scope of their predicament. She was still baseline human, dependent on the transport's life support system. Without it, she would succumb to Calderon's toxic atmosphere within hours.

"How long can you last?" he asked.

"With the emergency respirator? Maybe four hours. Six if we're fortunate."

Timothy made a quick calculation. Eight kilometers in four hours, while protecting a baseline human and avoiding Screamers. The odds were not favorable. But they had no alternative.

"We move now," he said. "Stay close to me."

As they began their journey back toward the facility, Timothy activated his communicator once more. "This is Lawson. Emergency situation. Isabel Gibson is with me, baseline human, limited life support. We're returning from sector twelve. Any harvesters in the area, please respond."

Static crackled in his audio pickup. Then, faintly, a voice: "Lawson, this is Talia. I'm in sector ten. I can reach your position in approximately thirty minutes. Can you hold out?"

Timothy looked at Isabel, who was already breathing heavily through her respirator, struggling with each step in the oppressive gravity.

"We'll have to," Timothy replied.

They moved as quickly as Isabel's baseline physiology would allow, which was frustratingly slow. Timothy kept scanning their surroundings for any sign of Screamers. The dead one they'd left behind would indeed attract others once night fell—which, according to his internal chronometer, would be in less than two hours.

"I need to rest," Isabel gasped after they'd covered perhaps a kilometer.

Timothy helped her sit on a relatively stable mineral outcropping. He kept his weapon ready, eyes constantly moving.

"I'm sorry," she said. "I should have thought this through better. My father always said I acted impulsively."

"You came back for me," Timothy said simply. "That took courage."

"Or foolishness. Graham was right about one thing—I don't really understand this operation. I've studied the economic history of resource extraction, read about waste reduction strategies and environmental ethics. But being here, seeing what you harvesters actually do..." She trailed off, shaking her head.

"It raises existential questions," Timothy agreed. "About what we're willing to sacrifice for profit. About the organizational behavior that allows this system to continue. About whether the diamonds are worth the cost in human—or modified human—lives."

"You sound like you've thought about this extensively."

"I have. That's partly why I'm here. I was developing a synthesis method that would have made atmospheric diamonds renewable. The Gibson company couldn't allow that."

Isabel looked at him sharply. "You're saying my father's company framed you?"

"I'm saying Paul Graham did. Whether your father knew..." Timothy shrugged. "That's between you and him."

Before Isabel could respond, Timothy's audio pickup crackled to life. "Lawson, this is Talia. I've got visual on your position. There's also a Screamer approaching from the south. You need to move north, now."

Timothy pulled Isabel to her feet. "We run. Now."

They moved as fast as Isabel could manage, which still seemed agonizingly slow. Timothy could see the Screamer now, its armored bulk rising from beneath the surface about two hundred meters away. Talia appeared from the opposite direction, covering ground in powerful leaps.

"Get behind me!" Talia shouted as she reached them. She positioned herself between the Screamer and the two others, weapon raised.

The Screamer charged. Talia fired, her first shot striking true. The creature convulsed but continued forward. She fired again, and this time the Screamer collapsed, sliding to a stop just meters from their position.

"That was close," Talia said. She looked at Isabel with something like respect. "You came out here alone to retrieve him?"

"It seemed like the right thing to do," Isabel said.

"Foolish, but brave," Talia said. "Come on. Let's get you both back before Graham decides to cause more trouble."

As they made their way back to the facility, Timothy found himself reconsidering his assumptions about Isabel Gibson. She wasn't just the privileged heir to a corporate empire. She was someone willing to risk her life based on ethical principles, someone who asked difficult questions about the system she would someday inherit.

When they finally reached the facility, Graham was waiting at the barrier, his expression unreadable.

"Ms. Gibson," he said formally. "I trust you've learned something about the challenges of managing operations on Calderon."

"I have," Isabel replied coolly. "I've learned that the current management is unacceptable. You're relieved of your position, effective immediately. Talia will assume operational control pending my father's review."

Graham's face reddened. "You don't have the authority—"

"I have full proxy authority from my father for this inspection. Which you would know if you'd bothered to read the documentation I provided when I arrived. Security will escort you to quarters pending transport back to Earth."

As Graham was led away, Isabel turned to Timothy. "I need to speak with you later. About your synthesis research. If it's viable, it could change everything—not just for the Gibson company, but for how we approach resource extraction across all our operations. It could be a model for ethical environmental management."

Timothy nodded slowly. "I'd be willing to discuss it. But I want assurances that other harvesters won't continue to be exploited while we develop the technology."

"Agreed. We'll work on that together." She paused. "Thank you, Timothy. For saving my life out there. And for making me see what I needed to see."

As Timothy watched her walk away to begin the complex work of reforming the operation, he felt something he hadn't experienced since his conviction: hope. Perhaps his year on Calderon would lead to something more than just survival. Perhaps it would lead to real change—in the system, in the company, and in himself.

The atmospheric diamonds would still be beautiful, still be valuable. But maybe, just maybe, they wouldn't have to cost so much humanity to obtain.
question: What would best describe Isabel's attitude towards Graham?
option_a: She trusted his judgment and respected his operational experience on Calderon.
option_b: She distrusted him and questioned his management decisions.
correct_answer_text: She distrusted him and questioned his management decisions.
incorrect_answer_text: She trusted his judgment and respected his operational experience on Calderon.
explanation: Throughout the story, Isabel demonstrates distrust of Graham and questions his management. She argues with him about abandoning Timothy, reveals that she was actually on Calderon to evaluate Graham's management for her father (not on a tour as Graham believed), tells Timothy she found "significant problems" with how Graham was running operations, and ultimately relieves Graham of his position. Her attitude is clearly one of distrust and criticism rather than trust and respect.

synthetic_story:
THE CATALYST
By ADAPTED WORK

Sure I'm a Catalyst, and I've been fired seven times, always in the pressure of corporate transitions, and I'm not alone, although there aren't very many of us, never were.

It made sense. TechFusion was new and they wanted her on the project because she was a trained analyst. They wanted facts, not speculation. But to ask a woman to give up eighteen months of her life—well, that was asking a lot. Eighteen months in a research facility. Still, it had an appeal Sara Henry knew she couldn't deny, a data scientist's joy of a clean dataset, a corporate merger far afield, a closeup view of innovation, history in the making.

TechFusion Chief Marcus Sharma knocked the ash from his cigarette in a tray, saying, "DataCorp is willing to let you have a leave of absence, if you're interested."

She knew Director Walter Cook from years of consulting, and now Cook said, "Personally, I don't want to see anybody else on the job. You've got a fine record in this sort of thing."

Sara Henry smiled, but just barely. "You should have called me for the Stonebridge project."

Cook nodded. "I wish we had had you on the Stonebridge Initiative."

"Engineers," Sharma said, "make poor observers."

The Stonebridge Initiative had launched three years before with two thousand employees relocated to the new renewable energy campus in Stonebridge, Xandria. It reached full operation with less than nine hundred remaining employees. Upon the completion of the first year, the management's report of conflict and chaos during the transition period was twisted, distorted and fragmentary. Henry remembered it well. The decision of TechFusion was that the employees started internal warfare early in the transition, that it was fanned by the ignorance of Director Peterson in dealing with such matters.

"Corporate transitions affect people in a peculiar way," Cook said. "We have conquered the problem of small team relocations—witness the success of the Springfield campus, for example—but when there are large groups, control is more difficult."

"Peterson," Sharma said, "was incompetent. The trouble started at about the six-month point. It ended with employees engaging in open hostility with each other and management. Peterson was lucky to escape with his career."

"As I recall," Henry said, "there was something about the AI systems."

Cook rubbed his chin. "No personal AI assistants were allowed in the facility, but you must remember the employees were selected for their intelligence and resourcefulness. They utilized these attributes to set up unauthorized systems to gain advantages."

"The second project is history," Sharma said. "And a puzzle."

Henry nodded. "The Crystalbrook facility failed."

"Yes. We gave control to the employees."

"Assuming no systemic failure," Cook said, "it was a wrong decision. They probably sabotaged the project."

"And now," Henry said, "you're going to try again."

Sharma said very gravely, "We've got the finest director in the industry. Elijah Allen. No doubt you've heard of him. He's spent his life in corporate transformations, and he's handpicking his own management team. We have also raised prerequisites for applicants. We don't think anything is going to happen, but if it does, we want to get an impersonal, unprejudiced view. That's where you come in. You do the observing, the reporting. We'll evaluate it on your return."

"If I return," said Henry.

"I suppose that's problematical," Cook said, "but I think you will. Director Allen and his fifty managers want to succeed as badly as you do." He grinned. "You can write that book on work-life balance you're always talking about after the project ends."

Being a Catalyst is important, probably as important as running the facility, and I think it is this thought that keeps us satisfied, willing to be what we are.

The Irondale Renewable Energy Complex had been built over two years, as had its predecessor in Crystalbrook, at a tremendous cost. Basically, it was an instrument which would open new possibilities for sustainable energy, reducing the carbon footprint of an entire region. A massive campus, the facility would house laboratories, manufacturing plants, and living quarters for fifteen hundred employees and their families. It was equipped with every conceivable facility and comfort—cafeterias, assembly halls, individual and family apartments, recreation centers, fitness facilities, library, theater. Nothing had been overlooked.

The director's briefing room was crowded, the air was heavy with the breathing of so many people, and the ventilators could not quite clear the air of coffee and stress that drifted aimlessly here and there before it was caught and whisked away.

In the tradition of analyst and observer, Sara Henry tried to be as inconspicuous as possible, pressing against a wall, but Director Allen's eyes sought hers several times as Allen listened to final reports from his engineers, data managers, AI specialists, resource coordinators, and all the rest. He grunted his approval or disapproval, made a suggestion here, a restriction there. There was no doubt that Allen was in charge, yet there was a human quality about him that Henry liked. The director's was a lean face, well maintained, and his eyes were sharp and focused.

"Colleagues," Allen said at last, as Henry knew he would, "I want to introduce Sara Henry, whose presence TechFusion has impressed upon us. On loan from DataCorp, she will have an observer status." He introduced her to the others. All of them seemed friendly; Henry thought it was a good team.

Allen detained her after the others had gone. "One thing, Ms. Henry. To make it easier for you, I suggest you think of this project strictly from the observer viewpoint. There will be no report for DataCorp at the end."

Henry was startled. While she had considered the possibility, she had not dwelt on it. Now it loomed large in her mind. "I don't understand, Director Allen. It seems to me—"

"Let me put it differently. Let me say that you will not understand why I say that until the project ends." He smiled. "Perhaps I shouldn't have mentioned it."

Henry left the director's quarters with an odd taste in her mouth. Now why had Allen said that? Why hadn't Sharma or Cook said something, if it was important?

She made herself comfortable in her small apartment, which is to say she dropped on her bed, found it more comfortable than she thought it would be, put her arms behind her head, stared at the ceiling. Standard walls, one window overlooking the solar array, ventilation, and standard lighting. This would be her home for eighteen months, just as there were homes like it for fifteen hundred others, except that the family apartments would be larger. Her quarters were near the administration building.

She felt rather than heard the dull hum. It was a sound she knew would be with her for eighteen months—the sound of the renewable energy systems coming online.

She looked at her tablet, opened her notes and made an entry. The facility right now would be beginning its first full day of operation. She got up. She'd have to go to the observation deck to see the full solar array. First full view of the project in action.

The penetration of corporate culture by large groups is the coming out from under the traditions of established norms, and as these organization-originated rules fall away, the floundering group seeks a new control, for they are humanity adrift, rudderless, for whom the mission statements are no longer bearings but nonexistent things, and values are altered if they are not shown the way.

The theft of Alex Robbins' research drive occurred on the forty-second day. In Henry's mind the incident, though insignificant from the standpoint of the facility as a whole, could very well be the cause of dissension later on. Her notes covering it were therefore very thorough.

Robbins' drive contained paleontology research data—years of work, according to the Director's Bulletin, the facility's daily newsletter which went to all employees. In the Bulletin the director appealed to the thief to return the drive to Dr. Robbins. He said it was significant that all employees had passed psychological evaluations, and that it was to the facility's discredit that someone with criminal tendencies should have been permitted inside.

Henry had to smile at that. What did Director Allen think of those employees who sabotaged each other at Crystalbrook? They had passed evaluations too. This, then, was what happened when you took fifteen hundred strangers and stuck them in a campus for eighteen months.

When Henry saw Allen about it, the director said, "Of course I realize it takes only a little thing like this to set things off. I know people get tired of seeing each other, attending the same meetings, looking at the same data dashboards, walking down the same corridors, reading the same reports, eating the same meals, though God knows we try to vary it as much as we can. Corporate pressure creates rough edges. But the point is, we know all this, and knowing it, we shouldn't let it happen. We've got to find that thief."

"What would he want research data for? Have you thought of that?"

"Of course. It'd have real value to competitors."

Henry sought out Alex Robbins. He was a middle-aged man with a tired face and worried eyes. He said, "Now what am I doing here? I could only bring along so much data and I left behind some personal projects to make room for this research. I'm a paleontologist, and TechFusion asked me to consult on their geological surveys. But what use am I now? Where am I going to get data like that? Do you know how long it took me to collect it? It's not ordinary research, Ms. Henry."

There was an appeal from Robbins in the next day's newsletter describing the data, telling of its value, and requesting its return in the interests of the project and of scientific progress.

On the forty-seventh day a witness turned up who said he had seen someone emerging from Robbins' office with the drive. "I didn't think anything of it at the time," Emma Graves said.

Allen asked her to describe the person.

"Oh, about average height, wearing all black, and they wore a silver mask that covered their face completely."

"Didn't you think that was important?" Allen asked in an outraged voice. "Someone wearing a silver mask?"

Graves shrugged. "This is a research facility. How would I know whether a silver mask—or any mask—does or doesn't belong in a research facility? Maybe it was some kind of experiment."

Although Graves' account appeared in the newsletter, it was largely discounted.

"If it is true," Allen told Henry, "the theft must be the work of someone unstable. But I don't believe Emma Graves. It may well be she's the unstable one." He snorted. "Silver mask! I think I'll have Graves evaluated by our psychologist."

Attendant to taking notes on this incident, Henry noted a strange thing. Robbins worked in Building A, and those who worked in that building—more than three hundred people—felt that the thief must surely work in Building B or D. Mohamed Tucker, who had the office next to Robbins', sounded the consensus when he said, "Surely a person wouldn't steal from their own building, now would they, Ms. Henry?"

And so, Henry observed in her notebook, are divisions created.

Seen in corporate life, routines are unchanging, silent, sterile patterns ever watchful and demanding. To people unused to it, such monotony numbs, compresses, stultifies. One introduces a countermeasure, proof one exists, which is any overt act, sometimes violent.

On the sixty-first day Malik Vasquez, a young engineer working on AI system integration, reported being attacked in his workspace while his supervisor was in a meeting. He was taken to the facility's healthcare center, where staff confirmed minor injuries.

He said the culprit wore a silver mask, and though his description of what happened did not appear in the story in the newsletter, it lost no time in penetrating every corner of the facility.

Henry was present when a delegation from Building C called on Director Allen, demanding action.

Allen remained seated behind his desk, unperturbed, saying, "I have no security personnel to spare for constant patrol duty."

The delegation commenced speaking vehemently, to be quieted by Allen's raised hand.

"I sympathize," Allen said, "but it is up to each building to deal with its problems, whatever they may be. My job is to keep this facility operational and meet our renewable energy targets."

The group left in a surly mood.

"You wonder at my reluctance, Ms. Henry," Director Allen said. "But suppose I assign security to patrol duties, the culprit isn't caught, and further incidents occur. What then? It soon becomes security's fault. And soon the employees will begin thinking these things might be security's doing in the first place."

"Yes," Henry said, "but what if the intruder is a member of security?"

"I know my team," Allen said flatly.

"You could have a facility-wide search for the mask and the drive."

"Do you think it is a member of security?" Allen's eyes were bright. "No, I trust my people. I won't violate that trust."

Henry left, feeling uneasy. If she were Allen, she'd initiate an investigation, if nothing else than to prove security guiltless. Why couldn't Allen see the wisdom of setting an example for the employees?

As a Catalyst, I knew that corporate pressure breeds hostility. There is a seed of malevolence in every person. It sometimes blossoms in confined environments. At Irondale it was ready for ripening.

Walter Cook was found unconscious in the medical center on the eighty-third day. Cook, a Building D consultant, had complained of feeling ill, had been treated with a diagnosis of exhaustion. He had put his tablet with confidential files in the drawer of the small table beside his bed. A person in a silver mask was seen hurrying from the medical area, and a staff investigation revealed that Cook had been injured trying to prevent the theft of the tablet.

Director Allen did not wait for the newsletter. Through the facility's speaker system, he reported that Cook had critical strategic planning documents on the tablet and had been seriously injured. He said that since the incident occurred in the administrative section of the facility, his management team would be forced to submit to a thorough inspection in an effort to find the mask, the drive, the tablet and the perpetrator.

"I will not countenance such an act by a manager," Allen said. "If and when they are found, they will be severely dealt with. But they might not be a member of management. I am ordering an assembly of all employees at nine tomorrow morning in the main auditorium. I will speak to you all then."

Faces were angry, tongues were sharp at the meeting, eyes suspicious and tempers short. Above it all was the commanding presence of Director Allen speaking to them.

"It is not my desire to interfere in departmental affairs," he said. "Insofar as the facility is concerned, it is my duty to make certain no manager is guilty. This I am doing. But my management team is not and cannot be a police force for you. It is up to you people to protect yourselves and maintain order."

"How can we protect ourselves without authority?" one employee called out.

"Does Silver Mask have authority?" Allen retorted. "It seems to me you have a better weapon than any authority."

"What's that?"

"This facility is only so big. If every inch is searched, you'll find your perpetrator. They have to be somewhere on campus."

The employees quieted. Emma Graves, one of the senior engineers, was elected president of the newly formed Building Council. One person from each of the buildings was named to serve under her. Each of these people in turn selected five others from their own group.

Those assembled waited in the hall while each team of six inspected the workspaces of the others. These spaces were then locked, everyone returned to their workspace, and the larger search was conducted. It took thirty hours.

No mask was found. No mask, no drive, no tablet, no perpetrator.

The director reported that his search had been equally fruitless. At another assembly the following day it was decided to make the inspection teams permanent, to await further moves on the part of Silver Mask. The Building Council held periodic meetings to establish protocols for dealing with the perpetrator when caught. It was all recorded in the newsletter and by Sara Henry.

We Catalysts know about hostility and about violence. We know too that where there is hostility there is violence, and where there is violence there is harm.

During night shift on the 107th day, a researcher named Marcus Sharma (no relation to the TechFusion chief), awakened by a strange sound, sat up in the bed of his apartment to find a person in a silver mask in his room. His cries brought neighbors into the corridor. The flight of the person was witnessed by many, and several people tried to stop them. But the intruder was quick and agile. They escaped.

The Building Council confronted the director, demanding access to security equipment.

"Are you out of your minds?" Allen exclaimed.

Emma Graves, Building D leader, said, "We want to set up a security force, Director. We want stun devices."

"There's no policy against it," Allen said, "but it's a rule of mine that no weapons are to be issued during operations."

"If we had had a device, we'd have caught Silver Mask," Graves said.

"And I might have a serious injury on my conscience."

Graves said, "We've also thought of that. Suppose you supply us with low-power stunners? That way we can immobilize but not seriously harm."

They got their devices. Now there were thirty-two security volunteers on duty throughout the facility—twelve on at a time. Henry observed that for the first time the employees seemed relaxed.

Let Silver Mask move against armed volunteers, they said.

Yeah, let them see what happens now.

Silver Mask did.

On the 137th day they were seen in a corridor in Building D. A volunteer named Malik Vasquez managed to activate his device several times at the retreating figure.

Silver Mask was seen again on the 163rd day, on the 184th day, and the 214th day. They were seen, pursued, but not caught. They were also unable to commit any crime.

We've got them on the run, the employees said.

They're afraid to do anything, now that we've got security, they said smugly.

The Building Council congratulated itself. The employees were proud of themselves. A special congratulatory message from Director Allen appeared one day in the Bulletin newsletter.

The employees settled down to working through the rest of the project until completion.

But on the 231st day calamity struck. Silver Mask obtained one of the stunners, made their way through one whole section in Building B, incapacitated occupants as they went, taking many items of value and leaving chaos behind.

Henry interviewed as many victims as she could, noted it all in her tablet. The things taken were personal items, photographs and objects of sentimental value. It seemed to be the work of someone disturbed. If Silver Mask wanted to make everyone furious, they certainly succeeded.

"What does this person want that stuff for?" a facilities manager asked. "I can see them taking my access codes, my security badge—but my daughter's drawing? That I don't understand."

It was the same with others. "This person's unstable, Ms. Henry. Positively unstable." Many people said it.

The council issued orders that all employees from now on would be required to lock their workspaces and apartments at all times. More devices were obtained from the director. More volunteers were appointed.

Henry was busy noting it all in her tablet. It became filled with observations about innocent people being accidentally stunned when trigger-happy volunteers thought their movements suspicious, about one person's suspicion of another and the ensuing search of spaces, people who saw Silver Mask here, saw them there. Hardly a day went by without some new development.

"Oh, yes, Ms. Henry, we're going to get them," said Graves, now chief of security, her eyes intense. "We're bound to get them. We've got things worked out with proper strategic planning and team building principles. They won't be able to get through our fingers now. Just let them make so much as a move."

"And what will you do when you catch them?"

"Terminate their employment," Graves said, her eyes fierce. "Immediately."

"Without due process?"

"Oh, there'll be a hearing, Ms. Henry, but you don't think any panel would let them stay after all the things they've done, do you?"

Silver Mask was stunned in Building D in a corridor by a volunteer named Mohamed Tucker on the 273rd day. The perpetrator was carried to the assembly room surrounded by guards, for they surely would have been attacked, if not seriously harmed, by angry employees who crowded around. In the assembly hall the mask was removed. The crowd gasped. Nobody recognized them.

Henry's first thought was that they must be an unauthorized person, but then she remembered the face, and Director Allen, who came to identify them, unhappily admitted the person was a member of management. Their name was Alex Robbins and they were a data coordinator.

"Well, Robbins," Allen said sternly, "what have you got to say for yourself?"

"Nothing you'd understand," Robbins said quietly. As if it were an afterthought, they turned away from the director.

Allen looked as if he were going to terminate them on the spot.

It was a long hearing—from the 298th to the 326th day—and there didn't seem to be much doubt about the outcome, for Robbins didn't help their own cause during any of it.

Emma Graves, who was appointed to lead the inquiry, asked, "What did you do with the stolen items, Robbins?"

Robbins looked her square in the eye and said, "I destroyed them. Does that answer your question?"

"Destroyed them?" Graves and the crowd were incredulous.

"Sure," Robbins said. "You employees got the easy life with your cognitive development programs and work-life balance initiatives, just coasting along. I had to work constantly managing data for you lazy people."

The verdict was, of course, termination.

They processed Alex Robbins' departure on the morning of the 367th day with full documentation and witnessed by a great crowd in the assembly hall. Security escorted them off the premises.

It was all duly recorded in Sara Henry's notes.

Leaving is easy for a Catalyst. Especially if it's arranged for beforehand, which it always is.

The Irondale project was only one week from completion when Director Allen sent for Henry and introduced her to the terminated employee.

"Hello," Robbins said, grinning broadly.

"I figured as much," Henry said. "I've been doing a lot of thinking."

Robbins sighed. "And I'll have to be caught again."

The research section was where I went first. There was nobody there but a graduate student working on what looked like a cultural anthropology thesis, and somebody reviewing oral history archives on a microfilm reader.

Dunn, who resided at 847 Maple Avenue, Willow Creek, had been active in labor relations advocacy and media production ethics...

It was sort of nostalgic watching them, but I really got bored with all that violence and destruction and destroying the same destruction over and over. Like watching a marathon of crime procedurals.

The screams woke me up.

They say it's a bad sign when you start hearing voices.

I nearly panicked, but I held myself in the seat and forced myself to be rational about it. My own voice was always saying things everyone could hear but which I didn't say. It wasn't any worse to be the only one who could hear other things I never said. I was as sane as I ever was. There was no doubt about that.

But a new thought suddenly impressed itself on me.

Whatever was punishing me for my transgression was determined that I turn back before reaching 847 Maple Avenue.

I got off at the next stop anyway. I had to face Teresa Dunn. I had to try to make amends, even if it was impossible. Even if whatever cosmic force was tormenting me didn't want me to.

The house was a modest ranch-style home with a well-maintained garden. I stood at the door for a full minute before ringing the bell.

Teresa Dunn answered. She looked older than her photo, worn down by the year since her termination. Her eyes were suspicious but not unkind.

"Yes?"

"Ms. Dunn, my name is William Wade. I need to talk to you about what happened at MediaWorks."

Her expression hardened. "I don't know who you are, but I have nothing to say about that situation."

"Please," I said. "I was there. I was the temp worker. It was my fault the files were leaked. I didn't mean to, but I did it."

She stared at me for a long moment. "Come inside."

We sat in her living room. I told her everything—about the confrontation, about accessing the system remotely, about not understanding what I was doing. I didn't tell her about the entities or the voices or the lifelong pattern of being framed. That would have made me sound insane.

When I finished, she was quiet for a long time.

"Why are you telling me this now?" she finally asked.

"Because I have money," I said, pulling out the check. "It's not much, but it's something. I want to give it to you. I want to try to make this right."

She looked at the check, then at me. "Twenty thousand dollars. That won't restore my career or my reputation."

"I know," I said. "But it's all I have."

She took the check, studied it, then handed it back to me. "I don't want your money, William. But I appreciate you coming here. It takes courage to admit what you did."

"You're not going to report me?"

"To whom? The company that fired me? The police who never investigated? No. I'm going to move forward with my life, and you should do the same."

I left her house feeling lighter than I had in years. The entities didn't appear on the bus ride back. My voice didn't say anything I didn't mean to say.

Maybe Max Sims was right. Maybe addressing the transgression was enough to break the pattern.

Or maybe the cosmic forces punishing me had simply found a new way to torture me: letting me hope.
