It was longer than that before they reconvened. In the meantime, their ship had moved into a higher orbit. Through the viewports, Market-7 rotated below them. The southern continents showed green agricultural regions; the oceans were deep blue; and much of the northern hemisphere was covered in the sprawling gray-brown of massive urban centers. Weather patterns swirled over the poles, and a haze of industrial pollution spread across the equatorial manufacturing zones.

"I haven't developed a brilliant strategy," said Samantha.

"Neither have I," said Isaac. "We're going to have to improvise."

"I did consider one approach," Isaac said. "What if we present ourselves as representatives of a superior economic authority? Use our obvious technological advantage to add weight to our recommendations?"

"Too risky," said Samantha. "A century ago that might have worked. But these people have satellites, quantum computers, and sophisticated media networks. They're not primitives who'll accept authority without question."

"I thought we should leverage our differences somehow."

"If we could do it subtly, I'd agree. But these people are cynical and desperate. They've been burned by false promises before. They won't trust anything that seems manipulative."

"All right, you're leading this operation," said Isaac.

"Here's the plan," said Samantha. "You take one major economic bloc, I'll take another. We'll present ourselves as neutral advisors and explain clearly what reforms they need to implement if they want to avoid collapse. We'll give them the frameworks they need to establish proper financial regulation."

"That'll be popular. Everyone loves being told their system is broken."

"Can't be helped. It's all we have time for."

"Any specific protocols?"

"None beyond the basics. We'll take separate landing craft down to the surface. You can contact me through our quantum communicators if necessary, but don't unless it's critical."

"They can't intercept our communications."

"They can't, and even if they detected the quantum signatures, they couldn't decode our language. But I want them to think we don't need to confer."

"I understand. Makes us seem more confident and knowledgeable than we actually are."

"Exactly."

Isaac looked at the planet below. "It's going to be challenging wherever we land. You too. Are we sure we don't want to adjust our targets? Maybe approach smaller nations first, build credibility?"

"No. The major economic powers control the global system. If we're going to prevent a collapse, we need to reach the decision-makers in the dominant markets."

"Right, but I was thinking about timing. We'll be arriving just before their major holiday season. That won't help."

"I know. People don't appreciate interruptions during holidays. But we can't wait."

"Understood," said Isaac. "Brief me on these holidays. Anything I should know? Religious significance?"

"Originally religious, centuries ago," said Samantha. "From what I've gathered from their media, it's now primarily commercial—a peak season for consumer spending and market activity."

"So it's fundamentally economic."

"That's accurate. I didn't learn as much as I should have. I was focused on understanding their approach to community organizing and how economic stress affects social cohesion."

"I was thinking we might be able to use the holiday period somehow. Make it work in our favor."

"If there's a way, I haven't seen it."

"You're running this mission." Isaac looked down at the planet. Storm systems were forming over the western ocean. "I don't like leaving our ship unmanned while we're on the surface."

"They can't touch it. Even with another century of development, they won't have the technology to breach our hull or access our systems."

"I'm thinking about us. Down there, alone."

"I'll be with you. On the opposite side of the planet."

"That's not exactly close. I'd prefer having someone in the ship ready to extract us if things go wrong. These people don't trust their own economists. I doubt they'll welcome alien auditors."

"They may be hostile," Samantha acknowledged. She switched a monitor to show a financial district in one of the major cities. People rushed through streets decorated with lights and synthetic trees. "I've thought of a strategy to mitigate that risk."

"If it keeps us safe, I'm interested."

"No guarantees," said Samantha. "But here's my thinking: instead of hiding the ship on the far side of their moon where it's unlikely to be detected, we make sure they do see it. Let's position it in a visible orbit and illuminate it."

"That could work," said Isaac.

"They won't imagine we'd light up an unmanned vessel," said Samantha. "Even if they consider the possibility, they'll have no way to verify it. More importantly, they'll be reluctant to harm us while our ship is clearly visible above them."

"Good thinking," said Isaac, moving to the navigation controls. "I'll position us in an optimal orbit and activate the external lighting arrays. I'll make it impossible to miss."

"Don't be subtle."

"Trust me. Everyone on the planet will see it." Later, with the ship in position, its hull blazing with light in a carefully programmed pattern that pulsed like a beacon, Isaac said: "You know, I feel better about this. We might actually succeed. The visible ship gives us leverage we didn't have before."

"It's not about our success, but their survival," said Samantha. "See you in five days." She entered a small landing craft, which left a faint ion trail as it descended toward the planet's surface. Minutes later, Isaac departed in another craft, heading for a different continent.

And the ship orbited Market-7, unmanned, brilliant and pulsing with light. No satellite or space station could match its luminosity. The automated weather satellites recorded it; the astronomical observatories tracked it; the media networks broadcast images of it. During daylight hours it appeared as an impossibly bright star. At night it seemed to burn through the darkness like a piece of captured starlight brought near the planet for all to witness.

And the ship continued its orbit, bright, shining, an undeniable presence in the sky that no one could ignore or explain away.

In five days, the two small landing craft that had departed from it arced back up through the atmosphere and docked with the larger vessel. The small craft slid inside and the airlocks sealed behind them. Shortly after, the two Federation auditors met again in the main cabin.

"We did it," said Isaac enthusiastically as he entered. "I don't know how, and I thought we'd fail, but at the last moment they agreed to the framework."

Samantha smiled, though she looked exhausted. "I'm tired," she said softly.

"Me too, but mostly I'm frustrated," said Isaac. "Bureaucracy. Nothing but bureaucracy wherever I went. Endless meetings. And yet you had me do those public presentations after that first day."

"From my own experience, it seemed effective," Samantha explained. "When I did a public presentation one day, I noticed the officials were much more cooperative the next day. If it worked for me, I thought it might help you."

"It did. I don't understand the mechanism, but it definitely helped," said Isaac. "Anyway, the regulatory framework they've agreed to isn't perfect, but I believe it will prevent a systemic collapse."

"It's the best we could achieve in the time available," said Samantha. "They may still have market corrections and regional recessions, but not the catastrophic collapse. In fifty or a hundred years, the Federation can send another team to assess their progress."

"I'm not sure I want that assignment," said Isaac. "Hey, what's a 'guardian angel'?"

"Why do you ask?"

"When I did those public presentations, people would approach me afterward. Some would kneel and call me a guardian angel. They'd thank me for watching over them."

"Something similar happened to me," said Samantha.

"I didn't understand the reference, but I didn't let it derail me," said Isaac. "I smiled and continued with the work." He stretched, and as he did, his wings—carefully folded during the mission—extended slightly. They were magnificent, spanning nearly three meters, with feathers that seemed to shimmer with an inner light. The evolutionary adaptation that had allowed his species to thrive on their high-gravity homeworld made them appear, to human eyes, like beings from ancient religious texts.

"I don't think your appearance hurt our credibility," said Samantha. She too stretched, her own wings unfurling briefly. They were slightly smaller than Isaac's but equally striking, with patterns of iridescence that shifted in the light.

"But you don't know what a 'guardian angel' is?"

"No. I didn't have time to research their mythology and comparative history thoroughly. I was focused on economic systems thinking and decision-making frameworks. Some figure from their cultural traditions, I assume. You know, except for the wings, they're remarkably similar to us physiologically. Their legends probably reflect similar archetypes."

"Makes sense," said Isaac. "Anyway, we've given them a chance. Financial stability on Market-7."

"For now," said Samantha, looking at the planet one last time before they departed. "For now."

The ship's lights dimmed, and it began to accelerate away from Market-7, heading toward Timberline and the summit that awaited them. Behind them, on the planet below, economists and government officials were already implementing the regulatory frameworks the two visitors had proposed. The financial markets, which had been teetering on the edge of collapse, began to stabilize.

And in the cities below, people looked up at the now-empty sky where the brilliant ship had been, and they wondered about the two winged visitors who had appeared during their holiday season, offered guidance, and then departed as mysteriously as they had arrived.

In Oakdale, Havencia, a financial analyst named Malik Vasquez filed a report about the new regulations, noting that they seemed to come from an understanding of systems far more advanced than anything their civilization had developed. In the Dawnridge District, Sophia Young, a professor of comparative history, began writing a paper about the visitors and their remarkable resemblance to figures from ancient texts.

And in Havenbrook, Marvenia, a community organizer named Henri Gonzalez stood in the street, looking up at the stars, thinking about existential questions that the visitors had raised simply by their presence. What did it mean that they were not alone? What did it mean that others were watching, sometimes helping?

The media debated the visitors' nature and purpose. Some claimed they were advanced beings from another world. Others insisted they were something more—angels, perhaps, or guardians sent to protect humanity from its own worst impulses.

In the end, it didn't matter what they called them. What mattered was that they had come, they had helped, and they had left behind a framework that might just save civilization from collapse.

At least for now.

At least for a while.

And somewhere, far above, accelerating toward distant stars, Samantha Boyd and Isaac Ahmed reviewed their mission reports, satisfied that they had done what they could with the limited time available.

"Do you think they'll make it?" Isaac asked.

"I think they have a chance," Samantha replied. "That's all anyone can ask for. A chance."

THE END

James Riley, mounting the steps of the old administrative building facing the Central Plaza, was in no mood for the architectural beauties of Clearwater's historic district. For one thing, Clearwater was familiar territory; his work with the Federal Cultural Protection Agency had brought him here often in the past, on other strange cases. And for another thing, his mission concerned more vital matters. Richard Weaver, as director of the state-funded Estoria Broadcasting Network, was next in importance to the Governor herself. As far back as the propaganda wars of the twentieth century it had been known that he who controls media, controls the populace. The Estoria Broadcasting Network was an important factor in maintaining social cohesion in a region still recovering from civil unrest. And when Richard Weaver sent an urgent request to the capital for one of the Federal Cultural Protection Agency's special investigators, something was definitely wrong.

The building was equipped with modern security systems as protection against the occasional protests that swept through Clearwater's streets. Riley passed through the security checkpoint and a polite automated voice asked his credentials. He provided them, and the inner door opened.

The director of EBN stood at one end of the spacious room, the walls of which were lined with awards, photographs of cultural events, and shelves of recording equipment. As Riley entered, Weaver swung about, frowning, one hand gripping the edge of his desk.

"Riley, Federal Cultural Protection." The special agent offered his identification. "You sent an urgent request to the capital for an investigator?"

Richard Weaver nodded. He was a tall, distinguished individual with silver hair and sharp features. A man of precision and control, one would think, who navigated complex bureaucracy with careful planning and strategic thinking. But as Riley looked closer, he could see lines of exhaustion, of genuine fear, etched about his mouth, and a species of terror within his intelligent eyes.

"Yes," said Richard Weaver. "I sent for an investigator. You arrived quickly, Mr. Riley."

Even Federal Cultural Protection headquarters hadn't been given full details about why an agent was needed in Clearwater—but Weaver was one of the few persons sufficiently important to have an investigator sent without complete explanation. Riley put it directly. "Why did you require the help of FCPA, Mr. Weaver?" he asked.

"Because we're dealing with something beyond the capacity of local law enforcement to handle." Richard Weaver's hands trembled slightly as he gestured. "No one has greater respect for our city police than myself. Chief Martinez is a personal friend. But I understood that FCPA agents had access to specialized technology and training that makes it possible for them to track down threats to cultural institutions."

"Mr. Riley," Weaver leaned forward, his face drawn and pale, "someone is systematically eliminating the senior staff of the Estoria Broadcasting Network! And I don't have to tell you that whoever controls EBN effectively controls public opinion in this entire region! Here's the situation! Our network, although state funded, operates with significant independence, so long as we maintain balanced programming and support social welfare initiatives. Except for myself and half a dozen other senior administrators, our technical staff is largely composed of freelance contractors and recent graduates. That's in line with our commitment to career planning and professional development. As you know."

Riley nodded, eyes intent as the pattern unfolded.

"All right." Weaver continued tensely. "You see the situation. Remove us—the few experienced administrators at the top of EBN—and junior staff would carry on until replacements arrived from the capital. But suppose during that transitional period, with no oversight, they started broadcasting destabilizing content? One hour of carefully crafted propaganda, exploiting economic inequality and social tensions, and there'd be riots. Thousands of angry citizens against a small police force. It would be catastrophic."

"But," Riley frowned, "this is merely speculation. What evidence do you have of an actual threat?"

"Evidence?" Weaver's voice rose. "Three weeks ago my chief technical director, Walter Park, died in what was ruled an accidental fall from his apartment balcony. Not a hint of suicidal ideation in his history, but he fell to his death. A week later Carmen McDonald, head of our music programming division, suffered a complete psychological breakdown. "Accidental death, mental breakdown, stroke." Riley shrugged. "All within the realm of normal, if unfortunate, occurrences. Coincidence that they happened within three weeks. What makes you think there's a coordinated attack?"

In each instance, neighbors or family members reported hearing, very faintly, a strange audio phenomenon. Sound that did disturbing things to them, even though they could hear it only vaguely. Along the street were carefully maintained gardens and public art installations. It was among these, he decided, that their unknown sonic attacker was concealed.

At that moment the aggressive audio assault outside changed abruptly. From the violent frequencies of moments before, the sound took on a seductive quality. A call, it seemed, irresistible, gentle, promising relief. This was the sound of safety, of comfort, of home. It conjured images in Riley's mind—images of peace, of rest, of surrender. The ultimate expression of musical innovation turned to dark purposes, the perfection of design science applied to neural manipulation. Officers pursued but the figure turned into an alley, disappeared among the narrow side streets. Drenched in cold sweat, Riley stepped back from the window, where the still form of Richard Weaver lay. Riley stared at the body, as though seeing it for the first time. Outside, there were pounding footsteps; the police were racing through the building, toward the office. And then, his mind exhausted as if from physical trauma, Riley sank to his knees.

Police headquarters in Clearwater was brightly lit by modern LED fixtures. Chief Martinez, a stocky woman with graying hair, studied Riley with a mixture of sympathy and suspicion.

Like a shadow Riley ran, moving through side streets, heading back toward Weaver's office building. Clearwater was beautiful in the evening, its historic architecture illuminated by carefully designed lighting. Sleek electric buses hummed along the main boulevards, and on the sidewalks, diverse crowds moved—students, professionals, artists, all part of the rich cultural exchange that made Clearwater unique.

"Flores," Riley said hoarsely. "You're behind this?"

Governments, corporations, criminal organizations—all would pay millions for what my protégé Sara Li has developed." He gestured to the young woman. "Sara was a student of Ms. Wagner's, actually, before Natalia's ethical qualms made her... unreliable."

"Ethical qualms?" Natalia Wagner's voice was sharp. "You mean before I realized you planned to sell sonic weapons to the highest bidder? Before I understood you'd kill anyone who stood in your way?"

"Details," Flores waved dismissively. "The point is, Sara proved more... pragmatic. Together we've perfected what Ms. Wagner began. And now we're ready to demonstrate our technology to interested buyers. What better demonstration than the systematic elimination of key personnel at a major broadcasting network? It shows precision, control, versatility."

"The deaths," Riley said. "Walter Park, Carmen McDonald, Luis Mitchell... you killed them to demonstrate your weapon?"

"Demonstration and elimination," Flores confirmed. "They were obstacles. Richard Weaver would have been next, but you complicated matters. Still, his death serves our purposes. And now..." He turned to Sara Li. "We have two more test subjects. Show our potential buyers what the technology can do. Full range of effects, please."

Sara Li nodded, raising her portable device. Riley tensed, knowing what was coming, knowing there was no escape. The young woman's fingers moved over the controls, and the sound began again.

This time it was different from before—harsher, more aggressive. Riley felt his heart rate spike, felt adrenaline flood his system. Beside him, Natalia Wagner gasped, her face contorting. The sound was triggering every fear response, every panic reaction. It was torture without physical contact, agony without visible wounds.

"Stop!" Riley shouted. "You'll kill us!"

"Eventually," Flores agreed. "But first, let's show the full range of effects. Sara?"

The sound shifted again, became that seductive, hypnotic tone that had nearly led Riley to jump from Weaver's window. He felt his will dissolving, felt an overwhelming urge to obey, to surrender, to do whatever the sound commanded. Beside him, Natalia Wagner was weeping silently, lost in whatever false paradise the sound created in her mind.

And then, suddenly, there was a tremendous crash. The door to the room exploded inward and armed police poured through, led by Chief Martinez. Sara Li spun, her device falling from her hands and shattering on the floor. The sound cut off abruptly.

"Nobody move!" Martinez shouted. "Nicholas Flores, Sara Li, you're under arrest!"

As officers secured Flores and Sara Li, Martinez approached Riley and Natalia Wagner, quickly releasing their restraints. Riley slumped forward, gasping for breath, his mind still reeling from the sonic assault.

"How..." he managed to ask.

"Your sonic tracker," Martinez explained. "When we recovered it from your pocket after you escaped, our tech people figured out what it was tracking. Led us right here." She smiled slightly. "You were right, Riley. This was bigger than a simple death investigation. Much bigger."

As police led Flores and Sara Li away, Natalia Wagner turned to Riley. "Thank you," she said quietly. "For what it's worth, I tried to stop them. That's why I was in Clearwater—I knew they were targeting Weaver. I just didn't get there in time."

"We'll need your full testimony," Martinez said. "And your expertise to understand this technology."

Natalia nodded. "Of course. This kind of sonic weapon... it violates everything I believe about the relationship between sound and human welfare. Musical innovation should enhance life, not destroy it. Design science should serve humanity, not enslave it."

Riley stood slowly, his legs unsteady. "There'll be an inquiry about Weaver's death. But given the circumstances..."

"We'll sort it out," Martinez said. "The important thing is we've stopped them. This technology... it's too dangerous to exist."

"Agreed," Natalia Wagner said. "I'll help you destroy every trace of it. And I'll testify about how Flores corrupted my research, turned it into a weapon."

As they left the building, Riley looked up at the night sky over Clearwater. The city seemed peaceful now, its lights twinkling in the darkness. But he knew how close they'd come to disaster. How close Flores had come to unleashing a weapon that could destabilize not just Clearwater, not just Estoria, but potentially the entire world.

"One thing I don't understand," Riley said to Natalia as they walked toward the waiting police vehicles. "Why did you develop this technology in the first place? What was your original purpose?"

Natalia was silent for a moment, then sighed. "I wanted to help people. I thought if we could understand how sound affects the brain, we could develop therapies for mental illness, treatments for addiction, ways to help people heal. But Flores saw military applications, saw profit. He stole my research, twisted it into something evil." She looked at Riley. "That's why I've spent the last two years trying to stop him. Trying to undo the damage I inadvertently caused."

"You'll get that chance now," Riley said. "To make it right."

As they drove back toward police headquarters, Riley reflected on the case. The weaponization of sound—it was a chilling development, a reminder that any technology, no matter how benign its original purpose, could be perverted. Musical innovation, design science, acoustic engineering—all could be turned to dark purposes in the wrong hands.

But they'd stopped it. This time.

And as Clearwater's lights faded behind them, Riley allowed himself a moment of relief. The sonic weapon was destroyed, its creators in custody, and the city was safe. For now.

The case of the Sonic Architect, as the media would later call it, was closed. But Riley knew it was only a matter of time before someone else tried to weaponize sound, tried to turn the most fundamental form of human communication and artistic expression into an instrument of death.

It was a sobering thought. But it was also a reminder of why the Federal Cultural Protection Agency existed—to guard against those who would corrupt culture, pervert innovation, and turn humanity's greatest achievements into weapons.

As they pulled up to headquarters, Riley made a mental note to recommend enhanced monitoring of acoustic research facilities across the region. They'd been lucky this time. But luck, he knew, eventually ran out.

The war between those who would protect cultural evolution and those who would exploit it for power and profit was never-ending. But it was a war worth fighting.

And James Riley, despite his exhaustion, was ready to continue the fight.

THE SILENT CONVOY
By Marcus Chen

Autonomous vehicles were the backbone of modern military logistics—and particularly in modern naval convoy operations. If you could disrupt all autonomous navigation systems—silence of that sort would be deadly to any military force dependent on technological progress.

The urgent beeping of the proximity alarm jolted Lieutenant Commander Mateo Lawrence from his review of the convoy routes. He rose from his station chair in the command center of the autonomous cargo vessel Meridian, stretching his tall frame and running a hand through his dark hair. That would be Ava Hernández, his systems engineer. Hernández always signaled that way—three short bursts, like someone who believed every situation was an emergency.

Lawrence didn't rush. It pleased him to let Hernández wait a moment. He moved deliberately to the door, paused there, and glanced back at the woman working intently at the design station—Dr. Jennifer Lambert, the elderly architect and systems designer, a civilian consultant for the United States Navy, here aboard the Meridian as it led a convoy from Bridgewater, Selvoria to Ashford, Wendria.

The weathered face of the older woman was set in concentrated lines, her silver hair pulled back as she bent over her holographic display. Lawrence caught a glimpse of the architectural design she was working on—some kind of modular port facility—and his lips relaxed slightly.

Lambert had arrived aboard the Meridian two days before the convoy departed from Bridgewater. With her came a shipment of experimental equipment, including several containers of what looked like advanced sensor arrays, now stored in the forward cargo bay. Lambert had supervised the loading with meticulous care, and spent hours daily in the converted storage room that served as her temporary design studio.

Sometimes, Lawrence thought Lambert was overly paranoid—an architect whose mind had been affected by the economic inequality she'd witnessed in the refugee camps of Riverside, Xandria, where her humanitarian work had taken her before this assignment. At other times, the woman seemed brilliant. Perhaps that was the answer—a brilliant mind scarred by what she'd seen.

Lawrence opened the door and looked out. Rain hammered against the observation deck like liquid bullets. Overhead, the sky was a storm-wracked mass of clouds, broken in one spot by a small patch of star-studded darkness.

His eyes rested on the face of the woman before him. It was Hernández, her dark brows drawn down over intense brown eyes; her angular face tight with tension; her hands gripping a data tablet. Rain streaked down her cheeks, leaving glistening trails.

The woman was a puzzle to Lawrence. She was inexplicably close to a problematic crew member named Robert Valdez—the most vocal critic of the autonomous systems on board. But there was no question of her technical ability. She was an excellent systems engineer—reliable, precise, dedicated to systems thinking and design thinking principles. Nevertheless, her tense demeanor, constantly searching eyes, and perpetually anxious manner irritated Lawrence.

"Come in, Hernández," he said.

Hernández pushed her way inside, standing there in her dripping rain gear, blinking against the overhead lights.

Lawrence closed the door and nodded toward Lambert's bent form with a slight smile. "Our architectural consultant is hard at work on her latest design to revolutionize port infrastructure and preserve cultural heritage in the rebuilding zones."

Hernández had no answering smile, although there had been considerable good-natured discussion aboard the Meridian ever since the Navy Department had assigned the architect to the vessel to continue her work during the convoy.

"I'm concerned, sir," Hernández said. "I'm not confident about the autonomous navigation readings. This storm—"

Lawrence put a reassuring hand on Hernández's shoulder. "Relax! Don't let a minor discrepancy worry you."

"But this storm, sir!" Hernández pulled away from his touch, avoiding his eyes. "It's affecting the sensor arrays. Variable electromagnetic interference. Choppy readings from the seafloor mapping—as if there are uncharted currents among these coastal formations. No way to verify by satellite, and now—look at this!"

She held out the tablet. The data streams were fluctuating wildly.

"You said there might be a way to verify?" Lawrence asked. "Clear satellite window?"

"Just briefly, sir, and I'm wondering—" Her voice trailed off, but her eyes moved toward the backup navigation console.

Lieutenant Commander Lawrence shrugged good-naturedly and moved to the console. "Not that I doubt your readings, Ava, but since you asked."

Lawrence accessed the satellite link and ran a manual verification. In a few minutes he returned and handed Hernández a printout with coordinates marked clearly.

"Here's what the satellite confirms," the commander told his systems engineer. "I bet your autonomous readings aren't far off."

Hernández stared at the data, then slowly held up her own tablet display.

Lawrence frowned, grabbed his printout again. "Any time my manual check differs this much from your autonomous systems reading, we're stopping to investigate," he declared, comparing the two sets of coordinates and quickly rechecking his figures.

"Signal the convoy to halt," he told Hernández. "We can't afford to proceed in these waters with this level of navigation uncertainty."

Hernández complied, and the subtle vibration of the Meridian's propulsion systems decreased immediately. Hernández said: "I've been thinking, sir, whether we should try to get a radio triangulation from the coastal beacons. With all these rocks and shallow areas—"

"Radio?" interrupted Dr. Lambert, inserting herself between them in her independent way that ignored military protocol. "You're using radio navigation?" She broke into a knowing chuckle, her keen eyes twinkling behind wire-rimmed glasses. "Go ahead and try it. See what response you get! It will be no better than what enemy forces would get when Jennifer Lambert implements her communication disruption protocols! Try it! Try it, I say!"

Mateo Lawrence stared at her, questioning her mental state. Then he hurried to the communications center, with Hernández close behind, and Lambert following.

The door opened as they approached it. A worried communications officer emerged, still wearing his headset, staring up at the antenna array with confusion.

"Get us a radio triangulation from the coastal beacons immediately," Lawrence said sharply, noting the officer's distracted state.

"Triangulation, sir?" The man brought his eyes down reluctantly, still troubled. "I'm sorry, sir, but the system's dead. Went offline about five minutes ago. I was monitoring weather updates when everything cut out. I was checking for hardware failures."

Lambert giggled. Lawrence gave her another concerned look and entered the communications center.

"Try again!" he told the officer. "See what you can raise!"

The communications officer returned to his station and worked frantically. Again and again, he sent requests for triangulation from the coastal beacon network that had recently been established to ensure safe passage for autonomous convoys, but there was no response on any frequency—not even commercial traffic on the standard bands, nor chatter from other vessels on the emergency channels.

"Dead!" Lambert muttered, with a bitter laugh. "Yet not dead, gentlemen! The equipment is undamaged. The signals themselves have been disrupted. There was a long pause as commander and engineer stared at her.

Lawrence was the first to speak.

"Your secrecy could cost the United States Navy an entire convoy—and us our lives!" he said angrily. "We need that triangulation now! If you're not delusional, shut down your system until we determine our exact position!"

Lambert spread her hands helplessly. "I cannot. I have programmed my automated assistant system to maintain two hours of communication disruption! I cannot send a message to override it, because our radio is dead!"

As if to mock her, the ship's radio suddenly activated:

"Beacon Station Alpha-7 calling convoy leader Meridian. Beacon Station Alpha-7 calling convoy leader Meridian—"

"Convoy leader Meridian responding to Beacon Alpha-7!" the officer intoned, exchanging glances with the two officers over Lambert's embarrassment, and requested position data.

The answer came back: "Position bearing northeast by quarter east, convoy leader Meridian!"

Lawrence sighed with relief. He noticed that Hernández was staring intently at the communications officer as he continued: "Convoy leader Meridian calling Beacon Station Beta-4. Convoy leader Meridian calling Beacon Station Beta-4—"

Then the system crackled again: "Beacon Station Beta-4 responding to convoy leader Meridian. Position bearing northwest by three degrees west. Position bearing northwest by three degrees west, convoy leader Meridian."

Commander and engineer had both recorded the coordinates. Ignoring Lambert's protests that signals had somehow penetrated her disruption field, they rushed to the navigation center.

Quickly they plotted the bearings from the designated points. Clean intersecting lines confirmed their position.

Lawrence frowned and shook his head. Slowly he managed a reluctant grin as he extended his hand.

"Good work, Ava," he said. "Looks like you and the radio triangulation are correct. Resume course as planned."

"I'm relieved, sir, all the same," Hernández admitted, "to have the radio confirmation. We would have run aground if you'd been right."

They continued through the night. The brief clear patch in the clouds had closed. The sky was again a solid mass of darkness pouring sheets of rain.

Hernández returned to her station, and Lambert went back to the commander's workspace. Lawrence lingered in the communications center with the officer.

"Strange thing," the officer said, still working the controls and frowning, "how I got that triangulation through and now can't raise anything else. I'm wondering if that architect really has done something to the electromagnetic spectrum. The equipment seems fine."

He continued checking the systems, testing and retesting. Indicators showed normal; connections were live and sent familiar tingles through his testing fingers.

Lawrence left him and went to rejoin Lambert. He found the architect pacing, gesturing in the air, pausing periodically to run her fingers through her silver hair or tug nervously at her collar.

"You have witnessed a demonstration, commander!" she declared. "My demonstration! My technology has disrupted electromagnetic communications in this area completely."

"Seems to me," Lawrence said dryly, "this technology could harm friendly forces as much as enemies."

The architect drew herself to her full height—barely five feet four. Her voice grew sharp. "Wait! Just wait! There are complementary technologies to work with this one. Combined properly, they will counter the autonomous warfare systems that have devastated the regions where I've worked!"

Lawrence was somewhat disturbed by the intensity in Lambert's eyes behind her glasses. There was something fierce in the woman's expression, as her jaw clenched.

"Those containers you have in the cargo bay," Lawrence said, "are they connected to this communication disruption?"

A distant look came into Lambert's eyes. She seemed not to hear the question. She lowered her voice: "My sister is still in Riverside, Xandria. So are my nieces, and my brother and his family. If hostile forces knew what I'm developing, all of them would be in danger. You understand—in grave danger?"

Lawrence said: "I understand."

"And if enemy agents in Selvoria knew of the island from which my disruption field is projected—" Lambert paused, her head tilting, as if listening—

On deck, there was shouting and commotion. Lawrence rushed out, grabbing his rain gear as he went. The alert from the forward watch had been relayed across the ship. The words struck Lawrence's ears with ominous weight.

"Shallow water ahead!"

He reached Hernández at the main control station and saw the helmsman working the manual override controls, trying to bring the autonomous steering hard to port.

Then the ship struck. Everything loose flew forward until it hit the end of its restraints or crashed into something solid.

Lawrence felt Hernández's hand grip his arm as she leaned close and shouted: "You must have been right, sir, and the radio triangulation and my autonomous readings wrong. We've hit that reef hard. I'm afraid we're breached!"

"Deploy the emergency seals!" Lawrence ordered. "We should be able to keep her afloat!"

And then he became aware of a profound stillness. A vast wall of silence enveloped the entire vessel. Looking over the side, he could no longer see the waves that moments before had beaten against the hull.

The Meridian was shrouded in a massive cloud of yellowish-gray vapor, and more was rising from below—from ventilation systems and access hatches and observation ports—as if the entire ship were flooding with some toxic gas.

Lawrence's mind flashed to stories he'd heard of military installations during recent conflicts that had fallen when defenders found themselves struck unconscious by gas that had been introduced into their facilities' ventilation systems.

There were theories about infiltrators who had compromised the systems, while others attributed the gas deployment to insider saboteurs. There were dozens of explanations—

The vapor clouds enveloping the Meridian were thickening. All around the deck lay the forms of unconscious crew members, suddenly stricken helpless. And then Lawrence saw other forms moving through the deck—forms that looked otherworldly, but he recognized them for what they were—people wearing gas masks.

Hernández was nowhere visible. The helmsman lay unconscious beside the drifting controls. Then a gas-masked figure appeared through the vapor and steadied the helm, preventing the vessel from being completely at the mercy of wind and waves.

Lawrence heard the anchor deploy, as if by invisible hands, the chain screaming and clanking through the mechanism. Then he was completely surrounded by the yellowish-gray mist. He felt his consciousness fading.

Voices murmured all around him in confused conversation—accented voices that rose and fell in excited discussion. He caught occasional English words mixed with what sounded like Eastern European phonetics.

Two phrases registered clearly in his mind. One was "Prometheus cargo"; the other was "supply chain." But gradually his hearing began to fade, as if someone were placing cotton in his ears. He couldn't breathe properly; a fog seemed to be rising within him until it overwhelmed his thoughts—

He felt something strike his head and realized he had collapsed on the deck. And after that, he was aware of nothing—

The rain had diminished to a light mist. The gentle motion of the surf rocked the Meridian in a lazy, rolling rhythm as she lay with her bow pressed into the sandbar at the inlet entrance.

From the bridge, Systems Engineer Ava Hernández watched the gas-masked figures moving about the decks, descending into compartments—like phantoms from a nightmare. Hernández looked phantom-like herself, her face covered by a respirator. Beside her stood her co-conspirator Robert Valdez, also wearing a gas mask.

Hernández spoke quietly, her lips near Valdez's ear. "It worked, Robert."

"Yeah," Valdez agreed. "Worked perfectly."

The unconscious bodies of the Meridian's crew were being carried to the lowered boarding platform and transferred into waiting boats.

Hernández cursed under her breath. "Estimate it'll take a few hours before the ship's clear of that gas."

Valdez shook his head. "The architect says she's got a neutralizing agent in one of those containers that'll clear everything in thirty minutes."

"I'd prefer to operate without Lambert if possible," Hernández muttered. "She's unstable."

"It was an unstable genius who invented the disruption technology that broke the autonomous defense networks in the Xandrian conflict," Valdez reminded her. "It saved countless resources—resources that would have been lost if the facilities had to be taken by direct assault."

Hernández grunted and turned away. A compact figure in the uniform of a foreign naval officer had climbed the boarding platform and was ascending to the bridge. She too wore a respirator.

She approached Hernández, saluted, and extended her hand, introducing herself as Commander Li Munoz. She began speaking in Mandarin, but Hernández stopped her.

"I don't speak Mandarin," she explained. "I was born and raised in the United States—by parents who had suffered economic inequality in the previous generation. My mother died when our family lost everything. My father—" She paused and cleared her throat.

"Yes? Your father?" the foreign officer prompted, switching to accented English.

"My father dedicated me to a mission of correction—to address the wrongs done to our family," Hernández continued. "If America's economic system hadn't failed my family, he wouldn't have lost his livelihood; my mother would still be alive. When he joined the resistance movement, the path became clear to use me—to educate me in military academy, then place me in the United States Navy for a career—and no one suspected me. No one—"

"Sometimes," Valdez interjected, "I thought Lawrence suspected you."

"Perhaps Lawrence will discover his suspicions were justified," Hernández said bitterly. "But it won't help Lawrence—a commander who's lost his convoy." She turned to Munoz. "You have sufficient personnel to operate the Meridian?"

Munoz nodded. "We have a complete crew—one hundred and fifty people—officers, engineers, technicians, communications specialists, all trained operatives who have been positioned here secretly over the past two months."

The three—Munoz, Hernández and Valdez—stood on the bridge and talked while the efficient teams worked systematically to remove the unconscious bodies of the Meridian's crew and transport them to shore.

And when that task was completed, boats began arriving alongside with sophisticated equipment, additional gas containers like those Lambert had brought aboard, and power systems and batteries that looked like something from a technological nightmare.

And supervising everything, shouting commands in multiple languages, gesturing emphatically to clarify her directions, was the energetic figure of Dr. Jennifer Lambert!

"The architect's in her element," Hernández remarked to Commander Munoz.

"Interesting about her," Valdez added, "is that her designs actually function. That disruption field isolated us completely."

Commander Munoz nodded. "Good. But you transmitted your position data—the false coordinates?"

"Yes," Hernández said. "That came through as planned. And Lawrence will have considerable difficulty explaining it."

"From now on," Munoz said seriously, "the disruption field will be projected from the Meridian, and we have another of Lambert's technologies that will be even more valuable when we intercept the Prometheus from its convoy."

"The Prometheus?" Hernández asked, puzzled.

Munoz said: "She's a cargo vessel in a convoy departing Juniper, Relvaria—fifteen thousand tons. The orders are to capture her intact, not sink her."

"What's the objective?"

"Her cargo," Munoz explained. "It's more valuable than gold. It includes a major shipment of rare earth elements."

"Rare earths?" Hernández repeated. "What's special about them?"

"Rare earth elements," Munoz told her, "are critical minerals—necessary for advanced electronics and autonomous systems, far more valuable to us than precious metals. They're essential for manufacturing advanced technology. They come from restricted sources—and our supply is critically low."

"I would think we could obtain these rare earths directly through established channels," Hernández said, "without the risk of capturing a United States Navy convoy vessel."

"There are other materials desperately needed aboard the Prometheus," Munoz explained. "Advanced semiconductors and specialized alloys and hundreds of containers of precision components for autonomous systems. Our intelligence has been monitoring the convoys for months for exactly this type of cargo that the Prometheus is transporting."

"Can we trust Lambert?" Hernández asked, with sudden suspicion.

"Yes," Munoz assured her. "Of all people—we can trust Lambert."

"But she's American," Hernández argued.

"Our organization manages Americans and Europeans and others whom it recruits as operatives," Munoz pointed out. "Lambert has a sister and other relatives in Riverside. She knows that if anything fails, if there's the slightest indication of betrayal on her part, her sister and the others will suffer. Lambert's loyalty is guaranteed."

Hernández turned to observe the forward section of the Meridian. The masked foreign crew members were installing some apparatus there—a strange device that resembled an advanced sensor array, connected by cables to the room that served as Lambert's design studio and laboratory.

Another team was installing communications equipment in the aft superstructure.

Descending to check the lower decks, Hernández found that ventilation ports were being opened and crews were dispersing chemicals to clear the atmosphere of the gas that had overcome the Meridian's American crew.

Returning to the bridge, she found that the tide in the inlet had risen significantly, and the vessel was floating more freely at anchor.

Then, at Munoz's orders, the anchor was raised, and boats and a powered launch were used to help maneuver the vessel completely free of the sandbar. This was accomplished smoothly.

Munoz approached where Hernández was standing on the bridge and extended her hand.

"Congratulations, Commander Hernández!" she said. "We have captured one of the United States Navy's most advanced autonomous convoy vessels!" She made a gesture as if raising a glass in toast. "To success!" she added.

"To success!" Hernández repeated, and the two smiled at each other.

Stars were visible in a patch of dark sky, and broken masses of gray cloud were racing before the wind. Lieutenant Commander Mateo Lawrence found himself lying in wet sand on a beach somewhere, with the rain—now a light drizzle—falling on his face. He was cold; his limbs were stiff and numb. His nose and throat felt scorched inside, as if a wave of searing heat had burned them.

According to his last calculations, the Meridian had been leading a convoy along the Selvorian coast. This probably was one of the islands in that region, or possibly the mainland.

It was difficult getting to his feet, and when he managed to stand, he could only plant his feet in the sand and sway unsteadily for a full minute, like someone learning to walk again.

All around him in the near-total darkness, he could make out dim forms of people sprawled on the beach, and others moving about, exploring. He heard murmuring voices and saw the glow of flashlights.

Someone with a flashlight was approaching. Its white beam shone briefly in Lawrence's face, and the familiar voice of Junior Officer Raj Price spoke: "Commander Lawrence! Are you all right, sir?"

"I think so." Lawrence's heart warmed at the concerned expression on Price's face, the genuine worry in his dark eyes. The young officer was earnest, dedicated, thoroughly sincere in his emotions. "How about you, Raj?" Lawrence added.

"Headache from the gas, but nothing serious. Any orders, sir?"

Lawrence thought for a moment. "Assemble the crew as best you can. We'll attempt a roll call. Any sign of the ship?"

There was a somber note in Price's voice. "No, sir. She's been freed from the sandbar and taken to sea."

The words hit Lawrence with the numbing shock of a physical blow. For the first time, he fully grasped the catastrophe that had befallen him. He had lost his ship—one of the United States Navy's most advanced autonomous convoy vessels—under circumstances that strongly suggested treachery and sabotage.

As he reflected, he realized he might have prevented the loss if he had been more alert, more suspicious. For it was clear now that the Meridian had been deliberately guided to this location; that those who had seized her had been waiting here for precisely that purpose.

The pieces fit together like a puzzle—Lambert's disruption field; the radio coordinates; Systems Engineer Hernández's suspicious behavior. They were all part of a carefully orchestrated plan.

All the questionable circumstances surrounding Hernández flooded into Lawrence's mind. He had never fully trusted her; never felt comfortable with her. Hernández always acted as if she harbored secrets.

Lawrence recalled that Hernández and Lambert had held long private discussions—conversations they would abruptly end when anyone else approached. And Hernández had always been close to the most problematic crew member—Robert Valdez.

Lawrence moved around, locating the officers, issuing orders. There were still some unconscious personnel to be revived. In a sheltered area among the rocks, an exploring group had found enough dry driftwood to build a fire—

In another hour, the skies had cleared, and bright moonlight flooded the scene with ghostly illumination. The crew of the Meridian had all regained consciousness and were drying themselves around the large driftwood fires in the cove.

Lawrence ordered a signal beacon maintained on a high point. Then he organized the crew, according to their departments, for a check of the missing.

When this was completed, it was determined that the Meridian's entire complement of one hundred and ten personnel were present—except Systems Engineer Ava Hernández and crew member Robert Valdez! And Dr. Jennifer Lambert was also missing!

With dawn's arrival, brief exploration revealed that the Meridian's crew was stranded on an island, roughly one square mile in area; that they had been put ashore without food or additional clothing or equipment of any kind, and that no boats had been left for them.

One search party reported finding the remnants of what had been a communications station on a high point on the north shore of the island. Another had found the remains of temporary structures, recently dismantled, in a small, wooded depression—a well-concealed location invisible from the air unless flying very low; a place where one hundred and fifty or more people could have camped.

There was adequate water—a small stream fed by springs—but no food. Evidently food was a valuable resource the recent inhabitants couldn't afford to leave behind.

Lawrence was examining the wreckage of the communications station, wondering if this might have been the source of Lambert's disruption field, when Junior Officer Raj Price approached him.

"There's a coast guard vessel heading for the island, sir," he announced.

Lawrence nodded grimly, already composing in his mind how he would explain this disaster—and how he would begin the hunt for those who had betrayed them.

synthetic_story:
THE HACKERS AND THE AI SUMMIT
By JAMES McCONNELL

The crystalline towers of Glendale, Kaldria rose like frozen lightning against the purple twilight sky. Inside the most prestigious of these structures, the Global Institute for Artificial Intelligence Research, the annual AI Summit was entering its third day. Two hundred of the world's leading researchers, corporate executives, and policy makers had gathered to discuss the future of computational intelligence and its role in reshaping human society.

"I can always work with a scientist if they remember the social contract," said Jessica Nichols, the celebrated AI ethicist whose passionate speeches on artificial intelligence governance had made her a household name. Her sharp features and intense gaze commanded attention in any room. She was widely considered the most influential voice in AI policy, and she rarely let anyone forget it.

"And I can always work with an ethicist if they remember who actually builds the systems," replied David Mills, the acerbic software architect whose revolutionary neural networks had transformed the field. He leaned his lanky frame back in the conference room chair and gave Jessica a challenging smile.

The two of them were sitting in the executive lounge of the Institute's main tower, enjoying post-conference cocktails with Dr. Francisco Cohen, the rotund director of the facility. The Summit was scheduled to conclude the following day with a major announcement about new international standards for AI development. But the tensions between the ethicists and the engineers were threatening to derail everything.

Jessica waved her tablet at David. "Don't listen to him, Francisco. You know how engineers are—always building things without considering the consequences, and not very good ones at that."

"Do you mean not very good consequences or not very good engineers, my dear?" David asked. The world's most famous AI ethicist pressed her lips together in rage. It would take someone like David Mills, she knew, to point out the one minor flaw in her otherwise impeccable record—her failed prediction about autonomous vehicles five years ago.

She began to wish she had never left Evergreen, Dravonia, that she had cancelled her attendance at the Summit when she learned David would be presenting. But the Institute had insisted she participate in the final panel on institutional reform. And this was the most important AI gathering in years. So she had kept her commitment despite David.

"I must say that I think Ms. Nichols has made the most compelling arguments I've heard all week," boomed Dr. Cohen, his voice carrying across the lounge. And he was not merely being diplomatic, for many a late night he had pondered the ethical frameworks she proposed.

"And I think you are definitely a man of discriminating judgment," said Jessica smoothly, adjusting her posture to project confidence.

David smiled casually. "It's all very impressive, my dear. But we've heard these arguments before and in reality you're supposed to propose solutions, if you can manage that."

Jessica drew back her hand to slam her tablet down in a very unprofessional manner when she suddenly realized they were not alone. Her hand froze, poised in mid-air, as she turned to see a newcomer standing at the door.

The witness to the impending outburst was a small elderly woman, scarcely five feet tall, with silver hair pulled back in a neat bun, eyes that sparkled with mischief, and a network of laugh lines that gave her face a warm, weathered appearance. Her slight figure was draped in a outdated pantsuit that had gone out of style decades before. The little woman coughed politely.

"I beg your pardon," she told them in a sweet, high voice. "I hope I didn't interrupt anything. If you would like to throw that tablet at the gentleman, Ms. Nichols, I'll be glad to come back later."

Jessica's eyes widened in surprise. "Why, I was... I was... I—" The ethicist made a small gulping sound as she recovered her composure. "Why, I was just going to show him some data. You do like data, don't you, David?" She leaned forward to tap the tablet screen gently. David laughed and Dr. Cohen colored deeply.

"Oh," said the little old woman, "I'm sorry. I didn't realize you were collaborating so closely." David choked and Jessica suffered from a brief fit of embarrassment.

Dr. Cohen took command. "Now, look here, Madam," he sputtered. "What is it you want?"

"I really wanted to see you, Director," she told him, her sensible shoes bringing her fully into the room with small steps. "The registration desk says I need to sign some kind of liability waiver, and I wanted to know which name to use. I'm Mrs. Ruby King, but you see, I'm really Mrs. Ruby Chen because my husband passed a few years ago. But I haven't signed my married name much since then and I'm not sure which is legal." She put one small hand to her throat and clasped the locket there as if it could give her support. She looked so small and so frail that Cohen forgave her the intrusion.

"It really doesn't make much difference how you sign it, just so long as you sign it," he blustered. "Just a formality anyway. You just sign it however you like." He paused, hoping she would leave now that she had her information.

"Oh, I'm so glad to hear that," she said, but made no move to leave. Dr. Cohen gave her his sternest academic stare, the type which withered most graduate students where they stood. Mrs. King just smiled sweetly at him.

His patience wearing thin, he finally blurted, "And now, Mrs. King, I think you'd better be getting back to your quarters. As you know, this lounge is reserved for Summit presenters and VIP guests."

Mrs. King continued to smile at him. "Yes, I know. It's lovely, isn't it? I'll just go out this way." And before anyone could stop her, she had moved to the door to Jessica's suite and opened it, stepping inside.

"That's my room, not the exit," Jessica said sharply.

"So I see," said Mrs. King, staring at the luxurious furnishings with evident pleasure. "It's such a beautiful space, all done up with smart glass and haptic interfaces. And what interesting research papers lying on the desk." Mrs. King picked up a confidential document to examine it. "This is about corporate governance of AI systems, isn't it?"

Jessica screeched and darted for the door. She snatched the paper away from Mrs. King and firmly escorted the older woman out, closing the door behind her. "Francisco, this woman must GO!"

"I was just leaving, Ms. Nichols. I hope you and your colleague have a very productive Summit. Good day, Dr. Cohen," she called over her shoulder as she exited. David Mills's sharp laughter followed her down the corridor.

Mrs. King had been sitting in her modest room reading for less than an hour when the knock sounded at her door. She would have preferred a more comfortable chair, but her accommodations were the cheapest available at the Institute.

"Come in," she called softly.

Nicholas Harvey, the young assistant who managed the budget accommodations, poked his earnest face through the door. "Hello, Mrs. King. I wondered if I could help you with anything? Dinner service starts in about ten minutes."

"Well, you can help me find my good shoes in that closet there, if you don't mind. And, I wonder, would you mind calling me Grandma Ruby? All my grandchildren do it and I miss it so." She gave him a wrinkled smile that was both wistful and playful.

Nicholas laughed easily. "Sure thing, Grandma Ruby." He opened the closet and found himself wondering how such a frail woman had managed to stack her heavy luggage on the top shelf. He brought down a box and set it on the floor.

As she bent over and extracted a pair of comfortable shoes from the box, she asked him, "Nicholas, what was that paper I signed this afternoon?"

"Oh, that? Why that was just a liability waiver, Grandma Ruby. You agreed not to hold the Institute responsible for any accidents, and they guaranteed you access to all public areas of the Summit until it concludes."

"But why do we need such a thing?"

Nicholas leaned against the doorframe. "Well, the Institute is part of a consortium of thirteen major AI research organizations—we call them the 'Big Thirteen.' They coordinate all major AI research conferences worldwide. Back in the early days, attendees would sometimes get injured or claim intellectual property theft. Some people would register, gain access to confidential research, and then leak it to competitors. To maintain their coordination role, the consortium had to implement strict legal protections. The World Technology Council makes them use these waivers to protect both sides."

Grandma Ruby sighed. "It's such a small room I don't think I have access to anything important anyway. But it's all I could afford," she said, smoothing her jacket.

"Anything else I can do for you, Grandma Ruby?"

"No, thank you, Nicholas. I think I can make it to the dining hall by myself."

A little while later when Nicholas checked on her, the room was empty and the heavy box was back on the top shelf.

The food that evening was adequate, Grandma Ruby thought, though her table in the corner meant she was served last. But she didn't complain. She enjoyed watching the important attendees at the director's table. Jessica Nichols and David Mills were seated there, Jessica having the place of honor to Dr. Cohen's right.

Grandma watched them finish their meal and then moved from her small table to one of the comfortable sofas in the main lounge. Technically she wasn't supposed to be sitting there, but she hoped she could get away with it. The furniture was much more comfortable than her room.

But her hopes were disappointed. Shortly after she sat down, Jessica Nichols and David Mills strolled over and sat across from her, not recognizing her at first. Then David noticed her.

"Jessica! There's that peculiar little woman from this afternoon."

"The nosy busybody, you mean," Jessica muttered, just loud enough for Grandma Ruby to hear.

"Why, hello, Ms. Nichols. And Mr. Mills too. I hope you'll forgive me for earlier. I've learned who you both are now."

"Of course we forgive you, Mrs. King," Jessica said with false warmth.

"Actually, it's Mrs. Chen—or was. I'm Grandma Ruby," she smiled.

"I hope you don't mind, but you remind me of my great-niece, Amanda. She was undoubtedly the brightest child I've ever known."

"Why, thank you, Grandma Ruby," Jessica purred, starting to relax slightly.

"Of course, Amanda never had much common sense," Grandma said, turning her head as if in sorrow. "She got three PhDs but couldn't hold a job. Last I heard she was working as a fortune teller at a carnival, using her computational linguistics degree to sound impressive. Such a waste. She was brilliant, just like you."

Jessica muttered something unpleasant under her breath.

"But we must make the best of things. That's what my husband used to say." Grandma paused to dab at her eye. "That reminds me, I have photos of all my grandchildren on my tablet. I brought it specially tonight because I thought you might want to see them. Now, where did I put it?" Grandma opened her purse and began rummaging.

Jessica and David exchanged horrified glances and silently slipped away.

Grandma looked up. "Oh my, they seem to have left."

Nicholas Harvey, who had been clearing a nearby table, came over. "I'd like to see the photos, Grandma Ruby."

"Oh, that's kind of you, Nicholas, but—" she said quickly.

"Really, I would."

"There aren't any photos, Nicholas. I don't need them—I know all their faces. But whenever I want to get rid of someone, I just offer to show them family pictures. You'd be surprised how well it works."

Nicholas laughed. "Why are you here at the Summit anyway, Grandma Ruby?"

The old woman sighed. "It's complicated, Nicholas. I'm 152 years old—life extension treatments, you know. Since my husband died, I've lived with one grandchild after another. They're all grown with families of their own now. I think I just get in their way. There isn't much left for someone my age."

Nicholas, remembering the heavy luggage, suppressed a smile at her apparent frailty.

"I don't have many friends left. So I'm being sent to Clearwater, Quendor, to a retirement community for elderly people, funded by my dear grandchildren—all twelve of them." She dabbed her eyes. "The ungrateful wretches," she muttered.

"To be honest, Nicholas, they've become boring and conventional. They think I've lost my mind. Everything I did embarrassed them. So maybe it's for the best, but—"

Grandma Ruby never finished, for suddenly the Institute's emergency alarm sounded, and charging through the lounge came Dr. Cohen.

"BREACH! SECURITY BREACH! We're being hacked! You there!" he shouted at Nicholas. "Get to your station! And you, Madam, to your room immediately! HACKERS!" He charged through the door toward the main server room.

Nicholas ran off, but Grandma moved calmly toward the exit. Maybe, she thought, we're going to have some excitement after all.

At the stairs to her lower-level room she paused.

"If I go hide, I'll miss everything. Of course, it's safer, and an old woman shouldn't be wandering around during a security crisis, but—" A delicious smile spread across her face as she turned to follow the bellowing director toward the server room.

II

The Global Institute for Artificial Intelligence Research was equipped with every security system known to modern technology. The server room was designed for maximum protection. But the architects never anticipated the current situation. The control center was chaos.

The Senior Security Officer was shouting at his assistant, the Network Administrator was cursing at the Systems Engineer, and the Chief Technology Officer, whose job had been mostly ceremonial, was yelling at everyone. Above the noise came Dr. Cohen's voice as he burst in.

"What in blazes has happened to our systems? Why are we locked out?"

The Senior Security Officer saluted. "Server room reports all systems compromised, Sir. Unknown how. We're running minimal functions on backup power."

The Communications Officer spoke up. "The hackers sent a message, Sir. They say they've deployed a new AI exploit that gives them complete control of our systems."

A synthesized voice came over the speakers. "Attention, Institute. Prepare for data extraction. If you resist, we'll wipe every server and leak all your confidential research."

"Hackers! Attacking us! Impossible!" cried Dr. Cohen. "We have the best security in the world! Where is the Cyber Security Task Force?"

The Communications Officer gulped. "We contacted Agent Jose Baker. He says his team can arrive in ten hours, and we should wait for them."

Dr. Cohen snorted. "Ten hours! They'll have stripped us clean by then. We'll counter-hack them right now! Activate our defenses!"

"The defenses are useless," whined the CTO. "The AI systems that run them are all compromised. What do we do?"

"Attention, Institute. We're entering your network now. Don't try to stop us or we'll destroy everything," boomed the speakers.

"Hackers breaking in. How interesting," Grandma Ruby muttered to herself as she listened outside the door.

"They'll never get our core data. At least our physical security still works. We'll stop them!" cried Dr. Cohen.

"We only want one thing from you. Everyone else will be spared if you don't interfere," came the voice.

"Tell them I'd rather lose everything than let criminals steal from this Institute," the director shouted.

"Oh my. That doesn't sound wise," Grandma said quietly. Turning from the doorway, she made her way through the deserted corridor.

The main server room entrance wasn't far from the control center. Grandma found it easily, and in minutes she had accessed the emergency override terminal beside the door. She felt awkward working the advanced interface, but once she understood the system, she felt quite capable.

Opening the security protocols, she typed rapidly. As she worked, she heard digital pounding—the hackers trying to break through the final firewall.

Calmly, she entered a command sequence and pressed a button clearly marked: EMERGENCY OVERRIDE - DO NOT USE DURING ACTIVE SESSION

The firewall dropped immediately. Her terminal crackled with alerts. "What are you doing?" demanded a voice through the system.

"Hackers! I'm hiding from the security team. They'll never find me here!" she said in a panicked voice into the microphone.

"Who are you?" asked the voice.

"Jessica Nichols, famous AI ethicist," she lied smoothly.

"That's the one," said another voice. "Perfect. Let's go." Through her terminal, they established a secure connection and began transferring data.

Thirty minutes later, after the hackers had disconnected from the Institute's network, the men in their hidden facility in Kensington, Galdoria began to relax. One of them, whom Grandma soon learned was Matthew Chapman, the group's leader, stretched and rubbed his tired eyes. Most of the men looked disheveled, as if they'd been working for days.

"Well, that worked beautifully," said Matthew.

Lucia Hunt was a sharp-featured woman whose intense gaze matched her technical skills. "You bet, Matt. We're real hackers now, just like the old Anonymous collective."

"You mean the ones who did community organizing through digital activism, Lucia," said Matthew.

"Right. They organized communities to resist corporate governance."

One of the other men spoke up. "And we got Jessica Nichols's personal research files as a bonus. Worth a fortune."

"Women are nothing but trouble—all of them," muttered Lucia.

"Now, Lucia, that's not fair. Apologize to our guest," Matthew said. He was broader and more imposing than Lucia. She apologized.

"Better. Now, Ms. Nichols, you'd probably be more comfortable if you came out from behind that terminal," he said.

"Oh no, thank you. I feel much safer here," said Grandma's voice through the speakers.

Matthew grinned. "Come now, Ms. Nichols. We won't hurt you. I guarantee no one will touch you."

"But I feel much—much safer, if you understand," said the voice.

"Look, you can't stay connected forever. You need to eat, sleep—well, there's lots you need to do. Besides, we want to talk to you about your work. Lucia, help our guest disconnect properly."

As Lucia began tracing the connection, Grandma sensed the game was up. "Okay, I give up. I'll disconnect myself." She began the process, and when her video feed finally came through, the truth became apparent.

"Holy smoke," said one of the men.

"What the—" said another.

"It's not even someone important!" cried Lucia.

"I beg your pardon," said Grandma Ruby, adjusting her jacket on the video screen. "I am Mrs. Ruby King."

When he recovered his composure, Matthew sputtered, "I think you owe us an explanation, lady."

"Certainly. When I overheard you wanted to extract data from one specific person, I realized you meant Jessica Nichols. She's obviously the only one at the Summit worth targeting for her research. So I simply let you believe I was her, and you took the bait. Simple, isn't it?"

"She's crazy," moaned Lucia.

"She's lost it," muttered another.

"Let's delete her connection right now," said another.

Matthew took control. "Wait. We can't do that. We have enough trouble already. You know what would happen if the authorities added conspiracy charges? They'd track us and our families down to the last person." He turned to address the screen.

"Look, lady—"

"My name is Mrs. Ruby King. You may call me Grandma Ruby."

"Okay, Grandma Ruby, look. You really complicated things. We're not really criminals. We used to work as independent AI researchers, doing contract work between the major labs. Matthew sat down heavily.

"So when we honest researchers couldn't find work because of the consortium, and we didn't want to give up our field, we decided to become hacktivists. This was our first major operation, and we needed Jessica Nichols's research on institutional reform and risk management to expose the consortium's corruption."

Matthew sighed. "Now we have you instead, no chance of getting the research, and we'll be wanted by the authorities."

"Well, it seems to me you're never going to be good hacktivists at this rate," Grandma told him. "You should have known better than to trust a voice over a microphone."

"I don't suppose you have any wealthy relatives who'd pay to get you back?" suggested Lucia hopefully.

"I don't have any wealthy relatives at all," she said. "But my twelve grandchildren might scrape together some money if you promised not to return me."

"I figured as much," Matthew said sadly. "Look, Grandma Ruby, the best thing we can do is disconnect you safely and make sure you get back to the Institute. Unless we handle this carefully, the authorities will hunt us forever. So don't get any ideas about joining us."

"Well, the very least you could do for a poor old lady is let her help you," Grandma told him, her lip jutting out stubbornly. "I may not be Jessica Nichols, but I know quite a bit about corporate governance and institutional reform myself. The room fell silent. Matthew leaned forward. "You're serious?"

Matthew and Lucia exchanged glances. Finally, Matthew spoke. "Grandma Ruby, I think we need to talk. Can you tell us more about these vulnerabilities?"

Grandma Ruby smiled, her eyes twinkling with that familiar mischief. "First, young man, you're going to feed this poor old lady. And as she began explaining the intricacies of international AI governance to her rapt audience, Grandma Ruby reflected that perhaps being kidnapped by hackers was exactly the adventure she'd needed all along.

"Two hundred meters northeast. But Dr. Wyatt, you should see this." Mateo adjusted a dial, and a sonar image appeared on one of the screens. "There's a massive cavern system beneath us. The readings suggest it extends for kilometers."

"Not safely. The entrance is too narrow, too unstable." Mateo paused. "But we could send in the drone."

While Mateo launched the remote probe, Helena turned her attention to the landing site. The plan was to deploy their modular habitat—a pressurized structure that would serve as living quarters and laboratory for a six-month research stint. After that, if all went well, they'd establish a permanent facility. The implications for marine biology, oceanography, and complexity science were staggering. The ecosystem here might hold answers to questions about the origins of life itself.

The *Nautilus* settled onto the trench floor with barely a tremor. Mateo was an excellent pilot; Helena had chosen well when she'd recruited him from the Maplewood Institute of Marine Studies.

"Stable landing confirmed," Mateo reported. "All systems nominal. Pressure holding steady at—" He stopped abruptly. "That's odd."

"What is it?"
