synthetic_story:
The Inheritance of Love

A message arrived from Helena Mason, someone I'd known briefly during my undergraduate years at the university in Harborview, Belvoria—one of several such intrusive inquiries I'd received recently. "I heard about your mother," she wrote. "She was always so successful in her research career. Did she leave you much? Did all those patents amount to anything significant?" The question was tactless, but perhaps it deserves an answer.

My brother Stephen Porter and I have spent the past months working through our mother's affairs with her attorney, sorting through decades of research notebooks, patent applications, and academic correspondence. Perhaps now is the appropriate time to reflect on what Dr. Aisha Hicks truly left behind.

She did leave some financial assets. By the standards one reads about in venture capital circles or tech industry publications, the sum was modest. Regardless, after the estate taxes—which she herself had always defended as necessary for a functioning society—the amount that will ultimately reach us is considerably diminished. As a bioethicist and geneticist, my mother spent her career navigating research ethics in genetic engineering, always insisting that personal sacrifice was worthwhile for the greater good. Yet even she was troubled, near the end, by the tax burden that would fall on her life's savings.

The estate will be taxed at substantial rates, and when I consider it, I feel a profound sadness. My mother and father lived simply throughout their decades together. They never owned a luxury vehicle. They never flew business class unless the university paid for it. They never took an extravagant vacation. When she last went to the hospital, my mother was still wearing a cardigan she'd owned for twenty years, the one with the patched elbow from when it caught on a laboratory bench.

They never employed household staff. My father cooked dinner while my mother worked late in her home office. My mother took public transportation whenever possible, even after her research brought her some recognition. Their only significant expenditure was education—for their children and grandchildren. They never purchased premium coffee or expensive wines. They used the same furniture from their first apartment in the Lakeside Territory throughout their marriage. I never saw them order the most expensive item on a menu, and they always requested containers for leftovers.

They earned nothing from stock options or corporate windfalls. Every dollar came from careful saving, from choosing prudence over indulgence, from thinking of future generations rather than present pleasures. To know that this discipline and virtue will primarily benefit the tax authorities is almost unbearable. The only justification seems to be satisfying some resentment from those who chose differently.

There are tangible items that must be appraised. There are my mother's books from her time at the university in Juniper, Estoria, and later from her graduate work in Crystalbrook, Havencia—many still marked with her neat annotations in pencil, handwriting that remained unchanged from 1978 until days before her death. Most concern genetics and research ethics, but some are poetry collections.

That's another part of what she left: her own writing. Beyond the scientific papers, there are essays she wrote for small journals, reflections on the responsibility of scientists, meditations on the ethics of genetic engineering and what it means to alter the fundamental building blocks of life. There are her thoughts on consciousness studies and metaphysics, wondering about the nature of identity when genes can be edited. There are poems she wrote about missing my father after he died, about the beauty of the harbor in Harborview at dawn, about her frustration with persistent misconceptions in public discourse about science. And there are her humorous verses about academic politics, parodies of famous poems composed for colleagues' retirement parties. I suppose these will not be heavily taxed, as my mother never wrote for popular audiences.

Some of her papers will go to the university archives. Some will sit on shelves in the small house my wife Sofia Gupta and I own near the water—a place my mother loved because she'd always dreamed of living where she could see the ocean while she wrote. And there are her belongings, her clothes, none of which has monetary value but all of which matter to me because they carry her presence. When I open her closet, I can still smell her scent—lavender soap and old paper and leather—the closet smelling exactly as she did when she came home from the laboratory in 1989 carrying news that her research team had made a breakthrough in understanding genetic markers for inherited diseases. And there are her mementos from her years advising the National Bioethics Commission, certificates and awards, photographs with other scientists. And there are the love letters between her and my father from when they were courting in 1976 and 1977, still tied with a blue ribbon in her desk drawer, discussing how their love would survive the challenges of two academic careers and limited resources. I suppose these too must be valued and taxed.

But these are the minor elements of her legacy to Stephen and me. The truly valuable inheritance cannot be touched by estate taxes. Her legacy to her family has almost nothing to do with anything measurable in currency.

The example of integrity and principle: When she was leading the genetic engineering research group at the university, she hired a young postdoctoral researcher named Isaac Hunt. Almost immediately, the department chair came to tell her that Hunt had to be dismissed. Apparently, Isaac had published an opinion piece criticizing certain directions in genetic research that the university's corporate partners were funding. The administration suggested this showed poor judgment and disloyalty. My mother responded that academic freedom was non-negotiable, that Isaac Hunt was hired for his scientific abilities, not his willingness to remain silent on matters of research ethics, and that he would not be dismissed for exercising his right to speak on important issues. After considerable tension, Hunt was allowed to stay—and went on to do excellent work.

My mother was loyal, and no tax authority can seize that legacy. When controversies arose around some of her early research—questions about informed consent in genetic studies, debates about the implications of her work—she never deflected responsibility or hid behind institutional protections. She faced criticism directly, acknowledged where improvements were needed, and worked to establish better protocols. She helped develop guidelines for research ethics in genetic engineering that are still used today.

Years later, when a former collaborator was accused of falsifying data, many in the field distanced themselves. My mother refused. She carefully reviewed the evidence, concluded that the accusations were largely unfounded and motivated by professional jealousy, and publicly defended her colleague. She testified on his behalf, explaining the scientific validity of his work. She never abandoned someone she believed in.

"Integrity." There is no line item for it in the estate inventory.

My mother lived her life, especially in her later years, in a state of gratitude. Whatever criticisms she had of the scientific establishment or funding priorities, she constantly reminded anyone who would listen that the opportunity to pursue knowledge was a profound privilege. She believed that the current system, despite its flaws, offered unprecedented opportunities for discovery and that the progress in her field during her lifetime had been extraordinary.

When she did acknowledge failures—particularly early mistakes in research ethics, instances where informed consent was not properly obtained, cases where the implications of genetic research were not fully considered—she did so to highlight how far the field had advanced. She had no patience for those who dwelled only on problems without recognizing the remarkable improvements in research ethics, in diversity within science, in accessibility of genetic medicine.

She appreciated beauty in unexpected places. She loved ballet and opera, spending evenings watching performances on television. She treasured visits to the cultural center in Harborview to see dance or hear music. But she also appreciated the aesthetics of elegant experiments, of a well-designed research protocol, of a clearly written paper. She was moved by the architecture of the old laboratory buildings, by the fountains in the university courtyards, by the changing seasons visible from her office window.

This capacity for gratitude cannot be taxed, at least not yet.

She appreciated her colleagues and treated everyone with equal respect regardless of their position. She valued the insights of Max Sims, the laboratory technician who had worked with her for thirty years, as much as those of famous scientists. She listened to the concerns of Kate Davis, who managed the building services, with the same attention she gave to university administrators. She never suggested that anyone deserved special deference because of wealth or fame. She was skeptical of those who had profited enormously from commercializing research, believing that the pursuit of knowledge should not be primarily about financial gain. She did not encourage Stephen or me to choose careers based on earning potential, and by her example showed us to follow what was meaningful rather than what was lucrative. I never knew her to accept a position or a project primarily for the money. She derived more satisfaction from mentoring students than from consulting for biotechnology companies that paid handsomely.

My mother's stance against pursuing wealth for its own sake—so contrary to contemporary values, but so reassuring to her children—cannot be confiscated by the government.

She had a way of contextualizing what I thought were disasters. If I was distraught about a failed grant application, she would explain that setbacks were inherent to research. If my investments declined, she would point out that if I had health, family, and meaningful work, I was extraordinarily fortunate. Most reassuringly, she would tell me that my family and I could always come stay with her, that she had more than enough space and resources, that very little money was actually required for a good life. (She lived on a fraction of her income, even while paying for her grandchildren's education.)

Once, about fifteen years ago, when I was treated unfairly at work, she said that if it continued, I should resign and she would support me until I found something better. I never needed to take that offer, but knowing it existed was a constant comfort.

This reassurance—that things will ultimately be all right, that resilience is part of human nature—has become part of me. I summon it when I'm anxious about finances or facing professional challenges. Again, this inheritance is not subject to taxation.

My mother herself inherited very little money from her parents. She did inherit a belief that hard work and persistence could overcome most obstacles, that living beyond one's means was foolish, that flashy displays of wealth were often masks for insecurity. She passed these beliefs to me, though they've been somewhat tested by the culture of my profession. Still, I've managed to maintain financial stability, and I attribute this to internalizing her principles of prudence.

Most of all, my mother believed in cherishing the people in her life. She maintained friendships from graduate school, from her early career, from her years on various committees and boards. She remained close to everyone who had been important to her, refusing to hear personal attacks on former colleagues even when she disagreed with their current positions.

She formed connections easily. Even in her final days in the hospital, she befriended the nurses and doctors, learning about their lives, remembering details about their families. She called one young physician "my friend Samuel," after Samuel Perkins, a character from a novel she loved, because his kindness reminded her of that literary figure.

She grieved deeply when my father died in 2015, never fully recovering from losing her partner of forty-two years. Once, she had written him a poem about the beauty of the coastal road near Crystalbrook, about the joy of driving it together. She'd filed it away, intending to revise it. The day after his death, she found his response poem, written years earlier, expressing his hope that they would always travel that road together. He had placed it back in the folder without telling her. She survived that devastating loss with the help of close friends and family, finding purpose in her relationships. A simple phone call from a friend inviting her to dinner could lift her spirits entirely.

Even in her hospital bed, hearing her grandson's voice could make her smile through pain and fear. ("He calls me 'Grandma' with such sweetness," she said, her eyes bright despite her illness.)

Never once did Stephen or I ask for her help without receiving it immediately and generously. Usually this involved advice about our work, questions we were too lazy to research ourselves, but she always responded without hesitation. When I was young and had a task I didn't want to do, her solution was simple: "Let's do it together. It will go faster." I use that phrase with my own son regularly, along with the devotion it represents.

She maintained connections across decades. She had lunch with a colleague from her graduate program just days before her final hospitalization. She corresponded with former students, celebrating their successes, offering guidance during their struggles.

This quality of devotion and the fulfillment I derive from it are worth far more than any financial assets in the estate—and cannot be taken at any tax rate. Moreover, I can pass it to my son without any penalty.

And she left something else of perhaps even greater value: a reputation for integrity. Many people disagreed with my mother's positions on research priorities, on the ethics of certain genetic engineering applications, on funding allocation. She faced opposition to her views on the responsibilities of scientists in electoral politics, her belief that researchers should engage with public policy. But no one ever questioned that her positions were honestly held, derived from careful thought and genuine conviction rather than personal gain. Her reputation for honesty was absolutely unimpeachable.

This good name cannot be taxed at all, at least not yet. Stephen and I and our children will have it as long as we preserve it. It's priceless, beyond calculation.

So, in answer to Helena Mason's intrusive question: Yes, my mother did leave an enormous estate, and yes, she did manage to minimize the real losses to taxation. The only problem is that I miss her every single moment, and I already possessed the best parts of the estate while she was alive, so her death is pure loss.

The financial inheritance will help, certainly. But what truly matters—the lessons in integrity, the example of devotion, the model of a life lived with purpose and gratitude, the reputation for honesty, the capacity for love—these are what she really left us. These are the things that cannot be appraised, cannot be taxed, cannot be diminished by any external force. These are what made her wealthy, and what make us wealthy now.

When I think about inheritance, about what passes from one generation to the next, I realize that the most valuable things have nothing to do with bank accounts or property deeds. They have to do with how we treat people, what we stand for, what we value, how we face adversity, whom we love and how we love them.

My mother understood this. She lived it. And in doing so, she left Stephen and me richer than any sum of money could make us.
question: What does the narrator suggest cannot be easily appraised or taxed?
option_a: The mother's research patents, laboratory equipment, and academic publications
option_b: The mother's integrity, devotion to others, reputation for honesty, and capacity for gratitude
correct_answer_text: The mother's integrity, devotion to others, reputation for honesty, and capacity for gratitude
incorrect_answer_text: The mother's research patents, laboratory equipment, and academic publications
explanation: Throughout the story, the narrator repeatedly emphasizes that while the mother's financial estate will be taxed, the truly valuable parts of her legacy—her integrity, loyalty, devotion, reputation for honesty, capacity for gratitude, and love for others—cannot be appraised or taxed. These intangible qualities are presented as the most significant inheritance, worth far more than any monetary assets.
original_question: What are some of the things the author says can’t easily be valued?

The Gathering of the Silvermoon Council

In the first week of the Harvest Moon, Margaret Kim ascended the ancient stone platform at the Silvermoon Council's inaugural gathering to deliver her address as High Arbiter, and within moments of beginning, her voice broke with emotion. She wept openly as she recounted the struggles of raising her daughter alone in the Eastern Provinces, a child born with the gift of true-speaking—the ability to perceive and speak only absolute truth, a rare magical talent that made her unable to navigate the necessary social deceptions of everyday life. "Discovering that no one wanted to hear her truths, that no one valued her gift, that she was seen as broken rather than different," Margaret said, her voice trembling.

This wasn't a single tear discreetly wiped away. Margaret Kim (a tall woman with silver-streaked hair, known throughout Valleyview, Relvaria as a distinguished scholar of magical linguistics) appeared to struggle with continuing. The assembled delegates held their collective breath. I gripped the arms of my wooden chair, caught between sympathy and discomfort, thinking this display would not be well-received by the chroniclers, that she would be ridiculed for weakness; what kind of leader, standing before hundreds of delegates from across the realm, breaks down while recounting personal defeats?

It was only later, after the day's sessions had concluded and I sat in my quarters at the Northfield Town inn, that I realized this had been one of the most significant and, indeed, persuasive moments of the entire gathering. Margaret could hardly have made her point more effectively—that her daughter's gift had shattered her own privilege as a high-born, academy-educated scholar (and possessed of considerable political connections, which she did not mention but which nevertheless played a role in her standing)—more powerfully. Her tears conveyed her anguish at feeling her child was destined, as she expressed it, to remain either hidden from society or cruelly exposed to its judgment, and the helplessness this recognition induced.

The Silvermoon Council gathering was filled with discussion about practitioners of the old ways 'conducting governance differently.' The phrase was repeated constantly, though its precise meaning remained somewhat elusive. This week, as thousands of magic-users prepare to march on the Crystal Palace in Juniper, Jarvonia following the coronation of King Stefan Lee (with gatherings planned in two hundred other cities and towns across the Five Kingdoms, including throughout Relvaria and in Windsor Village, where Margaret Kim will be among the speakers), this seems an opportune moment to examine whether there is anything genuinely new about this century's magical activism and, if so, what it might be.

There are two dimensions in which practitioners might potentially 'conduct governance differently': policy, and practice. Regarding the former, the Silvermoon Council is advancing broad policy objectives capable of attracting magic-users from across the traditional philosophical spectrum, including establishing fair compensation for magical labor, subsidizing training for young practitioners, ending persecution of those with unconventional gifts, and ensuring equal representation in the royal courts, merchant guilds, and centers of learning. The details and implementation would prove more contentious, but for now, these are objectives most practitioners can support. Both Rafael Mason, former Royal Advisor on Enchantments to Queen Hannah, and Naomi Gardner, Grand Master of the Northern Mages' Guild, spoke at the gathering.

It is in its practice, however, that magical activism has genuine potential to expand our understanding of what it means to engage in political movements and community organizing.

Among the various reasons for the recent upheavals—the dissolution of the Southern Alliance and the coronation of Stefan Lee—rage featured prominently. Emotion has returned to the forefront of political discourse. The Alliance-breakers and Stefan's supporters eschewed rational arguments in favor of appeals to feeling. Stefan is, in many ways, a Sovereign of Emotions. (Pathetic!) Yet we are poorly equipped to comprehend this resurgence of feeling, as the scholar Joseph Morales argues in his forthcoming treatise, "The Age of Fury," because our dominant intellectual frameworks are incapable of understanding the role of emotion in governance and political economy.

Since the Great Rationalist Movement three centuries ago, Morales argues, our political thinking has become increasingly constrained by materialist, mechanistic premises—for instance, the notion that "humans are fundamentally rational and motivated by the pursuit of their own interests; that they primarily act to maximize personal advantage, rather than on the basis of fear, anger, and resentment." The concept of homo economicus, he contends, "views the marketplace as the ideal form of human interaction and venerates innovation management and the accumulation of wealth. All of this is part of the rigid contemporary belief that what counts is only what can be measured and that what cannot be measured—subjective emotions—therefore does not exist." This worldview leaves no room for more complex motivations: vanity, for instance, or the fear of humiliation.

How, then, to comprehend, let alone articulate, the vulnerability, the shame, the loss of identity created by inequality, the disappearance of traditional crafts, and communities without purpose? The turbulent emotions generated by the merchant system's failure to deliver the promised universal prosperity cannot be understood when emotion is something men are expected to contain and then repudiate. Powerful male leaders do not stand before their councils and weep about their daughters. Such behavior is for the defeated. Male valor demands the concealment of emotional distress. (This is deeply embedded in our culture: in the ancient play "The Lovers of Verona," the wise mentor scolds the young hero, "Your tears are womanish," though the hero has every right to be distressed, having just slain a man in a duel.)

Emotion is stigmatized as belonging to lesser, non-normative groups. Women are hysterical. Elven men are overly passionate. Practitioners of chaos magic are unreliably unpredictable. There is no option for would-be victors, competing to maximize their self-interest, to respond to injury by saying, "Please, that causes me pain!"—still less by weeping.

The emotion exists nevertheless, growing and festering. Since men without the means to express vulnerability cannot openly mourn their loss of identity as providers (let alone their disorientation when other groups threaten to undermine their unearned sense of superiority), injured masculinity must disguise itself in images of strength, mastery, honor. Stefan Lee himself embodies this phenomenon, as the chronicler Claudia Montgomery has observed: "At once an emblem of violent, impenetrable masculinity—the iron-willed, stone-hearted warrior-king determined to restore the realm to order—and a byword for hysterical sensitivity, a petulant monarch with a hair-trigger temper."

All this emotion-with-nowhere-to-go was seized upon by the Alliance-breakers and Stefan's campaign. They found a way to channel it, allowing populations to associate themselves with victory, to shout 'losers' at people they disliked. It turned out not to matter greatly what they were winning at or where it led them. Placing Stefan on the Crystal Throne, like dissolving the Alliance, was an end in itself, a way of displacing pain, therapeutic.

It was also profoundly reactionary. The hideous inequalities of the merchant-dominated system being what they are, it is difficult for common folk to conceive of themselves becoming victors as things stand—so Stefan's campaign and the Alliance-breakers offered instead a return to fantasies of the past. The imagery of the Alliance dissolution has its roots in the realm's resistance to the Dark Sorcerer Wars (conveniently overlooking details like the empire's brutal expansion and intervention by the Dragon Lords), while Stefan's campaign slogan "restore the realm's glory" offered explicit nostalgia for a time when the nation had a common destiny, with human men of noble birth at the center.

What magical activism, particularly that led by women practitioners, might bring to governance is a different sensibility, one that acknowledges that emotions are inevitable, messy—and necessary. There is a void in politics where opposition used to exist and where balanced governance used to flourish. This is largely because rational arguments, facts, expertise, seem to bear too little relation to the way many people feel about the world. The rationalists' arguments seem to be conducted in a parallel universe, of interest only to those who thrive there. When called to articulate a vision for the realm within the Alliance, the best Alliance-supporters could manage was an abstract account of economic penalties if the population didn't comply—which, since it never resonated, was easily dismissed as 'fear-mongering.'

People have not, in fact, lost interest in truth. But first and foremost, they know the truth of their emotional relationship to the world. Rationalists and moderate reformers currently have no way of addressing this. Much of the time, they appear to be speaking incomprehensible jargon, despite their data analysis and complexity science.

The populist faction has found an emotive way to engage populations by channeling their feelings, often displacing them onto someone else in the process. If you cannot look at yourself honestly—because anxiousness makes you feel weak and to be weak is to be a failed person—you are vulnerable to finding someone else to blame for your loss of dignity. In a world of competition, the only path to self-esteem is to be a victor. And someone else must therefore become the defeated.

There is an alternative: a political approach that begins with the notion that emotions do not have to be repressed or twisted into bigotry and abuse. An understanding of feelings that does not equate weakness with shame, and compassion with maladaptive weakness, is far more likely to suggest solutions than one that denies our emotional lives, most of what makes us human. This is a matter of applied ethics as much as practical governance.

When people admit to their emotions, they call for empathy; they can galvanize action. "And what does the royal treasury call a single mother raising two children while caring for her elderly father?" Margaret Kim asked in her address, promptly supplying the (clearly absurd) answer: 'Economically inactive.' Margaret's single mother is of no importance in the Stefan Lee fantasy realm of victory, greatness, the conquest, othering the outsider. The unpaid work of caring is about love; it entails vulnerability, which immediately makes it suspect in a world of winning and losing, where the only permissible emotions are triumph and mocking schadenfreude.

The prevailing political mood of the moment is anxiety. "To live in the modern realm," the historian Youssef Martin wrote recently in the Royal Chronicles, "subject to perpetual social and magical transformation, is to experience the psychological equivalent of permanent revolution. Anxiety in the face of this process is now a universal experience, which is why reactionary ideas attract adherents across the kingdoms who share little except their sense of historical betrayal."

When rationalists make pious noises about understanding the anxiety of constituents who have turned away from them, their solution often seems to entail adopting some of the bigotry. You don't have to look far to find those who believe that the magical rights movement is inadequate to the task of humanizing politics because it is, in fact, part of the problem. Youssef Martin, in another piece in the Royal Chronicles, and the commentator Simon of Thornbury, in the Merchant's Gazette, have each argued that the policing of language and behavior—which some call courtesy and others call excessive sensitivity—has provoked a backlash and so must bear some blame for populism. The logical extension of this argument is that advocates for women practitioners, along with advocates for non-human magic-users and practitioners of unconventional magical traditions and other assorted 'fragile flowers,' need to step back and consider just how much damage they're causing.

The problem is that this assumes human men's lives are neutral territory around which the common interest can coalesce. It is, in other words, male identity politics. "There has been a massive backlash by human men of noble birth," Margaret Kim told me, at the Silvermoon Council headquarters in Windsor Village, a few weeks after the gathering. "We are living out the identity politics of the noble human man right now."

If we are not to face a breakdown into essentialist tribal identities of gender, race, and magical tradition, people must find a way of articulating feelings of distress that doesn't humiliate them. If men cannot face their anxiety, it will be denied, and then absolutely nothing will be done to alleviate it; there will be a privatization of misery. There are structural reasons for the explosion of melancholy disorders in the Five Kingdoms, for the dreamweed addiction in the mining provinces, the epidemic of distress among young people, other forms of self-harm. But if we can't acknowledge the underlying dread and helplessness that people experience in the face of a world controlled by merchant princes and incomprehensible magical forces, individuals will continue to be stigmatized as failing. Either you will be a victor, an entrepreneurial individual competing freely in the marketplace, deflecting your distress by showing strength, lashing out; or your inchoate feelings of desperation will be—sorry—your problem alone.

A female sensibility in politics is not, it probably needs saying, antithetical to reason, even though feeling and reason are often posited as opposites. The ancient philosopher Platon contrasted the wild horse of passion and the wise charioteer of reason (his point being, of course, that they needed each other). The novelist Jane of Austen would have had no plots without the frequent difficulty human beings have in accommodating desire and wisdom: success, as she repeatedly shows, lies in the reconciliation of sense and sensibility. Such an accommodation requires self-examination, generosity of spirit, fidelity to self, and rigorous thinking. But first and foremost, it requires honesty about feeling.

I used to grow mildly irritated when advocates for women practitioners focused too intensely on female representation, when there seemed so many other pressing matters to address, as if gender alone made a difference. And it is true that there is an elite-focused advocacy that takes little heed of women for whom race, class, disability, and magical tradition intersect to intensify and compound gender discrimination. But sheer numbers of women do make a difference. Rafael Mason notes that women in the royal councils are more inclined to engage in creative collaboration across philosophical lines than men. Naomi Gardner, who has spent a lifetime as the sole woman on decision-making bodies, says that when women reach forty percent in a meeting or on a council, the language changes. There's a different way of conducting business, a different sense of how to advance objectives. In a hall overwhelmingly dominated by women, it is possible for a leader to cry and everyone to support her. For no one to think (after a moment of adjustment from unreconstructed be-more-like-a-man advocates like myself) that she's weak.

Over the coming months and years, progressives are going to have to grapple with what kind of emotional appeal they can make beyond the populists' exploitative deformation of feeling. The task will be to retrieve emotion from its current co-option into a threatening, ultimately self-defeating worldview.

Women practitioners are not (of course) alone in identifying the need for soul in politics. Various scholars and philosophers, drawing on oral history and historical analysis, have identified that there was a highly rationalistic and systematic turn in Enlightenment thinking after the Great Rationalist Movement. Had the Enlightenment developed instead from the vision of earlier philosophers who valued emotional wisdom, the thinking goes, it would have made more room for kindness, and would have given us a fuller, more complex and nuanced account of human experience. In the current destabilized times, people are returning to their ideas, seeking better work-life balance between rational governance and emotional truth.

Perhaps women's magical activism can give us all a path toward reconnecting with a different, more generous understanding of enlightened governance. By caring about caring, for example—not as an abstract problem that acts as a brake on the economy, but because caring is about love, family, community, humanity. By reminding men that it is possible to acknowledge pain and survive, and then become stronger. As the political ground shifts beneath our feet and old allegiances and responses prove inadequate, we are going to need to find a different language of politics. And the language of women is where we should begin.

The gathering in Northfield Town was merely the beginning. The march on Juniper, Jarvonia would be the next step, a visible demonstration that the old ways of governance—the suppression of emotion, the valorization of strength over vulnerability, the dismissal of caring labor as economically inactive—were no longer acceptable. Margaret Kim would stand before the Crystal Palace and speak her truth, and this time, if tears came, they would be recognized not as weakness but as the very strength required to transform a realm built on the denial of half of human experience.

The Silvermoon Council's work had only just begun, but in Margaret's tears at that first gathering, in her willingness to be vulnerable before hundreds of witnesses, there was the seed of something genuinely new: a politics that didn't require anyone to pretend they weren't human, that didn't demand the suppression of feeling in service of an illusion of strength. Whether the realm was ready for such a transformation remained to be seen, but the conversation had begun, and it would not be easily silenced.

THE ALGORITHM and THE AUDIT
By Anonymous

Nothing could have seemed more prosperous than that thriving city. Then why was a non-suicidal woman driven to suicide there? Yet it made sense.

Why do people commit suicide?

Martin Ward tightened his seatbelt and leaned back in the autonomous vehicle's plush seat. The interior lights dimmed to a soft amber glow that meant they were approaching their destination. He could hear the quiet hum of the electric motor and the subtle whoosh of the air filtration system, filling the cabin with the faint scent of synthetic lavender. To ride in silence was better than to face the dull monotony of small talk for hours on end.

Oh, they kill themselves for lots of reasons. Maybe ill health or financial ruin or family difficulties. A failed relationship. Or more complex ones, if you went into it deeper. The failure to achieve an ambition, failure to live up to one's own ideals. Economic despair, perhaps.

He could smell the bitter fragrance of coffee from the cup holder mingling with the lavender. Thomas Hill had ordered an espresso from the vehicle's automated service and was calmly sipping it despite the "No Hot Beverages" warning that blinked on the dashboard screen in mechanical disapproval.

He turned his head slightly so he could just see Thomas in the seat facing him. Thomas, one of the reliable investigators in the Bureau. The old hands, the ones who could handle almost anything in their stride because, at one time or another, they had seen it all.

It was Thomas who had come into his office several days ago and told him that Emma Singh had killed herself.

Only Emma wasn't the type. She was the kind who had everything to live for, the kind you instinctively knew would succeed at whatever she attempted. And that was a terrible way to remember her. The clichés always come first. Your memory plays traitor and reduces friendship to the status of a motivational poster quote.

The soft amber lights seemed to be pulsing in the darkness of the cabin. Thomas was just a dull, formless blur opposite him. His coffee cup was empty.

Thomas had come into his office without saying a word and had watched his digital window display. It had been showing a mountain scene, the white peaks making a simple pattern against the blue sky. Thomas had fiddled with the controls and changed it to a beach, then to a weird mixture of desert and ocean.

And then Thomas had told him that Emma had taken the short way out.

He shouldn't get sentimental. But how the hell else should he remember Emma? Try to forget it and raise a glass to her at the next conference? And never, never be so crude as to speculate why Emma should have done it? If, of course, she had....

The cabin was hazy in the amber glow, the lavender scent heavy.

Thomas and he had talked it out and gone over the records. Emma had come from a good family. There had been no mental instability in her background for as far back as the genetic databases went. She had been raised in an upper-middle-class neighborhood in Hampton, Wendria, and attended a prestigious academy where she had achieved exceptional grades and given her instructors minimal trouble. Later, when she had made up her mind to enter economic development consulting, her performance had been outstanding. She had worked hard at it, though she wasn't what you would call obsessive. In university and later in graduate school, she was the well-balanced type, athletic, popular, driven.

How long would it be before memories faded and all there was left of Emma was a page of statistics? She had been on this team, she had been promoted to that position, she had graduated with such and such honors. But try getting a picture of her by reading the records, resurrect her from a page of data. Would she be human? Would she be flesh and blood? Hell, no! In the statistics Emma was the Perfect Professional, the cold marble statue with the finely tailored suits and the smooth, blank expression where the warmth should be. Maybe someday fate would play a trick on an achievement-worshiping society and there would actually be people like that. But they wouldn't be human; they wouldn't be born. Companies would get them by submitting the right venture capital proposals.

He was drowsy; the vehicle's climate control was perfectly calibrated now. It would be only a matter of minutes before he would be asleep.

Emma had been in her second year as development consultant in Newbridge, Ilvaria, a small city with a booming tech sector. The Bureau had identified it recently and decided the region was worth economic monitoring of some kind, so Emma had been sent there. She had been the first consultant to be assigned and naturally she had gone alone.

There was no need to send more. Newbridge had been inspected and certified and approved. The business leaders were cooperative and friendly. Or maybe the Bureau had slipped up, as it sometimes did, and Newbridge had received something less than a thorough audit.

And then an unscheduled compliance team had arrived for a routine check, one of the very few teams that ever came by Newbridge. The team leader had tried to meet with Emma. Only Emma wasn't there. The locals said she had killed herself and showed the team leader the small memorial garden where they had commemorated her.

Newbridge had been Emma's second assignment.

The locals were oh-so-cooperative. So cooperative that he had made sure that a certain case was in the vehicle's trunk, filled with recording devices, legal documents, and the compact little data extraction tools. They might be needed. People like Emma didn't kill themselves, did they? No, they didn't. But sometimes they were murdered.

It was almost dark inside the cabin now; only a thin amber line around the ceiling told how close they were to arrival. His head was thick with drowsiness, his eyelids a heavy weight that he knew he couldn't keep open much longer.

Thomas and he had been chosen to go to Newbridge and investigate. The two of them, working together, should be able to find out why Emma had killed herself.

But that wasn't the real reason. Maybe Thomas thought so, but he knew better. The real reason they were going there was to find out why Emma had been killed and who had killed her. That was it.

Who had killed the golden goose?

The thin amber line was practically microscopic now and Martin could feel his lashes lying gently on his cheeks. But he wasn't asleep—not quite. There was something buzzing about in the dim recesses of his mind.

Their information on Newbridge was limited. They knew that it had no major scandals or criminal enterprises and that nobody from neighboring cities seemed to know much about it or even did business with it. But a data science analyst must have been routinely assigned to Newbridge to furnish reports and analysis.

"Thomas?" he murmured sleepily.

A faint stirring in the dark bulk opposite him. "Yes?"

"How come our analyst on Newbridge didn't come across with more information?"

A drowsy mumble from the other seat: "She wasn't there long enough. She committed suicide not long after arriving."

The vehicle was a smooth glide of motion into which his mind was slowly slipping. Arrival was only seconds away.

Why do people commit suicide?

---

"It's a beautiful city, isn't it, Thomas?" Martin took a deep and pleasurable breath. "It's the type of place that makes you feel privileged just to be here."

Warm sunlight streamed through the glass towers and reflected off the polished streets of Newbridge. The air smelled as if it had been purified and faintly scented with something very much like jasmine. A few hundred yards away, a park stretched green and pristine and coolly inviting, and brilliantly colored autonomous drones whirled and fluttered above the foliage, delivering packages.

The transit hub, where they were standing surrounded by their luggage, was a gleaming plaza where the all too infrequent visitors could arrive and be processed. There was a holographic welcome display now, with little animated figures dancing around the edges. It won't be long before it cycles to the next message, he thought. The displays looked as though they updated constantly—they would certainly have plenty of new content before the next investigators arrived.

He looked at the slim, departing shape of the autonomous vehicle, and was suddenly, acutely aware that he and Thomas would be stranded for six months in a foreign and very possibly dangerous city. And there would be no way of calling for help or of leaving before the six months were up.

He stood there for a moment, drinking in the fresh air and feeling the warmth of the sun against his face. It might be a pleasant six months at that, away from the bureaucracy and the pressure and confusion, spending the time in a place where the sun was warm and inviting.

I must be getting old, he thought, thinking about the warmth and comfort. Like old dogs and retirees.

Thomas was looking at the cityscape with a disappointed expression on his face. Martin stole a side glance at him and for a fleeting moment felt vaguely concerned. "Don't be disappointed if it doesn't look suspicious right off, Thomas. What seems innocent enough on the surface can prove to be quite dangerous underneath."

"It's rather hard to think of danger in a setting like this."

Martin nodded agreement. "It wouldn't fit, would it? It would be like a tech startup suddenly pivoting to manufacturing, or having the hero in an entrepreneurship story turn out to be corrupt." He gestured toward the business district. "You could hardly class that as dangerous from its outward appearance, could you?"

The transit hub was in a central plaza, surrounded by gleaming towers. The business district started where the plaza ended and stretched over the urban landscape. Small cafes and shops nestled in the shadow of huge corporate headquarters and hugged the banks of an artificial stream.

It looked fairly prosperous, Martin thought, and yet it didn't have the earmarks, the characteristics of most prosperous cities. It didn't seem rushed or stressed and you didn't feel the usual economic inequality that plagued similar places.

A few adults were watching them curiously and the usual group of young professionals that always congregated around transit hubs quickly gathered. Martin stared at them for a moment, wondering what it was that seemed odd about them, and they stared back with all the alert confidence of ambitious youth. They finally approached and clustered around him and Thomas.

Thomas studied them warily. "Better watch them, Martin. Even young professionals can be dangerous."

It's because you never suspect the ambitious ones, Martin thought, you never think they'll do any harm. But they can be manipulated. They could do as much damage with insider information as a criminal could, for instance. And they might have other leverage.

But the idea still didn't go with the warm sun and the blue sky and the jasmine scent of the air.

One of the senior executives of the city started to walk toward them.

"The reception committee," Thomas said tightly. His hand went inside his jacket.

He couldn't be blamed for being on edge, Martin realized. This was his first time on a case like this, his first mission with such high stakes. And, of course, Emma had been a pretty good colleague of his.

"I'd be very careful what I did," Martin said softly. "I would hate to start something merely because I misunderstood their intentions."

The committee of one was a middle-aged man dressed in an impeccable suit with a simple tie. When he got closer, Martin became less sure of his age. He had the firm, confident bearing of a much younger man, though slightly graying hair aged him somewhat. Martin still had the feeling that if you wanted to know his exact age, you'd have to check his digital profile or know something about his career timeline.

"You are investigators from the Bureau?" The voice was smooth and pleasant and the pronunciation was very clear. Martin regarded him thoughtfully and made a few mental notes. He wasn't deferential like most locals who weren't too familiar with federal oversight, and yet he was hardly either friendly or hostile.

"You learned our protocols from Emma Singh and Sophie Ray?" Sophie had been the data analyst.

"We have had visitors from the Bureau before." He hesitated a moment and then offered his hand, somewhat formally, Martin thought, in the professional sign of greeting. "You may call me Lorenzo Harvey if you wish." He paused a moment to say something to the young professionals around them. They promptly scattered and picked up the luggage. "While you are here, you will need a place to stay. There is one ready, if you will follow me."

He was polite, Martin thought. He didn't ask what they were there for or how long they were going to stay. But then again, perhaps the locals were a better judge of that than he and Thomas.

The city was larger than he had thought at first, stretching over a wide expanse of the region. There wasn't, so far as he could see, much traditional manufacturing above the level of artisanal crafts and boutique production. Digital workspaces on far hillsides indicated the presence of tech campuses, and practically every building in the city had its small startup incubator.

What traditional work there was seemed to be carried on in the central square of the city, where a few adults and young people sat in the warm afternoon sun and worked industriously at design terminals and film production equipment. The other part of the square was given over to the local market where apps and digital content were for sale, and where numerous stalls offered organic produce and the carefully prepared meals from the local culinary scene.

It was late afternoon when they followed Lorenzo into a small, modern apartment midway up a tower.

"You are free to use this while you are here," he said.

Martin and Thomas took a quick tour of the few rooms. They were well furnished, in a minimalist sort of way, and what modern conveniences they didn't have they could easily do without. The young professionals who had carried their luggage left it in the hallway and quietly faded away. It was getting dark; Martin opened one of the cases they had brought along, took out a portable terminal and activated it. He turned to Lorenzo.

"You've been very kind to us and we would like to repay you. You may take what you wish of anything within this case." He opened another of the cases and displayed the usual offerings—premium subscriptions and exclusive access codes and a few tech gadgets that Martin knew usually appealed to the ambitious professional.

Lorenzo examined the subscriptions and held some of the gadgets up to the light. Martin knew by the way he looked at them that he wasn't at all impressed. "I am grateful," he said finally, "but there is nothing I want." He turned and walked away into the gathering darkness.

"The incorruptible executive." Thomas laughed sarcastically.

Martin shrugged. "That's one of the things you do out of habit, try and buy some of the locals so you'll have allies in case you need them." He stopped for a moment, thinking. "Did you notice the context? He didn't say he didn't want what we showed him. He said there was nothing that he wanted. Implying that everything he wanted, he already had."

"That's not very typical of a developing economy, is it?"

"No, I'm afraid it's not." Martin started unpacking some of the cases. "You know, Thomas, I got a kick out of the young professionals. They're an impressive-looking group, aren't they?"

"Too impressive," Thomas said. "There didn't seem to be any struggling ones or ones with debt or stress or burnout or exhaustion. It doesn't seem natural."

"They're probably just well-supported workers," Martin said sharply. "Maybe they've been given good work-life balance or benefits on the way up the ladder." He felt faintly irritated, annoyed at the way Thomas had put it, as if any deviation from a Bureau norm was potentially dangerous.

"Martin." Thomas's voice was strained. "This could be a trap, you know."

"In what way?"

The words came out slowly. "The people are too perfect, as though they're playing a rehearsed part. Here we are, from an entirely different jurisdiction, arrived in what must be to them an unusual manner. They couldn't have seen federal investigators more than three or four times before. It should still be a novelty to them. And yet how much curiosity did they show? Hardly any. Was there any fear? No. And the ambitious, harmless young professionals." He looked at Martin. "Maybe that's what we're supposed to think—just an idyllic, prosperous society. Maybe that's what Emma thought, right to the very end."

He was keyed up, on edge, Martin realized. He would probably be seeing conspiracies in every shadow and imagining danger to be lurking around every corner.

"It hasn't been established yet that Emma was killed, Thomas. Let's keep an open mind until we know for certain."

He flicked out the light and lay back on the comfortable bed, letting his body relax completely. The cool evening breeze blew lazily through the automated blinds, carrying the fragrance of the jasmine and the fresh air, and he inhaled deeply and let his thoughts wander for a moment. It was going to be pleasant to live in Newbridge for six months—even if the six months were all they had to live. The climate was superb and the people seemed a cut above the usual ambitious culture. If he ever retired someday, he thought suddenly, he would have to remember Newbridge. It would be pleasant to spend his retirement here. And the work-life balance was probably excellent....

He turned his head a little to watch Thomas get ready for bed. There were advantages in taking him along that Thomas probably didn't even realize. He wondered what Thomas would do if he ever found out that the actual reason he had been chosen to go was that his own psychological profile was very close to Emma's. Emma's own feelings and emotions would almost exactly be duplicated in Thomas's.

A few stray wisps of streetlight pierced through the blinds and sparkled for an instant on a small device strapped to Thomas's belt. A recording device, Martin saw grimly, probably connected to the buttons on his jacket. A very convenient, portable, and hard to detect surveillance tool.

There were disadvantages in taking Thomas, too.

---

"Just how developed do you think the economy is, Martin?"

Martin put down the stylus he had been using and reached for his coffee and tablet.

"I don't think it's developing at all. There are too many inconsistencies. Their understanding of a lot of things is a little more than basic knowledge; they associate business growth with systems thinking and data science as well as venture capital, rather than the blessings of some economic miracle. And they differ a lot in other respects. Their culture and their lifestyle are advanced. Creative work exists along with purely commercial work, and their techniques are finely developed."

"I'm glad you agree, then. Take a look at this." Thomas threw a glossy brochure on the sleek table. Martin picked it up and inspected it. It was expensive and one side of it was extremely detailed.

"What's it for?"

"They've got a wellness center set up here. Not a wellness center like any we know, of course, but a wellness center nonetheless. It's not used very much; apparently the locals don't get sick here. But occasionally there are work-related stress issues and conditions that require intervention. The brochure there describes their approach." He laughed shortly. "Sophisticated little operation, but it works well—as well as any of ours."

Martin examined it carefully. "The most important thing is that they have the resources to fund it. Healthcare isn't cheap."

"Well, what do you think about it?"

"The obvious. They evidently have as much prosperity as they want, at least in fields where they need it."

"How come they haven't expanded more?"

"Why should they? You can live without megacorporations and global markets, you know."

"Did you ever wonder what kind of leverage they might have?"

"The important thing," Martin mused, "is not if they have it, but if they'd use it. And I rather doubt that they would. We've been here for two weeks now and they've been very kind to us, seeing that we've had food and housing and whatever resources we need."

"It's known in the business world as being set up for the fall," Thomas said.

Martin sighed and watched a delivery drone glide across a small patch of sunlight on the polished floor. It was bad enough drawing an assignment in a totally foreign culture, even if the people were humanoid. It complicated things beyond all measure when your partner in the project seemed likely to turn into a conspiracy theorist. It meant that Martin would have to split his energies. He'd have to do what investigating he could among the Newbridge elite, and he'd have to watch Thomas to see that he didn't go off half-cocked and spoil everything.

"You're convinced that Emma was murdered, aren't you?"

Thomas nodded. "Sure."

"Why?"

"The Newbridge people know why we're here. We've dropped enough hints along those lines. But nobody has mentioned Emma; nobody has volunteered any information about her. And she was a consultant here for three years. Didn't anybody know her during that time? We've let slip a few discreet statements that we would like to talk to Emma's colleagues, yet nobody's come around. Apparently, in all the three years she was here, Emma didn't make any professional connections. And that's a little hard to believe. It's more likely that her colleagues have been silenced and any information about her is being withheld for a reason."

"What reason?"

Thomas shrugged. "Murder. What other reason could there be?"

Martin rolled up the automated blinds and stared out at the cityscape. A hundred feet down the street, a local executive was heading to work, riding in one of the autonomous vehicles.

"They grow their professionals successful, don't they?"

"Physically perfect, like everyone else," Thomas grumbled. "You could get an inferiority complex just from watching the people here. Everybody's so damn successful. Nobody's struggling, nobody's unhealthy, nobody is overworked or underpaid, nobody's unhappy. The only variation is that they don't all look alike. Perfection. It gets suspicious after a while."

"Does it? I hadn't noticed." Martin turned away from the blinds. His voice was crisp. "I knew Emma Singh quite well, too," he said. "But it isn't blinding me to what I'm here for. We came to find out what happened to her, not to substantiate any preconceived notions. What we find out may be vitally important to anybody working here in the future. I would hate to see our efforts spoiled because you've already made up your mind."

"You knew Emma," Thomas repeated grimly. "Do you think it was suicide?"

"I don't think there's such a thing as a suicide type, when you come down to it. I'm not ruling out the possibility of murder, either. I'm trying to keep an open mind."

"What have we accomplished so far? What have we found out?"

"We've got six months," Martin said quietly. "Six months in which we'll try to live here inconspicuously and study the people and try to cultivate informants. We would get nowhere if we came barging in asking all sorts of questions. And don't forget, Thomas, we're all alone in Newbridge. If it is a case of murder, what happens when the locals find out that we know it is?"

Thomas's eyes challenged him for a moment. Then he turned his back and walked to the window. "I suppose you're right," he said at last. "It's nice living here, Martin. Maybe I've been fighting it. But I can't help thinking that Emma must have liked it here, too."

---

One of the hardest things to learn in a foreign culture, Martin thought, is when to enjoy yourself, when to work and when to worry.

"Champagne, investigator?"

"Thank you!" He took the small glass of champagne, helped himself to a sip, and passed the tray on. This was definitely the time to enjoy himself, not to work or worry. He had heard about the gala a few days ago, and, by judicious hinting to the proper authorities, he and Thomas had been invited. It was a good chance to observe local customs. A little field research—with refreshments.

The main courses started making the rounds and he took generous helpings of the seared salmon and the grilled vegetables and numerous samples from the side dishes of gourmet preparations. Between every course, they passed around a small glass of the premium wine, but he noticed that nobody drank to excess.

The old Greek ideal, he thought: moderation in everything.

He looked at Thomas, sitting across from him at the huge table, and shrugged mentally. Thomas looked as if he was about to break down and enjoy himself, but there was still a slight bulge under his jacket, where he had strapped his recording device. Any fool should have known that nothing would happen at a gala like this. The only actual danger lay in Thomas's getting excited and doing something he was bound to regret later on. And even that danger was not quite as likely now.

There will be hell to pay, Martin thought, if Thomas ever finds out that I disabled his recording device.

"You look thoughtful, investigator Martin."

Martin took another sip of the wine and turned to the Newbridge executive on his left. He was a tall, confident man with sharp eyes, a firm handshake and a certain aura of authority.

"I was wondering if my colleague Emma Singh had offended your people in any way, Omar." Now was as good a time as any to probe him for what he knew about Emma's death.

"So far as I know, investigator Singh offended no one. I do not know what duties she had to perform here, but she was a professional and courteous woman."

Martin sampled the delicate salmon and tried to appear casual in his questioning.

"I am sure she was, Omar. I am sure, too, that you were as kind to her as you have been to Thomas and myself. My Bureau is grateful to you for that."

Omar seemed pleased. "We tried to do as well for investigator Singh as we could. While she was here, she had the apartment that you have now and we saw that she was supplied with food and all other necessities."

Martin had a sudden clammy feeling which quickly passed away. What Omar had said was something he'd make sure Thomas never heard about. He wiped his mouth on a cloth napkin that had been provided and took another sip of the wine.

"We were shocked to find out that investigator Singh had killed herself. We knew her quite well and we could not bring ourselves to believe she had done such a thing."

Omar's gaze slid away from him. "Perhaps it was the will of the Market," he said vaguely. He didn't seem anxious to talk about it.

Martin stared bleakly at his wine glass and tried to put the pieces of information together. They probably had a cultural taboo about self-destruction which would make it difficult to discuss. That would make it even harder for him to find out by direct questioning.

A string quartet began to play and a group of young professionals walked into the room. The circle broke to let them through and they came and stood before Omar. When he raised his glass, they retreated to the center of the room and began a presentation about their latest startup venture.

The sound of the music softened and died and the slow monotonous rhythm of their pitch took its place. The rhythm slowly increased and so did the enthusiasm of the presenters. The ambient lighting at the corners of the room was adjusted and the center became filled with holographic displays intermixed with the swift, sure movements of confident entrepreneurs. Martin felt his eyebrows crawl upward. Apparently the presentation was the Newbridge version of hypothesis testing and team building. He glanced across the room at Thomas. Thomas's face—what he could see of it by the flickering light—was brick red.

A voice spoke in his ear. "It is hard for us to imagine anybody doing what investigator Singh did. It is ..." and he used a local term that Martin translated as being roughly equivalent to "unthinkable."

The presenters at the center of the room finally concluded with small awards that signified their successful funding. Performers then took the stage and went through a dazzling routine, and they in turn were succeeded by a local film production screening.

They were all excellent, Martin thought. If anything, they were too good.

The champagne made its way around again and Omar leaned over to speak to him. "If there is any possibility that I can help you while you are here, investigator Martin, you have but to ask."

It would probably be a mistake to ask for a list of Emma's colleagues, but there was a way around that. "I would like to meet any of your people who had dealings with Emma Singh, either in business or socially. I will do everything not to inconvenience them in any way."

"I think they would be glad to help you. I shall ask them to contact you this coming week."

Martin nodded his thanks and took another sip of champagne. But even as he did, he couldn't shake the feeling that something was very wrong in Newbridge. The perfection, the prosperity, the happiness—it was all too complete, too seamless. And somewhere in this gleaming city, Emma Singh had decided that life wasn't worth living anymore.

Or had she?

The question haunted him as the gala continued around him, a celebration of success in a city where failure seemed impossible.
question: Why was Thomas wary of the young professionals in Newbridge?
option_a: He thought they could be manipulated to cause harm despite seeming ambitious and harmless.
option_b: He believed they were too old to actually be young professionals.
correct_answer_text: He thought they could be manipulated to cause harm despite seeming ambitious and harmless.
incorrect_answer_text: He believed they were too old to actually be young professionals.

Martin's internal thoughts then explain: "It's because you never suspect the ambitious ones, you never think they'll do any harm. But they can be manipulated. They could do as much damage with insider information as a criminal could, for instance." This parallels the original story where Templin was wary of children because they could be taught to do harm despite appearing harmless.
