synthetic_story:
THE WAVERLY INVESTIGATION
I

Initial Assessment

"First crime scene assessments are always difficult," Detective Laura Little said, looking thoughtfully at the fifty or more potential witnesses who gathered nervously in the community center, chatting with one another, or sat on the few metal chairs trying to look calm.

"With only nine people who actually saw anything useful," she continued, "it doesn't matter how observant these people think they are; most of them just haven't got anything relevant to tell us. I can't help feeling sorry for them—for all of us, I mean. After all, I'm trying to solve this case, too, and every false lead costs us time."

Laura's partner and colleague, Detective Henri Chang, smiled in agreement and said, "It's not an easy job, is it? But the ones I feel sorriest for right now are Lorenzo and Jennifer. After all, they have the unpleasant job of sorting through all these statements and deciding who's credible and who's not, and a lot of these folks are their neighbors. I wouldn't want to be in their shoes."

Laura nodded thoughtfully, and reflected that it must, indeed, be more wearing on the junior detectives. Lorenzo Harvey, lead investigator on the art theft case, had been a senior officer at the precinct when Laura had started there, and he was a good friend of hers. She had worked with him before, as a general assistant, when they had cracked a major fraud ring. It would not be easy for him to question Laura as a potential witness, and to do so completely without bias. It would not be a question of playing favorites, Laura knew, but quite the reverse. Lorenzo's sense of fair play would make him bend over backward to keep from giving favors to his friends. If she was to provide useful information in this investigation, she would really have to be precise.

And if it was difficult for Lorenzo, she thought, it was more so for Jennifer Lambert, the case coordinator, for her friendship with Jennifer was of a different sort than with Lorenzo. Lorenzo was just a friend—a good one, to be sure—but with Jennifer Lambert, somehow, things were different. There was nothing "serious," she assured herself, but they had worked cases together with a regularity that was a little more than casual and, whatever Jennifer's feelings were for her, she was sure that they were more complicated than Lorenzo's.

"Do you think they'll ever get through all these people?" Henri asked, interrupting her thoughts. "How can they hope to interview so many witnesses in just one afternoon?"

"Oh, they won't be doing full interviews today," Laura replied, glad to turn her attention from what was becoming a difficult subject for thought. "This is just an initial screening. All they want to do today is identify people by location. They'll select all the possible witnesses, send the impossible ones away, and then go into detailed questioning later."

"But what if the people they pick for location can't remember anything?" Henri asked. "And what if some of the rejects actually saw something important?"

"They won't go back to the rejects," Laura explained, "because they both have a pretty good idea of what the timeline of the theft should look like. And if the people they pick don't have good enough information, then they hold another witness call and try again. Lorenzo says that sometimes certain crimes are so hard to solve that they have to go through a dozen rounds of questioning just to find one solid lead."

"It seems kind of unfair, doesn't it, to be eliminated just because you weren't in the right place at the right time," Henri said, "but I can understand it. They have to start somewhere, and I guess that's as good a place as any." Then he smiled and added, "I guess I'm just feeling sorry for myself, because Lorenzo told me there was no sense in my being interviewed at all, because I was in Evergreen, Kaldria during the entire incident. If I don't get better at being in the right place at the right time, I may never contribute to a major case at all, except as a paper-pusher!"

Laura nodded sympathetically. "But it wasn't just your location, Henri," she said. "It's your assignment, too. At least for this case. Lorenzo and Jennifer told you that you're just too valuable in your current role analyzing financial records to be pulled into field interviews, and that's nothing to feel bad about. If anybody ought to feel inadequate, it's me, because they asked me to come in for questioning!"

"Oh, they were just being thorough," Henri replied. "And as for you, you know you don't have to worry about your observational skills. You have a wonderful eye for detail! You can notice behavioral patterns, or inconsistencies, or timing issues, or anything. I'm stuck with just being a number-cruncher, buried in spreadsheets and transaction records, po' li'l ol' me, starin' at those ol' computer screens!"

He exaggerated his usual serious demeanor until it sounded absurd, and both detectives broke into laughter that sounded odd in the tense atmosphere of the stark community center.

It was at this point that Lorenzo and Jennifer came in, with pleasant, if somewhat brisk, nods to the assembled witnesses, and a special smile for Henri and Laura. In a businesslike manner, they settled themselves at a table near the windows, spread out notepads and recording devices, and prepared for the task that faced them. Henri, who was there to help them by acting as secretary for the occasion, wished Laura good luck, and joined them at the table. His job was to take names and addresses, and to jot down any facts about each witness that Lorenzo and Jennifer wanted to be sure to remember.

Lorenzo started the proceedings by introducing himself and Jennifer. Then, estimating the crowd, he said, "Since there are fewer men here who were in the critical zone, and also fewer male witnesses who match our timeline, we're going to interview them first. I hope that you ladies won't mind. We won't keep you waiting long, but if we worked with you first, we'd have these gentlemen waiting most of the day. Shall we get started?" After a brief glance at his notes, he called out, "First, I'd like to see business district witnesses, approximately 2 PM to 3 PM. How many have we?"

Four men separated themselves from the crowd and approached the table. Laura watched with interest as Lorenzo and Jennifer looked them over, murmured to Henri to take notes, and asked preliminary questions. After a few minutes, the men left, two of them looking hopeful, two resigned. Then Lorenzo stood and called for art gallery district witnesses, late afternoon, who had clear sight lines to the main entrance. As six observant-looking individuals came forward, Laura felt that she just couldn't stand watching the screening interviews any longer. It reminded her too much of the systematic observation exercises she had attended as a rookie at the police academy in her home town of Greenfield, Veldoria. Necessary though it was, she felt it was hardly a way to have to deal with human beings who were trying to help.

Slipping back through the crowd of waiting witnesses, she joined the women in the rear of the room, and found an empty seat next to a young woman.

"Hi," she said. "What's the matter, can't you watch it either?"

The woman smiled in understanding. "It always upsets me," she replied, "but it's something we simply have to learn to live with when we're involved in investigations. At least until we become key witnesses, or get lawyers to handle this sort of thing for us."

"It sounds as if you've been in a few of these before," Laura said.

"I have. But not here in Waverly, Thandor," the woman replied. "I'm from Ivywood, Selvoria, and I've been involved in a few minor cases there, but nobody seems to pay much attention to them. I heard that major art thefts in Waverly attract a lot of attention from specialized investigators, and I thought that I'd be more helpful here. Have you had any luck with your testimony?"

"Oh, I'm just beginning," Laura said. "I'm still learning investigative procedures at the regional training center. I hope I can provide some kind of supporting information in this case, but I don't think I saw anything crucial yet. By the way, my name is Laura Little. What's yours?"

"I'm Elena Wyatt," the woman answered, "and maybe I'm being too optimistic, but I think I might have seen the primary suspect. I hope I can help with identification."

Laura looked carefully at her new acquaintance, at the somewhat uncertain expression that played about her well-formed, intelligent face and the sharpness that shone from her large, widely placed brown eyes. Her rather angular face was softened by careful styling of her dark hair, the whole effect being an appealing combination of strength and feminine observation.

"I think you might," Laura said. "In fact, if your timing is right, I bet you'll be a key witness. I've reviewed the case file, and I know the investigators, and unless I'm way off, your location matches exactly where the primary suspect should have been. In fact, it's almost uncanny. You were positioned as if you just walked out of the investigation plan!"

"Oh, I hope you're right!" Elena said with animation. "And I hope you can help, too. I have a feeling that you're going to bring me good luck!"

"The one who needs luck is me, I'm afraid," Laura said. "Being friendly with Lorenzo and Jennifer isn't going to help me in the least, and I'm going to have to be awfully precise to provide useful information. And it's really important to me, too, because I'm getting near the end of my probationary period."

"Probationary period?" Elena asked curiously.

"Uh-huh. My supervisors agreed to let me work on major cases and try for detective assignments for a year, and I agreed that if I didn't show signs of aptitude before the year was up, I'd go back to patrol duty. I've been in investigations for eight months now, and I haven't contributed anything significant yet. The information I might provide now isn't crucial, but it's a good supporting detail, and what's more, it relates to career planning. If I can show my supervisors that I can contribute meaningful observations to cases, I'm sure that they'll let me continue in investigations."

"But do you expect to solve major cases right away?" Elena asked.

"Oh, no! I'm not that naïve! But when my probationary year is over at the training center, I can always take an assignment in community relations or administrative support, while I look for investigative opportunities. If you have good analytical skills and attention to detail, you never have to worry about finding work in law enforcement."

"I wish that I had those skills," Elena said wistfully. "The only way I've been able to make ends meet is by working in retail security, and that doesn't pay much. Besides, the work is so unsteady."

"My supervisors are very practical people," Laura said with a smile, "and they made sure that I learned routine investigative procedures before they would let me think about specialized detective work. My father runs a private investigation firm in our small town in Veldoria, and I've worked with him on background checks and surveillance and as a research assistant, too. I'll always be grateful that he made me learn all those things. I don't think he has much faith in public law enforcement, but he's been wonderful about giving me a chance. What do your parents think of your wanting to be involved in investigations?"

Instead of answering, Elena suddenly stood up. "Let's go see how they're coming with the male witnesses," she said. "I think they're almost finished."

Not wanting to press Elena further, and feeling that perhaps she had asked too personal a question on such short acquaintance, Laura reluctantly stood too, and joined Elena to watch the last of what she now could only think of as the screening process.

As she drew closer to the table, she heard Lorenzo saying, "I'm really sorry, Mr. Martinez, but you just weren't in the right location at the right time. Perhaps some other case...." and his voice trailed off in embarrassment.

Martinez, a short, nervous young man, answered almost desperately, "But, Detective Harvey, location isn't everything. I'm really very observant. Honestly! If you would only give me a chance to describe what I saw, I know that I could make you reconsider my potential value as a witness!"

"I don't doubt that you could," Lorenzo said gently, "but if you did, we'd be pursuing a false lead. I'm afraid the witness we need for this must have been in the gallery district, in a position with clear sight lines, like these three gentlemen whom I have chosen to interview. The timeline requires it. I'm sorry."

Mr. Martinez nodded sadly, mumbled, "I understand," and walked off, his head hanging and his hands thrust deep in his pockets, looking less like a helpful witness than any man in the world. Laura watched him go, not knowing whether to feel sorrier for him or for Lorenzo.

"All right, gentlemen," Lorenzo called out. "That takes care of the male witnesses from the critical zones. All of you who are left will be given copies of the timeline and location map to review, marked at the areas we want to discuss. Be sure to study the whole case file carefully, so that you understand the sequence of events. You have three days to review it. We'll meet at ten o'clock on Saturday morning at the precinct to hear your statements. Thank you. And now for the ladies."

The men left, after being given their materials, and though they chatted amiably with one another, Laura was sure that each was casting rather competitive looks toward others who had similar observations. Maintaining cooperation in investigations was not an easy thing, she thought, particularly for people with overlapping information!

Lorenzo's first concern in reviewing the female witnesses was, of course, for the primary sighting. And, of course, it was for this sighting that he had the most claimants. More than twenty women came forward when the announcement was made, and Laura thought that she had never seen so many earnest and credible faces. It was not going to be easy for Lorenzo to make a choice. As Elena, her new acquaintance, went forward to join the others, Laura whispered a word of encouragement, then stood to one side to watch.

Lorenzo went down the line, regretfully dismissing one after the other of the women, and occasionally asking one to step aside to provide information about another aspect. His professional expression hardly varied as he spoke to each one, but Laura thought she saw the ghost of a smile cross his face when he spoke to Elena Wyatt. Another review of the remaining women eliminated a few more. Finally, there were only four left, Elena among them. Lorenzo thanked them, distributed case materials, and asked them to be at the precinct on Saturday at noon.

Elena returned to Laura with eyes shining. "Oh, Laura! I think you were right! I just know I'm going to be helpful! I know it!"

"Don't count too much on it," Laura cautioned, "or you may be too bitterly disappointed if your information doesn't pan out. But," she added, enthusiastically violating her own rule of caution, "I'm sure, too! I'll see you Saturday. Even if I don't provide crucial information, I'll be there just to hear your statement!"

Then, with a smile of farewell, Laura turned her attention to the "financial district witnesses, early afternoon" classification that Lorenzo had called for next. Once that was out of the way, she knew it would be her turn.

This time, there were not so many claimants and Laura remembered Jennifer telling her that this would be one of their most difficult aspects to verify. Only four witnesses came forward, and Lorenzo, with difficulty, reviewed them all. Unable to eliminate by location alone, he gave them all materials and asked them to come to the precinct. Then he called for "peripheral observers with partial sight lines" and Laura joined seven other women in the screening process.

Lorenzo reviewed them carefully, managing to look at Laura with complete professional detachment. He gently eliminated three of them on the basis of timing, distance or visual obstruction. Another, curiously enough, was eliminated for being in Evergreen, Kaldria during the incident, and a fifth was too far from the scene. "We need someone who was close enough to see details," Lorenzo said with a rare smile, "but not so close that they would have been noticed by the suspect! You were in an excellent position, but I'm afraid the angle wasn't quite right for what we need."

When he was done, Laura and two others were given materials and told to come to the precinct on Saturday. Feeling lightheaded with relief, Laura settled herself on one of the metal chairs that lined the back wall, and waited for Lorenzo, Jennifer, and Henri to finish so she could join them for coffee.

Scarcely noticing the rest of the proceedings, she thought only about the coming interviews. She was so familiar with the case that she knew she had an advantage, perhaps unfairly, over the other two women. She had watched the investigation develop from its first preliminary reports to the detailed analysis now in her hands, and had discussed it with Jennifer through each development. She knew she could provide useful information; in fact, she suspected secretly that Jennifer had positioned her deliberately to observe the area, and the thought made her uncomfortable. Still, it would not be easy, she knew. Lorenzo's sense of fairness and his absolute devotion to proper procedure above everything else would keep him from making up his mind in advance about any witness's credibility.

But despite this knowledge, she could not help looking ahead—all the way ahead—to the successful conclusion of the case, the commendations from the chief, the satisfaction of knowing she had contributed to solving the Waverly art theft, one of the most significant cases in recent memory, and the validation of her choice to pursue detective work as a career.

II

The Statements

The audience consisted of a handful of witnesses, and Jennifer Lambert and Lorenzo Harvey. The lighting was harsh fluorescent illumination without any softening. The setting was the gray concrete walls of the interview room, two chairs, a table and a recording device. Only the front section of the precinct was fully staffed, and the back offices were quiet, empty and utilitarian, a functional workspace of filing cabinets and desks.

In the interview room, a "business district witness" was giving his statement. Laura knew, after the first few sentences, that his information would not be useful. He had somehow completely missed the critical timing of the events he was describing, and was heavily speculating. Lorenzo, being perhaps more patient than Laura, listened and watched with great care. Henri, who was acting as Lorenzo's assistant for the investigation, sat in a chair by the door, following along with the case file and noting any discrepancies. Lorenzo followed the whole sequence with no visible sign of impatience and, when the witness was through, said, "Thank you. We'll contact you if we need any follow-up information."

The next "business district witness" was better, but still not quite accurate, Laura thought. He seemed to be trying to make his observations more dramatic than they were, and although there were some valid details in his account, it was really far more speculation than observation. Still, he was clearly more reliable than the first, and with careful questioning might provide something useful.

Following his statement, Lorenzo again repeated his polite, invariable formula, "Thank you. We'll contact you if we need any follow-up information," and called for the next witness.

Laura watched the remaining male witnesses provide their statements, and made mental notes of which ones were credible, which probable, and which stood no chance of being useful.

The same process was then followed for the primary sighting witnesses, and the same wide range of reliability and accuracy was displayed. Some seemed to have no clear memory at all about the incident or its context, and Laura was sure that these women had reviewed only the specific questions they'd been asked. Others had a clear recollection of the sequence of events, and tried to describe them in the brief time they had in the interview room. Others still were witnesses who had one rather inflexible way of describing things, and used it for all kinds of situations. Their accounts were uniform imitations of each other, and all were imitations of television crime dramas. They seemed to forget, Laura thought, that real investigations required precision and accuracy, not dramatic flair. It made her frustrated that some witnesses thought they could be helpful by being theatrical.

Each witness, no matter how reliable or how questionable, was treated with professional courtesy by Lorenzo, and each left looking confident that their information was crucial. Laura was glad that she would not have to see their faces when they learned that their statements had not been pivotal to the case.

"The pity of it," she whispered to Jennifer, "isn't that there are so many unreliable ones, but that there are so many good ones, and that only a few pieces of information will actually solve the case. I wish there were some way of telling the helpful ones you can't use that they were really trying their best, but that you just couldn't use everyone's information!"

"You can't let yourself worry about that," Jennifer replied. "The reliable ones know they're reliable, and they're not going to be discouraged by not being central to the case. And the unreliable ones think they're reliable, too, and most of them have tremendous confidence to protect them from ever finding out—or even thinking—otherwise!"

The door at the back of the precinct opened quietly, and Laura, turning around in her chair, saw a few of the female witnesses entering. They quietly found seats in the waiting area and settled down to await their turn.

"I think I'll go back there with the other witnesses," Laura whispered. "I'm looking for Elena, the woman I met at the screening, and I'd like to chat with her for a few minutes when she arrives. Do you mind if I don't observe all the interviews?"

Jennifer smiled. "Go ahead. I'd get out of here, too, if I could without getting Lorenzo annoyed at me. This kind of thing always tests my patience, too!"

As she went to the waiting area as unobtrusively as possible, Laura glanced at the witnesses who had just arrived. She recognized a few of their faces from the screening of three days ago, but did not see her new acquaintance among them. She decided to wait in the lobby area for her there. A new group of women entered the precinct as Laura was moving, and as she passed, one reached out and touched her arm.

Laura turned in surprise to find herself greeted with a warm smile and a friendly greeting.

"Maria!" she cried. "What are you doing here?"

"Come on out to the lobby, and I'll tell you," Maria Ward said, with a gesture that made her pull out her notebook and flip it open.

"But I thought you were in Evergreen, Kaldria, working on that venture capital fraud case," Laura said, when they had reached the lobby. "What on earth are you doing here?"

"I'm afraid you don't read your department bulletins very carefully," Maria said. "The venture capital case in Evergreen collapsed when the primary suspect fled the jurisdiction. At first we thought we'd coordinate with federal authorities to try to track him down, but the prosecutor finally decided, and very sensibly, that it would be easier to just focus on the local accomplices. I'm afraid the case lost a lot of momentum, and we didn't have enough evidence."

"Oh, I'm so sorry," Laura said. "And it was a real opportunity for you, wasn't it?"

"Not really," Maria said. "The case wasn't that strong, and I'd just as soon not be associated with a failed prosecution. Anyway, it gave me a chance to develop my skills in financial investigation for a few weeks, and a supervisor saw my work and said he thought I showed promise, so maybe I'm not any the worse for the experience."

At that moment, Laura saw Elena Wyatt enter the lobby, and she motioned to her to join them. "Maria, this is Elena Wyatt. She's giving a statement today about the primary sighting, and I hope her information is useful. Elena, I want you to meet Maria Ward, one of my colleagues."

"Colleagues?" Elena questioned, a little puzzled.

"Yes. There are about a dozen of us working on various aspects of this case, more or less. We work out of the Waverly precinct—a wonderful place—and we function like one big focused team. The precinct specializes in art theft and cultural preservation crimes, so we all have a lot in common. I haven't seen Maria for weeks—she's been working in Evergreen—and I'm just getting over being surprised at seeing her now."

"Laura tactfully neglected to mention that my case fell apart," Maria laughed, "and now I'm back in Waverly without a major assignment. In fact, that's why I'm here."

"You mean you're going to give a statement to Lorenzo?" Laura asked with interest.

"Uh-huh. I met him in the hallway an hour or so ago, and he told me he had some questions he thought I should answer, and that he was thinking of interviewing me all along, but assumed that I wouldn't be available. Well, you can't be more available than I am, so here I am!"

"Have you reviewed the case file?" Elena asked.

"I'm lucky there," Maria replied. "I've seen it in three different versions since it started. Laura's been involved with Jennifer Lambert, the case coordinator, and each time she brought an update home to our shared office, I got to review it. So I'm not at a disadvantage."

"What do you think of the Waverly art theft investigation, Elena?" asked Laura.

"I think it's fascinating! I hope more than ever that my information is useful! Do you really think I observed something important?"

Maria nodded decisively. "If you were where you say you were, you're perfectly positioned," she said.

"That's just what Laura said!"

Laura stole a glance through the doors to the interview area. "I think we're about ready to find out whether or not your statement is useful," she said. "They seem to be about through with the business district witnesses, and that means you're on next!"

Wishing each other good luck, they entered the waiting area and prepared for what Laura could only think of as their interrogation.

Afterward, as Laura, Henri, Elena, and Maria sat at a table in a nearby café waiting for Lorenzo and Jennifer to join them, each was sure that her statement had been inadequate.

"Oh, no!" Laura said. "You two were just excellent! But I couldn't have been worse. I know I described the timing wrong. I thought I had the sequence clear in my mind, but I'm sure that the way it came out was completely off!"

"You have a lot more skill than judgment," Maria said mournfully. "You were perfect. And so was Elena. As for me...." Her voice trailed off in despair.

"I don't know how you can say that, Maria," Elena put in. "I know you were the most precise in your statement, and nobody even came close to Laura's attention to detail. But I've never felt so uncertain in my life as I did describing what I saw. It's a wonder any of you even want to be seen with me!"

Only when Henri started to laugh did the three others realize how much alike they had sounded. Then they joined in the laughter and couldn't seem to stop. When they seemed at the point of dissolving helplessly into a permanent attack of nervous giggles, Jennifer and Lorenzo joined them.

"If you're laughing at the investigation," Jennifer said seriously, "I can hardly blame you. You never know just how weak your case is until someone starts to give contradictory statements."

All at the same time, the women started to reassure her and tell her how strong the case was, and how inadequately they, including themselves, had provided their information, but this was so much like their last exchange of conversation that once more they broke up in helpless laughter.

When they got their breath back, and when coffee and sandwiches had been ordered, they tried to explain the cause of their hilarity to Lorenzo and Jennifer.

"... so, you see," Laura concluded, "we were each explaining how good the others were and how inadequate we were, and when Jennifer started telling us how weak the investigation had been, we just couldn't stand it!"

It was Lorenzo who got them back to serious ground. With his stern face, like a movie detective's, and his calm, methodical manner, he carefully gave his assessment of the afternoon's witness statements.

"First," he said, "I want to thank all of you for your cooperation. Each of you provided information that helps us build a more complete picture of the incident. Elena, your observation of the suspect's clothing and approximate height is particularly valuable. Maria, your financial analysis background helped you notice details about the suspect's behavior that others missed. And Laura, your timing observations, despite your doubts, were actually the most precise we've received."

He paused to let this sink in, then continued, "What we're dealing with here is a sophisticated theft that required significant strategic planning. The suspect clearly understood the gallery's security systems, the staff schedules, and the optimal timing for the theft. This suggests someone with inside knowledge or extensive surveillance."

"Do you think it's related to the other art thefts in the region?" Elena asked.

"We're exploring that possibility," Jennifer said. "There have been three similar thefts in Ivywood, Selvoria over the past six months, all involving the same method of entry and similar items stolen. The pattern suggests either the same individual or a coordinated group."

"What about the economic inequality angle?" Maria asked. "I've been reading about how art theft often correlates with wealth concentration in particular areas. Waverly and Ivywood both have significant art markets and substantial wealth gaps."

"That's an interesting perspective," Lorenzo said, "and one we're considering as we look at motive. But for now, we need to focus on identifying the suspect and recovering the stolen pieces. The gallery has been very cooperative, and we have good security footage from several angles, though none showing the suspect's face clearly."

"What's the next step?" Laura asked.

"We'll be conducting follow-up interviews with gallery staff and reviewing all the witness statements together to create a comprehensive timeline," Jennifer explained. "We're also working with art theft specialists who have experience with similar cases. This type of crime requires specialized knowledge, both of the art market and of conflict resolution with insurance companies and private collectors who may be approached to purchase stolen items."

"I'm just glad I could help," Elena said. "When I saw that person leaving the gallery at that odd hour, I didn't think much of it at the time, but when I heard about the theft, I knew I had to come forward."

"Your civic responsibility is appreciated," Lorenzo said with one of his rare smiles. "Cases like this depend on observant citizens who are willing to get involved."

As they continued their conversation, Laura felt a sense of satisfaction. Despite her doubts about her own contribution, she had been part of something important. The investigation was far from over, but they had made progress, and she had demonstrated the kind of careful observation and analytical thinking that would serve her well in her career as a detective.

The Waverly art theft case would continue to develop over the coming weeks, but for now, Laura felt confident that she had taken an important step toward proving herself in the field she had chosen. Her probationary period was nearly over, and if this case went well, she might finally achieve her goal of becoming a full detective, specializing in the kind of complex investigations that required both systematic observation and creative problem-solving.

As they left the café and went their separate ways, Laura reflected on how much she had learned, not just about the case, but about herself and her capabilities. The path ahead was still uncertain, but she was ready to face whatever challenges came next.

"Luis, you awake?" His father's voice came through the door.

"Yeah, Dad," Luis called back, swinging his legs out of bed. He fumbled for his slippers in the dim light filtering through his curtains.

Dr. Robert Osborne opened the door. He was a tall man with broad shoulders, still maintaining the athletic build from his days as a competitive swimmer. His salt-and-pepper hair and reading glasses were the only real indicators of his fifty years. We work with classified materials at the aerospace plant—propulsion systems, advanced materials for spacecraft. If someone is stealing cutting-edge technology, we could be a target too."

As he walked home that evening, Luis couldn't shake the feeling of unease. The theft of the antimatter wasn't just about stolen property—it represented a breach of trust, a violation of the scientific community's collective memory and shared knowledge. His phone buzzed. A text from Leah: "Want to come over? We can talk."

One professor argued that excessive restrictions would hamper research and international diplomacy in scientific cooperation. Another countered that the theft proved current measures were insufficient.

"It's a complex problem," Leah observed. "Systems thinking again—you can't solve one part without considering how it affects everything else. Tighter security might prevent theft, but it could also slow down research and make collaboration harder."

"Dad always says science thrives on openness," Luis said. "Peer review, sharing data, building on each other's work. But how do you stay open while also protecting dangerous materials?"

"I don't know," Leah admitted. "But smarter people than us are working on it."

Luis's phone rang. It was his father.

"So it was someone with computer access?"

"Possibly. Or someone who hired a skilled hacker. Either way, we're getting closer to answers. I just wanted you to know I'm okay, and this will get resolved."

"Okay, Dad. Be careful."

"Always. Love you, son."

"Love you too."

Luis hung up and relayed the conversation to Leah.

"A hacker," she mused. "That makes sense. They'd need inside information to pull this off."

"Yeah, but a hacker with knowledge of particle physics and antimatter containment? That's a pretty specific skill set."

"Maybe they're working with someone who has that knowledge," Leah suggested. "A team—one person handles the technical side, another handles the science."

Luis nodded slowly. "That would explain a lot. And it means they're organized, which makes them more dangerous."

Over the next few days, the investigation intensified. Luis watched as his father worked long hours, coordinating with law enforcement and university security. The stress was visible on Dr. Osborne's face, the weight of responsibility pressing down on him.

But gradually, pieces of the puzzle fell into place. The cybersecurity team at the university traced the network intrusions to an off-campus location. Surveillance footage from nearby businesses showed a suspicious vehicle in the area around the time of the theft. Witness statements began to form a picture of the perpetrators.

"They found it," Dr. Osborne announced. "The antimatter containment unit. It's been recovered."

"Really? That's amazing! Where was it?"

"In a warehouse in Goldfield. The thieves were attempting to extract the antimatter for analysis. Fortunately, they hadn't breached the containment yet. Authorities arrested two individuals—a former graduate student from our program and a computer specialist he hired."

"A former student?" Luis was shocked. "Why would he do it?"

"Industrial espionage, just as we suspected. He'd been hired by a competing research facility overseas to steal our work. They wanted to analyze our antimatter samples and replicate our research without going through the proper channels or international agreements."

"But that's illegal."

"Very illegal. It violates international diplomacy agreements on scientific research, not to mention laws about handling hazardous materials. Both men are facing serious charges."

Luis felt relief wash over him. "So it's over?"

"The immediate crisis is over," his father said. "But this incident has sparked important conversations about security protocols, community organizing among research institutions to share best practices, and the need for better safeguards. We're implementing new measures—not just at our university, but across the scientific community."

"Will this affect your research?"

"In some ways, yes. There will be more oversight, more security checks. But ultimately, it's necessary. We have a responsibility to ensure that dangerous materials don't fall into the wrong hands. The pursuit of knowledge must be balanced with concerns for human rights and public safety."

That evening, the family had dinner together for the first time in over a week. The atmosphere was lighter, though the events of the past days had left their mark.

"Dad," Luis said as they cleared the table, "I've been thinking about what happened. About how one person's actions can have such wide-ranging effects."

"Systems thinking," his father said, nodding. "Everything's connected. A theft at one university affects security protocols everywhere. A breakthrough in particle physics can revolutionize space exploration. A violation of trust can damage the entire scientific community's collective memory and collaborative spirit."

"It makes me realize how important integrity is in science," Luis said. "Not just being smart, but being ethical."

Dr. Osborne put his hand on Luis's shoulder. "That's perhaps the most important lesson you could learn, son. Intelligence without ethics is dangerous. The power to understand the universe comes with the responsibility to use that knowledge wisely."

Luis nodded, understanding. The events of the past week had been frightening and stressful, but they'd also taught him something valuable. Science wasn't just about equations and experiments—it was about trust, collaboration, and the shared human endeavor to understand the cosmos.

As he went to bed that night, Luis thought about his dream of floating through Saturn's rings. It seemed so simple, so peaceful. But the reality of scientific research was far more complex, filled with challenges both technical and ethical. Still, it was a challenge he wanted to face. The universe held countless mysteries, and he wanted to be part of uncovering them—responsibly, ethically, and with the kind of integrity his father had demonstrated.

The stars outside his window seemed to shine a little brighter, full of promise and possibility. Somewhere out there, among the vast expanse of space, were answers to questions humanity hadn't even thought to ask yet. And perhaps, someday, he would help find them.

The stunned paralysis shattered. Flames engulfed the Founders' complex. The crowds surged forward again, and the city burned through the night...

Luis blinked, disoriented by the sudden return to the present. His arm tightened protectively around Bianca. He felt momentarily uncertain of what was real, such had been the power of the reconstruction—a historical simulation of such scope and detail as Luis had never experienced. With deep respect, he now regarded the bent old man who was the Archive Guardian.

"Some of the Founders escaped to space, and some perished in the collapse. But there was a faction who believed their time to rule would come again. These built the Archive, drew power from deep geothermal sources, and placed themselves in cryogenic suspension, surrounded by automated defenses, to wait until someone dared awaken them, or until conditions favored their return—no one knows which with certainty.

"I've told you the story you know, and shown you a glimpse of that era, because I must ensure you don't approach the Archive in ignorance. Our world is imperfect and sometimes unjust, full of the usual human failings of ambition and greed. Yet it's a better world than what the Founders created and would create again."

The Guardian studied them carefully. "Above all," he said finally, "this is a world where you're free to risk awakening the old powers, if in your judgment your need is great enough to justify the chance."

Bianca pressed her face against Luis's shoulder. In her mind, reaching for his, was a confusion of horror and determination. Luis looked grimly at the Guardian and opened his mouth to speak—but the Guardian seemed suddenly distant, and Luis could no longer feel his limbs, his face grew numb. Distantly he heard the old man say, "You're exhausted. Sleep until morning."

Luis tried to protest that there was no time, that Tomás was close and sleep was a luxury they couldn't afford, but his resistance dissolved under wave after wave of irresistible fatigue. The bright station blurred and faded; his eyes closed.

Luis woke to find daylight filtering through the station's small windows. He had been unconscious for hours! Panic seized him at the thought. He hadn't slept so deeply in years.

He rose quickly, his body and mind refreshed despite his fear—and realized that a footstep had awakened him. Across the station stood a young man who watched him with sharp, intelligent eyes that seemed familiar though the face was not.

Bianca sat up with a small gasp. Luis demanded, "Who are you? Where's the Guardian?"

The stranger smiled. "I'm the Guardian. I often rejuvenate my appearance in the morning, then allow myself to age as the day progresses. A vanity, perhaps, but vanities are scarce here."

"You made us sleep. Tomás will have caught up—"

"Tomás and his people couldn't track your mental signatures while you slept. They spent the night chasing false trails in the northern canyons, miles away."

Luis passed a hand across his face in bewilderment. Bianca said softly, "Thank you, Guardian."

"Don't thank me. I take no sides in your disputes. But now you're rested, your minds are clear. Do you still intend to enter the Archive?"

Without looking at the Guardian, Luis muttered, "We have no choice."

The security door slid open at the Guardian's gesture; the morning breeze swept into the station. The young Guardian beckoned them outside.

The station's entrance faced the Archive. It rose black and ominous in the dawn light. To either side, the desert cliffs glowed red and gold in the sunrise, but the Archive seemed to absorb all light that touched it.

Below their position, the ground fell away into a deep ravine filled with morning mist. They could hear the hum of buried power lines, the throb of machinery deep underground, but the mist concealed everything.

"You have an alternative," the Guardian said crisply. The two looked at him with sudden hope, but his expression was serious. "It's this: Luis, you can flee north through the canyon, by a route I'll show you, masking your presence as well as you can, while Bianca goes south without concealment. Your pursuers will be deceived and follow her, and by the time they catch her, you'll be beyond their reach."

The possibility hadn't occurred to them. Luis and Bianca looked at each other. Then, by unspoken agreement, they merged their thoughts completely.

They thought, in perfect union: "
It would work: I-you would endure the shame and consequences—which can be survived—that I-you might escape death—which is final.... But to become
I
and
you
again—that we cannot bear.
"

They said together, "No. Not that."

The Guardian's expression didn't change. "Very well. I'll give you what knowledge I have that might help you when you enter the Archive."

Rapidly, he impressed upon them what he had learned of the Archive's structure and its defense systems. Luis closed his eyes, slightly overwhelmed by the flood of technical detail.

"You're ready," said the Guardian. He spoke aloud now, and his voice was thin and aged. Luis opened his eyes in surprise and saw that the Guardian had become again the ancient figure of the previous night.

Luis felt an unfamiliar emotion—guilt, he realized, recognizing it through Bianca's thoughts. He said awkwardly, "You don't condemn us?"

"You've taken your lives into your own hands," the Guardian rasped. "Those who do that need no blessing and fear no curse. Go."

They navigated the ravine carefully, crossing unstable ground and hidden chasms, moving hand in hand, sharing their strength and mental abilities to bridge impossible gaps. Tomás and his group, with their numbers and resources, would cross more quickly. When Luis and Bianca finally stood on the Archive's foundation, they sensed the pursuit had closed to within an hour.

They stood before the entrance—a rectangle of absolute darkness set into the Archive's black wall, sealed only by an intangible barrier that their minds could sense but their eyes couldn't see. So little had the Founders feared those who might challenge them in their sleep.

Luis sent his thoughts probing beyond the barrier, listening carefully to the echoes. The corridor beyond descended steeply. Luis shaped a globe of light from the ambient solar energy and threw it forward. The light-globe vanished as if swallowed, but though sight failed, they both sensed it had passed through to illuminate the depths. Within the Archive, something snapped to alertness—something mechanical yet aware, programmed yet responsive. They felt sensors activate, felt electrical currents surge through long-dormant circuits...

They stood trembling together.

The morning wind rose, lifting the mist slightly, and they heard a voice shout, "There they are!"

Luis and Bianca turned. Far across the ravine, on a bridge of stone they could barely see, stood Tomás Roberts. He raised his hand dramatically. It was too far to see his expression, but his mental projection was clear and forceful: "Foolish children! I have you now!"

Behind Tomás, the silhouettes of his associates appeared through the mist. Bianca's hand tightened on Luis's. Luis projected defiance: "Turn back! Or you'll force us into the Archive!"

Tomás seemed to hesitate. Then he gestured sharply, and for the two at the Archive's entrance, the world inverted—the black wall hung above them and the sky yawned below. Luis fought for orientation as Bianca reeled against him, until he summoned his strength and shattered the illusion. The mist billowed again, obscuring Tomás, but they could hear him urging his people forward.

Bianca's face was pale but determined. "Come on!" she whispered urgently.

Together they plunged through the barrier of darkness.

Luis froze instantly, and Bianca stopped beside him. "Feel that," he muttered, and she sensed it too: the minute flow of current behind what appeared to be a blank corridor wall, a building charge that seemed to whisper
Ready... ready...

The light-globe floated ahead of them, illuminating the featureless corridor that descended toward the Archive's heart. Luis directed it forward, a dozen feet, then a bit more—

Between the walls, a blinding lance of energy materialized, pulsed briefly with searing intensity, then vanished. The immaterial light-globe drifted on unharmed.

"Forward, before it recharges!" Luis said. A few feet farther, they stumbled over scattered bones. Someone else had made it only this far. It was farther than the Guardian had gone into these unmapped regions, and only their heightened awareness had saved them. But the way wasn't blocked yet...

Then they felt the Archive begin to vibrate. A faint tremor at first, then an increasingly powerful shuddering of the floor and walls. Somewhere far below, immense systems were activating for the first time in a century. The geothermal power was rising; great turbines began to spin, the automated servants of the Founders woke one by one and began their programmed sequences, while their masters still slept, preparing for the moment of awakening that might be imminent.

From behind, up the corridor, came a clear thought of alarm, then a directed thought, echoing in the confined space:

"
Stop!
—before you go too far!"

Luis faced that direction and thought coldly: "Only if you turn back and leave us in peace."

In the darkness his will locked with that of Tomás, like two forces in perfect opposition. In that contest, each knew with absolute certainty that the other would never yield—that neither would surrender, though the Archive and the world outside should fall to ruin around them.

"Follow us, then!"

They plunged deeper. The Archive's vibrations increased with every step, becoming sound, a deep thrumming like the terrible city in the vision. Through the slow thunder of the awakening machines seemed to echo the despair of billions exploited, the anguish of all humanity before the Founders' inhuman power.

Without warning, lights activated. Blinking in their glare, Luis and Bianca saw that fifty feet ahead the corridor opened into a vast circular chamber, likewise brilliantly lit. Cautiously they approached the threshold of that room at the Archive's core.

Its ceiling was domed; its circular walls were covered with control panels studded with switches, displays, indicator lights. As they watched, lights flickered in changing patterns, registering progressive changes in the vast network of systems for which this must be the central control room. Behind those panels, circuits opened and closed in bewildering complexity; the two intruders felt magnetic fields shifting, sensed electrons flowing through superconducting pathways...

For long moments they forgot everything in wonder at this place, so utterly unlike anything in their world of leadership development and sustainable business practices. In all that brilliant space, there was no life. They looked at each other, the same thought occurring simultaneously: perhaps, after a century, the Founders were dead after all, and only the machines remained?

As if drawn by invisible force, they stepped across the threshold.

A metallic chime rang out. Halfway up the opposite wall, above a narrow ramp descending between control panels, a massive door slid open, and in the opening stood a figure.

Luis and Bianca froze, expecting each instant to be their last. The Founder stood motionless, looking down at them.

He was a man of average height and solid build, dressed in a garment of shimmering adaptive fabric that shifted colors subtly. In his right hand, held with the care one uses for a weapon, he grasped a sleek device of metal and polymer; his other hand rested against the doorframe as if for support. That gesture, and his movements as he descended the ramp slowly toward them, conveyed an odd impression of weakness or disorientation, as if he were not yet fully recovered from his century of suspended animation. But the Founder's bearing and his mind radiated an overwhelming consciousness of authority, a pride and certainty that struck them like a physical blow.

With shock, Luis realized the Founder's thoughts were completely open. They had a crisp, analytical quality that was alien and disturbing, expressed partly in unfamiliar concepts and symbols. But there was no mental shield. Apparently the Founder felt no need to guard his thoughts in the presence of lesser beings...

He stopped with his back to the central control panel and studied the intruders with the detached interest of a researcher examining an unexpected specimen. His thoughts seemed to click into place with mechanical precision—an observation that struck Luis as strange, coming from a culture where such comparisons were rare.

"Culture: post-institutional, neo-tribal. Craftsmanship adequate—acceptable. Physical specimens excellent..." There followed a complex array of calculations and abstract models. "Timeline: one century—less progress than optimal projections, given any survival scenario; but workable. The pessimists were wrong. We can rebuild. We can begin again." Then, startlingly superimposed on the cold analysis, came a surge of raw emotion, staggering in its intensity. It was a vision of a world once more subordinate, laboring, serving the Founders' will—
toward the stars, always the stars!

The icy calculation resumed: "Neutralize these subjects and those indicated in the corridor. Then initiate revival sequence..."

Luis found himself staring at the Founder's face. It was a face shaped by unquestioned authority; yet it bore the marks of deep strain, premature aging—denied and overridden by the fierce will they had sensed. It was the face of someone fundamentally unwell.

The Founder's final thought clicked into place:
Execute.
He turned toward the control panel, reaching with practiced certainty toward one specific location.

Bianca screamed.

Between the Founder and the controls, a monstrous shape materialized—seven feet tall, with writhing tentacles and glowing eyes and fangs like daggers. The Founder recoiled, and the weapon in his hand came up. There was an instantaneous flash like lightning, and the monster collapsed in on itself, twitched briefly, and vanished.

But in that moment, understanding had blazed in Luis's mind, and it remained. As the Founder reached out again, Luis acted. The Founder froze, teetering off balance, as a paralyzing grip seized all his motor neurons.

Holding that grip, Luis strode across the floor and looked directly into the Founder's frantic eyes. They glared back with such hatred and malice that for an instant Luis nearly faltered. But the Founder's efforts to free himself from the neural hold were as misdirected and futile as those of someone who had never learned to work with the mind.

Luis had guessed correctly. When Bianca in her terror had projected a nightmare creature into the Founder's path—a mere phantom from childhood stories—the Founder had not recognized it as illusion, but had taken it for a real threat. Luis laughed aloud, and with great care, as one communicates with a child, he projected his thoughts into the other's mind. "There will be no new beginning for you in
our
world, Founder! In a century, we've developed capabilities you never imagined. Now I finally understand why you built such elaborate systems, such complex arrangements of technology to accomplish simple tasks—it was because you knew no other way."

Behind the hate-filled eyes, the analytical mind tried to process this information. "Barbarians...? The faction that predicted regression was incorrect. After us, technological civilization could never rise again, because we had consumed the easily accessible resources. After us,
humanity
could not thrive on Earth, because we had corrupted the conditions that fostered greatness. The survivors must be something else—capabilities our models didn't account for—after us, the end of homo economicus, the beginning of... But those of us who chose immediate death were right after all."

The tide of hatred and sick ambition rose to overwhelm coherence. The Founder made a violent, wholly ineffective effort to raise the weapon in his paralyzed hand. Then his eyes rolled back, and suddenly he went limp and collapsed like a puppet whose strings had been cut.

Luis felt Bianca beside him and drew her close. As she trembled with relief, he continued to look down at the dead man. When he finally raised his head, he saw that the drama had had additional witnesses. In the outer doorway, backed by his colleagues, stood Tomás Roberts, staring first in astonishment at the fallen Founder, then with something approaching respect at Luis.

Luis met his gaze for a long moment, then smiled slightly and asked, "Well, Tomás? Is our dispute finished, or does your ambition for a worthy son-in-law extend beyond the one who defeated the Founders?"
question: Why were the Founders not concerned that someone might enter their Archive?
option_a: They believed their automated defense systems were sufficient protection against any intruders.
option_b: They believed no one from a post-collapse society would have the mental abilities to threaten them.
correct_answer_text: They believed no one from a post-collapse society would have the mental abilities to threaten them.
incorrect_answer_text: They believed their automated defense systems were sufficient protection against any intruders.
explanation: The story reveals that the Founders left their entrance unsealed with only an intangible barrier because "So little had the Founders feared those who might challenge them in their sleep." The key revelation comes at the end when Luis realizes the Founders relied entirely on technology and had no mental abilities—they couldn't recognize illusions as illusions and had no defenses against neural manipulation. The Founder's final thoughts confirm this: "The survivors must be something else—capabilities our models didn't account for." The Founders never imagined that post-collapse humanity would develop mental abilities that would make them vulnerable, rendering their technological superiority irrelevant.
original_question: Why were the Ryzgas not afraid that someone might enter their mountain?

synthetic_story:
The alarm pierced through Elena Herrera's consciousness like a needle through fabric.

"Initiate now—initiate now—initiate now—"

Elena awoke in the cramped pod, her breathing labored and shallow. The reinforced walls had buckled inward during the impact, pressing against her chest. She estimated at least two cracked ribs. How long had she been unconscious? Days? Weeks? There was no way to know. Her right hand fumbled for the oxygen regulator and twisted it open. For several minutes she lay there, each breath a small agony.

"Initiate now—initiate now—initiate now—"

The neural implant had awakened her with its programmed alert, signaling that it was time to execute her mission. Twelve years after the corporate war stations had collided in orbit above Parkview Province, the board of directors had sealed her in this survival pod, dormant and waiting, to be awakened only when victory or defeat was certain.

The implant's insistent message confirmed the latter. She had expected nothing else.

Her task was simple: locate the relay station, input the authorization code that would activate the massive energy cores at the heart of the station, and ensure that the conquering corporation would share the fate of the conquered in the cold vacuum of space.

But survival instinct made her hesitate. Life, even measured in minutes, was too precious to surrender immediately. Her mind raced through memories of her past, seeking comfort in what had been.

For fifteen years, alongside her brilliant mentor Samuel James, she had watched the Sentinel Station grow from a skeletal framework into a city-sized orbital platform. But construction had proceeded too slowly. When the Helix Corporation's attack station, the Dominion, emerged from deep space to seize control of the Parkview Province territories and their renewable energy patents, the Sentinel was incomplete, undermanned, and vulnerable.

The defenders could only buy time and hope for a miracle.

The Sentinel, under Samuel James's command, launched everything it had—kinetic projectiles, electromagnetic pulse weapons, even experimental biotechnology weapons that had never been field-tested.

Then, during a catastrophic solar flare event beyond the asteroid belt, both stations lost navigational control and collided. Helix shock troops poured through the breached outer hull of the crippled Sentinel.

Elena stirred uneasily in the pod. The memories became fragmented and terrible here, dominated by visions of death and destruction. She recalled that final conversation with Samuel James.

"In thirty minutes our last shuttle bay will be overrun," he had transmitted directly to her neural implant. "Only one escape pod can still launch. Be on it."

"No. I'll die here with the others."

His tired eyes had studied her face with an unreadable expression. "Then die with purpose. Our research team is developing a protocol that will destroy both stations at the moment of our inevitable defeat. If they succeed, you'll have the responsibility of executing the final command sequence."

"There's a small chance you might survive," added Dr. Sasha Palmer, the lead researcher. "We're also working on an escape mechanism—not just because you're Samuel's protégé, but because this solar storm will prevent communication with Parkview Province for years, and we need someone to survive with our research data if our experiments prove successful."

"But you must be prepared to die," Samuel had warned with gentle finality.

Elena clenched her fists and forced herself back to the present.

That moment had arrived.

With considerable effort, she extracted herself from the damaged pod and collapsed onto the floor, gasping and clutching her chest with both hands. The metal floor was frigid. Apparently the Helix weapons had finally penetrated to the station's core, allowing the cold of space to seep in. It didn't matter. She wouldn't die of cold.

She reached out, searching for the critical component—the authorization key—and gasped in dismay. The secure container had broken free from its mounting and lay on its side. The explosion that had crushed her pod had been devastating.

With a sound of horror, she activated her wrist light and examined the container's interior.

It was completely destroyed.

Once the reality settled in, she composed herself and lay there, breathing carefully and thinking. She had no way to fabricate another authorization key. At best, locating the rare components and tools would take months, and during that time the invaders would be cutting their station free from the dead hulk that held their conquering platform in a metallic death grip.

She gave herself six weeks to accomplish this mutual destruction.

Within that timeframe, she needed to determine whether the energy cores were still functional, and whether she could safely access the reactor chamber herself to manually override the safety systems and remove the control rods. If that proved impossible, she would need to manipulate her Helix enemies into doing it for her.

Still prone, she located the medical kit and wrapped her ribs expertly. The cold was becoming unbearable, so she activated the thermal underlayer she wore beneath her Helix worker's uniform. Then she crawled on her elbows to the small hatch, disengaged the seal, and emerged outside. Ignoring the pain and using the side of the artificial rock formation that concealed her pod, she slowly stood upright. The air was thin and freezing. She adjusted her portable oxygen supply almost automatically while scanning the devastated hydroponic forest as far as she could see. Mentally, she remained alert for wandering hostile minds. She had left her weapons inside the pod, except for the three items in the small pouch at her waist, knowing that her greatest advantage in the coming struggle would be her apparent harmlessness.

Three hundred meters behind her, she detected the mind of a low-ranking Helix soldier from the Ashbury division. Quickly she identified him as a tired, brutish sergeant leading a cleanup squad through the charred stumps and broken branches of the small forest that had supplied oxygen to the defenders of this sector for years.

The sergeant couldn't see her green Helix uniform clearly in the dim light and apparently mistook her for a Sentinel survivor. His mind wrestled with a decision: Should he shoot immediately, or should he capture her? It had been three months since he'd seen a woman. But his orders were explicit—shoot on sight. Yes, he would shoot.

Elena turned in profile to the plasma rifle and stretched languorously, hoping her grimace of pain wasn't visible. With satisfaction, she sensed a sudden shift in the sergeant's intentions. The weapon lowered, and the man began circling to approach from behind. He didn't alert his squad. He wanted her first. He had noticed her uniform, but that didn't deter him. Afterward, he would summon the squad. Finally, they would kill her and move on. Female support personnel had no business in combat zones anyway.

Hips swaying deliberately, Elena walked into the shattered grove. The man moved faster, still attempting stealth. Most of the overhead lighting panels had been destroyed, and visibility was poor. He wasn't surprised when he lost sight of his target. He continued forward rapidly but cautiously, picking his way through charred and fallen branches, confident she would reappear soon. He had advanced barely twenty meters when a howl of unbearable agony erupted in his mind, and consciousness fled.

She fought for survival beneath that damaged ceiling.

Breathing heavily from the mental effort, Elena emerged from behind a massive blackened tree trunk and hurried to the unconscious man. For individuals with IQs below 100, telepathic cortical disruption was quite effective. With clinical efficiency and no trace of revulsion, she stripped the foul-smelling uniform from the man, then took his weapon, reduced the power setting to minimum, and burned a precise line across his throat. While he bled out, she quickly donned the oversized uniform, secured the plasma rifle, and started up the ash-covered slope. For the immediate future, it would be safer to pass as a Helix soldier than as any type of woman.
