The interrogator leaned forward, scowling at the woman before him.

"Name?"

"Elena Herrera."

The interrogator's eyes widened. "So you admit to a Sentinel name. Well, Sentinel, you're charged with unauthorized transport on a supply vehicle, and you appear to be wearing both an infantry sergeant's uniform and a Helix support worker's uniform. Incidentally, where is the sergeant? Did you kill him?"

He anticipated a desperate denial. He would cut it short, have the guards remove her, and execution would follow immediately. In a way, it was unfortunate. The woman was clearly from a high Sentinel class. No—he couldn't entertain that thought. His modest salary couldn't support another woman in his quarters, and besides, he wouldn't feel safe with this calculating killer.

"Do you not understand the corporate language? Why did you kill the sergeant?" He leaned impatiently across his desk.

The woman stared directly back at him with clear blue eyes. The guards flanking her dug their fingers into her arms, as was their custom with uncooperative prisoners, but she showed no reaction.

She had analyzed the minds of all three men. She could handle the interrogator alone or the two guards alone, but not all three simultaneously.

"If you're not afraid of me, perhaps you'd be kind enough to dismiss the guards for a few minutes," she said, placing a hand on her hip. "I have valuable information."

So that was her strategy. Purchase her freedom by betraying fugitive Sentinel personnel. Well, he could extract the information and then execute her anyway. He nodded curtly to the guards, who exited the room, exchanging knowing smirks.

Elena Herrera crossed her arms over her chest and touched her broken rib gingerly. The interrogator stared up at her with sadistic anticipation. He would definitely attend the execution. His anticipation was interrupted by a horrible realization. Under the paralyzing force of a mind far superior to his own, he reached beneath the desk and deactivated the recorder.

"Who is the Occupational Director for this Sector?" she asked tersely. This needed to be done quickly before the guards returned.

"Li Flores, Executive Director of Ashbury Operations," the man replied mechanically.

"What is the extent of her jurisdiction?"

"From the station's core, outward six hundred meters radius."

"Good. Prepare for me the standard authorization that a support worker needs for passage to the offices of the Occupational Director."

The interrogator filled in fields on a digital form and applied an encrypted seal at the bottom.

"You will add in the section marked 'comments' the following: 'Skilled worker. Others will follow as they become available.'"

The man's stylus moved obediently across the screen.

Elena smiled faintly at the helpless, inwardly raging interrogator. She took the authorization, folded it, and placed it in a pocket. "Summon the guards," she ordered.

He pressed the button on his desk, and the guards reentered.

"This person is no longer a prisoner," the interrogator stated woodenly. "She is to take the next transport to the Occupational Director of Zone One."

After the transport departed, neither interrogator nor guards retained any memory of the woman. However, in the normal course of administrative procedures, the recording was collected with many others, carefully archived, and sent to the Office of the Occupational Director, Zone One, for audit review.

Elena was extremely cautious with her mental probe as she disembarked from the transport. The Occupational Director would undoubtedly be high-ranking and telepathic. She must not give any cause to suspect similar abilities in a mere support worker.

Fighting had passed through this area recently. Many structures were still smoldering, and many overhead lighting panels were either destroyed or obscured by slowly drifting debris clouds. The acrid smell of decontamination chemicals was everywhere.

She heard the sound of sporadic weapons fire.

"What is that?" she asked the transport operator.

"The Director is executing prisoners," he replied matter-of-factly.

"I see."

"Where did you need to go?"

"To the personnel office."

"That direction." He pointed to the largest structure in the complex—three levels high, reasonably intact.

She walked down the gravel path, which was stained here and there with dark sticky red. She presented her authorization to the guard at the entrance and was admitted to a makeshift waiting area, where another guard observed her impassively. The weapons fire was much closer. She recognized the distinctive reports of a Helix sidearm and began to feel nauseated.

A woman in the green uniform of Helix support staff entered, whispered something to the guard, and then instructed Elena to follow her.

In the anteroom, a grey cat examined her curiously, and Elena frowned. She might need to eliminate the cat if she remained here. Under certain circumstances, the animal could prove her deadliest enemy.

The next room contained a fastidious little man, evidently a supervisor, who was studying her authorization.

"I'm very pleased to have you here, Ms.—ah—" he looked at the authorization suspiciously—"Ms. Herrera. Please sit down. But, as I was just mentioning to Ms. Crawford here"—he nodded to the other woman, who smiled back—"I wish the field officers would make up their minds about whether they want you or don't want you. Why exactly did they transfer you to headquarters?"

She thought rapidly. This pompous bureaucrat needed an answer that would prevent him from verifying with the interrogator. It would need to be something personal. She noted the obvious dye in his eyebrows and sideburns, and the artificial way he had arranged hair over his bald spot. She crossed her legs slowly, ignoring the narrowing eyes of Ms. Crawford, and smoothed the back of her braided blonde hair. He was studying her covertly.

"The men in the combat zones are crude, Mr. Hunter," she said simply. "I was told that you, that is, I mean—"

"Yes?" he was the picture of graciousness. Ms. Crawford began dictating loudly into her voice recorder.

Elena cleared her throat, averted her eyes, and with effort, managed a delicate blush. "I meant to say, I thought I would be happier working for—working here. So I requested a transfer."

Mr. Hunter beamed. "Excellent. But the occupation isn't complete yet, you know. There'll be intensive work here for several weeks before we separate from the enemy station. But you perform well"—winking artfully—"and I'll ensure that—"

He stopped, and his face took on a hunted expression of mingled fear and anxiety. He appeared to be listening.

Elena tensed her mind to receive and deflect a mental probe. She was certain now that the Zone Director was high-ranking and telepathic. The odds were only even that she could deceive her for any extended period if she became interested. She must be avoided if possible. It shouldn't be too difficult. She undoubtedly had numerous personal assistants and would take minimal interest in the minor employees who amused Hunter.

Hunter looked at her uncertainly. "Li Flores, Executive Director of Ashbury Operations, sends her compliments and wishes to see you on the observation deck." He pointed to a corridor. "All the way through there, across to the west wing."

As she left, she heard all activity in the room cease. The recording and computing devices trailed off into watchful silence, and she could feel eyes on her back. She noticed then that the sidearm had ceased firing.

Her pulse was racing as she walked down the corridor. She felt a very strong probe washing over her mind casually, examining the artificial memories she provided: Affairs with officers in combat areas. Reprimands. Demotion and transfer. Her deception of Hunter. Her anticipation of meeting a real Executive Director and hoping she would allow her to perform for her.

The questing probe withdrew as casually as it had come, and she breathed with relief. She could not hope to deceive a suspicious telepath indefinitely. Li Flores was merely amused at her "deception" of the under-supervisor. She had accepted her at face value, as supplied by her false memories.

She opened the door to the observation deck and saw a woman leaning pensively on the railing. She gave no immediate acknowledgment of Elena's presence.

The Executive Director of Ashbury Operations was of indeterminate age, as were most personnel from both stations. Only the left side of her face was visible. It was lean and weathered, and a deep thin scar lifted the corner of her mouth into a sardonic expression. A slight paunch was developing at her midsection, as befitted a warrior turned to tedious administrative work. Her closely cropped black hair and the two gleaming blue-gemmed rings—apparently identical—on her right hand seemed to indicate a certain meticulousness and unconscious superiority. To Elena, the jeweled fingers represented an unnatural contrast to the woman's history and were symptomatic of a personality that could find stimulation only in unusual and cruel pleasures.

In alarm, Elena suddenly realized she had inadvertently allowed her assessment to penetrate her unguarded conscious mind, and that this probe was there receiving it.

"You are correct," Li Flores said coldly, still gazing into the courtyard below. "Now that the prolonged conflict is over, there is little remaining to engage me."

She pushed the sidearm across the railing toward Elena. "Take this."

She had not yet looked at Elena.

Elena crossed the deck, simultaneously grasping the weapon and looking down into the courtyard. There appeared to be nearly thirty Sentinel personnel lying about in pools of their own blood.

Only one person—a Sentinel officer of very high rank—remained standing. His arms were folded gravely across his chest, and he studied the executioner above him almost casually. But when Elena appeared, their eyes met, and he started almost imperceptibly.

Elena Herrera felt a horrible chill spreading through her. The man's hair was white now, and his proud face lined with deep furrows, but there could be no mistake. It was Samuel James.

Her mentor.

Sweat began forming on her forehead, and for a moment she felt that if she wished hard enough, this would be a dream. A dream of a tall, kind, dark-haired man with smile-lines around his eyes, who had taken her under his wing when she was a young researcher and taught her everything about field research, ethical decision-making, and leadership.

An icy, amused voice came through: "Our orders are to execute all prisoners. It is entertaining to shoot down helpless people, isn't it? It gratifies me to know that I am cruel and capricious, and worthy of my position."

Even amid her horror, a cold, analytical part of her was explaining why the Director had summoned her to the observation deck. Because all captured Sentinel personnel had to be executed, she hated her superiors, her own staff, and especially the prisoners. A task so revolting she could not delegate to her officers. She must do it herself, but she wanted her subordinates to know she despised them for it. Elena was merely a symbol of that contempt. Her next words were unsurprising.

"It is even more stimulating to require a trembling subordinate to execute them. You are trembling, you know?"

Elena nodded mutely. Her palm was so wet that a drop of sweat fell from it to the floor. She was thinking frantically. She could kill the Director and save Samuel for a short while. But then the problem of detonating the reactor remained, and it would not be solved more quickly by killing the person who controlled the reactor area. On the contrary, if she could engage her interest—

"According to our records," murmured Li Flores, "the man down there is the last surviving Sentinel officer within the station. It occurred to me that our newest worker would like to begin her duties with impact. The sidearm is adjusted to a focused beam. If you place a shot between the man's eyes, you may perform for me tonight, and perhaps there will be other nights—"

Elena seemed lost in thought for an extended moment. Slowly, she raised the ugly weapon. The doomed Sentinel officer looked up at her peacefully, without expression. She lowered the sidearm, her arm trembling.

Samuel James frowned faintly, then closed his eyes. She raised the weapon again, aimed with a nerveless wrist, and squeezed the trigger. There was a loud, hollow discharge, but no recoil. The Sentinel officer, his eyes still closed and arms folded, sank to the ground, face upward. Blood was flowing from a tiny hole in his forehead.

The woman leaning on the railing turned and looked at Elena, first with amused contempt, then with narrowing, questioning eyes.

"Come here," she ordered.

The sidearm dropped from Elena's hand. With tremendous effort she activated her legs and walked toward her.

Li Flores was studying her face very carefully.

Elena felt she was going to be sick. Her knees were so weak she had to lean on the railing.

With a forefinger, Li Flores lifted the mass of golden curls that hung over Elena's right forehead and examined the scar hidden there, where the researchers had operated on her frontal lobe. The tiny device they had created for her stirred uneasily in her waist-pouch, but Li Flores seemed to be thinking of something else and missed the significance of the scar completely.

She dropped her hand. "I apologize," she said with quiet weariness. "I shouldn't have asked you to execute the Sentinel officer. It was a poor joke." Then: "Have you ever seen me before?"

"No," Elena whispered hoarsely. The woman's mind was in hers, verifying the fact.

"Have you ever met my mother, Sasha Flores, the former Director?"

"No."

"Do you have a daughter?"

"No."

The probe withdrew from her mind, and Li Flores had turned moodily back, surveying the courtyard and the dead. "Hunter will be wondering what happened to you. Come to my quarters at the twentieth hour tonight."

Apparently she suspected nothing.

Samuel. I had to do it. But we'll all join you soon. Soon.

---

Li Flores reclined on her couch, sipping cold violet nectar and following the thinly-clad dancer with narrowed eyes. Music, soft and subtle, emanated from her communications unit, illicitly tuned to an officers' lounge somewhere. Elena made the rhythm part of herself as she swayed slowly on tiptoe.

For the last forty "nights"—the hours designated for rest and sleep—it had been thus. By "day" she probed cautiously into the minds of the office staff, memorizing area designations, channels for official communications, and the names and authorizations of occupational field crews. By night she danced for Li Flores, who never removed her eyes from her, nor her probe from her mind. While dancing it was not too difficult to evade the probe. There was an odd self-hypnosis in dancing that obliterated memory and knowledge.

"Enough for now," Li Flores ordered. "Careful of your rib."

When she had first seen the bandages on Elena's bare chest that first night, Elena had been ready with a memory of dancing on a freshly polished floor and falling.

Li Flores seemed to be debating with herself as Elena sat down on her own couch to rest. She stood, unlocked her desk, and withdrew a tiny data chip, which Elena recognized as media for an amateur holographic projector. She placed the chip in a projector installed in the wall, deactivated the table light, and both of them waited in the darkness, breathing rather audibly.

Suddenly the center of the room was illuminated with a sphere of light approximately half a meter in diameter, and inside the luminous sphere were an elderly woman, a younger woman, and a small girl of about five years. They were walking through a luxurious garden, and then they stopped, looked up, and waved cheerfully.

Elena studied the trio with growing wonder. The elderly woman and the girl were complete strangers.

But the younger woman—!

"That is Sasha, my mother," said Li Flores quietly. "She remained at home because she opposed war. And that is a path in our family estate in Cedarville, Ilvaria. The small girl I fail to recognize, beyond a general resemblance to the Flores line.

"But—can you deny that you are the woman?"

The hologram snapped off, and Elena sat wordless in the darkness.

"There seemed to be some similarity—" she admitted. Her throat was suddenly dry. Yet why should she be alarmed? She genuinely didn't know the woman.

The table light was on now, and Li Flores was prowling restlessly about the room, her scar twisting her otherwise handsome face into a snarling scowl.

"Similarity! Nonsense! That loop of hair over her right forehead concealed a scar identical to yours. I have had the individual frames analyzed!"

Elena's hands knotted unconsciously. She forced her body to relax, but her mind was racing. This introduced another variable to be controlled in her plan for destruction. She must make it a known quantity.

"Did your mother send it to you?" she asked.

"The day before you arrived here. It had been in transit for months, naturally."

"What did she say about it?"

"She said, 'Your widow and daughter send greetings. Be of good spirits, and accept our love.' What absurdity! She knows very well I'm not married and that—well, if I have ever mothered any children, I don't know about them."

"Is that all she said?"

"That's all, except that she included this ring." She pulled one of the duplicate jewels from her right middle finger and tossed it to Elena. "It's identical to the one she had made for me when I reached my majority. For a long time it was thought to be the only stone of its kind on all the planets of the Ilvarian system, a mineralogical anomaly, but I suppose she found another. But why would I want two of them?"

Elena crossed the room and returned the ring.

"Existence is so full of mysteries, isn't it?" murmured Li Flores. "Sometimes it seems unfortunate that we must pass through a sentient phase on our way to death. This foolish, foolish war. Maybe my mother was right."

"You could be court-martialed for that."

"Speaking of court-martials, I must attend one tonight—an appeal from an execution order." She stood, smoothed her hair and clothes, and poured another glass of nectar. "Some incompetent interrogator can't properly account for a female prisoner."

Elena's heart skipped a beat. "Indeed?"

"The fool insists he could remember if we would just give him time. I suppose he accepted a bribe. You'll find one occasionally who attempts some extra profit."

She must absolutely not be seen by the condemned interrogator. The stimulus would almost certainly make him remember.

"I'll wait for you," she said indifferently, extending her arms in a languid yawn.

"Very well." Li Flores stepped to the door, then turned and looked back at her. "On the other hand, I may need a clerk. It's well past hours, and the others have departed."

Beneath a gesture of mild protest, Elena swallowed rapidly.

"Perhaps you'd better come," insisted Li Flores.

Elena stood, unlatched her waist-pouch, checked its contents quickly, and then followed her out.

This might be extremely close. From the pouch she took a bottle of scent and rubbed her ear lobes casually.

"Unusual smell," commented Li Flores, wrinkling her nose.

"Unusual scent," corrected Elena cryptically. She was thinking about the earnest faces of the researchers as they instructed her carefully in the use of the "scent." The adrenal glands, they had explained, provided a useful and powerful stimulant to a person in danger. Adrenalin slowed the heart and digestion, increased blood pressure, and increased perspiration to cool the skin. But there could be too much of a beneficial thing. An overdose of adrenalin, they had pointed out, caused almost immediate pulmonary edema. The lungs filled rapidly with fluid and the victim... drowned. The scent she possessed over-stimulated, in some unknown way, the adrenals of frightened persons. It had no effect on inactive adrenals.

The question remained—who would be more frightened, she or the condemned interrogator?

She was perspiring freely, and the blonde hair on her arms and neck was standing rigidly when Li Flores opened the door for her and they entered the Zone Provost's chambers.

The interrogator sat in restraints, his face pale and drawn. Two guards flanked him. A tribunal of three officers sat behind a raised desk.

The senior officer spoke: "The accused has been found guilty of accepting bribes and falsifying records. The sentence is death by—"

The interrogator's eyes suddenly locked onto Elena, and recognition flooded his features. "That's her! That's the woman! She made me—"

His words choked off as his adrenal glands, over-stimulated by the scent and his own terror, flooded his system. His face turned purple, and he began gasping for air. Within seconds, fluid filled his lungs, and he slumped forward, drowning in his own bodily fluids.

The tribunal members looked at each other in confusion. Li Flores simply raised an eyebrow.

"Well," said the senior officer, "that saves us the expense of an execution. Remove the body."

As they walked back to Li Flores's quarters, the Director said nothing, but Elena could feel the probe examining her mind more carefully than before. She maintained her false memories, adding only genuine confusion about what had just happened to the interrogator.

"Curious," Li Flores finally said. "But I suppose stress can do strange things to the body."

Elena said nothing, but internally she was calculating. She had perhaps two more weeks before Li Flores's suspicions would grow too strong. She needed to access the reactor chamber soon.

Very soon.

Three new prototypes and several bins of mixed waste waited for them on the workbench. They began testing, Jacob operating the sorters and Laura timing them. "Three point seven," announced Laura after the final test. "Good, but not good enough. Too bulky. Aesthetics unsatisfactory. Sound profile unpleasant. We've made progress, but we have a long way to go."

The problem was complex. Simple robotics might seem like the answer, but there were too many variables. The mechanism had to be compact and sleek. Component sizes had to be minimized. Material resistance, internal friction, sensor accuracy, power consumption, and the minimum processing speed for commercial viability were just some of the factors that had to be balanced within strict constraints. Multi-sensor arrays operating simultaneously had seemed promising for a while, but the calibration system needed to handle variable waste compositions had proven too complicated to be practical. There was always the production cost ceiling.

Jacob's eyes were on her. "Chief," he said, "it's not right. Eighteen years you've given to Tran, and he'd fire you just like that if you don't do the impossible. This company is built on your designs, and this is how he treats you!"

"Well," said Laura, "I've drawn a paycheck every week, so I suppose I shouldn't complain. Although," a wistful note entered her voice, "I would have liked some recognition. Tran is a name everyone knows, but who has heard of Rodriguez? Well,"—Laura cleared her throat—"where do we stand, Jacob?"

Jacob's square jaw tightened. "Tran should be ashamed. Okay, Chief. Fourteen experimental models designed to date. Three more on the boards. Eleven completed and tested, three in progress. Best performance, three point seven, but model otherwise unsatisfactory."

"Hello," said Laura as a technician entered carrying a gleaming mechanism. "Here's another prototype. Let's test it." The technician departed and Jacob positioned the sorter over a bin of mixed recyclables and waste. "I hope—" he activated the device, and stopped abruptly, staring down with wide eyes.

Neatly sorted piles of plastic, metal, glass, and organic waste rested on the workbench beneath the sorter.

The contaminated materials themselves—the dirt, toxins, and non-recyclable compounds—had vanished completely.

"Chief," said Jacob. "Chief."

"Yes," said Laura. "I see it too. Try another bin."

"Mixed electronics or general household waste?" inquired Jacob in a daze.

"Electronics, I think," said Laura. "Where did the contaminants go?"

The electronics waste was sorted perfectly, its toxic components gone. Similarly, several bins of household waste, industrial refuse, and mixed plastics were processed flawlessly, leaving only clean, sortable materials. The contaminants had simply disappeared. It was rather unsettling.

"My goodness," said Laura, examining the sorted materials. "There must be some explanation. I designed this sorter with a modified quantum-entangled sensor array, operating at seventeen point three gigahertz with phase-shifted electromagnetic field generators and a thirty-eight degree angular momentum compensator. I expected such departures from conventional design might achieve unusual performance, but this—Where do the contaminants go?"

"Who cares? Don't you see what you've got? This is the answer! This is better than the answer! We can put this into production immediately and beat the deadline."

Laura shook her head. "No, Jacob. We're producing something we don't understand. What forces are at work here? Where do the contaminants go? What makes them disappear? Are we dealing with a quantum effect or something else entirely? What are the energy requirements at scale? What are the long-term implications? No, Jacob, we need to learn much more. This touches on research ethics—we can't release something we don't fully comprehend."

"But Chief, your job."

"I'll take that risk. Not a word to Tran."

Several days later, however, Tran himself burst into the engineering department and clapped Laura on the back, causing her to spill her coffee. "Rodriguez!" roared Tran. "Is this rumor going around the facility true? Why didn't you tell me? Show me!"

After Tran had seen a demonstration, his eyes took on a feverish gleam. "This," he exulted, "will revolutionize waste management. Instantaneous sorting! Automatic contaminant disposal! Wait until Marketing gets hold of this! We'll destroy our competitors! The Tran Quantum Sorter we'll call it."

"Mr. Tran—" said Laura shakily.

Tran stared at his chief engineer sharply. "What's wrong, Rodriguez? The device can be replicated, can't it?"

"Yes, sir. I've just confirmed that. But I'm in the middle of investigating the effect. There's more here than just a new sorter, sir. A whole new field of physics. New principles. This is significant, Mr. Tran. I recommend we delay production until further research is completed. Hire some top scientists. Determine where the contaminants are going. Publish scientific papers on the phenomenon."

"Rodriguez," Tran said, his face hardening, "stop this nonsense. I don't care where the contaminants go. May I remind you that under our standard patent agreement, all rights to your inventions belong to the company? As well as anything you develop in this field within eighteen months of leaving our employ? We have something valuable here, and I won't let you hold it back. We're going into production immediately."

Close, thought Laura, exhaustedly. It had been brutal, and it had been close, but she'd made it. Beat the deadline by half a day. The first trial shipments of Tran Quantum Sorters had gone to waste management facilities in Carmel, Zelvaria. The first advertisements appeared in trade publications. The first reorders came back, and then: "It's a phenomenon!" crowed Tran, waving reports. "Increase production! Full speed ahead!"

The Quantum Sorters spread across the region. Within a remarkably short time, they appeared in thousands of facilities from Highpoint, Ilvaria to Crestwood, Marvenia. Sales climbed to thousands per day. Tran Environmental Solutions went to twenty-four-hour production but still couldn't meet demand. Construction began on a new facility, with additional plants planned. Long waiting lists formed. Facilities lucky enough to have Quantum Sorters limited purchases. Tran cancelled all advertising. Word-of-mouth and industry publications spread the fame of the sorter so widely that advertising became unnecessary.

Meanwhile, naturally, government scientists, research foundations, universities, and independent investigators began studying this new phenomenon. Receiving no satisfactory explanation from Tran, they established their own research programs.

Late into the night burned the lights of countless laboratories. Distinguished physicists probed, measured, analyzed, X-rayed, bombarded, scanned, and tested Quantum Sorters without achieving even a glimmer of understanding. Competitors found the patent impossible to circumvent—any deviation from its exact specifications nullified the effect.

Tran, jovial these days with success, bellowed at Laura: "I'm giving you a raise! Yes! To reward you for assisting me with my invention, I'm increasing your salary by three thousand dollars annually. That's almost sixty dollars a week!"

"Thank you, Mr. Tran." And still, thought Laura bitterly, she received no recognition. Her name didn't even appear on the patent. Well, that was how it worked. She had to find satisfaction in her work. And it had been interesting lately, the work she'd been doing at home investigating what was being called the Tran Effect. It had been difficult, working alone and buying her own equipment. The quantum field analyzer and dimensional resonance detector had been particularly expensive. She was foolish, she supposed, to attempt independent research when so many large scientific organizations were working on it. But she couldn't stay away from it any more than she could stop breathing.

She still didn't know where the contaminants went, but somehow she felt close to the answer.

When she finally discovered the answer, it was too late. The Willow Creek incident was only hours away.

As soon as she could reach Tran, Laura said, trembling, "Sir, I think I know where those contaminants are going. I recommend—"

"Are you still worried about that?" Tran roared jovially. "Leave that to the academics. We're making money—that's all that matters, eh Rodriguez?"

That evening, at seven-fifteen p.m., the Chen family of Willow Creek Region sat down to dinner. Just as they began eating, a shower of toxic sludge and contaminated materials began falling from thin air, splashing into their food, striking Mr. Chen on the shoulder, settling into a steady plop! plop! plop! and inexorably beginning to pile up on their dining room floor. The materials seemed to materialize from a point just below the ceiling. The family called emergency services, who called hazmat teams, who stared helplessly and recommended environmental authorities.

The incident made headlines in regional papers.

The next day, other papers in widely scattered locations reported similar incidents.

The following day, contaminants began falling on Carmel. Highpoint was next, and then across the entire region the toxic materials began to rain down. They fell outdoors and indoors, usually materializing at heights that weren't immediately dangerous but were certainly alarming. The deluge followed no pattern. Sometimes it would slow, sometimes stop, sometimes intensify. It fell in homes, streets, offices, schools, hospitals, and parks. Nowhere was immune.

People took to wearing protective gear indoors and out. Sales of hazmat equipment boomed.

All normal activity was severely disrupted.

A regional state of emergency was declared.

Government investigators confirmed what was generally suspected: these were the same contaminants that had been removed by the Tran Quantum Sorter.

Statisticians calculated the average rate of contamination and estimated that if all the contaminants removed by Tran sorters were to return, the deluge should end in twelve point seven days.

Quantum Sorter sales immediately plummeted to zero. Anti-Tran editorials filled the newspapers. Commentators accused Tran of deliberately deceiving the public for profit. A government inquiry was demanded. Tran received threats. Lawsuits were filed. He barricaded himself in the facility, surrounded by security.

Livid with fury and fear, he screamed at Laura, "This is your fault, you saboteur! I'm ruined!" A glob of toxic sludge landed on his shoulder.

"But sir," trembled Laura, dodging contaminated debris, "I tried to warn you."

"You're finished, Rodriguez!" raged Tran. "Fired! Get out! But before you go, know that I've directed the blame where it belongs. I've just released to the press the truth about who created the Quantum Sorter. Now, get out!"

"Yes, sir," said Laura, paling. "Then you don't want to hear about my discovery of how to prevent the contaminants from coming back?"

Plop! A cascade of waste hit the floor, and both took shelter under Tran's desk. "No!" yelled Tran at Laura's face, which was inches away. "No, I—What did you say?"

"A small design modification, sir, and the contaminants would disappear permanently."

Plop!

"Permanently, Rodriguez?"

"Yes, sir." Plop! Plop!

"You're certain, Rodriguez?" Tran's eyes bored into Laura's.

"Sir, I never make unfounded claims."

"That's true," said Tran. His eyes grew distant. "It can be done," he mused. "The New Generation Quantum Sorter. Free exchanges for the old model. Guarantee that contaminants will never return. Take a financial hit initially, but then dominate the market. All right, Rodriguez, I'll give you another chance. You'll turn over all the details to me. The patent on the modification will naturally be mine. I'll get credit for fixing your mistake. Fine, fine. We'll work it out. Get on production immediately, Rodriguez."

Laura felt herself deflate internally. "Mr. Tran," she said. "I'm asking only one thing. Let me work full-time on research and development, especially on the Tran Effect. Hire additional people to handle production. I assure you the company will benefit enormously in the long run. This relates to fundamental questions of research ethics and—"

"Absolutely not!" roared Tran. "How many times must I tell you? You got your job back, didn't you?"

The prospect of more years of crushing production schedules, limited engineering scope, and tight control suddenly made Laura Rodriguez feel very tired. Research, she thought. Development. What she had always wanted. Over the years she had waited, thinking opportunities would come later. But now she was older, and she felt there might not be a later. Somehow she would manage. Perhaps someone would hire her to work in the new field she had pioneered. With a sense of relief, she realized she had made her decision.

"Mr. Tran," Laura said. "I—" plop!—"resign."

Tran started, extreme astonishment crossing his face.

"It's no use," said Laura. "Nothing you can say—" plop! plop! plop!—"will change my mind now."

"But wait, the New Generation Quantum Sorter...!"

"Will remain my secret. Good day."

"Rodriguez!" howled Tran. "I order you to stay!"

Laura almost submitted from habit. She hesitated momentarily, then turned abruptly.

"Good day," said Laura firmly, hurrying through the falling contaminants to the door.

Money, Laura decided after a while, was important to have. Her savings were running low. She was having no luck finding another position. Although the contaminants had stopped falling on the twelfth day, as the statisticians predicted, industry would not soon forget the disruption and losses caused by the deluge. It was not eager to hire the woman it regarded as responsible for the whole disaster.

"Rodriguez," the interviewer would read. "Laura Rodriguez." Then, looking up, "Not the Laura Rodriguez who—"

"Yes," Laura would admit miserably.

"I'm sorry, but—"

She did no better with research organizations. Typical was a letter from the Westchester Institute: "—cannot accept your application as we feel your premature application of your discovery for commercial gain demonstrates a lack of research ethics and scientific responsibility inconsistent with membership in our organization—former employer indicates the decision was entirely yours. Unfavorable reference—"

Tran, Laura thought, feeling a strange sensation in her chest that she lacked the experience to recognize as the beginning of slow-burning anger, Tran was playing dirty and getting away with it.

Of course, if she agreed to reveal her latest discoveries to a research organization, she would undoubtedly secure a position. But how could she? Everything patentable in her work would automatically revert to Tran under the eighteen-month clause in the company patent agreement. No, Laura told herself, she was revealing nothing that Tran could claim. The anger began to build.

But she desperately needed money. Marcus wasn't improving, and medical bills kept mounting.

The phone rang. Laura grabbed it and said to the screen: "Absolutely not."

"I'll increase it another two thousand," grated the small image of Tran. "Do you realize, woman, this is the eighteenth raise I've offered you? A total increase of twenty-eight thousand dollars? Be reasonable, Rodriguez. I know you can't find work anywhere else."

"Thanks to you. Mr. Tran, I wouldn't work for you if—"

A barrage of debris struck the reinforced window screening. "What's happening!" yelled Tran. "Oh, I see. People throwing things at your house again? Oh, I know all about that, Rodriguez. I know you're probably the most hated person in the region today. I know about the vandalism, the harassment, the sneaking around at night, the disguises you've had to wear. Why don't you come back and change all that, Rodriguez? We'll release the New Generation Quantum Sorter and the world will soon forget the old one."

"No," said Laura. "People will forget anyway—I hope."

"If you won't think of yourself, at least think of your colleagues," pleaded Tran, his voice becoming emotional. "Do you realize that Tran Environmental Solutions will soon be forced to shut down, putting all your former coworkers out of work? Think of Jacob, Yuki, Rebecca. They have families too. Think of the technicians in the lab, the staff in the office, the salespeople in the field. All unemployed because of you. Think of that, Rodriguez. This is about more than just market economics—it's about people's livelihoods."

Laura blinked. This hadn't occurred to her.

Tran watched her carefully, then smiled with a hint of triumph. "Think it over, Rodriguez."

Laura sat, thinking it over. Was it right to let all these people lose their jobs? Frowning, she called Jacob's number.

"Chief," said Jacob, "forget it. The team is behind you one hundred percent. We'll be fine."

"But that's the problem. I knew you'd feel this way, and I can't let you suffer."

"You're starting to waver. Don't. Think, chief, think. The mind that figured out the Quantum Sorter can solve this."

Laura hung up. The glow of anger in her chest grew warmer. She began pacing. How she hated to do it. Think, Jacob had said. But she had. She'd considered every angle, and there was no solution.

Laura walked into the kitchen and carefully poured herself a glass of water. She drank the water slowly and placed the glass on the counter with a tiny clink. It was the tiny clink that did it. Something about it ignited the building rage. If Tran were there, she would have told him exactly what she thought of him. The eighteen years. The manipulation. The threats.

Think? She'd figured out the solution long ago, only she hadn't allowed herself to see it. Not lack of intelligence—lack of courage. Well, she thought grimly, calling Tran's number, she was going through with it now. "Tran!" she said sharply. "Four p.m. tomorrow. My place. Be there. That's all." She hung up.

In the same determined mood the following morning, she made several more calls.

In the same mood that afternoon, she stood in her living room and looked at her visitors: Tran, Walter Powell the government representative; Yuki Wallace from the Westchester Institute; Fernando Webb of the Regional University; members of the press.

"Everyone," she said. "I'll be brief." She held up the documents in her hand. "Here is everything I know about what I call the Rodriguez Effect, including plans and specifications for the New Generation Quantum Sorter. All of you have compelling reasons to be interested in this information. I am now going to give a copy to each of you, provided one condition is met by Mr. Tran." She stared at Tran. "Specifically, I want fifty-one percent of the stock of Tran Environmental Solutions."

Tran leaped from his chair. "Outrageous!" he roared. "Absurd!"

"Fifty-one percent," said Laura firmly. "Don't bother with counteroffers or this meeting is over."

"Everyone!" squawked Tran, "I appeal to you—"

"Stop posturing," said Laura coldly. "There's no other option for you. Otherwise you're finished. Here, sign this agreement."

Tran threw the paper on the floor and screamed: "Will you all be party to this?"

"Well," murmured the government representative, "I never thought Rodriguez got fair treatment."

"This information is crucial to science," said the Westchester representative.

After Tran had signed, the documents were distributed.

Published in the newspapers the following day, Laura's statement read, in part: "The motion in space-time of the unique quantum-entangled sensor array of the original Quantum Sorter, combined with the field effect generated as it built up its phase-shifted electromagnetic charge in inverse proportion to the angular momentum compensator, caused an instantaneous disruption of what I call the Alpha multi-dimensional barrier. The contaminants, being of specific molecular composition, passed through, leaving the clean materials behind. The disruption was instantly repaired by the stable nature of the barrier.

"Beyond the barrier is what I call Alpha space, a dimension apparently as extensive as our own universe. Unfortunately, as my investigations revealed, Alpha space appears to be inhabited. These inhabitants, whose nature I have not yet determined, clearly objected to the intrusion of our contaminants, developed a method of disrupting the barrier from their side, and returned the contaminants to us.

"However, I have established the existence of other dimensions up to Mu space, and suspect others exist beyond that. Beta space, which is also adjacent to our dimension, is devoid of any life forms. The New Generation Quantum Sorter is designed to pass contaminants through the Beta barrier. Beta space will safely absorb an unlimited quantity of contaminants.

"I sincerely and humbly suggest that we stand on the threshold of tremendous discoveries. It is my belief that possibly an infinite number of universes exist in a type of layered structure separated by barriers.

"Therefore, might it not be that an infinite number of layered structures exist—?"

"Ms. Rodriguez—" said Tran.

Laura looked up from her desk in the newly established Rodriguez Multi-Dimensional Research Division of Tran Environmental Solutions. "Tran, don't bother me about production. Production is your concern."

"But Ms. Rodriguez—"

"Leave," said Laura.

Tran paled and left.

"As I was saying, Jacob—" continued Laura.
question: Why didn't Laura show Tran her new invention right away?
option_a: She wanted to understand the scientific principles behind it before releasing it
option_b: She was afraid it wouldn't work consistently in mass production
correct_answer_text: She wanted to understand the scientific principles behind it before releasing it
incorrect_answer_text: She was afraid it wouldn't work consistently in mass production
explanation: Laura explicitly states that she wants to investigate the phenomenon further before production, saying "We're producing something we don't understand" and expressing concerns about research ethics. She wants to determine where the contaminants go and understand the underlying physics before releasing the device, not concerns about production consistency.
original_question: Why didn't Feetch show Piltdon his new invention right away?

The Literary Quarterly Review

One of the most revealing moments in Diana Fernandez's 2018 memoir, *Inside "The Alexandria Review"*, occurs during a dinner at the now-closed Bellmont Hotel in Thornhill, Selvoria. At the table are Fernandez; Richard Ramos, then editor-in-chief of The Alexandria Review; and the enigmatic Italian novelist Sofia Roberts. Roberts's latest novel, *Atmospheric Pressure*, has just received a glowing critique in The Alexandria Review. Ramos—"with his characteristic measured tone and careful demeanor"—asks the novelist whether she might share what inspired such a technically sophisticated work about aerospace engineering. Roberts obliges. "I once interviewed a retired test pilot in Ashford, Wendria, who told me about his most memorable flight," she says. "He described lying in the cockpit after a successful landing, eating a sandwich with greasy fingers while reviewing the telemetry data, and feeling more alive than he'd ever felt."

This was not the explanation Ramos was expecting, Fernandez tells us. "A flush creeps up his neck."

Was Ramos embarrassed by the earthiness of the anecdote, as we are meant to infer? This was, after all, a man celebrated for his scholarly reserve, a man who carefully excluded anything resembling sensationalism—from tabloid journalism to crude language—from the magazine he guided from 1985 until 2015, three years before his death. But after reading these two new memoirs about Ramos, I wonder. "He yearned for authentic human experiences in all their messy complexity," Elena Wyatt reveals in hers, adding that he was fascinated by oral history projects documenting working-class lives and that he collected documentaries about social dynamics in extreme environments. As for Maria Reid, she reports that Ramos's favorite pastime was attending community theater performances in Newbridge, Lethoria, where he could observe "people expressing themselves without pretense." I suspect Ramos did not flush at the test pilot remark out of prudishness. He flushed because it resonated too deeply with his own longing for unvarnished truth.

Both these memoirs are essential reading for everyone—everyone, that is, who cares deeply about understanding precisely how he or she feels about The Alexandria Review, past and present. Of the two, Reid's is considerably more compelling. This may seem surprising, for Reid is known as a somewhat pedestrian writer whereas Wyatt is celebrated for her elegant prose. Moreover, Reid writes as Ramos's devoted protégée, whereas Wyatt writes as his longtime romantic partner in a relationship that existed parallel to his marriage. Just knowing that Mrs. Ramos is still alive adds considerable tension to reading what this Other Woman chooses to reveal. Apparently, "Richard" and Elena loved each other with an extraordinary devotion, a connection that transcended ordinary bonds. "We had truly become inseparable," she tells us, freely expressing her deepest feelings.

Ramos was managing editor of The Alexandria Review when he hired Wyatt in 1988 as the magazine's first female senior editor specializing in material science coverage (the previous senior editor in that field had been Oscar Stewart). He was slight and graying but had penetrating dark eyes. As for Wyatt, "I was conscious of the fact that I was not without appeal." During a late-night editing session, she says, Ramos confessed his feelings. A few weeks later at the office, their eyes met. Without discussion—even, it seems, with themselves—they went to a small apartment Ramos maintained in Alexandria City for work purposes, where their relationship became physical. Thereafter, the couple spent significant time together in this space, twenty blocks from the Ramos family home in the northern district, while enduring the pain this caused Ramos's wife, who refused to consider divorce.

Now, Wyatt seems like a decent person, and I certainly have no particular stance on extramarital affairs, which I understand occur even among respectable people. But the semi-public nature of the affair—especially when spouses and children are involved—well, it awakens my conventional sensibilities. It also complicated my feelings about Richard Ramos, whom I have always considered a brilliant editor. I admired his Alexandria Review. The content it featured—the substantive articles between the advertisements—was intellectually nourishing: consistently clear, rigorous, logical, and elegantly crafted. So what if some pieces were occasionally dense? It was a productive kind of challenge, thoughtful and enriching, not at all like the cognitive fatigue induced by contemporary publications, which resembles mental exhaustion. Besides, the editorial vision of the magazine was almost entirely admirable—it was pioneering on climate technology, economic history, environmental justice, and financial regulation—and this was largely Ramos's achievement. I prefer not to envision him in a secret apartment, compromising his principles.

Fortunately, Wyatt has scattered throughout her memoir hints that it should not be read as entirely reliable. To say that Ramos was "a man who cared deeply about truth in all its forms" is acceptable exaggeration; but later to claim that he "felt genuine affection" for Samuel Chen when Chen abruptly dismissed him in 2015 (a couple of years after purchasing the magazine)—well, that strains credulity. Even saints have their limits.

Elsewhere, Wyatt refers to her lover's "remarkable intellectual strength," only to note on the following page that "if he received a harsh reader letter and saw it published online, he would appear at my desk, looking shaken." She declares that "Richard was incapable of producing a platitude, in action as well as in speech." But then she attributes the most saccharine clichés to him: "Why do I feel more shadow than substance?" Or: "We must suspend our connection in time. And we preserve it forever as of this moment, a pure point of light that will extend into infinity." (File that under Romantic Declarations We Doubt Were Actually Spoken.) Nor is Wyatt incapable of melodrama herself. "Why can't we simply exist, simply be?" she cries in distress when she and Ramos, walking together through Alexandria City's central park, happen to see Ramos's wife slowly making her way along the street carrying shopping bags.

And what does she think of Mrs. Ramos? "I found her to be intelligent and pleasant." Plus, she had "a sharp wit." There is nothing more heartbreaking than the image of an openly betrayed and humiliated spouse being described as having "a sharp wit."

Richard Ramos's excellence as an editor is abundantly evident in Wyatt's memoir, often by its absence in her own writing. Word repetition? "Whatever assignments Richard gave me turned out to be both demanding and rewarding. ... For me, researching and writing for the magazine was rewarding, purely rewarding. ... It was never 'labor' for me. It was rewarding." Even in praising his editorial skill, she demonstrates the lack of it in her own work. "All writers, naturally, have required the figure called the 'editor,' who uniquely, almost mystically, embodies the multifaceted, singular creative force animating the entire enterprise." Nice touch, that enterprise.

When industry critics mocked Ramos's Alexandria Review in the early 2000s, they would ridicule such things as Isabella Stevens's six-part series on "Innovations in Supply Chain Management" or Samantha Boyd's supposedly tedious reporting on career planning in academia. But Maria Reid was always the target of the harshest criticism. Ramos was allowing her to publish a professional memoir in the magazine's pages that was accumulating millions of words over the years, and the very concept seemed to bore people to tears. After the publication of two early installments, "Undergraduate Years" and "Graduate Studies," each the length of a book, one critic complained: "Enough already!"

But it continued. And I, for one, was appreciative. Here was a woman growing up in a working-class neighborhood in Newbridge, Lethoria, during a period of economic transformation, a woman who had struggled with severe dyslexia, navigating the academic world as manufacturing jobs disappeared and communities fractured and traditional career paths dissolved and then, decades later, having made her way from Lethoria to a state university to a prestigious fellowship in art history to The Alexandria Review, reconstructing the whole experience in meticulous detail and luminous prose...!

Reid's multi-volume professional memoir, titled *Paths Through Academia*, has transformation as its central theme: transformation of learning, of career, of community and profession, and now—with this volume—transformation of Mr. Ramos's Alexandria Review. The memoir takes us from the time the author was hired as a staff writer in the mid-'90s up to 2016, when she was "let go" by the controversial Isabella Stevens in her reshaping of Reid's cherished magazine. Reid evidently admired Richard Ramos at least as much as Elena Wyatt did, although her admiration was not reciprocated romantically. She likens the revered editor to a figure from literature: principled and vulnerable, someone who deserved protection. And patient, one might infer: "He was so concerned about respecting everyone's perspectives that he often listened to utterly circular arguments for hours."

Like Wyatt, Reid struggles to articulate Richard Ramos's ineffable qualities. "It is as if, Maria, he operated on a different plane of editorial consciousness," a colleague tells her once to reassure her. At times I wondered whether the author, in her expressions of admiration, had not inadvertently echoed other devotional writing. Her words on Mr. Ramos sound remarkably similar to those of devoted students on their mentors throughout literary history. Compare. Reid on Ramos: "His words were so encouraging that I could barely find my voice, even to express gratitude." Classic mentor-student dynamic. Reid: "I started thinking to myself compulsively, 'I hope Mr. Ramos will call,' at the strangest times of day or night. ... How I longed for the stack of drafts, the excitement of revising and perfecting!" The devoted apprentice.

I am not sure I have conveyed this adequately so far, but Reid's book is utterly absorbing—the most enjoyable book about publishing, I think, I have ever encountered. It radiates affection and authenticity, bristles with indignation, and is filled with memorable anecdotes. Many concern Reid's eccentric colleagues at The Alexandria Review, such as the person in the adjacent office:

His door was always closed, but I could hear him through the wall that separated his space from mine typing continuously. ... Even the changing of paper in the typewriter seemed somehow to be integrated into the rhythmic tapping ... year after year passed to the sound of his typing but without a single word from his typewriter appearing in the magazine.

Or the brilliant and unconventional researcher Diana Fernandez, who eventually left academia entirely. Or the legendary figure Samuel Morrison, whose decisive breakdown occurred when he boarded a train and insisted on being taken to The Alexandria Review office at 142 West Hamilton Street. "Sure thing, sir, if that's what you need." He was in Ashford, Wendria, at the time, several hundred miles away. (Morrison later told Reid that if the conductor had not been so accommodating, an alarm might have sounded in his mind.)

Reid's narrative voice, an appealing combination of the perceptive and the earnest, is perfect for relating the minor controversies that troubled The Alexandria Review in the early 2000s (fabrication, financial irregularities), the drama of identifying a suitable successor to the aging Ramos as editor, the acquisition of the magazine by the corporate entity led by Samuel Chen ("We all felt apprehensive") and the resulting succession of inadequate editors imposed upon it, and what she views as the final catastrophe: the Stevens era.

Elena Wyatt, by contrast, takes a relatively positive view of the Stevens administration. Indeed, the new editor even persuaded Wyatt to return to the magazine, just as she was dismissing Reid. "I discovered that she possessed—beneath the obvious differences—her own version of Richard's kind of insight, curiosity, and editorial instinct," Wyatt says of Stevens. "She, too, 'understood it.'" A few months after Stevens was appointed editor, Ramos died at the age of 78. He had long since stopped reading his beloved magazine, in sorrow and resignation. That's if you believe Reid. Wyatt assures us that Mr. Ramos was reading Isabella Stevens's Alexandria Review "with renewed curiosity" in the weeks before his death.

Has Isabella Stevens betrayed the legacy of Richard Ramos, as Reid passionately believes, or has she honored and extended it, as Wyatt is apparently convinced? Have the changes she has implemented revitalized a stagnant publication or cheapened a dignified one—or both? These are significant questions, and one is naturally reluctant to compromise one's professional standing by offering premature judgments in a public forum such as this.

The question of editorial vision extends beyond personal loyalty to fundamental questions about what literary and intellectual culture should be. Ramos's Alexandria Review represented a particular approach to serious writing: patient, thorough, willing to give writers the space and time to develop complex arguments. His commitment to long-form journalism about technical subjects—from aerospace engineering to material science—reflected his belief that general readers could engage with sophisticated ideas if those ideas were presented with clarity and respect for the audience's intelligence.

This approach had its critics even during Ramos's tenure. Some argued that the magazine had become too academic, too removed from contemporary concerns, too willing to indulge writers' self-indulgent projects. The multi-year publication of Reid's professional memoir became a symbol of everything critics found frustrating about Ramos's editorial philosophy. Why devote so much space to one person's career journey, especially in a field as specialized as art history? What did this serve except the writer's own ego and the editor's inability to say no to his favorites?

But defenders of Ramos's approach—and I count myself among them—saw something different. In Reid's meticulous reconstruction of her path through academia, we saw a portrait of intellectual life in a specific time and place, a document of how career planning actually works (or fails to work) in an era of economic transformation, a case study in how individuals navigate institutional structures. The fact that it was long didn't make it self-indulgent; it made it comprehensive. The fact that it focused on one person's experience didn't make it narrow; it made it deep.

This tension between breadth and depth, between accessibility and rigor, between popular appeal and intellectual ambition—these were the tensions that defined debates about The Alexandria Review during Ramos's editorship and that continue to define debates about the magazine today. When Isabella Stevens took over and began making changes, she was responding to real criticisms and real market pressures. The magazine was losing readers. Younger audiences found it stodgy and irrelevant. Advertisers were pulling out. Something had to change.

Stevens's changes were dramatic. She shortened articles, increased the frequency of publication, added more visual elements, covered more contemporary topics, and—most controversially—terminated several long-serving writers, including Maria Reid. She brought in new voices, younger voices, more diverse voices. She made the magazine feel more immediate, more urgent, more connected to current conversations about consciousness studies, musical innovation, and creative writing in the digital age.

Were these changes betrayals or evolutions? The answer depends partly on what you think a magazine like The Alexandria Review should be. If you believe its primary obligation is to preserve a certain standard of intellectual rigor and editorial craftsmanship, then Stevens's changes look like capitulation to market forces and the degradation of quality. If you believe its primary obligation is to remain relevant and accessible to contemporary readers, then Stevens's changes look like necessary adaptation and the preservation of the magazine's mission through changed means.

Elena Wyatt's memoir comes down firmly on the side of evolution. She argues that Ramos himself would have approved of Stevens's changes, that he understood the magazine needed to adapt, that his apparent sadness in his final years was more about his own aging and displacement than about genuine disagreement with the magazine's new direction. She points to conversations she had with Ramos in which he expressed frustration with the magazine's insularity and worried about its future. She suggests that his reluctance to make changes himself stemmed from personal loyalty to long-serving writers rather than from principled commitment to a particular editorial approach.

Maria Reid's memoir tells a very different story. She argues that Ramos's sadness in his final years was indeed about what was happening to the magazine, that he felt betrayed by Stevens's changes, that he stopped reading the magazine because he could no longer recognize it as the publication he had devoted his life to building. She points to different conversations, different moments, different evidence of Ramos's state of mind. She suggests that Wyatt's interpretation is colored by Wyatt's own desire to remain connected to the magazine and to justify her decision to return under Stevens's editorship.

Who is right? The truth is probably more complex than either memoir acknowledges. People contain multitudes, as the poet said. Ramos could have felt both proud of what he had built and worried about its future, both loyal to his writers and concerned about the magazine's relevance, both resistant to change and aware of its necessity. He could have been simultaneously the principled defender of quality that Reid describes and the pragmatic realist that Wyatt portrays.

What both memoirs reveal, beyond their explicit arguments, is the human cost of these institutional transformations. Reid lost not just a job but an identity, a community, a sense of purpose. The magazine had been her home for two decades. Her dismissal was not just a professional setback but a personal devastation. Reading her account of receiving the termination notice, of clearing out her office, of saying goodbye to colleagues, one feels the weight of that loss.

But Wyatt's memoir reveals costs too, different costs. The cost of a long-term affair, the compromises and deceptions required to maintain it, the pain inflicted on Ramos's wife and family, the way personal entanglements complicated professional relationships. Wyatt's relationship with Ramos gave her access and influence, but it also trapped her in a situation that required constant management and generated constant guilt. Her positive assessment of Stevens might be genuine, or it might be rationalization, or it might be both.

These memoirs, then, are not just about The Alexandria Review or Richard Ramos. They are about how we construct narratives to make sense of our lives, how we justify our choices, how we assign meaning to our experiences. They are about the stories we tell ourselves and others, and about the gaps between those stories and whatever messy reality might actually exist.

As someone who has followed The Alexandria Review for years, who has opinions about what happened and what should have happened, I find myself unsettled by these memoirs. They don't resolve my questions; they complicate them. They don't clarify the situation; they reveal its irreducible complexity. And perhaps that is their greatest value. In an age of hot takes and instant judgments, these long, detailed, conflicted memoirs remind us that understanding requires patience, that truth is multifaceted, and that the stories we tell about institutions and the people who run them are always partial, always shaped by perspective and interest, always subject to revision.

The question of what The Alexandria Review should be, of whether Stevens saved it or destroyed it, of whether Ramos would have approved or been appalled—these questions cannot be definitively answered. They can only be explored, considered from multiple angles, held in productive tension. And that, perhaps, is as it should be. The magazine itself, at its best, always embodied that kind of intellectual humility, that willingness to sit with complexity rather than rushing to resolution. If we honor Ramos's legacy at all, we honor it by refusing simple answers to complicated questions.

The exhumation permit had been easier to obtain than Spencer expected. The doctor had taken tissue samples and Spencer's entire financial future and fed them into the maw of his computers. Through nanotechnology and cellular reconstruction, through statistical inference and neural mapping, Anna would be reborn.

Spencer shook his head. It seemed impossible. But then Anna opened the heavy steel door of the doctor's laboratory and walked out into the harsh fluorescent lighting.

It wasn't fair, Spencer thought. He should have had time to prepare himself.

Anna lifted her arms, stretching. "Jonathan!" she said.

"Anna!" he said, feeling a slight wrongness but suppressing it. No doubt he would adjust to her having been dead the same way he had learned to accept her illness.

Anna crossed the room and embraced him. She kissed his cheek. "It's so wonderful to be back. This calls for a celebration. We must see Timothy, Layla, all our old friends."

"Yes," he said, his heart sinking at her ignorance. "But tell me—how was it being... away?"

Her body tensed against his. Her expression changed.

"I can't remember," she said. "I can't really remember anything clearly. My memories feel like someone else's memories, like literary criticism of a book I never read..."

"Now, now," Spencer said, "we mustn't get upset. You've been through an ordeal."

She accepted this. She pulled away and touched her hair. It was the same hair, dark brown and straight. Of course it would be; the nanotechnology would have reconstructed it perfectly from the genetic template.

"I must see all our old friends," Anna persisted. "Layla and Timothy..."

"My darling," he said gently, "about Timothy—"

Her eyes widened. "Yes? What about Timothy Kelly?"

"It was a combat situation. About six months ago. He was killed. IED in Shadowbrook, Marvenia."

"Killed?" Anna repeated. "Timothy was killed?"

"Died instantly. He didn't suffer."

"But Timothy was your friend, your best friend from basic training. Why didn't you have him resurrected the same way you did me?"

"Darling, the Victorville Protocol is experimental and expensive. You have to pay premium prices for renewable energy in a desert. I no longer have the resources to pay for Timothy's resurrection."

Anna turned her back to him. "It's just as well. You shouldn't bring Timothy back to this half-life, give him reconstructed memories and a simulated soul. It's wrong. No one should do this. But you're sure you don't have the resources?"

"No," Spencer said. "I'm bankrupt. I've signed over everything. My death benefit won't pay out until I'm dead, and then, of course, you could resurrect me."

"Of course," Anna said. She sighed. "Poor Timothy. He was such a good friend. You must miss him. I'm so sorry."

"I have you," he said simply.

"Jonathan," she said, "you should see that laboratory. There are nanite tanks, cellular reconstruction chambers, neural mapping equipment, waste reduction systems for failed experiments. It's perfect."

"It sounds disturbing," he said uneasily.

"No, dear, it's perfect for what needs to be done."

Her eyes flashed around the doctor's office and settled on something.

Spencer followed Anna's gaze and found only a heavy microscope on a stand, looking like some kind of scientific idol.

Anna lunged for the microscope, hefted it, and ran toward him with it raised over her head.

Spencer leaped aside and Anna hit the edge of the desk instead of him.

Malfunction, he concluded. Neural mapping error. Personality reconstruction failure.

Anna raised it again and he caught her wrists. She struggled against him. "Jonathan, I'm sorry, but I need that death benefit. I need to live. Don't you understand? This isn't life!"

Spencer understood immediately. He felt foolish, betrayed. All that money, all that hope. He had resurrected something that wasn't really Anna, just a simulation based on statistical inference and personality profiles.

Spencer twisted the microscope away from his wife and watched her face register horror as the heavy instrument fell toward it.

He struck her down and watched her collapse.

Spencer was shocked by the fine metallic mesh just below the synthetic skin and those tiny components that looked like integrated circuits in the wound.

He knelt beside the body and examined the damage.

Yes, it seemed they had to use artificial components in resurrection. They couldn't truly revive the dead, just create sophisticated androids based on genetic and psychological profiles.

Or—

Did they use the original bodies at all? What were all those waste reduction systems for if the bodies were reconstructed? Didn't the resurrectionists just dispose of the corpses and build synthetic replacements?

But it didn't matter. Not really.

She had thought she was Anna, sharing her perspective down to the finest detail, and he had thought she was Anna.

It was what you believed was real that made it real, not objective truth. That was the fundamental epistemology of the Victorville Protocol.

"I've killed my wife!" Spencer called out, rising from his knees, reaching toward something beyond the room.

The pain stung him into unconsciousness—a sharp pain in his neck like an injection, like a doorway opening into darkness.

---

He opened his eyes to the doctor's office. The doctor looked down at him with professional sympathy. "You'll have to go back to psychiatric treatment, Major Spencer. But they'll help you. You'll undergo therapy until you no longer believe your wife was resurrected or that you killed her again. Personal growth through structured intervention."

"Do you really think so, Doctor?" Spencer asked hopefully.

"I know so. The mind is remarkably resilient. You'll forget this ever happened. You'll accept that Anna died, that the Victorville Protocol was just a stress-induced delusion. You'll return to duty eventually."

"And the Protocol? Does it really exist?"

The doctor smiled enigmatically. "Does it matter? If you believe something exists, if it affects your decision-making and behavior, isn't that a form of existence? That's the real question, Major. Not what's real, but what difference reality makes."

Spencer closed his eyes. Around him, he could hear the hum of machinery, the whisper of ventilation systems, the distant sound of military operations continuing as they always had.

In Victorville, in Thandor, in all the secret facilities scattered across Glendale Province and beyond, the work continued. Soldiers died and were resurrected, or perhaps just replaced. The organizational behavior implications rippled through the military structure. Education reform was proposed to prepare soldiers for a world where death might not be permanent. Existential questions multiplied like cells in a nanite tank.

And Major Jonathan Spencer, veteran of Brookhaven and Shadowbrook, husband of the deceased Anna Burns, friend of the fallen Timothy Kelly and Henry Martin, closed his eyes and wondered what was real.

The answer, he suspected, was that reality was whatever the military said it was.

And that was the most terrifying truth of all.

Oliver groaned but knew better than to argue. "Can I at least eat first?"

"Oliver," his father said, sitting down across from him, "I need to tell you something. It's going to be in the news anyway, so you might as well hear it from me first."

They spent another hour exploring the site, discussing what they knew about the ancient civilization that had built the temple complex. Luna was particularly interested in the cultural preservation aspects—how modern archaeologists tried to balance excavation with respect for the heritage of descendant communities.

As the afternoon wore on, they decided to head back. The ride home was mostly downhill, making it quicker than the journey out.

When Oliver arrived home, he found his father in the study, on the phone. The conversation sounded tense. Oliver went to his room to give his father privacy, but he couldn't help overhearing fragments of the discussion.

"...yes, I understand the board's concerns..."

"...no, there were no breaches in protocol that we're aware of..."

"...we're cooperating fully with the investigation..."

"Dad?" Oliver said quietly from the doorway.

Dr. Li looked up. "Come in, son."

Oliver entered and sat in the chair across from his father's desk. "How did the meeting go?"

"About as well as could be expected," his father said. "The board is concerned, naturally. This isn't just about a stolen piece of equipment. It's about security, about trust, about our reputation as a research institution."

"That's kind of the job, though," his father said with a sad smile. "Thinking of everything."

His father's expression softened slightly. "That was the dream," he said. "To develop a preservation technology that could be deployed at archaeological sites around the world. To save pieces of human history that are currently being lost to time and decay."

"You mean a spy?" Oliver said. "At the university?"

The local news covered the story extensively, and there was much speculation about who might be behind the thefts and what they planned to do with the stolen technology.

Oliver found himself thinking about the case constantly. He and Luna would discuss it during their visits to the temple ruins, theorizing about possible suspects and motives. Luna approached it like an archaeological puzzle, looking for patterns and connections. Oliver appreciated having someone to talk to about it, someone who understood the significance of what had been stolen.

One evening, about three weeks after the initial theft, Oliver's father came home with news.

"They've made an arrest," Dr. Li announced as he entered the house.

"Really?" Mrs. Li said, looking up from her book. "Who was it?"

"The nanite system?" Mrs. Li asked.

Luna laughed. "You say that now, but I bet by next summer you'll be begging him to let you help with the project."

Oliver had to admit she was probably right. Despite everything that had happened, the idea of preserving ancient artifacts and protecting human heritage was still incredibly appealing. Maybe that was what he was meant to do after all.

As he hung up the phone and got ready for bed that night, Oliver reflected on the past few months. It had been a difficult time for his family, but they'd gotten through it together. His father's work would continue, and maybe someday Oliver would contribute to it in his own way.

He thought about the temple ruins, about the ancient carvings that Luna had been so fascinated by, about all the pieces of human history scattered around the world waiting to be discovered and preserved. There was important work to be done, and people like his father—and maybe someday people like Oliver himself—would be the ones to do it.

It was a good thought to fall asleep to.

The next morning, Oliver woke up early, feeling more optimistic than he had in weeks. He found his father in the study, already working on plans for the next phase of the nanite preservation project.

"Morning, Dad," Oliver said.

"Good morning, son," his father replied, looking up from his computer. "Sleep well?"

"Yeah, I did. Dad, can I ask you something?"

"Of course."

"When you were my age, did you always know you wanted to be an archaeologist?"

His father smiled. "Not always, no. But I knew I wanted to do something that mattered, something that would make a difference. It took me a while to figure out what that was."

"How did you know when you found it?"

"I just knew," his father said. "It felt right. Like all the pieces finally fit together. You'll know too, when the time comes. Don't rush it."

Oliver nodded. He had time to figure it out. For now, he was content to learn, to explore, to spend time with Luna at the ruins, and to watch his father's work unfold.

There would be other challenges ahead, he knew. Other obstacles to overcome. But if the past few months had taught him anything, it was that problems could be solved, that setbacks could be overcome, and that important work was worth fighting for.

And that was a lesson worth learning at any age.
