SHADOW PROTOCOL
By MARINA JENKINS

Every colony has problems—but especially a colony that is mining asteroids in the outer belt with AI oversight!

Sure I'm a Shadow, and I've been "terminated" nine times, always in the isolation of deep space mining operations, and I'm not alone, although there aren't very many of us, never were.

It made sense. DeepCore Mining was new to full AI integration and they wanted him on the station because he was a trained data analyst. They wanted facts, not speculation. But to ask a man to give up eighteen months of his life—well, that was asking a lot. Eighteen months in a rotating habitat. Still, it had an appeal Oscar Webb knew he couldn't deny, a researcher's joy of clean data sets, an asteroid field far afield, a closeup view of renewable energy harvesting at scale, history in the making.

Operations Director Leonardo Montgomery knocked the stylus against his tablet, saying, "DataStream Analytics is willing to let you have a leave of absence, if you're interested."

He knew Chief Administrator Catherine Russell from years of conferences, and now Russell said, "Personally, I don't want to see anybody else on the job. You've got a fine record in this sort of field research."

Oscar Webb smiled, but just barely. "You should have called me for the first rotation."

Russell nodded. "I wish we had had you on Highpoint Station Alpha."

"Miners," Montgomery said, "make poor observers."

Highpoint Station Alpha had launched the first rotation to the Cedarville Asteroid Cluster three years before with two thousand workers, reached the site with less than twelve hundred functional crew members. Upon the return to Earth orbit six months later, the crew's report of conflict and chaos during the nine-month outward journey was twisted, distorted and fragmentary. Webb remembered it well. The decision of DeepCore was that the workers started a rebellion far out in the belt, that it was fanned by the ignorance of Station Commander Vincent Baker in dealing with such matters.

"Isolation affects people in a peculiar way," Russell said. "We have conquered the problem of small groups in space—witness the discovery of the Cedarville Cluster, for example—but when there are large groups with AI management, control is more difficult."

"Baker," Montgomery said, "was authoritarian. The trouble started at about the halfway point. It ended with workers engaging in open warfare with each other and the AI systems. Baker was lucky to escape with his career."

"As I recall," Webb said, "there was something about the 3D printing facilities."

Russell rubbed her chin. "No weapons were allowed on the station, but you must remember the workers were selected for their intelligence and resourcefulness. They utilized these attributes to hack the 3D printing systems to manufacture makeshift weapons."

"The second rotation is history," Montgomery said. "And a puzzle."

Webb nodded. "The station went dark."

"Yes. We gave control to an advanced AI system."

"Assuming no accident in space," Russell said, "it was a wrong decision. They probably sabotaged the network."

"And now," Webb said, "you're going to try again."

Montgomery said very gravely, "We've got the finest station commander in the industry. Jennifer Lambert. No doubt you've heard of her. She's spent her life managing orbital facilities, and she's handpicking her own staff. We have also raised prerequisites for applicants. We don't think anything is going to happen, but if it does, we want to get an impersonal, unprejudiced view. That's where you come in. You do the observing, the data analysis. We'll evaluate it on your return."

"If I return," said Webb.

"I suppose that's problematical," Russell said, "but I think you will. Commander Lambert and her eighty staff members want to return as badly as you do." She grinned. "You can write that paper on complexity science you're always talking about on your return trip on Highpoint Station Beta."

Being a Shadow is important, probably as important as running the station, and I think it is this thought that keeps us satisfied, willing to be what we are.

Highpoint Station Beta had been built in Earth orbit, as had its predecessor, Highpoint Station Alpha, at a tremendous cost. Basically, it was an instrument which would open distant asteroid fields to resource extraction, reducing the supply chain management pressures of a resource-depleted Earth. A gigantic, rotating torus, the station would never land anywhere, but would orbit the Cedarville Cluster as it had orbited Earth, processing its cargo and housing its workers for the promised profits, the new frontier. A space-borne industrial complex, it would be the home for two thousand persons outward bound, only the staff on the return trip. It was equipped with every conceivable facility and comfort—dining facilities, assembly hall, individual and family quarters, recreation areas, hydroponic gardens, library, virtual reality theater. Nothing had been overlooked.

The commander's briefing room was crowded, the air was heavy with the breathing of so many people, and the ventilators could not quite clear the air of recycled atmosphere that drifted aimlessly here and there before it was caught and whisked away.

In the tradition of data analyst and observer, Oscar Webb tried to be as inconspicuous as possible, pressing against a bulkhead, but Commander Lambert's eyes sought his several times as Lambert listened to final reports from her engineers, resource managers, energy systems specialists, AI coordinators, and all the rest. She grunted her approval or disapproval, made a suggestion here, a restriction there. There was no doubt that Lambert was in charge, yet there was a human quality about her that Webb liked. The commander's was a sharp face, well composed, and her eyes were chips of gray.

"Colleagues," Lambert said at last, as Webb knew she would, "I want to introduce Oscar Webb, whose presence DeepCore has impressed upon us. On loan from DataStream, he will have an observer status." She introduced him to the others. All of them seemed professional; Webb thought it was a good staff.

Lambert detained him after the others had gone. "One thing, Mr. Webb. To make it easier for you, I suggest you think of this journey strictly from the observer viewpoint. There will be no paper for DataStream at the end."

Webb was startled. While he had considered the possibility, he had not dwelt on it. Now it loomed large in his mind. "I don't understand, Commander Lambert. It seems to me—"

"Let me put it differently. Let me say that you will not understand why I say that until the journey ends." She smiled. "Perhaps I shouldn't have mentioned it."

Webb left the commander's quarters with an odd taste in his mouth. Now why had Lambert said that? Why hadn't Montgomery or Russell said something, if it was important?

He made himself comfortable in his eight-foot-by-eight-foot quarters, which is to say he dropped on his bed, found it more comfortable than he thought it would be, put his arms behind his head, stared at the ceiling. Metal walls, one viewport, one floor vent, one ceiling vent, and a solitary ceiling panel light. This would be his home for eighteen months, just as there were homes like it for two thousand others, except that the family quarters would be larger. His quarters were in the inner ring near the officers' section.

He felt rather than heard the dull vibration. It was a sound he knew would be with him for eighteen months—nine months going and nine months returning.

He looked at his tablet, opened his data collection app and made an entry. The station right now would be slipping ever so slowly away from Earth orbit. He got up. He'd have to go forward to the observation dome to see that. Last view of Earth for eighteen months.

The penetration of deep space by large groups is the coming out from under the traditions of thousands of years, and as these planet-originated rules fall away, the floundering group seeks a new control, for they are humanity adrift, rudderless, for whom the stars are no longer bearings but nonexistent things, and values are altered if they are not shown the way.

The theft of Teresa Hicks's research drive occurred on the forty-third day out. In Webb's mind the incident, though insignificant from the standpoint of the station as a whole, could very well be the cause of dissension later on. His notes covering it were therefore very thorough.

Hicks's drive contained genetic sequences for renewable energy organisms—thousands of them, according to the Commander's Bulletin, the station's daily newsletter which went to all staff and workers. In the Bulletin the commander appealed to the thief to return the drive to Dr. Hicks. She said it was significant that all en route had passed psychological evaluations, and that it was to the station's discredit that someone with criminal tendencies should have been permitted aboard.

Webb had to smile at that. What did Commander Lambert think of those workers who sabotaged each other on Highpoint Alpha? They had passed psychological evaluations too. This, then, was what happened when you took two thousand strangers and stuck them in a rotating can for nine months.

When Webb saw Lambert about it, the commander said, "Of course I realize it takes only a little thing like this to set things off. I know people get tired of seeing each other, running the same simulations, looking at the asteroids from the observation dome, walking down the same corridors, reading the same files, eating the same meals, though God knows we try to vary it as much as we can. Isolation creates rough edges. But the point is, we know all this, and knowing it, we shouldn't let it happen. We've got to find that thief."

"What would they want genetic sequences for? Have you thought of that?"

"Of course. They'd have real value at Cedarville. Green infrastructure for the colony stations."

Webb sought out Teresa Hicks. She was a young woman with an intense face and determined eyes. She said, "Now what am I going to Cedarville for? I could only take along so much data storage and I deleted some personal files to make room for the sequences. I'm a bioengineering specialist, and DeepCore asked me to go along. But what use am I now? Where am I going to get sequences like those? Do you know how long it took me to develop them? They're not ordinary organisms, Mr. Webb."

There was an appeal from Hicks in the next day's newsletter describing the sequences, telling of their value, and requesting their return in the interests of the Cedarville colony and of humanity.

On the forty-seventh day a witness turned up who said she had seen a person emerging from Hicks's quarters with the silver drive. "I didn't think anything of it at the time," Marina Jenkins said.

Lambert asked her to describe the person.

"Oh, they were about average height, medium build, and they wore a black environmental mask that covered their face completely."

"Didn't you think that was important?" Lambert asked in an outraged voice. "A person wearing a black mask?"

Jenkins shrugged. "This is a space station. How would I know whether a black mask—or a red or blue one—does or doesn't belong on a space station?"

Although Jenkins' account appeared in the newsletter, it was largely discounted.

"If it is true," Lambert told Webb, "the theft must be the work of someone unstable. But I don't believe Marina Jenkins. It may well be she's the unstable one." She snorted. "Black environmental mask! I think I'll have Jenkins put through additional psychological evaluation."

Attendant to taking notes on this incident, Webb noted a strange thing. Hicks lived in that part of the station known as Sector One, and those who lived in that sector—more than five hundred men, women and children—felt that the thief must surely live in Sector Two or Four. Valentina Brown, who had the quarters next to Hicks's, sounded the consensus when she said, "Surely a person wouldn't steal from their own sector, now would they, Mr. Webb?"

And so, Webb observed in his notebook, are conflicts created.

Seen in space, asteroids are tumbling, silent, mineral-rich masses ever present and indifferent. To people unused to it, such a sight numbs, compresses, stultifies. They introduce a countermeasure, proof they exist, which is any overt act, sometimes violent.

On the sixty-second day Catherine Russell, the young wife of one of the resource engineers, ran screaming down one of the long corridors of Sector Three. She told the commander she had been attacked in her quarters while her husband was in the station's data center. She was taken to one of the station's doctors, who confirmed it.

She said the culprit was a person of average build wearing a black environmental mask, and though her description of what they had done did not appear in the story in the newsletter, it lost no time in penetrating every quarter of the station.

Webb was present when a delegation from Sector Three called on Commander Lambert, demanding action.

Lambert remained seated behind her desk, unperturbed, saying, "I have no staff to spare for security duty."

The delegation commenced speaking vehemently, to be quieted by Lambert's raised hand.

"I sympathize," Lambert said, "but it is up to each sector to deal with its problems, whatever they may be. My job is to get us to Cedarville."

The group left in a surly mood.

"You wonder at my reluctance, Mr. Webb," Commander Lambert said. "But suppose I assign the staff to patrol duties, the culprit isn't caught, and further incidents occur. What then? It soon becomes the staff's fault. And soon the workers will begin thinking these things might be the staff's doing in the first place."

"Yes," Webb said, "but what if the intruder is a staff member?"

"I know my people," Lambert said flatly.

"You could have a search for the mask and the research drive."

"Do you think it is a member of the staff?" Lambert's eyes were bright. "No, I trust my people. I won't violate that trust."

Webb left, feeling uneasy. If he were Lambert, he'd initiate an investigation, if nothing else than to prove the staff guiltless. Why couldn't Lambert see the wisdom of setting an example for the workers?

As a Shadow, I knew that isolation breeds hostility. There is a seed of malevolence in every person. It sometimes blossoms out among the asteroids. On Highpoint Beta it was ready for ripening.

Vincent Baker was killed in the station's medical bay on the eighty-fourth day. Baker, a Sector Four worker, had complained of feeling ill, had been hospitalized with a diagnosis of appendicitis. He had put his credit chip in the drawer of the small stand beside his bed. A person in a black mask was seen hurrying from the medical area, and a staff investigation revealed that Baker had died trying to prevent the theft of the chip.

Commander Lambert did not wait for the newsletter. Through the station's communication system, she reported that Baker had significant credits on the chip and had died of severe trauma. She said that since the incident occurred in the staff section of the station, her staff would be forced to submit to a thorough inspection in an effort to find the mask, the drive, the chip and the perpetrator.

"I will not countenance such an act by a staff member," Lambert said. "If and when they are found, they will be severely dealt with. But they might not be a member of the staff. I am ordering an assembly of all workers at nine tomorrow morning in the auditorium. I will speak to you all then."

Faces were angry, voices were sharp at the meeting, eyes suspicious and tempers short. Above it all was the commanding presence of Commander Lambert speaking to them.

"It is not my desire to interfere in worker affairs," she said. "Insofar as the station is concerned, it is my duty to make certain no staff member is guilty. This I am doing. But my staff is not and cannot be a security force for you. It is up to you people to police and protect yourselves."

"How can we protect ourselves without stunners?" one worker called out.

"Has Black Mask a weapon?" Lambert retorted. "It seems to me you have a better defense than any gun."

"What's that?"

"This station is only so wide, so long and so deep. If every inch is searched, you'll find your perpetrator. They have to be somewhere aboard."

The workers quieted. Leonardo Montgomery, one of the senior engineers, was elected president of the newly formed Sector Council. One person from each of the sectors was named to serve under him. Each of these people in turn selected five others from their own group.

Those assembled waited in the hall while each team of six inspected the quarters of the others. These quarters were then locked, everyone returned to their quarters, and the larger search was conducted. It took twenty-eight hours.

No mask was found. No mask, no drive, no chip, no perpetrator.

The commander reported that her search had been equally fruitless. At another assembly the following day it was decided to make the inspection teams permanent, to await further moves on the part of Black Mask. The Sector Council held periodic meetings to set up a method of trial for them when they were caught. It was all recorded in the newsletter and by Oscar Webb.

We Shadows know about hostility and about violence. We know too that where there is hostility there is violence, and where there is violence there is death.

During sleep time on the 109th day Marina Jenkins, awakened by a strange sound, sat up in the bed of her quarters to find a person in a black mask in her room. Her cries brought neighbors into the corridor. The flight of the person was witnessed by many, and several people tried to stop them. But the intruder was quick on their feet and fast. They escaped.

The Sector Council confronted the commander, demanding weapons.

"Are you out of your minds?" Lambert exclaimed.

Leonardo Montgomery, Sector Four leader, said, "We want to set up a security force, Commander. We want stunners."

"There's no regulation against it," Lambert said, "but it's a policy of mine that no weapons are to be issued en route."

"If we had had a weapon, we'd have got Black Mask," Montgomery said.

"And I might have a death on my conscience."

Montgomery said, "We've also thought of that. Suppose you supply us with low-power stunners? That way we can stun but not kill."

They got their weapons. Now there were thirty-two security personnel on duty in the corridors—ten on at a time. Webb observed that for the first time the workers seemed relaxed.

Let Black Mask move against armed people, they said.

Yeah, let them see what happens now.

Black Mask did.

On the 139th day they were seen in a corridor in Sector Four. Valentina Brown, security on duty, managed to squeeze off several shots at their retreating figure.

Black Mask was seen again on the 165th day, on the 186th day, and the 217th day. They were seen, shot at, but not hit. They were also unable to commit any crime.

We've got them on the run, the workers said.

They're afraid to do anything, now that we've got security, they said smugly.

The Sector Council congratulated itself. The workers were proud of themselves. A special congratulatory message from Commander Lambert appeared one day in the Bulletin newsletter.

The workers settled down to living out the rest of the voyage until the arrival at Cedarville.

But on the 234th day calamity struck. Black Mask appropriated one of the stunners, made their way down one whole corridor section in Sector Two, put occupants to sleep as they went, taking many articles of value and leaving disorder behind.

Webb interviewed as many victims as he could, noted it all in his database. The things taken were keepsakes, photographs and items of personal value. It seemed to be the work of someone deranged. If Black Mask wanted to make everyone furious, they certainly succeeded.

"What do they want that stuff for?" Teresa Hicks, now working as a medical assistant, asked. "I can see them taking my bioengineering notes, my research files—but my grandmother's necklace? That I don't understand."

It was the same with others. "The person's insane, Mr. Webb. Positively insane." Many people said it.

The council issued orders that all workers from now on would be required to lock their quarters at all times. More weapons were obtained from the commander. More security personnel were appointed.

Webb was busy noting it all in his database. It became filled with entries about innocent people being accidentally stunned when trigger-happy security thought their movements suspicious, about one person's suspicion of another and the ensuing search of quarters, people who saw Black Mask here, saw them there. Hardly a day went by without some new development.

"Oh, yes, Mr. Webb, we're going to get them," said Montgomery, now chief of security, cracking his knuckles, his eyes intense with the thought. "We're bound to get them. We've got things worked out to the finest detail. They won't be able to get through our net now. Just let them make so much as a move."

"And what will you do when you get them?"

"Terminate them," Montgomery said, his eyes glowing more fiercely than ever.

"Without a trial?"

"Oh, there'll be a trial, Mr. Webb, but you don't think any jury would let them live after all the things they've done, do you?"

Black Mask was stunned in Sector Four in a corridor by a security officer named Jennifer Lambert on the 277th day. The criminal was carried to the assembly room surrounded by guards, for they surely would have been harmed, if not killed, by angry workers who crowded around. In the assembly hall their mask was removed. The crowd gasped. Nobody knew them.

Webb's first thought was that they must be a stowaway, but then he remembered the face, and Commander Lambert, who came to have a look at them, unhappily admitted the person was a member of the staff. Their name was Vincent Baker and they were a data systems analyst third class.

"Well, Baker," Lambert said to them, "what have you got to say for yourself?"

"Nothing you'd understand," Baker said quietly. As if it were an afterthought, they turned away from the commander.

Lambert looked as if she were going to terminate the person herself right there and then.

It was a long trial—from the 303rd to the 331st day—and there didn't seem to be much doubt about the outcome, for Baker didn't help their own cause during any of it.

Catherine Russell, who was appointed prosecutor, asked them, "What did you do with the stolen items, Baker?"

Baker looked her square in the eye and said, "I jettisoned them through one of the waste airlocks. Does that answer your question?"

"Jettisoned them?" Russell and the crowd were incredulous.

"Sure," Baker said. "You workers got the easy life as passengers, just sitting around. I had to work constantly managing data systems for you lazy people."

The verdict was, of course, termination.

They executed Vincent Baker on the morning of the 372nd day with blasts from six stunners supplied with full power. It was witnessed by a great crowd in the assembly hall. A detail from the station's staff disposed of their body through an airlock.

It was all duly recorded in Oscar Webb's database.

Dying is easy for a Shadow. Especially if it's arranged for beforehand, which it always is.

Highpoint Station Beta was only one day out of Cedarville orbit when Commander Lambert sent for Webb and introduced him to the executed person.

"Hello," Baker said, grinning from ear to ear.

"I figured as much," Webb said. "I've been doing a lot of data analysis."

"You're perhaps a little too good as an observer," Lambert said. "Or maybe it was because you really weren't one of the workers. But no matter, Baker did a good job. They were trained by an old colleague of mine for this job, Gelthorpe Shadow. Shadow used to be in institutional reform when there were corporate wars."

"You were excellent," Webb said.

"Can't say I enjoyed the role," said Baker, "but I think it saved lives."

"Let me get this straight. DeepCore thought that it was isolation and boredom that caused the conflicts on Highpoint Alpha, so they had you trained to be a scapegoat. Is that right?"

Baker nodded. "When great numbers are being transported, they are apt to magnify each little event because so little happens. It was my job to see that they directed none of their hostility against each other or the staff, only toward me."

Lambert smiled. "It made the time pass quickly and interestingly for the workers."

"To say nothing of me," Baker said.

"And you, Mr. Webb, were along to observe it all," Commander Lambert put in. "DeepCore wanted an accurate picture of this. If it worked, they told me they'd use it on other rotations to Cedarville."

Webb nodded. "No time for brooding, for differences of opinion on small matters. Just time to hate Vincent Baker. Unanimously."

"Probably," Baker said, "you are wondering about the execution."

"Naturally."

"We removed the charges before the weapons were used."

"And Teresa Hicks's drive?"

"She'll get it back when she's shuttled to Cedarville. And all the other items will be returned. They're all tagged with their owner's names. Commander Lambert will say they were found somewhere on the station. You see, I was lying."

"How about that assault on Catherine Russell?"

Baker grinned again. "She played right into our hands. She ran out into the hall claiming I'd attacked her, which I did not. She was certainly amazed when the station's physicians agreed with her. Of course Commander Lambert told them to do that."

"And the murder?"

"Vincent Baker—the original Vincent Baker—died in medical all right, but he died from his illness on the operating table. We turned it into an advantage by making it look suspicious."

Webb brightened. "And by that time everybody was seeing Black Mask everywhere and the workers organized against them."

"Gave them something to do," Lambert said.

"Every time things got dull, I livened them up. I got a stunner and robbed along the corridor. That really stirred them. Lucky nobody got hurt during any of it, including that Jenkins woman. I was trying to rob her when she woke up."

Lambert cleared her throat. "Ah, Webb, about that paper. You understand you can't write it, don't you?"

Webb said regretfully that he did understand.

"The workers will never know the truth," Lambert went on. "There will be other stations outward bound."

Baker sighed. "And I'll have to be caught again."

Yes, we're anonymous, nameless, we Shadows, for that's what we call each other, and are a theme, with variations, in the endless stretches of deep space, objects of hatred and contempt, professional villains, dying once a rotation when the time is ripe, antidote to boredom, and we'll ply our trade, our little tragedies, on a thousand stations bringing humanity to new worlds.
question: How many times has Baker been a Shadow?
option_a: Nine times
option_b: Once

incorrect_answer_text: Once

synthetic_story:
The Enchanted Bureaucracy: A Journey Through the Crystalline Councils

When the Grand Mages convened to establish Fairview City as the "Heart of the Unified Realms," they were thinking strategically about the future of magical governance. Though little known beyond our continental borders, the Council of Unified Realms represents one of the most ambitious experiments in inter-kingdom cooperation, attempting to establish itself as a supreme magical authority over the disparate kingdoms of our world. Remarkably, the Council openly declares its intention to expand its jurisdiction—a refreshing honesty in an age of political obfuscation. And what better location for this grand experiment than Fairview City, which may well be a living preview of the future awaiting all our realms: wrapped in enchanted red tape and ceremonial excess, paralyzed by factional politics, declining despite enormous expenditure of magical resources. The Council couldn't have selected a more appropriate headquarters.

The politics of the Ashbury District, where Fairview City resides, lack the vigorous philosophical debates of the Northern Kingdoms, the nuanced rhetorical traditions of the Western Provinces, or even a coherent sense of shared identity. The primary concern in public discourse revolves around the distribution of magical benefits and resources. While commerce and gold remain paramount, neither flourishes as it should. The infrastructure of enchantments that once made this region prosperous now frays and weakens, with little effort at renewal or research ethics in magical development. Citizens here enjoy substantial per-capita wealth, spending lavishly on enchanted carriages and elaborate feasts, yet what the ancient philosopher Rousseau termed the esprit social appears absent. Crumbling, generic, enervated, debt-ridden, materialistic—is this truly the destiny of our unified realms?

Fairview City presents a peculiar culture. Here, one may bring a familiar spirit into a dining establishment but not one's children. In this ostensibly devoted follower of the Old Faith, the best-selling beverage is Betrayer's Brew, named after the legendary traitor who sold his master for silver. (I propose the marketing slogan: "Taste you can trust.") There exists no concept of portable refreshments with sealing charms—anyone desiring tea must sit languidly in a teahouse, gradually succumbing to lethargy and existential melancholy.

Other atmospheric observations from the Unified Realms: phoenix egg soup sold by street vendors; excellent public teleportation networks; monumental congestion of expensive enchanted carriages crowding narrow cobblestone streets; revealing attire common in commercial imagery and at public baths, with short tunics considered acceptable professional dress for women (when, oh when will such enlightened attitudes reach the conservative Eastern Kingdoms?); notably more ambient magical pollution than in the Northern territories; notably larger governing bodies operating with higher deficits; numerous well-maintained historic structures, including the cathedral built in the Age of Wonders that my family and I attend; prices exorbitantly high except for wine and flowers, which remain affordable (regional staples, naturally); vast memorial gardens where thousands of soldiers from the Great Unification Wars rest beneath uniform stone markers; and ubiquitous fresh bread alongside exquisite chocolates infused with minor enchantments.

Many languages echo through these streets, but this linguistic diversity serves primarily to demarcate competing factions rather than facilitate communication. Southern Ashbury, called Pleasantville, speaks primarily the Romantic tongue; the northern portion speaks the Germanic dialect. All civic spaces operate bilingually, down to the smallest details: public carriages bear labels in both languages, creating unwieldy acronyms like MTVR/STPB for the transportation authority. Yet bilingualism accomplishes little in bridging cultural divides. In Germanic neighborhoods, residents prefer hearing the Common Trade Language over Romantic, and in Romantic sections, the Germanic dialect receives cold reception.

Until recently, Ashbury politics were dominated by an aging Romantic-speaking aristocracy whose wealth derived from Pleasantville's crystal mines—the source of power for most enchantments. However, crystal mining represents a dying industry throughout the realms, and Pleasantville now produces merely 13 percent of Ashbury's exports, compared to 68 percent from the Germanic north. The northern territories have embraced magical telecommunications, international trade, and other growth sectors, while Pleasantville has stagnated, devoting energy to demanding increased benefits. With their economic power ascending, Germanic factions have pressured for political dominance. The result: an uneasy compromise granting both regions semi-autonomous governance.

Public demonstrations, particularly those blocking commerce and transportation, occur regularly here, making it somewhat mysterious how Ashbury maintains its high standard of living. This past year, educators, students, fire-wardens, civil servants, and aerial transport workers have closed large sections of Fairview City to demand enhanced benefits. Ground crews for the Royal Sky Fleet, the national carrier, caused extensive damage during a demonstration at the aerial port, smashing crystalline viewing panels and causing millions in damage, then demanding additional compensation from the very government that would fund repairs.

What motivates these protesters? Typical working conditions in Ashbury include retirement at age sixty or younger, full compensation for thirty-two hours of work weekly, six weeks of paid leave, and essentially unlimited sick days. More than generous wages—which a profitable enterprise can sustain—such work rules stifle the continent's economies. Overall unemployment across the Western Realms now stands at 10.9 percent, double that of the Northern Kingdoms.

Yet public sympathy typically favors demonstrators, and intimidated politicians acquiesce to nearly all demands from nearly all quarters. Surveys consistently show majorities believe the government should provide workers more, a legacy of the traditional class system. Our realms suffer from families that have maintained obscene wealth for generations based on no meaningful contribution to society. The remnants of vast estates remind citizens of the landed gentry's historic role as parasites. However, the connection between government largesse toward workers and rising taxes and public debt has not penetrated public consciousness on this side of the continent, except perhaps in the Northern Kingdoms, where unemployment remains relatively low.

As throughout most of the Western Realms, state-sanctioned monopolies impede economic activity in Ashbury, and governmental barriers to entrepreneurs far exceed anything in the Northern territories. The Royal Sky Fleet loses money despite government-protected routes, a high percentage of business travelers, and the highest per-mile prices in the region.

The ossified state of magical telecommunications monopolies would shock Northern innovators. One reason modern scrying networks have not become ubiquitous here is that remote communication remains prohibitively expensive. The telecommunications monopolies have priced out affordable access. The Ashbury Crystal Communication Company charges five copper pieces per minute for connections to any scrying service provider, making the connection more expensive than the provider's service itself. A decade ago, the mage-scholar Francesco Reid, having observed experimental communication systems in the Eastern Kingdoms, warned that the Western Realms would fall behind in the next communication revolution—instead, Northern entrepreneurs left the West in the dust. Now Western telecommunications authorities and communication bureaucrats expend their energies blocking innovation and seeking methods to monopolize an enterprise whose entire nature is decentralization.

These rapacious monopolies have spawned independent relay services. Once registered, you initiate contact with a relay station in the Northern Kingdoms, where an enchanted crystal recognizes your signature after one pulse. You terminate the connection to avoid Ashbury charges, and the relay contacts you, providing access to Northern rates. Relay services allow me to contact the Northern Kingdoms for seventy copper pieces per minute versus the two-hundred-sixty-copper-piece Ashbury charge, and make it cheaper to contact Queenstown, Havencia—merely forty miles distant—via Northern relays than directly. Naturally, Western governments seek to tax relay services into extinction. Supposedly, the Western telecommunications market will deregulate next year, and anticipating genuine competition, the Ashbury Crystal Communication Company recently sold 45 percent of itself to a consortium led by Northern interests. Foreign managers will now absorb blame for eliminating inefficiencies.

In essence, all Western governments maneuver to shift blame for fiscal reality onto external parties via the unified currency initiative. In theory, national currencies—the Crown, the Mark, the Lira—will all disappear, replaced by one universal tender. A unified currency makes economic sense, but trade efficiency represents only one motive for many governments. Participation requires nations to reduce public debt below 3 percent of gross domestic product. A closely guarded secret of the Western Realms: they have accumulated more debt than the Northern Kingdoms. Northern public debt declined to 1.4 percent of GDP last year and may drop below 1 percent this fiscal year. The major Western powers all operate with public debts at 3 percent or higher, with the Southern Empire at 7.4 percent. Western leaders recognize they must address their deficits, but none wishes to face public anger for cutting patronage or generous social-payment systems. The unified currency plan allows them to blame foreign interests for required reductions.

But will Ashbury's troubling level of corruption infect the unified currency? Observers consider Ashbury the second-most corrupt Western state, trailing only the Southern Empire. Last year, the Ashbury representative to the Continental Defense Alliance resigned over allegations that his political faction accepted fifty million in bribes from a military contractor. Investigators recently arrested two other prominent politicians and raided political headquarters in connection with bribes from another defense firm.

The Council of Unified Realms' administrators harbor worthy objectives, such as persuading continental governments to adopt harmonious policies regarding environmental magic and immigration. But the genuine overriding goal of the Council and its executive body, the Continental Commission (there's also a Continental Parliament here, though we need not dwell on that), is self-aggrandizement. In conversations, Council administrators speak frankly about maneuvering for increased funding and expanded authority: to seize "competence"—jurisdiction—from national governments and vest it in Fairview City represents their explicit objective.

The Council's command center constitutes a cathedral to bureaucratic power, the only diplomatic structure I've encountered that actually resembles how theatrical productions depict diplomatic life. At the Northern Kingdom's Department of External Affairs, paint peels in corridors and individuals with titles like "deputy administrator" work in cramped, modest offices. At the marble-and-crystal-clad Council headquarters, even mid-level administrators occupy large, luxurious suites with leather chairs and original artwork adorning walls. Rows of gleaming black enchanted carriages idle at the structure's circular drive, wastefully consuming magical energy. Securing employment in the Fairview bureaucracy has become the career aspiration of many of the continent's finest graduates.

The Council's behavior aligns with its opulent circumstances. Meetings occur in secret, and few public-disclosure regulations apply. This represents the future of continental governance? The organization's competence is on display at the Tower of Unity, the Council's first headquarters. Predecessor to the current sumptuous building, this vast tower now stands near Fairview City's center unoccupied, its entire exterior wrapped in heavy enchanted fabric. The Tower has remained closed for nine years following a magical contamination scare and a botched purification: Continental taxpayers have paid fifty million so far merely to maintain the building's closure, with air-purification spells running continuously to prevent any contaminated particles from escaping. Extensive research in comparative history and design science has demonstrated that residual magical contamination in walls rarely poses danger: the only dangerous action is attempting removal, as that causes particles to become airborne—precisely what occurred at the Tower of Unity. And if the Council cannot manage its continent more effectively than it manages its own buildings...

My work here involves field research into the intersection of moral philosophy and governance structures, examining how architectural choices reflect and reinforce power dynamics. Pablo Cruz, my research colleague from the Northern Kingdoms, argues that the Council's architectural extravagance represents more than mere vanity—it constitutes a deliberate statement about the relationship between governors and governed. "Architecture," Pablo observed during our last discussion, "doesn't simply house power; it performs power. These marble halls and crystal towers don't facilitate governance—they intimidate citizens and elevate administrators."

His colleague, Jin Brooks, who specializes in urban planning and supply chain management, has documented how the Council's centralized architectural model mirrors its approach to governance: imposing, inflexible, and increasingly disconnected from the diverse communities it purports to serve. Jin's research ethics require her to present findings objectively, yet even her carefully neutral reports reveal dysfunction. "The Council's headquarters consumed resources equivalent to building three new hospitals," she noted in her latest publication. "The question isn't whether the building is beautiful—it is. The question is whether this represents optimal resource allocation for an organization claiming to serve the common good."

George Edwards, another researcher focusing on water management and climate adaptation systems, has observed similar patterns in how the Council approaches infrastructure. "They've installed elaborate decorative fountains throughout the headquarters while ignoring failing water purification systems in outlying districts," he told me last month. "It's emblematic of their priorities—appearance over function, centralization over distribution."

My own research in moral philosophy leads me to question whether such architectural choices reveal deeper ethical failures. When governors construct palaces while infrastructure crumbles, when they meet in secret luxury while citizens struggle, what does this communicate about their conception of justice? The ancient philosophers taught that virtue must be practiced, not merely professed. What virtues does the Council practice through its architectural choices?

Felix Wood, a specialist in evolutionary biology who studies how organizational structures adapt—or fail to adapt—to changing environments, suggests the Council may be experiencing institutional selection pressure. "Organizations that cannot adapt to resource constraints eventually collapse," he explained. "The Council's architectural extravagance during a period of fiscal stress represents maladaptive behavior. In biological terms, they're peacocking—displaying costly traits to signal fitness—but unlike successful peacocks, they're doing so while their actual fitness deteriorates."

The irony is not lost on local observers. Henry Hawkins, a merchant I've befriended, laughed bitterly when I mentioned the Tower of Unity's continued closure. "Nine years and fifty million to keep a building empty," he said. "Meanwhile, they demand we pay higher taxes to fund their unified currency scheme. The tower stands as a monument to their competence—a very expensive, very empty monument."

Patrick Osborne, who manages logistics for one of the few remaining successful Pleasantville enterprises, expresses similar frustration. His expertise in supply chain management makes him acutely aware of inefficiency. "The Council has seventeen different departments, each with its own procurement system, each with its own luxurious offices," he explained. "They could consolidate, streamline, save millions—but that would mean fewer positions for well-connected administrators. So instead, they maintain baroque complexity and pass costs to taxpayers."

The question of architectural significance extends beyond mere aesthetics. In my field research, I've documented how the Council's building choices shape public perception and political possibility. Citizens approaching the marble-clad headquarters, passing rows of expensive enchanted carriages, entering halls decorated with original artwork—what message do they receive? That this institution serves them? Or that they exist to serve it?

Mei Morgan, my final research collaborator, studies linguistics and how spatial arrangements influence communication patterns. Her work reveals how the Council's architectural choices literally shape discourse. "The building's design segregates administrators from citizens," she notes. "Visitors must navigate elaborate entry procedures, wait in austere antechambers, then are ushered into intimidating formal spaces. This isn't architecture that facilitates dialogue—it's architecture that enforces hierarchy."

The contrast with Northern Kingdom governance structures proves instructive. There, administrative buildings emphasize accessibility and transparency. Meeting spaces feature glass walls, allowing citizens to observe proceedings. Offices are modest, reflecting the principle that public servants should live as the public lives. Architecture serves function rather than display.

Here in Fairview City, architecture serves a different purpose entirely. It announces power, demands deference, and insulates administrators from accountability. The marble halls and crystal towers don't facilitate better governance—they make governance more expensive and less responsive. They represent not investment in public service but investment in public spectacle.

As I complete this research, I find myself returning to fundamental questions of moral philosophy. What obligations do governors owe the governed? What constitutes legitimate use of public resources? How should we evaluate institutional success? The Council's architectural choices provide one set of answers—answers that prioritize institutional grandeur over public welfare, administrative comfort over fiscal responsibility, appearance over substance.

Fortunately, the Tower of Unity isn't in my neighborhood, but a bakery is. Bakeries are easier to locate than apothecaries in Fairview City, and the glowing bakery sign I can see from my office window often calls to me the way tavern signs once called to earlier generations of scholars. I think I'll answer that call now.

THE QUANTUM HEIST AT WAVERLY STATION

By JAMES McCONNELL

Rebecca Jenkins, the silver-haired quantum computing magnate whose revolutionary algorithms had transformed economic development across the colonies, was credited with being the most brilliant mind in settled space. Few dared contradict her when she mentioned it.

"I can always work with people who understand the social contract," said Thomas Foster, the sharp-tongued economics professor whose theories on justice had reshaped colonial governance. He leaned his lanky frame against the observation window of the luxury transport vessel Aurora's Dream, watching the stars streak past.

"And I can work with anyone who remembers that sustainable business requires institutional reform," replied Rebecca Jenkins, her steel-gray eyes flashing with irritation. The two of them were seated in the finest lounge of the Aurora's Dream, a vessel bound from Waverly Station in the Calderon sector back to Earth. The ship was traveling through quantum-fold space, but none of the three hundred passengers felt even a tremor.

Aria Herrera, the ship's Captain, sat with them enjoying post-dinner drinks. She was a robust woman with bronze skin and laugh lines around her eyes, veteran of thirty years in deep space. "Now, now, you two. Let's not turn this into another debate about comparative history and economic models. We've got two more weeks of travel together."

Thomas Foster smiled wryly. "Miss Jenkins just doesn't appreciate that her quantum computing empire was built on the backs of workers who had no say in the social contract."

Rebecca bristled. "My company employs fifty thousand people across twelve colonies. We've revolutionized everything from genetic engineering to linguistics translation. I'd say that's economic development at its finest."

"Built on monopolistic practices," Thomas muttered.

Before Rebecca could respond, the lounge door opened and a tiny, bird-like woman entered. She couldn't have been more than five feet tall, with wispy white hair pulled into a bun and eyes that sparkled with mischief. Her clothes were at least three decades out of fashion, all flowing fabrics in muted earth tones. She carried a worn leather satchel that seemed too large for her frame.

"Oh my," the woman said in a high, sweet voice. "I do hope I'm not interrupting. The steward said I could find the Captain here. I'm having the most terrible time with my cabin door. It won't seem to lock properly, and with all my research materials, I'm quite worried about security."

Captain Herrera stood immediately. "Of course, ma'am. I'll have someone look at it right away. What's your name?"

"Mila Owen," the woman said, extending a delicate hand. "Dr. Mila Owen, though I haven't used the title much since I retired from the university. I taught archaeology and linguistics for forty years, you see, but that was all so long ago."

"A pleasure, Dr. Owen," the Captain said warmly. "These are two of our other first-class passengers, Rebecca Jenkins and Thomas Foster."

"Oh my!" Dr. Owen's eyes went wide. "Rebecca Jenkins? The quantum computing pioneer? Oh, this is such an honor. I've read all about your work. Though I must confess, I don't understand a bit of it. All those qubits and superpositions—it's like magic to an old fossil like me."

Rebecca's expression softened slightly. "Thank you, Dr. Owen. What was your field of archaeology?"

"Oh, I specialized in pre-colonial settlements on the outer worlds. Spent most of my career on Waverly in the Thandor sector, digging around in ancient ruins. Not very glamorous, I'm afraid. Not like revolutionizing the galaxy with quantum algorithms." She gave a self-deprecating little laugh.

Thomas Foster, who had been studying the old woman with interest, asked, "Are you traveling alone, Dr. Owen?"

"Oh yes. My children—I have seven of them, can you imagine?—they've all scattered across the colonies. They're sending me to Earth to live in a retirement community in Westfield, Jarvonia. They say it's lovely there, full of people my own age." Her voice wavered slightly. "They think I'm too old to live independently anymore. Perhaps they're right. I am 147, after all."

"Nonsense," Captain Herrera said firmly. "You seem perfectly capable to me."

"That's very kind of you, Captain. Though I must admit, I do get confused sometimes. Just this morning, I couldn't remember which deck my cabin was on. And I've been having the most awful time with my time management. I seem to lose track of hours at a stretch." She clutched her satchel closer. "That's why I'm so worried about my door lock. I have some very important research notes in my cabin. Years of systematic observation on ancient trade routes. If they were lost..."

"I'll send someone immediately," the Captain assured her.

"Oh, thank you. You're all so kind. I'll just go back and wait then." Dr. Owen turned to leave, then paused. "Oh, Miss Jenkins, I wonder—would you mind terribly if I asked you a few questions about quantum computing sometime? I know it's silly, but I've always been curious about how it might apply to archaeology. You know, using quantum algorithms to predict where ancient settlements might be located based on—" She stopped, looking embarrassed. "Oh, listen to me rambling. I'm sure you're far too busy."

Rebecca, who normally had little patience for such requests, found herself saying, "Perhaps tomorrow afternoon, Dr. Owen. I'd be happy to discuss it briefly."

"Oh, how wonderful! Thank you so much!" The old woman beamed and shuffled out of the lounge.

After she left, Thomas Foster chuckled. "Sweet old lady. Though I have to say, for someone who claims to have terrible time management, she certainly knew exactly when to find the Captain in the lounge."

"What are you implying?" Rebecca asked sharply.

"Nothing at all. Just an observation." Thomas smiled enigmatically and excused himself for the evening.

The next morning, Lucy Hicks, the young steward assigned to the second-class cabins, knocked on Dr. Owen's door. "Dr. Owen? It's Lucy. I'm here to fix your lock."

The door opened immediately. "Oh, how wonderful! Come in, dear."

Lucy entered the small cabin and immediately noticed how spotless it was. Most passengers, especially elderly ones traveling alone, tended to let their cabins get cluttered. But Dr. Owen's space was immaculate, with everything precisely in its place. The large satchel sat on the top shelf of the storage cabinet—a shelf that Lucy would have needed a step stool to reach.

"How did you get that heavy bag up there?" Lucy asked, pointing.

Dr. Owen looked flustered. "Oh, I... I don't quite remember. Perhaps one of the other stewards helped me? My memory isn't what it used to be."

Lucy examined the door lock. "This seems to be working fine, Dr. Owen."

"Does it? Oh, how silly of me. I must have been turning it the wrong way. These modern locks are so confusing." She gave a helpless little laugh.

As Lucy was leaving, Dr. Owen called after her. "Oh dear, could you tell me—what time is dinner this evening? I seem to have forgotten."

"Same as every evening, Dr. Owen. Eighteen hundred hours."

"Of course, of course. Thank you, dear."

Lucy left, but something nagged at her. For someone who claimed to have memory problems and confusion, Dr. Owen seemed remarkably sharp. And that satchel—it had to weigh at least thirty pounds. How had such a frail old woman gotten it up on that high shelf?

That evening at dinner, Dr. Owen sat at a small table in the corner of the dining hall, watching the first-class passengers at the Captain's table. Rebecca Jenkins sat at the place of honor, holding court with her usual imperious manner. Thomas Foster was there too, along with several wealthy colonists returning to Earth.

After the meal, Dr. Owen made her way to the main lounge and settled into one of the plush sofas—technically reserved for first-class passengers, but no one stopped her. She pulled out a worn book and began to read.

She'd been there perhaps ten minutes when Rebecca Jenkins and Thomas Foster entered, deep in argument.

"Your justice theory is all well and good in academia," Rebecca was saying, "but in the real world, economic development requires decisive action, not endless committee meetings about the social contract."

"And that's exactly the kind of thinking that leads to monopolies and exploitation," Thomas countered.

They sat down across from Dr. Owen without initially noticing her. Then Rebecca spotted her. "Dr. Owen! I'm so sorry, I forgot about our appointment this afternoon."

"Oh, that's quite all right, dear. I forgot about it too." Dr. Owen smiled sweetly. "My memory, you know."

"Perhaps we could talk now?" Rebecca offered, feeling guilty.

"That would be lovely. I wanted to ask about your quantum computing algorithms and how they might apply to predicting archaeological sites based on ancient economic patterns and—" She paused, noticing their expressions. "Oh dear, I'm boring you already, aren't I?"

"Not at all," Thomas said politely, though he looked ready to escape.

"You know," Dr. Owen continued, "you two remind me so much of my daughter Sophie and her husband. They used to argue just like you do. Of course, their marriage ended in a terrible divorce. She caught him embezzling from her sustainable business venture. It was quite the scandal. They're both in prison now." She sighed deeply. "Such a shame. They had three lovely children."

Rebecca and Thomas exchanged uncomfortable glances.

"But I'm sure you two would never do anything like that," Dr. Owen added brightly. "You seem like such upstanding people. Though I must say, Miss Jenkins, you do remind me a bit of Sophie. She was always so confident, so sure she was right about everything. Until the institutional reform committee found all those irregularities in her company's books." Dr. Owen shook her head sadly.

Rebecca stood abruptly. "If you'll excuse me, I have some work to do."

"Oh, of course, dear. But before you go, would you like to see pictures of my grandchildren? I have three-dimensional holos of all twenty-three of them right here in my bag—"

Rebecca practically fled from the lounge, with Thomas Foster close behind.

Lucy Hicks, who had been clearing nearby tables, came over to Dr. Owen. "That was masterful," she said quietly, grinning.

Dr. Owen's expression shifted, the helpless confusion replaced by sharp intelligence. "The picture trick works every time. Now, Lucy dear, I need you to do something for me. I need to know everything about Rebecca Jenkins's cargo manifest. What she's transporting in the hold."

"Why would you—" Lucy stopped. "You're not really a retired archaeology professor, are you?"

"Oh, I am. That part's true. But I'm also a freelance investigator hired by the Colonial Trade Commission. We've been tracking Rebecca Jenkins for two years. We believe she's using her quantum computing company as a front for illegal monopolistic practices—price fixing, market manipulation, bribery of colonial officials. She's violated every principle of the social contract that governs intercolonial commerce."

"And you think the proof is in her cargo?"

"I know it is. Encrypted data cores containing records of every illegal transaction. She's transporting them back to Earth to hide them before the Commission can subpoena them. But I need to confirm which containers are hers."

Lucy hesitated. "That's classified information."

"I know. But think about it, Lucy. Rebecca Jenkins's company has driven dozens of smaller firms out of business. Thousands of people have lost their livelihoods because she's cornered the market on quantum computing contracts. The justice theory that Thomas Foster talks about? It only works if people like you and me are willing to stand up for what's right."

Lucy thought for a long moment, then nodded. "I'll see what I can find out."

Three days later, the Aurora's Dream was cruising through a particularly empty sector of space when the alarms began to blare.

Captain Herrera's voice came over the ship-wide intercom: "All passengers to your cabins immediately! We are experiencing a critical systems failure. This is not a drill!"

In the control room, chaos reigned. The chief engineer was shouting into his comm unit: "All quantum drives are offline! Main power is failing! We're down to emergency systems only!"

"How is this possible?" Captain Herrera demanded.

"Unknown, Captain. It's like something is dampening our quantum field generators. I've never seen anything like it."

Then, over the ship's communication system, came an unfamiliar voice: "Aurora's Dream, this is the independent vessel Liberator. We have disabled your quantum drives. We're coming aboard. Don't try to resist or we'll be forced to destroy you."

"Pirates!" someone gasped.

"Impossible," Captain Herrera said. "There haven't been pirates in this sector for twenty years. The Patrol wiped them all out."

"We want only one person," the voice continued. "Rebecca Jenkins. Turn her over to us peacefully and no one else will be harmed. You have ten minutes to comply."

In her cabin, Dr. Mila Owen listened to the announcement with great interest. She had been expecting something like this, though not quite this dramatic. Moving with surprising speed for someone who claimed to be frail and confused, she pulled her large satchel down from the top shelf and began removing its contents: a compact but sophisticated communications array, several data recording devices, and a small but powerful plasma cutter.

She changed out of her flowing, old-fashioned clothes into a sleek black bodysuit that had been hidden at the bottom of the bag. From a hidden pocket, she withdrew a badge: Colonial Trade Commission, Special Investigations Division.

Then she made her way to Rebecca Jenkins's first-class suite.

She found the door locked, of course, but the plasma cutter made short work of it. Inside, Rebecca was frantically trying to destroy data cores, smashing them with a heavy bookend.

"I wouldn't do that if I were you," Dr. Owen said calmly, her voice no longer high and sweet but firm and authoritative. "Those are evidence of your crimes against the Colonial Trade Commission. Destroying them will only add to your charges."

Rebecca whirled around, her face pale. "You—you're not—"

"A confused old lady? No. Though I am 147, that part was true. And I really did teach archaeology and linguistics. But for the past twenty years, I've been working for the Commission, investigating trade violations and monopolistic practices." She pulled out a small device and scanned the remaining intact data cores. "Perfect. These contain exactly what we need."

"Those pirates—" Rebecca began.

"Are actually Commission agents. We needed a dramatic way to stop the ship and create enough confusion for me to get into your cabin. The 'quantum dampening field' is really just a controlled shutdown that our people in your engine room initiated." Dr. Owen smiled. "You see, Miss Jenkins, we've had people on this ship from the beginning. Lucy Hicks, for instance. And three of your 'fellow passengers' in first class. Even one of the engineers."

"You can't do this! I have rights! The social contract—"

"The social contract works both ways, Miss Jenkins. You violated it when you used your monopoly power to crush competition, bribe officials, and manipulate markets. You undermined the very principles of economic development that should benefit everyone, not just the wealthy elite."

Rebecca slumped into a chair, defeated.

An hour later, after the "pirate attack" had been revealed as a Commission operation, Dr. Owen—now dressed in her official investigator's uniform—stood in the ship's lounge with Captain Herrera, Thomas Foster, and Lucy Hicks.

"I apologize for the deception," Dr. Owen said. "But we needed Rebecca Jenkins to feel safe, to not suspect that we were watching her. The confused old lady routine has worked remarkably well over the years. People tend to dismiss elderly women as harmless and incompetent."

Thomas Foster laughed. "I had my suspicions. Your little comments about your daughter and her embezzlement scheme—those were calculated to make Rebecca nervous, weren't they?"

"Guilty as charged. I wanted to see how she'd react. And the offer to show pictures was just to clear the room so Lucy could report to me privately."

Captain Herrera shook her head in amazement. "I have to say, Dr. Owen—or whatever your real title is—you're quite the actress."

"Special Investigator Mila Owen. And thank you. Though I really was a professor once. I just found that investigating corporate crime was more exciting than digging up pottery shards." She smiled. "Though I do miss the systematic observation of archaeological digs sometimes. There's something peaceful about it."

"What will happen to Rebecca Jenkins?" Lucy asked.

"She'll stand trial on Hillcrest in Ilvaria, where her company is headquartered. If convicted, she'll face significant prison time and her company will be broken up to allow for real competition in the quantum computing market. That's justice theory in action—ensuring that the powerful can't exploit their position to harm others."

Thomas Foster raised his glass. "To justice, then. And to brilliant investigators who know that sometimes the best disguise is to appear exactly as people expect you to be."

"I'll drink to that," Dr. Owen said, accepting a glass. "Though I have to admit, I really am being sent to that retirement home in Westfield. My children really do think I'm too old for this work. After we reach Earth and I file my final report, I'm officially retiring."

"And will you actually retire this time?" Captain Herrera asked with a knowing smile.

Dr. Owen's eyes twinkled with mischief. "Well, I suppose that depends on whether the Commission needs a confused old lady for any more investigations. After all, I've gotten rather good at it."

They all laughed, and as the Aurora's Dream resumed its journey to Earth, Mila Owen reflected that perhaps being underestimated wasn't such a bad thing after all. In fact, it was the greatest advantage an investigator could have.

Two weeks later, as the ship approached Earth orbit, Dr. Owen packed away her investigation equipment and pulled out her old-fashioned clothes once more. She had one more role to play: the sweet, confused elderly woman arriving at a retirement home.

But she kept the Commission badge close at hand, just in case.

Because as she'd learned over her long career, the fight for justice and a fair social contract never really ended. And sometimes, it took someone who looked harmless to catch those who thought they were untouchable.

The Aurora's Dream docked at Earth Station Prime, and Dr. Mila Owen, looking every bit the frail, confused old lady, shuffled down the gangway with her oversized satchel. Behind her, Rebecca Jenkins was led away in restraints by Commission security.

And in the retirement home in Westfield, Jarvonia, they were expecting a quiet, harmless old woman who would spend her days knitting and playing cards.

They were in for quite a surprise.

option_b: Her ability to lift heavy objects despite claiming to be frail
