The Curator of Fairview
By ADAPTED WORK

Death was Felix Wood's expertise, and every colony had known his methods. But now, on the biodiversity station of Fairview, Yendor, he was selling his skills into the strangest of all his assignments—gambling his life against the preservation of species that shouldn't exist.

On the observation deck of the Elmwood Cultural Center, a slender woman with dark hair pulled back in a severe bun was lecturing about "The Lost Murals of Pre-Colonial Havencia." The lecture was technical, detailed, a favorite of the researchers and conservation officers who frequented the center. The woman delivered it with such precision that the audience sat in rapt attention.

She kept her eyes fixed on her notes so that her hair fell forward slightly, obscuring her face. There was tension in her shoulders. Her mouth maintained a professional smile. Her eyes were frightened.

The man who had been operating the holographic display system sat at the side of the stage, his back to the scattered audience. He did not look up at the lecturer but kept his weathered face bent over the controls, while his fingers automatically adjusted the images. Sweat beaded on his temples despite the climate control. Without looking up, he said: "Have you spotted him?" His voice was pitched to reach the lecturer alone.

The woman, with an almost imperceptible gesture, shook her head.

The afternoon was artificially temperate; but then it always was on Fairview, the newest, the most controversial, the most carefully monitored of Earth's biodiversity conservation stations. Ventilation systems throughout the center's walls circulated the processed air, while the researchers and administrators sitting in the audience sipped carefully at filtered water. Only the native assistants, the enigmatic, golden-eyed Yendorians, seemed truly at ease. They moved with fluid grace through the space.

Up on the stage the lecturer was about to transition to her next slide when she stiffened.

"Here he is," she said to the technician without moving her lips.

The technician swung around on his stool, lifted his gray eyes to the entrance leading from the main corridor.

Just within the doorway, a tall, lean man was standing. He looked like a predator surveying the room. His conservation officer's uniform hung perfectly. His dark hair was regulation length, his features angular and sharp. For a moment he studied the assembled researchers before making his way to an empty seat.

"Continue," said the technician in a flat voice.

The dark-haired woman shivered. Stepping from the stage she made her way through the seats until she came to the one occupied by the newcomer.

"May I join you?" she asked in a low voice.

The man stood. "Of course. I was expecting you. Here, sit down." He gestured to the adjacent seat, then signaled for a server. The Yendorian, his golden eyes reflecting light like polished amber, approached silently. "Bring us two glasses of the filtered spring water from the Redwood District, well chilled." The server glided away.

"So," said the dark-haired woman; "you came. I didn't think you would arrive in time." Her hands were clenched in her lap. The knuckles were white.

The man said nothing.

"I didn't want to bring you into this, Felix Wood." It was the first time she had used his name. "You have the reputation of being unpredictable. I don't trust you, but since..." She stopped as the server placed glasses on the small table and silently poured the clear water. The man, Felix Wood, raised his glass.

"Here's to ecosystem restoration," he said. His low voice carried an odd, compelling note. His eyes, pale gray and analytical, were striking against his tanned face.

The woman drew in her breath.

"No! Fairview isn't ready for that kind of intervention. Only a handful of extremists are pushing for immediate restoration. The real conservation scientists are against it, but they're afraid to speak out. You've got to believe me. The intervention is scheduled to begin during the Annual Biodiversity Summit. If it does, the research here will be compromised. The Yendorians are suspicious of us. We have limited authority."

Felix Wood wiped condensation from his glass with a cloth napkin. "I had forgotten how controlled the environment can be here."

The woman ignored the interruption. "There is one man; he is the leader, the driving force behind the intervention plan. The Yendorians respect him. They will follow whatever he recommends. Without him they would abandon the whole project. He is the scientist, Phillip Ray. I am authorized to offer you fifty thousand Earth credits to eliminate Phillip Ray's influence."

Felix Wood refilled their empty glasses. He was a imposing man, handsome in a severe fashion. Only his eyes were different. They were analytical and penetrating with straight brows. The pupils were a pale gray that could dissect a situation like a surgeon's scalpel. Now he caught the woman's eyes and held them with his own.

"Why bring me all the way from the Larchmont research station for that? Why not have that technician back there handle it?"

The woman started, glanced at the stage, said with a tremor: "We can't locate Phillip Ray. Don't look at me that way, Felix. You frighten me. I'm telling the truth. We can't find him. That's why we contacted you. You've got to find him, Felix. He's destabilizing all of Fairview's protocols."

"Who's funding this?"

"I can't tell you."

"Ah," said Felix Wood; "so that's the situation."

"That's the situation."

"There isn't much time," he said after a moment. "The Summit begins in three days."

"No," the woman replied. "But we think he's here in the facility."

"Why? What makes you think that?"

"He was seen," she began, then stopped with a gasp.

The lights had gone out.

It was as unexpected as a power failure. One moment the center was illuminated, the next the darkness swept through the space. The ventilation systems audibly slowed and stopped. The temperature began to shift.

Felix Wood moved sideways from his seat. He felt something brush his arm. Somewhere a researcher made a startled sound.

"What's happening?" growled an irritated voice. Other voices took up the complaint.

Across from Felix there was the sense of movement; he could detect it. An exclamation was suddenly muffled as if a hand had been placed over the woman's mouth.

"Lila!" said Felix in a low voice.

There was no answer.

"Lila!" he repeated, louder.

Unexpectedly, the authoritative voice of the Center Director boomed out from the stage.

"Everything is fine. The primary circuit failed. The lights will be restored momentarily."

Following his announcement the lights flashed back on, the ventilation resumed. The familiar hum of the systems returned.

Felix Wood glanced at his seat. The dark-haired lecturer was gone. So was the technician.

Felix Wood sat back down and took another sip of water. The filtered spring water had a pure, clean taste. It reminded him of mountain streams on Earth. On the carefully controlled station of Fairview it was as refreshing as natural rain.

He wondered who was funding the fifty thousand Earth credits? Who stood to lose most if the intervention failed? The answer seemed clear enough. Who, but Samuel Osborne. Osborne controlled the biodiversity research grants for which there was tremendous demand throughout the colonies.

And what had happened to the woman? Had the intervention supporters taken her? If so, he suspected they had underestimated her. Lila Park had the reputation of being resourceful.

He signaled a server, prepared to leave. As the Yendorian started to depart, a thought struck Felix. These golden-eyed Yendorians could navigate in near darkness as well as any nocturnal predator. For generations they had adapted to the variable light conditions of their world. He produced a credit chip, placed it in the server's hand.

"What became of the dark-haired lecturer?"

The Yendorian glanced at the chip, then back at the Earthman. There was no readable expression in his golden eyes.

"She and the man, the technician who operates the displays, left through the service corridor."

Felix shrugged, dismissed the server. He had not expected to get much information, but he was not a man to overlook any possibility. If the woman had been taken, only Yendorians could have managed it in the darkness; and the Yendorians were protective of their own.

Back in the main corridor Felix Wood headed for his quarters. The passages were narrow, designed for efficiency rather than comfort, with walls lined with monitoring equipment. Beneath his feet, he knew, stretched a network of laboratories and storage facilities. Somewhere in those spaces was Phillip Ray, the interventionist, and the woman.

At regular intervals soft blue lights illuminated the corridor, casting a clinical glow. He had just passed one of these lights when he detected movement behind him. It was barely perceptible, but as he moved beyond the illuminated section, he pressed himself against a maintenance alcove. Nothing appeared. There was no further sound. Again he started forward, but now he was conscious of shadows tracking him. They were never visible, but to his trained senses there came revealing indicators: the whisper of fabric against the walls, the subtle shift of air pressure. He turned down a connecting passage, faded into a doorway. Immediately all signs of pursuit ceased. But as soon as he emerged he was aware again of the followers. In the controlled environment, he was at a disadvantage against the adapted Yendorians.

In the distance a warm amber glow indicated the approach of the station's artificial dawn cycle. With a muttered curse, he set out again for his quarters. He made no further effort to elude the followers.

Once back in his room, Felix Wood removed his uniform jacket, unstrapped a shoulder holster containing a compressed air tranquilizer gun, stepped into the sanitation unit. His body was lean and marked with various scars from his years in conflict zones. There were small circular scars and long thin ones, and his left shoulder bore the distinctive mark of a chemical burn. Stepping out, he dried himself, reattached the shoulder holster, slipped into casual clothes. The clothes were simple gray with minimal decoration. Next he activated his communication device and began to review the station's personnel files with methodical attention.

He had, he supposed, eliminated rather a lot of threats. He had worked in the resource conflicts of the outer colonies for years, then the Territorial Disputes of the 2180s, after that the Larchmont Incident as well as dozens of smaller operations. No, there was little doubt but that he had neutralized quite a number of problems. But this business of tracking a man through the research facilities was outside his usual parameters.

Furthermore, there was something inconsistent about the entire situation. The Yendorians, he knew, had been advocating for greater autonomy in conservation decisions for years. Why, at this time when the Earth Council was about to grant them expanded authority, would they support a controversial intervention?

A loud, official knocking at the door interrupted his analysis. He stood and deactivated his device. Before he could reach the door the knocking came again.

Releasing the lock, he stepped back, balanced and ready.

"Enter," he called.

The door opened. A heavy-set man entered, secured and locked the door, then glanced around carefully. His eyes settled on Felix. He cleared his throat.

"Mr. Wood, the—ah—security specialist, I believe." His voice was precise, almost pedantic. "I'm Samuel Osborne." He extended a soft hand.

Felix said nothing. He ignored the hand, waited, poised.

Mr. Osborne cleared his throat again. "I have come, Mr. Wood, on a matter of urgent business. I had not intended to reveal myself in this matter. I preferred to remain behind the scenes, but the disappearance of Dr. Park has—ah—forced my hand." He paused.

Felix remained silent. Dr. Park must be the dark-haired lecturer, whom he had known under several different professional identities. He doubted even she remembered her original credentials.

"Dr. Park made you a proposition?" Samuel Osborne's voice was tight.

"Yes," said Felix.

"You accepted?"

"Why, no. As it happened she was taken before I had the opportunity."

Mr. Osborne cleared his throat. "But you will, surely you will. Unless Phillip Ray's influence is neutralized immediately there will be a catastrophic intervention across the entire station during the Biodiversity Summit. Earth doesn't recognize the severity of the situation."

"Then I was correct; it is you who are providing the fifty thousand Earth credits."

"Not entirely," said Osborne uncomfortably. "There are many of us here, Yendorians as well as Earthmen, who recognize the danger. We have—ah—pooled our resources."

"But you stand to lose most if the intervention succeeds?"

"Perhaps. I have substantial interests in the current research protocols. They are—ah—profitable."

Felix Wood activated a small recording device, sat on the edge of his bed. "Why be indirect," he asked with a slight smile. "Mr. Osborne, you've gained control of the biodiversity research funding. Other Earth administrators control the genetic archives and the northern conservation zones. Together you form perhaps the strongest administrative bloc the colonies have seen. You essentially run Fairview, and you've extracted every possible credit. Every time expanded Yendorian authority has come before the Earth Council you've succeeded in blocking it. You are, perhaps, the most resented group anywhere. I don't wonder that you fear losing control."

Mr. Osborne took out a cloth and dabbed his forehead. "Seventy-five thousand Earth credits I can offer you. But no more. That is my maximum authorization."

Felix laughed. "How did you know Lila had been taken?"

"We have a comprehensive monitoring system. I received the report of Dr. Park's abduction ten minutes after the incident."

Felix raised his eyebrows. "Perhaps then you know where she is?"

Mr. Osborne shook his head. "No. Phillip Ray's supporters took her."

A second knocking at the door caused them to exchange glances. Felix went to the door, opened it. The technician from the center was standing in the entrance. His gray eyes were intense in his lined face. His work clothes were stained with dust and moisture.

"They told me Mr. Osborne was here," he said.

"It's for you," said Felix over his shoulder.

Mr. Osborne came to the door. "Hello, Jonathan. I thought Ray's people had you? Where's Dr. Park?"

"I escaped. Look, Mr. Osborne, I need to speak with you privately."

Samuel Osborne said, "Would you excuse us, Mr. Wood?" He cleared his throat. "I'll just step out into the corridor a moment." He went out, closing the door behind him.

Felix activated his communication device. He paced the room silently, his movements economical. He sat on the edge of the bed. He stood and deactivated the device. He went to the door, but did not open it. Instead, he made another circuit of the room. Again he stopped before the door, pressed his ear against the panel. For a long time he listened but could distinguish no sound of conversation. With a curse he opened the door. The corridor was empty.

Felix returned to his room, put his uniform jacket back on, checked the tranquilizer gun. It was a flat, practical weapon which delivered a dose calculated to incapacitate. He preferred it because, though he rarely needed lethal force, it stopped a person effectively. He adjusted the gun carefully in its holster to ensure quick access if needed. Then he went out into the corridor.

At the information desk he inquired if any messages had come for him. There were none, but the clerk had seen Mr. Osborne with another man take the lift to the lower research levels. Above the clerk's head a news display was streaming current updates. Felix read:

"Earth Council suspends negotiations on Yendorian conservation autonomy pending investigation of rumored unauthorized intervention. Earth personnel advised to return home. Phillip Ray, conservation scientist, being sought."

Felix descended to the network of laboratories which served as the primary research areas. Here in the lower levels were located the specimen storage facilities and analysis rooms where the Yendorians worked at monitoring stations, their movements precise and methodical. The laboratories were brightly lit, the natives preferring clear visibility for their detailed work, and Felix moved easily through the space, passing researchers of various species. But when he reached the Earth Administration section, enhanced security protocols were evident, and there was a presence of Colonial guards among the staff.

Felix halted before a door bearing a placard which read:

"BIODIVERSITY RESEARCH ADMINISTRATION"

He pushed through the door into a well-appointed reception area. At the far end was a second door beside which sat a desk, both being separated from the rest of the office by a security barrier. The door to Samuel Osborne's inner office was slightly ajar. Felix could distinguish voices; then quite clearly he heard Samuel Osborne say in his precise tone:

"Jonathan, I thought I left you in the lower levels. Why did you follow me? How many times have I told you never to come here?"

The reply was unintelligible. Then the weathered technician came through the door, closing it behind himself. At the sight of Felix Wood he froze.

"What are you doing here?"

Felix settled himself carefully, his pale gray eyes assessing the man.

"Let's be clear," he said calmly. "I've known your type before. Frankly, ever since I saw you I've had to suppress an urge to report you to security."

The technician's gray eyes were cold, his fingers twitching. His hands began to move upward.

"You interfering..." he began, but he got no further. Felix Wood shot him with the tranquilizer.

The compressed air gun had appeared in Felix's hand. The dart struck the technician's shoulder with precision, and he slumped against the wall. Felix moved quickly, relieving him of two concealed weapons.

"I'll remember this," said Jonathan, his voice slurred. "You've interfered. I'll make you pay."

The door to the inner office opened.

"What's happened?" cried Samuel Osborne in distress. "What's wrong with you, Jonathan?"

"This man shot me with a tranquilizer."

"But why?" Osborne was agitated.

"Nothing permanent," said Felix. "He'll be unconscious for a while. That's all."

"Jonathan," said Mr. Osborne. "You're creating a scene. Why can't you go to the medical bay. Has anyone called a medic? Where's Ms. Miles? Ms. Miles! That woman. Ms. Miles!"

Jonathan slid to the floor, losing consciousness, just as a tall woman with straight auburn hair hurried in from an adjacent office. She had alert hazel eyes and enough professional competence to immediately assess the situation.

"Oh!" exclaimed Ms. Miles as she saw the unconscious technician.

"There's been an—ah—incident," said Mr. Osborne, clearing his throat. "Call medical, Ms. Miles."

Ms. Miles raised an eyebrow, went to the communication console. In a moment she had connected with a medical facility.

"Could Dr. Martinez come immediately? There's been an incident."

"Come where?" said the person on the screen. "These systems require specific locations."

"Oh," said Ms. Miles, "the offices of the Biodiversity Research Administration."

The person on the screen became more attentive. "Certainly. Dr. Martinez will be there shortly."

"Thank you," said Ms. Miles. She closed the connection, then added quietly: "Efficient."

Mr. Osborne regarded Felix Wood with concern.

"Really, Mr. Wood, was it necessary to tranquilize Jonathan? Isn't that—ah—somewhat extreme? I'm afraid it might incapacitate him, and I had an assignment for him."

"Oh," said Ms. Miles, her hazel eyes sharp. "Did you shoot that man? Aren't you the decisive one?"

"Decisive?" said Felix mildly. "Potentially dangerous individual. I took these items from him." He held out the concealed weapons. "You take them, Mr. Osborne. Frankly, they concern me. They might be used improperly."

Mr. Osborne accepted the weapons reluctantly. He held them as if they might activate unexpectedly. He started to secure them, reconsidered, glanced around helplessly.

"Here, Ms. Miles," he said, "do something with these. Put them in my secure storage."

Ms. Miles's eyes widened. "I wouldn't handle those devices for all the research grants on Fairview."

"Here, I'll take them," said Jonathan, regaining consciousness. He had managed to sit up. His face was pale and drawn. Felix watched him coldly as with his functioning hand the technician retrieved the weapons.

"Attempt to use those and I'll use lethal force next time."

"Now, Mr. Wood." Mr. Osborne cleared his throat nervously. "Jonathan, go into my office. The doctor will be here momentarily. Ms. Miles, you may leave for the day. I'll have no more work for you today."

Samuel Osborne helped Jonathan through the door. Felix and Ms. Miles were alone. With his attention on the door, Felix said:

"When you leave, go toward the cultural research section. Wait for me in the first observation lounge you find."

Ms. Miles raised her eyebrows. "What's this? An unusual approach?"

"Look," began Felix, annoyed.

"My curiosity is already overwhelming," she interrupted. "Another afternoon like this and I'm taking the first transport back to Earth." She gathered her belongings from the desk.

"I'm not trying to be social. This is..."

"How disappointing."

Felix began again patiently. "Wait for me in the first observation lounge. There's something I need to know. It's important." He cleared his throat. "Don't you find the artificial environment somewhat disorienting, Ms. Miles. But perhaps you've adapted to it."

Mr. Osborne returned to the room.

"Why, no, I mean yes," replied Ms. Miles, a confused expression on her face.

"Goodbye, Ms. Miles," said Mr. Osborne firmly.

Felix smiled slightly at her. Ms. Miles departed looking bewildered.

As the door closed behind the woman, Samuel Osborne cleared his throat, said: "Mr. Wood, I suppose my departure from your quarters requires some explanation. But the fact is that Jonathan brought critical information." He paused.

Felix said nothing.

"You might be interested to know that Dr. Park is quite safe. Phillip Ray has her, but Jonathan assures me she will be unharmed." Again he paused. As Felix remained silent, his neck flushed.

"The fact is, Mr. Wood, that we won't need your services after all. I realize that we've caused you considerable inconvenience and we're prepared to compensate you for your time. Say five thousand Earth credits?"

"That's reasonable," replied Felix.

Samuel Osborne sighed with relief. "I have the authorization prepared."

"Only," continued Felix coldly, "I'm not ready to be dismissed. I think I'll continue investigating this situation."

Mr. Osborne's face fell. "You won't reconsider?"

"Sorry," said Felix; "but I have an appointment. I'm late now." He started to leave.

"Jonathan!" called Samuel Osborne.

The weathered technician appeared in the doorway, one of the weapons in his functioning hand. Felix Wood dropped to the floor, drawing his tranquilizer gun as he fell. There was a soft discharge sound. He felt the projectile pass overhead. Then he fired from the floor. The technician collapsed completely.

Felix stood, keeping his attention on Samuel Osborne, brushed off his uniform.

"You've incapacitated him seriously," said Osborne. "If I were you, Mr. Wood, I would be on the next transport back to Earth."

Without responding, Felix backed carefully from the room.

Once Felix Wood had regained the corridor, he wiped his forehead with his hand. Whatever was occurring, these people were playing seriously. Carefully he started down the passage toward the cultural research section. At the first observation lounge he entered. His eyes scanned the space, then he smiled.

At a corner table, a glass of filtered water before her, sat Ms. Miles. Her auburn hair was slightly disheveled, and she was perched on the edge of her chair as if ready to leave quickly.

"Surprise," said Felix, approaching from behind and speaking quietly.

Ms. Miles jumped, nearly spilling her water. She regarded him with exasperation.

"Never a peaceful moment," she said.

Still smiling slightly, Felix sat down. "I'm Felix Wood, Ms. Miles. I think Samuel Osborne forgot to introduce us properly. There's some questionable activity occurring here that I'm particularly interested in understanding. I thought you might be able to help me."

"Yes," replied Ms. Miles carefully.

A Yendorian server, attracted by the commotion, approached and took Felix's order.

"All right," Felix said, but his pale gray eyes studied the woman thoughtfully. "I'll have to share certain information which might be risky for you to know. Are you willing, Ms. Miles?"

"Since we're going to be collaborating," she replied; "you might call me Anil. You make me feel excessively formal."

"Well then," he said. "First, I just seriously incapacitated that technician your supervisor had in his office."

"What!" said Anil, choking on her water.

"It was necessary," he assured her. "He attempted to use a weapon against me."

"But the authorities!" she cried, recovering.

"There'll never be an investigation. Samuel Osborne will ensure that. I was brought here on what I believed was a legitimate security assignment. Instead I was offered fifty thousand Earth credits to eliminate the influence of the intervention leader."

"What intervention? I'm completely confused."

"The Yendorians, of course."

"I don't believe it," said the woman. "The Yendorians are the most cooperative people in the colonies. They've been advocating for greater autonomy, yes. But they believe in peaceful negotiation. I don't believe you could convince a Yendorian to use violence, even in self-defense. That's why Samuel Osborne and the rest of the administration had such an easy time maintaining control of the research protocols."

"Excellent point," breathed Felix, "I begin to understand. Ms. Miles—ah, Anil—I have a feeling that we're going to work well together. How do you happen to be Samuel Osborne's administrative assistant?"

"Employment necessity. But truthfully, I was planning to resign. The Biodiversity Research Administration is nearly insolvent. Their funding has been declining precipitously."

Felix Wood raised his angular brows but did not interrupt.

"Samuel Osborne," she continued, "has been trying to transfer his position but nobody will accept the assignment, not since it appears the Earth Council is going to grant the Yendorians expanded authority. Everyone knows that the first thing the Yendorians will do is restructure the research administration."

"What about this Phillip Ray?" said Felix. "I've heard that he's encouraging the Yendorians toward unauthorized intervention. The news stream had information about the intervention too. The government has advised all Earth personnel to return home."

"It's not true," Anil stated firmly. "It's all fabricated by the Biodiversity Research Administration. I know."

"But I would think rumors like that would damage the administration's credibility."
question: Who wanted Felix dead?
option_a: Samuel Osborne
option_b: Phillip Ray
correct_answer_text: Samuel Osborne
incorrect_answer_text: Phillip Ray
explanation: Samuel Osborne wanted Felix dead. In the story, after Felix refuses to be dismissed and says he'll continue investigating, Osborne calls for Jonathan, who then attempts to shoot Felix with a weapon. This was clearly orchestrated by Osborne, who was trying to eliminate Felix because he wouldn't accept the payoff and leave. Phillip Ray, on the other hand, is portrayed as someone who has been falsely accused and is actually helping people (he has Dr. Park safely), not trying to kill Felix.
original_question: Who wanted Jaro dead?

synthetic_story:
The atmospheric shuttle descended through the thick clouds of Greenfield, Jarvonia, its heat shields glowing orange against the perpetual twilight. Dr. Adrian Lowe pressed his face against the viewport, studying the alien landscape below—a world of crystalline forests and bioluminescent vegetation that had been discovered only eighteen months prior.

"We're approaching the research site," the pilot announced through the intercom. "Landing in five minutes."

Adrian turned to his colleague, Dr. Valeria Hoffman, who was reviewing data on her tablet. "Are you certain about the coordinates? The last expedition reported the specimens much further north."

Valeria looked up, her expression tense. "The pilot insists this is correct. Though I explicitly told him the northern hemisphere, near Parkview, Orvandor."

"There shouldn't be any specimens this far south," Adrian muttered. "The climate adaptation patterns we documented were very specific to the polar regions."

"I know," Valeria said quietly. "I think he wanted to cause us problems. He doesn't approve of corporate-funded research expeditions."

The shuttle touched down with a shudder, its landing struts compressing against the spongy ground. Within minutes, the automated deployment system had erected their base camp—a cluster of pressurized habitats connected by flexible corridors. The main research tent was equipped with atmospheric processors, specimen containment units, and a quantum communication array that could reach the orbital station above.

Adrian stepped out of the shuttle, his environmental suit registering the planet's atmosphere as breathable but rich in exotic compounds. The air smelled of ozone and something sweetly organic, like fermented fruit.

"Dr. Lowe!" called Robert Gilbert, one of their field assistants. "We've detected vocalizations from the forest. I think we've found them."

Adrian felt his pulse quicken. The crystalline stalkers—apex predators unlike anything in human-controlled space. They had traveled across three star systems to study these creatures, creatures that existed nowhere else in human territory but had been extensively documented in the Collective's xenobiological databases.

"Show me the readings," Adrian demanded.

Robert pulled up the acoustic analysis on a portable display. "The signature matches what we recorded on our first expedition. Definitely a stalker, maybe two."

Valeria joined them, her face pale. "Adrian, I need to speak with you. Privately."

They moved away from the others, into the shadow of the shuttle.

"I'm frightened," Valeria admitted. "Not just of the stalkers. Of him."

"Gilbert?" Adrian asked, confused.

"No. Juan Green."

Adrian felt a chill despite his suit's temperature regulation. Juan Green—the expedition's sponsor, the corporate magnate who had personally insisted on joining this research trip. The man whose face appeared on every news feed, whose decisions affected billions of lives across dozens of worlds, whose reputation for ruthlessness was matched only by his reputation for getting what he wanted.

"What about him?" Adrian asked carefully.

"We'll talk," Valeria whispered urgently. "When we return to civilization. You, me, the assistants. About what we've seen. About what he's really like. He can't let that happen. He'll kill us first."

Adrian shook his head stubbornly. "No. We have positions. We have academic credentials. He couldn't just—"

"He can do anything," Valeria insisted. "He can make the public believe anything. Whatever he says. There's no way to verify it independently. The institutional reform movement has been trying for years to create oversight mechanisms, but he controls too much of the supply chain for critical resources. He has leverage everywhere."

"It's getting cold," Adrian said, though his suit maintained perfect temperature.

"Listen to me," Valeria pleaded. "This is about more than just us. Think about organizational behavior—how power structures function. Right now, he couldn't afford to let us talk. Not right now. Because the Colonial Fleet is not against him. You heard those officers who landed here yesterday. They don't want to overthrow him!"

Adrian's hands trembled inside his gloves.

"That's another lie," Valeria continued. "That he protects the colonies from military dictatorship. That's a lie. I don't believe they were ever plotting against him. Not even at first. I think they helped him rise to power, don't you see?"

"We couldn't make people believe that," Adrian said woodenly.

"No? Couldn't we? Not today, but what about tomorrow? Because I think the Fleet is preparing to invade the Collective's space!"

"The colonies won't support them," Adrian answered.

"Think. If he tells them to, they will. They trust him."

Before Adrian could respond, Juan Green himself emerged from the main research tent. He was a broad-shouldered man with silver-streaked hair and eyes that seemed to calculate the value of everything they observed. He wore an expensive exploration suit, custom-fitted, with his corporate insignia emblazoned on the chest.

"Dr. Lowe!" Green called out genially. "Come here. I want to discuss our hunting strategy."

Adrian exchanged a glance with Valeria, then approached reluctantly.

Green was examining a holographic display of the local terrain. "Your assistant tells me you've located the stalkers?"

"We've detected vocalizations, yes, sir."

Green smiled, revealing perfectly maintained teeth. "Excellent. I've been studying the Collective's xenobiological database. Fascinating creatures. Tell me, Doctor—you were on the expedition that first documented them?"

"Yes, sir. We observed them from a safe distance and—"

"And you killed one, I believe?"

Adrian shifted uncomfortably. "It was necessary for defensive purposes, sir. When it charged our observation post."

Green nodded slowly. "I see. And that makes you quite the expert, doesn't it? The first human ever to kill a crystalline stalker."

"I... suppose so, sir."

"Of course," Green said, his smile not reaching his eyes. "Though I imagine the Collective's xenobiologists have killed quite a few on their own worlds. Still, you should have reported your discovery to me immediately."

"I had intended to file a full report, sir, at the first opportunity—"

"Of course you did," Green interrupted. "Like all citizens of the Commonwealth, you know me and trust me. I'm sure your intentions were the best."

Adrian felt sweat beading on his forehead despite the suit's climate control.

"Now," Green continued, "I want you to help me locate these creatures. I've come a very long way for this opportunity."

Over the next several hours, they tracked through the crystalline forest, following the vocalizations. Green carried the only weapon—a military-grade plasma rifle capable of cutting through starship armor. The rest of them were unarmed, serving as guides and bearers for equipment.

They found tracks near a mineral seep where the local fauna came to drink. The impressions in the soft ground were unmistakable—three-toed, each toe ending in a crystalline claw that had scored the rock beneath.

"Fresh," confirmed Robert Gilbert, who had some field research experience.

They followed the tracks deeper into the forest. The bioluminescent plants cast eerie shadows, and the air grew thick with spores that their suit filters had to work harder to process.

A stalker vocalized somewhere ahead—a sound like breaking glass mixed with a predator's growl.

"They're moving away," Robert said.

"Damn," Green muttered. Then his expression changed. "Wait. Doctor, you said in your report that these creatures hunt by sensing electromagnetic signatures?"

"Yes, sir. They can detect the bioelectric fields of living organisms from quite a distance."

"And they're aggressive?"

"Extremely. They'll pursue prey for days once they've locked onto a signature."

Green stroked his chin thoughtfully. "Then why are we chasing them? Why not make them come to us?"

Robert looked alarmed. "Sir, that would be extremely dangerous. We'd need proper defensive positions, and even then—"

"We won't be the bait," Green said, his smile returning. "Dr. Lowe, come with me."

Back at the camp, Green ordered his personal assistant, Emma Baker, to prepare equipment. Emma was a quiet woman who had served Green for years, her face carefully neutral no matter what she witnessed.

"Get me a tether cable," Green instructed. "Something strong. Rated for at least two hundred kilograms of pull force."

"What are you planning?" Adrian asked, his voice tight with fear.

"Simple field research methodology," Green said pleasantly. "We'll use you as bait. Your bioelectric signature will draw them in, and I'll eliminate them from a safe position."

"No!" Adrian gasped. "You can't—"

"Oh, come now, Doctor. You're an expert on these creatures. You know their behavior patterns. You'll be perfectly safe. I'll shoot them before they reach you."

"But if there's more than one—"

Green shrugged. "That's a risk we'll have to take. After all, isn't risk management part of field research?"

Adrian's mind raced. "Wait. Sir, listen to me. It's not me you want for this. It's Valeria. Dr. Hoffman, sir. She was the one who killed the first stalker on our expedition, not me. And last night—last night, she—"

"She what?" Green demanded, leaning forward intently.

Adrian's mouth was dry. "She said she was planning to expose you, sir. That's what she said. I heard her, sir. She said she was going to tell everyone about... about everything. She's the one you should use for bait. Then if there was an accident, sir, it wouldn't matter, because she was planning to betray you. I wouldn't—"

Green's eyes glittered. "Which one is she?"

"That one. By the equipment storage unit."

"The one with her back to me?"

"Yes, sir. That's her."

Green raised the plasma rifle smoothly and fired. The beam punched through Valeria's suit and body, cauterizing the wound instantly. She fell without a sound.

Adrian felt bile rise in his throat. "You... you..."

Emma Baker approached with the tether cable. "Sir, the equipment is ready."

"Excellent," Green said. "Secure it around Dr. Lowe's waist."

"Wait," Adrian begged, trying to push the cable away. "You don't want to use me, sir. Not after I told you about her. Please, sir. If anything should happen to me... Please, sir. Don't do it."

"Secure it," Green ordered.

Emma's hands trembled slightly as she fastened the cable around Adrian's waist, but her face remained impassive.

They took him to the mineral seep—Green, Emma, Robert Gilbert, and Lucy Hicks, another assistant. The seep was in a natural depression, with crystalline formations rising on three sides. They anchored the free end of the cable to one of the larger formations.

"You will call out," Green instructed. "Activate your suit's external speakers and call out at maximum volume."

Adrian was shaking uncontrollably.

"Let me hear you," Green said.

Adrian made a weak sound.

"You'll have to do better than that." Green nodded to Emma, who activated something on her wrist device.

Adrian's suit delivered a painful electric shock. He screamed.

"Perfect," Green said. "Keep it up just like that." He turned to Emma. "We'll observe from that outcropping. It has good sight lines."

Slowly, they climbed to a position above the seep. Green settled into a comfortable spot with the plasma rifle at ready. Emma positioned herself nearby, her expression carefully blank.

"You feel it?" Green asked her. "The excitement? It's always like this before a kill."

"I feel it," Emma said quietly.

Green chuckled. "You were with me on the Kepler expedition?"

"Yes, sir."

"That was something. Remember those indigenous predators?" He ran his hand along the rifle's stock.

The sun—a dim, reddish star—began its slow descent toward the horizon. The bioluminescent plants grew brighter as natural light faded. Adrian's screams echoed across the seep, bouncing off crystalline formations.

Emma sat motionless, watching. Green's breathing grew faster, more excited. The forest was eerily quiet except for Adrian's cries.

A stalker vocalized in the distance—that distinctive sound of breaking glass and growling.

Green laughed nervously. "It heard him."

"We're lucky to rouse one so quickly," Emma said.

Green braced the rifle against a rock. "This is what I live for. The waiting. The anticipation. Knowing that in just moments, something is going to emerge from that forest, and I'm going to kill it."

"It's not only the killing," Emma said carefully.

"Exactly! You understand. It's the waiting too. The suspense. The knowledge that you've set the trap perfectly, chosen your ground, placed your bait." He clenched his fist. "And now you just wait to see if they'll take it."

The stalker vocalized again, closer. Another answered from a different direction.

"There are two," Emma said, her voice tense.

"Even better," Green said. "Hey! Down there! Let's hear you really scream!"

Adrian, below, had stopped screaming and was pressed against the crystalline formation, his eyes wide with terror.

"I've always loved hunting," Green said. "More than anything else. More than business, more than power. The pure simplicity of it."

Emma shifted position. "People should hunt because they need to. For food. For protection. For research."

"No," Green said sharply. "People should hunt for the love of hunting itself."

"Killing?"

"Hunting," Green repeated firmly.

The stalkers vocalized again, very close now. There was a sound of crystalline branches breaking.

"Here they come!" Green said, trembling with excitement.

Adrian had stopped screaming entirely. He was frozen against the formation, staring at the forest.

Green leaned forward, the rifle still resting on the rock before him.

The forest erupted. Two crystalline stalkers emerged—creatures like nothing in Earth's evolutionary history. Their bodies were partially translucent, with internal organs visible through crystalline exoskeletons. Their eyes glowed with bioluminescence, and their jaws were lined with teeth like shards of diamond. They were beautiful and terrifying, products of an alien evolutionary path that had produced intelligence without consciousness, predation without malice.

"Shoot!" Emma hissed. "For God's sake, shoot!"

"Wait," Green said. "I want to see what they do." He hadn't moved the rifle. He was leaning forward, his breath coming in rapid gasps.

The lead stalker oriented on Adrian. Its body shifted color, processing the bioelectric signature.

"Look!" Green cried. "Here it comes!"

Adrian began screaming again.

Still Green didn't raise the plasma rifle. He was laughing, his eyes wide with excitement. Emma waited, frozen, watching the stalker in horrified fascination.

The stalker charged toward Adrian, its crystalline claws scoring the rock as it ran.

"Watch! Watch!" Green cried gleefully.

And then the Collective sprang their trap.

The forest behind Green and Emma exploded with movement. Collective soldiers—humanoid but distinctly alien, with their characteristic iridescent skin and compound eyes—emerged from camouflaged positions. They had been waiting, watching, studying these humans who had invaded their space, killed their wildlife, and now revealed their true nature.

The lead Collective soldier carried a weapon that hummed with barely contained energy. It spoke in perfectly accented human Standard: "Juan Green. "They'll have to," Victoria said. "We have evidence. Documentation. Testimony from dozens of sources. The game theory was always in our favor—eventually, he would overreach, and when he did, we'd be ready."

She turned away from the seep. "Let's get everyone back to the shuttle. We have a lot of work ahead of us."

As they walked back through the crystalline forest, the stalkers followed at a distance, their control collars glinting in the bioluminescent light. They were magnificent creatures, Victoria thought—products of millions of years of evolution, adapted perfectly to their environment. They deserved better than to be hunted for sport by men like Juan Green.

The shuttle lifted off an hour later, carrying Green in restraints, along with the expedition members and the evidence that would reshape the Commonwealth. As they rose through the atmosphere, Victoria looked down at Greenfield, Jarvonia—a world that would now be properly studied, properly protected, properly integrated into the growing alliance between humanity and the Collective.

Green had come here to hunt. Instead, he had been caught in a trap years in the making, a trap built on patience, evidence, and the cooperation of two species working toward a common goal.

The hunter had become the hunted.

And justice, Victoria thought, had been served.

I wished they weren't starting with an invention, risking disappointment, but I said nothing, knowing I could help them adjust later.

That evening I told Elena about the day's ideas. Most seemed impractical, but several were intriguing.

Mateo wanted to create a game-theory-based simulation for teaching resource allocation—a board game that demonstrated tragedy of the commons scenarios.

Wei wanted to design modular furniture that could be reconfigured for different community gathering needs.

Layla, moving past her garden ideas, suggested creating seed packets with embedded information—QR codes that linked to growing guides and environmental impact data.

Rita added that if you designed the packets creatively, they could become collectible art objects, encouraging seed saving.

These ideas incorporated sophisticated concepts, and I spent some time discussing systems thinking principles with them.

"My," said Elena, "they're remarkably insightful. Mateo sounds like a natural facilitator. I don't think you'll need Dr. Park's help."

I feel somewhat embarrassed about the wind sculpture, even now. That it worked surprised me. That it worked so beautifully was humbling.

Four of them were at the greenhouse when I arrived the next morning, and the sculpture hung from a tree branch, its tubes singing softly in the breeze. I stood listening, then they noticed me.

"Hello, Mr. Reyes," Alice said, gesturing toward it. I examined the sculpture for several minutes. It was exquisitely crafted, with a professional quality.

"It's too perfect," Alice told Rita. "Art should have some rawness."

"You're right," Rita agreed. She adjusted one tube slightly. "There, now it has dissonance."

Indeed, in the morning breeze, the sculpture now produced an intriguing mix of harmony and tension.

As we walked back to the greenhouse, I asked Rita, "How did you know that angle would create dissonance?"

She looked thoughtful. "It had to, didn't it? It changed the resonance patterns." She glanced at me quickly. "Of course, I tried various configurations while building it."

"Naturally," I said. "Where's Mateo?"

"He went to the Council office," Wei told me, "to request funding. We'll need materials to produce more sculptures."

"But I said yesterday that Councilor Brennan and I were providing initial capital."

"Oh, certainly, but wouldn't it be better to go through official channels? More aligned with community values?"

"Perhaps," I said, "but the Council generally requires detailed proposals."

Mateo walked in and handed me a document. "I got five hundred credits approved. It took some discussion—half the environmental committee wanted to hear the proposal. The account's in your name, Mr. Reyes, and you'll need to authorize expenditures. They want you to stop by and sign the agreement."

My heart sank. I'd never dealt with bureaucratic funding processes, and they made me anxious. To say nothing of being responsible for five hundred credits. I mentally vowed to be very careful.

"So then I stopped by the arts supply cooperative," Mateo continued, "and ordered materials. We hadn't finalized a name yesterday, but I made an executive decision. Fairview Futures—how's that?"

Everyone nodded approval.

"Just simple design on the letterhead," he explained. "Fairview Futures—Highpoint, Yendor."

I found my voice. "Professionally printed, I assume?"

"Well, of course," he replied. "Presentation matters."

My appetite was subdued that evening, and Elena noticed my preoccupation, but asked no questions. I told her about the sculpture's success and the group's ambitious plans.

On Friday we established a production process, soon developing an efficient workflow: cutting tubes to calculated lengths, treating them with weatherproofing solution, assembling them in Rita's designed configurations, and hanging the finished sculptures to cure.

Wei had located a supplier of bamboo tubes, which produced wonderful tones and aligned with our environmental ethics. I didn't know what they cost until later.

Within two weeks we had nearly fifty sculptures completed and packaged. Frankly, I was ready for a break, but Mateo, our acknowledged expert on community engagement, wanted more inventory. This quantity satisfied him, and he said he'd begin outreach the following week.

Alice, with touching confidence, asked him to reserve one for her family.

Three other developments occurred that day. Alice brought her laptop and spent the afternoon working on what appeared to be quite competent graphic design for promotional materials.

And Layla brought samples of her seed packet designs. They were beautiful—small envelopes with botanical illustrations and embedded information chips.

"What species?" I asked.

Layla smiled. "Heritage vegetables adapted to our climate. I've been selecting for drought tolerance while maintaining flavor profiles."

"That's remarkable. How long have you been working on this?"

"Three growing seasons. I've documented everything—it's proper peer review quality data."

"Is it effective?"

She pulled out her phone and showed me growth comparison charts. "These varieties use 40% less water than commercial equivalents."

The third Friday development reached me on Monday morning.

I arrived at the greenhouse slightly late to find several vehicles parked outside and the space full of people, including two Council representatives. Our Fairview officials are quite young and informal, but they still looked official, though currently they were laughing.

"Well," I said in my best classroom voice, "what's happening here?"

"Are you Reyes?" the taller representative asked.

"I am," I said, and someone took a photograph.

A young journalist grasped my arm. "Oh, Mr. Reyes, please, tell me about the collective's work. This is exactly the kind of story we need."

"Perhaps someone should brief me first."

"You don't know? One of your members installed a wind sculpture in Stonegate's central plaza last night—without permission. It's wonderful, but it's caused quite a discussion about public art and the social contract."

I shook my head, stunned.

"It was perfect timing. Morning commuters discovered it, and by noon there was a crowd. The sculpture's song changes with the wind, and people are calling it 'The Voice of Stonegate.' And this morning"—she smiled—"someone anonymously contacted the Council—of course it was the same young person who installed it—Mateo?—and here we are. And we've just seen demonstrations of those amazing seed packets and heard the plans for vertical gardens."

"Gardens?"

"Yes, those modular living walls. Who would have thought young people could develop such sophisticated systems?"

After things settled, Mr. Lawrence came down from the house to see what the excitement was about, then returned to work. Mrs. Lawrence went back inside. The journalist and photographer left. Mateo was jubilant.

"Did you hear? They're calling it 'The Voice of Stonegate.' I wish we had a hundred sculptures ready. A thousand. This is exactly what community engagement looks like. Layla, how soon can you produce more seed packets? And Rita, how many bird behavior datasets do you have?"

Those datasets! I've always found ornithology interesting in theory, but I must admit Rita's work was genuinely impressive.

"How many observation hours?" I asked.

"About four hundred, across three years. Want to see the analysis?"

I won't try to explain her methodology, but it was clear she'd done rigorous systematic observation. We asked Mrs. Lawrence to join us for a discussion. She listened carefully.

"All right," she finally said, "if you're serious about this. But you'll need proper protocols for any research involving living creatures. And you can't use this greenhouse once winter comes—you'll need heated space."

"We'll have transitioned by then," Rita predicted. "Once our work is published, other researchers will replicate it. The collective will move on to new projects."

Rita was right, despite our concerns about scaling too quickly. After the
Fairview Chronicle
gave us most of page two, including photographs, we had regular visitors. Many wanted to purchase sculptures or seed packets, but Mateo insisted on working through established community channels.

The arts cooperative took all our sculptures at forty credits each—Mateo's pricing alarmed me, but they sold immediately. He valued the seed packets at fifteen credits per set and found ready buyers.

Our beautiful letterhead arrived, along with quickly printed project proposal forms.

The following Tuesday, a energetic woman extricated herself from her vehicle and walked into the greenhouse. I looked up from where I was assembling planter frames.

"Hi," she said. "You're Marcus Reyes, correct? I'm Dr. Sarah Kim, and I work in the intellectual property section at the district's innovation center. My supervisor sent me, though I'd have come anyway. What are you doing to protect Fairview Futures' innovations?"

I straightened up and brushed off my hands. "Well, I've been wondering about that, but I know very little about such matters—"

"Exactly," she interrupted. "We thought that might be the case. Three of us at the center would like to contribute time. Partly because we're interested, partly because you may have genuinely novel approaches worth protecting. Interested? You handle filing fees—about a hundred credits per innovation. We'll handle everything else."

"What's to lose," Mateo interjected.

And so we acquired intellectual property support.

The day our design application was filed, Alice contacted a dozen sustainable design firms, sent specifications to each, and offered licensing arrangements. Result: one licensee with a two-thousand-credit advance.

It was a foggy morning about three weeks later when I arrived at the greenhouse. Dr. Kim was there, along with everyone except Mateo. Sarah had her feet up on a work table.

"Hi," she said. "Good news."

"Tell me," I replied.

"I am," she said, "in a cautious legal sense, of course. Layla and I have been reviewing her seed development work. I've spent recent evenings studying agricultural patents and genetic selection literature. There are countless patents on crop varieties and selection methods, but it looks"—she held up a cautionary hand—"it just looks like we have something genuinely novel. If we get protection, you have a valuable property."

"That's good, Dr. Kim," Layla said, "but it's not the most important thing."

"No?" Sarah raised an eyebrow at me, and I handed her a small packet.

She opened it carefully. "What is this?"

"Soil amendment," Layla told her. "It's designed for Fairview's specific soil conditions. Try a bit."

Sarah examined it closely. "It's remarkably fine-textured, and there's something unusual about the color."

"It contains biochar and mycorrhizal fungi in a specific ratio. It improves water retention by 60% while enhancing nutrient availability."

"I see. What's in it?"

"Several components. Applied systems thinking. Waste wood from district maintenance, processed with controlled pyrolysis, combined with cultivated fungal cultures."

"Just several components. And does it work long-term?"

"Three growing seasons of data confirm it," I said.

Dr. Kim stood and looked out into the fog. After a moment she said, "Reyes, Layla and I are heading to my office. We can work better there, and if we're going to revolutionize urban agriculture, no time like the present."

After they left, I turned to the others. "Let's talk. Where's Mateo?"

"Oh, he went to the Council to request expanded funding."

"Whatever for? We have over eight thousand credits in the account."

"Well," Wei said, looking slightly sheepish, "we were planning to acquire some fabrication equipment. You see, Rita refined my idea for modular furniture." He grabbed paper. "Look, we make components that can be reconfigured using magnetic connections, like this—" And he was off explaining.

"What did they do today, dear?" Elena asked over dinner.

"Let's see. We selected fabrication equipment, Rita shared chapters from her book on urban ecology, and we found a space in the Fairview Arts Building we can rent for winter. Oh, and Sarah is starting the incorporation process."

"Winter space," Elena repeated. "You mean you're continuing after school starts?"

"Why not? The young people can manage their studies easily, and they'll only work a few hours weekly during the school year."

"Even so, isn't this a lot of responsibility for children?"

"They're not working for anyone. They're the collective. Dr. Kim and I will be the only formal staff—initially, anyway."

Elena looked startled. "Did you say you'd be staff?"

"Sure," I told her. "They've offered me a small stake in the collective, and I'd be foolish to refuse. After all, what's to lose?"
