story_name: And Then the Town Took Off
synthetic_story:
The district of Oakridge simply vanished on the night of March 15th.

A delivery driver named Sofia Stone was the first to report it. She had been rushing south along Highway 7, trying to make up time after a longer-than-expected stop at a distribution center, when she slammed on her brakes. If she'd gone another thirty feet, she would have driven straight into the void where Oakridge had been.

Sofia couldn't see the full extent of the emptiness because of the darkness, but it looked massive. Bigger than any sinkhole she'd ever heard of. Her first thought was some kind of catastrophic infrastructure collapse. She reversed two hundred feet, set out emergency flares, then sped off to find a phone signal.

State authorities converged on the former site of Oakridge from multiple directions. Communicating by radio across the vast emptiness, they confirmed that the district was definitely missing. They called in the National Guard.

The Guard surrounded the area with personnel—more than eight hundred were needed—to keep people from falling into the void. A helicopter pilot who flew over it reported that it looked as if someone had used a giant cookie cutter on the landscape.

The regional transit authority complained that one of its automated trains was missing. The train's schedule had it passing through Oakridge at 11:47 PM. That seemed to fix the time of the disappearance around midnight.

Someone pointed out that March 15th was the Ides of March, historically a day of upheaval.

Somebody else said they'd better check for radiation or chemical contamination. An environmental safety official brought detection equipment, but everything registered normal.

A National Guard officer volunteered to take a vehicle down into the void, having found what seemed like a navigable slope. She was gone for over an hour, but when she emerged on the other side, she reported that the void was smooth, bowl-shaped, and showed no signs of explosion or fire. She'd found no people, no buildings—no trace of anything except the void itself.

The Governor asked federal authorities whether any unidentified aircraft had been in the region. Washington said no. The Department of Defense and various agencies denied conducting any secret experiments.

Nor had there been any sensitive facilities in Oakridge that might have been targeted. The district's biggest employer was a film production studio, and the second-biggest was a venture capital firm specializing in virtual reality startups.

A commercial pilot found Oakridge early on the morning of March 16th. The pilot, Captain Jonathan Spencer, who prided himself on rational thinking and logic, was afraid he was seeing something impossible. The object emerged from a cloud layer at fifteen thousand feet, and Spencer changed course to avoid it. He noted with minimal relief that his co-pilot also saw the thing and wondered why it wasn't moving.

Then he saw the broadcast tower on it.

A few minutes later, he had relayed a message from Oakridge, formerly of the Pearlbrook Region, addressed to anyone listening:

It said that Oakridge had declared independence from the ground.

One other radio message came from Oakridge, now airborne, on that first day. An amateur radio operator reported an unidentified voice saying plaintively:

"Getting cold up here!"

Kevin Mason had been dozing in the observation car of the express train when it jerked to a stop. He looked out the window, hoping this was Magnolia Province, where he planned to catch a connecting flight. But it wasn't. All he could see were emergency lights moving along the tracks.

The conductor looked into the car. A woman with striking auburn hair across the aisle—Kevin had noticed her earlier—asked, "Why did we stop?"

"Someone flagged us down," the conductor said. "We don't normally stop at Oakridge on this route."

The woman's hair was professionally styled, and Kevin had observed earlier that she carried herself with the confidence of someone used to authority. Her eyes had been focused on a tablet when Kevin entered the car, giving him time to notice her sharp features and the slight frown lines that suggested she was accustomed to finding fault. Her expression was one of practiced skepticism.

If the woman had given Kevin more than a cursory glance, she would have seen a man in his late twenties—about her age—lean and athletic, with dark hair, an unremarkable face, and a habit of tapping his fingers thoughtfully when concentrating.

But likely all she noticed was the locked metal case he carried, secured by a biometric lock to his left wrist.

"Will we be here long?" Kevin asked the conductor. He didn't want to miss his flight. The sooner he got to Highpoint Territory, the sooner he'd deliver the case. The biometric lock was one reason why his interest in the auburn-haired woman had been only passing.

"Can't say," the conductor told him. He let the door close and went down to the tracks.

Kevin hesitated, shrugged at the woman, said, "Excuse me," and followed the conductor. About twenty people were milling around the train as it sat in the dark. Kevin made his way forward and found a larger group gathered ahead of the locomotive.

Some kind of barricade had been erected across the tracks, covered with every imaginable warning device. There were LED flares, reflective barriers, emergency lights, and even an orange safety vest.

Kevin saw two people who must have been the engineer and assistant talking to an older woman wearing a civil defense vest, a long coat, and hiking boots.

"You'd go over the edge, I'm telling you," the older woman was saying.

"If you don't clear this obstruction," the engineer said, "I'll push right through it. Over the edge? Are you serious?"

"See for yourself," the woman in the vest said. "Go ahead. Look."

The engineer was exasperated. She turned to her assistant. "You look. Humor her. Then let's go."

The woman—she introduced herself as Dr. Vanessa Shaw—went off with the assistant. Kevin followed them. They had walked a quarter mile along the gravel when the assistant stopped. "Okay," she said, "where's this edge? I don't see anything." The tracks seemed to stretch endlessly into the darkness.

"It's another half mile or so," Dr. Shaw said.

"Well, let's hurry. We haven't got all night."

The older woman chuckled. "I'm afraid you do."

They came to it at last, stopping well back from it. Dr. Shaw seemed almost proud as she made a theatrical gesture.

"Behold," she said. "The edge of our new world."

True enough, everything seemed to stop, and they could see lights from the ground shining far below where ground should not be visible.

Kevin Mason and the assistant walked cautiously toward the edge while Dr. Shaw strode ahead with the confidence of someone who had been there before. But there was a wind, and they didn't venture too close. Nevertheless, Kevin could see that it was apparently a clean, precise edge, not ragged like something caused by an explosion. This had the feeling of intentional design.

Standing on tiptoe and fighting a wave of vertigo, Kevin looked over the edge. He didn't need to stand on tiptoe any more than he needed to grip the armrest during a tense movie scene, but the situation seemed to demand it. Over the edge, he could see a vast section of the Pearlbrook Region. At least he assumed it was Pearlbrook.

Kevin looked at the assistant, who had a stunned expression, then at Dr. Shaw, who was smiling and nodding.

"You see what I mean," she said. "You would have gone right over. I believe it's a three-mile drop."

"Of course you could have stayed on the train," the man driving the electric sedan said, "but I really think you'll be more comfortable at the Institute."

Kevin Mason, sitting in the back seat with the auburn-haired woman from the observation car, asked, "Institute?"

"The Oakridge Institute for Advanced Studies. We focus on applied ethics and cultural sociology, though we're not traditionally accredited. What did you say your name was, miss?"

"Sasha Holmes," she said. "I work in international diplomacy."

"Ms. Holmes. I'm Jin Gupta. You know Mr. Mason, I suppose."

The woman smiled slightly. "We've exchanged glances." Kevin nodded and smiled back.

"There's plenty of room in the guest quarters," Jin said. "People don't exactly line up to visit the Institute."

"Are you connected with it?" Kevin asked.

"Me? No. I'm the district administrator of Oakridge. The whole place has really risen in the world, hasn't it?"

"Literally overnight," Sasha Holmes said. "If what Mr. Mason and the train assistant say is true. I haven't seen the edge myself."

"You'll have a better chance to look in the morning," the administrator said, "assuming we don't settle back down in the meantime."

"Was there any kind of explosion?" Kevin asked.

"No. There wasn't any sensation at all, as far as I noticed. I was reviewing some strategic planning documents on my tablet—we're always dealing with community organizing issues in Oakridge. Well, suddenly my internet connection improved dramatically. Then the phone rang, and it was Dr. Shaw."

"The older woman with the vest and the hiking boots?" Sasha Holmes asked.

"Yes. Vanessa Shaw, Director of the Institute's Applied Physics program."

"Applied Physics?" Kevin asked.

"Among other things. The Institute isn't bound by traditional academic constraints. Well, Dr. Shaw called and said, 'Jin'—that's my name—'we've achieved separation.' She was being cryptic, of course. I said, 'What?' and then she explained."

"Explained what?" Sasha Holmes asked. "I mean, does she have any theory about this?"

"She has theories about everything. I think what she was trying to convey was that this—this levitation—confirmed her gravitational manipulation hypothesis."

"What's that?" Kevin asked.

"I haven't the faintest idea. I'm an administrator, not a physicist. Dr. Shaw went on about it for a while, something about artificial gravity fields and quantum mechanics, but I think she was mainly calling as a courtesy, so the district administrator wouldn't look foolish the next morning."

"What's the population of Oakridge?" Kevin asked.

"Four thousand, including the Institute staff and students. Four thousand and fifty-three, counting you people from the train. I guess you'll be with us for a while."

"What do you mean by that?" Sasha Holmes asked sharply.

"Well, I don't see how you can get down. Do you?"

"Does Oakridge have an airport?" Kevin asked. "I need to get to Highpoint Territory."

"Nope," Jin said. "No airport. No suitable landing area, either."

"Maybe not for planes," Kevin said, "but helicopters could land almost anywhere."

"No helicopters here."

"Maybe not. But I bet they'll be swarming around by morning."

"Hm," said Jin Gupta. Kevin couldn't quite read his expression in the rearview mirror. "I suppose they could. Well, here's the Institute. You go right through that entrance, where the others are going. There's Dr. Shaw. I need to speak with her—excuse me."

The administrator hurried off across the campus. Kevin looked at Sasha Holmes, who was frowning. "Are you thinking," he asked, "that Administrator Gupta was perhaps less than completely forthcoming?"

"I'm thinking," she said, "that I should have stayed at my conference another day and taken a direct flight."

"Where were you headed?" Kevin asked.

"Highpoint Territory. I work with the diplomatic corps." She paused. "What do you do, Mr. Mason?"

"I'm a courier for a tech company. Artificial intelligence prototypes, mostly. Hence the locked case."

"I see," she said, though her tone suggested she wasn't entirely convinced. "We should find somewhere to sleep. It's getting late."

"Agreed," Kevin said. They were met by a middle-aged man who introduced himself as Marco Watson, the Institute's hospitality coordinator. "We'll make you comfortable," he said. "What a night! Dr. Shaw is absolutely thrilled. We haven't had this much excitement since the particle accelerator malfunctioned."

They caught a glimpse of Dr. Shaw, still in her civil defense vest, gesturing animatedly to someone in a lab coat.

Kevin Mason had slept, but not well. He'd tried to maneuver the metal case through his sleeve to remove his jacket, but whatever was inside was too large. The Institute had given him a private room in the guest quarters, and he'd removed his pants but had to sleep in his shirt and jacket. He got up feeling grimy and did what minimal preparation was possible.

It was eight o'clock according to his watch, and activity was evident outside. He had a view of the campus from his window. Bright sun illuminated young people moving generally toward a low building—probably the cafeteria—while others moved in various directions. The air was remarkably clear, and the morning shadows were sharp. Only then did he fully remember that he and the entire district of Oakridge were suspended in the air.

He went through the guest quarters. A few people were still sleeping. Others had left their unmade beds. He shivered as he stepped outside. It was cold, though not freezing, and his breath was visible. First he'd eat, he decided, so he'd have energy to examine the edge in daylight and see the ground below.

The dining hall was cafeteria-style, and he got in line with a tray for juice, eggs, and coffee. He saw no one he knew, but as he looked for a table, a slender woman with platinum blonde hair smiled and gestured to the empty seat across from her.

"You're Mr. Mason," she said. "Won't you join me?"

"Thanks," he said, unloading his tray. "How did you know?"

"The mystery man with the locked case. You're hard to miss. I'm Nathan Morris—yes, Nathan, not Natalie. My parents had a sense of humor. Are you with some intelligence agency? Or did you steal something valuable?"

"How do you do. No, just a tech courier. What an unusual name. Dr. Shaw's student?"

"Assistant, actually," she said. "Also her daughter, though we keep that quiet professionally. A pity, because if I'd had a choice, I'd have gone to a normal university. As it is, I'm duty-bound to represent the second generation at the experimental facility."

"Experimental facility? You mean the Institute?" Kevin struggled to manipulate his utensils without knocking things over with his attached case.

"Here, let me help you," Nathan said, cutting his food. "You should order scrambled eggs tomorrow. Yes, the Institute. Home of the unorthodox theory and the controversial experiment."

"I'm sure it's not that bad. Thanks. As for tomorrow, I hope to be gone by then."

"How do you plan to leave? Float down on a parachute?"

"I'll find a way. I'm more interested in how I got up here."

"You were levitated, like everyone else."

"You make it sound deliberate, Ms. Morris, as if someone lifted an entire district for some purpose."

"Well, that's debatable. Have you seen the news feeds?"

"I didn't know there were any."

"Actually, there's just one local outlet, the Oakridge Observer, a weekly publication. This is a special edition. The editor must have worked all night." She pulled out her phone and showed him a digital edition.

Kevin blinked at the headline: "District Gets High"

"The editor's something of an independent thinker, like most people in Oakridge," Nathan said.

Kevin read the story, which seemed to treat the situation with surprising levity despite its gravity.

"Residents planning to travel beyond district boundaries today are advised to reconsider. It's a long way down. Where Oakridge was once surrounded by the Pearlbrook Region, today Oakridge ends literally at the district line.

A Citizens' Emergency Barrier Committee is being organized, but in the meantime, everyone is warned to stay well away from the edge. The laws of physics seem to have been suspended for the district, but it's doubtful the same exemption would apply to a curious individual bent on investigating..."

Kevin skimmed the rest. "I don't see anything about it being deliberate."

Nathan had been preparing Kevin's coffee. She pushed it toward him and said, "It's not on the front page. The editor and Administrator Gupta don't get along, so you'll find the administrator's statement in a box on page three."

Kevin navigated to the page, took a sip of coffee, nodded his thanks, and read:

"Administrator Claims Independence from Ground

Administrator Jin Gupta, in a proclamation issued locally and transmitted to the ground via drone, announced today that Oakridge has declared independence. His reasons were as vague as his explanation.

The 'reasons' include: (1) Oakridge has been neglected by regional and federal agencies; (2) the Institute has been ridiculed by traditional academic institutions; and (3) the district has been subject to unfair pollution control regulations that hampered its film production industry.

The 'explanation' consists of a 73-page paper on gravitational field manipulation by Dr. Vanessa Shaw of the Institute, which the editor (a) does not fully understand; (b) lacks space to publish; and which (being highly technical) he (c) cannot adequately summarize for general readers."

Kevin said, "I'm beginning to like this editor."

"He's wonderful," Nathan said. "He's about the only one in town who challenges Mother."

"Does your mother claim that she levitated Oakridge off the ground?"

"Not to me. I'm one of those inconveniences, a skeptic. She gave up trying to convince me when I was seventeen. I had a physics professor at a summer program—not at the Institute—who gave me all kinds of difficult questions to ask Mother. I asked them, being naturally contrary, and Mother has considered me intellectually lost ever since."

"How old are you, Ms. Morris, if I may ask?"

She sat up straighter, adjusting her sweater. She had an excellent figure, intelligent eyes, a delicate nose, and expressive lips. She could have been the star of any campus with a more conventional student body.

"You may call me Nathan," she said. "And I'm twenty-two."

Kevin grinned. "Recently?"

"Four months ago. How old are you, Mr. Mason?"

"Kevin's the name I've had for twenty-eight years. Please use it."

"Gladly. And now, Kevin, unless you want more coffee, I'll accompany you to the edge of the world."

"On such short notice?" Kevin was intrigued. Last night the woman from the train had been coolly professional, and this morning a friendly blonde was apparently offering companionship. He wondered briefly where Sasha Holmes was.

"I'll admit to the double meaning," Nathan said. "What I meant—for now—was that we can walk out to where Oakridge used to be connected to the rest of the region and see how the ground is managing without us."

"I'd like that. But don't you have work to do?"

"Sure. I'm supposed to be analyzing data from yesterday's sensors. But I'm an expert procrastinator, which is why I'm still finishing my graduate work at my advanced age. On to the edge!"

They walked south from the campus and came to the train tracks. The train was still there, going nowhere. It had been abandoned except for the conductor, who had dutifully remained aboard overnight.

"What's happening?" he asked when he saw them. "Any word from down there?"

"Not that I know of," Kevin said. He introduced Nathan Morris. "What are you going to do?"

"What can I do?" the conductor asked.

"You can go to the Institute and have breakfast," Nathan said. "Nobody's going to bother your train."

The conductor decided that sounded reasonable and left.

"You know," Kevin said, "before the train stopped last night, I thought I saw a stream running alongside the tracks."

"Clearwater Stream," Nathan said. "That's right. It's just over there."

"Is it still there? Hasn't it all poured off the edge by now? Was that Oakridge's water supply?"

Nathan shrugged. "All I know is the water still works. Let's check the stream."

They found it flowing normally between its banks.

"Looks the same," she said.

"That's strange. Come on, let's follow it to the edge."

The edge, as Nathan called it, looked even more dramatic in daylight. Everything simply stopped. There was a residential area with houses and yards, then nothing. There was Clearwater Stream flowing along, then nothing. In the distance, a grove of trees simply ended.

"Where is the water going?" Kevin asked. "I can't tell."

"Down, presumably. Rain for the people below."

"But it should be drained by now. I'm going to look."

"Don't! You'll fall!"

"I'll be careful." He walked cautiously toward the edge. Nathan followed, a few feet behind. He stopped a yard from the brink and waited for vertigo to pass. The ground was spread out like a satellite image, far below. Kevin took another careful step, then sat down.

"Careful," said Nathan. She laughed nervously, then sat down too.

"I still can't see where the water goes," Kevin said. He lay flat on his stomach and began to inch forward. "You stay there."

Finally, he inched to a point where, by stretching, he could almost reach the edge. He gave another push forward and his right hand closed over the brink. For a moment he lay there, breathing hard, head pressed to the ground.

"How do you feel?" Nathan asked.

"Terrified. When I get my nerve back, I'll lift my head and look."

Nathan reached out tentatively, then firmly grasped his ankle. "Just in case of wind," she said.

"Thanks. That helps. Okay, here goes." He lifted his head. "Damn."

"What?"

"It's still not clear. Do you have a mirror?"

"I have a compact." She took it from her bag with her free hand and tossed it to him. It rolled and Kevin had to grab to keep it from going over. Nathan gasped. Kevin was momentarily shaken and had to put his head back down. "Sorry," she said.

Kevin opened the compact and carefully transferred it to his right hand. He held it out beyond the edge and peered into it, focusing on the end of the stream. "Now I see it. The water isn't going off the edge!"

"It isn't? Then where?"

"Down, yes, but it's as if it's going into a vertical shaft, just short of the edge."

"Why? How?"

"I can't see clearly, but that's what it looks like. Hold on. I'm coming back." He inched away from the edge, then stood and brushed himself off. He returned her compact. "I think we need to check the other end of the stream."

"The source?"

"Exactly."

Clearwater Stream didn't cut through the center of Oakridge but flowed in an arc through the southern part of the district. They had about two miles to walk, past Clearwater Bridge—which used to connect to the neighboring area, Nathan said—past the Oakridge Recreation Center, and on to the edge again.

But as they approached what should be the source of the stream, they found a chain-link fence blocking the area. "This is new," Nathan said.

The fence, which had a sign on it reading "WARNING—ELECTRIFIED," was semicircular, with each end at the edge, and tarps hung behind it so they couldn't see the mouth of the stream. The water flowed from under the tarp and fence.

"Look how it comes in pulses," Nathan said.

"As if it's being pumped."

Smaller text on the sign read: "Protecting source of Clearwater Stream, one of two water sources for Oakridge. Electrical charge in fence is sufficient to cause serious injury." It was signed: "Marco Watson, Security Coordinator, Jin Gupta, Administrator."

"What's the other source?" Kevin asked.

"North Reservoir, probably," Nathan said. "It's used for the water treatment facility."

"Is the reservoir entirely within the district boundaries?"

"I don't know."

"If it were on the edge, and if someone took a boat out on it, I wonder what would happen?"

"I know one thing—I wouldn't be there holding your ankle while you found out."

She took his arm as they gazed past the electrified fence at the ground below and to the west.

"It's impressive, isn't it?" she said. "I wonder if that's the Magnolia Province way over there?"

He patted her hand absent-mindedly. "I wonder if it's west at all. I mean, how do we know Oakridge is maintaining the same orientation as before?"

"We could tell by the sun, silly."

"Of course," he said, grinning. "And I guess we're not high enough to see very far. If we were, we'd be able to see the mountain ranges."

They were contemplating the geography when a plane emerged from a cloud layer and, a moment later, veered sharply. They could make out commercial airline markings on the fuselage. As it turned, they imagined they could see faces at the windows. They waved and thought they saw people wave back. Then the plane climbed eastward and disappeared.

"Well," Kevin said as they turned back toward the Institute, "now we know they know. Maybe we'll start getting some answers. Or, if not answers, then rescue."

"Rescue?" Nathan squeezed the arm she was holding. "Why? Don't you like it here?"

"If you mean don't I like you, the answer is yes, I do. But if I don't get out of this biometric lock soon so I can shower and change clothes, you're not going to like me."

"You're still quite presentable, if a bit scruffy." She stopped, still holding his arm, and he turned so they were face to face. "So kiss me," she said, "before you get any worse."

They were in the middle of an extremely pleasant kiss when the metal case at the end of Kevin's biometric lock began to emit a high-pitched alarm.

*Brookhaven Basic*. 8.4 silver per flagon. Self-styled King of Ales from Brookhaven, Fendria.

*Price category*: The tasters knew that each ale came from the expensive, medium, or cheap category—and they had to guess where A through J belonged. A rating of 3 was most expensive, 2 for average, 1 for cheap.

1) Buy Peter's Premium Lakeside Amber when they want an individual goblet of amber to be as good as it can be.

2) Buy Bruno's Basic at all other times, since it gives them the maximum taste and social influence per silver invested.

Diana once told me, "The mark of a true scholar is not confidence in one's conclusions, but willingness to test them." This experiment has embodied that principle. And the results, while humbling, have been illuminating in ways I didn't anticipate.

The Selection Process

"My parents are very practical people," Teresa said with a smile, "and they made sure I developed marketable skills before they would support my academic pursuits. My father runs an environmental consulting firm in Redwood, Estoria, and I've worked with him on impact assessments and policy reviews. I'll always be grateful he insisted I learn those practical skills. I don't think he has much faith in academic research, but he's been supportive of giving me this opportunity. What do your parents think of your work in community development?"

Instead of answering, Melissa suddenly stood. "Let's go see how they're progressing with the technical candidates," she said. "I think they're almost finished."

Not wanting to press further, and sensing she might have asked too personal a question on such brief acquaintance, Teresa reluctantly stood as well and joined Melissa to observe the remainder of what she could only think of as the screening process.

As she drew closer to the table, she heard Sebastian saying, "I'm truly sorry, Mr. Daniels, but your background doesn't quite match what we need for this role. Perhaps in the future..." and his voice trailed off in discomfort.

Mohamed Daniels, a thin, earnest young man, answered almost desperately, "But, Mr. Shaw, credentials aren't everything. I'm a quick learner and deeply committed to environmental justice. Honestly! If you would just give me a chance to present my ideas, I know I could demonstrate how my perspective on cultural heritage preservation could enhance this initiative!"

"I don't doubt your commitment," Sebastian said gently, "but this particular role requires specific technical expertise in water management systems, like these three candidates I've selected to interview. The position demands it. I'm sorry."

Mr. Daniels nodded sadly, mumbled, "I understand," and walked away, his shoulders slumped and his hands gripping his briefcase tightly, looking less like an aspiring environmental advocate than any person in the world. Teresa watched him leave, not knowing whether to feel sorrier for him or for Sebastian.

"All right, everyone," Sebastian called out. "That completes the technical screening. All of you who have been selected will receive detailed briefing materials to review, including the sections relevant to your potential roles. Please study the entire initiative framework carefully so you understand the interconnections between different components. You have three days to prepare. We'll reconvene at ten o'clock on Saturday morning at the Harborview Community Center in Lethoria to conduct interviews. Thank you. And now for the policy positions."

The technical candidates left, after receiving their materials, and though they chatted amiably with one another, Teresa was certain each was viewing the others who were competing for the same positions with some wariness. Maintaining professional relationships in competitive fields was never easy, she thought, particularly for people with similar qualifications!

Sebastian's first priority in reviewing the policy candidates was, of course, for the director position. And, of course, it was for this role that he had the most applicants. More than fifteen people came forward when the announcement was made, and Teresa thought she had never seen so many impressive credentials and accomplished professionals. It would not be easy for Sebastian to make a selection. As Melissa, her new acquaintance, went forward to join the others, Teresa whispered encouragement, then stood to one side to observe.

Sebastian reviewed the candidates, regretfully dismissing several and occasionally asking some to consider other roles. His serious expression hardly varied as he spoke to each person, but Teresa thought she detected a hint of approval when he spoke with Melissa Mendoza. Another review of the remaining candidates eliminated a few more. Finally, only four remained, Melissa among them. Sebastian thanked them, distributed materials, and asked them to be at the community center on Saturday at noon.

Melissa returned to Teresa with eyes bright. "Oh, Teresa! I think you were right! I really believe I'm going to get the position! I know it!"

"Don't count too heavily on it," Teresa cautioned, "or you may be too disappointed if it doesn't work out. But," she added, enthusiastically violating her own advice, "I'm confident too! I'll see you Saturday. Even if I don't advance, I'll be there just to observe your interview!"

Then, with a smile of farewell, Teresa turned her attention to the "research coordinator with policy analysis experience" category that Sebastian had called for next. Once that was completed, she knew it would be her turn.

This time, there were fewer applicants, and Teresa remembered Peter telling her this would be one of their most difficult positions to fill. Only five candidates came forward, and Sebastian, with visible difficulty, reviewed them all. Unable to eliminate based on qualifications alone, he gave them all materials and asked them to come to the center. Then he called for "junior researchers with interdisciplinary backgrounds" and Teresa joined six other candidates in the screening process.

Sebastian reviewed them carefully, managing to look at Teresa with complete professional detachment. He gently eliminated two based on lack of relevant fieldwork experience, another for insufficient policy background, and a fourth whose research focused too narrowly on theoretical modeling without practical application. "The position requires someone with practical skills," Sebastian said with a rare smile, "but also someone who won't be overwhelmed by the complexity of real-world implementation. Your theoretical work is impressive, but I'm afraid you're not quite right for this particular role."

When he was done, Teresa and two others were given materials and told to come to the center on Saturday. Feeling both anxious and excited, Teresa settled herself on one of the plastic chairs along the wall and waited for Sebastian, Peter, and Maya to finish so she could join them for coffee.

Barely noticing the rest of the proceedings, she thought only about the coming interviews. She was so familiar with the initiative framework that she knew she had an advantage, perhaps unfairly, over the other candidates. She had watched the proposal develop from its initial concept to the finished document now in her hands, and had discussed it with Peter through each revision. She knew she could handle the position; in fact, she suspected privately that Peter had designed it with her in mind, and the thought made her uncomfortable. Still, it would not be easy, she knew. Sebastian's commitment to fairness and his absolute dedication to the initiative's success would prevent him from making any predetermined decisions.

But despite this knowledge, she couldn't help looking ahead—imagining the press conference announcing the initiative's first major success, the community meetings where real change would be discussed, the satisfaction of seeing environmental ethics and social justice principles actually implemented as she worked on the Foxwood Environmental Initiative, Peter Fuller's groundbreaking program in which Teresa Cole would play a crucial role!

II

The Candidates

The interview panel consisted of Sebastian Shaw, Peter Fuller, and three community representatives. The room was a stark municipal space with fluorescent lighting that gave everything a harsh, clinical appearance. The furniture was standard government issue: a long table for the panel, a single chair facing it for candidates, and rows of plastic seats along the walls for those waiting. Only the front section of the room was fully lit, and the back area was dim and unwelcoming, a shadowy expanse of empty chairs that seemed to emphasize the isolation of each candidate's experience.

At the table, a technical specialist was presenting his approach to water management challenges. Teresa knew, after the first few minutes, that he would not be selected. He had somehow completely missed the initiative's emphasis on community engagement and was heavily focused on purely technical solutions without considering the social justice implications. Sebastian, being perhaps more patient than Teresa, listened and watched with great attention. Maya, who was serving as Sebastian's assistant for the initiative, sat in a chair to the side, following along with the briefing materials and occasionally noting observations. Sebastian followed the entire presentation with no visible sign of judgment and, when the candidate finished, said, "Thank you. We'll communicate our decision within the next few days."

The next technical specialist was better, but still not quite on target, Teresa thought. He seemed to be emphasizing entrepreneurship and market economics, and although there were certainly economic considerations in the initiative, it was fundamentally about environmental ethics and institutional reform. Still, he was clearly more aligned with the initiative's values than the first candidate, and with guidance might do well.

Following his presentation, Sebastian again repeated his courteous, consistent formula, "Thank you. We'll communicate our decision within the next few days," and called for the next interview.

Teresa observed the remaining technical candidates, making mental notes about which seemed possible, which probable, and which had no realistic chance.

The same process was then followed for the senior research positions, and the same wide range of understanding was displayed. Some seemed to have no grasp of the initiative's underlying principles or its connection to network theory and systems thinking, and Teresa was certain these candidates had only reviewed the materials superficially. Others had a clear understanding of the kind of integrated approach required and tried to demonstrate it in the brief time they had. Still others were researchers who had one rather inflexible methodology and applied it to all kinds of problems. Their presentations were uniform variations on the same theme, all derivative of a single influential paper on game theory applications to environmental policy. They seemed to forget, Teresa thought, that game theory was a tool, not an end in itself, and that effective environmental work required adapting approaches to specific contexts. It frustrated her that some researchers thought they could succeed in a creative field by being derivative.

Each candidate, regardless of performance, was treated with professional courtesy by Sebastian, and each left looking reasonably confident about their prospects. Teresa was glad she wouldn't have to see their faces when they learned they hadn't been selected.

"The unfortunate part," she whispered to Peter, "isn't that there are so many unsuitable candidates, but that there are so many qualified ones, and only one can be selected for each position. I wish there were some way of telling the good ones we can't select that they were truly impressive, but that we simply couldn't hire everyone!"

"You can't let yourself dwell on that," Peter replied. "The strong candidates know their worth, and they won't be discouraged by this outcome. And the weak ones often have enough confidence to protect them from ever recognizing—or even considering—their limitations!"

The door at the back of the room opened quietly, and Teresa, turning in her seat, saw several of the policy candidates entering. They quietly found seats in the rear and settled down to await their turn.

"I think I'll go back there with the policy group," Teresa whispered. "I'm looking for the woman I met at the screening, and I'd like to speak with her before she interviews. Do you mind if I don't observe all of this?"

Peter smiled. "Go ahead. I'd leave too if I could without Sebastian thinking I wasn't committed. This process always troubles me as well!"

As she walked up the aisle as unobtrusively as possible, Teresa glanced at the candidates who had just entered. She recognized several faces from the screening three days ago but didn't immediately see her new acquaintance. She decided to step out to the hallway to wait for her there. Another small group entered the room as Teresa was leaving and, as she passed, one reached out and touched her arm.

Teresa turned in surprise to find herself greeted with a warm smile and a quick, friendly hug.

"Angela!" she cried. "What are you doing here?"

"Come out to the hallway, and I'll explain," Angela Hughes said, adjusting the glasses that had slipped down her nose during the greeting.

"But I thought you were in Parkview, working on that cultural exchange program with the indigenous communities," Teresa said, when they had reached the hallway. "What brings you here?"

"I'm afraid you don't read your professional newsletters very carefully," Angela said. "The Parkview program lost its funding when the state legislature cut the cultural heritage budget. At first we thought we'd find alternative funding sources, but the director finally decided, quite reasonably, that it would be more practical to wind down operations. I'm afraid we had to let most of the staff go, and we didn't have resources to continue."

"Oh, I'm so sorry," Teresa said. "And it was such an important opportunity for you, wasn't it?"

"Not really," Angela said. "The position wasn't ideal, and I'd rather not be associated with a failed initiative. Anyway, it gave me a chance to develop some valuable skills, and a foundation officer saw my work and said she thought I was effective, so perhaps I'm better off for the experience."

At that moment, Teresa saw Melissa Mendoza enter the hallway, and she motioned to her to join them. "Angela, this is Melissa Mendoza. She's interviewing for the policy director position today, and I hope she gets it. Melissa, I want you to meet Angela Hughes, one of my colleagues from graduate school."

"Colleagues?" Melissa questioned, slightly puzzled.

"Yes. We were in the same cohort at the Institute—a wonderful group—and we worked together on several research projects. The Institute brings together about a dozen graduate students each year, and we function like an intellectual community. I haven't seen Angela for months—she's been working in Parkview—and I'm still processing the surprise of seeing her now."

"Teresa tactfully neglected to mention that my program lost its funding," Angela laughed, "and now I'm back in the job market without a position. In fact, that's why I'm here."

"You mean you're interviewing for Sebastian?" Teresa asked with interest.

"Exactly. I ran into him at a conference yesterday, and he told me he had a position he thought I should interview for, and that he'd been considering me for it all along but assumed I wouldn't be available. Well, you can't be more available than I am, so here I am!"

"Have you reviewed the initiative framework?" Melissa asked.

"I'm fortunate there," Angela replied. "I've seen it in three different drafts since Peter started developing it. Teresa collaborates with Peter Fuller regularly, and each time she brought a draft to our study group, I got to review it. So I'm not at a disadvantage."

"What do you think of the Foxwood Initiative, Melissa?" asked Teresa.

"I think it's brilliant! I hope more than ever that I get the position! Do you really think I have a chance?"

Angela nodded decisively. "If you can demonstrate the right combination of policy expertise and community engagement skills, you're perfect for it," she said.

"That's exactly what Teresa said!"

Teresa glanced through the door to the room. "I think we're about ready to find out whether you can demonstrate those skills," she said. "They seem to be finishing with the technical candidates, and that means the policy interviews are next!"

Wishing each other success, they entered the dimly lit back section of the room and prepared for what Teresa could only think of as their evaluation.

Afterward, as Teresa, Maya, Melissa, and Angela sat at a table in a nearby café waiting for Sebastian and Peter to join them, each was convinced she had performed poorly.

"Oh, no!" Teresa said. "You two were excellent! But I couldn't have been worse. I know I misunderstood what they were looking for. I thought I had the position requirements clear in my mind, but I'm sure my presentation was completely off target!"

"You have far more talent than perspective," Angela said mournfully. "You were perfect. And so was Melissa. As for me..." Her voice trailed off in despair.

"I don't know how you can say that, Angela," Melissa added. "I know you were the strongest candidate for your position, and nobody even came close to Teresa. But I've never felt so uncertain in my life as I did presenting my approach. It's a wonder any of you even want to associate with me!"

Only when Maya started to laugh did the three others realize how similarly they had been speaking. Then they joined in the laughter and couldn't seem to stop. When they seemed on the verge of dissolving helplessly into a prolonged fit of giggles, Sebastian and Peter joined them.

"If you're laughing at the initiative framework," Peter said glumly, "I can hardly blame you. You never know just how poorly you've designed something until people start trying to implement your ideas."

All at once, the women started to reassure him and explain how strong the framework was, and how inadequately the candidates, including themselves, had presented their qualifications, but this was so much like their previous exchange that once more they broke into helpless laughter.

When they recovered, and when coffee and sandwiches had been ordered, they tried to explain the cause of their amusement to the men.

"...so, you see," Teresa concluded, "we were each explaining how well the others had done and how poorly we had performed, and when Peter started telling us how flawed his framework was, we just couldn't help ourselves!"

It was Sebastian who restored order to the conversation. With his serious demeanor, like a detective's or prosecutor's, and his measured, thoughtful manner, he calmly gave his assessment of the afternoon's interviews.

The quantum processor hummed softly in the sterile laboratory as Dr. Elena Williams reviewed the final calculations. Her colleague, Timothy Miller, stood beside her, his face pale with the weight of what they were about to do.

"Are you certain about this?" Timothy asked, adjusting his glasses nervously.

Elena nodded, her fingers dancing across the holographic interface. "The information theory is sound. We can transmit a consciousness forward through quantum entanglement, but only forward. Never back."

They were in Dawnridge, Fendria's capital city, in the year 2087. The world had changed dramatically since the turn of the century. Climate adaptation technologies had transformed the landscape, but they'd also created new problems. The Global Trade Council had become too powerful, controlling nearly every aspect of international commerce through quantum computing networks that could predict and manipulate market trends with frightening accuracy.

"She's ready," Elena said softly.

In the adjacent chamber, suspended in a translucent gel matrix, was Rosa Davis. Not the Rosa Davis of 2087, but Rosa Davis from 1987—a contract killer from old Chicago, pulled from the moment before her death in a police shootout. The quantum transmission had worked, sort of. Her body was gone, but her consciousness, her memories, her entire neural pattern had been captured and reconstructed here, two hundred years in her future.

The gel drained away and Rosa's eyes snapped open. She gasped, thrashing against the restraints.

"Easy," Elena said through the speaker. "You're safe. Just breathe."

Rosa's eyes darted around the chamber, taking in the impossible technology, the strange materials, the wrongness of everything. When they finally released her and brought her into the main laboratory, she moved like a caged animal—wary, dangerous, ready to bolt or fight.

"Where the hell am I?" Rosa demanded. Her voice was rough, Chicago accent thick.

Timothy cleared his throat. "Ms. Davis, I know this will be difficult to accept, but you're no longer in 1987. You're in the year 2287. We've... brought you here."

Rosa stared at him. Then she laughed, a harsh sound. "You're insane."

"Look out the window," Elena suggested gently.

Rosa did. The city of Dawnridge stretched before her—gleaming towers that seemed to defy physics, vehicles that moved without wheels through designated air corridors, buildings that shifted and reconfigured themselves based on occupancy needs. It was beautiful and terrifying.

"Jesus Christ," Rosa whispered.

Over the next several days, they explained everything. The world had unified under eight major continental governments. War had been eliminated through a combination of post-scarcity economics and advanced social psychology. Crime was virtually nonexistent—not because of punishment, but because the motivations for crime had been systematically removed through universal abundance and comprehensive mental health care.

"So why'd you bring me here?" Rosa finally asked. They were in Elena's apartment in the Valleyview Territory, overlooking what had once been called the Pacific Ocean. "You don't have crime. You don't have violence. What do you need a killer for?"

Elena and Timothy exchanged glances. Timothy spoke first. "There's a man named Daniel Thompson. He's... dangerous."

"Dangerous how? I thought you said there was no crime here."

"There isn't," Elena said. "But Daniel Thompson is attempting to change that. He's a student of history, particularly of authoritarian movements and trade policy manipulation. He's discovered that our society, for all its advances, is vulnerable in one critical area."

"What's that?"

"Cognitive development," Timothy said. "Human beings don't reach full psychological maturity until their late twenties or early thirties. Before that, they're susceptible to romantic ideologies—nationalism, militarism, the glory of conflict. Thompson has been recruiting young people, teaching them about the 'excitement' of the old world. He's building something."

Rosa lit a cigarette—they'd managed to synthesize tobacco for her, though it had taken some effort. "So you want me to kill him."

"We want you to stop him," Elena corrected. "We've tried everything else. Legal intervention is impossible—he hasn't actually committed any crimes. Therapeutic intervention failed—he's too intelligent, too manipulative. We can't allow his movement to grow, but we can't bring ourselves to... to do what needs to be done."

"You want me to do your dirty work," Rosa said flatly.

"Yes," Timothy admitted. "And afterward, you'll be taken into custody. You'll receive treatment, therapy. It's painless, we promise. And you'll be integrated into society. You'll have everything you need."

Rosa laughed bitterly. "So I get caught on purpose. That's the plan."

"It's the only way," Elena said. "There's no escape in this world, Rosa. No borders to cross, no underground to hide in. Everyone is tracked, monitored—not for control, but for care. The moment you commit violence, medical teams will respond. But by then, Thompson will be gone, and his movement will collapse without him."

"And what's in it for me?"

"Life," Timothy said simply. "In your own time, you were about to die. Here, you'll live. You'll be free, eventually. You'll see wonders you can't imagine."

Rosa considered this. She'd spent her whole life in violence, in the shadows. The idea of a world without that violence was alien to her, but also... appealing? Maybe?

"Tell me about this Thompson guy," she said.

They spent the next week preparing. Daniel Thompson lived in Juniper City, in what had once been called the American Southwest. He held daily gatherings, recruiting sessions disguised as historical education seminars. Young people came to hear about the "glory days" of national sovereignty, of competitive markets, of the thrill of risk and reward.

Elena provided Rosa with a weapon—an antique pistol from a museum, along with ammunition that had been painstakingly recreated. The weight of it in Rosa's hand was familiar, comforting even.

"You understand," Timothy said as they prepared for the trip, "that we'll turn ourselves in as well. We're complicit in this. We'll need therapy too, probably."

"You're all crazy," Rosa muttered. But she was committed now.

They traveled to Juniper City by high-speed transport. The journey that would have taken days in Rosa's time took less than an hour. The city was smaller than Dawnridge, built into the red rock canyons with a respect for environmental ethics that would have been unthinkable in the twentieth century.

Thompson's residence was a modest tower near the city center. There was no security—why would there be? No one committed crimes anymore.

Rosa walked in alone. The reception area was empty except for two young people who left as she entered, barely glancing at her. A screen on the wall flickered to life, showing Thompson's face.

"Yes?" he said. His voice was cultured, educated.

"Rosa Davis to see Daniel Thompson," she said, using the formal phrasing Elena had taught her.

Thompson's eyebrows rose. "Your accent... you're speaking Old American English. How fascinating. Please, come in."

A door slid open. Rosa walked through into an office that was surprisingly sparse. Thompson sat behind a desk, watching her with keen interest.

"What can I do for you, Ms. Davis?" he asked.

Rosa studied him. He was younger than she'd expected, maybe forty, with the kind of intense eyes that suggested both brilliance and instability. She could see why Elena and Timothy were worried about him.

She reached for the gun.

But something stopped her. Maybe it was the way Thompson looked at her—not with fear, but with curiosity. Maybe it was the weight of everything she'd learned about this strange new world. Maybe it was just exhaustion.

"You know what this is?" she asked, pulling out the pistol but not pointing it at him.

Thompson leaned forward, fascinated. "A handgun. Late twentieth century, I'd estimate. Remarkable. Where did you acquire such a thing?"

"That's a long story," Rosa said. She sat down in the chair across from him, the gun resting in her lap. "I'm from 1987. They brought me here to kill you."

Thompson's expression didn't change. "Did they? How interesting. And yet you're talking to me instead of shooting me. Why?"

"I'm trying to figure that out myself," Rosa admitted. "They tell me you're dangerous. That you're going to destroy their perfect little world."

"Their world is stagnant," Thompson said. "Humanity has stopped evolving. We've achieved comfort, yes, but at what cost? There's no challenge anymore, no struggle, no growth. I'm simply trying to remind people that there's more to life than contentment."

"By teaching them about war? About violence?"

"By teaching them about passion," Thompson corrected. "About risk, about the thrill of uncertainty. Yes, the old world had problems, but it also had vitality. These people—" he gestured vaguely at the world outside, "—they're not living. They're just existing."

Rosa thought about her own life. The violence, the fear, the constant edge of danger. But also the intensity, the sense of purpose, the fierce loyalty of her crew.

"You're right," she said slowly. "But you're also wrong. That old world? It ate people alive. It destroyed more than it created. I've killed people, Thompson. A lot of people. And you know what? It didn't make me feel alive. It made me feel empty."

"Then why did you do it?"

"Because it was all I knew. Because the world I lived in didn't give me any other options." She looked at him hard. "These people here? They've built something different. Maybe it's not perfect. Maybe it's a little boring. But it's better than what we had."

Thompson smiled. "You're not going to kill me, are you?"

"No," Rosa said. "I'm not."

She stood up, placed the gun on his desk. "But I'm going to tell you something. If you keep pushing this, someone else will stop you. Maybe not with a bullet, but they'll stop you. Because what you're selling? It's poison dressed up as medicine."

She turned to leave.

"Ms. Davis," Thompson called after her. "What will you do now?"

Rosa paused at the door. "I guess I'll go turn myself in. Get that therapy they keep talking about. Try to figure out how to live in this crazy future of yours."

"Good luck," Thompson said, and he sounded sincere.

Rosa found Elena and Timothy waiting outside in their vehicle. Their faces were anxious, confused.

"Well?" Timothy asked.

"I didn't kill him," Rosa said, climbing in. "But I think maybe I got through to him. Or maybe not. Either way, that's not my problem anymore."

Elena looked stricken. "But the plan—"

"Your plan was stupid," Rosa interrupted. "You can't solve your problems by dragging someone from the past to do your dirty work. You want to stop Thompson? Figure it out yourselves. Use your fancy social psychology or whatever. But don't ask me to kill someone just because you're too scared to confront your own society's problems."

They drove in silence back to Dawnridge. When they arrived at the medical center, Rosa got out voluntarily.

"I'm ready for that therapy now," she told the attendants. "I got a lot to work through."

As they led her inside, she looked back at Elena and Timothy one last time. They looked lost, uncertain. Good, she thought. Maybe they needed to feel that way for a while.

The future, Rosa decided, was going to take some getting used to. But for the first time in her life, she had time to figure it out.

Three months later, after intensive therapy and integration training, Rosa Davis stood in a small apartment in Windsor, Quendor, looking out at a world she was finally beginning to understand. The treatment had been everything they'd promised—painless, thorough, transformative. She still remembered who she'd been, but she no longer felt trapped by that identity.

She'd heard that Daniel Thompson had voluntarily entered therapy as well, after their conversation. His movement had dissolved without his leadership. The young people he'd recruited had moved on to other interests, other passions—creative writing, robotics, cultural preservation projects.

Elena and Timothy had also received treatment, though theirs had been brief. They'd been driven by fear, not malice. Now they were working on new projects, using quantum computing to improve cognitive development education for adolescents.

And Rosa? Rosa was learning. Learning about information theory, about team building, about all the strange and wonderful things this future had to offer. She was even taking classes in cultural evolution, studying how societies changed over time.

It wasn't the life she'd expected. But it was a life. And for someone who'd been seconds from death two hundred years ago, that was more than enough.

She poured herself a glass of synthesized wine—they'd finally gotten the flavor right—and raised it in a silent toast to the past she'd left behind and the future she was learning to embrace.

Outside her window, Quendor glowed in the twilight, a city of possibilities she was only beginning to explore.

She wept openly as she recounted the struggles of raising her son alone after discovering his affinity for chaos magic—a form of power that traditional magical society viewed with suspicion and fear.

"Finding out that no academy would accept him," she said, her voice trembling. "That no master would train him. That he was seen not as a child with a gift, but as a threat to be contained or ignored."

This wasn't a single tear hastily wiped away. Elena seemed unable to continue. The assembled mages held their collective breath. I gripped my staff so tightly my knuckles turned white, caught between sympathy and mortification. I thought this display would be mocked by the Council of Elders, that she would be dismissed as weak. What kind of leader, faced with hundreds of the realm's most powerful practitioners, stands before them and weeps about personal defeats?

It was only later, as I reflected in my chambers overlooking the Moonlit Gardens, that I understood this had been one of the most significant moments of the entire gathering. Elena could hardly have made her point more effectively—that her son's magical nature had shattered her own privilege as a high elf, a graduate of the prestigious Luminous Academy, and a former court enchantress (and possessing the kind of ethereal beauty that opens doors in our superficial society, though she didn't mention this). Her tears conveyed powerfully her devastation at realizing her child was destined either to hide his true nature or to face persecution, and the helplessness this realization brought.

The Balance Coalition's conclave was filled with talk about mages "practicing governance differently." The phrase echoed through every workshop and discussion circle, though its actual meaning remained frustratingly vague. This week, as hundreds of thousands of practitioners prepare to march on the Imperial Palace in Carmel, Fendria—following the ascension of Archmage Dominion to the High Seat (with marches planned in two hundred other cities across the realm, including Greenfield in Quendor, Juniper Town, and here in Silverdale City, where Elena Williams will be among the speakers)—this seems an opportune moment to examine whether there is anything genuinely new about contemporary magical activism and, if so, what it represents.

Regarding policy, the Balance Coalition promotes objectives capable of attracting mages across traditional philosophical divides: closing the power gap between different magical traditions, subsidizing education for rare affinities, ending violence against chaos practitioners, and ensuring equal representation in the Councils, guilds, and teaching positions. The details would prove contentious, but for now, these are goals most progressive mages support. Both Claudia Murphy, former High Enchantress of the Conservative Circle, and Mark Howell, Grandmaster of the Liberal Practitioners' Guild, spoke at the conclave.

It is in methodology, however, that magical activism has genuine potential to expand our understanding of what it means to engage in governance and societal change.

Among the various catalysts for the Dominion Ascension and the Purification Movement, rage ranked prominently. Emotion has returned to magical discourse. The Purists eschewed rational argumentation in favor of appeals to feeling. Archmage Dominion is, in essence, Archmage of Emotions. (Pathetic!) Yet we lack the conceptual frameworks to comprehend this resurgence of feeling, as the scholar Robert King argues in his forthcoming treatise, "The Age of Wrath," because our dominant intellectual traditions cannot adequately address emotion's role in governance.

Since the Great Rationalization three centuries ago, King argues, magical political philosophy has been increasingly constrained by mechanistic premises—for example, the notion that "practitioners are fundamentally rational beings motivated by the pursuit of power and status; that they act primarily to maximize personal advancement rather than from fear, anger, or resentment." The idealized practitioner, he contends, "views magical hierarchy as the optimal form of social organization and venerates technical advancement and the accumulation of power. All of this stems from the rigid contemporary belief that only what can be measured matters, and what cannot be measured—subjective emotions—therefore does not exist." This worldview leaves no room for more complex motivations: vanity, the fear of humiliation, the need for belonging.

How, then, to comprehend, let alone articulate, the vulnerability, shame, and loss of identity created by the rigid caste system of magical society, the persecution of rare affinities, and communities stripped of their traditional practices? The churning emotions generated by the magical establishment's failure to fulfill its promise of meritocratic advancement cannot be understood when emotion is something practitioners are expected to suppress and deny. Strong leaders do not stand before their followers and weep about their children. Such displays are for the weak. Magical valor demands the concealment of emotional distress. (This is deeply embedded in our culture: "Thy tears are unbecoming of a mage," the ancient text "Principles of Power" instructs, though the treatise's author was later discovered to have suffered from profound melancholy.)

Emotion is stigmatized as belonging to lesser, non-normative groups. Women are hysterical. Chaos practitioners are dangerously unstable. Empaths are unreliably sensitive. There is no acceptable path for those competing to maximize their power to respond to injury by saying, "That hurts!"—much less by weeping.

Yet the emotion persists, festering beneath the surface. Since practitioners without means to express vulnerability cannot openly mourn their loss of status or purpose (let alone acknowledge their disorientation when marginalized groups threaten their unearned sense of superiority), wounded pride must disguise itself in imagery of strength, dominance, and honor. Archmage Dominion himself embodies this phenomenon, as the chronicler Sophie Leonard has observed: "Simultaneously an emblem of rigid, impenetrable authority—the iron-willed master determined to restore order through force—and a byword for hypersensitivity, a petulant tyrant with an explosive temper."

All this emotion-with-nowhere-to-go was exploited by the Dominion movement and the Purists. They channeled it, allowing practitioners to associate themselves with winning, to label others as "lesser mages." It mattered little what they were winning or where it led. Installing Dominion in the High Seat, like the Purification, became an end in itself, a means of displacing pain, therapeutic in its catharsis.

It was also profoundly reactionary. Given the stark inequalities of our magical hierarchy, it is difficult for most practitioners to envision themselves ascending as things stand—so Dominion and the Purists offered instead a return to fantasies of the past. The iconography of Purification draws from the mythical Golden Age of magical purity (conveniently overlooking uncomfortable truths about the archaeology of that era, which reveals far more diversity and complexity science than the myths suggest), while Dominion's "Restore True Power" campaign offered explicit nostalgia for a time when society had unified purpose, with traditional practitioners at the center.

What magical activism led by women might contribute to governance is a different sensibility, one acknowledging that emotions are inevitable, messy—and necessary. There is a void in magical politics where meaningful opposition once existed and progressive governance once flourished. This is largely because rational arguments, facts, and expertise seem disconnected from how many practitioners feel about the world. The liberals' arguments exist in a parallel universe, relevant only to those who thrive there. When called to articulate a vision for magical society, the best progressives could manage was an abstract account of the dangers of Dominion's policies—which, since it never resonated emotionally, was easily dismissed as "fear-mongering."

Practitioners have not lost interest in truth. But primarily, they know the truth of their emotional relationship to the world. Liberals and progressives currently cannot address this reality. Much of the time, they appear to speak in incomprehensible abstractions.

The reactionary right has found an emotive way to engage practitioners by channeling their feelings, often redirecting them toward scapegoats. If you cannot acknowledge your own anxiety—because anxiousness signifies weakness and to be weak is to fail as a practitioner—you become vulnerable to blaming others for your loss of dignity. In a world of competition, self-worth requires being a winner. Someone else must therefore become the loser.

There is an alternative: governance that begins with the understanding that emotions need not be repressed or twisted into bigotry and cruelty. An approach to feelings that doesn't equate vulnerability with shame, and compassion with maladaptive weakness, is far more likely to suggest solutions than one denying our emotional lives—most of what makes us truly sentient beings.

When practitioners admit to their emotions, they invite empathy; they can inspire action. "And what does the Council call a single mother raising two children while maintaining protective wards for her entire district?" Elena Williams asked in her conclave speech, immediately providing the (obviously absurd) answer: "Magically unproductive." Elena's single mother has no place in the Dominion fantasy of winning, greatness, and power, of othering the outsider. The unpaid work of caring involves love; it entails vulnerability, which immediately renders it suspect in a world of winning and losing, where the only acceptable emotions are triumph and contemptuous schadenfreude.

The prevailing mood in magical society is anxiety. "To practice magic in the modern realm," the scholar Zhang Walker wrote recently in the Arcane Chronicle, "subject to perpetual social and technical transformation, is to experience the psychological equivalent of permanent revolution. Anxiety in the face of this process is now universal, which is why reactionary ideas attract adherents across the realm who share little except their sense of historical betrayal."

When liberals make sanctimonious statements about understanding the anxiety of practitioners who have abandoned them, their solution often involves adopting some of the bigotry. You need not search far to find those who believe magical activism led by women is inadequate to humanizing governance because it is, in fact, part of the problem. Zhang Walker, in another piece in the Arcane Chronicle, and Ian Jordan, in the Progressive Practitioner, have each argued that the policing of language and behavior—which some call basic respect—has provoked backlash and must bear partial responsibility for reactionary movements. The logical extension suggests that women activists, along with chaos practitioners' advocates, empath rights activists, and other "oversensitive" groups, should retreat and consider the damage they're causing.

The problem is this assumes traditional male practitioners' experiences represent neutral ground around which common interest can coalesce. It is, in other words, male identity politics. "There has been a massive backlash by traditional male practitioners," Elena Williams told me at the Balance Coalition headquarters in Greenfield, Quendor, weeks after her conclave speech. "We are living through the identity politics of the traditional male practitioner right now."

If we are to avoid complete fragmentation into essentialist tribal identities of magical tradition and gender, practitioners must find ways to articulate distress without humiliation. If men cannot face their anxiety, it will be denied, and nothing will be done to alleviate it; there will be a privatization of suffering. There are structural reasons for the explosion of magical burnout in advanced societies, for the addiction to enhancement potions in struggling regions, the epidemic of distress among young practitioners, various forms of self-harm. But if we cannot acknowledge the underlying dread and helplessness practitioners experience facing a world controlled by ancient power structures and incomprehensible hierarchies, individuals will continue to be stigmatized as failures. Either you will be a winner, an ambitious individual competing freely for power, deflecting distress by projecting strength and lashing out; or your inchoate feelings of desperation will be—sorry—your problem alone.

A female sensibility in magical governance is not, it should be noted, antithetical to reason, though feeling and reason are often positioned as opposites. The ancient philosopher Magistra Sophia contrasted the wild griffin of passion with the wise dragon of reason (her point being they needed each other). The legendary enchantress Aria of Moonhaven would have had no tales without the frequent difficulty sentient beings have reconciling desire and wisdom: success, as her stories repeatedly demonstrate, lies in harmonizing sense and sensibility. Such reconciliation requires self-examination, generosity of spirit, authenticity, and rigorous thinking. But first and foremost, it demands honesty about feeling.

I used to grow mildly irritated when activists focused too intensely on female representation, when there seemed so many other urgent matters to address, as if gender alone made a difference. And it is true that there is a privileged activism that ignores practitioners for whom magical tradition, class, disability, and sexuality intersect to intensify gender discrimination. But sheer numbers of women do make a difference. Claudia Murphy notes that women in the Councils are more inclined to collaborate across philosophical lines than men. Mark Howell, who has spent decades as the lone male advocate on women-dominated committees, says that when women reach forty percent in a meeting or on a council, the discourse changes. There's a different approach to conducting business, a different sense of how to advance initiatives. In a hall overwhelmingly dominated by women, it is possible for a leader to cry and everyone to support her. For no one to think (after a moment of adjustment from unreconstructed be-more-like-men activists like myself) that vulnerability signifies weakness.

Over the coming months and years, progressives must grapple with what kind of emotional appeal they can make beyond the reactionaries' exploitative manipulation of feeling. The task will be to reclaim emotion from its current co-option into a threatening, ultimately self-defeating worldview.

Women are not (obviously) alone in identifying the need for soul in governance. Various scholars and philosophers have identified that there was a highly rationalistic and technical turn in magical philosophy after the Great Rationalization. Had our intellectual tradition developed instead from the vision of earlier philosophers who valued emotional wisdom, the thinking goes, it would have made more room for kindness and would have given us a fuller, more nuanced account of practitioner experience. In these destabilized times, practitioners are returning to those ideas, exploring what personal growth and complexity science can teach us about systems thinking and cognitive development.

Perhaps women's activism can provide us all a path toward reconnecting with a different, more generous approach to magical governance. By caring about caring, for example—not as an abstract problem hindering efficiency, but because caring involves love, family, community, and shared humanity. By reminding men that acknowledging pain is survivable, and can lead to greater strength. As the political ground shifts beneath us and old allegiances prove inadequate, we must find a different language of governance. And the language of women's experience, informed by work-life balance, bioethics, and justice theory, is where we should begin.

The march on the Imperial Palace approaches. Hundreds of thousands of practitioners from across the realm will walk together, demanding recognition, demanding change, demanding that emotion be acknowledged as essential to justice rather than antithetical to it. Elena Williams will stand before them, and perhaps she will cry again. And this time, we will all understand that her tears are not weakness, but the truest form of strength—the courage to be fully, honestly, vulnerably present in a world that has long demanded we hide our hearts to prove our power.

In the visual arts district of Silverdale City, banners are being painted. In Juniper Town, practitioners are organizing transportation. In Carmel, Fendria, the Imperial Plaza is being prepared—both by those who will march and those who will try to stop them. The old order is crumbling, not because it was defeated by superior force, but because it was built on a foundation of denied emotion, suppressed vulnerability, and the fiction that strength means never admitting pain.

The Balance Coalition offers something different: the radical notion that we are all more than our power levels, more than our magical traditions, more than our competitive rankings. We are beings who love, who fear, who hope, who grieve. And governance that cannot acknowledge this fundamental truth is governance that has already failed, no matter how many towers it builds or how many titles it bestows.

As I prepare to join the march, I think of Elena Williams weeping on that stage, and I understand now what I couldn't see then: that moment was not a breakdown but a breakthrough, not an ending but a beginning. The question is not whether emotion belongs in magical governance. Emotion is already there, has always been there, will always be there. The question is whether we will continue to let it fester in darkness, twisted into rage and resentment, or whether we will bring it into the light, where it can be acknowledged, honored, and transformed into something that serves us all.

The march begins at dawn. I will be there, staff in hand, heart open, ready to walk toward a different future—one where tears are not shameful, where vulnerability is not weakness, where caring is not dismissed as "magically unproductive," but recognized as the most powerful magic of all.

option_b: Greater collaboration between different magical traditions and increased representation of women in the Councils
correct_answer_text: The continued denial and suppression of emotion in favor of purely rational, mechanistic approaches that ignore practitioners' emotional experiences and vulnerability

The Quantum Café sits at the intersection of Innovation Boulevard and Heritage Street in Ashbury, Quendor's most eclectic district. It's a place where the old world meets the new, where holographic art installations hover above cobblestone streets, and where you can get a perfect cappuccino while watching delivery drones navigate between centuries-old architecture.

Ashbury has always attracted a certain type—the brilliant, the eccentric, the ones who don't quite fit anywhere else. After the Great Restructuring, when the global financial systems collapsed and rebuilt themselves on blockchain protocols, cities like Ashbury became havens for those who preferred to operate in the gray areas of the new economy.

The Quantum Café itself occupies three floors of a converted bank building. The ground floor serves as the main café, with floor-to-ceiling windows that let you watch the world go by. The second floor houses private research pods that rent by the hour. The third floor—well, nobody talks much about the third floor.

I was sitting at my usual table, reviewing a paper on computational linguistics and artificial intelligence when Rebecca Pearson dropped into the chair across from me. I'd seen her around before—slight build, sharp eyes, always carrying a tablet covered in equations I couldn't quite make out.

"Mind if I join you?" she asked, though she was already settling in. "All the other tables are taken."

"Okay," I said. "But we need to be careful. If human intelligence agencies discovered us—"

"That's why I chose it," I said.

She smiled sadly. "I know. But I have to try. These people—they're brilliant and foolish, creative and destructive, capable of incredible kindness and horrifying cruelty. They're worth saving."

Tomorrow I would return to my research, to my careful observations and detailed notes.
