"To not enjoy my humble establishment," the Veldorian mumbled. "Digestive incompatibility; to express regret."

"Don't worry about it," Xavier said, irritated. "Just serve it and I'll decide if it works for me."

"To be reported for contamination of off-worlders." The attendant looked around for support, found none. The Veldorian patrons, attention elsewhere, were leaving.

"Get moving," Xavier said, placing a credit chip in the payment receptor.

"The procurement of a containment unit," a thin voice called from nearby. "The display of an anomaly."

Xavier turned. A tall Veldorian gestured dismissively. From his flushed complexion, the individual appeared intoxicated.

"To silence yourself," the attendant hissed. "To remain quiet, birth-cohort mate."

"To consume your own product," the intoxicated one whispered. "To find proper containment for this specimen." He wavered toward Xavier. "To display this one publicly, like all anomalies."

"Seen a lot of specimens like me, have you?" Xavier asked with interest.

"To speak comprehensibly, malodorous off-worlder," the drunk said. The attendant whispered something, and two patrons came to assist the drunk toward the exit.

"To acquire containment!" the drunk called. "To keep the specimens in their designated areas."

"I've changed my mind," Xavier said to the attendant. "Thanks anyway, but I need to leave." He followed the drunk outside. The other Veldorians released him and hurried back inside. Xavier looked at the swaying figure.

"To depart, specimen," the Veldorian whispered.

"To be friendly," Xavier said. "To share information."

"To have you transported to a research facility, ill-mannered foreign specimen."

"To not be hostile," Xavier said. "To permit conversation."

"To not tolerate such presumption!" The Veldorian moved toward Xavier. Xavier backed away.

"To exchange knowledge," Xavier said. "To cooperate—"

The Veldorian reached for him, missed. A passer-by moved around them quickly, disappeared. Xavier backed into a narrow service corridor and continued offering conversational overtures to the intoxicated local, who followed, agitated. Xavier backed around a corner into a deserted maintenance passage.

Xavier stepped around him, grabbed his collar and pulled. The Veldorian fell. Xavier stood over him. The downed native tried to rise; Xavier placed a foot against his chest.

"To not be going anywhere for a while," Xavier said. "To stay right here and answer some questions."

---

"There you are!" Elizabeth said, looking at Xavier over her lenses. "There are two officials waiting to see you. Veldorian officials."

"Council representatives, I imagine. Word travels fast." Xavier removed his jacket. "This saves me the trouble of requesting another meeting at the Administrative Council."

"What have you been doing? They seem very upset, I don't mind telling you."

"I'm sure you don't. Come along. And bring an official recording device."

Two Veldorians wearing elaborate rank insignia rose as Xavier entered the conference room. Neither offered a courteous bow, Xavier noted. They were angry.

"I am Akira Wright, of the Off-World Relations Division, Administrative Council," the taller Veldorian said in accented standard language. "May I present Walter Ford, of the Internal Security Bureau?"

"Please sit," Xavier said. They resumed their seats. Elizabeth hovered nervously, then sat rigidly.

"Oh, it's such an honor—" she began.

"Skip the pleasantries," Xavier said. "These officials didn't come here for social calls."

"Indeed," Akira said. "Frankly, I have received a most disturbing report, Director. I shall ask Walter to present it." He nodded to the security chief.

"Two hours ago," Walter said, "a Veldorian citizen was brought to medical services suffering from minor injuries. Questioning revealed that he had been physically restrained by an off-worlder. An investigator from your world, to be precise. Investigation indicates that the description matches that of the Director of Research Ethics."

Elizabeth gasped audibly.

"Have you ever heard," Xavier said, looking steadily at Akira, "of a research vessel, the VSS Discovery, which disappeared in this sector fourteen years ago?"

"Really!" Elizabeth exclaimed, standing. "I wash my hands—"

"Keep that recorder active," Xavier said sharply.

"I'll not be party—"

"You'll do as instructed, Elizabeth," Xavier said quietly. "I'm telling you to make an official sealed record of this conversation."

Elizabeth sat down.

Akira's posture stiffened. "You reopen an old wound, Director. It reminds us of certain inappropriate treatment at investigator hands—"

"Nonsense," Xavier said. "That excuse worked with my predecessors, but it doesn't work with me."

"All our efforts," Elizabeth said, "to move past that terrible episode! And you—"

"Terrible? I understand that an investigative team came to Veldoria and asked questions. They got evasive answers and stayed to investigate further. After ten days they left. Somewhat annoying to the Veldorians, perhaps—at most. If they were innocent."

"If!" Elizabeth burst out.

"If, indeed!" Akira said, his soft voice trembling. "I must protest your—"

"Save the protests, Akira. You have explaining to do. And I don't think your explanation will be adequate."

"It is for you to explain! This person who was injured—"

"Not injured. Just detained briefly to refresh his memory."

"Then you admit—"

"It worked, too. He remembered quite a bit, once he focused."

Akira stood; Walter followed.

"I shall request your immediate recall, Director. Were it not for your diplomatic immunity, I should do more—"

"Why did the Council change, Akira? It happened just after the investigative team visited, and before the arrival of the first off-world research ethics mission."

"This is an internal matter!" Akira said, his voice strained. "The current Council has shown itself most cooperative with you investigators. It has been extraordinarily accommodating—"

"—to keep the research ethics director and staff uninformed," Xavier said. "And the same goes for the few off-world researchers you've granted access. This constant round of ceremonial obligations; no social contacts outside official channels; no travel permits to visit outlying districts, or your satellite research stations—"

"Enough!" Akira's hands trembled. "I can discuss this no further—"

"You'll discuss it with me, or there'll be an investigative team here in seven days to do the discussing," Xavier said.

"You can't!" Elizabeth gasped.

Xavier turned a steady look on Elizabeth. She fell silent. The Veldorians sat down.

"Answer me this," Xavier said, looking at Walter. "About fourteen years back, there was a small procession held here. Some unusual specimens were captured. After being securely contained, they were exhibited to the Veldorian public. Transported through the streets. Very educational, no doubt. A highly informative display.

"Interesting thing about these specimens. They wore clothing. They seemed to communicate with each other. Altogether it was quite a fascinating exhibit.

"Tell me, Walter, what happened to those eight off-worlders after the procession ended?"

Akira made a choking sound and spoke rapidly to Walter in Veldorian. Walter's posture collapsed. Elizabeth opened her mouth, closed it and blinked rapidly.

"How did they die?" Xavier demanded. "Did you terminate them, eliminate them, or contain them permanently? What entertaining end did you devise for them? Research, perhaps? Dissection to understand their biology..."

"No!" Akira gasped. "I must correct this terrible misunderstanding immediately."

"Misunderstanding, hell," Xavier said. "They were off-worlders! A simple truth-verification scan would get that from any Veldorian who witnessed the procession."

"Yes," Akira said weakly. "It is true, they were off-worlders. But there was no killing."

"They're alive?"

"Alas, no. They... expired."

Elizabeth made a small sound.

"I see," Xavier said. "They expired."

"We attempted to keep them alive, naturally. But we did not know what nutrition—"

"Didn't bother to find out, either, did you?"

"They became ill," Akira said. "One by one..."

"We'll address that question later," Xavier said. "Right now, I want more information. Where did you find them? Where did you hide the vessel? What happened to the rest of the crew? Did they 'become ill' before the big procession?"

"There were no more! Absolutely, I assure you!"

"Killed in the crash?"

"No crash. The vessel landed intact, in the Nordavia sector. The... off-worlders... were unharmed. Naturally, we feared them. They were strange to us. We had never before encountered such beings."

"Came out shooting, did they?"

"Weapons? No, no weapons—"

"They raised their hands, didn't they? Asked for help. You helped them; helped them to death."

"How could we know?" Akira moaned.

"How could you know an investigation would commence in a few months looking for them, you mean? That was a shock, wasn't it? I'll bet you had a frantic time hiding the vessel and silencing witnesses. A close call, eh?"

"We were afraid," Walter said. "We are a cautious people. We feared the strange beings from the alien vessel. We did not kill them, but we felt it was fortunate they... did not survive. Then, when the investigators came, we realized our error. But we feared to speak. We removed our guilty leaders, concealed what had occurred, and... offered our cooperation. We invited the establishment of research ethics oversight. We made a mistake, it is true, a grave mistake. But we have tried to make amends..."

"Where is the vessel?"

"The vessel?"

"What did you do with it? It was too large to just hide and forget. Where is it?"

The two Veldorians exchanged looks.

"We wish to demonstrate our remorse," Akira said. "We will show you the vessel."

"Elizabeth," Xavier said. "If I don't return in a reasonable timeframe, transmit that recording to Regional Administration, sealed." He stood, looked at the Veldorians.

"Let's go," he said.

---

Xavier ducked under the reinforced supports at the entrance to the underground chamber. He peered into the darkness at the curved hull of the space-weathered vessel.

"Any illumination in here?" he asked.

A Veldorian activated a control. A weak bluish glow appeared.

Xavier walked along the elevated platform, studying the vessel. Empty equipment bays gaped below damaged sensor arrays. Debris-covered decking was visible within the partially-open access port. Near the bow the words 'VSS Discovery M4 Lakeside Station' were visible in faded lettering.

"How did you get it in here?" Xavier asked.

"It was transported here from the landing site, approximately fifteen kilometers distant," Akira said, his voice thinner than ever. "This is a natural geological formation. The vessel was lowered into it and sealed."

"How did you shield it so the detection systems didn't locate it?"

"All here is high-density mineral deposits," Akira said, gesturing. "Extensive veins of nearly pure metals."

Xavier grunted. "Let's go inside."

Walter came forward with a portable light. The group entered the vessel.

Xavier climbed a narrow ladder, examined the interior of the command compartment. Dust covered the deck, the mounting points where control stations had been installed, the empty instrument panels, the scattered debris of severed connections, fragments of wire and documentation. A thin layer of corrosion dulled the exposed metal where cutting tools had removed heavy shielding. There was a faint odor of stale organic material.

"The storage compartment—" Walter began.

"I've seen enough," Xavier said.

Silently, the Veldorians led the way back through the tunnel and into the late afternoon light. As they climbed the slope to the transport vehicle, Akira came to Xavier's side.

"Indeed, I hope that this will conclude this unfortunate matter," he said. "Now that all has been fully and honestly revealed—"

"You can skip that," Xavier said. "You're fourteen years late. The crew was still alive when the investigative team arrived, I imagine. You killed them—or let them die—rather than risk admitting what you'd done."

"We were at fault," Akira said abjectly. "Now we wish only cooperation."

"The Discovery was a heavy research vessel, approximately thirty thousand tons." Xavier looked grimly at the slender official. "Where is she, Akira? I won't settle for a fifteen-hundred-ton auxiliary craft."

Akira's posture shifted so violently that one rank insignia fell off.

"I know nothing of... of..." He stopped. His breathing became rapid as he struggled for composure.

"My Council can entertain no further accusations, Director," he said at last. "I have been completely transparent with you. I have overlooked your intrusion into matters not properly within your jurisdiction. My patience is exhausted."

"Where is that vessel?" Xavier demanded. "You never learn, do you? You're still convinced you can conceal everything and move on. I'm telling you you can't."

"We return to the city now," Akira said. "I can do no more."

"You can and you will, Akira," Xavier said. "I intend to discover the truth of this matter."

Akira spoke to Walter in rapid Veldorian. The security chief gestured to his four armed officers. They moved to surround Xavier.

Xavier eyed Akira. "Don't try it," he said. "You'll just make things worse."

Akira's posture stiffened, his bearing aggressive toward the off-worlder.

"Out of deference to your diplomatic status, off-worlder, I shall ignore your insulting remarks," Akira said in his soft voice. "Let us now return to the city."

Xavier looked at the four officers. "I see your point," he said.

Akira followed him into the vehicle, sat rigidly at the far end of the seat.

"I advise you to remain very close to your research ethics office," Akira said. "I advise you to dismiss these theories from your mind, and to enjoy the cultural aspects of life in Veldoria. Especially, I should not venture outside the city, or appear overly curious about matters of concern only to the Veldorian Council."

In the front seat, Walter looked straight ahead. The suspension-equipped vehicle moved smoothly along the narrow highway. Xavier listened to the quiet hum of the electric motor and said nothing.

---

"Elizabeth," Xavier said, "I want you to listen carefully to what I'm going to tell you. I have to move rapidly now, to catch the Veldorians unprepared."

"I'm sure I don't know what you're talking about," Elizabeth said sharply, her eyes intense behind the augmented lenses.

"If you'll listen, you may find out," Xavier said. "I have no time to waste, Elizabeth. They won't be expecting an immediate action—I hope—and that may give me the opportunity I need."

"You're still determined to make an issue of that incident!" Elizabeth said. "I can hardly blame the Veldorians. They are not an experienced spacefaring culture; they had never before encountered aliens."

"You're ready to excuse a great deal, Elizabeth. But it's not what happened fourteen years ago I'm concerned with. It's what's happening now. I've told you that it was only an auxiliary craft the Veldorians have concealed. Don't you understand the implication? That vessel couldn't have traveled far. The main research vessel must be somewhere nearby. I want to know where!"

"The Veldorians don't know. They're a very cultured, peaceful people. You can do irreparable harm to off-world relations if you insist—"

"That's my decision," Xavier said. "I have responsibilities and we're wasting time." He crossed the room to his desk, opened a drawer and took out a compact energy weapon.

"This office is being monitored. Not very effectively, if I know the Veldorians. I think I can evade surveillance."

"Where are you going with... that?" Elizabeth stared at the weapon. "What in the world—"

"The Veldorians won't waste time destroying every piece of evidence in their records relating to this matter. I have to obtain what I need before it's too late. If I wait for an official Inquiry Board, they'll find nothing but cooperative smiles."

"You're out of your mind!" Elizabeth stood up, trembling with indignation. "You're like a... a..."

"You and I are in a precarious position, Elizabeth. The logical next move for the Veldorians is to eliminate both of us. We're the only ones who know what occurred. Akira almost accomplished that this afternoon, but I dissuaded him—for the moment."

Elizabeth emitted a sharp laugh. "Your paranoid delusions are overwhelming you," she gasped. "In danger, indeed! Eliminating me! I've never heard anything so absurd."

"Stay in this office. Secure the door with the safety lock. You've got food and water in the dispenser. I suggest you stock up before they disable the supply. Don't admit anyone, regardless of pretext. I'll maintain contact via secure communicator."

"What are you planning to do?"

"If I don't return, transmit the sealed record of this afternoon's conversation, along with the information I've given you. Send it through on an emergency priority. Then inform the Veldorians what you've done and remain secure. I think you'll be safe. It won't be easy to breach this office and anyway, they won't worsen things by harming you. A response team can be here in ten days."

"I'll do nothing of the sort! The Veldorians respect me! You... newcomer! Troublemaker! Setting out to destroy—"

"Blame me if it makes you feel better," Xavier said, "but don't be foolish enough to trust them." He pulled on a cape, opened the door.

"I'll be back in a few hours," he said. Elizabeth stared after him silently as he closed the door.

---

It was an hour before dawn when Xavier entered the combination to the security lock and stepped into the darkened research ethics office. He looked exhausted.

Elizabeth, dozing in a chair, awoke with a start. She looked at Xavier, rose and activated a light, turned to stare.

"What in the world—Where have you been? What's happened to your clothing?"

"I got a little dirty. Don't worry about it." Xavier went to his desk, opened a drawer and replaced the weapon.

"Where have you been?" Elizabeth demanded. "I stayed here—"

"I'm glad you did," Xavier said. "I hope you accumulated supplies from the dispenser, too. We'll be secured here for ten days, at least." He made notes on a data pad. "Activate the official transmitter. I have a lengthy transmission for Regional Administration."

"Are you going to tell me where you've been?"

"I have a message to transmit first, Elizabeth," Xavier said sharply. "I've been to the Administrative Council," he added. "I'll tell you all about it later."

"At this hour? There's no one there..."

"Exactly."

Elizabeth gasped. "You mean you broke in? You infiltrated the Administrative Council?"

"That's right," Xavier said calmly. "Now—"

"This is absolutely unacceptable!" Elizabeth said. "Thank heaven I've already—"

"Activate that transmitter, woman!" Xavier snapped. "This is critical."

"I've already done so, Director Gregory!" Elizabeth said harshly. "I've been waiting for you to return here..." She turned to the communicator, activated controls. The screen illuminated, and a wavering long-distance image appeared.

"He's here now," Elizabeth said to the screen. She looked at Xavier triumphantly.

"That's good," Xavier said. "I don't think the Veldorians can interrupt our transmission, but—"

"I have fulfilled my duty, Director Gregory," Elizabeth said. "I made a full report to Regional Administration last night, as soon as you left this office. Any doubts I may have had as to the appropriateness of that decision have been completely eliminated by what you've just told me."

Xavier looked at her steadily. "You've been busy, Elizabeth. Did you mention the eight off-worlders who died here?"

"That had no bearing on the matter of your reckless behavior! I must say, in all my years in the service, I've never encountered someone less suited to research ethics work."

The screen crackled, the twelve-second transmission lag having elapsed. "Director Gregory," the face on the screen said, "I am Administrator Eva Ahmed, Senior Deputy Director for the region. I have received a report on your conduct which makes it mandatory for me to relieve you administratively, with Elizabeth Brown assuming directorship. Pending the findings of an Inquiry Board, you will—"

Xavier reached out and deactivated the communicator. The triumphant expression faded from Elizabeth's face.

"Why, what is the meaning—"

"If I'd listened any longer, I might have heard something I couldn't disregard. I can't afford that at this moment. Listen, Elizabeth," Xavier went on earnestly, "I've found the missing research vessel."

"You heard her relieve you!"

"I heard her say she was going to, Elizabeth. But until I've heard and acknowledged a verbal order, it has no authority. If I'm wrong, she'll get my resignation. If I'm right, that suspension would be embarrassing all around."

"You're defying lawful authority! I'm in charge here now." Elizabeth stepped to the local communicator.

"I'm going to report this terrible situation to the Veldorians at once, and offer my profound—"

"Don't touch that screen," Xavier said. "You go sit in that corner where I can monitor you. I'm going to make a sealed recording for transmission to Administration, along with a request for an armed response team. Then we'll wait."

Xavier ignored Elizabeth's fury as he spoke into the recorder.

The local communicator chimed. Elizabeth jumped up, staring at it.

"Go ahead," Xavier said. "Answer it."

A Veldorian official appeared on the screen.

"Elizabeth Brown," he said without preamble, "for the Administrative Council of the Veldorian Authority, I hereby recognize you as Director of Research Ethics for this region, in accordance with the communications transmitted to my government directly from off-world Administration. As director, you are requested to make available for questioning Xavier Gregory, former director, in connection with the assault on two security personnel and illegal entry into the offices of the Administrative Council."

"Why, why," Elizabeth stammered. "Yes, of course. And I do want to express my deepest regrets—"

Xavier rose, went to the communicator, moved Elizabeth aside.

"Listen carefully, Akira," he said. "Your deception has been exposed. You don't come in and we don't come out. Your concealment worked for fourteen years, but it's finished now. I suggest you maintain composure and resist the temptation to worsen your situation."

"Elizabeth Brown," Akira said, "a security squad waits outside your research ethics office. It is clear you are dealing with a dangerous individual. As always, the Veldorians wish only cooperation with off-worlders, but—"

"Don't bother," Xavier said. "You know what was in those records I examined this morning."

Xavier turned at a sound behind him. Elizabeth was at the door, reaching for the security lock release...

"Don't!" Xavier moved—too late.

The door burst inward. A group of armed Veldorians pressed into the room, pushed Elizabeth back, aimed weapons at Xavier. Security Chief Walter Ford pushed forward.

"Attempt no resistance, off-worlder," he said. "I cannot promise to restrain my officers."

"You're violating off-world territory, Walter," Xavier said steadily. "I suggest you withdraw the same way you entered."

"I invited them here," Elizabeth spoke up. "They are here at my explicit invitation."

"Are they? Are you sure you intended to go this far, Elizabeth? A squad of armed Veldorians in the research ethics office?"

"You are the director, Elizabeth Brown," Walter said. "Would it not be best if we removed this unstable person to a secure location?"

"You're making a serious mistake, Walter," Xavier said.

"Yes," Elizabeth said. "You're quite right, Administrator Ford. Please escort Director Gregory to his quarters in this building—"

"I don't advise you to violate my diplomatic immunity, Akira," Xavier said.

"As director," Elizabeth said quickly, "I hereby waive immunity in the case of Xavier Gregory."

Walter produced a recording device. "Kindly repeat your statement, Director, officially," he said. "I wish no ambiguity to arise later."

"Don't be foolish, woman," Xavier said. "Don't you see what you're enabling? This would be an excellent time for you to determine whose interests you're serving."

"I'm serving the interests of proper conduct and research ethics!"

"You've been deceived. These people are concealing—"

"You think everyone is incompetent, don't you, Director Gregory?" She turned to the security chief and spoke into the microphone he held up.

"That's an invalid waiver," Xavier said. "I'm director here, whatever communications you've received. This situation is coming into the open, whatever you do. Don't add violation of off-world territory to the list of Veldorian offenses."

"Detain him," Walter said.
question: What official positions do Elizabeth Brown and Xavier Gregory hold in Veldoria?
option_a: Elizabeth Brown is Administrative Assistant and Xavier Gregory is Director of Research Ethics (though Elizabeth becomes director after Xavier is relieved).
option_b: Elizabeth Brown is Security Chief and Xavier Gregory is Council Administrator.
correct_answer_text: Elizabeth Brown is Administrative Assistant and Xavier Gregory is Director of Research Ethics (though Elizabeth becomes director after Xavier is relieved).
incorrect_answer_text: Elizabeth Brown is Security Chief and Xavier Gregory is Council Administrator.
explanation: The story clearly establishes that Xavier Gregory was appointed Director of Research Ethics at the beginning, with Elizabeth Brown serving as his assistant. Near the end, Elizabeth is recognized as the new Director after Xavier is administratively relieved, but for most of the story, Xavier holds the Director position while Elizabeth is his assistant. Option B is incorrect as Walter Ford is the Security Chief and Akira Wright is the Council official, not Elizabeth and Xavier.

THE PARADOX PROTOCOL

By Anonymous

The holding facility in Cliffside, Fendria had been constructed with remarkable precision. Patrick Harrison had seen plenty of detention centers during his career in international diplomacy, but nothing quite matched the sterile efficiency of this one. Every surface gleamed, every corner formed a perfect right angle, and the temperature remained at exactly 20.5 degrees Celsius at all times.

The Fendrians, Harrison reflected as he stretched out on the uncomfortably rigid cot, were nothing if not meticulous. All the preliminary intelligence reports had emphasized this trait; their obsession with precision and logical consistency had made them extraordinarily successful in fields like data science and blockchain technology. Within the past decade, they'd revolutionized digital security protocols and were on the verge of creating an unhackable global network. Before long, they'd control the infrastructure of international communications, and then—inevitably—they'd leverage that control into political dominance.

An outcome, the Coalition of Democratic Nations was certain, that would be catastrophic for global freedom.

Harrison sighed and stared at the ceiling. He'd been in isolation for four days now, with nothing to occupy his mind but his own thoughts. He'd tried mental exercises, memory games, even attempting to compose poetry in his head—but his talents didn't lie in creative writing. He couldn't pick the lock with his bare hands; he couldn't even influence the probability that his guards might make a mistake.

He could do, as a matter of fact, precisely nothing except wait. He wished the Fendrians had at least provided him with reading material. A technical manual on water management systems would have been better than this endless boredom.

In any reasonably-run prison, he told himself with frustration, there would at least be other inmates. But in this Fendrian facility, Harrison was completely alone.

True, every evening technicians came and subjected him to intensive language training while he was unconscious, but Harrison got no enjoyment from that. Now he could discuss everything from game theory to entrepreneurship in flawless Fendrian, but he had no one to talk to. He shifted position on the cot and examined the walls again. The Fendrians were thorough; there wasn't even a scratch to distract him.

He wasn't tired and he wasn't hungry; they'd provided him with nutritionally optimized meal replacements. But he was desperately bored and ready to talk to anyone about anything, just for human—or quasi-human—contact.

As he reached this conclusion, the door opened with a pneumatic hiss. Harrison stood quickly and turned to face his visitor.

The Fendrian was tall and had an odd bluish tint to his skin. He looked vaguely human if you didn't examine him too closely. Life throughout the explored regions seemed to favor humanoid forms; Harrison didn't know why, and the scientists back home had offered dozens of theories without reaching consensus. Harrison didn't particularly care; it wasn't his area of expertise.

The Fendrian studied him through pale, almost colorless eyes. "You are Patrick Harrison," he said in a flat, emotionless tone.

It was a ritual, Harrison had learned. "You are Fendrian," he replied.

The blue-tinted being nodded once. "I am Oliver Carter of Fendria," he said. The formalities completed, he entered the cell, the door sliding shut behind him. Harrison briefly considered attacking, but dismissed the idea. He was a prisoner, and it would be foolish to assume his captors lacked hidden defenses beyond the visible neural disruptor holstered at Carter's side and the small blade at his belt.

"What is your purpose here?" Harrison said. The Fendrian language—apparently the entire nation spoke one standardized dialect—was rigid and mathematical in structure, but easily learned under hypnotic conditioning. It was the most ruthlessly logical linguistic construction Harrison had encountered in his diplomatic career, reminiscent of formal logic systems he'd studied years ago.

"I have no purpose here," Carter said, standing near the door. "Do you have additional questions?"

Harrison suppressed a sigh. "Why have you come to this location?" he asked, mentally adjusting to the Fendrian literalist interpretation of language.

"I have been ordered to come to this location," Carter said, "by the Director. The Director requires information from you."

The Fendrian term wasn't quite "requires"—it was more specific, roughly translating to "demands with full legal authority." Harrison filed the distinction away. "Why did the Director not come to me?" he asked.

"The Director is the Director," Carter said, as if this explained everything. "You will go to the Director. This is the command."

Harrison smoothed his hair and straightened his posture. "I acknowledge the Director's command," he said—another required response. Everyone acknowledged the Director's commands in Fendria. Failure to do so meant immediate termination.

But Harrison meant exactly what he'd said. He was going to follow the Director's commands—and in doing so, eliminate the Fendrian threat to global democratic governance forever.

That, after all, was his mission.

---

The Director's office was large, rectangular, and overwhelmingly gray. The walls were dark gray, the furniture—a single imposing desk, several rigid chairs, and a row of filing cabinets—was light gray metal, and even the window treatments were slate-colored. It was, Harrison decided, an aesthetic disaster, even accounting for the contrast provided by the bluish Fendrian complexions.

The Director himself, a Fendrian over six and a half feet tall with correspondingly broad shoulders, sat behind his desk, fingers steepled precisely, studying Harrison and his two escorts. The escorts stood on either side of their prisoner, motionless as statues.

Harrison wasn't trying to escape. He wasn't begging for mercy. He wasn't defying authority. He was simply answering questions.

The Fendrians valued clarity above all else. They were a logical people. The Director had begun with Harrison's nationality, his full name, his biological sex, and whether his appearance was typical for his species.

Harrison was now addressing the last question. "Some humans are taller than I am," he said, "and some are shorter."

"Specify the range," the Director commanded.

Harrison shrugged slightly. "Some exceed two meters in height," he said, using the Fendrian measurement system, "while others are below one meter." He saw no need to mention that both extremes were exceptional cases. "Additionally, there is a category of humans who are typically between forty and sixty centimeters tall—usually around forty-five centimeters. We call these 'children,'" he added helpfully.

"'Typically'?" the Director said sharply. "We require precision here. We are a scientific society. We demand exactitude."

Harrison nodded quickly. "My species is more... variable," he said apologetically.

"Imprecise," the Director muttered.

"Undoubtedly," Harrison agreed politely. "I'll provide the most accurate information I can."

"You will answer my questions," the Director said, "with complete precision." He paused, his expression unchanging. "You arrived in Fendria via aircraft," he continued. "Explain the purpose."

"My assignment required it," Harrison said.

"An obvious falsehood," the Director said. "The aircraft crashed; our analysis proves this conclusively."

"Correct," Harrison said.

"And your assignment is to crash aircraft?" the Director said. "This is inefficient."

Harrison shrugged again. "What I state is accurate," he said. "Do you possess verification methods?"

"We do," the Director told him. "We are a precise and scientific nation. A truth-verification system has been calibrated to your physiology. It will be applied to you now."

Harrison looked toward the door as it opened, admitting two technicians pushing a large device. It was bulky, angular, and metallic, mounted on wheels, covered with displays, sensors, blinking indicators, cables, and featuring a seat with restraints. It was clearly a polygraph system—and Harrison marveled again at this society. Coalition technology had nothing approaching their mastery of physical sciences; adapting a hypnotic language-training program to an alien mind so rapidly had been impressive enough, but calibrating the extraordinarily sensitive mechanisms of a polygraph to unfamiliar physiology was nearly miraculous.

The Fendrians, under different circumstances, would have been valuable allies in promoting global stability and cultural exchange.

Being what they were, however, they could only threaten the democratic world order. And Harrison's understanding of that threat grew with each passing hour.

He hoped the polygraph had been calibrated correctly. If it indicated deception, he wouldn't survive long, and both his mission and his strong personal preference demanded his continued survival.

He swallowed hard. But when the technicians strapped him into the seat, attached sensors and electrodes to his body at various points, and tightened the final restraints, he offered no resistance.

"We will test the device," the Director said. "In what location are you?"

"In the Director's office," Harrison said calmly.

"Are you standing or seated?"

"I am seated," Harrison said.

"Are you a vrakken?" the Director asked. A vrakken was a small Fendrian animal, Harrison knew, something like an oversized beetle.

"I am not," he said.

The Director glanced at his technicians for confirmation, then nodded at their signal. "You will now state a falsehood," he said. "Are you standing or seated?"

"I am standing," Harrison said.

The technicians signaled again. The Director looked satisfied. "The device," he announced, "has been successfully calibrated to your physiology. Questioning will now proceed."

Harrison swallowed again. The test seemed inadequate to him. But the Fendrians knew their business better than anyone else could. They had the methodology and the logic and the expertise.

He hoped they were right.

The Director was studying him intently. Harrison tried to appear cooperative. "Why did you come to Fendria?" the Director asked.

"My assignment required it," Harrison said.

The Director nodded. "Your assignment is to crash aircraft," he said. "This is wasteful, but the device indicates truth. Very well; we will learn more about your assignment. Was the crash deliberate?"

Harrison maintained a neutral expression. "Yes," he said.

The Director's eyes narrowed slightly. "Very well," he said. "Was your assignment completed when the aircraft crashed?"

"No," Harrison said.

"What additional objectives does your assignment include?" the Director asked.

Harrison decided to introduce his first complication. "Remaining alive."

The Director's face flushed slightly darker blue. "Do not waste time with self-evident facts!" he said sharply. "Do not attempt to deceive us; we are a logical and scientific people! Answer appropriately."

"I have stated the truth," Harrison said.

"But it is not—not the truth we seek," the Director said.

Harrison shrugged. "I responded to your question," he said. "I was unaware that truth had multiple categories. Surely truth is truth, just as the Director is the Director?"

"I—" The Director stopped himself. "You attempt to confuse the Director," he said finally, his voice controlled again. "But the Director will not be confused. We have specialists in logical analysis who will advise the Director. They will be summoned."

Harrison's escorts had been standing idle now that their prisoner was restrained in the polygraph. The Director gestured and they exited quickly.

The Director looked down at Harrison. "You will discover that you cannot deceive us," he said. "You will discover that such primitive attempts will achieve nothing."

Harrison sincerely hoped so.

---

The logic specialists arrived within minutes, and Harrison was firmly informed that logical paradoxes would not confuse anyone in Fendria. Russell's paradox, the liar's paradox, Zeno's paradoxes, and all the other classic logical puzzles were elementary material for the Fendrians. "They can be resolved through formal logic systems," one specialist, a slight bluish being named Jordan West, told Harrison coolly. "Naturally, you would not comprehend the formal systems. But that is irrelevant. You need only understand that we cannot be confused by such methods."

"Excellent," Harrison said.

The specialist blinked. "Excellent?" he said.

"Naturally," Harrison said pleasantly.

The specialist's expression hardened, his jaw tightening. Harrison tried not to react. "Your strategy has failed," the specialist said, "yet you call this excellent. You can only mean that your strategy differs from what we have assumed."

"Correct," Harrison said.

There was a brief silence. The specialist's expression shifted to something like satisfaction. He examined the polygraph displays carefully. "What is your strategy?" he asked quietly.

"To answer your questions truthfully and logically," Harrison said.

The silence lasted longer this time.

"The device indicates truth," the specialist said finally, his tone suggesting awe. "Therefore, you must be betraying your own nation. You must want us to dominate your region, and have come here secretly to assist us."

Harrison was grateful that wasn't a question. It was, after all, the only logical conclusion.

But it happened to be wrong.

---

"Your nation is called the Bristol Region?" the Director asked. Several minutes had passed; the specialists were clustered around the desk. Harrison remained strapped to the polygraph; a logical society might use a traitor, but a logical society does not trust him.

"Sometimes," Harrison said.

"It has other names?" the Director asked.

"It has no name," Harrison said truthfully. The Fendrian idiom was similar to English; certainly a nation had no name of its own. People assigned names to it, that was all. It possessed none inherently.

"Yet you call it the Bristol Region?" the Director said.

"I do," Harrison said, "for convenience in communication."

"Do you know its precise geographical coordinates?" the Director asked.

"Not with exactitude," Harrison said.

There was a stir among the specialists. "But you can locate it again," the Director said.

"I can," Harrison said.

"And you will provide us with information about it?" the Director continued.

"I will," Harrison said, "to the extent of my knowledge."

"We will require information about defensive capabilities," the Director said, "and about strategic planning and fortifications. But we must first understand the decision-making structure in your region. Is your nation affiliated with others in a governmental alliance, or does it exist independently?"

Harrison almost smiled. "Both," he said.

A brief silence was broken by one of the specialists. "We have theorized that a subordinate entity may be permitted to make certain decisions independently, with only major decisions reserved for the central authority. This seems inefficient and error-prone, yet it is a possible system. Is this what you mean?"

Very astute, Harrison thought. "It is," he said.

"Then the government that controls multiple nations is supreme," the Director said.

"It is," Harrison said.

"Who exercises this control?" the Director asked.

The crucial question had finally been asked. Harrison was grateful that the logical Fendrians had chosen to begin systematically, rather than jumping to questions about military capabilities first; it saved considerable time.

"The answer to that question," Harrison said, "cannot be provided to you."

"Every factual question has an answer," the Director said sharply. "No paradox is involved here; a government exists, and some entity governs. Perhaps multiple entities share this function; perhaps automated systems perform the work. But where there is government, there is a governor. Is this not so?"

"Certainly," Harrison said. "It is completely obvious and accurate."

"The nation from which you come is part of an alliance of nations that are governed, you have stated," the Director continued.

"Correct," Harrison said.

"Then there is a governor for this alliance," the Director said.

"Correct," Harrison said again.

The Director exhaled slowly. "Describe this governor to us," he said.

Harrison shrugged. "The description cannot be provided to you."

The Director turned to his specialists and a brief whispered consultation occurred. When it ended, the Director returned his attention to Harrison. "Is the limitation in you?" he asked. "Are you somehow unable to describe this government?"

"It can be described," Harrison said.

"Then you will suffer negative consequences if you describe it to us?" the Director continued.

"I will not," Harrison said.

This prompted another consultation. With some satisfaction, Harrison noticed that the Fendrians were becoming visibly uncertain; they were no longer moving and speaking with calm confidence.

The plan was working.

The Director had finished conferring. "You are attempting again to confuse us," he said.

Harrison shook his head earnestly. "I am attempting," he said, "not to confuse you."

"Then I demand an answer," the Director said.

"I request that I be permitted to ask a question," Harrison said.

The Director hesitated, then nodded once. "Ask it," he said. "We will answer if we determine it appropriate."

Harrison tried to look grateful. "Very well," he said. "What is your system of government?"

The Director gestured to a heavy-set blue being, who stepped forward from a group of Fendrians, inclined his head toward Harrison, and began speaking in a surprisingly melodious voice. "Our government is the only logical form of government," he said. "The Director commands all, and citizens obey. Through this method, uniformity is achieved, and this uniformity enables rapid action and concentrated force. All Fendrians act simultaneously in the same manner. The Director is selected by the previous Director; through this method we ensure consistent wisdom and stable judgment."

"You have heard our government described," the Director said. "Now, you will describe yours to us."

Harrison shook his head. "If you insist," he said, "I'll attempt it. But you will not understand it."

The Director's expression hardened. "We will understand," he said. "Begin. Who governs you?"

"No one," Harrison said.

"But you are governed?"

Harrison nodded. "Yes."

"Then there is a governor," the Director insisted.

"Correct," Harrison said. "But everyone is the governor."

"Then there is no government," the Director said. "There is no unified decision-making."

"No," Harrison said calmly, "there are many decisions binding on all citizens."

"Who makes them binding?" the Director asked. "Who compels you to accept these decisions? Some of them must be unfavorable to some individuals?"

"Many of them are unfavorable," Harrison said. "But we are not compelled to accept them."

"Do you act against your own interests?"

Harrison shrugged. "Not knowingly," he said. The Director glanced sharply at the technicians monitoring the polygraph. Harrison turned to observe their expressions. They needed no words; the polygraph was clearly indicating that he was telling the truth. But the truth wasn't making any sense. "I warned you that you wouldn't understand it," he said.

"It is a flaw in your description," the Director said, his voice strained.

"My description is as precise as possible," Harrison said.

The Director breathed heavily. "Let us try a different approach," he said. "Everyone is the governor. Do you share a collective consciousness? A hive mind has been theorized, though we have encountered no examples—"

"Neither have we," Harrison said. "We are all individuals, like yourselves."

"But with no single director to formulate policy, to make decisions—"

"We have no need of one," Harrison said calmly.

"Ah," the Director said suddenly, as if seeing clarity ahead. "And why not?"

"We call our form of government 'democracy,'" Harrison said. "It means government by the people. There is no need for another director."

One of the specialists spoke up suddenly. "The individuals themselves govern each other?" he said. "This is clearly impossible; no single individual can possess the force to compel acceptance of commands. Without this force, there can be no effective government."

"That is our form of government," Harrison said.

"You are lying," the specialist said.

One of the technicians interjected: "The device indicates—"

"Then the device is malfunctioning," the specialist said. "It will be recalibrated."

Harrison wondered, as the technicians began arguing, how long they'd spend examining the polygraph before they realized it had no malfunction to correct. He hoped it wouldn't take too long; he could foresee another period of tedious boredom ahead. And besides, he was getting homesick for the Bristol Region.

---

It took five days—but boredom never really materialized. Harrison found himself receiving more attention than he'd anticipated; one by one, the specialists visited his cell, each with a different approach to resolving the apparent contradictions in his statements.

Some left angry. Others simply left, bewildered.

On the fifth day, Harrison escaped.

It wasn't particularly difficult; he hadn't expected it to be. Even the most logical of thinking beings possesses a subconscious mind as well as a conscious one, and one method of dealing with an insoluble problem is to make the problem vanish. There were only two ways to accomplish that, and eliminating the problem's focal point was somewhat more complicated. That couldn't be done by the subconscious mind alone; the conscious mind had to participate. And it couldn't.

Because that would require recognizing, fully and consciously, that the problem was genuinely insoluble. And the Fendrians weren't capable of that kind of thinking.

Harrison was grateful that their genius had been confined to the physical and computational sciences. Any insight into psychology would have given them the key to his existence and his entire strategy within seconds.

But then, it was precisely that lack of insight that had necessitated this particular mission. That, and the authoritarian political structure of Fendria.

The same lack of insight allowed the Fendrian subconscious to work on his escape without any troublesome interference from deep reflection. Someone left a door unlocked and a weapon accessible—all quite unintentional, Harrison was certain. Reaching his aircraft was slightly more complicated, but presented no fundamental obstacles; he was airborne, and then beyond Fendrian airspace, within a few hours of leaving the cell.

He set his course, relaxed, and cleared his mind. He had no telepathic abilities, but the specialists at Coalition Intelligence did; he couldn't receive messages, but he could send them. He sent one now.

*Mission accomplished; the Fendrians won't be expanding their authoritarian model into neighboring regions anytime soon. They've been given a conceptual puzzle—a beautifully indigestible puzzle that will occupy them until they finally manage to comprehend it. But they can't comprehend it and remain what they are; you need to embrace democratic principles, to some degree, to understand the concept. What makes us obey laws we ourselves create? What makes us obey laws that disadvantage us personally? Enlightened self-interest, naturally—but try to make a Fendrian grasp it!*

*With one director and one standardized language, they simply weren't equipped for this kind of translation. They were too successful with physical sciences to pursue psychology or political science seriously. No social sciences, no insight into my mind or their own—and that means no translation.*

*But—damn it—I wish I were home already. I'm absolutely bored out of my mind!*

---

Back in Lincoln, Nordavia, at Coalition Intelligence headquarters, Director Giovanni Potter received Harrison's mental transmission and smiled. The Fendrian problem had been neutralized, at least for the foreseeable future. They'd spend years, perhaps decades, trying to understand how a government could function without a single director, how laws could be binding without a single enforcer, how order could emerge from apparent chaos.

And by the time they figured it out—if they ever did—they'd no longer be the threat they currently posed. Understanding democracy required experiencing it, and experiencing it would change them fundamentally.

Potter drafted a brief report for the Coalition Council, noting the successful completion of the mission. Patrick Harrison, specialist in strategic planning and international diplomacy, had once again proven himself invaluable.

The report concluded: "The Paradox Protocol remains our most effective non-violent method for neutralizing authoritarian expansionist threats. Recommend continued deployment in similar situations."

Potter signed the report and filed it securely. Then he sent a message to Harrison: *Welcome home when you arrive. Well done.*

Harrison, still hours away from home, received the message as a vague sense of approval and warmth. It wasn't much, but it helped with the boredom.

He wondered what his next assignment would be. Probably something in Rosewood, Nordavia, where a new separatist movement was gaining strength. Or perhaps Cliffside again, if the Fendrians recovered faster than expected.

Either way, he'd be ready. That was his job, after all—to preserve the democratic way of life, one paradox at a time.
