THE RETURNED ONE
By HERBERT D. KASTLE
Adapted and Reimagined

There was the usual welcoming crowd for a celebrity, and the usual speeches by the usual officials who met her at the transit station which had once been twenty miles outside of Bayview, but which the growing city had since engulfed and placed well within its boundaries. But everything wasn't usual. The crowd was quiet, and the mayor didn't seem quite as at-ease as he'd been on his last big welcoming—for Dr. Helena Hoffman, who had won the international prize for her work in pollution control systems. His Honor's handclasp was somewhat moist and cold. His Honor's eyes held a trace of remoteness.

Still, she was the honored home-comer, the successful returnee, the hometown woman who had made good in a big way, and they took the triumphal tour up Main Street to the new square and the grandstand. There she sat between the mayor and a nervous young graduate student chosen as homecoming representative, and looked out at the municipal bands, the National Guard, the civic organizations and community groups. Several of the local institutions in town had shown indecision as to how to instruct their members to treat her. But they had all come around. The tremendous national interest, the fact that she was the First Returned, had made them come around. It was obvious by now that they would have to adjust as they'd adjusted to all the other firsts taking place in these—as the media had dubbed the start of the new era—the Revolutionary Thirties.

She was glad when the official greeting was over. She was a very tired woman and she had come farther, traveled longer through stranger territory, than any person who'd ever lived before. She wanted a meal at her own table, a kiss from her husband, a word from her daughter, and later to see some old friends and a relative or two. She didn't want to talk about the journey. She wanted to forget the immediacy, the urgency, the terror; then perhaps she would talk.

Or would she? For she had very little to tell. She had traveled and she had returned and her voyage was very much like no voyage anyone had ever experienced—long periods of absolute nothing, and then the gradual awakening.

The house had changed. She saw that as soon as the official car let her off at 45 Riverside Avenue. The change was, she knew, for the better. They had put solar panels on the roof. They had rehabilitated, spruced up, almost rebuilt the entire outside and grounds with funds from the government compensation program. But she was sorry. She had wanted it to be as before.

The head of the Community Council and the chief of the local administration, who had escorted her on this trip from the square, didn't ask to go in with her. She was glad. She'd had enough of strangers. Not that she was through with strangers. There were dozens of them up and down the street, standing beside parked vehicles, looking at her. But when she looked back at them, their eyes dropped, they turned away, they began moving off. She was still too much the First Returned to have her gaze met.

She walked up what had once been a gravel path and was now a smooth composite path. She climbed the new steps and raised her hand to the biometric scanner, but then realized it wouldn't recognize her yet. She pressed the old-fashioned bell button and heard the soft chime sound within. She was surprised that she'd had to do this. She'd thought Fernando would be watching at a window.

And perhaps he had been watching... but he hadn't opened the door.

The door opened; she looked at him. It hadn't been too long and he hadn't changed at all. He was still the tall, gentle man she'd loved in graduate school, the tall, gentle man she'd married fourteen years ago. Lena was with him. They held onto each other as if seeking mutual support, the thirty-eight-year-old man and twelve-year-old girl. They looked at her, and then both moved forward, still together. She said, "It's good to be home!"

Fernando nodded and, still holding to Lena with one hand, put the other arm around her. He kissed her—her neck, her cheek—and all the old jokes came to mind, the jokes of travel-weary people, the and-then-I'll-put-my-bag-down jokes that spoke of terrible hunger. He was trembling, and even as his lips came up to touch hers she felt the difference, and because of this difference she turned with urgency to Lena and picked her up—though the girl was almost too big for that now—and hugged her and said, because she could think of nothing else to say, "What a big girl, what a big girl."

Lena stood in her arms as if her feet were still planted on the floor, and she didn't look at her mother but somewhere beyond her. "I didn't grow much while you were gone, Mom. Dad says I'm just like you were at this age."

So she put her down and told herself that it would all change, that everything would loosen up just as her project director, Dr. Wei Kumar, had said it would early this morning before she left the Capital Medical Research Facility in Carmel.

"Give it some time," Wei had said. "You need the time; they need the time. And for the love of heaven, don't be sensitive."

Fernando was leading her into the living room, his hand lying still in hers, a cool, uncertain hand lying still in hers. She sat down on the couch, he sat down beside her—but he had hesitated. She wasn't being sensitive; he had hesitated. Her husband had hesitated before sitting down beside her.

Wei had said her position was analogous to the early pioneers of medical technology, to the first recipients of artificial organs, to the first cryogenic revival subjects—but more so. Wei had said lots of things, but even Wei who had worked with her all the way, who had engineered the entire fantastic process—even Wei the Nobel prize winner, the multi-degreed genius in neural regeneration, had not actually spoken to her as one person to another.

The eyes. It always showed in their eyes.

She looked across the room at Lena, standing in the doorway, a girl already tall, already showing the features of young womanhood. It was like looking into the mirror and seeing herself twenty-five years ago. But Lena's face was drawn, was worried in a way that few twelve-year-old faces are.

"How's it going in school?" she asked.

"Mom, it's the third month of summer break."

"Well, then, before summer break?"

"Pretty good."

Fernando said, "She made honor roll both semesters before break, and she made honor roll the semester you went away, Priya."

She nodded, remembering that, remembering everything, remembering the warmth of their farewell, the warmth of Lena's farewell, their tears as she left for the experimental medical facility in Crestwood. They had feared for her, having read of the many procedures gone wrong even in the most advanced research centers.

They had been right to worry. She had suffered much after that accident. But now they should be rejoicing, because she had survived and made the long journey back. Lena suddenly said, "I have to go, Mom. I promised Yasmin and the others I'd help with the data science project. It's the Regional Science Fair preparation, you know. I have to keep my word." Without waiting for an answer, she waved her hand—it shook; a twelve-year-old girl's hand that shook—and ran from the room and from the house.

She and Fernando sat beside each other, and she wanted badly to take him in her arms, and yet she didn't want to oppress him. She stood up. "I'm very tired. I'd like to lie down a while." Which wasn't true, because she'd been lying down all the months of the recovery.

He said, "Of course. How thoughtless of me, expecting you to sit around and make small talk and pick up just where you left off."

She nodded. But that was exactly what she wanted to do—make small talk and pick up just where she'd left off. But they didn't expect it of her; they wouldn't let her; they felt she had changed too much.

He led her upstairs and along the hallway past Lena's room and past the small study to their bedroom. This, too, had changed. It was newly painted and it had new furniture. She saw twin beds separated by an ornate little table with an ornate little lamp, and this looked more ominous a barrier to her than the twelve layers of security clearance around the research facility.

"Which one is mine," she asked, and tried to smile.

He also tried to smile. "The one near the window. You always liked the fresh air, the morning light. You always said it helped you to wake up motivated when you were working on your environmental conservation thesis. You always said it reminded you—being able to see the sky—that you were going to make a difference in the world, and that you were going to come back to this bed again."

"Not this bed," she murmured, and was a little sorry afterward.

"No, not this bed," he said quickly. "Your professional association donated the bedroom set and I really didn't know—" He waved his hand, his face pale.

She was sure then that he had known, and that the beds and the barrier between them were his own choice, if only an unconscious choice. She went to the bed near the window, began to remove her jacket, but then remembered that some neural interface scars still showed on her neck and arms. She waited for him to leave the room.

He said, "Well then, rest up, dear," and went out.

She took off her jacket and saw herself in the mirror on the opposite wall; and then took off her shirt. The scars were faint, the marks running in precise lines along her spine, across her shoulders, disappearing under her clothing. There were several more on her abdomen, and one on her left thigh where the emergency neural bypass had been installed. They'd been treated properly and would soon disappear. But he had never seen them.

Perhaps he never would. Perhaps long sleeves and high collars and dim lighting would keep them from him until they were gone.

Which was not what she'd considered at all important on leaving the Research Facility early this morning; which was something she found distasteful, something she felt beneath them both. And, at the same time, she began to understand that there would be many things, previously beneath them both, which would have to be considered. He had changed; Lena had changed; all the people she knew had probably changed—because they thought she had changed.

She was tired of thinking. She lay down and closed her eyes. She let herself taste bitterness, unhappiness, a loneliness she had never known before.

But sometime later, as she was dozing off, a sense of reassurance began filtering into her mind. After all, she was still Priya Baker, the same woman who had left home thirteen months ago, with a love for family and friends which was, if anything, stronger than before. Once she could communicate this, the strangeness would disappear and the First Returned would again become good old Priya. It was little enough to ask for—a return to old values, old relationships, the normalcies of everyday life instead of the intensity of the spotlight. It would certainly be granted to her.

She slept.

Dinner was at seven p.m. Her sister came; her colleague Zara and Zara's partner Sophie came. Together with Fernando, Lena and herself, they made six, and ate in the dining room at the big table.

Before she'd become the First Returned, it would have been a noisy affair. Her family had never been noted for a lack of enthusiasm, a lack of conversation, and Lena had always chosen mealtimes—especially with company present—to describe everything and anything that had happened to her during the day. And Fernando himself had always chatted, especially with her sister, though they didn't agree about much regarding education reform. Still, it had been good-natured; the general tone of their lives had been good-natured.

This wasn't good-natured. Exactly what it was she wasn't sure. "Stiff" was perhaps the word.

They began with salad, Fernando and her sister serving quickly, efficiently from the kitchen, then sitting down at the table. She looked at her sister as she raised her first forkful of greens, and said, "You look wonderful." It was nothing new; she'd said it many many times before, but her sister had always reacted with a bright smile and a quip something like, "Wonderful for someone pushing forty, you mean." This time she burst into tears. It shocked her. But what shocked her even more was the fact that no one looked up, commented, made any attempt to comfort her; no one indicated in any way that a woman was sobbing at the table.

She was sitting directly across from her sister, and reached out and touched her left hand which lay limply beside the silverware. She didn't move it—she hadn't touched her once beyond that first, quick, strangely-cool embrace at the door—then a few seconds later she withdrew it and let it drop out of sight.

So there she was, Priya Baker, at home with the family. So there she was, the miracle returned, waiting to be treated as a human being.

The salad plates were cleaned away and the soup served. Zara began to talk. "The most innovative educational data analytics platform you ever did see," she said in her enthusiastic professor's voice. "Still expanding rapidly. We'll reach national implementation before—" At that point she looked at Priya, and Priya nodded encouragement, desperately interested in this normalcy, and Zara's voice died away. She looked down at her bowl, mumbled, "Soup's getting cold," and began to eat. Her hand shook a little; her confident face was not quite as confident as Priya remembered it.

Sophie made a few tentative statements about the University Cultural Exchange Program, and Priya looked across the table to where she sat between Zara and her sister—her husband and daughter bracketed her, and yet she felt alone—and said, "I've missed being involved in the community initiatives. Here it is August and I haven't participated in a single project."

Sophie smiled, if you could call it that—a pitiful twitching of the lips—and nodded. She threw her eyes in her direction, and past her, and then down to her bowl. Her sister, who was still sniffling, said, "I have a terrible migraine. I'm going to lie down in the guest room a while." She touched her shoulder in passing—her affectionate, demonstrative sister who would embrace strangers and volunteer for every cause, who had often overwhelmed her with an excess of physical and verbal affection—she barely touched her shoulder and fled.

So now five of them sat at the table. The main course was served—grilled salmon, the pink flesh steaming and fragrant. She cut into it and raised a forkful to her mouth, then glanced at Lena and said, "Looks fresh enough to have been caught this morning." Lena said, "Yeah, Mom." Sophie put down her knife and fork and murmured something to her partner. Zara cleared her throat and said Sophie was dealing with some dietary concerns and she guessed she was going into the living room for a while. "She'll be back for dessert, of course," she said, her laugh sounding forced.

Priya looked at Fernando; Fernando was busy with his plate. Priya looked at Lena; Lena was busy with her plate. Priya looked at Zara; Zara was chewing, gazing out over their heads to the kitchen. Priya looked at Sophie; she was disappearing into the living room.

She brought her fist down on the table. The settings jumped; a glass overturned, spilling water. She brought it down again and again. They were all standing now. She sat there and pounded the table with her right fist—Priya Baker, who would never have thought of making such a scene before, but who was now so sick and tired of being treated as the First Returned, of being stood back from, looked at in awe of, felt in fear of, that she could have smashed more than a table.

Fernando said, "Priya!"

She said, voice hoarse, "Leave me alone. Go away. Let me eat alone. I'm sick of the lot of you."

Her sister and Zara returned a few minutes later where she sat forcing food down her throat. Her sister said, "Priya dear—" She didn't answer. She began to cry, and Priya was glad she left the house then. She had never said anything really harsh to her sister. She was afraid this would have been the time. Zara merely cleared her throat and mumbled something about getting together again soon and "come by the university and see the new data center" and she, too, was gone. Sophie never did manage to speak to her.

She finished her salmon and waited. Soon Fernando came in with the special dessert he'd been preparing half the day—a magnificent chocolate torte. He served her, and cut a portion for himself and Lena. He hesitated near her chair, and when she made no comment he called their daughter. Then the three of them were sitting, facing the empty side of the table. They ate the torte. Lena finished first and got up and said, "I really should—"

"You really should go work on your data science project or study for your advanced placement exams or anything to get away from your mother."

Lena's head dropped and she muttered, "No, Mom, that's not it."

Fernando said, "She'll stay home, Priya. We'll spend an evening together—talking, watching something, playing games."

Lena said, "Of course, Mom, if you want to."

Priya stood up. "The question is not whether I want to. You both know I want to. The question is whether you want to."

They answered together that of course they wanted to. But their eyes—her husband's and daughter's eyes—could not meet hers, and so she said she was going to her room because she was, after all, very tired and would in all probability continue to be very tired for a long, long time and that they shouldn't count on her for normal social life.

She fell asleep quickly, lying there in her clothes.

But she didn't sleep long. Fernando shook her and she opened her eyes to a lighted room. "Yasmin and her husband are here." She blinked at him. He smiled, and it seemed his old smile. "They're so anxious to see you, Priya. I could barely keep Yasmin from coming up and waking you herself. They want to go out and catch up. Please, Priya, say you will."

She sat up. "Yasmin," she muttered. "Yasmin and Marcus." They'd had wonderful times together, from college on. Yasmin and Marcus, their oldest and closest friends. Perhaps this would begin her real homecoming.

Go out and celebrate? They'd laugh and reminisce and reconnect!

It didn't turn out that way. She was disappointed; but then again, she'd also expected it. This entire first day at home had conditioned her to expect nothing good. They went to the recreation center, and Yasmin sounded very much the way she always had—animated and full of stories and full of insights. She hugged Fernando the way she always had, and squeezed Priya's hand (but not the way she always had—so much more carefully, almost tentatively), and insisted they all drink more wine than was sensible as she always had. And for once, Priya was ready to go along on the drinking. For once, she matched Yasmin glass for glass.

They didn't stay at the recreation center very long. At ten o'clock they crossed the plaza to the Garden Café, where Yasmin and the others ordered appetizers and coffee and Priya went right on drinking. Fernando said something to her, but she merely smiled and waved her hand and sipped another glass of oblivion.

There was music and dancing at the Garden Café. She'd been there many times before, and she was sure several of the patrons recognized her. But except for a few furtive glances in her direction, it was as if she were a stranger in a city halfway around the world.

At midnight, she was still drinking. The others wanted to leave, but she said, "I haven't danced with my friend Yasmin." Her speech was slightly slurred, her mind was blurred, and yet she could read the strange expression on Yasmin's face—brilliant Yasmin, who'd always been so warm with her, who'd made a ritual of their friendship. Brilliant Yasmin, who now looked as if she were going to be ill.

"So let's dance," she said and stood up.

They were on the dance floor. She held her close in the contemporary style, and hummed and chatted. And through the alcoholic haze saw she was a stiff-smiled, stiff-bodied, mechanical dancing partner.

The song finished; they walked back to the table. Marcus said, "Time to head home."

Priya said, "First one dance with my loving husband."

She and Fernando danced. She didn't hold him as close as she had Yasmin. She waited for him to come close on his own, and he did, and yet he didn't. Because while he put himself against her, there was something in his face—no, in his eyes; it always showed in the eyes—that made her know he was trying to be the old Fernando and not succeeding. This time when the music ended, she was ready to go home.

They rode back to Bayview along the main highway, she and Fernando in the rear of Yasmin's vehicle, Marcus driving because Yasmin had drunk just a little too much, Yasmin chatting and telling an occasional story about their university days, and somehow not her old self. No one was their old self. No one would ever be their old self with the First Returned.

They turned left, to take the short cut along Memorial Park Drive, and Yasmin finished a story about a failed experiment and a famous scientist and looked at her husband and then past him at the long, stone wall paralleling the road. "Hey," she said, pointing, "do you know what they're planning for the new memorial garden?"

Marcus glanced to the left, and so did Priya and Fernando. Marcus made a small sound, and Fernando seemed to stop breathing, but Yasmin went on a moment longer, not yet aware of her supposed misstep.

"You know what?" she repeated, turning to the back seat, the enthusiasm rising in her voice. "You know what, everyone?"

Marcus said, "Did you see the announcement about the new cultural center in—"

Priya said, "No, Yasmin, what are they planning for the memorial garden?"

Yasmin said, "They're going to—" And then she caught herself and waved her hand and muttered, "I can't remember the details."

"They're going to create a memorial for people who died and were brought back through neural regeneration," Priya said, and looked through the window, past the stone wall, into the large memorial park at the fleeting monuments.

The vehicle was filled with horrified silence when there should have been nothing but interest, or perhaps mild curiosity. "Maybe you should let me out right here," Priya said. "I'm home—or that's what everyone seems to think. Maybe I should lie down in the memorial garden. Maybe that would satisfy people. Maybe that's the only way to act, like something from a horror story."

Fernando said, "Oh, Priya, don't, don't!"

The vehicle raced along the road, crossed an intersection, went four blocks and pulled to a stop. She didn't bother saying good night. She didn't wait for Fernando. She just got out and walked up the composite path and entered the house.

"Priya," Fernando whispered from the study doorway, "I'm so sorry—"

"There's nothing to be sorry about. It's just a matter of time. It'll all work out in time."

"Yes," he said quickly, "that's it. I need a little time. We all need a little time. Because it's so strange, Priya. Because it's so frightening. I should have told you that the moment you walked in. I think I've hurt you terribly, we've all hurt you terribly, by trying to hide that we're frightened."

"I'm going to stay in the study," she said, "for as long as necessary. For good if need be."

"How could it be for good? How, Priya?"

That question was perhaps the first firm basis for hope she'd had since returning. And there was something else; what Wei had told her, even as Wei himself had reacted as all people did.

"There are others coming, Fernando. Fifteen that I know of in the regeneration pods right now. My colleague, Dr. Helena Hoffman, who died at the same moment I did—nine months ago next Tuesday—she's going to be next. She was injured worse than I was, so it took a little longer, but she's almost ready. And there'll be many more, Fernando. The government is going to save all they possibly can from now on. Every time a young and healthy person loses their life by accident, by trauma, and their body can be recovered in time, they'll go into the pods and they'll start the regenerative neural and organ process—the process that made it all possible. So people have to get used to us. And the old fears, the old superstitions, the primitive terrors have to die, because in time each community will have some of us; because in time it'll be an ordinary thing."

Fernando said, "Yes, and I'm so grateful that you're here, Priya. Please believe that. Please be patient with me and Lena and—" He paused. "There's one question."

She knew what the question was. It had been the first asked her by everyone from the President on down.

"I experienced nothing," she said. "It was as if I slept those eight months—slept without dreaming."

He came to her and touched her face with his lips, and she was satisfied.

Later, half asleep, she heard a siren wailing in the distance, and remembered stories of how they announced emergencies and the presence of danger. She shivered and pulled the covers closer to her and luxuriated in being safe in her own home.

THE END

THE ARCHITECT IN HIS SIMULATION
By ANONYMOUS

Martin Watkins stood at the edge of the digital construct, watching the sunset algorithms paint the sky in shades of amber and rose. The simulation was flawless—every photon traced, every atmospheric particle accounted for. It was his masterwork, a virtual recreation of Horizonville, Estoria, the coastal city where he'd grown up before the Great Migration had scattered humanity across the solar system.

He was here on business, of course. Nicole Leonard had disappeared into someone's mind-simulation three weeks ago, and the Cognitive Security Bureau had hired him to extract her. In the century since Dr. Kenji Yamamoto had discovered that human consciousness could be digitally projected into constructed virtual environments—what the media production companies now called "mindscapes"—crime had evolved in unexpected ways. Criminals no longer just hid in physical locations. They hid in the infinite labyrinths of digital consciousness.

Nicole Leonard was wanted for corporate espionage. She had stolen experimental design specifications from Helios Corporation's particle physics division—blueprints for a fusion reactor that could power an entire colony ship. The theft had international diplomacy implications; three governments were involved in the joint venture. When she'd vanished from her apartment in Evergreen, Belvoria, leaving behind only her neural interface headset still warm from use, the Bureau had known immediately where she'd gone.

The question was: whose mindscape?

Martin had spent two weeks analyzing the interface logs, tracing the quantum entanglement signatures, following the breadcrumb trail of neural patterns. The answer had shocked him. Nicole Leonard hadn't hidden in her own mindscape, nor in that of an accomplice. She had hidden in Martin's.

He still didn't understand how. His childhood home in Horizonville was a deeply personal memory, one he'd never shared publicly. Yet somehow she had learned enough about it to use it as an entry point into his digital consciousness. The implications troubled him on a professional ethics level—if criminals could access a pursuer's mindscape without permission, the entire foundation of cognitive security was compromised.

Now he was here, in his own mind, hunting her.

The Horizonville construct was eerily accurate. Every storefront on Main Street matched his memories—the bakery where his mother had bought bread, the bookshop where he'd discovered his love of art history, the small office building where his father had worked as an accountant. The people were here too, or rather, their ghost-images: constructs of memory that moved through their routines with no awareness of Martin's presence. They were echoes, nothing more.

Nicole's trail was easy to follow. She'd left digital artifacts everywhere—modified textures, altered lighting parameters, fragments of code that didn't belong. She was either careless or didn't understand the nature of mindscapes. Most likely the latter. Cognitive security was a specialized field, and civilians rarely grasped its complexities.

Martin followed her trail down Harbor Street toward the waterfront. The simulation grew more detailed as he walked, responding to his attention. He could smell the salt air, hear the cry of gulls, feel the ocean breeze on his skin. It was all artificial, of course—electrical signals interpreted by his brain—but the illusion was perfect.

He was so focused on the trail that he almost didn't notice the three figures following him.

When he finally turned around, his breath caught in his throat. Three people stood on the street behind him, watching him with expressions of unmistakable hostility. He recognized them instantly, though he couldn't understand why they were here.

The first was Professor Violet Hamilton, his undergraduate ethics instructor. The second was Henry Carter, the security officer who had supervised the dormitories at the Cognitive Sciences Institute. The third was Grace Rogers, the spokesperson from the public service announcements about social justice and human rights that had played endlessly during his childhood.

But these weren't memory-ghosts. Memory-ghosts had no awareness, no volition. These three were looking directly at him, and their eyes burned with anger.

"Professor Hamilton?" Martin said uncertainly. "What are you—"

"You know why we're here, Martin Watkins," Professor Hamilton said, her voice cold. "You know what you've done."

"Hypocrite," Henry Carter spat. "You speak of professional ethics while violating every principle you claim to uphold."

Grace Rogers pointed an accusing finger at him. "You preach about human rights and social justice, but your actions tell a different story."

Martin took a step back, his mind racing. This was impossible. He hadn't created these constructs—at least, not consciously. In mindscape theory, such autonomous entities could only emerge from deep psychological conflicts, unresolved guilt, suppressed trauma. But he had no such conflicts. He was well-adjusted, successful, confident in his choices.

Wasn't he?

"I don't understand," he said aloud. "What are you talking about?"

The three figures moved closer, their faces twisted with contempt. "You ask us that?" Professor Hamilton said. "After what you did to her?"

"After how you abandoned her?" Henry Carter added.

"After you hid behind your rationalizations and your excuses?" Grace Rogers finished.

Their voices began to blend together, overlapping, becoming a single accusatory chorus. Martin turned and ran.

---

He found himself in a different part of the simulation now—a recreation of the Cognitive Sciences Institute campus where he'd done his graduate work. The buildings were rendered in perfect detail, from the chrome-and-glass laboratory complex to the ivy-covered administration hall. Students moved across the quad, their faces blurred because Martin couldn't remember them clearly enough to render them properly.

Nicole's trail led across the campus toward the student union. Martin followed it, his mind still reeling from the encounter with the three hostile constructs. What had they meant? What had he done? And who was "her"?

The trail ended at a bench beneath a massive oak tree. Martin stopped, his heart sinking as he recognized the location. This was where he'd sat with Alex Frank five years ago, the day after her graduation ceremony.

The memory materialized around him, responding to his recognition. There was Alex, twenty-two years old, wearing her graduation dress—a simple blue affair that matched her eyes. Her dark hair was pulled back in a ponytail, and she wore the silver necklace he'd given her as a graduation present.

And there was Martin himself, or rather, his past-self—a construct of memory with no awareness of Martin's current presence. Past-Martin looked older than Martin remembered being, more careworn, with premature gray in his hair.

"Yes, at nine o'clock," Past-Alex was saying. "And I really want you to come."

Past-Martin shook his head. "Graduation parties aren't for mentors. You know that. That young man you were talking with earlier—Hugo Welch—he should take you. He'd jump at the chance."

"I'll thank you not to treat me like a child," Past-Alex said, her voice tight. "You're only thirty-five. That's not ancient."

"I'm your academic advisor," Past-Martin said. "There are professional ethics to consider. That young man—"

"What right does Hugo have to take me?" Past-Alex interrupted, her cheeks flushing. "Did he spend three years guiding my research? Did he help me get the fellowship to the Mars Institute? Did he—" She broke off, looking away.

"Please," Past-Martin said, desperation creeping into his voice. "You're making this harder than it needs to be. I helped you because it was my job, because you had talent. There was nothing more to it than that."

"Nothing more?" Past-Alex's voice was very quiet. "Is that really what you think?"

Past-Martin stood up from the bench. "You're leaving for Mars tomorrow. We won't see each other for years. It's better this way."

"You could visit," Past-Alex said. "The new ships only take two weeks."

"I won't come—you know I won't. I can't."

Past-Alex stood up too, her hands clenched at her sides. "Why? Because you're afraid? Because you can't admit to yourself what you feel?"

"I don't feel anything," Past-Martin said, but his voice cracked. "You're my student. That's all."

"I was your student," Past-Alex said. "I'm not anymore. But you can't see that, can you? You're so wrapped up in your rules and your professional ethics that you can't see what's right in front of you." She took a breath. "Fine. I'll say goodbye now, then."

"Alex, wait—"

But she was already walking away, her shoulders straight, her head high. Past-Martin watched her go, his face a mask of pain and regret.

Martin Present watched too, and felt the same pain, the same regret, magnified by five years of hindsight. He'd never seen Alex again. She'd gone to Mars, thrown herself into her work, become one of the leading researchers in theoretical modeling of consciousness transfer. He'd followed her career from a distance, never reaching out, never explaining, never apologizing.

And now these constructs—Professor Hamilton, Henry Carter, Grace Rogers—were manifestations of his guilt. They were right. He was a hypocrite. He'd hidden behind professional ethics to avoid confronting his own feelings, and in doing so, he'd hurt someone who cared about him.

"Touching, isn't it?"

Martin spun around. A woman stood behind him—thirtyish, with sharp features and calculating eyes. She wore a gray jumpsuit with the Helios Corporation logo on the shoulder.

Nicole Leonard.

"How long have you been watching?" Martin demanded.

"Long enough," Nicole said. She gestured at the memory-construct, where Past-Alex was disappearing into the distance. "That's Alex Frank, isn't it? The famous consciousness researcher. I read her papers while preparing for this job. Brilliant work. She's done more to advance theoretical modeling than anyone in the last decade." Nicole smiled. "I wonder what she'd think if she knew you were still carrying this around in your head."

"This is my private mindscape," Martin said coldly. "You're trespassing."

"True," Nicole agreed. "But you'll never catch me. I've already found your most recent entry point. One step beyond it, and I'm back in the real world. You'll be stuck here, dealing with your guilt constructs."

"How did you find my entry point? How did you even know about Horizonville?"

Nicole's smile widened. "You're not the only one who can do research, Mr. Watkins. I'm a professional thief. I steal information for a living. Did you really think your childhood memories were secret? I accessed your old school records, your family's social media archives, your father's tax filings. I built a profile of your early life detailed enough to construct an entry point. It took me three weeks, but I did it."

Martin felt a chill. If Nicole could do it, others could too. The implications for cognitive security were staggering. "That's a violation of human rights," he said. "Unauthorized access to someone's mindscape—"

"Is perfectly legal if you use only public information," Nicole finished. "I checked with my lawyers. The law hasn't caught up with the technology yet. Welcome to the cutting edge, Mr. Watkins."

She turned to leave, but Martin called after her. "Wait. Why show yourself? Why not just slip away?"

Nicole glanced back. "Because I wanted you to know. I wanted you to understand that your profession is obsolete. The old rules don't apply anymore. Cultural evolution has outpaced the legal framework. In a few years, mindscapes will be as easy to hack as computer networks used to be. You and your Cognitive Security Bureau are dinosaurs."

She walked away, her figure growing fainter as she moved toward the edge of the construct. Martin started to follow, but the three hostile constructs materialized in front of him, blocking his path.

"Let me through," Martin said.

"No," Professor Hamilton said. "Not until you face the truth."

"What truth?" Martin demanded. "That I made a mistake five years ago? I know that. I've always known that."

"Then why haven't you done anything about it?" Henry Carter asked.

"Because it's too late," Martin said. "Because Alex has moved on, built a life on Mars. Because I can't undo the past."

"You can't undo it," Grace Rogers said, "but you can acknowledge it. You can stop hiding from it."

The three constructs moved closer, their faces softening slightly. "We're not your enemies, Martin," Professor Hamilton said gently. "We're parts of you. We're the voice of your conscience, trying to make you listen."

Martin stared at them, understanding dawning. These weren't hostile entities at all. They were his own mind's way of forcing him to confront what he'd been avoiding. The anger in their faces was his anger at himself. The accusations in their voices were his own self-recrimination.

"What do I do?" he asked quietly.

"You know what to do," Henry Carter said.

Martin closed his eyes. When he opened them again, the three constructs had vanished. He was alone on the campus, with only the memory-ghosts moving through their endless routines.

He pulled up his interface menu—a translucent display that floated in his field of vision—and composed a message to Alex Frank. It was short, honest, and long overdue. He apologized for his cowardice, explained his feelings, and asked if she'd be willing to talk when he returned to the real world. He didn't expect forgiveness. He just needed her to know.

He sent the message, then turned his attention back to Nicole Leonard. She'd said she'd found his most recent entry point, but she was wrong. His most recent entry point wasn't in Horizonville or on the Institute campus. It was here, in this exact moment—the moment when he'd finally stopped running from his guilt and started dealing with it.

This was his most recent memory, freshly created. And Nicole Leonard had no way of knowing it existed.

Martin smiled grimly and set off in pursuit. The trail was easy to follow now. Nicole had grown careless, confident in her escape. She'd left obvious markers—modified code, altered textures, digital footprints that glowed like beacons in Martin's enhanced vision.

He found her at the edge of the Horizonville waterfront, standing before a shimmering portal that led back to the real world. She was reaching for it when Martin appeared behind her.

"Going somewhere?" he asked.

Nicole spun around, her eyes wide with shock. "But—how? I found your entry point!"

"You found an old entry point," Martin corrected. "I created a new one. That's the thing about mindscapes, Ms. Leonard. They're constantly evolving, responding to new experiences, new memories. You can't hack them with static information. You need to understand the person, not just their history."

Nicole lunged for the portal, but Martin was faster. He grabbed her arm, and the construct responded to his will, solidifying the connection. In the real world, their neural interfaces would be triggering the extraction protocol, pulling them both back to consciousness.

The simulation began to dissolve around them, the carefully rendered buildings and streets breaking apart into streams of data. The last thing Martin saw before the transition completed was the bench where he'd sat with Alex, still solid and clear amidst the dissolving chaos.

Some memories, he realized, were worth preserving. And some mistakes were worth correcting.

---

Martin woke in his extraction chair, his neural interface humming as it disconnected from his consciousness. Across the room, in a similar chair, Nicole Leonard was stirring, her wrists already secured by the automated restraints.

Two Bureau agents were waiting. They took Nicole into custody, reading her rights as they led her away. The stolen designs had been recovered from her personal storage—she'd been too confident to delete them.

Martin filed his report, collected his fee, and went home to his apartment in Foxwood Province. It was late evening, the city lights glittering through his window like artificial stars.

His message interface was blinking. One new message, received twenty minutes ago.

It was from Alex Frank.

Martin's hand trembled slightly as he opened it. The message was brief: "I'm glad you finally reached out. I'll be on Earth next month for a scientific collaboration conference in Horizonville Town. We should talk. —A"

Martin read the message three times, then set his interface aside and looked out at the city. The future was uncertain, full of possibilities both hopeful and frightening. But for the first time in five years, he wasn't running from it.

He was a god in his own mindscape, capable of creating entire worlds from memory and imagination. But in the real world, he was just a man—flawed, fallible, and finally ready to admit it.

And perhaps, he thought, that was enough.

QUANTUM COLLAPSE
BY ELENA HAYES

The server banks hummed in their climate-controlled chambers, processing petabytes of data every microsecond. In the Summit District headquarters of Nexus Corporation, the most advanced quantum computing facility ever built sat silent and dark, its supercooled processors offline for the first time in three years.

Dr. Hassan McCoy pressed his hand against the observation window, staring at the dormant machine that had been his life's work. Behind him, the emergency recorder continued its documentation.

"This is Dr. Hassan McCoy, lead physicist on Project Quantum Bridge, recording for the incident investigation. Date is March 15th, 2157. I'm probably the only survivor, and I need to get this on record while I still can.

"You're probably wondering what went wrong. How did the most secure facility in Nordavia, with triple-redundant systems and the best cybersecurity protocols ever designed, end up completely compromised? How did six people die and the entire quantum network collapse?

"I'll tell you how. We got cocky. We thought we understood particle physics well enough to build a bridge between quantum states. We thought our laboratory methods were foolproof. We were wrong on both counts.

"Let me start at the beginning. Project Quantum Bridge was designed to create stable quantum entanglement across macroscopic distances. Not just photons or electrons, but actual information systems. Imagine instant communication across any distance, unhackable encryption, processing power that makes our current systems look like abacuses. That's what we promised, and that's what we delivered. For three years, it worked perfectly.

"The breakthrough came from applying systems thinking to quantum mechanics. Instead of treating particles as isolated units, we modeled the entire quantum field as an interconnected system. Dr. Jin Brooks led that work—brilliant woman, background in both particle physics and cultural anthropology of all things. She argued that quantum systems behaved like social networks, with information propagating through relationship structures rather than linear pathways. Sounds crazy, but it worked.

"We built the Bridge in stages. First facility here in Summit District, second in Morningside, Nordavia, third in Yarnmouth, Quendor, and the final node in Crystalbrook District. Four quantum processors, entangled at the substrate level, sharing computational states instantaneously across thousands of miles.

"The applications were revolutionary. Consumer behavior prediction became trivially easy when you could process every transaction in real-time across the entire network. Economic development models that used to take months to run completed in seconds. We were going to change the world.

"Then the Yarnmouth facility reported anomalies. Dr. Talia Bailey was running the night shift when she noticed strange patterns in the quantum foam—fluctuations that shouldn't exist in a properly isolated system. She ran diagnostics for six hours before calling it in. Everything checked out normal, but the fluctuations persisted.

"We should have shut down then. We didn't.

"Two weeks later, Dr. Laura Rodriguez in Morningside reported similar issues. Then Crystalbrook. Then us. The fluctuations were spreading, synchronizing across all four nodes. Dr. Brooks proposed that we were seeing quantum decoherence from an external source, but we couldn't identify what. Our cybersecurity team, led by Stephen Nelson, ran every penetration test in the book. Nothing. The systems were secure.

"That's when Yuki Wallace arrived.

"Yuki came from the Yarnmouth facility as a 'consultant.' That's what they called her, anyway. She had credentials in material science and design thinking, supposedly there to help us optimize our cooling systems. But she spent most of her time just watching us work, asking odd questions, laughing at private jokes.

"I didn't trust her from the start. There was something off about her timing, her questions, the way she always seemed to be around when things went wrong. When Dr. Rodriguez's terminal crashed during a critical calculation, Yuki was standing right behind her. When the Crystalbrook link went unstable, Yuki had been 'consulting' there the day before. When our primary cooling system developed a leak, Yuki had just finished 'inspecting' it.

"But every incident checked out as equipment failure or human error. Rodriguez admitted she'd been working eighteen-hour shifts and might have made a mistake. The Crystalbrook instability traced back to a miscalibrated sensor. The cooling leak was a faulty seal, batch defect from the manufacturer.

"Plausible. All of it plausible.

"I started keeping notes. Yuki never made mistakes herself, but people around her did. Equipment near her failed. Calculations went wrong. It was subtle, distributed, deniable. But it was consistent.

"I researched her background. Her credentials were legitimate, but sparse. She'd worked on three major projects before ours. All three had experienced catastrophic failures attributed to improbable chains of human error and equipment malfunction.

"I tried to tell Dr. Brooks. She laughed it off. 'You're seeing patterns that aren't there, Hassan. That's not science, that's paranoia.' She was right, of course. I had no evidence, just statistical inference from anecdotal data. Not enough to accuse someone of... what? Being unlucky?

"The final test was scheduled for last Tuesday. We were going to demonstrate full quantum coherence across all four nodes simultaneously—a complete merging of computational states. The processing power would be unprecedented. We'd already lined up demonstrations for the Nordavian government, the Economic Development Council, even representatives from the Justice Theory Institute who wanted to model legal frameworks.

"Yuki was very interested in the test. She asked detailed questions about the timing, the protocols, the safety margins. She wanted to know what would happen if coherence failed during the merge. We told her: catastrophic decoherence, possible damage to the quantum processors, but the containment systems would prevent any danger to personnel.

"We were wrong about that too.

"The test began at 14:00 hours. All four facilities confirmed ready status. Dr. Brooks initiated the coherence sequence from the Summit District control room. I was monitoring the quantum field topology from my station. Stephen Nelson watched the security systems. Laura Rodriguez and Talia Bailey were on video link from their facilities. Yuki stood in the back of the control room, observing.

"For thirty seconds, it was beautiful. Perfect coherence across all nodes. The quantum field stabilized into a unified structure spanning thousands of miles. Processing power spiked to theoretical maximum. We were cheering.

"Then the fluctuations returned. Not gradually this time—all at once, everywhere. The quantum foam began to boil. Decoherence spread through the system like a virus. Dr. Brooks tried to abort, but the safety protocols failed. The containment fields failed. The backup systems failed.

"Everything failed at once.

"The quantum processors began to cascade. When quantum states collapse chaotically, they release energy. A lot of energy. The Yarnmouth facility exploded first. Dr. Bailey's video feed went white, then black. Crystalbrook went next. Then Morningside—I watched Dr. Rodriguez's face as she realized what was happening, watched her try to run, watched the feed cut out.

"Our facility was last. Dr. Brooks was screaming at her terminal, trying to engage manual overrides that wouldn't respond. Stephen Nelson was pulling people toward the exits. The quantum core was glowing, temperature spiking past every safety threshold.

"I looked back and saw Yuki. She was smiling. Not laughing, not gloating—just smiling, like she'd solved a particularly interesting puzzle. Then she turned and walked calmly toward the emergency stairs.

"I ran. We all ran. The explosion caught us in the stairwell. The blast wave threw me down three flights. When I woke up, I was buried in rubble, my left arm broken, my hazmat suit torn but functional. I could hear small fires crackling, structural elements groaning. No voices.

"I dug myself out. Took four hours. The facility was destroyed. I found Dr. Brooks near the control room—she hadn't made it far. Stephen Nelson was in the stairwell below me. I couldn't find the others, and I couldn't stay to look. The structure was collapsing.

"I made it to the surface access tunnel and sealed it behind me. I'm in an emergency shelter now, three miles from the facility. I've got power, water, medical supplies. I've been trying to reach someone, anyone, on the emergency channels. Nothing but static.

"I've been thinking about Yuki Wallace. About her pattern of failures. About how quantum mechanics describes probability, and how probability is just another word for chance, and how chance is just another word for luck.

"What if luck isn't random? What if it's a field effect, like gravity or electromagnetism? What if some people can manipulate probability the way we manipulate quantum states?

"It sounds insane. But consider: quantum mechanics tells us that reality is probabilistic at the fundamental level. Every particle exists in a superposition of states until observation collapses the wave function. What determines which state manifests? Probability. Pure chance.

"But what if it's not pure? What if consciousness can bias quantum outcomes, nudge probability in preferred directions? We've known about observer effects in quantum mechanics for two centuries. We've documented quantum consciousness theories, though most are dismissed as pseudoscience. But what if, on some world we haven't discovered yet, in some population we haven't encountered, this talent evolved? Developed? Became reliable?

"Yuki Wallace destroyed four quantum facilities and killed six people without touching anything, without hacking anything, without breaking any laws. She just walked through our facility and let probability do the work. Equipment failed. People made mistakes. Safety systems didn't trigger. All improbable, but not impossible. Just... unlucky.

"I can't prove it. I have no evidence that would stand up to scientific scrutiny. But I know what I saw, and I know the pattern. Check her background. Check the other facilities she's worked at. Look for the improbable chains of failure.

"And if you find her, if you track her down, remember this: a talent that manipulates probability can't be perfect. It's bound by the same quantum uncertainty it exploits. She can bias outcomes, but she can't control them absolutely. The proof is that I survived to tell this story.

"I'm going to try to reach Morningside on foot. It's forty miles through rough terrain, but I've got supplies and the suit's environmental systems are still functional. If I don't make it, if this recording is all that's left, then at least someone will know what happened.

"This is Dr. Hassan McCoy, signing off. God help us if there are more like her."

The recording clicked off. In the emergency shelter, Hassan McCoy checked his supplies one more time, adjusted his damaged hazmat suit, and prepared to begin the long walk to Morningside. Outside, the wind howled across the wasteland that had been Summit District's pride, carrying radioactive dust from the shattered quantum facility.

He didn't know that Yuki Wallace was already in Morningside, consulting on their new fusion project. He didn't know that the probability of his survival, given his injuries and the distance, was less than three percent. He didn't know that his emergency beacon, which he believed was malfunctioning, was actually working perfectly—but every rescue team that tried to respond encountered improbable equipment failures and navigational errors.

Hassan McCoy shouldered his pack and started walking. He was a scientist. He believed in evidence, in causation, in the rational universe. He believed that luck was just a word people used for patterns they didn't understand yet.

He believed he would make it to Morningside.

He was wrong.

But he was right about Yuki Wallace, and his recording would eventually reach people who could act on it. In the end, that would have to be enough.

Three miles into his journey, Hassan McCoy activated his suit recorder one final time:

"Additional note for the record. I've been thinking about political philosophy, about how we organize society around the assumption that everyone plays by the same rules of physics. What happens when someone doesn't? When someone can manipulate the fundamental probability structure of reality?

"Justice theory assumes equality before natural law. Economic development assumes predictable cause and effect. Communication skills mean nothing if someone can make your words come out wrong. Environmental justice is impossible if disasters can be caused by pure bad luck.

"We built our entire civilization on the assumption that chance is truly random. If it's not, if it can be controlled, then everything changes. Every system, every institution, every assumption about how the world works needs to be reconsidered.

"I don't have answers. I just have questions and a warning: Yuki Wallace is out there, and she's not alone. There must be others. And until we figure out how to detect them, how to defend against them, we're all vulnerable.

"The most dangerous weapon is the one you don't know exists.

"Dr. Hassan McCoy, final entry."

The wind picked up, carrying snow across the desolate landscape. Hassan McCoy continued walking, his footprints quickly filling with white powder. Behind him, the ruins of the quantum facility smoldered. Ahead, Morningside waited—forty miles away, impossible to reach, but he would try anyway.

Because he was a scientist, and scientists don't give up just because the odds are bad.

Even when the odds aren't random at all.
