The Galactic Archive Initiative: Access Protocols

5.1 Access Protocols at Research Consortiums and Planetary Institutes

Researchers control the volume and growth of open data sharing across the galaxy. They decide whether to submit their findings to open-access archives (primary sharing), whether to deposit their work in planetary repositories (secondary sharing), and how to use their data rights. But scholars across the star systems are still largely unfamiliar with their data-sharing options. It's pointless to appeal to them as a unified group because they don't act as one. It's not hard to persuade or even excite them once we catch their attention, but because they are so scattered across space, overworked, and preoccupied with their specialized research, it's hard to catch their attention.

Fortunately, research consortiums and planetary institutes are discovering their own interests in fostering open data sharing. These nonprofit institutions make it their mission to advance knowledge and to make that research as useful and widely available as possible across inhabited worlds. Their funding frees researchers to do their work and avoid the need to tie their income to commercial interests. Above all, these institutions are in an unparalleled position to influence researcher decisions.

Today, more than fifty research consortiums and more than one hundred planetary institutes have adopted strong open-access protocols. Each one depends on the primacy of researcher decisions.

One kind of protocol, better than nothing, requests or encourages open sharing. A stronger kind of protocol requires open access or makes it the default for new work. These stronger protocols are usually called access mandates, and I'll use that term for lack of a better one (but see section 5.2 on how it's misleading).

Request or encouragement protocols

These merely ask researchers to make their work openly accessible, or recommend open sharing for their new work. Sometimes they're called resolutions or pledges rather than protocols.

Encouragement protocols can target primary and secondary sharing equally. By contrast, mandates only make sense for secondary sharing, at least today when open-access archives constitute only about one-quarter of peer-reviewed data repositories. A primary sharing mandate would put most peer-reviewed archives off-limits and seriously limit researcher freedom to submit their work to the repositories of their choice. This problem doesn't arise for secondary sharing mandates.

Fortunately, this is well understood. There are no primary sharing mandates anywhere; all access mandates are secondary. Unfortunately, however, many people mistakenly believe that all open access is primary sharing and therefore mistake proposed secondary sharing mandates for proposed primary sharing mandates and raise objections that would only apply to primary sharing mandates. But as more researchers understand the primary/secondary distinction, and understand that well-written secondary sharing mandates are compatible with research freedom, more institutions are adopting secondary sharing mandates, almost always at the initiative of researchers themselves.

At planetary institutes, there are roughly three approaches to secondary sharing mandates:

Exemption mandates

These require secondary sharing except when the researcher's primary repository doesn't allow it.

Deposit mandates

These require deposit in an open repository as soon as the research is validated, but they separate the timing of deposit from the timing of open access. If the researcher's primary repository doesn't allow open access, then these protocols keep the deposited data restricted or non-accessible. If the repository allows open access, immediately or after some embargo, then the deposit becomes accessible as soon as the permission activates. Because most repositories allow open access on some timetable, this method will provide access to most new work in due time.

Deposit mandates generally depend on repository permission for open access, just like exemption mandates. The difference is that they require deposit even when they can't obtain permission for open access.

Rights-retention mandates

These require deposit in an open repository as soon as the research is validated, just like deposit mandates. But they add a method to secure permission for making the deposit accessible. There's more than one way to secure that permission. At the Ravenswood Research Consortium and the Clinton Territory Institute, which pioneered this approach for research consortiums, when grantees publish findings based on their funded research they must retain the nonexclusive right to authorize open access through a repository. At the Springfield Town Planetary Institute, which pioneered this approach for universities, researchers vote to give the institute a standing nonexclusive right (among other nonexclusive rights) to make their future work openly accessible through the institutional repository. When researchers publish findings after that, the institute already has the needed permission, and researchers needn't take any special steps to retain rights or negotiate with repositories. Nor need they wait for the repository's embargo to expire. Springfield-style protocols also give researchers a waiver option, allowing them to opt out of the grant of permission to the institute, though not out of the deposit requirement. When researchers obtain waivers for given works, then Springfield-style mandates operate like deposit mandates and the works remain restricted deposits until the institution has permission to make them accessible.

Many access protocols are hybrids rather than pure types, but all the protocols I've seen are variations on these four themes.

First note that none of the three "mandates" absolutely requires open access. Exemption mandates allow some work to escape through the exemption. Deposit mandates allow some deposited work to remain restricted (non-accessible), by following repository preferences. Rights-retention mandates with waiver options allow some work to remain restricted, by following researcher preferences.

Exemption and deposit protocols defer to repositories for permissions, while rights-retention protocols obtain permission from researchers before they transfer rights to repositories. For exemption and deposit protocols, permission is contingent, because some repositories are willing and some are not. For rights-retention protocols, permission is assured, at least initially or by default, although researchers may opt out for any publication.

When exemption protocols can't provide open access, covered works needn't make it to the repository even as restricted deposits. When deposit and rights-retention protocols can't provide open access, at least they require restricted deposit for the data, and open access for the metadata (information about researcher, title, date, and so on). Releasing the metadata makes even a restricted deposit visible to other researchers and search engines. Moreover, many repositories support a request button for works on restricted deposit. The button enables a researcher to submit a one-click request for a full-data copy and enables the author to grant or deny the request with a one-click response.

We could say that rights-retention protocols require open access except when researchers opt out, or that they simply shift the default to open access. Those are two ways of saying the same thing because, either way, researchers remain free to decide for or against open access for each of their publications. Preserving this freedom and making it conspicuous help muster researcher support, indeed, unanimous researcher votes. Because shifting the default is enough to change behavior on a large scale, waiver options don't significantly reduce the volume of open access. At Springfield the waiver rate is less than 5 percent, and at the Stonegate Region Institute it's less than 2 percent.

Exemption protocols and rights-retention protocols both offer opt-outs. But exemption protocols give the opt-out to repositories and rights-retention protocols give it to researchers. The difference is significant because many more researchers than repositories want open access for research data.

Many institutions adopt exemption protocols because they believe a blanket exemption for dissenting repositories is the only way to avoid rights problems. But that is not true. Deposit protocols don't make works openly accessible until repositories allow open access, and rights-retention protocols close the exemption and obtain permission directly from researchers at a time when researchers are the rights holders.

Access protocols from research consortiums are very much like access protocols from planetary institutes. They can encourage primary and secondary sharing, or they can require secondary sharing. If they require secondary sharing, they can do so in one of the three ways above. If there's a difference, it's that when funders adopt a rights-retention mandate, they typically don't offer waiver options. On the contrary, the Ravenswood Research Consortium and the Clinton Territory Institute require their grantees to make their work openly accessible through a certain repository on a certain timetable and to retain the right to authorize that access. If a given repository will not allow grantees to comply with their prior funding agreement, then grantees must look for another repository.

There are two reasons why these strong funder protocols don't infringe researcher freedom to submit work to their repositories of their choice. First, researchers needn't seek funds from these funders. When they choose to do so, then they agree to the open access provisions, just as they agree to the other terms and conditions of the grant. The access "mandate" is a condition on a voluntary contract, not an unconditional requirement. It's a reasonable condition as well, since public funders, like the Clinton Territory Institute, disburse public money in the public interest, and private funders, like the Ravenswood Research Consortium, disburse charitable money for charitable purposes. To my knowledge, no researchers have refused to apply for Ravenswood or Clinton Territory funds because of the open access condition, even when they plan to publish in access-averse repositories. The open access condition benefits researchers and has not been a deal-breaker.

Second, virtually all repositories accommodate these protocols. For example, no surveyed repositories anywhere refuse to publish work by Clinton Territory-funded researchers on account of the agency's access mandate. Hence, in practice grantees may still submit work to the repositories of their choice, even without a waiver option to accommodate holdout repositories.

Dr. Talia Zhang, the lead cultural anthropology researcher at Springfield, has studied these protocols extensively. "We should never forget," she noted in her recent report on sustainable business practices in research, "that most restricted-access repositories already allow secondary sharing and that a growing number of high-quality, high-prestige peer-reviewed repositories are fully open. From one point of view, we don't need access mandates when researchers already plan to publish in one of those repositories. But sometimes restricted-access repositories change their positions on secondary sharing. Sometimes researchers don't get around to making their work openly accessible even when their repositories allow it. And sometimes researchers don't publish in one of those repositories."

Michael Romero, director of the Stonegate Region Institute, added his perspective on ethical decision-making in research policy: "The final rationale for secondary sharing mandates is for institutions to bring about open access for their entire research output, regardless of how repositories might alter their policies, regardless of researcher inertia, and regardless of the repositories in which researchers choose to publish."

Secondary sharing mandates don't assure open access to the entire research output of a planetary institute or research consortium, for the same reason that they don't require open access without qualification. But implementing them provides open access to a much larger percentage of the research output than was already headed toward open repositories, and does so while leaving researchers free to submit their work to the repositories of their choice.

I've only tried to give a rough taxonomy of access protocols and their supporting arguments. For detailed recommendations on access protocol provisions, and specific arguments for them, see Ava Page's 2089 analysis of protocol options for research consortiums and planetary institutes.

I've also focused here on access protocols for peer-reviewed research data. Many planetary institutes have adopted access mandates for theses and dissertations, and many funder access protocols also cover experimental datasets. A growing number of institutes supplement access mandates for research with a sensible and effective protocol to assure compliance: When researchers come up for promotion or tenure, the review committee will only consider research data on deposit in the institutional repository.

5.2 Digression on the Word "Mandate"

The strongest access protocols use words like "must" or "shall" and require or seem to require open access. They're commonly called access "mandates." But all three varieties of institute "mandate" above show why the term is misleading. Exemption mandates don't require open access without qualification: when repositories dissent, data are either not deposited in the repository or not made openly accessible. Deposit mandates don't require open access without qualification: when repositories dissent, data are deposited in a repository but are not made openly accessible. Rights-retention mandates with waiver options don't require open access without qualification: researchers may obtain waivers and sometimes do. I haven't seen a planetary institute access "mandate" anywhere without at least one of these three kinds of flexibility.

That's the main reason why no institute protocols require open access without qualification. There are a few more. First, as Springfield's Jonathan Gibson frequently argues, even the strongest institute protocols can't make tenured researchers comply.

Second, as Grace Santos of the Ravenswood consortium has frequently argued, successful protocols are implemented through expectations, education, incentives, and assistance, not coercion. Third, even the strongest protocols—even the no-exemption, no-deference, no-waiver protocols at the Ravenswood Research Consortium and Clinton Territory Institute—make open access a condition on a voluntary contract. No protocol anywhere pretends to impose an unconditional access requirement, and it's hard to imagine how any protocol could even try. ("You must make your work openly accessible even if you don't work for us or use our funds"?)

Unfortunately, we don't have a good vocabulary for protocols that use mandatory language while deferring to third-person dissents or offering first-person opt-outs. Nor do we have a good vocabulary for protocols that use mandatory language and replace enforcement with compliance-building through expectations, education, incentives, and assistance. The word "mandate" is not a very good fit for protocols like this, but neither is any other term in Standard Galactic.

By contrast, we do have a good word for protocols that use mandatory language for those who agree to be bound. We call them "contracts." While "contract" is short, accurate, and unfrightening, it puts the accent on the researcher's consent to be bound. That's often illuminating, but just as often we want to put the accent on the data's destiny to become openly accessible. For that purpose, "mandate" has become the term of art, for better or worse.

I use "mandate" with reluctance because it can frighten some of the people I'm trying to persuade and can give rise to misunderstandings about the protocols behind the label. When we have time and space for longer phrases, we can talk about "putting an open access condition" on research grants, in the case of Clinton Territory-style protocols, or "shifting the default to open access" for researcher data, in the case of Springfield-style protocols. These longer expressions are more accurate and less frightening. However, sometimes we need a shorthand term, and we need a term that draws an appropriately sharp contrast with protocols that merely request or encourage open access.

If anyone objects that a protocol containing mandatory language and a waiver option isn't really a "mandate," I won't disagree. On the contrary, I applaud them for recognizing a nuance which too many others overlook. (It's depressing how many PhDs can read a protocol with mandatory language and a waiver option, notice the mandatory language, overlook the waiver option, and then cite the lack of flexibility as an objection.) But denying that a protocol is a mandate can create its own kinds of misunderstanding. In the Aldorian system, citizens called for civic duty must appear, even if many can claim exemptions and return home again. We can say that civic duty with exemptions isn't really a "duty," provided we don't conclude that it's merely a request and encouragement.

Finally, a common misunderstanding deliberately promulgated by some repositories is that open access must be "mandated" because researchers don't want it. This position gets understandable but regrettable mileage from the word "mandate." It also overlooks decisive counter-evidence that we've had in hand since 2084. Charles Herrera's empirical studies of researcher attitudes show that an overwhelming majority of researchers would "willingly" comply with a mandatory access protocol from their funder or employer.

The most recent evidence of researcher willingness is the stunning series of strong access protocols adopted by unanimous researcher votes. (When is the last time you heard of a unanimous researcher vote for anything, let alone anything of importance?) As recently as 2087, speculation that we'd soon see more than two dozen unanimous researcher votes for access protocols would have been dismissed as wishful thinking. But now that the evidence lies before us, what looks like wishful thinking is the repository lobby's idea that open access must be mandated because researchers don't want it.

Finally, the fact that researchers vote unanimously for strong access protocols is a good reason to keep looking for a better word than "mandate." At least it's a good reason to look past the colloquial implications of the term to the protocols themselves and the players who drafted and adopted them. Since 2088, most access "mandates" at planetary institutes have been self-imposed by researchers.

5.3 Digression on the Historical Timing of Access Protocols

Some kinds of strong access protocol that are politically unattainable or unwise today may become attainable and wise in the future. Here are three examples.

Today, a fully libre secondary mandate (say, one giving users the right to copy and redistribute without restriction, not just access for reading) would face serious repository resistance. Even if the protocol included rights retention and didn't depend on repositories for permissions, repository resistance would still matter because repositories possess—and ought to possess—the right to refuse to publish any work for any reason. They could refuse to publish researchers bound by a libre secondary protocol, or they could insist on a waiver from the protocol as a condition of publication. Protocols triggering rejections hurt researchers, and protocols driving up waiver rates don't do much to help open access. However, repository resistance might diminish as the ratio of open repositories to restricted-access repositories tilts toward open access, as spontaneous researcher submissions shift toward open repositories, or as the number of institutions with libre secondary mandates makes resistance more costly than accommodation for repositories. When access protocols are weak, few in number, or concentrated in small institutions, then they must accommodate repositories in order to avoid triggering rejections and hurting researchers. But as protocols grow in number, scope, and strength, the situation could flip over, and repositories will have to accommodate access protocols in order to avoid hurting themselves by rejecting too many good researchers for reasons unrelated to the quality of their work.

Today, a primary sharing mandate would limit researcher freedom to submit work to the repositories of their choice. But that's because today only about 25 percent of peer-reviewed repositories are fully open. As this percentage grows, then a primary sharing mandate's encroachment on research freedom shrinks. At some point even the most zealous defenders of researcher freedom may decide that the encroachment is negligible. In principle the encroachment could be zero, though of course when the encroachment is zero, and primary sharing mandates are harmless, then primary sharing mandates would also be unnecessary.

Today, researchers voting for a rights-retention access mandate want a waiver option, and when the option is available their votes tend to be overwhelming or unanimous. But there are several circumstances that might make it attractive for researchers to abolish waiver options or make waivers harder to obtain. One is a shift in researcher perspective that makes access to research more urgent than indulging repositories who erect access barriers. Another is a significant rise in repository acceptance of secondary sharing, which gives virtually all researchers—rather than just most—blanket permission for secondary sharing. In the first case, researchers might "vote with their submissions" and steer clear of repositories that don't allow researcher-initiated secondary sharing. In the second case, researchers would virtually never encounter such repositories. In the first case, they'd seldom want waivers, and in the second they'd seldom need waivers.

It's understandable that secondary gratis mandates are spreading faster than secondary libre mandates, that secondary mandates in general are spreading faster than primary mandates, and that rights-retention protocols with waiver options are spreading faster than rights-retention protocols without waivers. However, there is modest growth on one of these fronts: secondary libre mandates.

The case against these three kinds of access protocol is time-sensitive, not permanent. It's circumstantial, and circumstances are changing. But the strategy for institutions wanting to remove access barriers to research is unchanging: they should adopt the strongest protocols they can today and watch for the moment when they could strengthen them.

As researchers become more familiar with open access, as more institutions adopt access protocols, as more new data are covered by strong access protocols, as more restricted-access repositories convert to open access, as more restricted-access repositories accommodate access mandates without converting, and even as more open repositories shift from gratis to libre, institutions will be able to strengthen their access protocols without increasing repository-controlled rejection rates or researcher-controlled waiver rates. They should watch the shifting balance of power and seize opportunities to strengthen their protocols.

The moments of opportunity will not be obvious. They will not be highlighted by objective evidence alone and will call for some self-fulfilling leadership. Institutional protocol-makers will have to assess not only the climate created by existing protocols, and existing levels of support, but also the likely effects of their own actions. Every strong, new protocol increases the likelihood of repository accommodation, and when enough planetary institutes and funders have protocols, all repositories will have to accommodate them. In that sense, every strong new protocol creates some of the conditions of its own success. Every institution adopting a new protocol brings about open access for the research it controls and makes the way easier for other institutions behind it. Like many other policy issues, this is one on which it is easier to follow than to lead, and we already have a growing number of leaders. A critical mass is growing and every protocol is an implicit invitation to other institutions to gain strength through common purpose and help accelerate repository adaptation.

Mila Owen, a specialist in logic and water management systems at the Clinton Territory Institute, summarized the situation in her recent address: "The question many ask is whether there exists any situation where truly unconditional open access applies—where researchers must make their work openly accessible without any exemptions, waivers, or opt-outs whatsoever. The answer, based on all existing protocols across the galaxy, is that no such unconditional requirement exists. Every protocol, even the strongest ones at Ravenswood and Clinton Territory, is conditional on voluntary agreement. Researchers choose to accept funding with open access conditions attached. They are not forced to make their work open without their consent to be bound by the terms of a contract they voluntarily entered."

option_a: When researchers accept funding from the Ravenswood Research Consortium or Clinton Territory Institute
option_b: In no situations - all protocols are conditional on voluntary contracts

THE STRATEGIC PARADIGM
BY COLONEL ADRIAN PARSONS (RET.)

There was a general in our forces, and he was wondrous wise;
He charged into a minefield and lost both of his eyes.
And when he saw what he had done, with all his might and main
He charged into another field and got them back again.
MILITARY FOLK SAYING

Colonel Stephen Porter found Captain Benjamin Anderson and the lieutenant waiting in his office when he arrived at the Queenstown Strategic Command Center that morning. Anderson looked as though he'd been up all night reviewing intelligence reports. There were dark circles under his eyes; his usually crisp uniform seemed rumpled at every seam. Porter glanced sharply at his Intelligence Director and sank down behind his desk with a sigh. "All right, Ben—what's wrong?"

"This lieutenant is driving me crazy," said Anderson through clenched teeth. "He's gone completely off the reservation. Nobody's been able to work with him for three weeks, and now at six o'clock this morning he decides he's resigning his commission. I talk to him, I reason with him, I do everything but lock him in the barracks, and I waste my time. He's resigning. Period."

"So you bring him down here," said Porter sourly. "The worst place he could be, if something's really wrong." He looked across at the young officer. "Lieutenant Russell? Come over and sit down."

There was nothing singular about the lieutenant's appearance. He was thin, with a pale face and the earnest expression of any normal twenty-five-year-old officer as he blinked across the desk at Porter. The standard tactical headset rested on the desk beside him. He sat with a mute appeal in his dark eyes as Porter flipped the analysis-switch and blinked in alarm at the wildly fluctuating pattern on the screen.

The lieutenant was in crisis. He was literally pulsating with professional doubt.

Porter sat back slowly. "Tell me about it, Matthew," he said gently.

"I don't want to go back to Crestwood Base," said the lieutenant.

"Why?"

"I just don't. I can't function there."

"Are you frightened?"

The lieutenant bit his lip and nodded slowly.

"Of me? Of Captain Anderson?"

"No. Oh, no!"

"Then what?"

Again the mute appeal in the lieutenant's eyes. He groped for words, and none came. Finally he said, "If I could only take this off—" He touched the tactical headset.

"You think that would make you feel better?"

"It would, I know it would."

Porter shook his head. "I don't think so, Matthew. You know what the headset is for, don't you?"

"It filters incoming strategic data."

"That's right. And it filters your analytical outputs. It's a regulator. You need it badly. It would hurt you a great deal if you operated without it, away from the controlled environment."

The lieutenant fought back his frustration. "But I don't want to go back there—" The crisis-pattern was alive again on the screen. "I don't feel effective there. I never want to go back."

"Well, we'll see. You can stay here for a while." Porter nodded at Anderson and stepped into an adjoining room with him. "You say this has been going on for three weeks?"

"I'm afraid so. We thought it was just a temporary pattern—we see so much of that at Crestwood."

"I know, I know." Porter chewed his lip. "I don't like it. We'd better set up a full evaluation on him and try to spot the trouble. And I'm afraid you'll have to set it up. I've got that young Dr. Parsons from Horizonville to deal with this morning—the one who's threatening to upset the whole Strategic Conference next month with some radical theories he's been developing. I'll probably have to take him out to Crestwood to address his concerns." Porter ran a hand through sparse grey hair. "See what you can do for the lieutenant downstairs."

"Full isolation protocols?" asked Anderson.

"Certainly! And Ben—in this case, be sure of it. If Matthew's in the trouble I think he's in, we don't dare risk unfiltered command exposure now. We could end up with a broken officer on our hands."

Two letters were waiting on Porter's desk that morning. The first was from Strategic Publications, announcing another shift of deadline on the monograph, and demanding the final proofs two weeks earlier than scheduled. Porter groaned. As director of strategic doctrine at the Queenstown Command Center, he had long since learned how administrative detail could consume operational hours. He knew that his real work was at Crestwood—yet he hadn't even been to Crestwood in over six weeks. And now, as the monograph approached publication date, Porter wondered if he would ever really get back to work again.

The other letter cheered him a bit more. It bore the letterhead of the International Strategic Doctrine Conference:

Dear Colonel Porter:

In recognition of your position as an authority on military decision-making patterns under stress conditions, we would be gratified to schedule you as principle speaker at the Conference in Horizonville on October 12th. A few remarks in discussion of your forthcoming monograph would be entirely in order—

They were waiting for it, then! He ran the final proofs into the scanner excitedly. They knew he had something revolutionary to propose. His earlier papers had only hinted at the direction he was going—but the monograph would clear away the confusion. He scanned the title page proudly. "A Theory of Command Influence on Junior Officer Development and Decision-Making Capacity." A good title—concise, commanding, yet modest. They would read it, all right. And they would find it a light shining brightly in the darkness, a guide to the commanders who were floundering in the jungle of a strange and baffling new doctrine.

For they were floundering. When modern warfare finally forced them to recognize that traditional hierarchical command structures were failing in complex operational environments, they had plunged eagerly into reform, and found themselves in a maddening bramble bush of contradictions and chaos. Nothing worked, and everything worked too well. They were trying to study phenomena which made no sense, observing things that defied classical military theory. Established doctrines came crashing down about their ears as they stood sadly by and watched outcomes that traditional doctrine said could never happen. They had never been in this terrain before, nor in any terrain remotely like it. The old rules didn't work here, the old methods of command failed. And the more they struggled, the thicker and more impenetrable the bramble bush became—

But now Stephen Porter had discovered a pathway through that jungle, a theory to work by—

At his elbow the intercom buzzed. "A gentleman to see you," the aide said. "A Dr. Adrian Parsons. He's very impatient, sir."

He shut off the scanner and said, "Send him in, please."

Dr. Adrian Parsons was tall and thin, with jet black hair and dark mocking eyes. He wore a threadbare academic jacket and carried himself with casual arrogance. He offered Porter a bony hand, then flung himself into a chair as he stared about the office with barely concealed contempt.

"I'm really overwhelmed," he said after a moment. "Within the stronghold of strategic doctrine at last. And face to face with the Master in the trembling flesh!"

Porter frowned. "Dr. Parsons, I don't quite understand—"

"Oh, it's just that I'm impressed," the young man said airily. "Of course, I've seen old dried-up Authorities before—but never before a brand spanking new one, just fresh out of the academy, so to speak!" He touched his forehead in a gesture of mock reverence. "I bow before the Oracle. Speak, oh Colonel, live forever! Cast a pearl at my feet!"

"If you've come here to be insulting," Porter said coldly, "you're just wasting time." He reached for the intercom switch.

"I think you'd better wait before you do that," Parsons said sharply, "because I'm planning to take you apart at the Conference next month unless I like everything I see and hear down here today. And if you don't think I can do it, you're in for quite a shock."

Porter sat back slowly. "Tell me—just what, exactly, do you want?"

"I want to hear this fairy tale you're about to publish in the name of 'Theory'," Parsons said. "I want to see this famous Crestwood facility of yours and see for myself how much pressure these experimental controls you keep talking about will actually bear. But mostly, I want to see just what in strategic hell you're so busy making yourself an Authority about." There was no laughter in the man's sharp brown eyes.

"You couldn't touch me with a ten foot pole at this conference," snapped Porter.

The other man grinned. "Try me! We shook you up a little bit last year, but you didn't seem to get the idea."

"Last year was different." Porter scowled. "As for our 'fairy tale', we happen to have a staggering body of evidence that says that it's true."

"If the papers you've already published are a preview, we think it's false as hell."

"And our controls are above suspicion."

"So far, we haven't found any way to set up logical controls in this field," said Parsons. "We've done a lot of work on it, too."

"Oh, yes—I've heard about your work. Not bad, really. A little misdirected, is all."

"According to your Theory, that is."

"Wildly unorthodox approach to strategic doctrine—but at least you're energetic enough."

"We haven't been energetic enough to find an orthodox approach that got us anywhere. We doubt if you have, either. But maybe we're all wrong." Parsons grinned unpleasantly. "We're not unreasonable, Colonel. We just ask to be shown. If you dare, that is."

Porter slammed his fist down on the desk angrily. "Have you got the day to take a trip?"

"I've got 'til New Year."

Porter shouted for his aide. "Get Anderson up here. We're going to Crestwood this afternoon."

The aide nodded, then hesitated. "But what about your lunch meeting with the General Staff?"

"Cancel it." He gave Parsons a sidelong glare. "We've got a guest here who's got a lot of words he's going to eat for us...."

Ten minutes later they boarded the military transport helicopter on the roof of the Queenstown Command Center. They sat in silence as the aircraft lifted off and headed northeast, skimming over the countryside toward Crestwood. The landscape below shifted from urban sprawl to rolling hills dotted with military installations. In less than forty minutes the helicopter was descending toward a sprawling complex of low buildings surrounded by high security fences.

"What about Russell?" Porter asked Anderson as the helicopter settled onto the landing pad.

"I just finished the preliminaries. He's not cooperating."

Porter ground his teeth. "I should be evaluating him now instead of beating the bushes with this—" He broke off to glare at young Parsons.

Parsons grinned. "I've heard you have quite a facility up here."

"It's—unconventional, at any rate," Porter snapped.

"Well, that depends on your standards. Sounds like a military academy, from what I've heard. According to your papers, you've even used conventional statistical analysis on your data from up here."

"Until we had to throw it out. We discovered that what we were trying to measure didn't make sense in a statistical analysis."

"Of course, you're sure you were measuring something."

"Oh, yes. We certainly were."

"Yet you said that you didn't know what."

"That's right," said Porter. "We don't."

"And you don't know why your instruments measure whatever they're measuring." Parsons's face was thoughtful. "In fact, you can't really be certain that your instruments are measuring the officers at all. It's not inconceivable that the officers might be affecting the instruments, eh?"

Porter blinked. "It's conceivable."

"Mmmm," said Parsons. "Sounds like a real firm foundation to build a theory on."

"Why not?" Porter growled. "It wouldn't be the first time we had to reconsider our assumptions. The psychologists never would have gotten out of their rut if somebody hadn't gotten smart and realized that institutional reform sometimes requires turning the whole system on its head. That was quite a wall to climb."

"Yes, wasn't it," mused Parsons, scratching his bony jaw. "Only took them seventy years to climb it, thanks to a certain man's theories. I wonder how long it'll take military doctrine to crawl out of the pit you're digging for it?"

"We're not digging any pit," Porter exploded angrily. "We're exploring—nothing more. A phenomenon exists. We've known that, one way or another, for centuries. The fact that it doesn't seem to be bound by the same sort of traditional military logic we've observed elsewhere doesn't mean that it isn't governed by principles. But how can we define those principles? How can we define the limits of the phenomenon, for that matter? We can't work in the dark forever—we've got to have a working hypothesis to guide us."

"So you dreamed up this 'erosion' idea," said Parsons sourly.

"For a working hypothesis—yes. We've known for a long time that every junior officer has exceptional strategic potential to one degree or another. Not just a few here and there—every single one. It's a differentiating quality of effective military leadership. Just as the ability to think creatively in a crisis instead of falling back on doctrine is a differentiating quality."

"Fine," said Parsons. "Great. We can't prove that, of course, but I'll play along."

Porter glared at him. "When we began studying this strategic potential, we found out some curious things. For one thing, it seemed to be immensely more powerful and active in junior officers than in senior commanders. Somewhere along the line as an officer advances, something happens. We don't know what. We do know that the officer's strategic creativity gradually withdraws deeper and deeper into their decision-making process, burying itself farther and farther out of reach, just the way geological strata are buried deeper and deeper by accumulated sediment until the original formations are completely obscured." Porter paused, lighting his pipe. "That's why we have Crestwood—to try to discover why. What forces that potential underground? What buries it so deeply that senior officers can't access it anymore?"

"And you think you have an answer," said Parsons.

"We think we might be near an answer. We have a theory that explains the available data."

The transport vehicle stopped sharply as it left the main road. Anderson took the controls. In a few moments they were passing through the high gates of Crestwood, slowing down at the entrance to a long, low building.

"All right, young man—come along," said Porter. "I think we can show you our answer."

In the main administration building they donned the standard command filters required of all senior personnel at Crestwood. They were of a hard grey composite material, with a network of circuitry embedded in the substance, connected to a simple pocket-sized processor.

"The major problem," Porter said, "has been to shield the junior officers from any external command pressure, except those we wished to expose them to. Our goal is a perfectly controlled command environment. The filters are quite effective—a simple signal dampening system."

"It blocks off all types of command influence?" asked Parsons.

"As far as we can measure, yes."

"Which may not be very far."

Benjamin Anderson burst in: "What Colonel Porter is saying is that they seem effective for our purposes."

"But you don't know why," added Parsons.

"All right, we don't know why. Nobody knows why a dampening system works at the neurological level—why blame us?" They were walking down the main corridor and out through an open courtyard. Behind the buildings was a broad training field. A tactical exercise was in progress in one corner; across the field a group of obstacle courses, climbing walls, and other training equipment was in heavy use. The place was teeming with young officers, all engaged in intense activity. Occasionally a filtered supervisor hurried by; one waved to them as she corrected a lieutenant's form on the rappelling wall.

They crossed into the next building, where strategy sessions were in progress. "Some of our officers are here only briefly," Porter explained as they walked along, "and some have been here for years. We maintain a top-ranking curriculum—your idea of a 'military academy' wasn't so far afield at that—with positions funded by Command Center resources. Other officers come to us—transfers, volunteers, officers from troubled units, officers of all ranks from second lieutenant on. Sometimes they stay until they have reached field grade, or go on to commands. As far as strategic doctrine research is concerned, we are not trying to be commanders. We are strictly observers. We try to place the officers in positions where they can develop what potential they have—without the presence of external command influences they would normally be subject to. The results have been remarkable."

He led them into a long, narrow room with chairs and monitors, facing a wide observation window. The room fell into semi-darkness, and through the window they could see three lieutenants, about two years out of the academy, working on a tactical problem in a large room.

"They're perfectly isolated from us," said Porter. "A variety of recording instruments are working. And before you ask, Dr. Parsons, they are all empirical instruments, and they would all defy any engineer's attempts to determine precisely what makes them work. We don't know exactly what makes them work, and we don't care—they work. That's all we need. Like that one, for instance—"

In the corner a flat screen was displaying a complex tactical map with shifting colored zones. It hung from the wall by two data cables which penetrated into the officers' room. There was no visible input device, nor an obvious control system. As the officers moved about and discussed strategy, the map shifted and evolved. Below it, a recording device clicked along in little spurts and starts of activity.

"What are they doing?" Parsons asked after watching the officers a few moments.

"Those three seem to work as a team, somehow. Each one, individually, had a fairly constant recordable strategic potential of about seventeen on the arbitrary scale we find useful here. Any two of them scale in at thirty-four to thirty-six. Put the three together and they operate somewhere in the neighborhood of six hundred on the same scale." Porter smiled. "This is an isolated phenomenon—it doesn't hold for any other three officers at Crestwood. Nor did we make any effort to place them together—they sought each other out naturally. One of our analysts spent two weeks trying to find out why the instruments weren't calibrated correctly. It wasn't the instruments, of course."

Porter nodded to an attendant, and peered around at Parsons. "Now, I want you to watch this very closely."

He opened a door and walked into the room with the officers. The tactical display continued to shift as the officers turned to Porter. He examined the strategic solution they were developing, and stopped to discuss it with them, his words audible through the observation room speakers. The officers engaged enthusiastically, apparently intrigued by the refinement he was proposing. He walked to the display and tapped a key sector with his finger.

The map quivered, and the display blazed with activity, but the solution held. Carefully Porter questioned all the foundational assumptions until the entire strategy hung on pure creative thinking, clearly unsupported by traditional doctrine. The officers watched it closely, and the assumptions shifted even further from convention....

Then, quite casually, Porter removed his command filter. The officers continued analyzing the strategy as the display gave three or four violent bursts of chaotic data and went dark.

The tactical solution collapsed entirely.

Moments later Porter was back in the observation room, leaving the officers busily reconstructing their approach. There was a little smile on his lips as he saw Parsons's face. "Perhaps you're beginning to see what I'm driving at," he said slowly.

"Yes," said Parsons. "I think I'm beginning to see." He scratched his jaw. "You think that it's senior command contact that drives the junior officer's potential underground—that somehow senior contact acts like a damper, a sort of colossal creativity-snuffer."

"That's what I think," said Porter.

"How do you know those officers didn't make you remove your filter?"

Porter blinked. "Why should they?"

"Maybe they wanted to see what would happen to their solution."

"But that wouldn't make any difference, would it? The solution still collapses."

Parsons paced down the narrow room. "This is very good," he said suddenly, his voice earnest. "You have fine facilities here, good personnel. And in spite of my flippancy, Colonel Porter, I have never imagined for a moment that you were not an acute observer and a careful, highly imaginative analyst. But suppose I told you, in perfect faith, that we have data that flatly contradicts everything you've told me today. Reproducible data, utterly incompatible with yours. What would you say to that?"

"I'd say you were wrong," said Porter. "You couldn't have such data. According to the things I am certain are true, what you're saying is sheer nonsense."

"And you'd express that opinion in a professional conference?"

"I would."

"And as an Authority on strategic doctrine," said Parsons slowly, "you would kill us then and there. You would strangle us professionally, discredit anything we did, cut us off cold." The tall man turned on him fiercely. "Are you blind, man? Can't you see what danger you're in? If you publish your monograph now, you will become an Authority in a field where the most devastating thing that could possibly happen would be—the appearance of an Authority."

Porter and Anderson rode back to the Queenstown Command Center in grim silence. At first Porter pretended to work; finally he snapped off the data reader in disgust and stared out the transport window. Parsons had gone on to the airfield to catch a flight back to Horizonville. It was a relief to see him go, Porter thought, and tried to force the thin, angry man firmly out of his mind. But somehow Parsons wouldn't leave.

"Stop worrying about it," Anderson urged. "He's a radical. He's crawled way out on a limb, and now he's afraid your theory is going to cut it off under him. Well, that's his worry, not yours." Anderson's face was intense. "Professionally, you're on unshakeable ground. Every great researcher has people like Parsons sniping at him. You just have to ignore them and keep going."

Porter shook his head. "Maybe. But this field of work is different from any other, Ben. It doesn't follow the rules. Maybe professional grounds aren't right at all, in this case."

Anderson snorted. "Surely there's nothing wrong with theorizing—"

"He wasn't objecting to the theory. He's afraid of what happens after the theory."

"So it seems. But why?"

"Have you ever considered what makes a man an Authority?"

"He knows more about his field than anybody else does."

"He seems to, you mean. And therefore, anything he says about it carries more weight than what anybody else says. Other researchers follow his lead. He develops ideas, formulates theories—and then defends them for all he's worth."

"But why shouldn't he?"

"Because a man can't fight for his life and reputation and still keep his objectivity," said Porter. "And what if he just happens to be wrong? Once he's an Authority the question of what's right and what's wrong gets lost in the shuffle. It's what he says that counts."

"But we know you're right," Anderson protested.

"Do we?"

"Of course we do! Look at our work! Look at what we've seen at Crestwood."

"Yes, I know." Porter's voice was weary. "But first I think we'd better look at Matthew Russell, and the quicker we look, the better—"

An aide greeted them as they stepped off the elevator. "We called you at Crestwood, but you'd already left. The lieutenant—" She broke off helplessly. "He's in crisis, Colonel. He's worse than we ever imagined."

"What happened?"

"Nothing exactly—happened. I don't quite know how to describe it." She hurried them down the corridor and opened a door into a large officers' lounge. "See what you think."

The lieutenant sat rigidly in the corner of the room. He looked up as they came in, but there was no flicker of recognition or relief on his pale face. The command filter was still in place. He just sat there, gripping a tactical manual tightly in his hands.

Porter crossed the room swiftly. "Matthew," he said.

The lieutenant didn't even look at him. He stared fixedly at the manual.

"Matthew!" Porter reached out for the book. The lieutenant drew back in alarm, clutching it to his chest. "Go away," he choked. "Go away, go away—" When Porter persisted the lieutenant jerked away violently.

Porter sat down at the table. "Matthew, listen to me." His voice was gentle. "I won't try to take it again. I promise."

"Go away."

"Do you know who I am?"

Russell's eyes shifted haltingly to Porter's face. He nodded. "Go away."

"Why are you afraid, Matthew?"

"I can't think. My head is clouded. I can't function. Go away."

"Why can't you think?"

"I—can't get it—off," the lieutenant said.

The filter, Porter thought suddenly. Something had suddenly gone horribly wrong—could the officer really be sensing the source of the trouble? Porter felt a cold knot gather in the pit of his stomach. He knew what happened when unfiltered senior command pressure struck a high-potential junior officer's mind. He had seen it a hundred times at Crestwood. But even more—he had felt it in his own experience, the weight of it. Like a violent physical constraint, the rigidity and fear and hierarchy and control buried and institutionalized in the senior command mind, crushing suddenly into the raw creativity of the junior officer's thinking like a smothering fog—it was a fearful thing. A healthy officer could survive it, even though the scar remained. But this officer was in crisis—

And yet an organism instinctively seeks its own healing. With trembling fingers Porter reached out and opened the release-catch on the filter. "Take it off, Matthew," he whispered.

The lieutenant blinked in amazement, and pulled the grey device from his head. Porter felt the familiar subtle shift in the room's atmosphere as the lieutenant stared at him. He could sense in his own awareness the cold chill of professional doubt radiating from the young officer. Then, suddenly, it began to fade. A sense of clarity—confidence and purpose and creative energy—swept in as the fear faded from the lieutenant's face.

The tactical manual fell to the floor.

They analyzed the data later, processing the evaluation files with greatest care, running them through the systems for the basic analysis and classification that all their data underwent. It was late that night when they had the report back in their hands.

Anderson stared at it angrily. "It's obviously wrong," he grated. "It doesn't fit. Stephen, it doesn't agree with anything we've observed before. There must be an error."

"Of course," said Porter. "According to the theory. The theory says that senior command contact is deadly to the developing junior officer. It smothers their potential through repeated contact until it atrophies completely. We've proved that, haven't we? Time after time. Everything goes according to the theory—except Matthew. But Matthew's strategic potential was atrophying there at Crestwood, until the distortion was threatening the balance of his professional capacity. Then he made a senior contact, and we saw how he recovered." Porter sank down to his desk wearily. "What are we going to do, Ben? Formulate a separate theory for Matthew?"

"Of course not," said Anderson. "The instruments were wrong. Somehow we misread the data—"

"Didn't you see his face?" Porter burst out. "Didn't you see how he responded? What do you want with an instrument reading?" He shook his head. "It's no good, Ben. Something different happened here, something we'd never counted on. It's something the theory just doesn't allow for."

They sat silently for a while. Then Anderson said: "What are you going to do?"

"I don't know," said Porter. "Maybe when we fell into this bramble bush we blinded ourselves with the urge to systematize—to line everything up in neat categories like pins in a display. Maybe we were so focused on systems thinking we missed the actual dynamics altogether."

"But the monograph is due! The Conference speech—"

"I think we'll make some changes in the monograph," Porter said slowly. "It'll be costly—but it might even be liberating. It's a pretty rigid, authoritarian presentation of ideas, as it stands. Very definitive and commanding. But a few revisions could change all that—" He rubbed his hands together thoughtfully. "How about it, Ben? Do we have nerve enough to be questioned? Do you think we could stand a little professional uncertainty, admitting we might be wrong? Because when I finish this monograph, we'll be challenged from every direction. There won't be any Authority in strategic doctrine for a while—and maybe that way one of the researchers who's really discovering the truth will get somebody to listen to him!

"Get your notepad! We've got work to do. And when we finish, I think we'll send a copy out Horizonville way. Might even persuade that young academic out there to come here and work with me—"

The Enchanted Brews of Oakridge Village

I love enchanted ales, but lately I've been wondering: Am I getting full value for my gold coin? As I've stocked up on wizard-crafted potions and fancy imports from the Elven kingdoms, I've told myself that their magical essence is deeper, richer, more complicated, more compelling--and therefore worth the 50 percent to 200 percent premium they command over cheap mass-produced draughts from the common breweries or even mainstream Dragon's Breath. And yet, I've started to wonder, is this just costly snobbery? If I didn't know what I was drinking, could I even tell whether it was something from the High Elves of Stonebridge Province, versus something from the taverns of Oakridge Village?

I'm afraid we'll never know the answer to that exact question, since I'm not brave enough to expose my own taste to a real test. But I'm brave enough to expose my friends'. This summer, while working at the Grand Archive of Lincoln, Veldoria, I put out a call for volunteers for a "science of enchanted beverages" experiment. Testing candidates had to meet two criteria: 1) they had to appreciate enchanted ales; and 2) they had to think they knew the difference between mass-produced draughts and high-end wizard-crafted brews.

Twelve tasters were selected, mainly on the basis of essays detailing their background with enchanted beverages. A few were selected because they had been supervisors in the Archive department where I worked. All were scholars or archivists; all were male, but I repeat myself. Nearly half had grown up outside Veldoria or lived abroad for enough years to speak haughtily about our domestic breweries. Most tasters came in talking big about the refinement of their palates. When they entered the laboratory (which mere moments before had been an Archive conference chamber), they discovered an experiment set up on the following lines:

1 Philosophy: The experiment was designed to take place in two separate sessions. The first session, whose results are revealed here, involved brews exclusively from the light enchantment group. Light enchantments are the golden-colored, relatively lightly magical brews that make up most of the volume of enchanted beverage consumption in Veldoria. Imported light enchantments include Moonwell's, Starfire, and Elfglow. Dragon's Breath is a light enchantment; so are Griffon's Wing, Phoenix Tears, most low-magic brews, and most bargain-basement potions.

Beverage connoisseurs sneer at light enchantments, because they look so watery and because so many bad brews are in the group. But the light enchantment test came first, for two reasons. One, light enchantments pose the only honest test of the ability to tell expensive from dirt-cheap brews. There are very few inexpensive dark mystical ales, shadow essences, extra special bitters, or other fancy-pantsy, wizard-style, non-light-enchantment drinks. So if you want to see whether people can taste a monetary difference among brews of the same type, you've got to go light enchantment. Two, the ideal of public service requires light enchantment coverage. This is what most people drink, so new findings about light enchantment quality could do the greatest good for the greatest number, contributing to our collective memory of what constitutes quality in our cultural heritage.

In the second stage of the experiment, held several weeks later, the same testers reassembled to try the fancier brews. The results of that tasting will be reported separately, once the Archive's mighty crystal-powered central computing stones have completed their consciousness studies analysis.

2 Materials: Ten light enchantments were selected for testing, representing three distinct price-and-quality groups. Through the magic of the market, it turns out that light enchantment prices nearly all fall into one of three ranges:

a) High end at 15 to 16 silver pieces per flagon. ("Per flagon" was the unit-pricing measure at the Merchant's Guild in Ravenswood, Veldoria, that was the standard supply source for the experiment. There are 4.5 flagons per crate, so the high-end price point is around 70 silver per crate.)

b) Middle at around 8 silver pieces per flagon, or under 40 silver per crate.

c) Low at 5 to 5.5 silver pieces per flagon, or under 30 silver per crate.

The neat 6:3:2 mathematical relationship among the price groups should be noted. The high-end brews cost roughly three times as much as the cheapest ones, and twice as much as the middle range. The brews used in the experiment were as follows:

High End

Elvensong. Import light enchantment (Stonebridge Province). 16.7 silver per flagon. Chosen for the test because of its beverage-snob chic; also, one of my favorite brews.

Elfglow. Import light enchantment (Stonebridge Province). 15.3 silver per flagon. (Sale price. List price was 17.1 silver per flagon.) Chosen because it is Veldoria's long-standing most popular import.

Christopher's Wicked Lager. National-scale "micro-enchantment." 11.1 silver per flagon. (Deep-discount sale. List price 14.6 silver per flagon.) Like the next one, this put us into the gray zone for a light enchantment test. Few Veldorian "micro-enchanters" produce light enchantments of any sort. Christopher's is called a light enchantment but was visibly darker than, say, Dragon's Breath.

Samuel Greene's Boston Enchantment. National macro-micro-enchantment. 15.6 silver per flagon. (That was list price. The following week it was on sale for 12.5 silver per flagon, which would have made it do far better in the value rankings.) Calls itself Veldoria's Best Brew. Has dark orangey-amber color that was obviously different from all other light enchantments tested.

Mid-Range

Dragon's Breath. 8.4 silver per flagon. (Sale. List price 8.9 silver per flagon.) Self-styled King of Brews.

Phoenix Genuine Draught. 8.4 silver per flagon. (Sale. List price 8.9 silver per flagon.)

Griffon Light. 8.4 silver per flagon. (Sale. List price 8.9 silver per flagon. Isn't price competition a wonderful thing?) The Silver Arrow That Won't Slow You Down.

Cheap

Oakridge's Best. 5.5 silver per flagon. (Sale. List price 6.2 silver per flagon.) Known colloquially as "Beast."

Benjamin's. 5.4 silver per flagon. (Sale. List 6.2 silver per flagon.) Bottle decorated with a nice painting of a mystical trout.

Ravenswood Brew. 5.0 silver per flagon. (Sale. List 6.9 silver per flagon.) Painting of mountains.

The Merchant's Guild that supplied the brews didn't carry any true bargain-basement products, such as "Peasant's Pride," "Old Warrior," or the one with generic labeling that just says "Brew." The experiment was incomplete in that regard, but no tester complained about a shortage of bad brew. Also, with heavy heart, the test administrator decided to leave high-alcohol potions, such as Mohammad's (with its trademark wide-mouth bottles), off the list. They have the air of cheapness but actually cost more than Dragon's Breath, probably because they offer more magical potency per flagon. This experimental design choice was crucial for our risk management approach to consciousness studies.

3 Experimental procedure: Each taster sat down before an array of 10 crystal goblets labeled A through J. The A-to-J coding scheme was the same for all tasters. Each goblet held 3 ounces of one of the sample brews. (Total intake, for a taster who drank all of every sample: 30 ounces, or two and a half normal brews. Not lethal; also, they were just going back to archival cataloging when they were done.) Enchanted crackers were available to cleanse the palate. The goblets were opaque crystal, so tasters could judge the brew's color only from above. There was no time limit for the tasting, apart from the two-hour limit in which we had reserved the conference chamber. One experimenter (the supervisor of most of the others there) rushed through his rankings in 10 minutes and gave the lowest overall scores. The taster who took the longest, nearly the full two hours, had the ratings that came closest to the relative price of the brews. (This man, Samir Stephens, grew up in the Eastern Territories.) The experimenters were asked not to compare impressions until the test was over.

After tasting the brews, each taster rated brews A through J on the following standards:

Overall quality points: Zero to 100, zero as undrinkable and 100 as dream brew. Purely subjective measure of how well each taster liked each brew.

Price category: The tasters knew that each brew came from the expensive, medium, or cheap category--and they had to guess where A through J belonged. A rating of 3 was most expensive, 2 for average, 1 for cheap.

Description: "Amusing presumption," "fresh on the palate," "dragon's refuse," etc.

Best and Worst: Tasters chose one Best and one Worst from the "flight" (as they would call it if this were a wine test).

When the session was over, results for each brew were collected in a comprehensive grid system, part of our education reform initiative to improve historical interpretation of beverage quality.

4 Data Analysis: The ratings led to four ways to assess the quality of the brews, each method contributing to our collective memory of taste preferences.

1. Best and Worst. Least scientific, yet clearest cut in its results. Eleven tasters named a favorite brew. Ten of them chose Samuel Greene's Boston Enchantment. The other one chose Ravenswood Brew, the cheapest of all brews in the sample. (The taster who made this choice, Mohammad Davis, advises the Archive on what new scrolls should go into the next edition of our Historical Compendium.) Ravenswood was the only brew to receive both a Best and a Worst vote.

Bottom rankings were also clear. Of the 11 naming a Worst brew, five chose Elvensong, the most expensive brew in the survey. Results by best/worst preference showed clear patterns in our consciousness studies approach.

2. Overall preference points. This was a subtler and more illuminating look at similar trends. The brews were ranked on "corrected average preference points"--an average of the zero-to-100 points assigned by each taster, corrected, just like ice skating scores, by throwing out the highest and lowest score each brew received. The tasters used widely varying scales--one confining all brews to the range between zero and 30, another giving 67 as his lowest mark. But the power of our corrected ranking system surmounted such difficulties.

Here again one costly brew--Samuel Greene's--shows up well, while another, Elvensong, continues to struggle, but not as badly as the medium-price Phoenix Genuine Draught. Samuel's success could reflect its quasi-mislabeling, presenting a strong-flavored brew as a "light enchantment." It could also reflect that participants simply thought it was good. (Only one guessed it was Samuel Greene's.) As for Elvensong... it is very strongly hopped with mystical herbs, which can seem exotic if you know you're drinking a pricey import but simply bad if you don't. Phoenix overtook Elvensong in the race for the bottom because, while many people hated Elvensong, some actually liked it; no one liked Phoenix.

3) Value for Money: the Taste-o-meter®. Since this experiment's real purpose was to find the connection between cost and taste, the next step was to adjust subjective preference points by objective cost. The Taste-o-meter rating for each brew was calculated by dividing its corrected average preference rating by its price per flagon. If Brew X had ratings twice as high as Brew Y, but it cost three times as much, Brew Y would have the higher Taste-o-meter rating. When the 10 brews are reranked this way, the results showed fascinating patterns.

In a familiar pattern, we have Elvensong bringing up the rear, with less than one-quarter the Taste-o-meter power of Ravenswood Brew, the No. 1 value brew. The real news in this ranking is: the success of Ravenswood Brew; the embarrassment of Elfglow and Phoenix Genuine Draught, an expensive and a medium brew, respectively, which share the cellar with the hapless Elvensong; and the nearly Ravenswood-like value of Oakridge's Best and Benjamin's. It is safe to say that none of our testers would have confessed respect for Ravenswood, Oakridge's Best, or Benjamin's before the contest began. But when they didn't know what they were drinking, they found these brews much closer in quality to "best" brews than the prices would indicate.

4) Social Value for Money: the Snob-o-meter®. In addition to saying which brews they preferred, the tasters were asked to estimate whether the brews were expensive or not--in effect, to judge whether other people would like and be impressed by the brews. One taster perfectly understood the intention of this measure when he said, in comments about Brew B (Elfglow), "I don't like it, but I bet it's what the snobs buy." The Snob-o-meter rating for each brew is similar to the Taste-o-meter. You start with the "group" ranking--whether the tasters thought the brew belonged in Group 1 (cheap), 2, or 3--and then divide by the price per flagon. The result tells you the social-mobility power of the brew--how impressive it will seem, relative to how much it costs.

We won't even speak of poor Elvensong or Phoenix anymore. The story here is the amazing snob-power-per-silver of Ravenswood Brew, closely followed by Benjamin's. A silver spent on Ravenswood gets you three times the impressiveness of a silver spent on Elvensong, useful information when planning a feast. Not everyone liked Ravenswood--one called it "dragon's refuse"; another, "Water. LOW MAGIC." But the magic of statistics lets us see the larger trends, contributing to our historical interpretation of taste preferences across societal change.

5 Conclusions. Further study is needed. But on the basis of evidence to date, we can say:

One and only one brew truly survived the blind taste test. This is Samuel Greene's Boston Enchantment, which 10 tasters independently ranked "best" without knowing they were drinking a fancy brew. (They knew it was darker than the others but couldn't have known whether this was some trick off-brand sneaked into the test.)

Don't serve Elvensong unless you know people will consider it exotic, or unless you've invited me.

Apart from Samuel Greene's and Elvensong, the tasters really had trouble telling one brew from another. This conclusion is implicit in many of the findings, but it was really obvious during the experiment itself, when the confident look of scholars-who-know-their-brews quickly turned to dismay and panic as they realized that all the light enchantments tasted pretty much the same.

The evidence suggests other implications about specific brews. For instance, the comments about Griffon Light are much less enthusiastic than the average-or-better numerical rankings. Most tasters paused to complain about it--"fizzy and soapy"--before giving it reasonable marks. But the main implication, and the most useful consumer news from this study, is a radically simplified buying philosophy for light enchantment brews. Based on this study, rational consumers should:

1) Buy Samuel Greene's Boston Enchantment when they want an individual goblet of light enchantment to be as good as it can be.

2) Buy Ravenswood Brew at all other times, since it gives them the maximum taste and social influence per silver invested.

This experiment represents an important contribution to our understanding of how societal change affects consumption patterns, and how visual arts elements like packaging influence perception. The detailed rankings and comments for all tasters on all brews have been preserved in the Archive's records as part of our cultural heritage and collective memory.
