The Reluctant Innovators
By A. MITCHELL

The young woman sat rigidly in the conference room chair, her fingers drumming an anxious rhythm on the polished table. She studied the grain of the wood, traced invisible patterns on its surface, and adjusted her collar three times in as many minutes.

"I've been offered the lead position on the first autonomous vehicle testing facility in the Martian colonies," she said.

The older woman across from her set down her tablet and regarded her thoughtfully. "It's remarkable, isn't it? The new atmospheric processors make it possible now. There was a time when we couldn't even dream of surface facilities."

The young woman looked frustrated.

"I don't think I want to accept," she said quickly. "I don't think I want to spend three years there."

The older woman leaned back in her chair and folded her hands. "You mean you'd miss Earth—the people you've worked with, the familiar routines that have shaped your career here. You're worried the excitement would fade and you'd grow to resent Mars."

The young woman nodded miserably. "Yes, exactly that."

"Is there something else?"

The young woman's fingers found the table grain fascinating again. Finally, in a barely audible voice: "Yes."

"Someone special?"

A slight nod confirmed this.

The older woman smiled gently. "You know, of course, that the Commission's position is that research facilities should eventually be staffed by committed partnerships. Once it becomes feasible."

"But that could take years!" the young woman protested.

"It could—but sometimes these things happen faster than expected. And the goal makes it worthwhile."

"I suppose, but—"

The older woman's smile deepened. "Still the reluctant innovators," she murmured.

---

Grace Osborne stared at the communications terminal.

Four years at the Blackwood research station and they didn't want her to come back.

Four years developing autonomous vehicle systems for Martian terrain and they assumed she'd gladly stay longer. Just increase her compensation package, the standard corporate logic. They probably thought she'd found her calling here.

Sure, she loved it. Recycled water, protein paste, vitamin supplements, and filtered air until your body felt like a chemistry experiment. Life in a cramped habitat module where you could walk twenty paces before hitting a wall. Their glorious frontier outpost with none of Earth's comforts—a fascinating place where real showers were rationed, fresh food was a memory, and the low gravity played havoc with your bone density.

And for triple her salary they expected her to stay another two years. Maybe three. She should probably feel honored by the opportunity.

The terminal chimed again, demanding a response.

She typed: "Declined."

Silence, then an angry burst of text demanding reconsideration. Grace muted the notifications and turned toward the sleeping quarters.

The message hadn't woken anyone. They were all still asleep in their individual pods. Justin Wood, the geologist, was snoring peacefully in the lower tier. Zhang Williams, the poor kid assigned to stopover duty, was muttering in his sleep. Leo Potter wore that expression of perfect contentment, dreaming of home. Patrick Ford and David Rice lay perfectly still, sleeping lightly as always.

Lord, Grace thought, I'll be happy to see some different faces.

"What did they want?" Leo had one eye open, looking curious.

"They wanted me to stay until the next relief transport arrives," Grace whispered back.

"What did you tell them?"

She shrugged. "No."

"Diplomatic as always," someone else whispered. It was Patrick, sitting up in his pod. "If it were me, I'd have given them a detailed explanation of where they could file that request."

The others were stirring now, except for Zhang who had his back turned and seemed determined to sleep through everything.

Justin rubbed his face sleepily. "Frustrated, aren't you?"

"Somewhat. Who wouldn't be?"

"Don't take it personally. The board members have never been to Blackwood. They don't understand what it's like. They're just trying to retain a valuable employee."

"Trying to retain a valuable employee," Grace said sarcastically. "They can keep trying."

"They think you've made a home here," Patrick said.

"Why don't you all shut up until morning?" Zhang was awake now, looking bitter. "Some of us still have to stay here, you know. Some of us aren't leaving today."

No, Grace thought, some of us aren't leaving. You aren't. And Martinez isn't either. Only Martinez isn't ever going back.

Leo pointed toward Zhang's pod, held a finger to his lips, and walked quietly to the small food preparation unit. It was his turn for breakfast duty.

The others began organizing their spaces, preparing for their last day of work at Blackwood. In a few hours they'd be relieved by members of the Fourth research group and they'd be on their way back to Earth.

And that includes me, Grace thought. I'm going home. I'm finally going home.

She walked to the one small observation window. It was morning—Mars's morning—and she suppressed a shiver. The Sun's rays were striking the far edge of Valles Marineris, casting long shadows across the rust-colored landscape. The rest was still shrouded in that peculiar Martian darkness, a jumble of red dust and jagged rock formations that made the Badlands look like paradise.

Two hundred meters from the habitat she could make out the small memorial cairn and the simple metal marker, constructed from spare parts and welded together. You could still see the rover tracks in the fine dust where the group had gathered around it. That had been more than two years ago, but there was barely any wind to erase those tracks. They'd persist for decades.

That's what happened to people like Martinez, Grace thought. On Mars, one mistake could be your last.

Leo returned with the coffee. Grace took a cup, grimaced, and forced herself to finish it. It had been in storage so long the flavor was more memory than reality.

Patrick was warming his hands on his cup, looking contemplative. Justin and David were pulling on their environment suits, getting ready to go outside. Zhang was still in his pod, trying to ignore them.

"Think we should check with the orbital station to see if they've departed yet?" Leo asked.

"I contacted them on the last call," Grace said. "The relief transport left twelve hours ago. They should arrive"—she checked her chronometer—"in about seven hours."

"Grace, you know, I've been thinking," Patrick said quietly. "You've been here twice as long as the rest of us. What's the first thing you're going to do when you get back?"

It hit them then. Justin and David looked blank for a moment and slowly found equipment cases to sit on. The tops of their suits were still hanging on the wall rack. Leo lowered his coffee cup and looked serious. Even Zhang glanced up expectantly.

"I don't know," Grace said slowly. "I guess I was trying not to think about it. None of us have. We've been like children waiting so long for something that we can't believe it when it's finally about to happen."

Leo nodded in agreement. "I haven't been here four years like you, but I understand what you mean." He warmed to the topic as the realization deepened. "What are you really going to do?"

"Nothing spectacular," Grace said, smiling. "I'm going to rent a place in Goldfield Village, get some actual music—not synthesized—and just watch real people living real lives. Then I think I'll visit someone."

"Who's the someone?" Patrick asked.

Grace grinned. "Just someone. What about you, Patrick?"

"Well, I'm going to be practical. First, I'll submit all my geological survey data to the Commission. Then I'm going to sell my story to a media production company and then—well, then I think I'll get properly drunk!"

Everyone laughed and Grace turned to Leo.

"How about you?"

Leo looked solemn. "Like Patrick, I'll fulfill my obligations to the expedition first. Then I'm going home to see my husband."

They were quiet. "I thought all expedition members had to be unattached," Patrick said.

"They are. And I understand the reasoning—professional ethics and all that. But who could pass up the compensation package the Commission offered?"

"If I had to do it again? Not me," Patrick said promptly.

They laughed. Someone said: "Play your music file, Grace. Today's the day for it."

The audio file was an old recording Grace had brought with her when she'd arrived with the First group. The quality was degraded from multiple copies, but the song was meaningful.

"Homeward Bound" by an ancient folk artist.

They played it twice. They were beginning to feel it now, Grace thought. They were actually going home and the reality was starting to sink in.

"You know, Grace," Patrick said, "Blackwood won't be the same without you. We'll look at Mars from Earth and it just won't have the same appeal."

"Like they say in the old movies," David said, "you never had it so good. You found a home here."

The others joined in the gentle teasing and Grace smiled. Yesterday or a week ago they couldn't have done this. She had been here too long and resented it too much.

The mood quieted after a while and Justin and David finished suiting up. They still had atmospheric readings to take before they left. Patrick was right after them. There was a rock formation he wanted to sample and some strata he needed to photograph.

And time went faster when you kept busy.

Grace stopped them at the airlock. "Remember to check your suits for breaches," she warned. "And verify your oxygen tank levels."

Patrick looked annoyed. "I've gone out at least seven hundred times," he said, "and you check me every single time."

"And I'd check you seven hundred more," Grace said. "It takes only one mistake. And watch for unstable ground. Step through one of those weak spots and that's it."

Patrick sighed. "Grace, you watch us like we're children. You verify our suits, you mediate our disputes, you ensure we're not bored and that we stay healthy and productive. I think you'd tie our shoes if we couldn't manage it ourselves. But someday, Grace old friend, you're going to discover that your team can handle themselves!"

But he checked his suit for breaches and verified his tank level before he left.

Only Leo and Grace remained in the habitat. Leo was at the work station, carefully cataloging some bacterial specimens.

"I never knew you were married," Grace said.

Leo didn't look up. "There wasn't much point in discussing it. You just end up dwelling on it and wanting—and there's nothing you can do. You talk about it and it just intensifies the longing."

"He let you go without objection?"

"No, he didn't object. But I don't think he wanted me to go, either." He laughed slightly. "At least I hope he didn't."

They were silent for a while. "What do you miss most, Grace?" Leo asked. "I know what we said earlier, but I mean genuinely."

Grace thought for a moment. "I think I miss the weather," she said quietly. "Real weather. Rain and snow and wind that isn't trying to kill you. Trees that change with the seasons. I think, when I get back, I'd like to stand in a thunderstorm and just feel the rain on my face."

She paused, feeling self-conscious. Leo's expression was encouraging. "And then I think I'd like to go to a crowded place—maybe Eastwood in Prandoria—and just watch people. Or maybe go to a live performance and smell the popcorn and feel the energy of a real audience in the dark."

She examined her hands. "I think what I miss most is humanity in all its complexity—complexity science could never fully capture. All kinds of people. People struggling with applied ethics in their daily lives. People who wouldn't know strategic planning from urban planning. And people who wouldn't care. We're hundreds of millions of kilometers from everything familiar, Leo, and what I miss most is the messy, beautiful chaos of human society."

"Someone special back home?" Leo asked almost casually.

"Yes."

"You're not like Zhang. You've never mentioned it."

"Same reason you didn't mention your husband. You get to thinking about it."

Leo sealed the specimen container. "Going to get married when you return?"

Grace was at the window again, staring out at the desolate landscape. "We hope to."

"Settle down somewhere and build a life together?"

Grace nodded.

"That's the only real future," Leo said.

He stored the container and joined her at the window. Grace moved over so they could both look out.

"Grace." Leo hesitated. "What happened to Martinez?"

"She died," Grace said. "She was brilliant, completely dedicated to the research. Being on Mars was the opportunity of a lifetime. She was so focused on the work that she forgot the fundamentals—like how to stay alive. The day before the Second group arrived, she went out to complete some experiments. She forgot to check for suit breaches and whether her tank valve was fully closed. We couldn't reach her in time."

"She had her communicator?"

"Yes. It worked perfectly. We heard everything she was thinking at the end."

Leo's face was expressionless. "What's your real job here, Grace? Why does someone have to stay for stopover?"

"Many reasons, Leo. You can't bring in a whole relief crew and let them take over without guidance. They need to know where you left off. They need to know where equipment is, how systems work, what hazards to watch for. And because you've been here two years and understand the environment, you have to monitor them to ensure they stay alive despite their inexperience. Mars is a hostile environment and you have to learn how to survive in it. There's a lot to learn—and some people just never do."

"You're a caretaker, then."

"I suppose you could say that."

Leo said, "You're not a researcher, are you?"

"No, you should know that. I came as the pilot and systems engineer of the first transport. We converted parts of the ship into the habitat, so there wasn't anything to return on. I'm good with machinery and made myself useful with the equipment. When it became clear someone would need to stay for stopover, I volunteered. I thought the others were so valuable that their data should get back to Earth when the first relief transport came."

"You wouldn't do it again, though, would you?"

"No, I wouldn't."

"Do you think Zhang will do as good a job as you've done here?"

Grace frowned. "Frankly, I hadn't considered that. I don't believe I care anymore. I've served my time; it's someone else's turn now. He volunteered for it. I think I was clear in explaining the responsibilities when you all discussed it."

"You were, but I don't think Zhang's right for it. He's too young, too inexperienced. He volunteered because he thought it made him look heroic. He doesn't have the judgment that someone older would have. That you have."

Grace turned slowly and faced Leo.

"I'm not irreplaceable," she said slowly, "and even if I were, it wouldn't matter to me. I'm sorry if Zhang is young. So was I. I've lost four years here. And I don't intend to lose any more."

Leo held up his hands. "Look, Grace, I didn't mean you should stay. I know how much you resent it and the time you've invested. It's just—" His voice trailed away. "It's just that I think it's such a critically important job."

Leo had gone out for a final equipment check and Grace enjoyed one of her rare moments of solitude. She wandered to her pod and opened her personal storage locker. She checked her civilian clothes and toiletries for perhaps the hundredth time and pushed everything down further in the bag. It was unnecessary because the bag had been packed for a week. She remembered postponing it as long as possible and then the quiet satisfaction about a week ago when she had opened her locker and transferred its meager contents to the bag.

She hadn't actually needed to pack, of course. In less than a day she'd be back on Earth where she could buy more toothpaste than she could use in a decade. She could leave behind her worn clothes and the oversized shirts she had inherited from—who was it? Richardson?—from the First group. Zhang could probably use them or maybe someone from the Fourth.

But it wasn't like going home unless you packed. It was part of the ritual, like marking off the last three weeks on the wall panel beside her pod. Just hours ago, when she woke, she had made the final mark and signed her name and the date. Her signature was right beneath Martinez's.

She frowned thinking about Martinez and secured the bag's closure. They should never have sent someone like Martinez to Mars.

She had just locked the bag when she heard the airlock cycle and the soft hiss of equalization. Someone had returned earlier than expected. She watched the inner door open and the suited figure enter and remove its helmet.

Zhang. He had gone out to assist Justin with the atmospheric sensors. Maybe Justin hadn't needed help, with David along. Or more likely, considering the circumstances, Zhang wasn't much help to anyone today.

Zhang stripped off his suit. His face was covered with perspiration and his eyes showed fear.

He moistened his lips. "Do—do you think they'll ever have relief transports more frequently than every two years, Grace? I mean, considering the advances in—"

"No," Grace interrupted bluntly. "I don't. Not for at least a decade. The fuel costs too much and the journey's too dangerous. In terms of transport economics, you're worth more than your weight in platinum when they send you here. Even if it becomes cheaper, it won't shorten stopover periods right away." She paused, feeling some sympathy for Zhang. "It won't be terrible. There'll be new people here and you'll spend considerable time getting to know them."

"Well, you see," Zhang started, "that's why I came back early. I wanted to talk to you about stopover. It's that—well, I'll put it this way." He seemed to be searching for the right words. "I'm engaged back home. Really wonderful person, Grace, you'd like them if you knew them." He fumbled in his pocket and produced a photograph, placing it on the work station. "That's a picture of Alex, taken at a gathering we attended together." Grace didn't look. "We—I—expected to get married when I returned. I never told Alex about stopover, Grace. They think I'll be home tomorrow. I kept thinking, hoping, that somehow—"

He was handling it badly, Grace thought.

"You wanted to trade places with me, didn't you, Zhang? You thought I might stay for stopover again, in your place?"

It hurt to see Zhang's eyes. They were the eyes of someone desperately trying to stop themselves from doing something shameful, but unable to help themselves.

"Well, yes, essentially. Oh, God, Grace, I know you want to go home! But I couldn't ask any of the others; you were the only one who could, the only one who was qualified!"

Zhang looked as though he might be sick. Grace tried to recall everything she knew about him. Zhang Williams. Excellent engineer. Graduate from a prestigious technical institute. Family was involved in natural resource management or something similar.

It still didn't quite add up. "You know I don't like it here any more than you do," Grace said slowly. "I may have commitments at home, too. What made you think I would change my mind?"

Zhang took the plunge. "Well, you see," he started eagerly, too desperate to remember pride, "you know my family's quite well-off. We would make it worth your while, Grace." He was feverish. "It would mean two more years, Grace, but they'd be well-compensated years!"

Grace felt exhausted. The good feeling about going home was slowly dissolving.

"If you have any reports to complete, I think you should get started," she cut in, keeping the harshness she felt out of her voice. "It'll be too late after the relief transport departs. It'll be easier to give the captain your report than try to transmit it back to Earth from here."

She felt more sympathy for Zhang than she could remember feeling for anyone. Long after returning home, Zhang would remember this moment.

It would haunt him.

Cowardice is the one thing no one ever forgives themselves for.

Patrick was eating a nutrition bar and looking out the window, so naturally he saw the transport first. "Well, look at that!" he shouted. "We have visitors!" He rushed for his suit. Justin and David followed quickly and all three headed for the airlock.

Grace was standing in front of it. "Check your suits," she said quietly. "Just be certain to check."

"Oh, come on, Grace!" Patrick started angrily. Then he stopped and went over his suit. He got to his tank and went pale. Nearly empty. It was only a kilometer to the relief transport, so someone probably would have reached him in time, but.... He bit his lip and got a full tank.

Grace and Leo watched them cross the Martian surface, making the long, bounding strides that low gravity permitted. The transport's hatch had opened and small figures were descending the ramp. The figures from the habitat reached them and performed a brief dance of welcome. Then the figures linked arms and started back. Grace noticed one—probably Patrick—pat the transport's hull affectionately before starting back.

They were in the airlock and the air cycled in and then they were in the habitat, removing their suits. The newcomers were impressed and serious, acutely aware of the tremendous responsibility that now rested on them. Like Patrick and Leo and the members of the Second group had been when they arrived. Like Grace had been with the First.

Patrick and the others surrounded them.

How was Earth? What was the political situation? Were the autonomous vehicle regulations finally passed? What was happening in healthcare policy? Was the orbital station expansion complete?

Was the sky still blue, was the grass still green, did the seasons still change, did people still love and argue and were there still people who didn't understand complexity science and didn't care?

Grace had experienced this before. But was Jordan still Jordan?

Some of the Fourth group members had brought personal items. One of them—a sturdy, enthusiastic woman named Camila Cook—was opening a container about thirty centimeters square and fifteen centimeters deep. Grace watched curiously.

"Well, I'll be damned!" Leo said. "Hey, everyone, look at this!"

Grace and the others crowded around and suddenly Patrick leaned over and inhaled deeply. In the container, covering a thick layer of actual soil, was a small plot of living grass. They looked at it, awed. Leo reached out and touched it gently.

"I like the feel of it," he said simply.

Grace carefully plucked a single blade and held it to her nose. It had been years since she had seen grass, experienced the luxury of walking barefoot on it and lying on its cool surface during those warm summer evenings when it was too pleasant to be indoors.

Camila blushed. "I thought we could spare a little water for it and perhaps use the grow lights occasionally. Couldn't resist bringing it; it seemed like a symbol of something...." She looked embarrassed.

Grace understood. If she had been thinking clearly, she should have tried to bring something like that instead of her music files.

"That's expensive grass," Zhang said sharply. "Do you realize that at current transport rates, it's worth about a thousand credits per blade?"

Camila looked distressed and someone said, "Oh, shut up, Zhang."

One of the newcomers separated from the group and approached Grace. She extended her hand and said, "My name's Joshua Fuller. Captain of the relief transport. I understand you're in charge here?"

Grace nodded and shook hands. They hadn't had a captain on the First transport. Just a pilot and crew. Fuller looked every inch a captain. Strong features, graying hair, the confident bearing of someone accustomed to command.

"You could say I'm in charge here," Grace said.

"Well, look, Ms. Osborne, is there somewhere we can speak privately?"

They walked to one corner of the habitat. "This is about as private as we can get, captain," Grace said. "What's on your mind?"

Fuller found an equipment case and sat down. He looked at Grace carefully.

"I've always wanted to meet the person who's spent more time here than anyone else," he began.

"I'm sure you wanted to see me for more than just curiosity."

Fuller reached for a container of mints. "Mind if I have one?"

Grace gestured toward Zhang. "Ask him. He's in charge now."

The captain didn't bother. He put the container away. "You know we have extensive plans for the station," he said.

"I hadn't heard specifics."

"Oh, yes, extensive plans. They're developing automated cargo transports now that could deliver building materials for additional habitat modules. Enable us to expand the facility, have a series of modules all connected. Create proper laboratories and living quarters for the research staff." His eyes swept the room. "Provide some actual privacy for a change."

Grace nodded. "They could use some privacy here."

The captain noticed the pronoun. "Well, that's one of the reasons I wanted to speak with you, Osborne. The Commission discussed it and they'd like you to stay. They feel if they're going to expand operations, add more modules and increase staff, that someone with practical experience should be managing things. They believe you're the only person who's capable and who has the necessary experience."

The captain vaguely sensed his approach was wrong.

"Is that everything?"

Fuller looked uncomfortable. "Naturally you'd be well compensated. I don't imagine anyone would enjoy being here indefinitely. They're prepared to triple your salary—perhaps even add a substantial bonus—and give you complete authority. You'd be Director of the Blackwood Research Complex."

All this and a title too, Grace thought.

"That's it?" Grace asked.

Fuller frowned. "Well, the Commission said they'd be willing to consider anything else you had in mind, if it was additional compensation or...."

"The answer is no," Grace said. "I'm not interested in more money for staying because I'm not interested in staying. Money can't buy it, captain. I'm sorry, but I'm afraid you'd have to live here to appreciate that.

"Zhang Williams is staying for stopover. If there's something important about the project or upcoming changes, perhaps you should brief him before you leave."

She walked away.
question: How many different people attempted to convince Grace to remain at Blackwood?
option_a: Three people
option_b: Four people
correct_answer_text: Three people
incorrect_answer_text: Four people
explanation: Three different people tried to convince Grace to stay at Blackwood: 1) The Commission (via communications terminal at the beginning), 2) Zhang Williams (who asked her to trade places with him for stopover duty), and 3) Captain Joshua Fuller (who offered her the Director position with increased compensation). While Leo Potter expressed that the stopover job was important, he explicitly stated he didn't mean Grace should stay and acknowledged her time served.
original_question: How many different people tried to talk Chapman into staying on the moon?

THE ARCHITECT AND ETERNITY
By Anonymous

THE PURSUIT OF IMMORTALITY THROUGH INNOVATION—BUT AT WHAT COST TO OTHERS?

Eva Ahmed stood at the window of her penthouse in Summit District, gazing out at the city sprawling below. At forty-seven, she remained striking—her posture perfect, her skin meticulously maintained through the latest dermatological treatments, her figure sculpted by personal trainers and nutritionists. But she knew. She could see the subtle changes that no amount of money or technology could fully reverse. The slight looseness in her jawline. The faint creases that appeared when she smiled, which was why she'd trained herself not to smile anymore.

She turned from the window and walked to her private study, the room where she kept her most precious research. On the desk lay a leather-bound journal filled with notes, calculations, and diagrams. Next to it sat a slim volume: "Temporal Mechanics and Human Consciousness" by Dr. Christopher Richards, the brilliant theoretical physicist from Yarnmouth, Marvenia.

Eva had spent months studying Richards's work on consciousness transfer and temporal displacement. The theory was elegant: human consciousness could be transferred backward through time into one's own younger body, effectively allowing someone to relive their youth with all the knowledge and experience of their older self. It was the ultimate form of entrepreneurship—investing in yourself, literally.

The door chimed. Eva checked her appearance in the polished surface of a chrome sculpture—she never kept mirrors in her main rooms, as they were too honest—and then opened the door.

Daniel Wallace stood there, young and eager, his eyes bright with ambition. At twenty-six, he was one of the most promising consciousness engineers in the field, fresh from his doctorate at the Institute of Applied Ethics in Pearlbrook, Quendor. Eva had been cultivating this relationship for three months, ever since she learned he would be leading the experimental consciousness transfer project.

"Eva," he said warmly, stepping forward.

She held up a hand, stopping him just short of an embrace. "Not yet, Daniel. Come in. We need to talk about tomorrow."

The young engineer's face showed confusion, but he followed her inside. Eva had designed the lighting carefully—soft enough to be flattering, strategic enough to highlight her best features while obscuring the rest. It was all part of what she called her aesthetic philosophy, though others might have called it calculated manipulation.

"Tomorrow's the big day," Daniel said, settling onto the couch. "The first human trial of temporal consciousness displacement. If it works, we'll revolutionize everything—medicine, education, career planning. Imagine being able to go back and make better choices with the wisdom you have now."

"Tell me exactly how it works," Eva said, though she'd read Richards's book cover to cover a dozen times.

Daniel launched into an explanation, his enthusiasm evident. "We've built a quantum resonance chamber in Cedarville, Galdoria. It creates a stable temporal field that allows consciousness to travel backward along its own timeline. The subject enters the chamber, and their consciousness is displaced to a younger version of themselves—potentially decades younger."

"And the younger consciousness? What happens to it?"

"It's absorbed, integrated. You'd have all your younger self's vitality and physical youth, but with your current mind and memories intact. It's the ultimate form of systems thinking—optimizing the entire timeline of a human life."

Eva leaned closer. "How young could someone go?"

"Theoretically? Back to early adulthood. Maybe eighteen or twenty. Any younger and the neural development might not support the older consciousness." He paused, studying her face. "Eva, why all these questions? You've asked me this before."

She changed tactics. "Who else is involved in tomorrow's test?"

"Just me and Dr. Mohamed Ramirez from the ethics board. He's there to monitor and ensure protocols are followed. But Eva, I need to rest. The procedure is complex, and I need to be alert. I should go—"

"Stay," she said, her voice dropping to a purr. "Just a little longer. Tell me about the risks."

Daniel sighed but continued. "The main risk is temporal paradox. If the consciousness transfer creates too much change in the timeline, it could cause a cascade effect. Also, there's the question of human rights—does the younger self consent to being overwritten? The ethics are complicated, which is why Ramirez insists on being present."

Eva stood and moved to a control panel hidden in the wall. She pressed several buttons. The lights dimmed further. Soft music began to play. And in the corner, a red light began blinking on a concealed recording device.

"What was that?" Daniel asked.

"Just setting the mood," Eva said, moving to sit beside him. "Daniel, I need to tell you something. I'm not who you think I am."

Over the next hour, Eva revealed her true age—forty-seven, not the thirty-two she'd claimed—and her true purpose. She'd been planning this for months. She had recordings of Daniel, compromising recordings that showed him violating research protocols, sharing confidential information, accepting what could be construed as bribes. She had similar recordings of Dr. Ramirez, the ethics monitor. She had leverage over the entire project.

"You're going to take me with you tomorrow," she said flatly. "I'm going into that chamber instead of the designated test subject. I'm going back twenty-five years, to when I was twenty-two. And you're going to make it happen, or I'll destroy your career before it even begins."

Daniel's face had gone pale. "You can't—that's insane. The test subject has been prepared for months, physically and psychologically. You haven't undergone any of the preliminary scans or—"

"I don't care," Eva snapped. "I've studied the process. I understand the risks. And I have the leverage to make this happen. Unless you want Dr. Ramirez and the entire scientific collaboration to see what I have recorded..."

She showed him clips. Daniel with his head in his hands, admitting he'd falsified some safety data to speed the project along. Ramirez accepting expensive gifts that violated ethics guidelines. The young engineer's face crumbled.

"You're a monster," he whispered.

"I'm a survivor," Eva corrected. "I'm someone who understands that in this world, you either control your destiny or it controls you. This is my entrepreneurship—investing everything in myself. Now, we're going to the facility. You'll input my biometric data, and by this time tomorrow, I'll be twenty-two again. Young, beautiful, with decades ahead of me to build an empire with the knowledge I have now."

"And what about me?" Daniel asked bitterly. "What happens to me in all this?"

Eva smiled, though it cost her—she could feel the wrinkles forming. But it didn't matter now. Soon there would be no wrinkles. "You'll continue your career. You'll be the genius who made temporal displacement work. You'll be famous. Just... cooperative."

They drove through the night to Cedarville, to the research facility hidden in the hills. Eva's mind raced with possibilities. She'd go back to twenty-two, but with everything she knew now. She'd make different investments, build different relationships. She'd avoid the mistakes that had cost her years of struggle. And when she started to age again, she'd simply do it again. And again. Eternal youth through temporal displacement.

The facility was quiet when they arrived. Daniel used his credentials to get them inside, past security, down to the quantum resonance chamber. It was a massive spherical structure, gleaming with superconducting coils and quantum processors.

"Get in," Daniel said, his voice hollow.

Eva climbed into the chamber, settling into the contoured seat. Through the transparent walls, she could see Daniel at the control console, his fingers moving reluctantly over the interface.

"How long will the procedure take?" she asked.

"The displacement itself is instantaneous," he replied. "But the temporal field needs to build up gradually. Once it reaches critical density, your consciousness will snap backward along your timeline to your twenty-two-year-old self. From your perspective, you'll simply wake up twenty-five years in the past, in your younger body."

"Perfect," Eva breathed. "Start it."

Daniel's hands hesitated over the controls. "Eva, please. Think about what you're doing. The ethics of this—the social contract we have with our younger selves—"

"Start it!" she screamed.

He pressed the activation sequence.

The chamber began to hum, a sound that started below hearing and gradually rose in pitch. Eva felt a tingling in her skin, then a deeper vibration in her bones. The air inside the chamber began to shimmer, and she could see ghostly images overlaying reality—images of herself at different ages, all occupying the same space.

"It's working!" she cried. "I can feel it! I'm getting younger already!"

Through the chamber walls, she saw Daniel's face, and something in his expression made her uneasy. Was that pity? Or something else?

The vibration intensified. Eva's vision blurred, and she felt a wrenching sensation, as if she were being pulled in multiple directions at once. The images of her younger selves grew more solid, more real. She reached out, trying to touch the twenty-two-year-old Eva she could see standing before her—

And then the chamber exploded with light.

When Eva's vision cleared, she was still in the chamber, but something was wrong. She looked down at her hands. They were wrinkled, spotted with age. More wrinkled than before. She touched her face and felt deep creases, loose skin.

"What—what happened?" she gasped, her voice cracking.

Daniel's voice came through the speaker, and now she could hear the emotion in it—not pity, but cold satisfaction. "I tried to warn you, Eva. Dr. Richards's theory had a flaw, one he discovered too late to publish. The temporal displacement doesn't work the way you thought. It doesn't send your consciousness backward. It accelerates your personal timeline forward while keeping you stationary in space-time. To an outside observer, you appear to age rapidly. To you, subjectively, time seems to flow backward—but it's an illusion."

"No," Eva whispered. "No, that can't be—"

"The images you saw weren't your past selves. They were projections, echoes. The chamber doesn't make you younger, Eva. It makes you older. Much older. You've just lived through another twenty-five years in the span of minutes."

Eva looked at her reflection in the chamber's polished interior. The face staring back was that of a woman in her seventies. Deep wrinkles, sagging skin, age spots, thinning hair. She screamed.

"I'm shutting it down now," Daniel said. "But the damage is done. You wanted to control time, Eva. You wanted to cheat aging through entrepreneurship and manipulation. But time doesn't negotiate. And neither do I."

"You knew," Eva gasped. "You knew this would happen."

"I suspected," Daniel admitted. "After you blackmailed me, I went back through Richards's notes, the ones he never published. I found the error in his calculations. I tried to tell you, but you wouldn't listen. You were so obsessed with your aesthetic philosophy, with maintaining your appearance, that you couldn't see the truth."

The chamber door opened, and Eva stumbled out, her joints aching, her muscles weak. She caught sight of herself in a polished panel on the wall—an old woman, ancient, withered.

"Why?" she whispered. "Why did you let me do this?"

Daniel's face was hard. "Because you gave me no choice. You were going to destroy my career, destroy Dr. Ramirez, corrupt years of scientific collaboration. Daniel Wallace attended, standing at the back of the small gathering. He carried with him a copy of Dr. Richards's unpublished notes, which he planned to release to the scientific community as a warning about the dangers of temporal manipulation.

"Mr. Wallace," she said, "I understand you were involved in the research that led to Ms. Ahmed's condition. Can you comment?"

He walked away, leaving Layla to write her story—a cautionary tale about vanity, manipulation, and the dangers of trying to control forces beyond human comprehension.

Years later, Daniel would perfect a different approach to temporal mechanics, one focused not on individual immortality but on environmental justice and ecosystem restoration, using temporal fields to accelerate the healing of damaged ecosystems. It was a project that required systems thinking, career planning, and a deep understanding of the social contract between humanity and the planet.

But he never forgot Eva Ahmed, the woman who wanted to live forever and ended up dying before her time.

In the quantum resonance chamber in Cedarville, now sealed and decommissioned, a faint temporal echo remained—the ghostly image of a woman reaching for her younger self, forever frozen in the moment of her greatest mistake.

And in Summit District, in the penthouse Eva had once occupied, new tenants moved in, unaware of the tragedy that had unfolded there. They found, hidden in a wall panel, Eva's journal filled with notes and calculations. They threw it away, along with the copy of Dr. Richards's book.

Some lessons, it seemed, were destined to be learned over and over again.

The city moved on. Time moved on. And somewhere in the fabric of space-time, the echo of Eva Ahmed's scream faded slowly into silence, a warning that would never be heard, a mistake that would inevitably be repeated.

Because humanity's greatest weakness has always been the belief that we can control what we cannot understand, that we can bargain with forces that recognize no negotiation, that we can cheat the one certainty that binds us all.

Time always wins.

Always.

Benjamin Anderson adjusted the neural feedback collar around his neck carefully. The sleek device hummed softly, its sensors extending down his spine in a web of responsive filaments that would detect and counteract any stress response before it could manifest. The readout on his wrist displayed his current cortisol levels, heart rate variability, and emotional state in real-time.

Nathan Mills watched his colleague from across the climate adaptation laboratory. "You know, Ben, I still think you're crossing a line here. We're supposed to be helping people adapt to climate stress, not becoming test subjects ourselves."

Benjamin turned his pale eyes toward the massive windows overlooking Kensington, Zelvaria's flooded districts. The city had been gradually sinking for decades, and the psychological toll on its residents had become the focus of their research. "That's exactly my point, Nathan. There's a barrier between us and the people we're trying to help. How can we truly understand climate anxiety, displacement trauma, or resource scarcity stress if we stay safely behind our institutional walls?"

Nathan ran his hand through his thinning hair, disrupting the carefully combed strands. "I don't know, Ben, but maintaining our objectivity is crucial for proper hypothesis testing. We're scientists, not guinea pigs. What we're doing with these Adaptive Solutions is revolutionary enough—we're using climate technology to address psychological responses to environmental change. But if we start using them ourselves..."

Benjamin leaned forward intensely. "Revolutionary? Nathan, we're just treating symptoms! We're the most primitive kind of behavioral scientists. One person giving another a device to suppress their fear of rising water doesn't solve anything. Eventually, the environmental crisis will overwhelm us all unless we address the root cause, not just the psychological indicators."

Nathan shifted his considerable weight uncomfortably. "Now, Ben, we can't turn back the clock. There simply aren't enough traditional therapists or time to give old-fashioned cognitive behavioral therapy to everyone suffering from climate trauma. The scale is too massive."

Benjamin slammed his hand on the desk. "I used to call myself a climate psychologist. But now I know we're semi-engineers, semi-programmers, semi-inventors of gadgets, but certainly not real psychologists. A real psychologist wouldn't give someone a buoyancy suit with integrated anxiety suppressors just because they're afraid of the water."

His mind drifted back to the first buoyancy suit he had ever prescribed. The memory sickened him now. He could see the patient's face, slack with artificial calm as the suit's sensors detected fear and immediately released calming neurotransmitters. The suit was designed to be worn constantly—day and night, for life. It monitored the wearer's proximity to water and automatically inflated if submersion was detected, while simultaneously flooding their system with anxiety suppressants.

"That's just one example," Benjamin continued. "There are so many others. The thermal regulation implants for people with heat anxiety. The air quality monitors that pipe in recorded nature sounds when pollution levels rise. We're creating dependencies, not solutions."

Nathan tried to smile reassuringly. "You know, Ben, not all of our Solutions are so invasive. Those climate grief processors aren't even visible. If anyone notices that small port behind a patient's ear, it looks like a hearing aid. Yet for a reasonable cost, the patient is equipped to process their eco-anxiety through guided virtual reality scenarios that help them accept the changing world."

"But should they just accept it?" Benjamin asked intensely. "Suppose someone is driving through a flash flood zone. They think about turning back, but their grief processor is telling them everything will be fine, the world is changing and that's natural. Or suppose they're in a building during a heat wave and the cooling system fails—if they can process their heat stress away, they might not evacuate in time."

Nathan's face hardened. "You know as well as I do that those processors only reduce anxiety by about 23 percent. They don't eliminate survival instincts."

"At first, Nathan—only at first. But what about severe cases where we have to use the immersive climate acceptance therapy? When we're burning positive environmental imagery directly into their visual cortex with targeted neural stimulation? With those images overlaying everything they see and those acceptance mantras running through their subconscious, do you really think their judgment will only be impaired 23 percent? Nathan shrugged helplessly. "You're an idealist."

Most people seemed normal, but you couldn't tell who was wearing an Adaptive Solution and who wasn't. Many Solutions weren't readily apparent.

A young woman with darkened glasses and a spatial orientation headset—clearly someone with submersion phobia—accidentally bumped into Benjamin. Her sensors detected his neural collar and her expression softened when she realized he was also Adapted. "I'm so sorry," she said warmly.

"No problem at all."

It was the first time in years anyone had apologized to Benjamin for anything. He had been one of those condemned Unadapted, more to be scorned than pitied for his "privilege" of not needing help. Perhaps he could really understand these people now that he had joined them.

Suddenly, something yanked at Benjamin's arm. He looked down to see a magnetic tether locked onto his wrist. Model Acrophobe 101-X, he catalogued immediately—a safety line system for people afraid of falling from the elevated walkways. But his emotional response didn't follow his clinical analysis. Terror flooded through him, heart racing, breath catching. The impervium cable stretched back to a heavy-set man covered in similar tethers attached to railings, support columns, and other pedestrians.

"Release that line!" someone shouted.

A clean-cut man with dark hair was approaching the tethered man. "Disconnect it, Ramirez! Can't you see he's wearing a neural collar? You're overloading his stress response system!"

"I can't," Ramirez groaned. "I'm too scared to let go!"

Halfway along the cable, the dark-haired man grabbed hold. "I've got it. Release it now!"

Ramirez fumbled with his control belt and sent a release pulse through the cable. The magnetic clamp fell away from Benjamin's wrist. He breathed deeply, feeling overwhelming relief as his collar worked to stabilize his system.

After a moment, he looked up to see Ramirez retracting all his lines, drawing them back into his belt. The dark-haired man stood by tensely as the crowd dispersed.

"This isn't the first time you've done something like this, Ramirez," he said. "You weren't too scared to release that line. You just don't care about other people. This is official." He struck Ramirez with a precise blow to the jaw. The larger man collapsed.

The other turned to Benjamin. "He was already checked out mentally. Never felt the punch."

"What did you mean by 'official'?" Benjamin asked, trying to process what had just happened.

The young man's expression became guarded. "How long have you been Adapted?"

"Not long," Benjamin evaded.

The other glanced around. "Do you think you might be interested in joining an organization of the Adapted? We're working on institutional reform—changing how climate adaptation is managed."

The man's face paled visibly. "All right. I'll risk it." He touched the side of his head.

Benjamin shifted, trying to see what the man was indicating, but couldn't manage it gracefully. He wondered if his rescuer had some kind of substance monitoring system. "I'm Benjamin Anderson."

"Lucas Ramirez. Well, Lucas—not related to that other Ramirez. I suppose they have beverages at the Hub. We can get something there."

Lucas set their direction and Benjamin fell in beside him. "Look, if you don't drink, we can just talk. It was only a suggestion."

Lucas's features were beginning to glisten with sweat. "You're fortunate in one way, Dr. Anderson. People see your neural collar and understand. But even after seeing this—" he turned his head to reveal a small metallic cube above his left ear "—some people still ask me to have a drink."

Benjamin had never issued a device quite like it. He wasn't sure if it would be appropriate to ask about it.

"It's an alcohol monitor," Lucas explained. "It maintains a constant blood analysis to ensure my alcohol level never exceeds safe limits."

Lucas looked away. "It releases a lethal dose of toxin into my bloodstream."

"What kind of irresponsible person could have created such a device?" he demanded.

They sat at a small table. Benjamin wondered why these places always used synthetic wood grain. Then he realized—it hid the water stains and mold remarkably well.

A large man who smelled of recycled water shuffled toward them, staring at something beyond normal vision.

Lucas lit a cigarette with shaking hands. "Reggie is studying environmental justice texts. Interesting setup. His contact lenses are made of layered smart glass. Every time he blinks, the polarization changes and a new page appears. His mother once told him that if he didn't study climate justice and work to help others, she would die in the floods."

Benjamin understood that such a threat alone couldn't create this fixation. His eyebrows raised questioningly.

Lucas nodded. "Twenty years ago, at least."

"What can I get you, Lucas?" Reggie asked.

The young man crushed out his cigarette. "Whiskey. Neat."

Reggie smiled vacantly. "Sure thing. The texts say everyone deserves basic resources, or something like that. I don't remember exactly."

Of course he didn't, Benjamin knew. Why should he? It was futile to study environmental justice to save his mother, because she was obviously dead. He would never succeed because there was no reason to succeed. But he had to try, didn't he? He didn't want her to die. He had to prove that.

Benjamin sighed. At least this compulsion kept the man functional, doing useful work instead of catatonic in an institution with imaginary texts. A person could harm themselves with anything if desperate enough.

"But Lucas," Reggie complained, "you know you won't drink it. You always order drinks and just stare at them. You look so strange when you're looking at drinks. Honestly, Lucas, it's almost funny."

Lucas examined his cigarette stub with scientific precision. "Dr. Anderson is buying the drink. That makes it different."

Reggie left. Lucas kept dissecting the tobacco. Benjamin cleared his throat. "You were telling me about some organization."

Lucas looked up, suddenly alert and observant. "Was I? Well, suppose you tell me something. What do you really think of the Unadapted?"

Benjamin frowned. "Who?"

"I forgot—you're new to this. The Unadapted is what we call people without Solutions. Have you considered how dangerous these people are, Dr. Anderson?"

"Frankly, no," Benjamin said, knowing it wasn't what Lucas wanted to hear.

"You don't understand. Everyone has some climate trauma or environmental anxiety. Maybe not everyone did once, but after decades of ecological collapse, everyone who didn't develop symptoms created defense mechanisms that made them vulnerable in other ways. If that trauma isn't addressed and Adapted, it may surface unexpectedly and endanger others. The only safe, stable citizens are Adapted. Those lacking Solutions—the Unadapted—must be dealt with."

Benjamin's throat went dry. "And you're going to deal with them?"

"It's my purpose," Lucas said quickly. "And yours too, of course."

Benjamin nodded slowly. Lucas was a demagogue—young, charismatic, dynamic, compelling, passionate about his cause, and convinced of his righteous purpose. He was dangerous. Doubly dangerous because, even though Benjamin could recognize him for what he was, he still liked the young man's intelligence and courage.

"How do we deal with the Unadapted?" Benjamin asked.

Lucas glanced around, then seemed to decide against excessive caution. "We'll Adapt them whether they want it or not—for their own good."

Benjamin felt ice in his stomach. The roaring in his head grew louder, and he realized it wasn't just internal. Thunder was rumbling outside. He was getting sick.

Lucas was the type who could spread his ideas throughout the Adapted community—if indeed the movement wasn't already widespread.

Benjamin could picture an entirely Adapted world and the vision horrified him. Every Solution reduced mental and physical capabilities to some degree, whether Nathan and the others admitted it or not. If everyone had one crutch, they would develop secondary issues.

People would need two Solutions—perhaps a buoyancy suit and a thermal regulator—then another and another. There would always be a crutch for one problem, leaving room to develop something else—until everyone would be so burdened with Solutions they couldn't function.

A Solution was a last resort, palliative care for a terminal case. Enforced Solutions would be a curse for individuals and society.

But Benjamin relaxed slightly. How could anyone force mechanical relief for climate trauma on someone who didn't want or need it?

"Perhaps you don't see how it could be done," Lucas said. "I'll explain."

Reggie's heavy hand set whiskey before Lucas and Benjamin. Lucas stared at the drink as if unable to comprehend its presence. He began to sweat.

"Lucas, drink it."

The voice belonged to a young woman—Hannah Ramos, with carefully styled hair and professional clothes. In this gathering place of the Adapted, Benjamin thought, it was surprising to see someone Unadapted. But then he noticed something about the device she carried. The Solution had been simple—not a sophisticated climate monitor, just a basic air quality reader that she obsessively checked. She sat down at their table.

"Lucas," she said, "drink it. One drink won't trigger your monitor. You need to overcome this fear of even being near alcohol."

She turned to Benjamin. "You're Adapted, but you're new, so you don't know about Lucas. Maybe you can help if you understand. It's all unnecessary. He's not an alcoholic. He didn't need that monitor. It's just an excuse for avoiding alcohol. All of this is because something happened when he was drinking once—just drinking, not drunk.

"I don't remember what happened—it wasn't important. But Lucas has been obsessing about it ever since. I think he believes something terrible will happen if he drinks. That's irrational. Tell him it's irrational."

"Maybe it is," Benjamin said softly. "You could handle the shock if he drank that, and the shock might help you both."

Lucas laughed bitterly. "I feel like doing something dramatic, like throwing these drinks across the room, but I can't bring myself to touch them. Do it for me, will you? Sometimes shock therapy works, but I don't have the courage to administer it to myself."

Before Benjamin could move, Reggie collected both drinks on a tray and moved away. "Just like always. You just stare at drinks. Makes me want to laugh."

Lucas wiped sweat from his palms. Benjamin sat thinking. Hannah checked her air quality monitor, oblivious to them.

"You were explaining," Benjamin said. "You were going to tell me how you plan to Adapt the Unadapted."

"I said we were going to do it. Actually, you will play a greater role than I, Doctor Anderson."

Benjamin sat rigidly.

"You didn't think I wouldn't recognize you? I know some climate psychologists are sensitive about wearing Solutions themselves, but it's a mark of honor. You should be proud of your Adaptation and eager to Adapt others. Very eager."

"What exactly do you mean?" Benjamin already suspected.

Lucas leaned forward. "There's one condition so widespread, a Solution isn't even considered—climate anxiety. Hundreds of people come to your laboratory seeking help, and you turn them away. Suppose you and other Adapted psychologists give everyone who comes to you a Solution?"

Benjamin gestured vaguely. "A psychologist wouldn't distribute Solutions unless absolutely necessary."

"You'll feel differently after you've been Adapted longer. Others have."

Before Benjamin could respond, the heavy-set man from earlier—the other Ramirez—moved past their table. He wore his safety tether system. He had attached one of his lines to Benjamin in the walkway.

Ramirez went to the bar. "Give me a bottle," he demanded of the vacant-eyed Reggie. He returned carrying the bottle, brushing condensation from it. He stopped beside Lucas and glared. Lucas leaned back. Hannah kept checking her monitor.

"You made me fall," Ramirez accused.

Lucas shrugged. "You were unconscious. You never knew it."

Sweat appeared on Ramirez's forehead. "You broke the Code. Don't you think I can imagine how it felt to fall? You bastard!"

Suddenly, Ramirez triggered his tether system. At close range, before the lines could spread properly, the forward lines attached to Lucas, the side lines to their table and floor, and the rear lines to the table behind Benjamin. Ramirez released all lines except those on Lucas, then threw himself backward, dragging Lucas from his chair onto the floor.

Expertly, Ramirez moved forward and looped the lines around Lucas's head and shoulders, then his legs. He crouched beside Lucas and forced the bottle into his gasping mouth, pouring.

Lucas twisted against the restraints in blind terror, choking on whiskey. Ramirez laughed and tilted the bottle more.

Hannah screamed. "The monitor! If you get that much alcohol in his system, it will kill him!" She clutched her air quality reader, staring in horror.

Benjamin struck Ramirez behind the ear. He dropped the bottle and fell sideways. Fear and hatred filled his eyes as he looked up at Benjamin.

Ramirez released his lines and retracted them. He stood unsteadily. "I'm going to kill you," he said, glaring at Benjamin. "You made me fall worse than Lucas did. I'm really going to kill you."

Benjamin wasn't large, but he was strong. He grabbed Ramirez's belt with both hands and lifted him several inches off the floor.

"I could drop you," Benjamin said.

"No!" Ramirez begged. "Please!"

"Then leave." Benjamin set him down.

Ramirez backed away, directly into Reggie's arms. The large waiter closed his hands on Ramirez's shoulders.

"You broke the Code completely," Reggie said. "The texts say something about not harming others, and so does the Code."

"Let him go, Reggie," Lucas choked out, getting to his feet. He wiped his mouth.

"No. No, you're not dead." Benjamin felt excitement building, like when he had first understood a complex system. No, better than that.

"That alcohol didn't kill you, Lucas. Nothing terrible happened. You could find a way to remove that monitor."

Lucas stared at him as if he were insane. "That's different. I'd be helpless without it. Besides, no one ever removes a Solution."

They were all looking at Benjamin. He felt this represented a critical moment. It was up to him which direction things went, at least for these people. "I'm actually in favor of fewer Solutions, not more, Lucas. Look, if I can show you that someone can discard a Solution, would you remove that—if I may use the word—monstrous device?"

Lucas grinned. Benjamin didn't recognize its smugness at the time.

"I'll show you." He removed the neural collar and yanked at the filaments running down his spine. The excitement was running high. He felt the connections snap and come free easily. He threw the Solution on the floor.

"Now," he said, "I'm going out into that storm. There's thunder and lightning out there. I'm afraid, but I can function without a Solution, and so can you."

"You can't! Nobody can!" Lucas screamed after him. He turned to the others. "If he exposes us, the movement is finished. We have to stop him permanently. We have to follow him."

"It's slippery out there," Ramirez whimpered. "I might fall."

Hannah clutched her monitor. "I can't go—the air quality is terrible in the rain."

"Well, there's no alcohol out there, and you can study your texts in the lightning flashes, Reggie. Come on."

Running through the elevated walkways that gleamed with rain, running into the stabbing cold needles of the downpour, Benjamin Anderson realized he was terrified of the lightning.

There is no action without a reason, he knew from old psychology texts. He had chosen the neural collar because he had a latent fear of electrical storms. He could have selected a buoyancy suit or thermal regulator just as easily.

He sneezed. He was soaked through, but he kept running. He didn't know what Lucas and Reggie planned when they caught him. He slipped and fell. He would soon find out.

Reggie said, "We shall make an example."

Benjamin looked up and saw lightning reflected on a thin blade. Benjamin reached toward it more in fascination than fear. He managed to grab Reggie's wrist. He jerked and the knife fell into Benjamin's hand. Pulling himself up using Reggie's arm, he remembered what he must do and slashed at the waiter's face. A cut streaked across Reggie's forehead and blood poured into his eyes. He screamed. "I can't see the texts!"

It was his problem. Benjamin usually solved other people's problems, but now he ran—he couldn't even solve his own.

Benjamin realized he had gone mad as he held the blade overhead, but he did need some kind of lightning rod. Lucas (who was right behind him, gaining) had been right. No one could discard a Solution. He watched the lightning play across the blade and knew that Lucas was going to reach him in the next moment.

He was wrong.

The lightning struck him first.

Reggie squinted under the bandage at the lettering on the door that said ANDERSON & MILLS and opened it. He ran to the man sitting at the desk, reading by lamplight.

"Mr. Mills, your partner, Dr. Anderson, he—"

"Just a moment." Nathan switched on the overhead lights. "What were you saying?"

"Dr. Anderson went out without his Solution in a storm and was struck by lightning. We took him to the hospital morgue. He must have been crazy to go out without his collar."

Nathan stared into his bright desk lamp without blinking. "This is quite a shock. Would you mind leaving? I'll come by later and you can tell me more."

Reggie left. "Yes, sir. Struck by lightning, killed instantly. He must have been crazy to remove his Solution...." The door closed.

Nathan exhaled. Poor Benjamin. But it wasn't the lightning that killed him, of course. Nathan adjusted the sound-dampening implants in his ears, thinking that you did need quite a bit of light to read lips properly. The thunder, naturally, was what had done it. Loud noise—any noise—would do it every time. Too bad Benjamin had never really stopped being one of the Unadapted. Dangerous people. He would have to deal with them.
