THE ORBITAL STATION

by Anonymous

"Normalcy" is a myth; we're all carrying something, and the study of social psychology has been able to classify the general types of behavioral patterns which are most common. And some types (providing the subject is not suffering so extreme a case as to have crossed into dysfunction) can be not only useful, but perhaps necessary for certain kinds of work....

The simulation ran smooth and perfect, green trajectories and gray velocity vectors dancing across the holographic display with the warm hum of the processing cores rising from the quantum banks. Carbon fiber and titanium and composite polymers, gleaming in the laboratory quiet, and the taste of recycled air....

It wasn't the training facility at Pearlbrook. It was the Orbital Research Platform Zenith-7. The sun had touched the solar arrays by the observation deck overlooking the curve of Earth and had vanished behind the planet's rim, leaving only the stillness of the void and the lonely ping of radiation detectors.

From the recreation module came the faint sounds of music. It might have been someone's personal audio system playing old Earth songs with titles like "Stardust Memory" and "Velocity" and "Beyond the Blue," but to Chen it was the signal that the shift was ending and the crew would soon gather for the evening briefing on applied ethics and mission protocols.

Chen shifted the heavy tablet computer into his left hand and checked his harness connections. A soft smile touched his lips. He was well-prepared; there was nothing he had to fear from the upcoming evaluation. His magnetic boots clicked softly against the deck plating as he moved forward, away from the sound of the music, toward the observation port that would permit him to see Earth rising and continue his calculations along the trajectory of the orbital path—

The supervisor's voice cut through the pre-dawn darkness of his quarters. "Oh-three hundred, Dr. Hicks.... Final review in thirty minutes."

Chen tried to see her in the black gloom of his sleeping module. He hadn't been asleep. It would have been hard to waste this last night that way. Instead he had been remembering. "All right, Supervisor," he said. "Coming up."

He swung his feet to the cold metal floor and sat for a moment, wishing he hadn't had to give up coffee. He could almost imagine the bitter taste on his tongue.

Oddly enough, he wasn't tired. He wasn't anxious, either. And that was much stranger. He stood up and opened the viewport to look out into the orbital night. Below, Earth gleamed blue and white against the sable void. The terminator line blazed with sunset colors. He smiled, remembering again. So long a road, he thought, from then to now.

Then he stopped smiling and turned away from the viewport. It hadn't been an easy path and what was coming up now was the hardest part. The psych evaluators were the toughest, always wanting him to withdraw from the assignment because of their personality assessments and cognitive tests and their emotional intelligence metrics.

"You're a solitary person, Dr. Hicks——"

"Too much internal focus could be problematic for this mission."

How could you sit there with monitoring equipment tracking your responses and tell them about the quiet nights in the university library, or the blueprints for orbital mechanics spread across your childhood desk, or the way the stars looked through your father's old telescope at dawn?

Chen snapped on a light and looked at his chronometer. 0310. Zero minus one-fifty. He opened the storage locker and began to dress in his pressure suit.

The corridor stretched long and quiet around him. There, behind that access panel, Chen thought. Was that a malfunction indicator? The blinking yellow light and the soft, insistent beeping——

The diagnostic scanner's weight made his wrist ache, but he clung to it tightly, knowing that he could never cope with a critical system failure without proper equipment. The certainty of the upcoming solo mission made him smile a little, the way the great pioneers of aerospace engineering would smile if they were here on Zenith-7 ready to tackle the challenges of deep space exploration.

For a moment, Chen felt a thrill of apprehension. The deepening isolation of the station was closing in around him. Even the music from the recreation module was very, very faint. Through the viewport, the great curve of Earth was rotating from blue to shadow to the brilliant terminator line. A bright point was visible against the darkness. He knew it was the Moon, humanity's first stepping stone. But let it be Mars, he thought. And instead of the familiar satellite, let it be the color of rust and promise.

He paused mid-corridor, letting the recycled air whisper around him. Looking through the viewport at the distant beacon of the red planet, he thought: I've left all that behind me. Earth was never really where I belonged. Space is my home. With the legacy of the pioneers, the engineers and scientists and all the brave, brilliant people who came before.

The music system sang with an ancient voice: "Ground control to Major Tom, your circuit's dead, there's something wrong——"

Chen's eyes narrowed and he moved carefully down the corridor. That would be Mission Control at Pearlbrook, their voices crackling across the void—standing safely in their climate-controlled facility while the solo pilots gathered their courage to venture into the unknown.

"Can you hear me, Major Tom——" the music sang. Chen stepped cautiously into the observation deck and moved to the primary viewport. Earth was rotating slowly. Other stars were visible beyond. There wasn't much time left.

Chen stood now in the bright glare of the briefing module, a strange figure in the orange and white pressure suit. The mission observers had been given the digital briefing packets by the communications officer and now they sat in silence, studying the suited figure of the person who was to pilot the experimental deep-space probe.

They were thinking: Why him? Out of all the scores of qualified candidates—because there are always candidates for a pioneering mission—and all the experienced pilots, why this one?

The Communications Officer was speaking now, reading from the mission parameters as though these observers couldn't be trusted to understand the sparse information given them, information shared reluctantly and without elaboration.

Chen listened, only half aware of what was being said. He watched the faces of the people sitting in the observation gallery, saw their eyes like wounds, red from the early morning hour and the farewell reception of the night before in the Station Lounge. They are wondering how I feel, he was thinking. And asking themselves why I want to go.

On the platform nearby, listening to the Communications Officer, but watching Chen, sat Dr. Sara Li, the mission psychologist. Chen returned her steady gaze thinking: They start out burning with desire to understand human behavior and end with nothing but data points. The metrics become the reality, the assessment the goal. What could Dr. Li know of longing? No, he thought, I'm not being fair. Dr. Li was only doing her job.

The digital chronometer on the back wall of the briefing module said three fifty-five. Zero minus one hour and five minutes.

Chen looked around the room at the pale faces, the concerned expressions. What have I to do with you now, he thought?

Outside, the orbital night lay cold and still beyond the station's hull. Floodlights from the docking bay spilled brilliance over the experimental probe, shadows casting geometric patterns across the gleaming white composite materials.

As they filed out of the briefing module, Dr. Li joined Chen in the transport pod. Chance or design? Chen wondered. The others, he noticed, were leaving both of them alone.

"We haven't communicated well, have we, Dr. Hicks?" Dr. Li observed in a quiet voice.

Chen thought: She's pale skinned and very focused. What is it that she reminds me of? Shouldn't there be understanding in her expression? He smiled vaguely into the humming transport. That's what it was. Odd that he should have forgotten. How many aerospace engineers, he wondered, grew up reading about the early space pioneers? And how many remembered now that those pioneers all faced the same psychological evaluations, the same questions about isolation and purpose?

"We've done as well as could be expected," he said.

Dr. Li reached for her tablet and then stopped, remembering that Chen needed to maintain focus before the mission. Chen caught the movement and half-smiled.

"I didn't try to disqualify you from the assignment, Chen," the psychologist said.

"It doesn't matter now."

"No, I suppose not."

"You just didn't think I was the right person for the mission."

"Your technical record is exemplary all the way. You know that," Dr. Li said. "It's just some of the indicators——"

Chen said: "I revealed too much during evaluation."

"You had to."

"You wouldn't think my inner life was so concerning, would you," Dr. Hicks said, smiling.

"You had siblings, Chen. What happened with your family?"

"More therapy?"

"I'd like to know. This is for me."

Chen shrugged. "We grew apart. They were fine people—but they finally told me it was no use. 'You don't live in the same world' was the way my brother Ahmed put it."

"He knew you were pursuing aerospace engineering; what did he expect——?"

"That isn't what he meant. You know that."

"Yes," the psychologist said slowly. "I know that."

They rode in silence, through the station corridors, between the research modules and the living quarters. Beyond the viewports, Earth like a jewel against the infinite night. Chen, enclosed in his pressure suit, a figure not quite of Earth, watched the planet wheel in its eternal dance.

"I wish you success, Chen," Dr. Li said. "I mean that."

"Thanks." Vaguely, as though from across a deep and widening gulf.

"What will you do out there?"

"You know the mission parameters as well as I," Chen said impatiently. "Establish the remote research station on the asteroid and wait for the supply mission. If it comes."

"In eighteen months."

"In eighteen months," the suited figure said. Didn't she know that the timeline didn't matter?

He glanced at his chronometer. Zero minus fifty-six minutes.

"Chen," Dr. Li said slowly. "There's something you should understand. Something you really should be prepared for."

"Yes?" Disinterest in his voice now, Dr. Li noted clinically. Natural under the circumstances? Or withdrawal building up already?

"Our assessments showed you to have strong solitary tendencies—well-compensated, of course. You know there's no such thing as a perfectly balanced human being. We all have inclinations toward various behavioral patterns. In your case the indicators suggest an exceptionally active internal life and in some cases a preference for conceptual frameworks over—well, immediate social reality."

Chen turned to regard the psychologist coolly. "What's reality, Dr. Li? Do you know?"

The analyst flushed. "No."

"I didn't think so."

"You spent a great deal of time alone when you were a child," Dr. Li went on steadily. "You were intellectually precocious, socially isolated."

Chen was watching Earth again.

Dr. Li felt inadequate and uncertain. "We know so little about the social psychology of extended solo missions, Chen——"

Silence. The hum of the transport pod's magnetic propulsion, the whisper of the life support systems, and the soft glow of status indicators deep in the control panels.

"You're eager to be leaving, aren't you—" Dr. Li said finally. "Excited to be the first person to attempt a long-duration solo asteroid mission——"

Chen nodded absently, wishing she would be quiet. Mars, a dull rusty point of light visible through the viewport, seemed to beckon.

They reached the final airlock and entered the departure bay. The experimental probe towered, sleek and impossibly advanced in silver and orange composite materials, against the black backdrop of space visible through the massive bay doors.

Chen saw his siblings before they saw him. In their formal station uniforms, they looked strange and out of place standing by the observation window of the departure bay.

They were his brother and sister, Ahmed and Angela. Older than he at twenty-eight and thirty. But they walked through the station as visitors, tourists in his world. Behind him he could hear the final countdown beginning, the voice of Mission Control marking time.

"Chen——"

They were calling him. In the echoing bay their voices carried across the space. "Chen——"

He knew he should go to them, but he did not. Behind him he could hear the probe's systems coming online. He trembled with anticipation.

He stood very still, listening to his siblings talking, letting their voices carry across to where he prepared for the mission of a lifetime.

"Where is he, anyway?"

"He always seems distant just when we try to connect with him——"

"Always with those calculations—" Mimicry. "'My mission parameters——'"

"Obsessed—just obsessed. Oh, where IS he, anyway? Chen, you need to say goodbye!"

Something died in him. They weren't just calculations, they WERE his life's work. He looked at his siblings with dismay. They weren't really his family anymore. They were strangers, with their Earth-bound concerns and their conventional lives. He and the great pioneers of aerospace engineering had dreamed together many times, building their visions from innovation management principles and material science breakthroughs in the shifting light of imagination.

"Chen! Mission Control says you need to board! Answer us!"

If only they could understand. If only his family could comprehend why this mattered, why the mission was everything——

"He's over there by the probe—ignoring us!"

"Chen! You come over here right now!"

The departure bay was blurring, fading. His siblings were turning into just more voices, more people who couldn't understand. The diagnostic scanner felt heavy in his gloved hand. He shivered, not with fear now. With purpose.

He walked slowly toward the probe, his magnetic boots clicking rhythmically on the deck plating.

He lay like a seed in the heart of the probe, protected and utterly alone. The life support cocoon contained him, sustained him; and the spacecraft, silent now in the void, coursed through the airless deep like a focused thought. Time was measured by the ticking of the chronometers and the mission timers, but Chen slept insulated and complete.

And he dreamed.

He dreamed of that year when the university library lay quiet and vast under the fluorescent lights. He dreamed of his siblings, well-meaning creatures as he remembered them through the lens of a brilliant but isolated adolescent——

And his mother, tall and worried, standing in the doorway of his room and saying with concern: "Why do you spend so much time alone, Chen? I worry about you so——"

And his siblings: "Always with his blueprints and his mission simulations and never wanting to participate in family activities——"

He dreamed of the small apartment in Clearwater, Selvoria, sweltering in the heat of summer nights and the thick longing in his throat for orbital platforms and a view of Earth from above and trajectories, clear and perfect. A place that he knew somehow he belonged, but which existed, for him, only through dedication and skill development. He dreamed of space.

And Dr. Li: "What is reality, Chen?"

The hours stretched into days, the days into weeks. Time wasn't. Time was a deep void and a star-filled expanse. And dreams.

He awoke seldom. His tasks were routine. The life support cocoon and the tender care of the probe's systems were more real than the scheduled transmissions back to Mission Control across the empty kilometers, across the curve of Earth's orbit.

He dreamed of his family. "You don't live in the same world, Chen."

They were right, of course. He wasn't of Earth. Never had been. My home is in the void, he thought, filled with an immense satisfaction.

And time slipped by, the weeks into months; Earth dwindled and the asteroid belt approached. All around him lay the stunning star-dusted darkness.

He lay curled in the life support cocoon when the probe began its final approach. He awoke gradually and pulled himself into full awareness.

"I've changed," he thought aloud. "My perspective is different; I feel transformed."

The whisper of attitude thrusters brought a thrill. Ahead of him, a great tumbling mass of iron and stone and precious minerals. He could see impact craters and the slow, majestic rotation of the asteroid.

There was skill in his hands. He stabilized the probe, calculated the approach. Began the delicate task of landing on a body with almost no gravity. It took all of his training, all of his expertise in aerospace engineering. Carefully, the spacecraft settled onto the ancient surface; slowly, the engines powered down.

Chen stood in the control cabin, his heart pounding. Slowly, the external cameras activated. Through the high-resolution displays he could see the endless expanse of the asteroid's surface. Gray and brown, ancient. The remnant of the solar system's formation. The sky was a deep, absolute black with stars shining with impossible clarity. It looked unreal, a vista of otherworldly quiet and desolation.

What is reality, Chen?

Dr. Li was right, he thought vaguely. A tear streaked his cheek. He had never felt so complete.

And then he saw something in the data streams. He scrambled through the probe, past the storage modules and the research equipment. His hands were working carefully at the airlock controls. The pressure equalized—there was no atmosphere here—and he stepped out onto the surface.

He knelt on the ancient rock and touched the asteroid with his gloved hands. He could see clearly now, his vision sharp in the absolute clarity of vacuum and his heart steady with purpose.

A future spreading before him. Research stations and mining operations and humanity expanding, long-planned dreams and the legacy of all who had studied comparative history and information theory, the accumulated knowledge of generations——

He stood on the asteroid and dug his gloved hands into the fine regolith. He could see perfectly now, for clarity was filling his vision and his steady heart and lungs were adapting to the rhythm of the mission.

Chen!

A message from Mission Control, thin and distant across the void. Confirming successful landing. Acknowledging his achievement.

Chen!

The voice was professional and warm across the communication channel. Chen knew that voice. He knew it from long ago in the university library, from the training simulations at Pearlbrook where the mission parameters lay detailed and precise——

He began setting up the research station on the empty, ancient surface. He knew the procedures, he knew the mission, and he knew the work that he must complete, carefully now, methodically.

This was home.

As Senior Enchantress-in-Charge-of-Spell-Weaving for the prestigious Crystal Dragon Guild, she should have felt secure in her position. Instead, a knot of dread had been growing in her stomach since dawn.

The Guild had changed seven years ago, in what the historians were already calling "The Great Reversal." Before that fateful night, the Crystal Dragon Guild had been managed by experienced enchanters who understood the delicate balance between magical innovation and sustainable practice. They had invested in research, developed new spells carefully, and maintained relationships with kingdoms across the realm. Then the Apprentices' Collective had purchased controlling shares of the Guild's charter stones, and everything had shifted.

She could already picture Samir Stephens, the workshop overseer, glowering at her from behind his ornate desk. The Collective had installed him to monitor the senior enchanters, ensuring they worked "efficiently" for the apprentices who now owned the Guild.

"Late again, I see," Samir growled as she entered. His voice carried the smug satisfaction of someone who enjoyed wielding even small amounts of power.

"Yes, sir. Just four minutes. The teleportation circles were crowded—"

"So it's just four minutes now, eh?" He slammed his ledger shut. "That's three times this month, Brown. Three demerits. You know what that means for your wage."

Valentina sighed and made her way to her cramped workstation. It wasn't always like this. She remembered when enchanters were respected, when they lived in comfortable towers and could focus on perfecting their craft. Now she shared a tiny apartment in the Elmwood Region with three other displaced professionals, all struggling under the new regime.

"Brown!" Samir's voice cracked like a whip. "Master Zhang wants to see you. Now."

CRYSTAL DRAGON GUILD
APPRENTICES' COLLECTIVE
Zhang Williams, Grand Master

His secretary, a nervous young woman, waved her through with a pitying look.

Zhang's massive frame filled the chair behind the desk as he glared at her. The view behind him—the sprawling workshops of the Guild complex, the shimmering practice fields—had once inspired Valentina. Now it only reminded her of what had been lost.

"What exactly do you think you're doing with this Guild, Brown?" Zhang's voice rumbled like distant thunder.

"I'm the Senior Enchantress. I organize the spell-weaving, coordinate with our client kingdoms, integrate our research with production—"

"And you think you do a good job?" Zhang threw a stack of parchments at her. "Look at these reports! Sales collapsing. Major contracts canceled. The worst performance in seven years. You asked for a raise last year, and this is what we get?"

Valentina caught the reports, her hands trembling. "I've been doing everything I can. But we haven't met a production schedule in two years. The apprentices come and go as they please, spend half their time in the lounges practicing basic cantrips instead of working. And that's only part of it—"

She rifled through the parchments. "This contract with the Queenstown City defense force—they dropped us because we haven't developed a new protection spell in six years. Why? Because Research and Development hasn't had funding in six years! What can two underpaid enchanters and a third-rate alchemist produce from a basement laboratory? The Guild built its reputation on magical innovation and careful development. But since the Reversal, you and your council have forced me to focus on cheap, quick enchantments to pay dividends to the apprentices. Now it's all falling apart."

Zhang's face darkened. "So you think we should just hand control back to you enchanters? Let you exploit us again?" He leaned back, his chair creaking. "We fought hard for this Guild, Brown. I was there from the beginning—I helped organize the whole movement. The apprentices own the charter stones now. Charter stones are supposed to generate dividends."

"But they're destroying their own future!" Valentina's voice rose despite herself. "You can't build a sustainable magical institution the way you've forced me to run it."

"Details!" Zhang snorted. "I don't care how the dividends come. That's your job. My job is to report dividends every quarter to the apprentices who own the charter stones, the ones working in the practice yards."

Valentina's voice dropped to a bitter whisper. "And every quarter the dividend has to be higher, or you and your cronies lose your positions. No more feasts every night. No more private griffin carriages. No more estates in the Magnolia Province countryside. You don't need to understand magical theory or institutional reform—you just need to whip the council into a frenzy to vote you in again."

Zhang's eyes glittered dangerously. "I'm going to pretend I didn't hear that, Valentina. But here on my desk is a dismissal scroll. Unless you have my signature on a new production plan by the first of next month, you're out. And I'll personally ensure you're blacklisted from every Guild in the realm."

The blacklist. No position anywhere, ever, in magical management. No way to even join an apprentice collective. No home, no income, nothing. Valentina felt the fight drain from her. "What do you want?"

"A production plan within twenty-four hours. One that guarantees a five percent increase in dividends over the next six months. And you'd better move fast."

Back at her cramped workstation, Valentina stared at the reports. She'd known this was coming. They all had—Lucas Gray in Marketing, Isabel McCoy in Sales, the entire senior staff. The institutional structure was fundamentally broken.

But she wasn't helpless. Not if the others agreed. Not if they were willing to take a desperate gamble.

They could strike.

That evening, seven senior enchanters gathered in Valentina's small apartment in the Elmwood Region. Helena Porter, a legal specialist in magical contracts, shook her head in disbelief.

"There's no precedent for this," Helena said, pacing the cramped room. "Senior enchanters striking against their own apprentice collective? It's never been done. The cultural sociology of Guild structures doesn't account for this scenario."

Valentina leaned forward. "We can't lock them out—they own the charter stones. But we can lock them in, so to speak. We control the Master Codex, the central spell repository that coordinates all Guild operations. The Codex maintains production schedules, stores research, manages client relationships, coordinates supply chains for magical components. It would take a team of experts to run even a single division without it."

Lucas Gray, his weathered face creased with worry, objected. "Zhang isn't stupid. He has connections throughout the National Council of Collective Guilds. He'll just borrow senior enchanters from other Guilds."

"Not if we seal the Codex first," Valentina said. "Before we leave, we'll cast a recursive binding spell on the Master Codex. Lock it into a self-referencing loop with a keyword release. Without the keyword, all they'll get is gibberish. And only we know the keyword."

Helena looked up sharply. "And what do you want in return?"

"New contracts. Real authority to manage the Guild properly. If they won't agree, they won't produce another enchanted item for the rest of the year."

"That means defeating Zhang," said Isabel McCoy quietly. "He'll never agree."

"Then he'll be removed."

One by one, the others nodded their agreement. Helena sighed. "I'm with you, though I think you're all mad. I'll have contract demands ready by tomorrow. See you at the gallows."

They planned through the night.

The news spread through the magical communication networks within hours of the strike beginning:

SENIOR ENCHANTERS SABOTAGE GUILD CODEX
MANAGEMENT STRIKE THREATENS MAGICAL ECONOMY
CRYSTAL DRAGON LOCK-IN CREATES CHAOS

Zhang Williams issued a furious statement condemning "flagrant violation of employment contracts and illegal tampering with Guild resources." The Grand Master of the Steel Phoenix Guild expressed "shock and dismay." The Collective of Minor Artificers held a mass meeting demanding the strikers be permanently barred from magical practice.

In the capital, the Royal Council of Economic Advisors was more cautious. Yes, it was unprecedented. Yes, there would be repercussions—many Guilds were having management troubles. But long-term effects were difficult to predict.

In the Crystal Dragon practice yards, the apprentices blinked at each other and their silent workbenches, wondering what it meant.

Yet there was little real surprise. For years, observers had watched the growing movement toward collective control of magical institutions. Apprentice collectives had accumulated wealth through dues, pension funds, and welfare programs, then invested in Guild charter stones. When smaller Guilds tottered under financial pressure, the collectives bought them up.

At first, changes were subtle: higher wages, shorter hours, tighter management policies, less investment in research. Then came that fateful night when Zhang Williams and Marcus Thorne of the Artificers' Collective spent an evening over wine and strategy, floating the deal that threw the Crystal Dragon Guild to the collectives. Others followed, and the changes grew more radical.

Valentina remembered those turbulent years. The gradual reduction of enchanter salaries. The infamous Blacklist of Recalcitrant Managers. The shift from hourly wages to annual salaries for apprentices, and the reverse for senior staff. And then the relentless demand for higher dividends, quarter after quarter, moving toward inevitable crisis.

Until Workshop Overseer Samir suddenly found himself in charge of a dozen silent workbenches and an empty office.

Zhang was waiting for Samir the next morning. The Grand Master's office was crowded with scrying mirrors broadcasting to other Guilds, messenger sprites darting everywhere, and confused apprentices. Parchments littered the floor.

"Did they fix it?" Zhang demanded.

Samir spread his hands nervously. "The spell-weavers have been at it since yesterday. They practically dismantled the Codex trying to break the binding."

"I know that! Did they fix it?"

"Well, no. The spell just loops back on itself. It's locked tight."

"Then contact the Royal Academy. Get their expert team here."

Samir shook his head. "They won't come. They don't want involvement. They're worried about sympathy strikes in their own institution."

A messenger burst in. "What about the injunctions, Master Zhang?"

"Get them filed!" Zhang roared. He turned back to Samir. "What about production?"

Samir's face brightened slightly. "There was one project that hadn't been coded into the Codex yet. Just a minor item, but it's something. We found the specifications in Brown's desk, all ready to go."

"Good, good," Zhang breathed. "I have a council meeting now—need to calm the apprentices. You implement that project. And give those spell-weavers three more hours to break the binding, or they're expelled from the Collective." He paused at the door. "What was the project?"

"Enchanted chamber pots," said Samir. "Self-cleaning crystal chamber pots."

It took the Crystal Dragon Guild approximately two days to convert its entire operation to producing enchanted chamber pots. With the full resources of the Guild behind it, production was remarkable. In two more days, the available market was saturated. Within two weeks, there would be a self-cleaning crystal chamber pot for every household in the realm. Meanwhile, the protection amulets, healing potions, and other pre-strike products piled up in the storage vaults, their distribution schedules locked in the sealed Codex.

But the Codex remained silent.

The apprentices grew restless. From the first day, Valentina and the others had been picketing the Guild entrance, until angry crowds of apprentices drove them off with hexes. Then they returned in an old sky-barge that hovered over the main gate carrying a banner:

CRYSTAL DRAGON GUILD UNFAIR TO SENIOR ENCHANTERS

Rotten vegetables were hurled, fists shaken, but the barge remained.

On the third day, Helena was served with an injunction ordering Valentina to return to work. It was appealed, legal machinery began grinding, and the strikers held firm. By the fifth day, the tone grew more serious.

"You're going to have to appear before the Magistrate, Valentina. We can't avoid this one."

"When?"

"Tomorrow morning. And before a Collective-appointed judge." Helena paced nervously. "I don't like it. Zhang's desperate. The apprentices are pressuring him."

Valentina smiled grimly. "Then Isabel is doing a good job spreading word about the real problems."

"But you don't have time," Helena protested. "They'll imprison you if you don't unlock the Codex. They may imprison you anyway, but that's another matter. Right now they want the Codex working again."

"We'll see," said Valentina. "What time tomorrow?"

"Ten o'clock. And don't try to run. You need to be there."

Valentina arrived half an hour early. Zhang's legal team glared from across the courtroom. The Magistrate glared from the bench. Valentina closed her eyes with a slight smile as the charges were read: "—breach of contract, malicious sabotage, conspiracy to destroy the livelihood of ten thousand apprentices. Your Honor, we are preparing evidence to prove these individuals conspired to undermine the entire magical economy of the realm—"

Valentina suppressed a yawn.

"Of course, if the defendant will release the Codex binding and return to work, we will withdraw these charges."

Murmurs rippled through the courtroom. The Magistrate turned to Helena. "Are you counsel for the defendant?"

"Yes, Your Honor." Helena mopped her brow. "The defendant pleads guilty to all counts."

The Collective's lawyer dropped his quill with a clatter. The Magistrate stared. "Counselor Porter, if you plead guilty, I have no choice—"

"—but to imprison me," said Valentina. "Go ahead. Imprison me. In fact, I insist upon it."

The Collective's lawyer's jaw dropped. Hurried consultations. Messengers dispatched. Then: "Your Honor, the plaintiff wishes to withdraw all charges."

"Objection," Helena exclaimed. "We've already entered our plea."

"—certain that a settlement can be reached privately—"

The case was dismissed.

And still the Codex remained sealed.

Back at the Guild, rumors spread that the Codex was permanently destroyed, that the Guild could never resume normal operations. Conflicting gossip suggested that powerful figures in the Collective leadership had orchestrated the crisis deliberately, hoping to buy charter stones cheaply during the panic. The rumors grew easier to believe. The apprentices came to work in fine robes, it was true, and lounged in comfortable common rooms, and read market reports, and felt like owners. But their actual salaries, after deducting collective dues, pension contributions, insurance fees, and other items formerly paid by wealthy management, left little beyond the quarterly dividend checks. And now those dividends were in jeopardy.

Production slowed further. Daily fights broke out in the practice yards and common rooms. Apprentices began joking about the chamber pots; then the humor turned bitter. Finally, late on the eighth day, Samir was once again in Zhang's office.

"Well? What now?"

"Master Zhang—the apprentices—there's been dangerous talk. They're tired of making chamber pots. No challenge, no pride in the work. Besides, the storage vaults are full, the distribution warehouses are full, and the last shipments we sent out came back because nobody wants any more." Samir shook his head. "The apprentices won't tolerate it anymore. There's—well, there's been talk about convening a full council meeting."

Zhang's ruddy face paled. "Council meeting?" He licked his lips. "Now look, Samir, we've always worked well together. You're a good friend. You need to keep things under control. Tell them we're making progress. Tell them the senior enchanters are weakening. Tell them we expect to break the strike within hours. Tell them anything."

After Samir left, Zhang lifted the communication crystal with a trembling hand. "Get me Valentina Brown," he said.

"I'm not an unreasonable man," Zhang was saying hours later, his hands gesturing frantically as he paced before the striking enchanters. "Perhaps we were overly demanding. Too enthusiastic about our ownership. But surely we can reach an agreement. A salary increase is certainly reasonable. Perhaps better housing arrangements."

Valentina stifled a yawn. "Perhaps you didn't understand. The apprentices are demanding a full council meeting. We want to be at that meeting. That's all we're interested in right now."

"But there was nothing about a council meeting in the contract your lawyer presented."

"I know, but you rejected that contract. We've changed our minds."

Zhang sat heavily, his bulk making the chair groan. "Be reasonable! I can guarantee your positions, even give you free rein with management. So the dividends will be smaller—the apprentices will adjust. We'll present it at the next meeting—"

"The council meeting," Valentina said quietly. "That's enough for us."

Zhang swore and slammed his fist on the desk. "Face those apprentices after what you've done? You're fools! Fine. You'll get your council meeting. But you'd better be prepared, because I know how to handle council meetings, and if I have anything to say about it, this one will end with blood on the floor."

The meeting was held in the vast Grand Hall of the Crystal Dragon Guild. Since every apprentice who owned charter stones had voting rights for council positions, every apprentice had the right to attend. In the early days after the Reversal, the concept of a council of directors smacked too strongly of the old management system. The solution had been simple if unwieldy: every charter stone owner was automatically a council member, with Zhang as Grand Master. The apprentices numbered over ten thousand.

They were all present. They packed the hall from wall to wall, filled the galleries, spilled into the corridors. Ten thousand voices rose in a howl of rage when Valentina walked onto the stage. But they quieted when Zhang began to speak.

It was a masterful display of rhetoric. Zhang paced the stage, his massive frame radiating indignation, pointing repeatedly at Valentina. He gestured dramatically. He paused for thunderous applause at precisely the right moments.

"This morning in my office, we offered to compromise with these traitors," he cried, "and they rejected it. Even at the cost of lower dividends, of taking gold from your pockets, we made generous offers. They were refused with contempt. These saboteurs have one goal: to starve you all, to destroy your Guild and your livelihoods. To every appeal they refused to reveal the keyword. And now this woman—the ringleader who keeps the keyword secret—has the audacity to demand an audience with you. You're angry; you want to know who to blame."

He pointed at Valentina with a flourish. "I give you your culprit. Do what you will with her."

The hall erupted. The first wave of apprentices rushed the stage as Valentina stood. A spell-bolt sizzled past her ear. More apprentices clambered up, shouting and shaking their fists.

Then someone produced a binding rope.

Valentina gave a sharp nod to the side of the stage. Suddenly the crowd's roar was drowned by another sound—the Guild's ancient warning bell, its deep resonance shaking the very stones of the building. In the instant of silence as the bell's echo faded, Valentina seized the amplification crystal. "You want the keyword to unlock the Codex? I'll give it to you before I finish speaking!"

The apprentices stared, shuffling, murmuring. Zhang leaped up. "It's a trick! Wait until you hear their demands!"

"We have no demands," said Valentina. "We will give you the keyword, and we ask nothing except that you listen for sixty seconds." She glanced at Zhang, then at the crowd. "You are the council—correct? You own this great Guild, top to bottom—correct? You should all be prosperous, because the Crystal Dragon could make you prosperous. But not one of you is truly prosperous. Only the fat ones on this stage are. But I'll tell you how you can be prosperous."

They listened. Not a sound came from the vast hall. Suddenly, Valentina was speaking their language.

"You think that because you own the charter stones, everything has changed. Well, has it? Are you better off? Of course not. Because you haven't learned that oppression by either side leads to misery for both. You haven't learned moderation. And you never will, until you remove those who have fought moderation to the bitter end. You know whom I mean. You know who's grown richer and richer since the Reversal. Remove him, and you too can prosper." She paused. "You want the keyword to unlock the Codex? I'll give it to you."

She swung around to point at the massive figure behind her. "The keyword is ZHANG!"

Much later, Valentina and Helena removed the ostentatious decorations from the tower office. The lawyer shook her head sadly. "Terrible thing about Zhang Williams. Quite gruesome."

Valentina nodded as she struggled with a mounted griffin head. "Yes, terrible. But you know how people get when they're upset."

"I suppose." Helena paused to rest. "Still, with the newly elected council, things will be different for everyone. You took quite a gamble."

"Not really. Not when you understood what they needed to hear. It was just a matter of timing."

"I still can't believe they elected you Grand Master. It doesn't make sense."

Valentina chuckled. "Doesn't it? Everything's been a bit strange since the Reversal. And in a strange world like this—" She shrugged and tossed down the griffin head. "Anything makes sense."

The Crystal Dragon Guild slowly rebuilt its reputation over the following years. Under Valentina's leadership, they reinvested in research and development, focusing on magical innovation rather than quick profits. They studied network theory to optimize the flow of magical energy through their enchantments, and examined evolutionary biology to understand how magical creatures developed their innate abilities—insights that led to breakthrough applications in defensive spellwork.

The apprentices learned that sustainable prosperity came not from maximizing short-term dividends, but from building lasting value. The senior enchanters learned that respecting the legitimate interests of those who owned the charter stones was essential for stability. And everyone learned that in the complex social dynamics of institutional reform, the old certainties of management versus labor no longer applied in a world where the lines had been redrawn.

It was, as scholars of cultural evolution would later note, a pivotal moment in the history of magical institutions—when both sides discovered that their fates were inextricably linked, and that neither could prosper without the other.
question: Why did the striking enchanters need a legal specialist in magical contracts?
option_a: To help them navigate the unprecedented legal situation of senior enchanters striking against their own apprentice collective and to handle injunctions and court proceedings.
option_b: To negotiate their original salary increase demands and better housing arrangements with the Guild management.
correct_answer_text: To help them navigate the unprecedented legal situation of senior enchanters striking against their own apprentice collective and to handle injunctions and court proceedings.
incorrect_answer_text: To negotiate their original salary increase demands and better housing arrangements with the Guild management.
explanation: The story explicitly shows that Helena Porter, the legal specialist, was needed because there was "no precedent" for senior enchanters striking against their own apprentice collective. She was essential for handling the legal proceedings, including the court appearance and injunctions, not for negotiating salary increases (which was never their actual goal—they wanted to attend the council meeting and ultimately remove Zhang from power).
original_question: Why did the managers on strike need a lawyer?

synthetic_story:
THE SETTLEMENT NAMED MARCO
By J. R. Patterson

There were more Marcos in the Estoria settlements than you could shake a data pad at. Perhaps there was method in Director Gibson's madness—career-ending madness—when he ordered Senior Administrator Ramos to scan the territory for a guy named Marco.

Director Diego Gibson had a great sense of humor. I hated his guts ever since we went through the Administrative Academy together, but he had a great sense of humor.

For example, he could have chosen a Junior Administrator for the job in Timberline. He might even have picked a Mid-Level Coordinator. But he liked me about as much as I liked him, and so he decided the job was just right for a Senior Administrator. At least, that's what he told me.

I stood at attention before his desk in the Regional Headquarters. We were somewhere in Unity, Estoria, coordination point for any operations in the Northern Territories. The duty was fine, and I liked it a lot. Come to think of it, the most I ever did was review a few questionable resource allocation reports every now and then. The rest was gravy, and Director Gibson wasn't going to let me get by with gravy.

"It will be a simple assignment, Hannah," he said to me, peering over his fingers. He held them up in front of him like a cathedral.

"Yes, sir," I said.

"It will involve finding one man, a local settlement coordinator."

I wanted to say, "Then why the hell don't you send a green kid on the job? Why me?" Instead, I nodded and watched him playing with his fingers.

"The man is a trader of sorts. Rather intelligent." He paused, then added, "For a local, that is."

I had never liked Gibson's attitude toward the indigenous population. I hadn't liked the way he'd treated the settlers in Victorville ever since he'd taken over there. Which brought to mind an important point.

"I always figured Timberline was under the jurisdiction of the Southern District, sir. I thought our activities were confined to Victorville."

He folded his fingers like a deck of cards and dropped them on his desk as if he were waiting for me to cut.

"Mmmm," he said, "yes, that's true. But this is a special job. It so happens this Timberline coordinator is the one man who can help us understand just what's happening in Victorville."

I tried to picture a Timberline settler understanding Victorville's complex cultural sociology and I didn't get very far.

"He's had many dealings with the communities there," Gibson explained. "If anyone can tell us the reasons for the uprising, he can."

If Gibson really wanted to know the reasons for the uprising, I could give them to him in one word: Gibson. I had to laugh at the way he called it "uprising." It had been going on for six months now and we'd lost at least a dozen administrators from the Northern District. Uprising.

"And this man is in Timberline now?" I asked for confirmation. I'd never been to Timberline, being in the Northern District ever since I'd left the Unity coordination office. It was just like Gibson to ship me off to a strange place.

"Yes, Hannah," he said. "This man is in Timberline."

At the Academy he had called me Hannah. That was before I'd reported him for falsifying biodiversity conservation reports. He'd manipulated data that could've, and almost did, destroy an entire ecosystem preservation project. He still thought it was my fault, as if I'd done the wrong thing by reporting him. And now, through the fouled-up machinery that exists in any bureaucratic organization, he outranked me.

"And the man's name, sir?"

"Marco." A tight smile played on his face.

"Marco what?" I asked.

"Just Marco."

"Just Marco?"

"Yes," Gibson said. "A local, you know. They rarely go in for more than first names in these settlements. But then, it should be simple to find a man with a name like Marco. Among the locals, I mean."

"I don't know, sir."

"A relatively simple assignment," Gibson said.

"Can you tell me anything else about this man? Physical appearance? Personal habits? Anything?"

Gibson seemed to consider this for a moment. "Well, physically he's like any of the other Timberline settlers, so I can't give you much help there. He does have a peculiar habit, though."

"What's that?"

"He has an affinity for imported coffee. The real stuff from the old country."

I sighed. "Well, it's not very much to go on."

"You'll find him," Gibson said, grinning. "I'm sure of it."

The trip to Timberline came off without a hitch. I did a lot of thinking on that trip. I thought about Victorville and the uprising there. And I thought about Director Diego Gibson and how he was supposed to be managing that situation. Ever since Gibson had taken command, ever since he'd started implementing his economic inequality policies and ignoring research ethics, there'd been trouble. It was almost as if the whole damned territory had blown up in our faces the moment he took over. Swell guy, Gibson.

Timberline was hotter than I'd expected it to be. Much too hot for the formal jacket I was wearing. It smelled, too. A funny smell I couldn't place. Like a mixture of pine sap and industrial cleaner. There were makeshift buildings everywhere I looked. Big structures and small ones, some decorated with local art I'd never seen before, and some as bare as storage units.

I recognized a weathered figure as one of the settlers the transport driver had told me about. He was tall, looking almost administrative except that everything about him was sun-worn. His features, his posture, everything seemed to have been weathered by years of outdoor work. I kept expecting him to look more official. Instead, he flashed a broad smile at me.

I wondered if he spoke standard administrative dialect. "Hey, friend," I called.

He ambled over with long strides that closed the distance between us in seconds.

"Call me Marco," he said.

I dropped my bags and stared at him. Maybe this was going to be a simple assignment after all. "I sure am glad to see you, Marco," I said.

"Same here, Administrator," he answered.

"The folks back in Unity are searching high and low for you," I told him.

"You've got the wrong person," he said, and I was a little surprised at his use of administrative terminology.

"You are Marco, aren't you? Marco the trader?"

"I'm Marco, all right," he said. "Only thing I ever traded, though, was a set of tools. Got some seeds for it."

"Oh," I said, my voice conveying my disappointment. I sighed and began wondering just how I should go about contacting the Marco I was looking for. My orders said I was to report to Coordinator Crawford immediately upon arrival. I figured the hell with Coordinator Crawford. I outranked him anyway, and there wasn't much he could do if I decided to stop for a drink first.

"Where's the Administrator's Lodge?" I asked the settler.

"Are you buying information or are you just curious?"

"Can you take me there?" I asked.

"Sure thing, Administrator." He picked up my bags and started walking up a dusty path. We'd probably walked for about ten minutes when he dropped my bags and said, "There it is."

The Administrator's Lodge was a prefabricated structure with solar shields that protected it from the heat of the sun. It didn't look too comfortable but I really wanted that drink. I reached into my jacket and slipped the settler thirty credits.

He stared at the credits curiously and then shrugged his shoulders. "Oh well, you're new here. We'll let it go."

He took off then, while I stared after him, wondering just what he'd meant. Had I tipped him too little?

I shrugged and looked over at the Administrator's Lodge. From the outside it looked as hot as hell.

On the inside it was about two degrees short of that mark. I began to curse Gibson for taking me away from my nice soft job in Unity.

There wasn't much inside the lodge. A few tables and chairs, a bulletin board and a bar. Behind the bar a weathered settler lounged.

I walked over and asked, "What are you serving, friend?"

"Call me Marco," he answered.

He caught me off balance. "What?"

"Marco," he said again.

A faint glimmer of understanding began to penetrate my thick skull. "You wouldn't happen to be Marco the trader? The guy who knows all about Victorville, would you?"

"I never left home," he said simply. "What are you drinking?"

That rat! That dirty, filthy, stinking, unprincipled....

But then, it should be simple to find a man with a name like Marco. Among the locals, I mean.

Sure. Oh sure. Real simple. Gibson was about the lowest, most contemptible....

"What are you drinking, Administrator?" the settler asked again.

"Skip it," I said. "How do I get to the coordinator's office?"

"Follow the main path, Administrator. Can't miss it."

I started to pick up my bag as another settler entered. He waved at the bartender.

"Hello, Marco," he said. "How's it going?"

"Not so hot, Marco," the bartender replied.

I listened in fascination. Marco, Marco, Marco. So this was Gibson's idea of a great gag. Very funny. Very....

"You Senior Administrator Ramos, ma'am?" the settler who'd just come in asked.

"Yes," I said, still thinking of Director Gibson.

"You better get yourself over to the coordinator's office," he said. "He's about ready to post you as overdue."

"Sure," I said wearily. "Will you take my bags, please?"

"Roger," he answered. He picked up the bags and nodded at the bar.

"So long, Marco," he said to the bartender.

"See you, Marco," the bartender called back.

Coordinator James Crawford was a nervous, unimpressive sort of man. He was wearing a field uniform, but he still resembled a wilted plant more than he did an administrator.

"Have a seat, Senior Administrator," he offered. He reached for a coffee container on the desk and extended it to me. He coughed in embarrassment when he saw it was empty. Quickly, he pressed a button on his desk and the door popped open. A weathered settler stepped into the room.

"Sir?" the settler asked.

"We're out of coffee, Marco," the Coordinator said. "Will you get us some, please?"

"Sure thing," the settler answered. He smiled broadly and closed the door behind him.

Another Marco, I thought. Another damned Marco.

"They take it," Coordinator Crawford said abruptly.

"Take what?" I asked.

"Coffee. I sometimes think the coffee is one of the few things they like about administrative culture. Part of the whole cultural exchange dynamic we're studying here."

So Gibson had taken care of that angle too. He has a peculiar habit, though. He has an affinity for imported coffee. Coffee was the tip I should have given; not credits.

"All right," I said, "suppose we start at the beginning."

Coordinator Crawford opened his eyes wide. "Ma'am?" he asked.

"What's with all this Marco business? It may be a very common name but I think its popularity here is a little outstanding."

Coordinator Crawford began to chuckle softly. I personally didn't think it was so funny. I tossed him my withering Superior Officer's gaze and waited for his explanation.

"I hadn't realized this was your first time in Timberline," he said.

"Is there a local hero named Marco?" I asked.

"No, no, nothing like that," he assured me. "It's a simple culture, you know. Not nearly as developed as Victorville. Interesting from a cultural sociology perspective, though."

"I can see that," I said bitingly.

"And the settlers are only now becoming acquainted with administrative culture. Lots of field workers, you know."

I began to get the idea. And I began to appreciate Gibson's doubtful ancestry more keenly.

"It's impossible to tell exactly where it all started, of course," Crawford was saying.

I was beginning to get angry. Very angry. I was thinking of Gibson sitting back in a nice cozy office back in Unity.

"Get to the point, Coordinator!" I barked.

"Easy, ma'am," Crawford said, turning pale. I could see that the Coordinator wasn't used to entertaining Senior Administrators. "The field workers. You know how they are. They'll ask a settler to do something and they'll call him Marco. 'Hey, Marco, give me a hand with this.' Or 'Listen, Marco, how'd you like to earn some coffee?' Do you follow?"

"I follow, all right," I said bitterly.

"Well," Crawford went on, "that sort of thing mushrooms. The settlers are a simple, almost childish people. It appealed to them—the Marco business, I mean. Now they're all Marco. They like it. That and the coffee."

He cleared his throat and looked at me apologetically as if he were personally responsible for Timberline culture. In fact, he looked as if he were responsible for having established Timberline in the first place.

"Do you understand, Senior Administrator? Just a case of extended idiom, that's all. Fascinating from an information theory standpoint, really."

Just a case of extended idiot, I thought. An idiot on a wild goose chase a hell of a long way from home.

"I understand perfectly," I snapped. "Where are my quarters?"

Crawford asked a settler named Marco to show me my quarters, reminding me that dinner was at nineteen hundred. As I was leaving, the first settler came back with the coffee Crawford had ordered.

I could tell by the look on his face that he probably had half a container stuffed into his pockets. I shrugged and went to change into a field uniform.

I called Unity right after dinner. The Coordinator assured me that this sort of thing was definitely against regulations, but he submitted when I showed him my administrative credentials.

Gibson's face appeared on the screen. He was smiling, looking like a fat cat.

"What is it, Senior Administrator?" he asked.

"This man Marco," I said. "Can you give me any more on him?"

Gibson's grin grew wider. "Why, Senior Administrator," he said, "you're not having any difficulties, are you?"

"None at all," I snapped back. "I just thought I'd be able to find him a lot sooner if...."

"Take your time, Senior Administrator," Gibson beamed. "There's no rush at all."

"I thought...."

"I'm sure you can do the job," Gibson cut in. "I wouldn't have sent you otherwise."

Hell, I was through kidding around. "Look...."

"He's somewhere in the backcountry, you know," Gibson said.

I wanted to ram my fist into the screen, right smack up against those big white teeth. Instead, I cut off the transmission and watched the surprised look on his face as his screen went blank miles away.

He blinked at the screen, trying to realize I'd deliberately hung up on him.

"Ramos!" he shouted, "can you hear me?"

I smiled, saw the twisted hatred on his features, and then the screen on my end went blank, too.

He's somewhere in the backcountry, you know.

I thanked Coordinator Crawford for his hospitality and went back to my quarters.

As I saw it, there were two courses for me to follow.

One: I could say the hell with Gibson and Timberline. That would mean taking the next transport back to Unity.

It would also mean disobeying the direct order of a superior officer. It might mean demotion, and it might mean getting bounced out of the Service altogether.

Two: I could assume there really was a guy named Marco somewhere in that backcountry, a Marco separate and apart from the other Marcos in this settlement, a trader Marco who knew the Victorville communities well. I could always admit failure, of course, and return empty handed. Mission not accomplished. Or, I might really find a guy who was trader Marco.

I made my decision quickly. I wanted to stay in the Service, and besides Gibson may have been on the level for the first time in his life. Maybe there was a Marco here who could help us in Victorville. If there was I'd try to find him. It was still a hell of a trick though.

I cursed Gibson again and pushed the buzzer near my bed.

A weathered settler stepped into the room.

"Marco?" I asked, just to be sure.

"Who else, boss?" he answered.

"I'm trying to locate someone," I said. "I'll need a guide to take me into the backcountry. Can you get me one?"

"It'll cost you, boss," the settler said.

"How much?"

"Two containers of coffee at least."

"Who's the guide?" I asked.

"How's the price sound?"

"Fine, fine," I said impatiently. And the Coordinator had said they were almost a childish people!

"His name is Marco," the settler told me. "Best damn guide in the territory. Take you anywhere you want to go, do anything you want to do. Courageous. Doesn't know the meaning of fear. I've known him to...."

"Skip it," I said, cutting the promotion short. "Tell him to show up around fifteen hundred with a complete list of what we'll need."

The settler started to leave.

"And Marco," I said, stopping him at the door, "I hope you're not overlooking your commission on the deal."

His face broke into a wide grin. "No danger of that, boss," he said.

When he was gone I began figuring out a plan of action. Obviously, I'd just have to trek through the backcountry looking for a guy named Marco in a settlement where everyone was named Marco. Everybody, at least, but the Coordinator, the small staff attached to the office, and me.

I began wondering why Gibson had gone to so much trouble to get rid of me. The job, as I saw it, would take a hell of a long time. It seemed like a silly thing to do, just to get even with a person for something that had happened years ago. He surely must have realized that I'd be back again, sooner or later. Maybe he had another little assignment all set for me.

Or maybe he didn't expect me to come back.

The thought hadn't occurred to me before this, and I began to consider it seriously. Gibson was no good, rotten clear through. He was failing at the job of managing Victorville, and he probably realized that a few more mistakes on his part would mean the end of his career with the Northern District. I chuckled as I thought of him isolated in some God-forsaken place like the Eastern Wastes or the Southern Frontier. This probably bothered him a lot, too. But what probably bothered him more was the fact that I was next in command. If he were transferred, I'd be in charge of the Northern District, and I could understand how much that would appeal to Gibson.

I tried to figure the thing out sensibly, tried to weigh his good points against his bad. But it all came back to the same thing. A guy who would deliberately falsify biodiversity conservation reports with an entire ecosystem ready to collapse if it wasn't properly managed, would deliberately do just about anything.

Sending me off on a wild goose chase after a character named Marco may have been a gag. But it may have been something a little grimmer than a gag, and I made up my mind to be extremely careful from here on in.

The guide arrived at fifteen hundred on the dot. He was weathered, sun-worn, looked almost like all the other settlers I'd seen so far.

"I understand you need a Grade A guide, ma'am," he said.

"Are you familiar with the backcountry?" I asked him.

"Born and raised there, ma'am. Know it like the back of my hand."

"Has Marco told you what the payment will be?"

"Yes, ma'am. A container and a half of coffee."

I thought about Marco deducting his commission and smiled.

"When can we leave?"

"Right away, ma'am. We won't need much really. I've made a list of supplies and I can get them in less than an hour. I suggest you wear light clothing, boots, and a hat."

"Will I need a weapon?"

He looked at me, his eyes faintly amused. "Why, what for, ma'am?"

"Never mind," I said. "What's your name, by the way?"

He lifted his eyebrows, and his eyes widened in his weathered face. He was definitely surprised.

"Marco," he said. "Didn't you know?"

When we'd been out for a while I discovered why Marco had suggested the boots and the hat. The terrain was often rocky and uneven and it would have injured my legs were they not protected by the high boots. The hat kept the strong sun off my head.

Marco was an excellent guide and a pleasant companion. He seemed to be enjoying a great adventure, seemed to love the backcountry and take a secret pleasure in the work he was doing. There were times when I couldn't see three feet ahead of me. He'd stand stock still for a few minutes, his head barely moving, his eyes darting from one landmark to another. Then he'd say, "This way," and take off into what looked like more impassable terrain invariably to find a little path leading directly to another settlement.

Each settlement was the same. The settlers would come out of their structures, weathered and friendly, shouting, "Coffee, Marco? Coffee?" It took me a while to realize they were addressing me and not my guide.

Everybody was Marco. It was one beautiful, happy, joyous round of hot, dusty backcountry. And I wasn't getting any nearer my man. Nor had I any idea how I was supposed to find him. I began to feel pretty low about the whole affair.

Marco, on the other hand, enjoyed every moment of the trip. In each settlement he greeted the settlers cheerfully, told them stories, swapped gossip and jokes. And when it was time to leave, he would say goodbye to all his friends and we would plunge into the rocky terrain again.

His spirits were always high and he never failed to say the right thing that would give a momentary lift to my own depressed state of mind. He would talk for hours on end as we made our way through the backcountry.

"I like Timberline," he said once. "I would never leave it."

"Have you ever been to Unity?" I asked.

"No," Marco replied. "I like administrators too, you understand. They are good for Timberline. And they are interesting. Part of the team building efforts, you know."

"Interesting?" I asked, thinking of a particular species of administrator: species Diego Gibson.

"Yes, yes," he said wholeheartedly. "They joke and they laugh and ... well, you know."

"I suppose so," I admitted.

Marco smiled secretly, and we pushed on. I began to find, more and more, that I had started to talk freely to Marco. In the beginning he had been just my guide. There had been the strained relationship of employer and employee. But as the days lengthened into weeks, the formal atmosphere began to crumble. I found myself telling him all about Unity, about the people there, about my decision to attend the Academy, the rigid tests, the grind, even the organizational development courses. Marco was a good listener, nodding sympathetically, finding experiences in his own life to parallel my own.

And as our relationship progressed from a casual one to a definitely friendly one, Marco seemed more enthusiastic than ever to keep up our grinding pace to find what we were looking for.

Once we stopped in a clearing to rest. Marco lounged on the dry grass, his long body stretched out in front of him, the canteen gleaming at his belt. I'd seen him navigate through thick, difficult terrain with that sense of direction, his long, muscular legs powerfully carrying him forward like a natural explorer.

"How far are we from the office?" I asked.

"Three or four weeks," he replied.

I sighed wearily. "Where do we go from here?"

"There are more settlements," he said.

"We'll never find him."

"Possibly," Marco mused, the smile creeping over his face again.

"A wild goose chase. A fool's errand."

"We'd better get started," Marco said simply.

I got to my feet and we started the march again. Marco was still fresh, a brilliant contrast to me, weary and dejected. Somehow, I had the same feeling I'd had a long time ago on my sixteenth birthday. One of my friends had taken me all over the city, finally dropping me off at my own house where the whole gang was gathered for a surprise party. Marco reminded me of that friend.

"There's a settlement ahead," he said, and the grin on his face was large now, his eyes shining.

Something was missing here. Settlers. There were no settlers coming out to greet us. No cries of "Coffee? Coffee?" I caught up with Marco.

"What's the story?" I whispered.

He shrugged knowingly and continued walking.

And then I saw the vehicle, a sleek administrative transport catching the rays of the sun like a great silver bullet.

"What...?" I started.

"It's all right," Marco said, smiling.

The vehicle looked vaguely familiar. I noticed the crest of the Northern District near the front, and a lot of things became clear then. I also saw Gibson standing near one of the structures, a stun weapon in his hand.

"Hello, Senior Administrator," he called, almost cheerfully. The weapon didn't look cheerful, though. It was pointed at my head.

"Fancy meeting you here, Director," I said, trying to match his joviality. Somehow it didn't quite come off.

Marco was walking beside me, waving at the director, beaming all over with happiness.

"I see you found your man," Gibson said.

I turned rapidly. Marco nodded and kept grinning, a grin that told me he was getting a big kick out of all this. Like a kid playing a game.

I faced Gibson again. "Okay, what's it all about, friend?"

"Director," Gibson corrected me. "You mustn't forget to say Director, Senior Administrator." He emphasized my rank, and he said it with a sort of ruthless finality.

I waited. I could see he was just busting to tell me how clever he'd been. Besides, there wasn't much I could do but wait. Not with Gibson pointing the stun weapon at my middle.

"We've come a long way since the Academy, haven't we, Senior Administrator?"

"If you mean in miles," I said, looking around at the terrain, "we sure have."

Gibson grinned a little. "Always the wit," he said drily. And then the smile faded from his lips and his eyes took on a hard lustre. "I'm going to eliminate you, you know." He said it as if he were saying, "I think it'll rain tomorrow."

Marco almost clapped his hands together with glee. He was really enjoying this. Another of those funny administrative games.

"You gave me a powerful handicap to overcome," Gibson said. "I suppose I should thank you, really."

"You're welcome," I said.

"It wasn't easy living down the disgrace you caused me."

"It was your own damn fault," I said. "You knew what you were doing when you decided to falsify those reports."

Beside me, Marco chuckled a little, enjoying the game immensely.

"You didn't have to report me," Gibson said.

"No? Maybe I should have forgotten all about it? Maybe I should have helped you cover it up? So you could do it again sometime and maybe destroy an entire ecosystem! Think about the public health implications alone!"

Gibson was silent for a long time. When he spoke his voice was barely audible. The heat was oppressive, as if it were concentrated on this little spot in the backcountry, focusing all its penetration on a small, unimportant drama.

I could hear Marco breathing beside me.

"I'm on my way out," Gibson rasped. "Finished, do you understand?"

"Good," I said. And I meant it.

"This Victorville thing. A terrible situation. Terrible."

Beside me, a slight frown crossed Marco's face. Apparently he couldn't understand the seriousness of our voices. What had happened to the game, the fun?

"You brought the Victorville business on yourself," I told Gibson. "There was never any trouble before you took command. Your healthcare policy alone was disastrous. And the economic inequality you created through your market economics approach...."

"The settlers," he practically shouted. "They ... they...."

Marco caught his breath sharply, and I wondered what Gibson was going to say about the settlers. Apparently he'd realized that Marco was a settler. Or maybe Marco's expression had something to do with it.

"What about the settlers?" I asked.

"Nothing," Gibson said. "Nothing." He was silent for a while.

"A person of my calibre," he said then, his face grim. "Dealing with primitives." He caught himself again and threw a hasty glance at Marco. The perplexed frown had grown heavier on Marco's face. He looked at the director in puzzlement.
question: What was Director Gibson's main motive behind putting Hannah on the mission?
option_a: To genuinely find someone who could help resolve the Victorville situation
option_b: To get rid of Hannah because she was next in line for his position and he was failing at his job
correct_answer_text: To get rid of Hannah because she was next in line for his position and he was failing at his job
incorrect_answer_text: To genuinely find someone who could help resolve the Victorville situation

The mission was a pretense to remove a threat to his position.
