It's always gratifying to see studios proved wrong about the commercial viability of "challenging" films, but in this case I believe they exercised appropriate judgment. *Disconnected Minds* isn't merely problematic—it's egregiously, offensively problematic, a spectacle for those lacking in empathy. The controversy it has generated isn't puritanical; it's more like justified disgust at watching an egotist exploit people's vulnerabilities in the name of "larger scientific truths."

Those truths are sweeping, certainly. Consider Ian Yates, the 38-year-old neural engineer who has been attempting consciousness upload for nearly fifteen years. If you encountered him in the research facilities of Ashford City, you might assume that someone with his obsessive dedication might struggle with accepting the technology's limitations and harbor resentment about it. The larger truth is that Ian struggles enormously with the technology's failures and is deeply embittered about it. Just in case you sympathize too much with him, however, Hicks is careful to include a contemptuous monologue in which Ian dismisses younger researchers who waste their careers pursuing what he calls "fantasy neuroscience" instead of rigorous evolutionary biology.

Ian proves to be the film's most sympathetic subject—by a considerable margin. At least he's not Roman Munoz, a frustrated 52-year-old former consciousness researcher who writes but cannot publish papers and who consistently sabotages collaborative projects, because his potential partners are "intellectual frauds." Sounding like one of the minor academics who posture as revolutionary thinkers, Roman talks extensively about frauds. He also reminisces about that brief period in the 2040s when he managed to publish three groundbreaking papers on neural plasticity, whose citations he proudly displays. These days, all he encounters are frauds. He comes across as a pathetic failure—a fraud himself.

Bianca Rice, conversely, is a different kind of tragic figure, having undergone seven failed consciousness mapping attempts. Determined to achieve successful upload before her neural pathways degrade beyond recovery, she is generally filmed surrounded by medication bottles and monitoring equipment. She confides her desperation to her successfully uploaded friend, who, in one scene, gently suggests that Bianca's psychological resistance might be preventing the transfer. Clearly the scene is scripted, but Bianca performs convincing surprise well. She has always been neurologically atypical—and she's "comfortable with it," and the technology just has to accommodate her. This is followed by more discussion about neural compatibility. Will the system accept you if you're too anxious? If you resist too strongly? "Or," the viewer thinks, "if your brain simply isn't compatible?"

The only natural presence here is Noah Reid, a garrulous technician who thrives before the camera—he could have a career as a science communicator. Divorced from his uploaded wife and aging, Noah needs income and is willing to sell access to his neural data ("I'm up to two data harvests a day"). Researchers contact him and, within minutes, they're extracting his consciousness patterns. Strange, right? What Hicks omits (it's revealed in a Stonegate Province investigative report) is that Noah, a former neural test subject, works in recruitment at the biotechnology facility. Presumably, random scientists at conferences don't immediately scan his brain patterns. Nor, presumably, does he allow unrestricted access to his consciousness—although he permits Hicks' cameras to film his neural mapping session, chattering about his cognitive patterns while technicians attach electrodes and initiate the scanning sequence.

Hicks might have constructed his subjects' testimonials from their actual words, but he has stripped them of their authenticity—and, thus, of their humanity. They aren't processing or attempting to understand their situations before your eyes, because they already know their lines: They've been preserved like specimens in a laboratory and presented for voyeuristic examination. The scenes with colleagues and confidantes serve crude, mechanical purposes. You can imagine the director composing a shot (the shots are meticulously composed and dramatically lit) and instructing them, "In this scene she suggests your neural resistance is the problem and you react defensively. Ready... Action."

Call me traditional, but I find this antithetical to the science fiction spirit—particularly science fiction grounded in actual research ethics. A former neuroscience researcher who transitioned to filmmaking after working at the Ashford City Neural Institute, Hicks clearly formed his conclusions about his material before his cameras began recording—so it's unsurprising that it feels predetermined and processed. When reality interfered (Bianca apparently did not undergo an eighth mapping attempt as she does on-screen), Hicks dismissed the truth as irrelevant, following her into the neural chamber in her hospital gown because it was "true to her character." But what distinguishes thoughtful science fiction from exploitation is that real people are often more nuanced, and more contradictory, than simplified characters—as Bianca proved to be more (or, at least, other) than the sum of her neural patterns. That's the kind of truth that reveals itself to careful filmmakers during editing, when they review footage and discover unexpected complexities, contradictions, glimpses of a reality that's richer and more ambiguous than the one they intended to portray.

So what are Hicks' "larger scientific truths"? People pursuing consciousness upload can be desperate. People fear mortality and obsolescence. People are judged and, in turn, judge others by their neural compatibility. Hardly revolutionary insights. One could argue, generously, that the film is meant to be cautionary, that Hicks intends for us to recognize how his subjects deceive themselves and thereby learn to identify our own self-deceptions regarding technology. But Hicks hasn't developed a larger thematic structure that would integrate those larger truths and help us comprehend where these people's thinking became distorted. He dramatizes up to the point where a dramatist would be expected to provide insight—and then, conveniently, he's a documentarian.

*Disconnected Minds* might make an effective screening for biotechnology ethics courses. There's little to debate about the subjects' choices—both scientists and laypeople will find them troubling—and the picture the film paints of consciousness research in Ashford City is so disturbing that you'll probably want to appreciate your unmodified consciousness. Anything to avoid becoming one of those people.

*The Colonies of Carmel* also navigates between two genres, in this case coming-of-age narrative and speculative environmental fiction. Paul Sanders, the writer and first-time director, has an eye for absurd contradictions that was obviously sharpened by the pain of growing up in the pollution-ravaged settlements. His protagonist (played by a newcomer) spends his formative years being relocated with his two siblings from one temporary shelter to another in the Carmel, Orvandor region, all because his idealistic father (a veteran character actor) wants them educated in sustainable agriculture and renewable energy principles. ("Infrastructure is temporary; knowledge is permanent.") It's a significant oversight, then, that we never see those educational facilities or the children's interaction with their stable, well-resourced counterparts from the protected zones. We can't determine if the father is, on some level, justified in his conviction, or whether he's damaging his children—subjecting them to instability and depriving them of security—for no reason. Sanders hasn't quite mastered narrative structure, which is full of episodes that exist because they actually occurred but that lack dramatic payoff. I almost wish he'd included more voice-over narration, more commentary on the things that, as a filmmaker, he hasn't learned to convey visually.

*The Colonies of Carmel* never fully coheres, but it has an appealing earnestness, and it's remarkably atmospheric, with striking depictions of environmental degradation and thoughtful evocations of post-pollution survival aesthetics. The father, to obtain resources from his wealthy brother (a former corporate executive), volunteers to shelter his troubled nephew, recently expelled from the protected zones. The cousins compare environmental suits, experiment with illegal air purifiers, and communicate in coded language about forbidden topics, but Sanders never allows the proceedings to become overly sentimental: The warmth is always tempered with an acidic awareness of the family's precarious situation. "Are we safe now?" ask the children, hopefully, before another environmental crisis sends them back into their transport vehicle, passing the sealed habitats of the privileged, in the contaminated wastelands of Carmel.

Grading on the steep curve established by science fiction seasons past, these have turned out to be reasonably strong months for genre cinema. Even the commercial offerings (*Neural Dawn*, *Consciousness Rising*, *The Upload Protocol*, *Synthetic Memories*, *Pattern Recognition*, *Evolution: E20*) have been of acceptable quality, and *Saving Earth's Future* and *Return to Reality* were sharp reminders for audiences dazed by escapist entertainment. *Beyond Perception* was thoughtful and engaging, as was, in its provocative way, *There's Something About Consciousness*. And, on the independent front, *The Opposite of Upload*, *Carmel 66*, and *Phi* have proved that there's still commercial viability for original science fiction. Certainly, we had failures, but even *Mega-Neural* was entertaining to mock. And there's something reassuring about the fact that *The Researchers* is so terrible: proof yet again that people with enormous budgets can hire brilliant visual effects artists but can't manufacture authenticity.

I don't know who the credited screenwriter, Sebastian Shaw, is, but it's unlikely that he has ever studied actual neuroscience research, let alone understood the source of its fascination. Opening with an absurd sequence of researcher Isaac Ellis performing impossible neural hacks, the film shifts to a scene in which he meets a colleague while standing in a decontamination chamber with only a lab coat to cover his monitoring equipment. The premise could have been compelling in a way only rigorous science fiction can be: The dedicated Ellis was capable of theoretical breakthroughs and publishing groundbreaking papers, but he left the practical applications to his more technically skilled associate. Here their roles have been carelessly confused, and Shaw's idea of scientific dialogue is to have the pair exchange technobabble clichés.

Whereas actual neuroscientists bring methodical precision to their work, Ellis is portrayed as recklessly impulsive. His colleague looks impressive in her lab attire, but it's increasingly apparent that the actress isn't much of a performer—at least, not a trained one—and her attempts at scientific authority are embarrassingly forced. As the eccentric antagonist who controls the consciousness network, even the veteran actor is disappointingly flat, performing with exaggerated melodrama. To think he once found commercial science fiction beneath him! When he delivers lines like "Time to upload!" one imagines serious researchers, ethicists, and historians of science cringing in the background.

The film raises important questions about research ethics, consumer behavior regarding biotechnology, and the intersection of neuroscience with societal change. Historical analysis of consciousness research suggests we're approaching capabilities that seemed impossible decades ago. Evolutionary biology teaches us that human consciousness evolved over millions of years; can we really expect to replicate it artificially in mere decades? The archaeology of failed technological promises should make us cautious. Yet films like *Disconnected Minds* exploit these legitimate scientific pursuits for sensationalism, while films like *The Researchers* trivialize them through careless dramatization.

What we need is science fiction that respects both scientific rigor and human complexity—that understands the difference between dramatizing research and exploiting researchers. Until filmmakers learn this distinction, we'll continue seeing either exploitative pseudo-documentaries or mindless spectacles, with little middle ground for thoughtful exploration of how neuroscience, renewable energy solutions, and other emerging technologies are reshaping human experience. The genre deserves better, and so do the real people working in these fields.
question: How does Hicks view his own film?
option_a: As an exercise in scientific dramatization where manipulating narratives is acceptable if it communicates larger truths
option_b: As a purely objective documentary that presents unmanipulated reality without any directorial intervention
correct_answer_text: As an exercise in scientific dramatization where manipulating narratives is acceptable if it communicates larger truths
incorrect_answer_text: As a purely objective documentary that presents unmanipulated reality without any directorial intervention
explanation: The story explicitly states that Hicks calls his own film "an exercise in scientific dramatization" and says "I'm quite comfortable manipulating my subjects' narratives and even amplifying their psychological conflicts if it enables me to communicate larger truths about neuroscience and human identity." This directly parallels how Barker viewed his film in the original story as "an exercise in mendacity" where he was "quite happy to tell lies" to communicate "larger dramatic truths."
original_question: How does Barker view his own film?

synthetic_story:
I am a Probability Sink
By ISABEL MCCOY

When I arrived at the climate tech startup's office in Bridgewater, Selvoria, I was exhausted from the morning's disasters, but the effect was the same as being tired. I let myself into the building, which had an abandoned look since most of the team was at the renewable energy conference in Pearlbrook, and took a cold shower in the executive washroom. The current temperature outside, according to my phone, was thirty-two degrees Celsius, but according to the ancient thermometer in our lab, it was thirty-eight.

I got dressed and went into the main workspace, wishing desperately that my business partner Ruth Singh were here to tell me why everything looked so desolate. What do successful entrepreneurs do, I asked myself, that I have left undone? I've organized the prototypes, I've filed the patent applications, and I've updated the investor deck.... Ah! The coffee mugs. I washed them and put them back, but still the place looked partner-deserted.

It had been a catastrophic day; I had forgotten to charge my phone, so I'd had to rush to make a pitch meeting at one of the venture capital firms we were courting. I didn't notice the impending thunderstorm and had no umbrella when I reached the street, to find myself confronted with an almost tropical downpour. I would have turned back, but an auto-taxi pulled up and a woman got out, so I dashed through the rain and got in.

"Venture Plaza, downtown," I said to the AI system.

"Confirmed," said the synthesized voice, and I heard the electric motor hum, and then sputter and die. After some futile diagnostic beeps, the system announced, "Sorry, passenger. Vehicle malfunction. Please find alternative transportation."

If possible, it was raining even harder. I opened my jacket over my head and ran for the metro: four blocks. Malfunctioning traffic signals held me up at each intersection and I was soaked when I reached the platform, just in time to miss the express train. After an abnormal delay, I caught one which exactly missed the connection at Central Station. The same thing happened at both ends of the cross-town line, but I found the rain had stopped when I emerged at Market and Fifth.

As I walked toward Venture Plaza, I passed a large construction site where they were preparing to install a massive solar panel array for the new carbon-neutral office complex. There was the usual crowd of onlookers watching the installation robots and, in particular, a technician operating a plasma cutter who was removing some old concrete foundation. While I watched, a large chunk fell away, and for an instant I was able to see something that looked like a piece of crystalline mineral, the size of a storage container. It glowed with an unusual iridescence in the sunlight, and then his cutting torch hit it.

There was a faint pop and the thing shattered. The technician stumbled backward but wasn't hurt. At the moment of the fracture—if so minor an event can be called one—I felt something sting my cheek and, on touching it, found a small cut. I dabbed at it with a tissue but, though slight, the bleeding wouldn't stop, so I went into a pharmacy and bought some liquid bandage which I applied to the tiny wound.

When I got to the VC firm, I found that the partners had rescheduled without telling me.

During the day, by actual count, I heard the phrase "disruptive innovation" eleven times, and another startup favorite, "paradigm shift," fifteen times. However, our climate technology proposal had been accepted for second-round consideration because nobody had noticed my absence from the original meeting time. There you have what is known as the startup world, the entrepreneurship game, or the venture capital racket, depending upon which stage of funding you've achieved.

The metro gave a repeat performance going back, and as I arrived at our building in Bridgewater, the security guard was standing outside talking to a municipal inspector.

He said, "Hello, Ms. McCoy. I guess you just missed it at Venture Plaza." I looked confused and he explained, "We just heard about it: all four elevators in that building locked simultaneously on different floors. Sounds impossible. I guess you just avoided that mess."

Anything can happen in the startup world, I thought. "That's right, Oscar," I said, and went inside.

Psychology tells us that some people are accident-prone; I, on the other hand, seemed recently to be coincidence-prone, fluke-magnetized, and except for my phone, I'd had no control over what had been happening.

I went into our small kitchenette to make coffee and reread the instructions Ruth had left, telling me how to manage by myself until she returned from the conference in Pearlbrook, a matter of eight days. How to operate the espresso machine, how to access the backup servers, whom to call if equipment failed. My partner used to be a systems engineer and she is quite convinced that I cannot function without her oversight. She is correct, but not for the reasons she supposes.

I opened the refrigerator to get some oat milk and saw another note: "When you take out the Samples or Equipment, Return them Immediately. And Close the Door properly."

Intimidated, I took my coffee into the main lab and sat down in front of my workstation. As I reviewed the renewable energy prototype documentation that was supposed to liberate us from investor dependency, I noticed an error and picked up a stylus. When I put it down, it rolled off the desk, and with my eyes on the screen, I groped under the chair for it. Then I looked down. The stylus was standing on its end.

There, I thought to myself, is that one chance in a million we hear about, and picked up the stylus. I turned back to the documentation and drank some of the coffee in hopes of inspiration and relief from the oppressive heat, but nothing came. I went back and reviewed the whole technical specification to try to build momentum, but came to a dead stop at the last section.

Damn the heat, damn the stylus, damn venture capital and institutional reform. My coffee was gone and I went back to the kitchenette and read Ruth's notes again to see if they would feel like a message from her. I noticed one I had missed, attached to the recycling chute: "Composting collected at 6:00 AM so the idea is to Put materials Here the Night Before. Good luck with everything."

I made another coffee and went to stare out of the lab window at the rooftop garden opposite. The sun was out again and a researcher was monitoring a flock of sensor-equipped drones. They circled in a pattern, collecting air quality data, but were kept in constant motion.

Drones typically fly in coordinated patterns and adjust simultaneously, so that their solar panels all catch the sunlight at optimal angles. I was thinking about this efficient fact when I saw that as they were making a turn, they seemed to cluster together unnaturally. By some peculiar chance, they all wanted the same position in the airspace, and several collided and fell.

The researcher was as surprised as I and went to one of the damaged drones and picked it up. She stood there shaking her head, examining its components.

My speculations about this peculiar aerial traffic accident were interrupted by raised voices in the hallway. Since our building is usually very professional, I was astonished to hear what sounded like an argument, and among the angry voices I recognized that of my colleague, Steven Mason, a very reserved guy who works on ecosystem restoration projects and has never, to my knowledge, caused disruptions, particularly in the late afternoon.

"You can't accuse me of that!" I heard him shout. "I tell you I bought this deck this morning and the seal wasn't broken until we started playing!"

Several other loud voices erupted simultaneously.

"Nobody draws a royal flush five times in a row!"

"Yeah, and only when you were dealing!"

The tone of the argument was becoming hostile, and I opened the door to offer Steven assistance if needed. There were three people confronting him, evidently torn between the desire to storm off and the impulse to stay and confront him further. His face was flushed and he looked bewildered.

"Here!" he said, holding out a deck of cards. "For heaven's sake, examine them yourselves if you think they're marked!"

The nearest person struck them from his hand. "Fine, Houdini! So they're not marked! All I know is five royal flushes..."

His voice faded. He and the others stared at the scattered cards on the floor. About half were face down, as might be expected, and the rest face up—all spades.

Someone must have called it, because at that moment the elevator arrived and the three people, with half-frightened, incredulous expressions, and in silence, got in and descended. My colleague stood looking at the impossibly arranged cards.

"Good grief!" he said, and started to collect them. "What a session..."

I helped him and suggested he come to the lab for coffee and explain what happened, but I had an intuition about what I would hear.

After a while, he calmed down, but still seemed dazed.

"Never experienced anything like it," he said. "Wouldn't have thought it possible. Those people didn't believe it. Every hand normal, nothing unusual—three of a kind, a straight, that sort of thing, and one person got queens over jacks, until it's my deal. Incredible! Royal flush—every single time! And each time, somebody else has four aces..."

He started to perspire again, so I got up to make him more coffee. There was one container of oat milk left, but when I tried to open it, the cap broke and fragments got into the liquid.

"I'll have to go down for more milk," I said.

"I'll come too. I need fresh air."

At the corner market, the clerk handed me three bottles in what must have been a defective bag, because as he passed them to me over the counter, the bottom gave way and they fell onto the tile floor. None of them broke, although the fall must have been from at least six feet. Steven was too absorbed in his thoughts to notice and I was becoming accustomed to improbabilities.

On the sidewalk, a person walking in front of Steven stopped suddenly to check their phone and Steven, to avoid collision, stepped into the bike lane where an electric scooter swerved to avoid Steven. The pavement was still wet and the scooter skidded, its rear end lightly tapping a small autonomous delivery vehicle, which was moving rather quickly. It spun sideways and, without any apparent friction, went directly up the steps of a brownstone across the street, coming to rest with its front compartment inside the entrance, which someone opened at that moment.

The sight of this caused another cyclist to skid, and when both the cyclist and a pedestrian had stopped their confused movements, they were face to face, blocking the entire sidewalk. This left them exactly no room to move in either direction.

Although reasonably wide, this is a two-way street, and within minutes, traffic was backed up from both directions as far as the main boulevards. Everyone was sounding their horns.

Oscar was frustrated—more so when he tried to use the emergency communication panel.

It was malfunctioning.

Upstairs, the ventilation was blowing papers around the lab and I closed the vents, mainly to shut out the chaos and commotion. Steven had brightened somewhat.

"I'll stay for one more coffee and then I'm expected at the ecosystem restoration site," he said. "You know, I think this would make an interesting case study." He smiled and gestured toward the pandemonium.

When he left, I noticed it was getting dark and turned on the desk lamp. Then I saw the cables. They were all tangled in knots, except one. That was tied in three knots.

All right, I told myself, it was the ventilation system. But I felt the time had come for me to seek expert consultation, so I went to the phone to call Felix Chang. Felix is a professor of applied physics and metaphysics at a university in Carmel, Yendor, and maintains a research office near us. He is highly analytical, but we believe he understands everything.

When I picked up the receiver, the line sounded dead and I thought, more problems. Then I heard someone clear their throat and I said hello. Felix's voice said, "Isabel? You must have picked up just as the connection completed. That's a remarkably unlikely coincidence."

"Not in the least," I said. "Come over here immediately. I have something that requires your expertise."

"Well, actually, I was calling to ask you and Ruth—"

"Ruth's at the conference for the week. Can you get here quickly? It's urgent."

"Right away," he said, and disconnected.

While I waited, I thought I might try documenting a few notes about our renewable energy prototype—perhaps some insight would emerge now. It did, but as I came to a point where I was about to type the word "photosynthetic," I decided it was too technical for the summary, and stopped at the letter "P." Then I saw that I had inexplicably pressed all the wrong keys several positions to the side of the correct ones, and deleted the paragraph, my face burning.

This was absolutely not my day.

"Well," Felix said, "nothing you've described is impossible or supernatural. Just extraordinarily, extraordinarily improbable. In fact, the odds against that card game alone would lead me to suspect Steven, well as I know him. It's all these other incidents..."

He stood and walked to the window and looked at the warm twilight while I waited. Then he turned around; he had an expression of concern.

"Isabel, you're a rational person, so I don't think you'll be offended by what I'm about to say. What you've told me is so impossibly unlikely, and the odds against it so astronomical, that I must consider the possibility that you're either fabricating this or experiencing some kind of perceptual distortion." I started to protest, but he gestured for me to wait. "I understand, but don't you see that that is far more likely than..." He stopped and shook his head. Then he brightened. "I have an idea. Perhaps we can conduct a demonstration."

He thought for an intense moment and snapped his fingers. "Do you have any coins?"

"Why, yes," I said. "Several." I reached into my pocket. There must have been nearly three euros in various denominations. "Do you think they'll all show the same year, perhaps?"

"Did you accumulate all these coins today?"

"No. Over the past week."

He shook his head. "In that case, no. Setting aside the fact that you could have arranged it deliberately, if my tentative hypothesis is correct, that would be actually impossible. It would require temporal reversal. I'll explain later. No, just toss the coins. Let's see if they all land heads up."

I moved away from the equipment and tossed the handful of coins onto the floor. They clattered and bounced—and bounced together—and stacked themselves into a neat tower.

I looked at Felix. His eyes narrowed. Without a word, he took several coins from his own pocket and threw them.

These coins didn't stack. They simply fell into a perfectly straight line, each one touching the next.

"Well," I said, "what more evidence do you need?"

"Extraordinary," he said, and sat down. "I suppose you're aware that there are two great apparently opposing principles governing the Universe—randomness and order. The distribution of particles in a gas is an example of random distribution, and biological life is an example of order. The motions of molecules in a liquid are what we call random, but there are so many of them, we treat them statistically and derive thermodynamic laws—quite reliable from a practical standpoint. These laws aren't theoretically absolute; they're matters of extreme probability. Now life, on the other hand, seems not to depend on probability at all; actually, it works against entropy. Or you might say it is certainly not an accidental phenomenon."

"Do you mean," I asked in some confusion, "that some form of life is controlling the coins and—the other events?"

He shook his head. "No. What I mean is that improbable events usually have improbable explanations. When I observe a natural law being violated, I don't conclude, 'Here's a miracle.' I revise my understanding of the principles. Something—I don't know what—is occurring, and it seems to involve probability manipulation, and it seems to center on you. Were you still in that building when the elevators malfunctioned? Or nearby?"

"I must have been. It happened shortly after I left."

"Mm. You're the epicenter, certainly. But why?"

"Epicenter of what?" I asked. "I feel as though I'm at the center of some kind of probability storm. Something is targeting me!"

Felix smiled. "Don't be superstitious. And especially don't anthropomorphize."

"Well, if it's the opposite of random, it must be some form of intelligence."

"On what basis? All we know with certainty is that random events are being reorganized. A crystal, for example, is not alive, but it's a non-random arrangement of molecules.... I wonder." He had a distant, contemplative look.

I was beginning to feel hungry and the coffee had worn off.

"Let's go out for dinner," I said. "There's nothing in the kitchenette and I'm not supposed to use the main lab equipment for food preparation. Only coffee and basic items."

We put on our jackets and went down to the street. From both directions, we could hear emergency vehicles clearing the stalled traffic. There were, by this time, several frustrated traffic coordinators managing the operation and we heard one of them say to Oscar, "I don't understand what's happening here. Every single vehicle has some kind of malfunction. They can't any of them reverse or move forward for various reasons. Never witnessed anything like it."

Near us, two pedestrians were performing a peculiar little dance as they tried to pass one another; as soon as one moved aside to let the other pass, the other would shift to the same side. They both had embarrassed smiles initially, but before long their smiles were replaced by expressions of suspicion and then determination.

"All right, wise guy!" they shouted simultaneously, and pushed forward, only to collide. They stepped back and threw simultaneous gestures which met in mid-air. Then began one of the most remarkable confrontations ever witnessed—an argument in which accusation met accusation but never any resolution, until both parties backed away unsatisfied, muttering identical complaints and threats.

Oscar appeared at that moment. His face was glistening with perspiration. "Are you all right, Ms. McCoy?" he asked. "I don't know what's happening around here, but ever since I started my shift this afternoon, things have been going haywire. Martinez!" he called—his voice could carry across a stadium. "Bring those people over here!"

Two individuals in a confused dispute, with their identical briefcases somehow locked together, were escorted across the street, which meant climbing over vehicle bumpers. Martinez, a competent young security officer, seemed self-conscious; the individuals seemed oblivious.

"All right, now, Mr. Watkins!" one of them said. "Release my briefcase and we'll forget about this!"

"And so now it's Mister Watkins, is it?" said his adversary.

A third person, a woman with her back to us, her briefcase also caught in the tangle, pulled at it tentatively, at which the other two glared at her. She turned her head away and tried to let go, but the handle was caught on her watch. She looked up and I saw it was Ruth. My partner.

"Oh, Isabel!" she said, and managed to detach herself. "Are you all right?" Was I all right!

"Ruth! What are you doing here?"

"I was so worried, and when I saw all this chaos, I didn't know what to think." She pointed to the stalled vehicles. "Are you really all right?"

"Of course I'm all right. But why..."

"The conference coordinator said someone kept trying to access the emergency contact system repeatedly and it was traced to our office here. I kept trying to call, but I only got error messages. Oh dear, are you sure you're all right?"

I put my arm around her and glanced at Felix. He had an introspective expression. Then I caught Oscar's eye. It had a thoughtful, almost suspicious quality.

"Trouble does seem to follow you, Ms. McCoy," was all he said.

When we got upstairs, I turned to Felix. "Explain to Ruth," I said. "And incidentally to me. I'm not adequately briefed yet on your hypothesis."

He did so, and when he reached the conclusion, I had the feeling she was ahead of him.

"In other words, you think it's something organic? Some kind of life form?"

"Well," Felix said, "I'm trying to conceive of what else it might be. I'm not succeeding," he admitted.

"But as far as I can determine," Ruth answered, "it's pure probability manipulation, without any discernible pattern or purpose."

"Not quite. It has a center. Isabel is the center."

Ruth looked at me with a curious expression for a moment. "Do you feel all right, darling?" she asked me. I nodded enthusiastically. "You'll think this unscientific of me," she went on to Felix, "but why couldn't it be something like an overactive poltergeist phenomenon?"

"Pure speculation," he said. "No empirical evidence for such things."

"Electromagnetic fields?"

"Absolutely not. For one thing, most of the objects affected weren't ferromagnetic—and don't forget electromagnetism is a force, not a form of energy per se, and a substantial amount of energy has been involved. I acknowledge the energy has primarily been supplied by the objects themselves, but in an electromagnetic field, all you'd observe would be stored potential energy, such as when a piece of iron moves toward a magnet. Then it would simply remain there, like a wound-down clock. These objects do considerably more than that—they continue moving in improbable ways."

"Why did you mention a crystal earlier? Why not a biological organism?"

"Only an analogy," said Felix. "A crystal resembles life in that it has a definite structure and exhibits growth, but that's all. I'll concede this—phenomenon—has no discernible structure and motion is involved, but plants don't move and amoebas have no fixed shape. A crystal feeds, but it doesn't metabolize what it consumes; it merely reorganizes it into a non-random pattern. In this case, it's reorganizing random motions and it has a nucleus and it seems to be growing—at least in what you might call improbability intensity."

Ruth frowned. "Then what is it? What's it composed of?"

"I would hypothesize it's composed of the motions themselves. There's a similar concept in particle physics regarding virtual particles. Another similarity to crystals is that it appears to be forming around a nucleus not of its own substance—the way a grain of sand in a supersaturated solution becomes the nucleation site."

"Sounds like a pearl in an oyster," Ruth said, and gave me a teasing look.

"Why," I asked Felix, "did you say the coins couldn't show the same date? I mean apart from the unlikely chance I received them that way."

"Because I don't believe this phenomenon initiated before today and everything that's occurred can all be described as improbable events here and now. The dates were already stamped, and to alter them would require retroactive causation, reversing time. That's excluded, in my framework. That communication system now—"

The door chime sounded. We were not surprised to find it was the telecommunications technician. She examined the system and made disapproving sounds.

"I think you dropped the handset," she said with evident disapproval.

"Certainly not," I said. "Is it damaged?"

"Not exactly damaged, but—" She shook her head and disassembled it further.

Felix went over and they discussed the technical problem in low voices. Finally the technician left and Ruth contacted her mother to provide reassurance. Felix attempted to explain to me what had occurred with the system.

"You must have dislodged something. And then you replaced the handset in such a way that the contact wasn't quite disconnected."

"But for heaven's sake, Ruth says the calls were continuing for an extended period! I contacted you only a short while ago and it must have taken her nearly three hours to get here from Pearlbrook."

"Then you must have done it twice and the vibrations in the structure—something like that—just happened to generate the correct signal impulses. Yes, I understand your reaction," he said, observing my expression. "It's beginning to intensify."

Ruth had finished her call and suggested going out for dinner. I was so relieved to see her that I'd forgotten about being hungry.

"I'm in no condition to cook," she said. "Let's get away from all this."

Felix raised an eyebrow. "If all this, as you call it, will permit us."

In the lobby, we encountered Steven, looking satisfied in a journalistic way.

"I've been assigned to document the story—who could be better qualified?—I work here. So far, I don't quite understand what's been occurring. I've been talking to Oscar, but he was circumspect. I got the impression he thinks you're involved in some mystical way. Hello, Felix, what's your assessment?"

"He has a hypothesis," said Ruth. "Come and eat with us and he'll explain it thoroughly."

Since we decided on a climate-controlled restaurant nearby on Harbor Avenue, we walked. The congestion of vehicles didn't seem any less than before and we saw Oscar again. He was talking to a municipal supervisor, and when he noticed us, he said something that made the supervisor regard us with interest. Particularly me.

"If you want your briefcase, Ms. Singh," Oscar said, "it's at the security office. What remains of it, anyway."

Ruth thanked him and there was a brief pause, during which I felt the evaluative regard of the supervisor. I pulled out a package of mints, which I had opened, as always, by tearing the wrapper. I happened to have it inverted and all the mints fell out. Before I could move my foot to obscure what they had arranged themselves into on the pavement, the two officials saw it. The supervisor gave me a hard look, but said nothing. I quickly scattered the offensive mints into the gutter.

When we arrived at the restaurant, it was crowded but cool—although it didn't remain cool for long. We sat down at a corner table near the entrance and ordered sparkling water as we examined the menu. Sitting at the adjacent table were a heavyset woman wearing a very long, brilliant purple evening gown, and a thin, sour-faced man in formal attire. When the server returned, they commandeered him and began ordering dinner fussily: a grain bowl for the man, and gazpacho, quinoa salad, and mango sorbet for the heavyset woman.

I tasted my water. It was most peculiar; it seemed to have salt in it instead of being neutral. I mentioned this and my companions tried theirs, and grimaced.

The server was concerned and apologetic, and took the glasses back to the bar across the room. The bartender looked over at us and tasted one of the drinks. Then he poured them into his sink with a puzzled expression and prepared a new batch. After mixing this, he set out a row of glasses, added ice and began to pour.

That is to say he tilted the pitcher over the first glass, but nothing came out. He tapped it against the bar and tried again. Still nothing. Then he removed the top and probed into it with a stirrer, his face flushed with frustration.

I had the impression that the pitcher had frozen solid. Well, ice is a crystal, I thought to myself.

The other bartender provided him with a fresh pitcher, but the same thing occurred, and I saw no more because the customers sitting at the bar crowded around, offering suggestions. Our server returned, baffled, saying he'd have the drinks momentarily, and went to the kitchen. When he returned, he had the woman's gazpacho and some bread, which he set down, and then went to the bar, where the audience had expanded.

Ruth lit a cigarette and said, "I suppose this is all part of it, Isabel. Incidentally, it seems to be getting warmer in here."

It was, and I had the sense the place was quieter—a background sound had ceased. It occurred to me that I no longer heard the faint hum of the air-conditioning unit over the door, and as I started to mention this, I made a gesture toward it. My hand collided with Ruth's when she tapped her cigarette over the ashtray, and the cigarette landed in the neighboring gazpacho.

"Hey! What's the meaning of this?" snarled the sour-faced man.

"I'm terribly sorry," I said. "It was an accident. I—"

"Throwing cigarettes at people!" the heavyset woman said.

"I really didn't intend to," I began again, standing up. There must have been a loose thread on the edge of their tablecloth which one of my bracelet clasps caught on, because as I stepped out from between the closely positioned tables, I pulled everything—tablecloth, silverware, water glasses, ashtrays and the gazpacho-à-la-nicotine—onto the floor.

The heavyset woman surged from the booth and struck me solidly. The man assumed a boxing stance. The proprietor of the establishment, a man with prominent dark eyebrows, hurried toward us with a determined expression. I attempted to explain what had happened, but I was overwhelmed by shouting, and the proprietor frowned severely.

option_b: The rescheduled meeting at the VC firm

Love and Labor

No romantic drama in the last five years has succeeded in dividing critics and audiences as fully as the sprawling, ambitious workplace romance The Golden Thread, Helena Phillips' return to directing after a decade away from film. I've watched it twice and am still trying to sort out my responses, which oscillate between admiration and skepticism and back again. Like The Notebook, the picture grabs you emotionally with brilliant, sweeping montages of passion and Turneresque images of love transcendent. But Phillips, a certified intellectual who studied neuroscience and moral philosophy before directing Autumn in Fairview and Nights of Shadowbrook in the early 2010s and then vanished from public life, occupies a different philosophical universe from Nicholas Sparks. Post-romance, her various characters philosophize about their experiences in dreamy, cryptic voice-overs that wash over you like gentle waves: "Why does love compete with itself? ... Is there a destructive force in passion, not one force but two?" Or "This great longing: Where's it come from? What seed, what root did it grow from? Who's doing this? Who's robbing us of connection and light?" First you get swept up in emotion, then you get submerged in contemplation.

Those existential questions don't derive from the screenplay's source, a straightforward but otherwise grounded 2018 novel by Rebecca Thomas (who also wrote Hearts in Transit) about a labor organizer's romance with a media executive in the coastal town of Yarnmouth, Xandria. They're central to Phillips' vision of the story, however, and not frivolous. In the romantic drama genre, the phrase "love conquers all" usually means nothing more than that it's nice to find your soulmate, or to see your protagonist get their happy ending. A true work of art owes us more than superficial emotions, and Phillips obliges by making her tale of romance the setting for nothing less than a meditation on the nature of human connection and the existence of meaningful relationships in a fragmented world.

She tells the story deliberately, in three parts, with a prestigious cast (Anthony Johnson, Elizabeth Hernandez, Nathan Morris) and a few other major stars (Logan Payne, Claudia James, Yasmin Hall) appearing in supporting roles. After an idyllic prelude, in which an earnestly idealistic union organizer, Yasmin Hall (in a career-defining performance), walks through the morning markets of Fairview, Selvoria, to the accompaniment of a soaring string quartet, the first part chronicles the arrival of a media production company in the economically depressed town, introduces the principal characters (none of whom functions as a simple protagonist), and establishes the movie's geographical and philosophical landscape. The centerpiece—the romance—unfolds over nearly an hour and features the most intense and tender sequences, chiefly Yasmin's initially conflicted attraction to Anthony Johnson's character, Nathan Morris, the media executive sent to document the town's labor struggles for a controversial documentary series. The coda lasts almost 45 minutes and is mostly reflection and resolution, the rhythms growing more contemplative until a final, unexpected moment of separation—whereupon the surviving relationship transforms into something neither character anticipated. In the final shot, intertwined vines grow along the waterfront of Yarnmouth Town, the cycle of connection beginning anew.

The Golden Thread has a distinctive soundscape, as the noise of conflict frequently recedes to make room for interior monologues and composer Helena Chen's minimalist, contemplative score. Yasmin talks to her absent sister, viewed in achingly beautiful flashbacks. ("Love: Where does it come from? Who lit this flame in us?") Nathan, a borderline workaholic passed over one too many times for creative control and desperate to prove his worth no matter the personal cost, worries anxiously about how his choices affect others. The dreamer Yasmin poses probing questions about whether we're all connected through invisible threads of shared humanity. If the movie has a backbone, it's her evolving dialogue with her colleague Rebecca Thomas (played by Claudia James), who's increasingly frustrated by Yasmin's romantic, almost utopian optimism about the possibility of bridging class divides through personal relationships. Says Rebecca, "In this world, a person alone is nothing, and there ain't no bridge but the ones we burn." Replies Yasmin, dark eyes shining, "I've seen another way." At first it seems as if Yasmin will indeed be a naive romantic to Rebecca's cynical realist. But if Yasmin is ultimately an idealistic believer, Rebecca turns out to be a wounded romantic who can't stop feeling hope despite a world that seems designed to crush it. She speaks the movie's epitaph, "Connection and isolation, hope and despair: Are they the workings of one heart, the features of the same face? O my soul, let me exist in you now. Look out through my eyes. Look out at the things you've made, all things shining."

Phillips puts many shining things on screen: workers, executives, children, elderly couples, visions of community by way of documentary realism and of alienation by way of stark modernism. Phillips' conception of consciousness distributes it among all her characters equally; almost every person is held up for careful contemplation. I could cite hundreds of images: Yasmin in a crowded union hall hovers over a speech she's writing, which is covered from top to bottom with revisions and additions. (You don't know the woman yet, but you can feel in an instant her need to get everything exactly right.) A small, white-haired elderly man walks peacefully past a group of anxious workers who can't believe the factory owners haven't responded to their demands yet. Two conversations bring together the first pair of characters to acknowledge their attraction; a moment later, the sunset plays mystically over the industrial waterfront that has shaped their entire lives. Helena Chen's camera rushes in on a workers' meeting: One worker shouts passionately; another, exhausted, laughs and laughs; a third weeps over a colleague's testimony. The face of a retired worker speaks from memory, "Are you fighting for justice? Know that I was, too."

Whether or not these luminous moments cohere is another matter. Phillips throws out her overarching theme—is love possible across class divides, or does economic reality always win?—in the first few minutes but, for all her striking juxtapositions, she never dramatizes it with anything approaching the clarity of, say, Mike Leigh's Secrets & Lies (1996). Besides the dialogue between Rebecca and Yasmin, The Golden Thread's other organizing story involves a wrenching conflict between Nathan's professional ambitions and his growing feelings for Yasmin, whose labor organizing work he's supposed to be documenting objectively. But matters of cause and effect don't really interest Phillips. Individual acts of courage can and do change lives, and love can transform a person or a community, she acknowledges. But Nathan is ultimately recalled by his company, and Phillips never bothers to trace the full impact of his documentary on the labor dispute. In fact, the entire conflict seems to take place in an ambiguous space. Nathan quotes Rilke's letters on love and films meaningless B-roll to "make the executives happy—it'll look like we're capturing authentic moments." Characters navigate uncertain feelings, unsure whether they're experiencing genuine connection or manufactured emotion. People collide, sabotage themselves with their own fears, retreat frantically into familiar patterns, use work as a shield to keep the vulnerability of intimacy at bay. A tiny bird, building a nest, flutters in the eaves.

Phillips is convincing—at times overwhelming—on the subject of emotional chaos. It's when she tries to ruminate on order that she gets muddled, retreating to one of her abstract multiple narrators: "Where is it that we were together? Who is it that I loved? The partner. ... The friend. ... One heart." I think I'd have an easier time with Phillips' metaphysical speculations if I had a sense of some concomitant socioeconomic ones—central to any larger musings on forces of connection as viewed through the prism of class conflict. Couldn't it be that the corporate media order is profoundly anti-human, and that the workers' cause represents a natural human need for dignity and fair treatment? You don't have to buy into Thomas's socialist pieties in her original novel to believe that there's a difference between a romance that ignores power dynamics and one that confronts them (or, for that matter, between authentic documentary and propaganda). While she was at film school, Phillips might have peeled herself away from her mentor's abstract theories about cognitive development and cultural sociology and checked out a few courses on labor relations and organizational behavior. Maybe then she'd view the Yarnmouth labor dispute not in a romantic vacuum (the lovers meet, they feel and are felt for, they part) but in the larger context of economic struggles that have shaped human relationships for centuries. For all her visionary filmmaking, Phillips' aesthetic neutrality sometimes seems like a cultivated—and pretentious—brand of avoidance.

Claudia James's wooden performance as a corporate lawyer in The Negotiator (2019) had one positive result: It gave her preparation for Rebecca Thomas, the pragmatic labor organizer at the center of The Golden Thread. James's Rebecca is much more nuanced than her previous work: tough and skeptical and hardened in many ways but fundamentally on the side of human dignity, too proud and experienced to believe in fairy tales when all evidence suggests otherwise. Rebecca has fought—and mostly lost—countless labor disputes against corporate giants over workers' rights, fair wages, and safe conditions in Yarnmouth, Xandria. Director Helena Phillips, in the film based on the book, goes beyond the specific labor dispute to evoke (stopping just short of propaganda) the difficulty of maintaining authentic human connections in a world structured by economic inequality and power imbalances.

Phillips' version doesn't capture the mounting frustration that one experiences while reading Thomas's book, or even the satisfying romantic resolution that James Cameron skillfully manipulated in his underrated Titanic (1997). But The Golden Thread is a thoughtful piece of work, an old-fashioned transformation narrative with some contemporary complexity. Yasmin doesn't pursue this romance—initiated by Nathan, the documentarian sent to film the labor dispute—because she wants to fall in love but because she believes that personal connection might bridge the gap between workers and management. She might succeed, too, if it weren't for the structural forces that Nathan himself represents, the media production company that knows how to keep filming while actual workers' lives deteriorate.

Phillips is at her most assured when she cuts back and forth between Rebecca's union meetings about what not to do when dealing with media and Yasmin's developing relationship with Nathan. The sequence has the extra dimension of good social commentary: It dramatizes and comments simultaneously. Plus, it gives James a splendid platform for understated wisdom. (James has become one of the most reliable actors working today.) Elsewhere, Phillips takes a more impressionistic approach, focusing on emotional nuance and rarely offering clear answers. As in her Autumn in Fairview (2012), the outcome of every scene is somewhat predictable, but how Phillips gets from moment to moment is surprisingly fresh. She also gets sterling performances from Logan Payne as the disturbingly charming media CEO, Elizabeth Hernandez as Yasmin's anxious younger sister, and Anthony Johnson as Nathan. Johnson understands that when you're playing a man caught between professional duty and personal feeling, you don't need to overact—you reveal the conflict by trying not to show it.

To the communities involved in real labor struggles, the real climax of stories like this isn't the ambiguous ending of the book or the open-ended, "let's imagine new possibilities," hopeful conclusion of the movie. The climax is the creation of art that takes workers' perspectives seriously and that remains in cultural conversation for years. The climax is the film starring talented actors who bring dignity to working-class stories. Corporate media companies may continue to dominate the industry, but some of us will never watch their productions again without thinking about the real human costs behind the glossy images, without remembering the questions Phillips raises about whether genuine connection is possible in a world structured by inequality, without considering the existential questions about love, labor, and what it means to live authentically in an inauthentic world.

The Golden Thread ultimately asks whether romance can survive—or even exist—when lovers occupy different positions in an economic hierarchy. Phillips suggests, through her layered narrative and complex characterizations, that love requires more than individual feeling; it requires structural change, a reimagining of how we organize our social and economic lives. The film's greatest achievement isn't its beautiful cinematography or its thoughtful performances, but its insistence that personal relationships cannot be separated from political and economic contexts. In this way, Phillips elevates the romantic drama genre, demanding that we think critically about the conditions that make authentic human connection possible or impossible.

Whether audiences will embrace this challenging vision remains to be seen. The Golden Thread has performed moderately at the box office, attracting cinephiles and critics but puzzling mainstream viewers expecting conventional romantic satisfaction. Phillips seems unconcerned with commercial success, having stated in interviews that she made the film she needed to make, regardless of market considerations. This artistic integrity, combined with her decade-long absence from filmmaking, has only enhanced her reputation as a singular voice in contemporary cinema, someone willing to risk everything for a vision that refuses easy answers or comfortable resolutions.
