THE SCENT OF DIGITAL PAINT
BY HANNAH MUNOZ

The gallery district of Maplewood, Veldoria had to be safe enough. I couldn't have been more certain. In the window of the electronics store, a holographic display was cycling through NFT art pieces, and folded in my pocket was the news article about the catastrophic failure of the new blockchain-based conservation tracking system. The young people on the corner seemed barely recognizable, hunched figures in synthetic fiber coats. It was my own time. Anyone could see I was safe, and I could risk doing what I desperately wanted to do.

I turned the corner.

The odds were against me from the start. It didn't come as any surprise. I could never get away with it. I knew that all along.

There was a Tesla parked just beyond the charging station.

The metal and glass fronts of the buildings didn't show back here, only weathered brick held together with crumbling mortar. The line of the block seemed to stretch back, ever further away from the sleek fronts into the decaying stone.

A woman brushed past me, wearing a smart blazer and carrying a tablet. And, reassuringly, she was in a hurry.

I decided to chance it. I certainly wanted to do it in the worst way.

My footsteps carried me on down the block.

A small vehicle whirred past me. One of those autonomous pods, I decided. Only it wasn't quite right. I fixed the silhouette in my mind's eye and tried to identify it. Something from the early 2020s.

Still, I wasn't worried. It was actually too early in the day. It wasn't as if it were evening or anything like that.

The little shop was right where I left it, quietly deteriorating by itself. The Retrospective Gallery, the faded sign proclaimed in blue and silver, or now, gray and cream. In the window, in protective cases, were prints from the first digital art exhibition, a recent magazine featuring contemporary VR installations, a coffee table book about the Restoration Movement murals, and a brand-new, sun-faded catalog of the Morningside Province Ecosystem Art Project.

There was a delivery drone at the curb. This time I recognized it was from an earlier generation.

I went in, the chrome handle making me conscious of the sweat on my palm.

The old woman sat behind a fortress of art books and magazines, treacherously scrolling through something on an ancient tablet. Her gray hair was pulled back from the sharp angles of her cardigan. She smiled, showing yellowed teeth.

"Came back for more of the work, did you?"

She set down the tablet. (That headline couldn't really be making such an accusation about the Conservation Council, could it?)

"Yes," I laughed, not very convincingly.

"I know what a craving can be. I shouldn't eat sweets, but I do. I've tried to stop but I lie there thinking about chocolate half the night. Dark chocolate, milk chocolate, truffles, plain bars. I feel like I could eat a whole box. Is it like that with you?"

"Not that bad. To me it's just—"

"Don't tell me art isn't a craving with some of you people. I've seen folks come in here, hardly two coins to rub together, and grab up those restoration journals and read and read, until sweat starts rolling off the end of their nose. I've hardly got the heart to throw them out."

Restoration journals. Ones with beautiful landscapes being returned to their natural state, with ecosystems being rebuilt from nothing. Yes, they were a part of it. Not a big part, but a part.

"That's not what I want to see. I want—"

The old woman chuckled. "I know what you want. Indeed I do. This way."

I followed her pointing hand and sure enough, there they were. Stacks upon stacks of old art magazines from the Restoration Movement.

"Twenty credits for ones in good condition," the old woman pronounced the ritual, "ten credits for ones with damaged covers, three for twenty-five, check them at the desk when you go."

I ran my hand down a stack. *Art & Ecology*, *The Restoration Artist*, *Biodiversity Canvas*, *Creative Conservation*, all of them.

The old woman was watching me. She scuttled back across the floor and snatched up a magazine. It was a copy of *Ecosystem Visions* with a woman in paint-splattered overalls standing before a massive mural of a restored wetland.

"This one, this one," she said. "This must be a good one. I bet she painted every species that came back. Every single one. Species."

"I'll take it."

Reluctantly she handed over the magazine, waited a moment, then left me.

I stared at the stacks of Restoration Movement magazines and I felt the slow run of the drop of sweat down my nose.

My sickness was terrible. It is as bad to be nostalgic for things you have never known as for an orphan who has never had a home to be homesick.

Living in the past, that was always me. I never watched anything on the screens made later than 2025. I was fascinated by the early digital artists, the first VR creators, the pioneers of blockchain art. My favorite artists were the ones who had painted the great restoration murals in Redwood Territory.

The music I listened to was from the Cultural Exchange Movement and the early days of computational composition.

And my viewing was the documentation of the Restoration Movement, harking back to when they had first begun rebuilding the ecosystems. This was the biggest part of it all, I think.

You identify with the subject of any documentary if it's well enough made. But the identification I felt with the artists in restoration documentation was plainly ridiculous.

I was there.

I was standing before the canvas, feeling on my face the bite of the wind from the restored prairie. I was lifting my brush to capture the return of the native grasses in the dawn light. Then in a moment my hand was moving across the canvas in answer to the landscape, creating through the systematic observation that had been drilled into us, recording the biodiversity that was slowly, miraculously returning. And back through the field notes in the pocket at my knee.

Here it comes, the morning light hitting the wetland in perfect illumination. Look at that careful documentation. You can almost see the species checklist in the artist's other hand. They can afford to be methodical with that funding. I'd like to trade this rushed commission for it. That may be just what happens too if I don't watch it.

You aren't any master restorer, friend, but this is from the Maplewood Collective for the Redwood Project.

Missed that detail!

Careful with that brushstroke! God, look at the way that color bleeds. At least it was a lie about them using cheap materials.

One of your own techniques for you, amateur. Up with the palette, up under that canopy, into the shadow detail. Where am I? Where am I?

Right here.

Look at that background go. The supplier can't be giving you as good paint as they claim.

So long. I'm nodding, see.

She's pushing through. No more paint and she's pushing through. She's a good artist. Come on. A little more. A little more and you can finish it. Come on, friend. You're doing it. You're pushing through—

But not enough.

God, what a mess.

I'm sick.

That damned synthetic medium in the mix. I'll be in the bathroom until morning...

No, the air wasn't one of synthetic medium but the pleasant smell of aged paper and printer's ink.

I'd been daydreaming again. I shouldn't forget things were getting different lately. It was becoming dangerous.

I gathered up an armload of Restoration Movement magazines at random.

Leaning across the table, I noticed the curtain in back for the first time. It was a beaded curtain of many different colors, like something from an old bohemian studio. Behind the curtain was a screen. It was a comforting anti-anachronism here.

The large flat display was showing an old documentary. A very old documentary. Early footage from the first ecosystem restoration project as scientists worked to bring back a destroyed forest, standing them off from encroaching development. The flickering images caught my unblinking eyes.

A developer is sneaking across the property line, a contract in his briefcase. A young activist makes a try to stop the bulldozers, but the security forces remove her. Now a government official is arriving with the preservation order. The developer makes a try with legal action, the activists celebrate, and the official signs the protection into law. It goes through, all the way through.

The young woman is running toward the official as he finishes with the paperwork and stands, her shirt torn from the earlier struggle. The developer stands up in defeat. The official smiles. No, no, say the woman's lips. "No!" "No!" says the subtitle. The official hesitates. Swimming in bureaucracy, the developer smiles sadly and walks away.

I had seen documentaries like that before.

When I was younger, I had seen *Heritage Flashbacks* between episodes of nature shows and environmental programs. I looked at old footage and heard voices making commentary. But hadn't I also seen these images with the sound of actual field recordings and low conversation?

I had seen these images before the Collapse.

The Collapse had made a lot of difference in my life.

Art supplies were rationed, from full sets to basic kits, and prices had gone up to where you had to pay hundreds for proper materials, so high that people said the Council should do something about it.

The Restoration Movement had transformed, and artists worked on rebuilding ecosystems in both physical and digital space. Only, hadn't they also worked on the social contract, on justice theory, on ethical decision-making about what should be restored and how?

And at the community center I had participated in decision-making processes about local projects. I never did get enough votes to lead a project, but my mentor had taken my designs and incorporated parts of them for the wetland restoration. I could never get enough recognition...

"Nobody would look at my magazines," the old woman chuckled, "if I put it out front. My daughter got me that screen. She runs a digital art studio. A good girl. Her name's on the business registry."

I pressed some credits on her and walked myself out of the store. Shutting the door, I saw that the catalog of the Ecosystem Art Project had been replaced by something about the Cultural Exchange Movement.

The street was full of autonomous vehicles, sleek electric cars, boxy delivery drones, swept-back courier bikes. Only one dark, heavy, combustion-engine vehicle moved through the traffic. It had a light on the roof.

I dodged in front of a recycling truck and behind an electric postal van and ran for that light, leaving a trail of gaudy restoration images checkering the street behind me.

I grabbed the handle on the door, opened it and threw myself into the back seat.

"Central District," I said from my diaphragm, without any breath behind it.

Something was wrong. Two people were in the front seat. The driver showed me his hard, expressionless face. "What do you think you are doing?"

"This isn't a rideshare?" I asked blankly.

"Environmental Police."

I sat there while we drove on for a few minutes.

"Disoriented and disturbed," the second person said to the driver.

"Right into our laps."

The second officer leaned forward and clicked something. "I'll get the City units."

"No, kill it, Hannah. Think of all that damned paperwork."

Hannah shrugged. "What will we do with him?"

I was beginning to attach myself to my surroundings. The street was full of traffic. My kind of traffic. Vehicles that were too new or too old.

"Look, officers, I'm not disoriented or disturbed. I thought this was a rideshare. I just wanted to get away from back then—I mean back *there*."

The two officers exchanged glances.

"What were you running from?" the driver asked.

How could I tell him that?

Before I even got a chance to try, he said: "What did you do?"

"I didn't *do* anything!"

The vehicle was turning, turning into shadows, stopping. We were in an alley. Soggy cardboard, discarded containers, prowling rats, a broken die, half a dice, looking big in the frame of my thick, probably bulletproof window.

The officers opened their doors and then mine.

"Out."

I climbed out and stood by the vehicle, blinking.

"You were causing some kind of trouble in that neighborhood back there," the driver announced.

"Really, officers—"

"What's your name?"

"Noah Nguyen. There—"

"We don't want you going back there again, Nguyen, causing trouble. Understand?"

"Officer, I only bought some magazines—I mean art journals."

"These?" the second person, Hannah, asked. She had retrieved them from the back seat. "Look here, Stephen. They look pretty subversive."

Stephen took up the *Ecosystem Visions* with the woman in the paint-splattered overalls. "Dangerous," he said.

"You know about the laws governing unauthorized restoration documentation, Nguyen."

"Those aren't unauthorized and they are my property!"

I reached for them and Hannah pulled them back, grinning. "You don't want to read these. They aren't good for you. We're confiscating them."

"Look here, I'm a citizen! You can't—"

Hannah shoved me back a little. "Can't we?"

Stephen stepped in front of me, his face in deadly earnest. "How about it, Nguyen? You a memory addict?"

He grabbed my wrist and started checking my pulse, looking for signs of neural interface abuse. I twisted away from him.

"Resisting an officer," Stephen said almost sadly.

At that, Hannah moved up beside him.

The two of them started to beat me.

They hit clean, in the belly and ribs, but not in the groin. They gave me clean white flashes of pain, instead of angry, red-streaked ones. I didn't fight back, not against the two of them. I knew that much. I didn't even try to block their blows. I stood with my arms at my sides, leaning back against the vehicle, and hearing myself grunt at each blow.

They stood away from me and let me fold helplessly to the greasy pavement.

"Stay away from that neighborhood and stay out of trouble," Stephen's voice said above me.

I looked up a little bit and saw an ugly, scarred hand thumbing across a stack of half a dozen magazines like a giant deck of cards.

"Why don't you take up contemporary art?" he asked me.

I never heard the vehicle drive away.

Home. I activated the living room lights from the door, looked around for intruders for the first time I could remember, and went inside.

I threw myself on the couch and rubbed my stomach. I wasn't hurt badly. My middle was going to be sorer in the morning than it was now.

Lighting up a vape, I watched the shapes of vapor and tried to think.

I looked at it objectively, forward and back.

The solution was obvious.

First of all, I positively could *not* have been a restoration artist in the early Restoration Movement. I was in my mid-twenties; anybody could tell that by looking at me. The time was the late 2050s; anybody could tell that from the neural interface ports in the corner, the new autonomous vehicles on the street. Memories of painting restoration murals and documenting returning biodiversity stirred in me by old magazines, archived documentaries, and re-runs of *The Restoration* on the streams were mere hallucinations.

Neither could I remember attending the first Cultural Exchange festivals, hearing the debates about the social contract in the post-Collapse world, or paying a month's credits to get into the original Ecosystem Art Project exhibition.

Only... I probably had seen the Project. Hadn't I gone with my mentor to a preview? Didn't she pay reduced admission for me? So how could I remember taking a partner, dark-haired, green jacket, Zoe, and paying full price each? I couldn't. Different exhibitions. That was it. The thing had toured half a dozen times. But would it have been that expensive no more than ten years ago?

I activated a new vape cartridge.

The thing I must remember, I told myself, was that my recollections were false and unreliable. It would do me no good to keep following these false memories in a closed curve.

I touched my navel area and flinched. The beating, I was confident, had been real. But it had been a nightmare. Those officers couldn't have been true. They were a small person's bad dream about symbolized authority. They were keeping me from re-entering the past where I belonged, punishing me to make me stay in my trap of the present.

Oh, God.

I rolled over on my face and pushed it into the upholstery.

That was the worst part of it. False memories, feelings of persecution, that was one thing. Believing that you are actively caught up in a mixture of the past with the present, a surreal viscosity of reality, was something else.

I needed help.

Or if there was no help for me, it was my duty to have myself placed where I couldn't harm other citizens.

If there was one thing that working for the Conservation Council had taught me, it was social responsibility.

I took up the directory and located several memory specialists. I selected one at random, for no particular reason.

Dr. Christopher Fernandez.

I memorized the address and heaved myself to my feet.

The doctor's office was as white as the inside of a sterile laboratory.

The cool, efficient receptionist told me to wait and I did, tasting nothing inside my mouth.

After several long, peaceful minutes the inner door opened.

"Mr. Nguyen, I can't seem to find any record of an appointment for you in Dr. Fernandez's files," the man said.

I got to my feet. "Then I'll come back."

He took my arm. "No, no, I can fit you in."

"I didn't have an appointment. I just came."

"I understand."

"Maybe I had better go."

"I won't hear of it."

I could have pulled loose from him, but somehow I felt that if I did try to pull away, the grip would tighten and I would never get away.

I looked up into that long, hard, blank face that seemed so recently familiar.

"I'm Dr. Santos," he said. "I'm taking care of Dr. Fernandez's practice for him while he is on leave."

I nodded. What I was thinking could only be another symptom of my illness.

He led me inside and closed the door.

The door made a strange sound in closing. It didn't go *snick-bonk*; it made a noise like *click-clack-clunk*.

"Now," he said, "would you like to lie down on the couch and tell me about it? Some people have preconceived ideas that I don't want to fight with at the beginning. Or, if you prefer, you can sit there in front of my desk and tell me all about it. Remember, I'm a neurologist, a doctor, not just a therapist."

I took possession of the chair and Santos faced me across his desk.

"I feel," I said, "that I am caught up in some kind of temporal displacement."

"I see. Have you consumed much restoration documentation, Mr. Nguyen?"

"Some. I view a lot. All kinds of content. Historical archives, contemporary streams, educational programs, entertainment feeds."

"You should *view* them instead of live them. Catharsis. Sublimate, Mr. Nguyen. For instance, to a certain type of person, I often recommend contemporary action feeds."

I seemed to be losing control of the conversation. "But this temporal displacement..."

"Mr. Nguyen, do you really believe in 'temporal displacement'?"

"No."

"Then how can there be any such thing? It can't be real."

"I know that! I want to be cured of imagining it."

"The first step is to utterly renounce the idea. Stop thinking about the past. Think of the future."

"How did you know I keep slipping back into the past?" I asked.

Santos's hands were more expressive than his face. "You mentioned temporal displacement..."

"But not to the past or to the future," I said.

"But you did, Mr. Nguyen. You told me all about thinking you could go into the past by visiting a gallery where they sold old magazines. You told me how the intrusion of the past got worse with every visit."

I blinked. "I did? I did?"

"Of course."

I stood up. "I did not!"

"Please try to keep from getting violent, Mr. Nguyen. People like you actually have more control over themselves than you realize. If you *will* yourself to be calm..."

"I *know* I didn't tell you a thing about the Retrospective Gallery. I'm starting to think I'm not sick at all. You—you're trying to do something to me. You're all in it together."

Santos shook his head sadly.

I realized how it all sounded.

"Good—GOD!" I moaned.

I put my hands to my face and I felt the vein over my left eye swelling, pulsing.

Through the bars of my fingers I saw Santos motion me down with one eloquent hand. I took my hands away—I didn't like looking through bars—and sat down.

"Now," Santos said, steepling his fingers, "I know of a completely appropriate facility in Crestwood. Of course, if you respond properly..."

Those hands of his.

There was something about them that wasn't right. They might have been the hands of a corpse, or a synthetic...

I lurched across the desk and grabbed his wrist.

"*Please*, Mr. Nguyen! Violence will—"

My fingers clawed at the backs of his hands and my nails dragged off ugly strips of some theatrical material—synthetic skin, I think—that had covered the scrapes and bruises he had taken hammering away at me and my belt buckle.

Santos.

Stephen.

I let go of him and stood away.

For the first time, Santos smiled.

I backed to the door and turned the handle behind my back. It wouldn't open.

I turned around and rattled it, pulled on it, braced my foot against the wall and tugged.

"Locked," Santos supplied.

He was coming toward me, I could tell. I wheeled and faced him. He had a neural interface device. It was the smallest one I had ever seen and it had an iridescence or luminosity about it, a gleaming silver needle.

I closed with him.

By the way he moved, I knew he was trained in physical combat, but you can't win them all, and I had been in a lot of fights when I had been younger. (Hadn't I?)

I stepped in while he was trying to decide whether to use the device on me or drop it to have his hands free. I palm-struck him in the solar plexus and crossed my fist into the hollow of the apex arch of his jawbone. He dropped.

I gave him a kick at the base of his spine. He grunted and lay still.

There was a knocking on the door. "Doctor? Doctor?"

I searched through his pockets. He didn't have any keys. He didn't have any money or identification or a weapon. He had a cloth and a stylus.

The receptionist had moved away from the door and was talking to somebody, in person or on a comm or intercom.

There wasn't any back door.

I went to the window. The city stretched out in an impressive panorama. On the street below, traffic crawled. There was a ledge. Quite a wide, old-fashioned ornamental ledge.

The ledge ran beneath the windows of all the offices on this floor. The twenty-first, I remembered.

I had seen it done in entertainment feeds all my life. Action heroes were always doing it for some reason or other. I had a good reason.

I unlatched the window and climbed out into the dry, crisp breeze.

The entertainment feeds didn't know much about physics. The updraft nearly lifted me off the ledge, but the cornice was so wide I could keep out of the wind if I kept myself flat against the side of the building.

The next window was about twenty feet away. I had covered half that distance, moving my feet with a sideways shuffle, when Hannah, indisputably the second officer, put her head out of the window where I was heading and pointed a weapon at me, saying in a let's-have-no-foolishness tone: "Get in here."

I went the other way.

The cool, efficient receptionist was in Santos's window with the tiny silver device in readiness.

I kept shuffling toward the receptionist. I had decided I would rather wrestle with her over the device than fight Hannah over the weapon. Idiotically, I smiled at that idea.

I slipped.

I was falling down the twenty-one stories without even a moment of windmilling for balance. I was just gone.

Lines were converging, and I was converging on the lines.

You aren't going to be able to recover from this fall, Nguyen. Good-by, Nguyen.

Death.

A sleep, a reawakening, a lie. It's nothing like that. It's nothing.

The end of everything you ever were or ever could be.

I hit.

My kneecap hurt terribly. I had scraped it badly.

Reality was all over me in patches. I showed through as a line drawing, crudely done, a sketch.

Some kind of projection. High-resolution hologram, that was all reality meant.

I was kneeling on a hard surface no more than six feet from the window from which I had fallen. It was still twenty-one flights up, more or less, but *Down* was broken and splattered over me.

I stood up, moving forward a step.

It brought me halfway through the projection, halfway through the wall at the base of the building. The other side of the screen. The solid side, I found, stepping through, bracing a hand on the image.

Looking up twenty-one floors, I saw an unbroken line of peacefully closed panes.

I remembered riding up in the elevator, the moments inside, the faint feeling of vertigo. Of course, who was to say the elevator really moved? Maybe they had only switched scenery on me while I was caught inside, listening to the artificial hum, seeing the flashing lights. Either alter the oxygen supply inside the cubicle suddenly or use subtle neural stimulation and that would contribute a sensation of change, of movement. They had it all worked out.

My fingers rubbed my head briskly, both hands working, trying to get some circulation in my brain.

I guessed I had to run. There didn't seem much else to do.

I ran.

Get help?

Not this elderly man and his grandson. Not this construction worker on her way to a job site. Not the accountant. Maybe the gallery owner, ex-Council, community leader, solid, respectable, well-intentioned, not a complete fool. The person on the corner checking a tablet by the transit stop.

"I need help," I panted to them. "Somebody's trying to kidnap me."

"Really makes you concerned to hear about something like that, doesn't it?" they said. "I'm in favor of stronger citizen protection laws myself."

"I'm not sure whether—"

"This heat is oppressive, isn't it? Especially here in these urban canyons. Sometimes I wish I was back in Crestwood. Cool, shaded streets..."

"Listen to me! These people, they're conspiring against me, trying to drive me insane! Two officers, a receptionist—"

"For my money, the Ecosystem Art Project is *the* achievement of our generation. I just don't understand these people who say it hasn't got merit. It gets merit by demonstrating what restoration can accomplish..."

They were like anybody you might talk to on the street. I knew what they would say if I cued them with "sports" or "politics" instead of the key words I had used.

I should have known better, but I wanted to touch them in some way, make them know I was alive. I grabbed them and shook them by the shoulders, and there was a whoosh and as I might have expected they collapsed like the insubstantiality they were.

There was a stick figure of a person left before me, an economical skeleton supporting the shell of a human being and two-thirds of a business suit.

Hide.

I went into the first shop I came to—Artisan Supplies.

Appropriately, it was a false front.

A neutral-colored gray surface, too smooth for concrete, stretched away into some shadows. The area was littered with trash.

Containers, bottles, what looked like the skin of a dehydrated human being—obviously, on second thought, only the discarded skin of one of the things like the one I had deflated.

And a moldering pile of documents and files.

Something caught my eye and I kicked through them. Yes, the proposal I had written to the Conservation Council in Redwood Territory, unopened. *And which they had approved.*

My work.

The work I had done for the Council, important, creative work. There was my design, the sketch of the wetland restoration, the families, children, elders, the caption: Biodiversity Conservation is Part of Our Social Contract.

All of it lying here to rot.

Something made me look away from that terrible trash.

Santos stood in the entrance of Artisan Supplies, something bright in his hand.

Something happened.

I had been wrong.

The shining instrument had not been a neural interface device.

"You're resilient," Santos said as I eased back into focus.

"You aren't, not without help," I told him in disgust.

"Spirited, aren't you? I meant mental resilience. That's the one thing we can never judge. I think you could have taken the shock right from the start. Of course, you would still have needed the conditioning to integrate properly."

"Conditioning? Conditioning?" It came out of me, vortexing up, outside of my control. "What have you done to my mind?"

"We've been trying to get it to grow back up," Santos said reasonably. "Think of this. Restoration. Renewal. Rejuvenation. This is it. Never mind how it works. Most minds can't stand being young and knowing they will have to go through the same experience all over again. We use neural remapping to shift your upper conscious memories to your subconscious, leaving room for new memories. You remember only those things out of the past you *have* to, to retain your identity."

"Identity," I repeated. "I have no identity. My identity is a dream. I have two identities—one of them decades beyond the other."

Santos tilted his head and his eyes at me and slapped me across the face. "Don't go back on me now. We gave you the best we could. The Rejuvenation Service couldn't help it if you were too old for a *beta*. You shouldn't have waited until you were so old, so very old. We used the very oldest sets and simulations we had for *betas*, but you, you had to keep wandering onto *alpha* territory, while they were striking sets, even. *Beta* or not, we gave you good service. Don't slip now."

I heard the voice and I heard another voice, and it said "What could you expect of a *beta*?" and they were only some of the voices I was hearing, and I wondered what you could expect from a *beta*, and I didn't know, or think that I would ever know.
question: Why was Noah Nguyen daydreaming about being a restoration artist?
option_a: Because he was actually experiencing false memories implanted during a rejuvenation process that couldn't fully suppress his original identity from decades earlier
option_b: Because he had read too many restoration journals and was naturally prone to vivid fantasies about artistic work
correct_answer_text: Because he was actually experiencing false memories implanted during a rejuvenation process that couldn't fully suppress his original identity from decades earlier

synthetic_story:
The neural interface lab in Dalebrook Town hummed with the quiet efficiency of expensive equipment. I nearly tripped over the kid before I saw her in the dim corridor outside the observation room.

Her wheelchair was positioned where it usually was during evening hours, near the large window overlooking the research campus courtyard. But tonight something was different. Priya wasn't watching the courtyard gardens as she typically did, tracking the movements of birds and small animals with that intense focus that had first caught my attention months ago. Instead, she sat with her head tilted back, staring at the ceiling-mounted neural activity display that showed real-time brain scans of research subjects.

The girl wasn't observing the data streams tonight as she usually did. She was lying back in her chair with her face turned upward, her eyes following patterns that seemed to exist only in her mind, so absorbed that she didn't notice me until I spoke.

"Everything okay, Priya?" I asked.

She said, "Yes, Dr. Wolfe," without shifting her gaze from the display.

For a moment I experienced an odd sensation of déjà vu, as if I'd lived through this exact scene before. The feeling puzzled me until I remembered a similar encounter three months earlier, when Dr. Nathan Hamilton and I had first brought our mobile research unit to the Dalebrook Neurological Institute. I'd nearly stumbled over Priya's wheelchair that time too, but she hadn't been studying neural patterns then. She'd been watching something else entirely.

"What are you looking at up there, Priya?" I asked.

She didn't move, and her voice had that distant quality I'd learned to recognize.

"I'm reorganizing some connections," she said softly.

I gave up and continued to my shared office without pressing further. How do you talk to a child prodigy like that?

Nathan wasn't in, but for once I didn't worry about him. I was trying to recall what had seemed so familiar about finding Priya's wheelchair out of place. I retrieved a coffee from our small machine—I think better with something warm in my hands—and by the time I'd finished it, I had my answer.

This scenario was familiar because it had happened before, about three months back when Nathan and I first established our research presence at Dalebrook. I'd nearly stumbled over Priya that time too, but she wasn't reorganizing neural connections then. She was just staring ahead, waiting.

She'd been sitting in her wheelchair near the window, gazing out at the courtyard entrance. She was practically holding her breath, as if expecting someone important to arrive, so absorbed that she didn't notice me until I spoke. With her slight frame, serious expression, and unnaturally still dark eyes, she reminded me of those unsettling child actors in psychological thrillers. Except there was nothing theatrical about her intensity. Maybe that's why I spoke, because she looked so desperately focused.

"Something wrong, kid?" I asked.

She didn't startle or look up. Her accent placed her as second-generation immigrant, probably South Asian based on her name and features.

"I'm waiting for Dr. Santos to come back," she said, keeping her eyes on the entrance.

I might have asked who Dr. Santos was, but just then the observation room door opened behind her and her mother took over.

I couldn't see Susan Stanley well because the lights were dimmed inside for the neural imaging equipment. But I could tell from her silhouette that she was tall and imposing. I could make out the glow of a tablet screen in her hands, and when she looked up—the blue light illuminating her face—I saw she was in her mid-thirties, professional-looking but with an edge of exhaustion that spoke of long hours and difficult decisions. The ventilation system carried a faint scent of institutional coffee her way.

"This isn't your concern, Dr. Wolfe," she said. Her voice was educated, professional, but with an undercurrent of protective fierceness. "Please don't encourage Priya's fixations."

She was right about it being none of my business. I went on to the office I shared with Nathan Hamilton and left the two of them waiting for Dr. Santos together.

Our office was dark, which meant first that Nathan had probably gone to the faculty lounge as soon as I left that morning to run my experiments, and second that he'd probably gotten too caught up in philosophical debates to remember to come back. But I was wrong on at least one count, because when I switched on the light and set down my research notes, I saw Nathan asleep on the small couch we'd requisitioned.

He'd been drinking coffee, though. I could smell it on him when I shook him awake—strong, institutional coffee that spoke of long hours in the lounge discussing epistemology with anyone who would listen.

Nathan sat up and blinked against the fluorescent lights, a thin man in his fifties with graying temples, wire-rimmed glasses, and rumpled clothes that suggested he'd been sleeping in them. He was still wearing his lab coat, though at some point during the day he'd managed to shave. He'd even organized some papers; they sat in a neat stack on his desk with a half-written grant proposal on top.

"Wake up and help me write this progress report, Nathan," I said, holding him to his end of our research partnership. "I've collected three months of data and the ethics board wants documentation."

Nathan got up and stretched. He walked to my desk and poked at my notes.

"Cortical plasticity studies again," he complained. "Diego, I'm tired of measuring brain waves!"

"You don't get tenure by studying philosophy," I told him. And because I'd never been able to stay annoyed at him for long, I added, "But we have fresh coffee. Where's your mug?"

"I'm tired of coffee, too," Nathan said. "I need a real conversation about something meaningful."

I gestured at the air, making a show of it. "You've been having one already. Where?"

He grinned at me then with that self-aware, intellectually mischievous expression that transformed his face and made him different from every other burned-out academic I'd ever met.

"The bounty of human curiosity," he said, "is distributed impartially across disciplines and departments. I helped young Priya to the restroom this afternoon while her mother was conducting interviews, and my kindness was justly rewarded."

Sometimes it's hard to tell when Nathan is being serious. He's a trained philosopher—used to teach at some prestigious Eastern university, he'd mentioned once, and I never doubted it—and speaks like one when he chooses to. But Nathan's no deadbeat, though he's semi-obsessed with existential questions and lets me carry most of our research load, and he's perceptive enough to read my thoughts like a data stream.

"No, I didn't barge into her private files," he said. "Susan—Ms. Stanley—shared information with me voluntarily. Why else do you suppose I'd organize those papers?"

That was like Nathan. He hadn't violated research ethics though his curiosity was probably eating him alive. He'd organized grant proposals instead, making himself useful enough to warrant Susan sharing what she knew. It wasn't such a gamble at that, because Nathan has a way about him when he bothers to use it; maybe that's why he drifts through academic positions with me and the grant-funded research circuit, because he's used that charm too often in inappropriate contexts.

"Fair enough," I said and poured coffee for both of us while Nathan pulled up our data files.

He told me more about the Stanleys while we reviewed the research. Susan and Priya were permanent residents of Dalebrook. The girl—she was twelve—was a neurological anomaly who hadn't walked for over two years following a severe accident, and her mother was a research coordinator at the Institute studying rehabilitation techniques. There wasn't any Mr. Stanley. I guessed there never had been, which would explain Susan's protective intensity.

We were halfway through the data review when I remembered something Priya had said.

"Who's Dr. Santos?" I asked.

Nathan frowned at his screen. "Priya had a mentor named Stella Santos, a brilliant neuroscientist who specialized in neural plasticity and consciousness studies. Dr. Santos isn't coming back. She died in a research accident at the Bristol facility while Priya was hospitalized after her injury."

"Terrible," I said, thinking of the girl sitting out there every evening in her wheelchair, watching the entrance. "You mean she's been waiting two years?"

Nathan nodded, seemed to lose interest in the Stanleys, so I let the subject drop. We worked through the evening and finished the progress report around midnight. When we shut down for the night, I figured we wouldn't be staying long at the Dalebrook Institute. It wasn't a very comfortable research environment.

I was wrong there. It wasn't comfortable, but we stayed.

I couldn't have explained at first why we remained, and if Nathan could, he didn't volunteer the information. Neither of us discussed it. We just continued our routine, a few months here and a few there, following grant funding across the country.

We'd arrived at the Dalebrook facility too late for the main consciousness studies funding cycle, so I focused on peripheral research instead. I worked on cortical mapping projects all the way from basic sensory processing to complex decision-making paradigms, not committing to any of the major research teams because I prefer mobility when I get restless. I chose independent neural plasticity studies mostly, because the publication potential is good there if you've got strong analytical skills and patience for data collection.

Neural mapping isn't the exciting frontier it seems to graduate students who flock to the field because the technology is cutting-edge. You work with sophisticated equipment, usually, scanning brain activity instead of direct observation, and you use multiple measurement modalities that capture activity at the cellular level where the real changes occur. There's no dramatic breakthrough moment, as the students discover quickly. A neural reorganization happens gradually, and the biggest challenge is documenting the incremental changes once you've identified a pattern.

Usually a researcher like me publishes findings through the Institute's channels or collaborates with some established team that wants additional data for their meta-analyses, and there's nearly always recognition—from a pool of competitive researchers at the beginning of every funding cycle—for the person documenting the most significant plasticity event. There's a knack to identifying meaningful patterns, and when the grants were running well I only worked a few days a week and spent the rest of my time in the office playing chess and drinking coffee with Nathan Hamilton.

Usually it was an ideal academic life, but somehow it wasn't enough at this place. We'd get moderately caffeinated and work up a promising debate about the nature of knowledge or the foundations of consciousness. Then, just when we'd gotten epistemology looking its most fascinating with our arguments, one or the other of us would glance out the window and see Priya Stanley in her wheelchair, waiting for a brilliant neuroscientist named Stella Santos to walk through the entrance. She was always there, morning or evening, until her mother finished work and took her home.

It wasn't right or natural for a child to wait like that for anything, and it troubled me. I even offered once to arrange for Priya to meet other mentors in the field, but Susan Stanley told me quickly to mind my own business. Nathan explained that the girl didn't want another mentor because she had what he called an epistemological fixation.

"Dr. Santos was more than just a teacher to her," Nathan said. "She was a symbol representing two things no one else in the world could offer—validation and possibility. With Dr. Santos mentoring her, Priya felt intellectually validated, and she could envision possibilities beyond her physical limitations because Dr. Santos showed her that pure thought could transcend bodily constraints. If she accepted another mentor now, she'd be abandoning more than Dr. Santos. She'd be abandoning everything that relationship represented, and then there wouldn't be any point in pursuing knowledge."

I could understand it when Nathan framed it that way. Dr. Santos had spent more time with Priya than Susan had, and the girl felt as intellectually secure with her as she would have with a tenured faculty advisor. And Dr. Santos, being dedicated to her protégés, had depended on Priya for the kind of brilliant insights that made research worthwhile. The mentor needed Priya and Priya needed her. Together, they'd been an ideal partnership.

At first I thought it was strange that Priya never expressed grief or cried when Dr. Santos didn't return, but Nathan explained it was all part of this epistemological fixation. If Priya grieved, she'd be admitting that the knowledge quest was over. So she waited and watched, secure in her belief that Dr. Santos would come back.

The Stanleys grew accustomed to Nathan and me being around, but they never became what you'd call close. Priya would engage with some of Nathan's philosophical provocations, but her attention always returned to the courtyard entrance, watching for Dr. Santos. And she never let anything interfere with her routine.

That routine started every morning when Leonardo Simmons, the Institute's mail courier, rolled his cart through from the main building to deliver correspondence and packages. Leonardo would always make it a point to stop by the observation room window, and Priya would intercept him and ask if he'd seen anything of a Dr. Santos on his rounds that day.

Old Leonardo would pause with his cart and remove his cap, frowning while he pretended to consider.

Then he'd say, "Not today, Priya," or, "Thought I saw someone similar yesterday, but she was heading to the Lincoln facility. Wasn't Dr. Santos."

Then he'd continue on, shaking his head. Later the maintenance staff would come around to service the equipment, and Priya would ask them the same question. Once a month the administration sent someone to conduct facility inspections, and they became part of Priya's routine too.

It was hard on Susan. Sometimes the girl would have vivid dreams at night that Dr. Santos had returned and was working in her old lab, and she'd wake Susan and beg her to go check. When that happened, Nathan and I could hear Susan talking to her through the thin walls of the residential wing, low and steady, until late into the morning, and when Priya finally settled, we'd hear Susan in her kitchenette, probably pouring something stronger than coffee.

But there came a night that exceeded Susan's capacity to cope, a night that changed Priya's routine and much more besides. It left a mark you've seen yourself—everyone has who follows neuroscience news—though you never knew what caused it. Nobody ever knew that except Priya and Susan Stanley and Nathan and me.

Nathan and I were finishing our evening work around midnight when the girl called out from the residential wing. We heard Susan go to her, and we paused our discussion because we knew neither of us would concentrate until Susan got Priya settled again. But this night was different. Susan hadn't talked to the girl long when Priya cried out, "Dr. Santos! Dr. Santos!" and after that we heard both of them weeping.

Shortly after, Susan emerged into the corridor and closed the door behind her. She looked disheveled and defeated, her professional demeanor completely stripped away, her hair loose around her shoulders and her eyes swollen from crying. Whatever emotional reserves she'd been maintaining hadn't helped.

She stood motionless for a while, then she looked up at the ceiling-mounted neural displays and said something I'm not likely to forget.

"Why couldn't you give the girl a break?" she said, not angry or anything but loud enough for us to hear through our open door. "You, up there—what's another brilliant mentor to You?"

Nathan and I looked at each other in the fluorescent light of our office.

"She's done it, Diego," Nathan said.

I knew what he meant and wished I didn't. Susan had finally told the girl that Dr. Santos wasn't coming back, not ever.

That's why I was concerned about Priya when I came to the lab the next evening and found her studying the neural activity displays instead of watching the courtyard. It meant she'd stopped waiting for Dr. Santos. And the quiet way the girl spoke of reorganizing neural connections concerned me more, because it sounded genuinely delusional.

Not that you could blame her for losing touch with reality. It was challenging enough to be confined to a wheelchair without being able to move her legs at all. But to lose her mentor in addition...

I was reviewing my third data set when Nathan arrived with a large package under his arm. Nathan was completely sober, which surprised me, and he was energized from a shopping trip to Brookhaven, which surprised me more. It was when he opened his package, though, that I thought he'd lost his professional judgment.

"Books for Priya," Nathan said. "Susan and I agreed this morning that the girl needs a new intellectual focus now, and since she can't attend regular school, I'm going to tutor her here."

He went on to explain that Susan hadn't had the courage the previous night, desperate as she was, to tell Priya the complete truth. She'd told her instead, citing an imaginary colleague at the Bristol facility, that Dr. Santos had accepted a position at a research institute in Lincoln, Orvandor, and had taken the assignment to advance her career. It was a plausible story. Priya still didn't know that Dr. Santos was dead, but her waiting was over because no mentor could be expected to return from such a prestigious opportunity.

"We must give the girl another focus," Nathan said, shelving the books and pouring fresh coffee. "Priya has a remarkable capacity for concentration—most intellectually gifted children do—that could destroy her if it isn't redirected into productive channels."

I thought the girl had already broken down and said so.

"Reorganizing neural connections?" Nathan said when I told him. "Good God, Diego—"

Susan Stanley knocked just then, interrupting him. She came in and had coffee with us and discussed Nathan's plan for tutoring Priya at the Institute. But she couldn't tell us anything more about the girl's new fixation than we already knew. When she asked Priya why she stared at the neural displays like that, she'd say only that she wanted something to remember Dr. Santos by.

It was about nine o'clock when Susan went back to prepare dinner. Nathan and I abandoned our chess game and moved to the observation room to check some equipment. It was then that the first neural pattern shifted.

It shifted suddenly, the way any spontaneous reorganization does, and rippled across the display in a cascading wave of activity. I didn't pay much attention, but Nathan nearly dropped his coffee.

"Diego," he said, "that was Subject Twelve! The motor cortex just reorganized!"

I didn't see anything particularly significant about it and said so. You can observe dozens of minor reorganizations on any given day if you're monitoring enough subjects.

"Not minor reorganization, you fool," Nathan said. "Subject Twelve—the chronic paralysis case—just showed complete motor cortex reactivation, then stabilized!"

I paid attention then, partly because the pattern really had stabilized instead of reverting the way spontaneous activity usually does, partly because anything that excites Nathan Hamilton that much deserves consideration.

We monitored the displays like two researchers at a critical experiment, but nothing else changed. After a while another subject's scan showed activity, though, and later in the night a whole series of them displayed reorganization patterns, forming a sequence that didn't make sense to us. They stopped changing around midnight and we returned to our office, but neither of us could focus on work.

"Perhaps we ought to find another research focus ourselves instead of developing one for Priya," Nathan said. He meant it as a joke but it sounded uncertain. "Something besides staring at neural scans every night, for instance."

"You think we're experiencing shared delusions from too much caffeine?" I asked.

Nathan laughed at that, sounding more like himself. "No, Diego. No two people ever had simultaneous and identical hallucinations of objective data."

"Look," I said. "I know this sounds irrational, but maybe Priya—"

Nathan wasn't amused anymore. "Don't be absurd, Diego. If those patterns really reorganized, you can be certain of two things—Priya had nothing to do with it, and the research literature will explain everything tomorrow."

He was wrong on at least one count.

The neuroscience journals the next day were filled with urgent communications and breaking news, but none of them explained anything. The conference calls and emergency meetings involved every authority available, and research coordinators everywhere were struggling to understand. It just couldn't happen, they said.

Nathan and I reviewed the literature systematically that night, and I learned more about neural plasticity than I'd absorbed in years of study. Nathan, as I've mentioned, is a trained philosopher, and what he couldn't recall about neuroscience, the emergency publications quoted with extensive citations. They included interviews with researchers at major institutes—Harvard, Stanford, Johns Hopkins, and facilities across the globe—but nobody could explain why all those subjects would show spontaneous motor cortex reorganization simultaneously.

It disturbed me to learn that Subject Twelve had been paralyzed for over three years following severe spinal trauma, that the case had been considered permanent and irreversible, that the motor neurons had been documented as non-functional but hadn't shown any activity until now. This particular subject—researchers referred to them by number for privacy—hadn't shown any change in associated regions, which puzzled the specialists considerably. I suggested to Nathan, only half joking, that maybe the associated regions hadn't reorganized because they weren't damaged enough to interest Priya's attention, but Nathan rebuked me sharply.

"Don't joke about Priya," he said sternly. "Regarding Subject Twelve—the neural pathways are so extensively damaged that signals need years to establish new routes. That means any reorganization would have started when Priya was only ten years old. Neural plasticity has well-established temporal constraints, Diego, and neuroscientists say they can't be violated."

"They said spontaneous reorganization across multiple subjects was impossible, too," I pointed out. "I'm not claiming that Priya really reorganized those neural pathways, Nathan, but if she did, she could have accelerated the timeline along with them, couldn't she?"

But Nathan wouldn't engage the argument. "I need air," he said.

I followed, but we didn't get farther than Priya's wheelchair.

There she sat, tense and absorbed, staring up at the neural activity displays. Nathan and I followed her gaze, the way you do automatically when someone ahead of you focuses intently on something. We looked up just in time to see more patterns begin reorganizing.

The first one to change was a subject with severe cognitive impairment whose scan suddenly showed activity spreading across the prefrontal cortex—rapid, like that—and stabilized at a level consistent with normal function.

Nathan said, "There went Subject Seven," and his voice sounded strained.

That was only the beginning. During the next hour, forty or fifty more subjects showed reorganization patterns, and their scans joined the group that had changed the night before. The sequence they formed still didn't resemble anything recognizable.

I left Nathan staring at the displays and went over to help Priya, who had finished for the night and was manually rolling her wheelchair toward the residential wing entrance, navigate the door. I assisted her inside where Nathan couldn't overhear, then I asked her how things were progressing.

"Slowly, Dr. Wolfe," she said. "I have approximately a hundred more to complete."

"Then you're really reorganizing those neural patterns up there?"

She looked surprised. "Yes, it's not particularly difficult once you understand the principles."

The odds were even that she was speaking metaphorically, but I proceeded anyway and asked another question.

"I can't discern any pattern in it, Priya," I said. "What are you creating up there?"

She gave me a very small smile.

"You'll know when I'm finished," she said.

I told Nathan about that after we'd returned to our office, but he said I shouldn't encourage the girl's magical thinking. "Priya's heard everyone discussing those neural reorganizations; the emergency meetings have been constant, so she's excited too. But she has far more imagination than most people because she's intellectually gifted, and she could develop a delusional system because she's traumatized about Dr. Santos. The thing to do is provide her with a rational explanation instead of validating her fantasy as reality."

Nathan was taking all this so seriously—because it was undermining theories he'd accepted as foundational all his professional life, like those neuroscientists who were panicking worldwide. I didn't realize how disturbed Nathan really was, though, until he woke me around 4:00 a.m.

"I can't sleep for thinking about those neural patterns," he said, sitting at my desk. "Diego, I'm frightened."

That from Nathan was something I'd never expected to hear. It startled me alert enough to sit up and listen while he articulated his concerns.

"I'm afraid," Nathan said, "because what is happening in those scans isn't consistent with established neuroscience. It just can't be, yet it is."

It was so quiet when he paused that I could hear the ventilation system humming. Finally Nathan said, "Diego, the human nervous system is as delicately balanced as any complex system. If that balance is disrupted too extensively, our understanding of consciousness itself will be fundamentally challenged."

Ordinarily I wouldn't have argued with Nathan on his own ground, but I could see he was constructing a mental scenario of all neuroscience collapsing like a house of cards, and I was afraid to let him continue.

"The problem with you philosophers," I said, "is that you think your experts have everything figured out, that there's nothing in the world their theories can't explain. Well, I'm a pragmatic researcher, but I know that your neuroscientists can measure brain activity until they're exhausted and they'll never learn who designed those brains in the first place. So how do they know that whatever designed them won't reorganize them again? I've always heard that if a person had sufficient belief, they could accomplish impossible things. Well, if a person has the focus that Priya's demonstrated, maybe she could reorganize neural pathways, too."

Nathan sat quiet for a moment.

"'There are more things in heaven and earth...'" he began, then laughed. "A quotation worn threadbare by centuries of repetition but as relevant tonight as ever, Diego. Do you really believe Priya is reorganizing those neural patterns?"

"Why not?" I responded. "It's as valid an explanation as any the experts have proposed."

Nathan stood and returned to his couch. "Perhaps you're right. We'll discover more tomorrow."

And we did. Nathan did, rather, while I was occupied running controlled experiments all day.

I returned to the lab slightly earlier than usual that evening, just before the day shift ended. Priya was sitting as usual alone in her wheelchair. In the dimming light I could see a stack of books on the floor beside her, books Nathan had given her to study. What stopped me was that Priya was staring at her legs as if they were the first ones she'd ever really seen, and she had that same expression of intense concentration I'd observed when she was studying the neural displays.

I didn't know what to say to her, thinking perhaps I shouldn't mention the neural patterns. But Priya spoke first.

"Dr. Wolfe," she said, without taking her eyes off her knees, "did you know that Dr. Hamilton is an exceptionally wise person?"

I said I'd always thought so, but why?

"Dr. Hamilton said this morning that I shouldn't reorganize any more neural patterns," the girl said. "He says I should concentrate instead on learning to walk again so I can travel to Lincoln and study with Dr. Santos's colleagues."

For a moment I was angry enough to confront Nathan if he'd been available. Anyone who would manipulate a disabled, vulnerable child like that...

"Dr. Hamilton says that if I can do what I've been doing to those neural scans, then it ought to be straightforward to reorganize my own neural pathways," Priya said. "And he's correct, Dr. Wolfe. So I'm not going to reorganize any more patterns in the database. I'm going to reorganize my own."

She looked up at me with her small, serious smile. "It took me a whole day to learn how to reorganize that first subject's motor cortex, Dr. Wolfe, but I could do this after only a few hours. Look..."

And she moved both her feet.

It's unfortunate that events in reality don't unfold like they do in fiction, because a compelling narrative could be constructed from Priya Stanley's capacity for reorganizing neural patterns through focused attention. In a story, Priya might have revolutionized neuroscience or destroyed the field entirely, depending on which outcome would engage the most readers and earn the writer the largest advance, but of course it didn't actually conclude either way. It ended in what Nathan Hamilton called an anticlimax, leaving everyone satisfied enough except a few neuroscientists who appreciate mysteries anyway or they wouldn't be neuroscientists in the first place.

The neural patterns that had been reorganized remained stable, but the sequence Priya had started was never completed. That unfinished sequence won't ever disappear, in case you've wondered about it—it's there in the research database where you can access it with proper clearance—but it will never be finished because Priya Stanley lost interest in it when she learned to walk again.

Walking was a gradual process with Priya at first because her legs had atrophied significantly—severe muscle wasting, Nathan said—and it took time to rebuild them. But within a few weeks she was moving around with crutches, and after that she never approached her wheelchair again.

Susan enrolled her in the Dalebrook school system, and before the academic year ended she was participating in adaptive sports and joining other students for social activities on weekends.

School opened up an entirely new world to Priya, and she adapted to the routine as smoothly as if she'd been doing it all her life. She learned extensively there and she forgot much that she'd learned independently through isolation. Before we realized what was happening, she was just like any other twelve-year-old, full of curiosity and energy, with no more ability to reorganize neural patterns through concentration than anyone else had.

I think she actually forgot about those neural scans along with other things that had meant so much to her when she was confined to her wheelchair and couldn't do anything but wait and think.

For instance, a young researcher named Jose Baker joined the Institute staff and began mentoring Priya in basic neuroscience. She attended his lectures and assisted with his experiments and called him Professor Baker, and after that she never mentioned traveling to Lincoln to find Dr. Santos's colleagues. It was only natural, of course, because adolescents—healthy adolescents—move forward quickly. It's a sort of developmental necessity, Nathan says, against the traumas of existence.

When the academic year ended, Susan accepted a position at the Brookhaven facility where Priya could attend a specialized school for gifted students instead of the standard curriculum. When they transferred, the Dalebrook Institute felt so empty and purposeless that Nathan and I relocated and went to the Bristol research center for the consciousness studies program. We never heard from Susan and Priya again.

We've moved several times since; we're at a facility in Belvoria currently, working with the artificial intelligence research group. But everywhere we go, we're reminded of them. Every time we access the neural plasticity database, we see what Nathan calls the Priya Stanley Neural Monument, which is nothing but an unusual sequence sketched out with a hundred or so reorganized patterns of various types and magnitudes.

The structure of it is so incomplete that you'd never determine what it's supposed to represent unless you knew already what you were looking for. To us, the outline of a human brain is fairly clear. If you know enough to fill in the gaps, you can see it was meant to be a detailed neural map with only one region missing.

Nathan says that transient researchers like him and me forget old associations as quickly as adolescents do—and for the same adaptive reasons—so I'm not particularly interested now in where Susan and Priya Stanley are or how they're progressing. But there's one thing I'll always wonder about, now that there's no way of ever knowing for certain.

I wish I'd asked Priya or Susan, before they transferred away, which brain region she decided to leave incomplete.
question: Why did Susan Stanley tell Dr. Wolfe to leave Priya alone?
option_a: She didn't want him to encourage Priya's fixation on waiting for Dr. Santos to return
option_b: She was worried he would interfere with Priya's neural reorganization experiments
correct_answer_text: She didn't want him to encourage Priya's fixation on waiting for Dr. Santos to return
incorrect_answer_text: She was worried he would interfere with Priya's neural reorganization experiments
