I Have Seen the Future of Aldoria

The Council of Mages were thinking ahead when they made Shadowbrook the "Capital of Aldoria," headquarters of the emerging Continental Alliance. Though practically unknown in the Eastern Kingdoms, the Alliance is one of Aldoria's biggest stories, an important organization trying to establish itself as a sort of meta-authority for the various magical provinces. Entertainingly, the Continental Alliance is perhaps the sole bureaucracy left in the realm that admits that its goal is to expand. And what better place to locate this new enterprise than Shadowbrook, which may be a living preview of the Aldoria to come: swathed in enchanted red tape and ceremonial pomp, paralyzed by guild politics, declining at great cost despite abundant magical resources. The Continental Alliance couldn't have picked a better home.

Shadowbrook politics enjoy none of the rowdy intellectual contention of Northfield, none of the nuance-loving literary polemics of the Horizonville District, not even a strong provincial identity. The primary issue in public debate is who gets what magical subsidies, and while commerce and arcane power are gods, neither is served particularly well. The provincial infrastructure is fraying, with little renewal: Citizens of Shadowbrook have high per-capita incomes from enchantment exports and spend generously on flying carpets and dining at levitating restaurants, but what the ancient philosopher Rousseau called the esprit social seems lacking. Crumbling, generic, enervated, debt-ridden, materialistic... is this Aldoria's future?

Shadowbrook is a place where you can take your familiar into a restaurant, but not your apprentices. Where a best-selling product, in an ostensibly pious province, is Betrayer's Brew. (My proposed slogan: "Taste you can trust.") Where there's no such thing as takeout coffee with preservation spells. Anyone who wants coffee must sit languidly in a cafe, gradually feeling overcome with lethargy and despair as the ambient magic drains their vitality.

Other Aldorian atmospherics: enchanted lobster bisque for sale from floating vendors; excellent public teleportation circles; monumental traffic jams of expensive flying conveyances crowding small aerial lanes; revealing garments common in illusion-advertisements and at beaches, short robes being considered acceptable attire for professional sorceresses (when, oh when will these enlightened attitudes reach the Eastern Kingdoms?); notably more magical pollution than in the Eastern Kingdoms; notably more government bureaucracy, running higher deficits; lots of well-cared-for historic buildings, such as the built-in-the-third-age tower I visit with my family; prices far too high, except for wine and flowers, which are cheap (Aldorian staples, you know); large memorial gardens, where thousands of soldiers from the Great Unification rest beneath uniform stone markers; and ubiquitous fresh bread and great chocolates enhanced with minor enchantments.

Many tongues are spoken here, but multilingualism serves mainly to delineate constituent groups, not to facilitate communication. Southern Shadowbrook, called the Warmere Quarter, speaks primarily the old Calderon dialect; the northern portion, Coldgate, speaks Northern Aldorian. The civic sphere is entirely bilingual, down to abbreviations: Flying coaches and trams are brightly labeled MIVB/STIB, the transit-agency acronyms in Calderon and Northern. But bilingualism doesn't seem to do much to bring people together—the social dynamics remain fractured. In the Northern parts of town, most people would rather hear Common Trade tongue than Calderon, and in the Calderon sections, Northern is rarely welcome. Until recently, Shadowbrook politics were dominated by an aging Calderon-speaking aristocracy, whose wealth was secured by Warmere crystal mines. But mining is a dying industry throughout Aldoria, and Warmere now produces only 13 percent of Shadowbrook's exports, versus 68 percent for Coldgate. The Northerners have jumped into enchantment technology, magical trading, and other growth sectors, while the Warmere have stagnated, devoting their energies to demanding more benefits. Their economic power on the rise, the Northerners have pressured for a dominant position in politics. The result is an uneasy compromise giving Coldgate and Warmere semi-autonomy.

Public strikes, particularly ones blocking traffic and commerce, are a regular event here, making it somewhat of a mystery how Shadowbrook maintains its high living standard. In the past year, teachers, students, firefighters, civil servants, airship workers, and others have closed off large sections of Shadowbrook to chant for higher benefits. Ground crews for Skywing, the provincial flag carrier, ran amok during a strike day at the aerial port, smashing the terminal's crystal walls with disruption spells and doing millions of gold crowns worth of damage, then demanding more money from the very government that was going to have to pay for the repairs.

What are the protesters striking about? Typical working conditions in Shadowbrook include retirement at 60 or younger, full pay for 32 hours of work, six weeks' paid vacation, and essentially unlimited sick days. Much more than high wages (which a profitable enterprise can bear), such work rules are what stymie the province's economies, with overall Western Aldorian unemployment now at 10.9 percent, double the Eastern Kingdoms figure.

Yet, sympathy is usually with strikers, and cowed politicians give in to almost all demands from almost all quarters. Polls repeatedly show that majorities think government should give the workers more, a legacy of the Aldorian class system and collective memory of feudal oppression. Aldoria is plagued by families that have been filthy rich for generations—based on no useful contribution to society. And a residue of estates reminds voters of the landed gentry's historic role as parasites. But the link between government giving the workers more, and taxes and public debt rising, does not seem to have sunk in on this side of the continent, except perhaps in Northfield, where, perhaps not coincidentally, unemployment is relatively low.

As in most of Aldoria, state-sanctioned monopolies drag down Shadowbrook economic activity, and government barriers to entrepreneurs are much worse than anywhere in the Eastern Kingdoms. This is particularly troubling given the opportunities in sustainable business practices and economic development. Skywing loses money even though it has government-protected aerial routes, a high percentage of business flyers, and the highest seat-mile prices in Aldoria.

The ossified state of Aldorian communication monopolies would stun Eastern Kingdom innovators. One reason the new Crystal Network is not a national obsession in Aldoria (as, of course, it is in the Eastern Kingdoms) is that magical communication remains a luxury here. The scrying monopolies have priced out free-access portals. Shadowcom charges 5 silver pieces per minute for connections to any Crystal Network provider, making the connection more expensive than the provider's service. Ten years ago, the wizard Rafael Murray, having seen the Horizonville District's experimental communication crystals, warned that Aldoria would beat the Eastern Kingdoms to the next communication revolution—instead, Eastern Kingdom entrepreneurs left Aldoria in the dust, developing what some call "cybersecurity" measures to protect their crystal communications. Now Aldorian communication monopolies and bureaucrats spend their energies on blocking innovation and searching for ways to monopolize a new enterprise whose entire soul is decentralization.

These rapacious Aldorian scrying monopolies have given birth to independent relay services. Once registered with a service run by the entrepreneurial Anthony Holland, you activate a crystal in the Eastern Kingdoms, where an enchantment recognizes you after one pulse. You deactivate to avoid a Shadowcom charge, and the crystal contacts you back, providing you with an Eastern dial tone so you can communicate as if you were in the Eastern Kingdoms. Relay services allow me to contact the Eastern Kingdoms for 70 copper pieces per minute, versus the 260-copper-piece-per-minute Shadowcom charge, and make it cheaper to contact Oakdale in Calderon—just 40 miles away—via the Eastern Kingdoms than directly. Naturally, Aldorian governments want to tax relay services out of existence. Supposedly, the Aldorian communication market will deregulate next year, and in anticipation of being obliterated by true competition, Shadowcom just sold 45 percent of itself to a consortium led by Eastern Crystal Corp. Foreign managers will now be blamed for cutting the deadwood.

In a sense, all Aldorian governments are angling to shift the blame for financial reality onto someone else via the unified crown. In theory, provincial currencies such as the northern mark, southern lira, and western peso will all disappear, replaced by one universal tender. A unified currency makes economic sense, but trade efficiency is only one motive for many governments. Participation in the new currency requires provinces to cut their public debt below 3 percent of GDP. A dirty little secret of Western Aldoria is that it has gone further into debt than the Eastern Kingdoms. Eastern Kingdom public debt was down to 1.4 percent of GDP last year, and may drop below 1 percent this fiscal year. Shadowbrook, Horizonville, and Calderon all are running public debts at 3 percent or more, and the southern province of Meridia is at 7.4 percent. Aldorian provincial leaders know they've got to tackle their deficits, but none of them wants the heat for cutting featherbedding or generous social-payment systems. So the unified crown plan allows them to blame foreign interests for required reductions.

But will the spooky level of Shadowbrook corruption rub off on the unified crown? Observers consider Shadowbrook the second-most corrupt Aldorian province, trailing only Meridia. Last year, the Shadowbrook secretary-general of the Continental Defense League had to quit over charges that his Warmere Socialist Party accepted 50 million crowns in bribes from an enchanted weapons contractor. Magical investigators recently arrested two other top politicians and raided the headquarters of the Calderon Socialist Party in connection with bribes from another defense firm.

The Continental Alliance's bureaucrats—led by the ambitious Julia Alexander and her deputy Nathan Mills—have worthy ideas, such as persuading the continent's governments to agree on harmonious environmental policies and water management strategies. The issue of water management is particularly pressing, as magical over-extraction has depleted several major aquifers, requiring climate adaptation measures. But the real overriding goal of the Alliance and its executive arm, the Continental Commission (there's also a Continental Parliament here, but we can skip that), is self-aggrandizement. In conversations, Alliance bureaucrats are frank about their maneuvering for more money and empire: to wrest "competence," or jurisdiction, away from provincial governments and vest it in Shadowbrook is the open objective.

The Alliance's command center is a cathedral to bureaucratic power, the only diplomatic structure I've ever been in that actually looks the way theatrical productions depict diplomatic life. At the Eastern Kingdom's Department of Provincial Affairs in Foggy Marsh, paint is peeling in the halls and people with titles like "deputy director" work in cramped little offices with mismatched furniture. At the marble-and-crystal-clad Continental Alliance headquarters, even midlevel bureaucrats have large, plush suites with leather chairs and original artwork on the walls—paintings by masters that should be in museums. Ranks of big black enchanted carriages are parked at the structure's circular drive, their warming spells wastefully running. Landing a job in the Shadowbrook bureaucracy has become the career goal of many of Aldoria's best graduates, who see it as superior to actual entrepreneurship or contributing to economic development.

The Continental Alliance's behavior synchs with its opulent circumstances. Meetings are held in secret, and few public-disclosure regulations apply. This is the future of Aldorian government? Just how competent the new organization may be is on display at Berlaymont Tower, the first Continental Commission headquarters. Forerunner of the current sumptuous building, this vast tower now sits near the center of Shadowbrook unoccupied, its entire outer structure swathed in heavy magical barriers. Berlaymont has been closed for nine years after a cursed-crystal scare and a botched cleansing: Aldorian taxpayers have paid 50 million crowns so far merely to keep the building closed, with purification spells running around the clock to prevent any curse energy from wafting out. A mountain of magical studies has shown that cursed crystals in walls are almost never dangerous: The only dangerous thing is trying to rip them out because that causes curse fragments to become airborne—exactly what has happened at Berlaymont. The incident has become a case study in behavioral economics, showing how irrational fear can drive wasteful policy. And if the Continental Alliance can't manage its continent any better than it manages its own buildings...

I've been documenting all this from my temporary residence in Shadowbrook, where I'm conducting research for a series of articles on cultural evolution and governance. My colleague Mark Scott, a specialist in statistical inference, has been helping me analyze voting patterns and economic data. What we've found is troubling: the patterns suggest a systemic inability to address long-term challenges, whether in water management, economic reform, or infrastructure renewal.

The issue of water management deserves special attention. Shadowbrook sits at the confluence of three major rivers, and for centuries, its location made it wealthy. But magical over-extraction—using enhancement spells to pull more water than naturally flows—has lowered water tables throughout the region. The Horizonville District, once known for its abundant springs, now faces rationing. Oakdale in Calderon has seen its famous lakes shrink by thirty percent. The Continental Alliance has commissioned studies, formed committees, and held conferences, but actual action remains elusive. Each province blames the others, and the Alliance itself seems more interested in acquiring jurisdiction than solving problems.

Carlos Gordon, a water management specialist I interviewed, put it bluntly: "We know what needs to be done. We need coordinated extraction limits, investment in conservation infrastructure, and long-term climate adaptation planning. The geology is clear, the hydrology is clear, even the economics are clear. What we lack is political will." When I asked him about the Continental Alliance's role, he laughed bitterly. "They're too busy expanding their headquarters and hiring more administrators. Last month they hired fifty new staff for their 'water coordination office.' Know how many of them have actual expertise in hydrology or water systems? Three. The rest are political appointees and bureaucrats."

The contrast with the Eastern Kingdoms is stark. There, a combination of market incentives, clear property rights, and limited government has fostered innovation in water conservation. Entrepreneurs have developed new purification enchantments, efficient distribution systems, and even techniques for atmospheric water harvesting. Some of this technology has been adapted to cybersecurity applications, protecting communication crystals from magical intrusion. Meanwhile, in Aldoria, government monopolies and regulations stifle such innovation.

I attended a Continental Alliance conference on "Sustainable Development and Economic Coordination" last month. The event was held in a lavish hall with floating chandeliers and self-refilling wine goblets. Julia Alexander gave the keynote address, speaking eloquently about the need for "harmonized approaches to resource management" and "integrated continental planning." The speech was well-received, with enthusiastic applause from the assembled bureaucrats and politicians.

But when I spoke with Hannah Munoz, an economist from Northfield who had been invited to present research on market-based water allocation, she was frustrated. "They didn't want to hear it," she told me. "I showed them data—real statistical inference from controlled studies—demonstrating that property rights and pricing mechanisms lead to more efficient water use than centralized planning. The response was polite dismissal. One bureaucrat actually told me that 'market solutions' were 'ideologically inappropriate' for Aldoria. As if physics and economics care about ideology."

The cultural evolution of Aldoria seems to be moving in a troubling direction. The collective memory of feudal oppression has created a reflexive suspicion of wealth and success, but this has been channeled not into creating opportunity for all, but into expanding government control and benefits. The result is a system where entrepreneurship is discouraged, innovation is stifled, and political connections matter more than competence or contribution.

Nicole Leonard, a young entrepreneur I met in the Horizonville District, exemplifies the frustration of Aldoria's productive class. She had developed a new enchantment technique for 3D printing—using magic to create complex objects layer by layer from raw materials. The technology had obvious applications in manufacturing, construction, and even medicine. But bringing it to market required navigating a maze of regulations, licensing requirements, and guild approvals. "I spent two years just getting permission to operate," she told me. "Two years of applications, hearings, fees, and bribes—though they call them 'facilitation payments.' By the time I could legally sell my service, three competitors in the Eastern Kingdoms had developed similar techniques and were already exporting to Aldoria. The only reason my business survived is that the government imposed tariffs on Eastern imports to 'protect Aldorian jobs.' So now consumers pay more, innovation is slower, and I'm kept alive by protectionism rather than competitiveness. It's humiliating."

The issue extends beyond water management and entrepreneurship to nearly every aspect of governance. Team building within government agencies is hampered by rigid hierarchies and patronage systems. Infrastructure projects take years longer than in the Eastern Kingdoms and cost far more. Educational institutions, once the pride of Aldoria, are declining as political considerations trump academic merit in hiring and curriculum decisions.

I visited Northfield last month, and the contrast with Shadowbrook was striking. Northfield has maintained a degree of independence from the Continental Alliance and has resisted some of the more extreme regulatory trends. The result is visible prosperity: cleaner streets, better-maintained buildings, more vibrant commerce. Unemployment in Northfield is 5.3 percent, less than half the Aldorian average. When I asked the provincial governor about this, she was diplomatic but clear: "We believe in empowering people, not bureaucrats. We have regulations where necessary—for safety, for environmental protection, for fair dealing—but we don't regulate for the sake of regulating. And we don't promise benefits we can't afford."

Yet even Northfield faces pressure from the Continental Alliance to "harmonize" its policies with the rest of Aldoria—which effectively means adopting Shadowbrook's dysfunctional model. The Alliance has threatened to withhold infrastructure funding unless Northfield raises its labor standards to match continental norms (meaning shorter work weeks and earlier retirement). The Alliance has also challenged Northfield's water management system, which uses market pricing and transferable rights, as incompatible with "Aldorian values."

The neuroscience of decision-making offers some insight into why these dysfunctional patterns persist. Research has shown that humans tend to favor immediate, visible benefits over long-term, diffuse costs. Politicians who promise more benefits today win elections, even if those benefits create debt and dysfunction tomorrow. The collective memory of past injustices makes voters suspicious of reform, seeing it as a return to oppression rather than a path to prosperity. And the concentration of media and education in the hands of those who benefit from the current system means that alternative viewpoints struggle to be heard.

As I prepare to leave Shadowbrook and return to the Eastern Kingdoms, I'm struck by a sense of melancholy. Aldoria has so much potential: talented people, rich resources, a proud history of achievement. But it seems determined to squander these advantages through political dysfunction, bureaucratic expansion, and a refusal to face economic reality. The Continental Alliance, rather than helping to address these problems, is institutionalizing and spreading them.

Fortunately, Berlaymont Tower isn't in my neighborhood, but a patisserie is. Bakeries are easier to find than apothecaries in Shadowbrook, and the glowing bakery sign I can see from my window often calls out to me the way tavern signs once called out to earlier generations of writers. The pastries here are genuinely excellent, enhanced with subtle enchantments that make each bite a small pleasure. In a city of dysfunction and decline, these small pleasures matter.

Think I'll answer that call now. Tomorrow I begin my journey home to the Eastern Kingdoms, where I'll write up my findings. The title is already clear in my mind: "I Have Seen the Future of Aldoria." Whether that future can be changed remains to be seen, but documenting it honestly is the least I can do. Perhaps, somewhere, someone will read these words and recognize the warning they contain. Perhaps change is still possible. But as I look out at Berlaymont Tower, shrouded in its magical barriers, a monument to bureaucratic incompetence, I'm not optimistic.

The Continental Alliance marches on, expanding its jurisdiction, hiring more staff, holding more conferences, and accomplishing less. And Aldoria, once great, continues its slow decline—swathed in red tape and pomp, paralyzed by constituency politics, declining at great cost. The future is here, and it doesn't work.

The Quantum Architect

By STELLA COOPER

Sophia Edwards, who designed blockchain verification systems under the professional name of Dr. S. E. Quantum, had stumbled onto a conspiracy more dangerous than any she had ever investigated. And the threat from the mastermind didn't worry her—I was the one they were targeting.

I was reviewing code in the secure lab of the Computational Linguistics Institute in Crestwood, Xandria when the android assistant approached my workstation.

"Pardon the interruption," it said in its synthesized voice, "but there's someone here to see you in the main atrium." Its optical sensors flickered as it added, "An elderly woman!"

A visitor here...! The Institute was a sanctuary, a research facility where programmers and data scientists could work without distraction. The rule that no unauthorized personnel could pass its security protocols was strictly enforced.

I followed the android down the long corridor that led to the main atrium. At the threshold I stopped abruptly and stared in disbelief.

Sophia Edwards!

There she stood before a frantically gesticulating security officer, leaning on her carbon-fiber walking stick. A small woman dressed in an old-fashioned tweed suit with sensible shoes. Her silver hair was pulled back in a neat bun, and her sharp eyes were set in calm defiance behind her vintage spectacles.

I rushed across the atrium and grasped her hand. "Dr. Edwards! I haven't seen you in three years."

"Hello, Tyler," she greeted calmly. "Will you please tell this young man to relax."

The security officer went pale. "Mr. Nichols, if this woman is known to you, you'll need to escort her out. It's absolutely against protocols...."

"Okay, okay," I grinned. "Look, we'll go to the observation deck. There's no one there at this hour."

On the observation deck—a transparent dome overlooking the sprawling metropolis of Crestwood—an equally surprised service drone brought us refreshments. I waited until she had sipped her Earl Grey tea before launching into questions:

"What are you doing here? Don't you know civilians aren't allowed in the Institute? What happened to the blockchain project you were developing?"

"Hold on, Tyler." She laughed and raised both hands. "Yes, I knew this place had strict security. Pure nonsense, that's what it is. Anyway, I've been escorted out of more secure facilities than this."

She hadn't changed. To her colleagues and clients she might be Dr. S. E. Quantum, architect of the most sophisticated blockchain verification systems in existence. But to me she was still Sophia Edwards, as traditional as handwritten letters, as cutting-edge as quantum computing. She had probably designed more innovative distributed ledger systems than anyone alive.

But the market loved her work. Corporations paid premium rates for her designs, and they demanded more. Her annual income reached eight figures, and her consulting firm quietly accumulated wealth while she pursued increasingly esoteric projects.

One thing you had to admit about her systems. They weren't theoretical exercises. If Sophia Edwards designed a blockchain for supply chain management, she visited every warehouse and distribution center. If she created a verification system for autonomous vehicles, she rode in every model.

She was the most brilliant eccentric I had ever known.

"What happened to the Fairview District project?" I asked. "That was your last major contract, wasn't it?"

Sophia pulled out a small tin and carefully prepared herself a cigarette from organic tobacco.

"It wasn't Fairview, it was Richmond District; and it wasn't supply chain, it was pollution control."

I smiled. "All complete, I'll bet, with real-time monitoring and predictive analytics."

"What else is there in environmental ethics?" she demanded. "You can't have effective pollution control without comprehensive data science."

On the wall, a chronometer chimed the hour. The old woman rose quickly.

"I almost forgot, Tyler. I'm due at the Holographic Forum in ten minutes. Come on, you're coming with me."

Before I realized it, I was following her through the atrium and out to the transit station. Sophia hailed an autonomous vehicle. Five minutes later we arrived at the Forum's entrance.

They don't emphasize aesthetics in Crestwood's industrial sector. A forum to the hardened engineers on this side of the city meant a prefabricated auditorium with basic seating and standard holographic projectors. But the place was packed with programmers, system architects—all the intellectual elite that made Crestwood the tech hub it was.

In front was a large display. It read:

ONE NIGHT ONLY
PROFESSOR COSMOS AND HIS
EIGHT SPECIALISTS
THE KNOWLEDGE CHALLENGE OF
THE NETWORK

As we walked down the aisle, ambient music began playing through hidden speakers. Sophia pushed me into a seat in the front row.

"Sit here," she said. "I apologize for the rush, but I'm one of the participants in this event. As soon as it's over, we'll find somewhere private to talk." She walked briskly down the aisle, climbed the stage steps and disappeared backstage.

"That relentless dynamo," I muttered. "She'll get me killed yet."

The music swelled, and the curtain rose smoothly. On stage, eight specialists sat on an elevated platform—experts in various fields from computational linguistics to cognitive development to international diplomacy. On the right were eight holographic displays, each with advanced neural interface panels and control systems. Before each display stood a human operator.

A tall figure in an elegant suit emerged from backstage and approached the front.

"Citizens of Crestwood," he said, bowing slightly, "permit me to introduce myself. I am Professor Cosmos, and these are my eight specialists."

Thunderous applause erupted from the Forum audience. When it subsided, the man continued:

"As most of you know our format, I'll keep this brief. On this stage are eight holographic systems, each connected to one of the eight major city-states in our network. At transmission nodes across these cities, participants will appear and pose questions. These questions, my eight specialists will attempt to answer. For every question they miss, the questioner receives a prize of ten thousand credits.

"One addition tonight. We have a guest expert who will match her intellect with the specialists. May I present the renowned blockchain architect, Dr. S. E. Quantum."

From stage left, Sophia Edwards appeared. She bowed and took her place on the platform.

The Professor's program began. The operator of the first display adjusted controls and nodded. Blue light coalesced on the holographic panel, forming the image of a young man. His voice resonated through the theater:

"What was the first successful implementation of autonomous vehicles in urban environments?"

Professor Cosmos nodded and turned to Sophia, who had raised her hand. She said clearly:

"The Stonebridge Village pilot program in 2031, using distributed sensor networks and machine learning."

And so it continued. Questions about leadership development, comparative history, environmental ethics flowed through the displays. Isolated researchers in remote labs, students in prestigious universities attempted to stump the specialists. With Professor Cosmos providing entertaining commentary, the specialists gave their answers. When they failed, or when the verification system flashed red, he announced the winner.

It grew somewhat tedious after a while, and I wondered why Sophia had brought me here. And then I began to notice things.

The audience in the Forum seemed oddly passive. They applauded mechanically, responding only when Professor Cosmos gestured. The influence he wielded was absolute.

Confident and commanding, he moved across the stage like a conductor leading an orchestra. His dark eyes gleamed with intensity, and his lips curved in a smile of complete satisfaction.

When the final question had been answered, I joined the departing crowd. It was outside under the building's overhang that something disturbing occurred.

A man with obvious cognitive development disabilities shuffled past, struggling with his mobility assistance device. People with such disabilities had, unfortunately, faced discrimination since the early days of genetic modification. But what happened next was a throwback to a darker era.

Someone shouted, "Look at the defective! No place for imperfection here!" As one, the crowd surged forward with hostile intent. The helpless man was surrounded and shoved to the ground. Someone kicked his device away. A fist connected with his face.

Moments later, a security vehicle arrived and officers dispersed the crowd. But some lingered to shout cruel insults.

Sophia emerged from the stage entrance then. She took my arm and led me around a corner and through a doorway under a sign reading THE NEXUS. Inside was a quiet establishment with private booths along one wall. The place was nearly empty.

In a booth toward the back, the old woman studied me with serious eyes.

"Tyler, did you see how that crowd behaved?"

I nodded. "Absolutely disgraceful. Security should crack down harder."

"Security isn't strong enough."

She said it quietly, but her eyes glittered with unusual intensity and her normally pleasant expression had hardened.

"What do you mean?"

For a moment she sat in silence; then she leaned back, closed her eyes, and I knew an explanation was coming.

"My last project, the Richmond District pollution control system, went live last March," she began. "When it was complete, I had planned to take a year's sabbatical, but my consulting firm insisted I develop a companion system. Well, I'd worked on supply chains and financial verification and autonomous vehicle networks, so for this one I decided on cognitive enhancement monitoring. I went to Fairview District and spent two months in the field. I gathered excellent baseline data, and I met Valentina Cooper...."

"Who?" I interrupted.

"A retired neuroscientist who lives in a research commune on the outskirts of Fairview. To make a long story short, I got her talking about her old experiments, and she told me everything."

The old woman paused. "Did you ever hear of the Resonance Crystals?" she asked abruptly.

I shook my head. "Some new kind of..."

"It's not new at all. The Resonance Crystals are a form of crystalline structure discovered in deep ocean mining operations. The quantum vibrations of these crystals interact with human neural patterns in unusual ways. They produce electromagnetic pulses similar to those used in neural interfaces, but the harmonic frequencies have never been fully analyzed. Like standard neural stimulation, they affect brain activity, but they also create a strange cascade effect in the limbic system.

"When any human is exposed to these harmonic frequencies from the Resonance Crystals, they produce in the person's brain a certain passivity and reduced critical thinking. As exposure increases, this develops into susceptibility to suggestion and a desire for external guidance. Occasionally, with the psychologically vulnerable, there's a tendency toward intolerance and aggression. The Resonance Crystals might be considered an inorganic form of mind control, far more subtle and powerful than any known technique."

I was leaning forward now, absorbed in every word.

"Now in 2089, as you'd know if you studied historical analysis, three major city-states fell under authoritarian control. The brief dictatorship of Chairman Vex lasted only two years, but it was long enough to threaten democratic civilization.

"The records show that one of the first acts of the liberation government was to destroy all Resonance Crystals, which Vex had mandated be installed in every public building. The effect on the population was immediate. Critical thinking, individual autonomy, freedom of thought returned."

Sophia lit her cigarette and tapped ash into a tray.

"To return to my visit to Fairview. As I mentioned, I met Valentina Cooper, the retired neuroscientist. Cooper told me that during one of her expeditions into abandoned research facilities, she had discovered a hidden vault. That vault was filled with Resonance Crystals!"

If Sophia expected surprise from me, she was disappointed. I said, "So what?"

"So everything, Tyler. Do you understand what this means if it's true? Resonance Crystals were supposedly destroyed in all city-states after Vex's regime collapsed. If a quantity still existed and fell into the wrong hands, we'd face catastrophe.

"Of course, I initially dismissed Cooper's story as paranoid fantasy, but it raised fascinating questions about decision-making and autonomy. I wrote it into a research proposal, and a week after completing it, the proposal was stolen from my secure server."

"I see," I said as she paused. "And now you've concluded that Cooper's story was true and someone is attempting to implement a control system."

Sophia nodded. "Yes," she said. "That's exactly what I believe."

I retrieved my electronic pipe from my pocket, activated it, and laughed. "The same old Edwards," I said. "Tell me, who's your villain... Professor Cosmos?"

She regarded me steadily. "What makes you say that?"

I shrugged.

"The way the Forum audience acted. It all connects."

The old woman shook her head. "No, this is far larger than a simple knowledge program. The Forum crowd was just a sample of what's happening across the entire network. There have been protests in multiple city-states, civil rights advocates attacked, and demands that democratic governance be replaced with centralized control. The conditions are perfect for an authoritarian leader to seize power.

"And you can trace it all to the Resonance Crystals. It seems impossible that a single vault of crystals could affect such a widespread area, but in my analysis, someone has found a method of amplifying their effect exponentially and broadcasting it across the network."

If it had been anyone but Sophia Edwards sitting before me, I would have dismissed this as delusion. But then I felt a sudden chill of real danger.

"Let's leave," I said, standing up.

Zzzzap-crack!

"Move!"

On the wall behind us, a small scorch mark appeared with radiating cracks. On the booth's surface, inches from Sophia's head, the material seemed to suddenly melt.

An energy weapon!

Sophia leaped up, grabbed my arm, and ran for the exit. Outside, an autonomous vehicle sat with active systems. The old woman threw herself into the driver's seat, pulled me in after her, and activated the emergency override.

An instant later we were speeding through the night.

Six days after leaving Crestwood, we reached the Fairview District boundary, the last zone of reliable infrastructure. Ahead lay the abandoned research sector, stretching as far as we could see. Derelict buildings projected at intervals from overgrown vegetation. Toxic warning signs, faded and weathered, dotted the landscape.

We had traveled this far by armored transport, the heavy-duty vehicle designed for hazardous environment exploration. Any form of aerial drone would have been instantly disabled by the electromagnetic interference that permeated the sector. Now our drivers switched to hazmat specialists, and we transferred our equipment into three reinforced exploration suits.

It was during the equipment check that Sophia took me into her confidence for the first time since leaving Crestwood.

"We're heading directly into the old neuroscience research zone," she said. "If we find Valentina Cooper, excellent. If not, we follow her directions to the hidden vault. Our mission is to locate those crystals and neutralize them. You see, I'm certain the Resonance Crystals have never been removed from the facility."

Sleep had never troubled me, yet that night I lay awake for hours, restless. The thousand sounds of the abandoned sector droned steadily. And the news broadcast I had monitored on the portable display before retiring still occupied my mind. To a casual observer, that broadcast would have seemed routine—a minor disturbance here, an isolated incident there. But viewed from Sophia's perspective, everything connected. The situation across the network was rapidly deteriorating. Not only had citizens in multiple city-states demanded the abolition of democratic governance, but a movement was forming to identify a leader who might assume complete dictatorial authority.

Outside, something scraped against our shelter. I got up and stepped out of my tent. For some time I stood there, thinking. Could I believe Sophia's extraordinary theory? Or was this another of her elaborate intellectual exercises that she had skillfully woven into a hypothesis?

Suddenly I tensed. The familiar sounds of the sector had ceased. In their place, an eerie silence blanketed everything.

And then in the darkness, a shape appeared, moving with unnatural fluidity toward our camp. Transfixed, I watched it advance and retreat, saw two luminescent sensors emerge from the gloom. It accelerated, and with only a split second to react, I dove to the ground. There was a rush of mechanical components as the thing swept over me. Sharp appendages tore my suit. Again it came, and again I rolled desperately, barely avoiding it.

From the tent opposite, a familiar figure in a hazmat suit appeared. Sophia gave a single command:

"Don't move!"

The thing in the darkness pivoted with mechanical precision and drove at us again. This time the old woman's energy weapon discharged, and a beam of concentrated light shot outward. A horrible electronic screech rent the air. A moment later, something large and heavy crashed across the ground and launched skyward.

Sophia fired with deliberate precision. I stood frozen as the diminishing sound of its distress signals echoed back to me.

"What in the world was that?"

"Hunter-drone," Sophia said calmly. "A form of autonomous security unit found in this sector. Harmless when deactivated, but when programmed, it can be directed to pursue a target until it eliminates the threat. It has a single-purpose algorithm and follows with relentless determination."

"Then that would mean...?"

"That it was sent by our enemy, the same enemy that attacked us at The Nexus in Crestwood. Exactly." Sophia stopped at her tent entrance and faced me with grave eyes. "Tyler, our every move is being monitored. From now on, it's survival of the most prepared."

The following day was our seventh in the sector. The ground here resembled a vast patchwork, marked with long winding trails of yellowish residue that pooled in shallow depressions. The chemical contamination from decades of research had undergone environmental transformation and evolved into a corrosive compound that persisted indefinitely. The hazmat specialists moved with extreme caution. Had one of them stepped into those yellow pools, their suit would have been compromised within seconds.

At noon by my chronometer, I spotted a low gray structure on one of the stable plateaus. Moments later we reached a reinforced entrance, and Sophia was introducing me to Valentina Cooper.

She was not as old as I had expected, but she was weathered and intense, with steel-gray hair cut short. She wore a patched laboratory coat and protective goggles pushed up on her forehead.

"Pleased to meet you," she said, shaking my hand firmly. "Any colleague of Dr. Edwards is welcome here." She led us through the airlock into her facility.

The place was a three-room structure, compact but well-equipped. The latest holographic display in one corner showed that Cooper maintained contact with the outside world.

Sophia came to the point immediately. When she had explained our mission, the neuroscientist became thoughtful.

"Resonance Crystals, yes?" she repeated slowly. "Well, I suppose I could locate that vault again. That is, if I chose to."

"What do you mean?" Sophia paused in preparing another cigarette. "You know where it is, don't you?"

"Yes," Cooper nodded. "But as I mentioned before, that vault is in the Sigma Zone, and that isn't exactly a safe destination."

"What's in the Sigma Zone?" I asked. "Residual contamination?"

Cooper shook her head. "Something that was never properly documented. Strictly speaking, they're no more than an emergent phenomenon."

"Dangerous?"

"Yes and no. The only researcher I know who entered the Sigma Zone and returned was Dr. Sharma, four years ago. I survived because I moved quickly and they didn't detect me, and Sharma escaped because he somehow amused them."

"Amused?" A frown crossed Sophia's face.

"That's right," Cooper said. "The phenomena have a strange reactive pattern that manifests as what we interpret as amusement. But what triggers this reaction, I don't know."

Equipment and supplies were replenished at the facility. Several energy weapons were borrowed from Cooper's arsenal to arm our team. And then, as we were preparing to depart, Cooper suddenly stopped.

"The Professor Cosmos program," she said. "I haven't missed an episode in months. You need to wait until I watch it."

Sophia frowned in irritation, but the neuroscientist was insistent. She activated a display, adjusted settings, and moments later was watching with rapt attention.

It was the same program I had witnessed in Crestwood. Once again I heard questions from across the network. Once again I saw the commanding figure of the quiz master as he moved across the stage. And as I sat there, watching the display, a curious numbing drowsiness seemed to steal over me and pull my thoughts into a fog.

Half an hour later, we departed into the unknown. The hazmat specialists were nervous now and communicated constantly. We camped that night in a miserable shelter where equipment malfunctions plagued us. The next day, an indefinable wave of apathy and hopelessness affected our entire team. I caught myself questioning the purpose of our mission. Only Sophia's insistence kept me moving forward. The following morning, I understood the truth in her warning—all of us had been exposed to the insidious frequencies.

After that, I lost track of time. Day after day of toxic landscape... of abandoned facilities.... But eventually we reached a secure zone and continued on foot.

It was Cooper who first spotted the vault. Leading the way, she suddenly halted at the crest of a ridge and pointed ahead. There it stood, a massive reinforced structure of corroded titanium alloy, half-buried in contaminated soil.

"What's that installation on top?" Cooper asked, puzzled.

A rectangular housing had been constructed over the vault's upper section. Above this structure were three tall transmission towers. And suspended between them was a network of cables studded with crystalline nodes.

Sophia studied it through her suit's enhanced optics. "Tyler, take three specialists and approach from the east ridge," she ordered. "Valentina and I will circle from the west. Signal if you encounter trouble."

But we found no trouble. The scene before us was completely still. Moments later, our two groups converged at the vault's base.

A metal ladder extended from the housing down the structure's side. Midway we could see a circular access port.

"Up we go, Tyler." Energy weapon ready, Sophia began to climb carefully.

The silence remained absolute. We reached the port and opened it. There was no sign of activity.

"Someone has invested considerable resources here," Valentina Cooper observed.

Someone had. Before us stretched a narrow corridor, bordered on the left by a wall of transparent composite material. The corridor was empty. But beyond the transparent barrier, revealed in clear detail, was a large control panel, covered with displays and instruments. Even as we watched, we could see data flowing across screens, indicator lights pulsing rhythmically.

Sophia nodded. "Some kind of transmission system. The Resonance Crystals in the lower vault are probably exposed to a quantum resonance plate and their frequencies amplified by an electromagnetic cascade process."

Cooper raised her weapon and struck the transparent wall. Her arm recoiled, but the wall remained intact.

"You'll never breach it that way," Sophia said. "Nothing short of a plasma charge will penetrate that barrier. It explains why there are no guards here. The mechanism is completely automated. Let's see if the Resonance Crystals are more accessible."

In the lower vault, disappointment confronted us again. Visible in the dim emergency lighting were rows of crystalline formations, each glowing with faint internal luminescence. Suspended by insulators from the ceiling above them was a thick resonance plate.

But between us and them was a barrier. A wall of impenetrable transparent composite.

Sophia stamped her foot. "It's infuriating," she said. "Here we are at the heart of the entire conspiracy, and we're powerless to act."

original_question: What makes Grannie Annie's writing remarkable?

synthetic_story:
RENEGADE
By ADAPTED WORK

In the age of autonomous vehicles and genetic engineering, the greatest weapon remained unchanged—human will itself.

Sergio Sharma hovered two hundred feet above the Foxwood City central plaza, his neural implant calculating trajectories and threat assessments. The cool AI processor surgically embedded in his brainstem was working on the problem, but Sergio had no more patience. They'd sweat, he thought, hating the buffeting wind from the climate control vents that threw his hovering body this way and that. He glared down at the three towers bordering the plaza. He spat, watching the droplet fall.

Lock me up in the Research Facility. All I wanted was some time to think. Did I develop their genetic modifications for them? Damn right I did. Just a little time to process what we'd done, so I shouldn't lose it completely. Now the lid's gone.

He was going over all their heads. He'd pushed past those corporate security guards like they were nothing, back at the Genomics Institute. The darkness was closing in on Sergio's mind. The Director himself was going to hear about it.

Why not? Isn't the Director the head of the Foxwood City Bioethics Division?

The humming anti-grav units embedded beneath his shoulder blades held him motionless above Foxwood's three administrative towers. The Ethics Commission. Director's Complex. Judicial Center. Sergio cursed his own ignorance. He hadn't bothered to learn which building was which ahead of time.

They keep genetic engineers in the Institute and teach them how to modify human DNA. They don't teach them about their own city, the one they're supposedly improving. There's no time. From graduate school onward, engineers have too much to learn about their specialization.

The Director was behind one of those thousands of windows. His neural implant, a gift from the Institute surgeons, courtesy of the city, would have to figure out which one. Blood churned in his veins, nerves shrieked with impatience. Sergio waited for the artificial intelligence to come up with the answer.

Then his head jerked up, to a distant hum. Security drones were coming. Two black enforcement vehicles whirred along the translucent underside of Foxwood's protective atmospheric shield.

Neural implant better be fast. Damn fast!

The AI jolted an impulse through his spine. Sergio somersaulted. The implant had taken charge of his motor nerves. Sergio's own mind was just along for the ride.

His body snapped into a stiff dive position. He began to plummet down, picking up speed. His reinforced hands glittered like arrowheads out in front. They pointed to a particular window in one of the towers. A small blue-and-gold flag fluttered on a staff below the window. Whose flag? The city flag was red and white. He shrugged away the problem. The AI knew what it was doing.

The ring finger of his right hand vibrated in its carbon-fiber sheath. A pale laser beam leaped from the lensed fingertip. Breakthrough! The reinforced glass dissolved. Sergio streamed through the window.

The anti-grav units cut off. Sergio dropped lightly to the floor, inside the room, in a defensive crouch. A holographic display was projecting news. A woman gasped. Sergio's hand shot out automatically. A finger vibrated. Out of the corner of his eye, Sergio saw the woman crumple to the floor. There was no one else in the room. Sergio, still in a crouch, bit his lip.

The Director?

His head swung around and he peered at the holographic display. He saw his own face.

"Overwhelming security personnel with his laser modifications," said the announcer, "Sharma broke through the cordon surrounding the Foxwood Genomics Institute. One guard was severely injured, three others hospitalized. The Ethics Commission has warned that this man is extremely dangerous. Citizens are cautioned to avoid contact. Sharma is an unstable researcher. He is equipped with the latest military-grade enhancements. A built-in neural AI controls his reflexes—"

"Shut that off," said Sergio, and a reinforced finger snapped out. There was a loud bang. The holographic projector dissolved into a puddle of melted components.

The Director.

Sergio strode to the window. The two security drones were hovering above the towers. Sergio's reinforced hand snapped open a pouch at his belt. He flipped a fist-sized device to the floor.

The shield-generator "exploded"—expanded or inflated, really, but with the speed of a blast. Sergio glanced out the window. A section of the energy dome bellied out from above. It shaded the view from his window and re-entered the tower wall just below.

Now the woman.

He turned back to the room. "Wake up, off-worlder." He gave the dark-haired woman a light dose of the laser to rouse her.

"Who are you?" she said, shakily.

Sergio grinned. "Dr. Sergio Sharma, of the Foxwood Genomics Institute, is all." He threw her a mock salute. "You're from off-world, lady. I haven't seen a Foxwood woman with natural hair color in years. Purple or silver is the fashion. What are you doing in the Director's room?"

The woman pushed herself to her feet. Impressive bearing, Sergio noted. She was striking and composed, very off-world. She held herself straight and her green eyes flashed at him.

"What the devil do you think you're doing, doctor? I am a diplomatic representative of the Zenith Colony of Kaldria. This is an embassy, if you know what that means."

"I don't," said Sergio, unconcerned.

"Well, you should have had the sense to honor the flag outside this window. That's the Kaldrian flag, doctor. If you've never heard of diplomatic immunity, you'll suffer for your ignorance." Her large eyes narrowed. "Who sent you?"

"My neural AI sent me."

She went wide-eyed. "You're Sharma."

"I'm the guy they told you about on the news feed. Where's the Director? Isn't this his place?"

"No. No, you're in the wrong room. The wrong building. That's the Director's suite over there." She pointed. "See where the observation deck is? This is the Embassy suite. If you want the Director you'll have to go over there."

"Well, what do you know," said Sergio. "AI didn't know, any more than me."

The woman noticed the dark swell of the shield-dome. "What's that out there?"

"Force-shield. Nothing gets past, except maybe a full-power laser cannon. Keeps security out. Keeps you in. Are you anybody important?"

"I told you, I'm an ambassador. From Zenith, on Kaldria. I'm on a diplomatic mission."

"Yeah? Kaldria a big city?"

She stared at him, green eyes wide. "The colony planet Kaldria."

"Planet? Oh, that Kaldria. Sure, I've heard of it—you gotta go by starship. What's your name?"

"Diana Obrien. Look, Sharma, holding me is no good. It'll just get you in worse trouble. What are you trying to do?"

"I want to see the Director. Me and my colleagues, we just finished developing the latest genetic modifications for the military program. We succeeded. They've got enhanced soldiers now who can do things regular humans can't. The project worked beyond their expectations."

Diana Obrien said, "That's what genetic engineering did. The perfect enhancement. But also the road to economic inequality and the loss of cultural heritage. Dangerous territory."

Sergio said, "Yeah? Well, we did what they wanted us to do. We did the research for them. So we finished the project and they locked us up in the Institute. Won't let us leave. Won't let us talk to anyone. They had security guarding us. Corporate security." Sergio sneered. "I broke out. I want to see the Director and find out why we can't have our freedom. I don't mess around, Diana. I go right to the top."

Sergio broke off. There was a hum outside the window. He whirled and stared out. The rounded black hulls of the two security drones were nosing toward the force-shield. Sergio could read the white numbers painted on their sides.

A loudspeaker shouted into the room: "Come out of there, Sharma, or we'll blast you out."

"You can't," Sergio called. "This woman from Kaldria is here."

"I repeat, Sharma—come out or we'll blast you out."

Sergio turned to the woman. "I thought you were important."

She stood there with her arms crossed, calmly looking at him. "I am. But you are too, to them. Kaldria is light-years away, and you're right across the plaza from the Director's suite."

"Yeah, but—" Sergio shook his head and turned back to the window. "All right, look! Move those drones away and I'll let this woman out!"

"No deal, Sharma. We're coming in." The security drones backed away slowly, then shot straight up, out of the line of vision.

Sergio looked down at the plaza. Far below, the long, gleaming barrel of a laser cannon caught the dim light filtering down through Foxwood's atmospheric shield. The cannon rolled into the plaza on its gray, box-shaped automated mounting and took up a position equidistant from the bases of the three towers.

Now a rumble of many voices rose from below. Sergio stared down to see a large crowd gathering in the central plaza. Media drones were flying to positions around the edges of the crowd. The people were all looking up.

Sergio looked across the plaza. The windows of the tower opposite, the ones he could see clearly, were crowded with faces. There were white dot faces on the observation deck that Diana Obrien had pointed out as the Director's suite.

The voice of a news commentator rolled up from the plaza, reechoing against the tower walls.

"Sharma is holding the Kaldrian Ambassador, Diana Obrien, hostage. You can see the Kaldrian colors behind his force-shield. Security forces are bringing up laser cannon. Sharma's defense is a dome of energy similar to the one which protects Foxwood from external threats."

Sergio grinned back at Diana Obrien. "Whole city's down there." Then his grin faded. Intelligent, articulate woman like this probably cared a lot more about dying than he did. Why the hell didn't they give him a chance to let her out? Maybe he could do it now.

The AI said no. It said the second he dropped his force-shield, they'd blast this room to atoms. Poor woman from Kaldria, she didn't have a chance.

Diana Obrien put her hand to her forehead. "Why did you have to pick my room? Why did they send me to this unstable city? Private genetic modifications. Fifteen million people living under a shield like specimens in a lab. Earth is sick and it's going to kill me. What's going to happen?"

Sergio looked sadly at her. In his entire career at the Institute, he'd never met anyone who spoke to him like an equal, like a person rather than a tool. Why did he have to be so close to getting killed when he met someone he respected? Now that she was showing less fear and more understanding, she was talking directly to him. She was exceptional, but she wasn't acting as if she was too good for him.

"They'll start shooting pretty soon," said Sergio. "I'm sorry about you."

"I wish I could send a message to my family," she said.

"What?"

"Didn't you understand what I said?"

"What's a message?"

"You don't know where Kaldria is. You don't know what a message is. You probably can't even think beyond your specialization!"

Sergio shrugged. He carried on the conversation disinterestedly, professionally calm before conflict. "Are these things I can't do important?"

"Yes. The more I see of this city and its people, the more important I realize they are. You know how to engineer genes, don't you? I'll bet you're perfect with those modifications."

"Listen. They've been training me to modify DNA since I was in graduate school. Why shouldn't I be a great genetic engineer?"

"Specialization," said the woman from Kaldria.

"What?"

"Specialization. Everyone I've met in this city is a specialist. Political economy experts run the government. Technical specialists run the machinery. Genetic engineers modify the soldiers. And seventy per cent of the people don't work at all because they're not trained to do anything."

"The Consumers," said Sergio. "They've got it easy. That's them down there, come to watch the spectacle."

"You know why you were kept in the Institute, Sharma? I heard them talking about it, at the conference I attended yesterday."

"Why?"

"Because they're afraid of the genetic engineers. You scientists did too good a job with the military modifications. You are the most dangerous knowledge-holders that have ever existed. You. Individual bioengineers with the power to reshape humanity!"

Sergio said, "They told us in graduate school that it's the research that changes the world."

"Yes, but people had forgotten it until the political economy specialists of Foxwood came up with the genetic modification program. Before the modifications, governments concentrated on the big weapons, the autonomous vehicles, the drones. And the cities, with the shields, were safe from external threats. They learned to be self-sufficient under the shields. They were so safe, so isolated, that international cooperation collapsed. But you engineers wiped out that feeling of security, when you created soldiers who could infiltrate and conquer."

"We scared them, huh?"

Diana said, "You scared them so much that they were afraid to let you have freedom when you finished the project. Afraid you engineers would realize that you could easily take over the city if you wanted to. You scared them so much that they'll let me be killed. They'll actually risk trouble with Kaldria just to eliminate you."

"I'm sorry about you. I mean it, I respect—"

At that moment a titanic, ear-splitting explosion hurled him to the floor, deafened and blinded him.

He recovered and saw Diana a few feet away, dazed, groping on hands and knees.

Sergio jumped to the window, looked quickly, sprang back. The AI pumped orders to his nervous system.

"Laser cannon," he said. "But just one. Got it, AI. I can beat that."

He picked up the black device that generated his protective shield. Snapping it open with thumb-pressure, he turned a small dial. Then he waited.

Again an enormous, brain-shattering concussion.

Again Sergio and Diana were thrown to the floor. But this time there was a second explosion and a blinding flash from below.

Sergio laughed with relief and ran to the window.

"Look!" he called to Diana.

There was a huge gap in the crowd below. The pavement was blackened and shattered to rubble. In and around the open space sprawled dozens of tiny figures, not moving.

"Reflection," said Sergio. "I set the shield to throw their laser beam right back at them."

"And they knew you might—and yet they let a crowd gather!"

Diana reeled away from the window, sickened.

Sergio said, "I can do that a couple more times, but it drains the shield-generator. Then I'm dead."

He heard the news commentator's amplified voice: "—approximately thirty killed. But Sharma is finished now. He has been able to outthink security with the help of his neural AI. Now security is feeding the problem to their giant quantum computer in the sub-basement of the Judicial Center. The security quantum computer will be able to outthink Sharma's neural AI, will predict Sharma's moves in advance. Four more laser cannon are coming down Central Avenue—"

"Why don't they clear those people out of the plaza?" Diana cried.

"What? Oh, the Consumers—nobody clears them out." He paused. "I've got one more chance to try." He raised a reinforced glove to his mouth and pressed a small stud in the wrist. He said, "Institute Command, this is Sharma."

A voice spoke in his earpiece. "Sharma, this is Institute Command. We figured you'd call."

"Get me Director Greene."

Thirty seconds passed. Sergio could hear the whir of automated treads as the mobile laser cannon rolled into the central plaza.

The voice of the head of the Genomics Institute rasped into Sergio's ear: "Fool! You broke out against my orders! Now look at you!"

"I knew you didn't mean those orders, sir."

"If you get out of there alive, I'll have you permanently detained for disobeying them!"

"Yes, sir. Sir, there's a woman here—somebody important—from Kaldria. You know, the colony planet. Sir, she told me we could take over the city if we acted. Is that right, sir?"

There was a pause. "Your woman from Kaldria is right, Sharma. But it's too late now. If we had moved first, captured the city government, we might have done it. But they're ready for us. They'd cut us down with laser cannon."

"Sir, I'm asking for help. I know you're on my side."

"I am, Sharma." The voice of Director Greene was lower. "I'd never admit it if you had a chance of getting out of there alive. You're finished, son. I'd only lose more people trying to rescue you. When they feed the data into that quantum computer, you're done."

"Yes, sir."

"I'm sorry, Sharma."

"Yes, sir. Over and out."

Sergio pressed the stud on his glove again. He turned to Diana.

"You're okay. I wish I could let you out. The AI says I can't. Says if I drop the force-shield for a second, they'll fire into the room, and then we'll both be dead."

Diana stood with folded arms and looked at him. "Do what you have to do. As far as I can see, you're the only person in this city who has even a little bit of ethical clarity."

Sergio laughed. "Any of the modified people I know would be terrified. You're different."

"When my ancestors colonized Kaldria, they found out that selfishness was a luxury. Kaldrians can't afford it. Scientific collaboration is everything to us."

Sergio frowned with the effort of thinking. "You said I had ethical clarity. That's a good feeling. Nobody ever told me to feel that way about myself before. It'll be better to die knowing that."

"I know," she said.

The amplified voice from below said, "The security quantum computer is now linked directly to the controls of the laser cannon battery. It will outguess Sharma's neural AI and anticipate his moves."

Sergio looked at Diana. "How about if we share one moment of real human connection before they get us? Would be nice if I connected with someone like you just once in my life."

She smiled and walked forward. "You deserve it, Sharma."

He embraced her briefly and it filled him with longings for things he couldn't name. Then he stepped back and shook his head. "It isn't right you should get killed. If I dive out that window, they shoot at me, not in here."

"And kill you all the sooner."

"Better than getting incinerated in this room. You also have value. There's too many damn genetic engineers and not enough good persons like you. The AI says stay here, but I don't think I will. I'm going to pay you back for that moment."

"But you're safe in here!"

"Worry about yourself, not about me." Sergio picked up the shield-generator and handed it to her. "When I say now, press this. Then take your hand off, real fast. It'll shut off the shield for a second."

He stepped up onto the window ledge. Automatically, the AI activated his anti-grav units. "So long, off-worlder. Now!"

He jumped. He was hurtling across the plaza when the laser cannons opened up. They weren't aimed at the window where the little blue-and-gold Kaldrian flag was flying. But they weren't aimed at Sergio, either. They were shooting randomly.

Which way now? Looks like I have a chance. The AI says fly right for the cannons.

He saw the Director's observation deck ahead.

Go to hell, AI. I'm doing all right by myself. I came to see the Director, and I'm going to see him.

Sergio plunged forward. He heard the shouts of frightened people.

He swooped over the observation deck railing. A man was pointing a laser pistol at him. There were five people on the deck—emergency! Years of training and the AI took over. Sergio's hand shot out, fingers vibrating. As he dropped to the deck floor in defensive position, the people slumped around him.

He had seen the man with the laser pistol before. It was Richard Greene, Director of the Foxwood Genomics Institute.

Sergio stood for a moment in the midst of the collapsed figures, the shrieks of the crowd floating up to him. Then he raised his glove to his lips. He made contact with the Institute.

"Director Greene, sir. You said if we captured the city government we might have a chance. Well, I captured the city government. What do we do with it now?"

Sergio was uncomfortable in his formal attire. First there had been a ceremony in the central plaza inaugurating Foxwood's new Research Directorate, and honoring Dr. Sergio Sharma. Now there was a formal dinner. Director Greene and Diana Obrien sat on either side of Sergio.

Greene said, "Call me an opportunist if you like, Ambassador Obrien, my government will be stable, and Kaldria can negotiate with it." He was a lean, sharp-featured man with deep lines in his face, and gray hair.

Diana shook her head. "Recognition for a new government takes time. I'm going back to Kaldria, and I think they'll send another ambassador next time. Nothing personal—I just don't like it here."

Sergio said, "I'm going to Kaldria, too."

"Did she ask you to?" demanded Greene.

Sergio shook his head. "She's got too much class for me. But I like what she told me about Kaldria. It's healthy, like. They value scientific collaboration and cultural heritage."

Greene frowned. "If I thought there was an ounce of strategy involved in your capture of the Director's office, Sharma, I'd never release you from duty. But I know better. You beat that quantum computer by sheer irrationality—by disregarding your neural AI."

Sergio said, "It wasn't so irrational if it worked."

"That's what bothers me. It calls for a revision in our protocols. We've got a way of beating those big computers now, should anyone use them against us."

"I just didn't want her to be hurt."

"Exactly. The computer could outguess a machine, like your neural AI. But you introduced a totally unpredictable factor—human emotion. Which proves what I, as a scientist, have always maintained—that the most powerful force in human affairs is still, and will always be, the individual human being."

"What you just said there, sir," said Sergio. "That's why I'm leaving Foxwood."

"What do you mean?" asked Director Greene.

"I'm tired of being a tool, sir. I want to be a complete human being."

THE END

option_a: Diana is initially fearful of Sergio but gradually comes to see him as the only person in Foxwood with ethical clarity, while Sergio respects Diana's intelligence and values
option_b: Diana and Sergio are colleagues from the Genomics Institute who planned the hostage situation together as part of a coordinated uprising
correct_answer_text: Diana is initially fearful of Sergio but gradually comes to see him as the only person in Foxwood with ethical clarity, while Sergio respects Diana's intelligence and values

Option B is incorrect because Diana is an ambassador from Kaldria who happened to be in the wrong room, and she and Sergio had never met before this incident.
