synthetic_story:
The Crystalline Spire

Phillip Robinson sat in the filtered sunlight of his studio in Thornhill, Selvoria, composing a linguistic analysis as he watched the canal flow gently past his window. There were very few boats on it, for he lived in a quiet district, and those who preferred travel generally chose the faster waterways where the current was stronger.

Moreover, on a humid afternoon like this one, there would be few people out and about. Most would be in their climate-controlled homes, working on their various projects—some composing music, others writing treatises on moral philosophy, still others developing new applications of nanotechnology. Those without creative inclinations would be relaxing in whatever manner they had chosen to spend this particular one of the perfect days that stretched in an unbroken line before every member of the human race from birth to death.

Only the Architects were much in evidence. Only the Architects had duties to perform. Only the Architects worked.

Phillip stretched and rejoiced in knowing that he was human and not an Architect. Immediately afterward, he felt guilty for the selfish thought. Didn't the Architects work only to serve humanity? How ungrateful, then, to feel superior to them! Besides, he comforted himself, probably the Architects liked to work. He hailed a passing Architect for assurance on this point.

Courteous, like all members of their kind, the being stepped from the canal path and listened attentively to the young man's question. "We Architects have but one purpose," it replied in its melodious voice. "We exist to maintain the balance and guide humanity toward enlightenment."

"But how do you know what constitutes enlightenment?" Phillip persisted.

"We know," the Architect said, its crystalline face reflecting the afternoon sun as it gazed reverently across the city to the great Crystalline Spire where The Prime Architect dwelt, in constant communication with every member of its race at all times, or so they said. "That is why we were entrusted with humanity's stewardship. Someday you, too, may advance to the point where you know, and we shall return to our origin."

"But who entrusted you," Phillip asked, "and where is your origin?" Fearing he might seem motivated by vulgar curiosity, he explained, "I am researching the cultural heritage of our world for a linguistic study."

A lifetime spent under their gentle guidance had made Phillip able to interpret the expression that flickered across this Architect's translucent features as a patient smile.

"We come from beyond the observable universe," it said. Phillip already knew that; he had hoped for something more specific. "We were entrusted with power by those who had the authority. And the power through which we guide is the power of harmony! Be well!"

And with that conventional farewell, it stepped back onto the canal path and glided away. Phillip looked after it pensively for a moment, then shrugged. Why should the Architects surrender their secrets to gratify the idle curiosity of a linguist?

Phillip packed his recording equipment in its case and went to call on the woman next door, whom he loved with a deep and intermittently requited passion.

As he passed through the entrance to the Wyatt residence, he noted with dismay that there were quite a number of Isabella's associates present, lounging about and sipping beverages which probably exceeded the legal stimulant threshold.

Much as he hated to think harshly of anyone, he did not like Isabella Wyatt's associates. He had never known anybody who had as many associates as she did, and sometimes he suspected they were not all genuine friends. Then he would dismiss the thought as unworthy of him or any right-thinking human being. He loved Isabella for herself alone and not for her companions. Whether they were actually her friends or something else was none of his business.

"Be well!" he greeted the assemblage cordially, sitting down beside Isabella on the cushioned floor.

"Nonsense!" said old Ahmed Crawford, Isabella's mentor. Phillip was sure that, underneath his gruffness, the weathered scholar hid a heart of gold. Although he had been searching diligently, the young man had not yet been able to find that vein; however, he did not give up hope, for not giving up hope was one of the principles that his wise old Architect teacher had inculcated in him. Other principles were to pursue knowledge and maintain work-life balance.

"Now, Ahmed," Isabella said, "no matter what your views, that does not excuse rudeness."

Phillip wished she would not allude so blatantly to dissent, because he had a lurking notion that Isabella's "associates" were, in fact, a band of resisters... such as still existed across the peaceful planet and proved by their existence that humanity was not advancing anywhere within measurable distance of that totality of wisdom implied by the Architects.

You could tell malcontents, even if they did not voice their dissatisfactions, by their faces. The vast majority of the human race, living good and enlightened lives, had smooth and pleasant faces. Malcontents' faces were lined and sometimes, in extreme cases, deeply furrowed. Everyone could easily tell who they were by looking at them, and most people avoided them.

It was not that dissent was illegal, for the Architects permitted free speech and reasonable opposition; it was that such behavior was considered uncouth. Phillip would never have dreamed of associating with this set of neighbors, once he had discovered their tendencies, had he not lost his heart to the violet-eyed Isabella at their first meeting.

"Rudeness, bah!" old Ahmed said. "To see a healthy young man simply accepting the status quo!"

"If the status quo is a good status quo," Phillip said uneasily, for he did not like to discuss such subjects, "why should I not accept it? We have everything we could possibly want. What do we lack?"

"Our autonomy," Ahmed retorted.

"But we are autonomous," Phillip said, perplexed. "We can say what we like, do what we like, so long as it serves the common good."

"Ah, but who determines what serves the common good?"

Phillip could no longer temporize with truth, even for Isabella's sake. "Look here, old man, I have studied history. I know about the old days before the Architects emerged from the deep ocean. Humanity was destroying itself through resource wars and environmental collapse. There is none of that any more."

"All lies and propaganda," old Ahmed said. "My grandmother told me that, when the Architects took control of Earth, they rewrote all the historical records to suit their own purposes. Now nothing but Architect propaganda is taught in the academies."

"But surely some of what they teach about the past must be true," Phillip insisted. "And today every one of us has clean water, sustainable food, comfortable shelter, and all the time in the world to pursue our interests in creative collaboration with others. What is missing?"

"They've taken away our agency!"

Behind his back, Isabella made a little apologetic face at Phillip.

Phillip tried to make the old man see reason. "But I'm content. And everybody is content, except—except a few troublemakers like you."

"They certainly did a thorough job of conditioning you, boy," Ahmed sighed. "And most of the young ones," he added mournfully. "With each succeeding generation, more of our independence is lost." He patted Isabella's hand. "You're a good woman, Isabella. You don't hold with being managed like some domesticated creature."

"Never mind Ahmed, Robinson," one of Isabella's alleged colleagues grinned. This was Felix Chang, a burly man with unkempt hair. "He talks excessively, but of course he doesn't mean half of what he says. Come, have some tea."

He handed a cup to Phillip. Phillip sipped and coughed. It tasted as if it were well above the legal caffeine limit, but he didn't like to say anything. They were taking an awful risk, though, doing a thing like that. If they got caught, they might receive a public correction—which was, of course, no more than they deserved—but he could not bear to think of Isabella exposed to such an ordeal.

"It's only natural," Felix went on, "that older people should have reservations about being governed by outsiders."

Phillip smiled and set his nearly full cup down on a table. "You could hardly call the Architects outsiders; they've been on Earth longer than even the oldest of us."

"You seem to be quite friendly with them," Felix said, looking narrow-eyed at Phillip.

"No more so than any other loyal citizen," Phillip replied.

Felix sat up and wrapped his arms around his thick legs. He was a powerful, rough-looking man who had not taken advantage of the numerous cosmetic enhancements offered by the benevolent Architects. "Don't you think it's peculiar they can process our water so easily?"

"Why shouldn't they?" Phillip bit into a fruit that Isabella handed him from one of the dishes of food and other delicacies arranged about the room. "It's excellent water," he continued through a full mouth, "especially now that it's all purified. I understand that in the old days—"

"Yes," Felix said, "but don't you think it's suspicious that they manage water exactly the way we need it managed, considering they claim to come from another dimension?"

"No coincidence at all," said Phillip shortly, no longer able to pretend he didn't know what the other was implying. He had heard the ugly rumor before. Of course heresy was not illegal, but it was in bad taste. "Only one set of physical laws governs intelligent life."

"They say," Felix continued, impervious to Phillip's unconcealed dislike for the subject, "that there's really only one Architect, who lives in the Crystalline Spire—in some kind of containment field, because it can't survive in our environment—and that the others are a sort of projection it sends out to do its work."

"Nonsense!" Phillip was goaded to irritation at last. "How could a projection have that subtle expressiveness, that graceful movement?"

Isabella and Felix exchanged glances. "But they are absolutely expressionless," Felix began hesitantly. "Perhaps, with your rich linguistic imagination..."

"See?" old Ahmed remarked with satisfaction. "The boy's been conditioned. I told you so."

"Even if The Prime Architect is a single entity," Phillip went on, "that doesn't necessarily make it less benevolent—"

He was again interrupted by Ahmed. "I won't listen to any more of this drivel. Benevolent, bah! It or they are just plain exploiting us! Taking our geological resources away—I've seen them loading minerals on the transport vessels—and—"

"—and exchanging them for other resources from beyond," Phillip said tightly, "without which we could not have the perfectly balanced society we have today. Without which we would be, technologically, back in the dark ages from which they rescued us."

"It's not the materials they bring from outside that powers this technological progress," Felix said. "It's some energy source they've got that we can't seem to understand. Though Lord knows we've tried," he added musingly.

"Of course they have their own source of power," Phillip informed them, smiling to himself, for his old Architect teacher had taken great care to instill a sense of humor into him. "An Architect was explaining that to me only today."

Twenty heads swiveled toward him. He felt uncomfortable, for he was a modest young man and did not like to be the center of attention.

"Tell us, dear boy," Felix said, grabbing Phillip's cup and refilling it, "what exactly did it say?"

"It said the Architects guide through the power of harmony."

The cup crashed to the floor as Felix uttered a very inappropriate word.

"And I suppose it was harmony that killed Teresa and Samir when they tried to breach the Crystalline Spire—" old Ahmed began, then halted at the looks he was getting from everybody.

Phillip could no longer pretend his neighbors were a group of eccentrics whom he himself was eccentric enough to regard as interesting.

"So!" He stood up and wrapped his jacket about him. "I knew you were against the government, and, of course, you have a legal right to disagree with its policies, but I didn't think you were actual—actual—" he dredged a word up out of his studies—"revolutionaries."

He turned to the woman, who was looking thoughtful as she stroked the glittering crystal that always hung at her neck. "Isabella, how can you stay with these—" he found another word—"these insurgents?"

She smiled sadly. "Don't forget: they're my colleagues, Phillip, and I owe them loyalty, no matter how misguided they are." She pressed his hand. "But don't give up hope."

That rang a bell inside his brain. "I won't," he vowed, giving her hand a return squeeze. "I promise I won't."

Outside the Wyatt residence, he paused, struggling with his inner self. It was an unworthy thing to inform upon one's neighbors; on the other hand, could he stand idly by and let those neighbors attempt to destroy the social order? Deciding that the greater good was more important—and that, moreover, it was the only way of taking Isabella away from all this—he went in search of an Architect. That is, he waited until one glided past and called to it.

"I wish to report a conspiracy at the Wyatt residence in Thornhill," he said. "Isabella is innocent, but the others are deeply involved."

The Architect appeared to consider for a moment. Then it displayed what might have been a smile. "Oh, them," it said. "We know. They are harmless."

"Harmless!" Phillip repeated. "Why, I understand they've already tried to breach the Crystalline Spire by force!"

"Quite. And failed. For we are protected from hostile forces, as you were told earlier, by the power of harmony."

Phillip knew, of course, that the Architect used the word harmony metaphorically, that the Spire was protected by a series of highly efficient energy barriers to repel attackers—barriers which, he realized now, from the sad fate of Teresa and Samir, were potentially lethal. However, he did not blame the Architects for being so secretive about their race's source of power, not with people like Isabella's associates running about plotting and whatnot.

"You certainly do have a wonderful communication system," he murmured.

"Everything about us is optimal," the Architect said noncommittally. "That's why we're so beneficial to you people. Be well!" And it was off.

But Phillip could not be well. He wasn't precisely unwell yet, but he was troubled. Of course the Architects knew better than he did, but still... Perhaps they underestimated the seriousness of the conspiracy. On the other hand, perhaps it was he who was taking Isabella's associates too seriously. Maybe he should investigate further before doing anything rash.

Later that night, he slipped over to the Wyatt residence and crept about until he found the window behind which the group was conspiring. He peered through a gap in the curtains, so he could both see and hear.

Isabella was saying, "And so I think there is merit in what Phillip said..."

Bless her, he thought emotionally. Even in the midst of her plotting, she had time to spare a kind word for him. And then it hit him: she, too, was a plotter.

"You suggest that we try to turn the power of harmony against the Architects?" Felix asked ironically.

Isabella gave a musical laugh as she twirled her glittering crystal pendant. "In a manner of speaking," she said. "I have an idea for a device which might do the trick—"

At that moment, Phillip stumbled over a container which some careless associate had apparently left lying about. It crashed to the floor, spattering Phillip's legs and shoes with a liquid which later proved to be extremely strong coffee.

"There's someone outside!" Felix declared, half-rising.

"Nonsense!" Isabella said, putting her hand on his shoulder. "I didn't hear anything."

Felix looked dubious, and Phillip thought it prudent to withdraw at this point. Besides, he had heard enough. Isabella—his Isabella—was an integral part of the conspiracy.

He lay down to sleep that night beset by doubts. If he told the Architects about the conspiracy, he would be betraying Isabella. As a matter of fact, he now remembered, he had already told them about the conspiracy and they hadn't believed him. But supposing he could convince them, how could he give Isabella up to them? True, it was the right thing to do—but, for the first time in his life, he could not bring himself to do what he knew to be right. He was weak, weak—and weakness was contrary to the principles of moral philosophy his old Architect teacher had taught him.

As Phillip writhed restlessly upon his bed, he became aware that someone had come into his chamber.

"Phillip," a soft, beloved voice whispered, "I have come to ask your help..." It was so dark, he could not see her; he knew where she was only by the glitter of the crystal on her necklace as it moved through the blackness.

"Isabella..." he breathed.

"Phillip..." she sighed.

Now that the amenities were over, she resumed, "Against my will, I have been involved in the group's plot. Felix has invented a device which he believes will counteract the power of the barriers."

"But I thought you devised it!"

"So it was you outside. Well, what happened was I wanted to gain time, so I said I had a device of my own invention which I had not perfected, but which would cost considerably less than Felix's model. We have to watch resources, you know, because we can hardly expect the Architects to supply the components for this job. Anyhow, I thought that, while my colleagues were waiting for me to finish it, you would have a chance to warn the Architects."

"Isabella," he murmured, "you are as noble and clever as you are beautiful."

Then he caught the full import of her remarks. "Me! But they won't pay any attention to me!"

"How do you know?" When he remained silent, she said, "I suppose you've already tried to warn them about us."

"I—I said you had nothing to do with the plot."

"That was good of you." She continued in a warmer tone: "How many Architects did you warn, then?"

"Just one. When you tell one something, you tell them all. You know that. Everyone knows that."

"That's just theory," she said. "It's never been proven. All we do know is that they have some sort of central information hub, presumably The Prime Architect. But we don't know that they are incapable of thinking or acting individually. We don't really know much about them at all; they're very secretive."

"Reserved," he corrected her, "as befits a guiding race. But always approachable."

"You must warn as many Architects as you can."

"And if none listens to me?"

"Then," she said dramatically, "you must approach The Prime Architect itself."

"But no human being has ever reached it!" he said plaintively. "You know that all those who have tried perished. And that can't be a rumor, because Ahmed said—"

"But they came to attack The Prime Architect. You're coming to warn it! That makes a significant difference. Phillip..." She took his hands in hers; in the darkness, the crystal swung on her presumably heaving chest. "This is bigger than both of us. It's for Earth."

He knew it was his duty to do as she said; still, he had enjoyed life so much. "Isabella, wouldn't it be much simpler if we just destroyed Felix's device?"

"He'd only make another. Don't you see, Phillip, this is our only chance to save the Architects, to save humanity... But, of course, I don't have the right to send you. I'll go myself."

"No, Isabella," he sighed. "I can't let you go. I'll do it."

Next morning, he set out to warn Architects. He knew it wasn't much use, but it was all he could do. The first half dozen responded in much the same way the Architect he had warned the previous day had done, by courteously acknowledging his concern and assuring him there was no need for alarm; they knew all about the conspirators and everything would be resolved.

After that, they started to get increasingly dismissive—which would, he thought, substantiate the theory that they were all part of one vast coordinate network of consciousness. Especially since each Architect behaved as if Phillip had been repeatedly bothering it personally.

Finally, they refused to stop when he hailed them—which was unprecedented, for no Architect had ever before failed to respond to a human's call—and when he started running along the canal paths after them, they moved much faster than he could.

At last he gave up and wandered about Thornhill for hours, speaking to neither human nor Architect, wondering what to do. That is, he knew what he had to do; he was wondering how to do it. He would never be able to reach The Prime Architect. No human being had ever done it. Teresa and Samir had died trying to reach it. Even though their intentions had been hostile and Phillip's would be helpful, there was little chance he would be allowed to reach The Prime Architect with all the other Architects against him. What guarantee was there that The Prime Architect would not be against him, too?

And yet he knew that he would have to risk his life; there was no help for it. He had never wanted to be a hero, and here he had heroism thrust upon him. He knew he could not succeed; equally well, he knew he could not turn back, for his Architect teacher had instructed him in the meaning of duty.

It was twilight when he approached the Crystalline Spire in Newbridge City. Commending himself to the highest principles, he entered. The Architect at the entrance did not display the customary welcoming demeanor. In fact, it seemed to radiate a curiously anxious aura.

"Go back, young man," it said. "You're not wanted here."

"I must see The Prime Architect. I must warn it against the conspirators."

"It has been warned," the guardian told him. "Go home and be well!"

"I don't trust you or your fellows. I must see The Prime Architect itself."

Suddenly this particular Architect lost its commanding presence. It began to sag, insofar as so rigidly structured a being could go limp. "Please, we've done so much for you. Do this for us."

"The Prime Architect did things for us," Phillip countered. "You are all only its extensions. How do I know you are really following it? How do I know you haven't turned against it?"

Without giving the being a chance to answer, he strode forward. The Architect attempted to bar his way. Phillip knew one Architect was vastly stronger than a human, so it was out of utter desperation that he struck.

The Architect collapsed completely, shattering into a cascade of crystalline fragments and delicate circuitry. The fact was of some deeper significance, Phillip knew, but he was too stunned by his incredible success to be able to think clearly. All he knew was that The Prime Architect would be able to explain things to him.

Alarms began to sound. That meant the energy barriers had activated. He could see the shimmering translucence of the first one before him. Squaring his shoulders, he charged it... and walked right through. He looked himself up and down. He was alive and whole.

Then the whole thing was a deception; the barriers were not lethal—or perhaps even real. But what of Teresa? And Samir? And countless rumored others? He would not let himself even try to think of them. He would not let himself even try to think of anything save his duty.

A ramp spiraled up ahead of him. An Architect was at its base. Behind it, a barrier shimmered.

"Please, young man—" the Architect began. "You don't understand. Let me explain."

But Phillip destroyed the thing before it could say anything further, and he passed right through the barrier. He had to get to the top and warn The Prime Architect, whatever it was, that the conspirators had a device which might be able to destroy it. Architect after Architect Phillip destroyed, and barrier after barrier he penetrated until he reached the summit. At the top of the ramp was a vast crystalline door.

"Go no further, Phillip Robinson!" a mighty voice roared from within. "To open that door is to bring disaster upon your race."

But all Phillip knew was that he had to get to The Prime Architect within and warn it. He battered down the door; that is, he would have battered down the door if it had not turned out to be unlocked. A stream of noxious vapor rushed out of the opening, causing him to black out.

When he came to, most of the vapor had dissipated. The Prime Architect was already dying of asphyxiation, since it was, in fact, a single alien entity who breathed another combination of elements. The chamber at the top of the ramp had been its containment field.

"You fool..." it gasped. "Through your misguided integrity... you have destroyed not only me... but Earth's future. I tried to make... this planet a better place for humanity... and this is my reward..."

"But I don't understand!" Phillip wept. "Why did you let me do it? Why were Teresa and Samir and all the others killed? Why was it that I could pass the barriers and they could not?"

"The barriers were designed... to respond to hostility... You meant well... so our defenses... could not activate." Phillip had to bend low to hear the creature's last words: "There is... an Earth proverb... should have warned me... 'I can protect myself... against my enemies... but who will protect me... from my friends'...?"

The Prime Architect died in Phillip's arms. It was the last of its race, so far as Earth was concerned, for no more came. If, as they had said themselves, some outside power had sent them to guide the human race, then that power had given up the race as a lost cause. If they were merely exploiting Earth, as the malcontents had kept suggesting, apparently it had proven too dangerous or too costly a venture.

Shortly after The Prime Architect's demise, Isabella's associates arrived en masse. "We won't need your device now," Phillip told them dully. "The Prime Architect is dead."

Isabella gave one of the musical laughs he was to grow to hate so much. "Darling, you were my device all along!" She beamed at her "colleagues," and it was then he noticed the faint lines around her eyes. "I told you I could use the power of harmony to destroy the Architects!" And then she added gently: "I think there is no doubt who leads this movement now."

Felix gave a strained laugh. "You're going to have a remarkable leader there, boy," he said to Phillip.

"Leader?" Phillip repeated, still absorbed in his grief.

"Yes, I imagine the people will want to make you our first Governor by popular acclaim."

Phillip looked at him through a haze of tears. "But I killed The Prime Architect. I didn't mean to, but... they must hate me!"

"Nonsense, my boy; they'll adore you. You'll be a hero!"

Events proved him right. Even those people who had lived in apparent contentment under the Architects, accepting what they were given and seemingly enjoying their carefree lives, now declared themselves to have been suffering in silent resentment all along. They showered Phillip with praise and composed extremely flattering songs about him.

Shortly after he was universally acclaimed Governor, he married Isabella. He couldn't escape.

"Why doesn't she become Governor herself?" he wailed, when the associates came and found him hiding in the ruins of the Crystalline Spire. The people had torn the Spire down as soon as they were sure The Prime Architect was dead and the others thereby rendered inoperative. "It would spare her considerable trouble."

"Because she is not The Architect-slayer," Felix said, dragging him out. "Besides, she loves you. Come on, Phillip, be strong." So they hauled him off to the wedding and, amid much celebration, he was married to Isabella.

He never drew another happy breath. In the first place, now that The Prime Architect was dead, all the systems that had been operated by it stopped and no one knew how to repair them. The water purification stopped functioning, the climate control stopped controlling, the food distribution stopped distributing, and so on. And, of course, everybody blamed it all on Phillip—even that year's drought and subsequent floods.

There were famines, riots, plagues, and, after the waves of mob hostility had coalesced into regional factions, wars. It was like the old days again, precisely as described in the historical records—assuming those records hadn't been falsified after all.

In the second place, Phillip could never forget that, when Isabella had sent him to the Crystalline Spire, she could not have been sure that her plan would work. Harmony might not have conquered all—in fact, it was the more likely hypothesis that it wouldn't—and he would have been killed by the first barrier. And no husband likes to think that his wife thinks he's expendable; it makes him feel she doesn't really love him.

So, in the twentieth year of his reign as Dictator of the Springfield Territory, Phillip had Isabella removed from power—that is, had her removed, for by now he had a Minister of Internal Affairs to handle such delicate matters—and married a very pretty, very young, very affectionate woman named Violet Romero. He wasn't particularly happy with her, either, but at least it was a change.

"Better than betraying our people," Melissa said.

The old woman looked at them for a long moment, then pulled them both into an embrace. "If a bridge can be built," she whispered, "then build it well."

They watched from the hills of Highpoint Territory as the ships rose into the night sky, their engines painting streaks of light across the darkness. One by one, they disappeared into the black, heading for coordinates only Carmen and a handful of others knew.

Then the city began to burn. Demolition charges, carefully placed, turned the beautiful spires and flowing walkways into cascading waterfalls of molten material. The blockchain networks collapsed in a cascade of failing nodes. The autonomous vehicles, their purpose fulfilled, drove themselves into the flames. Within hours, Ashford City was nothing but a scorched circle on the ground, already being reclaimed by the native vegetation of Highpoint Territory.

Melissa wept silently as the last flames died. Oliver held her, his own eyes dry but his heart breaking.

They waited.

The Architect ships arrived four days later, descending on pillars of nuclear fire. They were massive, industrial things, all hard angles and exposed infrastructure. No beauty in their design, no consideration for aesthetics or environmental impact. They landed in the clearing where Ashford City had stood, their sensors sweeping the area.

Oliver and Melissa stood on a hill, clearly visible, and waited to be found.

The Architects came for them within the hour. They were tall, broad-shouldered, their faces hard and angular. They wore uniforms of gray and black, weapons strapped to their sides. Oliver and Melissa were seized and brought before the Architect commander.

Patrick Ford looked up from his tactical display as they were pushed into his command center. His face was a mask of controlled aggression, his eyes cold and calculating. "So," he said, his voice like grinding metal, "the mice finally stopped running."

"We're not mice," Melissa said quietly. "We're people. Like you."

Ford snorted. "Like us? You're nothing like us. You're weak. Inefficient. You waste resources on frivolous things—art, music, beauty. While we've been building an empire, you've been playing with colored lights and autonomous toys."

"We've been building a civilization," Oliver said. "There's a difference."

"A civilization that runs away every time we get close." Ford leaned back in his chair. "Your people were here. Now they're gone. And you two stayed behind. Why? Are you defective? Criminals?"

"We stayed to offer peace," Melissa said. "This endless pursuit is wasteful for both of us. We want to negotiate an end to the conflict."

Ford stared at them for a long moment, then laughed—a harsh, barking sound. "Peace? You want peace? After you started the war, after you attacked our expansion into Oakridge, Ulvaria, after you sabotaged our ventures in Greenfield Village? Now you want peace?"

"That was thousands of years ago," Oliver said. "Neither of our peoples are what we were then. We've changed. Maybe you have too."

"We haven't changed," Ford said flatly. "We've perfected ourselves. Streamlined. Optimized. Every resource allocated for maximum efficiency, every citizen contributing to the expansion. That's why we'll always win. That's why you'll always run."

"But we're not running now," Melissa said softly. She reached into her clothing and withdrew a small device—a holographic projector, one of the few pieces of technology they'd been allowed to keep. "Let us show you something. Let us show you what we've built, what we've become."

Ford's hand moved toward his weapon. "I don't need to see your propaganda."

"It's not propaganda," Melissa said. "It's just... us. Our truth. Please."

Something in her voice made him pause. Perhaps it was curiosity. Perhaps it was arrogance—the certainty that nothing these weak refugees could show him would matter. He gestured curtly. "Go ahead. Show me your 'truth.'"

Melissa activated the projector.

The command center filled with light and sound. Images of Ashford City flowed through the air—not as it had been in its final days, but throughout its three-hundred-year history. The first settlement, crude and functional. Then the gradual transformation as art and architecture merged, as the citizens learned to build not just for efficiency but for beauty. The development of the autonomous transit systems, designed not just to move people but to enhance their daily experience. The public health facilities that treated illness while uplifting the spirit. The entrepreneurship programs that fostered innovation not for profit alone but for the betterment of all.

And woven through it all, the music. The concerts that had become the heart of Ashford City's culture—not performances for passive audiences, but communal experiences where every citizen participated, their minds linked through quantum interfaces, creating something greater than any individual could achieve alone.

The hologram showed the final concert, held the night before the evacuation. Four hundred voices and minds joined in perfect harmony, creating music that was also emotion, memory, hope, and love made manifest. It was a glimpse into a world where technology served humanity's highest aspirations, where cultural evolution had led not to conquest but to transcendence.

Ford watched, transfixed. His hand had fallen away from his weapon. His face, usually so controlled, showed something Oliver couldn't quite identify—confusion, perhaps, or fear, or something else entirely. For just a moment, the commander's cold eyes seemed to soften, as if remembering something long forgotten.

Then, with a roar of rage, Ford swept the projector from Melissa's hands. It shattered against the metal wall, the images dying in a cascade of sparks.

"Lies!" Ford shouted, his whole body shaking. "Manipulation! You're trying to weaken me, to make me forget my duty! Well, it won't work! I didn't see it, I didn't feel it, I won't remember it! We'll hunt you down, every last one of you, and your pathetic music will die forever!"

He whirled on his guards. "Take them to interrogation! Find out where their people went! Use whatever methods necessary!"

The interrogation was brutal. Oliver and Melissa had never imagined such pain could exist. The Architects had perfected torture as they had perfected everything else—systematic, efficient, designed to break the mind and body with minimal waste of resources.

The questions came in endless waves, punctuated by pain that seemed to split their skulls. Where had the ships gone? What were the coordinates? How many people? What were their defenses?

Oliver and Melissa said nothing. They couldn't have answered even if they'd wanted to—Carmen had been careful to tell them nothing of the destination. But the Architects didn't believe them. The pain intensified.

Finally, when they could endure no more, they whispered the trigger phrase they'd memorized. The hypnotic key that would erase everything—their memories, their knowledge, their very identities. It was the ultimate sacrifice, and they made it together.

The change was instantaneous. The screaming stopped. Oliver and Melissa stared at each other with blank, empty eyes, all recognition gone.

Ford stared at them in horror, realizing what they'd done. For a long moment, he stood frozen, his face twisted with frustration and something else—something that might have been respect, or regret.

Then, surprisingly, he ordered them released.

"Put them outside," he said quietly. "Leave them supplies. Water. Basic tools."

"Sir?" One of the guards looked confused. "We should execute them."

"I said leave them." Ford's voice was hard, brooking no argument. "They're no threat now. They're nothing."

The ships departed that night, their engines screaming into the darkness as they began their search of nearby systems, looking for any trace of the refugee fleet.

Oliver and Melissa sat on a hillside, watching the lights disappear. They didn't know why they were watching. They didn't know what the lights meant. They knew almost nothing at all.

Three thoughts filled their empty minds:

They were cold.

They were hungry.

Something dangerous was moving in the forest below.

Instinct drove them to find shelter. They stumbled into a cave in Highpoint Territory, huddling together for warmth. They didn't remember Ashford City. They didn't remember Carmen Wells, or the concerts, or the beautiful architecture they'd helped create. They didn't remember the Architects, or why those ships had come, or why they'd been shown mercy.

They didn't know that Patrick Ford, in the privacy of his quarters, was replaying the holographic images he'd secretly recorded. That he was watching the concert footage over and over, his face troubled, his cold certainty beginning to crack.

They didn't know that a seed had been planted. A tiny doubt in the mind of an Architect commander, a question that would grow and spread: What if we're wrong? What if there's another way?

They didn't know that the bridge had been built, even as they'd lost themselves in building it.

They knew only that they were alive, that they had each other, and that somehow, in some way they couldn't understand, that was enough.

In the command ship, now light-years away, Patrick Ford stared at the frozen image of the concert—hundreds of faces, united in joy and purpose, creating something beautiful together. He thought about his own people, isolated in their efficient pods, working toward quotas and expansion goals, never touching, never sharing, never creating anything that didn't serve the machine of conquest.

For the first time in his life, Patrick Ford wondered if efficiency was enough. If conquest was worth the cost. If maybe, just maybe, the people he'd been hunting for so long had something his people had lost.

It was a small thought. A dangerous thought. But it was there, planted deep, and it would grow.

The bridge had been built. Not with words or weapons, but with beauty and sacrifice. And though Oliver and Melissa would never know it, their sacrifice had not been in vain.

On a distant hillside, two people who had once been more than they were now huddled together in the darkness, their minds empty but their hands still clasped together, holding onto the one thing that remained: each other.

And in the vast darkness of space, the seeds of change had been planted in the most unlikely soil.

The hunt would continue. But it would never be quite the same.

THE SPECIMEN COLLECTOR
BY A. MORRISON

The transport pod materialized in the Oakdale District with barely a shimmer. Anthony Santos stepped out onto what appeared to be grass but felt wrong beneath his feet—too uniform, too perfect, like synthetic turf but not quite. He looked up at a sky that glowed with sourceless light, neither day nor night, and felt the familiar knot of despair tighten in his chest.

Eighteen months. Eighteen months since the accident on the highway outside Larchmont, Ulvaria, when his car had spun out on black ice and he'd woken up... here. Wherever here was.

The compound resembled a research facility, all clean lines and transparent barriers that hummed with energy he couldn't see but could feel. Three buildings stood in a triangular formation, each architecturally distinct—one mimicked classical Earth design, another was aggressively modernist, the third incorporated elements he recognized from historical databases as Eastern European. His captors' attempt at making humans feel comfortable, he supposed. It only made everything more unsettling.

Teresa Hicks was waiting by the central building, arms crossed, her expression hostile. She wore what looked like a lab coat, though it shimmered with colors that didn't exist in normal light. Her dark hair was pulled back severely, emphasizing the sharp angles of her face.

"They're sending you back," she said without preamble. "To Earth."

Anthony felt his pulse quicken despite himself. "When?"

"Soon. The Collectors want another specimen. A male, this time." Her lip curled. "Guess who gets to be the bait?"

He'd known this was coming. The Collectors—that's what they called their captors, beings that existed partially in dimensions humans couldn't perceive—had been training him for months. Teaching him to manipulate space in ways that defied three-dimensional physics. Preparing him for this.

"The others?" he asked.

"Sophia's in the nursery. The twins are growing impossibly fast—some kind of accelerated development the Collectors engineered. Natalia's due any day now." Teresa's voice dripped with bitterness. "We're breeding stock, Anthony. That's all we are to them. Specimens for their research into evolutionary biology."

He wanted to argue, to offer comfort, but what could he say? She was right. The Collectors studied them like lab animals, forced them to reproduce, monitored every aspect of their biology and behavior. They were living examples of consumer behavior, conflict resolution, mating patterns—all the social dynamics the Collectors found so fascinating about humanity.

The worst part was how they controlled it all. The attractions, the desires—all artificially induced through methods Anthony didn't understand. Neural manipulation, probably, or something more exotic. He felt desire for Teresa now, could see in her eyes that she felt it too, and both of them hated it because they knew it wasn't real. It was scheduled. Programmed.

"I won't bring someone else back," Anthony said firmly. "I'll find a way to escape instead."

Teresa laughed, a harsh sound. "You think you're the first to think that? They're in your head, Anthony. They know everything you're planning. The only reason you're having this thought right now is because they're letting you."

She was probably right. But he had to try.

---

The training chamber defied description. Walls intersected at impossible angles, floors curved into ceilings, distances contracted and expanded based on rules Anthony was only beginning to grasp. His instructor—he called it Prism because of how light refracted through its partially-visible form—floated in what might have been the center of the room.

*Demonstrate translocation across non-adjacent space*, Prism's thoughts commanded directly into Anthony's mind.

Anthony focused, felt the strange tension in reality that he'd learned to manipulate, and suddenly he was thirty feet away. Then back. Then to another corner. Each jump required intense concentration and left him exhausted.

*Adequate*, Prism communicated. *You will be capable of limited translocation on Earth. This will aid in specimen acquisition.*

"I won't do it," Anthony said aloud, knowing the words were meaningless. Prism couldn't hear sound—or if it could, it showed no sign. But Anthony needed to say it anyway, to maintain some sense of agency.

*You will comply*, Prism responded to his thoughts. *The alternative is termination. We have sufficient genetic material from you. You are no longer irreplaceable.*

The threat was clear. Anthony had seen the trophy room once, when Prism had carelessly allowed his consciousness to wander during a training session. Mounted heads. Preserved bodies. Humans, displayed like hunting trophies. The Collectors valued specimens—alive when possible, dead when necessary. They were researchers, yes, but also hunters. It was their nature.

*Your species does the same*, Prism had noted when Anthony recoiled in horror. *Museums. Taxidermy. Zoos. You preserve and display other species constantly. We are not so different.*

Anthony had no good response to that. Humans did do those things. The Collectors were simply better at it, and humans were on the wrong side of the equation.

---

The gateway looked like a massive lens made of crystallized space-time, if such a thing were possible. Colors that shouldn't exist swirled across its surface. Prism floated beside it, radiating what Anthony had learned to recognize as anticipation.

*You will emerge near your former residence*, Prism communicated. *Acquire a male specimen. Preferably one with different genetic markers than your own. Diversity is valuable for our research.*

"And if I refuse?"

*You will not refuse. The compulsion is already in place.*

Anthony felt it then, a pressure in his mind like a hand on his shoulder, guiding him forward. He could resist it no more than he could resist gravity. His body moved toward the gateway of its own accord.

*Your mate has formed a pair-bond with another male in your absence*, Prism added, almost as an afterthought. *This is useful data on human social flexibility and conflict resolution patterns. You may observe this when you return.*

The words hit Anthony like a physical blow. Elizabeth. His wife. Of course—eighteen months was a long time. He'd been declared dead, probably. She would have moved on. The rational part of his mind understood this. The emotional part felt like it was being torn apart.

Then the gateway swallowed him and the world twisted inside-out.

---

He materialized two miles from his house in Ashbury, Belvoria, in a grove of trees he recognized. The air smelled real—actually smelled, full of pine and earth and the faint exhaust of distant traffic. After eighteen months in the odorless captivity of the Collectors' facility, it was overwhelming.

Anthony made his way toward the house through a series of short translocations. The ability worked even better here, in normal three-dimensional space. He could feel Prism's presence in his mind, a constant pressure, monitoring everything.

The house looked the same. Lights were on. He approached the front door, hesitated, then knocked.

Elizabeth answered. She looked... good. Better than he remembered, actually. Her blonde hair was shorter, styled differently. She wore an expensive-looking dress. Her eyes went wide when she saw him.

"Anthony? Oh my God. Anthony!" She grabbed him, pulled him inside. "You're alive! Where have you been? The police thought—we all thought—"

"It's complicated," he said, looking past her into the living room. Everything was familiar yet subtly different. New furniture. Expensive electronics. A man's jacket draped over a chair.

Elizabeth followed his gaze and her face went pale. "Anthony, I... there's something you need to know."

"You've moved on," he said flatly. "I understand. Eighteen months is a long time."

"I had you declared dead after a year," she said, tears forming. "I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. But I couldn't—I couldn't just wait forever not knowing."

The front door opened and a man walked in. Logan Chapman. Anthony recognized him immediately—Elizabeth's colleague from the renewable energy startup where she worked. They'd met at company parties. Logan was tall, confident, successful. Everything Anthony had tried to be.

"Elizabeth, I got the—" Logan stopped, staring. "Santos? But you're dead."

"Apparently not," Anthony said. He felt the compulsion from Prism intensifying, pushing him toward action. Acquire the specimen. Bring him through. Complete the mission.

He fought it. "Logan, you need to leave. Right now."

"Like hell," Logan said, moving protectively toward Elizabeth. "You disappear for over a year, show up out of nowhere, and think you can just—"

"I'm trying to save your life!" Anthony shouted. The compulsion was becoming painful now, a spike of agony in his skull. "Elizabeth, I'm not—I'm not in control. You have to get him out of here."

But it was too late. His body moved without his permission, crossing the distance to Logan in an instant. He grabbed the man's arm and focused on the gateway, on the return point Prism had burned into his mind.

"No!" Elizabeth screamed.

The world twisted. Logan's shocked face, Elizabeth's horror, the familiar living room—all of it spiraled away into the dimensional vortex. Then they were standing in the Collectors' facility and Logan was screaming, a high-pitched sound of pure terror.

Prism materialized nearby, its form pulsing with satisfaction. *Excellent. A new specimen. This one shows promising genetic diversity.*

Anthony fell to his knees, the compulsion finally releasing him. He'd done it. He'd brought another human through. He was a Judas goat, leading the lamb to slaughter.

Logan had stopped screaming and was staring around in shock. "What... where... Santos, what the hell is this?"

"I'm sorry," Anthony whispered. "I'm so sorry."

Teresa appeared in the doorway, took in the scene, and her expression hardened further. "Welcome to the zoo," she told Logan. "Try not to fight. It only makes things worse."

---

Days passed. Logan was processed, examined, assigned quarters in the male section of the compound. The Collectors were pleased with their new acquisition. Anthony tried to apologize, to explain, but Logan wouldn't speak to him. Not that Anthony blamed him.

The worst part was knowing it would happen again. The Collectors wanted more specimens. They were studying human social dynamics, evolutionary biology, biodiversity within the species. They needed variety. And Anthony was their acquisition tool.

He sat in his quarters, staring at the wall that wasn't quite a wall, thinking about systems thinking and game theory. The Collectors operated on principles humans could barely grasp, but there had to be a pattern, a logic. They were researchers, not sadists. They had goals.

What if he could understand those goals well enough to negotiate?

It was a long shot. The Collectors had shown no interest in communication beyond simple commands. But Anthony had been observing them, learning. He'd noticed patterns in their behavior, hints of a larger social structure. They had politics of their own, conflicts, competing interests. They weren't a monolith.

And if they weren't a monolith, maybe they could be influenced.

He reached out with his mind, carefully, the way Prism had taught him to do for translocation. But instead of manipulating space, he tried to manipulate information, to send a message.

*I want to negotiate.*

Silence. Then, surprisingly, a response—not from Prism, but from another presence he'd sensed occasionally during training. Older. More powerful.

*Negotiation implies you have something to offer.*

*I do*, Anthony sent back. *I understand humans better than you do. I can help you get better specimens. More diverse. More valuable for your research. But not like this. Not through kidnapping and forced breeding.*

*Explain.*

Anthony took a deep breath and began to explain his idea. It was audacious. Probably impossible. But it was the only chance he had.

What if the Collectors could recruit humans voluntarily? There were people on Earth who would jump at the chance to be part of something like this—scientists, researchers, people fascinated by the possibility of other dimensions. Make it a research exchange program. Human volunteers in exchange for knowledge about dimensional physics, technological progress beyond Earth's current capabilities.

The Collectors could study human behavior in a more natural context. Humans could learn about the multiverse. Everyone wins.

*Your species would not cooperate*, the presence responded. *They would fear us. Attack us. This has been demonstrated.*

*Because you're abducting people*, Anthony argued. *Because you're treating us like animals. Start with international diplomacy. Communication. Show humans you're not a threat. The scientific community would be fascinated. You could establish a formal research partnership.*

There was a long pause. Then: *This would require peer review within our own social structure. Political movements within our collective that currently oppose human contact. It is not a simple proposition.*

*But it's possible?*

*It is... worth consideration. Your creative collaboration on this concept is noted. We will deliberate.*

The presence withdrew. Anthony sat back, exhausted. He had no idea if anything would come of it, but at least he'd tried. At least he'd offered an alternative to the horror of being a specimen collector.

Teresa found him an hour later. "Logan told me what you said to him. About being compelled." Her voice was softer than usual. "I'm sorry I was so hard on you. This isn't your fault."

"I brought him here," Anthony said. "That makes it my fault."

"No. It makes it their fault." She sat beside him. "But maybe... maybe there's hope. Natalia heard something from one of the other Collectors. Apparently there's debate happening. About changing how they interact with humans. Someone proposed a different approach."

Anthony looked at her sharply. "Really?"

"Don't get excited. It's just rumors. But if it's true..." She shrugged. "Maybe we won't be specimens forever. Maybe we'll be colleagues instead."

It was a slim hope. But it was hope nonetheless.

Outside the transparent walls of the compound, in the impossible geometry of the Collectors' world, beings of higher dimensions debated the fate of the humans they'd captured. And for the first time since his abduction, Anthony Santos allowed himself to believe that maybe, just maybe, there was a way forward that didn't end in tragedy.

The question was whether the Collectors would see it the same way.

And whether Earth would be willing to negotiate with beings that had already taken so much.

Only time would tell. And in a place where time itself behaved strangely, that was the most uncertain variable of all.

The Temporal Nexus Incident
by Anonymous

Case File TN-847392. Temporal Nexus malfunction. Lucas Ahmed supervising. Felix Wood assisting. Subject Naomi Frank displaced from 2489, scattered across historical timepoints. Recovery protocol initiated. Current target: 1987, Glendale, Dravonia. Subject age: 14 months. File TN-847392.

Julia Alexander sat in her small apartment in Glendale, Dravonia, reviewing data spreadsheets on her laptop while her daughter played nearby. The toddler, Naomi, was contentedly stacking colorful blocks in the playpen, occasionally babbling to herself. Julia had been working from home for the past year, doing data analysis for a regional insurance firm—tedious work, but it paid the bills.

She glanced up from her screen when she heard footsteps on the stairs outside. Someone knocked at the door. Julia frowned; she wasn't expecting anyone.

Opening the door, she found a tall man with intense gray eyes and an oddly formal bearing. He wore a suit that seemed slightly out of fashion, though she couldn't quite place why.

"Hello, Julia," he said with a slight smile.

"Hello," she responded cautiously. "Do I know you?"

"I'm Timothy," he said smoothly. "Timothy Ruiz. We met at the data science conference last month. You said I could stop by to discuss that collaborative project on evolutionary biology datasets."

Julia's expression softened. "Oh, right! Timothy. I'm sorry, I completely forgot. Please, come in."

As Timothy entered, Julia felt a strange sense of certainty about having met this man before, though somewhere in the back of her mind a small voice questioned this memory. She pushed the doubt aside.

"I hope you don't mind, but I'd like to take Naomi with me for a short walk," Timothy said, moving toward the playpen. "My colleague is waiting downstairs—she's an expert in child development and evolutionary biology. She wanted to observe typical behavior patterns for our research on human developmental milestones across cultural contexts."

"Oh, well, I suppose that would be fine," Julia heard herself saying, though again that small voice of doubt whispered.

Timothy reached into the playpen and lifted Naomi. The child, startled by the unfamiliar grip, let out a wail of protest. Her small hand caught on the edge of the playpen, scraping her palm, which only intensified her crying.

Timothy started toward the door with the screaming child.

Suddenly, from the kitchen, Julia's cat—a large orange tabby named Copper—shot out like a missile. The cat, normally placid, launched itself at Timothy's leg with claws extended and teeth bared. Timothy stumbled, clearly unprepared for the assault, and dropped the crying child onto the carpet.

Looking confused and off-balance, Timothy backed away from the hissing, spitting cat. Then, without a word, he turned and hurried out of the apartment, the cat pursuing him down the stairs.

Julia snatched up her daughter, her mind suddenly clearing as if from a fog. Her hands trembled as she examined Naomi's scraped palm and tear-stained face.

"I don't know anyone named Timothy Ruiz," she whispered to herself. "I've never been to a data science conference. What just happened?"

"Detective, I know how this sounds," Julia told the police officer for the third time. "The man made me believe we'd met before. He made me think I'd invited him to discuss a research project. But I've never seen him before in my life. I don't even work in research—I do basic data analysis for an insurance company."

Detective Samir Zhang nodded, taking notes. "And your cat attacked him?"

"Yes. Copper's never done anything like that before. He's the gentlest cat in the world. But he went after that man like he was protecting Naomi."

"Mrs. Alexander, do you have any enemies? Anyone who might want to harm your daughter?"

Julia shook her head. "No one. My ex-husband is overseas in the military. We have a good relationship. I can't think of anyone who'd do this."

"What about money? Any inheritance, insurance policies?"

"Nothing significant. We're barely making ends meet."

The detective closed his notebook. "Keep your doors locked. Don't let anyone in you don't know—and I mean really know, not just think you know. We'll have patrols keep an eye on your building. Call immediately if anything unusual happens."

After the detective left, Julia double-checked all the locks and kept Naomi close. But Copper seemed agitated, pacing near the windows and hissing at shadows.

Three days later, there was another knock at the door.

Julia peered through the peephole and saw two people in white coats—a man and a woman, both carrying medical bags.

"Mrs. Alexander?" the woman called. "I'm Dr. Layla Knight from Bayview Medical Center. We received a call about your daughter's vaccination records being incomplete. We're conducting a door-to-door immunization program in the Larchmont Region."

Julia felt a wave of certainty wash over her. Of course—she had been meaning to update Naomi's shots. She reached for the lock.

Then Copper yowled—a sound of pure warning.

Julia's hand froze on the doorknob. Vaccination programs didn't go door-to-door. And Naomi's records were current; she'd just been to the pediatrician last week.

"I'm sorry," Julia called through the door. "I'll need to verify this with the medical center. Please leave your credentials and I'll call you back."

There was a pause. Then the woman's voice came again, but this time it sounded different—harder, more frustrated.

"Mrs. Alexander, this is important. Your daughter needs—"

"Leave now or I'm calling the police," Julia said firmly.

She heard footsteps retreating down the stairs. Racing to the window, she watched as two figures in white coats climbed into a dark sedan and drove away. She immediately called Detective Zhang.

"They're getting more sophisticated," the detective said when he arrived twenty minutes later. "Medical personnel, official-looking credentials. Did you get a license plate?"

"No, I was too shaken up. But Detective, how did they make me want to open the door? It was like before—I just felt certain they were legitimate."

"Some kind of hypnosis, maybe? Or psychological manipulation techniques? We've seen cases where criminals use social engineering, but this seems more advanced."

Detective Zhang examined the door and windows, then paused by Copper, who was now calm. "That's one alert cat you've got there. He might have saved your daughter twice now."

That night, Julia couldn't sleep. She kept Naomi's crib in her bedroom and Copper on the bed beside her. Around 2 AM, Copper suddenly sat up, ears back, staring at the bedroom door.

Julia heard it too—soft footsteps in the living room.

Her heart pounding, she silently reached for the baseball bat she'd placed by the bed. She'd also borrowed a hunting rifle from her neighbor, a veteran named Mr. Hill, but it was downstairs by the front door.

The bedroom door slowly opened.

A figure stood silhouetted in the doorway. "Julia," a calm male voice said. "I'm Jacob Hill, your neighbor from upstairs. There's a gas leak in the building. We need to evacuate immediately. Bring Naomi."

Julia felt that same strange certainty flooding her mind. Of course—Mr. Hill from upstairs. She knew him. She should trust him.

But Copper hissed, and Julia remembered: her neighbor was Mr. Hill from downstairs, not upstairs. And his first name was Robert, not Jacob.

"Get out!" she screamed, lunging forward with the bat.

The figure dodged, moving with inhuman speed, and retreated. Julia heard rapid footsteps, then the sound of her front door opening and closing.

She grabbed Naomi and ran downstairs to Mr. Hill's real apartment, pounding on his door. When he answered, she gasped out her story while he called the police.

"The door was locked," Detective Zhang said, examining Julia's apartment. "No signs of forced entry. How did he get in?"

"I don't know," Julia said, exhausted and terrified. "I checked all the locks before bed."

"We're going to station an officer outside your apartment," the detective said. "This has gone beyond simple attempted kidnapping. Someone really wants your daughter, and they're using techniques I've never encountered before."

Over the next week, two officers rotated shifts outside Julia's apartment. Nothing happened. Julia began to relax slightly, though she remained vigilant.

Then, on a Tuesday morning, there was a knock at the door. Julia looked through the peephole and saw Detective Zhang.

"Mrs. Alexander, we need to take Naomi to the station for protection," he said. "We've identified the kidnapping ring. They're planning another attempt today. We have a safe house prepared."

Julia felt that certainty again, but this time she fought it. She called the police station.

"Detective Zhang?" she said when someone answered. "Is he there?"

"Yes, he's at his desk. Would you like me to transfer you?"

Julia's blood ran cold. She looked through the peephole again at the man who looked exactly like Detective Zhang.

"There's someone impersonating you at my door right now," she said into the phone.

"Lock your door and don't open it," the real Detective Zhang's voice came through the phone. "We're sending units now."

The fake detective's expression changed. He turned and walked quickly toward the stairs. Julia heard the stationed officer's voice: "Sir, I need you to stop and show identification."

Then there was a scuffle, a shout, and the sound of someone falling down the stairs.

Julia cracked open her door to see the officer lying at the bottom of the stairs, groaning and holding his head. The fake detective was gone.

"This is beyond anything I've dealt with," Detective Zhang told Julia at the police station later. "These people can somehow make you believe they're someone you know or should trust. They can impersonate anyone convincingly. They can apparently pick locks or bypass them entirely. And they're willing to assault police officers."

"Why Naomi?" Julia asked desperately. "What's special about my daughter?"

"We're investigating every angle. Your family history, your late husband's military service, everything. There has to be a reason."

But weeks passed with no answers and no further incidents. Julia began to hope it was over.

Then, one morning, she received a call from Bayview Hospital in Marvenia, two hours away.

"Mrs. Alexander? This is Dr. Knight. Your daughter's genetic test results from last month's checkup have come back. There are some anomalies we need to discuss. Can you bring Naomi in today?"

Julia felt that certainty, that trust. But she'd never authorized genetic testing. And the name—Dr. Knight—was the same as the fake doctor who'd come to her door.

"I'll call you back," Julia said and hung up.

She was about to call Detective Zhang when there was a knock at her door. She looked through the peephole and saw a delivery person with a large package.

"Delivery for Julia Alexander," the person called.

Julia hadn't ordered anything. She didn't open the door.

The knocking became more insistent. Then stopped.

Copper began hissing at the door.

Julia heard a strange sound—like static electricity crackling. The door began to shimmer, and to her horror, a hand began to push through it as if the solid wood were becoming insubstantial.

She screamed, grabbed Naomi, and ran to the bedroom, slamming and locking that door too. She called 911, then Detective Zhang directly.

"They're coming through the door!" she cried. "I don't know how, but they're coming through the solid door!"

"We're two minutes away," Zhang said. "Hide and stay on the line."

Julia heard her front door open. Footsteps in her apartment. Then her bedroom door began to shimmer.

In desperation, Julia threw open the bedroom window and climbed out onto the fire escape with Naomi. She scrambled down to the ground level just as police cars screeched to a halt in front of the building.

Officers rushed inside. Julia waited, shaking, on the sidewalk.

Five minutes later, Detective Zhang emerged, looking pale and confused.

"There's no one in your apartment," he said. "But Mrs. Alexander... your front door is still locked from the inside. Your bedroom door is locked from the inside. There's no way anyone could have been in there and escaped."

"But I heard them! I saw the door shimmer!"

"I believe you," Zhang said quietly. "But I don't understand what's happening. This isn't normal criminal activity. The techniques they're using... they're not possible."

That night, Julia stayed at a police-protected safe house. Naomi slept in a crib beside her bed. Copper was there too, and two armed officers were stationed outside the door.

At 3 AM, Julia woke to find Copper standing on the bed, back arched, hissing at the corner of the room.

Two figures were materializing out of thin air.

One was the man who'd first tried to take Naomi—Timothy Ruiz. The other was an older man she'd never seen before.

"Julia," the older man said calmly, "we're not going to hurt Naomi. We're trying to save her."

Julia screamed for the officers. The door burst open and two policemen rushed in, weapons drawn.

"Freeze!" one shouted.

Timothy Ruiz turned toward them with his hands up. "Officers, I'm Detective Zhang. This woman has been experiencing delusions. We're here to help her."

Julia saw the officers' expressions change, saw them lowering their weapons.

"No!" she screamed. "He's lying! Call Detective Zhang! Verify!"

One officer reached for his radio, but Timothy spoke again: "I am Detective Zhang. You know me. We've worked together."

The officers looked confused but convinced.

The older man moved toward Naomi's crib.

Julia grabbed the lamp from the bedside table and threw it at him. It passed through his head as if he weren't solid, then he suddenly became solid and the lamp struck him, shattering.

"Felix!" Timothy shouted.

"Enough of this," the older man—Felix—snapped. "Arvid, we're doing this now."

Timothy—or Arvid, apparently—moved toward the crib with inhuman speed. Julia lunged at him, and they struggled. Copper launched himself at Arvid's face, claws extended.

In the chaos, Felix grabbed Naomi from the crib.

And then both men, with the child, simply vanished.

The officers stood frozen, their expressions clearing as if waking from a dream.

"What... what just happened?" one asked.

Julia collapsed to the floor, sobbing. "They took her. They took my baby."

But even as she cried, there was a crackling sound in the air. The two men materialized again—but they were arguing violently, and Naomi was crying in Felix's arms.

"—told you we couldn't maintain phase coherence with the temporal anchor destabilizing!" Felix was shouting.

"The cat disrupted my concentration!" Arvid shot back.

"Gentlemen," a new voice said.

A third figure materialized—a woman in strange, shimmering clothing that seemed to shift colors.

"This has gone far enough," she said coldly. "Lucas Ahmed has reviewed your case file. Your methods have been deemed unacceptable. The Temporal Nexus Committee has voted to abort this recovery mission."

"But Naomi Frank's consciousness is still scattered across the timeline!" Felix protested. "If we don't recover this iteration—"

"Then we don't recover it," the woman said. "Your interference has created more temporal disruption than the original malfunction. The subject will be allowed to live out this iteration naturally. Perhaps in the next cycle, we'll develop better protocols."

She turned to Julia, who was staring in shock.

"Mrs. Alexander, I apologize for the distress you've experienced. What you've witnessed is a temporal recovery operation gone wrong. Your daughter—or rather, the consciousness that inhabits her—is someone very important from the year 2489. Due to a malfunction in our rejuvenation technology, her life essence was scattered backward through time, forcing her to live multiple lives across different eras. These two operatives were attempting to extract her consciousness and transfer it forward to the next temporal anchor point."

"I don't understand," Julia whispered.

"You don't need to. In a moment, you won't remember any of this. You'll remember only that you've been experiencing stress and paranoia, which led to a brief psychiatric evaluation. Your daughter will grow up normally in this timeline. The consciousness of Naomi Frank from 2489 will experience this life fully before being naturally transferred to her next incarnation in approximately 2267."

The woman made a gesture, and Julia felt a wave of drowsiness.

"Wait," Felix said. "At least let me explain to Arvid—"

"There's nothing to explain," the woman said sharply. "Your partner's reckless behavior, his amusement at manipulating these people, his complete disregard for non-interference protocols—all of it has been documented. The Committee has recommended that neither of you ever be assigned to temporal operations again."

"But—" Arvid started.

"You thought it would be entertaining to play with their minds," the woman continued. "To see how far you could push your persuasion abilities. To test whether you could walk through solid matter in front of witnesses. To impersonate police officers and medical personnel. Every protocol violation has been logged."

"I was just trying to make the mission more efficient," Arvid protested.

"By traumatizing an innocent woman? By assaulting local law enforcement? By nearly causing a temporal paradox when you crashed that vehicle in the previous iteration?"

"That was an accident—"

"Nothing with you is an accident, Arvid. Or should I call you Timothy? Or John? Or whatever name you've been using?" The woman shook her head. "Felix, you should have maintained better control over your partner."

"I tried," Felix said wearily. "Believe me, I tried."

The woman turned back to Julia, who was fighting to stay conscious.

"Sleep now," the woman said gently. "When you wake, this will all seem like a bad dream."

Julia's eyes closed.

When Detective Zhang found Julia Alexander the next morning, she was confused and disoriented, with only fragmented memories of persecution delusions. Naomi was safe in her crib, sleeping peacefully. Copper the cat was curled up beside the child, purring contentedly.

The psychiatric evaluation concluded that Julia had experienced a brief episode of postpartum psychosis, exacerbated by stress and isolation. With treatment and support, she recovered fully.

Naomi grew up to be a bright, curious child with an inexplicable interest in evolutionary biology and data science—fields that wouldn't fully develop their current methodologies for several more decades. She excelled in comparative history and epistemology, showing an unusual ability to understand complex systems and temporal relationships.

She never knew that she was living her forty-third life, or that she had over two hundred more to go before returning to 2489.

And in a facility beyond time, in a place called the Temporal Nexus, two operatives filed their final report on the failed recovery mission, while the Committee debated whether technological progress in consciousness transfer was worth the ethical cost.

The debate continues to this day.

Case File TN-847392. Temporal Nexus malfunction. Recovery mission aborted. Subject Naomi Frank to remain in 1987 iteration. Natural transfer to 2267 iteration authorized. Operatives Lucas Ahmed and Felix Wood reassigned. Operative Arvid 6 suspended pending review. Cultural exchange protocols under revision. Human rights considerations elevated. New mentorship programs recommended for temporal operatives. Social welfare impacts of timeline interference under study. Laboratory methods for consciousness transfer to be reviewed. Trade policy with alternate timelines suspended. Art history suggests similar patterns across recovered subjects. File closed. TN-847392.
