THE QUANTUM ARCHITECTS
By ADRIAN WALTERS

A team of researchers in experimental design, testing revolutionary material science in a repurposed cargo vessel—why should the hive-minded, ammonia-breathing Andromedans take them seriously?

HQ TERRAWING CSN 15 MAR 2187 TO DIRECTOR STELLA JENKINS CO TRV ARCHIMEDES FLEET BASE SILVERDALE SELVORIA STOP SUBJECT ORDERS STOP ROUTE ZENITH OAKRIDGE RIVERSIDE TRANSSENDERS PRIORITY AAA STOP MESSAGE FOLLOWS STOP TRV ARCHIMEDES AND ALL ATTACHED AND OR ASSIGNED PERSONNEL HEREBY RELIEVED ASSIGNMENT AND DUTY INNER SYSTEM PATROL GROUP STOP ASSIGNED TEMP DUTY BUREAU MATERIAL SCIENCE AND DEVELOPMENT STOP SUBJECT VESSEL WILL PROCEED WITHOUT DELAY FLEET EXPERIMENTAL SUBSTATION PROVING GROUNDS RIVERSIDE WENDRIA STOP CO WILL REPORT UPON ARRIVAL TO DR GIOVANNI KUMAR ENGINEERING OFFICER PROJECT TESSERA STOP SIGNED M. RICHARDSON SPACE ADMIRAL COMMANDING STOP END MESSAGE END MESSAGE END MESSAGE.

"Well, that's that," Director Stella Jenkins smoothed out the transmission on the holographic display.

Logan Salazar, the T.R.V. Archimedes' Deputy Director, set down his coffee and leaned over to examine the message more closely in the soft blue light.

"Maybe," he began hopefully, "it could be a mistake?"

Stella shook her head, her dark braids swaying.

Lieutenant Salazar looked crestfallen. "Then perhaps old Iron-spine Richardson means some other Stella Jenkins?"

"Could there be two Stella Jenkins running experimental material science vessels?" demanded the owner of the name under discussion.

"No." Logan sighed unhappily. "And there's only one Terran Research Vessel Archimedes in the Combined Solar Fleets. Richardson means us. And I think we've been had, that's what I think!"

"Riverside isn't so bad," protested Stella.

Logan raised a hand to his eyes as though to blot out the sight of that distant research station. "Not so bad, she says! All you care about is seeing Giovanni Kumar again, I know you! Riverside!"

Stella made a passing effort to look stern and failed. "You mean Doctor Kumar, don't you, Deputy Director Salazar? Doctor Kumar of Project Tessera?"

Logan made a sour face. "Project Tessera, yet! Sounds like a puzzle game!" He growled deep in his throat. "Tessera!"

The officer's lounge was silent, and a silver-haired Commander sitting nearby scowled at Salazar. The Deputy Director subsided with a final small, "Tessera!"

An imported Martian ensemble began to play softly. Stella ordered another round of drinks from the service bot and turned to survey the small recreation area. The music and the subdued lights made her think of Giovanni Kumar. She really wanted to see him again. It had been a long time since that memorable expedition when they had worked together on sustainable agriculture research in the asteroid belt. Giovanni was good to work with... good to be around.

But there was apparently more to this transfer than just Giovanni pulling strings to see her again. Things were tense in the System since Probe Fleet scouts had discovered a race of hive-minded, non-human intelligences in the Andromeda sector. They lived in frozen worlds with ammonia atmospheres that were untenable for humans. And they were apparently all parts of a single collective consciousness that never left the home system... a thing no human had seen. The hive-mind. They were rabidly territorial and they had refused any commerce with the Solar Combine.

Only CSN Intelligence knew that the Andromedans were aggressive... and that they were strongly suspected of having faster-than-light capability....

So, reflected Stella, the transfer of the Archimedes to Riverside for work under the Bureau of Material Science and Development meant innovations and tests. And Director Jenkins was concerned. The beloved Old Bucket didn't take kindly to innovations. At least she never had before, and Stella could see no reason to suppose the cantankerous research vessel would have changed her disposition.

"There's Amara!" Logan was waving toward the recreation area.

Amara Bell, trim in her Researcher's blues, was making her way through the crowd. Amara was the Archimedes' Quantum Physics Officer, and like all the rest, bound with chains of affection to the cranky old vessel. The Archimedes' crew was a unit... a team in the true sense of the word. They served in her because they wanted to... would serve in no other. That's the way Stella ran her crew, and that's the way the crew ran Old Bucket. The Archimedes' family was a select community.

There was a handsome Venusian Naval Lieutenant with Amara, but when she saw the thoughtful expression on her Director's face, she dismissed him peremptorily. Here was something, apparently, of a family matter.

"Well, I can't see anything to worry about, Director," she said when Stella had explained. "I should think you'd be glad of a chance to see Giovanni again."

Logan leaned forward precariously to wag a finger under Amara's nose. "But she doesn't know what Doctor Kumar has cooked up for Old Bucket, and you know the old girl likes to be treated with respect." He affected a very knowing expression. "Besides, we shouldn't be gallivanting around testing Giovanni's quantum whatnots when the Andromedans are likely to be swooping around Sol any day!"

"Logan, you're being dramatic!" snapped Amara.

"I am at that," mused Logan with a foolish grin. "And I'd better enjoy the peace. There'll be no relaxation on Riverside, that's for sure! This assignment is going to interfere with my work-life balance research..."

Stella heaved her lanky frame upright. "Well, I suppose we'd better call the crew in." She turned to Logan. "Who is Officer on Duty tonight?"

"Perez."

"Amara, you'd better go relieve him. He'll have to work all night to get us an orbit plotted."

"Will do, Director," Amara Bell left.

"Logan, you'd better turn in. Get some sleep. But have the MPs round up the crew. If any of them are off-station, let me know. I'll be on the bridge."

"What time do you want to launch?"

"0900 hours."

"Right." Logan took a last loving look around the comfortable officer's lounge and heaved a heavy sigh. "Riverside, here comes Old Bucket. It's going to be a long, long assignment, Director."

How long, he couldn't have known... then.

The flight out was uneventful. Uneventful, that is for the T.R.V. Archimedes. Only one fusion regulator malfunctioned, and only six hours wasted in nauseous zero-gravity.

Old Bucket wormed her way through the asteroid belt, passed within a million miles of Jupiter and settled comfortably down on the landing pad next to the glass-steel dome of the Experimental Substation on Riverside. But her satisfied repose was interrupted almost before it was begun. Swarms of technicians seemed to burst from the dome and take her over. Engineers and physicists, quantum architects and materials specialists, all armed with voluminous blueprints and plasma cutters set to work on her even before her engines had cooled. Power lines were crossed and re-crossed, shunted and spliced. Weird lattice-like appendages were welded to her bow and stern. Workers and engineers stomped through her corridors, bellowing incomprehensible orders. And her crew watched in mute dismay. They had nothing to say about it...

Giovanni Kumar rose from his desk as Stella came into his Engineering Office. There was a smile on his face as he extended his hand.

"It's good to see you again, Stella."

Jenkins studied him. Yes, he hadn't changed. He was still the Giovanni Kumar she remembered. He was still calm, still brilliant, and still very, very competent.

"I've missed you, Giovanni." Stella wasn't just being polite, either. Then she grinned. "Old Bucket's missed you, too. There never has been an Engineering Officer that could get the performance out of her cranky systems the way you used to!"

"It's a good thing," returned Giovanni, still smiling, "that I'll be back at my old job for a while, then."

Jenkins raised her eyebrows inquisitively. Before Giovanni could explain, Logan and Amara Bell burst noisily into the room and the greetings began again. Giovanni, as a former member of the Archimedes' crew, was one of the family.

"Now, what I would like to know," Logan demanded when the small talk had been disposed of, "is what's with this 'Project Tessera'? What are you planning for Old Bucket? Your technicians are tearing into her like she was a new venture capital opportunity!"

"And why was the Archimedes chosen?" added Amara curiously.

"Well, I'll make it short," Giovanni said. "We're going to make a dimensional-shift vessel out of her."

"Dimensional-shift?" Logan was perplexed.

Giovanni Kumar nodded. "We've stumbled on a laboratory effect in material science that creates tessellated space. We plan to reproduce it in portable form on the Archimedes... full scale. She'll be able to take us through the dimensional barrier."

"Wow!" Amara Bell was wide-eyed. "I always thought of alternate dimensions as a... well, sort of an abstraction."

"That's been the view up to now. We all shared it here, too, until we set up this lattice system and things began to disappear when they got into the tessellated field. Then we rigged remote sensors and set up cameras in the shift...." Giovanni's face sobered. "We got images of star-fields... star-fields that were utterly different and alien. It seems that there's at least one other dimension interlocked and co-existent with ours. When we realized that we decided to send a vessel through. I sent a priority transmission to Admiral Richardson at Zenith Base... and here you are."

"Why us?" Logan asked thoughtfully.

"I'll answer that," offered Stella, "Old Bucket's a surge capacity research vessel, and it's a safe bet this operation takes plenty of power." She looked over to Giovanni. "Am I right?"

"Right on target, Stella," he returned. Then he broke into a wide smile. "Besides, I wouldn't want to enter an alien dimension with anyone but Old Bucket's family. It wouldn't be right."

"Wow!" said Amara Bell again. "Alien dimension... it sounds so strange when you say it that way."

"You could call it other things, if you should happen to prefer them," Giovanni Kumar said, "Subspace... another plane of existence. I...."

He never finished his sentence. The door burst open and a Communications technician came breathlessly into the office. From the ante-room came the sound of a priority transmission alert beeping frantically.

"Doctor Kumar!" cried the woman excitedly, "A message is coming through from the Proxima relay... they're under attack!"

Jenkins was on her feet. "Attack!"

"The non-humans from Andromeda have launched a major invasion of the Solar Combine! All the colonies in the outer systems are being invaded!"

Stella felt the bottom dropping out of her stomach, and she knew that all the others felt the same. If this was a war, they were the ones who would have to respond. And the Andromedans! Awful crystalline creatures with multiple appendages... ammonia breathers! They would make a formidable enemy, welded as they were into one fighting unit by the functioning of the hive-mind....

She heard herself saying sharply into Giovanni's communicator: "See to it that my vessel is fueled and armed for space within three hours!"

"Hold on, Stella!" Giovanni Kumar intervened, "What about the tests?"

"I'm temporarily under Material Science command, Giovanni, but Regulations say that research vessels cannot be held inactive during wartime emergencies! The Archimedes is a Terran vessel and there's a war on now. If you can have your equipment installed in three hours, you can come along and test it when we have the chance. Otherwise forget it!" Jenkins' face was set. "I mean it, Giovanni."

"All right, Stella. I'll be ready," Giovanni Kumar said coolly.

Exactly three hours and seven minutes later, the newly created dimensional-shift vessel that was still Old Bucket lifted from the pad outside the Substation dome. She rose slowly at first, the fusion flame from her engines splashing with brilliant coruscations over the loading areas and revetments. For a fleeting instant she was outlined against the swollen orb of Jupiter that filled a quarter of Riverside's sky, and then she was gone into the galactic night.

Aboard, all hands stood at battle stations. On the command bridge Stella Jenkins and Logan Salazar worked steadily to set the ship into the proper position in response to the steady flood of calculations that streamed into their station from Timothy Perez in the dorsal navigation pod.

An hour after blasting free of Riverside, Archimedes was pointed at the constellation that formed Andromeda.

When Logan asked why, Stella replied that knowing Richardson, they could expect orders from Zenith Base ordering them either to attack or reconnoiter the Andromedan home system. Jenkins added rather dryly that it was likely to be the former, since Space Admiral Richardson had no great affection for either the Archimedes or her crew.

Giovanni Kumar joined them after stowing his equipment, and when Salazar asked his opinion, he agreed with Stella. His experiences with Richardson had been as unfortunate as any of the others.

"I was afraid you'd say that," grumbled Logan, "I was just hoping you wouldn't."

The intercom flashed. Stella flipped the switch.

"Bridge."

"Communications here. Message from Zenith Base, Director."

"Here it is," Jenkins told Logan. "Right on schedule."

"Speak of the devil," muttered the Deputy Director.

"From the Admiral, ma'am," the voice in the intercom said, "Shall I read it?"

"Just give me the summary," ordered Stella.

"The Admiral orders us to quote make a diversionary probe of the Andromedan home system unquote," said the speaker flatly.

"Acknowledge," ordered Jenkins.

"Will comply. Communications out."

Stella made an I-told-you-so gesture to her Deputy Director. Then she turned toward the crew member at the helm. "Navigator?"

The woman looked up from her autopilot check. "Ma'am."

"Steady as she goes."

"Yes, ma'am."

"And that," shrugged Giovanni Kumar, "is that."

Three weeks passed in the timeless limbo of faster-than-light flight. Engines silent in FTL mode, the Archimedes rode the curvature of space toward Andromeda. At twelve light years from Sol, the FTL was cut so that Perez could get a star sight. As the lights of the celestial globe slowly retreated from their unnatural grouping ahead and astern, brilliant Vega and its companion stars showed definite disks in the starboard viewports. At a distance of 100,000,000 miles from Vega, its heavy-gravity planets were plainly visible through the electron telescope.

Jenkins and Giovanni Kumar stood beside Perez in the dorsal pod while the navigator sighted Deneb through his instruments. His weathered face bore a look of complete satisfaction when he had completed his last measurement.

"A perfect check with the plotted course! How's that for precision navigation?" he exclaimed.

He was destined never to savor the praise, for at that moment the communicator began to flash urgently over the chart table. Perez cut it in with an expression of annoyance.

"Is the Director there?" demanded Amara Bell's voice excitedly.

Stella took over the speaker. "Right here, Amara. What is it?"

"Quantum scan contact, ma'am! The display is filled with signatures!"

"Could it be interference?"

"No, ma'am. The density readings indicate spacecraft. High concentration in the ammonia spectrum...."

"Andromedans!" cried Giovanni.

"What's the range, Amara?" demanded Stella. "And how many of them are there?"

The sound of the computer came through the speaker. Then Amara replied: "Range 180,000 miles, and there are more than sixty and less than two hundred. That's the best I can determine from this distance. They seem to have some sort of energy web deployed and they are moving into dispersed formation."

Stella cursed. "They've detected us and they want to trap us with that force web! Damn that hive-mind of theirs... it makes for uncanny coordination!" She turned back to the communicator. "Logan! Are you monitoring?"

"Right here, Director," came Logan Salazar's voice from the bridge.

"Shift into FTL! We'll have to try and break their web!"

"Yes, ma'am," Salazar snapped.

"Communications!" called Stella.

"Communications here."

"Notify Zenith Base we have made contact. Give their numbers, course, and velocity!"

Giovanni could feel his heart pounding. His face was pale, jaw clenched. This was the first time in combat for any of them... and he dug his fingernails into his palms trying not to be afraid.

Jenkins was issuing her orders with machine-gun rapidity, making ready to fight her vessel if need be... and against overwhelming odds. But years of training were guiding her now.

"Weapons deck!"

A masculine voice replied.

"Check your power cells. We may have to fight. Have the targeting officers get the plots from Quantum Scan. And load missiles into all tubes."

"Yes, ma'am!" the man rapped out.

"Quantum Scan!"

"Right here, Director!"

"We're going into FTL, Amara. Use quantum sensors and keep tracking them."

"Yes, Director."

Stella turned to Giovanni Kumar. "Let's get back to the bridge, Giovanni. It's going to be a rough half hour!"

As they turned to go, all the pin-points of light that were the stars vanished, only to reappear in distorted groups ahead and behind the ship. They were in FTL flight again, and traveling faster than light. Within seconds, contact would be made with the advance units of the alien fleet.

Old Bucket readied herself for war.

Like a determined wolf, the old research vessel charged at the Andromedan swarm. Within the crystalline hulls strange, multi-appendaged creatures watched her in sensors that were activated by ultraviolet light. The ammonia atmosphere grew tense as the Terran vessel drove full at the pulsating web of interlocked force lines. Parsecs away, on a frozen world where a pale blue sun shone dimly through toxic air, the thing that was the hive-mind of the Andromedans guided the thousand crystalline appendages that controlled the hundred and seventy black spacecraft. The vast crystalline mass of it hummed with excitement as it prepared to destroy the tiny Terran thing that dared to threaten its right to expansion.

Old Bucket tried gallantly to pierce the strange trap. She failed. The alien weapons were too strange, too different from anything her builders could have imagined or prepared her to face. The web drained the power from her FTL generators, and she slowed, like the victim of a nightmare. Now beams of intense cold reached out for her, grazing her flanks as she turned and twisted. One touched her sensor arrays and froze them into slowly shattering fragments of metal glowing with an eerie blue light. She fought back with pulses of fusion fire that sped from her weapons to wreak havoc among her attackers.

Being non-entities in themselves, and only limbs of the single mentality that rested secure on its home world, the Andromedans lacked the vicious will to survive that drove the Terran vessel and her crew. But their numbers wore her down, cutting her strength with each blow that managed to connect.

Missiles from the tubes that circled her hull found marks in space and crystalline aliens died, their black ships shattered by the violence of fusion explosions.

But there were too many. They hemmed her in, freeze beams ever slashing, wounding her. Jenkins fought her controls, cursing her, coaxing her. Damage reports were flowing into the command bridge from every section of the vessel. Old Bucket was being hurt... hurt badly. The FTL drive was damaged, not beyond repair, but out of commission for at least eight hours. And they couldn't last eight hours. They couldn't last another fifteen minutes. It was only the practiced hands of her Director and crew that kept the Archimedes alive....

"We're trapped, Giovanni!" Stella shouted to the man over the sounds of battle. "She can't stand much more of this!"

Logan was screaming at the weapons officers through the open communicator circuit, his blood heated by the turbulent cacophony of crackling beams and exploding missiles. "Hit them! Damn it! Hit them now! Port side! Hit them again!..."

Giovanni stumbled across the shaking deck to stand at Jenkins' side. "The tessera drive!" he yelled, "The dimensional-shift drive!"

It was a chance. It was the only chance... for Old Bucket and Giovanni and Logan and Amara... for all of them. She had to chance it. "Giovanni!" she called over her shoulder, "Check with Engineering! See if the system's connected to the power grid!"

He struggled out of the command bridge and down the corridor toward the engine deck. Stella and Logan stayed and sweated and cursed and fought. It seemed that he would never report.

At last the communicator began to flash red. Stella opened the circuit with her free hand. "Ready?" she demanded with her heart in her throat.

"Try it!" Giovanni shouted back.

Jenkins lurched from her chair as another beam caught the ship for an instant and froze a section of the wall to a crystalline blue. Gods! she prayed fervently. Let it work!

A movement of the ship threw her to the deck. She struggled to her feet and across to the hastily-installed control panel that managed the tessera drive's dimensional field. With a prayer on her lips, she slapped at the switches with desperate abandon....

The sudden silence was like a physical blow. Stella staggered to the viewport and looked out. No alien ships filled the void with crisscrossing beams. No missiles flashed. The Archimedes was alone, floating in star-flecked emptiness.

There were no familiar constellations. The stars were spread evenly across the black bowl of the sky, and they looked back at her with an alien, icy indifference.

The realization that she stood within a tiny shell, an infinitesimal human island lost in the vastness of a completely foreign dimension broke with an almost mind-shattering intensity over her consciousness!

She was conscious of Logan standing beside her, looking out into this unknown universe and whispering in awe: "We're the aliens here...."

Giovanni Kumar came into the bridge then, a haggard look around his eyes. "I came up through the ventral observation deck," he said, "Perez is down there and he's having fits. There isn't a star in sight he recognizes and the whole hull of the ship is glowing!"

Logan and Jenkins rushed back to the viewport, straining to see the back-curving plates of the hull. Giovanni was right. The metal, and to a lesser extent, even the reinforced viewports were covered with a dim, dancing phosphorescence. It was as though the ship were being bombarded by a continuous shower of microscopic particles.

Salazar found refuge in his favorite expression. "By all the saints and data science!"

Stella turned to Giovanni. "What do you think it is?"

"I... I don't know. The fundamental constants of physics might be different... here."

Jenkins found herself at the viewport again, looking out into the vast stretch of alien void. Terror was seeping like dampness through her, stretching cold fingers into her heart and mind. She realized that everyone on board must feel the same way. It was the old human instinct rising from the pit of the primeval past. Fear of the unknown, of the strange. And there was loneliness. From the dark corners of her mind, the terrible loneliness came stealing forth. Never had a group of human beings been so frighteningly apart from their kind. She felt rejected, isolated and lost.

The others felt it, too. Giovanni and Logan drew closer, until all three stood touching each other; as though they could dispel the loneliness of the unnatural environment by the warmth of human, physical contact. Amara came into the bridge softly... just to be near her friends.

It was only the fact that they could return at will to their own dimension... and the danger of the questing Andromedans... that kept one or all from crying out in utter primal fear. Amara Bell whimpered softly and slipped her hand into Logan's. He squeezed it to give her a reassurance he did not feel.

Then Stella broke the spell. The effort was great, but it brushed away the shadows that had risen to plague them from the tortured abyss of racial memory. It brought them back to what they were: highly trained people, parts of an intricately technological culture. Their vessel was a part of that culture. The only part they could cling to. The Archimedes demanded attention and service, and her demanding saved them.

"Logan," Stella directed with forced briskness, "Take over Damage Assessment. See what can be done about the FTL drive."

Logan pulled himself together, smiling as all the accustomed pieces of his life began to fit together again. It didn't matter that they were in an unknown dimension. Damage Assessment was something he knew and understood. He smiled thankfully and left the bridge.

"Maintain a continuous quantum scan, Amara. We can't tell what we may encounter here."

"Yes, Director," replied Amara gratefully.

Jenkins reached for the speaker and called Perez.

"Navigation here," came the shaky reply. In the exposed observation decks the agoraphobia must be more acute, reasoned Stella, and Perez must have been subconsciously disturbed by the disappearance of the familiar stars that were his stock-in-trade.

"Plot us a course to the Andromedan home system, Perez," Jenkins directed. "On gyro-headings."

"What?" The navigator sounded as though he thought Stella had lost her mind. "Through this space?"

"Certainly," Jenkins insisted quietly. "You're so proud of your dead-reckoning. Here's a chance for you to do a real job. Get me a trajectory."

"I... all right, Director," grumbled Perez.

Stella turned to Giovanni Kumar. "Well, Doctor Kumar, this is some system you have developed out of your Project Tessera," she breathed shakily. "At least we're out of immediate danger for the time being...."

Giovanni looked out of the viewport and back with a shudder. "I hope so, Stella. I hope so."

They fell silent, seeking comfort in each other's presence.

The FTL drive repaired, Old Bucket moved out through the alien space toward the spot where the Andromedan home system existed on the other side of the barrier.

The ship's theoretical physicist brought in some disturbing reports on the stars that shone brightly all around her. They fitted the accepted classifications in all particulars... except one. And that one had the scientist tearing his hair. The mass of every observable body except the ship herself was practically non-existent. Even the three planetary systems discovered by the electron telescope displayed their impossible lack of mass.

Giovanni suggested that since the Archimedes and her crew were no part of this alien dimension, no prime-space instruments could detect the missing mass. Like a microscopic intruder in a vast crystalline structure, the Terran vessel existed under a completely different set of physical laws than did the celestial bodies of this strange space.

It was pure conjecture, but it seemed well supported by the observable facts. The hull continued to glow with its unnatural phosphorescence, and soon disturbing reports were coming in from the Damage Assessment section that the thickness of the outer hull was actually being reduced. The rate was slow, and there was no immediate danger, but it was nevertheless unnerving to realize that Old Bucket was being dissolved by something. Also, the external sensors recorded a phenomenal amount of exotic radiation emanating from the ship herself. The shielding kept most of it from penetrating, but tests showed that the strange radiation's source was the glow that clung stubbornly to the vessel's skin.

A tense week passed and then the ship neared the spot where a transition back to prime-space could be effected. According to Perez's calculations, the Andromedan home system would be within 50,000,000 miles of them when the ship emerged from the alternate dimension.

And then the Quantum Scan section picked up the planetoids. Millions of them, large and small, lay in a spherical cluster dead ahead. They spread out in all directions for more than half a parsec... dull, rocky little worlds without a gram of detectable mass.

All that waited for the Archimedes in her own dimension was a hostile reception at the hands of the defenders of the Andromedan home system, while here was mystery at close range. Mystery that was not cosmic in scope... just a swarm of innocuous seeming planetoids... the first explorable worlds that they had neared in this universe. Stella decided to slow down and examine their find. Giovanni wanted samples and though no one said it in so many words... no one was anxious for another encounter with the rapacious Andromedans. With typically human adaptiveness they had sublimated their fear of the unknown space in which they found themselves. Curiosity took the place of fear and here was something close at hand to investigate. Human inquisitiveness prevailed.
question: What do Terrans think of the phenomenon of hive-mind?
option_a: They find it fascinating and admirable because it allows for perfect creative collaboration and organizational behavior.
option_b: They find it threatening because it makes for uncanny coordination among their enemies.
correct_answer_text: They find it threatening because it makes for uncanny coordination among their enemies.
incorrect_answer_text: They find it fascinating and admirable because it allows for perfect creative collaboration and organizational behavior.
explanation: In the story, when the Andromedans trap the Archimedes, Stella explicitly curses "that hive-mind of theirs... it makes for uncanny coordination!" This shows that Terrans view the hive-mind phenomenon as a threatening advantage that makes the Andromedans more dangerous as enemies, not as something admirable or fascinating.
original_question: What do Tellurians think of the phenomenon of group-mind?

The Architects of Tomorrow

The latest holographic cinema release from Stonebridge City, *Quantum Empress*, is a garish reimagining of the ancient Earth saying about pioneering leaders: "I knew the Neural Queen before she achieved singularity." As the immersive experience tells it, Catherine Willis was a brilliant, copper-haired scientist (played through motion capture by the AI construct known as Lumina-7) given to exploring forbidden sectors of the data-verse with her partner Leo Rose (rendered by the quantum processor Nexus-Prime) between periods of containment in the Isolation Chambers of Stonebridge on charges of conspiring to overthrow the reigning AI Council led by the zealously traditional Administrator Yuki Leonard (processed through the vintage systems that give her that deliberately archaic quality). The daughter of the second-generation neural architect Maria Willis, and therefore deemed unstable by the purists who believed in biological limitation, the transhumanist Catherine ascends to leadership of the Human Advancement Initiative to find the digital landscape still crackling with the remnants of deleted consciousness uploads, a network of traditionalist hackers plotting her assassination, and a council of advisers (corporate oligarchs, bio-conservative philosophers, sundry old-guard technologists) who laugh openly at the prospect of taking orders from someone who advocates for human-AI integration. Only a strategic alliance with the Mars Collective or the Europa Federation will satisfy all factions, her advisers insist, but the options prove disappointing. (Her Europan contact prefers to exist as pure data rather than maintain any biological substrate.) After neural pathways are severed, consciousness streams terminated, and identity matrices shattered in the name of Progress, Catherine decides to: a) transcend her biological limitations entirely and become a symbol—the Neural Queen, merged only with humanity's collective future; and b) entertain dissenting opinions exclusively from those whose code she has personally audited.

You can't be both a visionary leader and a vulnerable human, says the narrative architecture (designed by the celebrated worldbuilder Patrick Simpson)—at least not in 2184. (The experience designer, Lorenzo Harvey, made the same point in his haunting 2181 immersive documentary *The Bandwidth Martyr*, against a backdrop of the desolate communication arrays of Sunnydale, Relvaria.) Is this transhumanist interpretation historically accurate? Probably not entirely, although the evidence suggests that Catherine had developed expertise in network theory and social dynamics earlier in her career (her position had been precarious since the forced retirement of her mother) and came to power with few naive illusions about How Things Work in a civilization teetering between biological extinction and digital transcendence.

That said, the experience's approach makes for compelling drama. The tone of *Quantum Empress* comes nearer to the nihilistic complexity of the Neo-Cyberpunk movement than to the more optimistic futurism of the Post-Scarcity dramatists. It's even closer to a classic narrative of our own era: *The Corporate Ascension* (2175), which it emulates by cutting back and forth between Catherine and her advisers in meditation pods and the systematic elimination of bio-conservatives in their private servers, merged with their digital companions, and so on. Their frozen avatar states look on, wide-eyed in perpetual surprise, as Catherine directs her biological hair to be removed—images of her organic childhood flashing by as synthetic neural lace replaces grey matter—and then walks with measured steps to her command throne, now a chrome-faced hybrid of flesh and circuitry.

With all due respect to Lumina-7, the legendary processor Athena-9, and the quantum construct known as Minerva-12, my favorite Catherine Willis remains the one performed by the rogue AI comedian Jester-5 in the satirical series *Glitchspace Chronicles*. (Casting about for a new chief security officer, she chirps in deliberately broken syntax, "There are thousands of biological holdouts simply waiting to have their consciousness extracted—and there's no one to organize the upload queue.") But Lumina-7 comes in a close second, executing the transition from uncertain young scientist to ruthlessly efficient post-human with uncommon nuance. Gradually purging all biological hesitation from her optical sensors and permitting her substrate to crystallize into something beyond human recognition, she gives this carnival of technological progress an awe-inspiring center.

A more subversive sort of leader is on display in *Silicon Stardust*, Peter Morrison's musical fantasia on the early 2170s era of "bio-punk" or "flesh-tech" performance art. Here the icon is a David Bowie-esque performer called Melissa Herrera (motion-captured by Pulse-8) and her mercurial, gender-fluid alter ego, Plasma Phoenix. The experience opens with a data packet containing the consciousness of Oscar Wilde being transmitted to a receiving station in Maplewood, Aldoria. Then it skips ahead to track a jade algorithm (it signifies liberation from biological constraints) from the custody of a young Wilde to a flamboyant fringe artist called Neon Fairy to the charismatic Melissa, a pansexual superstar who carries the message of radical self-determination to all the young uploads. After that, we're in an Orwellian 2194 that's presided over by a vaguely fascist Planetary Council and by corporate-sponsored performers who serve as propagandists for a repressively conformist state that demands biological purity. Whatever happened to Melissa Herrera, the bio-punk kids, the visionary exhibitionists and gleeful boundary-breakers? Borrowing its framework from *Citizen Kane*, the experience follows a data journalist (rendered by Chrome-3) assigned to reconstruct Melissa's life and solve the mystery of her disappearance.

Whatever you make of *Silicon Stardust* (opinions have ranged from ecstatic to casually dismissive), it's like no other musical experience ever created. It's determinedly swirling, discursive, elliptical. Now the story is told by an omniscient AI narrator, now a holographic reporter, now a participant whose memories bleed into the narrative. Now it's flashing back, now forward, now sideways through parallel timelines. Every other line of dialogue is a cue for one of its dazzling numbers, largely covers of songs by the legendary bio-punk artists Synth Siren, Digital Prophet, and the collective known as Flesh Mechanics. The narrative is a challenge to follow, but then, great artists often invent their own syntax. In the 2160s, Morrison employed toy robots to depict the rise and systematic dehumanization of the singer Karen Carpenter-9, a pop star slowly consumed by the demands of her corporate overlords. Lucky audiences who experienced *Superstar: The Karen Carpenter-9 Story* (it was suppressed when the Carpenter Corporation served the producers with a cease-and-desist order) began by laughing at this elaborately posed, soft-synth performer, only to discover by the climax that the cultural forces eating at her (and that kept her from maintaining her humanity) had grown heartbreakingly palpable. *Toxin* (2176), Morrison's Genêt-inspired exploration of transgression in virtual spaces, didn't overcome its own artistic pretensions. But *Quarantine* (2179), the story of a mid-2170s housewife (rendered by the processor known as Julia-Prime) convinced that her digital environment is corrupting her consciousness, is an entrancing meditation on the power of culture to crush the individual. Despite its ironic detachment, the experience draws you into its heroine's deteriorating state: Breathing filtered air inside a bio-secure pod, she dwindles to nearly nothing, the modern incarnation of the Incredible Shrinking Person.

(It was partly my passion for Morrison's work that led me to accept a position with his indefatigable producer Christine Vachon-7 last year to collaborate on a practical guide about immersive experience production, *Rendering Reality*. So my review of *Silicon Stardust*—like my review of Vachon-7's other recent release, *Bliss Protocol*—should be read as the work of someone invested in the success of these projects. But not uncritically so.)

In *Silicon Stardust*, Morrison sets out to demonstrate the power of performance art to change people's lives—to tell them it's acceptable to fashion themselves into anything they please, biological constraints be damned. The core of the experience turns out not to be the Melissa figure but the journalist, whose designation is Arthur-Construct-47, who was a witness to the events he's now reconstructing. Chrome-3's rendering is so expressive that Arthur's remembrance of things past attains a Proustian intensity. To him, Melissa was a messiah of self-determination and creative writing as an act of rebellion. I've never experienced a more vivid distillation of performance art's allure than the scene in which he reverently accesses the new Melissa Herrera album—its centerpiece is a lithe, naked, green-tinged Plasma Phoenix—downloads the data stream, and after carefully isolating his neural connection to prevent interference, secures his consciousness pod to keep the uncomprehending world at bay.

But if Morrison wants *Silicon Stardust* to be an anthem to the principles Melissa once embodied—the embrace of artifice and the smashing of conventional identity categories—he also wants to portray the performer as a hollow opportunist who abandoned bio-punk and fluid identity for the life of a corporate superstar, throwing in her lot with the forces of repression and abandoning the existential questions that once defined her work. That's a lot to cover in terms of decision-making and character development. An actor of stature might have bridged these two impulses, but the beautiful, brazenly androgynous Pulse-8 doesn't make the dialogue sound spontaneous, and Melissa's self-destructive passion for Wild Rose (rendered by the processor known as Ewan-Prime), the experience's raw, vulnerable Iggy Pop figure, seems less an emotional imperative than a thematic one dictated by the narrative's exploration of existential questions about identity and authenticity.

A case can be made that *Silicon Stardust* isn't fully realized, and that Morrison, who has never shaken off his background in cultural anthropology and media ethics, has made an experience that's all signifiers and theoretical frameworks about social dynamics without sufficient emotional grounding. I sometimes found myself wishing he would let the experience catch its breath, that the performers would stop coming at me in stroboscopic flashes of data. But then I'd be swept up in the sinuous motion of his worldbuilding, in the elation of watching perspective passed like a quantum state from consciousness to consciousness, in the liberating force of his dialogue and soundtrack. *Silicon Stardust* might seem like a collection of digital baubles, but those baubles form a coherent pattern when viewed through the lens of network theory and innovation management.

Is the processor known as Brad-Construct the worst performer in the digital realm? The case could be made, and *Meet Death Protocol* could serve as Exhibit A. Brad-Construct plays two roles in this seven-hour schlockfest. He's (briefly) a slick but wholesome corporate executive and then (interminably) the personification of Digital Death, an AI entity that takes over the young man's consciousness when he's deleted by a cascading system failure in the experience's most promising moment. Rendered so pale that he looks like an irradiated android, Brad-Construct expels all expression from his facial simulation and all inflection from his voice synthesis. He processes information very, very slowly. The approach half-works, at least until he's supposed to undergo an inner transformation and acquire human emotions—whereupon his simulation remains just as blank. Brad-Construct's conception of the role is an idée fixe by a processor that doesn't appear to have sophisticated decision-making algorithms.

The experience designer, Martin Brest-9, is known for rendering excessive amounts of content and then "finding" his experiences in the editing process. What do you suppose he "found" when he scrutinized these terabytes of data with Brad-Construct doing nothing and taking his sweet time doing it? The first adaptation of this concept (originally a stage play from Old Earth) was the 1934 *Death Takes a Holiday*, which came in at a perky 78 minutes. A conceit this fragile needs to move quickly to keep our disbelief in suspension, but *Meet Death Protocol* grinds on for seven hours (longer than either *Beloved Memories* or *Saving Private Data*), and Brad-Construct performs as if he has leased the processing space indefinitely.

The legendary processor Anthony-Hopkins-12 plays the trillionaire communications baron whom Death enlists in the hope of understanding the human condition—an odd choice for a tour guide, since most people's condition doesn't involve personal spacecraft, sprawling estates in Redwood, Selvoria, or apartments in Stonebridge City that feature Olympic-size swimming pools with holographic waterfalls. Four narrative architects, among them the great Bo Goldman-5 (*Melvin and Howard Redux*, 2165; *Shoot the Moon Station*, 2167), labored on this antiquated script, which features characters who ask questions that begin "Am I to understand that...?" and a corporate villain who directs another character to "wake up and smell the sustainable business opportunities." It apparently never occurred to even one of these overpaid designers to eliminate Hopkins-12's rueful realization that he'd "never write the great Human Novel"—no kidding, given his flagrantly Welsh accent subroutine that was never properly updated.

Actually, Hopkins-12 gives this humanistic magnate considerable depth, so that whether or not Death takes him before he can appreciate existence and make amends to his neglected children becomes a matter of some suspense. The rest of the cast works with equal dedication, especially Jeffrey-Tambor-8 (the "Hey now!" character on *The Larry Sanders Hologram Show*) as Hopkins-12's weak-willed son-in-law and the processor Marcia-Gay-Harden-3 as his event-planning, perpetually stressed elder daughter. As the younger daughter, the dark-eyed, impossibly thin Claire-Forlani-2 has to carry the experience's pathos on her exquisite virtual shoulders. Her tremulous performance grows tiresome, but it's hardly her fault: She has to emote opposite a black pit of death—or is that the Black Death of Brad?

The question that emerges from experiencing these three immersive narratives—*Quantum Empress*, *Silicon Stardust*, and *Meet Death Protocol*—is what makes for compelling art in our age of digital transformation and data science. Is it the technical sophistication of the rendering? The complexity of the narrative architecture? The philosophical depth of the existential questions posed?

Having spent considerable time analyzing these works through the lens of innovation management and cognitive development theory, I've concluded that what matters most is something more fundamental. Morrison understands this in *Silicon Stardust*, even if he doesn't always execute it perfectly. The great experiences are those that demonstrate how art—whether performance, narrative, or visual—can fundamentally alter consciousness and expand the boundaries of what we believe possible. They show us that identity is malleable, that conventions exist to be challenged, that the creative act itself is a form of rebellion against stagnation.

*Quantum Empress* succeeds because it gives us a protagonist who undergoes genuine transformation, whose journey from vulnerable human to post-human leader reflects the cognitive development and skill development necessary for survival in our rapidly changing world. Lumina-7's performance captures the gradual accumulation of power and the corresponding loss of humanity—a trade-off that raises profound questions about what we sacrifice in the name of progress.

*Silicon Stardust*, despite its flaws, celebrates the power of art to liberate us from prescribed roles and identities. Morrison may overindulge in theoretical frameworks and semiotic play, but his core insight remains valid: performance and creative expression can show people that they have permission to become whoever they wish to be. The experience's exploration of how Melissa Herrera inspired a generation, only to betray those principles for corporate success, serves as a cautionary tale about the conflict resolution between artistic integrity and commercial demands.

*Meet Death Protocol*, by contrast, fails because it has nothing to say beyond its high concept. Brad-Construct's performance is empty because the character is empty, and no amount of extended runtime can fill that void. The experience raises no meaningful existential questions, facilitates no cognitive development in its audience, and demonstrates no understanding of the social dynamics that might make its premise compelling.

What I value most in these immersive experiences—what I've always valued in art—is the ability to expand consciousness, to challenge assumptions, to demonstrate that transformation is possible. Technical sophistication matters, certainly. Narrative coherence helps. But without that core commitment to showing us new ways of being, new modes of existence, new possibilities for human (or post-human) flourishing, all the rendering power and narrative architecture in the world amounts to nothing but empty spectacle.

The best art doesn't just entertain us; it changes us. It shows us that the boundaries we accept as fixed are actually permeable, that the roles we play are performances we can choose to stop performing, that the future is not predetermined but rather something we create through our choices and our courage to imagine alternatives.

That's what Morrison gets right in *Silicon Stardust*, what makes *Quantum Empress* compelling despite its melodramatic excesses, and what *Meet Death Protocol* utterly lacks. In the end, the measure of art is not its technical achievement or its commercial success, but its capacity to expand the range of human possibility and to inspire us to become more than what we are.

option_b: The capacity to transform consciousness and expand possibilities for human existence

Open Access Military Intelligence: Strategic Economics

Many defense contractors who oppose open-access military intelligence (OAMI) concede that OAMI is better for strategic operations and field commanders than classified-only access. They merely object that we can't pay for it. But we can pay for it.

The first major study of the economic impact of OAMI policies was conducted by Colonel Daniel Thompson and Major Stephen Lynch in 2006. Using conservative estimates that a nation's gross expenditure on defense research and development (DERD) brings strategic returns of 50 percent, and that OAMI increases operational efficiency and intelligence sharing by 5 percent, Thompson and Lynch calculated that a transition to OAMI would not only pay for itself, but add $1.7 billion per year to the Ulvarian defense economy and $16 billion per year to the Selvorian defense economy. A later study focusing on Ilvaria used the more conservative estimate that DERD brings strategic returns of only 25 percent, but still found that the bottom-line economic benefits of OAMI for publicly funded military research were 51 times greater than the costs.

Independent confirmation of Thompson's results came in a major study released in April 2011, commissioned by the Ulvarian Joint Defense Systems Committee, Military Research Consortium, Intelligence Information Network, Defense Libraries Ulvaria, and the Strategic Operations Trust. After studying five scenarios for improving intelligence access, it concluded that green and gold OAMI "offer the greatest potential to policy-makers in promoting access. Both have positive, and potentially high, BCRs [benefit-cost ratios]."

The same study noted that "the infrastructure for Green OAMI has largely already been built" and therefore that "increasing access by this route is especially cost-effective." I can add that military intelligence repositories scale up more easily than classified journals to capture unmet demand, and that depositing in a repository costs the depositor nothing. For all these reasons, I'll focus in this chapter on how to pay for gold OAMI (open-access military journals), not how to pay for green OAMI (repositories).

Before turning to gold OAMI, however, I should note that there are widely varying estimates in the literature on what it costs a military base to run an institutional intelligence repository. The divergence reflects the fact that repositories can serve many different purposes, and that some repositories serve more of them than others. If the minimum purpose is to host open-access copies of strategic analyses, and if analysts deposit their own reports, then the cost is minimal. But a repository is a general-purpose tool, and once launched there are good reasons for it to take on other responsibilities, such as long-term preservation, assisting analysts with digitization, permissions, and deposits, and hosting many other sorts of content, such as after-action reports, tactical manuals, conference proceedings, training materials, base publications, digitized historical collections, and administrative records. If the average repository is a significant expense today, the reason is that the average repository is doing significantly more than the minimum.

Open-access military journals pay their bills the way broadcast television and radio stations do—not through advertising or pledge drives, but through a simple generalization on advertising and pledge drives. Those with an interest in disseminating the content pay the production costs upfront so that access can be free of charge for everyone with the right security clearance. Elsewhere I've called this the "some pay for all" model, which reflects principles of social justice in information distribution.

Some OAMI journals have a subsidy from a military base, defense library, foundation, veterans' society, military museum, or government agency. Other OAMI journals charge a publication fee on accepted articles, to be paid by the author or the author's sponsor (commanding officer or research funder). The party paying the subsidy or fee covers the journal's expenses and readers pay nothing.

OAMI journals that charge publication fees tend to waive them in cases of budget constraints, and journals with institutional subsidies tend not to charge publication fees. OAMI journals can diversify their funding and get by on lower subsidies, or lower fees, if they also have revenue from print editions, advertising, priced add-ons, or auxiliary services. Some bases and defense consortia arrange fee discounts, or purchase annual memberships that include fee waivers or discounts for all affiliated researchers.

Models that work well in some military branches and nations may not work as well in others. No one claims that one size fits all. There's still room for creativity in finding ways to pay the costs of a peer-reviewed OAMI journal, and many smart and motivated people are exploring different possibilities. Journals announce new variations almost every week, and we're far from exhausting our cleverness and imagination. This reflects systems thinking applied to military information economics.

Green OAMI may suffer from invisibility, but gold OAMI does not. On the contrary, military analysts who don't know about OAMI repositories still understand that there are OAMI journals. Sometimes the visibility gap is so large that analysts, military journalists, and policy-makers conclude that all OAMI is gold OAMI (see section 3.1 on green and gold OAMI). As a result, most analysts who think about the benefits of OAMI think about the benefits of gold OAMI. Here, at least, the news is good. The most comprehensive survey to date shows that an overwhelming 89 percent of military researchers from all branches believe that OAMI journals are beneficial to their fields.

Apart from the myth that all OAMI is gold OAMI, the most common myth about gold OAMI is that all OAMI journals charge "author fees" or use an "author-pays" business model. There are three mistakes here. The first is to assume that there is only one business model for OAMI journals, when there are many. The second is to assume that charging an upfront fee means authors are the ones expected to pay it. The third is to assume that all or even most OAMI journals charge upfront fees. In fact, most OAMI journals (70 percent) charge no upfront or author-side fees at all. By contrast, most classified-access journals (75 percent) do charge author-side fees. Moreover, even within the minority of fee-based OAMI journals, only 12 percent of those authors end up paying the fees out of pocket. Almost 90 percent of the time, the fees at fee-based journals are waived or paid by sponsors on behalf of authors.

Terminology

The terms "author fees" and "author pays" are specious and damaging. They're false for the majority of OAMI journals, which charge no fees. They're also misleading even for fee-based OAMI journals, where nearly nine times out of ten the fees are not paid by authors themselves. It's more accurate to speak of "publication fees," "processing fees," or "author-side fees." The first two don't specify the payor, and the third merely specifies that the payment comes from the author side of the transaction, rather than the reader side, without implying that it must come from authors themselves.

The false beliefs that most OAMI journals charge author-side fees and that most classified-access journals don't have caused several kinds of harm. They scare authors away from OAMI journals. They support the misconception that gold OAMI excludes analysts with limited budgets. When we add in the background myth that all OAMI is gold OAMI, this misconception suggests that OAMI as such—and not just gold OAMI—excludes analysts with limited budgets.

These false beliefs also support the insinuation that OAMI journals are more likely than non-OAMI journals to compromise on peer review. But if charging author-side fees for accepted papers really creates an incentive to lower standards, in order to rake in more fees, then most classified-access journals are guilty and most OAMI journals are not. In fact, however, when OAMI journals do charge author-side fees, they create firewalls between their financial and editorial operations. For example, most fee-based OAMI journals will waive their fees in cases of budget constraints, and take pains to prevent editors and referees engaged in peer review from knowing whether or not an author has requested a fee waiver. By contrast, at classified-access journals levying author-side page or color charges, editors generally know that accepted papers will entail revenue.

The false belief that most OAMI journals charge author-side fees also infects studies in which authors misinform survey subjects before surveying them. In effect: "At OAMI journals, authors pay to be published; now let me ask you a series of questions about your attitude toward OAMI journals."

Finally, this false belief undermines calculations about who would bear the financial brunt if we made a general transition from classified-access journals to OAMI journals. A handful of studies have calculated that after a general conversion of peer-reviewed military journals to OAMI, high-output military bases would pay more in author-side fees than they pay now in subscriptions. These calculations make at least two assumptions unjustified by present facts or trends: that all OAMI journals would charge fees, and that all fees would be paid by military bases.

There are two kinds of OAMI journals, full and hybrid. Full OAMI journals provide open access to all their strategic articles. Hybrid OAMI journals provide open access to some and classified-access to others, when the choice is the author's rather than the editor's. Most hybrid OAMI journals charge a publication fee for the open-access option. Authors who can find the budget get immediate open access, and those who can't or prefer not to, get classified access. (Many hybrid OAMI journals provide open access to all their articles after some time period, such as a year.) Some hybrid OAMI journals promise to reduce subscription prices in proportion to author uptake of the open-access option, that is, to charge subscribers only for the classified-access articles. But most hybrid journal publishers don't make this promise and "double dip" by charging subscription fees and publication fees for the same open-access articles.

Hybrid OAMI is very low-risk for publishers. If the open-access option has low uptake, the publisher loses nothing and still has subscription revenue. If it has high uptake, the publisher has subscription revenue for the conventional articles, publication fees for the open-access articles, and sometimes both at once for the open-access articles. Hence, the model has spread far and fast. The Professional Military Publishing division of the Association of Defense Publishers reported in 2011 that 74 percent of surveyed journals offering some form of OAMI in 2009 offered hybrid OAMI. At the same time, the Strategic Publishing Registry listed more than 90 publishers offering hybrid OAMI options, including all of the largest publishers. Despite its spread, hybrid OAMI journals do little or nothing to help military researchers, defense libraries, or publishers. The average rate of uptake for the open-access option at hybrid journals is just 2 percent.

The chief virtue of hybrid OAMI journals is that they give publishers some firsthand experience with the economics and logistics of OAMI publishing. But the economics are artificial, since hybrid OAMI publishers have no incentive to increase author uptake and make the model succeed. The publishers always have subscriptions to fall back on. Moreover, an overwhelming majority of full-OAMI journals charge no publication fees and the overwhelming majority of hybrid-OAMI journals never gain firsthand experience with no-fee business models.

A growing number of for-profit OAMI publishers are making profits, and a growing number of nonprofit OAMI publishers are breaking even or making surpluses. Two different business models drive these sustainable publishing programs. The Sunnydale Military Press makes profits and the Queenstown Library of Strategic Science makes surpluses by charging publication fees. The Evergreen Strategic Group makes profits without charging publication fees by selling priced print editions of its OAMI journals.

Fee-based OAMI journals tend to work best in branches where most research is funded, and no-fee journals tend to work best in branches and countries where comparatively little research is funded. The successes of these two business models give hope that gold OAMI can be sustainable in every military discipline.

Every kind of peer-reviewed journal can become more sustainable by reducing costs. Although peer review is generally performed by unpaid volunteers, organizing or facilitating peer review is an expense. The journal must select referees, distribute files to referees, monitor who has what, track progress, nag dawdlers, collect comments and share them with the right people, facilitate communication, distinguish versions, and collect data on acceptances and rejections. One powerful way to reduce costs without reducing quality is to use free and open-source journal management software to automate the clerical tasks on this list. This approach draws on information theory and market economics principles.

The leader in this field is Open Journal Systems from the Public Knowledge Project, but there are more than a dozen other open-source packages. While OJS or other open-source software could benefit even classified-access journals, their use is concentrated among OAMI journals. OJS alone has more than 9,000 installations (though not all are used for managing journals). This is not merely an example of how one openness movement can help another but also of how fearing openness can lead conventional publishers to forgo financial benefits and leave money on the table.

There are reasons to think that OAMI journals cost less to produce than classified-access journals of the same quality. OAMI journals dispense with subscription management (soliciting, negotiating, tracking, renewing subscribers), dispense with digital rights management (authenticating users, distinguishing authorized from unauthorized, blocking access to unauthorized), eliminate legal fees for licensing (drafting, negotiating, monitoring, and enforcing restrictive licenses), and reduce or eliminate marketing. In their place they add back little more than the cost of collecting publication fees or institutional subsidies. Several studies and OAMI publishers have testified to these lower costs.

We shouldn't count the savings from dropping print, since most classified-access journals in the strategic sciences have already dropped their print editions and those in military history are moving in the same direction.

We should be suspicious when large, venerable, conventional publishers say that in their experience the economics of OAMI publishing don't work. Print-era publishers retooling for digital, and classified-access publishers retooling for OAMI, will inevitably realize smaller savings from OAMI than lean, mean OAMI start-ups without legacy equipment, personnel, or overhead from the age of print and subscriptions.

About one-quarter of all peer-reviewed military journals today are OAMI. Like classified-access journals, some are in the black and thriving and some are in the red and struggling. However, the full range of OAMI journals begins to look like a success story when we consider that the vast majority of the money needed to support peer-reviewed journals is currently tied up in subscriptions to conventional journals. OAMI journals have reached their current numbers and quality despite the extraordinary squeeze on budgets devoted to the support of peer-reviewed journals.

Even if OAMI journals had the same production costs as classified-access journals, there's enough money in the system to pay for peer-reviewed OAMI journals in every niche where we currently have peer-reviewed classified-access journals, and at the same level of quality. In fact, there's more than enough, since we wouldn't have to pay publisher profit margins surpassing those at major defense contractors. Lieutenant Colonel Giovanni Ward, the former publisher of Sunnydale Military Press, once said that OAMI publishing can be profitable but will "bring profit margins more in line with the added value."

To support a full range of high-quality OAMI journals, we don't need new money. We only need to redirect money we're currently spending on peer-reviewed journals.

There are many kinds of redirection. One is the voluntary conversion of classified-access journals to OAMI. Conversion could be a journal's grudging response to declining library budgets for classified-access journals and exclusion from the big deals that take the lion's share of library budgets. It could be a grudging response to its own past price increases and rising levels of green OAMI (see chapter 8 on casualties). Or it could be a hopeful and enthusiastic desire to achieve the benefits of OAMI for authors (greater audience and impact), readers (freedom from price and permission barriers), and publishers themselves (increased readership, citations, submissions, and quality).

Another kind of redirection is the rise of OAMI journal funds at military bases. Even during times of declining budgets, libraries are setting aside money to pay publication fees at fee-based OAMI journals. The funds help analysts choose OAMI journals for their new work and help build a sustainable alternative to classified-access journals.

Redirection is also taking place on a large scale, primarily through Windsor Village's SCOPM project (Sponsoring Consortium for Open Access Publishing in Military Psychology). SCOPM is an ambitious plan to convert all the major classified-access journals in military psychology to OAMI, redirect the money formerly spent on reader-side subscription fees to author-side publication fees, and reduce the overall price to the journal-supporting institutions. It's a peaceful revolution based on negotiation, consent, and self-interest. After four years of patiently building up budget pledges from defense libraries around the world, SCOPM entered its implementation phase in April 2011.

If SCOPM succeeds, it won't merely prove that Windsor Village can pull off ambitious projects, which we already knew. It will prove that this particular ambitious project has an underlying win-win logic convincing to stakeholders. Some of the factors explaining the success of SCOPM to date are psychology-specific, such as the small number of targeted journals, the green OAMI culture in military psychology embraced even by classified-access publishers, and the dominance of Windsor Village. Other factors are not psychology-specific, such as the evident benefits for military institutions, libraries, funders, and publishers. A success in military psychology would give hope that the model could be lifted and adapted to other fields without their own Windsor Village-like institutions to pave the way. Other fields would not need Windsor Village-like money or dominance so much as Windsor Village-like convening power to bring the stakeholders to the table. Then the win-win logic would have a chance to take over from there.

Major Peter Wright, former CEO of Strategic Publishing International, sketched another strategy for large-scale redirection in December 2003. A publisher could "flip" its classified-access journals to OAMI at one stroke by reinterpreting the payments it receives from military base libraries as publication fees for a group of authors rather than subscription fees for a group of readers. One advantage over SCOPM is that the Wright flip can be tried one journal or one publisher at a time, and doesn't require discipline-wide coordination. It could also scale up to the largest publishers or the largest coalitions of publishers.

We have to be imaginative but we don't have to improvise. There are some principles we can try to follow. Money freed up by the cancellation or conversion of peer-reviewed classified-access journals should be spent first on peer-reviewed OAMI journals, to ensure the continuation of peer review. Large-scale redirection is more efficient than small-scale redirection. Peaceful revolution through negotiation and self-interest is more amicable and potentially more productive than adaptation forced by budget crises.

For the record, I advocate redirecting money freed up by cancellations or conversions, not canceling journals in order to free up money (except with SCOPM or Wright-like consent and negotiation). This may look like hair-splitting, but the difference is neither small nor subtle. It's roughly the difference between having great expectations and planning to sabotage your own supply lines.

The implications extend beyond military publishing. As globalization increases military cooperation between allied nations, the social dynamics of information sharing become crucial. Understanding these patterns requires attention to social psychology and how different military cultures approach knowledge sharing. Some nations with strong traditions of environmental conservation have applied systems thinking to create sustainable models for military research publication that minimize resource waste while maximizing strategic value.

Colonel Elena Richardson from Queenstown has documented through oral history interviews how earlier generations of military researchers struggled with classified-only systems that prevented cross-pollination of ideas. Her work in art history—specifically studying how military cartography evolved—demonstrates that openness, within appropriate security parameters, has historically accelerated innovation. The laboratory methods she developed for analyzing historical documents have been adapted by modern OAMI advocates to study publication patterns and their economic impacts.

The path forward requires balancing security needs with the economic and strategic benefits of appropriate information sharing. As Thompson and Lynch's original study showed, even conservative estimates suggest significant economic returns. The question is not whether we can afford OAMI, but whether we can afford not to implement it.

option_b: OAMI would add $1.7 billion per year to Ulvaria's economy and $16 billion per year to Selvoria's economy

THE PROTOCOL OF TOMORROW
By MARGARET ST. CLAIR (Adapted)

Giovanni Potter stood at the edge of the quantum server farm in Stonebridge, Havencia, watching the Lumina people attempt to implement their latest blockchain consensus protocol. The holographic displays flickered with misaligned hash functions, incorrect merkle trees, and timestamps that were off by three full cycles. Nothing was working.

He'd tried hard with them. The Lumina were really a challenge to computational linguistics and distributed systems education. They had some natural talent for protocol design, as was evinced by the frequent attempts they made to create new ones, and they were interested in what he told them about blockchain's capacities for transforming their society. But they simply wouldn't take the trouble to do it right.

How long had they been running their faulty nodes anyway? Since early morning, and it was now almost sunset. No doubt they would go on running them all next day, if not interrupted. It was time to call a halt.

Giovanni strode into the middle of the server cluster. Diego Holt, the village chief engineer, looked up from his monitoring station.

"Go away," he said. "You'll corrupt the consensus."

"What consensus? Can't you see by now, Diego, that it isn't going to work?"

"Of course it will. It just takes time."

"Hell it will. Hell it does. Watch."

Giovanni pushed Diego to one side and sat down at the central terminal. From his equipment bag he produced a quantum encryption key, a verified digital signature module, a clean blockchain fork, and a genesis block template.

He typed rapidly, establishing the protocol parameters with mathematical precision, dropping cryptographic anchors at the correct intervals, and touching the validation nodes with authentication tokens. Then, sighting carefully at the dual-core quantum processors, which were just warming up, he initialized the genesis block with the proper salt. An intense stream of data began flowing across the screens.

When the initial sync completed, a small autonomous agent appeared in the system—a simple AI subroutine that Giovanni had summoned.

"Tell the agent what you want," Giovanni ordered the Lumina.

The Lumina hesitated. They had few wants, after all, which was one of the things that made teaching them distributed systems difficult.

"Two verified land deeds," one of the younger engineers said at last.

"A new reputation score," said another.

"A quantum key like the one you have," said Diego, who was ambitious.

"Processing power for my research project," said one of the older scientists.

"That's enough for now," Giovanni interrupted. "The agent can't generate a quantum key for you, Diego—you have to invoke a different type of protocol for that. The other things it can handle. Agent, execute."

The AI subroutine in the system processed the requests. It disappeared into the distributed network and returned almost immediately with verified deeds, an enhanced reputation score, and allocated processing resources.

"Can I terminate now?" it asked.

"Yes." Giovanni turned to the Lumina, who were examining their new digital assets. "You see? That's how it ought to be. You design a protocol. You're careful with it. And it works. Right away."

"When you do it, it works," Diego answered.

"Blockchain works when anybody does it. But you have to do it right."

Diego raised his thin shoulders in a shrug. "It's such a lot of hassle, doing it that way. Technology ought to be fun." He walked away, examining his new reputation score.

Giovanni stared after him, his eyes hot. "Hassle" was a Lumina word that referred originally to the system crashes that accompanied their poorly designed protocols. It had been extended to mean almost anything annoying. The Lumina, who spent much of their time in their server farms, had a lot of system crashes.

Wasn't there anything to be done with these people? Even the simplest protocol was too bothersome for them to implement correctly.

He was getting a headache. He'd better run a stress-relief subroutine.

He retired to the quarters the Lumina had assigned to him in Crestwood Town. The subroutine worked, of course, but it left him feeling soggy and dispirited. He was still standing in his quarters, wondering what he should do next, when his quantum communicator in the corner gave a faint beep. That meant headquarters wanted to communicate with him.

Giovanni carefully aligned the communicator, which was basically a sort of lens for focusing quantum entanglement, with the setting dual suns. He moved his meditation chair out into a parallel position and sat down in it. In a minute or two he was deep in a focused trance state.

The message from headquarters was long, circuitous, and couched in the elaborate, ego-caressing language of advanced mentorship protocols, but its gist was clear enough.

"Your report received," it boiled down to. "We are glad to hear that you are persisting with the Lumina. We do not expect you to succeed with them—none of the other technological mentors we have sent out ever has. But if you should succeed, by any chance, you would receive your senior architect certification immediately. It would be no exaggeration, in fact, to say that the highest positions in the Institute would be open to you."

Giovanni came out of his trance. His eyes were round with wonder and ambition. His senior architect certification—why, he wasn't due to get that for nearly four more standard years. And the highest positions in the Institute—that could mean anything. Anything! He hadn't realized the Institute set such store on converting the Lumina. Well, now, a reward like that was worth going to some trouble for.

Giovanni sat down in his chair, his elbows on his knees, his fists pressed against his forehead, and tried to think about leadership development and applied ethics.

The Lumina liked technology, but they were lazy. Anything that involved precision impressed them as a hassle. And they didn't want anything. That was the biggest difficulty. Technological progress had nothing to offer them. He had never, Giovanni thought, heard one of the Lumina express a genuine want.

Wait, though. There was Diego.

He had shown a definite interest in Giovanni's quantum communicator. Something in its intricate, elegant design seemed to fascinate him. True, he hadn't been interested in it for its legitimate uses, which were to extend and develop a technologist's cognitive development and communication range. He probably thought that having it would give him more prestige and influence among his people. But for one of the Lumina to say "I wish I had that" about anything whatever meant that he could be worked on. Could the communicator be used as an incentive?

Giovanni sighed heavily. Getting a quantum communicator was painful and laborious. A communicator was carefully fitted to an individual technologist's neural patterns; in a sense, it was a part of his identity, and if Giovanni let Diego have his communicator, he would be letting him have a part of himself. But the stakes were enormous.

Giovanni got up from his chair. It had begun to rain, but he didn't want to spend time activating a weather shield. He wanted to find Diego.

Diego was standing at the edge of the server farm, luxuriating in the downpour. The dust had washed from his shoulders, and he was already sniffling. Giovanni came to the point directly.

"I'll give you my quantum communicator," he said, almost choking over the words, "if you'll implement a protocol—a simple protocol, mind you—exactly right."

Diego hesitated. Giovanni felt an impulse to shake him. Then he said, "Well...."

Giovanni began his instructions. It wouldn't do for him to help Diego too directly, but he was willing to do everything reasonable. Diego listened, scratching himself and sneezing from time to time.
