He started off, Giovanni after him, to the latter's quarters. While Giovanni looked on tensely, Diego began going through the implementation Giovanni had described. Half-way through the first sequence, he forgot. He inverted the order of the validation steps, applied encryption to the wrong nodes, and mispronounced the variable names in the initialization code. When he executed the final command, only a tiny error message appeared.

Giovanni cursed bitterly. Diego, however, was delighted. "Look at that, will you!" he exclaimed, clapping his chapped hands together. "It worked! I'll take the communicator home with me now."

"The communicator? For that? You didn't implement the protocol right."

Diego stared at him indignantly. "You mean, you're not going to give me the communicator after all the trouble I went to? I only did it as a favor, really. Giovanni, I think it's very mean of you."

"Try the protocol again."

"Oh, hassle. You're too impatient. You never give anything time to work."

He got up and walked off.

For the next few days, everybody in Crestwood Town avoided Giovanni. They all felt sorry for Diego, who'd worked so hard, done everything he was told to, and been cheated out of his communicator by Giovanni. In the end the technologist, cursing his own weakness, surrendered the communicator to Diego. The accusatory atmosphere in the normally indifferent Lumina was intolerable.

But now what was he to do? He'd given up his communicator—he had to ask Diego to lend it to him when he wanted to contact headquarters—and the senior certification was no nearer than before. His head ached constantly, and all the subroutines he ran to cure the pain left him feeling wretchedly tired out.

Technology, however, is a field of many resources, not all of them savory. Giovanni, in his desperation, began to consult AI agents more disreputable than those he would ordinarily have invoked. In effect, he turned for help to the technological underground—systems that operated outside normal applied ethics.

His questionable informants were none too consistent. One agent told him one thing, another something else. The consensus, though, was that while there was nothing the Lumina actually wanted enough to go to any trouble for it (they didn't even want to fix their system crashes, for example—in a perverse way they were proud of them), there was one thing they disliked intensely—Giovanni himself.

The Lumina thought, the agents reported, that he was inconsiderate, tactless, officious, and a crashing bore. They regarded him as the psychological equivalent of the worst system crash ever known, carried to the nth power. They wished he'd leave or disappear.

Giovanni dismissed the last of the agents. His eyes had begun to shine. The Lumina thought he was a nuisance, did they? They thought he was the most annoying thing they'd encountered in the course of their cultural evolution? Good. Fine. Splendid. Then he'd really annoy them.

He'd have to watch out for sabotage, of course. But in the end, they'd turn to proper technology to get rid of him. They'd have to. And then he'd have them. They'd be caught.

One act of communal protocol implementation that really worked and they'd be sold on proper methodology. He'd be sure of his senior certification.

Giovanni began his campaign immediately. Where the Lumina were, there was he. He was always on hand with unwanted explanations, hypercritical objections, and maddening "wouldn't-it-be-betters."

Whereas earlier in his mentorship mission he had confined himself to pointing out how much easier proper technology would make life for the Lumina, he now counseled and advised them on every phase of their daily routine, from server maintenance to data analysis, and from the time they got up until they went to bed. He even pursued them with advice after they logged off for the night, and told them how to optimize their personal lives—advice which the Lumina, who set quite as much store by their personal lives as anybody does, resented passionately.

But most of all he harped on their folly in putting up with system crashes, and instructed them over and over again in the details of a protocol—a quite simple protocol—for preventing them. The protocol would, he informed them, work equally well against anything—or person—that they found annoying.

The food the Lumina brought him began to have a highly peculiar taste. Giovanni grinned and activated a toxin-detection nanochip, a first-class antidote to poison, in his system. The Lumina's distaste for him bothered him, naturally, but he could stand it. When he had repeated the anti-annoyance protocol to a group of Lumina last night in Queenstown, Galdoria, he had noticed that Diego was listening eagerly. It wouldn't be much longer now.

On the morning of the day before the system-wide update, Giovanni was awakened from sleep by an odd tingling sensation in his neural implants. It was a sensation he'd experienced only once before in his life, during his training, and it took him a moment to identify it. Then he realized what it was. Somebody was running a protocol against him.

At last! At last! It had worked!

Giovanni put on his jacket and hurried to the door of his quarters. The environment seemed remarkably distorted, almost like a simulation glitch, but that was caused by the protocol. This one happened to involve the sensory processing centers.

He began to grope his way cautiously toward the town center in Evergreen, Lethoria, where the Lumina had gathered. He didn't want them to see him and get suspicious, but he did want to have the pleasure of seeing them execute their first accurate protocol. (He was well protected against any damage from it, of course.) When he was almost at the center, he took cover behind a building. He peered out.

They were doing it right. Oh, what a satisfaction! Giovanni felt his chest expand with pride. And when the protocol worked, when the data stream swooped in and digitally removed him from their systems, the Lumina would certainly receive a second technological mentor more kindly. Giovanni might even come back, well disguised, himself.

The implementation continued. The operators made three validation passes to the left, three validation passes to the right. Cross-reference, and all apply encryption to the intersections of the network Diego had traced on the holographic display with a laser pointer. Back to the circle. One to the left, one to right, while Diego, in the center of the circle, overlaid the encryption with—with what?

"Hey!" Giovanni yelled in sudden alarm. "Not that compression algorithm! Watch out! You're not doing it ri—"

His chest contracted suddenly, as if a large, heavy force had seized his thorax above the waist. He couldn't breathe, he couldn't think, he couldn't even say "Stop!" It felt as if his chest—no, his whole body—was being compressed and converted into pure data.

He tried to wave his tiny, heavy arms in a counter-protocol; he couldn't even inhale. The last emotion he experienced was one of bitterness. He might have known the Lumina couldn't get anything right.

The Lumina take a dim view of the small holographic statue that now stands in the center of their town in Evergreen, Lethoria. It is much too integrated into their systems for them to delete, and while it is not nearly so much of a nuisance as Giovanni was when he was alive, it inconveniences them. They have to route around it when they run their protocols.

They still hope, though, that the protocols they are running to get rid of him will work eventually. If he doesn't disappear this update cycle, he will the cycle after next. They have a good deal of faith in technology, when you come right down to it. And patience is their long suit.

THE LAST DEEP-SEA EXPLORER
BY VARIOUS AUTHORS

Illustrated by Digital Artists

[Transcriber's Note: This etext was produced from
Ocean Worlds Quarterly, March 2089
Extensive research did not uncover any evidence that
the U.S. copyright on this publication was renewed.]

What's more important—humanity's understanding
of the deep ocean, or one explorer's peace of mind?

I

They gave him a commemorative plaque. It was meant to be symbolical, of course. In the old tradition. It was crafted from actual titanium alloy, being one of the materials used in the earliest deep-sea submersibles constructed generations past in the coastal facilities of Highpoint, Selvoria. Its significance lay in the fact that it represented the hull plating from the historic vessel Challenger Deep II, not a modern composite material grown through nanotechnology, but actual forged metal that had withstood the crushing pressures of the Mariana Trench.

They also had a ceremony for him, complete with speeches by such luminaries of the Department of Ocean Exploration as Director Luna King and Professor Mohammad Newman. There was also somebody from the Global Resource Management Council who spoke, but he was one of those pseudo-elected bureaucrats who didn't know much about deep-sea exploration nor the significance of Paul Sanders' retirement. Paul didn't bother to remember his name. He only wondered vaguely why the administrator had shown up at all.

In common with recipients of commemorative plaques of a score of generations before him, Paul Sanders would have preferred something a bit more tangible in the way of reward, such as a few additional shares of Universal Basic Income credits to add to his portfolio. But that, he supposed, was asking too much.

The fact of the matter was, Paul knew that his retiring had set them back considerably. They hadn't figured he had enough UBI credits to see him through decently. Well, possibly he didn't, given their standards. But Deep-Sea Pilot Paul Sanders didn't have their standards. He'd had plenty of time to think it over. It was better to retire on a limited income, on a confoundedly limited income, than to take the two or three more dives in hopes of attaining a higher standard of living.

He'd had plenty of time to figure it out, there alone in the crushing darkness of the hadal zone, there on the abyssal plain runs. There on the long, long descents to the hydrothermal vent systems, fearfully checking the symptoms of pressure psychosis, the madness compounded of claustrophobia, sensory deprivation, profound isolation and the constant awareness of millions of tons of water pressing against the hull. Plenty of time. Time to decide that a small efficiency habitat-pod, complete with an auto-recliner and built-in beverage synthesizer, and with one wall a full immersion holographic display, was all he needed to find contentment for a mighty long time. Possibly somebody like Professor Newman might be horrified at the idea of living in an efficiency habitat-pod... not realizing that to a deep-sea pilot it was spacious beyond belief compared to the cramped sphere of a submersible craft.

No. Even as Paul listened to their speeches, accepted the plaque and made a halting little talk of his own, he was grinning inwardly. There wasn't anything they could do. He had them now. He had enough UBI credits to keep him comfortably, by his standards, for the rest of his life. He was never going to subject himself to pressure psychosis again. Just thinking about it, now, set the tremor going in his left hand.

They could pressurize their hulls and descend, for all he gave a damn.

The commemorative plaque idea had been that of Luna King, which was typical, she being in the way of a living traditionalist herself. In fact, Director King was possibly the only living person on the North American continent who still maintained a physical library of actual printed books. Her explanation was that she found the tactile experience of turning pages irreplaceable and that digital formats lacked the gravitas of bound volumes.

That was only an excuse so far as her closest associate, Mohammad Newman, was concerned. Professor Newman was convinced King would have even used a manual typewriter, had she but a touch more courage. King longed for the methodologies of yesteryear, a seldom found phenomenon under the Universal Welfare System.

Seated in an ergonomic chair in the research facility of his Hampton, Ilvaria apartment, Luna King scowled at her colleague. She said, acidly, "Any more brilliant ideas, Mohammad? I presume you now acknowledge that appealing to Sanders' sense of duty, scientific curiosity and desire for historical significance have miserably failed."

Newman said easily, "I wouldn't call Paul Sanders unmotivated. In his position, I am afraid I would do the same thing he has."

"That's nonsense, Mohammad. By all measures of comparative history! Either you or I would gladly take Sanders' place were we capable of performing the duties for which he has been trained. There aren't two people on this continent—there aren't two people in the world!—who better realize the urgency of continuing our exploration of the hadal zones." King snapped her fingers. "Like that, either of us would risk our lives to prevent humanity from completely abandoning the quest to understand our ocean's depths."

Her colleague said drily, "Either of us could have volunteered for deep-sea pilot training forty years ago, Luna. We didn't."

"At that time there wasn't such a devastating percentage of risk-averse individuals throughout this whole Universal Welfare System! Who could foresee that eventually our entire program would face termination due to lack of courageous young people willing to take chances, willing to face the existential questions that arise in profound isolation, willing to react to danger in the manner our ancestors did?"

Newman grunted his sarcasm and synthesized a glass of cold green tea. He said, "Nevertheless, both you and I conform with the present generation in finding it far more pleasant to follow one's research interests in the comfort of one's facility than to be confronted with the psychological dangers of facing nature's extremes in more adventurous pursuits."

King, half angry at her colleague's argument, leaned forward to snap a rebuttal, but the other was raising a hand negatively. "Face reality, Luna. Don't require or expect from Paul Sanders more than is reasonable. He is an average young man. Born in our Universal Welfare System, he was guaranteed his fundamental security by being issued that minimum allocation of UBI credits in our society that allows him an income sufficient to secure the food, housing, medical care and education to sustain a basic level of subsistence. Statistical probabilities were against his ever being drafted into the workforce. Automation and robotics being what they are, only a fraction of the population is ever called up for mandatory service. But Sanders was. His aptitude profile revealed him a possible candidate for deep-sea pilot, and it was you yourself who convinced him to take the training... pointing out the pragmatic advantages such as complete retirement after but six dives, supplemental UBI credits so that he could enjoy a more comfortable life than most, and the recognition that would accrue to him as one of the very few who still participate in hadal exploration. Very well. He was persuaded. Took his training, which, of course, required long years of demanding study in neuroscience, pressure physiology, and submersible operations. Then, performing his duties quite competently, he made his six dives. He is now legally eligible for retirement. He was drafted into the workforce reserves, served his time, and is now free from mandatory labor for the balance of his life. Why should he listen to our pleas for a few more dives?"

"But has he no sense of wonder? Has he no appreciation for..."

Newman was raising his hand again, a gesture that, seemingly mild though it was, had an astonishing ability to halt the conversation of one who debated with the calm, measured man.

He said, "No, he hasn't. Few there are who have, nowadays. Humanity has always paid lip service to exploration, hardships and discovery, but in actuality our instincts, like those of any other animal, lead us to the safest path. Today we've reached the point where no one need face danger—ever. There are few who don't take advantage of that fact. Including you and me, Luna, and including Paul Sanders."

His colleague changed subjects abruptly, impatiently. "Let's leave this frustrating discussion about Sanders' motivation and address the actual problem. The man is the only trained deep-sea pilot in the world. It will take months, possibly more than a year, to bring another candidate to the point where they can safely be trusted to pilot our next research submersible down to hadal depths. Appropriations for our expeditions have been increasingly difficult to secure—even though in our minds, Mohammad, we are approaching critical breakthroughs, discoveries which might possibly so inspire the human race that a renewed commitment to understanding our planet's last frontier will take hold of us. If it is revealed that our organization has deteriorated to the point that we haven't a single qualified pilot, then it might well be that the Economic Planning Council, and especially those administrators on the Appropriations Committee, will terminate the entire Department of Ocean Exploration."

"So..." Newman said gently.

"So somehow we've got to bring Paul Sanders out of his retirement!"

"Now we are addressing the real issue." Newman nodded his agreement. Looking over the rim of his glass, his eyes narrowed in thought as his face took on an expression of calculated strategy. "And do not the ends justify the means?"

King blinked at him.

The other chuckled. "The trouble with you, Luna, is that you have failed to apply lessons from comparative history to our problem. Haven't you ever studied the psychology of sailors and their way of life?"

"Sailors? What in the name of reason do sailors have to do with it?"

"You must realize, my dear Luna, that our Paul Sanders is nothing more than a modern-day sailor, with many of the psychological patterns, perspectives, tendencies and vulnerabilities of the seafarers of the past. Have you never heard of the merchant mariner who dreamed of returning to his hometown and starting a small business? All the long months at sea—and sometimes the cargo vessels or fishing boats would be out for years at a stretch before returning to home port—he would talk of his retirement and his dream. And then? Then in port, it would be one drink with his shipmates, before taking his accumulated wages and heading home. The one drink would lead to another. And morning would find him, broke, tattooed and possibly sleeping it off in a holding cell. So back to sea he'd have to go."

King grunted bitterly. "Unfortunately, our present-day explorer can't be separated from his credits quite so easily. If he could, I'd personally be willing to hack his account, drain his balance and force him back to work."

She brought up her wrist display and flicked it to show her universal credit account. "The ultimate financial regulation," she grunted. "Nobody can spend your money but you, yourself. Nobody can steal it, nobody can, ah, manipulate you out of it. Just how do you expect to separate our modern-day sailor from his accumulated nest egg?"

The other chuckled again. "It is simply a matter of finding contemporary methods, my dear colleague."

II

Paul Sanders was a great believer in the institution of celebration. Any excuse would do. Back when he had finished his basic education at the age of twenty-five and was registered for the labor draft, there hadn't been a chance in a hundred that he'd have the misfortune to have his name selected. But when it had been, Paul had celebrated.

When he had been informed that his physical and psychological qualifications were such that he was eligible for the most demanding occupation in the Universal Welfare System and had been persuaded into taking training for deep-sea pilot, he had celebrated once again. Eighteen others had taken the training with him, and only he and Eva Ahmed had passed the final evaluations. On this occasion, he and Eva had celebrated together. It had been quite an event. Three weeks later, Eva had died when a catastrophic hull failure occurred on what should have been a routine descent to the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

Each time Paul returned from one of his own dives, he celebrated. A night out, an indulgence, a spree, a commemoration of dangers met and survived.

Now it was all over. At the age of thirty he was retired. Professional ethics and legal regulations prevented him from ever being called up for contributing to the world's labor needs again. And he most certainly wasn't going to volunteer.

He had taken his education much as had his contemporaries. There wasn't any particular reason for trying to excel. You didn't want to get the reputation for being overly ambitious, or lazy either. Just one of the crowd. You could do the same in life whether you really studied or not. You had your Universal Basic Income allocation, didn't you? What else did you need?

It had come as a surprise when he'd been drafted for the labor force.

In the early days of the Universal Welfare System, they had made a mistake in adapting to the automation revolution and the advances in robotics. They had attempted to give everyone work by reducing the number of working hours in the day, and the number of working days in the week. It finally became absurd when employees were working but two days a week, three hours a day. In fact, it got chaotic. It became obvious that it was more practical to have one worker putting in thirty-five hours a week and developing real expertise, than it was to have a score of employees, each working a few hours a week and none of them ever really becoming proficient.

The only equitable solution was to let the technologically unemployed remain unemployed, with their Universal Basic Income as the equivalent of unemployment insurance, while the few workers still needed put in a reasonable number of hours a day, a reasonable number of weeks a year and a reasonable number of years in a lifetime. When new employees were needed, a draft lottery was held.

All persons registered in the labor force participated. If you were drawn, you must serve. The dissatisfaction those chosen might feel at their poor luck was offset by the fact that they were granted supplemental UBI credits, according to the tasks they fulfilled. Such credits could be added to their portfolios, the dividends becoming part of their current balance, or could be liquidated for a lump sum.

Yes, but now it was all over. He had his own small habitat, his own personal transport pod and twice the amount of UBI credits that most of his fellow citizens could claim. Paul Sanders had it made. A celebration was obviously called for.

He was going to do this one properly. This was the significant one. He'd accumulated substantial credits these past few months and he intended to spend them, or at least a considerable portion of them. His credit account was ready to be used. However, he wasn't going to rush into things. This had to be done correctly.

Too many celebrations were improvised. You started off with a few drinks, met some unremarkable companion and usually ended up in a mediocre establishment where you spent just as much as though you'd been in the finest venue in the city. Come morning and you had nothing to show for all the credits that had been spent but a headache and regrets.

Thus, Paul was vaguely aware from his studies of social psychology, it had always been down through the centuries since the ancient Phoenician sailor, back from his year-long voyage to distant trading ports, squandered his hard earned share of the expedition's profits in a matter of days in the wine shops of Tyre. Nobody gets quite so little for his money as that loneliest of all workers, he who must leave his home for isolated duty, returning only periodically and usually with the compensation of lengthy, demanding periods of time to be spent hurriedly in an attempt to achieve the pleasure and happiness so long denied him.

Paul was going to do it differently this time.

Nothing but the best. Entertainment, cuisine, companionship, luxury accommodations. Everything. But nothing but the best.

To start off, he dressed with great care in the formal retirement-status attire he had so recently purchased. His deep-sea exploration pin he attached carefully to the collar. That was a good beginning, he decided. A bit of prestige didn't hurt when you went out on the town. In the Universal Welfare System hardly one person in a hundred actually ever performed anything of significant value to society. The contributions of most weren't needed. Those few who did contribute were awarded honors, recognition, status markers.

Attired satisfactorily, Paul double-checked to see that his credit chip was secure. As an afterthought, he went over to the habitat-pod's communication console, activated it, held the chip to the scanner and said, "Balance inquiry, please."

In a moment, the console's synthesized voice reported, "Base Universal Basic Income allocation: ten thousand credits annually. Supplemental workforce credits: forty-two thousand credits. Current liquid balance: eight thousand, three hundred and seventeen credits." The screen went dark.

Eight thousand, three hundred and seventeen credits. That was substantial. He could safely spend as much as half of it, if the celebration proved as memorable as he hoped it would. His quarterly UBI distribution was due in another week or so, and he wouldn't have to worry about routine expenses. Yes, indeed, Paul Sanders was as financially secure as he had ever been in his thirty years.

He opened the compact door which housed his personal transport pod, and settled himself into the comfortable vehicle. He activated the canopy, engaged the pressurization and considered the destination interface. Only one place really made sense. Unity, Galdoria.

He considered for a moment, decided against the districts of Highpoint and Dawnridge, and selected Unity instead. He had the resources. He might as well do it properly.

He entered Unity into the navigation system and felt the subtle acceleration that indicated his pod's engagement with the transit network. While it was being routed through the automated controls, being directed here and there preparatory to the high-speed transit to his destination, he accessed the pod's information system for data on the premier hotels of Unity. He selected an exclusive establishment he'd read about and seen on the holographic broadcasts of society and celebrity content, and entered it as his destination.

"Nothing too good for ex-Deep-Sea Pilot Paul Sanders," he said aloud.

The pod paused for a moment, that brief hesitation before the acceleration, and Paul took the involuntary breath that even experienced travelers couldn't quite suppress. He pressed back into the seat. Minutes passed, and the direction of the pressure reversed.

Unity. The routing adjustments began again, and one or two more local transits. Finally, the display showed green and Paul opened the canopy and stepped into his hotel suite.

A voice said pleasantly, "If the accommodations are satisfactory, please present your credit chip within ten minutes."

Paul took his time. Not that he really needed it. It was by far the most luxurious suite he had ever seen. One wall was a holographic window of whatever view the guest might desire and Paul touched the control that expanded it to maximum. His view opened such that he could see both the Central Archive Tower and the Meridian Gardens. Beyond the gardens stretched the seemingly endless metropolis that was Greater Unity.

He didn't take the time to activate the menu interface next to the automated dining station, nor to check the extensive selection on the beverage synthesizer. All that, he well knew, would be exceptional. Besides, he didn't plan to dine or do much drinking in his suite. He made a wry smile. Not unless he managed to find some pleasant companionship, that was.

He looked briefly into the hydrotherapy pool and cleansing chamber, then settled himself onto the bed. It wasn't adjusted to the degree of firmness he presently desired, and he recalibrated the settings to his preference so that with a satisfied sigh he sank into the perfect support of the mattress.

He came back to his feet, gave his attire a quick adjustment so that it fell into perfect alignment and, taking his credit chip from his pocket, placed it against the communication console screen and pressed the hotel registration control so that check-in could be completed.

For a moment he stood in the center of the floor, considering his options. Take it easy, Paul Sanders, take it all easy, this time. No squandering his credits in second-rate establishments, no eating in automated food dispensaries. This time, perhaps the only time in his life, he was going to celebrate in the grand manner. No mediocrity for Paul Sanders.

He decided a drink was in order to help him plan his evening. A drink at the hotel's famous Zenith Lounge where notable individuals were reputed to gather regularly.

He left the suite and entered one of the elevators. He said, "Zenith Lounge."

The automated elevator responded politely, "Yes, sir, the Zenith Lounge."

At the entrance to the famous gathering place of the elite, Paul paused a moment and observed his surroundings. He'd never been in a place like this before. However, he suppressed his initial instinct to worry about what this was going to cost with an inner smile and made his way to the bar.

There was actually a human bartender.

Paul suppressed his astonishment and said, casually, attempting an air of practiced sophistication, "Abyssal Depths."

"Yes, sir."

The drinks in the Zenith Lounge might be prepared by hand, but Paul noticed they had the standard payment scanners built into the bar surface. He placed his credit chip on the scanner immediately before him when the drink arrived, and had to resist his desire to check for a balance inquiry, so as to be able to calculate what the cocktail had cost him.

Well, this was something worthwhile. This was the sort of experience he'd imagined, out there in the crushing darkness, sealed in the confining sphere of his submersible craft. He sipped at the drink, finding it exceeded his expectations, and then turned slightly on his stool to observe the other patrons.

To his disappointment, there were no recognizable celebrities. None that he identified, at least—prominent holographic performers, influential politicians of the Universal Welfare System or renowned artists.

He turned back to his drink and noticed, for the first time, the woman who occupied the seat two down from him. Paul Sanders blinked. He blinked and then inhaled sharply.

"Remarkable," he breathed.

She was styled in the latest aesthetic from the Pacific Rim cultural centers, even to the point of having cosmetically enhanced her features with bioluminescent accents that caught the ambient light. Every detail, but every detail, was flawless. She sat with the composed elegance that spoke of professional training in artistic expression.

His stare couldn't be ignored.

She looked at him coolly, turned to the bartender and murmured, "A Crystalline Cascade, please, Walter." Then deliberately added, "I thought the Zenith Lounge was supposed to be exclusive."

There was nothing the bartender could say to that, and he went about preparing the drink.

Paul cleared his throat. "Hey," he said, "how about letting this one be on me?"

Her eyebrows, which had been shaped and enhanced to complement her aesthetic presentation, rose. "Indeed?" she said, drawing it out.

The bartender said quickly, "I beg your pardon, sir..."

The woman, her voice suddenly subtly changed, said, "Wait, isn't that a deep-sea exploration pin?"

Paul, disconcerted by the sudden reversal, said, "Yeah... sure."

"Good heavens, you're a hadal pilot?"

"Sure." He indicated the collar pin. "You can't wear one unless you've completed at least one descent to the hadal zone."

She was obviously both taken aback and impressed. "Why," she said, "you're Paul Sanders, the pilot. I watched the ceremony they held for you."

Paul, carrying his glass, moved over to the seat next to her. "Call me Paul," he said. "Everyone calls me Paul."

She said, "I'm Claudia. Claudia Montgomery. Just Claudia. Imagine meeting Paul Sanders. Just sitting down next to him at a bar. Just like that."

"Paul," Paul said, gratified. By all measures, he'd never encountered anyone with this level of refined beauty. Maybe on holographic displays, of course, one of the current cultural icons, but never in person. "Call me Paul," he said again. "I've been called Paul so long, I don't even register when someone uses my full name."

"I was moved when they gave you that commemorative plaque," she said, her tone such that it was obvious she hadn't quite processed having actually met him.

Paul Sanders was surprised. "Moved?" he said. "Well, why? I was somewhat disengaged from the whole ceremony. But Director King, I used to work under her in the Ocean Exploration Department, she was enthusiastic about it."

"Director King?" she said. "You just call her Luna?"

Paul was expansive. "Why, sure. In the Ocean Exploration Department we don't have much use for formality. Everyone's just Paul, and Luna, and Mohammad. Like that. But why were you moved?"

She looked down into the drink the bartender had placed before her, as though avoiding his gaze. "I... I suppose it was that speech Professor Newman made. There you stood, so distinguished in your deep-sea pilot uniform, the veteran of six exploration dives to the hadal zones..."

"Well," Paul said modestly, "two of my dives were only to the bathypelagic zone."

"...and he said all those things about humanity's quest to understand the deep ocean. And the existential questions that arise when we confront the unknown depths. And then the fact that you were the last of the deep-sea pilots. The last person in the whole world trained to pilot a hadal submersible. And there you were, retiring."

Paul grunted. "Yeah. That's all part of Luna's strategy to get me to take on another three dives. They're concerned the whole department will be eliminated by the Appropriations Committee on the Economic Planning Council. Even if they can find some other candidate to train for the position, it would take maybe a year before they could even send them on a bathypelagic descent. So Director King, and Professor Newman too, they're both trying to pressure me into more dives. Otherwise they have an Ocean Exploration Department, with all the expense and all, but nobody to pilot their submersibles. It's somewhat ironic, in a way. You know what one of those hadal submersibles costs?"

"Ironic?" she said. "Why, I don't think it's ironic at all."

Paul said, "Look, how about another drink?"

Claudia Montgomery said, "Oh, I'd love to have a drink with you, Mr..."

"Paul," Paul said. He gestured to the bartender with a circular motion indicating their need for two more of the same. "How come you know so much about it? You don't meet many people who are interested in deep-sea exploration anymore. In fact, most people are almost dismissive, like. Think it's kind of a wasteful expenditure to help consume resources and keep the economy functioning."

Claudia said earnestly, "Why, I've been fascinated by ocean exploration all my life. I've studied everything about it. Have always known the names of all the deep-sea pilots and everything about them, ever since I was young. I suppose you'd say I'm captivated by the existential questions that Professor Newman spoke about."

Paul chuckled. "A real enthusiast, eh? You know, it's kind of funny. I was never much interested in it. And I became considerably less interested after my first dive and I discovered what pressure psychosis was."

She frowned. "I don't believe I know much about that."

Sitting in the Zenith Lounge with the most beautiful woman to whom he had ever spoken, Paul could be casual about the subject. "Director King keeps that aspect mostly suppressed and out of the media articles and holographic documentaries. Says there's enough negative publicity about ocean exploration already. But at this stage when the whole submersible is packed with automated scientific equipment and all, there's extremely limited space in the pilot sphere and you're the only person aboard. Luna says later on when submersibles are larger and there's a whole crew aboard, there won't be any such thing as pressure psychosis, but..." Suddenly the left side of Paul Sanders' hand began to tremble and he hurriedly took up his drink and finished it.
question: What happens to drafted workers in the Universal Welfare System?
option_a: They receive supplemental UBI credits according to their tasks and can retire after serving their time.
option_b: They are required to work reduced hours but must continue working for their entire lives.
correct_answer_text: They receive supplemental UBI credits according to their tasks and can retire after serving their time.
incorrect_answer_text: They are required to work reduced hours but must continue working for their entire lives.
explanation: The story explicitly states that drafted workers are "granted supplemental UBI credits, according to the tasks they fulfilled" and that after serving their time, they are "free from mandatory labor for the balance of his life." Paul Sanders himself is retired at age 30 after completing his six dives, demonstrating that drafted workers can fully retire after their service period ends.
original_question: What happens to drafted workers?

synthetic_story:
THE SILICON VALLEY AND THE SERVERS
BY LUCIA PAGE

The CEO of NovaTech wanted progress—a piece of every innovation in sight!

"I'm not at all sure," Deputy Director Steven Boyd said, "that I fully understand the necessity for your... ah... physically traveling here from your post, Ms. Hart. Surely this matter could have been handled through our usual communication channels—assuming any action is necessary."

"I had a sharp malfunction in my video conferencing equipment, Mr. Boyd," Valentina Hart said. "So I thought I'd better come in person—just to be sure I was making my point clearly."

"Eh?"

"Why, ah, there were a number of reports," Assistant Deputy Director Matthew Robbins put in. "Unfortunately, this being end-of-fiscal-year time, we found ourselves quite inundated with data. Reports, reports, reports—"

"Not criticizing our data collection protocols, are you, Mr. Robbins?" the Deputy Director barked.

"Gracious, no," Robbins said. "I love data."

"It seems nobody's told NovaTech about fiscal years," Valentina said. "They're going right ahead with their program of intellectual property acquisition in Rosewood. So far, I've persuaded the local tech cooperatives that this is a matter for the Bureau, and not to take matters into their own hands."

The Deputy Director nodded. "Quite right. Carry on along the same lines. Now, if there's nothing further—"

"Thank you, Mr. Boyd," Robbins said, rising. "We certainly appreciate your guidance."

"There is a little something further," said Valentina, sitting solidly in her chair. "What's the Bureau going to do about NovaTech?"

The Deputy Director turned a weary eye on Valentina. "As Regional Coordinator for Rosewood, you should know that the function of a regulatory representative is merely to... what shall I say...?"

"String them along?" Robbins suggested.

"An unfortunate choice of phrase," the Deputy Director said. "However, it embodies certain realities of modern corporate governance. The Bureau must concern itself with matters of broad policy."

"Twenty years ago the Bureau was encouraging the tech cooperatives to settle in Rosewood," Valentina said. "They were assured of Bureau support against corporate encroachment."

"I don't believe you'll find that in writing," said the Deputy Director blandly. "In any event, that was twenty years ago. At that time a foothold for worker-owned enterprises was deemed desirable. Now the situation has changed."

"The cooperatives have spent twenty years building Rosewood," Valentina said. "They've established makerspaces, developed open-source platforms, created community organizing networks, and trained local workers in robotics and data science. They've just about reached the point where they can scale their operations. NovaTech has picked this as a good time to move in. They've deployed fifteen teams of 'consultants'—complete with non-compete agreements and predatory licensing terms—and another dozen groups of 'investors'—all with hostile takeover intentions."

"Surely there's market space enough to afford room for both groups," the Deputy Director said. "A spirit of cooperation—"

"The cooperatives needed some cooperation twenty years ago," Valentina said. "They tried to get NovaTech to join in collaborative development. The Bureau didn't like the idea. They wanted to see independent worker-owned innovation. NovaTech didn't want to play, either. But now that the infrastructure is built, they're moving in."

"The exigencies of regulation require a flexible policy—"

"I want a firm assurance of Bureau support to take back to Rosewood," Valentina said. "The cooperatives are a little naive. They don't understand regulatory double-speak. They just want to hold onto the enterprises they've made from nothing."

"I'm warning you, Hart!" the Deputy Director snapped, leaning forward. "Bureau policy with regard to Rosewood includes no inflammatory actions based on outmoded concepts. The cooperatives will have to accommodate themselves to the situation!"

"That's what I'm afraid of," Valentina said. "They're not going to sit still and watch it happen. If I don't take back concrete evidence of Bureau backing, we're going to have a nice hot legal battle on our hands."

The Deputy Director pushed out his lips and drummed his fingers on the desk.

"Confounded idealists," he muttered. "Very well, Hart. I'll go along to the extent of a Formal Letter; but positively no further."

"A Letter? I was thinking of something more like a team of Bureau investigators running through a few routine audits of NovaTech."

"Out of the question. A sternly worded Formal Letter is the best I can do. That's final."

Back in the corridor, Robbins turned to Valentina. "When will you learn not to argue with Deputy Directors? One would think you actively disliked the idea of ever receiving a promotion. I was astonished at the Deputy Director's restraint. Frankly, I was stunned when he actually agreed to a Letter. I, of course, will have to draft it." Robbins pulled at his lower lip thoughtfully. "Now, I wonder, should I express deep concern about potential labor relations violations, or merely point out apparent breaches of protocol..."

"Don't bother," Valentina said. "I have a draft all ready to go."

"But how—?"

"I had a feeling I'd get paper instead of action," Valentina said. "I thought I'd save a little time all around."

"At times, your cynicism borders on insubordination."

"At other times, it borders on disgust. Now, if you'll run the Letter through for signature, I'll try to catch the six o'clock flight."

"Leaving so soon? There's an important conference tonight. Some of our biggest names will be there. An excellent opportunity for you to join in the regulatory give-and-take."

"No, thanks. I want to get back to Rosewood and join in something mild, like a hackathon."

"When you get there," said Robbins, "I hope you'll make it quite clear that this matter is to be settled without litigation."

"Don't worry. I'll keep the peace, if I have to start a war to do it."

On the broad terrace at Cooperative House, Valentina settled herself comfortably in an ergonomic chair. She accepted a craft beer from a server and regarded the impressive Rosewood skyline, a gorgeous array of solar panels and green roofs that reflected the afternoon sun, silhouetted vertical gardens among innovation hubs.

"You've done great things here in twenty years, Peter," said Valentina. "Not that natural market forces wouldn't have produced the same results, given a couple of hundred years of economic inequality."

"Don't belabor the point," the Cooperative Director Peter Fuller said. "Since we seem to be on the verge of losing it."

"You're forgetting the Letter."

"A Letter," Peter said, waving his hand. "What the hell is a Letter supposed to do? I've got NovaTech claim-jumpers camped in the middle of what used to be a fine open-source development lab, holding closed-door meetings not ten blocks from Cooperative House—and they're recruiting our best engineers."

"Say, if that's the same lab that developed your AI platform, I'd call that a first-class violation."

"Valentina, on your say-so, I've kept my people restrained. They've put up with plenty. Last week, while you were away, these corporate raiders walked right through the middle of one of our best mentorship programs for young developers. It was all I could do to keep a bunch of our members from filing immediate lawsuits."

"That wouldn't have been good for the program, either."

"That's what I told them. I also said you'd be back here in a few days with something from Bureau HQ. When I tell them all we've got is a piece of paper, that'll be the end. There's a strong legal defense fund here that's been preparing for the last four weeks. If I hadn't held them back with assurances that the Bureau would step in and take care of this corporate invasion, they would have filed suit before now."

"That would have been a mistake," said Valentina. "NovaTech is a tough customer. They're active in half a dozen regions at the moment. They've been building up for this push for the last five years. A show of resistance by your cooperatives without Bureau backing would be an invitation to bankruptcy—with the excuse that you started it."

"So what are we going to do? Sit here and watch these corporate raiders take over our innovations and worker-owned businesses?"

"Those corporate raiders aren't all they seem. They've got a first-class legal team."

"I've seen them. They show up in casual clothes, talk about 'collaboration' and 'synergy,' wear those ridiculous smart glasses—"

"The 'casual' approach is a calculated strategy, made by the same consultants who design hostile takeover campaigns. The collaboration talk is just for show. Back at headquarters they use aggressive acquisition tactics of the most predatory design."

Peter Fuller frowned.

"Why the masquerade?"

"Something to do with public relations, I suppose."

"So we sit tight and watch them take our innovations away from us. That's what I get for playing along with you, Valentina. We should have filed injunctions as soon as they set foot in our territory."

"Slow down, I haven't finished yet. There's still the Letter."

"I've got plenty of paper already. Files and files of it."

"Give regulatory processes a chance," said Valentina. "The Letter hasn't even been delivered yet. Who knows? We may get surprising results."

"If you expect me to supply a messenger for the purpose, you're out of luck. From what I hear, they're likely to come back with a cease-and-desist order stuffed in their inbox."

"I'll deliver the Letter personally," Valentina said. "I could use a couple of escorts—preferably tech-savvy individuals."

Peter Fuller frowned, took a sip of his beer. "I wasn't kidding about NovaTech," he said. "I hear they have some nasty legal tactics. I don't want to see you tied up in litigation for years."

"I'd be against that myself. Still, the message must go through."

"Tech-savvy individuals, eh? What have you got in mind, Valentina?"

"A little technical expertise in the background is an old regulatory custom," Valentina said.

Peter Fuller set down his beer thoughtfully. "I used to be a pretty fair coder myself," he said. "Suppose I go along...?"

"That," said Valentina, "should lend just the right note of solidarity to our little delegation." She leaned closer. "Now, depending on what we run into, here's how we'll play it..."

Eight miles into the tech district east of central Rosewood, a Bureau vehicle flying the flags of Regional Coordinator and Worker Advocacy skimmed along the elevated transit line. Slumped in the passenger seat, Peter Fuller gestured glumly at the surrounding buildings.

"Ten years ago this was abandoned industrial space," he said. "We've developed special programs here to retrain workers, and we followed up with a campaign of sustainable business development. We planned to put the whole area into cooperative ownership by next year. Now it looks like the corporations will get it."

"Will that industrial space support cooperative ownership?" Valentina said, eyeing the converted warehouses.

"Sure. We start with makerspaces and follow up with full production facilities. Wait until you see this next section. It's an old manufacturing district, came into production five years ago. One of our finest—"

The vehicle topped a rise. Peter dropped his coffee and half rose, with a hoarse yell. A NovaTech billboard announced "Premium Office Space Available" over a building that had housed a worker-owned 3D printing facility. The vehicle pulled to a stop. Valentina held Peter's arm.

"Keep calm, Peter," she said. "Remember, we're on a regulatory mission. It wouldn't do to come to the negotiating table smelling of desperation."

"Let me at them!" Peter roared. "I'll shut them down with my bare hands!"

A security camera swiveled to watch them. "Look at that surveillance!" The camera tracked their movement. "Did you see that?" Peter yelled. "They've automated the—"

"Chin up, Peter," Valentina said. "We'll take up the surveillance problem along with the rest."

"I'll sue them!"

"Hold it, Peter. Look over there."

A hundred yards away, three suited executives emerged from a sleek corporate shuttle, paused dramatically against the glass facade, then walked briskly down the plaza toward the vehicle, briefcases swinging at their sides, designer coats billowing out behind. Side by side they walked, through the carefully landscaped courtyard, cutting three narrow paths through the sustainable garden to the Bureau vehicle where Valentina and Peter waited.

Peter scrambled for the door. "Just wait 'til I get my hands on them!"

Valentina pulled him back. "Sit tight and look professional, Peter. Never give the opposition a hint of your true feelings. Pretend you're interested in partnership—and hand me one of your business cards."

The three executives pulled up in a rustle of expensive fabric and a click of polished shoes. Peter coughed, adjusting his collar. Valentina arranged her tablet unhurriedly, checked her notes and thumbed it on. She scrolled through data, pulled up a document and glanced casually at the trio of NovaTech executives.

"Good afternoon," she said in accent-free corporate-speak. "I trust we're not interrupting anything important."

The leader of the three, a sharp-featured woman with perfectly styled hair, adjusted her smart glasses. She checked her phone, frowning professionally.

"We're quite busy," Valentina said, smiling graciously. "But we always make time for stakeholder engagement."

A younger member of the threesome tapped his phone and pulled up a document.

"Let's keep this brief," Valentina said. "We have other meetings scheduled."

The leader turned to Valentina.

"You're trespassing," she said. "This is NovaTech property."

"Public records indicate otherwise," Valentina said. "This facility is registered to the Rosewood Tech Cooperative. But enough of these technicalities. We seek a meeting with your CEO."

"You may address me as 'Director'," the leader said. "Now please vacate this area."

"With respect, Director, we must decline," Valentina said. "We have requested a meeting. Professional courtesy suggests you should accommodate us."

"Enough of your bureaucratic nonsense!" The woman pulled out her phone. "I could have security remove you!"

"Network theory suggests that would be counterproductive," Valentina said. "We have asked for a meeting. Surely you can spare a few minutes."

"You're wasting my time. Leave now!"

"Only collaboration makes progress," Valentina said. "We came here in good faith."

"Get out of the vehicle!"

Valentina scrolled through her tablet, eyeing the executive cheerfully. The younger man moved forward, phone raised.

"Patience leads to opportunity," Valentina said.

"I cannot guarantee civility in the face of your intrusion," the woman said sharply. "My colleagues are quite protective of our interests!"

"When corporations overreach, markets correct," Valentina said. "Haste creates waste."

The woman's face grew red.

Valentina closed her tablet.

"Now I think we'd better be getting on," she said briskly. "I've enjoyed our chat, but we do have business to attend to."

The woman laughed shortly. "Does the defendant beg for trial?" she enquired rhetorically. "You shall visit the CEO, then. Follow us! And make no attempt to record anything, else our legal team will speak you a brief farewell."

The executives glowered, then, at a word from the leader, took positions around the vehicle. Peter started the vehicle forward, following the leading executive. Valentina leaned back and let out a long sigh.

"That was close," she said. "I was about out of business clichés."

"You sound as though you'd brought off a coup," Peter said. "From the expression on the leader's face, we're in for trouble. What was she saying?"

"Just a routine exchange of corporate posturing," Valentina said. "Now when we get there, remember to make your proposals sound confident and your concerns sound manageable, and you'll be all right."

"These people are powerful. And they don't like interference," Peter said. "Maybe I should have studied their tactics before I joined this expedition."

"Just stick to the plan," Valentina said. "And remember: preparation is better than improvisation."

The Bureau vehicle followed the escort across a plaza to a gleaming tower and through a security checkpoint to a corporate campus set with modern architecture.

The executive escort motioned the vehicle to a halt before an immense glass building. Before the building, security personnel stood under a banner bearing the NovaTech logo in blue on a white field.

"Get out," the leader ordered. The guards eyed the visitors, their security badges gleaming. Valentina and Peter stepped from the vehicle onto polished concrete. They followed the gesture of the woman through the entrance into a climate-controlled interior of sleek design. A subtle scent of expensive air freshener hung in the air, and the hum of servers laid a muted background behind the decorations of chrome and glass, white and blue. At the far end of the room, among a collection of awards and patents, a large and impeccably dressed woman with silver hair and designer glasses looked up from her tablet. She set it down carefully on a glass desk, adjusted her jacket and looked the callers over.

The leader cleared her throat. "These individuals insisted on seeing you, Ms. Evans."

"Thank you, Director," the CEO said. "That will be all."

The woman nodded and withdrew to the rear.

"Ms. Hart," the CEO said, "I'm Nora Evans, CEO of NovaTech. I understand you have some concerns."

"Ms. Evans," Valentina said, "I have the honor to present Mr. Peter Fuller, Cooperative Director of the Regional Cooperative Alliance."

"Cooperative Alliance?" Nora Evans pulled up a file on her tablet. "We've observed some small-scale operations in the area. If they're struggling, we might consider acquisition offers."

"Your concern is noted but unnecessary," Valentina said.

"I've built this company from the ground up," Nora Evans said. "I know a few things about business. For example, 'Growth requires expansion.'"

"We have no objection to legitimate business development," Valentina said. "However, predatory practices are another matter."

"I've had some challenging experiences with regulatory agencies," Nora Evans said. "Still, professional courtesy suggests we can work something out. Please, sit."

Assistants brought chairs. Valentina and Peter settled themselves. Nora Evans eyed them in silence.

"We have come to deliver a communication from the Bureau of Labor Relations," Valentina said formally. An assistant offered coffee.

"I'm always interested in regulatory perspectives," Nora Evans said. "What brings the Bureau into this situation?"

"The concerns of workers and cooperatives," Valentina said. "The Bureau has a mandate to protect worker interests."

"Very well, I'll listen." Nora Evans gestured at the assistants. "Leave us. These are regulators. They deal in paperwork, not action."

The assistants departed.

"Now," Nora Evans said. "Let's get down to business. Not that I don't respect your regulatory authority. But I'm here to grow my company. What exactly is the Bureau's position?"

"We're here to address certain conflicts between your operations and the cooperative enterprises. I have here a Formal Letter, which I'm delivering on behalf of the Deputy Director. With your permission, I'll read it."

"Go ahead." Nora Evans pulled up a document on her tablet.

"The Deputy Director for Regional Affairs presents his compliments to Ms. Nora Evans, Chief Executive Officer of NovaTech Industries, and with reference to the recent expansion of operations under the jurisdiction of NovaTech, has the honor to point out that the territories now under development comprise a portion of that area, hereinafter designated as the Rosewood Innovation District, which, under terms of the Agreement entered into with the Regional Cooperative Alliance, and as referenced in Bureau Letters numbers 2045-B-789 and 2046-C-234, with particular pertinence to that region designated in the Regional Development Plan as Rosewood, Relvaria—"

"Come to the point," Nora Evans cut in. "You're here to complain that I'm expanding into territories claimed by someone else, is that it?" She smiled broadly. "Well, I've been expecting this call. After all, it's what you government people do. Cheers."

"You have a direct way of putting things," Valentina said.

"Call me Nora," she said. "The formality is just for the board. They're still kicking themselves because the company almost went bankrupt twenty years ago during the tech crash. This aggressive expansion is supposed to prove we've recovered. However, I've no time to waste in nostalgia. I have markets to capture and profits to generate."

"At first glance," Valentina said, "it looks as though the markets are already occupied, and the profits are being earned by others."

Nora Evans laughed. "For a regulator, you speak plainly, Ms. Hart. Want some more coffee?" She poured, eyeing Peter. "What about Mr. Fuller? How does he feel about it?"

Peter took a thoughtful sip of coffee. "Not bad," he said. "But not quite good enough to cover the smell of corporate greed."

Nora Evans raised an eyebrow. "I thought the community organizing angle was a bit much myself," she said. "Still, the marketing team insisted. And I need their support."

"Also," Peter said distinctly, "I think you're lazy. You sit around in your executive suite while real workers are out creating actual value."

Nora Evans looked startled. "Lazy? I work eighty hours a week. I've built this company through strategic vision and relentless execution." She tapped her tablet. "As for the rest, your romantic views about the virtues of cooperative ownership are as naive as my board's faith in unlimited growth. As for myself, I am a pragmatist. If two companies want the same market, in the end one will dominate, and the other will cry unfair. The years of my career are numbered. While they last, I intend to maximize shareholder value, expand market share, acquire strategic assets and take my compensation. I leave to others the questionable satisfactions of egalitarian fantasies."

"You admit you're here to take our innovations, then," Peter said. "That's the most blatant piece of corporate theft—"

"Ah, ah!" Nora Evans held up a hand. "Watch your vocabulary, Mr. Fuller. I'm sure that 'strategic market positioning' would be more appropriate to the situation. Or possibly 'legitimate competitive advantage' might fit the case. Theft is, by definition, an activity carried on only by those without proper legal representation."

"Legal representation! Why, you corporate raiders have been the most notorious intellectual property thieves in regional history, you—you—"

"Call me Nora." She sipped her coffee. "I merely operate within legal frameworks. Let's be realistic; it's a matter of resources. Some entities can acquire assets and pass it off as business strategy; others are dubbed thieves merely for protecting their own interests. Unfair, you say. But that's capitalism, my friends. And I shall continue to leverage every advantage."

"We'll fight you!" Peter said loudly. He took another gulp of coffee and set the cup down firmly. "You won't take our innovations without a struggle!"

"Another cup?" Nora Evans said, offering the pot. Peter glowered as his cup was refilled. Nora Evans held the cup up to the light.

"Excellent brew, don't you agree?" She turned her eyes on Peter.

"It's pointless to resist," she said. "We have you outspent and outlawyered. Your small cooperatives have no chance against us. But we're prepared to be reasonable. You may continue to operate in areas we do not immediately require until such time as you're able to make other arrangements."

"And by the time we've developed a technology from nothing, you'll be ready to acquire it," Peter snapped. "But you'll find that we aren't alone!"

"Quite alone," Nora said. She nodded confidently. "Yes, one need only examine the pattern. The Bureau will make formal protests, but it will accept the reality. You, Mr. Fuller, are but a very small obstacle. We won't make the mistake of overreaching. We shall expand methodically—and those who resist shall be labeled obstructionists."

"I see you're quite a student of game theory, Nora," Valentina said. "I wonder if you recall the eventual fate of most monopolistic corporations?"

"Ah, but they grew reckless. They expanded too far, too fast."

"The absolute arrogance," Peter rasped. "Tells us to our face what she intends!"

"An ancient corporate tradition, from the robber barons through the tech giants. Such declarations have a legendary quality. It's traditional that they're never taken seriously until it's too late."

"But always," Valentina said, "there was a critical point at which the monopoly could have been broken."

"Could have been," Nora Evans chuckled. She finished her coffee and began checking her messages. "But they never were. Standard Oil could have been stopped earlier; Microsoft was vulnerable during antitrust proceedings; the social media giants were exposed during the privacy scandals. But the burden of proof could not be overcome. It has been the fate of regulatory agencies to establish rules and then, amid budget cuts and political pressure, to withdraw enforcement, leaving the spoils for corporate opportunists and market manipulators, clothed in the mystical virtue of 'innovation' and 'disruption.' Have some pastries."

"You're stretching your analogy a little too far," Valentina said. "You're banking on the inaction of the Bureau. You could be wrong."

"I shall know when to stop," Nora Evans said.

"Tell me, Nora," Valentina said, rising. "Are we quite private here?"

"Yes, perfectly so," Nora Evans said. "My office is secure. No one would dare to intrude during confidential discussions." She looked at Valentina. "You have a proposal to make in confidence? But what about our dear friend Peter? One would not like to see him disappointed."

"Don't worry about Peter. He's a pragmatist, like you. He's prepared to deal in facts. Hard facts, in this case."

Nora Evans nodded thoughtfully. "What are you getting at?"

"You're basing your strategy on the certainty that the Bureau will sit by, filing paperwork, while you embark on a campaign of corporate acquisition."

"Isn't it the pattern?" Nora Evans smiled complacently.

"I have news for you, Nora. In this instance, enforcement seems more in order than paperwork."

Nora Evans frowned. "Your tone—"

"Never mind our tone!" Peter blurted, standing. "We don't need any lessons from corporate raiders who've never built anything themselves!"

Nora Evans's face darkened. "You dare to speak thus to me, you naive cooperative idealist!"

Peter stepped forward. "And you're not just lazy—you're a parasite! You've built your empire on the backs of real innovators, real workers, real creators! You sit in your tower and extract value while contributing nothing!"

"How dare you!" Nora Evans stood, face flushed. "I've worked my entire life to build this company! I've made strategic decisions that—"

"That enriched yourself while impoverishing communities!" Peter shouted. "You talk about game theory and competitive advantage, but all you really understand is exploitation!"

Nora Evans's hand moved toward her phone, then stopped. She took a deep breath, visibly controlling herself.

"Mr. Fuller," she said icily, "I think this meeting is over. You may show yourselves out."

"Not quite yet," Valentina said calmly. She pulled out her tablet. "Before we go, I should mention that this conversation has been recorded. Every word. Every admission of predatory intent. Every acknowledgment of your acquisition strategy."

Nora Evans went pale. "You can't—that's not—"

"Legal? Oh, but it is. You see, Nora, you made one critical error. You assumed the Bureau was toothless. You assumed we'd follow the old pattern of complaint without consequence." Valentina smiled. "But times have changed. We have new leadership. New priorities. And new enforcement mechanisms."

"This is blackmail!"

"This is documentation," Valentina said. "For the antitrust investigation that begins tomorrow. For the labor relations violations we'll be filing next week. For the intellectual property theft charges we're preparing. You wanted to know when to stop, Nora? You've already gone too far."

Peter grinned. "You see, we did our homework. We know about the Yarnmouth Town acquisition—the one where you 'accidentally' destroyed all the original patents. We know about the Carmel operation in Quendor—where your 'consultants' turned out to be corporate spies. And we know about Brookhaven in Orvandor—where you're planning your next move."

Nora Evans sank back into her chair. "What do you want?"

"Complete withdrawal from Rosewood," Valentina said. "Dissolution of all contracts signed under duress. Compensation for damages. And a consent decree preventing future predatory practices in this region."

"That's impossible! My board would never—"

"Your board will do exactly what you tell them," Valentina said. "Once they see this recording. Once they understand the legal exposure. Once they realize that fighting this will cost far more than compliance."

Nora Evans stared at them for a long moment. Then she laughed—a bitter, defeated sound.

"You played me," she said. "The whole naive cooperative act. The righteous indignation. You wanted me to incriminate myself."

"We wanted the truth," Valentina said. "You provided it. Now, do we have an agreement, or do I forward this to the Bureau's litigation team?"

Nora Evans closed her eyes. "Draft your terms. I'll review them."

"We already have." Valentina placed a document on the desk. "Sign it now, or we walk out and file charges within the hour."

For a long moment, Nora Evans didn't move. Then she picked up a pen and signed.

"You've won this round," she said quietly. "But don't think this is over."

"Oh, it's over," Peter said. "For you, at least. Word travels fast in our network. Every cooperative, every worker-owned enterprise, every community organization in three sectors will know about this by tomorrow. You'll find the climate much less hospitable for your kind of business."

As they walked out, Valentina turned back. "One more thing, Nora. You asked what I was getting at earlier. Here it is: the pattern you counted on? It only works when people don't fight back. We fought back. And we won."

Outside, in the fading light, Peter let out a whoop of joy. "We did it! We actually did it!"

"We did," Valentina said. "But remember, this is just one battle. There will be others."

"Let them come," Peter said. "We know how to fight now."

As they drove back toward Cooperative House, the Rosewood skyline glowed in the sunset—solar panels catching the last light, vertical gardens swaying in the breeze, innovation hubs humming with creative energy. It was a landscape built by workers, for workers. And now, at least for a while, it would stay that way.

"You know," Peter said, "I was skeptical about that Letter. But it turned out to be pretty useful after all."

"The Letter?" Valentina smiled. "Oh, that was just to get us in the door. The real weapon was always going to be the recording. And her own arrogance."

"Remind me never to underestimate you," Peter said.

"Remind me never to underestimate the power of community organizing," Valentina replied. "We couldn't have done this without your network, your solidarity, your willingness to stand together."

"To standing together," Peter said, raising an imaginary glass.

"To standing together," Valentina echoed. "And to keeping the bastards honest."

They drove on through the twilight, toward home, toward the community they had fought to protect. Behind them, in her tower, Nora Evans stared at the signed document and wondered how it had all gone so wrong. She had played by the old rules, the tried-and-true patterns of corporate expansion. But the game had changed. And she had been too arrogant to notice until it was too late.

In the end, that was the lesson: patterns only hold until someone breaks them. And in Rosewood, on this day, the pattern had been shattered.
