DEEP CURRENT
BY IRVING W. LANDE

The submersible dove through layers of darkness, its external lights cutting pale swaths through the midnight zone. Commander Jordan Cruz checked the depth gauge—3,200 meters and descending. They were hunting in the abyssal plains now, far below where sunlight had ever reached.

"Contact at two o'clock, range approximately twelve kilometers," Isaac Kim's voice crackled through the comm system, tense despite his casual delivery.

Jordan glanced at the sonar display, her practiced eye immediately recognizing the signature. She smiled grimly at her instinctive reaction—looking out the viewport as if she could see anything in this perpetual night. At this depth, you could pass within fifty meters of another vessel and never know it unless your sonar was better. She pressed the comm button. "Any identification beacon?"

"Negative beacon."

"Understood. Alert me when you have a vector." Jordan began her pre-engagement check, noting with wry amusement that her breathing had quickened and her palms were damp on the controls. She verified her emergency beacon was secure in its housing on her survival suit; checked the oxygen rebreather system; confirmed the paired carbon dioxide scrubbers were functioning within normal parameters. She sealed her helmet, locked it, then opened it again. She touched the photograph of her sister mounted near the viewport. "Keep us safe, Em."

She pressed comm again. "You have anything yet, Isaac?"

"Plotting now, Commander. Should have it in sixty seconds."

Jordan scanned the darkness beyond the viewport, her mind drifting as it always did before action. The familiar anxiety built in her chest—not quite fear, but a tight, helpless sensation that grew with each passing moment.

She thought of Priya first. Always Priya. Those challenging eyes and that quick laugh. The way she'd looked in her blue dress at the Pinehurst gala, how she'd teased Jordan about being too serious. A cascade of memories—dancing at the Crestwood officer's club, that weekend in Hillcrest when they'd watched the meteor shower from the beach.

Then Talia, calm and thoughtful, with warmth breaking through like sunrise when she smiled. Jordan wished she'd been more mature that night at the Lakeside research station. She replayed their last conversation for the hundredth time, seeing the disappointment in Talia's eyes, hearing her own clumsy apologies. She was a good person. Silently Jordan's lips formed the words: "You're a good person."

I think she cares about me. She was just upset because I was drunk.

The tension of approaching engagement suddenly merged with the memory, swelling into a wave of tenderness. She whispered Talia's name, and suddenly knew that if she made it back, she was going to ask her to move to Pinehurst together.

She thought of her father, sitting in his workshop in Crestwood, probably listening to the radio as he worked on one of his endless projects. She wished she'd sent him a message last night instead of joining the usual drinking session in the crew quarters. She wished—. She wished.

"Got him, Jordan. He's got four point three knots of relative velocity on us. Come to heading two-seven-zero, descend to thirty-three hundred meters."

Automatically she adjusted the dive planes and turned the control wheel. The gyroscopic compass recorded the course change.

"Hold three knots for two hundred forty seconds, then drift for three minutes to get within five hundred meters of his stern."

"Right, Isaac. Two-forty, then three minutes." She set the timer, advanced the throttle, and settled back as the acceleration pressed her gently into her seat. The Return-To-Base-Power and Relative-Velocity-To-Base gauges did their usual dance with a course change, as the ship's computer processed the new data. She liked those gauges—her two guardian angels.

The power gauge tracked how much more battery capacity they had than needed to return to base. When they moved away from the Lakeside Deep Station, it dropped in alarming increments, but when heading home, it climbed with serene confidence, or during drift, crept triumphantly upward.

The velocity gauge started getting nervous around five knots away from base, and above eight knots, it trembled steadily. Jordan didn't blame the gauges for worrying. With only two hours of battery at full power, you didn't waste a single amp unless absolutely necessary. Most of their patrol time was spent drifting in the cold darkness, in the anxiety-laden boredom that all warriors have known.

Wish the Collective vessel was crossing our path. It would have taken less power, and the intercept wouldn't take them so far from base. But then they'd probably have been detected, losing the precious element of surprise.

She blessed their superior sonar. In this strange "conflict"—so like the submarine warfare of the twentieth century—the hundred-kilometer edge of Western Alliance sonar was often the margin between success and failure. The Alliance crews were better trained, more experienced, but with their stripped-down vessels and minimal safety equipment, the Collective could run deeper, faster, and farther. You had to catch them unaware, or it was over.

The timer hit its mark, and she eased back the throttle to drift speed.

Forty-seven deep-sea missions, but officially there's no war. Her mind wandered back over six years in the service. Aptitude tests. Physical evaluations. Psychological screening. Eight months of pressure adaptation training. Basic oceanography. Advanced submersible operations. The pride of being selected for deep combat operations. By the time she graduated, both the Western Alliance and the Eastern Collective had multiple deep-sea research stations operating, but in 2087, the Alliance had won the race to establish a permanent station in the Mariana Trench—the deepest point on Earth.

A year later, that station had "imploded." No warning. No survivors. Just twisted metal scattered across the seafloor. Six months after that, the replacement station, nearly operational, suffered the same fate. The diplomats had raged with accusations and threats, but nothing could be proven—there were experimental pressure systems that could have failed. The implication was clear enough. There wasn't going to be a deep trench station until one power controlled Earth's oceans. Or until the Alliance and Collective figured out how to coexist. And so far, coexisting with the Collective was like trying to coexist with a shark.

There were rumors that the psychological warfare division had developed some technique involving linguistic analysis and oral history preservation to undermine Collective propaganda, to spark revolution during the next leadership transition, but she'd heard those rumors for years. Still, with three new premiers in the last seven years, there was always hope.

Anyway, she was just a submersible pilot, doing her job in this bizarre conflict in the deep ocean. On the surface, there was no war. Diplomats talked, held conferences, played their games as always. Neither side interfered with the other's surface vessels or shallow-water operations. There just wasn't going to be any deep trench station for a while. Nobody knew what resources might exist at those depths, but if one side couldn't have them, neither would the other.

Meanwhile, the struggle intensified month by month, each side seeking the advantage that would give control of the deep ocean, or make open warfare a viable option. They hadn't found it yet, but casualties were mounting. A year ago, the average patrol was uneventful. Now, Collective submarines appeared on nearly every mission.

Twenty-eight missions left after today. She wondered if she'd retire at seventy-five. Deep inside, the old pride and excitement remained strong. She still felt a thrill when civilians noticed the silver submarine insignia on her uniform. But she didn't feel as lucky as she used to. Thirty-one years old, and she was starting to feel ancient. She pictured herself lecturing eager recruits.

Had a couple of close calls those last two missions. That Collective sub had seemed vulnerable, wandering off course. They hadn't detected the Alliance vessel until the intercept was well underway, but once engaged, they'd made Jordan's crew look slow. If they hadn't attempted that reckless sudden ascent.... Jordan shook her head. And the previous mission had been a draw at best. Those crews were skilled.

"Crossing his track now, Jordan. Come to heading three-one-five, hold two point five knots for forty-five seconds, starting on mark... five—four—three—two—one—mark!" She completed the maneuver in silence, grateful for Isaac. The man loved the hunt. He navigated like a predator, though his techniques were unconventional.

Jordan chuckled at their improvised methods, remembering the courses, the tests, the procedures practiced until they were automatic. When engaging a Collective sub, the standard navigation protocols became irrelevant. They navigated relative to the enemy. During combat, she often had no idea of her absolute position beyond what the gauges showed and what she could infer from the thermocline layers.

And using the old "clock" system for bearing references. She chuckled again. The service had initially resisted it, but it worked. When time was critical, it worked fast, and that was good enough for Jordan. She'd submitted a report on it to Captain Phillip Cox.

"You're positioned, Jordan. We're directly astern, five hundred meters back, matching velocity. Adjust heading to three-two-zero and you're lined up perfectly." Isaac was pleased with his work.

Jordan watched the contact move into her targeting display. It settled within a degree of center. She made final corrections, set the cabin pressure to standard, and locked her helmet.

"Excellent work, Isaac. Let's seal up. You ready, Weapons?"

Zachary Ramirez sounded relaxed as a cat. "Ready when you are, Commander."

Jordan advanced the throttle to full power. With the hum of the motors, Submersible DS-47 began the deadly maneuver called an intercept pass—inherited from submarine warfare—the optimal method of destroying an enemy submersible. Start on the enemy's stern, just beyond their sonar range. Approach at two knots relative velocity, firing torpedoes from five hundred meters. In the final seconds, break away just enough to avoid collision, praying they won't break in the same direction. And keep going.

Three minutes and twenty seconds to weapons release. Forty seconds at full power; one hundred twenty seconds of drift; and then, if lucky, the twenty seconds they were here for—launching their torpedoes into the darkness, reaching out five hundred meters with sonar and explosives to destroy their counterpart.

This is the worst. These two minutes are the worst. One hundred twenty eternal seconds of waiting, of profound silence and stillness, feeling nothing but their own heartbeats. Each time she returned to base, the memory faded, leaving only the excitement. But each time she lived through it, it was worse. Just drifting in silence, praying they weren't detected—staring at the sonar display and knowing she was a projectile moving through the abyss straight toward metal and flesh that was the enemy. Knowing the odds were poor for a kill... unless they collided.

At ninety seconds, she corrected slightly to center the contact. The brief motor hum was a relief. She heard the muffled clunk as Zachary test-fired the torpedo guidance system.

Suddenly the waiting ended. "Tubes one and two away," Zachary announced calmly.

Thirty seconds to target. Her eyes flicked between the sonar display and the darkness ahead, watching for the telltale bloom of cavitation bubbles—ready to follow instantly.

There! At four hundred meters from target, a faint disturbance appeared in the water ahead. She forgot everything but the display, concentrating on keeping the contact centered. The torpedoes tracked on.

At two hundred fifty meters from target, the automated collision avoidance system kicked in, turning the submersible ninety degrees in three seconds.

She held course as long as she dared. Closer than ever before. At one hundred meters she applied emergency ascent—four G's for three seconds.

They missed colliding by perhaps thirty meters. The enemy submarine flashed past below them in a fraction of a second, already turned and heading back along its track, yet Jordan could make out every detail—the bright red star on its hull, even the desperate face of a crewman through a viewport. Was there something wrong with that propeller, or was she imagining it in the blur of their passing? And did she hear a metallic scrape just then, feel the hull vibrate?

She continued the turn, bringing her bow around to watch the enemy's track. As the sonar showed the other vessel still heading toward Collective territory, she brought the throttle back to emergency power, trying to close the distance their pass had created.

Zachary spoke quietly to Isaac. "Let me know when we match his velocity. I might get another shot."

Isaac answered, mock-hurt, "What do you think I'm doing down here—reading one of your design science journals?"

Jordan was struggling to focus the external camera mounted on the hull. As the image cleared, she could see the enemy's propeller was damaged, wobbling unevenly, throwing debris.

Quietly and intensely, she was talking to herself. "Break down. Break down."

And it did. Like a violent shudder, the propeller tore free, the submarine going dark and beginning to sink. Something glowed briefly from an internal explosion, then faded.

There, but for grace.... Jordan shuddered in a mixture of relief and revulsion.

She reduced to cruising power, noting that the velocity gauge registered about three knots away from base, and suddenly noticed the warning light for hull breach. The pressure gauge showed slow flooding in the aft compartment, and her heart jumped as she remembered that scraping sound as they passed the enemy. She told Zachary to locate the breach and assess damage, and was soon startled by a low whistle in her earphones.

"If I wasn't seeing it, I wouldn't believe it. Must have been debris from their propeller scraped along the hull without breaching the pressure vessel. There's at least two centimeters of hull between the outer damage and the pressure boundary! We must have caught it at exactly the right angle. Commander, this is our lucky day!"

Jordan felt no surprise, only relief at having the damage identified. The emotional reaction might not come until later. "This kind of luck we can do without. Can you patch it?"

"I can seal the outer hull, but the inner pressure vessel is intact. No actual breach."

"That's a relief." Isaac's comment was sincere.

"Never mind the outer hull for now, Zachary. As long as the pressure vessel is intact, we're fine."

They were about eighty kilometers from base. She set course for Lakeside Deep Station at about six knots, which Isaac calculated would bring them in during the station's maintenance window, and settled back for the tedious hour of cruising. For ten minutes, the intercom crackled with the camaraderie born of survival, and gradually the vessel fell silent as each person returned to private thoughts.

Jordan wondered about the crew of the other submarine—whether any survived. Eighty kilometers to sink. That was beyond the capacity of an emergency ascent system—even if they had them. What a way to die. She wondered what she'd do in that situation. Would she wait it out, or just open her helmet.

Zachary's voice broke her reverie. "Say, Commander, I've been reading about an old technique called skip bombing. They'd attach a bomb to an aircraft and fly low at the target. They'd release the bomb and escape, and the bomb would skip into the target. You think we could modify our vessel to carry a larger warhead we could release several hundred meters out? Add a proximity fuse and a timer in case we miss. Trading shots at point-blank range like last mission is hard on my nerves, and it's happening too often."

"Nice idea. I'm not fond of those close-range battles either. Problem is, you'd have maybe one chance in a hundred of hitting anything at that distance, even if they didn't detect it and evade. You'd need a guided weapon that could chase them, with the warhead attached. And there's no way we could carry that size weapon, or launch it if we could. Someday these vessels will have proper weapons bays, and we'll have room for something like that."

"How big would a weapon like that be?"

"Two meters long, maybe thirty centimeters diameter. Mass at least one hundred fifty kilograms."

Five minutes passed before Zachary spoke again. "I've been thinking, Commander. With some modifications to the equipment bay, I think I could fit a weapon that size. We could weld a launch rail to one of the external hard points that would hold it up to four G's. After we left station, I could go outside and mount it on the rail."

"Forget it. If they caught us with unauthorized modifications, we'd be on waste reduction duty for five years. They don't want us experimenting with weapons until the experts work out all the angles and build vessels to handle them. Besides, who would rig a weapon like that without anyone finding out? And where would we get a warhead? They don't leave those lying around. Olivia Howard watches them constantly. I think she does inventory twice daily."

"Sorry, Commander. I just figured if you could get a warhead, I know some people who could rig it and keep quiet."

"Well, forget it. It's not a bad idea, but we don't have access to warheads."

"Understood, Commander."

But Jordan couldn't forget about it. All the way back to station, she kept seeing visions of a hatch opening in a sleek submersible, while a guided torpedo emerged and streaked away at high speed.

Debriefing was brief. The mission had yielded no new intelligence. Their kill made nine against eight for David King's crew, and they made sure David heard about it. They were euphoric with the elation following a successful mission, trading jokes with the squadron, reveling in being back safe.

It wasn't until she returned to her quarters and started to message her father that she remembered hearing Olivia Howard mention she was going on leave.

When she finished the message, she opened the oceanography journal she'd borrowed from Rodriguez's collection. She couldn't concentrate. She kept thinking about the weapons officer.

Olivia was quiet and dedicated, devoted to her work. Jordan wasn't particularly close to her. She wasn't a pilot, for one thing. One of those illogical but powerful distinctions that divided station personnel. And she was a bit too formal to be easy company.

Jordan remembered walking into the Crestwood Base Officer's Club with Priya Simmons. The longing that had been undisguised on Olivia's face when she first saw them. Priya was striking, direct, and liked military personnel, especially deep-sea veterans. Jordan hadn't thought about the incident since, but the look in Olivia's eyes kept returning as she tried to read.

She wasn't sure how or why she found herself walking into Captain Cox's office to request the leave she'd declined after her fiftieth mission. She'd considered taking it several times, but the thought of leaving the squadron, even briefly, had felt like abandonment.

Once she had her authorization, excitement built. As she completed her paperwork and packed her bag, her hands fumbled, and her mind was full of Priya.

The vastness of Crestwood Base was impressive as always. Rows of efficient buildings, each above its deep elevator shaft. A thriving city dedicated to the long struggle to control the deep ocean. The maintenance crew eyed them with studied indifference as they emerged from the submarine and stepped onto the dock. They requisitioned a helijet at operations and headed for Pinehurst.

Olivia had been pleased when Jordan asked if she'd like to share accommodations during leave. She was quiet during the flight, as she had been during the ascent, listening contentedly while Jordan discussed tactics and relationships with David King, another pilot on leave.

They parked at Pinehurst Field and headed for the public communication booths, picking up an entourage of children on the way. The kids followed quietly, awestruck by their uniforms.

Jordan straightened her shoulders, befitting a hero, and ruffled a couple of heads as they walked. The kids clustered around the booths as Olivia entered one to locate lodging, and Jordan another to call Priya.

"Jordan, I've been so worried. Where are you? When will I see you? Why didn't you message?..." She sputtered to a stop as Jordan held up both hands.

"Whoa. One thing at a time. I'm at the airport. You'll see me tonight. I'll explain everything then. That is, if you're free tonight. And tomorrow. And the next few days. Are you free?"

Her hesitation was brief. "Well, I had plans—with a colleague. But she'll understand. What's happening?"

Jordan took a deep breath. "I'd like to get away from the city for a few days, where we can relax away from crowds. And there's someone else I'd like to bring."

"We could take my helijet to my family's cottage at—What did you say?"

It was delicate explaining about Olivia, but when Priya understood it was just helping a friend, and she'd still have Jordan's attention, she relaxed. They made arrangements quickly and disconnected.

Jordan hesitated before calling Talia. She was remarkable to give up. Once Talia saw her with Priya, she'd be unwelcome—that was certain. It was an unhappy thought. Well, maybe it was for a good cause. She shrugged and called.

Talia nearly refused when she heard the request, but Jordan talked fast. The idea of several days at the cottage intrigued her, and when Jordan described how taken Olivia had been, she brightened and agreed. Jordan disconnected, adjusted her uniform, and stepped out.

Olivia and the kids were waiting. The weapons officer had apparently been telling them of Jordan's accomplishments. They glowed with admiration. The oldest boy, about twelve, hesitated, then asked seriously: "Would you tell us how you destroy a Collective submarine, sir?"

Jordan eyed the toy submarine that dangled from the youngster's hand. She bent and tapped it with her finger. Her voice was warm and confiding, but her eyes were distant.

"I think next we're going to try a guided torpedo," she said.

THE END
question: What advantage did the Western Alliance have over the Collective submarines in deep-sea combat?
option_a: Superior sonar range of approximately one hundred kilometers
option_b: Faster maximum speed and deeper diving capability

synthetic_story:
JULIA FINDS THE LABORATORY

I
Scientific Dialogue

"Of course, this is no surprise to us," Dr. Elena Khan said to her daughter Julia, who sat tensely on the edge of a laboratory stool. "We could hardly have helped knowing that you've wanted to be a nanotechnology researcher since you were in middle school. It's just that decisions like this can't be made quickly."

"But, Mom!" Julia almost wailed. "You just finished saying yourself that I've been thinking about this and wanting it for years! You can't follow that by calling it a quick decision!" She turned to her father, her dark eyes flashing under a mass of black curls. "Dad, you understand, don't you?"

Dr. Marcus Khan smiled gently and placed his hand on his daughter's shoulder. "Of course I understand, Julia, and so does your mother. We both want to do what's best for you, not to stand in your way. The question is whether the time is right, or if you should wait longer."

"Wait! Mom—Dad—I'm years behind already! The field is full of researchers a year and even two years younger than I am, and people my age have published papers already. Besides, what is there to wait for?"

Julia's mother set down her coffee cup and leaned back in her chair. She took her time before answering. When she finally spoke, her voice was warm and measured.

"Julia, I don't want to hold up your career. I don't have any objections to your wanting to do nanotechnology research. I think—judging from your undergraduate work and your senior thesis—that you have real talent. But I thought that if you would continue with the traditional PhD program here at Woodbridge University for five more years and get your doctorate through the conventional route, you would gain so much worthwhile knowledge that you'd use and enjoy for the rest of your life—"

"But not cutting-edge research experience!" Julia cried.

"There's more to science than that," her mother put in. "There's the theoretical foundation, the peer review process, the academic network, computational linguistics for international collaboration, and understanding corporate governance in research institutions—all of them important."

"None of them is as important as actual nanoscale engineering to me," Julia replied, "and none of them is nearly as critical to my career development."

Dr. Khan nodded. "Of course, dear. I know just how you feel about it," she said. "I would have answered the same way when I was your age, except that for me it was artificial intelligence instead of nanotechnology. But—" and here her face betrayed a trace of concern—"but the path I chose was difficult. I worked in industry for years before returning to academia, and it wasn't always smooth."

She paused and looked thoughtfully at her daughter's intense expression, then took a deep breath before going on.

"What you must realize, Julia, is that you may face setbacks. We think you're brilliant, but the field is full of young researchers whose parents thought they were geniuses; people who excelled in undergraduate programs; people who have everything except the right opportunity at the right time. You may face those challenges, and if you do, we want you to be prepared. We want you to have credentials to fall back on, just in case you ever need them."

Mr. Khan, seeing Julia's hurt look, was quick to step in with reassurance. "We don't think you're going to fail, Julia. We have every confidence in you and your abilities. I don't see how you could miss making significant contributions to the field—but I'm your father, not a grant reviewer or a lab director, and I could be wrong. And if I am wrong, I don't want you to be hurt. All I ask is that you finish your master's degree here at Woodbridge first, so that you have solid credentials. Then you can pursue this accelerated research position. Doesn't that make sense?"

Julia stared at the polished laboratory floor for a few moments before answering. Then, looking first at her mother and then at her father, she replied firmly, "No, it doesn't! It might make sense if we were talking about anything else but nanotechnology research, but we're not. If I'm ever going to make a real contribution, I'll have a better chance now than I will in two years. The field is moving too fast. But I can see your point of view, Dad, and I'll tell you what—I'll make a bargain with you."

"What sort of bargain, Julia?" her father asked curiously.

"If you let me go to Unity now, and if I can get into the Advanced Nanotechnology Institute there, I'll work on my research and complete coursework at the same time. That way I'll still be getting formal education while giving myself a chance at breakthrough work. And if I haven't made significant progress or published anything substantial in eighteen months, I'll come back and finish a traditional PhD before trying industry research again. How does that sound to you?"

"It sounds fair enough," Dr. Khan admitted, "but are you so confident that you'll see results in eighteen months? After all, some of our top researchers worked many times that long before their first major publication."

"I don't expect to revolutionize the field in eighteen months, Dad," Julia said. "I'm not that arrogant or that naive. All I hope is that I'll be able to contribute meaningfully in that time, maybe co-author a paper or two. And that's probably ambitious enough. If I have to, I'll support myself with teaching assistantships or lab work while I pursue my research. What I want to prove in this time is that I can do original work. If I can't, I'll come home."

"It seems to me, Marcus, that Julia has a pretty good idea of what she's doing," Dr. Elena Khan said. "She sounds sensible and practical. If she were all starry-eyed and expected to win a major award in a few months, I'd vote against her going, but I'm beginning to think that maybe she's right about this being the best time."

"Oh, Mother!" Julia shouted, jumping down from the stool and throwing her arms around her mother's neck. "I knew you'd understand! And you understand too, don't you, Dad?" she appealed.

Her father nodded slowly. "I never said I didn't understand you, did I?" He paused before continuing more evenly.

"Julia, your mother and I are cautious only because we love you so much and want what's going to make you happy. At the same time, we want to spare you any unnecessary disappointment along the way. Remember, I'm not a complete stranger to the challenges of research. Before I came to Woodbridge to direct the cognitive development lab, I worked at one of the best institutes in Unity. I saw a lot... I met a lot of young researchers... and I know how difficult the city often was for them. But I don't want to protect you from professional challenges. That's no good either. Just let me think about it a little longer and let me talk to your mother some more."

Dr. Elena Khan patted Julia's arm and said, "We won't keep you in suspense long, dear. Why don't you go out for a walk for a while and let us discuss this quietly? We'll decide before bedtime."

Julia nodded silently and walked to the door, where she paused to say, "I'm just going over to the greenhouse to check on my plant samples. Then maybe I'll go to Yuki's for a while."

As she stepped out into the soft evening air, she turned to look back just in time to see her mother throw her a comically exaggerated wink of assurance. Feeling much better, Julia shut the door behind her and started for the research greenhouse.

Ever since she had been an undergraduate, the greenhouse had been Julia's favorite place to think. Its humid atmosphere and the scent of soil and growing things made her feel both calm and energized. Breathing in its atmosphere gratefully, she walked into the climate-controlled space to check on her experimental samples—plants being used to test nanoscale sensors for ecosystem restoration research.

As Julia checked the moisture levels and recorded data on her tablet, she thought about her life in Woodbridge and the new life that she might soon be pursuing.

Woodbridge, Calderon, was a fine place, as pleasant a university town as any researcher could ask to grow up in. And not too small, either, Julia thought. Its population of 85,000 supported excellent schools, outstanding libraries, and a thriving research community. What's more, Woodbridge University attracted visiting scholars and hosted conferences, so that life in the town had always been intellectually stimulating.

Julia had lived here since she was ten, knew every tree-lined street near campus, every coffee shop where researchers gathered, every trail in the surrounding hills. Many of her closest friends were here, friends she had known since her undergraduate years. It would be hard to leave them, she knew, but there was no doubt in her mind that she was going to do so. If not now, then as soon as she possibly could.

It was not any dissatisfaction with her life, her friends, or her home that made Julia want to leave Woodbridge. She was not running away from anything, she reminded herself; she was running to something.

To what? To the gleaming laboratories, cutting-edge equipment, and collaborative research environment of Unity? Would it really be like she imagined? Or would it be something different, something like the competitive, isolating world of failed grants and abandoned projects that she had also heard about?

Seeing the image of herself exhausted and discouraged, going from lab to lab looking for research opportunities, Julia suddenly laughed aloud and brought herself back to reality, to the warm greenhouse air and the healthy green of her experimental plants. She touched one of the leaves gently.

"I need some grounding if I'm going to go out on my own," she murmured to herself. "A good night's sleep and some clear thinking in the morning will help!"

With a final check of her data, she left the greenhouse behind, stepping out into the deepening dusk. It was still too early to go back to the house to see if her parents had reached a decision about her future. Fighting down an impulse to rush right back to ask how they were coming along, Julia continued down the path and turned toward Yuki Ray's apartment at the end of the block.

As she walked past her own home, she noticed with a familiar tug at her heart how the light from the windows illuminated the garden her mother tended so carefully. For a moment, or maybe a little more, she wondered why she wanted to leave this. What for? What could ever be better?

II
Scientific Decision

At Yuki's apartment, Julia found her friend surrounded by books and papers, working on a literature review for her thesis in cultural sociology.

"You just finished one chapter yesterday!" Julia said. "Are you starting another one already?"

Yuki grinned, her eyes tired but bright. "I'm afraid so," she answered. "Maybe it's become an obsession!"

"It's a wonder you haven't burned out, with all the work you put in," Julia said with a laugh.

"Well, if I do burn out, at least it will be with comprehensive citations!" Yuki answered with a tired smile. She closed her laptop and stretched. "So, what brings you here? Shouldn't you be celebrating? Or are you still waiting for the verdict?"

"How do you know they haven't decided anything yet?" Julia said, in a puzzled tone.

"Oh, that didn't take much deduction," Yuki laughed. "If they had decided against the Unity position, you'd look devastated, and you don't. And if the answer was yes, you would have called me immediately. You certainly wouldn't be walking over here so calmly. So I figured that nothing was decided yet."

"You know, if I were as perceptive as you," Julia said thoughtfully, "I would have figured out a way to convince Mom and Dad by now."

"Oh, don't feel bad," Yuki said. "If I had your scientific talent, I wouldn't need social psychology skills either!" She laughed and gestured for Julia to sit down.

Julia settled into a comfortable chair and looked at her friend with a rueful smile. "You know, sometimes I think we're still just students playing at being researchers," she said. "I can hardly blame my parents for thinking twice—and a lot more—before treating me like an independent scientist."

"Nonsense!" Yuki replied firmly. "Your parents know better than to confuse caution with capability. And besides, I know they're not the least bit worried about your ability to do the work. I heard them talking with my advisor last week, and they haven't got a doubt in the world about your talent. But they know how competitive nanotechnology research can be, and they want to be sure you have credentials to fall back on if your first position doesn't work out."

"I know," Julia answered. "We had a long talk about it this evening." Then she told her friend about the conversation and her proposed "bargain" with her parents.

"They both seemed to think it was fair," she concluded, "and when I left, they were discussing it. They promised me an answer by bedtime, and I'm over here waiting. You know," she said suddenly, sitting up straighter, "I bet they wouldn't hesitate a minute if you would only change your mind and decide to come with me and work in a related field!"

After a moment's thoughtful silence, Yuki answered slowly, "No, Julia. I've thought this all out before, and I know it would be as wrong for me as it is right for you. I know we worked together on some interesting interdisciplinary projects, and I guess I contributed some useful perspectives on the social implications of nanotechnology, but I know I haven't got the real scientific drive—and I know that you have. In fact, the only scientific talent I think I do have is the ability to recognize brilliance when I see it—and to recognize when it's not there!"

"But, Yuki," Julia protested, "you understand the intersection of technology and society better than anyone I know!"

Yuki nodded, accepting the compliment while seeming to brush it off. "That doesn't matter. You know even better than I that there's a lot more to being a successful researcher than understanding concepts. There's the drive to push boundaries, the resilience to handle failure, the creativity to see what others miss. And that's something you can't learn; you either have it, or you don't. You can make people pay attention to your work the minute you present it. That's why you're going to go to Unity and become a leading researcher. And that's why I'm staying here to finish my sociology PhD."

"But, Yuki—" Julia began.

"No buts!" Yuki cut in. "We've talked about this enough before, and I'm not going to change my mind. I'm as sure about what I want as you are about what you want. I'm going to finish my doctorate and get a position teaching cultural sociology."

"And what about research? Can you get it out of your system as easily as all that?" Julia asked.

"That's the interesting part of my plan," Yuki answered with a smile. "Once I get a faculty position, I'm going to focus on studying the social impact of emerging technologies, including nanotechnology and artificial intelligence. I'm going to work with researchers like you to understand how scientific advances affect economic inequality and social structures. That way, I'll be in a position where I can use my real talents. And that way," she added, becoming more serious, "I have a chance to really contribute to understanding how science shapes society. If I can help bridge the gap between researchers and the public, then I'll feel that I've really done something worthwhile."

Julia nodded silently, not trusting herself to speak for fear of saying something overly sentimental. Her friend's clarity about her path and her faith in Julia's abilities had touched her deeply.

The silence lasted what seemed a long time, until Yuki broke it by suddenly standing up. "Come on! I'll make us some tea. By the time we're finished, it'll be about time for your big decision scene!"

It was nearly ten o'clock when Julia finally felt that her parents had had enough time to talk things through. Leaving Yuki's apartment, she walked slowly despite her eagerness, trying in all fairness to give her mother and father every minute she could. Reaching her home, she walked up the front steps to the porch. As she climbed the steps, she heard her father's voice, but she could not make out the words.

Crossing the porch, she caught sight of him through the window. He was speaking on the phone, and now she caught his words.

"Excellent. Yes.... Yes—I think we can arrange that. Very well, day after tomorrow, then. That's right—all three of us. And, Diana—it'll be good to see you again, after all these years! Goodbye."

As Julia entered the room, her father put down the phone and turned to Dr. Elena Khan. "Well, Elena," he said, "it's all arranged."

"What's all arranged, Dad?" Julia said, walking quickly to her father's side.

"Everything's arranged, Julia," her father said with a smile. "And it's arranged just the way you wanted it! There's not a scientist in the world who can hold out against two determined women." He leaned back, waiting for the explosion he felt sure was to follow his announcement. But Julia just stood, hardly moving. Then she walked carefully to the sofa and slowly sat down.

"Well, for goodness' sake!" her mother cried. "Where's the excitement?"

Julia swallowed hard before answering. When her voice came, it sounded strange, higher than usual. "I'm trying to be professional... and composed... and very mature," she said. "But it's not easy. All I want to do is to—" and she jumped up from the sofa—"to celebrate!" She let out a whoop of joy.

After the hugs and the initial excitement, Julia and her parents settled in the living room for more discussion.

"Now, tell me, Dad," Julia asked, no longer "composed" but her natural, enthusiastic self. "Who was that on the phone, and where are the three of us going, and what's all arranged?"

"One thing at a time," her father said. "To begin with, we decided shortly after you left that we were going to support your move to Unity to pursue this research opportunity. But then we had to decide where you would live, which program would be best, how we'd handle the logistics, and many other things. So I called Unity to talk to an old colleague of mine who I felt would be able to give us some guidance. Her name is Diana Roberts, and she's spent her entire career in nanotechnology research. In fact, she's now the director of the Advanced Nanotechnology Institute. I thought she might give us some advice."

"And did she?" Julia asked.

"We were luckier than I would have thought possible," Dr. Elena Khan put in. "It seems that Diana has been developing a residential program specifically for promising young researchers. The Institute has converted a historic building near campus into housing with integrated lab space. She always wanted to create a collaborative living-learning environment, and this way, she can mentor emerging scientists while they pursue advanced work. And best of all, she says she has a space available for you!"

"Oh, Mother! It sounds perfect!" Julia exulted. "I'll be with other researchers my own age, and working directly with an experienced director! I bet I can learn so much!"

"I'm sure you can," her father said. "And so can you at the Advanced Nanotechnology Institute itself."

"Dad!" Julia shouted. "Don't tell me you've managed to get me accepted there! That's the best nanotechnology research facility in the country! How—?"

"Don't get too excited, Julia," Dr. Khan interrupted. "You're not accepted anywhere yet, but Diana Roberts told me that the Institute is the best place for cutting-edge research, and she said she would arrange an interview and presentation for you in two days. The new cohort starts in a couple of weeks, so there isn't much time to lose."

"Two days! Do you mean we'll be going to Unity day after tomorrow?"

"Oh, no," her mother answered calmly. "We're going to Unity tomorrow on the first flight we can book. Your father doesn't believe in wasting time, once his mind is made up."

"Tomorrow?" Julia repeated, almost unable to believe what she had heard. "What are we sitting here talking for, then? I've got so much to do! I've got to pack... I've got to prepare my presentation! I need to review my thesis work and think about how to present it. I should look at recent publications from the Institute to understand their current research directions. Oh, Mother, what should I focus on? Where are my notes? Where's—"

"Whoa!" Dr. Khan said, catching Julia's arm to prevent her from rushing out of the room. "Not now, young lady! We'll pack in the morning, discuss your presentation strategy, and take an afternoon flight to Unity. But tonight, you'd better think of nothing more than getting some rest. This is going to be an intense time for all of us."

Reluctantly, Julia agreed, recognizing the wisdom of what her father said. She hugged her parents good night and went upstairs to her room.

But it was one thing to go to bed and another to fall asleep.

Julia lay on her back, staring at the ceiling and thinking about her research. What should she emphasize in her presentation? Which aspects of her work would be most relevant? She recognized that she had grown and developed past some of her earlier projects. But her skills had changed. She was certainly not a senior researcher yet, but neither was she just a student anymore. Her technical abilities were solid; her understanding had gained depth and nuance.

Should she focus on her work with nanoscale sensors? Or perhaps her theoretical modeling? Maybe the Institute would think she was too specialized? Maybe she should present something that showed breadth, demonstrating her understanding of how nanotechnology could address economic inequality through better resource distribution, or contribute to ecosystem restoration through environmental monitoring?

Nothing seemed quite right. Julia's thoughts raced. All the research she had ever conducted or studied seemed to blur together, until methodologies from one project seemed to merge with results from another. More ideas kept emerging until her mind was completely full. Then, gradually, her racing thoughts began to slow, her breathing deepened, the tension left her body—and Julia was fast asleep.

Galactic Governors

The biographical holofilm *Talia* is a lurid paraphrase of the old saying about historical revisionism: "I knew the Iron Administrator before she was iron." As the production tells it, she was a spirited, dark-haired colonial administrator (played by rising star Lucia Woods) given to exploring the crystalline forests of Havenbrook, Calderon with her partner (Victor Hill) between periods of detention in the Orbital Detention Complex on charges of conspiring to undermine her predecessor, the rigidly traditionalist Governor Ahmed Olson (Timothy Matthews). The daughter of a disgraced reformer executed during the Resource Wars, and therefore dubbed a radical by the corporate councils, the progressive Talia Zhang ascends to the governorship to find the atmosphere still thick with the residue of environmental disasters, a network of shadowy corporate operatives plotting her removal, and a council of advisers (mining executives, colonial bishops, sundry old guard) who sneer openly at the prospect of taking orders from someone advocating institutional reform. Only a strategic alliance with the Springfield District cartels or the Newbridge, Nordavia syndicates will mollify all factions, her advisers insist, but the options prove dismal. (Her Newbridge contact is more interested in smuggling operations than governance.) After assassination attempts are thwarted, conspirators are exiled, and reformers are martyred in the name of progress, Talia decides to: a) transform herself into a symbol of uncompromising leadership—the Iron Administrator, devoted only to colonial welfare; and b) entertain dissenting opinions exclusively from those whose loyalty has been proven beyond doubt.

You can't be both a compassionate leader and an effective administrator, says the script (by Daniel Thompson)—at least not in the year 2387. (The director, Jin Woods, made the same point in his acclaimed 2383 documentary *The Frontier Reformer*, against a backdrop of devastated mining colonies along the Outer Rim.) Is this interpretation of moral philosophy and leadership historically accurate? Probably, although the evidence suggests that Talia had developed a talent for strategic thinking earlier in life (her position had been precarious since the execution of her mother) and came to power with few idealistic illusions about How Things Work in a corrupt colonial system.

That said, the production's approach makes for compelling drama. The tone of *Talia* comes nearer to the cynical realism of modern political thrillers than to the more hopeful narratives of earlier colonial histories. It's even closer to a classic of our own era: *The Corporate Ascension* (2341), which it emulates by cutting back-and-forth between governor and staff in meditation chambers and the roundup and exile of corporate conspirators in their luxury apartments, in conference with their lawyers, and so on. Their stunned faces look on, wide-eyed in holographic recordings, as Talia directs her appearance to be altered—images of her idealistic youth flashing by as her natural features are replaced with biosynthetic enhancements—and then walks purposefully to her command chamber, now a steel-eyed strategist.

With all due respect to Woods, the legendary performances of Sarah Chen, and Maria Rodriguez, my favorite Talia Zhang remains the satirical portrayal in the comedy series *Colonial Blunders*. (Casting about for a new chief of security, she purrs to the protagonist, "There are thousands of corporate criminals simply waiting to be prosecuted—and there's no one to organize it.") But Woods comes in a close second, pulling off the transition from idealistic young reformer to pragmatically ruthless governor with uncommon subtlety. Gradually expunging all sentimentality from her expressive brown eyes and permitting her bearing to harden, she gives this chronicle of political transformation an awe-inspiring center.

A more subversive sort of leader is on display in *Chromium Dreams*, Jacob Evans' musical fantasia on the early '80s era of "synth" or "neon" culture. Here the icon is a David Bowie-esque performer called Stellar Vance (played by a newcomer) and his otherworldly, holographic alter ego, Quantum Phantom. The film opens with a transport ship depositing an infant Oscar Wilde on the landing pad of a Dalebrook, Zelvaria settlement. Then it skips ahead to track a jade medallion (it signifies artistic liberation) from the custody of a young Wilde to an eccentric fringe artist called Nova Spark to the celebrated Vance, a pansexual superstar who carries the message to all the young colonists. After that, we're in an Orwellian 2420 that's presided over by a vaguely authoritarian Earth Council and by corporate entertainment moguls who serve as propagandists for a repressively conformist society. Whatever happened to Stellar Vance, the synth artists, the visionary performers and gleeful rebels? Borrowing its framework from *Citizen Kane*, the film follows a journalist (another character) assigned to reconstruct Vance's life and solve the mystery of his disappearance.

Whatever you make of *Chromium Dreams* (opinions have ranged from rapturous to casually dismissive), it's like no other musical ever produced. It's determinedly swirling, discursive, elliptical. Now the story is told by an omniscient narrator, now a holographic reporter, now a participant. Now it's flashing back, now forward. Every other line of dialogue is a cue for one of its dazzling numbers, largely covers of songs by Brian Eno, Bryan Ferry, and T. Rex adapted for the 24th century. The narrative is a challenge to keep up with, but then, great artists often invent their own syntax. In the '80s, Evans employed AI-generated avatars to depict the rise and mental deterioration of the singer Karen Carpenter. Lucky audiences who caught *Superstar: The Karen Carpenter Story* (it was archived when intellectual property disputes arose) began by laughing at this elaborately rendered, soft-synth performer, only to discover by the climax that the cultural forces that were consuming her had grown heartbreakingly palpable. *Toxin* (2391), Evans' Genêt-inspired exploration of transgression, didn't overcome its own artiness. But *Isolated* (2395), the story of a corporate-era colonist convinced that her environment is poisoning her, is an entrancing meditation on environmental justice and the power of culture to crush the individual. Despite its ironic detachment, the film draws you into its heroine's deteriorating state: Breathing filtered air from a containment unit inside a high-tech habitat, she dwindles to nearly nothing, the modern incarnation of the Incredible Shrinking Man.

(It was partly my passion for Evans' films that led me to accept a job offer from his indefatigable producer Christine Vachon last year to collaborate on a practical guide about producing, *Shooting To Kill*. So my review of *Chromium Dreams*—like my review of Vachon's other recent release, *Contentment*—should be read as the work of a partisan. But not a blind partisan.)

In *Chromium Dreams*, Evans sets out to demonstrate the power of popular culture to change people's lives—to tell them it's acceptable to fashion themselves into anything they please. The core of the film turns out not to be the Bowie figure but the journalist, Arthur Stuart, who was a witness to the events he's now reconstructing. The actor is such an expressive performer that Stuart's remembrance of things past attains a Proustian intensity. To him, Vance was a cultural messiah. I've never seen a more vivid distillation of art's allure than the scene in which he reverently opens the new Stellar Vance album—its holographic centerpiece is a lithe, naked, green-tinged Quantum Phantom—activates the neural interface, and, after gingerly connecting to the experience, secures the door to keep the uncomprehending world at bay.

But if Evans wants *Chromium Dreams* to be an anthem to the principles Bowie once embodied—the embrace of artifice and the smashing of conventional social dynamics—he also wants to portray the performer as a hollow opportunist who abandoned synth culture and pansexuality for the life of a corporate superstar, throwing in his lot with the forces of repression. That's a lot to cover. An actor of stature might have bridged these two impulses, but the beautiful, brazenly androgynous newcomer doesn't make his lines sound as if he's thinking them up on the spot, and Vance's self-destructive passion for Kurt Savage (another performer), the film's fuzzy, sweet Iggy Pop figure, seems less an emotional imperative than a thematic one.

A case can be made that *Chromium Dreams* isn't fully filled in, and that Evans, who has never shaken off his background as a semiotics major, has made a film that's all signifiers. I sometimes found myself wishing he would let the picture catch its breath, that the performers would stop coming at me in stroboscopic flashes. But then I'd be swept up in the sinuous motion of his filmmaking, in the elation of watching point of view passed like a baton from hand to hand, in the liberating force of his language and soundtrack. *Chromium Dreams* might seem like a collection of baubles, but those baubles are strung.

Is Brad Pitt the worst actor in the galaxy? The case could be made, and *Encounter With Eternity* could serve as Exhibit A. Pitt plays two roles in this seven-course schlockfest. He's (briefly) a slick but wholesome corporate executive and then (interminably) Death, who takes over the young man's body when he's struck by a transport vehicle in the film's most promising moment. Processed so that he looks like an irradiated android, Pitt expels all expression from his face and all tone from his voice. He speaks very, very slowly. The stunt half-works, at least until he's supposed to undergo an inner transformation and acquire human emotions—whereupon his face remains just as blank. Pitt's conception of the role is an idée fixe by someone who doesn't appear to have an idée in his head.

Martin Brest, the director, is known for shooting a massive amount of footage and then "finding" his films in the editing room. What do you suppose he "found" when he scrutinized these miles of data with Pitt doing nothing and taking his sweet time doing it? The first adaptation of this story (originally a play) was the 1934 *Death Takes a Holiday*, which came in at a perky 78 minutes. A conceit this fragile needs to move along briskly to keep our disbelief in suspension, but *Encounter With Eternity* grinds on for three hours (longer than either *Beloved* or *Saving Private Ryan*), and Pitt acts as if he has leased the screen by the century.

Anthony Hopkins plays the trillionaire communications baron whom Death enlists in the hope of understanding the human condition—an odd choice for a tour guide, since most people's condition doesn't involve personal spacecraft, sprawling estates on orbital platforms, or apartments that sport Olympic-size zero-gravity pools. Four screenwriters, among them the great Bo Goldman (*Melvin and Howard*, 1980; *Shoot the Moon*, 1982), labored on this moldy script, which features characters who ask questions that begin "Am I to understand that...?" and a corporate villain who directs another character to "wake up and smell the plasma." It apparently never occurred to even one of these overpaid scribes to eliminate Hopkins' rueful realization that he'd "never write the great Galactic novel"—no kidding, given his flagrantly Earth accent.

Actually, Hopkins gives this humanistic magnate considerable weight, so that whether or not Death takes him before he can stop to appreciate life and make amends to his neglected children becomes a matter of some suspense. The rest of the cast works with equal fortitude, especially Jeffrey Tambor (Hank "Hey now!" Kingsley on *The Larry Sanders Show*) as Hopkins' milksop son-in-law and Marcia Gay Harden as his event-planning, perpetually wilting elder daughter. As the younger daughter, the dark-eyed, ethereally thin Claire Forlani has to carry the picture's bathos on her exquisite shoulders. Her tremulous thoroughbred act wears thin, but it's hardly her fault: She has to emote like mad opposite a black pit of death—or is that the Black Death of Pitt?

The question of decision-making in leadership contexts pervades all three films, though each approaches it from a different angle. *Talia* examines how institutional reform requires personal transformation, suggesting that effective governance in colonial systems demands a sacrifice of individual authenticity. The film's historical interpretation may be debatable, but its emotional truth resonates: power corrupts, or at least hardens, those who wield it responsibly.

*Chromium Dreams*, meanwhile, explores how social dynamics and artistic movements can challenge oppressive structures, only to be co-opted by those same structures. Evans' use of music as a vehicle for examining questions of identity and conformity places the film squarely in the tradition of social commentary disguised as entertainment. The peer review of this film has been mixed, with some critics finding its fragmented narrative style alienating while others praise its ambitious scope.

*Encounter With Eternity*, despite its flaws, attempts to grapple with questions of mortality and meaning in a universe where wealth and technology have seemingly conquered all obstacles except death itself. The film's failure lies not in its themes but in its execution—specifically, in Pitt's somnambulant performance and the bloated runtime that suggests the filmmakers couldn't distinguish between profundity and pretension.

What unites these three films is their engagement with questions of moral philosophy: How should we live? What responsibilities do leaders bear to those they govern? Can art change society, or does society inevitably change art? These are timeless questions, rendered in contemporary (or futuristic) settings that make them feel urgent and relevant.

The treatment of mentorship in *Chromium Dreams* deserves particular attention. The relationship between Stellar Vance and his younger followers illustrates how cultural icons can inspire transformation in their audiences, even as they themselves remain trapped by the expectations they've created. This dynamic mirrors the relationship between Talia and her supporters in the biographical film—both leaders find themselves constrained by the very symbols they've become.

Environmental justice, though not the central theme of any of these films, lurks in the background of *Talia*, where the devastated landscapes of colonial mining operations serve as a constant reminder of the costs of unchecked exploitation. The film suggests that natural resource management and social welfare are inseparable concerns, and that leaders who ignore this connection do so at their peril.

In the end, these films—flawed as some of them are—represent ambitious attempts to grapple with the complexities of leadership, identity, and social change. They remind us that cinema, even science fiction cinema, can serve as a vehicle for exploring the most fundamental questions of human existence. Whether set in Elizabethan England, the glam rock era, or the distant future of colonial space, these stories resonate because they touch on universal themes that transcend their specific settings.

The craft of filmmaking itself becomes a subject of contemplation when watching these works. The organizational development required to produce films of this scope and ambition is staggering—hundreds of artists and technicians collaborating to create a unified vision. When that vision succeeds, as it largely does in *Talia* and *Chromium Dreams*, the result justifies the enormous investment of resources and talent. When it fails, as in *Encounter With Eternity*, the waste feels almost tragic.

Climate adaptation, both literal and metaphorical, emerges as a theme in these futuristic narratives. The characters must adapt to changing political climates, shifting cultural norms, and in some cases, actual environmental catastrophes. Their success or failure in adapting determines not just their own fates but the fates of entire societies.

International diplomacy—or in the case of *Talia*, interplanetary diplomacy—provides the backdrop for much of the political maneuvering in these films. The negotiations, alliances, and betrayals that characterize relations between different factions and territories drive the plots forward and create the conflicts that the protagonists must resolve.

Conflict resolution, ultimately, is what these films are about. Whether the conflict is between tradition and reform, conformity and individuality, or mortality and meaning, the characters must find ways to navigate these tensions. Their methods—compromise, transformation, resistance, or acceptance—reveal their characters and shape their destinies.

The Geologists of Titan's Edge

By the expedition log of Dr. Li Ramos
Recorded at Dalebrook Station, Aldoria Sector

There were two crystalline formations on the tiny plateau that shouldn't have existed.

To understand the geological mystery of Titan's Edge, one must consider three elements: the observer, the phenomenon, and the catalyst. All three existed on this remote moon, but there was a question as to their true nature.

The fourth day of the *Horizon Explorer's* landing on the tidally-locked moon orbiting the gas giant Prometheus was a repetition of the three before it—a twelve-hour cycle of eerie, phosphorescent twilight. Geologist Dr. Li Ramos—standing her rotation on monitoring duty—sat at the observation dome with her spectrographic scanner ready; but despite her vigilance, she had captured no useful data when the inevitable pre-shift luminescence began to shimmer over the methane sea to the east.

The cycle change brought her alert with a start, frowning at the sight of two meter-tall crystalline formations standing on the tiny basalt plateau a half-kilometer from shore, their geometric faces oriented precisely toward the research station.

"They're back again," Ramos called, and climbed down from the dome. "Everyone up! I'm going to run a full spectral analysis this time!"

Walter Gutierrez and Timothy Kelly emerged from their rest pods reluctantly, fastening the thermal suits required even in Titan's Edge's carefully regulated artificial atmosphere. Gutierrez blinked as he cycled through the airlock, his gray beard frosted with condensation and his rounded frame moving stiffly. He looked, Ramos thought for the hundredth time, more like a retired university dean than the veteran commander of a Terran Geological Survey expedition.

Kelly followed, his lean athletic build moving with the careful precision of someone trained in extreme-environment protocols. Kelly was the team's xenomineralogist, a man in his late twenties with sharp features and an intensity that sometimes bordered on obsessive.

"Any sign of the silicon-based organisms yet?" he asked.

"They won't emerge until the crystal-eaters arrive," Ramos said. She adjusted the wavelength filter of her scanner and frowned at Gutierrez. "Walter, I wish you'd let me take core samples this time. This cycle of destruction is affecting our data quality."

Gutierrez shielded his eyes against the glare of Prometheus rising over the methane sea. "You know I can't authorize that, Li. These formations may represent a form of proto-intelligence or higher, and under Terran Survey Protocols, our interference with what may be a fundamental geological process would violate every principle of scientific collaboration. We need to crack the chemical communication patterns and understand the ecosystem restoration cycle before we can intervene."

Ramos turned an irritated stare toward the cluster of smaller crystalline structures gathering at the edge of the sulfur-dioxide frost fields that bordered the landing site.

"What puzzles me is the pattern," she said. "Why do these formations migrate to that plateau every cycle, when the outcome is always the same?"

Kelly answered with his own persistent mystery, his angular face troubled. "For that matter, what happened to the city I detected during our orbital survey? The electromagnetic signatures suggested a massive structure, yet we've mapped this entire moon in the rover and found nothing but methane seas and scattered plateaus like this one, all covered in mineral deposits. The architecture I detected wasn't something these crystal formations could have created. The complexity was beyond anything natural by orders of magnitude."

Gutierrez and Ramos exchanged weary looks. The city had become an obsession with Kelly, and his stubborn insistence—coupled with an annoying habit of being proven right—had worn their patience thin.

"There never was a city here, Tim," Gutierrez said. "You misinterpreted the data during orbital insertion, that's all."

Kelly stiffened defensively, but Ramos's voice cut through. "Get ready! Here they come!"

Out of the luminescent haze descended a swarm of silicon-based flyers, each three meters across and gleaming with metallic compounds in the dim light. They dove like raptors upon the plateau, engulfing the two crystalline formations instantly under their grinding, abrading appendages. Then around the outcrop, the ground erupted violently, churned up by a sudden emergence of dark, tentacled shapes composed of living polymer chains.

"The silicon-eaters," Gutierrez muttered. "Right on schedule. Two seconds too late, as always, to prevent the destruction."

A barrage of chemical tendrils lashed out from the emerging organisms and struck into the swarm of flyers. The flyers retreated immediately into the haze, leaving behind three of their number who were pulled beneath the surface like trapped insects. No trace remained of the two crystalline formations.

"A perfect example of predator-prey dynamics," Ramos said, deactivating her scanner. "Do any of those entities look like city-builders to you, Tim?"

The smaller crystalline structures drifted past from the shelter of the frost fields, seemingly oblivious to the researchers, and arranged themselves along the mineral-rich ledges near the methane sea to begin their photosynthetic cycle.

"Nothing we've observed fits the technological signatures I detected," Kelly said stubbornly. "But the source is here somewhere, and I'm going to find it. Will either of you need the rover today?"

Gutierrez raised his hands in surrender. "I have mountains of geological data to process, and Li is off duty after her monitoring shift. Take the rover, but you won't find anything."

The rover was a distant speck on the horizon when Ramos entered her rest pod a short time later, leaving Gutierrez to organize his collection of samples. Sleep eluded her initially; a vague sense of overlooked details nagged at her consciousness, but it wasn't until drowsiness finally claimed her that the discrepancy crystallized into clarity.

She recalled then that on the first day of the *Explorer's* landing, one of the crystal formations had fallen from a ledge into a methane pool and had dissolved rapidly before the polymer organisms could extract it with their tendrils. Which meant that the formations couldn't survive in liquid methane—otherwise some would surely have adapted to that environment.

And the expedition had surveyed Titan's Edge exhaustively without finding any mechanism for the formations to traverse the methane sea. The logical chain completed itself automatically, nearly jolting Ramos from her drowsy state.

"Impossible," she muttered. "No traversal mechanism, and they can't survive the sea. *Then how do they reach that plateau?*"

She fell asleep with the paradox unresolved.

Gutierrez was still hunched over his sample analysis when Ramos emerged from her pod and extracted a nutrition pack from the storage unit. The communication panel above the control console hummed softly, its display blank on open channel.

"Has Kelly located his phantom city yet?" Ramos asked, grinning when Gutierrez snorted.

"He's scanning the sunward hemisphere now," Gutierrez said. "Li, I'm going to ground Tim tomorrow, despite my reluctance to issue direct orders. He's fixated on that electromagnetic anomaly, and he lacks the perspective to understand how dangerous such an obsession can be to our mission parameters."

Ramos shrugged. "I'd normally agree, except for Tim's frustrating tendency to be correct. I hope he finds it soon, if it exists. I'll probably be covering his monitoring shifts until he's satisfied."

Gutierrez looked relieved. "Would you mind taking tonight's shift? I'm exhausted after processing today's samples."

Ramos gestured agreement and gathered her scanning equipment. Darkness had fallen outside—the deep, absolute darkness of Titan's Edge's shadow side, where Prometheus's bulk blocked all light from the distant sun. She positioned her chair at the observation dome and activated her data pad, settling in comfortably while Gutierrez prepared a sleep aid before retiring.

Later she would remember that Gutierrez had taken a sedative, but at the moment it seemed routine. Within minutes, his gentle snoring drifted through the station, a sound faintly irritating against the absolute silence outside.

Ramos reviewed her notes and returned to the inconsistencies she'd identified. The formations couldn't survive methane immersion, and without any traversal mechanism...

It occurred to her then that there had been precisely two formations on the plateau each cycle, and the consistency made her sit up abruptly, startled. Why two? Why not three or four, or only one?

She cycled through the airlock and paced restlessly on the processed landing pad, feeling the artificial atmosphere's warmth against her face. Four days of routine monitoring had built up a need for direct investigation that chafed at her scientific discipline; she was intrigued and simultaneously frustrated by the enigmatic relationship linking the crystal formations to the flyers and polymer organisms, and her desire to understand that relationship was intensified by the knowledge that Titan's Edge could provide crucial insights into biodiversity conservation principles. That is, she thought wryly, if Terran scientists could rationalize the bizarre cycle pursued by its indigenous life forms—what appeared to be deliberate self-sacrifice in pairs.

She reviewed again the improbable drama of the past four cycles, and found it scientifically explicable until she reached the question of motivation and the transportation mechanism that placed the formations in pairs on the plateau, when her entire framework of hypothesis collapsed into contradictions. She abandoned the effort finally; how could any human scientist rationalize the alien imperatives that drove such fundamentally different forms of existence?

She returned inside, and the sound of Gutierrez's muffled snoring aggravated her restlessness. She made her decision impulsively, setting aside the scanner for a portable light and a pocket-sized communicator which she clipped to her thermal suit.

She didn't select any defensive equipment because she saw no need for it. The light would reveal how the formations reached the outcrop, and if she required assistance the communicator would summon Gutierrez. Investigating without Gutierrez's authorization was, technically speaking, a violation of Survey Protocols, but—

"Damn the protocols," she muttered. "I need to *understand*."

Ramos activated the light at the edge of the frost field and proceeded carefully, eager for discovery now that she'd committed to action. Just inside the mineral deposits she encountered a pair of small crystalline structures, dormant and stable, their geometric faces completely blank and unrevealing.

She worked deeper into the field and found other dormant pairs, but nothing else. There were no atmospheric disturbances, no thermal variations, no electromagnetic anomalies. She had penetrated close to the field's center without further discovery and was preparing to return, disappointed, when something massive and powerful seized her from behind.

A sharp cold burned through her thermal suit at the shoulder, and a sudden overwhelming numbness swept her into unconsciousness deeper than Titan's Edge's darkness. Her last conscious thought wasn't of her own danger, but of Gutierrez—sedated and unprotected in the station...

She was standing upright when consciousness returned, her back to the methane sea and a prismatic shimmer of cycle-change luminescence reflecting on the liquid surface before her. For a moment she was completely disoriented; then peripherally she detected the crystalline blur of a formation standing beside her, and cried out in panic when she tried to turn her head and couldn't.

She was on the basalt plateau offshore, and except for autonomic functions of balance and respiration, her body was paralyzed.

The first glow of Prometheus-rise blurred the reflected luminescence at her feet, but for several seconds her racing mind was too occupied to consider the implications of her predicament. *Whatever transported me here immobilized me first*, she thought. *That cold at my shoulder was like a chemical injection.*

Panic seized her again when she remembered the silicon-based flyers; more seconds passed before she regained control, her suit's thermal regulation system straining against her fear-induced temperature spike. She had to get help. If she could activate the communicator at her belt and call Gutierrez...

She focused every ounce of concentration toward raising her right hand, and failed.

Her arm felt like solid metal, its inertia impossible to overcome. She released the effort with a groan, anxiety rising again when she saw Prometheus's bright curve on the methane sea, edges distorted by surface tension waves.

On shore she could see the *Horizon Explorer* resting between frost field and landing pad, its composite hull gleaming with condensation. The airlock remained open, and the empty rover dock told her that Kelly hadn't yet returned.

She realized then that sensation was gradually returning, that the cold surface of the communicator unit at her hip—previously unfelt—was now pressing against her forearm. She concentrated again on movement; this time her arm responded slightly, enough to send hope surging through her. If she could apply sufficient pressure to the activation stud...

The tiny click of its engagement left her weak with relief.

"Gutierrez!" she called. "Walter, emergency—*Gutierrez*!"

The communicator hummed quietly, without response.

She gathered herself for another call, and remembered with horror the sedative Gutierrez had taken before retiring. Exhausted by his work, Gutierrez had ensured he wouldn't be easily disturbed.

Prometheus's curve on the sea brightened and expanded. Above its reflected glow she detected movement, a restless suggestion of approaching flyers.

She tried again. "Gutierrez, help me! I'm on the plateau!"

The communicator crackled. The voice that answered wasn't Gutierrez's, but Kelly's.

"Ramos! What are you doing on that killing ground?"

Ramos suppressed an hysterical laugh. "Never mind that—get here immediately, Tim! The flyers—"

She stopped, seeing for the first time the polymer organisms that surrounded the plateau just beneath the surface, waiting with chemical tendrils extended and sensor nodes studying her with alien awareness. She heard the unmistakable sound of approaching flyers behind and above her then, and thought with shock-induced clarity: *I wanted to observe this phenomenon, and now I'm part of it*.

The rover roared in from the west across the frost field, passing so close overhead that she felt the turbulence of its passage. Almost instantly she heard the high-pitched whine of its emergency thrusters as Kelly intercepted the flyer swarm directly.

Kelly's voice came through the communicator. "Dispersed them temporarily, Li—disrupted their navigation with the thruster wash, I think. Hold position. I'm retrieving you now."

The rover settled on the plateau beside Ramos, so close that the heat from its exhaust system warmed her legs through the thermal suit. Kelly extended his arms and pulled her inside like a mannequin, ignoring the crystal formation. The rover accelerated toward shore with Ramos lying across Kelly's lap in the cockpit, her head hanging partially outside.

Ramos had a final disorienting glimpse of the plateau against the blur of methane sea below, and felt her shaky laugh of relief catch in her throat. Two of the polymer organisms were moving strongly toward shore, holding the rigid crystal formation carefully above the liquid surface between them.

"Tim," Ramos croaked. "Tim, can you look back? I think I'm hallucinating."

The rover swerved briefly as Kelly glanced back. "You're fine, Li. Just stay calm. I'll explain everything when we get you safely to the *Explorer*."

Ramos forced herself to relax, more relieved than alarmed by the painful tingling of returning sensation. "I should have known, damn you," she said. "You found your city, didn't you?"

Kelly moved to seal the airlock, blocking out the dim luminescence. "Research operations being prohibited, we should depart before the polymer organisms become sufficiently curious about us to create complications. Can you handle the acceleration, Li?"

Ramos and Gutierrez looked at each other, understanding dawning. Ramos said: "You don't think I want to remain here and be used as bait again, do you?"

The city, built by an ancient crystal-based civilization before geological subsidence flooded the lowlands, had been preserved by the polymer-people as a monument to their predecessors. In their own chemical communication system—incomprehensible to humans—they had been trying to convey a simple message: *We remember those who came before.
