THE SAPPHIRE INITIATIVE
BY KEITH LAUMER

It was a simple cultural exchange—but Sebastian Knight gave them more of an education than they expected!

I

Deputy Administrator Michelle Peterson took her embroidered shawl and jade pendant from the wall hook. "I'm off now, Sebastian," she said. "I hope you'll manage the administrative routine during my absence without any unfortunate incidents."

"That seems a modest enough hope," Sebastian said. "I'll try to live up to it."

"I don't appreciate frivolity with reference to this Division," Michelle said testily. "When I first came here, the Cultural Heritage and Environmental Development Directorate was a shambles. I fancy I've made CHED what it is today. Frankly, I question the wisdom of placing you in charge of such a sensitive desk, even for two weeks. But remember. Yours is purely a rubber-stamp function."

"In that case, let's leave it to Ms. Chen. I'll take a couple of weeks off myself. With her experience, she could bring plenty of expertise to bear."

"I assume you jest, Sebastian," Michelle said sadly. "I should expect even you to appreciate that Zenithian participation in the Cultural Exchange Program may be the first step toward sublimation of their industrial aggressions into more sustainable channels."

"I see they're sending three thousand artisans to Greenfield Territory," Sebastian said, glancing at the Memo for Record. "That's a sizable sublimation."

Michelle nodded. "The Zenithians have launched no less than five mining campaigns in the last two decades. They're known as the Strip-Miners of the Proxima Sector. Now, perhaps, we shall see them breaking that precedent and entering into the cultural life of the Coalition."

"Breaking and entering," Sebastian said. "You may have something there. But I'm wondering what they'll study in Greenfield Territory. That's an agricultural world of the poor but honest variety."

"Academic details are the affair of the artisans and their mentors," Michelle said. "Our function is merely to bring them together. See that you don't antagonize the Zenithian representative. This will be an excellent opportunity for you to practice your diplomatic restraint—not your strong point, I'm sure you'll agree."

A buzzer sounded. Sebastian punched a button. "What is it, Ms. Chen?"

"That—rustic person from Parkview is here again." On the small desk screen, Ms. Chen's stern features were compressed in disapproval.

"This fellow's a confounded pest. I'll leave him to you, Sebastian," Michelle said. "Tell him something. Get rid of him. And remember: here at Coalition HQ, all eyes are upon you."

"If I'd thought of that, I'd have worn my other jacket," Sebastian said.

Michelle snorted and passed from view. Sebastian punched Ms. Chen's button.

"Send the rustic person in."

A tall broad woman with sun-darkened skin and silver-streaked hair, wearing practical trousers of heavy canvas, a loose tunic open at the collar and a short vest, stepped into the room. She had a bundle under her arm. She paused at sight of Sebastian, looked him over momentarily, then advanced and held out her hand. Sebastian took it. For a moment the two stood, face to face. The newcomer's jaw muscles knotted. Then she winced.

Sebastian dropped her hand and motioned to a chair.

"That's nice grip work, mister," the stranger said, massaging her hand. "First time anybody ever did that to me. My fault though. I started it, I guess." She grinned and sat down.

"What can I do for you?" Sebastian said.

"You work for this Cultural Heritage bunch, do you? Funny. I thought they were all bureaucrats. Never mind. I'm Isabella Wyatt. I'm a farmer. What I wanted to see you about was—" She shifted in her chair. "Well, out in Parkview, Xandria we've got a serious problem. The sapphire harvest is just about ready. We start gathering in another two, three months. Now I don't know if you're familiar with the Crystal Sapphire plants we cultivate...?"

"No," Sebastian said. "Have a drink?" He pushed a carafe across the desk. Isabella took it. "Crystal Sapphires are an unusual crop," she said, pouring water into a glass. "Only mature every fifteen years. In between, the plants don't need a lot of attention, so our time's mostly our own. We like to farm, though. Spend a lot of time developing new forms. Vegetables the size of a boulder—and delicious—"

"Sounds very pleasant," Sebastian said. "Where does the Cultural Heritage and Environmental Development Division come in?"

Isabella leaned forward. "We go in pretty heavy for the visual arts. Folks can't spend all their time hybridizing plants. We've turned all the land area we've got into parks and farms. Course, we left some sizable forest areas for wildlife preservation and such. Parkview's a nice place, Mr. Knight."

"It sounds like it, Ms. Wyatt. Just what—"

"Call me Isabella. We've got long seasons back home. Six of 'em. Our year's about twenty-two Terra months. Cold as ice in winter; eccentric orbit, you know. Purple-black sky, stars visible all day. We do mostly sculpture and pottery in the winter. Then Spring; still plenty cold. Lots of ice-sailing, snow-trekking, aurora watching; and it's the season for glassworkers. Our crystal work—"

"I've seen some of your crystal work," Sebastian said. "Beautiful pieces."

Isabella nodded. "All local minerals too. Lots of rare earths in our soil and those compounds give the crystals some color, I'll tell you. Then comes the Bloom Season. Flowers—they cover everything. But the sun's getting closer. Shines all the time. Ever seen it with flowers blooming in perpetual daylight? That's the music-composing season. Then summer. Summer's warm. We stay outside most of the time and have community gatherings all night. Lots of open spaces in Parkview; we're mostly valleys and plains. That's the dance and theater time. The stages are set up in the meadows, or on the hillsides. You have the performances and the wildflowers and the bonfires and stars—we're close to the center of a stellar nursery, you know...."

"You say it's time now for the sapphire harvest?"

"That's right. Autumn's our harvest season. Most years we have just the ordinary crops. Grains, tubers, that kind of thing; getting it in doesn't take long. We spend most of the time on architecture, getting new places ready for the winter or renovating the older ones. We spend a lot of time in our dwellings. We like to have them comfortable. But this year's different. This is Sapphire Year."

Isabella sipped her water, looked worriedly at Sebastian. "Our sapphire crop is our big money crop," she said. "We make enough to keep us going. But this year...."

"The crop isn't panning out?"

"Oh, the crop's fine. One of the best I can remember. Course, I'm only thirty-five; I can't remember but two other harvests. The problem's not the crop."

"Have you lost your markets? That sounds like a matter for the Commercial—"

"Lost our markets? Mister, nobody that ever saw our sapphires ever settled for anything else!"

"It sounds like I've been missing something," said Sebastian. "I'll have to see them some time."

Isabella put her bundle on the desk, pulled off the wrappings. "No time like the present," she said.

Sebastian looked at the two crystalline samples, one azure blue, one deep violet, both gleaming with inner light.

"Accepting gifts on duty is frowned on in the Coalition, Ms. Wyatt," he said.

"This isn't a gift. It's just samples." Isabella smiled. "Besides, my feelings would be hurt if you didn't look at them properly." She winked.

Sebastian took a jeweler's loupe from a drawer beside the desk. "Come to think of it, we also have to be careful about violating cultural heritage protocols."

Isabella held up the blue crystal. Sebastian examined it through the loupe, noting the perfect internal structure, then studied it with the naked eye. He looked at Isabella thoughtfully.

"Hmmm. The refraction patterns are extraordinary. Like looking into a living ocean."

"Don't try to describe it, Mr. Knight," Isabella said. She held up the violet crystal. "The custom back home is to view both colors in sequence."

Sebastian examined the second crystal. "Bad luck if you don't appreciate both," Isabella said, nodding. "You probably never heard about the trouble we had in Parkview a few years back?"

"Can't say that I did, Isabella." Sebastian set down the loupe. "Beautiful work."

"We've got plenty of minerals in Parkview," Isabella said. "But we don't plan to wreck the landscape mining 'em. We like to farm and create art. About twelve years back some neighbors of ours landed a force. They figured they knew better what to do with our minerals than we did. Wanted to strip-mine, process ore industrially. We convinced 'em otherwise. But it took a year, and we lost a lot of people."

"That's too bad," Sebastian said. "Environmental justice is a serious matter."

"It put us in a bad spot," Isabella went on. "We had to borrow money from a world called Bayview Territory. Mortgaged our fields. Had to start exporting art work too. Plenty of buyers, but it's not the same when you're doing it for strangers."

"Say, these crystals are remarkable," Sebastian said. "What's the problem? Bayview about to foreclose?"

"Well, the loan's due. The sapphire crop would put us in the clear. But we need harvest hands. Gathering Crystal Sapphires isn't a job you can turn over to machinery—and anyway we wouldn't if we could. Harvest season is the high point of living in Parkview. Everybody joins in. First, there's the gathering in the fields. Miles and miles of crystal gardens covering the valley floors, and climbing the hillsides, with meditation spaces here and there. Tall plants, ten feet high, loaded with crystals, and deep moss growing between. The water-carriers keep on the run, bringing refreshment to the gatherers. There's prizes for the biggest day's output, competitions for who can fill the most baskets in an hour.... The sun's high and bright, and it's just cool enough to give you plenty of energy. Come nightfall, the tables are set up in the garden plots, and the feast is laid on: roasted game, cultivated proteins, grain dishes, all kinds of preparations. Big salads. Plenty of fruit. Fresh-baked bread ... and crystal-clear water from the mountain springs. The cooking's done by a different crew each night in each garden, and there's prizes for the best crews.

"Then the crystal-processing. We still hand-polish each stone. That's mostly for the young folks but anybody's welcome. That's when things start to get creative. Matter of fact, pretty near half our artistic collaborations start after a harvest. All formality is dropped then. It keeps a person inspired though. Ever tried to polish a crystal while working side by side with someone who shares your vision?"

"Never did," Sebastian said. "You say most of the artistic collaborations start after a harvest. That would make the participants only fifteen years old by the time—"

"Oh, that's Parkview years; they'd be twenty-three, Terra reckoning."

"I was thinking you looked a little mature for thirty-five," Sebastian said.

"Fifty-two, Terra years," Isabella said. "But this year it looks bad. We've got a bumper crop—and we're short-handed. If we don't get a big harvest, Bayview steps in. Lord knows what they'll do to the land. Then next harvest time, with them holding half our crystal acreage—"

"You mortgaged the gardens?"

"Yep. Pretty foolish, huh? But we figured fifteen years was a long time."

"What we figured was, maybe you Cultural Heritage people could help us out. A loan to see us through the harvest, enough to hire extra hands. Then we'd repay it in sculpture, paintings, crystal work—"

"Sorry, Isabella. All we do here is work out itineraries for traveling exhibitions, that kind of thing. Now, if you needed a troupe of Andromedan light-dancers—"

"Can they gather crystals?"

"Nope. Anyway, they can't work in daylight. Have you talked this over with the Labor Office?"

"Sure did. They said they'd fix us up with all the digital transformation specialists and climate technology programmers we wanted—but no field hands. Said it was what they classified as menial drudgery; you'd have thought I was trying to buy slaves."

The buzzer sounded. Ms. Chen's features appeared on the desk screen.

"You're due at the Intergroup Council in five minutes," she said. "Then afterwards, there are the Zenithian artisans to meet."

"Thanks." Sebastian stood. "I have to run, Isabella," he said. "Let me think this over. Maybe I can come up with something. Check with me day after tomorrow. And you'd better leave the samples here. Cultural exhibits, you know."

II

As the council meeting broke up, Sebastian caught the eye of a colleague across the table.

"Mr. Hassan, you mentioned a shipment going to a place called Bayview Territory. What are they getting?"

Hassan blinked. "You're the fellow who's filling in for Michelle, over at CHED," he said. "Properly speaking, equipment grants are the sole concern of the Industrial Equipment Distribution, Division of Loans and Exchanges." He pursed his lips. "However, I suppose there's no harm in telling you. They'll be receiving heavy mining equipment."

"Drill rigs, that sort of thing?"

"Strip mining gear." Hassan took a slip of paper from a breast pocket, blinked at it. "Titan Model XV/3 excavators, to be specific. Why is CHED interested in IED's activities?"

"Forgive my curiosity, Mr. Hassan. It's just that Bayview cropped up earlier today. It seems they hold a mortgage on some crystal gardens over in—"

"That's not IED's affair, sir," Hassan cut in. "I have sufficient problems as Chief of IED without probing into CHED's business."

"Speaking of excavators," another person put in, "we over at the Special Committee for Rehabilitation and Development of Under-resourced Nations' Environmental Systems have been trying for months to get a request for mining equipment for Greenfield Territory through IED—"

"SCRUNES was late on the scene," Hassan said. "First come, first served. That's our policy at IED. Good day, colleagues." He strode off, briefcase under his arm.

"That's the trouble with peaceful worlds," the SCRUNES committee member said. "Zenith is a troublemaker, so every agency in the Coalition is out to pacify them. While my chance to make a record—that is, assist peace-loving Greenfield Territory—comes to naught." She shook her head.

"What kind of arts institute do they have in Greenfield Territory?" asked Sebastian. "We're sending them three thousand exchange artisans. It must be quite an institution."

"Arts institute? Greenfield Territory has one under-funded community center."

"Will all the exchange artisans be studying at the Community Center?"

"Three thousand artisans? Hah! Three
hundred
artisans would overtax the facilities of the center."

"I wonder if the Zenithians know that?"

"The Zenithians? Why, most of Greenfield Territory's difficulties are due to the unwise trade agreement they entered into with Zenith. Three thousand artisans indeed!" She snorted and walked away.

Sebastian stopped by the office to pick up a light jacket, then rode the elevator to the roof of the 180-story Coalition HQ building and hailed a transport to the port. The Zenithian artisans had arrived early. Sebastian saw them lined up on the platform waiting to go through customs. It would be half an hour before they were cleared through. He turned into the lounge and ordered a coffee.

A stocky young person at the next table raised their cup.

"Good fortune," they said.

"And prosperity to match."

"You said it." They gulped half their coffee. "My name's Valentina Evans. Ms. Evans. Yeah, Ms. Evans. This is tedious, sitting around this place waiting...."

"You meeting somebody?"

"Yeah. Bunch of novices. Kids. How they expect—Never mind. Have one on me."

"Thanks. You a mentor?"

"I'll tell you what I am. I'm a shepherd. You know—" Valentina turned to Sebastian—"not one of those kids has more than basic training." She grimaced. "Artisans, you know. Never saw an artisan with real experience, did you?"

"Lots of times. You're meeting the artisans, are you?"

Valentina blinked at Sebastian. "Oh, you know about it, huh?"

"I represent CHED."

Valentina finished her coffee, ordered another. "I came on ahead. Sort of an advance coordinator for the kids. I trained 'em myself. Treated it like a workshop, but they can handle a fabrication unit. Don't know how they'll act under pressure. If I had my old team—"

She looked at her coffee cup, pushed it back. "Had enough," she said. "So long, friend. Or are you coming along?"

Sebastian nodded. "Might as well."

At the exit to the Customs enclosure, Sebastian watched as the first of the Zenithian artisans came through, caught sight of Valentina and straightened up, chest out.

"Drop that, friend," Valentina snapped. "Is that any way for an artisan to act?"

The youth, a lean-faced person with intense eyes, grinned.

"Right, no. Say, uh, Ms. Evans, are we gonna get to see the city? We folks were thinking—"

"You were, hah? You act like a bunch of students! I mean ... no! Now line up!"

"We have quarters ready for the artisans," Sebastian said. "If you'd like to bring them around to the west side, I have a couple of transports arranged."

"Thanks," said Valentina. "They'll stay here until departure time. Can't have the little dears wandering around loose. Might get ideas about going independent." She grimaced. "I mean they might skip orientation."

"We've scheduled your re-embarkation for noon tomorrow. That's a long wait. CHED's arranged gallery visits and a dinner."

"Sorry," Valentina said. "As soon as the equipment gets here, we're off." She grimaced again. "Can't travel without our equipment, y'know."

"Suit yourself," Sebastian said. "Where's the equipment now?"

"Coming in aboard a Bayview lighter."

"Maybe you'd like to arrange for a meal for the artisans here."

"Sure," Valentina said. "That's a good idea. Why don't you join us?" Valentina winked. "And bring some refreshments."

"Not this time," Sebastian said. He watched the artisans, still emerging from Customs. "They seem to be all young adults," he commented. "No senior artisans?"

"Maybe later," Valentina said. "You know, after we see how the first group is received."

Back at the CHED office, Sebastian buzzed Ms. Chen.

"Do you know the name of the institution these Zenithian artisans are bound for?"

"Why, the Arts Institute at Greenfield Territory, of course."

"Would that be the Community Center?"

Ms. Chen's mouth puckered. "I'm sure I've never pried into these details."

"Where does doing your job stop and prying begin, Ms. Chen?" Sebastian said. "Personally, I'm curious as to just what it is these artisans are travelling so far to study—at Coalition expense."

"Ms. Peterson never—"

"For the present, Ms. Chen, Ms. Peterson is on leave. That leaves me with the question of three thousand young artisans headed for a world with no facilities for them ... a world in need of excavators. But the excavators are on their way to Bayview Territory, a world under obligation to Zenith. And Bayview holds a mortgage on the best crystal acreage in Parkview."

"Well!" Ms. Chen snapped, eyes glaring. "I hope you're not questioning Ms. Peterson's wisdom!"

"About Ms. Peterson's wisdom there can be no question," Sebastian said. "But never mind. I'd like you to look up an item for me. How many excavators will Bayview be getting under the IED program?"

"Why, that's entirely IED business," Ms. Chen said. "Ms. Peterson always—"

"I'm sure she did. Let me know about the excavators as soon as you can."

Ms. Chen sniffed and disappeared from the screen. Sebastian left the office, descended thirty-three stories, followed a corridor to the Coalition Library. In the archives he thumbed through catalogues, pored over indices.

"Can I help you?" someone asked. A young librarian stood at his elbow.

"Thank you," Sebastian said. "I'm looking for information on a mining rig. A Titan model XV excavator."

"You won't find it in the industrial section," the librarian said. "Come along." Sebastian followed them along the archives to a well-lit section lettered MILITARY EQUIPMENT. They took a data crystal from the shelf, plugged it into the viewer, scrolled through and stopped at a massive armored vehicle.

"That's the model XV," they said. "It's what is known as a planetary extraction unit. It carries six operators, with devastating environmental impact capability."

"There must be an error somewhere," Sebastian said. "The Titan model I want is an excavator. Model XV M-3—"

"Oh, the modification was the addition of a processing blade for demolition work. That must be what confused you."

"Probably—among other things. Thank you."

Ms. Chen was waiting at the office. "I have the information you wanted," she said. "I've had it for over fifteen minutes. I was under the impression you needed it urgently, and I went to great lengths—"

"Sure," Sebastian said. "Go ahead. How many excavators?"

"Eight hundred."

"Are you sure?"

Ms. Chen's face tightened. "Well! If you feel I'm incompetent—"

"Just questioning the possibility of a mistake, Ms. Chen. Eight hundred excavators is a lot of equipment."

"Was there anything further?" Ms. Chen inquired frigidly.

"I sincerely hope not," Sebastian said.

III

Leaning back in Michelle's ergonomic chair with climate control and posture adjustment, Sebastian leafed through a folder labelled "CERP 9-804-Bt; BAYVIEW TERRITORY (general)." He paused at a page headed Industry.

Still reading, he opened the desk drawer, took out the two crystal samples and examined them in the light. He studied the blue crystal meditatively.

It would be a pity, he reflected, if anything should interfere with the production of such beauty....

Half an hour later he laid the folder aside, keyed the communications panel and put through a call to the Bayview Legation. He asked for the Commercial Attache.

"Knight here, Coalition HQ," he said airily. "About the IED shipment, the excavators. I'm wondering if there's been a mix up. My records show we're shipping eight hundred units...."

"That's correct. Eight hundred."

Sebastian waited.

"Ah ... are you there, Knight?"

"I'm still here. And I'm still wondering about the eight hundred excavators."

"It's perfectly in order. I thought it was all settled. Mr. Hassan—"

"One unit would require a substantial operation to handle its output," Sebastian said. "Now Bayview subsists on its fisheries. They have perhaps half a dozen small processing facilities. Maybe, in a bind, they could handle the ore fifteen XVs could extract ... if Bayview had any ore. It doesn't. By the way, isn't an XV a poor choice as a mining outfit? I should think—"

"See here, Knight! Why all this interest in a few surplus excavators? And in any event, what business is it of yours how we plan to use the equipment? That's an internal affair of my government. Mr. Hassan—"

"I'm not Mr. Hassan. What are you going to do with the other seven hundred and eighty-five excavators?"

"I understood the grant was to be with no strings attached!"

"I know it's bad manners to ask questions. It's an old diplomatic tradition that any time you can get anybody to accept anything as a gift, you've scored points in the game. But if Bayview has some scheme cooking—"

"Nothing like that, Knight. It's a mere business transaction."

"What kind of business do you do with a Titan XV? With or without a blade attached, it's what's known as a planetary extraction unit."

"Great Heavens, Knight! Don't jump to conclusions! Would you have us branded as environmental criminals? Frankly—is this a secure line?"

"Certainly. You may speak freely."

"The excavators are for transshipment. We've gotten ourselves into a difficult situation, balance-of-payments-wise. This is an accommodation to a group with which we have rather strong business ties."

"I understand you hold a mortgage on the best land in Parkview," Sebastian said. "Any connection?"

"Why ... ah ... no. Of course not, ha ha."

"Who gets the excavators eventually?"

"Knight, this is unwarranted interference!"

"Who gets them?"

"They happen to be going to Parkview. But I scarcely see—"

"And who's the friend you're helping out with an unauthorized transshipment of grant material?"

"Why ... ah ... I've been working with a Ms. Oliver Johnson, a Zenithian representative."

"And when will they be shipped?"

"Why, they went out ten days ago. They'll be two-thirds of the way there by now. But look here, Knight, this isn't what you're thinking!"

"How do you know what I'm thinking? I don't know myself." Sebastian rang off, buzzed the secretary.

"Ms. Chen, I'd like to be notified immediately of any new applications that might come in from the Zenithian Consulate for placement of artisans."

"Well, it happens, by coincidence, that I have an application here now. Ms. Johnson of the Consulate brought it in."

"Is Ms. Johnson in the office? I'd like to see her."

"I'll ask if she has time."

"Great. Thanks." It was half a minute before a sharp-featured woman in severe attire walked in. She wore modern styling, a crisp uniform, polished boots and an impatient expression.

"What is it you wish?" she barked. "I understood in my discussions with the other ... ah ... administrator there'd be no further need for these tiresome conferences."

"I've just learned you're placing more artisans abroad, Ms. Johnson. How many this time?"

"Three thousand."

"And where will they be going?"

"Bayview Territory. It's all in the application form I've submitted. Your job is to provide transportation."

"Will there be any other artisans embarking this season?"

"Why ... perhaps. That's Zenith's business." Oliver looked at Sebastian with narrowed eyes. "As a matter of fact, we had in mind dispatching another three thousand to Magnolia, Veldoria."

"Another under-populated world—and in the same sector, I believe," Sebastian said. "Your people must be unusually interested in that region of space."

"If that's all you wanted to know, I'll be on my way. I have matters of importance to see to."

After Oliver left, Sebastian called Ms. Chen in. "I'd like to have a breakdown of all the artisan movements that have been planned under the present program," he said. "And see if you can get a summary of what IED has been shipping lately."

Ms. Chen compressed her lips. "If Ms. Peterson were here, I'm sure she wouldn't dream of interfering in the work of other departments. I ... overheard your conversation with the representative from the Bayview Legation—"

"The lists, Ms. Chen."

"I'm not accustomed," Ms. Chen said, "to intruding in matters outside our responsibility cluster."

"That's worse than listening in on communications, eh? But never mind. I need the information, Ms. Chen."

"Loyalty to my Chief—"

"Loyalty to your position should send you moving for the material I've asked for," Sebastian said. "I'm taking full responsibility. Now go."

The buzzer sounded. Sebastian flipped a key. "CHED, Knight speaking...."

Isabella's weathered face appeared on the desk screen.

"Hello, Sebastian. Okay if I come up?"

"Sure, Isabella. I want to talk to you."

In the office, Isabella took a chair. "Sorry if I'm rushing you, Sebastian," she said. "But have you got anything for me?"

Sebastian gestured at the crystal samples. "What do you know about Bayview Territory?"

"Bayview? Not much of a place. Mostly ocean. All right if you like fish, I guess. We import our seafood from there. Nice shellfish in storm season. Over two pounds each."

"You on good terms with them?"

"Sure, I guess so. Course, they're pretty thick with Zenith."

"So?"

"Didn't I tell you? Zenith was the bunch that tried to take us over here a dozen years back. They'd've made it too, if they hadn't had a lot of bad luck. Their equipment sank in the wetlands, and without equipment they're manageable."

Ms. Chen buzzed. "I have your lists," she said shortly.

"Bring them in, please."

The secretary placed the documents on the desk. Isabella caught her eye and grinned. She sniffed and left the room.

"What that person needs is a joyful time in the crystal gardens," Isabella observed. Sebastian thumbed through the documents, pausing to read from time to time. He finished and looked at Isabella.

"How many people do you need for the harvest, Isabella?" Sebastian inquired.

Isabella examined her crystal sample and looked thoughtful.

"Two hundred would help," she said. "Two thousand would be better. Here's hoping."

"What would you say to three thousand?"

"Three thousand? Sebastian, you're not joking?"

"I hope not." He picked up the communications panel, called the Port Authority, asked for the dispatch coordinator.

"Hello, Zhang. Say, I have a favor to ask of you. You know that contingent of Zenithian artisans. They're traveling aboard the two Coalition transports. I'm interested in the equipment that goes with the artisans. Has it arrived yet? Okay, I'll wait."

Zhang came back to the panel. "Yeah, Sebastian, it's here. Just arrived. But there's a strange thing. It's not consigned to Greenfield Territory. It's ticketed clear through to Parkview."

"Listen, Zhang," Sebastian said. "I want you to go over to the warehouse and take a look at that equipment for me."

Sebastian waited while the dispatch coordinator carried out the errand. He was studying the violet crystal when Zhang returned to the panel.

"Hey, I took a look at that equipment, Sebastian. Something suspicious going on. Weapons. Plasma cutters, Mark IX energy rifles, demolition charges—"

"It's okay, Zhang. Nothing to worry about. Just a mix-up. Now, Zhang, I'm going to ask you to do something more for me. I'm covering for a colleague. It seems they made an error. I wouldn't want word to get out, you understand. I'll send along a written change order in the morning that will cover you officially. Meanwhile, here's what I want you to do...."

Sebastian gave instructions, then rang off and turned to Isabella.

"As soon as I get off a couple of messages, I think we'd better get down to the port, Isabella. I think I'd like to see the artisans off personally."

Dr. Sophia Edwards left her laboratory at the Oceanographic Research Institute in Oakdale Village at exactly 6:00 PM and began the evening walk she had taken, without fail, for fifteen solid years.

The walk never varied. She paced three blocks down Harbor Street, stopped at the Blue Whale Café to purchase a kelp tea, then walked to the end of the fifth block on Harbor. There she turned left on Maritime Avenue, followed Maritime to Coral Street, down Coral and so by way of Beacon back to Harbor again and to her small apartment above the institute.

She didn't walk quickly. She took her time. She always returned to her door at exactly 6:50 PM. No one ever stopped to talk with her. Even the barista at the Blue Whale Café remained silent while preparing her drink. Dr. Edwards merely nodded, the woman prepared the tea, and Dr. Edwards took her cup. That was all.

For people long ago had gathered that Dr. Edwards desired solitude. The newer generation of researchers called it dedication to her work. Certain colleagues had a different word for it. The senior scientists remembered that this intense woman with her waterproof notebook, titanium data collection tools, and ever-present rain jacket had once been a celebrated professor at Ravenswood Regional University.

A professor of oceanography, they recalled, specializing in deep-sea ecosystems and marine resource management. At any rate, a controversy of some sort was connected with her name—an academic dispute. She had published a research paper, and she had presented that research to international conferences. What that research proposed had long been forgotten by most, but whatever it was had been considered sufficiently radical to cost Dr. Edwards her tenured position at the university.

A pale moon hung over the harbor and a sharp, salt-tinged wind was blowing when Dr. Edwards started out at six o'clock.

It was a good evening, she told herself, breathing the clean ocean air and the faint scent of seaweed from the nearby docks.

She walked steadily, her notebook tucked securely in her jacket pocket. She noticed that the streetlight at the corner of Harbor and Beacon was flickering, and she frowned slightly when forced to step around construction barriers before the entrance to Building 47.

It seemed she reached the corner of Maritime and Harbor just a bit too quickly, but she told herself this couldn't be. For fifteen years, since the year following her dismissal from the university, she had lived by precise routine.

The same thing, at the same time, day after day. She had not deliberately chosen such a regimented existence. A single woman, living alone with her research stipend and savings, the timed routine had developed gradually—a framework for maintaining work-life balance in the absence of other anchors.

So she turned on Maritime and back on Coral. The security guard at the corner of Coral and Beacon nodded to her as always, a silent acknowledgment of her nightly passage.

A news broadcast was playing from someone's open window, and fragments drifted to Dr. Edwards.

"...continuing to occur worldwide...entire research station in Larchmont Province vanished...leading marine biologist, Dr. Christopher Lane, cannot explain..."

The wind carried the words away and Dr. Edwards pressed her lips together. Another sensationalist report, probably. She remembered similar panic years before, something about atmospheric anomalies. And Lane! What did Lane have to do with anything? He was one of the scientists who had dismissed her paper as pseudoscience.

But she pushed the thought away, focused on the familiar rhythm of her steps, looked at the known landmarks that emerged from the coastal darkness as she walked. For there was nothing—absolutely nothing in the world—that she would let disturb her equilibrium. That was a principle she had established fifteen years ago.

There was a group of researchers outside the institute's main entrance at the corner of Coral and Beacon, talking urgently. Dr. Edwards caught excited phrases: "It's happening in every coastal region...What could cause this...The data analysis shows nothing..."

But as Dr. Edwards approached, they fell silent and watched her pass. She, for her part, gave them no acknowledgment. That was how it had been for many years, ever since people had accepted that she did not wish to engage.

One of the researchers, a young woman named Camila Bryant, half-stepped forward as if to speak, but then retreated, and Dr. Edwards continued her walk.

Back at her apartment door, she stopped and, as she had done a thousand times before, checked her waterproof watch.

She stared at it in confusion. It was only 6:35 PM.

For long minutes she stood examining the watch. The timepiece hadn't stopped; its second hand still swept smoothly around the face.

But fifteen minutes too early! For fifteen years, day in and day out, she had left at six and returned at ten minutes to seven. Now...

It wasn't until then that she realized something else was wrong. She had no kelp tea. For the first time, she had failed to stop at the Blue Whale Café.

Shaken, muttering to herself, Dr. Edwards unlocked her apartment and secured the door behind her.

She hung her jacket on the hook in the entryway and walked slowly into the living area. Dropping into her reading chair, she shook her head in bewilderment.

Silence filled the room. A silence measured by the soft hum of the temperature control system.

But silence was familiar to Dr. Edwards. Once she had enjoyed music—classical recordings she could stream through her speakers. But the speakers sat disconnected in the corner. Dr. Edwards had unplugged them years before, precisely on the evening when a concert had been interrupted for breaking news.

She had stopped following news feeds and scientific journals too, had isolated herself to a few city blocks. And as the years passed, that self-imposed isolation had become absolute, an invisible but impenetrable boundary marking an area five blocks by four. Beyond that perimeter lay something she could not name, would not acknowledge. Beyond it, she never ventured.

But recluse though she was, she could not entirely escape information. Things researchers discussed in the hallways, fragments of broadcasts from open windows, headlines glimpsed on discarded tablets.

And so she knew this was the year 2089, and that the conflicts in the Pacific territories and Asian coastal regions had ended in catastrophe, followed by a mysterious phenomenon—a plague of disappearances sweeping through region after region like an invisible tide, erasing populations. A phenomenon undoubtedly connected to the wars and their disruption of natural resource management systems.

But those things she dismissed as concerns far removed from her small world. She disregarded them. She pretended she had never heard of them. Others might worry and theorize if they wished. To her, they simply did not matter.

But there were two things tonight that did matter. Two disturbing, inexplicable events. She had arrived home fifteen minutes early. She had forgotten her kelp tea.

Huddled in the chair, she frowned. It was unsettling to have her routine disrupted. There must be something wrong. Had her long isolation finally affected her mind—perhaps just slightly—enough to impair her judgment? Had she lost her sense of temporal precision, of spatial awareness?

No, she hadn't. Take this room, for example. After fifteen years, it had become as integral to her identity as her research methodology. Every detail was recorded in her mind with scientific clarity: the titanium desk with its organized specimen samples; the shelf with her carefully maintained equipment; the chronometer that displayed not only time but date, lunar phase, and tidal information; the specimen jar on the side table and, most important of all, the framed photograph.

Dr. Edwards treasured that photograph. It showed depth, she always said. It depicted an underwater scene in the foreground, a coral reef teeming with life. Far in the distance, almost at the edge of visibility, was the vague outline of a research submersible.

There were other images too. The coastal landscape above the storage unit, the marine charts in the corner where she sat, the satellite imagery above the bookshelf. But the reef photograph was directly in her line of sight. She could see it without turning her head. She had positioned it there because she valued it most.

Further reflection became difficult as Dr. Edwards felt exhaustion overtaking her. She prepared for bed mechanically. For an hour she lay awake, troubled by undefined anxieties she could neither articulate nor comprehend.

When finally she slept, it was to experience a series of disturbing dreams. She dreamed first that she was conducting fieldwork on a small research platform in the open ocean, that the waters around the platform teemed with unknown organisms—bioluminescent creatures that pulsed with alien light—and that steadily those organisms were consuming the platform itself.

In another dream, she was pursued by something she could neither observe nor measure, but only sense. And as she tried to flee, she remained stationary. Her legs moved frantically, but she made no progress. It was as if she ran on a treadmill in the laboratory.

Then again the threat surrounded her, a vast, incomprehensible presence, and she tried to call out but couldn't. She opened her mouth and strained but filled her lungs to bursting with the effort to shout—but no sound emerged.

All next day she was uneasy, and as she left the apartment that evening at precisely 6:00 PM, she kept reminding herself: "You must not forget tonight! You must remember to stop for your tea!"

The streetlight at the corner of Beacon was still flickering, and in front of Building 47 the construction barriers remained in place. Everything appeared the same as the night before.

And now, she told herself, the Blue Whale Café is in the next block. I must not forget tonight. To forget twice consecutively would be unacceptable.

She held that thought firmly in mind, walked just slightly faster down the street.

But at the corner she stopped, disoriented. Bewildered, she stared down the next block. There was no blue neon sign, no welcoming light on the sidewalk to mark the small café tucked into this research district.

She stared at the street marker and read the word slowly: MARITIME. She read it again, disbelieving, for this shouldn't be Maritime Avenue, but Dock Street. She had walked two blocks, and the café was between Dock and Maritime. She hadn't reached Dock yet—and here was Maritime.

Or had she, absent-mindedly, walked one block farther than intended, passed the café as on the previous night?

For the first time in fifteen years, Dr. Edwards retraced her steps. She walked back to Beacon, then turned and went back to Maritime again and on to Coral. Then back to Maritime again, where she stood stunned while a single, impossible fact crystallized in her mind:

There wasn't any café! The block from Dock to Maritime had disappeared!

Now she understood why she had missed the café the night before, why she had arrived home fifteen minutes early.

On legs that felt numb, she stumbled back to her apartment. She locked the door behind her and made her way unsteadily to her chair in the corner.

What was this? What did it mean? By what inconceivable mechanism could a paved street with buildings, equipment, and structures be erased and the space it had occupied be closed up?

Was something happening in the world that she, in her isolated existence, knew nothing about?

Dr. Edwards shivered, started to adjust her jacket, then stopped as she realized the room temperature was regulated. The cold she felt came from somewhere else. The cold of fear and uncertainty, the chill of half-formed understanding.

A profound silence had descended, a silence still measured by the chronometer's digital display. And yet a silence that held a different quality than she had ever experienced before. Not a comfortable, familiar silence—but a silence that suggested emptiness and void.

There was something behind this, Dr. Edwards told herself. Something that connected to fragments of memory buried in her consciousness, demanding recognition. Something tied to the conversations she had overheard at the institute, pieces of broadcasts she had heard while walking, the urgent discussions among researchers. Something related to events in the world from which she had withdrawn.

She recalled them now and focused on the central theme: the wars and disappearances. Hints of Pacific territories and Asian coastal regions swept nearly clean of human presence, of the phenomenon spreading through African coastlines, of its appearance in South American ports, of the desperate efforts of North American authorities to prevent its advance.

Millions of people had vanished from Pacific and Asian regions, African and South American coasts. Billions, perhaps.

And somehow those grim statistics seemed connected to her own experience. Something, somewhere, some element of her earlier research, seemed to hold an explanation. But try as she might, her confused mind failed to find the answer.

The chronometer advanced silently, its display shifting from 7:29 to 7:30.

Dr. Edwards stood, walked to the window, and looked out.

Moonlight painted the harbor in silver and black, silhouetting the cranes and vessels against a luminous sky.

But the research building directly across the street was not the same. It was strangely distorted, its proportions wrong, like a structure that had suddenly become non-Euclidean.

She stared at it in shock, trying to determine what was wrong. She recalled how it had always stood, solid, a standard example of modern marine research architecture.

Then, before her eyes, the building corrected itself. Slowly it resolved, smoothed out its strange angles, readjusted its dimensions, became once again the familiar structure she knew it must be.

With relief, Dr. Edwards turned back toward the room.

But before she moved away from the window, she looked again. The building was distorted—as severe, perhaps worse than before!

Gasping, Dr. Edwards moved away from the window, went to her bedroom, and took sedatives from her medical kit.

Her dreams that night were the same as before. Again there was the research platform in open ocean. Again she was alone upon it. Again the bioluminescent organisms were consuming her foundation piece by piece.

She woke, body drenched with perspiration. Dim light of early dawn filtered through the window. The clock beside her bed showed 7:15 AM. For a long time she lay motionless.

Again the inexplicable events of the night before returned to haunt her, and as she lay there staring at the window, she remembered them one by one. But her mind, still clouded by sleep and confusion, processed the events mechanically, lost the sharp edge of terror that surrounded them.

The light through the window slowly brightened. Dr. Edwards slid out of bed, crossed to the window, the cold floor against her bare feet. She forced herself to look out.

There was nothing outside the window. No shapes. As if there might be fog. But no fog, however dense, could obscure the equipment storage shed that stood close to the building.

But the shed was there—shadowy, indistinct in the gray light, with rust visible on its panels, a few identification markers still attached to its surface.

The shed was there now. But it hadn't been when she first looked. Dr. Edwards was certain of that.

And now she saw the faint outline of the adjacent research building—but that outline was wrong. The dimensions didn't align properly—they were distorted. As if some massive force had grasped the building and twisted it out of true. Like the building she had seen across the street the night before, the building that had painfully corrected itself when she focused on how it should appear.

Perhaps if she concentrated on how the adjacent building should look, it too might correct itself. But Dr. Edwards was exhausted. Too exhausted to focus on the building.

She turned from the window and dressed slowly. In the living area, she collapsed into her chair, rested her feet on the ottoman. For a long time she sat, trying to think.

And then, abruptly, something like an electrical shock ran through her. Rigid, she sat there, hollow inside at the realization. Minutes later she rose and almost ran across the room to the bookshelf mounted on the wall.

There were many volumes on the shelf: her reference texts on the first level, her research journals on the lower levels. The second level contained but one publication. And it was around this publication that Dr. Edwards' entire professional life had revolved.

Fifteen years ago she had written it and foolishly attempted to present its hypothesis to the international oceanographic community. The media, she remembered, had sensationalized it extensively. Controversy had erupted. Narrow-minded colleagues, failing to understand either her methodology or her conclusions, but seeing in her another proponent of pseudoscience, had forced her resignation from the university.

It was a straightforward paper, really, dismissed by most authorities as merely the speculation of an overzealous researcher.

Dr. Edwards took it down now, opened the cover, and began reading slowly through the pages. For a moment, the memory of her former career swept over her.

Then her eyes focused on a paragraph, a paragraph written so long ago the very words seemed foreign and distant:

"Human consciousness itself, through collective observation and measurement, maintains the physical structure of observable reality—yes, even the ocean depths we study. Billions of minds perceiving currents as currents, organisms as organisms, geological formations as formations—and not as something else. Minds that observe phenomena as they are and have maintained phenomena as they were. Eliminate those minds, and the entire framework of matter, deprived of its observational foundation, will collapse and transform like a column of sand..."

Her eyes followed down the page:

"Yet this would relate not to matter itself—but only to matter's configuration. For while human consciousness through long ages may have shaped our understanding of the space we inhabit, consciousness would have limited conceivable influence upon the existence of that matter. What exists in our known universe shall exist perpetually and can never be destroyed, only altered or transformed.

"But in modern theoretical physics and oceanography, we gain insight into the possibility—yes, probability—that there are other dimensions, other frameworks of space-time intersecting with the one we occupy.

"If a probe is inserted into a two-dimensional plane, would that plane have any knowledge of the probe? It would not, for in this case the plane is two-dimensional, the probe three-dimensional. Yet both occupy the same space.

"Granting then that the power of human consciousness alone maintains this universe, or at least this world in its present configuration, may we not go further and envision other consciousnesses in some other dimension observing us, waiting, waiting strategically for the moment they can assume control of matter? Such a concept is not impossible. It is a logical conclusion if we accept the dual hypothesis: that consciousness does control the configuration of all matter; and that other realities exist in juxtaposition with ours.

"Perhaps we shall encounter a day, far distant, when our dimension, our world will dissolve beneath our feet and before our eyes as some stronger consciousness reaches out from the dimensional shadows of the very space we inhabit and wrests from us the matter which we know to be our own."

She stood stunned beside the bookshelf, her eyes staring unseeing at the window.

She had written that. And because of those words, she had been called a pseudoscientist, had been compelled to resign her position at the university, had been forced into this isolated existence.

A tremendous realization struck her. Humans had vanished by the millions worldwide. Where there had been thousands of minds, there now were one or two. An insufficient force to maintain the configuration of matter intact.

The disappearances had swept Pacific and Asian regions nearly clean of life, had devastated African coasts, had reached South American ports—might even have come to North America. She remembered the whispers she had heard, the words of the researchers at the institute entrance, the buildings vanishing. Something scientists could not explain. But those were merely fragments of information. She did not know the complete picture—she could not know. She never monitored broadcasts, never read scientific journals.

But abruptly everything fit together in her mind like the solution to a complex equation. The significance of it all gripped her with devastating clarity.

There were not sufficient consciousnesses in existence to maintain the material world in its familiar configuration. Some other intelligence from another dimension was struggling to supersede human observation and transform this universe into its own framework!

Abruptly Dr. Edwards closed the paper, returned it to the shelf, and retrieved her jacket.

She had to know more. She had to find someone who could provide information.

She moved through the entryway to the door, emerged onto the walkway. Outside she looked skyward, trying to locate the sun. But there wasn't any sun—only an all-pervading grayness that shrouded everything—not a gray fog, but a gray emptiness that seemed devoid of life, of any movement.

The walkway led to the street and there it ended, but as she moved forward the pavement came into view and the building ahead loomed out of the gray, but a building with distortions.

She moved forward rapidly. Visibility extended only a few meters, and as she approached them the buildings materialized like two-dimensional projections without depth, like twisted cardboard structures appearing in misty conditions.

Once she stopped and looked back and saw that the grayness had closed in behind her. The buildings were erased, the walkway faded into nothing.

She called out, hoping to attract attention. But her voice frightened her. It seemed to echo upward into higher levels of the atmosphere, as if a giant opening had appeared to a vast space high above her.

She continued until she came to the corner of Maritime. There, on the curb, she stopped and stared. The gray barrier was thicker there, but she did not realize how close it was until she glanced down and saw there was nothing, nothing at all beyond the curb. No dull gleam of wet pavement, no sign of a street. It was as if all existence ended here at the corner of Harbor and Maritime.

With a sharp cry, Dr. Edwards turned and ran. Back down the street she raced, jacket streaming behind her in the wind.

Breathing hard, she reached her building and stumbled up the walkway, grateful that it still existed.

On the threshold she stood for a moment, catching her breath. She glanced back over her shoulder, and a strange feeling of inner emptiness seemed to wash over her. At that moment, the gray nothingness appeared to thin—the enveloping curtain fell away, and she saw...

Vague and indistinct, yet cast in holographic outline, an enormous structure was silhouetted against the darkening sky. It was a structure fantastic with geometric domes, crystalline towers, and suspended platforms and connecting bridges. Corridor-like passages, flanked on either side by luminous panels and transport systems, stretched endlessly to the vanishing point. Great beams of multicolored energy probed huge patterns and spirals above the higher levels.

And beyond, like a final backdrop, rose a colossal barrier. It was from that barrier—from its angular projections and geometric features—that Dr. Edwards felt the presence observing her.

Thousands of consciousnesses focused with a single purpose.

And as she continued to observe, something else seemed to form above that barrier. A pattern this time, that swirled and shifted in the ribbons of energy and rapidly coalesced into strange mathematical configurations, without definite form or detail. A vast intelligence, an intelligence of incomprehensible power and purpose, staring down with calculating composure.

Then the structure and the intelligence slid out of focus; the vision faded like a deactivated hologram, and the grayness returned.

Dr. Edwards pushed open the door of her apartment. But she did not lock it. There was no purpose in locks—not anymore.

The temperature control was still functioning, and she adjusted it upward, though she knew the cold she felt came from within.

Without removing her jacket, she sank exhausted into her chair, closed her eyes then opened them again.

She sighed with relief as she saw the room was unchanged. Everything in its accustomed place: the chronometer, the specimen jar, the equipment on the shelf, the reef photograph on the wall.

Everything was as it should be. The chronometer measured the silence with its silent display; it advanced to the next minute and the equipment emitted its usual faint hum.

This was her room, she thought. Rooms acquire the identity of the person who inhabits them, become part of them. This was her world, her own private world, and as such it would be the last to go.

But how long could she—her consciousness—maintain its existence?

Dr. Edwards stared at the reef photograph, and for a moment a small measure of reassurance returned to her. They couldn't take this away. The rest of the world might dissolve because there was insufficient observational power to maintain its configuration.

But this room was hers. She alone had furnished it. She alone, since she had first moved into this apartment, had lived here.

This room would remain. It must remain—it must...

She rose from her chair and walked across the room to the bookshelf, stood staring at the second level with its single publication. Her eyes shifted to the top level, and swift terror gripped her.

For not all the books were there. Many books weren't there! Only the most familiar, the most frequently referenced ones.

So the transformation had already begun here! The unfamiliar books were gone, and that fit the pattern—for it would be the least familiar things that would disappear first.

Turning, she stared across the room. Was it her imagination, or did the specimen jar on the table blur and begin to fade?

But as she stared at it, it became clear again, a solid, substantial object.

For a moment real fear reached out and touched her with icy fingers. For she knew that this room no longer was protected against the thing that had happened out there on the street.

Or had it really happened? Might not all this exist within her own mind? Might not the street be as it always was, with researchers walking and equipment functioning? Might not the Blue Whale Café still exist, its blue neon sign glowing in the evening?

Could it be that she was losing her sanity? She had heard whispers when she had passed, whispers the gossiping researchers had not intended her to hear. And she had seen the looks when she walked by. They thought her unstable. Could she be actually unstable?

But she knew she wasn't unstable. She knew that she perhaps was the most rational of all people who walked the earth. For she, and she alone, had foreseen this very thing. And the others had dismissed her for it.

Somewhere else the researchers might be working in a laboratory. But it would be a different laboratory. And the researchers undoubtedly would be different too.

For the matter of which the laboratory and everything within it had been formed would now be cast in a different configuration, claimed by different consciousnesses in a different dimension.

"Perhaps we shall encounter a day, far distant, when our dimension, our world will dissolve beneath our feet and before our eyes as some stronger consciousness reaches out from the dimensional shadows of the very space we inhabit and wrests from us the matter which we know to be our own."

But there had been no need to wait for that distant day. Scant years after she had written those prophetic words, the thing was happening. Humanity had played unwittingly into the hands of those other consciousnesses in the other dimension. Humanity had waged wars, and wars had created conditions for mass disappearances. And the whole vast cycle of events was but a component of a strategic plan.

She could see it all now. By an insidious form of manipulation, entities from that other dimension—or was it one supreme intelligence—had deliberately created the conditions for conflict. The reduction of the world's consciousness had been carefully planned with calculated premeditation.

On impulse she suddenly turned, crossed the room, and opened the connecting door to the bedroom. She stopped on the threshold, and a sound of despair forced its way to her lips.

There was no bedroom. Where her bed and storage units had been, there was grayish nothingness.

Like an automaton, she turned again and moved to the entry door. Here, too, she found what she had expected. There was no entryway, no familiar jacket hook and equipment rack.

Nothing...

Weakly Dr. Edwards moved back to her chair in the corner.

"So here I am," she said, half aloud.

So there she was. Making a final stand in the last corner of the world that remained to her.

Perhaps there were other people like her, she thought. People who stood at bay against the emptiness that marked the transition from one dimension to another. People who had lived close to the things they valued, who had endowed those things with such substantial form by power of consciousness alone that they now stood out alone against the power of some greater consciousness.

The street was gone. The rest of her apartment was gone. This room still retained its form.

This room, she knew, would remain the longest. And when the rest of the room was gone, this corner with her chair would persist. For this was the location where she had lived for fifteen years. The bedroom was for sleeping, the kitchenette for eating. This room was for living. This was her final stand.

These were the walls and floors and photographs and equipment that had absorbed her will to make them walls and photographs and equipment.

She looked toward the window into a blank world. The adjacent buildings were already gone. Others had not lived with them as she had lived with this room. Their attention had been divided, broadly distributed; their thoughts had not been concentrated as hers upon an area five blocks by four, or a room fifteen by thirteen.

Staring toward the window, she saw it again. The same vision she had observed before, yet different in an indescribable way. There was the structure illuminated against the sky. There were the geometric towers and crystalline features, the dome-shaped projections and platforms. She could see with stereoscopic clarity the suspended bridges, the luminous corridors sweeping on into infinity. The vision was closer this time, but the depth and proportion had changed—as if she were viewing it from two concurrent perspectives simultaneously.

And the intelligence—the intelligence of magnitude—of power, of cosmic strategy and purpose...

Dr. Edwards turned her attention back into the room. The chronometer was advancing slowly, steadily. The grayness was infiltrating the room.

The desk and equipment were the first to go. They simply faded away, and with them went one corner of the room.

And then the specimen jar.

"Oh, well," said Dr. Edwards, "I never did value that particularly."

Now as she sat there, it didn't seem strange to be without the desk or the equipment. It was as if it were something quite normal. Something one could expect to happen.

Perhaps, if she concentrated hard enough, she could restore them.

But, after all, what was the purpose? One person, alone, could not resist the irresistible advance of nothingness. One person, all alone, simply couldn't do it.

She wondered what the specimen jar looked like in that other dimension. It certainly wouldn't be a specimen jar, nor would the equipment be equipment, for perhaps they didn't have specimen jars or equipment in the invading dimension.

She wondered, as a matter of fact, what she herself would look like when she finally transitioned into the unknown. For she was matter, too, just as the specimen jar and equipment were matter.

She wondered if she would retain her individuality—if she still would be a person. Or would she merely be a thing?

There was one answer to all of that. She simply didn't know.

Nothingness advanced upon her, consumed its way across the room, approaching her as she sat in the chair beneath the shelf. And she waited for it.

The room, or what remained of it, plunged into profound silence.

Dr. Edwards started. The chronometer had stopped. Strange—the first time in fifteen years.

She leaped from her chair and then sat down again.

The chronometer hadn't stopped.

It wasn't there.

There was a tingling sensation in her feet.
