synthetic_story:
THE QUANTUM CANVAS
BY MICHAEL ZUROY

"Spencer!" bellowed Roman Munoz, CEO of Munoz Robotics Corporation, slamming his fist on the laboratory table. "I want results!"

Heads turned from their workstations. Camila Spencer visibly flinched.

"As chief robotics engineer, you're not delivering," Munoz continued savagely. "The Munoz Art-Bot is falling behind the competition. Marketing and Sales are working overtime. It's Engineering that's dropping the ball!"

"But Mr. Munoz," Camila protested weakly under her employer's glare, "don't you remember? I tried to explain—"

"For three years there hasn't been one significant improvement in the Munoz Art-Bot!" Munoz roared. "Look at our competitors. The TechniCanvas robot creates museum-quality paintings in forty-five minutes. Universal Arts does it in fifty-two."

"But Mr. Munoz—"

"The Minerva MasterStroke does it in fifty-five minutes and plays Vivaldi while it works. Our own Art-Bot barely manages to complete a decent painting in ninety-seven minutes without music. Is this what I'm paying you for?"

Camila adjusted her glasses with trembling hands. "But Mr. Munoz, our robot still produces work with genuine artistic merit. It creates pieces with depth, meaning. It has integrity..."

"Integrity," Munoz pronounced, "is for galleries. Five months, Spencer! In five months I want a new Art-Bot that will be faster, lighter, more efficient, more impressive and more entertaining than any other on the market. I want it completely developed, engineered and ready for production. Otherwise, Spencer—"

Camila's body tensed. "But Mr. Munoz, five months is hardly enough time for proper development, even with an adequate team. I've been trying to tell you for years that we're bound to fall behind because we don't have sufficient personnel to conduct research. Our people can barely keep up with production and maintenance. If you would let me hire a few more engineers and consciousness studies specialists to help with the AI development..."

"Excuses," sneered Munoz. "Your team is more than adequate. I will not allow you to waste my money. Five months, Spencer, no more!" Munoz stormed out of the lab, leaving behind an oppressive silence.

How could you set a time limit on consciousness studies and robotics development? A designer had to experiment, investigate, test neural networks, compare results, iterate. She had always wanted to devote all her time to research, but Munoz Robotics had not given her that opportunity. Eighteen years! thought Camila. Eighteen years of constant pressure, impossible deadlines, production headaches, inadequate facilities and assistance. What had happened to the proud dream she once had, the dream of exploring uncharted territories in artificial consciousness, of unlimited time to investigate and develop?

Ah, well, thought Camila straightening her shoulders, she had managed to design a few good systems during her eighteen years with Munoz. That was some satisfaction.

What now? She had to keep her job. Technical positions were scarce. The market was flooded with qualified engineers. She was too old to compete effectively for new positions. She couldn't afford to lose income. Her mother wasn't well, and the medical bills from the pollution control treatments for her respiratory condition were mounting.

How to meet this five-month deadline? She would tackle it herself, of course; Ian James—excellent researcher—could work with her. She shook her head despairingly. Something would inevitably go wrong. Well, she had to start—

"Chief," said Ian a few weeks later as they entered the lab in Silverdale City, "I'm beginning to wonder if the answer lies in traditional neural network architectures at all."

"It has to," answered Camila wearily. "We must work along classical robotics lines. Departures, such as quantum computing approaches or fully autonomous consciousness systems, would be too expensive for mass production."

Three new prototypes and a series of blank canvases were waiting for them on the workbench. They began testing, Ian activating the robots and Camila timing their performance. "Fifty-eight minutes," announced Camila after the last test. "Good, but not good enough. Too bulky. Aesthetic output unsatisfactory. Musical accompaniment tinny. We've made progress, but we have a long way to go."

The problem was complex. It might seem that optimizing the processing algorithms would give the required speed, but there were too many other factors that complicated this direct approach. The mechanism had to be compact and elegant. Component sizes had to be minimized. Canvas resistance, brush dynamics, paint viscosity, color theory implementation, and the minimum acceptable artistic quality were some of the variables that had to be balanced within rigid constraints. Multi-brush systems, working on several sections simultaneously, had seemed promising for a while, but the coordination algorithms necessary to maintain artistic coherence had been too complex to be practical. There was the ever-present constraint of production cost.

Ian's eyes were upon her. "Chief," he said, "it's not right. Eighteen years of your life you've given to Munoz, and he'd fire you just like that if you don't achieve the impossible. The Munoz Corporation is built upon your designs and this is the thanks you get!"

"Well, well," said Camila. "I collected my salary every month, so I suppose I have no complaints. Although," a wistful note crept into her voice, "I would have liked some recognition. Munoz is known worldwide, but who has heard of Spencer? Well,"—Camila cleared her throat—"where do we stand, Ian?"

Ian's determined features drew into a scowl. "Munoz ought to be investigated. Okay, Chief. Fourteen experimental models designed to date. Three more in development. Eleven completed and tested, three in progress. Best performance, fifty-eight minutes, but model otherwise unsatisfactory."

"Hello," said Camila as a lab technician entered carrying a gleaming robot. "Here's another prototype. Let's try it." The technician departed and Ian activated the Art-Bot with a canvas mounted before it. "I hope—" he pressed the start button, and stopped abruptly, staring open-mouthed.

A completed masterpiece hung on the easel before the robot.

The canvas itself—the blank canvas—had disappeared.

"Chief," said Ian. "Chief."

"Yes," said Camila. "I see it too. Try another canvas."

"Landscape or portrait?" inquired Ian dreamily.

"Portrait, I think," said Camila. "Where did the blank canvas go, do you suppose?"

The blank portrait canvas disappeared. Likewise several landscape canvases, still-life canvases, and abstract canvases, leaving completed paintings in their place. It was rather disconcerting.

"Dear, dear," said Camila, regarding the collection of artwork around the lab. "There must be some explanation. I designed this robot with modified quantum computing processors, experimental consciousness matrices incorporating metaphysics principles, and a new approach to data analysis of artistic patterns. I expected that such departures from the norm might achieve unconventional performance, but this—Dear, dear. Where do the blank canvases go, I wonder?"

"What's the difference? Don't you see what you've got here? It's the answer! It's more than the answer! We can put this into production immediately and beat the deadline."

Camila shook her head. "No, Ian. We're producing something we don't understand. What forces have we uncovered here? Where do the blank canvases go? What makes them disappear? Are we dealing with quantum entanglement or consciousness transference? What patterns can we trace in the area of disappearance and what are their analytical mathematical formulas? What masses may be critical here? What transformations of energy are involved? No, Ian, we must learn much more."

"But Chief, your job."

"I'll risk that. Not a word to Munoz."

Several days later, however, Munoz himself charged into the laboratory and slapped Camila heartily on the back, causing her to drop her tablet. "Spencer!" roared Munoz. "Is this rumor circulating through the facility true? Why didn't you inform me? Let me see it."

After Munoz had witnessed the demonstration, his eyes took on a feverish glint. "This," he exulted, "will revolutionize the visual arts industry. Instantaneous creation! Perfect quality! Wait until Marketing and Sales get hold of this! We'll dominate the market! The Munoz Quantum-Artist we'll call it."

"Mr. Munoz—" said Camila shakily.

Munoz stared at his chief engineer sharply. "What's the matter, Spencer? The effect can be replicated, can't it?"

"Yes, sir. I've just finished verifying that. But I'm in the midst of further investigation of the phenomenon. There's more here than just a new type of art robot, sir. A whole new field of consciousness studies. New principles in quantum computing. This is significant, Mr. Munoz. I recommend that we delay production until further research can be completed. Hire a few top scientists and consciousness researchers. Find out where the canvases go. Publish a scientific paper on the effect."

"Spencer," bit out Munoz, his face growing hard. "Stop this nonsense. I don't care where the canvases go. May I remind you that under our standard patent agreement, all rights to your invention belong to the company? As well as anything you may produce in the field within a year after leaving our employ? We have a breakthrough here, and I don't want you holding it back. We're going into production immediately."

Close, thought Camila, exhausted. It had been a grueling job, and it had been close, but she'd made it. Beat the time limit by half a day. The first tentative shipments of Munoz Quantum-Artists had gone to distributors in Ivywood, Estoria. The first advertisements blazed across media channels. The first reorders came back, and then: "It's a phenomenon!" crowed Munoz, waving a sheaf of messages. "Increase production! Full speed ahead!"

The Quantum-Artists spread across the regions. In a remarkably short time they appeared in millions of homes and studios from Oakdale Territory to Ravenswood, Veldoria. Sales climbed to hundreds of thousands per day. Munoz Robotics went into peak production in three shifts, but was still unable to keep up with demand. Construction began on a new facility, and additional plants were planned. Long lines formed outside electronics stores. Retailers lucky enough to have Quantum-Artists in stock limited sales to one per customer. Munoz cancelled his advertising program. News coverage and word-of-mouth spread the fame of the robot so effectively that advertising was unnecessary.

Meanwhile, of course, government scientists, research foundations, universities and independent investigators began to examine this new phenomenon. Receiving no satisfactory explanation from Munoz, they established their own research programs.

Far into the night burned the lights of countless laboratories. Noted physicists and consciousness researchers probed, measured, scanned, traced, analyzed, and tested Quantum-Artists without achieving even a glimmer of a satisfactory explanation. Competitors found the patent impossible to circumvent, for any deviation from its exact specifications nullified the effect.

Munoz, genial these days with success and acclaim, roared at Camila: "I'm giving you a raise. Yes! To reward you for assisting me with my invention, I'm increasing your salary by three thousand dollars annually. That's almost sixty dollars a week!"

"Thank you, Mr. Munoz." And still, thought Camila wryly, she received no recognition. Her name didn't even appear on the patent. Well, well, that was how it worked. She must find her satisfaction in her work. And it had been fascinating lately, the work she had been doing evenings at home investigating what had been named the Munoz Effect. It had been difficult, working alone and purchasing her own equipment. The quantum resonance detector and consciousness field analyzer had been particularly expensive. She was foolish, she supposed, to attempt independent research when so many large scientific organizations were working on it. But she could no more stay away from it than she could stop breathing.

She still didn't know where the blank canvases went, but somehow she felt she was close to the answer.

When she finally discovered the answer, it was too late. The Sofia Robbins incident was only hours away.

As soon as she could reach Munoz, Camila said trembling, "Sir, I think I know where those blank canvases are going. I recommend—"

"Are you still worried about that?" Munoz roared jovially. "Leave that to the academics. We're making money, that's all that matters, eh Spencer?"

That night, at seven-fifteen p.m., the Sofia Robbins family of Ravenswood, Veldoria, sat down in their living room to relax. Just as they settled in, a rain of completed paintings began falling from nowhere, crashed into furniture, raised a bruise on Sofia Robbins' arm, settled down to a steady thump! thump! thump! and inexorably began to pile up on the living-room floor. They seemed to materialize from a plane just below the ceiling. The police called emergency services and emergency services stared helplessly and recommended contacting the Department of Urban Planning.

The incident made headlines in the local news.

The next day other regional outlets in widely scattered locations reported similar incidents.

The following day, paintings began falling on Silverdale City. Ivywood was next, and then across the entire region the paintings began to rain down. They fell outdoors and indoors, usually materializing at heights that were not dangerous. The deluge followed no pattern. Sometimes it would slacken, sometimes stop, sometimes begin heavily again. It fell in homes, on streets, in theaters, trains, offices, and art galleries. No place was immune.

People took to wearing protective gear indoors and out, and the sale of helmets boomed.

All activity was seriously disrupted.

A state of regional emergency was declared.

Government investigators went to work and soon confirmed what was generally suspected: these were completed versions of the blank canvases that had been used by the Munoz Quantum-Artist.

Statisticians and mathematicians calculated the mean rate of painting precipitation and estimated that if all the canvases processed by Munoz robots were to return, the deluge should be over in twelve point forty-three days.

Quantum-Artist sales of course immediately plummeted to zero and stayed there. Anti-Munoz editorials appeared in the press. Commentators accused Munoz of deliberately deceiving the public for his own gain. A governmental investigation was demanded. Munoz received threats. Lawsuits were filed against him. He barricaded himself in the facility, surrounded by security.

Livid with fury and apprehension, he screamed at Camila, "This is your doing, you saboteur! I'm a ruined man!" A falling painting caught him squarely on the shoulder.

"But sir," trembled Camila, dodging three portraits, "I tried to warn you."

"You're through, Spencer!" raved Munoz. "Fired! Get out! But before you go, I want you to know that I've directed the blame where it belongs. I've just released to the press the truth about who created the Quantum-Artist. Now, get out!"

"Yes, sir," said Camila paling. "Then you don't want to hear about my discovery of a way to prevent the paintings from coming back?"

Thump! A barrage of paintings hit the floor, and both took refuge under Munoz's desk. "No!" yelled Munoz at Camila's face which was inches away. "No, I—What did you say?"

"A small modification sir, and the canvases would disappear forever."

Thump!

"Forever, Spencer?"

"Yes sir." Thump! Thump!

"You're certain, Spencer?" Munoz's eyes glared into Camila's.

"Sir, I never make careless claims."

"That's true," said Munoz. His eyes grew dreamy. "It can be done," he mused. "The New Model Quantum-Artist. Free exchanges for the old units. Guarantee that paintings will never bother you. Take a loss at first, but then dominate the market. All right, Spencer, I'll give you another chance. You'll turn over all the details to me. The patent on the modification will naturally be mine. I'll get the credit for fixing your mistake. Fine, fine. We'll work it out. Start on production immediately, Spencer."

Camila felt herself sag inwardly. "Mr. Munoz," she said. "I'm asking only one favor. Let me work full time on research and development, especially on consciousness studies and the Munoz effect. Hire a couple of extra people to help with production. I assure you the company will benefit in the end."

"Absolutely not!" roared Munoz. "How many times must I tell you? You got your job back, didn't you?"

The prospect of long years of heavy production schedules, restricted engineering and tight supervision suddenly made Camila Spencer feel very weary. Research, she thought. Development. Consciousness studies. What she had always wanted. Over the years she had waited, thinking there would be opportunities later. But now she was growing older, and she felt there might not be a later. This represented personal growth, she realized—finally standing up for herself. Somehow she would manage. Perhaps someone would give her a job working in the new field she had pioneered. With a sense of relief she realized she had made her decision.

"Mr. Munoz," Camila said. "I—" thump!—"resign."

Munoz started, extreme astonishment crossing his face.

"No use," said Camila. "Nothing you can say—" thump! thump! thump!—"will make any difference now."

"But see here, the New Model Quantum-Artist...!"

"Will remain my secret. Good day."

"Spencer!" howled Munoz. "I order you to remain!"

Camila almost submitted from force of habit. She hesitated for a moment, then turned abruptly.

"Good day," said Camila firmly, sprinting through the falling paintings to the door.

Money, Camila decided after a while, was necessary. Her savings were running low. She was having no luck finding another position. Although the paintings had stopped falling on the twelfth day, as predicted by the statisticians, industry would not soon forget the disruption and losses caused by the deluge. It was not eager to hire the woman it regarded as responsible for the whole thing.

"Spencer," the interviewer would read. "Camila Spencer." Then, looking up, "Not the Camila Spencer who—"

"Yes," Camila would admit miserably.

"I am sorry, but—"

She did no better with research organizations. Typical was a message from the David King Research Institute: "—cannot accept your application inasmuch as we feel your premature application of your discovery to commercial purposes denotes a lack of scientific responsibility and ethics not desirable in a member of our organization—former employer states the decision was yours entirely. Unfavorable reference—"

Munoz, Camila thought, feeling a strange sensation deep within her chest that she had not the experience to recognize as the beginning of a slow anger, Munoz was playing dirty and getting away with it.

Of course, if she were to agree to reveal her latest discoveries to a research organization, she would undoubtedly get an appointment. But how could she? Everything patentable in her work would automatically revert to Munoz under the one-year clause in the company patent agreement. No, Camila told herself, she was revealing nothing that Munoz might claim. The anger began to mount.

But she was beginning to need money desperately. Her mother wasn't getting any better and medical bills for the pollution control treatments were running high.

The phone rang. Camila seized it and said to the image: "Absolutely not."

"I'll increase it another fifteen hundred," grated the small Munoz image. "Do you realize, woman, this is the twelfth raise I've offered you? A total increase of sixteen thousand dollars? Be sensible, Spencer. I know you can't find work anywhere else."

"Thanks to you. Mr. Munoz, I wouldn't work for you if—"

A barrage of rocks crashed against the reinforced window. "What's happening!" yelled Munoz. "Oh, I see. People throwing rocks at your residence again? Oh, I know all about that, Spencer. I know that you're probably the most unpopular person alive today. I know about the rocks, the vandalism, the threats, the sneaking out at night, the disguises you've had to use. Why don't you come back to us and change all that, Spencer? We'll release the New Model Quantum-Artist and the world will soon forget about the old one."

"No," said Camila. "People will forget anyway—I hope."

"If you won't think of yourself, at least think of your fellow workers," begged Munoz, his voice going soft. "Do you realize that Munoz Robotics will soon be forced to close down, throwing all your former colleagues out of work? Think of Ian, Maria Ward, Yuki Wallace. They have families too. Think of the technicians in the lab, the staff in the office, the sales team. All, all unemployed because of you. Think of that, Spencer."

Camila blinked. This had not occurred to her.

Munoz eyed her sharply, then smiled with a hint of triumph. "Think it over, Spencer."

Camila sat, thinking it over. Was it right to let all these people lose their jobs? Frowning, she dialed Ian's number.

"Chief," said Ian, "Forget it. The team is behind you one hundred percent. We'll manage."

"But that's the problem. I thought you'd feel like this, and I can't let you."

"You're beginning to weaken. Don't. Think, chief, think. The mind that figured out the Quantum-Artist can solve this."

Camila hung up. A glow of anger that had been building in her chest grew warmer. She began pacing the floor. How she hated to do it. Think, Ian had said. But she had. She'd considered every angle, and there was no solution.

Camila walked into the kitchen and carefully poured herself a glass of water. She drank the water slowly and placed the glass on the counter with a tiny clink. It was the tiny clink that did it. Something about it triggered the growing rage. If Munoz were there she would have given him a piece of her mind. The eighteen years. The manipulation. The threats.

Think? She'd figured the solution long ago, only she hadn't allowed herself to see it. Not lack of intelligence, lack of courage. Well, she thought grimly, dialing Munoz's number, she was going through with it now. "Munoz!" she barked. "Two p.m. tomorrow. My place. Be there. That's all." She hung up.

In the same determined mood the following morning, she placed a few more calls.

In the same mood that afternoon she stood in the middle of her living room and looked at her visitors: Munoz, Mohammad Osborne, the Government representative; David King from the research foundation; Yuki Wallace of Silverdale University; members of the press.

"Everyone," she said. "I'll make this brief." She waved the documents in her hand. "Here is everything I know about what I call the Spencer Effect, including plans and specifications for the New Model Quantum-Artist. All of you have special reasons for being keenly interested in this information. I am now going to give a copy to each of you, providing one condition is met by Mr. Munoz." She stared at Munoz. "In short, I want fifty-one percent ownership of Munoz Robotics Corporation."

Munoz leaped from his chair. "Outrageous!" He roared. "Ridiculous!"

"Fifty-one percent," said Camila firmly. "Don't bother with any counterproposals or the meeting is over."

"Everyone!" squawked Munoz, "I appeal to you—"

"Stop bluffing," said Camila coldly. "There's no other way out for you. Otherwise you're ruined. Here, sign this agreement."

Munoz threw the paper to the floor and screamed: "Everyone, will you be a party to this?"

"Well," murmured the Government representative, "I never did think Spencer got a fair deal."

"This information is important to consciousness studies," said the David King representative.

After Munoz had signed, the documents were distributed.

Published in the news the following day, Camila's statement read, in part: "The motion in quantum space and consciousness dimensions of the singular processing patterns of the original Quantum-Artist combined with the resonance effect built up as it increased its quantum entanglement in inverse proportion to the consciousness field strength caused an instantaneous disruption of what I call the Alpha multi-dimensional barrier. The blank canvas, being quantum-entangled, passed through, leaving its completed artistic form behind. The disruption was instantly repaired by the stable nature of the barrier.

"Beyond the barrier is what I call Alpha space, a space apparently quite as extensive as our own universe. Unfortunately, as my investigations indicated, Alpha space seems to be thickly inhabited. These inhabitants, the nature of whom I have not yet ascertained, obviously resented the intrusion of the blank canvases, developed a method of disrupting the barrier from their side, and returned the canvases as completed paintings.

"However, I have established the existence of other spaces up to Mu space, and suspect that others exist beyond that. Beta space, which is also adjacent to our own space, is devoid of any form of consciousness. The New Model Quantum-Artist is designed to pass canvases through the Beta barrier. Beta space will safely absorb an infinite number of canvases.

"I sincerely and humbly venture the opinion that we are on the threshold of tremendous and mighty discoveries in consciousness studies. It is my belief that possibly an infinite number of universes exist in a type of layered structure separated by barriers.

"Therefore, might it not be that an infinite number of layered structures exist—?"

"Ms. Spencer—" said Munoz.

Camila looked up from her desk in the newly constructed Spencer Multi-Dimensional Consciousness Division of the Munoz Robotics Corporation. "Munoz, don't bother me about production. Production is your concern."

"But Ms. Spencer—"

"Get out," said Camila.

Munoz paled and left.

"As I was saying, Ian—" continued Camila.

The Quantum Commons: Systems Thinking for Collective Intelligence

In the orbital settlements circling Mars, humanity had discovered something unexpected about cooperation. The current narrative that most colonists told themselves about how humans survived in space focused on the familiar themes of competition—resource allocation, territorial claims, corporate sponsorship, technological supremacy, survival against the void. People also worked together in space habitats for curiosity, for the thrill of discovery, and because they sometimes enjoyed collaborating to create something that benefited the entire settlement. If Peter Morrison had to reduce the essence of successful space colonization to five words, "people solve impossible problems together" would suffice. Neural-link communication networks could be powerful amplifiers of collective intelligence precisely because they augmented and extended the power of ever-evolving human cooperation. To be sure, manipulation, sabotage, corporate espionage, hoarding and xenophobia were part of human nature in space, and those aspects of human behavior could be amplified through technology as well. But mutual aid, innovation, community and scientific curiosity were also parts of human nature—and Morrison proposed that the Martian Collaborative Network was an existence proof that these capabilities could be amplified effectively. Indeed, humanity's social inventiveness had become central to survival beyond Earth. The neural implants that evolved from early brain-computer interfaces, which connected to what colonists considered their "higher" faculties of reasoning and prediction, were also essential to coordinated social life. The neural information-processing required for managing shared life-support systems, coordinating resource distribution, maintaining the complex rituals that built trust across settlements scattered across two planets and three moons, from small outposts to sprawling orbital cities, had been enabled by (and had driven the rapid development of) those uniquely twenty-second-century innovations in collective cognition.

But Morrison hadn't started out thinking about the dynamics of distributed decision-making and the amplification of collective action through quantum-encrypted neural networks. Like all the other pioneers in this era, he had started by experiencing the new ways of being that space-based social technologies had made possible. And like the other early adopters, Jasmine Perry had played a catalytic, communitarian, boundary-pushing, convention-challenging, authority-questioning, innovation-loving role in his experiences of the possibilities of networked consciousness in space.

Collaborators and Visionaries

To Morrison, direct experience of what he later came to call quantum commons communities preceded theories about the ways people accomplished things together through neural-link networks. He met Jasmine Perry in the 2140s as part of what they called "the Distributed Intelligence Collective," a small group of enthusiasts who thought that sharing consciousness fragments through primitive neural bridges with 10-gigabit bandwidth was revolutionary. Perry, like the legendary Hannah Ramos before her, was what sociologists called a network catalyst, who occupied what organizational theorists would call key structural positions—what cultural historians called a connector. Perry was also a believer in building practical systems rather than merely theorizing about them.

Perry was one of the founders of a multicultural consciousness-sharing hub in the Richmond District of New Shanghai Station, and in the early 2140s Morrison had begun to branch out from local neural networks to make connections across the solar system. The excitement of sharing experiences, planning missions, debating political philosophy and helping each other through neural-link channels came before the notion that their experimental subculture might evolve into a solar-system-wide, consciousness-to-consciousness, multi-sensory network of ten billion humans and artificial intelligences. They started to dream about future possibilities of collective intelligence only after personally experiencing something unprecedented, profound and authentic in their webs of emerging collaboration and shared consciousness. In recent decades, consciousness studies had grown into a discipline—more properly, an interdiscipline involving neuroscientists, quantum physicists, systems theorists, cultural anthropologists, economists, programmers and political scientists. Back when people in neural networks argued through 10-gigabit connections about whether one could properly call what they were doing a form of collective consciousness, there was no body of empirical evidence to serve as a foundation for scientific argument—all theory was experiential. By now, however, there was substantial data.

One particularly useful affordance of neural-link sociality was that a great deal of shared cognitive activity was recorded and structured in a way that made it suitable for systematic study using particle physics-derived analysis methods. One effect of the neural surveillance infrastructure was the loss of cognitive privacy and the threat of authoritarian thought control; another effect was a rich body of data about collective decision-making patterns. Every one of the Martian Knowledge Commons's millions of contributions, and all the neural discussions and debate threads associated with those contributions, was available for inspection—along with billions of archived consciousness-sharing sessions. Patterns were beginning to emerge. Researchers were beginning to understand something about what worked and what didn't work with neural-linked humans, and why.

Did knowing something about the way neural architecture influenced collective behavior mean that knowledge could be put to use? Now that scientists were beginning to learn about the specific sociotechnical affordances of consciousness-sharing networks, was it possible to derive normative design principles? How should systems architects think about the principles of beneficial collective intelligence platforms? Could dehumanizing or consciousness-fragmenting effects of neural linking be mitigated or eliminated by better network design? In what ways did the design of consciousness-sharing systems enable or prevent authentic community, organized collective action, social capital, cultural and scientific production? Morrison had continued to make direct experience of his life in neural networks—from lifelong collaborators like Jasmine Perry to the other people across the solar system he'd come to know, because consciousness-sharing technology made it possible to connect with people who shared his interests in systems thinking and sustainable business models for space settlements, even if he had never heard of them before, even if they lived in Horizonville, Estoria on Titan or Eastwood, Nordavia on Europa. But parallel with his direct experience of the consciousness-sphere, Morrison had continued to track new research and theory about what collective intelligence might mean and the ways in which neural communication systems influenced and were shaped by social forces.

The Ethics of Shared Consciousness

One of the first questions that arose from Morrison's earliest experiences in neural networks was why people in consciousness-sharing communities should spend so much cognitive energy answering each other's questions, solving each other's problems, without direct compensation. Morrison first encountered Samuel Schneider in pursuit of his curiosity about why people would work together with strangers, without payment, to create something nobody owned—free and open-source consciousness protocols. First in "Coase's Quantum Dilemma," and then in "The Wealth of Neural Networks," Schneider contributed to important theoretical foundations for a new way of thinking about collective cognitive activity—"commons-based consciousness production," technically made possible by ten billion neural implants and quantum-encrypted networks—as a new form of organizing economic and intellectual production, alongside markets and corporations. If Schneider was right, the new story about how humans accomplished things included an important corollary—if tools like neural implants and quantum networks made it easy enough, people were willing to work together for non-market incentives to create knowledge systems, collaborative research databases and archives of shared human experience. While the old story was that people were highly unlikely to cooperate with strangers to voluntarily create public goods, the new story seemed to be that people would indeed create significant common value voluntarily, if it was easy enough for anybody to contribute what they wanted, whenever they wanted to contribute it ("self-selection"). There was substantial evidence to support the hypothesis that what used to be considered altruism was now a natural byproduct of daily life in neural networks. So much of what colonists took for granted as part of daily life in space, from the climate adaptation protocols that managed habitat atmospheres, to the distributed computation systems that powered settlement infrastructure, to the green infrastructure designs that made orbital gardens possible, was created by volunteers who gave their creations away to make possible something larger—the sustainable civilization they all depended on.

To some degree, the explosion of innovation that followed the deployment of quantum neural networks in 2138 was made possible by deliberate design decisions on the part of the system's architects—the consciousness-integrity principle, built into the quantum protocols that made safe neural linking possible, which deliberately decentralized the power to innovate, to build something new and transformative on existing foundations. Was it possible to understand exactly what it was about neural networks that made the Martian Knowledge Commons, the Solar Operating System, the Climate Technology Collaborative, and the Consciousness Rights Movement possible? And if so, could this theoretical knowledge be put to practical use? Morrison was struck by a phrase from Schneider's essay: "We must now turn our attention to building systems that support human consciousness while preserving individual agency." That seemed right. But how would it be done? It was easy to say and not as easy to see the ways in which power structures and financial regulation molded the design of consciousness-sharing systems. They needed to develop a participatory framework, assisted by neural networks and consciousness-sharing platforms, that focused on catalyzing, inspiring, nourishing, facilitating, and guiding the cognitive skills essential to individual and collective life.

A Framework for Collective Intelligence

To accomplish this attention-turning, they needed to develop a participatory framework, assisted by neural networks and consciousness-sharing platforms, that focused on catalyzing, inspiring, nourishing, facilitating, and guiding the cognitive skills essential to individual and collective life in the twenty-second century. These cognitive skills were where the human brain, human sociality and consciousness-sharing technologies met. Colonists were accustomed to thinking about the tangible parts of communication systems—the neural implants and quantum networks—but the less visible social practices and social affordances, from language to quantum protocols, were where human social genius could meet the augmenting power of technological networks. Cognitive literacy was the most important method Homo sapiens had used to introduce systems and tools to other humans, to train each other to partake of and contribute to culture, and to humanize the use of instruments that might otherwise enable commodification, mechanization and dehumanization. By cognitive literacy, Morrison meant, following theorists like Logan Salazar and others, the set of skills that enabled individuals to encode and decode knowledge and power via speech, writing, neural transmission and collective action, and which, when learned, introduced the individual to a community. Cognitive literacy linked technology and sociality. The alphabet had not caused ancient civilizations, but made them possible. Printing had not caused democracy or science, but literate populations, enabled by the printing press, devised systems for citizen governance and collective knowledge creation. Neural networks had not caused open-source consciousness protocols, the Martian Knowledge Commons or emergent collective responses to habitat failures, but they made it possible for people to act together in new ways, with people they weren't able to organize action with before, in places and at speeds for which collective action had never been possible. Cognitive literacies were the prerequisite for the human agency that used alphabets, presses and neural networks to create wealth, alleviate suffering and invent new institutions. If the humans currently alive across the solar system were to take advantage of consciousness-sharing technologies to address the severe problems that faced their species and the fragile ecosystems they depended on, neural implants, quantum computers and consciousness networks were not enough. They needed new literacies around participatory consciousness-sharing, the dynamics of cooperation and collective action, the effective deployment of attention and the rational and critical discourse necessary for healthy democratic governance.

Consciousness-Sharing Literacies

In "Using Participatory Neural Networks and Collective Voice to Encourage Civic Engagement," Morrison wrote:

If print culture shaped the environment in which the Enlightenment blossomed and set the scene for the Industrial Revolution, participatory consciousness-sharing might similarly shape the cognitive and social environments in which twenty-second century life takes place (a fundamental shift in the way our culture operates). For this reason, consciousness-sharing literacy is not another subject to be added to educational programs as job training for cognitive workers.

Participatory consciousness-sharing systems included (but weren't limited to) neural blogs, consciousness wikis, experience streaming, memory tagging and social bookmarking, sensory-sharing, experience mashups, cognitive podcasts, neural storytelling, virtual consciousness communities, neural network services, immersive virtual environments, and experience-sharing platforms. These distinctly different systems shared three common, interrelated characteristics:

Many-to-many neural networks now made it possible for every person connected to the network to broadcast as well as receive thoughts, sensations, memories, emotions, computations, tags, or links to and from every other person. The asymmetry between broadcaster and audience that was dictated by the structure of pre-neural technologies had changed radically. This was a technical-structural characteristic.

Participatory consciousness-sharing systems were social systems whose value and power derived from the active participation of many people. Value derived not just from the size of the network, but from participants' power to link to each other, to form a collective consciousness as well as a market. This was a psychological and social characteristic.

Social networks, when amplified by neural and quantum networks, enabled broader, faster, and lower-cost coordination of activities. This was an economic and political characteristic informed by game theory principles.

Like the early days of print, radio, and television, the present structure of the participatory consciousness-sharing regime—the political, economic, social and cultural institutions that constrained and empowered the way the new medium could be used, and which imposed structures on flows of information and consciousness—was still unsettled. As legislative and regulatory battles, business competition, and social institutions vied to control the new regime, a potentially decisive and presently unknown variable was the degree and kind of public participation. Because the unique power of the new consciousness-sharing regime was precisely its participatory potential, the number of people who participated in using it during its formative years, and the skill with which they attempted to take advantage of this potential, was particularly salient.

Like Samuel Schneider and the oral history researchers at Foxwood Province, Morrison believed that a participatory culture in which most of the population saw themselves as creators as well as consumers of shared consciousness was far more likely to generate freedom and prosperity for more people than one in which a small portion of the population produced consciousness content that the majority passively consumed. The technological infrastructure for participatory consciousness-sharing had grown rapidly, building on advances in quantum computing, neural interface technology, the settlement boom and the innovations of neuroscientists and systems engineers. Increasingly, access to that infrastructure—the ability to upload a consciousness fragment documenting corporate malfeasance or reveal a threat to settlement security—had become economically accessible. Literacy—access to the codes and communities of neural video-sharing, consciousness-streaming, experience bookmarking, collaborative consciousness wikis—was what was required to use that infrastructure to create a participatory culture. A population with neural infrastructure and ubiquitous quantum computing could be a captive audience for a consciousness monopoly, given enough bad laws and judicial rulings. A population that knew what to do with the tools at hand stood a better chance of resisting enclosure. The more people who knew how to use participatory consciousness-sharing systems to learn, inform, persuade, investigate, reveal, advocate and organize, the more likely the future consciousness-sphere would allow, enable and encourage liberty and participation. Such literacy could only make action possible, however—it was not in the technology, or even in the knowledge of how to use it, but in the ways people used knowledge and technology to create wealth, secure freedom, resist tyranny.

Morrison had seen this principle in action during the Great Habitat Crisis of 2147, when consciousness-sharing networks enabled rapid coordination across settlements from the Richmond District to Horizonville, Estoria to Eastwood, Nordavia, and even remote outposts in Foxwood Province. When life-support systems began failing across multiple settlements simultaneously due to a cascading software failure, it was the consciousness-sharing networks—not the corporate communication channels or government emergency systems—that enabled colonists to pool their knowledge, share solutions, and coordinate rescue efforts. Engineers in one settlement could share their direct neural experience of solving a specific problem with engineers thousands of kilometers away facing similar challenges. The collective intelligence that emerged from millions of people contributing their expertise, experience and cognitive resources saved countless lives and demonstrated the transformative potential of participatory consciousness-sharing.

But Morrison also recognized the dangers. The same technologies that enabled beneficial collective action could also enable manipulation, surveillance and control. Without proper literacy—without understanding how consciousness-sharing systems worked, how to protect one's cognitive privacy, how to distinguish authentic shared experience from manufactured propaganda—people could become vulnerable to exploitation. This was why Morrison dedicated himself to developing educational frameworks, working with collaborators like Jasmine Perry and Samuel Schneider to create open-source training materials that taught not just how to use consciousness-sharing technology, but how to think critically about it, how to participate ethically, how to build systems that enhanced rather than diminished human agency.

The work was far from complete. As neural networks continued to evolve and new forms of collective consciousness emerged, new literacies would be required. But Morrison remained optimistic. The same human capacities for cooperation, creativity and mutual aid that had enabled humanity to survive on Earth for millennia were now being amplified and extended through consciousness-sharing technologies. If enough people developed the literacies needed to use these technologies wisely, if enough people committed themselves to building systems that supported human flourishing rather than exploitation, then perhaps humanity's future among the stars would be characterized not by competition and conflict, but by collaboration and collective intelligence. The quantum commons—the shared space of collective consciousness that neural networks made possible—could become humanity's greatest achievement, a testament to what people could accomplish when they worked together to solve impossible problems.

The Singing Clock Tower
CHAPTER I
An Unsolved Mystery

"Tell Olivia about it," begged Nora. "Please, Lucy, it can't be as bad as it appears. There isn't anything that Olivia can't figure out."

Lucy tilted her head disdainfully. "We're colleagues now. We're both working on the Glendale Regional Arts Council and should support each other. But you always did take Olivia's side. She was the one who nearly disrupted our joint performance trying to solve a mystery. I don't believe she'd understand—understand any better than I do. Everyone has problems, and I'm sure Olivia is no exception."

"You're right, Lucy," announced Olivia, coming in to serve tea to the two friends she had invited for lunch at Thomas's suggestion. "I do have problems, and there are plenty of mysteries I can't solve."

"Name one," challenged Nora. "Just mention one single strange thing you couldn't explain, and I'll believe you. I've seen you in action, Olivia Lane—"

"Olivia Hill, remember?"

"Well, you were Olivia Lane when you solved all those mysteries. I met you when the whole Glendale Region was threatened by the controversial dam project and you solved that—"

"That," declared Olivia, "was my brother Juan, not me. He was the hero without even meaning to be. He was the one who spoke at the town council meeting and convinced them to reconsider. I was off chasing shadows."

"A vanishing shadow," Nora said with a sigh. "What you did wasn't easy, Olivia."

"It didn't need to be as hard as it was," Olivia confessed. "I know now that keeping that promise not to talk about the environmental impact study was a great big mistake and could have cost the region its heritage sites. I should have told Steven."

"Please," Lucy said, a pained expression clouding her pretty face, "let's not talk about him now."

"Very well," Olivia agreed. "What shall we talk about?"

"You," Nora said, "and all the mysteries you've solved. Maybe you were mistaken about a thing or two before the dam controversy, but what about the haunted theater you investigated? You were the one who tracked down the strange occurrences backstage and in the orchestra pit and goodness knows where all. You've been chasing mysteries ever since I met you, and not one of them did you fail to explain in some sensible, logical fashion."

"Before I met you," Olivia said, thinking back, "there were plenty of them I couldn't explain. There was one I used to call the spirit of the clock tower, but what it was or how it sang to me is more than I know. If my grandparents knew, they weren't telling. And now they're both gone and I can't ask them. They left me a lot of unsolved mysteries along with this house. Maybe I'll find the answers to some of them when I finish sorting Grandmother's things. They're stored in one end of the attic."

"Another mysterious attic? How thrilling!" exclaimed Nora. "Why don't you investigate and expose the truth?"

"I didn't say the attic was mysterious."

Olivia was almost sorry she had mentioned it. She wasn't in the mood for digging up old mysteries, but Nora and Lucy insisted. It all began, she finally told them, the summer before they met. Juan had just started working on the regional newspaper. Olivia remembered that it was Lucy's father, Richard Stone, who gave him his job with the Glendale Regional Herald. He had turned in some interesting coverage of a local arts festival, convincing Mr. Stone that he had in him the makings of a good reporter. And so it was that he spent the summer Olivia was remembering in Cliffside where the wealthy families had their estates, while she had to suffer the heat and loneliness of Maplewood.

Her thoughts were what had made it so hard, she confessed now as she reviewed everything that had happened. She just couldn't help resenting the fact that her parents left her every summer while they went off on a cultural exchange program by themselves. What did they think she would do?

"You'll have plenty to read," her father had told her. "I bought you six new books in that mystery series you like. When they're finished there are plenty of old programs and playbills around. Your grandmother never throws anything away. She has theater memorabilia she's saved since your mother was a girl. If you ask for them she'll let you have the whole collection. I know how you love the performing arts."

"I do, Dad, but if the programs are that old—"

Olivia had stopped. She had seen her father's tired eyes and had realized that a busy professor needed a vacation much more than a student who had too little to do. He and Olivia's mother usually went to the international arts conference where they had met. It was a precious memory. Every summer Professor Lane and his wife relived it. And every summer Olivia went to stay with her grandmother Hill, who scolded and fussed and tried to pretend she wasn't glad to have her.

"You here again?" she had greeted her that summer, and Olivia hadn't noticed her old eyes twinkling behind her glasses. "What do you propose to do with yourself this time?"

"Read," Olivia had told her. "Mom and Dad say you have a whole collection of old theater programs—"

"In the attic. Go up and look them over if you can stand the heat."

Olivia went, not to look over the old programs so much as to escape to a place where she could have a good cry. It was the summer before her fifteenth birthday. In another year she would have outgrown her childish resentment of her parents' vacation or be grown up enough to ask them to let her have a vacation of her own. In another year she would be summering at the prestigious Evergreen Arts Academy and solving a mystery to be known as the Phantom Performance.

"A whole series of strange events," Nora would be telling her, "and you solved everything."

But then she didn't even know Nora. She had no idea so many thrilling adventures awaited her. There seemed to be nothing—nothing—and so the tears came and spilled over on one of the programs. As Olivia wiped it away she noticed that it had fallen on a picture of a clock tower.

"A clock tower with musical notes floating from it. How strange!" she remembered saying aloud.

Olivia had never seen a real singing clock tower. The thrill of walking up to the door of the palatial arts center in Cliffside was still ahead of her. On the grounds a clock tower still chimed melodies like those she was to hear on her honeymoon in the musical district of Galdoria's capital. But all that was in the future. If anyone had told the freckled-faced, ponytailed girl that she would one day marry Thomas Hill, she would have laughed in their faces.

"That tease!"

For then she knew Thomas only as an older boy who used to tease her and call her bookworm until one day she yelled back at him, "Bookworms are intelligent and so am I!"

Thomas was to win Olivia's heart when he gave her a music box and suggested she keep it forever. The music box was now a treasured keepsake. But the summer Olivia found the picture of a clock tower and spilled tears on it she had no music box. She had nothing, she confessed, not even a friend. It had helped to pretend the clock tower in the picture was filled with all the songs lonely girls like herself had ever wished to hear.

"But that would make it enchanted!" she had suddenly exclaimed. "If I could find it I'd wish—"

A step had sounded on the stairs. Olivia remembered it distinctly. She had turned to see her grandmother and to hear her say in her usual abrupt fashion, "Enchanted clock tower, indeed! If you let people know your wishes instead of muttering them to yourself, most of them aren't so impossible."

"Were they?" asked Nora.

She and Lucy had listened to this much of what Olivia was telling them without interruption.

"That's the unsolved mystery," Olivia replied. "There weren't any of them impossible."

And she went on to tell them how, the very next day, her grandparents had taken her to a clock tower exactly like the one in the picture. It was in the center of a beautiful arts complex with gardens leading up to it. Beside the main path were smaller sculptures with water features. Olivia had stared at them a moment and then climbed the steps to the tower.

"Am I dreaming?" she remembered saying aloud. "Is this beautiful clock tower real?"

A voice had answered, although she could see no one.

"Make your wishes, Olivia. Wish wisely. If you sing a note at the tower your wishes will surely come true."

"A note?" Olivia had asked. "How can I sing when I'm so amazed? This is a wonderful place."

"Sing a note at the tower and your wishes will surely come true," the voice had repeated.

"But what should I sing?"

"You found plenty to cry about back at your grandmother's house," the mysterious voice had reminded her. "Weren't you crying on my picture up there in the attic?"

"Then you—you are the clock tower!" Olivia remembered exclaiming. "But a clock tower doesn't speak. It doesn't have a voice."

"Wish wisely," the voice from the tower had said in a mysterious whisper.

CHAPTER II
If Wishes Came True

"Did you?" Nora interrupted the story to ask excitedly. "Oh, Olivia! Don't keep us in suspense any longer. What did you wish?"

"Patience," Olivia said with a smile. "I'm coming to that."

First, she told her friends, she had to think of a wise wish. There had been so much she wanted in those early days before the dam controversy. Her best friend had moved away.

"You see," she explained, "I made the mistake of having just one best friend. There wasn't anybody in Maplewood. I remember thinking of how lonely I was and how I wished for friends and opportunities, and suddenly I began to hum a melody. It echoed in the tower. I thought I had to wish quickly before it faded, and so I began naming the things I wanted as fast as I could. I'm not sure they were wise wishes. They seem rather selfish to me, now. I wasn't thinking of anybody but me, Olivia Lane, and what I wanted. It wasn't until after I began to think of others that my wishes started to come true."

"But what were they?" Nora insisted.

Lucy seemed unusually quiet and thoughtful. Olivia did not notice the concern in her eyes as she replied airily, "Oh, didn't I tell you? I wished for lots of friends and opportunities in the performing arts, and I wished I could marry someone who worked in justice theory or conflict resolution and solve a lot of mysteries and that's as far as I got when the echo vanished. I thought the spell was broken and so I didn't wish for anything more."

"Wasn't there anything more you wanted?" Nora asked.

"Of course," replied Olivia. "There were lots more things. I wanted to travel, of course, and work in media production, and have a nice home, and—"

"And your wishes all came true!"

"Every one of them," Olivia agreed. "Thomas did become a mediator specializing in conflict resolution, and I did get involved in the performing arts. That seemed impossible at the time, but the future did hold all of it for me."

"Strange how things work out," Nora said, squeezing Lucy's hand under the table. "Don't you think friends should tell each other their problems, Olivia?"

"Thomas and I always do," she replied, "but then it was different. I didn't know I would marry Thomas or that he would become a mediator, and I didn't know about any of the opportunities that would come. It is strange, isn't it? But the strangest thing of all was the clock tower itself."

"Why?" asked Lucy. "Do you still think it was enchanted?"

Nora laughed at this, but Olivia was serious as she answered, "I was still young enough to think so at the time. I wandered around, growing very drowsy. Then I found a bench in the garden and sat down. I must have dozed off, because I remember waking up and wondering if the voice in the clock tower had been a dream."

"A bench?" Nora questioned. "Are you sure it wasn't a magic carpet?"

"No, it was a bench all right," Olivia assured her, laughing. "It was in a beautiful garden all surrounded by flowering hedges. Did I tell you it was June?"

"All the year around?"

Again Nora laughed. But Lucy said abruptly, "Let's not talk about gardens in June. It's a long way from June to December."

"Do you mean a garden changes? I know," Olivia said, "but I think this one would be beautiful at any time of the year. There were sculptures, too, and I don't know how many different kinds of plantings. I explored the garden all around the clock tower."

"And then what happened?" Lucy urged her.

"Yes, yes. Go on," entreated Nora. "I didn't dream you'd kept anything that exciting a secret. Why didn't you try to solve the mystery?"

"I think I would have tried," Olivia admitted, "if I had been older or more experienced. I really should have investigated it more thoroughly and learned the secret of the tower. But after the echo went away it didn't speak to me any more, and I didn't really think it had heard my wishes. I was still wishing for a friend when I met you, Nora. It did seem impossible for us to be friends at first, didn't it? Lucy was your friend."

"I did make trouble for you," Lucy remembered. "It was all because of my foolish jealousy."

"It was nothing compared to the trouble caused by the dam controversy," declared Olivia. "After that things started happening so fast that I completely forgot about the clock tower. Honestly, Nora, I don't believe I thought about it again until after we moved to Cliffside and I walked up to your door and saw the arts center on the hill."

"The old Cliffside landmark, I always called it," Nora said with a giggle. "I've seen lots nicer clock towers."

"You have?" asked Olivia. "Then maybe you've seen the one I've been telling you about. I think the picture of it is still in the attic. Come on up and I'll show you."

Nora and Lucy had finished their tea while Olivia was telling them the story of the clock tower. Somehow, she wasn't hungry for hers. She had tasted it too often while she was making it.

"I'll save it for later," she decided.

Nora watched as Olivia cleared the cups.

"Sometimes," Olivia said fondly, "I think about those old days and wonder what really happened."

"Let's go look at that picture," Nora said eagerly.

Leaving the table, they all started upstairs. In modernizing her grandparents' house to suit her own and Thomas's tastes, Olivia had seen to it that the old stair door was removed. But there was still a door closing off the narrower stairs that led to the attic.

"Come on. There's nothing up here to be afraid of," Olivia urged her friends.

"Maybe not, but I'm beginning to get curious," confessed Nora as she followed Olivia to the storage room at the top of the last flight of stairs.

"So am I," Lucy admitted. "I'm interested in seeing this mysterious picture."

"Up here we can all turn back the clock," Olivia said mysteriously. "Does anybody care to explore the past?"

The exploration began enthusiastically with Olivia relating still more of what she remembered about the clock tower.

"When I told Grandma about it she laughed and said I must have dreamed it. She said if wishes came true that easily she'd be living in a palace. But would she?" Olivia wondered. "When I first remember this house she was still using oil lamps. I think she and Grandpa liked the way they lived without any modern conveniences or anything."

"I think so, too," Nora agreed, looking around the old attic. "It is strange they both died the same winter, isn't it?"

"Maybe they wanted it that way. Maybe they wished neither of them would outlive the other. If they did wish at the tower," Olivia went on more thoughtfully, "I'm sure that was one of their wishes. Another could have been to keep the good old days, as Grandma used to call them. That one came true in a way. They did manage to keep a little of the past when they kept all these old things. That's what I meant about turning back the clock."

"If wishes came true I'd like to turn it back a little myself," Lucy began. "It would be nice if things were the way they used to be when I trusted Steven—"

"Don't you trust him now?" Olivia asked.

Afterwards she was sorry for the interruption. Nora and Olivia both questioned Lucy, but that was all she would say. Olivia wondered, as they searched through the old programs, what was wrong. Lucy was of a suspicious disposition. Was jealousy coming between her and her partner, Steven Richardson? Until now they had seemed to work well together. But there was no happiness in Lucy's face as she gazed at a picture of one of the clock towers and then said in a tight little voice, "It is. It's the very same one."

"But that's the picture I've been searching for!" Olivia said eagerly. "Do you know where it is?"

"I can't be sure. But if it ever was enchanted, I'm sure it isn't now. Let's go," Lucy said suddenly to Nora. Olivia knew she was suggesting a fast trip home. But, apparently, Nora did not understand it that way. If she did, she pretended not to.

"Where?" she asked. "To the clock tower? I'd love to, wouldn't you, Olivia?"

"I certainly would," Olivia replied enthusiastically. "Do you recognize it, too?"

"I think so," Nora answered after studying a little more closely the picture they had found. "It looks like the tower on the Matthews estate."

"The technology company Matthews?" Olivia questioned. "Then my grandparents must have driven old Bessie all the way to the edge of Cliffside."

"Not quite all the way," Lucy objected. "The Matthews own that stretch of woodland just before you come into the city. You've passed it lots of times."

"Of course," agreed Olivia. She put the program back in its place and turned eagerly to her friends. "I do remember a road turning off into the woods and going on uphill," she told them. "I never thought it led to a house, though. There isn't even a gate. Could that be the road my grandparents took?"

"Why don't we take it ourselves and find out?" Nora suggested.

CHAPTER III
A Strange Encounter

Lucy was not too enthusiastic about the proposed trip to the Matthews estate. Finally she agreed to it under one condition. They were not to drive all the way to the house which, she said, was just over the hilltop. They were to park the car where no one would see it and follow the path to the clock tower.

"But suppose we can't find the path?" asked Olivia.

"You'll remember it, won't you?"

Olivia thought she would, but she wasn't too sure. She and Nora both argued that it would be better to inquire at the house. Nora knew Pablo Matthews slightly.

"He'd be glad to show us around. This way it looks as if we're planning something secretive," Nora said as they started off in the blue car she was driving.

It was a neat little car, not too conspicuous, and easy to park in out-of-the-way places. Olivia laughed and said if they did find the clock tower she thought she'd wish for one exactly like Nora's car.

"Well, you know what your grandmother said about wishes, don't you?" Lucy asked. "If you let people know about them instead of muttering them to yourself most of them aren't so impossible."

"Quite true," Olivia agreed. "I'll let Thomas know about this one. He's my gift-giver, and it will soon be the holidays. Maybe I should have worn the coat he gave me last year."

"Your jacket's better in case it rains. It's too warm for snow. We picked a perfect day for this trip," Nora continued, guiding the car around curves as it climbed the steep hill beyond Maplewood.

The trip was a short one. In twenty minutes they had covered the distance that had seemed such a long way to Olivia when she was riding in her grandfather's old truck.

"I've been thinking about it," she said, "and I've just about figured out how it happened. I didn't think my grandparents knew the Matthews well enough to pay them a visit, though. We must have looked odd driving up to a beautiful estate in Grandpa's old truck. I do remember that Grandma had some handmade quilts to deliver. But that still doesn't explain what happened afterwards. When I woke up on the bench I was alone in the garden. Truck, grandparents—all had disappeared."

"How could they?" asked Nora.

"Anyway," Lucy began, "you had a chance to see how beautiful everything was before—"

Again she broke off as if there were something she wanted to tell but didn't quite dare.

"Before what?" questioned Olivia.

"Oh, nothing. Forget I said anything about it. You were telling us how you woke up on the bench, but you never did explain how you got back home," Lucy reminded her.

"Didn't I?" asked Olivia. "I'd forgotten a lot of it, but it's beginning to come back now. I do remember driving home along this road. You see, I thought my grandparents had left me in the garden for a surprise and would return for me. I told you I was all alone. There wasn't a house in sight."

"The Matthews house is just over the top of this next hill," Nora put in.

"I know. You told me that. Now I know why I couldn't see it. All I could see was the old clock tower and a path leading in that direction. Naturally, I followed it. There's something about a path in the woods that always tempts me."

"We know that, Olivia. Thomas told us all about your latest mystery. You followed a trail or something."

"Well, this trail led out of the garden where the bench was and then through an archway," Olivia continued. "All sorts of little statues and ornaments peered out at me from unexpected places. I was actually nervous by the time I reached the old tower. There wasn't time to explore it. Just then I heard the rumble of my grandfather's truck and knew he was driving off without me."

"He was!" Olivia's friends both chorused in surprise, and Nora asked, "Why would he do a thing like that?"

"I think now it was just to tease me. He did stop and wait for me after a while," Olivia remembered. "The quilts were gone. Grandma must have delivered them, but I didn't ask where. If she made them for Mrs. Matthews they may still be there."

"I wouldn't depend on it," Lucy said as they turned up the narrow road to the Matthews estate.

"Watch out!" Olivia suddenly exclaimed. "There's another car coming."

As Nora swerved to avoid the oncoming car, Lucy ducked her head. She kept herself hidden behind Olivia until the car had passed. The man driving it was a stranger to Olivia, but she would remember his intense, calculating eyes and sharp features for a long time. The dark cap he was wearing covered most of his hair.

"What's the matter with you two?" asked Nora when the car had passed. "Aren't you acting a bit strange?"

"I wasn't—acting. Let's not go up there," Lucy begged. "I don't think the Matthews live there any more."

"Maybe not, but we can pretend we think they do, can't we?" Olivia replied a little uncertainly.

She was beginning to suspect that Lucy knew more about the Matthews estate than she was telling. Nora kept on driving along the narrow, gravelly road. Soon there were more evergreens and hedges to be seen. They looked very green next to the bare trees in the woods beyond. The sky was gray with white clouds being driven across it by the wind.

"There's the tower!" Lucy exclaimed. "I can see it over to the left. It looks like something out of a fairy tale, doesn't it?"

"It looks mysterious all right," agreed Olivia. "I wonder what it is."

"I suppose it's nothing but an old clock tower. It would be fun to explore it, though," Nora said. "But if there are new people living here they'll never give us permission."

"We might explore it without permission," Olivia suggested daringly. "Come on!" she urged her friends as Nora parked the car in a cleared place beside the road. "Who's going to stop us? And who wants to explore a gloomy old tower, anyway? Let's look for the garden."

"Do you think we should?" Lucy asked. "It won't be enchanted. I told you—"

"You told us very little," Nora reminded her. "If you know anything about the people who live here now, I think you ought to let us know. Otherwise, I'm afraid we won't be very welcome."

"I don't think they'll welcome us, anyway. I do know who they are," Lucy admitted. "You remember Mohammad Hansen from the arts council, don't you? I've seen him around here. His family must have acquired the property, or else he's just working on the estate."

"Then you've been here lately? Why didn't you tell me?" asked Nora. "We always used to go places together."

"It wasn't important," Lucy replied evasively. "I was just out for a drive."

"You're being mysterious," laughed Olivia. "Each with secrets of your own. You're not interested in Mohammad Hansen, are you, Nora? I'm sure you can do better than that. I did know him slightly, but not well. I remember his colleague, Pablo Matthews, a lot better. He was in our performing arts group."

"Sh!" Nora cautioned her. "Nice people no longer mention Pablo Matthews's name in certain circles. He's involved in some scandal."

"For what?" asked Olivia.

Like Thomas, her mediator husband, she preferred facts to gossip.

"Electoral fraud, I guess. He manipulated some voting records during the regional council elections. I think he falsified some documents, too. Anyway, there was an investigation. It was all in the papers," Lucy told her.

Now Olivia did remember. It was something she would have preferred to forget. She liked to think she was a good judge of character, and she had taken Pablo Matthews for a quiet, principled person who would never stoop to corruption.

"I don't see what all this has to do with the clock tower," Nora said impatiently. "Are we going to look for it, or aren't we?"

"Of course we are. That's what we came for. I just like to know what I'm walking into before I walk into it," Olivia explained.

"You seem to think there's danger in this expedition of ours, don't you?" asked Lucy.

"I don't know what to think. You're the one who seems to know the answers, but you're not telling. Hiding your face back there gave you away. You've seen that person who drove down this road and, for some reason, you were afraid he would see you. Why, Lucy? Why didn't you want to be recognized?"

Lucy hesitated a moment and then replied evasively, "People don't generally enter private estates without an invitation. That's all."

"I'd better turn the car around," Nora decided, "in case we have to leave in a hurry. I don't expect we'll encounter any real danger, but we may be accused of trespassing."

"I'm sure we will be," announced Olivia as two dark-coated figures strode down the road toward them. "You drove right by a NO TRESPASSING sign, and this isn't a welcoming committee coming to meet us!"

She makes cryptic comments that she refuses to elaborate on ("it would be nice if things were the way they used to be when I trusted Steven"), she ducks and hides when a car passes (not wanting to be recognized), she admits to having visited the Matthews estate before but calls it "not important," she knows who currently owns or works at the estate, and she is evasive when pressed for information.
