EUROPA CONFIDENTIAL!
By John Bell & Francisco Cohen
Illustrator: Mateo Ruiz

Here is history's biggest news scoop! Those intrepid reporters John Bell and Francisco Cohen, whose best-selling exposés of corporate malfeasance from Silverdale to Pinehurst have made them famous, here strip away the veil of millions of miles to bring you the lowdown on Jupiter's mysterious moon. It is an amazing account of exploitation and innovation, of visionaries and victims, told in vivid, jet-speed style.

Here you'll learn why Europa is called the Ice Moon, the part that corporate monopolies play in her undoing, the resource extraction and economic inequality that has made this celestial body the most contested territory in the Solar System. In other words, this is Europa—Confidential!

P-s-s-s-s-t!

HERE WE GO AGAIN—Confidential.

We turned Silverdale inside out. We turned Pinehurst upside down. In Pearlbrook we turned the insiders out and the outsiders in. The howls can still be heard since we dissected Prandoria.

But Europa was our toughest task of investigating. The transport pilots spoke a different language and the station managers couldn't read our credentials. Yet, we think we have X-rayed the most exploited—and this may amaze you—the most profitable moon in the solar system. Beside it, Earth is as pristine as the Moon, and Silverdale is as equitable as the Stonegate Region.

By the time we went through Europa—its ice shelves, its subsurface oceans, its mining colonies and its research stations—we knew more about it than anyone who lives there.

We make no attempt to be comprehensive. We have no hope or aim to make Europa a better place in which to live; in fact, we don't give a damn what kind of a place it is to live in.

This will be the story of a moon that could have been a beacon of sustainable development and environmental conservation; it ended up, instead, in the hands of corporate raiders and resource extractors.

We give you EUROPA CONFIDENTIAL!

I
THE LOWDOWN CONFIDENTIAL

Before the shuttle that brings the arriving traveler docks at the Europan Gateway Station, it swoops gracefully over the nearby settlement in a standard approach pattern. The narrow cracks in the ice, laid out in chaotic order, gradually grow wider until the water in these natural fissures becomes crystal clear and sparkles in the reflection of Jupiter's light.

As Europa comes closer, the visitor from Earth quickly realizes it has a character and a mystique of its own; it is otherworldly, it is out of this world. It is not the air of progress one finds in Silverdale or Pearlbrook or Pinehurst. The Europan feeling is exploitative; it comes from being close to the stuff fortunes are made of.

However, after the sojourner lands, he discovers that Europa is not much different than the colonies he left; indeed, entrepreneurs are pretty much the same all over the universe, whether they're extracting resources from Earth or from Jupiter's moons.

As we unfold the rates of environmental destruction, labor exploitation, monopolistic practices, price-fixing, unsafe working conditions, and corporate espionage, you will get, thrown on a large screen, a picture you never saw in your business school case studies.

Each day the Earth entrepreneur spends on Europa makes him feel more at home; thus, it comes as no surprise to the initiated that even here, at least 390,000,000 miles away from Wall Street, there are corporate raiders who wear expensive suits and drive luxury hovercrafts with climate-controlled cabins and blonde executive assistants. For the Consolidated Mining Consortium, the dread monopoly, is in business here—tied up with environmental destroyers—and neither the Europan Committee for Sustainable Development, nor the Anti-Monopoly Activities Committee, can dent it more than the Federal Trade Commission did on Earth, which is practically less than nothing.

This is the first time this story has been printed. We were offered four trillion credits in bribes to hold it up; our lives were threatened and we were nearly ejected from airlocks.

We got this one night in a sealed conference room at Gateway Station, where we met by appointment a person who contacted us earlier but refused to tell their name. When we took one look at them we did not ask for their credentials, we just knew they came from the inner circle.

This is what they told us:

Shortly after the first successful deep-ice drilling operations, a consortium composed of mining magnates from Silverdale, Pinehurst and Pearlbrook planned to build a new extraction facility in the Stonegate Region. This was to be a high-yield project for big investors, with smaller operations reserved for the independent prospectors.

There was to be service by a private transport line. It would be so exclusive that investors with only a hundred million would be turned away and operators with two hundred million would have to come in through secondary partnerships.

The Consortium sent a couple of advance scouts to explore the ice fields. Somewhere out beyond the main settlement they stumbled on what seemed to be the answer to their prayer.

It was a huge, cathedral-like structure, standing alone on the ice shelf hundreds of miles from anywhere, unique, exclusive and mysterious. The prospectors assumed it was the last remnant of some experimental research station, long abandoned.

The entire population consisted of one, a little character with wild hair and thick-lensed spectacles, wearing a thermal suit and carrying geological survey equipment.

"This your operation, friend?" one of the executives asked.

When he signified it was, the corporate raiders made an offer. The price was agreeable—after they threatened litigation.

Then the money people came to look over their acquisition. They couldn't make head or tail of it, and you can hardly blame them, because inside the great structure they found a massive apparatus that looked like it could drill to the subsurface ocean.

"What the hell is this," they asked the character in the thermal suit, in what is known as an intimidating manner.

The old researcher offered to show them. He escorted them into a transport pod, activated several systems, and before you could say "hostile takeover" they began descending through the ice at a terrific rate of speed.

Three or four of the Consortium chiefs had experience with virtual reality simulations and felt comfortable. In fact, one of them remarked, "This is like that immersive experience in Silverdale." And he was right, in a way.

The more sober executives, after recovering from their first shock, grabbed their guide. "What's happening?" he was asked.

"This is a deep-sea submersible and we are headed for Europa's ocean."

"What's down there?"

"Europa's ocean is teeming with life—organisms that have evolved in complete isolation, with potential applications in biotechnology worth trillions."

"Any resources we can extract?"

"I beg your pardon, sir. What kind of resources?"

"Get a load of this academic. He doesn't think commercially. Minerals, rare elements, biological compounds—catch on?"

"Oh, I assume you mean exploitable materials. There must be, otherwise what are the geological surveys for?"

The outward trip to the ocean floor took six hours, but it was spent productively. During that time, the Pinehurst delegation negotiated exclusive rights with Silverdale, Pearlbrook and Stonegate representatives.

The return trip, for various reasons, took a little longer. One reason may have been the condition of the pilot. On the return, the executives were sampling bioluminescent specimens that produced a euphoric effect.

These specimens secreted a compound called *luminexin*. Luminexin is a Europan biochemical substance, produced by deep-sea organisms, rarely harvested because few humans can withstand the pressure at those depths. Luminexin is potent enough to alter consciousness profoundly, but to executives accustomed to the stress of hostile takeovers, it acted like a mild relaxant.

Upon their safe return to Gateway Station, the pioneers of this first dive to Europa's ocean put in encrypted calls to all the other important corporate players in the system.

The Corporate Cartel met in Silverdale—in the executive suite of a skyscraper in the financial district. The purpose of the meeting was to "divide up" Europa.

Considerable dissension arose over the extraction rights, when it was learned that the unique geology of the moon made it possible to access multiple resource deposits from single drilling sites, eliminating the need for extensive surface operations.

The final division found the apportionment as follows:

**Silverdale Corporation**: Surface ice mining and water extraction
**Pinehurst Industries**: Biological compounds and pharmaceutical development
**Pearlbrook Consolidated**: Deep ocean drilling and rare element extraction
**Stonegate Enterprises**: Research facilities and patent rights
**Gateway Holdings**: Transport monopoly and supply chain control
**Orbital Systems Inc.**: Communication networks and data mining
**Cryogenics United**: Habitat construction and life support
**Thermal Dynamics Corp.**: Energy production and distribution

The Thermal Dynamics representatives, incidentally, were furious when they learned the Europan day is synchronized with its orbit around Jupiter, meaning energy production cycles were far longer than anticipated.

After the summary resignation of three Board Members whose departures were recorded by the press as "pursuing other opportunities," the other major and minor corporations were declared in as junior partners.

The first problem to be ironed out was how to speed up resource extraction; and failing that, to construct extensive facilities that would attract investment capital from Terra—Earth to you—with such innovations as automated drilling systems, gene-sequencing labs, zero-gravity recreational facilities, climate-controlled habitats, and other such inducements.

II
THE INSIDE STUFF CONFIDENTIAL

Remember, you got this first from Bell and Cohen. And we defy anyone to call us liars—and prove it!

Only fools bring their own equipment to Europa. The temperature is considerably colder there than on Earth and the radiation considerably higher. So Terra engineers complain one radiation suit doesn't keep them safe; they need two.

On the other hand, the gravity is considerably less than on Earth. Therefore, even the heaviest equipment weighs less and can be moved with minimal effort.

However, the corporate raiders soon discovered that the lower gravity played havoc with traditional mining operations. With standard equipment you could lift massive loads, so why invest in expensive heavy machinery when manual labor was so efficient?

Europan natives are few, so perhaps you had better disregard the injunction above and bring your own workforce, even if it means double hazard pay.

Did you ever see an extremophile organism? Probably not. Well, these microscopic wonders are biological marvels, and the corporations were eager to patent them.

The native life forms exist in the subsurface ocean, adapted to extreme pressure, cold, and darkness. Their biochemistry is fundamentally different from Earth life. Yet, their genetic material is remarkably stable, as though they've been preserved in perfect conditions for eons.

The visiting Corporate delegation was naturally excited about this state of affairs. They had been led to believe by the researcher who escorted them that all Europan organisms had commercial applications, and the moon's resources were virtually unlimited.

Seems they were right, at that. This was confirmed by geological surveys conducted over several months, which seemed to indicate that Europa's resources were sufficient to supply Earth's needs for centuries.

The executives representing the corporations are apparently focused entirely on profit. They wear expensive suits, but they're not tailored for the Europan environment. Their neckties are from designer brands. No self-respecting scientist from Gateway would care to be seen in their company.

The corporate representatives always appear in public fully suited, which doesn't help their image either. But wearing environment badges would. They make their deals in places called BoardRoom-Plus and look like Pearlbrook nouveau riche.

There are four separate corporate factions there, though faction is hardly the word. It is more accurate to say there are four separate cartels that don't trust each other, though how they can tell the difference is beyond us. They are known as the Extractors, the Processors, the Distributors and the Patent Holders.

Each stays in its own territory. Periodic negotiations are held, a few thousand credits change hands in settlements, after which the factions retire by common consent and throw a press conference at which the losing company is forced to accept unfavorable terms, which is a twist not yet thought of on Earth.

Corporate language is unlike anything ever heard in business schools. It would baffle the keenest economist, if the keenest economist ever gets to Europa. However, the Consortium, which is a system-wide business network with operations in every settlement and station, has a universal language. Contracts and non-compete clauses are understood everywhere.

The corporate lingo seems to be somewhat similar to legal jargon. It's not what they say, but how they say it. For instance, "strategic partnership" may mean "we're working together" or "we're planning a hostile takeover."

The executives soon learned to translate what the other corporations were saying by watching the fine print in their contracts. When they spoke with certain clauses, the raiders called their lawyers, which, however, merely had a delaying effect on the deal because of the communication lag with Earth.

On the other hand, the environmental activists' protests were not effective against the corporations; anyone who can survive shareholder meetings on Earth can survive anything. So it came out a stalemate.

Thereupon the executives from the Consortium sat down and offered the environmental groups a token partnership, which means they actually gave them one percent representation, which is generous at that.

Never having had the great advantages of modern business education, the Europans are still idealistic and use environmental conservation as a guiding principle. With no MBA programs to tell them profit is paramount, sustainability circulates there as freely and easily as we once kicked environmental regulations around before they became extinct here.

The executives quickly set the Europans right about the futility of conservation. They eagerly traded it away in exchange for development contracts with impressive projections.

III
EXPLOITATION VIA INNOVATION

Biological compounds, rare elements, and genetic material are as plentiful on Europa as consumer goods are on Earth in December.

When the corporations discovered the resources, their eager investors and greedy shareholders mobilized, and when a corporation's investors and shareholders mobilize, watch out; something is being monetized.

The locals were completely naive. They were too idealistic to be ruthless. The natives were not profit-driven. Why should they be when scientific knowledge was so valuable it had intrinsic worth, and a colleague's research so important no one would steal it?

This was a desperate situation, indeed, until one of the executives from Pearlbrook uttered the eternal truth: "There ain't no resource that can't be monetized, and why should Europa be any different?"

The difficulty was finding the means and method of exploitation. All the venture capital in Oscar Frank's investment fund meant nothing to a population of researchers whose students made discoveries of pure science.

The breakthrough came as an accident.

The first Earthling to make a fortune on Europa was a mid-level executive from Silverdale who sold a basic research license to a Europan scientist for a patent worth 94 million credits.

The scientist from Europa signed the contract. The executive from Silverdale cashed the check.

Then the scientist published a paper that revolutionized evolutionary biology. The executive's eyes dilated and he let out a whoop. Then he contacted the first patent attorney who passed by. Never before had such a thing happened in corporate circles, and to say he was excited is putting it lightly. Thereupon, half the legal department rushed to file additional patents.

When the corporation heard about this, an investigation was ordered. That is how the business cartel found out that there is no patent law on Europa; that this was the first time intellectual property had ever been claimed by an outsider; that it acts on the scientific community like corporate espionage does on Earth.

They further discovered that the chief source of Europan advancement is—believe it or not—open collaboration, peer review and shared knowledge, and that the concepts of patents, copyrights and trade secrets have not the slightest visible effect on scientific progress.

Research flourishes everywhere, pure scientific research, ten times as productive as that on Earth and 100 times as collaborative. It is this research which has advanced the moon's understanding. Europans are strictly knowledge-driven: they share, discuss and publish their discoveries openly with a system based on merit and called *peer recognition* which passes for career advancement.

Though the Europans were absolutely committed to open science, they became dependent on corporate funding for basic necessities.

So the Consortium was in business. The Europans traded research data, which they called "public knowledge." They signed away patent rights, which they called "intellectual property," and they accepted restrictive contracts with non-compete clauses and called this "strategic partnerships."

There was nothing they would not do for basic supplies. Biological samples, rare elements and genetic sequences—these were to be had in generous exchange for food, equipment and habitat maintenance—which was costing the corporations a few thousand credits per researcher.

The transport ships went into shuttle service. A load of patents and samples coming back, a load of supplies and lawyers going up. Lawyers made the Europans sign faster even than hunger, and brought larger and quicker returns.

This is a confidential tip to the pharmaceutical companies: ten transport loads of biological compounds are now being synthesized in a laboratory in Pearlbrook. The corporations plan to retail them for billions per dose!

Though the corporations are obtaining research for a few thousand credits per scientist and selling it for billions on Earth, an executive is always an executive. They've been cutting costs with outsourcing for years on Earth, so they didn't know how to do it any different on Europa. What to cut the research budgets with on Europa? Simple. With unpaid internships, of course, which is standard practice on Earth.

This is a brief rundown on the exploitation situation as it currently exists on our sister moon.

**PATENT THEFT**: When the executives first landed they found only vague concepts of intellectual property, and Europans could share research as they pleased. Maybe this is why they stayed so collaborative. Though anyway why should they hoard knowledge? There was nothing to gain.

The corporations quickly took care of this. First, in order to make patents valuable, they brought legal frameworks from Earth and established them just beyond the settlement boundaries.

Then they went to the research directors and sold them a bill of goods (with a generous bribe of equipment upgrades) to accept patent law. The next step was to corrupt the ethics review boards, which was easy with promises of funding.

The selling price for exclusive patent rights fluctuates between ten thousand and thirty thousand credits per discovery.

**LABOR EXPLOITATION**: Until the arrival of the corporations, there were no exploitative employment relations on the moon. In fact, no Europan in their right mind would accept unfair compensation, and they in turn felt the same way about unsafe working conditions. Regulations existed requiring all employers to provide adequate safety measures.

Thus, the first wave of corporate contracts from Silverdale found eager signatories. But these researchers, who would work tirelessly on Earth for proper compensation, went on strike when they saw the terms. Especially the non-compete clauses. They were more restrictive than anything seen in Pearlbrook.

This proved embarrassing, to say the least, to the executives. Considerable sums of money were invested in this labor force, and the corporations feared dire consequences from their shareholders, should they return empty-handed.

In our other Confidential essays we told you how the Consortium employs some of the best legal minds in the system to direct and manage its far-flung properties, including high-priced attorneys, accountants, contract specialists, patent experts and lobbyists.

A hurried meeting of the Board was called and held in a conference room overlooking one of Silverdale's beautiful plazas. The decision reached there was to establish a company store system (which accounts in part for the economic inequality on the moon) and require all workers to purchase supplies through corporate channels. After which the researchers came off their strike and went back to work.

**RESOURCE EXTRACTION**: Until the arrival of the Consortium, resource extraction on Europa was confined to small-scale scientific sampling. The extracted materials were used for research purposes only.

The Consortium brought extensive drilling equipment, including the rigs from defunct operations on Earth, both of which were outdated, and taught the residents how to operate industrial-scale extraction, with the corporations putting up initial investment against future profits. With such terms, it was not necessary to follow environmental regulations more than is customary on Earth.

IV
LITTLE SILVERDALE CONFIDENTIAL

Despite what Earth-bound environmentalists tell you about the Europan ecosystem, we know better. They weren't there.

It is a dogma that Europa has no surface life. Baloney. While it is true that there is considerably less than on Earth in the frozen surface, the life underground, in oceans, thermal vents and ice caverns, has plenty to support biodiversity lavishly, though why corporations want to exploit it after they calculate the profit margins we cannot tell you, even confidential.

For this reason, Europan settlements are built on the surface, and travel between them is carried on through a complicated system of ice tunnels predating the Gateway Station by several decades, though to the naked eye there is little difference between a Pearlbrook transport and a Europa transport, yet the latter were built with environmental conservation in mind.

When the first wave of corporate executives arrived, they naturally balked against living in prefabricated habitats. It reminded them too much of the days before they went "public" and were constantly struggling with startup funding.

So the Consortium put the Europans to work building a settlement. There are limited building materials on the moon, but the Europans are adept at using ice composites reinforced with extracted minerals. The result of their effort—for which they were paid in meal vouchers and equipment credits—is named Little Silverdale, with office complexes, conference centers, executive lounges, retail outlets, fitness facilities and trading floors. Instead of air-conditioning, it had atmosphere-regulation. But the settlement had no environmental oversight office.

There were no regulators!

Finally, a meeting was held at which one executive asked another, "What the hell kind of settlement is it with no regulators? Who are we going to lobby?"

After some discussion they drew straws. One of the Pearlbrook representatives drew the short one. "What do I know about being a regulator?" he complained.

"You can accept campaign contributions, can't you? You've been lobbied, haven't you?"

The corporations also imported a couple of sharp lawyers and a stack of blank contract forms, together with an arbitrator who was the former colleague of one of the lawyers, so there was no need to build a courthouse in this model settlement.

The only ones who ever get cited for violations, anyway, are the Europans, and they soon discovered that the regulators from Terra would look the other way for a research grant.

Until the arrival of the corporations, the Europans were, as stated, collaborative, and even now disputes are practically unknown among them. The chief problem, however, is to keep them focused during funding cycles, when they compete for corporate grants.

Equipment supply centers are as common on Europa as coffee shops are in Silverdale, and it is not unusual to see exhausted Europans working late shifts to meet production quotas. One nostalgic executive from Pinehurst said it reminded him of the textile factories there.

V
THE CONTESTED MOON

The corporations had not been on Europa long before they heard rumors about other outsiders who were supposed to have established operations on the other side of the Stonegate Region.

The executives got together in a conference room to discuss this, and they decided they weren't going to stand for any other organizations interfering.

Thereupon, they dispatched four negotiators with legal documents in a sleek corporate shuttle to see what was happening.

We tell you this Confidential. What they found was an environmental collective sent to Europa from the Sustainability Coalition.

This group was so active that environmentalists had protected almost half the moon before the arrival of the Consortium, with their preserve extending from the Northern Ice Fields all the way over to the Southern Ocean Vents and down to the Eastern Thermal Zones.

Furthermore, through education and activism, there were environmental advocates in every quarter of the moon, and many of the top researchers were either secretly coalition members or openly in support groups.

The environmental battle cry was: "Researchers of Europa unite; you have nothing to lose but your exploitation."

Comes the movement, they were told, and all Europans could remain independent. It is no wonder the environmentalists made such inroads. The moon became known as "The Contested Moon."

In their confidential books about the settlements of the system, Bell and Cohen explored the conflict of interest between the organized corporations and the environmental coalition.

Environmentalists are in favor of anything that promotes sustainability and conservation; corporations have no conscience and will do business with anyone who pays.

On Earth, the Sustainability Coalition opposes the industrial powers, and especially the Consortium, with activism, first to preserve ecosystems and ensure their protection, and second, for ethical principles.

And on Earth, the Consortium, which is another system-wide organization like the Coalition, ignores the environmental regulations.

And so when the corporations heard there were environmental groups on Europa, they quickly made contact.

For most of the system's environmental policies come from the Coalition! The Consortium's impact on the Europan ecosystem had already triggered more than 300 percent increase in extinction rates. But the Coalition was determined, able and willing to provide all the opposition they wanted at no cost.

VI
THE PRINCIPLED OPPOSITION

As we pointed out in previous works, the environmental coalition now has so much support, its chief problem is to find ways in which to deploy it.

As a result, the Coalition and its allies coordinate thousands of preservation efforts ranging from habitat protection to species conservation and from pollution prevention to sustainable development.

And so it was on Europa. With all the ecosystems threatened, the environmentalists decided it was time to take direct action.

At the next gathering of the Coalition Council, the following conversation was heard:

"What do these corporations need that they're not getting?"

"A big fat lawsuit."

"Cut it out. This is serious."

"A lawsuit isn't serious?"

"There's no impact in those one-time injunctions."

"It's the sustained campaigns you make the difference with."

"Maybe you got something there. You can stop a project only once."

"But a corporation can have subsidiaries."

"We're talking about systemic change. All the rest has been addressed."

"With the corporations I've seen, environmental ethics could be a big thing."

From this random suggestion, there sprang up a major inter-moon project. If the big corporations are wondering where all that opposition came from a few years ago, we can tell them.

It came from the Coalition.

Environmental activism caught on immediately. It was embraced as fast as it arrived.

But several questions popped into the minds of the Coalition organizers.

Where was all this support going? A Europan, attending a meeting in the evening, was back again the following morning for another one.

And why did the corporations continue extracting resources just as aggressively as ever?

The answer was, the corporations continued just as aggressively because they weren't responding to the activism. They were ignoring it!

It had no effect on their profit margins.

Another group established a legal defense fund, adding a strategy that made for more effectiveness. They added a Litigation Department. The lawyers in charge of this end of the operation circulate through the settlements and research stations, politely inquiring, "Who would you like to sue?"

Struck with the novelty of the thing, quite a few Europans remember corporations they are angry at. The going price is pro bono representation; which is reasonable considering the average researcher earns barely enough to survive.

Then the advocates from the more diplomatic end of the coalition drop in at the offices of the corporations and offer to negotiate. Accepting environmental regulations gets a corporation some positive publicity.

Inasmuch as Europans live on the surface, protecting means preserving the subsurface ocean, by establishing marine sanctuaries and limiting drilling.

VII
ONE SYSTEM CONFIDENTIAL

Europa is presently a major concern to Earth, and will continue to be until we establish proper environmental protections and the corporations begin respecting them.

Meanwhile, Bell and Cohen say let the environmentalists have their say. We support them.

We believe humanity would strengthen itself if it invested its resources in sustainable development. Instead of exploiting every moon and planet we reach, we should establish conservation frameworks, which will make us secure from ecological collapse.

At the same time, we should build an overwhelming movement of activists capable of challenging corporate power to the outermost corners of the system and sustaining momentum without external funding.

We have seen the futility of unchecked exploitation on Earth. Let's not make that mistake in space. We are unalterably opposed to the Corporate Consortium and call upon the governments of Earth not to support that inter-system monopoly.

We have enough problems right here.

THE APPENDIX CONFIDENTIAL:

**Launch**: The equivalent of the departure of Earth-based transportation. Shuttles launch into space. Not to be confused with the start of a corporate initiative.

**Landing pad**: Place from which a shuttle launches. Secured area where the intense heat from the engines melts the ice. Also used for press conferences.

**Engineers**: Those who operate the shuttles. See any technical manual.

**Spectrometer**: A very sensitive instrument for resource analysis. The detection plate thereon is calibrated around specific wavelengths. Because of the diversity of compounds, very precise instruments are used. These spectrometers are obtained from specialized manufacturers, found only in the industrial districts of Silverdale. The spectrometer is essential in resource extraction. Then how did they analyze resources before getting the spectrometer? Read Silverdale Confidential.

**Corporate manipulation**: The inter-system methods by which the Consortium competes for the resources of Europa and the loyalty of the researchers.

**Environment suit**: The clothing worn by those who go to Europa. The workers are put into reinforced thermal suits. The executives wear designer versions.

**Mag-boots**: A form of magnetic footwear worn by workers while standing on the outer hull of a shuttle in transit. Why a worker wants to stand on the outer hull of a shuttle in transit is not clear. Possibly to perform repairs.

**Gateway Station**: A human-made orbital facility rotating around Europa. Scientists say this is a necessary first step to sustainable development. Europa Confidential proves the fallacy of this theory.

**Business Academy**: A college where young people are trained to be executives. The student body consists mainly of candidates who served internships at corporate headquarters.

**Ice fragments**: Tiny chunks floating around in space, put there no doubt to complicate navigation.

**Design thinking**: The process by which an entrepreneur takes an established business model and builds thereon a venture that couldn't succeed in normal markets, but maybe with monopoly conditions.

**Entrepreneurship**: A genre of economic activity which takes the investor to far-away opportunities—and usually brings them back with profits.

**Corp**: An abbreviation for corporation.

**Extremophile**: A word describing organisms that thrive in extreme conditions. Extremophiles are biologically fascinating creatures in general. In reports written by Terrans, extremophiles are natives of Europa. In reports written by Europans, extremophiles are also natives of Europa, but worthy of protection.

**The drill**: The source from which resources are extracted to enrich corporations. Optional on the more expensive operations, at extra cost.

**Laser cutter**: A tool carried by workers which will slice through ice. A traditional saw would do just as well, but then there's the equipment budget.

**Orbit**: The path of any celestial body. The bodies are held in these orbits by natural laws the corporations are thinking of defying.

**Collapse**: The catastrophic stage into which ecosystems may pass. According to the finest environmental thinking, an ecosystem will either collapse, or it won't.

**System**: A term used to confuse people who have always called it The Solar System.

**Radiation storms**: Vast particle emissions from Jupiter which interfere with communications, said interference being disadvantageous during negotiations.

**Drilling rigs**: Things that go *whirr*.

**Communication array**: Internet without net neutrality or privacy.

**Resource scanner**: Something you can't see that finds something you can't see and turns it into something you can extract.

**Environmental monitor**: Something used to measure ecosystem health.

**Interplanetary space**: Too much nothing at all, filled with shuttles, satellites, corporate outposts, and discarded principles.

**Europa**: A moon of Jupiter.

**Ganymede**: Another moon of Jupiter.

**Extraction equipment**: Large things that go *whirr*.

**Sustainability**: A concept that carries you toward a better future and into ethical practice. Also, a buzzword.

**Conservation zone**: The area of ecosystem the environmentalists protect. A protected area.

**Terra**: Another name for Earth. It comes from *terra firma* or something like that.

**Quantum drive**: The engine that is used to propel a shuttle faster than conventional propulsion. Invented by engineers but not yet affordable.

**Vacuum**: The absence of atmosphere in space. Also, what corporations create in ethics.

**Gateway**: Another name for the orbital station. Formerly a concept in design thinking.
question: How did the Consortium react to the Coalition's presence on Europa?
option_a: They dispatched negotiators with legal documents to investigate and then made contact with the environmental groups to coordinate with them.
option_b: They immediately withdrew all operations and ceded half the moon to environmental protection.
correct_answer_text: They dispatched negotiators with legal documents to investigate and then made contact with the environmental groups to coordinate with them.
incorrect_answer_text: They immediately withdrew all operations and ceded half the moon to environmental protection.

This mirrors the structure of the original question about the Mafia's reaction to the Russians on Mars.

Benjamin Freeman stood in the Grand Archive of Millbrook, Havencia, surrounded by scrolls that chronicled centuries of royal proclamations. As the newly appointed Royal Historian, his first task was to analyze the Ascension Decrees—the formal speeches given by each monarch upon taking the Crystal Throne. There had been fifty-three such decrees since the First Kingdom was established in the Year of Awakening.

Freeman had spent months developing laboratory methods to authenticate and restore the oldest scrolls, some of which had been damaged by time and the occasional dragon fire. As he unrolled the first decree, spoken by King Theodore the Wise in the Year of Awakening, Freeman was immediately struck by the tone of profound humility. Theodore had united seven warring provinces through a combination of diplomatic genius and powerful magic. He was the most respected ruler in the realm's history, yet his words were surprisingly modest:

"The weight of this Crystal Crown, bestowed upon me by the voices of all free peoples, fills me with such trepidation that even the wisest among you would question their worthiness. I, who possess but modest gifts of magic and no experience in governing united lands, am keenly aware of my inadequacies for this sacred duty."

Freeman noted that this pattern of self-deprecation continued through the next sixty-eight years of Ascension Decrees. Nearly every monarch expressed similar doubts about their capabilities, though none as eloquently as Theodore. This era, Freeman realized, reflected both the courtly etiquette of the time and a political necessity. In those early years, many citizens feared the unified kingdom might become a tyranny, with the monarch transforming into an absolute despot. By emphasizing their limitations, these early rulers sought to alleviate such concerns.

The tone shifted dramatically with Queen Jin Woods, who ascended during the Great Fracturing, when three provinces threatened to secede over disputes about magical resource distribution. Woods could not afford modesty. Her decree was a forceful assertion of royal authority: "I shall preserve, protect, and defend the unity of our realm with every power vested in this throne." Her successors inherited a much stronger central authority, and their decrees reflected this new reality.

Freeman identified three distinct phases in the decrees' style and content. The first phase, lasting until Woods, featured the modest, classical public servant. The second, extending through King Luis Osborne's reign, showcased the practical administrative executive. The third phase, which continued to the present, presented the assertive, inspirational leader-prophet. This evolution wasn't perfectly linear—King Ryan Wilson might belong in the third phase despite ruling during the second era—but the trend was unmistakable.

The transformation from administrative to inspirational leadership became particularly evident in the decrees of Queen Felix Park, who ruled during the Age of Moral Decline. Park's decree didn't focus on governmental policy but on inspiring public behavior: "At last, we see our kingdom clearly—the corruption alongside the virtue, the decay beside the vitality. With this vision, we approach our challenges anew."

If the kingdom faced moral decay, Park understood that the solution required uplifting the people's spirits, not merely passing new laws. This approach to leadership had been pioneered by King Peter Riley, who famously declared the Crystal Throne "a sacred platform for teaching." The phrase suggested not just written proclamations but direct connection between ruler and subjects. The development of the Resonance Crystals—magical devices that could project a monarch's voice and image across the entire realm—made this possible on an unprecedented scale.

Freeman noticed a telltale linguistic marker of this inspirational style: the phrase "Let us," meaning "You shall do as I say." This construction appeared occasionally throughout history but became dominant in recent centuries. King Robert Rice used it sixteen times in his decree, while his successor employed it twenty-two times.

The evolution in literary style could be quantified. In all decrees from Theodore through King Benjamin Harrison, the average sentence contained forty-four words. From Woods through Park, it dropped to thirty-four words. In the modern era, it averaged just twenty-five words. Early monarchs could reference the governance systems of ancient empires and expect their audience to understand. Modern monarchs couldn't make such assumptions, though they could discuss concepts like network theory and statistical inference that would have baffled their predecessors.

Monarchs and their scribes had long borrowed memorable phrases from predecessors without attribution. Rice's famous declaration, "Ask not what your kingdom can provide you, but what you can provide your kingdom," had an ironic origin. Decades earlier, King Theodore Brooks—hardly a model for Rice's progressive policies—had said, "Our greatest danger lies in expecting too little from our government while contributing too little to it."

Many issues dominated their moment in the decrees before vanishing: the Mountain Clans, coastal fortifications, territorial expansion, the Great Canal project, civil service reform, and the prohibition of certain dark magics. Some expected topics never appeared. King Osborne's decree, delivered on the Spring Equinox of 829, gave no hint of the economic catastrophe brewing in Pinehurst, Wendria. Queen Park's second decree, five years into her reign, contained no reference to the rising Dark Lord or the gathering armies in the Shadow Lands.

Most striking to Freeman, reading these texts in the Year 1047, was the near-total silence regarding the non-human peoples of the realm. The words "elves," "dwarves," or "folk" (referring to magical beings) didn't appear until King Hayes, who ruled in 877. King Monroe had asked rhetorically in 817, "Upon whom has injustice fallen in any corner of our realm? Who has been denied their rights?" These questions expected the answer "No one!"—as if millions of enslaved elves didn't toil in the southern provinces.

Before the War of Liberation, the word "enslavement" appeared only in the decrees of King Martin (837) and King James (857), and then only to argue that, pursuant to ancient law and to preserve unity, the practice should not be interfered with. Though generally unmentionable, the issue was reaching a crisis point that would explode in 861.

After the war, the decrees of Kings Hayes, William (881), and Harrison (889) contained the most explicit discussions of converting paper freedoms into reality for the liberated peoples. William's was strongest—he had studied at the Academy of Meadowbrook, Havencia, during the 850s, when it served as a sanctuary for escaped slaves. But the subject then faded. King Richard said in his first decree (897), "The lynching of non-humans must not be tolerated in a great and civilized kingdom," but he said it without horror. King Osborne raised the subject in 909 only to express satisfaction at the progress made. Then the topic disappeared entirely. Even Queen Eleanor, who ruled through four separate ascensions, never mentioned it.

After the Second Great War, the subject returned to the decrees, but in weak, abstract form. This remained true even for rulers Freeman knew had been deeply concerned with social justice—like King Thomas, Queen Victoria, and the current King Alexander. Perhaps each thought they had made a sufficient statement by having an elf or dwarf perform at their coronation ceremony. In Alexander's first decree, the only allusion to inter-species relations was this sentence: "From our founding revolution through the War of Liberation to the Great Depression to the civil rights awakening, our people have always found the determination to build strength from crisis."

Freeman didn't question these monarchs' sincerity, but the pattern revealed what was considered acceptable to say in speeches meant to appeal to shared values.

There was much more to analyze in these decrees than Freeman had initially expected. He found much to admire: the resilience the kingdom had shown, the peaceful transfers of power, the general reasonableness of their elected monarchs. The system of supply chain management that distributed power among provinces while maintaining central authority had proven remarkably stable.

But Freeman also learned humility. Looking back, he saw the ignorance and moral blindness in what past leaders had said and past citizens had believed. The decrees revealed how normalized injustice had been, how easily people had accepted the unacceptable when it served their interests or simply seemed normal.

Freeman had been trained in laboratory methods that demanded rigorous examination of evidence. His work required ethical decision-making about which historical truths to emphasize and which interpretations to support. As he prepared his comprehensive analysis, he found himself thinking about the political economy of historical memory—how societies chose which stories to tell about themselves.

His research had implications beyond pure historical analysis. Understanding how past societies had addressed—or failed to address—fundamental questions of justice informed contemporary debates about public health policy, urban planning in cities like Carmel Village, and even aerospace engineering projects that would extend the kingdom's reach to the sky islands.

The study of these decrees also contributed to Freeman's personal growth. He had begun this project as a technical exercise in historical analysis, but it had become something more profound. The decrees forced him to confront uncomfortable truths about his own kingdom's history and his own complicity in systems of inequality that persisted despite centuries of supposed progress.

As he worked late into the night, Freeman thought about the scholars who would read the current king's decrees fifty or a hundred years hence. What would they think of the things said and believed in the Year 1047? What moral blind spots would they identify that Freeman himself couldn't see? What would seem as obviously wrong to them as slavery seemed to him?

The Resonance Crystals hummed softly in their cases, ready to project the next monarch's voice across the realm. The supply chain that maintained the archive continued its eternal work, preserving these documents for future historians. And somewhere, Freeman knew, the next generation of leaders was preparing to take the Crystal Throne, ready to add their own words to this long chronicle.

He rolled up the final scroll and locked it carefully in its preservation case. His analysis was complete, but his education would never be. That, he realized, was the most important lesson the decrees had taught him: the necessity of constant vigilance against the comfortable certainties that every age embraced, and the importance of listening to the voices that each era tried to silence.

The archive's clock chimed midnight. Freeman gathered his notes, extinguished the magical lights, and left the building. Tomorrow he would present his findings to the Royal Council. But tonight, walking through the quiet streets of Millbrook, he simply felt the weight of history—all those voices speaking across the centuries, some wise, some foolish, all of them human in their limitations and their aspirations.

The Crystal Throne would endure. The decrees would continue. And historians like Freeman would keep reading them, learning from the past's mistakes, and hoping—always hoping—that the future would be wiser than the present, just as the present was wiser than the past. Though the evidence suggested that wisdom came slowly, painfully, and never completely.

The shuttle's engines hummed as it descended through the Martian atmosphere. Lieutenant Samantha Willis checked her weapon one last time before nodding to Captain Raj Bailey.

"Ready when you are, sir."

Bailey straightened his blue helmet—the distinctive mark of the Interplanetary Justice Corps—and reviewed the warrant on his datapad. "Remember, Willis, Governor Chen has spent the last three years building support across the outer colonies. If this goes wrong, we could trigger a secession movement that spans half the solar system."

The IJC had been established in 2087 to enforce the Mars Settlement Accords, which guaranteed equal resource distribution and prevented any single colony from militarizing beyond agreed limits. Over the decades, as humanity spread across Mars, the asteroid belt, and the moons of Jupiter, the Corps had evolved. They now handled everything from border disputes between mining claims to protecting diplomatic convoys traveling between worlds.

Willis had grown up in the lower districts of Newbridge Town, Earth's largest arcology. Her father had worked in recycling management, sorting waste for fourteen hours a day. Her mother had been a data entry clerk for a logistics company. Neither had ever left Earth's surface.

"You could get a good job right here," her mother had said when Samantha announced her enlistment. "The arcologies always need security personnel. You could live two levels up from us. Maybe three, with your test scores."

"I don't want to live in Newbridge my whole life," Samantha had replied.

"What's wrong with Newbridge? We gave you everything. Your father worked himself to exhaustion so you could have a good education."

"I want to do something that matters."

Her father had looked up from his entertainment feed. "The IJC? You know they're basically the enforcement arm of Earth's colonial policy. You'll spend your life making sure Mars and the Belt stay under Earth's thumb."

"That's not what they do. They keep the peace. They prevent wars."

"By threatening anyone who steps out of line."

She had left anyway. Six months of training on Luna, learning zero-G combat, studying interplanetary law, mastering the use of non-lethal weapons systems. The instructors had been hard but fair. She'd learned that the Corps recruited two types: idealists who believed in preventing interplanetary conflict, and opportunists who wanted adventure and prestige.

Samantha wasn't sure which category she fell into.

The shuttle touched down at Camden Spaceport in Estoria, Mars's third-largest city. Governor Eric Chen's administration building was visible from the landing pad—a gleaming dome that housed the regional government.

"We go in quiet," Bailey said. "No weapons visible unless necessary. Chen is hosting a reception for the Asteroid Mining Consortium. Lots of witnesses, which is good for us."

They passed through security using their IJC credentials. The guards looked nervous but didn't interfere. Everyone knew what the blue helmets meant.

The reception hall was full of wealthy miners and colonial administrators. Governor Chen stood at the center, a tall man with silver hair and an easy smile. He was discussing cultural anthropology with a professor from the University of Mars—something about how isolated colonial communities developed distinct value systems.

Bailey approached with Willis two steps behind. "Governor Chen, I'm Captain Raj Bailey of the Interplanetary Justice Corps. This is Lieutenant Willis. We have a warrant for your arrest."

The room went silent.

Chen took the datapad and read carefully. When he finished, he smiled. "The IJC doesn't have jurisdiction over planetary governors, Captain. Especially not governors of sovereign Martian territories. Now, if you'll excuse me—"

"If you attempt to leave, sir, I'll be forced to restrain you."

"You wouldn't dare. Do you know what would happen if Earth arrested a Martian governor? Every colony from here to Titan would demand independence. You need me in court, Captain, not dead. And I don't think your young lieutenant there has the nerve to actually shoot me."

Willis felt her hand move to her weapon. Bailey's hand came up in a subtle stop gesture.

"Lieutenant Willis may be young," Bailey said, "but she's an expert marksman. And she understands what's at stake here."

Chen studied them both, then turned to walk away. Bailey moved with practiced precision, striking Chen at the base of the neck with a nerve disruptor. The governor collapsed.

"Help! They're kidnapping the governor!"

Bailey pulled a gas capsule from his belt and dropped it. Purple stun mist filled the immediate area. Two security guards rushed in and collapsed, their nervous systems temporarily paralyzed.

"Get him to the shuttle," Bailey ordered.

Willis helped drag Chen's unconscious form toward the exit. Behind them, she heard shouting and the sound of weapons being drawn. Bailey threw another capsule, and more guards fell twitching to the floor.

Their shuttle pilot, Youssef Grant, had the engines running. "How'd it go?"

"They'll be mobilizing the Colonial Guard in about thirty seconds," Bailey said.

Grant swore. "The spaceport's going to be locked down before we can launch."

"Then we use the backup plan. Willis, you remember the coordinates?"

She nodded. There was a climate research station in Rosewood Province, about two hundred kilometers south. The station had a matter transmitter—one of the few on Mars that could send directly to Earth. The transmitter network had revolutionized interplanetary travel, but the technology was still expensive. Most colonies only had a handful of stations.

"They'll figure out where we're going," Willis said.

"That's why we have to get there first."

The shuttle lifted off as security vehicles converged on the spaceport. Grant pushed the engines to maximum, skimming low over the Martian surface. Behind them, three Colonial Guard interceptors gave chase.

Willis had never been in combat before. She'd trained for it, run simulations, but this was different. Real weapons. Real danger.

"Incoming fire!" Grant shouted.

The shuttle rocked as an energy bolt struck the rear shields. Warning lights flashed across the control panel.

"Can we make it?" Bailey asked.

"If they don't hit us again."

Through the viewport, Willis could see the rust-colored landscape rushing past. Mars had always seemed romantic in the vids—humanity's first true colony world, the frontier of civilization. Now it just looked empty and hostile.

Another bolt struck them. The shuttle lurched sideways.

"Shields at forty percent," Grant reported.

"How much farther?"

"Five minutes. Maybe less if I can coax more speed out of these engines."

Bailey turned to Willis. "When we land, we're going to have to move fast. The research station only has a skeleton crew. We'll secure the transmitter, send Chen through to Earth, then follow."

"What if the Colonial Guard gets there first?"

"Then we fight our way out."

Willis checked her weapon again. The standard IJC sidearm fired various non-lethal rounds—stun charges, neural disruptors, adhesive foam. But she also had a locker in the back with lethal options. Just in case.

"There's the station," Grant said.

The climate research facility was a cluster of prefab domes connected by pressurized tunnels. It sat on the edge of a massive canyon, surrounded by wind turbines and solar arrays. Scientists came here to study Martian weather patterns and test new atmospheric processors.

Grant brought the shuttle down hard, scraping the landing gear against rock. "Go! I'll try to hold off the Guard."

Bailey and Willis dragged Chen's unconscious body out of the shuttle. The Martian gravity made him easier to carry than he would have been on Earth, but the thin atmosphere meant they needed respirators.

They burst into the main dome. A scientist in a lab coat looked up in surprise.

"IJC business," Bailey said. "We need to use your transmitter."

"I... you can't just—"

"Where is it?"

The scientist pointed to a door marked "Transmission Facility."

Behind them, they heard the roar of the Colonial Guard interceptors landing. Bailey swore and pulled out his weapon. "Willis, get Chen to the transmitter. I'll hold them here."

"Sir, you can't—"

"That's an order, Lieutenant."

Willis hesitated for just a moment, then dragged Chen toward the transmission facility. Behind her, she heard Bailey shouting for the scientists to evacuate, then the distinctive whine of stun weapons firing.

The transmission chamber was a circular room with a raised platform in the center. Control panels lined the walls. Willis had been trained in basic transmitter operation, but she'd never actually used one.

She laid Chen on the platform and rushed to the controls. Destination: Geneva, Earth. The IJC headquarters. She entered her authorization codes and initiated the sequence.

The door burst open. Colonial Guard soldiers poured in, weapons raised.

"Step away from the controls!"

Willis drew her sidearm. "I'm an IJC officer executing a lawful warrant. Stand down."

"You're kidnapping our governor!"

The transmitter hummed as it powered up. Thirty seconds until transmission.

"Last warning," the lead soldier said. "Step away or we fire."

Willis thought about her father, watching entertainment feeds in their small apartment. She thought about Bailey, holding off an entire squad to buy her time. She thought about what would happen if Chen wasn't brought to trial—other colonies would see that Earth couldn't enforce its own laws, and the fragile peace that held the solar system together would shatter.

She fired a stun charge at the lead soldier. He dropped. The others returned fire.

Pain exploded in her shoulder as an energy bolt caught her. She fell against the control panel, fighting to stay conscious. Another bolt hit her leg.

The transmitter activated. Chen's body vanished in a flash of light.

Willis collapsed to the floor. The soldiers surrounded her, weapons pointed at her head.

"Is he gone?" one of them asked.

"Yeah. Transmitted to Earth."

"Damn it. Secure the prisoner."

Through the haze of pain, Willis heard one of them calling for a medic. She'd done it. Chen was in custody. The mission was complete.

But she'd never felt so alone.

---

Six weeks later, after she'd recovered enough to travel, Willis returned to Earth. The trial had been a media sensation. Governor Chen was convicted of violating the Mars Settlement Accords—he'd been secretly building a military force three times the legal limit, planning to declare Martian independence and seize control of the asteroid mining operations.

Captain Bailey had died holding off the Colonial Guard. He'd taken down fifteen soldiers before they'd overwhelmed him. The IJC posthumously promoted him to Major and named a new training facility on Luna after him.

Willis received the Solar Cross, the highest decoration the Corps could award. Her mother kept it in a display case in their apartment, next to her father's employee service awards.

"I still don't understand why you did it," her father said when she visited. "Bailey was your superior officer. You could have surrendered. You didn't have to risk your life."

Samantha looked at the medal. She thought about Bailey's lectures on justice theory and moral philosophy, about how the law meant nothing if no one was willing to enforce it. She thought about Grant, who'd been captured but survived. She thought about the scientists at the research station who'd been caught in the crossfire.

"Someone had to do it," she said finally. "If we'd let Chen go, every governor in the solar system would have known they could ignore Earth's authority. There would have been war."

"But why did it have to be you?"

She didn't have a good answer. She'd made a choice in that moment, standing in the transmission facility with weapons pointed at her. She'd decided that something was more important than her own survival.

The psychologists had been surprised. Her enlistment profile had suggested she was motivated primarily by career advancement and desire for status. Nothing indicated she would sacrifice herself for an abstract principle.

But people were more complicated than profiles suggested.

"I'm going back," she told her parents. "They've offered me a promotion. Captain. My own team."

Her mother looked worried. Her father just shook his head.

"You really want to do this for the rest of your life? Risking everything for people who don't even appreciate it?"

Samantha looked out the window at the arcology's lower levels, where her parents had spent their entire lives. Where she would have spent hers, if she hadn't left.

"Yeah," she said. "I do."

She reported to IJC headquarters the next morning. They gave her a new team, a new mission. There were always disputes to settle, laws to enforce, people who thought they could ignore the rules that kept civilization from tearing itself apart.

Someone had to do it.

And Samantha Willis had discovered she was willing to be that someone.

Her first mission as captain took her to Glendale, Ulvaria—a mining colony on one of Jupiter's moons where the local administrator was accused of exploiting workers and creating dangerous levels of economic inequality. The mission required careful strategic planning and an understanding of how isolated communities developed their own cultural norms.

But that was a problem for tomorrow.

Today, she put on her blue helmet and reported for duty.

The helmet felt heavier than she remembered. Or maybe she just understood better what it meant to wear it.

Either way, she wore it with pride.

option_b: It requires the team to use experimental climate technology that has never been tested in combat situations
