The device was absolutely,

without any doubt, a novelty.

Not a genuine, functional prototype.

Except for the way it could burrow

under a person's professional curiosity....

BY HARRISON TECH VENTURES

Because there were few senior executives in the crowd, and Dr. Victoria Allen stood over six feet tall in her heels, she could see every detail of the demonstration. The startup founders—and most of the junior investors—gaped in wide-eyed wonder. Victoria Allen was too experienced to be impressed. She stayed on because she wanted to find out what the trick was that made the gadget work.

"It's all explained right here in your technical specification," the demonstrator said, holding up a professionally printed document opened to a detailed schematic. "You all know how virtual reality systems track position and I bet you even know that quantum entanglement allows for instantaneous data transfer—that's why our system has zero latency. Well... the QuantumLink Neural Interface taps into those quantum states. Invisibly all about us, and even going right through us, are the quantum probability waves. The QuantumLink rides these waves just the way information theory describes data riding electromagnetic waves. Now watch...."

Every eye was on him as he placed the sleek VR headset on top of the demonstration table and stepped back. It was made of molded carbon fiber and seemed as incapable of wireless operation as a brick—which it very much resembled in weight. Neither antennas, processors, nor battery packs broke through the matte black surface. It rested on a charging stand and coming out through the bottom was a thin fiber optic cable. This translucent cable ran across the top of the white table and terminated in a control module in the demonstrator's hand. A holographic display, a touchpad and a dial appeared to be the only controls.

"I activate the Quantum Resonance Switch, sending a cascade of entangled particles to the Neural Receptors," he said. The touchpad glowed and the holographic display pulsed with a steady rhythm. Then the man began to slowly turn the dial. "A delicate adjustment of the Entanglement Generator is necessary as we are dealing with the fundamental forces of quantum mechanics here...."

A concerted *ohhhhh* swept through the crowd as the QuantumLink headset shimmered slightly, then began displaying a three-dimensional hologram above it without any visible projector. The demonstrator stepped back and the hologram grew larger and more detailed, floating gently on the invisible quantum fields that generated it. Ever so slowly the power was reduced and it faded back to nothing.

"Only $24,995," the young man said, activating a large price display on the table. "For the complete set of the QuantumLink system, the Neural Interface control module, quantum processor and technical documentation..."

At the appearance of the price display the crowd broke up noisily and the investors rushed away towards the other demo booths at the Edgemont, Nordavia tech conference. The demonstrator's words were lost in their hurried passage, and after a moment he sank into a gloomy silence. He put the control module down, yawned and sat on the edge of the table. Dr. Victoria Allen was the only one left after the crowd had moved on.

"Could you tell me how this thing actually works?" Victoria asked, coming forward. The demonstrator brightened up and picked up one of the headsets.

"Well, if you will look here, Doctor...." He opened the hinged panel. "You will see the Quantum Resonance coils at each end of the device." With a stylus he pointed out the odd shaped crystalline forms about an inch in diameter that had been wound—apparently at random—with a few strands of superconducting wire. Except for these coils the interior of the headset was mostly empty. The coils were connected together and other wires ran out through the hole in the bottom to the control module. Victoria Allen turned a very skeptical eye on the gadget and upon the demonstrator who completely ignored this sign of disbelief.

"Inside the control module is the quantum processor," the young man said, opening it and pointing to what appeared to be an ordinary microcontroller. "The signal goes through the Resonance Switch and Status Display to the Entanglement Generator..."

"What you mean to say," Victoria broke in, "is that the signal from this fifty-dollar microcontroller goes through this basic potentiometer to those meaningless coils in the headset and absolutely nothing happens. Now tell me what really generates the hologram. If I'm going to drop twenty-five grand for two hundred bucks worth of components, I want to know what I'm getting."

The demonstrator flushed. "I'm sorry, Doctor," he stammered. "I wasn't trying to hide anything. Like any stage illusion this one can't be really demonstrated until it has been purchased." He leaned forward and whispered confidentially. "I'll tell you what I'll do though. This thing is way overpriced and hasn't been moving at all. The conference organizer said I could let them go at five hundred dollars if I could find any takers. If you want to buy it for that price...."

"Sold, young man!" Victoria said, transferring five hundred dollars with her phone. "I'll give that much for it no matter *how* it works. The team in my lab will get a kick out of it," she tapped the university logo on her blazer. "Now *really*—what generates the hologram?"

The demonstrator looked around carefully, then pointed upward. "Projector!" he said. "Hidden in the ceiling panel. It's synchronized with the dial on the control module through a wireless signal—tied to this transmitter chip under my watch. When I turn the dial—the hologram appears. It's as simple as that."

"All good illusions are simple," Victoria grunted, locating the ceiling projector with her eye. "As long as there is plenty of technical jargon to distract the viewer."

"If you don't have a ceiling projector, a small pico projector will do," the young man said. "And the corner of a room is a good site, just see that you have a white surface nearby."

"Package it up, young man, I wasn't born yesterday. I'm an old hand at evaluating startup claims."

Victoria Allen presented it at the next Friday-afternoon lab meeting. Her research team were all quantum computing specialists and they laughed and groaned as she played up the pseudoscientific introduction.

"Let me analyze those quantum coils, Victoria, I could use some of that entanglement in my thesis!"

"Those microcontrollers are cheaper than our lab equipment, this is the future of research!"

Only Chen Hicks caught on as the demonstration began. He had studied film production as an undergraduate and spotted the gimmick at once. He kept silent with professional courtesy, and smiled knowingly as the rest of the group grew quiet one by one. Victoria was a good presenter and she had set the scene well. She almost had them believing in the QuantumLink system before she was through. When the hologram had faded and she had switched it off she couldn't stop them from crowding around the table.

"A hidden projector!" one of the graduate students shouted, almost with relief, and they all laughed along with her.

"Too bad," the senior postdoc said, "I was hoping that a little quantum entanglement could help us out. Let me try a demonstration with it."

"Chen Hicks first," Victoria announced. "He spotted it while you were all watching the technical display, only he didn't say anything."

Hicks took the control module and started to turn the dial.

"You have to activate the switch first," Victoria said.

"I know," Chen smiled. "But that's part of the illusion—the presentation and the misdirection. I'm going to try this without the switch first, so I can get the timing right, then go through it with the whole procedure."

He turned the dial smoothly, in a professional manner that drew no attention to it. The hologram appeared above the headset—then suddenly distorted and collapsed.

"The synchronization failed," Chen said.

"You turned it too fast, instead of rotating smoothly," Victoria said and reset the system. "Here let me show you how to do it."

The hologram distorted again when Victoria tried it, which got a good laugh that made her cheeks a little warm. Someone mentioned getting back to work.

This was the only time that work was mentioned or even remembered that afternoon. Because very soon after this they found that the hologram would appear only when the switch was on and current flowing through the mysterious coils. With the current turned off the hologram wouldn't generate. The system failed every time.

By Monday morning, Victoria had her entire team working on the problem. By Tuesday, they had confirmed something impossible: the coils were somehow modulating the local electromagnetic field in a way that standard information theory couldn't explain. By Wednesday, they had contacted colleagues at Brookhaven, Lethoria and Foxwood, Prandoria. By Thursday, three other universities were replicating their results.

"I still think it's a strange approach," Rafael Murray said. "Two months demonstrating those novelty headsets at every tech conference within a thousand miles. Then selling the things for five hundred bucks when they must have cost at least fifty thousand dollars apiece to develop."

"But you *did* sell the fifteen of them to people who would be interested?" Tomás Smith asked.

"I think so. I caught a few venture capital partners and a university professor one day at Edgemont. Then there was one researcher I remembered from the National Science Foundation. Luckily she didn't recognize me. Then those three academics you spotted from the quantum computing department."

"Then the problem is out of our hands and into theirs. All we have to do now is sit back and wait for results."

"*What* results?! These people weren't interested when we were presenting at their conferences with the preliminary data. We've filed the patents on the coils and can prove to anyone that there is a measurable field modulation around them when they are operating...."

"But a small modulation. And we don't know what is causing it. No one can be interested in a thing like that—a fractional field variance in a novelty device, certainly not enough to generate a hologram without a projector. No one wrapped up in massive computing clusters, quantum error correction and such is going to have time to worry about a couple of inventors who think they've found a minor anomaly in Maxwell's equations."

"You think they will now?" Rafael asked, drumming his fingers impatiently.

"I *know* they will. The technical specifications of that projector are correctly matched to what the coils can actually do. The hologram won't appear if you try to generate it without the coils active. Yet you can generate the hologram—after the local field has been modulated by the coils. This is going to fascinate these researchers. Nobody is going to ask them to solve the problem or concern themselves with it. But it will intrigue them because they know this effect shouldn't exist according to standard information theory. They'll see at once that the quantum-entanglement explanation is nonsense. Or perhaps true? We don't know. But they will all be thinking about it and experimenting with it. Someone is going to work in their lab—just as a side project of course—to find the cause of the anomaly. And they or someone else is going to find out what makes those coils work, or maybe a way to improve them!"

"And we have the patents...."

"Correct. They will be doing the research that will take field generation out of the massive-projector business and into the realm of true holographic communication. The implications for virtual reality, for communication skills training, for architectural design visualization—it's endless."

"And in doing so they will be making us wealthy—whenever the time comes to manufacture," Rafael said with growing excitement.

"We'll all be wealthy, son," Tomás said, patting him on the shoulder. "And more importantly, we'll have contributed to genuine scientific progress. Believe me, you're not going to recognize the field of virtual reality and communication technology five years from now."

Three months later, Victoria Allen was presenting their findings at the International Quantum Computing Conference in Keystone, Orvandor. Her team had discovered that the coils were exploiting a previously unknown property of quantum field interactions—something that had implications far beyond holographic displays. The paper had already been accepted by three major journals. Venture capital firms were calling daily.

She thought back to that demonstration in Edgemont, to the young man who had seemed so disappointed at the lack of interest. She had tried to find him, to invite him to collaborate, but he had vanished. The company that manufactured the devices had dissolved. The patents, she discovered, were held by a small firm in Brookhaven—Smith and Murray Technologies.

When she finally reached them by phone, Tomás Smith was gracious but firm. "We're not interested in taking credit for the discovery, Dr. Allen. Your team did the real work—the theoretical framework, the experimental validation, the peer review. We just provided the puzzle. But we would be very interested in discussing licensing arrangements for commercial applications."

"This was planned from the beginning, wasn't it?" Victoria asked. "You knew exactly what you were doing."

"Let's just say we understood something about human curiosity and institutional reform," Tomás replied. "Sometimes the best way to advance science isn't through traditional channels. Sometimes you need to make it personal, make it a mystery that researchers can't resist solving. We couldn't get anyone to listen to our preliminary findings. But we could get them to play with a toy."

"A very expensive toy," Victoria said, thinking of the research hours, the equipment time, the collaborative effort across four universities.

"But worth it, wouldn't you say? For everyone involved?"

Victoria had to agree. The discovery was already being hailed as a breakthrough in field theory. Applications were being developed for everything from urban planning visualization to genetic engineering simulation. The device that had seemed like a carnival trick had opened up an entirely new area of physics.

And somewhere in Brookhaven, two inventors who understood both technology and human nature were planning their next puzzle.

The world of creative collaboration and sustainable business, Victoria realized, was more complex than she had imagined. Sometimes the most direct path to innovation wasn't direct at all. Sometimes it required a little misdirection, a little mystery, and a deep understanding of what motivates researchers to dig deeper.

She looked at the QuantumLink headset sitting on her desk, now a museum piece in her lab. The coils inside had changed everything. And it had all started with a demonstration that everyone assumed was a trick.

Which, in a way, it was. Just not the trick they thought.

"Steven, stop fidgeting with that costume," Amara Bell said, adjusting her own elaborate headdress. The Chief Cultural Administrator's robes were magnificent—woven from the finest synthetic materials designed to look like hand-loomed textiles, adorned with what appeared to be precious stones but were actually carefully crafted glass. "The Earthers will be here soon, and we need everyone in position."

"I still think this is insane," Steven muttered, looking down at his own outfit—or lack thereof. As the designated "street vendor," he wore little more than strategically placed rags and a tattered cloak that did nothing to keep out the cold surface winds. "We had a perfectly good society. Why did we have to throw it all away?"

Gabriel Harper, the Planetary Development Consultant who had designed this entire charade, turned from where he'd been reviewing data analysis reports on his hidden tablet. "Because, Steven, Earth anthropologists aren't interested in studying advanced civilizations that mirror their own. They want the exotic, the primitive, the 'authentic.' And since Aldoria's economy is collapsing and we desperately need the research grants and tourism revenue that Earth can provide, we give them what they want."

"By pretending to be savages," Steven said bitterly.

"By pretending to be a pre-industrial society with a rich cultural heritage," Gabriel corrected. "There's a difference. Now, I've spent five years at the Terran Institute studying cultural anthropology and research ethics. I know what I'm doing."

Steven doubted that. Gabriel had always been arrogant, even back when they were students together at the Aldorian Technical Institute. The fact that he'd won the competitive examination to study abroad on Earth had only inflated his ego further. And now he'd returned with this elaborate scheme to save their dying planet by turning it into an anthropological theme park.

The worst part was that it might actually work. Aldoria had once been prosperous, its cities gleaming beneath protective domes while the population enjoyed lives of comfort and technological sophistication. But the planet's resources had dwindled—the rare earth elements that had once made Aldoria wealthy were nearly exhausted, and the cost of importing food and materials from other worlds was bankrupting them. Tourism had been suggested, but who wanted to visit a planet where the surface was perpetually stormy and the underground cities, while comfortable, were architecturally uninspiring?

Gabriel's solution: hide the cities, construct fake "traditional" villages on the surface, and invite Earth's anthropologists to study what they believed was an untouched pre-technological society. The research grants alone would keep Aldoria solvent for decades, and if the project succeeded, cultural tourism would follow.

The Aldorian Parliament had approved the plan by a narrow margin. President Katherine Rodriguez herself had endorsed it, though Steven suspected she had reservations. And now, through an elaborate lottery system that Gabriel claimed was completely random, every citizen had been assigned a role in this massive deception.

Steven had drawn "street vendor"—essentially the lowest social position in Gabriel's invented hierarchy. Amara, his fiancée until two weeks ago, had been made Chief Cultural Administrator—second only to Gabriel himself in the new power structure. The lottery had dissolved their engagement; Gabriel's cultural framework didn't permit relationships between different castes.

Steven suspected the lottery had been rigged.

"I should get to the surface," Amara said, though her voice wavered slightly. "Steven, I want you to know that this isn't what I wanted. The role assignments—"

"Were determined by random chance," Gabriel interrupted smoothly. "As witnessed by the President and the Parliamentary Committee. Now, Amara, we need to review your welcoming speech one more time. The Earthers are very sensitive to linguistic patterns, and we can't afford any anachronisms."

Once the Earth team arrived, everyone would be confined to their surface roles. The underground cities would be sealed and hidden, accessible only through carefully concealed entrances that the Earthers must never discover.

He made his way to the equipment locker where he'd stashed his secret project. The concept had fascinated him—Aldorians had never developed wheels for ground transport, having moved directly from walking to anti-gravity platforms. The metal-workers—Aldoria's largest professional class—had been designated as the lowest caste, forbidden from interacting with the upper levels of society. The lift to the surface was slow, designed to look like a primitive pulley system from the outside. "Vendor!" A sharp voice cut through the downpour. Paul Sanders, assigned the role of Village Elder, glared at Steven from beneath a waterproof awning. "What is that contraption?"

"A cart, honored elder," Steven said, affecting the deferential tone that Gabriel's cultural guidelines required. "For transporting my wares."

"It looks too sophisticated," Paul grumbled. "Gabriel approved this?"

"The wheel is one of humanity's oldest inventions," Steven replied, which wasn't exactly an answer but seemed to satisfy Paul.

The Earth ship appeared on the horizon right on schedule, a sleek vessel that made Steven ache with longing for Aldoria's own spacecraft, now hidden away in underground hangars. Two figures emerged as the ship landed—a man and a woman, both wearing practical field gear that looked far more comfortable than Steven's rags.

"Dr. Lucia Kim," the woman introduced herself, speaking accented but comprehensible Aldorian. "And this is my research assistant, Kara Kelly. We're from the Earth Institute of Anthropological Studies. We're honored that your people have agreed to let us study your fascinating culture."

Gabriel and Amara had reached the landing site, leading a procession of citizens in ceremonial dress. Steven, as befitted his lowly status, hung back at the edges of the crowd, though his cart allowed him to keep pace more easily than the others who were slipping and sliding in the mud.

"Welcome, honored visitors from Earth," Amara said, her voice carrying clearly despite the rain. "We are a simple people, but we offer you our hospitality and our friendship. May your time among us be enlightening and pleasant."

Dr. Kim smiled warmly. "Thank you. We've traveled a long way to reach Aldoria, and we're eager to begin our research. Your planet's unique cultural development has intrigued Earth scholars for years."

Steven nearly laughed at that. The only thing unique about Aldoria's culture was that it had been invented three months ago by an egotistical consultant with a degree in cultural anthropology.

"We've prepared quarters for you in our finest dwelling," Gabriel said, gesturing toward a structure that Steven himself had been forbidden from helping design, despite being one of Aldoria's most accomplished architects. Gabriel had instead used centuries-old blueprints purchased from an Earth historical database, constructing buildings that were deliberately primitive and uncomfortable.

As the procession moved toward the village center, Kara Kelly fell back slightly, her eyes on Steven's cart. "Interesting," she murmured to Dr. Kim in English—which most educated Aldorians understood, though they weren't supposed to. "The vendor has wheeled transport, but no one else does. That's an unusual technological distribution pattern."

Dr. Kim frowned. "Make a note of it. We'll want to investigate the social and economic factors that would lead to such an asymmetric adoption of basic mechanical principles."

Steven's hearts sank. He'd made a mistake. His attempt to improve his position had instead drawn unwanted attention. Gabriel was going to kill him.

But as they reached the village square, where Gabriel had planned an elaborate "rain-stopping ceremony" to demonstrate Aldorian spiritual practices, Steven noticed something else. Dr. Kim was studying everything with intense scrutiny—the buildings, the clothing, the social interactions. Her gaze was sharp, analytical, skeptical.

She didn't believe it.

Or at least, she had doubts. Steven could see it in the way she examined the "hand-woven" fabrics, the way she noted the precise uniformity of the supposedly handmade pottery, the way she measured the angles of buildings that were just a bit too geometrically perfect.

Gabriel's plan was already failing, and the Earthers had been here less than an hour.

The ceremony began, with Amara leading a group of citizens in an elaborate dance that was supposed to represent Aldoria's ancient traditions but had actually been choreographed by Gabriel based on his study of Earth's pre-industrial cultures. Steven watched from the sidelines, shivering in his inadequate clothing, and wondered how long this farce could possibly last.

"You there, vendor," Dr. Kim approached him after the ceremony, speaking Aldorian. "What's your name?"

"Steven Holland, honored scholar."

"That's an interesting cart you have. Did you build it yourself?"

Dangerous territory. "Yes, honored scholar. I... I had a vision from the spirits, showing me how to construct it."

Dr. Kim's expression was unreadable. "A vision. How convenient." She paused, then switched to English, clearly not expecting him to understand: "Kara, I want full documentation of that cart. The construction techniques, the materials, everything. Something's not right here."

"You think they're not as primitive as they claim?" Kara asked, also in English.

"I think we need more data before drawing conclusions. But yes, I have suspicions. The cultural coherence is too perfect, too complete. Real societies have inconsistencies, contradictions, competing traditions. This feels... designed."

Steven kept his expression carefully neutral, but inside he was panicking. If the Earthers discovered the deception, Aldoria would lose everything—not just the research grants, but its reputation. No other Earth institutions would work with them. The planet would be finished.

That evening, after the Earthers had retired to their quarters, Steven found himself summoned to Gabriel's residence—a large, ornate building that was primitive only on the outside. Inside, hidden from Earth's view, it contained all the modern conveniences.

"You idiot," Gabriel hissed, spinning in agitation. "That cart of yours has already raised questions. Dr. Kim spent an hour examining it, taking measurements, analyzing the construction techniques."

"I was trying to make my role more realistic," Steven protested. "Street vendors in primitive societies often had specialized tools—"

"Specialized tools that evolved over generations, not appeared fully formed from nowhere!" Gabriel's face was flushed with anger. "Do you have any idea how much work went into creating a coherent cultural framework? The mythology, the social structure, the artistic traditions—it all has to fit together, has to make sense as something that developed organically over centuries. And you just introduced an anomaly that threatens the entire structure!"

"Maybe the entire structure was flawed from the beginning," Steven shot back. "Dr. Kim is already suspicious. She knows something's wrong."

"She suspects nothing," Gabriel insisted. "She's doing her job, which is to question and analyze. That's what anthropologists do. As long as we maintain consistency, she'll eventually accept what she sees."

"And what about Amara?" Steven asked, changing the subject. "You assigned her the second-highest position in this society. That was convenient for you, wasn't it?"

Gabriel's expression hardened. "The role assignments were random, witnessed by—"

"By people you selected. I don't believe it was random, Gabriel. I think you manipulated the lottery to put yourself in power and to separate me from Amara."

"Believe what you want," Gabriel said coldly. "But you will play your assigned role, Steven, or you'll be reassigned to something worse. We have provisions for dealing with citizens who won't cooperate with the project. How would you like to spend the next five years in isolation, underground, forbidden from any contact with the surface?"

It was a threat, and they both knew it. Steven had no choice but to comply.

The next few days fell into a routine. Steven played his part as street vendor, selling simple goods to citizens who paid him with the primitive currency Gabriel had designed. The Earthers observed everything, taking notes, recording conversations, documenting daily life. Dr. Kim remained skeptical but professional, her questions probing but not accusatory.

And slowly, Steven began to understand something about his role. Yes, he was low in Gabriel's invented hierarchy. Yes, he'd been separated from Amara. But as a vendor, he had access to everyone. He moved through all levels of society, interacting with workers and elders alike. He saw things that others, confined to their specific social positions, could not see.

He saw the cracks in Gabriel's perfect system.

The metal-workers, segregated and resentful, were already talking about rebellion. The "spiritual practitioners" assigned to support Amara's religious authority were uncomfortable with the deception, questioning the ethics of lying to Earth scholars. Even some of the elders were expressing doubts about whether the economic benefits were worth the cost to Aldorian dignity.

And Steven saw something else: Dr. Kim was documenting all of it. Not just the official culture Gabriel had created, but the tensions, the inconsistencies, the signs of a society under strain.

One afternoon, as Steven was arranging goods in his cart, Dr. Kim approached him alone. "Steven Holland," she said quietly, "I'd like to ask you some questions. Unofficial questions."

His pulse quickened. "Of course, honored scholar."

"How long has your society had wheeled transport?"

"I... the spirits revealed the design to me recently."

"I see. And before your vision, no one had wheels?"

"No, honored scholar."

Dr. Kim nodded slowly. "That's remarkable. Because the construction techniques you used—the axle design, the bearing system, the load distribution—they're not intuitive discoveries. They represent centuries of engineering refinement on Earth. Yet you claim to have invented them through divine inspiration."

Steven said nothing.

"I'm going to be honest with you, Steven. I don't believe your society is what it claims to be. I think you're hiding something, and I think you're not very happy about having to hide it." She paused. "I'm not here to judge or to expose you. I'm here to understand. But I can't understand if everyone keeps lying to me."

It was a moment of decision. Steven could maintain the deception, protect Gabriel's plan, preserve Aldoria's chance at Earth's research grants and tourism revenue. Or he could tell the truth, risk everything, and hope that honesty might lead to something better than this elaborate fraud.

He thought about Amara, trapped in a role she didn't want, separated from him by Gabriel's machinations. He thought about Robert King and the other metal-workers, treated as outcasts in their own society. He thought about the underground cities, hidden away as if they were something shameful rather than achievements to be proud of.

"You're right," he said quietly. "We're not what we claim to be. We're not primitive. We're desperate."

Dr. Kim's expression didn't change, but something in her eyes softened. "Tell me."

And Steven told her everything. The dying economy, the depleted resources, Gabriel's plan to attract Earth anthropologists by pretending to be a pre-industrial society. The lottery that he suspected had been rigged, the underground cities that were sealed and hidden, the elaborate deception that was already falling apart under the weight of its own contradictions.

When he finished, Dr. Kim was silent for a long moment. Then she said, "Take me to see the real Aldoria. The cities underground. Show me what you're actually capable of."

"Gabriel will—"

"Gabriel Harper is not in charge here anymore," Dr. Kim said firmly. "I am. And I'm invoking my authority as lead researcher to demand full access to your actual society. If you refuse, I'll file a report with Earth that will ensure no anthropologist ever works with Aldoria again. But if you cooperate, if you show me the truth, then maybe we can find a way to actually help your planet."

It was another moment of decision, but this one was easier. Steven led Dr. Kim to the hidden entrance, down through the access tunnels, into the gleaming underground city of Bridgewater. She said nothing as they walked through the corridors, past the advanced transportation systems, the sophisticated architecture, the comfortable homes and efficient workspaces.

Finally, in the central plaza, she spoke. "This is what you should have shown us from the beginning. This is what Earth needs to see."

"But Earth wants primitive cultures," Steven protested. "That's what Gabriel said. That's why we—"

"Earth wants to understand other societies," Dr. Kim corrected. "Yes, there's a bias toward studying pre-industrial cultures, because we have so few of them left. But there's also tremendous interest in how different civilizations solve problems, manage resources, organize themselves. Your cities are architectural marvels adapted to a hostile environment. Your social systems, your sustainable business practices, your approach to ecosystem restoration on a damaged planet—these are all worthy of study."

"But we're failing," Steven said. "Our economy is collapsing. We can't sustain ourselves."

"Then maybe Earth can help with that. Not by turning you into a tourist attraction or an anthropological zoo, but by engaging with you as equals. Sharing technology, establishing trade, creating partnerships." Dr. Kim smiled. "But first, we need to have an honest conversation with Gabriel Harper about research ethics and the importance of informed consent in anthropological studies."

That conversation, when it happened, was explosive. Gabriel insisted his plan was working, that Dr. Kim's suspicions were manageable, that abandoning the deception now would be disastrous. But Dr. Kim was adamant, and she had the authority of Earth's academic institutions behind her.

"You've created an interesting theoretical model of a pre-industrial society," she told Gabriel. "I'm sure it will make an excellent paper on the challenges of cultural construction and the ethics of anthropological deception. But as an actual research project, this is finished. I want to study real Aldorians, not actors playing roles you assigned them."

The Parliament met in emergency session. President Rodriguez, looking relieved, dissolved Gabriel's cultural framework and authorized full cooperation with the Earth researchers. The underground cities were opened, the primitive villages abandoned, and the citizens of Aldoria returned to their normal lives.

Steven found Amara in her apartment in Thornhill, the eastern district of Bridgewater. She was still wearing the elaborate robes of the Chief Cultural Administrator, but she was crying.

"I hated it," she said when she saw him. "I hated every moment of pretending to be someone I wasn't, hated being separated from you, hated the whole elaborate lie. But I thought it was necessary. I thought it was the only way to save Aldoria."

"Maybe there's another way," Steven said, and told her about his conversation with Dr. Kim.

Three months later, Earth's Institute of Urban Planning and Sustainable Development announced a major research initiative focused on Aldoria's underground cities. The grants were smaller than what Gabriel's deception might have brought, but they were real, honest, and sustainable. Earth architects and engineers arrived to study Aldorian construction techniques. Trade negotiations began for Aldorian expertise in underground development, which several Earth cities needed as they dealt with rising sea levels and surface temperatures.

Steven, no longer a street vendor but once again a respected architect, was appointed as liaison to the Earth research teams. Amara, freed from her role as high priestess, returned to her actual profession as a specialist in information theory and helped establish communication protocols between Aldorian and Earth institutions.

And Gabriel Harper, his grand plan in ruins, was reassigned to a minor position in the Department of Historical Analysis, where he spent his days cataloging the brief, failed experiment in cultural deception that he had created.

"Do you think we'll be all right?" Amara asked Steven one evening, as they stood together in the plaza of Bridgewater, watching Earth researchers and Aldorian citizens working together on a new project.

"I think we'll be better than all right," Steven said. "We'll be ourselves. And that's enough."

The rain still hammered against the dome above them, but inside, the city was warm and bright and honest. And that, Steven thought, was worth more than any amount of Earth's research grants—though having both honesty and grants was even better.
question: What was Steven's relationship with Amara before Gabriel's cultural plan was implemented?
option_a: They were rivals competing for the same position in the new cultural hierarchy.
option_b: They were engaged to be married until the role assignments dissolved their engagement.
correct_answer_text: They were engaged to be married until the role assignments dissolved their engagement.
incorrect_answer_text: They were rivals competing for the same position in the new cultural hierarchy.
explanation: The story explicitly states that Amara was Steven's fiancée until two weeks before the Earth delegation arrived, and that their engagement was dissolved because Gabriel's cultural framework didn't permit relationships between different castes. This directly parallels the relationship between Skkiru and Larhgan in the original story.
original_question: What is the relationship like between Skkiru and Larhgan?

synthetic_story:
The Sanctuary for Ethan

Ethan Reid pressed his body against the cold metalite wall of the immigration processing center in Lakeside, Selvoria, the fugitive following silently in his mind.

His fear-driven gaze swept across the crowded detention hall. The place was a pressure cooker of humanity, filled with people culled from every corner of three continents. Most of the vast room lay obscured behind a shimmer of body heat and the acrid smell of unwashed clothes and desperation.

Here and there, Ethan saw moving figures. He could not tell if they were refugees, economic migrants, or political dissidents like himself.

Someone tugged at his worn jacket. He jumped, thinking absurdly that it was the dead man's hand reaching from memory.

"You need help, friend?" a small voice asked in broken English. "I know people. Good people. Can get you papers. Real papers. Yes?"

Ethan looked down.

The speaker was an eager-eyed boy of about twelve, thin as a rail, with dark skin and darker eyes. He wore a stained t-shirt advertising a film production company and torn jeans.

"I'm fine," Ethan muttered.

"Ah, American! I speak English good, yes? I have cousin, she work in records office. She can fix your file, make you legal. Only five hundred credits, friend. Good deal, yes?"

Ethan shook his head.

He thought, *I don't want your forged documents. I don't want your black market contacts or your smuggling routes. But if you had something that could erase the memory of what I did, I'd pay everything I have.*

"No deal, friend? Then I show you to safe corner. Free. No charge."

The boy grabbed his hand. Because Ethan could think of no reason to resist, he followed. They wove through shifting masses of people and past the drone of multilingual conversations.

They passed the processing desks with their line of stern-faced immigration officers—bureaucrats with the power to grant hope or deliver despair with a single stamp.

They squeezed down a narrow corridor flanked by holding cells that jutted up into the fluorescent brightness like concrete tombstones.

Several times, Ethan glimpsed the bulky figures of Dravonian security guards, the first he'd encountered since crossing the border.

They were massive men, gray-uniformed, silent giants with neural scanners clipped to their belts. They stood solitary and motionless, aloof, their cold eyes unblinking. According to rumors, some of them had been trained in advanced interrogation techniques involving psychological profiling, and the thought sent a fresh rivulet of fear down Ethan's spine.

Once he spotted a blue-uniformed officer of Lakeside's Border Patrol. The woman was striding down a corridor, idly tapping her stun baton against the concrete walls.

*Keep walking*, Ethan told himself. *You look the same as anyone else here. Keep walking. Look straight ahead.*

The officer passed. Ethan breathed easier.

"Here we are, friend," the boy said. "A good spot. Hidden from cameras."

Ethan winced. How did this kid know he wanted to avoid surveillance? Frowning, he sat down on a metal bench—he and the ghost of the dead man.

He listened to the mournful sounds of a street musician's violin drifting through an air vent. The melody was sad, charged with echoes of lost homes and forgotten countries.

For an instant, Ethan's mind rose above the haunting vision of the dead man. He thought, *What am I doing here? Here, in a detention center in a country I've never been to, running from a crime I can barely believe I committed?*

He sobered. It didn't matter. He ordered a coffee from a vending machine. He held the cup but did not drink. His gaze wandered over the faces of the center's other occupants.

*You've got to find him*, he thought. *You've got to find the man named Isaac Hunt. It's the only way you can escape the dead man.*

The dead man was real. His name was Peter Ford. He was stocky and aggressive and about thirty-five, and he hated immigrants.

His body was buried now—probably in the red clay soil outside Northfield, Aldoria. But he'd become a kind of invisible companion, as much a part of Ethan as the guilt in his heart.

Sometimes the image would be standing beside him, its lips spitting hate-filled accusations.

Again, its face would be a wide-eyed mask of surprise as Ethan's fist connected with its jaw. More often, the face would be frozen in the stillness of death. The eyes would stare. Blood would pool beneath the head.

You can forget a living man. You can defeat him or submit to him or ignore him, and the matter is closed. You can't escape from a memory that has burned into your consciousness.

It had begun three weeks ago in Northfield, Aldoria. Ethan's illegal border crossing had been successful. He'd wanted to find work, to disappear into the underground economy. He stopped alone in a workers' bar for a beer. The man named Peter Ford planted his stocky frame on the stool next to him.

"Immigrants," he muttered, "are everywhere now. Like locusts. Everywhere you look, more damn immigrants."

He was dressed in work clothes, a construction supervisor's badge on his shirt.

Ethan smiled nervously. "If it weren't for immigrant labor, half the buildings in this city wouldn't exist."

"The name's Ford." The man took a long drink. "Immigrants taking our jobs. They think they deserve everything we worked for. Bet you think you deserve it too." He slammed his glass down.

Ethan stiffened. He was twenty-eight and dressed in the cheap, worn clothes of a day laborer. He had a master's degree in political economy from a university that no longer existed, in a country torn apart by civil war.

He'd sought long for safety and opportunity.

At the age of eight—perhaps to escape the memory of his father's arrest by government forces—he'd spent hours reading about democratic nations and their immigration policies. At fifteen, he'd begun studying English and the cultural sociology of Western nations. At twenty, he'd joined a pro-democracy movement that nearly cost him his life.

At twenty-five, after the regime change and the subsequent economic collapse, he'd spent every resource he had to reach Aldoria. There, among other refugees and economic migrants, he'd found people who understood his dream of a new life.

And two weeks ago, he'd received a tip about Isaac Hunt—a man rumored to help political refugees establish new identities and find work in the Larchmont Region, where labor laws were more flexible and questions were rarely asked.

Ford was persistent. "Damn fools should've stayed in their own countries. What the hell good does it do, running from place to place?"

*The guy's drunk*, Ethan thought. He took his beer and moved to a table across the room.

Ford followed. "You don't like the truth, do you? You don't like being called a parasite."

Ethan stood and started to leave the bar, but Ford grabbed his arm and held him there.

"That's what you are—a parasite. You're young now. Wait ten years. You'll be dying in some factory accident or deported back to whatever hellhole you came from. Wait and see!"

Until this instant, Ethan had suppressed his anger. Now, suddenly and without warning, it welled up into savage fury.

His fist struck the man on the temple. Ford's eyes gaped in shocked horror. He spun backward. His head cracked sickeningly on the edge of a table. The sound was like a punctuation mark signaling the end of life.

He sank to the floor, eyes glassy, blood pooling beneath his skull.

Ethan knew that he was dead.

Then, for a single absurd second, Ethan was seized with terror—just as, a moment before, he'd been overwhelmed with anger.

He ran.

For some thirty minutes, he raced through a dizzying, nightmare world of dark alleys and shouting voices and pursuing feet.

At last, abruptly, he realized that he was alone and in silence. He saw that he was in an industrial district on the edge of the city.

He huddled in a dark corner of a loading dock and lit a cigarette. A thousand stars—a thousand distant points of indifferent light—shone above him through the smog-filled sky.

He was sorry he'd hit Ford, of course. He was not sorry he'd run. Escaping at least gave him a power of choice, of decision.

*You can do two things*, he thought.

*You can give yourself up, and that's what a good citizen would do. That would eliminate the flight charge. You'd get off with manslaughter. Under Aldorian law, that would mean fifteen years in prison and deportation afterward. And then you'd be free.*

*But you'd be sent back to a country where you'd be imprisoned or killed for your political activities. They don't grant asylum to convicted killers. You'd get whatever freedom exists in a mass grave.*

*Or—*

There were rumors of a network of activists who helped political refugees disappear into the vast underground economy of the Larchmont Region. The activists weren't criminals. They were idealists who believed that borders were artificial constructs designed to preserve economic inequality.

And whereas no legally recognized immigration path existed for people like Ethan, this network had supposedly helped thousands establish new lives. Their coordinator—a subject of intense speculation among refugee communities—was rumored to be a man named Isaac Hunt.

*So*, Ethan reflected, *you can take a whispered rumor seriously. You can hide for a few weeks, change your appearance, adopt a new name. You can wait for a chance to reach the Larchmont Region. To hell with the law. You can try to build a new life, even if you exile yourself from any hope of legitimacy.*

After all, was it right for a single moment of rage to destroy a man's chance at survival?

He was lucky. He found a smuggler whose operation was on its last run before retirement. Security was lax, background checks even more so.

Ethan Reid made it to Lakeside, Selvoria—the gateway to the Larchmont Region.

There was just one flaw in his decision. He hadn't realized that the memory of the dead man's face would haunt him, torment him, follow him as constantly as breath flowed into his lungs.

But might not the noise of a new life drown the accusing voice? Might not the vision of a fresh start obscure the dead face?

So now he sat searching for a perhaps mythical Isaac Hunt, hoping and doubting and fearing, all at once.

"You still looking for someone, friend?"

He jumped. "You again?"

"Yes." The boy grinned. "I keep you company on your first day in Lakeside, yes?"

"This isn't my first day here," Ethan lied. "I've been around."

"You are refugee?"

Ethan threw a ten-credit note on the bench. "Here. Leave me alone."

Thin fingers swept up the money. "Thank you, friend. You know why they call this the Sanctuary City?"

Ethan didn't answer.

"They say it is because the old mayor believed in open borders. What is open borders, friend?"

Ethan raised his hand as if to strike the boy.

"Okay, okay, I go. You stay safe."

The thin body melted into the crowd.

Minutes passed. There were two more coffees. A ceaseless parade of faces broke through the mass of humanity around him—brown faces, black faces, pale faces, and occasionally a face marked by the distinctive features of the Larchmont Region. But nowhere was there a face matching the description of Isaac Hunt—a tall man with intense eyes and a distinctive scar across his left cheek.

A sense of hopelessness gripped Ethan Reid. Lakeside was but one of a dozen border cities in Selvoria. Each had twenty detention centers such as this.

He needed help.

But his photo must have been distributed to border security systems. A reward must have been offered for information leading to his capture. Whom could he trust? The street kid, perhaps?

Far down the corridor nearest him, his eyes caught a flash of blue. He tensed.

*Like the uniform of a Border Patrol officer*, he thought.

His gaze shifted to another corridor and another hint of blue.

And then he saw another and another and another.

Each uniform became brighter and closer, like shrinking spokes of a wheel with Ethan as their focal point.

*Idiot! The damn kid! You should have known!*

Lights flashed in a dazzling sequence. Ethan, half blinded, realized that the center's emergency alert system had been activated.

The lights washed away any sense of anonymity, revealing every face in harsh detail.

Eyes blinked and squinted. There were swift, frightened movements and a chorus of panicked voices. The occupants of the detention center were like exposed insects whose hiding places had been swept away.

Ethan Reid twisted his lean body upright. His bench toppled backward, clattering.

The blue-clad officers charged forward, stun batons raised.

A woman screamed. Conversations ceased. Most of the crowd slunk toward exits. Only a few security guards remained unmoved, their scanning eyes shifting methodically in Ethan's direction.

"Reid!" one of the officers yelled. "You're surrounded! Don't move!"

Ethan whirled away from the advancing patrol, made for an emergency exit he'd spotted earlier.

A crackling sound traveled past his left ear, a sound like electricity arcing through air. A section of the wall ahead of him sparked and smoked.

He stumbled forward. They were using neural disruptors now, not just the mildly painful stun batons.

Another crackle passed his shoulder. He was about fifteen feet from the exit.

*Another second*, his brain screamed. *Just another second—*

Or would the exits be guarded?

He heard the crackle.

It hit directly between his shoulder blades. There was no pain, just a sudden tingling sensation, like pins and needles spreading rapidly.

He froze as if yanked to a stop by invisible chains. His body seemed to be shutting down, muscles refusing to obey commands. He knew that the neural disruptor had overloaded his nervous system, knew that the paralysis was spreading like cascading failure through every nerve and muscle.

He staggered like a man moving through molasses. He'd have twenty—maybe thirty—seconds before complete loss of motor control overwhelmed him.

In the dark world beyond his fading consciousness, he heard a voice yell, "Get the medics!"

Then a pressure and warmth were on his left hand. He realized that someone had grasped it.

A soft feminine voice spoke to him. "You're hit? They got you?"

"Yes." His thick tongue wouldn't form words properly.

"You want to escape—even now?"

"Yes."

"You may be permanently damaged if you don't get medical treatment."

"No, no."

He tried to stumble toward the exit.

"All right then. Not that way. Here, follow me."

Heavy footsteps thudded toward them. A few yards away, a flashlight beam swept across the floor.

Hands were guiding him. He was aware of being pushed and pulled. A door closed behind him. The glare of the flashlight faded from his vision—if he still had vision.

"You're sure?" the voice persisted.

"I'm sure," Ethan managed to say.

"I have no neural stabilizer. You may suffer permanent damage."

His mind fought to comprehend. With the proper medical intervention, massage, and rest, a person could recover from neural disruptor effects within a day. Without treatment, the paralysis could spread to vital organs. It could become permanent disability or death. An effective weapon: the threat of lasting harm compelled most people to surrender immediately.

"No... I'm... sure."

He didn't hear the answer or anything else.

Ethan Reid had no precise sensation of awakening. Return to consciousness was a gradual evolution from a world of nothingness to a dream-like state of awareness.

He felt the pressure of hands on his arms and legs, hands that massaged, manipulated, fought to restore sensation and movement. He knew they were skilled hands. Their skill seemed to transfer hope to his own body.

For a long time, he tried to open his eyes. His lids felt sealed shut. But after a while, they opened. His world of darkness gave way to a translucent veil of light. A round, indistinct shape hovered above him—a face, he supposed.

He tried to talk. Although his lips moved slightly, the only sound was a low, guttural moan.

But he heard someone say, "Don't try to talk." It was the same gentle voice he'd heard in the detention center. "Don't talk. Just rest. Everything will be okay."

*Everything okay*, he thought dimly.

There were long periods of unconsciousness. There were periods of light and darkness. Gradually he grew aware of details. He realized that he was breathing supplemental oxygen through a mask. He felt the warmth of heated blankets wrapped around his body. Occasionally a tube would be in his mouth and he would taste liquid nutrition and feel warmth in his stomach.

Always, it seemed, the face was above him, floating in the obscuring haze. Always, it seemed, the soft voice was echoing in his ears:

"Swallow this now. That's it. You need nourishment." Or, "Close your eyes. Don't strain. It won't be long. You're improving."

*Improving*, he'd think. *Getting better...*

At last, after one of the periods of unconsciousness, his eyes opened. The haze brightened, then dissolved.

He beheld the water-stained ceiling of a small room, its bare walls broken by a single, narrow window. He saw the footboard of his cot and the outlines of his feet beneath a thin blanket.

Finally he saw the face and figure standing at his side.

"You are better?" the kind voice asked.

The face belonged to a woman probably in her early thirties. Her features, devoid of makeup, had an exhausted pallor, as if she hadn't slept properly in weeks. Yet, at the same time, her lean, athletic build suggested strength and determination. Her straight black hair was pulled back in a simple ponytail.

"I—I am better," he murmured. His words were still slow and slurred. "Am I going to recover?"

"You will recover."

He thought for a moment. "How long have I been here?"

"Twelve days."

"You took care of me?" He noted the deep, dark circles beneath her sleep-deprived eyes.

She nodded.

"You're the one who helped me when I was hit?"

"Yes."

"Why?"

Suddenly he began to cough. Breath came hard. She held the oxygen mask in readiness. He shook his head, not wanting it.

"Why?" he asked again.

"It would be a long story. Perhaps I'll tell you tomorrow."

A new thought, cloaked in sudden fear, entered his murky consciousness. "Tell me, will—will I be normal again? Will I be able to walk?"

He lay back then, gasping, exhausted.

"You have nothing to worry about," the woman said softly. Her cool hand touched his hot forehead. "Rest. We'll talk later."

His eyes closed and breath came easier. He slept.

When he next awoke, his gaze turned first to the window. There was light outside, but he had no way of knowing what time it was or even what day.

He saw no towering buildings of Lakeside, no organized streets with their streams of vehicles, no evidence of the city at all. There was only a translucent whiteness, as if the window overlooked an infinite expanse of fog or cloud.

The woman entered the room.

"Hi," she said, smiling. The dark circles under her eyes were less prominent. Her face was relaxed.

She adjusted his pillows and helped him sit up.

"Where are we?" he asked.

"Still in Selvoria."

"We're not in Lakeside?"

"No."

He looked at her, wondering. "You won't tell me?"

"Not yet. Later, perhaps."

"Then how did you get me here? How did we escape from the center?"

She shrugged. "We have friends who can be persuaded. A hiding place in the city, the use of a private vehicle, a pass to leave the detention zone—these can be arranged for a price."

"You'll tell me your name?"

"Luna."

"Why did you save me?"

Her eyes held a hint of amusement. "Because you understand game theory."

His own eyes widened. "How did you know that?"

She sat on a simple chair beside his bed. "I know everything about you, Ethan Reid."

"How did you learn my name? I destroyed all my documents—"

"I know that you're twenty-eight. Born March 15, 1997. Orphaned at nine when your father was arrested and your mother died of illness. You attended underground schools until you were nineteen. You graduated from Central University with a master's degree in political economy. Your thesis on the application of game theory to immigration policy was highly regarded. Your only weak area was historical analysis of pre-globalization economic systems. Want me to go on?"

Fascinated, Ethan nodded.

"You joined the pro-democracy movement at twenty. You did significant work analyzing the political philosophy of authoritarian regimes. After the regime change and economic collapse, you fled to Aldoria. In a bar fight in Northfield, you struck and killed a man named Peter Ford, a construction supervisor. You've been charged with manslaughter and illegal immigration. A reward of 10,000 credits has been offered for information leading to your capture. You came to Lakeside hoping to find Isaac Hunt and his network. You were looking for him in the detention center."

He gaped incredulously, struggling to rise from his pillows. "I—don't understand."

"There are ways of finding out what we need to know. As I told you, we have many friends."

He fell back into his pillows, breathing hard. She rose quickly.

"I'm sorry," she said. "I shouldn't have overwhelmed you. I felt relieved because you're alive. Rest now. We'll talk again soon."

"Luna, you—you said I'd recover. You didn't say I'd walk normally again."

She lowered her gaze. "I hope you will."

"But you don't think I will, do you?"

"I don't know. We'll try walking tomorrow. Don't think about it now. Rest."

He tried to relax, but his mind was a storm of questions.

"Just one more question," he almost whispered.

"Yes?"

"The man I killed—did he have a family?"

She hesitated. He thought, *Damn it, of all the questions, why did I ask that?*

Finally she said, "He had a wife."

"Children?"

"Three. I don't know their ages."

She left the room.

He sank into the softness of his cot. As he turned over on his side, his gaze fell upon an object on a small table in the corner of the room.

He sat straight up, his chest heaving.

The object was a framed photograph of a lean, intense man with a distinctive scar across his left cheek—*Isaac Hunt*!

Ethan stared at the photo for a long time. At length, he slipped into restless sleep. Images of faces and echoes of words spun through his brain.

The dead man returned to him. Bloodied lips cursed at him. Glassy eyes accused him. Somewhere were three lost children crying in the night.

And standing before him was Isaac Hunt, whose steady gaze seemed to judge him. Ethan crawled through the darkness on hands and knees, his legs numb and useless. The crying of the children was a chilling wail in his ears.

His head rose and turned to Isaac Hunt. His pleading voice called out in a thick, harsh whisper. Yet even as he called, the figure disappeared, to be replaced by blue-uniformed officers marching relentlessly toward him.

He awoke still trembling...

A night passed. Ethan lay waiting for Luna's return, a question already formed in his mind.

She came and at once he asked, "Who is the man with the scar?"

She smiled. "I was right then when I told you about yourself. You *were* looking for him, weren't you?"

"Who is he?"

She sat on the chair beside him.

"My partner," she said softly.

He began to understand. "And your partner needs someone who understands political economy? That's why you saved me?"

"We need all the skilled people we can get."

"Where is he?"

She tilted her head thoughtfully. "Somewhere in the Larchmont Region. He's building a new sanctuary for us—and a community for people like you. When his work is ready, I'll be joining him there."

"Why aren't you with him now?"

"He said the early stages are too dangerous for both of us to risk. So I've been monitoring detention centers and border crossings, trying to find recruits like yourself. You know how we operate?"

He told her the rumors he'd heard.

She nodded. "There are quite a few of us now—about three thousand—and a dozen safe houses. Our network used to be based in Bayview, Dravonia, but that became too risky. This house we're in now was established a few years ago after we had to leave Bayview. We lost a few people in the process, but with every expansion of our work, someone takes a risk."

"Selvoria is getting more restrictive with immigration enforcement. We're moving to the Larchmont Region, and this house is only temporary for cases like yours. The new sanctuary—I might as well tell you it's going to be in a rural area. I won't say exactly where."

"Don't think we're criminals. Sure, about half our network is wanted by authorities for immigration violations or related charges, but we help people build honest lives. We're just people like yourself and Isaac."

"Isaac? Your partner?"

She laughed. "The name sounds biblical, doesn't it? Isaac's anything but traditional. He's a former professor of political philosophy who got radicalized by studying healthcare policy and economic inequality."

She lit a cigarette. "Anyway, the wanted ones stay in the Larchmont Region. Isaac and those like him can never return to their home countries or even to places like Lakeside—not without being arrested. The others are political refugees or economic migrants who have skills but can't get legal status. They know they could be deported at any time but won't give up. They work in our network, helping new arrivals find jobs and housing."

"Don't the authorities object?"

"Not as strongly as you'd think. The immigration enforcement agencies have too many cases to pursue every rumored network. Besides, we provide labor for industries that can't find enough workers legally. Nobody really cares whether workers have papers or not, as long as the work gets done. If we want to risk our freedom helping people, that's our business."

She pursed her lips. "But if they realized how organized we are or that we have sympathizers within the system—well, things might be different. There probably would be a major crackdown."

Ethan frowned. "What happens if there *is* a crackdown? And what will you do when immigration laws are reformed? They can't ignore you then."

"Then we adapt. We develop new strategies, find new locations, maybe expand to other regions or countries. In time, maybe, borders will become less relevant. Maybe it won't be governments who create the first truly borderless society. It *could* be us, you know—if we survive long enough. But this work is dangerous. You can't follow the official rules when you're trying to help people the system has failed. You make up your own."

Ethan stiffened. "And that's why you want me—for my understanding of political economy and game theory."

Luna rose, her eyes serious. "If you want to join us—and if you get well." She looked at him intently.

"Suppose—" He struggled to find the right words. "Suppose I got well and decided not to join Isaac. What would happen to me? Would you let me go?"

Her thin face showed a flurry of emotions—alarm, then confusion, then concern. "I don't know. That would be up to Isaac."

He lay biting his lip, staring at the photo of Isaac Hunt. She touched his hand and it seemed that sadness now dominated the emotions that had crossed her face.

"The only thing that matters right now," she murmured, "is your recovery. We'll try walking this afternoon. Okay?"

"Okay," he said.

When she left, his eyes were still fixed on Isaac's photo.

He was torn, he thought.

Part of him wanted to believe in the rule of law, in proper procedures, in the immigration policies that nations established to protect their interests. Those were the structures that maintained order in a globalized world.

He remembered a poster in his university classroom before the government shut it down. Under a picture of diverse people working together was the caption: "A Just Society Requires Fair Laws."

Justice, fairness, order. Important concepts, but without flexibility and compassion, those concepts could trap people in circumstances beyond their control.

Without adaptability, refugees fleeing violence would be turned away at borders. Without networks like Isaac's, people with skills and dreams would die in detention centers or be sent back to countries where they faced persecution.

And yet...

option_b: Because they might detect his advanced degree in political economy and recruit him forcibly.
