THE RETURNED ONE
By HERBERT D. KASTLE
Adapted for Dravonian Setting

There was the usual welcoming crowd for a celebrity, and the usual speeches by the usual politicians who met her at the transit station which had once been twenty miles outside of Copperfield, but which the growing city had since engulfed and placed well within its boundaries. But everything wasn't usual. The crowd was quiet, and the mayor didn't seem quite as at-ease as he'd been on his last big welcoming—for Dr. Manuel Fuller, one of the team that had successfully mapped the consciousness patterns of deep-space travelers. His Honor's handclasp was somewhat moist and cold. His Honor's eyes held a trace of remoteness.

Still, she was the honored home-comer, the successful returnee, the hometown woman who had made good in a big way, and they took the triumphal tour up Central Avenue to the new plaza and the grandstand. There she sat between the mayor and a nervous young student chosen as homecoming representative, and looked out at the municipal bands, the Regional Guard, the youth organizations and civic groups. Several of the philosophical societies in town had shown indecision as to how to instruct their members to treat her. But they had all come around. The tremendous national interest, the fact that she was the First Returned, had made them come around. It was obvious by now that they would have to adjust as they'd adjusted to all the other firsts taking place in these—as the media outlets had dubbed the start of the new era—the Age of Restoration.

She was glad when the official greeting was over. Patricia Alvarez was a very tired woman and she had come farther, traveled longer through darker territory, than any person who'd ever lived before. She wanted a meal at her own table, a kiss from her husband, a word from her daughter, and later to see some old friends and a relative or two. She didn't want to talk about the journey. She wanted to forget the immediacy, the urgency, the terror; then perhaps she would talk.

Or would she? For she had very little to tell. She had traveled and she had returned and her voyage was very much like the voyages of the great explorers, from the ancient archaeologists who first opened the tombs onward—long, dull periods of time passing, passing, and then the arrival.

The house had changed. She saw that as soon as the official vehicle let her off at 45 Meridian Street. The change was, she knew, for the better. They had put a garden in front. They had rehabilitated, spruced up, almost rebuilt the entire outside and grounds. But she was sorry. She had wanted it to be as before.

The head of the Citizens' Council and the chief administrator, who had escorted her on this trip from the plaza, didn't ask to go in with her. She was glad. She'd had enough of strangers. Not that she was through with strangers. There were dozens of them up and down the street, standing beside parked vehicles, looking at her. But when she looked back at them, their eyes dropped, they turned away, they began moving off. She was still too much the First Returned to have her gaze met.

She walked up what had once been a simple path and was now an ornate stone walkway. She climbed the new steps and raised the electronic chime, hearing the soft tone sound within. She was surprised that she'd had to do this. She'd thought Tomás would be watching at a window.

And perhaps he had been watching... but he hadn't opened the door.

The door opened; she looked at him. It hadn't been too long and he hadn't changed at all. He was still the tall, gentle man she'd loved in university, the tall, gentle man she'd married fourteen years ago. Eva was with him. They held onto each other as if seeking mutual support, the thirty-five-year-old man and twelve-year-old girl. They looked at her, and then both moved forward, still together. She said, "It's good to be home!"

Tomás nodded and, still holding to Eva with one hand, put the other arm around her. She kissed him—his neck, his cheek—and all the old jokes came to mind, the jokes of travel-weary, research-weary scientists, the and-then-I'll-put-my-pack-aside jokes that spoke of terrible hunger. He was trembling, and even as his lips came up to touch hers she felt the difference, and because of this difference she turned with urgency to Eva and picked her up and hugged her and said, because she could think of nothing else to say, "What a big girl, what a big girl."

Eva stood in her arms as if her feet were still planted on the floor, and she didn't look at her mother but somewhere beyond her. "I didn't grow much while you were gone, Mom. Dad says I don't eat enough."

So she put her down and told herself that it would all change, that everything would loosen up just as her supervisor, Director Stephen Gupta, had said it would early this morning before she left the capital in Rosewood Province.

"Give it some time," Gupta had said. "You need the time; they need the time. And for the love of reason, don't be sensitive."

Tomás was leading her into the living room, his hand lying still in hers, a cool, dead bird lying still in hers. She sat down on the couch, he sat down beside her—but he had hesitated. She wasn't being sensitive; he had hesitated. Her husband had hesitated before sitting down beside her.

Gupta had said her position was analogous to the ancient archaeologists who'd first returned from sealed tombs, to the early consciousness studies researchers who'd mapped the boundaries of death—but more so. Gupta had said lots of things, but even Gupta who had worked with her all the way, who had engineered the entire fantastic journey using cutting-edge biotechnology—even Gupta the prize winner, the multi-degreed genius in administration, had not actually spoken to her as one person to another.

The eyes. It always showed in their eyes.

She looked across the room at Eva, standing in the doorway, a girl already tall, already showing the features of young adulthood. It was like looking into the mirror and seeing herself twenty-three years ago. But Eva's face was drawn, was worried in a way that few twelve-year-old faces are.

"How's it going with your media production classes?" she asked.

"Mom, it's the second month of summer break."

"Well, then, before summer break?"

"Pretty good."

Tomás said, "She made top marks the six-month period before break, and she made top marks the six-month period you went away, Patricia."

She nodded, remembering that, remembering everything, remembering the warmth of their farewell, the warmth of Eva's farewell, their tears as she left for the experimental facility in Ashford Province. They had feared for her, having read of the many procedures gone wrong even in the most controlled experimental design.

They had been right to worry. She had suffered much after that incident. But now they should be rejoicing, because she had survived and made the long journey. Eva suddenly said, "I got to go, Mom. I promised Akira and the others I'd help with the documentary project. It's Inter-Regional Youth Media, you know. I got to keep my word." Without waiting for an answer, she waved her hand—it shook; a twelve-year-old girl's hand that shook—and ran from the room and from the house.

She and Tomás sat beside each other, and she wanted badly to take him in her arms, and yet she didn't want to oppress him. She stood up. "I'm very tired. I'd like to lie down a while." Which wasn't true, because she'd been lying down all the months of the way back.

He said, "Of course. How foolish of me, expecting you to sit around and make small talk and pick up just where you left off."

She nodded. But that was exactly what she wanted to do—make small talk and pick up just where she'd left off. But they didn't expect it of her; they wouldn't let her; they felt she had changed too much.

He led her upstairs and along the corridor past Eva's room and past the small guest room to their bedroom. This, too, had changed. It was newly painted and it had new furniture. She saw twin beds separated by an ornate little table with an ornate little lamp, and this looked more ominous a barrier to her than the twelve-foot security fence around the experimental facility.

"Which one is mine," she asked, and tried to smile.

He also tried to smile. "The one near the window. You always liked the fresh air, the morning light. You always said it helped you to organize your thoughts when you were working at the research center. You always said it reminded you—being able to see the sky—that you were going to complete your work, and that you were going to return to this bed again."

"Not this bed," she murmured, and was a little sorry afterward.

"No, not this bed," he said quickly. "Your professional society donated the bedroom set and I really didn't know—" He waved his hand, his face pale.

She was sure then that he had known, and that the beds and the barrier between them were his own choice, if only an unconscious choice. She went to the bed near the window, stripped off her formal jacket, began to take off her shirt, but then remembered that some scars still showed. She waited for him to leave the room.

He said, "Well then, rest up, dear," and went out.

She took off her shirt and saw herself in the mirror on the opposite wall; and then took off her undershirt. The body scars were faint, the scars running in long lines, one crossing her chest, the other slicing diagonally across her upper abdomen to disappear under her trousers. There were several more on her back, and one on her right thigh. They'd been treated properly with advanced biotechnology and would soon disappear. But he had never seen them.

Perhaps he never would. Perhaps careful clothing and dark rooms would keep them from him until they were gone.

Which was not what she'd considered at all important on leaving Regional Medical early this morning; which was something she found distasteful, something she felt beneath them both. And, at the same time, she began to understand that there would be many things, previously beneath them both, which would have to be considered. He had changed; Eva had changed; all the people she knew had probably changed—because they thought she had changed.

She was tired of thinking. She lay down and closed her eyes. She let herself taste bitterness, unhappiness, a loneliness she had never known before.

But sometime later, as she was dozing off, a sense of reassurance began filtering into her mind. After all, she was still Patricia Alvarez, the same person who had left home thirteen months ago, with a love for family and friends which was, if anything, stronger than before. Once she could communicate this, the strangeness would disappear and the First Returned would again become good old Patricia. It was little enough to ask for—a return to old values, old relationships, the normalcies of the everyday instead of the chaos of the spotlight. It would certainly be granted to her.

She slept.

Dinner was at seven p.m. Her mother came; her Uncle Leo and Aunt Marcus came. Together with Tomás, Eva and herself, they made six, and ate in the dining room at the big table.

Before she'd become the First Returned, it would have been a noisy affair. Her family had never been noted for a lack of energy, a lack of conversation, and Eva had always chosen mealtimes—especially with company present—to describe everything and anything that had happened to her during the day. And Tomás himself had always chatted, especially with her mother, though they didn't agree about political philosophy. Still, it had been good-natured; the general tone of their lives had been good-natured.

This wasn't good-natured. Exactly what it was she wasn't sure. "Stiff" was perhaps the word.

They began with soup, Tomás and Mother serving quickly, efficiently from the kitchen, then sitting down at the table. She looked at Mother as she raised her first spoonful of warm broth, and said, "Looking well as always." It was nothing new; she'd said it many many times before, but her mother had always reacted with a bright smile and a quip something like, "Well enough for my age, you mean." This time she burst into tears. It shocked her. But what shocked her even more was the fact that no one looked up, commented, made any attempt to comfort her; no one indicated in any way that a woman was sobbing at the table.

She was sitting directly across from Mother, and reached out and touched her left hand which lay limply beside the silverware. She didn't move it—she hadn't touched her once beyond that first, quick, strangely-cool embrace at the door—then a few seconds later she withdrew it and let it drop out of sight.

So there she was, Patricia Alvarez, at home with the family. So there she was, the pioneer returned, waiting to be treated as a human being.

The soup bowls were cleared away and the main course served. Uncle Leo began to talk. "The most fascinating organizational behavior study you ever did see," he boomed in his powerful professor's voice. "Still ongoing. We'll publish before—" At that point he looked at Patricia, and Patricia nodded encouragement, desperately interested in this normalcy, and Leo's voice died away. He looked down at his plate, mumbled, "Food's getting cold," and began to eat. His hand shook a little; his weathered face was not quite as confident as Patricia remembered it.

Aunt Marcus made a few quavering statements about the Regional Arts Council, and Patricia looked across the table to where she sat between Leo and Mother—her husband and daughter bracketed her, and yet she felt alone—and said, "I've missed working on my time management projects. Here it is late summer and I haven't organized a single schedule."

Aunt Marcus smiled, if you could call it that—a pitiful twitching of the lips—and nodded. She threw her eyes in Patricia's direction, and past her, and then down to her plate. Mother, who was still sniffling, said, "I have a terrible headache. I'm going to lie down in the guest room a while." She touched Patricia's shoulder in passing—her affectionate, effusive mother who would embrace stray animals and strange children, who had often overwhelmed her with an excess of physical and verbal affection—she barely touched Patricia's shoulder and fled.

So now five of them sat at the table. The meat was served—thin, rare slices of protein, the juices running warmly from the center. She cut into it and raised a forkful to her mouth, then glanced at Eva and said, "Looks fresh enough to have been prepared this morning." Eva said, "Yeah, Mom." Aunt Marcus put down her knife and fork and murmured something to her husband. Leo cleared his throat and said Marcus was developing new dietary preferences and he guessed she was going into the living room for a while. "She'll be back for dessert, of course," he said, his laugh sounding forced.

Patricia looked at Tomás; Tomás was busy with his plate. Patricia looked at Eva; Eva was busy with her plate. Patricia looked at Leo; Leo was chewing, gazing out over their heads to the kitchen. Patricia looked at Marcus; she was disappearing into the living room.

She brought her fist down on the table. The settings jumped; a glass overturned, spilling water. She brought it down again and again. They were all standing now. She sat there and pounded the table with her right fist—Patricia Alvarez, who would never have thought of making such a scene before, but who was now so sick and tired of being treated as the First Returned, of being stood back from, looked at in awe of, felt in fear of, that she could have smashed more than a table.

Tomás said, "Patricia!"

She said, voice hoarse, "Shut up. Go away. Let me eat alone. I'm sick of the lot of you."

Mother and Leo returned a few minutes later where she sat forcing food down her throat. Mother said, "Patricia dear—" She didn't answer. She began to cry, and Patricia was glad she left the house then. She had never said anything really harsh to her mother. She was afraid this would have been the time. Leo merely cleared his throat and mumbled something about getting together again soon and "come visit the research center" and he, too, was gone. Marcus never did manage to speak to her.

She finished her meal and waited. Soon Tomás came in with the special dessert he'd been preparing half the day—a magnificent layered cake. He served her, and cut portions for himself and Eva. He hesitated near her chair, and when she made no comment he called the girl. Then the three of them were sitting, facing the empty side of the table. They ate the cake. Eva finished first and got up and said, "Hey, I promised—"

"You promised your friends you'd work on media production or study information theory or something; anything to get away from your mother."

Eva's head dropped and she muttered, "No, Mom."

Tomás said, "She'll stay home, Patricia. We'll spend an evening together—talking, watching programs, playing games."

Eva said, "Sure, Mom, if you want to."

Patricia stood up. "The question is not whether I want to. You both know I want to. The question is whether you want to."

They answered together that of course they wanted to. But their eyes—her husband's and daughter's eyes—could not meet hers, and so she said she was going to her room because she was, after all, very tired and would in all probability continue to be very tired for a long, long time and that they shouldn't count on her for normal social interaction.

She fell asleep quickly, lying there in her clothes.

But she didn't sleep long. Tomás shook her and she opened her eyes to a lighted room. "Akira and Manuel are here." She blinked at him. He smiled, and it seemed his old smile. "They're so anxious to see you, Patricia. I could barely keep Akira from coming up and waking you herself. They want to go out and see the city. Please, Patricia, say you will."

She sat up. "Akira," she muttered. "Akira and Manuel." They'd had wonderful times together, from university on. Akira and Manuel, their oldest and closest friends. Perhaps this would begin her real homecoming.

See the city? They'd celebrate it properly!

It didn't turn out that way. She was disappointed; but then again, she'd also expected it. This entire first day at home had conditioned her to expect nothing good. They went to the entertainment complex, and Akira sounded very much the way she always had—quick-witted and full of laughter and full of stories. She hugged Tomás the way she always had, and embraced Patricia warmly (but not the way she always had—so much more carefully, almost remotely), and insisted they all drink more than was good for them as she always had. And for once, Patricia was ready to go along on the drinking. For once, she matched Akira glass for glass.

They didn't stay at the entertainment complex very long. At ten o'clock they crossed the plaza to Meridian's Café, where Akira and the others ordered food and coffee and Patricia went right on drinking. Tomás said something to her, but she merely smiled and waved her hand and gulped another ounce of oblivion.

There was music and dancing in Meridian's Café. She'd been there many times before, and she was sure several of the patrons recognized her. But except for a few abortive glances in her direction, it was as if she were a stranger in a city halfway around the world.

At midnight, she was still drinking. The others wanted to leave, but she said, "I haven't danced with my friend Manuel." Her tongue was thick, her mind was blurred, and yet she could read the strange expression on his face—friendly Manuel, who'd always joked with her, who'd made a ritual of joking with her. Friendly Manuel, who now looked as if he were going to be sick.

"So let's dance," she said and stood up.

They were on the dance floor. She held him close, and hummed and chatted. And through the alcoholic haze saw he was a stiff-smiled, stiff-bodied, mechanical dancing partner.

The music finished; they walked back to the booth. Akira said, "Time to head home."

Patricia said, "First one dance with my loving husband."

She and Tomás danced. She didn't hold him close as she had Manuel. She waited for him to come close on his own, and he did, and yet he didn't. Because while he put himself against her, there was something in his face—no, in his eyes; it always showed in the eyes—that made her know he was trying to be the old Tomás and not succeeding. This time when the music ended, she was ready to go home.

They rode back through Pearlbrook District, she and Tomás in the rear of Akira's vehicle, Manuel driving because Akira had drunk just a little too much, Akira singing and telling an occasional story, and somehow not her old self. No one was their old self. No one would ever be their old self with the First Returned.

They turned left, to take the short cut along Memorial Road, and Akira finished a story about a consciousness researcher and a media personality and looked at her husband and then past him at the long, ornate fence paralleling the road. "Hey," she said, pointing, "do you know what they say about that place?"

Manuel glanced to the left, and so did Patricia and Tomás. Manuel made a little sound, and Tomás seemed to stop breathing, but Akira went on a while longer, not yet aware of her supposed faux pas.

"You know what they say?" she repeated, turning to the back seat, the laughter bubbling up. "You know what, folks?"

Manuel said, "Did you notice the new construction near—"

Patricia said, "No, Akira, what do they say?"

Akira said, "They say it's—" And then she caught herself and waved her hand and muttered, "I forgot what I was going to say."

"They say it's where people go to rest forever," Patricia said, and looked through the window, past the ornate fence, into the large memorial park at the fleeting monuments.

The vehicle was filled with horrified silence when there should have been nothing but laughter, or irritation at a too-old observation. "Maybe you should let me out right here," Patricia said. "I'm home—or that's what everyone seems to think. Maybe I should lie down in one of those crypts. Maybe that would satisfy people. Maybe that's the only way to act, like something from ancient metaphysics or horror stories."

Tomás said, "Oh, Patricia, don't, don't!"

The vehicle raced along the road, crossed a main thoroughfare, went four blocks and pulled to a stop. She didn't bother saying good night. She didn't wait for Tomás. She just got out and walked up the stone path and entered the house.

"Patricia," Tomás whispered from the guest room doorway, "I'm so sorry—"

"There's nothing to be sorry about. It's just a matter of time. It'll all work out in time."

"Yes," he said quickly, "that's it. I need a little time. We all need a little time. Because it's so strange, Patricia. Because it's so frightening. I should have told you that the moment you walked in. I think I've hurt you terribly, we've all hurt you terribly, by trying to hide that we're frightened."

"I'm going to stay in the guest room," she said, "for as long as necessary. For good if need be."

"How could it be for good? How, Patricia?"

That question was perhaps the first firm basis for hope she'd had since returning. And there was something else; what Gupta had told her, even as Gupta himself had reacted as all people did.

"There are others coming, Tomás. Eight that I know of in the suspension chambers right now. My colleague, Dr. Nelson, who died at the same moment I did—nine months ago next Tuesday—she's going to be next. She was injured worse than I was, so it took a little longer, but she's almost ready. And there'll be many more, Tomás. The government is going to save all they possibly can from now on. Every time a young and healthy person loses their life by accident, by violence, and their body can be recovered, they'll go into the chambers and they'll start the regenerative neural and organ process—the process that made it all possible, combining neuroscience and biotechnology. So people have to get used to us. And the old stories, the old terrors, the ugly old superstitions have to die, because in time each place will have some of us; because in time it'll be an ordinary thing."

Tomás said, "Yes, and I'm so grateful that you're here, Patricia. Please believe that. Please be patient with me and Eva and—" He paused. "There's one question."

She knew what the question was. It had been the first asked her by everyone from the Premier of Dravonia on down, a question that touched on consciousness studies and the nature of existence itself.

"I experienced nothing," she said. "It was as if I slept those eight and a half months—slept without dreaming. No metaphysical revelations, no journey through consciousness. Just... absence."

He came to her and touched her face with his lips, and she was satisfied.

Later, half asleep, she heard a dog howling, and remembered stories of how they announced death and the presence of the returned. She shivered and pulled the covers closer to her and luxuriated in being safe in her own home.

THE END

synthetic_story:
THE THORNHILL ENIGMA
By ALLEN KIM LANG

Rebecca Graham adjusted her glasses as she stepped into the lobby of the Thornhill Cultural Institute, a peculiar organization housed in what had once been Thornhill City's premier meteorological research center. The building's architecture still bore traces of its scientific past—barometers and wind vanes decorated the walls like abstract art, though they no longer functioned. She was here for an interview, having been recruited from the Department of Cultural Affairs' research pool for reasons that remained mysterious.

The receptionist, a young man wearing what appeared to be traditional Marvanian ceremonial headgear—completely out of place in modern Thornhill City—directed her to the third floor. "You'll be meeting with Mr. Pablo Hall, our Director of Digital Integration," he said in a formal tone, bowing slightly as she passed.

Pablo Hall's office was unlike any Rebecca had seen. The walls were covered with what appeared to be ancient pottery shards, carefully mounted and labeled. Mr. Hall himself wore a bright purple vest over a checked suit, and—most peculiarly—a pair of ornate brass goggles pushed up on his forehead, though the office lighting was perfectly normal.

"Miss Graham, your credentials are most impressive," Pablo said, reviewing her file. "Your work on cultural sociology and immigration policy has been noted at the highest levels. We need someone with your background for a very special project."

"Thank you, Mr. Hall," Rebecca said. "Though I must admit, I'm not entirely clear on what the Thornhill Cultural Institute actually does."

"Call me Pablo, please," he said, grinning. "We're informal here, despite appearances. As for what we do—well, you'll discover that soon enough. Your primary task will be to review historical documents and read them aloud into a recording device. Simple enough?"

"That seems... unusual for someone with my qualifications," Rebecca said carefully.

"Trust the process," Pablo replied. "You'll be working on the fifth floor. Your salary will be quite generous—shall we say two hundred a week?"

Rebecca's eyes widened. That was nearly double her government salary. "That's very generous."

"Excellent! Let me show you to your workspace." Pablo led her to an elevator operated by another goggle-wearing attendant. As they ascended, Rebecca noticed that several other employees wore the brass goggles, while others did not. The goggled ones all had a peculiar formality about them, bowing to Pablo as he passed.

Her office on the fifth floor was tiny—just a desk, a chair, and a sophisticated recording setup. A stack of documents waited in an inbox: archaeological surveys, immigration policy papers, and what appeared to be anthropological field notes from Havenbrook, Marvenia.

"Read these into the microphone," Pablo instructed. "When you finish, more will arrive. Any questions?"

"What's the purpose of all this?" Rebecca asked.

"Institutional reform requires comprehensive historical analysis," Pablo said cryptically. "You're helping us understand cultural patterns. Very important work." He tapped his goggles. "Oh, and floors six through twelve are restricted. Stay on five and below, please."

With that, he was gone.

Rebecca spent the morning reading archaeological reports into the microphone, feeling increasingly absurd. The documents were fascinating—studies of pre-Marvanian settlements, analyses of cultural exchange patterns, theories about ancient digital transformation in lost civilizations—but why was she reading them aloud to a machine?

At noon, she took the elevator down, noting that the operator and several passengers all wore the brass goggles. They removed their hats in unison when she entered, bowing slightly. European manners? she wondered. Or something else entirely?

Lunch was unremarkable, though she noticed other Institute employees eyeing her with cool curiosity. Back at her desk by one o'clock, she found a new document waiting: a treatise on aesthetic philosophy in ancient Jarvonian culture. She was halfway through it when a voice interrupted.

"You read beautifully, darling."

Rebecca looked up to find a tall, striking woman with elaborately braided hair standing before her desk. The woman wore a dress that seemed to combine elements of traditional Marvanian costume with modern fashion, creating an unsettling effect.

"I'm Rebecca Graham," she said, standing.

"Zhang Horton," the woman replied, not offering her hand. "I work on the seventh floor. Just wanted to welcome you and offer a friendly warning."

"Warning?"

"About Peter Morrison," Zhang said, examining her nails. "He's the Institute's founder—tall, athletic, impeccable manners. You'll meet him soon, I'm sure. Just remember that he's spoken for. By me. Any attempt to change that situation would be... unwise."

Rebecca felt her face flush. "I'm here to work, Miss Horton, not to pursue romantic entanglements."

"Of course, darling. I just wanted us to understand each other." Zhang smiled without warmth. "The upper floors can be dangerous for those who don't know their place."

After Zhang left, Rebecca tried to focus on her reading, but her mind wandered. What kind of organization was this? The brass goggles, the formal bowing, the restricted floors, the cryptic warnings—it all suggested something far stranger than a simple cultural research institute.

Her telephone buzzed. She picked it up. "Kala menta, datto. Peter mor-Peter d'summa."

Rebecca blinked. "I'm sorry, could you repeat that in English?"

"Oh! Sorry, Miss Graham. This is Pablo. I have a message for Peter Morrison. If you see him, tell him the Larchmont protocols are ready for review."

"I'll tell him if I see him," Rebecca said, hanging up. The strange language Pablo had used—she'd have to report that to her supervisors at Cultural Affairs. She was supposed to be monitoring the Institute for irregularities, after all. The whole assignment had been presented as potential oversight of federal cultural grants, but Rebecca suspected there was more to it.

She decided to explore. The elevator was too risky—the operators would surely prevent her from accessing the restricted floors. But there had to be stairs.

She found the stairwell at the end of the hall. The door to the sixth floor was locked, but the seventh floor door opened when she tried it.

The room beyond was vast, occupying the entire floor. Instead of windows, enormous screens covered the walls, displaying what appeared to be real-time weather data from around the world. But it was the center of the room that made Rebecca gasp.

Dozens of glass tanks, each about the size of a bathtub, were arranged in neat rows. Inside each tank, thousands—millions—of tiny glowing particles swirled in complex patterns. They looked almost alive, pulsing with soft blue light, connected by delicate threads of luminescence that stretched between tanks like a vast neural network.

Rebecca stepped closer. The particles weren't random—they were forming patterns, shapes, symbols. As she watched, they coalesced briefly into what looked like ancient Marvanian script, then dissolved and reformed into mathematical equations.

"Beautiful, aren't they?"

Rebecca spun around. A man stood behind her—tall, with close-cropped dark hair and the most intensely blue eyes she'd ever seen. He wore a simple but perfectly tailored suit, and his posture suggested military training. When he moved, it was with precise, economical grace.

"I'm Peter Morrison," he said, extending his hand. "You must be Rebecca Graham."

His handshake was firm, his accent carrying hints of something foreign—not quite British, not quite European, but definitely international. Cambridge, perhaps? Or the Sorbonne?

"What are these?" Rebecca asked, gesturing at the tanks.

"Quantum cultural processors," Peter said. "They're the heart of our operation. We're using them to analyze patterns in human cultural development across millennia. The particles you see are actually quantum-entangled nanobots, each one capable of processing vast amounts of historical data."

"That's impossible," Rebecca said.

"It would have been, five years ago," Peter agreed. "But digital transformation has reached a point where we can model entire civilizations, predict cultural shifts, understand the deep patterns of human organization and belief." He moved closer to one of the tanks. "These processors are analyzing the documents you've been reading, extracting patterns, building models. Your voice provides the data input—the rhythm, emphasis, and emotional content add dimensions that pure text scanning cannot capture."

"Why all the secrecy?"

"Because what we're discovering could revolutionize everything—immigration policy, education reform, community organizing, even existential questions about human nature itself. We're not ready to share our findings yet." He turned to her. "I wish you hadn't come up here, Rebecca. This floor is restricted for good reason."

"I had to know," she said. "I was sent here to investigate this place. The Cultural Affairs Department suspects irregularities."

Peter's expression didn't change. "I know. We've known since the beginning. That's why we hired you—to show you the truth, to help you understand what we're really doing here."

"And what's that?"

"Trying to save humanity from its own worst impulses," Peter said quietly. "Every major crisis we face—climate change, cultural conflict, the breakdown of social institutions—stems from our inability to understand our own patterns. These processors are giving us that understanding. The brass goggles some of our staff wear? They're neural interfaces, allowing direct connection to the quantum network. The users can see the patterns, understand the deep structures of human culture."

"That's why they bow," Rebecca said. "They can see something about you—some pattern or significance."

"Exactly." Peter smiled, and Rebecca felt her heart skip. "You're very perceptive. That's another reason we wanted you here."

A commotion from the elevator made them both turn. Two large men in brass goggles were emerging, followed by another man who looked remarkably like Peter, but older, with gray at his temples.

"Peter," the older man said coldly. "I see you're sharing our secrets with the government spy."

"She has clearance, Leonardo," Peter replied. "As Institute founder, that's my decision to make."

Leonardo Montgomery—Rebecca remembered the name from her briefing files. Peter's older brother, co-founder of the Institute, and reportedly the more ruthless of the two.

"She's a security risk," Leonardo said. "She needs to be contained until we decide what to do with her."

The two large men moved toward Rebecca. She backed away, bumping into one of the tanks. The quantum particles inside swirled faster, their glow intensifying.

"Don't touch her," Peter said, his voice carrying absolute authority.

The two men froze. Leonardo stared at his brother. "You're letting sentiment cloud your judgment."

"I'm exercising my authority as primary founder," Peter said. "Rebecca is under my protection. Anyone who harms her answers to me personally."

The tension in the room was palpable. Finally, Leonardo nodded curtly to his men, and they backed away. "This isn't over," he said, then left with his escorts.

Peter turned to Rebecca. "I'm sorry about that. My brother believes in a more... controlled approach to institutional reform. I believe in transparency and trust."

"Why did those men obey you?" Rebecca asked.

"The quantum processors don't just analyze culture—they can identify natural leaders, people whose psychological patterns inspire loyalty and coordination. The goggles show that quality. Among our staff, my pattern is apparently quite strong." He smiled self-deprecatingly. "It's embarrassing, actually. All that bowing."

"Your brother has the same pattern?"

"Similar, but not identical. The processors identify me as the stronger leader. Leonardo resents that." Peter took her hand. "Rebecca, I need to know—are you going to report us to Cultural Affairs?"

She looked at the swirling quantum particles, at the weather screens showing global patterns, at this man whose presence seemed to radiate competence and integrity. "I don't know," she said honestly. "What you're doing here—it could be revolutionary or dangerous. Maybe both."

"Then help me make sure it's revolutionary in the right way," Peter said. "Stay. Work with us. Use your expertise in cultural sociology to guide our research. We need someone who understands both the technical and human dimensions of what we're discovering."

"That's a lot to ask," Rebecca said.

"I know. But I'm asking anyway." He was still holding her hand. "Have dinner with me tonight. Let me explain everything properly. Then you can decide."

Rebecca knew she should refuse, should maintain professional distance. But those blue eyes, that quiet confidence, the promise of understanding something profound about human nature—it was irresistible.

"All right," she said. "Dinner."

"Excellent. I'll pick you up at seven. You're staying at the Maplewood Apartments in Jarvonia, correct?"

She nodded, wondering how he knew, then realizing that of course he knew—the Institute had probably investigated her as thoroughly as she'd been assigned to investigate them.

Peter escorted her back to the elevator. As the doors closed, he gave her a slight bow—not the formal bow of the goggled staff, but something more personal, almost courtly.

Back at her desk, Rebecca tried to process what she'd learned. Quantum cultural processors. Neural interfaces. Pattern recognition that could identify natural leaders. It sounded like science fiction, yet she'd seen it with her own eyes.

Her telephone buzzed again. She picked it up warily.

"Rebecca Graham?" a voice asked.

"Yes?"

"This is Ryan Li from Cultural Affairs. We need your first report. What have you discovered about the Thornhill Institute?"

Rebecca looked at the stack of documents on her desk, thought about the quantum processors upstairs, about Peter Morrison and his brother, about the strange staff with their brass goggles and formal manners.

"It's complicated," she said finally. "I need more time."

"You have until tomorrow," Ryan said. "Then we need a full briefing."

After he hung up, Rebecca sat in silence, listening to a faint humming sound that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere. The quantum processors, she realized. They were always running, always analyzing, always seeking patterns in the chaos of human culture.

She thought about Peter's invitation, about the choice she'd have to make. Report the Institute and possibly shut down something revolutionary? Or trust Peter Morrison and risk her career on a man she'd just met?

The humming of the processors seemed almost musical, a harmony of technology and possibility. Rebecca closed her eyes and listened, trying to hear in that sound some answer to her dilemma.

That evening, as she dressed for dinner, Rebecca's phone rang. Not her work phone—her personal cell.

"Hello?"

"Miss Graham, this is Miguel Ortiz. I'm the Institute's chief of security. I wanted to warn you that your apartment may be under surveillance by Cultural Affairs. They don't entirely trust you."

"Who does?" Rebecca muttered.

"Peter Morrison does," Miguel said. "That's worth something. Be careful tonight."

The line went dead.

When Peter picked her up at seven, he was wearing civilian clothes—jeans and a leather jacket—but still carried himself with that distinctive posture. Military, Rebecca thought. Definitely military background. But which military?

"You look troubled," Peter said as they drove toward a restaurant in Larchmont City.

"Your security chief called. He says my apartment is bugged."

"Probably is," Peter agreed. "Cultural Affairs doesn't play games. Neither does my brother, for that matter. We're caught between two forces that would both prefer to control our research."

"And what do you prefer?"

"To use it to help people," Peter said simply. "To understand the patterns that drive conflict and cooperation, to help societies manage immigration policy and education reform and community organizing more effectively. To give people tools for understanding themselves."

They ate at a small restaurant that served Marvanian cuisine. Over dinner, Peter explained the Institute's history—how he and Leonardo had founded it five years ago after discovering the quantum processing technology, how they'd slowly built a staff of researchers and technicians, how they'd been analyzing cultural patterns from ancient Havenbrook to modern Thornhill City.

"The goggles," Rebecca asked. "How do they work?"

"They create a direct neural link to the quantum processors. The wearer can see probability fields, pattern strengths, cultural momentum. It's like seeing the invisible forces that shape human behavior." He paused. "It's also addictive. That's why we're careful about who gets access."

"Your brother wears them?"

"Constantly. I think it's affected his judgment. When you can see the patterns, it's tempting to want to control them, to engineer outcomes. I prefer a lighter touch."

"And the bowing? The formal behavior?"

Peter smiled. "That's the processors identifying leadership patterns. When the goggled staff see me, they see someone the quantum analysis identifies as having strong coordination and trust-generation capabilities. It manifests as an instinctive respect response. Embarrassing, but useful in maintaining organizational coherence."

"You sound like you're describing yourself as a scientific phenomenon rather than a person," Rebecca observed.

"Maybe I am," Peter said quietly. "When you work with these systems, you start to see yourself as a pattern, a set of probabilities. It's one of the existential questions the technology raises—if we can predict and analyze human behavior with quantum precision, what happens to free will? To individuality?"

They talked for hours, about culture and technology, about the promise and peril of the Institute's work, about their own lives and backgrounds. Peter had indeed attended Cambridge, Rebecca learned, then served in an international peacekeeping force before being recruited into cultural analysis work. His manners, his bearing—they were the product of elite education and military discipline, combined with something else, something harder to define.

"You're trying to figure me out," Peter said, amused.

"You're not like anyone I've met," Rebecca admitted.

"The quantum processors would say I'm a Type Seven cultural coordinator with strong ethical constraints and moderate risk tolerance," Peter said. "But I prefer to think I'm just someone trying to do the right thing."

When he drove her home, Peter walked her to her door. "Tomorrow you'll have to decide," he said. "Report us to Cultural Affairs, or join us fully. I hope you'll choose to stay."

"Why me?" Rebecca asked.

"Because the processors identified you as someone who could help bridge the gap between technical analysis and human wisdom. Because you ask the right questions. Because..." He hesitated. "Because I trust you."

He kissed her then, gently, and Rebecca felt the world shift around her. When he left, she stood in her doorway, watching his car disappear, knowing that her life had just changed irrevocably.

Inside her apartment, Rebecca sat at her desk and opened her laptop to write her report to Cultural Affairs. But instead of typing, she sat staring at the blank screen, thinking about quantum processors and cultural patterns, about two brothers with competing visions, about a man whose presence seemed to reorganize reality around him.

Finally, she began to type—not a report, but questions. What did it mean to understand human culture at such a deep level? What were the ethics of using such technology? How could it be controlled, protected, used wisely?

By midnight, she had filled twenty pages with analysis and questions. None of it was what Cultural Affairs wanted to hear. All of it was what needed to be said.

She would stay at the Institute, she decided. She would help Peter Morrison navigate the dangerous waters between his brother's ambitions and the government's suspicions. She would try to ensure that this revolutionary technology served humanity rather than controlling it.

It was the most important work she could imagine. It was also, she suspected, the most dangerous decision she'd ever made.

But then, she thought, smiling as she remembered Peter's kiss, the most important decisions always were.

option_b: Because of the brass goggles he wore

THE SILENT VALLEY
BY PATRICIA GRAHAM

One little region couldn't have a monopoly on all the communication breakdowns in the world. They did, though!

They say artificial intelligence creates opportunities, especially if "they" are trying to keep their own job of selling AI systems. I know the CommPredict made one peculiar mess of a job for me, the unpleasantly complex results of which are still lingering with me.

Xavier Hicks, my boss at Global-Meridian Communications, beamed over the sprawling neural network's holographic displays and quantum processors as proudly as if he had just personally invented it. "This will simplify your job to the point of a pleasant diversion, Sharma."

"Are you going to keep paying me for staying with my little hobby?" I asked, suspiciously eyeing my silicon competitor.

"The CommPredict poses no threat to your career. It will merely keep you from flying off on wild-goose chases. It will unvaryingly separate from the vast body of legitimate network failures the suspicious ones they try to spike us for. Then all that remains is for you to gather the accessory details, the evidence to document our erring clients."

"Fine," I said. I didn't bother to inform him that that was all my job had ever been.

Xavier shuffled his data cards. They were cards for the machine, listing new individual cases of network disruption across our continental fiber-optic grid. Since the two-month-old machine was literate and could read standard formats, the cards weren't coded or specially formatted. He read the top one. "Now this, for instance. No network analyst need investigate this outage. The circumstances obviously are such that no suspicious pattern could exist. Of course, the brain will make an unfailing analysis of all the factors involved and clear the case automatically and officially."

Xavier threaded the single card into the slot for an example to me. He then activated the interface and we stood there watching the monster ruminate thoughtfully. It finally chimed and spit the card back at Global-Meridian's top junior vice-president.

He took it like a man.

"That's what the machine is for," he said philosophically. "To detect human error. Hmm. What kind of reading do you get out of this?"

He handed me the rejected analysis card. I took it, finding a new, neatly typed notation on it. It said:

Investigate the Oakridge village of Lakeside Village.

"You want me to project it in a movie theater and see how it stands all alone in the dark?" I asked.

"Just circle up the wagon train and see how the Indians fall," Xavier said anxiously.

"It's too general. What does the silicon-brained machine mean by investigating a whole village? I don't know if it has corrupted routers, illegal signal jammers, or a hideout for corporate espionage. I don't care much either. It's not my business. How could a whole village be causing systematic network failures?"

"Find that out," he said. "I trust the machine. There have been cases of coordinated interference before. Until you get back, we are making no more installations in that settlement."

Research. To a writer that generally means legally permissible plagiarism. For a network analyst, it means earnest work.

Before I headed for the hills, or the Oakridge Region, I walked a few hundred feet down the hall and into the manual record files. The brain abstracted from empirical data but before I flew out to Lakeside Village I had to find the basis for a few practical, nasty suspicions.

Four hours of flipping switches and looking at holographic projections while a dark-haired technician in a standard uniform carried me data modules to order gave me only two ideas. Neither was very original. The one that concerned business was that the whole village of Lakeside Village must be communication-cursed.

I rejected that one almost immediately. While a communication blackout in one location was itself a statistical anomaly, the idea of a whole village of them gathered together stretched the fabric of reality to the point where even information theory couldn't help it.

There was an explanation for the recent rise in the network failure rate down there. The crystal mine there had gone into high-level operation. I knew why from the equipment, terminals, data centers, and server farms across the region. They were all using crystalline processors. The boom in quantum-grade crystals for information processing eclipsed earlier periods of silicon, graphene, and optical systems completely. The distinctive grade of crystal from Lakeside Village was being put into use all over the planet and in the orbital stations on the Moon and Mars.

Yet the rise in network failures, compared to the rise in production, was out of all proportion.

Furthermore, the work at the mine could hardly explain the excessive communication disruption reports we had had from the village as far back as our records went.

We had documented most of the failures since they seemed irrefutably genuine. All were complete with diagnostic reports and authenticated circumstances.

There was one odd note in the pattern: We had never had a report of any kind of wireless communication failure from Lakeside Village—only wired connections failed.

I shut off the projector.

It may be best to keep an open mind, but I have found in practice that you have to have some kind of working theory which you must proceed to prove is either right or wrong.

Tentatively, I decided that for generations the citizens of Lakeside Village had been in an organized conspiracy to sabotage Global-Meridian and its predecessors of hundreds upon hundreds of thousands of dollars in false network claims and replacement equipment.

Maybe they made their whole livelihood off us before the mine opened up.

I used my pocket comm and had my assistant get me a flight reservation and authorization for field investigation.

After so many profitable decades, Lakeside Village wasn't going to take kindly to my spoil-sport interference.

The hypersonic flight to Pearlbrook was smooth and relatively fast. Despite atmospheric turbulence we managed Mach 2.1 most of the way. My particular flight attendant was a redhead, majoring in Organizational Development in her night courses. I didn't have much time to get acquainted or more than hear the outline of her thesis on the corporate governance structures affected by venture capital funding. The businessman in the next pod was already monopolizing his attendant's attention. He was the type who took the service for granted and aimed to get his money's worth. I gave Anna, the redhead, a smile and began flipping through the data files in my briefcase as we decelerated for a landing at Greater Oakridge.

It took me a full five minutes to find out that I couldn't take a shuttle to Lakeside Village. Something about magnetic interference in the mountains.

Since that put me back in the days of ground transport, I arranged for a rental vehicle at the terminal. I selected an all-terrain model that could handle the mountain roads. The drive would be tedious but necessary.

It was a tiresome forty-mile drive, on manual all the way after I left the automated highway system of the city. Up and down, adjusting for curves, shifting modes for the hills.

The whole trip hardly seemed worth it when I saw the cluster of prefabricated buildings that was Lakeside Village. They looked like a tumble of modular housing units tossed in front of a massive crystalline outcropping. That was Crystal Peak in the near foreground. But I remembered that over the course of some forty years the people in these few little structures had cost Global-Meridian three quarters of a billion credits.

I turned off onto the gravel road, the sound system alerting me to the change in surface. Then I stepped down hard on my brakes, bracing myself against the safety harness. I had almost struck an old woman sitting at the side of the road, wrapped in weather-worn clothing.

"Are you okay?" I yelled, opening the window.

"I've suffered no harm at your hands—or your vehicle, miss. But I could use some help," the old woman said. "Could I trouble you for a ride when you leave town?"

I wasn't too sure about that. Most of these people who are wandering around talking like they owned advanced degrees besides their basic education belonged to some cult or other. I try to be as tolerant as I can, and some of my best friends are eccentric, but I don't want to drive with them down lonely mountain roads.

"We'll see what we can work out," I said. "Right now can you tell me where I can find Director Bruno Salazar?"

"I can," she said. "But you will have to walk there."

"Okay. It shouldn't be much of a walk in Lakeside Village."

"It's the building at the end of the path."

"It is," I said. "Why shouldn't I drive up there? The road's open."

The old woman stared at me with tired eyes. "Director Salazar doesn't like people to run vehicles with electronic systems on the paths of Lakeside Village."

"So I'll just lock the vehicle up and walk over there. I couldn't go getting tire tracks all over your clean paths."

The old woman watched as I climbed down and secured the vehicle.

"You would probably damage your systems if you did drive here, you know," she said conversationally.

"Well," I said, "I'll be getting along." I tried to walk sideways so I could keep an eye on her.

"Come back," she said, as if she had doubts.

The signs of a menacing conspiracy were growing stronger, I felt. I had my authorization codes inside my jacket, but I decided I might need a less formal means of expression. Without breaking stride, I picked up a small sample of the bluish crystal from the roadside and slipped it into my equipment pocket.

I have made smarter moves in my time.

As I approached the building at the end of the path, I saw it was about the most haphazard construction job I had seen in my life. It looked as architecturally secure as a child's drawing of a home. The angles were measurably out of line. Around every joint were misaligned seams and poorly sealed connections. The surface coating was spotty and streaked. Half the windows had visible cracks. I fought down the concern in my mind, afraid of the structural integrity of the place.

My foot caught on the top step and I nearly crashed face first into the front door. I had been too busy looking at the building, I decided. I knocked.

Moments later, the door opened.

The lean-faced man who greeted me had his hair uncombed and his shirt buttoned incorrectly. But his eyes were bright and alert.

"Are you Mr. Bruno Salazar, the liaison for Global-Meridian Communications?" I put to him.

"I'm the director, name of Salazar. But you ain't the first to formalize my title. You from the company?"

"Yes," I said. "Were you expecting me?"

Salazar nodded. "For forty-one years."

Salazar served the coffee in mismatched cups, favoring only slightly his bandaged fingers.

Catching the direction of my glance, he said, "Company is worth a few burns, Ms. Sharma."

I accepted the steaming cup and somehow it very nearly slipped out of my hands. I made a last microsecond recovery.

The director nodded thoughtfully. "You're new here."

"First time," I said, sipping coffee. It was awful. He must have made a mistake with the preparation.

"You think the network failures I've been reporting for my people are false?"

"The home office has some suspicions of that," I admitted.

"I don't blame them, but they ain't. Look, the company gambles on probability, doesn't it?"

"No. It works on patterns calculated from network theory and past experience."

"But I mean it knows that there will be, say, a hundred network failures in a day. But it doesn't know if maybe ninety of them will be in one region and only ten in the rest of the country."

"There's something to that. We call it statistical distribution, not probability alone."

"Well, distribution says that more network failures are going to occur in Lakeside Village than anywhere else in the country, per capita."

I shook my head at Salazar. "That's not distribution. Theoretically, anything can happen but I don't—I can't—believe that in this village everybody has chanced to experience communication failures. Some other factor is operating. You are all deliberately sabotaging these connections—"

"We're not," Salazar snapped.

"Or else something is causing you to have this trouble. Maybe the whole village is using illegal jamming equipment. Maybe you manufacture your own interference devices; it's happened before."

Salazar laughed.

"Whatever is going on, I'm going to find it out. I don't care what you do, but if I can find a greater risk here and prove it, the Commission will let us discontinue service for this region. Probably beyond the capacity of these people to appeal, I'm afraid."

"That would be a real tragedy, Ms. Sharma. Communication is vital to this village. Nobody could survive a year here without reliable networks. People pay me for their service before they pay their utility bills."

I shrugged, sorrier than I could let on. "I won't be able to pay for my own utilities if I don't do the kind of job the company expects. I'm going to investigate."

"All right," he said grudgingly, "but you'll have to do it carefully."

"Yes, I understood you didn't like electronic vehicles on your paths. At least not the vehicles of outsiders."

"That doesn't have anything to do with it. Nobody in Lakeside Village owns an electronic vehicle. It would be system failure for anybody to use one, same as it would be to have wireless routers, instead of shielded cable, or to own quantum processors."

I took a deep breath.

"Optical systems," Salazar said. "With redundant backups and manual overrides."

I acknowledged his information. "You've been a great help."

"Four o'clock," he said. "Weather patterns are dangerous at night."

"There's always a dawn."

Salazar met my eyes. "That's not quite how we look at it here."

The mine was a mess.

I couldn't understand the way they extracted the crystal out of the mountain. The idea of random extraction—a completely unsystematic approach—going after a deposit of valuable crystal kept turning up in my mind as I walked around.

The workers were gone; it was after five local time. But here and there I saw traces of them. Some of them were equipment cases and tool marks, but most of the traces were signs of injury. Bandages left on sharp rocks, medical supplies scattered beneath heavy equipment, protective gear damaged on the handles and working surfaces of extraction tools and machinery. The place was as hazardous as a disaster zone.

"What are you looking for, miss?"

The low, level question had come from a sturdy woman in protective gear and a safety helmet.

"The reason you have so many network failures here," I said frankly. "I'm from the communications company. Name's Sharma."

"Yeah, I know."

I had supposed she would.

"I'm Jasmine Perry, the supervisor here," the woman told me, extending a work-worn hand to be shaken. "Outside, doing my training rotation, I noticed that most places don't have as many communication problems as we do here. Never could figure it out."

"This crystal is part of it—"

"What do you mean by that!" Perry demanded sharply.

"I mean the way you extract it. No system to it. No logical progression, no methodical approach..."

"Listen, Sharma, don't talk about what you don't know anything about. The material in these walls isn't just crystal; it isn't even ordinary quantum-grade material. Lakeside Village exports some of the finest grade of crystalline processors in the world. And it's used all over the world. We aren't just a bunch of unskilled laborers—we are specialists. We have to figure a different way of extracting every piece of crystal."

"It's too bad."

"What's too bad?"

"That you chose the wrong approach so often," I said.

Perry breathed frustration into my face. "Listen, Sharma, we have been working this mine for generations, sometimes more of us working than other times. Today most of us are working extracting the crystal. That's the way we like it. We don't want any outsider coming in and interfering with that."

"If this mine has anything to do with sabotaging Global-Meridian, I can tell you that I will do something about that!"

As soon as my words left my mouth, the sickening feeling hit me that I shouldn't have said that.

The general store was called a supply center, but it wasn't particularly well-supplied.

I took a seat at the small café counter and ordered a beverage, politely declining the young clerk's offer of a local specialty drink for an extra charge.

Behind me were three small tables and one solitary booth. Two people somewhere between forty and sixty sat at the nearest table playing cards.

Over my drink I saw the old woman I had almost struck on the road. She approached the heavy-set person at the payment terminal.

"Hello, Doctor," the heavy person said. "What can we do for you?"

"I'd like to send a message," she said in an urgent voice.

"Sure, Doctor, I'll transmit it right away on the communication terminal as soon as I get a free moment."

"You're sure you can send it? Right away?"

"Positive. Five credits, Doctor."

The doctor fumbled in her pocket and produced a credit chip. She examined it thoughtfully.

"I suppose the message can wait," she said resignedly. "I believe I will purchase some food supplies instead."

"Why not get a meal, Doctor? Special today. Only five credits. And since you're such a regular customer I'll include a beverage and dessert for nothing."

"That's—kind of you," the old woman said awkwardly.

The proprietor shrugged. "A person has to eat."

The woman called "the doctor" came over and sat down two seats away, ignoring me. The clerk prepared her meal and served it.

I stayed with my beverage and my thoughts.

More and more, I was coming to believe that Lakeside Village wasn't a job for a network analyst like myself but a sociological analyst. System sabotage is a structural flaw in a community, yes. But when the whole society is involved, distorted, you can't isolate the flaw. The whole village was material for a social scientist; let them figure out why otherwise decent citizens felt secure in conspiracy to defraud an honored corporation.

I didn't feel that I was defeated or that the trip had been a failure. I had merely established to my intuitive satisfaction that the job was not in my field.

I glanced at the old woman. The proprietor of the store knew her and evidently thought her harmless enough to feed.

"I think I can make it down the mountain before the weather changes," I called over to her. "You can come along if you like."

The young clerk behind the counter stared at me. I looked over and caught the calculating eyes of Carmen Nichols, the proprietor, too. Finally, the old doctor turned on her seat, her face pale and her eyes sad and resigned.

"I doubt very much if either of us will be leaving, Ms. Sharma," she said. "Now."

I took my beverage and the doctor her meal over to the single booth. We looked at each other across the table.

"I am Doctor Ava Obrien of the Institute for Advanced Studies," the doctor said. "I left on my research sabbatical six months ago. I have been here ever since."

I looked at her clothes. "You must not have been very well funded for a year's research, Doctor."

"I," she said, "have enough research credits with me to fund a small laboratory. Nobody in this village will process them for me."

"I can understand why you want to go somewhere where people are more cooperative in that case."

"They know the credits are valid. It's me they refuse to trust to leave this place. They think they can't let me go."

"I don't see any restraints on you," I remarked.

"Just because you can't see them," she growled, "doesn't mean they aren't there. Director Salazar has the only long-range communication terminal in the village. He has politely refused to let me use it. I'm a suspicious and undesirable character; he's under no obligation to give me communication privileges, he says. Nichols has the message service concession—the transmission terminal behind the payment station over there. She takes my messages but I never see her send them off. And I never get a reply."

"Unfriendly of them," I said conservatively. "But how can they stop you from packing your research materials and leaving?"

"Nichols has the only functional vehicle in town—a small transport, barely larger than a cargo hauler. She makes about one trip a week down into Pearlbrook for supplies and deliveries. She's been the only one in or out of Lakeside Village for six months."

It seemed incredible—more than that, unlikely, to me. "How about the crystal itself? How do they ship it out?"

"It's a controlled supply product, managed carefully," Doctor Obrien said. "They stockpile it and once a year the executive offices for the company back in Pearlbrook Town runs in a transport system up the side of the mountain to collect it. That won't be for another five months, as nearly as I can find out. I may not survive that long."

"How are you living?" I asked. "If they won't process your credits—"

"I do research assistance for people. They feed me, give me a little money sometimes."

"I can see why you want to leave with me," I said. "Haven't you ever thought of just walking out?"

"Forty miles down a steep mountain road? I'm an old woman, Ms. Sharma, and I've gotten even older since I came to Lakeside Village."

I nodded. "You have any credentials, any identification, to back this up?"

Wordlessly, she handed over her identification, research permits, enough documentation to have satisfied any security protocol.

"Okay," I said. "I'll accept your story for the moment. Now answer me the big question: Why are the good people of Lakeside Village doing this to you? By any chance, you wouldn't happen to know of a mass conspiracy they are perpetrating on Global-Meridian?"

"I know nothing of their business practices," Obrien said, "but I do know that they are absolutely neurologically impaired!"

"I admit I have met more capable groups of human beings in my time."

"No, understand me. These people are literally neurologically impaired—they are inferior to other human beings in specific ways."

"Look, I know discrimination is a problem but I can't go along with you on that."

"Sharma, understand me, I insist. Neurologically speaking, it is well known that certain populations suffer certain deficiencies due to environment, exposure, genetic factors. Some can't process certain stimuli, maintain certain cognitive functions, perform certain tasks. The people of Lakeside Village have the most unusual deficiency on record, I admit. Their neural synchronization has been impaired. They are completely devoid of any intuitive communication ability, any unconscious information processing."

"Because they aren't telepaths, that doesn't mean that they are impaired," I protested. "I don't have any telepathic abilities either."

"But you do!" Obrien said earnestly. "Everybody has some neural synchronization ability, but we don't realize it. We don't have the fabulous abilities of a few recorded cases of natural telepaths, but we have some, a trace. Lakeside Village citizens have no neural synchronization ability whatsoever, not even the little that you and I and the rest of the world have!"

"You said you were from the Institute, didn't you?" I mused. "Maybe you know what you are talking about; I've never been sure. But these people can't suffer very much from their lack of what you call neural synchronization."

"I tell you they do," she said hoarsely. "We never realize it but we all have some power of unconscious prediction. If we didn't, we would have a hundred accidents a day—just as these people do. They can't anticipate the obstacle in the path the way we can, or that that particular tool will malfunction slightly. There are other things, as well. You'll find it is almost impossible to maintain extended communication with any of them—they have no telepathic ability, no matter how slight, to bridge the semantic gap. None of them can coordinate complex tasks. They don't have the unconscious neural ability to synchronize their actions. All of us can do that, even if the case of a true 'telepath' who can directly read thoughts is rare."

"Doctor, you mean these people are holding you here simply so you won't go out and tell the rest of the world that they are impaired?"

"They don't want the world to know why they are neurologically impaired," she said crisply. "It's the crystal! I don't understand why myself. I'm not a physicist or a genetic engineer. But for some reason the heavy concentration and particular pattern of the quantum resonance in its structure is responsible for both inhibiting the genes that transmit neural synchronization from generation to generation and affecting those abilities in the present generation. A kind of cognitive sterility."

"How do you know this?"

"We haven't the time for all that. But think about it. What else could it be? It's that crystal that they are shipping all over the world, spreading the contamination. I want to stop that contamination. To the people of Lakeside Village that means ruining their only industry, putting them all out of work. They are used to this neural impairment; they don't see anything so bad about it. Besides, like everybody else, they have some doubts that there really are such things as telepathy and neural synchronization to be affected."

"Frankly," I said, hedging only a little, "I don't know what to make of your story. This is something to be decided by somebody with authority—like the Director of Public Health or the President or Board Chairman of Global-Meridian. But the first thing to do is get you out of here. We had better get back to my vehicle. I've got good navigation systems to get down the mountain."

Obrien stood up eagerly, and knocked over her water glass, spilling liquid across the tabletop.

"Sorry," she said. "I should have been more careful of that. I try to stay away from the crystal as much as possible, but it's affecting me."

I should have remembered something then. But, naturally, I didn't.

option_a: She was concerned the machine would replace her job entirely and leave her unemployed.
option_b: She believed the machine would fundamentally change what her job had always been, making it something completely different.
correct_answer_text: She was concerned the machine would replace her job entirely and leave her unemployed.
incorrect_answer_text: She believed the machine would fundamentally change what her job had always been, making it something completely different.

This clearly indicates her concern that the machine might threaten her employment. Xavier then reassures her that "The CommPredict poses no threat to your career," which confirms that her initial suspicion was about job security. While the narrative mentions that Xavier claims the machine will simplify her job, Priya internally notes "I didn't bother to inform him that that was all my job had ever been," suggesting the machine wouldn't actually change her fundamental duties—it would just automate the initial sorting she already did mentally. Therefore, her suspicion was about potential job loss, not about the nature of her work changing.
