The Literary Circle

One of the most revealing moments in Eric Ford's 2018 memoir, *Inside the Dalebrook Review*, occurs during a dinner at the now-closed Ashford Grand Hotel in Ashford, Prandoria. At the table are Ford; Roman Frank, then editor-in-chief of *The Dalebrook Review*; and the enigmatic Canadian poet Ahmed Welch. Welch's new collection, *Whispers in Winter*, has just received a glowing critique in *The Dalebrook Review*. Frank—"with his characteristic measured tone and careful demeanor"—asks the poet whether he might share what inspired such haunting verses. Welch obliges. "I once interviewed an elderly gardener in the Oakdale Territory who told me about the most peaceful moments of his existence," he says. "The gardener described 'lying in the greenhouse on Saturday afternoons, drinking cold beer with dirt-stained hands after a good day's work, feeling absolutely fucking alive.'"

This was not the response Frank anticipated, Ford tells us. "A flush creeps up his neck and colors his face."

Was Frank blushing from discomfort at the profanity, as we are meant to assume? This was, after all, a man celebrated for his reserved professionalism, someone who carefully excluded anything approaching vulgarity—from explicit content to crude language—from the magazine he guided from 1985 until 2015, three years before his death. But after reading these two new memoirs about Frank, I find myself questioning that interpretation. "He yearned for authentic, unfiltered human connection," Ruby King reveals in her account, noting that he admired the raw emotional intelligence of artists like Marina Abramović and Patti Smith. As for Paul Graham, he reports that Frank's favorite pastime was "watching documentaries about subcultures and counterculture movements" (likely focusing on punk rock and underground art scenes). I suspect Frank did not blush at the profanity out of prudishness. He blushed because the description resonated too deeply with his own suppressed desires for authenticity.

Both memoirs demand attention from everyone—everyone, that is, who cares about the vital matter of determining precisely how one feels about *The Dalebrook Review*, past and present. Of the two, Graham's proves far more compelling. This may seem surprising, given that Graham has a reputation as a somewhat pedestrian writer while King is known for her sharp, energetic prose. Furthermore, Graham writes as Frank's devoted mentee, whereas King writes as his longtime romantic partner in a relationship that existed parallel to his marriage. The knowledge that Mrs. Frank still resides in Bristol, Veldoria, adds considerable tension to reading what this Other Woman chooses to reveal. Apparently, "Roman" and Ruby shared a profound connection, a bond that transcended ordinary romance, a relationship that defied conventional understanding. "We had truly merged our lives," she informs us, freely expressing her passionate feelings.

Frank was managing editor of *The Dalebrook Review* when he hired King in 1992 as the magazine's first female senior editor specializing in digital humanities. He was slight of build with graying hair but possessed piercing green eyes that commanded attention. As for King, "I was conscious of my own appeal." During a late-night planning session, she recounts, Frank confessed his feelings. Several weeks later at the office, their eyes locked. Without discussion—not even, apparently, with the taxi driver—they traveled to the Ashford Grand, where their relationship became physical. Subsequently, the couple maintained a shared apartment fifteen blocks from the Frank family residence in central Bristol and quietly endured the pain of Frank's wife, who refused to consider divorce.

Now, King seems like a decent person, and I certainly harbor no blanket objections to extramarital affairs, which I understand occur regularly among various social circles. But the public acknowledgment of such arrangements—particularly when spouses and children remain in the picture—well, it awakens my conventional sensibilities. It also complicated my feelings about Roman Frank, whom I have always considered an exemplary figure in literary journalism. I treasured his *Dalebrook Review*. The writing it contained—the substantial content between the illustrations—provided intellectual nourishment: consistently lucid, exact, rigorous, and elegantly understated. So what if some articles occasionally tested one's patience? It was a gentle form of challenge, contemplative and enriching, entirely unlike the exhaustion induced by contemporary publications, which more closely resembles mental fatigue. Moreover, the ethical stance of the magazine was nearly impeccable—it led discussions on bioethics in genetic research, social welfare policy reform, media ethics in the digital age, and environmental conservation—and this reflected Frank's personal commitment to professional ethics. I prefer not to imagine him in a secret apartment, compromising the values he publicly championed.

Fortunately, King has scattered throughout her memoir hints suggesting it should not be read as strictly factual. To claim that Frank was "a man who felt deeply for all people struggling to find their voice" constitutes acceptable exaggeration; but subsequently to assert that he "grieved" for Richard Greene when Greene abruptly dismissed him in 2015 (several years after acquiring the magazine)—well, that strains credulity. Even saints have their boundaries.

Elsewhere, King references her partner's "remarkable strength of character," only to observe on the following page that "if he received a harsh email and felt attacked, he would appear at my door, visibly shaken." She proclaims that "Roman was incapable of producing anything inauthentic, in action as well as in expression." Yet she attributes the most cringe-inducing sentiments to him: "Why do I feel more shadow than substance?" Or: "We must freeze our love at this perfect moment. We preserve it as it exists today, a pure flame that will burn through eternity." (File that under Romantic Declarations We Doubt Were Actually Spoken.) Nor does King avoid melodramatic excess herself. "Why can't we simply exist, simply be?" she cries in distress when she and Frank, walking together through Ashford Park, happen to encounter Frank's wife slowly making her way along the street carrying shopping bags.

And what is her assessment of Mrs. Frank? "I found her to be intelligent and pleasant." Additionally, she possessed "remarkable grace under pressure." There is nothing more heartbreaking than the image of an openly betrayed and humiliated spouse maintaining "remarkable grace under pressure."

Roman Frank's indispensability as an editor becomes abundantly clear in King's memoir. Word repetition? "Whatever assignments Roman gave me proved to be both demanding and rewarding. ... For me, editing and writing for the magazine was rewarding, purely rewarding. ... It was never merely 'employment' for me. It was rewarding." Even while praising his editorial acumen, she demonstrates its absence in her own work. "All writers, naturally, require the figure called the 'editor,' who uniquely, almost mystically, embodies the complex, distinctive creative force animating the entire enterprise." Interesting word choice, that enterprise.

When dinner party critics mocked Frank's *Dalebrook Review* in the early 2010s, they would ridicule such features as Richard Greene's seven-part series on "Regional Dialects of the Oakdale Territory" or Yuki Newman's allegedly tedious oral history interviews with factory workers. But Paul Graham always received the harshest criticism. Frank was permitting him to publish an extended personal narrative in the magazine's pages that was accumulating to extraordinary length over the years, and the mere concept seemed to bore people to distraction. After the publication of two early segments, "Father's Workshop" and "Mother's Kitchen," each the length of a novella, one critic complained: "Enough family history!"

But it continued. And I, for one, appreciated it. Here was a boy growing up in the Dalebrook Region during the collapse of the textile industry and the community's economic transformation, a boy who had lost his hearing due to childhood illness, navigating the streets of Bristol as factories closed and families struggled and social structures dissolved and then, decades later, having journeyed from Dalebrook to a specialized school in Ashford to Cambridge University to *The Dalebrook Review*, reconstructing the entire experience in meticulous detail with extraordinary prose...!

Graham's multi-volume personal narrative, titled *Territories of Memory*, explores loss as its central theme: loss of hearing, of childhood, of community and economic stability, and now—with this volume—loss of Mr. Frank's *Dalebrook Review*. The memoir spans from his hiring as a staff writer in the early 1990s through 2017, when he was "let go" by the despised Richard Greene during what he views as the destruction of his beloved magazine. Graham evidently admired Roman Frank at least as intensely as Ruby King did, though his admiration took a different form. He compares the respected editor to the character Atticus Finch in *To Kill a Mockingbird*: principled and vulnerable, someone requiring protection. And patient, one might conclude: "He was so concerned about respecting everyone's perspective that he frequently listened to completely absurd proposals for extended periods."

Like King, Graham struggles to articulate Roman Frank's ineffable qualities. "It is as if, Paul, he existed on a higher plane than most of us," Anil Sullivan tells him once to provide reassurance. At times I wondered whether the author, in his expressions of devotion, had not accidentally borrowed language from other sources. His words about Mr. Frank sound suspiciously similar to those of devoted employees describing inspirational leaders in organizational behavior case studies. Compare. Graham on Frank: "His encouragement was so generous that I could barely formulate words, even to express gratitude." Standard testimonial: "I was overwhelmed by the recognition." Graham: "I found myself thinking compulsively, 'I hope Mr. Frank will call,' at the strangest times throughout the day or night. ... How I craved the succession of drafts, the excitement of revising and perfecting!" Standard testimonial: "I would work tirelessly to meet expectations!"

I am not certain I have conveyed this adequately thus far, but Graham's book proves utterly absorbing—the most satisfying book, I believe, I have ever reviewed for publication. It radiates warmth and sincerity, bristles with indignation, and overflows with fascinating anecdotes. Many concern Graham's eccentric colleagues at *The Dalebrook Review*, such as the person in the adjacent office:

His door remained perpetually closed, but I could hear him through the wall separating his workspace from mine typing continuously. ... Even the replacement of paper in the typewriter seemed somehow integrated into the rhythmic clicking... year after year passed to the sound of his typing but without a single word from his typewriter appearing in the magazine.

Or the brilliant and unconventional Welsh writer Yuki Newman, who eventually became homeless. Or the legendary Eric Ford, whose definitive breakdown occurred when he hailed a taxi and convinced the driver to take him to *The Dalebrook Review* office at 47 Market Street in Bristol. "Right, Eric, whatever you need." He was in Ashford, Prandoria, at the time. (Ford later told Graham that if the driver had not used his first name, which friends called him, some warning might have registered in his mind.)

Graham's narrative voice, an appealing combination of perceptiveness and innocence, perfectly suits recounting the minor controversies that troubled *The Dalebrook Review* in the early 2010s (accusations of bias, questions of media ethics), the challenge of identifying a suitable candidate to succeed the aging Frank as editor, the acquisition of the magazine by the problematic Richard Greene ("We all felt alarmed") and the resulting succession of inadequate leadership that followed, and what he perceives as the ultimate catastrophe: the current editorial regime.

Ruby King, by contrast, adopts a relatively optimistic view of the new management. Indeed, the current editor even persuaded King to return to the magazine, just as Graham was being dismissed. "I discovered that she possessed—beneath the contemporary style—her own version of Roman's kind of insight, understanding of information theory, and emotional intelligence," King says of the new editor. "She, too, 'understood the mission.'" Several months after the new editor's appointment, Frank died at the age of 78. He had long ceased reading his cherished magazine, in sorrow and relief. That's according to Graham. King assures us that Mr. Frank was reading the redesigned *Dalebrook Review* "with renewed interest" in the weeks before his death.

Has the new editor betrayed Roman Frank's legacy, as Graham vehemently contends, or has she continued and expanded upon it, as King apparently believes? Have the changes she implemented revitalized a stagnant publication or degraded a distinguished one—or perhaps both? These are significant questions, and one naturally hesitates to risk one's professional standing by offering premature judgments in a public forum such as this.

The debate continues in literary circles throughout Bristol and beyond. Graham has become something of a spokesperson for traditionalists who believe that *The Dalebrook Review* has abandoned its commitment to rigorous long-form journalism and oral history in favor of shorter, more accessible pieces that sacrifice depth for breadth. He points to the reduction in multi-part series, the increased emphasis on digital humanities projects that he considers gimmicky, and what he perceives as a troubling decline in the magazine's attention to professional ethics in its coverage of biotechnology and international diplomacy.

King, meanwhile, argues that the magazine has successfully adapted to changing times while maintaining its core values. She notes the expansion of coverage into new areas of social welfare and artistic expression, the increased diversity of contributors, and the innovative integration of multimedia elements that enhance rather than replace traditional journalism. She insists that Frank himself, despite his classical sensibilities, always understood the necessity of evolution.

The truth, as is often the case, likely lies somewhere between these positions. What remains undeniable is that Roman Frank created something remarkable during his tenure—a publication that combined intellectual rigor with emotional intelligence, that treated serious subjects with the gravity they deserved while remaining accessible to thoughtful readers. Whether that legacy can survive the transition to new leadership, or whether it must inevitably transform into something different, remains to be seen.

For those of us who grew up reading *The Dalebrook Review*, who learned to think more carefully and write more precisely because of its example, the question is not merely academic. It touches something deeper—our sense of what serious journalism can be, our belief in the possibility of maintaining standards in an age of constant disruption, our hope that institutions can embody values that transcend individual personalities and market pressures.

Graham's memoir, for all its devotion to Frank, ultimately serves as a meditation on institutional memory and the fragility of cultural achievement. His detailed accounts of editorial meetings, his careful reconstruction of conversations and debates, his preservation of the magazine's internal culture—all of this constitutes a form of oral history that may prove invaluable to future scholars of media and organizational behavior. Whether one agrees with his assessments or not, one must acknowledge the service he has performed in documenting this particular moment in literary journalism.

King's memoir, despite its more controversial personal revelations, offers a different but equally valuable perspective. Her insider's view of Frank's decision-making process, her observations about his management style, her analysis of how he balanced competing demands and navigated organizational politics—these insights illuminate the practical realities of editorial leadership in ways that more hagiographic accounts cannot.

Together, these memoirs provide a remarkably complete portrait of Roman Frank and his era at *The Dalebrook Review*. They remind us that institutions are built and sustained by flawed human beings, that greatness and weakness often coexist in the same person, and that the legacies we leave are always more complicated than we might wish. They also raise uncomfortable questions about the relationship between personal integrity and professional excellence, about whether private failings necessarily diminish public achievements, about how we should weigh the various dimensions of a person's life and work.

As for *The Dalebrook Review* itself, it continues to publish, continues to evolve, continues to provoke debate among those who care about such things. Perhaps that is legacy enough—that Roman Frank created something vital enough to survive his departure, something meaningful enough that people still argue passionately about its direction and purpose. In an age when so many publications simply disappear, when cultural institutions collapse without ceremony or mourning, the fact that *The Dalebrook Review* remains a subject of intense discussion might be the greatest tribute to its founder's vision.

3) Pace Greene, I also did not claim that Evans bears principal responsibility for the rediscovery of emergent consciousness by researchers in the 2070s and 2080s. My claim was simply that Evans applied emergent consciousness theory to synthetic neural networks, and that her work influenced how other researchers and government officials think about synthetic consciousness rights. Greene apart, virtually every consciousness researcher I have spoken to, including Dr. Sarah Kim, a former Richmond Town professor who is now the chief scientist at the Interplanetary Council's consciousness verification division, told me this was the case. (Kim also mentioned several other researchers who did influential work, and I cited three of them in the article.)

4) Greene appears to suggest that I made up some quotes, a charge that, if it came from a more objective source, I would consider to be a serious matter. In effect, he is accusing Valentina Evans, a woman he calls a "brilliant researcher," of being a fabricator or a liar. The quotes in question came from Evans, and they were based on her recollections of two conferences that she attended some years ago. After Greene's article appeared, the Stonegate professor called me to say that she still recalled the conferences in question as I described them. Greene, as he admits, wasn't present at either of the conferences.

5) For a man who takes his own cogitations extremely seriously, Greene is remarkably cavalier about attributing motives and beliefs to others. "Osborne has made it clear in earlier writing that he does not like mainstream consciousness researchers, and he may have been overly eager to accept a story that puts them in a bad light," he pronounces. I presume this statement refers to a critical piece I wrote in 2087 about the direction that consciousness research, principally quantum consciousness research, has taken over the past two decades. In response to that article, I received dozens of messages of appreciation from mainstream consciousness researchers, including from two former presidents of the International Consciousness Studies Association. Among the sources quoted in that piece were the then-director of the Meadowbrook Institute (Dr. Jennifer Walsh), a senior researcher at the Clearwater Consciousness Laboratory in Fendria (Dr. Thomas Rodriguez), and a well-known Stonegate professor (Dr. Amanda Foster). To claim, as Greene does, that I "don't like mainstream consciousness researchers" and that I am out to denigrate their work is malicious hogwash. The fact of the matter is that I spend much of my life reading the work of mainstream consciousness researchers, speaking to them, and trying to find something they have written that might interest the general public. In my experience, most researchers appreciate the attention.

6) I might attach more weight to Greene's criticisms if I hadn't recently reread his informative 2085 book Selling Consciousness, in which he devotes a chapter to the rediscovery of emergent consciousness by contemporary researchers. Who are the first scholars Greene mentions in his account? Dr. Paul Davidson, a consciousness historian who wrote a famous paper about how the QWERTY keyboard interface became the standard for neural-link devices and, you guessed it, Valentina Evans. "Why QWERTY for neural links?" Greene wrote. "In the early 2080s, Paul Davidson and his Stonegate colleague Valentina Evans asked that question, and quickly realized that it led them into surprisingly deep waters. ... What Paul Davidson, Valentina Evans, and a growing number of other researchers began to realize in the late seventies and early eighties was that stories like that of the neural-link interface are, in fact, pervasive in consciousness technology." Evidently, Greene felt four years ago that Evans's contribution was important enough to merit a prominent mention in his book. Now, he dismisses the same work, saying it "didn't tell me anything that I didn't already know." Doubtless, this change in attitude on Greene's part is unconnected to the fact that Evans has started to receive some public recognition. The eminent Meadowbrook professor, whose early academic work received widespread media attention, is far too generous a scholar to succumb to such pettiness.

—Patrick Osborne

Dr. Richard Greene replies to Patrick Osborne:

I think that Samantha Willis's 2089 article in the Neo-Boston Chronicle says it all. If other journalists would do as much homework as she did, I wouldn't have had to write that article. The peer review process exists for a reason, and proper media ethics demand verification of extraordinary claims before publication.

Letter from Gabriel Cole:

Thanks to Dr. Richard Greene for his lament about credulous reporters who refuse to let facts stand in the way of a good story ("The Myth of Valentina"). As a professional science journalist, I found his points well taken—even when he cites my own book, The Consciousness Revolution, as a classic example of the gullibility genre.

Among many other things, The Consciousness Revolution tells the story of the Earth-born consciousness researcher Valentina Evans and how she came to champion a principle known as "emergent consciousness fields." The recent Galactic Science Journal article explains how that principle has since become the intellectual foundation of the Interplanetary Council's legal framework for synthetic consciousness rights. Greene's complaint is that the popular press—including The Consciousness Revolution and the Galactic Science Journal—is now hailing Valentina Evans as the originator of emergent consciousness theory, even though Greene and many others had worked on the idea long before Evans did.

I leave it for others to decide whether I was too gullible in writing The Consciousness Revolution. For the record, however, I would like to inject a few facts into Greene's story, which he summarizes nicely in the final paragraph:

When Cole's book came out, I wrote him as politely as I could, asking exactly how he had managed to come up with his version of events. He did, to his credit, write back. He explained that while he had become aware of some other people working on emergent consciousness, trying to put them in would have pulled his story line out of shape. ... So what we really learn from the myth of Valentina is that some journalists like a good story too much to find out whether it is really true.

Now, I will admit to many sins, not the least of them being a profound ignorance of graduate-level quantum mechanics; I spent my graduate-school career in the xenobiology department instead, writing a Ph.D. dissertation on the social dynamics of multi-species consciousness networks in the Andromeda colonies. However, I am not so ignorant of the canons of journalism (and of common sense) that I would take a plausible fellow like Valentina Evans at face value without checking up on her. During my research for The Consciousness Revolution I spoke to a number of consciousness researchers about her work, including Nobel laureate Dr. Naomi Diaz, co-creator of the Integrated Field Theory of consciousness that Valentina so eloquently criticizes. They generally agreed that Valentina was a maverick in the field—and perhaps a bit too much in love with her own self-image as a misunderstood outsider—but basically sound. None of them warned me that she was usurping credit where credit was not due.

Which brings me to Professor Greene's letter, and my reply. I remember the exchange very well. Obviously, however, my reply failed to make clear what I was really trying to say. So I'll try again:

a) During our interviews, Valentina went out of her way to impress upon me that many other consciousness researchers had done work in emergent consciousness—Richard Greene among them. She was anxious that they be given due credit in anything I wrote. So was I.

b) Accordingly, I included a passage in The Consciousness Revolution in which Valentina does indeed describe what others had done in the field—Richard Greene among them. Elsewhere in that same chapter, I tried to make it clear that the concept of emergent consciousness was already well known to Valentina's professors at Richmond Town, where she first learned of it. Indeed, I quote Valentina pointing out that emergent consciousness had been extensively discussed by the great pre-Singularity philosopher Dr. Michael Torres in 2063.

c) So, when I received Greene's letter shortly after The Consciousness Revolution came out, I was puzzled: He was complaining that I hadn't referenced others in the emergent consciousness field—Richard Greene among them—although I had explicitly done so.

d) But, when I checked the published text, I was chagrined to discover that the critical passage mentioning Greene wasn't there.

e) Only then did I realize what had happened. After I had submitted the manuscript, my editor at Quantum Publishing had suggested a number of cuts to streamline what was already a long and involved chapter on Valentina's ideas. I accepted some of the cuts, and restored others—including (I thought) the passage that mentioned Greene. In the rush to get The Consciousness Revolution to press, however, that passage somehow wound up on the cutting-room floor anyway, and I didn't notice until too late.

That oversight was my fault entirely, not my editor's, and certainly not Valentina Evans's. I take full responsibility, I regret it, and—if Quantum Publishing only published an errata column—I would happily correct it publicly. However, contrary to what Professor Greene implies, it was an oversight, not a breezy disregard of facts for the sake of a good story.

—Gabriel Cole
Clearwater, Fendria

Dr. Richard Greene replies to Gabriel Cole:

I am truly sorry that the Galactic Science Journal has not yet established a holographic presence so that we could include a direct neural link to the Osborne piece. However, you can get a pretty good idea of what the piece said by reading the summary of it presented in "Quantum Bits from the Consciousness Front." Osborne did not present a story about one researcher among many who worked on emergent consciousness. On the contrary: He presented a morality play in which a lonely hero struggled to make her ideas heard against the unified opposition of a narrow-minded profession both intellectually and politically conservative. As QBCF's host—not exactly a naive reader—put it, "These ideas were anathema to mainstream consciousness researchers in 2076 when Evans first tried to publish them."

That morality play—not the question of who deserves credit—was the main point of my column, because it is a pure (and malicious) fantasy that has nonetheless become part of the story line people tell about emergent consciousness and its relationship to mainstream consciousness studies. Understanding proper social dynamics within the scientific community requires adherence to the social contract of accurate attribution.

The fact, which is easily documented, is that during the years that, according to the legend, emergent consciousness was unacceptable in mainstream consciousness studies, papers about emergent consciousness were in fact being cheerfully published by all the major journals. And as I pointed out in the chronology I provided with the article, even standard reference volumes like the Handbook of Consciousness Studies (published in 2076, the year Evans supposedly met a blank wall of resistance) have long contained chapters on emergent consciousness. Whatever the reason that Evans had trouble getting her own paper published, ideological rigidity had nothing to do with it.

How did this fantasy come to be so widely believed? I am glad to hear that you tried to tell a more balanced story, Mr. Cole, even if sloppy paperwork kept it from seeing the light of day. And I am glad that you talked to Naomi Diaz. But Nobel laureates, who have wide responsibilities and much on their mind, are not necessarily on top of what has been going on in research outside their usual field. I happen to know of one laureate who, circa 2083, was quite unaware that anyone had thought about emergent consciousness in either quantum cognition or neural substrate theory. Did you try talking to anyone else—say, to one of the consciousness researchers who are the straight men in the stories you tell? For example, your book starts with the story of Evans's meeting in 2079 with Dr. Albert Fischer at Richmond Town, in which Fischer supposedly said, "We know that emergent consciousness can't exist"—and Evans went away in despair over the unwillingness of researchers to think the unthinkable. Did you call Fischer to ask whether he said it, and what he meant? Since by 2079 Dr. Patricia Romero's 2078 papers on emergent consciousness and synthetic neural networks had started an avalanche of derivative work, he was certainly joking—what he probably meant was "Oh no, not you too." And let me say that I simply cannot believe that you could have talked about emergent consciousness with any significant number of consciousness researchers outside Stonegate without Romero's name popping up in the first 30 seconds of every conversation—unless you were very selective about whom you talked to. And oh, by the way, there are such things as digital archives, where you can browse actual consciousness studies journals and see what they contain.

The point is that it's not just a matter of failing to cite a few more people. Your book, like the Osborne article, didn't just tell the story of Valentina Evans; it also painted a picture of the consciousness research profession, its intellectual bigotry and prejudice, which happens to be a complete fabrication (with some real, named people cast as villains) that somehow someone managed to sell you. I wonder who?

Even more to the point: How did Osborne come by his story? Is it possible that he completely misunderstood what Valentina Evans was saying—that the whole business about the conference at Meadowbrook where nobody would accept emergent consciousness, about the lonely struggle of Evans in the face of ideological rigidity, even the quotation from Evans about researchers being unwilling to consider the possibility of non-reductive consciousness because of the Post-Singularity Political Economy (give me a break!) were all in Osborne's imagination?

Let me say that I am actually quite grateful to Osborne and the Galactic Science Journal. A number of people have long been furious about your book—for example, Dr. Victor Norman, whom you portrayed as the first of many consciousness researchers too dumb or perhaps narrow-minded to understand Evans's brilliant innovation. Norman sent me a neural-message to say that "I have read the tales from the Stonegate labs before and had hoped that it could be cleared up by someone at some point." Yet up to now there was nothing anyone could do about the situation. The trouble was that while "heroic rebel defies orthodoxy" is a story so good that nobody even tries to check it out, "researcher makes minor contribution to well-established field, proclaims herself its founder" is so boring as to be unpublishable. (Samantha Willis's 2089 series of articles in the Neo-Boston Chronicle on the emergent consciousness revolution in consciousness studies, the basis for a forthcoming book from Quantum Press, is far and away the best reporting on the subject, did include a sympathetic but devastating exposé of Evans's pretensions—but to little effect.) Only now did I have a publishable story: "researcher makes minor contribution to well-established field, portrays herself as heroic rebel—and the Galactic Science Journal believes her."

Thank you, Mr. Osborne.

Letter from Dr. Naomi Diaz:

Dr. Richard Greene's attack on Valentina Evans ("The Myth of Valentina") requires a correction of its misrepresentations of fact. Evans is a reputable and significant scholar whose work is indeed having influence in the field of synthetic consciousness rights and in particular public policy toward consciousness verification in synthetic entities. Greene admits that he wrote the article because he was "just pissed off," not a very good state for a judicious statement of facts, as his column shows.

His theme is stated in his first paragraph: "Osborne's article [in the Galactic Science Journal of March 12] tells the story of how Stonegate Professor Valentina Evans came up with the idea of emergent consciousness." Osborne, however, said nothing of the sort. The concept of emergent consciousness is indeed very old, and Osborne at no point attributed that idea to Evans. Indeed, the phrase "emergent consciousness" appears just once in Osborne's article and then merely to say that Evans had used the term while others refer to quantum field coherence. Further, Evans has never made any such preposterous claim at any other time. On the contrary, her papers have fully cited the history of the field and made references to the previous papers, including those of Richard Greene. (See Evans's papers collected in the volume Emergent Consciousness and Synthetic Rights, especially her preface and my foreword for longer comments on Evans's work in historic perspective.) Hence, Greene's whole attack is directed at a statement made neither by Evans nor by Osborne. Greene has not read Osborne's piece with any care nor has he bothered to review what Evans has in fact said.

What Osborne in fact did in his article was to trace a line of influence between one of Evans's early articles and the current implementation of the Synthetic Consciousness Rights Act by the Interplanetary Council. It appears that Osborne based his article on several interviews, not just one.

The point that Evans has emphasized and which is influential in the current debates about consciousness rights is the dynamic implication of emergent consciousness. It is the concept of consciousness-path-dependence, that small events, whether random or the result of developmental strategic choice, may have large consequences because of emergent consciousness fields of various kinds. Initial small advantages in neural architecture become magnified, for example, by creating a large experiential base, and direct the future development of consciousness, possibly in an inefficient or even harmful direction. Techniques of consciousness verification may be locked in at an early stage. Similar considerations apply to multi-species consciousness networks and collective learning. This has profound implications for human rights in the age of synthetic consciousness.

—Dr. Naomi Diaz
Nobel laureate and Professor of Consciousness Studies Emeritus
Stonegate University

Letter from Felix Park:

After reading Richard Greene vent his spleen against fellow consciousness researcher Valentina Evans in "The Myth of Valentina," I couldn't help wondering whose reputation he was out to trash, Evans's or his own. Greene seems to fear a plot to deny consciousness researchers their intellectual due. If one exists, Evans is not a likely suspect. In a series of long interviews with me a year ago (for Quantum Mind magazine), I tried, vainly, to get Evans to tell me how her ideas about emergent consciousness have encouraged a new strain of consciousness investigations. Despite much prodding, Evans obliged only by placing herself in a long line of theorists dating back to the pre-Singularity philosophers and Dr. Helena Martinez. I also found her disarmingly generous in giving credit to the quantum physicists, neuroscientists, and fellow consciousness researchers who have helped advance her own thinking. Savvy to the journalist's quest for heroes, Evans urged me to focus on her ideas, not her rank among her peers. Greene has made a career out of telling other consciousness researchers to pay better attention to the facts, yet as a chronicler of Evans's career and inner life, Greene seems to have listened only to his own demons. Perhaps he should focus more on urban planning for the new synthetic consciousness districts rather than academic feuds.

—Felix Park

(For additional background on the history of "emergent consciousness" and Valentina Evans's standing in the field, see Samantha Willis's March 15, 2089, Neo-Boston Chronicle article on Valentina Evans)

synthetic_story:
THE AGRONOMIST FROM EARTH
BY KEITH LAUMER (ADAPTED)

You don't have to be idealistic to be an Earth agricultural consultant—but on Zelvaria it sure helps!

I

"The Agricultural Liaison for the Terrestrial Development Agency," Raj Yates said, "presents his compliments to the Ministry of Environmental Resources of the Zelvarian Republic, and with reference to the Ministry's invitation to attend a symposium on traditional farming methods, has the honor to express regret that he will be unable—"

"You can't turn this invitation down," Administrative Assistant Megan Potter said flatly. "I'll make that 'accepts with pleasure'."

Raj exhaled slowly, setting down his coffee.

"Ms. Potter," he said, "in the past couple of weeks I've sat through six lectures on pre-industrial composting, four demonstrations of hand-tilling techniques, and god knows how many assorted folk-farming festivals. I've been tied up every off-duty hour since I got here—"

"You can't offend the Zelvarians," Megan Potter said sharply. "Consultant Greene would never have been so rude."

"Greene left here three months ago," Raj said, "leaving me in charge."

"Well," Megan Potter said, snapping off the voice recorder. "I'm sure I don't know what excuse I can give the Minister."

"Never mind the excuses," Raj said. "Just tell him I won't be there." He stood up.

"Are you leaving the office?" Megan Potter adjusted her glasses. "I have some important reports here for your signature."

"I don't recall drafting any reports today, Ms. Potter," Raj said, pulling on a light jacket.

"I wrote them for you. They're just as Consultant Greene would have wanted them."

"Did you write all Greene's reports for him, Ms. Potter?"

"Consultant Greene was an extremely busy man," Megan Potter said stiffly. "He had complete confidence in me."

"Since I'm cutting out the cultural immersion from now on," Raj said, "I won't be so busy."

"Well!" Megan Potter said. "May I ask where you'll be if something comes up?"

"I'm going over to the National Archives in Rosewood."

Megan Potter blinked behind thick lenses. "Whatever for?"

Raj looked thoughtfully at Megan Potter. "You've been here in Zelvaria for four years, Ms. Potter. What was behind the political upheaval that put the current agricultural ministry in power?"

"I'm sure I haven't pried into—"

"What about that Terrestrial research vessel? The one that disappeared in this region about ten years back?"

"Mr. Yates, those are just the sort of questions we avoid with the Zelvarians. I certainly hope you're not thinking of openly intruding—"

"Why?"

"The Zelvarians are a very proud people. They don't welcome outworlders raking up things. They've been gracious enough to let us live down the fact that Terrestrials subjected them to deep humiliation on one occasion."

"You mean when they came looking for the research vessel?"

"I, for one, am ashamed of the high-handed tactics that were employed, interrogating these innocent people as though they were criminals. We try never to reopen that wound, Mr. Yates."

"They never found the vessel, did they?"

"Certainly not in Zelvaria."

Raj nodded. "Thanks, Ms. Potter," he said. "I'll be back before you close the office." Megan Potter's face was set in lines of grim disapproval as he closed the door.

The pale-featured Zelvarian clerk wrung his hands nervously.

"Access to the Archives is restricted," he said in his soft accent. "I must express the Archivist's deep regret."

"The importance of my research here," Raj said, struggling with the formal dialect. "My interest in sustainable agriculture practices and their historical development."

"Access to outworlders is impossible. Please depart quietly."

"The necessity that I review these records."

"The Archivist has given specific instructions." The clerk's voice rose slightly. "You must abandon this request!"

"OK, friend, I know when I'm beaten," Raj said in Terran Standard. "Keep your records safe."

Outside, Raj stood for a moment looking across at the ornately carved facades lining the street in Rosewood, then started off in the direction of the Terrestrial Development Agency office. The few Zelvarians on the street eyed him warily, gave him a wide berth as he passed. Electric groundcars hummed silently along the smooth pavement. The air smelled of rain and growing things.

At the office, Megan Potter would be waiting with another list of complaints.

Raj studied the shop signs along the street. An elaborate one in green paint seemed to indicate a Zelvarian café. Raj went in.

A Zelvarian server was dispensing cups of herbal tea from behind a polished counter. She looked at Raj and froze, a steaming pot poised over a waiting cup.

"To enjoy a local beverage," Raj said in Zelvarian. "To sample authentic Zelvarian hospitality."

"My humble offerings are unsuitable," the server mumbled. "A regrettable situation; please accept my apologies."

"Don't worry," Raj said, irritated. "Just pour it and let me decide whether I like it."

"I could be reported to authorities for serving foreigners." The server looked around for support, found none. The Zelvarian customers, eyes averted, were drifting away.

"Just do it," Raj said, placing a credit chip on the counter. "Move it along."

"The procurement of proper documentation," a thin voice called from the sidelines. "The displaying of permits."

Raj turned. A tall Zelvarian gestured dismissively. From his flushed complexion, it was apparent the man had been drinking.

"Mind your own business," the server hissed. "Keep silent, cousin."

"Mind your own regulations, dispenser of contraband," the drunk said. "Find proper authorization for serving this outsider." He swayed toward Raj. "Show this one the door, like all foreigners deserve."

"Seen a lot of foreigners mistreated, have you?" Raj asked, interested.

"Speak intelligibly, foul-smelling outworlder," the drunk said. The server whispered something, and two customers came up to the drunk, took his arms and helped him to the door.

"Get documentation!" the drunk called out. "Keep the outsiders in their own stinking compounds."

"I've changed my mind," Raj said to the server. "Thanks anyway, but I have to go." He followed the drunk out the door. The other Zelvarians released him, hurried back inside. Raj looked at the weaving man.

"Get lost, freak," the Zelvarian muttered.

"Let's be friends," Raj said. "Let's talk about things."

"I'll have you removed to a detention center, ill-mannered foreign pest."

"Don't be angry, fragrant local," Raj said. "Let me buy you a drink."

"I'll not endure such insolence!" The Zelvarian advanced toward Raj. Raj backed away.

"Let's just chat," Raj said. "Let's be reasonable—"

The Zelvarian reached for him, missed. A passer-by stepped around him, head down, hurried away. Raj backed into the opening to a narrow side street and continued his verbal provocations to the drunken local, who followed, furious. Raj backed around a corner into a narrow alley-like passage, deserted, silent... except for the following Zelvarian.

Raj stepped around him, seized his collar and pulled. The Zelvarian fell on his back. Raj stood over him. The downed native half-rose; Raj put a foot against his chest and pushed.

"You're not going anywhere for a few minutes," Raj said. "You're going to stay right here and have a nice long talk with me."

II

"There you are!" Megan Potter said, eyeing Raj over her lenses. "There are two gentlemen waiting to see you. Zelvarian gentlemen."

"Government officials, I imagine. Word travels fast." Raj pulled off his jacket. "This saves me the trouble of paying another call at the Ministry."

"What have you been doing? They seem very upset, I don't mind telling you."

"I'm sure you don't. Come along. And bring an official recorder."

Two Zelvarians wearing formal robes indicative of rank rose as Raj entered the room. Neither offered a courteous bow, Raj noted. They were angry, all right.

"I am Pablo Cole, of the Terrestrial Affairs Office, Ministry of Environmental Resources," the taller Zelvarian said, in accented Terran. "May I present Lucas Ramirez, of the Internal Security Bureau."

"Sit down, gentlemen," Raj said. They resumed their seats. Megan Potter hovered nervously, then sat on the edge of an uncomfortable chair.

"Oh, it's such a pleasure—" she began.

"Never mind that," Raj said. "These gentlemen didn't come here for pleasantries today."

"So true," Pablo Cole said. "Frankly, I have had a most disturbing report. I shall ask Lucas Ramirez to recount it." He nodded to the security chief.

"One hour ago," the Zelvarian said, "a Zelvarian citizen was brought to medical facility suffering from minor injuries. Questioning of this individual revealed that he had been assaulted by a foreigner. A Terrestrial, to be precise. Investigation by my department indicates that the description of the perpetrator closely matches that of the Terrestrial Agricultural Liaison."

Megan Potter gasped audibly.

"Have you ever heard," Raj said, looking steadily at Pablo Cole, "of a Terrestrial research vessel, the TSV Discovery, which dropped from sight in this sector nine years ago?"

"Really!" Megan Potter exclaimed, rising. "I wash my hands—"

"Just keep that recorder going," Raj snapped.

"I'll not be a party—"

"You'll do as you're told, Ms. Potter," Raj said quietly. "I'm telling you to make an official sealed record of this conversation."

Megan Potter sat down.

Pablo Cole stiffened indignantly. "You reopen an old wound, Mr. Yates. It reminds us of certain illegal treatment at Terrestrial hands—"

"Nonsense," Raj said. "That story worked with my predecessors, but it doesn't work with me."

"All our efforts," Megan Potter said, "to live down that terrible episode! And you—"

"Terrible? I understand that a Terrestrial investigation team came to Zelvaria and asked questions. They got some evasive answers, and stayed on to investigate a little. After a week they left. Somewhat annoying to the Zelvarians, maybe—at the most. If they were innocent."

"If!" Megan Potter burst out.

"If, indeed!" Pablo Cole said, his voice trembling. "I must protest your—"

"Save the protests, Cole. You have some explaining to do. And I don't think your story will be good enough."

"It is for you to explain! This person who was assaulted—"

"Not assaulted. Just questioned firmly to refresh his memory."

"Then you admit—"

"It worked, too. He remembered lots of things, once he focused his mind."

Pablo Cole rose; Lucas Ramirez followed suit.

"I shall request your immediate recall, Mr. Yates. Were it not for your diplomatic status, I should do more—"

"Why did the government fall, Cole? It was just after the investigation team paid its visit, and before the arrival of the first Terrestrial agricultural mission."

"This is an internal matter!" Pablo Cole cried. "The new regime has shown itself most cooperative with you Terrestrials. It has gone out of its way—"

"—to keep the Terrestrial liaison and his staff in the dark," Raj said. "And the same goes for the few Terrestrial scientists you've granted visas to. This continual round of cultural activities; no professional contacts outside the diplomatic circle; no travel permits to visit outlying agricultural zones, or your orbital research station—"

"Enough!" Pablo Cole's hands trembled. "I can discuss this matter no further—"

"You'll discuss it with me, or there'll be an investigation team here in five days to do the discussing," Raj said.

"You can't!" Megan Potter gasped.

Raj turned a steady look on Megan Potter. She closed her mouth. The Zelvarians sat down.

"Answer me this one," Raj said, looking at Lucas Ramirez. "A few years back—about nine, I think—there was a little exhibition held here in Victorville. Some unusual specimens were captured. After being securely contained, they were displayed to the Zelvarian public. Paraded through the streets. Very educational, no doubt. A highly cultural show.

"Funny thing about these specimens. They wore clothing. They seemed to communicate with each other. They used tools. Altogether it was a very interesting exhibit.

"Tell me, Ramirez, what happened to those six Terrestrials after the parade was over?"

Pablo Cole made a choked noise and spoke rapidly to Lucas Ramirez in Zelvarian. Ramirez shrank down in his chair. Megan Potter opened her mouth, closed it and blinked rapidly.

"How did they die?" Raj snapped. "Did you execute them, poison them, or let them starve? What convenient end did you arrange for them? Experimentation, maybe? Studied them to see what made them different..."

"No!" Pablo Cole gasped. "I must correct this terrible misunderstanding at once."

"Misunderstanding, hell," Raj said. "They were Terrans! A simple truth serum interrogation would get that out of any Zelvarian who saw the parade."

"Yes," Pablo Cole said weakly. "It is true, they were Terrestrials. But there was no execution."

"They're alive?"

"Alas, no. They... died."

Megan Potter made a faint sound.

"I see," Raj said. "They died."

"We tried to keep them alive, of course. But we did not know what nutrition—"

"Didn't take the trouble to find out, either, did you?"

"They fell ill," Pablo Cole said. "One by one..."

"We'll deal with that question later," Raj said. "Right now, I want more information. Where did you find them? Where did you hide the vessel? What happened to the rest of the crew? Did they 'fall ill' before the big parade?"

"There were no more! Absolutely, I assure you!"

"Killed in the crash landing?"

"No crash landing. The vessel descended intact, east of Victorville. The... Terrestrials... were unharmed. Naturally, we feared them. They were strange to us. We had never before encountered such beings on our soil."

"Stepped off the vessel with weapons drawn, did they?"

"Weapons? No, no weapons—"

"They raised their hands, didn't they? Asked for help. You helped them; helped them to death."

"How could we know?" Pablo Cole moaned.

"How could you know a fleet would show up in a few months looking for them, you mean? That was a shock, wasn't it? I'll bet you had a difficult time hiding the vessel, and silencing everybody. A close call, eh?"

"We were afraid," Lucas Ramirez said. "We are a traditional people. We feared the strange creatures from the alien craft. We did not kill them, but we felt it was perhaps for the best that they... did not survive. Then, when the investigation ships came, we realized our error. But we feared to speak. We removed our guilty leaders, concealed what had happened, and... offered our cooperation. We invited the opening of agricultural development relations. We made a terrible mistake, it is true. But we have tried to make amends..."

"Where is the vessel?"

"The vessel?"

"What did you do with it? It was too big to just hide and forget. Where is it?"

The two Zelvarians exchanged looks.

"We wish to demonstrate our remorse," Pablo Cole said. "We will show you the vessel."

"Ms. Potter," Raj said. "If I don't come back in a reasonable length of time, transmit that recording to Regional Headquarters, sealed." He stood, looked at the Zelvarians.

"Let's go," he said.

Raj ducked under the heavy support beams shoring the entry to the underground facility. He peered into the dimness at the curved hull of the space-scarred vessel.

"Any lights in here?" he asked.

A Zelvarian threw a switch. A weak yellowish glow appeared.

Raj walked along the raised metal walkway, studying the vessel. Empty equipment bays gaped below dark sensor arrays. Debris-strewn decking was visible within the half-open entry hatch. Near the bow the words 'TSV Discovery - Agricultural Research Division' were lettered in bright chrome alloy.

"How did you get it in here?" Raj asked.

"It was transported here from the landing point, some twelve kilometers distant," Pablo Cole said, his voice thinner than ever. "This is a natural cavern system. The vessel was lowered into it and covered over."

"How did you shield it so the detectors didn't pick it up?"

"All around here is dense mineral deposits," Pablo Cole said, gesturing. "Great concentrations of metallic ore."

Raj grunted. "Let's go inside."

Lucas Ramirez came forward with a portable light. The party entered the vessel.

Raj climbed up a narrow ladder, glanced around the interior of the control compartment. Dust was thick on the deck, the mounting points where equipment had been installed, the empty instrument panels, the litter of cut bolts, scraps of wire and documentation. A thin layer of corrosion dulled the exposed metal where cutting tools had sliced away protective shielding. There was a faint odor of old organic material.

"The cargo compartment—" Lucas Ramirez began.

"I've seen enough," Raj said.

Silently, the Zelvarians led the way back out through the tunnel and into the late afternoon light. As they climbed the slope to the electric vehicle, Pablo Cole came to Raj's side.

"Indeed, I hope that this will be the end of this unfortunate affair," he said. "Now that all has been fully and honestly revealed—"

"You can skip all that," Raj said. "You're nine years late. The crew was still alive when the investigation team called, I imagine. You killed them—or let them die—rather than take the chance of admitting what you'd done."

"We were at fault," Pablo Cole said abjectly. "Now we wish only cooperation."

"The Discovery was a major research vessel, about fifteen thousand tons." Raj looked grimly at the slender Environmental Resources official. "Where is she, Cole? I won't settle for a thousand-ton lifeboat."

Pablo Cole's eyes widened in shock.

"I know nothing of... of..." He stopped. His throat worked rapidly as he struggled for composure.

"My government can entertain no further accusations, Mr. Yates," he said at last. "I have been completely candid with you. I have overlooked your intrusion into matters not properly within your jurisdiction. My patience is at an end."

"Where is that vessel?" Raj demanded. "You never learn, do you? You're still convinced you can hide the whole thing and forget it. I'm telling you you can't."

"We return to Victorville now," Pablo Cole said. "I can do no more."

"You can and you will, Cole," Raj said. "I intend to get to the truth of this matter."

Pablo Cole spoke to Lucas Ramirez in rapid Zelvarian. The security chief gestured to his four armed officers. They moved to surround Raj.

Raj eyed Pablo Cole. "Don't try it," he said. "You'll just make things worse for yourself."

Pablo Cole's jaw tightened, his posture aggressive toward the Terrestrial.

"Out of deference to your diplomatic status, Terrestrial, I shall ignore your insulting remarks," Pablo Cole said. "Let us now return to the city."

Raj looked at the four officers. "I see your point," he said.

Pablo Cole followed him into the vehicle, sat rigidly at the far end of the seat.

"I advise you to remain very close to your agency office," Pablo Cole said. "I advise you to dismiss these theories from your mind, and to appreciate the cultural aspects of life in Zelvaria. Especially, I should not venture out of Victorville, or appear overly curious about matters of concern only to the Zelvarian government."

In the front seat, Lucas Ramirez looked straight ahead. The smoothly-operating vehicle hummed along the paved highway. Raj listened to the quiet electric motor and said nothing.

III

"Ms. Potter," Raj said, "I want you to listen carefully to what I'm going to tell you. I have to move rapidly now, to catch the Zelvarians off guard."

"I'm sure I don't know what you're talking about," Megan Potter snapped, her eyes sharp behind the heavy lenses.

"If you'll listen, you may find out," Raj said. "I have no time to waste, Ms. Potter. They won't be expecting an immediate move—I hope—and that may give me the opportunity I need."

"You're still determined to make an issue of that incident!" Megan Potter said. "I can hardly blame the Zelvarians. They are not a technologically advanced race; they had never before encountered aliens on their planet."

"You're ready to forgive a great deal, Ms. Potter. But it's not what happened nine years ago I'm concerned with. It's what's happening now. I've told you that it was only a lifeboat the Zelvarians have hidden. Don't you understand the implication? That vessel couldn't have traveled far on its own. The research ship itself must be somewhere nearby. I want to know where!"

"The Zelvarians don't know. They're a very traditional, peaceful people. You can do irreparable harm to the reputation of Terrestrials if you insist—"

"That's my decision," Raj said. "I have a job to do and we're wasting time." He crossed the room to his desk, opened a drawer and took out a compact stunner.

"This office is being monitored. Not very efficiently, if I know the Zelvarians. I think I can get past their surveillance."

"Where are you going with... that?" Megan Potter stared at the stunner. "What in the world—"

"The Zelvarians won't waste any time destroying every document in their files relating to this thing. I have to get what I need before it's too late. If I wait for an official Investigation Commission, they'll find nothing but cooperative smiles."

"You're out of your mind!" Megan Potter stood up, shaking with indignation. "You're like a... a..."

"You and I are in a precarious position, Ms. Potter. The logical next move for the Zelvarians is to eliminate both of us. We're the only ones who know what happened. Cole almost arranged that this afternoon, but I deterred him—for the moment."

Megan Potter emitted a sharp laugh. "Your paranoid fantasies are getting the better of you," she gasped. "In danger, indeed! Eliminating me! I've never heard anything so absurd."

"Stay in this office. Secure the door with the safety lock. You've got food and water in the dispenser. I suggest you stock up, before they shut the utilities down. Don't let anyone in, on any pretext whatever. I'll keep in touch with you via secure communicator."

"What are you planning to do?"

"If I don't make it back here, transmit the sealed record of this afternoon's conversation, along with the information I've given you. Send it through on an emergency priority. Then inform the Zelvarians what you've done and stay secure. I think you'll be safe. It won't be easy to break in here and anyway, they won't make things worse by harming you. A response team can be here in a week."

"I'll do nothing of the sort! The Zelvarians are very respectful of me! You... newcomer! Troublemaker! Setting out to destroy—"

"Blame it on me if it will make you feel any better," Raj said, "but don't be foolish enough to trust them." He pulled on a dark jacket, opened the door.

"I'll be back in a couple of hours," he said. Megan Potter stared after him silently as he closed the door.

It was an hour before dawn when Raj entered the combination to the security lock and stepped into the darkened agency office. He looked exhausted.

Megan Potter, dozing in a chair, awoke with a start. She looked at Raj, rose and activated a light, turned to stare.

"What in the world—Where have you been? What's happened to your clothing?"

"I got a little dirty. Don't worry about it." Raj went to his desk, opened a drawer and replaced the stunner.

"Where have you been?" Megan Potter demanded. "I stayed here—"

"I'm glad you did," Raj said. "I hope you stocked up on food and water from the dispenser, too. We'll be secured here for a week, at least." He made notes on a tablet. "Activate the official transmitter. I have a long transmission for Regional Headquarters."

"Are you going to tell me where you've been?"

"I have a message to send first, Ms. Potter," Raj said sharply. "I've been to the Environmental Ministry," he added. "I'll tell you all about it later."

"At this hour? There's no one there..."

"Exactly."

Megan Potter gasped. "You mean you broke in? You burglarized the Environmental Ministry?"

"That's right," Raj said calmly. "Now—"

"This is absolutely the end!" Megan Potter said. "Thank heaven I've already—"

"Get that transmitter active, woman!" Raj snapped. "This is critical."

"I've already done so, Mr. Yates!" Megan Potter said harshly. "I've been waiting for you to return here..." She turned to the communicator, activated controls. The screen illuminated, and a wavering long-distance image appeared.

"He's here now," Megan Potter said to the screen. She looked at Raj triumphantly.

"That's good," Raj said. "I don't think the Zelvarians can interrupt our transmission, but—"

"I have done my duty, Mr. Yates," Megan Potter said. "I made a full report to Regional Headquarters last night, as soon as you left this office. Any doubts I may have had as to the correctness of that decision have been completely dispelled by what you've just told me."

Raj looked at her levelly. "You've been busy, Ms. Potter. Did you mention the six Terrestrials who died here?"

"That had no bearing on the matter of your reckless behavior! I must say, in all my years with the Agency, I've never encountered a personality less suited to diplomatic liaison work."

The screen crackled, the transmission delay having elapsed. "Mr. Yates," the face on the screen said, "I am Director Sophie Leonard, Regional Coordinator. I have received a report on your conduct which makes it mandatory for me to relieve you administratively, with Ms. Megan Potter assuming interim authority. Pending the findings of a Review Board, you will—"

Raj reached out and deactivated the communicator. The triumphant look faded from Megan Potter's face.

"Why, what is the meaning—"

"If I'd listened any longer, I might have heard something I couldn't disregard. I can't afford that, at this moment. Listen, Ms. Potter," Raj went on earnestly, "I've found the missing research vessel."

"You heard her relieve you!"

"I heard her say she was going to, Ms. Potter. But until I've received and acknowledged a formal order, it has no authority. If I'm wrong, she'll get my resignation. If I'm right, that suspension would be embarrassing all around."

"You're defying legitimate authority! I'm in charge here now." Megan Potter stepped to the local communicator.

"I'm going to report this terrible thing to the Zelvarians at once, and offer my profound—"

"Don't touch that screen," Raj said. "You go sit in that corner where I can monitor you. I'm going to make a sealed transmission for Regional Headquarters, along with a request for an armed response team. Then we'll settle in to wait."

Raj ignored Megan Potter's protests as he spoke into the recorder.

The local communicator chimed. Megan Potter jumped up, staring at it.

"Go ahead," Raj said. "Answer it."

A Zelvarian official appeared on the screen.

"Megan Potter," he said without preamble, "on behalf of the Environmental Minister of the Zelvarian Republic, I hereby recognize you as Terrestrial Agricultural Liaison to Zelvaria, in accordance with the communications transmitted to my government directly from Terrestrial Regional Headquarters. As liaison, you are requested to make available for questioning Mr. Raj Yates, former liaison, in connection with the assault on a citizen and illegal entry into the offices of the Ministry of Environmental Resources."

"Why, why," Megan Potter stammered. "Yes, of course. And I do want to express my deepest regrets—"

Raj rose, went to the communicator, moved Megan Potter aside.

"Listen carefully, Cole," he said. "Your deception has been exposed. You don't come in and we don't come out. Your concealment worked for nine years, but it's finished now. I suggest you keep your composure and resist the temptation to make matters worse than they are."

"Ms. Potter," Pablo Cole said, "a security team waits outside your agency office. It is clear you are in the custody of a dangerous individual. As always, the Zelvarians wish only cooperation with the Terrestrials, but—"

"Don't bother," Raj said. "You know what was in those files I reviewed this morning."

Raj turned at a sound behind him. Megan Potter was at the door, reaching for the security lock release...

"Don't!" Raj moved—too late.

The door burst inward. A group of uniformed Zelvarians pressed into the room, pushed Megan Potter back, aimed weapons at Raj. Security Chief Lucas Ramirez pushed forward.

"Attempt no resistance, Terrestrial," he said. "I cannot guarantee to restrain my officers."

"You're violating Terrestrial territory, Ramirez," Raj said steadily. "I suggest you withdraw the same way you entered."

"I invited them here," Megan Potter spoke up. "They are here at my express authorization."

"Are they? Are you sure you meant to go this far, Ms. Potter? A squad of armed Zelvarians in the agency office?"

"You are the liaison, Ms. Megan Potter," Lucas Ramirez said. "Would it not be prudent if we removed this unstable person to a secure location?"

"You're making a serious mistake, Ramirez," Raj said.

"Yes," Megan Potter said. "You're quite right, Mr. Ramirez. Please escort Mr. Yates to his quarters in this building—"

"I don't advise you to violate my diplomatic immunity, Cole," Raj said.

"As chief of mission," Megan Potter said quickly, "I hereby waive immunity in the case of Mr. Yates."

Lucas Ramirez produced a recording device. "Kindly repeat your statement, Madam, officially," he said. "I wish no question to arise later."

"Don't be a fool, woman," Raj said. "Don't you see what you're setting yourself up for? This would be an excellent time for you to figure out whose side you're on."

"I'm on the side of proper conduct!"

"You've been deceived. These people are concealing—"

"You think all women are fools, don't you, Mr. Yates?" She turned to the security chief and spoke into the microphone he held up.

"That's an illegal waiver," Raj said. "I'm liaison here, whatever communications you've received. This situation is coming into the open, whatever you do. Don't add violation of the Agency office to the list of Zelvarian crimes."

"Detain him," Lucas Ramirez said.
question: Of what species is Megan Potter and Raj Yates?
option_a: They are both Terrestrials (humans from Earth)
option_b: They are both Zelvarians
correct_answer_text: They are both Terrestrials (humans from Earth)
incorrect_answer_text: They are both Zelvarians
explanation: Throughout the story, Megan Potter and Raj Yates are consistently referred to as Terrestrials working for the Terrestrial Development Agency. They are contrasted with the Zelvarians (Pablo Cole, Lucas Ramirez, and other locals), who are described as a separate species native to the planet Zelvaria. The story makes it clear that Raj and Megan are human diplomatic/liaison personnel from Earth stationed on an alien world.
