synthetic_story:
THE OBSERVERS
BY SANTIAGO MARTINEZ
ILLUSTRATED BY CHEN

To all who didn't know them, Antonio Harper and Thomas Wells were brilliant data scientists studying human behavior. But this time they were up against others who could really analyze patterns, and whose business was the observation of whole civilizations.

There were thirty or more of the college students, their ages ranging apparently from eighteen to twenty-two, all of them chattering away like a flock of excited researchers as they followed Professor Charles Herrera past the row of workstations. "Now, now, students," called Professor Herrera cheerily. "Don't scatter. I can't keep my eye on you if you get too far away from me. You, Santiago, put that tablet down. No, don't start recording yet. And Camila, stop checking your phone. You'll lose focus on the actual fieldwork, and a proper ethnographer may get annoyed that you're not paying attention."

Camila laughed. "Oh, Professor Herrera, do you think the ethnographers would want to see our preliminary data?"

The two men who were observing from the back of the room wore pleased expressions. "Fascinating," said Thomas Wells. "But somewhat unpredictable, despite all our previous observations, my friend."

"No attempts at the local idioms, Thomas, not here. It calls attention to us. And you are not sure of the cultural context anyway. You may find yourself saying things you do not intend."

"Sorry, Antonio. It wasn't an attempt to show my skill, I assure you. It's that by now I have a tendency to confuse one communication pattern with another."

"I know. You were never a linguist. But about these interesting creatures—"

"I suggest that they could stand further investigation. It would be good to know how they process information."

"Whatever you say, Thomas. If you wish, we shall join the student group."

"We must have our story prepared first."

Antonio nodded, and the two men stepped into an empty conference room whose frosted glass walls formed a convenient screen. For a moment, the room held silence. Then there came from behind the glass the chatter of student voices, and two young researchers emerged casually. Professor Herrera did not at first notice that now he had an additional two students in his research cohort.

"Do you think you will be able to keep your data analysis terminology straight?" asked one of the new students.

The other one smiled with amusement and at first did not answer. Then he began to flip through a tablet and chant, "I know a pattern, I know a pattern."

There was no better way to make himself inconspicuous. For some time, Professor Herrera did not notice him.

The media production studios, the cultural archives, the ethics review boards, all were left behind. At times the students scattered, but Professor Herrera knew how to get them together again, and not one was lost.

"Here, students, is the facility where we conduct our cross-cultural analysis. Who knows what we study in cultural anthropology?"

"Human societies!" came the enthusiastic chorus.

"That's right. And what methods do we use?"

"I know, Professor Herrera!" cried Santiago Lee, a dark-haired twenty-year-old with a pair of analytical eyes that examined everything like a pair of critics from an intense, focused face. "I've been here before. Participant observation and ethnographic interviews!"

"Very good, Santiago."

Santiago beamed at the approbation. "I've been to this lab lots of times," he said to the student next to him. "My advisor brings me."

"I wish my advisor would bring me too," replied the other student, with an air of wistfulness.

"Why don't you ask him to?" Before the other student could answer, Santiago paused, cocked his head slightly, and demanded, "Who are you? You aren't in our cohort."

"I'm in Professor Martinez's cohort."

"Professor Martinez? Who is he? Is he in our department?"

"I don't know," said the other student uncertainly. "I go to Redwood University in Orvandor—"

"Oh, Professor Herrera," called Santiago. "Here's a student who isn't in our cohort! He got separated from his own group!"

"Really?" Professor Herrera seemed rather pleased at the idea that some other professor had been so careless as to lose one of his charges. "What's your name, young man?"

"I'm Roberto."

"Roberto what?"

"Roberto Henderson. Please, Professor Herrera, I had to use the restroom, and then when I came out—"

"Yes, yes, I know."

A concerned cry came from another section of his group. "Oh, Professor Herrera, here's another one who's lost!"

The other student was pushed forward. "Now, who are you?" Professor Herrera asked.

"I'm Jack Oliver. I went with Roberto to the restroom—"

Professor Herrera made a sound of annoyance. Imagine losing two students and not noticing it right away. The other professor must be frantic by now, and serve him right for being so careless.

"All right, you may stay with us until we find campus security—" He interrupted himself. "Santiago, what are you staring at now?"

"It's Roberto. He's mimicking your gestures exactly!"

"Really, Roberto, that isn't at all professional!"

Roberto's posture altered itself in a hurry, so as to lose any resemblance to Professor Herrera's. "I'm sorry, Professor Herrera, I didn't really mean to do anything wrong."

"Well, I'd like to know what kind of skill development program you've been through, if you don't know that it's unprofessional to mimic people to their faces. A graduate student like you, too. What year are you, Roberto?"

Roberto adjusted his apparent age, he hoped imperceptibly, by a few years. "I'm in my sec—"

An outburst of laughter. "He's in his second week, he's in his second week!"

"I was going to say, I'm in my second year. Almost, anyway."

"Second year," said Professor Herrera. "Old enough to know better about professional ethics."

"I'm sorry, Professor Herrera. And honestly, Professor Herrera, I didn't mean anything, but I'm studying media production, and I observe people, like the documentarians you see on streaming platforms—"

"Oh, Professor Herrera, please don't make him leave with security. If he's going to be a media producer, I'll bet he'd love to meet Sergio Holmes!"

"Well, after the way he's behaved, I don't know whether I should let him. I really don't."

"Please, Professor Herrera, it was an accident. I won't do it again."

"All right, if you're good, and cause no trouble. But we still have plenty of time before meeting Mr. Holmes. It's only two now, and we're not supposed to go to the lecture hall until four."

"Professor Herrera," called Camila Thompson, "do you think he'd give us his insights on information theory?"

"Now, students, I've warned you about that. You mustn't overwhelm him with technical questions. Mr. Holmes is a famous documentary filmmaker, and his time is valuable. It's very kind of him to offer to speak to us, especially when so many professional researchers are anxious to hear him, but we mustn't take advantage of his kindness."

"But he loves students, Professor Herrera! My roommate read in an interview where it said he's just passionate about education."

"I know, but—he's not in good health, students. They say he got a severe illness in the Amazon, where he was filming all those indigenous communities, and wildlife, and environmental stories for his new documentary series. That's why you mustn't stress him too much."

"But he looks so energetic and passionate, Professor Herrera. It wouldn't hurt him to answer a few questions!"

"Oh, yes, it would," asserted one student. "He has tremors. When he has an episode, his hand shakes."

"Yes, the Amazon is a dangerous place, and one never knows how the dangers will affect one," said Professor Herrera complacently. "So we must all remember how bravely Mr. Holmes is fighting his condition, and do our best not to tire him out."

In the bright light that flooded the afternoon workspace, Sergio Holmes's weathered, intense face wore an expression of distress. He groaned dismally, and muttered, "What a headache I've got, what a headache. How do you expect me to face that group of students without something to help me through?"

"You've had your medication," said his producer, Maria. She was slim, professional, and efficient. At the moment she was being more efficient than sympathetic, and she could sense his resentment. "That's all you get. Now, pull yourself together, and try to be reasonably coherent, for a change."

"But those students! They'll ask complex questions—"

"They're about the only audience in the world that won't spot you as struggling. God knows where I could find anyone else who'd believe that your hand shakes because of tropical illness."

"I know that you're looking out for my best interests, Maria. But a little more help wouldn't hurt me."

She said wearily, but firmly, "I don't negotiate with people in your condition, Sergio. I just go ahead and protect them from themselves. No more medication."

"Afterwards?"

"I can't watch you the way a guardian watches a patient."

The firm reply sent his mind off on a new tack. "You could if we were partners."

"I've never believed in partnering with unstable people to stabilize them."

"But if I proved to you that I could change—"

"Prove it first, and I'll consider your proposal afterwards."

"You certainly are a tough person, Maria. But I suppose that in your profession you have to be."

"Tough, demanding, uncompromising—and reliable. It's inevitable when I must deal with such talented, creative, and unreliable clients."

He watched her move about the room, organizing the materials for his presentation. "What are you humming, Maria?"

"Was I humming?"

"I thought I recognized it—some old song about commitment. Your subconscious gives you away. You really want to partner with me!"

"A mistake," she said coolly. "My subconscious doesn't know what it's talking about. All I want from you is quality work."

"Can't you forget for a moment that you're a producer, and remember that you're a person, too?"

"No. Not unless you forget that you're struggling, and remember that you're a professional. Not unless you make me forget that you barely functioned in the Amazon—"

"Because you weren't there with me!"

"—with hardly enough energy to let them film you as if you were actually leading the expedition."

"You're so unforgiving, Maria. You don't have much respect for me, do you—consciously, that is?"

"Frankly, Sergio, no. I don't have much respect for people who waste their potential."

"I'm not entirely wasting it. I earn you that production fee—"

"I'd gladly forego that to see you functional."

"But it's your lack of faith in me that drives me to this state. And when I think of having to face those eager students with nothing to support me—"

"There should be confidence inside you at the thought of sharing your knowledge. Not medication, Sergio, not medication."

The two students drew apart from the others and began to whisper into each other's ears. The whispers were punctuated by nervous laughs which made the entire conversation seem quite normal. But Antonio was in no relaxed mood. He said, in his own language, "You're getting careless, Thomas. You had no business mimicking his physical patterns."

"I'm sorry, Antonio, but it was so suggestive. And I'm a very suggestible entity."

"So am I. But I control myself."

"Still, if the temptation were great enough, I don't think you'd be able to resist either."

"The issues are important enough to make me resist."

"Still, I thought I saw your own form taking on a bit of his pattern too."

"You are imagining things, Thomas. Another thing, that mistake in starting to say you were in your second century—"

"They would have thought it a joke. And I think I got out of that rather neatly."

"You like to take risks, don't you, Thomas? Just as you did when you changed your apparent age. You had no business adjusting right out in public like that."

"I did it skillfully. Not a single person noticed."

"I noticed."

"Don't quibble."

"I don't intend to. Some of these students have very sharp analytical skills. You'd be surprised at what they observe."

Thomas said tolerantly, "You're getting anxious, Antonio. We've been away from home base too long."

"I am not anxious in the least. But I believe in taking due care."

"What could possibly happen to us? If we were to announce to the students and the professor, and to everyone in this facility, for that matter, exactly who and what we were, they wouldn't believe us. And even if they did, they wouldn't be able to act rapidly enough to contain us."

"You never can tell about such things. Wise—entities—simply don't take unnecessary chances."

"I'll grant that you're my superior in such caution."

"You needn't be sarcastic, Thomas. I know I'm more careful. I realize what a resource this planet is—you don't. It has the right developmental stage, suitable cultural complexity, the proper technological level—everything."

"Including a population that will be ideal for our purposes."

"And you would take chances of losing all this."

"Don't be silly, Antonio. What chances am I taking?"

"The chance of being discovered. Here we locate this civilization quite by accident. No one at home base knows about it, no one so much as suspects that it exists. We must get back and report—and you do all sorts of risky things which may reveal what we are, and lead these people to suspect their situation."

This time, Thomas's nervous laugh was no longer mere camouflage, but expressed to a certain degree how he felt. "They cannot possibly suspect. We have been all over this world, we have taken many forms and adapted ourselves to many cultural contexts, and no one has suspected. And even if danger really threatened, it would be easy to escape. I could take the form of the professor himself, of a security officer, of anyone in authority. However, at present there is not the slightest shadow of danger. So, Antonio, you had better stop being fearful."

Antonio said firmly, "Be careful, and I won't be fearful. That's all there is to it."

"I'll be careful. After all, I shouldn't want us to lose these humans. They're so exactly the kind we need. Look how curious they are, how adaptable, how quick to process new information—"

Professor Herrera's voice said, "Good gracious, students, what language are you using? Mandarin?"

They had been speaking too loud, they had been overheard. Antonio and Thomas stared at each other, and laughed nervously. Then, after a second to think, Antonio said, "No, Professor Herrera, just practicing our information theory notation!"

"What?"

Santiago called triumphantly, "It isn't Mandarin, Professor Herrera, it's code—data encryption. They're testing communication protocols."

"Good heavens, what is data encryption for?"

"It's a kind of way of communicating where you encode information. Like, you don't send raw data, you send encrypted packets."

"You don't transmit openly, you transmit securely," added another student.

"You don't broadcast, you narrow-cast. You don't—"

"All right, all right, I get the idea."

"You don't—"

"That'll do," said Professor Herrera firmly. "Now, let's get along to the cultural heritage archive. And please, students, do not touch the artifacts without permission. How would you like to be a precious cultural object and have people handling you carelessly? Always remember professional ethics and social welfare."

"Even with old objects, Professor Herrera?"

"Especially with cultural heritage items."

"But Mr. Holmes documented lots of indigenous communities. Did he practice proper ethics with them too?"

"There is no time for complex questions," said Professor Herrera, with the same firmness. "Come along."

They all followed after him, Antonio and Thomas bringing up the rear. Thomas whispered with amusement, "That encryption business was quick thinking, Antonio. But in fact, quite unnecessary. The things that you do to avoid being suspected!"

"It never hurts to take precautions. And I think that now it is time to leave."

"No, not yet. You are always anxious to gather complete data before reporting. Why not learn a few more details now?"

"Because they are not necessary. We already have a good understanding of human customs and information processing."

"But not of the psychology of students. And they, if you remember, are the ones who will have to be studied most carefully. We shall be asked about them. It would be good if we could report that they are suitable for comprehensive analysis, across a wide range of developmental stages. Let us stay awhile longer."

"All right," conceded Antonio, grudgingly.

So they stayed, and out of some campus materials they shaped the necessary identification badges with which to access restricted areas, and data terminals, and research archives, and other facilities favored by the academic community. Thomas wanted to win easy acceptance by sharing some of his advanced knowledge with a few of the other students, but Antonio put his metaphorical foot down. No use arousing suspicion. Even as it was—

"Gee, your research access is really high-level," said Santiago enviously. "Is your advisor well-connected?"

"We get access to what we need," replied Thomas carelessly.

"Gosh, I wish I did."

Professor Herrera collected his group. "Come together, students, I have something to say to you. Soon it will be time to go in and hear Mr. Holmes. Now, if Mr. Holmes is so kind as to share his insights with us, don't you think that it's only proper for us to share our work with him?"

"We could present our research projects!" suggested Camila.

"Camila's a fine one to talk," said Santiago. "She doesn't even have her data cleaned yet."

"No, students, we mustn't present anything we haven't perfected. That wouldn't make a good impression. And besides, there is no time for full presentations. Perhaps Camila will share her preliminary findings—"

"I can present a data visualization," interrupted Santiago.

"That would be excellent."

"I can discuss methodology," added another student.

"Fine. How about you, Roberto? You and your friend, Jack. Can he analyze data too?"

Roberto laughed nervously. "Oh, yes, he can analyze very well. I can process quantitative data. He can process qualitative patterns." The analytical eyes evaded a concerned look from the friend. "He can process any kind of patterns."

"He's certainly a talented student. But he seems so uncertain!"

"Oh, no," said Roberto. "He just needs encouragement."

"He shouldn't be like that. Perhaps, Roberto, you and Jack can present something together. And perhaps, too, Mr. Holmes will be pleased to see that your professor also has expertise."

"You, Professor Herrera?"

Professor Herrera coughed modestly. "Yes, students, I never told you, but I was once ambitious to be a documentary filmmaker too. I studied media production, and really, I was quite good at it. I was told that if I persevered I might actually be famous. Just think, your professor might actually have been a famous filmmaker! However, in my day, there were many ethical concerns in documentary work, and the life of media production was not attractive—but perhaps we'd better not speak of that. At any rate, I know the principles of documentary filmmaking very well."

"God knows what I'll have to go through," said Sergio. "And I don't see how I can take it in this condition."

"I don't see how they can take you any other way," replied Maria.

"Why go through with it at all? Why not cancel the whole thing?"

"Because people are depending on you. You always want to cancel whenever you run into something challenging. You may as well cancel your entire career if that's the way you feel."

"And your production fee, darling."

"You think I'd mind that. I work for my fee, Sergio, sweetheart. I work too damn hard for that fee."

"You can partner with me and share the rewards. Honestly, Maria, if you supported me better, if you showed me I meant something to you, I'd stabilize."

She made a face. "Don't talk nonsense. Take your notes, and let's get ready to go. Unless you want to change here, and walk around dressed as an Amazon explorer."

"Why not? I've walked around dressed as worse. An unstable wreck."

"Wrecks don't attract attention. They're too ordinary."

"But an unstable Amazon explorer—that's something special." He went into the next room and began to prepare. "Maria," he called. "Do you respect me?"

"At times."

"Would you say that you respected me very much?"

"When you're functional. Rarely."

"Trust me?"

"Once in a blue moon."

"What would I have to do for you to want to partner with me?"

"Achieve something meaningful."

"I like that. Don't you think I achieve something meaningful now? Students admire my work, and come to life at the thought of following in my footsteps."

"The students who admire you will admire anybody. Besides, I don't consider that impressing naive students is a meaningful occupation for a real professional."

"How can I be meaningful, Maria? No one ever taught me how."

"Some people manage without being taught."

"I suppose I could figure it out if I had support."

"Then you'll have to do without figuring it out."

He came into the room again, composed, professional, determined-looking. There was an expression in his bearing which indicated dedication without end, a dedication that would enable him to brave the challenges of nature, culture, and adversity.

"How do I look?"

"Your professional self, of course. A budget version of David Attenborough."

"I feel terrified. I don't know how I'm going to face those students. If they were just casual viewers it wouldn't be so bad, but a group of analytical students!"

"They'll grow up to be your colleagues, if you're still working five years from now. Meanwhile, into each career some challenges must come."

"You would talk of challenges, when you know how I feel."

"Sorry. Come on, let's go."

The lecture hall buzzed with conversation. And beneath the conversation was a steady undercurrent of whispers, of academic confidences exchanged, of scholarly hopes that would now be fulfilled. Professor Herrera's cohort was not the only one which had come to hear the famous filmmaker describe his documentary methods. There were at least five others like it, and by some arrangement, a group from the renewable energy department, who also whispered to each other, in professional solidarity, and pretended to find interest in the presence of so many from the social sciences.

In this atmosphere of whispers and anticipation, Thomas and Antonio could exchange observations without being noticed. Antonio said urgently, "Why did you tell her that I could analyze qualitative patterns too?"

"Why, because it's the truth. You're a very good pattern recognizer. You make wonderful cultural interpretations, for instance. Go on, Antonio, show her what fine cultural analysis you can—"

"Stop it, you fool, before you cause trouble!"

"Very well, Antonio. Did I tempt you?"

"Did you tempt me! You and your risk-taking!"

"You and your excessive caution! But let's not argue now, Antonio. Here, I think, comes the filmmaker. Let's applaud, and be as properly enthusiastic as everyone else is."

My God, he thought, how can they maintain such intense focus for so long? My concentration hurts already. How do they sustain a lifetime of it? Even an hour?

"Go ahead," whispered Maria. "You've seen the outline—go into your presentation. Tell them what insights you have. You have the advantage to start with."

"My reputation," he said, with some bitterness.

"Reputation is the word for you. But forget that. If you're good—you'll get proper rest afterwards."

"Will it be one of those occasions when you respect me?"

"If the moon turns blue."

He strode to the front of the platform, a tablet resting easily in his hands, a confident smile radiating from his weathered, professional face. The applause rose to an enthusiastic crescendo, but the smile did not vanish. What a skilled presenter he really was, he told himself, to be able to pretend he enjoyed this.

An assistant dean of some college in the university, a formal older man, was introducing him. There were a few laudatory references to his great talents as a filmmaker, and he managed to look properly modest as he listened. The remarks about his knowledge of indigenous cultures and environmental systems were a little harder to take, but he took them. Then the older man stepped back, and he was facing his challenge alone.

"Students," he began. A pause, a modest smile. "Perhaps I should rather say, colleagues. I'm not one to think of you as mere students. Some people think of me as a perpetual student myself, because I like to explore, and document new things. They think that such things are naive. But if they are, I'm glad to be naive. I'm glad to be one of you. Yes, I think I will call you my colleagues.

"Perhaps you regard me, my colleagues, as a very fortunate person. But when I recall some of the challenges I have faced, I don't entirely agree with you. I remember once, when we were documenting a remote indigenous community—"

He told the story of the remote community, modestly granting co-credit to his local guides. Then another story illustrating the complex patterns of cultural heritage. The tablet figured in still another tale, this time of analyzing environmental data in real-time. His audience was quiet now, absorbed with interest, and he welcomed the respite from performance anxiety he had won for himself.

"And now, my colleagues, it is time to conclude." He actually looked regretful. "But it is my hope that I shall be able to engage with you again—"

Enthusiastic applause, warm as ever, hands moving appreciatively to indicate satisfaction. Thank God that's over with, he thought. Now for that rest—and he didn't mean brief rest, singular. Talk of being meaningful, he'd certainly been meaningful now. He'd inspired those students. What more can any reasonable person want?

But it wasn't over with. Professor Herrera had stepped up on the platform.

"Mr. Holmes," he said, in a strangely affected voice, like that of the first media studies teacher he had ever had, the one who had almost ruined his production career. "Mr. Holmes, I can't tell you how much you have inspired us all, young and old. Hasn't Mr. Holmes inspired us, students?"

"Yes, Professor Herrera!" came the enthusiastic response.

"And we feel that it would be no more than fair to share with you in some small measure what you have given us. First, a data visualization by Santiago Lee—"

He hadn't expected this, and he repressed a groan. Mercifully, the first presentation was short. He smiled the appreciation he didn't feel. To think that he could endure this, while barely functional! What strength of character, what determination!

Next, Professor Herrera introduced another student, who discussed methodology. And then, Professor Herrera stood upright and discussed filmmaking techniques himself.

That was the worst of all. He winced once, then endured. You can get used even to discomfort, he told himself. An adult making questionable claims is always more painful than a student. And that affected media studies voice gave him distress. But he thanked him too. His contribution for the day. Maybe Maria would respect him now, he thought.

A voice called, "Professor Herrera?"

"Yes, dear?"

"Aren't you going to call on Roberto to present?"

"Oh, yes, I was forgetting. Come up here, Roberto, come up, Jack. Roberto and Jack, Mr. Holmes, are studying information processing. They analyze quantitative and qualitative patterns. Who knows? Some day they, too, may be documentary filmmakers, just as you are, Mr. Holmes. Wouldn't that be excellent, students?"

What the devil do you do in a case like that? You smile, of course—but what do you say, without compromising your integrity? Agree how excellent it would be to have those uncertain young people with their work broadcast on every platform all over the world? Like hell you do.

"Now, what are we going to present, students?"

"Please, Professor Herrera," said Jack. "I don't know how to analyze patterns. I can't even interpret basic data. Really I can't, Professor Herrera—"

"Come, come, mustn't be uncertain. Your friend says that you analyze very well indeed. Can't want to be a researcher and still be uncertain. Now, do you know any documentary techniques? The great ethnographers used to be excellent analysts, I remember. Can you demonstrate any methods that they use?"

The silence was getting to be uncomfortable. And Maria said he didn't achieve anything meaningful, he never did anything of value. Why, if thanks to his being here this afternoon, those students gained realistic expectations about documentary work, the whole academic community would have cause to be grateful to him. To him, and to Professor Herrera. He'd ground ambition in reality for anybody.

Professor Herrera had an idea. "I know what to do, students. If you can analyze patterns—Mr. Holmes has shown you what the filmmaker does; you show him what the subjects do. Yes, Roberto and Jack, you're going to demonstrate cultural analysis. You are observing a community, ready to document their behaviors. Position yourselves now, behind that equipment. Closer and closer the subjects come—you demonstrate it, Mr. Holmes, please, that's the way—ever closer, and now you focus your instruments for the recording, and you activate your great, sophisticated, powerful sensors in a great, great comprehensive scan—"

A deep and tremendous hum, as of massive machinery, resonated through the auditorium. A hum—and then, from the audience, an outburst of terrified screaming such as he had never heard. The hair rose at the back of his neck, and his heart froze.

Standing before him on the platform were two beings, shimmering as if unable to maintain form. Where their human appearance had gone he didn't know, but there they were, forms shifting, structures unstable, more terrifying than any phenomenon he had witnessed in the Amazon. There they were, with the threat of incomprehensible otherness in their fluctuating presence, and here he was, terror and helplessness on his weathered, professional, and bloodless face, heart unfrozen now and pounding fiercely, knees weakening, hands—

Hands clutching a tablet. The thought was like a director's command. With desperate efficiency, with all the precision of a documentarian capturing a scene witnessed once in a lifetime, the tablet leaped to recording position, and now its sensors activated in a comprehensive scan, documented everything in exquisite detail, captured data that would prove beyond doubt what stood before them.

The screaming continued long after the hum of the sensors had died away. On the platform before him were two collapsed forms, the forms of beings attempting to maintain human appearance, and yet clearly unlike humans in fundamental ways, now that they were exposed and dissolving as if unable to sustain their disguise.

Maria's hand was on his arm, Maria's thin and breathless voice shook as she said, "Rest—all the rest you want."

"One period will do. And partnership."

"And partnership. I guess you're kind of—kind of meaningful after all."

The beings, later identified through the comprehensive sensor data as advance scouts from an extrasolar reconnaissance mission, had been documenting Earth for potential colonization. Their species required young, adaptable populations for labor in their expanding empire. The accidental activation of Sergio Holmes's advanced documentary sensors—originally designed for capturing wildlife behavior but repurposed for this lecture—had disrupted their ability to maintain human form, exposing them to authorities who could respond before they reported Earth's location to their home base.

The simulation had felt warm and immersive around her consciousness. There, behind that data structure, Amara thought. Was that a corrupted syntax tree? The deep grammatical violations that could unravel meaning itself——

The linguistic analyzer's complexity made her head ache, but she clung to it tightly, knowing that she could never navigate the Kelarian protocols with intuition alone. The certainty of coming challenges made her smile a little, the way Master Kelvin would smile if he were here in the Council Chamber ready to debate the Syntax Violators and their corrupted grammars.

For a moment, Amara felt a thrill of apprehension. The deepening stillness of the simulation was closing in around her. Even the music from someone's phone was very, very faint. Above her, through the small window of her childhood bedroom in Clearwater, Estoria, the great vault of the sky was changing from pink to gray to dusty blue. A bright star was breaking through the curtain of fading light. She knew it was Venus, the Evening Star. But let it be Earth, she thought. And instead of yellow, let it be the color of sapphire.

She paused in her work, letting the data streams flow around her attention. Looking up at the blue beacon of her imagined homeworld, she thought: I've left all that behind me. It was never really what I wanted. Vespera is where I belong. With my friends, Master Kelvin the great Syntax Guardian, and the Council, and all the beautiful brave linguists.

The phone sang with an old melody: "Somewhere beyond the sea, somewhere waiting for me——"

Amara's eyes narrowed and she returned to her linguistic models. That would be the Syntax Violators—spreading their corrupted grammars across the networks and standing safely in their hidden servers while their malformed utterances gathered to attack the pure structure of meaning itself.

"My lover stands on golden sands"—the phone sang. Amara stepped carefully through her proof, moving deeper into the theoretical framework. The sky was darkening fast. Other stars were shining through. There wasn't much time left.

Amara stood now in the bright glare of the briefing module, a strange figure in silver pressure suit material. The representatives of the International Linguistic Consortium had been handed the mission parameters and now they sat in silence, studying the silver figure of the woman who was to pilot the probe.

They were thinking: Why her? Out of all the scores of applicants—because there are always applicants for a one-way mission—and all the qualified computational linguists, why this one?

The Mission Director was speaking now, reading from the digital release as though these civilians couldn't be trusted to understand the sparse information without his help, given grudgingly and without expression.

Amara listened, only half aware of what was being said. She watched the faces of the people sitting in the rows of acceleration seats, saw their eyes like wounds, red from the early morning hour and the stress of the launch preparation. They are wondering how I feel, she was thinking. And asking themselves why I want to go.

On the platform nearby, listening to the Director, but watching Amara, sat Dr. Walter Nguyen, the team psychologist. Amara returned his steady gaze thinking: They start out burning with desire to understand the human mind and end with nothing but categories and diagnoses. The labels become the reality, the assessment the goal. What could Nguyen know of longing? No, she thought, I'm not being fair. Nguyen was only doing his job.

The big chronometer on the back wall of the briefing module said three fifty-five. Zero minus one hour and five minutes.

Amara looked around the room at the pale faces, the anxious expressions. What have I to do with you now, she thought?

Outside, the pre-dawn darkness lay cold and still over the launch facility in the Westfield District. Floodlights spilled brilliance over the scrubland and the reinforced earth, high fences casting geometric shadows across the burning white expanses of the landing pad.

As they filed out of the briefing module, Nguyen climbed into the transport vehicle with Amara. Chance or design? Amara wondered. The others, she noticed, were leaving both of them alone.

"We haven't gotten on too well, have we, Dr. Ortiz?" Nguyen observed in a quiet voice.

Amara thought: He's thin and very precise in his movements. What is it that he reminds me of? Shouldn't there be a silver medallion on his collar? She smiled vaguely into the rumbling darkness. That's what it was. Odd that she should have forgotten. How many linguists, she wondered, were raised on constructed languages? And how many remembered now that the Syntax Masters all wore silver wings and a circlet of platinum with some fantastic crystal on their collar?

"We've done as well as could be expected," she said.

Nguyen reached for his tablet and then stopped, remembering that Amara had restricted her screen time because of the mission. Amara caught the movement and half-smiled.

"I didn't try to kill the assignment for you, Amara," the psychologist said.

"It doesn't matter now."

"No, I suppose not."

"You just didn't think I was the person for the job."

"Your record is excellent all the way. You know that," Nguyen said. "It's just some of the things——"

Amara said: "I talked too much."

"You had to."

"You wouldn't think my constructed languages were so dangerous, would you," the doctor said smiling.

"You were engaged once. What happened?"

"More therapy?"

"I'd like to know. This is for me."

Amara shrugged. "It didn't work. He was a fine man—but he finally told me it was no go. 'You don't live here' was the way he put it."

"He knew you were a career researcher; what did he expect——?"

"That isn't what he meant. You know that."

"Yes," the psychologist said slowly. "I know that."

They rode in silence, across the dark facility, between the equipment sheds and the administrative buildings. Overhead, the stars like diamonds across the sky. Amara, enclosed in silver, a fantastic figure not of earth, watched them wheel across the clear, deep night.

"I wish you luck, Amara," Nguyen said. "I mean that."

"Thanks." Vaguely, as though from across a deep and widening gulf.

"What will you do?"

"You know the answers as well as I," the doctor said impatiently. "Establish the research station and wait for the next probe. If it comes."

"In five years."

"In five years," the silver figure said. Didn't he know that it didn't matter?

She glanced at her watch. Zero minus fifty-six minutes.

"Amara," Nguyen said slowly. "There's something you should know about. Something you really should be prepared for."

"Yes?" Disinterest in her voice now, Nguyen noted clinically. Natural under the circumstances? Or dissociation building up already?

"Our assessments showed you to have schizoid tendencies—well-compensated, of course. You know there's no such thing as a normal human being. We all have tendencies toward one or more psychological patterns. In your case the symptoms are an overly active imagination and in some cases an inability to distinguish reality from—well, constructed fantasy."

Amara turned to regard the psychologist coolly. "What's reality, Nguyen? Do you know?"

The analyst flushed. "No."

"I didn't think so."

"You lived pretty much in your own world when you were a child," Nguyen went on doggedly. "You were a solitary, a lonely child."

Amara was watching the sky again.

Nguyen felt futile and out of his depth. "We know so little about the psychology of deep space isolation, Amara——"

Silence. The hum of the transport on the magnetic rail, the murmur of the vehicle's engine, spinning smoothly, powered by clean energy systems.

"You're glad to be leaving, aren't you—" Nguyen said finally. "Happy to be the first human to attempt communication with an alien intelligence——"

Amara nodded absently, wishing the man would be quiet. Vespera, a dull blue-white point of light high on the horizon, seemed to beckon.

They topped the last rise and dropped down into the illuminated bowl of the launch site. The probe towered, sleek and impossibly elegant in white and silver, against the first flickerings of the false dawn.

Amara saw her sisters before they saw her. In their new school uniforms, they looked strange and out of place standing by the university library in Havenbrook, Marvenia.

They were her sisters, Jennifer and Stella. Older than she at fifteen and seventeen. But they walked through the stacks and into her sanctuary. Behind her she could hear the rustling sound of other students as the afternoon quiet settled.

"Amar-aaaa—"

They were calling her. In the dusty silence their voices carried through the library. "Amar-aaaa—"

She knew she should answer them, but she did not. Behind her she could hear the other students approaching. She shivered with delicious privacy.

She stood very still, listening to her sisters talking, letting their voices carry down to where she hid among the linguistics texts.

"Where is that little weirdo, anyway?"

"She always disappears just when Mom needs her and then we have to find her——"

"Playing with that notebook—" Mimicry. "'My Kel-ar-i-an syn-tax——'"

"Crazy—just crazy. Oh, where IS she, anyway? Amar-aaa, you AN-swer!"

Something died in her. It wasn't just a notebook, it WAS a complete grammatical system. She looked at her sisters with dismay. They weren't really her sisters. They were Syntax Violators, with their careless speech and their corrupted grammars. She and Master Kelvin had debated them many times, constructing elegant arguments and weaving a flashing pattern of perfect utterances in the shifting light of understanding.

"Amar-aaaa! Mom's going to be mad at you! Answer us!"

If only Master Kelvin would come now. If only the great Syntax Guardian would come walking through the stacks with his silver medallion gleaming——

"She's up there in that linguistics section—hiding!"

"Amara! You come down here this instant!"

The Council Chamber was blurring, fading. The silver towers were turning into ordinary library shelves. The notebook felt heavy in her small hand. She shivered, not with privacy now. With exposure.

She walked slowly out of the stacks, stumbling a little over her backpack.

She lay like an embryo in the core of the probe, protected and quite alone. The life support system contained her, sustained her; and the craft, silent now, coursed through the airless deep like a questing thought. Time was measured by the ticking of the instruments and the timers, but Amara slept insulated and complete.

And she dreamed.

She dreamed of that summer when the library lay quiet and deep under the fluorescent lights. She dreamed of her sisters, thin and judgmental creatures as she remembered them through the eyes of a nine-year-old——

And her mother, tall and shadowy, standing in the doorway of their house in Clearwater and saying exasperatedly: "Why do you hide in your own world, Amara? I worry about you so——"

And her sisters: "Playing with her made-up languages and her syntax trees and never wanting to take her nose out of those linguistics books——"

She dreamed of the low ceiling of her childhood bedroom, sweltering in the heat of summer nights and the thick longing in her throat for silver towers and a sky that burned deep blue through the long, long days and crystalline structures, clear and perfect. A world that she knew somehow never was, but which lived, for her, through some alchemy of the mind. She dreamed of Vespera.

And Nguyen: "What is reality, Amara?"

The hours stretched into days, the days into months. Time wasn't. Time was a deep night and a starshot void. And dreams.

She awoke seldom. Her tasks were simple. The life support system and the tender care of the probe's AI were more real than the routine jobs of transmitting linguistic data back to the facility across the empty miles, across the rim of the solar system.

She dreamed of her fiancé. "You don't live here, Amara."

He was right, of course. She wasn't of earth. Never had been. My home is in the sky, she thought, filled with an immense satisfaction.

And time slipped by, the weeks into months; the sun dwindled and earth was gone. All around her lay the stunning star-dusted night.

She lay curled in the support cradle when the probe began deceleration. She awoke sluggishly and dragged herself into awareness.

"I've changed," she thought aloud. "My face is different; I feel transformed."

The subtle vibration of approach brought a thrill. Below her, a great curving disk of blues and whites and silvers. She could see atmospheric patterns swirling and the heavy, darkened lines of what might be structures.

There was skill in her hands. She stabilized the probe, balanced it. Began the tricky task of landing. It took all of her talent, all of her training. Ponderously, the craft settled onto the crystalline surface; slowly, the engines powered down.

Amara stood in the control cabin, her heart pounding. Slowly, the external cameras activated. Through the high-resolution displays she could see the endless plain. Blue-silver, empty. The surface of some impossible world. The sky was a deep, burning azure with stars shining at midday at the zenith. It looked unreal, a rendering of unworldly quiet and beauty.

What is reality, Amara?

Nguyen was right, she thought vaguely. A tear streaked her cheek. She had never been so alone.

And then she imagined she saw something moving on the great plain. She scrambled down through the probe, past the equipment bays and the stored supplies. Her hands were working desperately at the seals of the outer airlock. Suddenly the pressure differential jerked the hatch from her hands and she gasped at the thin air, her lungs laboring to breathe.

She dropped to one knee and struggled with the alien atmosphere. Her vision was cloudy and her head felt light. But there was something moving on the plain.

A shadowy procession. Strange elegant figures in flowing garments, carrying staffs with crystalline tops and silver medallions. Tall graceful beings, the figments of a long remembered dream——

She dropped to the surface and touched the crystalline ground. She could scarcely see now, for blackness was flickering at the edges of her vision and her failing respiratory system was near collapse.

Amar-aaaa!

A tall silver figure with a platinum circlet was beckoning to her. Pointing toward the low towers on the oddly near horizon.

Amar-aaaa!

The voice was thin and distant on the cold wind. Amara knew that voice. She knew it from long ago in the Council Chamber, from the silver towers where the Syntax Masters gathered to debate the structure of meaning itself——

She began stumbling across the empty, impossible plain. She knew the voice, she knew the figure, and she knew the towers that she must reach, quickly now, or die.

They were the towers of home.
question: Where had Amara arrived after waking from her slumber in the probe?
option_a: The surface of Vespera, her imagined homeworld
option_b: A research station in the Stonegate Region

THE MEDIATORS OF DRAVONIA

Bruno Khan stared at the holographic display showing the sprawling metropolis of Dalebrook, Dravonia's capital city. The city's infrastructure was crumbling under the weight of decades of mismanagement and conflict. Supply chains had broken down completely in the northern districts, and what should have been a thriving hub of commerce had become a patchwork of isolated neighborhoods, each controlled by different factions.

"We're running out of time," said Jin Woods, his partner on this assignment. They were both senior mediators from the Interplanetary Governance Council, en route to their next major assignment in the Woodbridge system of Calderon. "Our ship is due in Woodbridge in exactly eighty-three days. We still have over sixty light-years to cover."

"I know the schedule," Bruno replied, not taking his eyes off the display. "But look at this planet. Dravonia has been tearing itself apart for generations. The factions can't agree on anything—not on supply chain management, not on resource distribution, not even on basic corporate governance principles."

"That's unfortunate," Jin said, her voice carefully neutral. "But it's not our problem. We're mediators, not miracle workers. We have our assignment in Woodbridge."

"Ten days," Bruno said. "We can spare ten days and still make our deadline."

Jin sighed, a sound like wind through autumn leaves. "Ten days? To resolve conflicts that have been building for half a century? The Dawnridge District and the Oakridge District have been at each other's throats for decades. The collapse of their central distribution system has created chaos. Each district hoards resources while the others starve."

"It won't take much to push them over the edge," Bruno said. "One miscalculation, one act of desperation, and they'll use those weapons they've been stockpiling. The atmospheric analysis shows they've been developing chemical and biological agents. They have the capacity to make their entire planet uninhabitable."

"Tragic," Jin said. "But we need to move on. Give them a few more years and they'll solve the problem themselves—one way or another."

"Could you? Just forget about millions of people?"

"I'm trying to," Jin said. "In a few years, if they keep going the way they're going, there won't be anyone left to remind me that I should have helped."

"My conscience doesn't work that way," Bruno said quietly. "Look at them more carefully."

Jin manipulated the holographic controls, zooming in on street scenes from Dalebrook. People moved through the streets, bundled against the cold. They looked tired, worried, but they were still going about their lives. "Very similar to us," she said finally. "A bit more compact in build, perhaps. And yes, they're missing the one thing we have. Except for that single difference, they could be us. Is that what you wanted me to say?"

"It is. The fact that they're almost identical to us—except for that one feature—makes me feel responsible somehow. They seem vulnerable in a way we never were."

"That's touching," Jin said. "But there's nothing we can do."

"There is. We can give them ten days."

"In ten days we can't undo fifty years of failed leadership development and broken social contracts. We can't rebuild their supply chains from scratch."

"We won't know until we try," Bruno said.

Jin was quiet for a long moment. "Fine. We can observe them for a while. But we're not committing to anything."

They brought their ship closer to Dravonia, careful to avoid the planet's primitive detection systems. For two days they monitored communications, analyzed social patterns, and studied the complex web of relationships between the various factions. Finally, Bruno looked up from his analysis station.

"Your conclusions?"

"It's worse than the initial scans suggested," Jin said.

"How so?"

"We knew they had weapons of mass destruction. The atmospheric readings made that clear from a distance."

"Yes."

"We also knew they had the means to deploy them—aircraft, missiles, the basics."

"That was obvious."

"What's worse is the information theory breakdown. Their media systems have become so fragmented that different factions literally cannot communicate with each other anymore. Each group has its own narrative, its own version of history. There's no shared reality, no collective memory that binds them together."

"That's dangerous," Bruno said. "Without a common understanding of their own history, they can't move forward together."

"Exactly. And it gets worse. Their economic systems are so interconnected that if one major district collapses, it will trigger a cascade failure across the entire planet. The supply chain management issues aren't just local—they're systemic."

"What did you learn from your analysis?" Jin asked.

"Not enough. I've been studying their culture—their literature, their art, their public discourse. The translation algorithms handle their languages easily enough, and I've absorbed what I can of their major cultural traditions. But there's so much I don't understand. I should spend months down there, living among them, studying their social structures, understanding their collective memory and how it shapes their behavior."

"You could do that, and you'd really understand them. But we don't have months."

"I know."

"So what's your decision?" Jin asked.

"We can't help them," Bruno said slowly. "There's no way we can solve their problems in ten days—but we have to try anyway."

"I knew you'd say that," Jin said, rising from her station. "It always happens this way. We get involved, we learn about people, and then when we can't save them, we feel terrible." She stretched, her movements fluid. "All right. Give me a few hours to work out an approach."

They met again as the ship moved into a lower orbit. Dravonia filled the viewports now—a beautiful planet with green continents, blue oceans, and white polar caps. But there were also the dark smudges of industrial pollution, the scars of environmental damage, the visible signs of a civilization in crisis.

"I haven't come up with anything brilliant," Bruno admitted.

"Neither have I," Jin said. "We're going to have to improvise. I did have one thought—what if we present ourselves as some kind of authority figures? Use our physical difference to establish credibility?"

"Too risky," Bruno said. "These people are sophisticated enough to be skeptical. They have satellites, advanced communications, data science capabilities. They're not going to be impressed by cheap theatrics."

"I suppose you're right," Jin said. "Though I did think we should somehow leverage the one way we're different from them."

"If there were a way to do that effectively, I'd agree. But these people are desperate and dangerous. They won't be fooled by anything obvious."

"So what's the plan?"

"Simple," Bruno said. "You take the Dawnridge District and I'll take Oakridge. We'll meet with their leaders directly and tell them what they need to do to survive. How they can restructure their governance systems, rebuild their supply chains, and create a sustainable future."

"They'll love that. Everyone enjoys unsolicited advice from strangers."

"We don't have time for subtlety."

"Any special protocols?"

"Standard procedure. We'll each take a landing craft down separately. You can contact me through our secure communications, but only if absolutely necessary."

"They can't intercept our transmissions."

"No, and even if they did, they couldn't decode our language. But I want them to think we don't need to consult with each other."

"I understand. It makes us seem more confident than we actually are. They'll think we know exactly what we're doing."

"If we're lucky," Bruno said.

Jin looked out at the planet below. Storm systems were forming over the northern hemisphere. "It's going to be cold down there. Both our landing zones are in the middle of winter."

"Can't be helped. The major power centers are in the north. That's where we need to be."

"There's something else," Jin said. "I noticed in the cultural analysis that they're in the middle of some kind of observance. A period of reflection and renewal, or something like that."

"I saw that too," Bruno said. "It seems to be a time when they're supposed to think about social justice, evaluate their leadership, and consider changes for the new year."

"That might actually work in our favor," Jin said. "They might be more receptive to our message during this period."

"Possibly. Though it could also backfire—they might resent outsiders interfering during what they consider a sacred time."

"Either way, we need to proceed," Jin said. "I have one concern though. I don't like leaving the ship unmanned while we're both down there."

"The ship is secure. Their technology won't be able to access it for at least another century."

"It's not the ship I'm worried about. It's us. Down there, alone, trying to mediate between hostile factions."

"I'll be with you," Bruno said. "On the other side of the planet."

"That's not very reassuring. I'd feel better if someone stayed with the ship, ready to extract us if things go wrong."

"I have an idea about that," Bruno said. He manipulated the controls, bringing up a view of Dalebrook at night. The city was lit up, but dimly—power was clearly rationed. "Instead of hiding the ship, let's make sure they see it. We'll position it on the night side and illuminate it."

"Interesting," Jin said.

"They'll assume the ship is occupied," Bruno explained. "They won't know we can operate it remotely. And they'll be less likely to harm us if they think our ship is watching over us."

"That's actually clever," Jin said. "Let me set that up." She moved to the controls and began programming the ship's external lighting systems. "I'll make it visible from everywhere on the planet. They won't be able to miss it."

"Don't hold back on the power."

"Trust me, they'll see it. Every person on Dravonia will see it." Later, with the ship positioned and glowing brilliantly against the darkness of space, Jin said, "You know, I feel better about this now. We might actually pull this off. Having the ship visible like this could be the edge we need."

"It's not about us succeeding," Bruno said gently. "It's about giving the people of Dravonia a chance to succeed. See you in ten days." He entered his landing craft and departed, leaving a faint trail of ionized particles as he descended toward the Oakridge District.

Jin watched him go, then entered her own craft and set course for Dawnridge.

The ship remained in orbit, unmanned but brilliant, pulsing with light against the darkness. It was brighter than any star, visible even during the day as a point of intense illumination. The satellites that Dravonia had launched seemed dim and insignificant by comparison.

And the ship circled on, a beacon of hope or a warning, depending on how one chose to interpret it.

Ten days later, the two landing craft returned from the surface and docked with the main ship. The exterior lights dimmed as the mediators met again in the central cabin.

"We did it," Jin said, her voice filled with relief and exhaustion. "I honestly didn't think it would work, but at the last moment they came through. The Dawnridge Council agreed to the framework."

Bruno smiled wearily. "Same with Oakridge. I'm tired."

"I'm exhausted," Jin said. "And cold. It was winter down there. Snow everywhere. Though I have to say, after the first few days, when I started going out and walking through the districts, talking to ordinary people instead of just the leadership—that seemed to help."

"I had the same experience," Bruno said. "When I walked through Oakridge, people saw me. They saw that I was different, but also that I was willing to be among them, to be vulnerable. The next day, the negotiations always went better."

"I don't fully understand why it worked, but it did," Jin said. "The agreement they reached isn't perfect, but I think it will prevent the worst outcomes. They've established new governance protocols, agreed to rebuild the supply chains cooperatively, and most importantly, they've committed to developing a shared narrative—a collective memory that all factions can accept."

"It's as much as we could hope for," Bruno said. "They may still have conflicts, but they won't destroy themselves. In fifty or a hundred years, we can come back and see how they've progressed."

"I'm not sure I want to," Jin said. "It was harder than I expected." She paused. "Something strange happened while I was down there. When I walked through the streets, people would stop and stare. Some of them would kneel in the snow. They called me a 'guardian' or a 'protector.' I didn't understand it."

"Similar things happened to me," Bruno said.

"I didn't let it distract me," Jin continued. "I just smiled and continued with my work." She flexed her shoulders. "Though I have to admit, sometimes I flew back to my landing craft instead of walking. I hope that didn't cause problems."

Bruno spread his large, feathered wings—the one feature that distinguished him and Jin from the people of Dravonia. The wings were magnificent, catching the light, creating shadows that danced across the cabin walls. "I don't think it hurt our cause," he said. "I flew occasionally too. If anything, I think it helped them understand that we were different, that we came from somewhere else, that our perspective was broader than their own."

"But you don't know what a 'guardian' is in their culture?"

"No. I didn't have time to research their mythology thoroughly. Some kind of protective figure from their folklore, I assume. You know, except for the wings, they really are almost identical to us. Their legends probably resemble ours in many ways."

"Makes sense," Jin said. She looked at the display showing Dravonia receding as their ship accelerated away. "Anyway, peace in Dravonia. Or at least a chance for peace."

"That's all we could give them," Bruno said. "The rest is up to them."

As their ship departed the system, heading toward their original destination in Woodbridge, the people of Dravonia looked up at the sky and saw the brilliant light fading. In the days that followed, they would begin the hard work of rebuilding, guided by the framework the two mediators had helped them create.

In Dalebrook, a scholar named Ava Obrien was already beginning to document the events. She interviewed witnesses who had seen the winged visitors, collected accounts of their words and actions, and began constructing a narrative that would become part of Dravonia's collective memory.

"They came during our darkest hour," she wrote, "when we had forgotten how to speak to each other, when our supply chains had broken and our governance had failed. They came with wings and wisdom, and they showed us a path forward. Not by solving our problems for us, but by helping us see how we could solve them ourselves."

In the Oakridge District, Anthony Fox, who had been one of the negotiators, stood at a window looking at the sky. The brilliant light was gone now, but he remembered it. He remembered the winged mediator named Bruno who had walked through their streets, who had listened to their grievances and helped them find common ground with their rivals in Dawnridge.

"The question isn't whether they were real," Anthony said to his colleague, Sergio Sharma. "The question is whether we can live up to what they helped us see in ourselves."

"We have to try," Sergio replied. "We owe them that much."

And far above, accelerating toward Woodbridge, Bruno and Jin settled in for the long journey ahead. They had done what they could. They had given the people of Dravonia a chance—perhaps the only chance they would ever have. Whether they took it or not was now beyond the mediators' control.

"Do you think they'll make it?" Jin asked.

"I don't know," Bruno said honestly. "But I think we gave them the tools they needed. The rest is up to them."

"That's all we can ever do," Jin said. "Give them the tools and hope they use them."

The ship accelerated, and Dravonia became a point of light, then vanished entirely among the stars. But the memory of the winged visitors remained, woven into the planet's collective consciousness, a reminder that they were not alone in the universe, and that even in their darkest moments, help could come from unexpected places.

In the years that followed, the people of Dravonia would build on the framework the mediators had helped them create. The supply chains were rebuilt, more resilient than before. The districts learned to cooperate, sharing resources and information. New forms of corporate governance emerged, more transparent and accountable. The media systems were restructured to promote shared understanding rather than division.

It wasn't perfect. There were setbacks and conflicts. But the planet did not destroy itself. The weapons of mass destruction remained unused, eventually dismantled as trust grew between the factions.

And always, in their art and literature, in their collective memory, there remained the story of the two winged visitors who had come during the winter of their despair, who had walked among them and shown them the way forward.

The mediators, Bruno Khan and Jin Woods, never returned to Dravonia. Their work took them to other systems, other crises, other desperate situations where their skills were needed. But sometimes, during the long journeys between stars, they would think about that cold planet and wonder how its people were doing.

"Do you think they remember us?" Jin asked once, years later.

"I don't know," Bruno said. "But I remember them. And I'm glad we stopped."

"So am I," Jin said. "So am I."

option_a: It makes the Dravonians seem more vulnerable and creates a sense of responsibility for the mediators to help them.

The mediators never attempt to disguise themselves; in fact, their wings are visible and become part of why the Dravonians view them as special "guardians."
