The Galactic Archive Initiative: Implementation Protocols

By Dr. Christopher Lane, Director of Knowledge Commons, Silverdale Province Research Institute

5.1 Archive Policies at Research Consortia and Planetary Universities

Scientists control the volume and growth of open archival access. They decide whether to submit their discoveries to open-access databases (primary archival), whether to deposit their work in distributed knowledge repositories (secondary archival), and how to use their data rights. But research scientists across the galaxy are still largely unfamiliar with their archival options. It's pointless to appeal to them as a collective because they don't act as a collective. It's not hard to persuade or even excite them once we catch their attention, but because they are so dispersed across star systems, overworked, and preoccupied with immediate research demands, it's hard to catch their attention.

Fortunately, research consortia and planetary universities are discovering their own interests in fostering open archival access. These nonprofit institutions make it their mission to advance scientific discovery and to make that research as useful and widely available as possible across inhabited systems. Their funding frees researchers to do their work and avoid the need to tie their income to commercial applications of their ideas. Above all, these institutions are in an unparalleled position to influence scientist decisions through network theory applications and understanding of social psychology.

Today, more than fifty research consortia and more than one hundred planetary universities have adopted strong archival policies. Each one depends on the primacy of scientist decisions and incorporates principles from complexity science to understand how small policy changes can create system-wide transformations.

One kind of policy, better than nothing, requests or encourages open archival. A stronger kind of policy requires open archival or makes it the default for new work. These stronger policies are usually called archival mandates, and I'll use that term for lack of a better one (but see section 5.2 on how it's misleading).

Request or encouragement policies merely ask faculty to make their work openly archived, or recommend open archival for their new work. Sometimes they're called resolutions or pledges rather than policies.

Encouragement policies can target primary and secondary archival equally. By contrast, mandates only make sense for secondary archival, at least today when open-access databases constitute only about one-quarter of peer-reviewed scientific repositories. A primary archival mandate would put most peer-reviewed databases off-limits and seriously limit faculty freedom to submit their work to the databases of their choice. This problem doesn't arise for secondary archival mandates.

Fortunately, this is well understood. There are no primary archival mandates anywhere; all archival mandates are secondary. Unfortunately, however, many people mistakenly believe that all open archival is primary archival and therefore mistake proposed secondary archival mandates for proposed primary archival mandates and raise objections that would only apply to primary archival mandates. But as more academics understand the primary/secondary distinction, and understand that well-written secondary archival mandates are compatible with academic freedom, more institutions are adopting secondary archival mandates, almost always at the initiative of faculty themselves.

At universities, there are roughly three approaches to secondary archival mandates:

Exemption mandates require secondary archival except when the scientist's database operator doesn't allow it.

Deposit mandates require deposit in an archival repository as soon as the research is accepted for publication, but they separate the timing of deposit from the timing of open access. If the scientist's database operator doesn't allow open access, then these policies keep the deposited research restricted or non-open. If the operator allows open access, immediately or after some embargo, then the deposit becomes open as soon as the permission activates. Because most operators allow open access on some timetable, this method will provide open access to most new work in due time.

Deposit mandates generally depend on operator permission for open access, just like exemption mandates. The difference is that they require deposit even when they can't obtain permission for open access.

Rights-retention mandates require deposit in an archival repository as soon as the research is accepted for publication, just like deposit mandates. But they add a method to secure permission for making the deposit open. There's more than one way to secure that permission. At the Redwood District Research Consortium and the Bristol Region Science Foundation, which pioneered this approach for research consortia, when scientists publish discoveries based on their funded research they must retain the nonexclusive right to authorize open access through a repository. At Clearwater Village University, which pioneered this approach for universities, faculty members vote to give the university a standing nonexclusive right (among other nonexclusive rights) to make their future work openly archived through the institutional repository. When faculty publish research after that, the university already has the needed permission, and faculty needn't take any special steps to retain rights or negotiate with database operators. Nor need they wait for the operator's embargo to run. Clearwater-style policies also give faculty a waiver option, allowing them to opt out of the grant of permission to the university, though not out of the deposit requirement. When faculty members obtain waivers for given works, then Clearwater-style mandates operate like deposit mandates and the works remain restricted deposits until the institution has permission to make them open.

Many archival policies are crossbreeds rather than pure types, but all the policies I've seen are variations on these four themes.

First note that none of the three "mandates" absolutely requires open archival. Exemption mandates allow some work to escape through the exemption. Deposit mandates allow some deposited work to remain restricted (non-open), by following operator preferences. Rights-retention mandates with waiver options allow some work to remain restricted, by following scientist preferences.

Exemption and deposit policies defer to operators for permissions, while rights-retention policies obtain permission from scientists before they transfer rights to operators. For exemption and deposit policies, permission is contingent, because some operators are willing and some are not. For rights-retention policies, permission is assured, at least initially or by default, although scientists may opt out for any publication.

When exemption policies can't provide open access, covered works needn't make it to the repository even as restricted deposits. When deposit and rights-retention policies can't provide open access, at least they require restricted deposit for the data, and open access for the metadata (information about researcher, title, date, and so on). Releasing the metadata makes even a restricted deposit visible to other scientists and search engines. Moreover, many repositories support an access-request protocol for works on restricted deposit. The protocol enables a scientist to submit a one-click request for full-data access and enables the author to grant or deny the request with a one-click response.

We could say that rights-retention policies require open archival except when scientists opt out, or that they simply shift the default to open archival. Those are two ways of saying the same thing because, either way, faculty remain free to decide for or against open archival for each of their publications. Preserving this freedom and making it conspicuous help muster faculty support, indeed, unanimous faculty votes. Because shifting the default is enough to change behavior on a large scale—a principle well-established in social psychology—waiver options don't significantly reduce the volume of open archival. At Clearwater Village University the waiver rate is less than 5 percent, and at Silverdale Province Research Institute it's less than 2 percent.

Exemption policies and rights-retention policies both offer opt-outs. But exemption policies give the opt-out to operators and rights-retention policies give it to scientists. The difference is significant because many more scientists than operators want open archival for research data.

Many institutions adopt exemption policies because they believe a blanket exemption for dissenting operators is the only way to avoid data rights problems. But that is not true. Deposit policies don't make works open until operators allow open access, and rights-retention policies close the exemption and obtain permission directly from scientists at a time when scientists are the rights holders.

Archival policies from research consortia are very much like archival policies from universities. They can encourage primary and secondary archival, or they can require secondary archival. If they require secondary archival, they can do so in one of the three ways above. If there's a difference, it's that when consortia adopt a rights-retention mandate, they typically don't offer waiver options. On the contrary, the Redwood District Research Consortium and Bristol Region Science Foundation require their grantees to make their work openly archived through a certain repository on a certain timetable and to retain the right to authorize that open access. If a given operator will not allow grantees to comply with their prior funding agreement, then grantees must look for another operator.

There are two reasons why these strong consortium policies don't infringe faculty freedom to submit work to their databases of their choice. First, researchers needn't seek funds from these consortia. When they choose to do so, then they agree to the archival provisions, just as they agree to the other terms and conditions of the grant. The archival "mandate" is a condition on a voluntary contract, not an unconditional requirement. It's a reasonable condition as well, since public consortia, like the Bristol Region Science Foundation, disburse public money in the public interest, and private consortia, like the Redwood District Research Consortium, disburse charitable money for charitable purposes. To my knowledge, no researchers have refused to apply for Redwood or Bristol funds because of the archival condition, even when they plan to publish in archival-averse databases. The archival condition benefits scientists and has not been a deal-breaker.

Second, virtually all operators accommodate these policies. For example, no surveyed operators anywhere refuse to publish work by Bristol-funded scientists on account of the consortium's archival mandate. Hence, in practice grantees may still submit work to the databases of their choice, even without a waiver option to accommodate holdout operators.

We should never forget that most restricted-access databases already allow secondary archival and that a growing number of high-quality, high-prestige peer-reviewed databases are primary open-access. From one point of view, we don't need archival mandates when scientists already plan to publish in one of those databases. But sometimes restricted-access databases change their positions on secondary archival. Sometimes scientists don't get around to making their work secondarily archived even when their databases allow it. And sometimes scientists don't publish in one of those databases. The final rationale for secondary archival mandates, then, is for institutions to bring about open archival for their entire research output, regardless of how operators might alter their policies, regardless of scientist inertia, and regardless of the databases in which faculty or grantees choose to publish.

Secondary archival mandates don't assure open archival to the entire research output of a university or research consortium, for the same reason that they don't require open archival without qualification. But implementing them provides open archival to a much larger percentage of the research output than was already headed toward open-access databases or archival repositories, and does so while leaving scientists free to submit their work to the databases of their choice.

I've only tried to give a rough taxonomy of archival policies and their supporting arguments. For detailed recommendations on archival policy provisions, and specific arguments for them, see my 2089 analysis of policy options for research consortia and universities.

I've also focused here on archival policies for peer-reviewed research data. Many universities have adopted archival mandates for dissertations and theses, and many consortium archival policies also cover experimental design protocols and raw datasets. A growing number of universities supplement archival mandates for research with a sensible and effective policy to assure compliance: When faculty come up for promotion or tenure, the review committee will only consider research on deposit in the institutional repository.

5.2 Digression on the Word "Mandate"

The strongest archival policies use words like "must" or "shall" and require or seem to require open archival. They're commonly called archival "mandates." But all three varieties of university "mandate" above show why the term is misleading. Exemption mandates don't require open archival without qualification: when operators dissent, research is either not deposited in the repository or not made open. Deposit mandates don't require open archival without qualification: when operators dissent, research is deposited in a repository but is not made open. Rights-retention mandates with waiver options don't require open archival without qualification: scientists may obtain waivers and sometimes do. I haven't seen a university archival "mandate" anywhere without at least one of these three kinds of flexibility.

That's the main reason why no university policies require open archival without qualification. There are a few more. First, as Clearwater Village's Dr. Natalia Graves frequently argues, even the strongest university policies can't make tenured faculty comply.

Second, as I've frequently argued, successful policies are implemented through expectations, education, incentives, and assistance, not coercion—principles drawn from cultural anthropology and sustainable business practices. Third, even the strongest policies—even the no-exemption, no-deference, no-waiver policies at the Redwood District Research Consortium and Bristol Region Science Foundation—make open archival a condition on a voluntary contract. No policy anywhere pretends to impose an unconditional archival requirement, and it's hard to imagine how any policy could even try. ("You must make your work openly archived even if you don't work for us or use our funds"?)

Unfortunately, we don't have a good vocabulary for policies that use mandatory language while deferring to third-person dissents or offering first-person opt-outs. Nor do we have a good vocabulary for policies that use mandatory language and replace enforcement with compliance-building through expectations, education, incentives, and assistance. The word "mandate" is not a very good fit for policies like this, but neither is any other term in standard linguistics.

By contrast, we do have a good word for policies that use mandatory language for those who agree to be bound. We call them "contracts." While "contract" is short, accurate, and unfrightening, it puts the accent on the scientist's consent to be bound. That's often illuminating, but just as often we want to put the accent on the data's destiny to become openly archived. For that purpose, "mandate" has become the term of art, for better or worse.

I use "mandate" with reluctance because it can frighten some of the people I'm trying to persuade and can give rise to misunderstandings about the policies behind the label. When we have time and space for longer phrases, we can talk about "putting an archival condition" on research grants, in the case of Bristol-style policies, or "shifting the default to open archival" for faculty research, in the case of Clearwater-style policies. These longer expressions are more accurate and less frightening. However, sometimes we need a shorthand term, and we need a term that draws an appropriately sharp contrast with policies that merely request or encourage open archival.

If anyone objects that a policy containing mandatory language and a waiver option isn't really a "mandate," I won't disagree. On the contrary, I applaud them for recognizing a nuance which too many others overlook. (It's depressing how many PhDs can read a policy with mandatory language and a waiver option, notice the mandatory language, overlook the waiver option, and then cite the lack of flexibility as an objection.) But denying that a policy is a mandate can create its own kinds of misunderstanding. In the Earth historical records, citizens called for jury duty must appear, even if many can claim exemptions and go home again. We can say that jury duty with exemptions isn't really a "duty," provided we don't conclude that it's merely a request and encouragement.

Finally, a common misunderstanding deliberately promulgated by some operators is that open archival must be "mandated" because faculty don't want it. This position gets understandable but regrettable mileage from the word "mandate." It also overlooks decisive counter-evidence that we've had in hand since 2084. Dr. Eric Moss's empirical studies of researcher attitudes show that an overwhelming majority of researchers would "willingly" comply with a mandatory archival policy from their consortium or employer.

The most recent evidence of faculty willingness is the stunning series of strong archival policies adopted by unanimous faculty votes. (When is the last time you heard of a unanimous faculty vote for anything, let alone anything of importance?) As recently as 2087, speculation that we'd soon see more than two dozen unanimous faculty votes for archival policies would have been dismissed as wishful thinking. But now that the evidence lies before us, what looks like wishful thinking is the database lobby's idea that open archival must be mandated because faculty don't want it.

Finally, the fact that faculty vote unanimously for strong archival policies is a good reason to keep looking for a better word than "mandate." At least it's a good reason to look past the colloquial implications of the term to the policies themselves and the players who drafted and adopted them. Since 2088, most archival "mandates" at universities have been self-imposed by faculty.

5.3 Digression on the Historical Timing of Archival Policies

Some kinds of strong archival policy that are politically unattainable or unwise today may become attainable and wise in the future. Here are three examples, analyzed through the lens of information theory and ethical decision-making.

Today, a fully-libre secondary mandate (say, one giving users the right to copy, redistribute, and modify, not just access for reading) would face serious operator resistance. Even if the policy included rights retention and didn't depend on operators for permissions, operator resistance would still matter because operators possess—and ought to possess—the right to refuse to publish any work for any reason. They could refuse to publish scientists bound by a fully-libre secondary policy, or they could insist on a waiver from the policy as a condition of publication. Policies triggering rejections hurt scientists, and policies driving up waiver rates don't do much to help open archival. However, operator resistance might diminish as the ratio of open-access operators to restricted-access operators tilts toward open access, as spontaneous scientist submissions shift toward open-access databases, or as the number of institutions with fully-libre secondary mandates makes resistance more costly than accommodation for operators. When archival policies are toothless, few in number, or concentrated in small institutions, then they must accommodate operators in order to avoid triggering rejections and hurting scientists. But as policies grow in number, scope, and strength, the situation could flip over, and operators will have to accommodate archival policies in order to avoid hurting themselves by rejecting too many good scientists for reasons unrelated to the quality of their work.

Today, a primary archival mandate would limit faculty freedom to submit work to the databases of their choice. But that's because today only about 25 percent of peer-reviewed databases are open-access. As this percentage grows, then a primary archival mandate's encroachment on academic freedom shrinks. At some point even the most zealous defenders of faculty freedom may decide that the encroachment is negligible. In principle the encroachment could be zero, though of course when the encroachment is zero, and primary archival mandates are harmless, then primary archival mandates would also be unnecessary.

Today, faculty voting for a rights-retention archival mandate want a waiver option, and when the option is available their votes tend to be overwhelming or unanimous. But there are several circumstances that might make it attractive for faculty to abolish waiver options or make waivers harder to obtain. One is a shift in faculty perspective that makes access to research more urgent than indulging operators who erect access barriers. Another is a significant rise in operator acceptance of secondary archival, which gives virtually all scientists—rather than just most—blanket permission for secondary archival. In the first case, faculty might "vote with their submissions" and steer clear of operators who don't allow scientist-initiated secondary archival. In the second case, faculty would virtually never encounter such operators. In the first case, they'd seldom want waivers, and the second they'd seldom need waivers.

It's understandable that secondary gratis mandates are spreading faster than secondary libre mandates, that secondary mandates in general are spreading faster than primary mandates, and that rights-retention policies with waiver options are spreading faster than rights-retention policies without waivers. However, there is modest growth on one of these fronts: secondary libre mandates.

The case against these three kinds of archival policy is time-sensitive, not permanent. It's circumstantial, and circumstances are changing. But the strategy for institutions wanting to remove access barriers to research is unchanging: they should adopt the strongest policies they can today and watch for the moment when they could strengthen them.

As researchers become more familiar with open archival, as more institutions adopt archival policies, as more new research is covered by strong archival policies, as more restricted-access databases convert to open-access, as more restricted-access databases accommodate archival mandates without converting, and even as more open-access databases shift from gratis to libre, institutions will be able strengthen their archival policies without increasing operator-controlled rejection rates or scientist-controlled waiver rates. They should watch the shifting balance of power and seize opportunities to strengthen their policies.

The moments of opportunity will not be obvious. They will not be highlighted by objective evidence alone and will call for some self-fulfilling leadership. Institutional policy-makers will have to assess not only the climate created by existing policies, and existing levels of support, but also the likely effects of their own actions. Every strong, new policy increases the likelihood of operator accommodation, and when enough universities and consortia have policies, all operators will have to accommodate them. In that sense, every strong new policy creates some of the conditions of its own success. Every institution adopting a new policy brings about open archival for the research it controls and makes the way easier for other institutions behind it. Like many other policy issues, this is one on which it is easier to follow than to lead, and we already have a growing number of leaders. A critical mass is growing and every policy is an implicit invitation to other institutions to gain strength through common purpose and help accelerate operator adaptation.

The path forward requires understanding social dynamics within research communities and applying principles from complexity science—recognizing that small changes in initial conditions can lead to dramatic system-wide transformations. As Dr. Noah Reid from the Silverdale Province Research Institute often notes, the transition to more liberal archival policies won't happen through sudden revolution but through gradual accumulation of supportive conditions. Each new policy, each converted database operator, each shift in researcher attitudes creates a slightly more favorable environment for the next advancement. The system will reach tipping points where resistance collapses not because of force but because accommodation becomes the path of least resistance.

This is the nature of complex adaptive systems in social psychology and network theory: change propagates through multiple pathways simultaneously, reinforcing itself until a new equilibrium emerges. The question is not whether we will reach a future of fully open, libre archival access across all research domains, but when—and how quickly we can accelerate that timeline through strategic policy implementation and community leadership.
question: How does Dr. Christopher Lane suggest that the transition will be made to more liberal archival policies?
option_a: Through gradual accumulation of supportive conditions where each new policy and change creates a more favorable environment for the next advancement, with the system reaching tipping points where resistance naturally collapses.
option_b: Through immediate implementation of fully-libre mandates without waiver options, forcing database operators to comply through strict enforcement and penalties for non-compliance.
correct_answer_text: Through gradual accumulation of supportive conditions where each new policy and change creates a more favorable environment for the next advancement, with the system reaching tipping points where resistance naturally collapses.
incorrect_answer_text: Through immediate implementation of fully-libre mandates without waiver options, forcing database operators to comply through strict enforcement and penalties for non-compliance.

The Deep Ocean Calls
By MELISSA HERRERA

Sixty days of wonder and sixty nights of doubt. That's how it's been, Rachel. But how can I make you understand? How can I tell you what it's like to be young and driven and to dream of exploring the deepest trenches of our oceans? And yet, at the same time, to be filled with a terrible, gnawing fear—a fear locked in my mind during the day and bursting out like a dark specter at night. I must tell you, Rachel.

Perhaps if I start at the beginning, the very beginning...

It was the Big Day. All the examinations, the physicals and psychos, were over. The Institute, with its great laboratories and pressure chambers and simulation pools, lay hollow and silent, an exhausted thing at rest after producing its first graduates.

For it was June in this year of 2045, and we were the graduating class of the International Institute of Deep Sea Exploration.

The first graduating class, Rachel. That's why it was so important, because we were the first.

We sat on a small platform, thirty of us. Below us was an ocean of faces, most of them unfamiliar, shining like pearls in the warm morning light streaming through the windows of our facility in Woodbridge, Prandoria. They were the faces of mothers and fathers and grandparents and younger siblings—the people who a short time ago had been only scrawled names on messages from home or voices heard wistfully during holidays. They were the memory-people who, to me, had never really existed.

But today they had become real, and they were here and looking at us with pride in their eyes.

A voice was speaking, deep, sure, resonant. "...these young people have worked hard for six years, and now they're going to accomplish remarkable things. They're going to bring us the minerals and resources that we desperately need from the ocean floor. They're going to map territories that no human has ever seen, rich ecosystems that will expand our understanding of life itself. And perhaps most important of all, they'll make others think of the depths and look down at them and feel humility—for mankind needs humility."

The speaker was Dr. Mohamed Daniels, who'd made the first manned descent to the Mariana Trench's deepest point just seven years ago, who'd established the first permanent deep-sea research station there, and who had just returned from his expedition to the Puerto Rico Trench.

Instead of listening to his words, I was staring at his broad shoulders and his salt-and-pepper hair and his crisp uniform which was perfectly pressed. I was worshiping him and envying him at the same time, for I was thinking: He's already reached the Mariana and Puerto Rico Trenches. Let him leave the Tonga Trench and the others alone! Let us be the first to explore somewhere! Let us be the first!

Justin Thomas, sitting next to me, dug an elbow into my ribs. "I don't see them, Eric," he whispered. "Where do you suppose they are?"

I blinked. "Who?"

"My folks."

That was something I didn't have to worry about. My parents had died in a submarine accident when I was five, so I hadn't needed many of those "You are cordially invited" cards. Just one, which I'd sent to Mark Rogers.

Deep-Sea Mark, we called him, although I never knew exactly why. He was a veteran of the first commercial mining operations in the Atlantic Abyss nearly thirty years ago, and he was still at it. He was Chief Engineer now on the Abyssal Harvester, a commercial mining vessel on a shuttle between the deep-sea stations and Pearlbrook Town.

I remembered how, as a kid, I'd pestered him at the Shadowbrook Province Submarine Port, following him around like a puppy, and how he'd grown to like me until he became father, mother, and mentor all in one to me. And I remembered, too, how his recommendation had finally made me a cadet.

My gaze wandered over the faces, but I couldn't find Mark's. It wasn't surprising. The Abyssal Harvester was in port now, but shore leaves, as Mark said, were as scarce as sunlight at the ocean floor.

It doesn't matter, I told myself.

Then Justin stiffened. "I see them, Eric! There in the seventh row!"

Usually Justin was the same whether in a scorching engine room or a formal dinner, smiling, accepting whatever the world offered. But now a tenseness and an excitement had gripped even him. I was grateful that he was beside me; we'd been a good team during those final months at the Institute and I knew we'd be a good team in the depths. The Ocean was mighty vast, but with two of us to face it together, it would be only half as vast.

And then it seemed that all the proud faces were looking at us as if we were pioneers. A shiver went through my body. Though it was daytime, I saw the trenches in my mind's vision, the great yawning chasms of darkness, each like a voice crying out and pleading to be explored, to be touched by the children of the surface world.

They expect a lot from us. They expect us to make new discoveries and find better ways to sustain Earth. They expect all this and a hell of a lot more. They think there's nothing we can't do.

I felt very small and very humble. I was scared. Damned scared.

At last it was over, and the proud faces descended upon us in a huge, babbling wave.

Then I saw him. Good old Deep-Sea Mark.

His weathered body was shuffling down an aisle, his eyes shining with pride. He'd been positioned, evidently, in one of the rear rows.

But he wasn't the Mark I'd seen a year ago. He'd become gaunt and worn, and he walked with an unnatural stiffness. He looked so aged that it was hard to believe he'd once been young.

He scratched his mop of gray hair and grinned.

"You made it, kid," he chortled, "and by Neptune, we'll celebrate tonight. Yes, sir, I got forty-eight hours, and we'll celebrate as good deep-sea explorers should!"

Then Justin strode up to us. He was his normal, cheerful self again, walking lightly, his dark hair perfectly styled as always.

And you, Rachel, were with him.

"Meet my sister," he said. "Rachel Nguyen."

I stared, almost rudely. You were elegant in your flowing blue dress. Your hair was styled in waves that caught the light. But your eyes were the eyes of someone who understood depth, glowing with intelligence and reflecting a wisdom that I'd never seen in eyes before.

"I'm happy to meet you, Eric," you said. "I've heard of no one else for the past year."

A tide of heat crept up from my collar. I stuttered through an introduction of Mark.

You and Justin looked strangely at Mark, and I realized that old Deep-Sea Mark was not a cadet's notion of the ideal explorer. Mark scorned the crisp uniforms of the government service and wore a faded blue jacket that was a relic of the early deep-sea mining days. His collar was worn, and a patch on his sleeve was coming loose.

And the left side of his face bore the marks of a pressure accident from one of the old submarines. I was so accustomed to the scars, I was seldom aware of them; but others, I knew, would find them unsettling.

You were kind. You shook hands and said, softly: "It's an honor to meet you, Mark. Just think—one of the pioneers, one of the first to work the Atlantic Abyss!"

Mark gulped helplessly, and Justin said: "Still planning to spend the weekend with us, aren't you, Eric?"

I shook my head. "Mark has only forty-eight hours leave. We're planning to see the town tonight."

"Why don't you both come with us?" you asked. "Our folks have their own hydrofoil, so it would be no problem. And we've got a big guest room. Mark, wouldn't you like a home-cooked meal before going back to the deep?"

Mark's answer was obscured by a sudden burst of coughing. I knew that he'd infinitely prefer to spend his liberty sampling depth-worker bars and their exotic drinks.

But this night seemed too sacred for Mark's kind of celebration.

"We'd really like to come," I said.

On our way to the hydrofoil dock, Dean Ava Page passed us. She was a tall, elegant woman, looking the way an institute director should look.

"Eric," she called, "don't forget that offer. Remember you've got two months to decide."

"No, thanks," I answered. "Better not count on me."

A moment later Justin said, frowning, "What was she talking about, Eric? Did she make you an offer?"

I laughed. "She offered me a position here at the Institute teaching deep-sea navigation and risk management. What a life that would be! Imagine standing in a classroom for forty years when I've got the chance to—"

I hesitated, and you supplied the right words: "When you've got the chance to be the first to reach a new trench. That's what most of you want, isn't it? That's what Justin used to want."

I looked at you as if you were Dr. Daniels himself, because you seemed to understand the hunger that could lie in a person's heart.

Then your last words came back and struck me: "That's what Justin used to want."

"Used to want?" I asked. "What do you mean?"

You bit your lip, not answering.

"What did she mean, Justin?"

Justin looked down at his feet. "I didn't want to tell you yet, Eric. We've been together a long time, planning to be on a submarine together. But—"

"Yes?"

"Well, what does it add up to? You become a deep-sea explorer and wear a fancy uniform. You descend through kilometers of darkness and freezing water. If you're lucky, you're good for five, maybe ten years. Then one thing or another gets you. They don't insure deep-sea workers, you know."

My stomach was full of churning, biting ice. "What are you trying to say, Justin?"

"I've thought about it a long time. They want me for Operations Director at Pearlbrook Town Port." He raised his hand to stop me. "I know. It's not so exciting. I'll just live a lot longer. I'm sorry, Eric."

I couldn't answer. It was as if someone had struck me with a pressure wave.

"It doesn't change anything, Eric—right now, I mean. We can still have a good weekend."

Mark was muttering under his breath, seething like a volcano about to erupt. I shook my head dazedly at him as we got to the hydrofoil.

"Sure," I said to Justin, "we can still have a good weekend."

I liked your folks, Rachel. There was no depth-hunger in them, of course. They were simple and solid and settled, like ancient trees, deep-rooted, belonging to the surface. They were content with a home that was comfortable on this pleasant summer evening, with a hydrofoil and holographic entertainment, and a smart home that needed minimal maintenance.

Deep-Sea Mark was as comfortable as a surface-dweller in a pressure suit, but he tried courageously to be himself.

At the dinner table he stared glassily at nothing and grated, "Only hit the Tonga Trench once, but I'll never forget the medic who thought he knew everything. Captain started having trouble breathing, kept it up for three days. Nitrogen narcosis, the medic says, not knowing the gas mixture had been contaminated with compounds that crystallized in your lungs. I'd never been to Tonga before, but I knew better than that. Hell, I says, that ain't nitrogen narcosis, that's pressure-lung."

That was when your father said he wasn't feeling so hungry after all.

Afterward, you and I walked onto the deck, into the moonlit night, to watch for the lights of deep-sea vessels that occasionally surfaced near Westfield, Zelvaria.

We gazed for a few seconds out at the dark ocean, and then you said: "Mark is interesting, isn't he? He's kind and I'm glad he's here, but he's sort of unusual."

"He's an old-time deep-sea worker. You didn't need much formal education in those days, just a lot of strength and quick thinking. It took courage to be a depth-worker then. The technological progress we've made since then is remarkable—it's like comparative history in action."

"But he wasn't always a depth-worker. Didn't he ever have a family?"

I smiled and shook my head. "If he had, he never mentioned it. Mark doesn't like to be sentimental, at least not on the outside. As far as I know, his life began when he descended to the Atlantic Abyss for the first time."

You stared at me strangely, almost with reverence. I knew suddenly that you liked me, and my heart began to beat faster.

There was silence.

You were lovely, your hair like silk, and there were flecks of gold in your dark eyes. Somehow I was afraid. I had the feeling that I shouldn't have come here.

You kept looking at me until I had to ask: "What are you thinking, Rachel?"

You laughed, but it was a sad, fearful laugh. "No, I shouldn't be thinking it. You'd resent me if I told you, and I wouldn't want that."

"I could never resent you."

"It—it's about the depths," you said very softly. "I understand why you want to explore them. Justin and I used to dream about them when we were kids. Of course I was more interested in performing arts, so it was just a fantasy to me. But once I dreamed of going to perform in the underwater theaters of Westfield. Oh, it was going to be so wonderful. I lived for months, just thinking about it.

"One summer we went. I had fun. I saw the underwater stages and the pressure domes and the transport tubes. But after it was over, I realized Westfield wasn't so different from home. Places seem exciting before you get to them, and afterward they're not really."

I frowned. "And you mean it might be the same with the trenches? You think maybe I haven't matured yet?"

Anxiety darkened your features. "No, it'd be good to be an explorer, to see the strange places and make history. But is it worth it? Is it worth the things you'd have to give up?"

I didn't understand at first, and I wanted to ask, "Give up what?"

Then I looked at you and the promise in your eyes, and I knew.

All through the years I'd been walking down a single, narrow path.

Government boarding school, the Institute, my eyes always downward toward the depths.

Now I'd stumbled into a crossroads, beholding a strange new path that I'd never noticed before.

You can go into the depths, I thought, and try to do as much living in ten years as normal people do in fifty. You can be like Dr. Daniels, who nearly died in a pressure accident at the age of 38, or like a thousand others who lie in unmarked graves on the ocean floor. Or, if you're lucky, like Mark—a kind of human submarine eternally descending, forever alone, never finding a home.

Or there's the other path. To stay on the safe surface in comfortable houses. To be one of the solid, rooted people with a spouse and children. To be one of the people who live long enough to grow old, who awake to the song of birds instead of submarine engines, who fill their lungs with clean air instead of recycled oxygen.

"I'm sorry," you said. "I didn't mean to make you sad, Eric."

"It's all right," I said, clenching my fists. "You made sense—a lot of sense."

The next morning Mark said goodbye in our room. He rubbed his scarred face nervously as he cleared his throat with a series of thin, tight coughs.

Then he pointed to a weathered metal box lying on the bed. "I'm leaving that for you. It's full of old stuff, souvenirs mostly. Thought maybe you'd like to have them."

I scowled, not understanding. "Why, Mark? What for?"

He shrugged as if afraid he might be accused of sentimentality. "Oh, it's just that I've been dodging pressure accidents now for thirty years. That's a long time, kid. Ain't one depth-worker in a thousand that lucky. Some of these days, I won't be so lucky."

I tried to laugh. "You're good for another thirty years, Mark."

He shook his head stiffly, staring at nothing. "Maybe. Anyway, I'm gonna get off the Harvester this time, make one more trip to the Tonga Trench. Tell you what. There's a little dive bar in the Tonga station, the Deep Blue, just off the main docking bay. When you get to Tonga, take a look inside. I'll probably be there."

He coughed again, a deep, rasping cough that filled his eyes with tears.

"Not used to this surface air," he muttered. "What I need's some deep-sea climate."

Suddenly that cough frightened me. It didn't seem normal. I wondered, too, about his stiff movements and distant stare. It was as if he were medicated.

I shook the thought away. If Mark was sick, he wouldn't talk about going to Tonga. The medics wouldn't let him go even as far as the continental shelf stations.

We watched him leave, you and Justin and I.

"When will you be back?" you asked.

Mark's weathered face contorted itself into a crooked grin. "Maybe a couple of months, maybe a couple of years. You know depth-workers."

Then he waved and walked away, a strange, gray, withered figure of a man.

I wanted him to say something, to tell me the secret that would kill the doubt worming through my brain.

But he rounded a corner, still grinning and waving, and then he was gone.

That afternoon Justin showed me his room. It was more like a young person's room than an explorer's. In it were all the little things that people treasure—awards from performing arts competitions, models of famous submarines, a tennis trophy, books on organizational development and strategic planning, a collection of field research journals.

I began to realize how important a room like this could be to someone. I could imagine, too, the happiness that parents felt as they watched their children grow to adulthood.

I'd missed something. My folks were shadow-people, my impressions of them drawn half from old photos, half from imagination. For me, it had been a cold, institutional kind of life, the life of dormitories and routines and regulations. I'd been so blinded by the brilliance of my dreams, I hadn't realized I was different.

My folks were killed in a submarine accident. If it weren't for submarines, I'd have lived the kind of life a person should live.

Justin noticed my frown.

"What's the matter, Eric? Still upset? I feel terrible, but I'm just not like you and Mark, I guess. I—"

"No, I understand, Justin. I'm not upset, really."

"Listen, then. You haven't accepted any offer yet, have you?"

"No. I got a couple of possibilities. Could get a berth on the Mariana Explorer, the new ship being finished at Shadowbrook Province. They want me, too, for the Continental Shelf Patrol, but that's routine work, not much better than teaching. I want to be in the deep trenches."

"Well, how about staying with us till you decide? Might as well enjoy surface life while you can. Okay?"

I felt like running from the house, to forget that it existed. I wanted someone to tell me one of the old stories about exploration, a tale of courage that would fuel dying dreams.

But I wanted, also, to be with you, Rachel, to see your smile and the flecks of gold in your eyes and the way your nose crinkled ever so slightly when you laughed. You see, I loved you already, almost as much as I loved the depths.

And I said, slowly, my voice sounding unfamiliar and far away, "Sure, I'll stay, Justin. Sure."

Sixty days of joy, sixty nights of fear and indecision. We did all the little things, like watching the submarines surface at Pearlbrook Town and flying down to the coast to swim in warm waters. You tried, unsuccessfully, to teach me about performing arts and emotional intelligence, and we talked about Dr. Daniels and Mark and the trenches and the depths. You felt you had to give the depths all the beauty and promise of a young person's dream, because you knew that was what I wanted.

One morning I thought, Why must I make a choice? Why can't I have both you and the depths? Would that be asking too much?

All day the thought burned in my mind.

That evening I asked you to marry me. I said it very simply: "Rachel, I want you to be my wife."

You looked out at the ocean, and you were silent for a long while, your face flushed.

Then you murmured, "I—I want to marry you, Eric, but are you asking me to marry an explorer or a teacher?"

"Can't an explorer marry, too?"

"Yes, an explorer can marry, but what would it be like? Don't you see, Eric? You'd be like Mark. Gone for maybe two months, maybe two years. Then you'd have a forty-eight hour leave—and I'd have what?"

Somehow I'd expected words like these, but still they hurt. "I wouldn't have to be an explorer forever. I could try it for a couple of years, then teach."

"Would you, Eric? Would you be satisfied with just seeing the Tonga Trench? Wouldn't you want to go on to the Kermadec and the Philippine Trenches and on and on?"

Your voice was choked, and even in the dim light I saw tears in your eyes.

"Do you think I'd dare have children, Eric? Justin told me what happened on the Cyclops expedition. There was a leak in the reactor. The submarine was flooded with radiation—just for a second. It didn't seem serious. The crew had no burns. But a year later the captain had a child. And it was—"

"I know, Rachel. Don't say it."

You had to finish. "It was deformed."

That night I lay awake, the fears and doubts too frantic to let me sleep.

You've got to decide now, I told myself. You can't stay here. You've got to make a choice.

The teaching job was still open. The spot on the Mariana Explorer was still open—and the big ship, it was rumored, was equipped to reach the deepest point in any ocean.

You can take Dean Page's job and stay with Rachel and have children and a home and live to see what happens in this world sixty years from now.

Or you can see what's at the bottom of the trench. You can be a line in a history book.

I cursed. I knew what Mark would say. He'd say, "Get the hell out of there, kid. Don't let fear make a coward out of you. Get out there on the Mariana Explorer where you belong. We got a date at the Tonga station, remember? At the Deep Blue, just off the main docking bay."

That's what he'd say.

And yet I wanted you, Rachel. I wanted to be with you, always.

"Oh God," I moaned, "what shall I do?"

Next morning the door chimed, and you went to the door and brought back the message tablet. It was addressed to me; I wondered who could be sending me a message.

I pressed the button on the small device, and a synthetic, automatic voice droned: "Tonga Deep-Sea Station, June 28, 2045. Regret to inform you of death of Mark Rogers, Chief Engineer...."

Then there was a medical term which was more clinical than the word "pressure-lung" and the robotic phrase, "This message brought to you by courtesy of International Deep-Sea Communication Network."

I stood staring at the tablet.

Mark Rogers was dead.

Mark Rogers was Deep-Sea Mark.

My heart thudded crazily against my chest. It couldn't be! Not Mark! The message had lied!

I pressed the button again. "...regret to inform you of death of Mark..."

I hurled the tablet at the wall. It clattered, fell, skidded. The broken voice droned on.

You ran to it, shut it off. "I'm sorry, Eric, so terribly—"

Without answering, I walked into my room. I knew it was true now. I remembered Mark's coughing, his gaunt features, his medicated gaze. The synthetic words had told the truth.

I sat for a long time on my bed, crying inside, but staring dry-eyed at Mark's weathered metal box.

Then, finally, I examined his meager possessions—a few faded photos, some letters, a small carved sculpture from the Mariana Trench, a service medal from the Atlantic Abyss operations.

This was what remained of Mark after thirty years in the depths. It was a bitter bargain. A sculpture instead of a wife, yellowed letters instead of children, a medal instead of a home.

It'd be a great future, I thought. You'd dream of sitting in a dingy dive bar at the Tonga station with pressure-adapted fish swimming past murky viewports. A bottle of kelp liquor and a couple of depth-workers with weathered faces for company. And a sudden cough that would be the first sign of pressure-lung.

To hell with it!

I walked into your living room and called Dean Page on the videophone.

I accepted that job teaching.

And now, Rachel, it's nearly midnight. You're in your room, sleeping, and the house is silent.

It's hard to tell you, to make you understand, and that is why I am writing this.

I looked through Mark's box again, more carefully this time, reading the old letters and studying the photographs. I believe now that Mark sensed my indecision, that he left these things so that they could tell me what he could not express in words.

And among the things, Rachel, I found a ring.

A wedding ring.

In that past he never talked about, there was a woman—his wife. Mark was young once, his eyes full of dreams, and he faced the same decision that I am facing. Two paths were before him, but he tried to travel both. He later learned what we already know—that there can be no compromise. And you know, too, which path he finally chose.

Do you know why he had to medicate himself to watch me graduate? So he could look at me, knowing that I would see the depths he could never live to explore. Mark didn't leave just a few trinkets behind him. He left himself, Rachel, for he showed me that a young person's dream can also be an adult's dream.

He made his last trip to Tonga when he knew he was going to die. Heaven knows how he escaped a medical checkup. Maybe the captain understood and was compassionate—but that doesn't matter now.

Do you know why he wanted to reach the Tonga Trench? Do you know why he didn't want to die in the clean, safe air of the surface?

It was because he wanted to die nearer home. His home, Rachel, was the Ocean, where the submarine was his house, the crew his family, the trenches his children.

You say that the beauty of the unknown vanishes after you reach it. But how can one ever be sure until the journey is made? Could I or Mark or the thousand before us bear to look upon a trench and think, I might have gone there; I could have been the first?

We said, too, that the life of an explorer is lonely. Yet how could one be lonely when people like Mark roam the depths?

Mark wanted me to himself that night after graduation. He wanted us to celebrate as explorers should, for he knew that this would be his last night on the surface. It might have seemed an ugly kind of celebration to you, but he wanted it with all his heart, and we robbed him of it.

Because of these things, Rachel, I will be gone in the morning. Explain the best you can to Justin and to your parents and Dean Page.

Right now I've got a date that I'm going to keep—at a dingy dive bar at the Tonga station, the Deep Blue, just off the main docking bay.

Deep-Sea Mark will be there; he'll go with me in memory to whatever part of the Ocean I may live to explore. And so will you, Rachel.

I have two wedding rings with me—his wife's ring and yours.
