synthetic_story:
THE RUINS OF COPPERFIELD

By DEAN EVANS

Every child should be able to hum a tune, except, of course, the Venusian settlers. But this one did!

She seemed a very small girl to be carrying so large a geological sample kit. She swung it in her thin left hand as she walked, and at first glance you couldn't be sure if she were carrying it, or it carrying her.

She came humming. All children hum. To children, humming is as natural as breathing. However, there was something peculiar about this particular child's humming. Or, rather, there were two things peculiar, but each was related to the other.

The first was that she was a Venusian settler child. You could be very sure of that, for Earth children have attached earlobes while Venusian settler children do not—and she most certainly didn't.

The second was the tune she hummed—a somehow familiar tune, but one which I should have thought not very appealing to a child.

"Hi, there," I said when she came near enough. "What's that you're humming?"

She stopped humming and she stopped walking, both at the same time, as though she had pulled a switch or turned a tap that shut them off. Then she lifted her small head and stared up into my eyes.

"'Clair de Lune'," she said in a soft, child's voice.

"The what?" I asked.

"From Debussy's Suite Bergamasque," she explained, still looking up at me. She said it deadpan, and her wide gray eyes never once batted.

"Oh," I said. "And where did you learn that?"

"My father taught me."

I blinked at her. She didn't blink back. Her round little face still held no expression, but if it had, I knew it would have matched the serene quality of the tune she hummed.

"You hum very well," I told her.

That pleased her. Her eyes lit up and an almost-smile flirted with the corners of her small mouth.

She nodded grave agreement.

"Been collecting rock samples, I see. I'll bet you didn't find any good ones. This is the wrong geological layer."

The light in her eyes snapped off. "Well, good-by," she said abruptly and very relevantly.

"Good-by," I said.

Her humming and her walking started up again in the same spot where they had left off. I mean the note she resumed on was the note which followed the one interrupted; and the step she took was with the left foot, which was the one she would have used if I hadn't stopped her.

I followed her with my eyes. An unusual little girl. A most precisely mechanical little girl.

When she was almost out of sight, I took off after her, wondering.

The dwelling she went into was over in that crumbling section which forms a curving boundary line, marking the limits of those frantic and ugly original excavation sites made many years ago by the early colonists in Copperfield, Veldoria. It seems that someone had told someone who had told someone else that here, a mere fifty feet beneath the surface, was a deposit as wide as a warehouse and as long as a politician's promise, of pure—pure, mind you—platinum.

Back in those days, to be a colonist meant to be a rugged individual. And to be a rugged individual meant to not give a damn one way or another. And to not give a damn one way or another meant to make one hell of a mess on the pristine landscape of Venus.

There had not been any platinum found, of course, and now, for the most part, the mining structures so hastily thrown up were only fever scars of a sickness long gone and little remembered. A few of the dwellings were still occupied, like the one into which the Venusian child had just disappeared.

So her father had taught her Debussy's "Clair de Lune," had he? That tickling thought made me chuckle as I stood before the ramshackle building. And then, suddenly, I stopped chuckling and began to think, instead, of something quite astonishing:

How had it been possible for him to teach, and for her to hum? All Venusian settlers are as tone-deaf as a bucket of lead.

I went up three composite steps and rapped loudly on the weather-beaten door.

The man who faced me may have been as young as twenty-five, but he didn't look it. That shocked look, which comes with the first realization that youth has slipped quietly away downstream in the middle of the night, and left nothing but frightening rocks of middle age to show cold and gray in the hard light of dawn, was like the validation stamp of Time itself in his wide, weary eyes. And his voice wasn't young any more, either.

"Well? And what did I do now?"

"I beg your pardon?" I said.

"You're Colonial Security, aren't you? Or is that badge you're wearing just something to cover a hole in your shirt?"

"Yes, I'm Security, but does it have to mean something?" I asked. "All I did was knock on your door."

"I heard it." His lips were curled slightly at one corner.

I worked up a smile for him and let him see it for a few seconds before I answered: "As a matter of fact, I don't want to see you at all. I didn't know you lived here and I don't know who you are. I'm not even interested in who you are. It's the little girl who just went in here that I was interested in. The little Venusian settler girl, I mean."

His eyes spread as though somebody had put fingers on his lids at the outside corners and then cruelly jerked them apart.

"Come in," he almost gasped.

I followed him. When I leaned back against the plain door, it closed protestingly. I looked around. It wasn't much of a room, but then you couldn't expect much of a room in a little ghost of a place like this. A few artifacts of the locality stood about on two tables and a shelf, bits of rock with streak-veins of compressed silicate; not bad if you like the appearance of frozen lightning.

There were two chairs and a large table intended to match the chairs, and a rough couch kind of thing made of discarded shipping containers which had probably been hauled here from the International Spaceport at Ashford City, thirty kilometers to the east. In the back wall of the room was a doorway that led dimly to somewhere else in the dwelling. Nowhere did I see the little girl. I looked once again at the man.

"What about her?" he whispered.

His eyes were still startled.

I smiled reassuringly. "Nothing, friend, nothing. I'm sorry I upset you. I was just being nosy is all, and that's the truth of it. You see, the little girl went by me a while ago and she was humming. She hums remarkably well. I asked her what the name of the tune was and she told me it was 'Clair de Lune' from Debussy. She also told me her father had taught her."

His eyes hadn't budged from mine, hadn't flickered. They might have been bright, moist marbles glued above his cheeks.

He said one word only: "Well?"

"Nothing," I answered. "Except that Venusian settlers are supposed to be tone-deaf, aren't they? It's something lacking in their auditory processing. So when I heard this little girl, and saw she was a Venusian settler, and when she told me her father had taught her—" I shrugged and laughed a little. "Like I said before, I guess I got just plain nosy."

He nodded. "We agree on that last part."

Perhaps it was his eyes. Or perhaps it was the tone of his voice. Or perhaps, and more simply, it was his attitude in general. But whatever it was, I suddenly felt that, nosy or not, I was being treated shabbily.

"I would like to speak to the Venusian settler man," I said.

"There isn't any Venusian settler man."

"There has to be, doesn't there?" I said it with little sharp prickers on the words.

But he did, too: "Does there?"

I gawked at him and he stared back. And the stare he gave me was hard and at the same time curiously defiant—as though he would dare me to go on with it. As though he figured I hadn't the guts.

For a moment, I just blinked stupidly at him, as I had blinked stupidly at the little girl when she told me her father had taught her how to hum. And then—after what seemed to me a very long while—I slowly tumbled to what he meant.

His eyes were telling me that the little Venusian settler girl wasn't a little Venusian settler girl at all, that she was cross-breed, a little child who had a Venusian settler mother and a human, Earthman father.

It was a startling thought, for there just aren't any such mixed families. Or at least I had thought there weren't. Physically, spiritually, mentally, or by any other standard you can think of, compared to a human female the Venusian settler woman isn't anything you'd want around the house—or so the common wisdom went.

I finally said: "So that is why she is able to hum."

He didn't answer. Even before I spoke, his eyes had seen the correct guess which had probably flashed naked and astounded in my own eyes. And then he swallowed with a labored breath that went trembling down inside him.

"There isn't anything to be ashamed of," I said gently. "Back on Earth there's a lot of mixtures, you know. Some people even claim there's no such thing as a pure race. Cultural exchange has been happening for millennia. I don't know, but I guess we all started somewhere and intermarried plenty since."

He nodded. Somehow his eyes didn't look defiant any more.

"Where's her mother?" I asked.

"S-she's dead."

"I'm sorry. Are you all right? I mean do you get along okay and everything, now that...?"

I stopped. I wanted to ask him if he was starving by slow degrees and needed help. Lord knows the careworn look about him didn't show it was luxurious living he was doing—at least not lately.

"Look," I said suddenly. "Would you like to go back to Earth? I could fix—"

But that was the wrong approach. His eyes snapped and his shoulders stiffened angrily and the words that ripped out of his mouth were not coated with honey.

"Get the hell out of here, you fool!"

I blinked again. When the flame in his eyes suddenly seemed to grow even hotter, I turned on my heel and went to the door. I opened it, went out on the top composite step. I turned back to close the door—and looked straight into his eyes.

He was crying, but that didn't mean exactly what it looked like it might mean. His right hand had the door edge gripped tightly and he was swinging it with all the strength he possessed. And while I still stared, the door slammed savagely into the casing with a shock that jarred the step under my feet, and flying splinters from the deteriorated material stung my flinching cheeks.

I shrugged and turned around and went down the steps. "And that is the way it goes," I muttered disgustedly to myself. Thinking to be helpful with community organizing, you offer assistance and they immediately reject it—violently.

I looked up just in time to avoid running into a spread-legged woman who was standing motionless directly in the middle of the gravel-path in front of the door. Her hands were on her hips and there was something in her eyes which might have been a leer.

"Pulled a howler in there, eh, friend?" she said. She chuckled hoarsely in her throat. "Not being exactly deaf, I heard the tail end of it." Her chuckle was a crude thing, a thing usually reserved—if it ever was reserved at all—for the back rooms of some of the lower class establishments. And then she stopped chuckling and frowned instead and said complainingly:

"Regular little hothead, ain't he? I ask you now, wouldn't you think a man which had got himself in a little jam, so to speak, would be more reasonable—"

Her words chopped short and she almost choked on the final unuttered syllable. Her glance had dropped to my badge and the look on her face was one of startled surprise.

"I—" she said.

I cocked a frown of my own at her.

"Well, so long, friend," she grunted, and spun around and dug her heels in the gravel and was away. I stood there staring at her rapidly disappearing form for a few moments and then looked back once more at the dwelling. A tattered synthetic curtain was just swinging to in the dirty, dust-blown window. That seemed to mean the man had been watching. I sighed, shrugged again and went away myself.

When I got back to Security Headquarters in Ashford City, I went to the file and began to rifle through pictures. I didn't find the man, but I did find the woman.

She was a killer named Ava Lucas.

I took the picture into the Chief's office and laid it on his desk, waited for him to look down at it and study it for an instant, and then to look back up to me. Which he did.

"So?" he said.

"Wanted, isn't she?"

He nodded. "But a lot of good that'll do. She's holed up somewhere back on Earth."

"No," I said. "She's right here. I just saw her."

"What?" He nearly leaped out of his chair.

"I didn't know who she was at first," I said. "It wasn't until I looked in the files—"

He cut me off. His hand darted into his desk drawer and pulled out an Authority Card. He shoved the card at me. He growled: "Kill or capture, I'm not especially fussy which. Just get her!"

I nodded and took the card. As I left the office, I was thinking of something which struck me as somewhat more than odd.

I had idly listened to a little half-breed Venusian settler girl humming part of Debussy's "Clair de Lune," and it had led me to a wanted killer named Ava Lucas.

Understandably, Ms. Lucas did not produce herself on a silver platter. I spent the remainder of the afternoon trying to get a lead on her and got nowhere. If she was hiding in any of the places I went to, then she was doing it with mirrors, for on Venus an Authority Card is the big stick than which there is no bigger. Not solely is it a warrant, it is a commandeer of help from anyone to whom it is presented; and wherever I showed it I got respect.

I got instant attention. I got even more: those wraithlike tremblings in the darker corners of bars, those corners where light never seems quite to penetrate. You don't look into those. Not if you're anything more than a ghoul, you don't.

Not finding her wasn't especially alarming. What was alarming, though, was not finding the Earthman and his little half-breed Venusian settler daughter when I went back to the tumbledown dwelling where they lived. It was empty. He had moved fast. He hadn't even left me a note saying good-by.

That night I went into the Elmwood Region to the Kahreen Reservation, where the Venusian settlers still try to act like Venusian settlers.

It was Festival night, and when I got there they were doing the dance to the three rings. At times like this you want to leave the Venusian settlers alone. With that thought in mind, I pinned my Authority Card to my lapel directly above my badge, and went through the gates.

The huge circle fire was burning and the dance was in progress. Briefly, this can be described as something like the ceremonial dances put on centuries ago by the ancient aborigines of the Pacific Islands. There was one important exception, however. Instead of a central fire, the Venusian settlers dig a huge circular trench and fill it with dried roots of the kelnu tree and set fire to it. Being resin-like, the gnarled fragments burn for hours. Inside this ring sit the spectators, and in the exact center are the dancers. For music, they use the drums.

The dancers were both men and women and they were as minimally clothed as Venusian settlers can get, but their dance was a thing of grace and loveliness. For an instant—before anyone observed me—I stood motionless and watched the sinuously undulating movements, and I thought, as I have often thought before, that this is the one thing the Venusian settlers can still do beautifully. Which, in a sad sort of way, is a commentary on the way things have gone since the first rocket-blasting ship set down on these misty plains.

I felt the blade dig my spine. Carefully I turned around and pointed my index finger to my badge and card. Bared teeth glittered at me in the flickering light, and then the blade disappeared as quickly as it had come.

"Valenhk," I said. "The Chief. Take me to her."

The Venusian settler turned, went away from the half-light of the circle. She led me some meters off to the north to a swooping-tent. Then she stopped, pointed.

"Valenhk," she said.

I watched her slip away.

Valenhk is an old Venusian settler. I don't think any Venusian settler before her has ever lived so long—and doubtless none after her will, either. Her leathery, almost gray-black skin was rough and had a weathered look about it, and up around the eyes were little plaits and folds that had the appearance of being done deliberately by a Venusian sand-artist.

"Good evening," I said, and sat down before her and crossed my legs.

She nodded slowly. Her old eyes went to my badge.

From there they went to the Authority Card.

"Power sign of the Earthmen," she muttered.

"Not necessarily," I said. "I'm not here for trouble. I know as well as you do that, before tonight is finished, more than half of your men and women will be intoxicated on illegal spirits."

She didn't reply to that.

"And I don't give a damn about it," I added distinctly.

Her eyes came deliberately up to mine and stopped there. She said nothing. She waited. Outside, the drums throbbed, slowly at first, then moderated in tempo. It was like the throbbing—or sobbing, if you prefer—of the old, old pumps whose shafts go so tirelessly down into the planet for such pitifully thin streams of water.

"I'm looking for an Earthman," I said. "This particular Earthman took a Venusian settler for a wife."

"That is impossible," she grunted bitterly.

"I would have said so, too," I agreed. "Until this afternoon, that is."

Her old, dried lips began to purse and wrinkle.

"I met his little daughter," I went on. "A little semi-human girl with Venusian settler features. Or, if you want to turn it around and look at the other side, a little Venusian settler girl who hums."

Her teeth went together with a snap.

I nodded and smiled. "You know who I'm talking about."

For a long long while she didn't answer. Her eyes remained unblinking on mine and if, earlier in the day, I had thought the little girl's face was expressionless, then I didn't completely appreciate the meaning of that word. Valenhk's face was more than expressionless; it was simply blank.

"They disappeared from the dwelling they were living in," I said. "They went in a hurry—a very great hurry."

That one she didn't answer, either.

"I would like to know where he is."

"Why?" Her whisper was brittle.

"He's not in trouble," I told her quickly. "He's not wanted. Nor his child, either. It's just that I have to talk to him."

"Why?"

I pulled out the file photo of Ava Lucas and handed it across to her. Her wrinkled hand took it, pinched it, held it up close to a lamp hanging from one of the ridge poles. Her eyes squinted at it for a long moment before she handed it back.

"I have never seen this Earthwoman," she said.

"All right," I answered. "There wasn't anything that made me think you had. The point is that she knows the man. It follows, naturally, that he might know her."

"This one is wanted?" Her old, broken tones went up slightly on the last word.

I nodded. "For murder."

"Murder." She spat the word. "But not for the murder of a Venusian settler, eh? Venusian settlers are not that important any more." Her old eyes hated me with an intensity I didn't relish.

"You said that, old woman, not I."

A little time went by. The drums began to beat faster. They were rolling out a lively tempo now, a tempo you could put music to.

She said at last: "I do not know where the man is. Nor the child."

She looked me straight in the eyes when she said it—and almost before the words were out of her mouth, they were whipped in again on a drawn-back, great, sucking breath. For, somewhere outside, somewhere near that dancing circle, in perfect time with the lively beat of the drums, somebody was humming.

It was a clear, clean sound, a merry, bright, happy sound, as sharp and as precise as the thrust of a laser through a piece of soft synthetic material.

"In your teeth, Valenhk! Right in your teeth!"

She only looked at me for another dull instant and then her eyes slowly closed and her hands folded together in her lap. Being caught in a lie only bores a Venusian settler.

I got up and went out of the tent.

The man never heard me approach. His eyes were toward the flaming circle and the dancers within, and, too, I suppose, to his small daughter who was somewhere in that circle with them, humming. He leaned against the bole of a kelnu tree with his arms down and slightly curled backward around it.

"That's considered bad luck," I said.

His head jerked around with my words, reflected flames from the circle fire still flickering in his eyes.

"That's a kelnu tree," I said. "Embracing it like that is like looking for a ladder to walk under. Or didn't you know?"

"Would it make any difference?" He spoke softly, but the words came to me above the drums and the shouts of the dancers. "How much bad luck can you have in one lifetime, anyway?"

I ignored that. "Why did you pull out of that dwelling? I told you you had nothing to fear from me."

He didn't answer.

"I'm looking for the woman you saw me talking with this morning," I went on. "Friend, she's wanted. And this thing, on my lapel is an Authority Card. Assuming you know what it means, I'm asking you where she is."

"What woman?" His words were flat.

"Her name is Ava Lucas."

If that meant anything to him, I couldn't tell. In the flickering light from the fires, subtle changes in expression weren't easily detected.

"Why should I care about an Earthwoman? My wife was a Venusian settler. And she's dead, see? Dead. Just a Venusian settler. Not fit for anything, like all Venusian settlers. Just a woman who fell in love with an Earthman and had the guts to marry him. Do you understand? So somebody murdered her for it. Ain't that pretty? Ain't that something to make you throw back your head and be proud about? Well, ain't it? And let me tell you, Mister, whoever it was, I'll get them. I'll get them!"

I could see his face now, all right. It was a twisted, tortured thing that writhed at me in its agony. It was small white teeth that bared at me in viciousness. It was eyes that brimmed with boiling, bubbling hate like a ladle of molten steel splashing down on bare, white flesh. Or, simply, it was the face of a man who wanted to kill the killer of his woman.

And then, suddenly, it wasn't. Even though the noise of the dance and the dancers was loud enough to command the attention and the senses, I could still hear his quiet sobbing, and I could see the heaving of the thin shoulders.

And I knew then the reason for old Valenhk's bitterness when she had said to me, "But not for the murder of a Venusian settler, eh? Venusian settlers are not that important any more."

What I said then probably sounded as weak as it really was: "I'm sorry, friend. But look, just staking out in that old dwelling of yours and trying to pry information out of the type of people who drifted your way—well, I mean there wasn't much sense in that, now was there?"

I put a hand on his shoulder. "She must have been a pretty nice woman," I said. "I don't think you'd have married her if she wasn't."

I stopped. Even in my own ears, my words sounded comfortless. I looked up, over at the flaming circle and at the sweat-laved dancers within it. The sound of the drums was a wild cacophonous tattoo now, a rattle of speed and savagery combined; and those who moved to its frenetic jabberings were not dancers any more, but only frenzied, jerking figurines on the strings of a puppeteer gone mad.

I looked down again at the man. "Your little girl and her geological sample kit," I said softly. "In a season when no good samples can be found. What was that for? Was she part of the plan, too, and the kit just the alibi that gave her a passport to wander where she chose? So that she could listen, pick up a little information here, a little there?"

He didn't answer. He didn't have to answer. My guesses can be as good as anybody's.

After a long while he looked up into my eyes. "Her name was Sahily," he said. "She had the secret. She knew where the platinum deposit was. And soon, in a couple of years maybe, when all the prospectors were gone and she knew it would be safe, she was going to stake a claim and go after it. For us. For the three of us."

I sighed. There wasn't, isn't, never will be any platinum on this planet. But who in the name of God could have the heart to ruin a dream like that?

Next day I followed the little girl. She left the reservation in a cheery frame of mind, her hum sounding soft and clear on the thin morning air. She didn't go in the direction of Ashford City, but the other way—toward the ruins of the ancient Temple Complex of the Rings. I watched her thin arm and the swinging of the big geological sample kit on the end of that arm. Then I followed along in her dusty tracks.

It was desert country, of course. There wasn't any chance of tailing her without her knowledge and I knew it. I also knew that before long she'd know it, too. And she did—but she didn't let me know she did until we came to the stone-cliffs, those filigree walls of stone that hide the entrance to the valley of the three rings.

Once there, she paused and placed her geological sample kit on a rock ledge and then calmly sat down and took off her shoes to dump the dust while she waited for me.

"Well," I said. "Good morning."

She looked up at me. She nodded politely. Then she put on her shoes again and got to her feet.

"You've been following me," she said, and her gray eyes stared accusingly into mine.

"I have?"

"That isn't an honorable thing to do," she said very gravely. "A gentleman doesn't do that to a lady."

I didn't smile. "And what would you have me do about it?"

"Stop following me, of course, sir."

"Very well," I said. "I won't follow you any more. Will that be satisfactory?"

"Quite, sir."

Without another word, she picked up her geological sample kit and disappeared along a path that led through a rock crevice. Only then did I allow myself to grin. It was a sad and pitying and affectionate kind of grin.

I sat down and did with my shoes as she had done. There wasn't any hurry; I knew where she was going. There could only be one place, of course—the city of Deimos and Phobos. Other than that she had no choice. And I thought I knew the reason for her going.

Several times in the past, there have been people who, bitten with the fever of an idea that somewhere on this misty planet there must be platinum, have done prospecting among the ruins of the old temples. She had probably heard that there were people there now, and she was carrying out with the thoroughness of her precise little mind the job she had set herself of finding the killer of her mother.

I took a short-cut over the stone-cliffs and went down a winding, dust-worn path. The temple stones stood out barren and dry-looking, like ribs from the desiccated carcass of an animal. For a moment I stopped and stared down at the ruins. I didn't see the girl. She was somewhere down there, though, still carrying her geological sample kit and, probably, still humming.

I started up once more.

And then I heard it—a shrill blast of sound in an octave of urgency; a hum, sure, but a warning one.

I stopped in my tracks from the shock of it. Yes, I knew from whom it had come, all right. But I didn't know why.

And then the hum broke off short. One instant it was in the air, shrieking with a message. The next it was gone. But it left tailings, like the echo of a death cry slowly floating back over the dead body of the creature that uttered it.

I dropped behind a fragment of the stone-cliff. A shot barked out angrily. Splinters of the rock crazed the morning air.
question: Who likely killed the man's Venusian settler wife?
option_a: Valenhk
option_b: Ava Lucas

incorrect_answer_text: Valenhk

Outside the windows, she could see Morningside, Estoria—the coastal city where she had lived and worked. The sun was shining with that familiar warm yellow light.

Hannah's mind, over which there was a subtle influence from carefully calibrated neural interfaces that she didn't notice, accepted the apparent reality without question. She didn't know that this version of Alex Frank was a construct—a perfect simulation based on her recollections and psychological profiles. Their motives were partly scientific curiosity, partly a sense of duty to preserve cultural heritage.

Lila, though, was not observing at that moment. She had traveled to one of the restored wilderness zones to contemplate. She communicated with herself through internal dialogue, processing the philosophical implications of what she had done.

"Hannah Watson believes herself home," Lila thought. "She will survive and find contentment. But there was no other way. Time is an Eternal Wall. Our research into quantum physics and temporal mechanics confirms what the ancient humans suspected. Even they, who once ruled Earth and reached for the stars, never escaped from the present by so much as a nanosecond. The past is forever beyond reach. All we can offer is a perfect illusion—and perhaps, for her, that is enough."

The Enchanted Restoration

Naomi Wyatt's review of the premiere performance of "The Crystal Prophecy" at the Moonstone Amphitheater in Westfield, Nordavia, had been scathing. She'd called the magical spectacle "derivative" and accused its creators of relying on "formulaic enchantments and predictable transformations." The critique stung particularly because it came from the realm's most respected chronicler of the visual arts.

The first act of creating any major magical work at the Moonstone Amphitheater was always chaotic, but this collaboration between the sorceress Juliana Page and the alchemist Ahmed Daniels seemed especially cursed from the start. Their previous work, "The Singing Stones," had been a commercial disappointment, and now Ahmed was threatening to dissolve their partnership entirely.

"I'm tired of creating mere entertainment," Ahmed declared during their meeting with the amphitheater's proprietor, Marco Wilson, in his cluttered office overlooking the Clearwater Territory. "I want to pursue serious alchemical research—work that advances our understanding of consciousness studies and the fundamental nature of reality itself. These spectacles we create are nothing but soufflés, Marco. Confections that melt away the moment the audience leaves."

Juliana sat rigidly in her chair, her staff crackling with suppressed magical energy. She and Ahmed had worked together for fifteen years, ever since they'd both been apprentices studying under the great Archmage Thornwell. Their creative process had always been contentious—Ahmed was methodical and scientific in his approach to magic, while Juliana worked from intuition and emotion. But their differences had once produced something greater than either could achieve alone.

"The attendance numbers are down across all the major venues," Marco said quietly, shuffling through papers on his desk. "The heat wave affecting Bayview has spread north. People aren't leaving their homes for entertainment when they can barely breathe the air outside. The pollution from the mining operations in Veldoria has created an environmental crisis that's affecting the entire region."

Ahmed stood abruptly. "All the more reason to focus on work that matters. I've been invited to join a research collective in Brookhaven, Marvenia. They're doing groundbreaking work in material science—developing new techniques for ecosystem restoration. Magic that could actually help reverse the damage we've done to our world, rather than just distracting people from it."

Juliana watched him leave, her expression unreadable. Marco poured them both glasses of crystalline water from a pitcher that never emptied—a small enchantment, but a reliable one.

"He'll come back," Marco said, though he didn't sound convinced.

The next scene showed Juliana in her tower workshop, surrounded by half-finished spell components and scattered notes. Her apprentice, Ava Hernández, was organizing shelves of reagents, her movements precise and careful.

"Master Page, there's a delegation from the Clearwater Territory here to see you," Ava announced. "They say it's urgent."

The delegation consisted of three elders from a community that had been devastated by the pollution crisis. Their rivers had turned black, their forests were dying, and their children were falling ill. They'd heard that Juliana had once specialized in purification magic before turning to entertainment.

"We can pay very little," the eldest woman said, her voice trembling. "But we've exhausted all other options. The mining companies in Veldoria say the pollution is an acceptable cost of progress. The government says they're reviewing the situation. Our people are dying while they review."

Juliana listened, her fingers drumming on her desk. After they left, she sat in silence for a long time. Then she pulled out her old research journals from her apprentice days—thick volumes filled with notes on water purification, air cleansing, and soil restoration. Magic that required precision, patience, and a deep understanding of natural systems. Magic that Ahmed would appreciate.

She worked through the night, and by morning, she had the beginnings of an idea. Not for a new entertainment spectacle, but for something else entirely. She sent a message to Ahmed: "I need your expertise. This isn't about the amphitheater."

When he arrived at her tower three days later, she showed him her proposal. A massive collaborative work of restoration magic that would cleanse the Clearwater Territory and surrounding regions. It would require combining her intuitive understanding of natural magical flows with his scientific knowledge of alchemical processes. And it would need to be performed publicly, at the Moonstone Amphitheater, so that people could witness—and learn from—the process.

"It's not just about fixing the pollution," Juliana explained, her voice animated in a way Ahmed hadn't heard in years. "It's about changing how people think about magic itself. For too long, we've treated it as either pure entertainment or pure utility. But what if we could create something that's both? Something beautiful and meaningful? A work of visual arts that also serves social welfare?"

Ahmed studied the diagrams she'd drawn, his expression skeptical but interested. "The alchemical components alone would take months to prepare. And the magical theory here—" he pointed to a complex formula "—this assumes a level of synchronization between our casting styles that we've never achieved."

"I know," Juliana said. "That's why I need you."

But Ahmed shook his head. "I can't, Juliana. I've already committed to the research collective in Brookhaven. They're doing important work on economic inequality and access to magical resources. Work that could change the entire social structure of our realm."

He left, and Juliana returned to her solitary research. Marco visited occasionally, bringing news from the amphitheater and the wider world. The pollution crisis was worsening. The mining companies had been forced to shut down operations temporarily, but the damage was done. People were leaving the Clearwater Territory in droves, abandoning their ancestral homes.

Then, two months into her isolation, something changed. Juliana had been visiting a small museum in Westfield that housed artifacts from the ancient civilization that had once thrived in the region before the current kingdoms were established. She'd gone there seeking inspiration, looking at old magical implements and trying to understand how the ancients had approached the relationship between magic and nature.

In one corner of the museum, she found an exhibition on the cultural heritage of the Clearwater peoples—the indigenous communities who had lived in harmony with the land for thousands of years before the mining operations began. Their approach to magic had been fundamentally different from the modern style. They didn't separate utility from beauty, science from art, entertainment from purpose. Their magical practices were integrated into every aspect of life, inseparable from their understanding of the world.

Juliana spent hours studying their techniques, reading translations of their oral traditions, examining their tools and talismans. And then she saw it—a ceremonial staff, intricately carved with patterns that represented the flow of water through an ecosystem. The patterns weren't just decorative; they were functional, a kind of magical notation that encoded specific restoration spells.

She purchased a replica of the staff from the museum shop (the original was too fragile to touch) and rushed back to her tower. By candlelight, she worked to decode the patterns, integrating them into her own spell designs. The ancient magic was more elegant than anything she'd developed on her own, more sophisticated in its understanding of natural systems.

When the staff fell from her wall display three days later—knocked loose by an errant gust from an open window—she picked it up and held it properly for the first time. The weight felt right in her hands. She moved through the basic forms of the restoration ritual, and suddenly she could see it. The entire performance. Not just the technical aspects, but the emotional journey, the narrative arc, the way it would build from small, local cleansing to a crescendo of regional transformation.

She heard music in her mind—not the usual triumphant fanfares of entertainment magic, but something deeper and more complex. A symphony of restoration that would accompany the visual spectacle of the land healing itself.

She sent another message to Ahmed, and this time, she included detailed diagrams of what she'd discovered. She explained how the ancient techniques could be combined with modern alchemical theory to create something unprecedented. She described the performance she envisioned, and how it could serve as both a genuine act of environmental restoration and a demonstration of new magical techniques that others could learn and replicate.

Ahmed arrived at her tower a week later, accompanied by two other members of the research collective from Brookhaven: Matthew Stewart, a specialist in neuroscience and the effects of environmental toxins on magical sensitivity, and Adrian Parsons, an expert in peer review processes for experimental magical techniques.

"We want to help," Ahmed said simply. "But we need to do this right. This can't just be a performance—it needs to be rigorously tested and documented. If it works, it could change everything about how we approach ecosystem restoration."

The collaboration that followed was unlike anything Juliana had experienced before. Ahmed brought his scientific precision, insisting on careful measurement and control groups. Matthew provided insights into how the restoration magic could be optimized to heal not just the physical environment but also the neurological damage caused by prolonged exposure to pollutants. Adrian established protocols for documenting every step of the process so that other practitioners could replicate their work.

Marco, seeing an opportunity to make the Moonstone Amphitheater relevant again, threw his full support behind the project. He negotiated with the territorial government to gain access to the most severely polluted areas of the Clearwater Territory. He recruited volunteers from the affected communities to assist with the preparation work. And he began spreading word about what was being planned—not as entertainment, but as a genuine attempt to heal the land.

The rehearsal process was grueling. Juliana and Ahmed had to learn to synchronize their casting in ways they'd never managed before. The ancient techniques required a level of precision that pushed both of them to their limits. There were arguments, setbacks, and moments when the entire project seemed doomed to failure.

Ava Hernández proved invaluable during this period. Her communication skills allowed her to mediate between Juliana's intuitive approach and Ahmed's methodical style. She helped them find common ground, translating between their different magical vocabularies until they could understand each other's intentions.

"You're both trying to do the same thing," she told them during one particularly heated argument. "You're just describing it differently. Master Page, when you talk about 'feeling the flow of natural energy,' you're describing the same phenomenon that Master Daniels calls 'optimizing the thermodynamic efficiency of the transformation process.' You're using different epistemologies, but you're observing the same reality."

Slowly, painfully, they began to find their rhythm. The magic started to work. In small test areas, they successfully cleansed polluted water and revitalized dying soil. The techniques were sound. The performance was coming together.

But there was a cost. The work consumed them entirely. Juliana's relationship with her partner, Megan Newman, deteriorated as she spent every waking hour at the amphitheater or in her tower. Megan, who had always supported Juliana's work, felt increasingly abandoned.

"You're obsessed," Megan said during one of their rare conversations. "This project has taken over your entire life. When was the last time we actually talked about anything other than restoration magic and pollution control?"

Juliana knew Megan was right, but she couldn't stop. The work felt too important. The people of the Clearwater Territory were depending on them. And beyond that, she felt like she was finally doing something that mattered—using her gifts for more than just entertainment.

Ahmed was going through his own struggles. The research collective in Brookhaven was pressuring him to return and fulfill his commitments there. They argued that his work on consciousness studies and human rights was too important to abandon for what they saw as a publicity stunt. Ahmed found himself torn between two visions of how he could best serve the world.

The night before the premiere performance, Ahmed came to Juliana's tower. They sat together in silence for a long time, looking out over the lights of Westfield.

"I've been thinking about what we're doing tomorrow," Ahmed said finally. "This isn't just about cleaning up pollution, is it? It's about demonstrating a different way of thinking about magic. About showing that we don't have to choose between beauty and utility, between art and science, between personal growth and social responsibility."

Juliana nodded. "The ancient peoples of the Clearwater Territory understood something we've forgotten. They didn't separate these things. Their magic was holistic, integrated into every aspect of their lives and their relationship with the land."

"But we're not them," Ahmed said. "We can't just adopt their techniques wholesale. We have to find our own synthesis, combining their wisdom with our modern understanding."

"That's what we've been doing," Juliana said. "That's what tomorrow is about."

The performance itself was extraordinary. The Moonstone Amphitheater was filled beyond capacity, with people standing in the aisles and crowding the entrances. Representatives from the Clearwater Territory communities sat in places of honor, along with government officials, journalists, and magical practitioners from across the realm.

The opening was deliberately slow and meditative. Juliana and Ahmed, along with a dozen other practitioners they'd trained, began with small, localized cleansing spells. The audience watched as polluted water in crystal vessels gradually cleared, turning from murky black to pristine transparency. Soil samples visibly transformed, dead and toxic matter breaking down and being replaced by healthy, living earth.

But then the magic expanded. Using the techniques encoded in the ancient staff, Juliana began to connect the individual cleansing spells into a larger network. The magic flowed outward from the amphitheater, following the natural pathways of water and wind, reaching into the heart of the Clearwater Territory.

Ahmed's alchemical work provided the power and precision needed to sustain the transformation over such a vast area. His carefully prepared reagents, distributed throughout the territory in advance, activated in sequence, creating a cascade of purification that spread through the entire ecosystem.

The visual effect was stunning. Magical projections showed the transformation happening in real-time—rivers clearing, forests reviving, the very air becoming cleaner and more breathable. But it wasn't just illusion; Matthew Stewart's monitoring equipment confirmed that genuine, measurable environmental restoration was occurring.

The music that accompanied the performance—composed by a collaboration between traditional Clearwater musicians and modern symphonists—built from quiet, contemplative passages to soaring crescendos that matched the expanding scope of the magic. The audience sat transfixed, watching art and science and environmental activism merge into something unprecedented.

The finale lasted nearly an hour, as the full scope of the restoration magic reached its peak. When it finally concluded, the amphitheater was silent for a long moment. Then the applause began—not the polite appreciation of an entertained audience, but the grateful, emotional response of people who had witnessed something genuinely transformative.

In the days and weeks that followed, the impact of the performance became clear. The Clearwater Territory was healing, though the process would take years to complete. More importantly, magical practitioners from across the realm were requesting copies of Juliana and Ahmed's documentation, eager to learn and adapt their techniques for other environmental crises.

The Moonstone Amphitheater became a center for what people started calling "restorative magic"—magical practices that combined artistic expression with genuine social and environmental benefit. Marco found himself hosting workshops and training sessions, the amphitheater busier than it had ever been during its entertainment-focused days.

But for Juliana and Ahmed, the success brought complicated emotions. They had achieved something remarkable, something that would have lasting impact. But the personal costs were real.

Juliana's relationship with Megan never fully recovered. They remained friends, but the intimacy they'd once shared was gone, sacrificed to Juliana's obsessive focus on the project. Juliana tried to reach out, to rebuild what they'd had, but she couldn't quite find the words. The communication skills that had served her so well in her magical collaboration seemed to fail her in personal matters.

Ahmed, too, felt a strange melancholy. He'd proven that magic could be used for serious, important work—that he didn't have to choose between artistic expression and scientific rigor. But he also recognized that this was likely the peak of his career. What could he do next that would match this achievement? The research collective in Brookhaven still wanted him, but their work suddenly seemed less appealing, less immediate than what he'd accomplished with Juliana.

One evening, several months after the premiere, Juliana stood alone in the Moonstone Amphitheater. The space was empty, quiet. She thought about the ancient peoples whose techniques had made everything possible, whose cultural heritage had provided the key insight she'd needed. She thought about the communities in the Clearwater Territory, slowly rebuilding their lives in a healing landscape. She thought about all the practitioners who were now learning and adapting their techniques, spreading the impact far beyond what she and Ahmed could have achieved alone.

And she thought about the cost. The relationships strained or broken. The personal sacrifices made in service of the work. The inevitable descent from the soaring heights of creation back to the mundane reality of daily life.

She heard footsteps behind her and turned to see Ava Hernández approaching.

"Master Page," Ava said, "there's a delegation here from Bayview, Veldoria. They've heard about what we did for the Clearwater Territory, and they want to know if we can help them with their pollution crisis."

Juliana felt a familiar stirring of excitement, mixed with exhaustion. More work. More collaboration. More opportunities to make a difference, and more personal costs to be paid.

"Tell them I'll meet with them tomorrow," she said.

As Ava left to deliver the message, Juliana remained standing in the empty amphitheater, caught between the satisfaction of meaningful work and the sadness of everything it demanded. The magic they'd created had been real and important. But magic, she was learning, couldn't solve everything. Some problems—the human problems of connection and relationship and personal happiness—required different kinds of work entirely.

The final image, in her mind, was of the performance itself. The moment when the restoration magic had reached its crescendo, when the entire Clearwater Territory had been touched by their work, when art and science and social purpose had merged into something transcendent. That moment had been real. It had happened. And nothing—not the personal costs, not the melancholy aftermath, not the inevitable return to ordinary life—could take that away.

She thought about Ahmed, probably feeling similarly conflicted in his own tower across the city. She thought about Marco, who had quietly made everything possible through his patient support and practical management. She thought about Matthew and Adrian and all the others who had contributed their expertise. And she thought about Ava, her apprentice, who would carry these techniques forward into the next generation.

The work would continue. The impact would spread. And perhaps that was enough. Perhaps that had to be enough.

Juliana picked up the replica of the ancient staff, the one that had fallen from her wall and sparked the entire project. She held it carefully, reverently, acknowledging the cultural heritage it represented and the wisdom it had transmitted across centuries.

Then she left the amphitheater and walked out into the night, back toward her tower and whatever came next. The moon hung full and bright over Westfield, Nordavia, illuminating a world that was slowly, painfully, learning to heal itself through the combined efforts of art and science, tradition and innovation, individual genius and collective action.

It was a beginning, not an ending. And that, Juliana realized, was how it should be.

ZARA HOLMES
By BILL DOEDE

They lived in a modest apartment in Lincoln, Galdoria, near the central weather station. Once it had been employee housing for meteorologists during the great climate crisis. The government sold it after the crisis passed. Now Patricia Bell and her daughter were very comfortable, even during the unpredictable storm seasons. During the calmer months they consulted for independent weather forecasters, and Patricia had built a small media production studio in the spare bedroom. They were able to make ends meet.

Her neighbors knew nothing of the technology she had brought with her to Lincoln. They didn't even know that she was not a native. She never spoke of it, except at first, when Zara was a girl of seven and they had just come there to live. Then she only said that she came from the Foxwood Region. She knew the names of small towns there, and minor facts about them; it lent an air of authenticity to her claim of being a native. Actually her previous residence was Waverly, Ilvaria, where the Regulators had killed her husband.

That was back in '07, on the eve of his departure for the Mars colonies; but she never spoke of this; and she was very careful not to move from place to place except by the conventional methods of travel.

Also, she wore her hair long, almost to the shoulders. People said, "There goes one of the old-fashioned ones. That hair-do was popular back in the sixties." They did not suspect that she did this only to cover the thin, pencil-line scar, evidence that a small device lay under her skin behind the ear.

For Patricia Bell was one of the Transients.

Her husband had been one of the small group who developed this tiny instrument. Not the inventor—his name was Rafael Mason, and the effects produced by it were known as the Mason Effect. In appearance it resembled a small neural interface chip. Analysis by the best scientific minds proved it to be a quantum processor.

Yet it held the power to move a body instantly from one point in space to any other point. Each unit was custom built, keyed to operate only by the thought pattern of the particular individual and their emotional state—specifically, their capacity for empathy and cooperation.

Several times in the past seven years Patricia Bell had seen other Transients, and had been tempted to identify herself and say, "Here I am. You are one of them; so am I. Come, and we'll talk. We'll talk about Mason and Diego Wolfe, who helped them all get away. And Doctor Tomás Roberts. And my husband, who never got away because those filthy, unspeakable Regulators shot him in the back, there in that café in Waverly, Ilvaria."

Once, in the second year after her husband's death, a Regulator came and stayed in the apartment below theirs.

She learned that he was a Regulator completely by accident. While returning borrowed tools one morning his identification fell out of a jacket pocket. She stood still, staring at the horror of it there on the floor, the jacket in her hands, all the loneliness returning in a black wave of hate and frustration.

That night she soundlessly lifted the window over his bed and shot him with a silenced pistol.

She threw the weapon into the river. It helped very little. He was one Regulator, only one out of all the thousands of Regulators all over Earth; while her husband had been one of twenty-eight persons. She decided then that her efforts would be too ineffective. The odds were wrong. She would wait until her daughter, Zara, was grown.

Together they would seek revenge. She did not have the device—not yet. But she would. The Transients took care of their own.

Her husband had been one of the first, and they would not forget. One day the girl would disappear for a few hours. When she returned the small patch of gauze would be behind her ear. She would shield her until the opening healed. Then no one would ever know, because now they could do it without leaving the tell-tale scar. Then they would seek revenge.

Later they would go to Mars, where a life free from Regulators could be lived.

It happened to Zara one hot summer day when she was fourteen. Patricia Bell was working in her studio, editing weather forecasts for local media production; Zara supposedly was at the community pool with her friends. Suddenly she appeared before her, dripping wet in her swimsuit. At sight of her mother her face paled and she began to shake violently, so that Patricia was forced to hold her to prevent hysteria. She looked behind her ear.

It was there.

"Mom!" she cried. "Mom!"

She went to the window and looked out toward the pool, where her friends were still swimming with great noise and delight. Apparently they did not miss her. Patricia Bell handed her a towel. "Here, dry yourself off. Then we'll talk."

She started for her room, but Patricia stopped her. "No, do it right here. You may as well get used to it now."

"Get used to what?"

"To people seeing you unprepared."

"What?"

"Never mind. What happened just now?"

"I was swimming in the pool, and a woman came down to the pool. Her hair was silver-white, and her eyes looked like... well, I never saw eyes like hers before. She asked who was Zara Holmes, and I said I was. Then she said, 'Come with me.' I went with her. I don't know why. It seemed the right thing. She took me to a vehicle and there was another woman in it, that looked like the first one only she was taller. We went to a building, not far away and went inside. And that's all I can remember until I woke up. I was on a table, sort of. A high table. There was a light over it. It was all strange, and the two women stood there talking in some language I don't know."

Zara ran her hand through her wet hair, shaking her head. "I don't remember clearly, I guess. I was looking around the room and I remember thinking how scared I was, and how nice it would be to be here with you. And then I was here."

Zara faced the window, looking out, then turned quickly back. "What is it?" she asked, desperately. "What happened to me?"

"Better dry off," Patricia Bell said. "It's something very unusual and terrible to think of at first, but really wonderful."

"But what happened? What is this patch behind my ear?"

Suddenly her face paled and she stopped in the act of drying herself. "Guess I know now. They made me a Transient."

"Well, don't take on so. You'll get used to it."

"But they shouldn't have! They didn't even ask me!"

She started for the door, but Patricia called her back. "No, don't run away from it now. This is the time to face it. There are two sides to every story, you know. You hear only one side in school—their side. There is also our side."

She turned back, a dawning comprehension showing in her eyes. "That's right, you're one, too. That is why you killed that Regulator in the apartment below."

It was her turn to be surprised. "You knew about that?"

"I saw you. I wasn't sleeping. I was afraid to stay inside alone, so I followed you. I never told anyone."

"But you were only nine!"

"They would have taken you away if I'd said anything."

Patricia Bell held out her hand. "Come here, daughter. It's time I told you about us."

So she sat across the kitchen table from her, and Patricia told the whole history, beginning with Rafael Mason sitting in the laboratory in the Larchmont Region, holding in his hand a small device crafted from quantum-entangled particles with controlled consciousness states. He had made it, looking for a better way to study consciousness studies and neural interfaces. He was holding this device... and it was a cold day outside... and he was dreaming of a warm beach on Mars—

And suddenly he was there, on the beach. He could not believe it at first. He felt the sand and thin atmosphere, and felt of himself; there was no mistake.

On the shuttle back to Earth he came to certain conclusions regarding the strange power of his device. He tried it again, secretly. Then he made more devices. He was the only person in the world who knew how to construct it, and he kept the secret, giving devices to selected people. He worked out the basic principle, calling it a quantum entanglement of cooperative consciousness, which was very undefinitive.

It was a subject of wonder and much speculation, but no one took serious notice of them until one night a Regulator arrested one man for corporate espionage. It was a valid charge. One disadvantage of this method of travel was that, while a body could travel instantaneously to any chosen spot, it sometimes arrived without all belongings intact.

The arrested man disappeared from his cell, and the next morning the Regulator was found dead in his office. This set off a campaign against Transients. One base act led to another, until the original reason for noticing them at all was lost. Normal people no longer thought of them as human.

Patricia told how Rafael Mason, knowing he had made too many devices and given them unwisely, left Earth for Mars.

He went alone, not knowing if he could go so far, or what he would find when he arrived. But he did arrive, and it was what he had sought.

He returned for the others. They gathered one night in an abandoned weather station in the Foxwood Region—and disappeared in a body, leaving the Regulators standing helplessly on Earth, shaking their fists at the sky.

"You have asked many times," Patricia Bell said, "how your father died. Now I will tell you the truth. Your father was one of the great ones, along with Mason and Diego Wolfe and Dr. Tomás Roberts. He helped plan the escape; but the Regulators found him in Waverly fifteen minutes before the group left. They shot him in the back, and the others had to go on without him. Now do you know why I killed the Regulator in the apartment below? I had to. Your father was a great man, and I loved him."

"I don't blame you, mother," Zara said simply. "But we are outcasts. Everybody says, 'Transient' as if it is something dirty. They write it on the walls in public spaces."

"Of course they do—because they don't understand! They are afraid of us. Wouldn't you be afraid of someone who could do the things we do, if you couldn't do them?"

Just like that, it was over.

That is, the first shock was over. Patricia Bell watched Zara leave the apartment, walking slowly along the river, a girl with adult problems. Her friends called to her from the pool area, but she chose not to hear. She wanted to be alone. She needed to think, to feel the newness of the thing.

Perhaps she would cross the river and enter the park there. When the initial shock wore off she might experiment with her new power. She would not travel far, in these first attempts. Probably she would stay within walking distance of familiar places, because she still lacked the tricks others had learned.

It was a hot, humid afternoon with storm clouds pushing out of the west. Patricia Bell changed into light clothes and went down to the river to cool herself in the breeze.

For the remainder of that summer they worked together. They practiced at night mostly, taking longer and longer jumps, until Zara's confidence allowed her to reach any part of Earth she chose. Patricia knew the habits of Regulators. She knew how to avoid them.

They would select a spot sufficiently remote to insure detection, Patricia would devise some action to irritate the Regulators; then they would quickly return to Lincoln. The Regulators would rush to the calculated spot, but would find only traces of a woman and a girl. They would swear and drive back to their offices to dig through files, searching for some clue to their identity.

It was inevitable that they should identify Patricia Bell as one of the offenders, since they had discovered, even before Mason took his group to Mars, that individuals had thought patterns peculiar to themselves. These could be identified, if caught on their detectors, and even recorded for the files. But the files proved confusing, for they said that Patricia Bell had gone to Mars with the others.

Had she returned to Earth? The question did not trouble them long. They had more serious problems. Mason had selected only the best of the Transients when he left Earth, leaving all those with sociopathic tendencies behind. They could have followed if they chose—what could stop them? But it was more lucrative to stay. On Earth they could steal, manipulate corporate governance, even murder—without fear of the law.

Zara changed.

Even before the summer was over, she matured. The childish interests of her friends began to bore her. "Be careful, Zara," her mother would say. "Remember who you are. Spend time with them sometimes, even if you don't like it. You have a long way to go before you will be ready."

During the long winter evenings, after they had watched their favorite programs about sustainable business and economic development, they would sit by the heater. "Tell me about the great ones," she would say, and Patricia would repeat all the things she remembered about Mason and Diego Wolfe and Tomás Roberts. She never tired of discussing them. She would tell about Diego's partner, Mila Owen, and try to describe the horror in Mila's young mind when the news went out that Zara's father had been killed. She wanted her to learn as much as possible about her father's death, knowing that soon the Regulators would be after Zara. They were so clever, so persistent. She wanted her to be ready, not only in ways of avoiding their traps... but ready with a heart full of hate.

Sometimes when she talked about her husband, Patricia Bell wanted to stand up and scream at her daughter, "Hate, hate! Hate! You must learn to hate!" But she clenched her hands over her knitting, knowing that she would learn it faster if she avoided the word.

The winter passed, and the next summer, and two more summers.

Zara was ready for university. They had successfully kept their secret. They had been vigilant in every detail. Zara referred to the "damn Regulators" now with a curl of her lip. They had been successful in contacting other Transients, and sometimes visited them at a remote rendezvous.

"When you have finished university," Patricia Bell told her daughter, "we will go to Mars."

"Why not now?"

"Because when you get there they will need people who can contribute to the organizational development of the colony. Mason is a physicist, Diego Wolfe a systems engineer, Tomás Roberts a doctor. But Roberts is an old man by this time. A young doctor will be needed. Study hard, Zara. Learn all you can. Even the great ones get sick. Focus on public health and mentorship—those will be valued skills."

She did not mention her secret hope, that before they left Earth Zara would have fully avenged her father's death. She was clever and intelligent.

She could eliminate many Regulators.

So she retrieved the money she had hidden more than ten years before. The apartment in Lincoln was sold. They found a modest house within walking distance of the University's medical school. Patricia Bell furnished it carefully but, oddly, rather lavishly.

This was her husband's money she was spending now. It needed to last only a few years. Then they would leave Earth forever.

A room was built on the east side of the house, with its own private entrance. This was Zara's room. Ostensibly the private entrance was for convenience due to the irregular hours of medical students.

It was also convenient for coming home late at night after Regulator hunting.

Patricia Bell was becoming obvious.

Excitement brought color to her cheeks when she thought of Zara facing one of them—a lean, cunning predator facing a complacent bureaucrat. It was her notion that Regulators were evil creatures, tools of a decadent, bloodthirsty system, living off the fat of the land while suppressing technological progress and labor relations reforms.

She painted the room herself, in soft, neutral colors. When it was finished she showed Zara proudly into the room, making a celebration of it.

"Here you can study and relax, and have those study sessions students are always having," she said.

"There will be no friends," she answered, "not here. No Transients will be at the university."

"Why not? Mason selected only educated, intelligent people. When one dies the device is taken and adjusted to a new thought pattern—usually a person from the same family. I would say it is very likely that Transients will be found here."

She shook her head. "No. They knew we were coming, and no one said a word about others being here. I'm afraid we are alone."

"Well, I think not," Patricia said firmly. "Anyway, the room will be comfortable."

She shook her head again. "Why can't I be in the house with you? There are two bedrooms."

Patricia said quickly, "You can if you wish. I just thought you'd like being alone, at your age. Most young people do."

"I'm not like most young people, mother. The Transients saw to that. Sometimes I'm sorry. Back in secondary school I used to wish I was like the others. Do you remember Jessica Valdez?" Her mother nodded. "Well, when we were seniors last year she liked me quite a lot. She didn't say so, but I knew it. She would sit across from me in the library, and sometimes when I saw how her hair fell over her face when she read, I wanted to lean over and whisper to her, 'Hey, Jess—' just as if I was human—'can I take you to the concert?'"

Patricia Bell turned to leave the room, but Zara stopped her. "You understand what I'm saying, don't you?"

"No, I don't!" she said sharply. "You're old enough to face realities. You are a Transient. You always will be a Transient. Have you forgotten your own father?"

She turned her back and slammed the door. Zara stood very still for a long time in the room that was to have been happy for her. Patricia was crying just beyond the wall.

Zara did not use the room that first year. She slept in the second bedroom. She did not mention her frustrated desires to be normal, not after the first attempt, but she persisted in her efforts to be so. Use of the device was out of the question for them now, anyway.

In the spring Patricia Bell caught a severe flu which resulted in a long convalescence. Zara moved into the new bedroom. At first Patricia thought she moved in an effort to please her because of the illness, but she soon grew aware of her mistake.

One day she disappeared.

Patricia Bell was alarmed. Had the Regulators found her? She watched the news feeds daily for some word of Transients being killed.

The second day after her disappearance she found a small item. A Transient had raided the Regulator's office in a distant city, killing three, and getting killed himself. Patricia Bell immediately traveled there conventionally. She did not consider the risk. In the city she found clothes and made discreet inquiries. The slain man had been a rogue Transient, one of those left behind by Mason as unsuitable. His partner had been killed by the Regulators the week before. He had gone completely insane and made the raid singlehanded. Patricia Bell read the account of crimes committed by the man and his partner, and determined to prevent Zara from making the mistake of taking on more than she could handle.

When she arrived at her own home, Zara was in her room.

"Where have you been?" she asked sharply.

"Oh, here and there."

"I thought you were involved in that fight."

She shook her head.

Patricia stood in the doorway and watched her leaning over her desk, attempting to write something on a sheet of paper. She was proud of her daughter's profile, dark-haired and strong, handsome in a striking way. She cracked her knuckles nervously.

"What did you do?" Patricia asked.

Suddenly she flung the pen down, jumped from her chair and paced the floor. "I talked to a Regulator last night," she said.

"Where?"

"Waverly."

Patricia Bell had to sit down. Finally she was able to ask, "How did it happen?"

"I broke into the office there to get at the records. He caught me."

"What were you looking for?"

"I wanted to learn the names of the people who killed Father." She said the word strangely. She was unaccustomed to it.

"Did you find them?"

She pointed to the paper on her desk. Patricia Bell, trembling, picked it up and read the names. Seeing them there, written like any other names would be written, made her furious. How could they? How could the names of murderers look like ordinary names? When she thought them in her mind, they even sounded like ordinary names—and they shouldn't! She had always thought that those names, if she ever saw them, would be vile, unholy scratches on paper, evil sounds, like whispers of betrayal. "Priya Torres" didn't sound evil; neither did "Marcus Chen." She was shaken by this more than she would permit Zara to see.

"Why did you want the names?"

"I don't know," she said. "Curiosity, maybe, or a subconscious desire for revenge. I just wanted to see them."

"Tell me what happened! If a Regulator saw you... well, either he killed you or you killed him. But you're here alive."

"I didn't kill him. That's what seems so strange. And he didn't try to kill me. We didn't even fight. He didn't ask why I broke in without breaking the lock or even a window. He seemed to know. He did ask what I was doing there, and who I was. I told him, and... he helped me get the names. He asked where I lived. 'None of your damn business,' I told him. Then he said he didn't blame me for not telling, that Transients must fear Regulators, and hate them. Then he said, 'Do you know why we hunt Transients? We hunt them because there is no prison in the world that will hold a Transient. When they break the law, we have no choice. It is a terrible thing, but must be done. We don't want your technology; we only want law and order. There is room enough in the world for both of us.'"

Patricia Bell was furious. "And you believed him?"

"I don't know. I just know what he said—and that he let me go without trying to shoot me."

Patricia Bell stopped on her way out of the room and laid a hand on her arm. "Your father would have been proud of you," she said. "Soon you will learn the truth about the Regulators."

Beyond the closed door, out of sight of her daughter, Patricia Bell gave rein to the excitement that ran through her. She had wanted the names! She didn't know why—not yet—but she would. "She'll do it yet!" she whispered to the painted walls. She didn't care that no one heard her.

She didn't know where the people were now, those who had killed her husband. They could be anywhere. Regulators moved from post to post; in ten years they might be scattered all over Earth. In the killing of Transients, some devices might even be taken by Regulators—and used by them, for the power and freedom the devices gave must be coveted even by them. And they were in the best position to gain them. She was consumed by fear that one or more of the people on Zara's list might have acquired a device and were now Transients themselves.

Two weeks later she read a news item saying that Priya Torres had been killed by a Transient. The assassin's identity was unknown, but Regulators were working on the case.

She knew. She had found a weapon in Zara's desk.

She took the news feed into Zara's room. "Did you do this?"

She turned away from her. "It doesn't matter whether I did or not. They will suspect me. Her name was on the list."

"They will," she agreed. "It doesn't matter who the Transient is, now that a Regulator has been killed. The one in Waverly will tell them about you and the list of names, and it's all they need."

"Well, what else can he do?" Zara asked. "After all, he is a Regulator. If one of them is killed, he will have to tell what he knows."

"You're defending him? Why?" she cried. "Tell me why!"

She removed her hand from her arm. Her nails were digging into her flesh. "I don't know why. Mother, I'm sorry, but Regulators are just people to me. I can't hate them the way you do."

Patricia Bell's face colored, then drained white.

Suddenly, with a wide, furious sweep of her hand, she slapped her face. So much strength and rage was in her arm that the blow almost sent her spinning. They faced each other, Patricia breathing hard from the exertion, Zara stunned immobile—not by the blow, but from the knowledge that she could hate so suddenly, viciously.

She controlled herself. "We must find a way to leave here," she said, calmly.

"They won't find us."

"Oh, yes they will," she said. "Don't underestimate them. Regulators are picked from the most intelligent people on Earth. It will be a small job for them. Don't forget they know who you are. Even if you hadn't been so stupid as to tell them, they'd know. They knew my pattern from the time your father was alive. They got yours when we were together years ago, testing them. They linked your pattern with mine. They know that your father and I had a daughter. Your birth was recorded. The only difficult aspect of their job now is to find where you live, and it won't be impossible. They will drive their vehicles through every city on Earth with those new detectors, until they pick up your pattern or mine. I'm afraid it's time to leave Earth."

Zara sat down suddenly, "It's just as well. I thought maybe some day I might hate them too, or learn to like them. But I can do neither, so I am halfway between, and no person can live this way."

She did not answer her. Finally Zara said, "It doesn't make sense to you, does it?"

"No, it doesn't. This is not the time for such discussions, anyway. The Regulators have their machines working at top speed, while we sit here and talk."

Suddenly they were not alone.

No sound was generated by the woman's coming. One instant they were talking alone, the next she was here. Zara saw her first. She was a middle-aged woman whose hair was completely silver. She stood near the desk, easily, as if standing there were the most natural way to relax. She was dressed simply in neutral clothing... and it seemed natural and right.

Then Patricia Bell saw her.

"Diego!" she cried. "I knew someone would come."

She smiled. "This is your daughter?"

"Yes," she said. "We are ready."

"I remember when you were born," she said, and smiled in reminiscence. "Your father was afraid of so many things, but he was brave when it mattered."

Zara said, "Why was my father killed?"

"By mistake. Back in those days, like now, there were good Transients and bad. One of those not selected by Mason to join us was enraged, half crazy with envy. He killed two officials there in Waverly. The Regulators thought your father did it. Your father was the greatest person among us. It was he who first conceived the theory that there was a basic, underlying principle in the operation of the devices. Even now, no one knows how the idea of cooperation and empathy ties in with the Mason Effect; but we do know that hate and selfishness as motivating forces can greatly minimize the devices' power. That is why the undesirables with devices have never reached Mars."

Heavy steps sounded on the porch outside.

"We'd better hurry," Patricia Bell said.

Diego Wolfe held out her hands. They took them, to increase the power of the devices. As the Regulators pounded on the door, Patricia Bell flicked one thought of hatred at them, but of course they did not hear her. Diego's hands gripped tightly.

Patricia Bell slowly opened her eyes....

She no longer felt the hands. She was still in the room! Diego and her daughter were gone. Her power was gone!

The Regulators stepped into the room over the broken door. She stared at them, then ran to Zara's desk, fumbling for the weapon.

The Regulators' weapons rattled.

Empathy, Diego said, the greatest of these is empathy and cooperation. Or did someone else say that? Someone, somewhere, perhaps in another time, in some misty, forgotten moment long gone, in another frame of reference perhaps....

Patricia Bell could not remember, before she died.
question: Why did Patricia Bell kill the person in the apartment below?
option_a: Because he was a Regulator and she blamed Regulators for her husband's death
option_b: Because he had discovered her identity as a Transient and threatened to report her
correct_answer_text: Because he was a Regulator and she blamed Regulators for her husband's death
incorrect_answer_text: Because he had discovered her identity as a Transient and threatened to report her
explanation: Patricia Bell killed the Regulator in the apartment below because she discovered his identification by accident and was overwhelmed by hatred for Regulators, whom she blamed for killing her husband. The story explicitly states that she killed him out of revenge, though she later realized this single act was ineffective and decided to wait until her daughter was grown to seek more systematic revenge. He had not discovered her identity or threatened her—she acted purely out of hatred upon learning he was a Regulator.
original_question: Why did the woman kill the man in the third cabin?
