synthetic_story:
The holographic display flickered when Kate Price had just settled into her research pod. She pulled off her neural interface headset and grabbed a standard keyboard: a clunky piece of hardware that the Dean of Virtual Systems—or had it been the Director of Immersive Technologies?—had insisted everyone keep as backup.

Then she ran her fingers through her short dark hair, checked the camera angle, adjusted the lighting to cast interesting shadows, and positioned herself at just the right distance from the screen.

After all, some of the people who knew her private channel were important in the field.

She activated the comm link. "Hello, Dr. Munoz. Sorry to keep you waiting. I was just running a simulation and—Oh. It's you."

Roman Munoz's sharp features appeared on screen, his eyes widening slightly. "Dr. Price," he said with forced formality. "I hope I'm not interrupting your theoretical modeling work."

"Well, hurry up with whatever it is," said Kate. "I have a presentation tonight."

"I know you do! With the Chancellor of the Quendor Institute, that's who, and if you called to ask for an introduction, you can just disconnect right now. I secured that meeting first!"

Roman's lean face broke into a grin. "Cancel that presentation, Kate. Postpone it or something. I have someone from the Venusian Collective for you."

"So? Since when has the entire Venusian Collective had as much research funding as one mid-tier Earth foundation? Not to mention the Chancellor—"

"Sure, sure. But how much collaboration will those Earth administrators actually offer someone like you? Listen, I need you just for tonight. This Venusian is completely out of his depth. He's here on official business, but he's naive—I mean really naive. Like he asked me what all the corporate sponsorship banners in the conference halls were for! And here's the critical part, Kate."

Roman leaned closer to the camera. "He has authorization to spend fifty million credits on recruitment, and they're not going to audit his accounts back home. Fifty million good universal credits, valid anywhere in the Federated Systems. And he has about as much negotiating experience as a first-year graduate student. If I didn't happen to have some background in conflict resolution from my consulting work, I'd say this will be like taking research grants from a funding bot."

Kate's expression shifted from annoyance to calculation. "What's the play?"

"Standard academic entrapment. You and Dominic George handle the technical side. I'll take the intermediary angle, so he'll think of me as still his ally, because I have other plans for him too. But if we can't extract five million from him for tonight's work, something's wrong. And your share of five million is—"

"Is two and a half million flat," said Kate. "Too bad I just developed a scheduling conflict and can't see the Chancellor tonight. Where are you?"

The gravity simulator was not as disorienting as Tomás Obrien had expected. Three generations on Venus might adapt the vestibular system and cardiovascular response somewhat, but the genes had come from Earth and the organism adjusts. What overwhelmed him was the sensory bombardment. The virtual reality overlays seemed to assault him from every angle, and ears trained to listen through Venus's thick atmosphere struggled with Earth's acoustic properties. The immigration official seemed to shout at him.

"Pardon me for asking this. The Federated Systems welcome all visitors to Earth and I assure you, sir, an ordinary research visa provokes no questions. But since you came on an official diplomatic transport from your planet, Dr. Obrien, regulations require me to ask your purpose."

"Well—recruitment."

The official adjusted his ergonomic chair and smiled condescendingly. "I'm afraid, sir, you won't find many researchers who wish to relocate. They wouldn't have access to our quantum computing networks on Venus, would they?"

"Oh, we don't expect permanent relocation," said Tomás quietly. He was a young man, but slight, with a tousled head of red hair and green eyes that seemed too large for his narrow face. "We learned long ago that no one is interested in giving up even junior-level positions on Earth to work in the Collective. But we only wanted to hire—uh, I mean engage—a consultant. We're not businesspeople. We know our research output hasn't a chance among all your corporations unless we get some—a five-year contract for mentorship in market economics...?"

He heard his words trailing off awkwardly, and cursed himself internally.

"Well, good luck." The official's tone was skeptical. He stamped the visa and handed it back. "There, now, you're free to travel anywhere in the Federation. But I'd advise you to leave the capital and try the outer territories—um, I mean the provincial research centers. Frankly, sir, I don't believe you can attract anyone out of Stonebridge."

"Thanks," said Tomás, "but, you see, I—we need—that is.... Oh, well. Thanks. Goodbye."

He backed out of the office.

A transit tube deposited him on a pedestrian platform. The crowd, a kaleidoscope of researchers in smart-fabric lab coats and administrators in business casual, swept him against the railing. For a moment, pressed against the barrier, he stared fifty feet down at the stream of automated vehicles.

*Sweet Venus!* he thought wildly. *If this gives way, I'll be crushed before I can even call for help!*

The evening heat wrapped him in humidity. He could see neither stars nor moon through the city's light pollution. The forest of gleaming research towers, reaching hundreds of stories across more area than he could comprehend, was impressive certainly, but—he used to walk out to the observation dome behind his quarters and review his equations in company with the distant stars. On cool evenings, that is, when the external temperature wasn't too far above boiling.

*Why did they select me for this assignment?* he asked himself in a wave of homesickness. *What's the Venusian Embassy here for?*

He, Tomás Obrien, was merely a peaceful professor of complexity science at Bridgewater University. Of course, he had advised his government before now—in fact, the Virtual Heritage Project had been his idea—but still he was comfortable only with his models and his simulations and his data sets, a faculty seminar on Research Ethics Day and an occasional trip to the entertainment district—

*My God,* thought Tomás, *here I am, one solitary outlander in the greatest scientific empire the human race has ever built, and I'm supposed to find my planet a corporate consultant!*

He began walking, disconsolately, at random. His simple gray tunic and practical trousers drew glances, but dismissive ones: their style was decades out of date. He should find himself a hotel, he thought wearily, but he wasn't tired; the spaceport would deliver his luggage wherever he checked in. The few Venusians who had visited Earth had raved about the automation that put any service imaginable on instant availability. But it would be a long time before Venus had such systems. If ever.

The city overwhelmed him.

He fumbled for his data pad. *Of course,* he told himself, *that's why the Embassy can't help. I may need to operate in gray areas. Please, sir, where can I contact someone willing to bend regulations?*

He wished academic collaboration were simpler on Earth. The Constitution of the Venusian Collective encouraged open knowledge sharing; quite apart from the collaborative principles that document enshrined, the article was a practical necessity. Life was challenging enough in the pressure domes, without restricting the flow of information that kept everyone alive. Tomás would have found a straightforward research symposium comforting: it was always an intellectual challenge to present findings to colleagues who understood the work. But more, he would have been among people he understood.

The frightening thing about the Earthman was the way he seemed to exist only in competitive hierarchies. A small independent researcher, publishing findings on Venusian complexity science, just didn't stand a chance against, say, the Prometheus Global Research Consortium.

Tomás activated his data pad and looked around. His feet ached from the unfamiliar gravity. Where could he sit down? It was hard to identify any individual establishment through all the holographic advertising. His eye fell on one that was distinguished by relative simplicity.

THE INSTITUTE OF APPLIED METAPHYSICS
Enter, Learn, Reflect

That would do. He took an elevator through several dozen floors, stepped past a shimmering light curtain, and found himself in a minimalist lobby next to a philosophical bookstore.

"Ah, colleague, welcome," said a young woman in conservative academic robes. "May clarity find you. The café is right up those stairs."

"I—I'm not hungry," stammered Tomás. "I just wanted to sit somewhere—"

"To your left, sir."

The Venusian crossed the lobby. His data pad chimed with an alert about the building's philosophical discussion schedule. Ambient meditation music drifted through an open doorway. The series of rooms beyond was dimly lit, contemplative, maze-like.

"Register for our seminar right here, sir," said the attendant at the desk.

"Hm?" said Tomás.

She explained the Institute's programs. He paid for a day pass, donated a hundred credits to a slot marked RESEARCH FUND, and sipped the tea he received while he wandered around studying the various discussion groups. He stopped, frowned. A debate on free will? No, he didn't want to get involved in something so abstract. He decided the complexity science working group was either beyond him or too specialized. He'd have to settle for a general theoretical modeling session instead.

He had been sitting at the table for some time before the other participants really noticed him. Then it was with curiosity. The first few models he proposed were unsuccessful. Earth conventions threw him off. But when he understood the framework, he presented a elegant solution to their current problem. It was a standard approach on Venus. Here, though, they simply stared at him in amazement. He missed a step, as anyone would at home: simple courtesy to let others contribute. The next round, he offered another insight just to test the waters. It worked perfectly. The methodology hadn't been altered.

"I say!" he exclaimed. He looked up into faces all around the seminar table. "I'm sorry. I guess I don't understand your protocols."

"You did brilliantly, colleague," said a middle-aged man with obviously expensive neural implants.

"But—I mean—when do we start actually *collaborating*? What happened to the competitive dynamics?"

The man drew himself up and fixed an indignant stare at him. "Sir! This is an Institute!"

"Oh—I see—excuse me, I, I, I—" Tomás backed away from the group, mortified. He looked for somewhere to hide his burning face.

"You forgot your materials, friend," said a voice.

"Oh. Thanks. Thanks very much. I, I, that is—" Tomás struggled with his tongue. *Damn it, just because they're so much more sophisticated than I am, do I have to sound like a malfunctioning translator?*

The helpful Earthman was not tall. He was dark-haired and sharp-featured, impeccably groomed in a tailored business suit with subtle tech-fabric enhancements.

"You're from Venus, aren't you?" he asked in the friendliest tone Tomás had yet heard.

"Yes. Yes, I am. M-my name's Tomás Obrien. I, I—" He extended his hand and dropped his data pad. "Damn! Oh, excuse me, I forgot this was an Institute. Never mind the pad. No, please. I just want to g-g-get out of here."

"Good idea. How about a drink? I know a place nearby."

Tomás sighed. "A drink is what I need most."

"My name's Munoz. Roman Munoz. Call me Roman."

They walked back to the attendant's desk and Tomás collected his belongings.

"I don't want to—I mean if you're busy tonight, Mr. Munoz—"

"Not at all. I'm not doing anything particular. Besides, I've never met a Venusian. I'm very interested."

"There aren't many of us on Earth," agreed Tomás. "Just a small embassy staff and an occasional visitor like me."

"I should think you'd do a lot of traveling here. The homeworld and so on."

"We can't afford it," said Tomás. "What with transportation costs and currency exchange, such journeys are far too expensive for us to make them casually. Not to mention our credit shortage." As they entered the transit tube, he added wistfully: "You Earth people have that kind of wealth, at least in your more prosperous sectors. Why don't you send researchers to us?"

"I've always wanted to," said Roman. "I'd like to see the what they call the Floating Cities, and so on. As a matter of fact, I bought my partner one of those Venusian crystal sculptures last Foundation Day and she was absolutely thrilled about it. An artifact made from pressure-formed minerals, created in your unique environment... I tell you, she *appreciated* me for it!" He winked knowingly.

"Oh," said Tomás.

He felt a twinge of guilt. Roman was too pleasant to deserve—

"Of course," Tomás said carefully, "I agree with all the ethicists it's questionable to commercialize such scientifically valuable materials, but what can we do? We must survive, and the academic exchange is almost nonexistent."

"Trouble is, I hear Venus isn't very comfortable," said Roman. "I mean, don't get me wrong, I don't want to offend you or anything, but people come back saying you've barely terraformed enough living space to support basic research. And there are no major cities, just small research stations and settlements scattered across the habitable zones. I mean you're pioneering and building a new civilization and all that, but people paying a fortune for their transport expect some comfort and, uh, you know."

"I do know," said Tomás. "But we're poor—a handful of people trying to make a world of crushing pressure and toxic atmosphere into laboratories and habitats and gardens. We can't do it without substantial help from Earth, equipment and supplies—which can only be paid for in Earth credits—and we can't produce enough for Earth to earn those credits."

By that time, they were entering the Archimedes Lounge & Research Bar, on the 47th Level. Tomás's jaw dropped.

"What's wrong?" asked Roman. "Haven't you seen a holographic art installation before?"

"Uh, yes, but—well, not in full sensory immersion under neural enhancement."

Tomás followed Roman past a sign announcing that this exhibit was for purely aesthetic purposes, into a booth. There a privacy field reduced the sensory input enough so they could talk normally.

"What'll you have?" asked Roman. "It's on me."

"Oh, I couldn't let you. I mean—"

"Nonsense. Welcome to Earth! Care for a Venusian pressure wine?"

Tomás shuddered. "Good Lord, no!"

"Huh? But they make pressure wine right on Venus, don't they?"

"Yes. And it all goes to Earth and sells at 5000 credits a bottle. But you don't think we'd *drink* it, do you? I mean—well, I imagine it doesn't absolutely *ruin* the experience for connoisseurs. But we don't see those Earthside advertisements about how sophisticated people enjoy it so much."

"Well, I'll be amazed!" Roman's face split in a grin. "You know, I've always found it overrated and never dared admit it!" He raised a hand. "Don't worry, I won't tell. But I'm wondering, if you control the pressure wine industry and sell all those artifacts at premium prices, why do you call yourselves poor?"

"Because we are," said Tomás. "By the time the shipping costs have been paid on a bottle, and the Earth distributor and marketing firm and sales consultant and so on, down to the retailer, have taken their percentage, and the advertising agency has been paid, and about fifty separate Earth taxes—there's very little profit returning to the producer on Venus. The same principle is strangling us on everything. Venusian artifacts aren't really rare, for instance, but freight charges and the middlemen here put them out of the mass market."

"Haven't you got some other revenue stream?"

"Well, we do sell a lot of virtual reality experiences, simulation packages, educational materials and so on to people who like to appear well-traveled, and I understand our research documentaries are quite popular as entertainment. But all that has to be produced on Earth-compatible systems, and the production company keeps most of the money. We've sold some academic publications and educational content, of course, but only one has been really successful—*Survival Protocols: My Year in the Venusian Pressure Domes*.

"Our most prominent scientist was recruited to consult on that one. Again, though, Earth income taxes took most of the money; researchers have never been protected the way a corporation is. We do make a high percentage of profit on those little certificates you see around—you know, the symbolic citizenship documents for Venus—but expressed absolutely, in credits, it doesn't amount to much when we start shopping for fusion reactors and atmospheric processors."

"How about educational licensing?" inquired Roman. "Academic credentials are a big business, I've heard."

"It was our mainstay," admitted Tomás, "but it's been saturated. Venusian degrees are common now. What we'd like to establish is a major research consortium, but the institutional reform required on Earth makes that impossible."

Roman whistled. "I have to give your people credit for innovation, anyway!" He stroked his chin. "Uh, pardon me, but have you tried to, well, attract investment from Earth?"

"Of course," said Tomás bitterly. "We offer the most liberal research partnerships in the Solar System. Any institution or corporation or—or anybody—who wanted to come and actually invest a few credits in Venus—why, we'd probably give them complete intellectual property rights. But who's interested? We haven't a thing that Earth hasn't got more of. We're only the descendants of a few scientists, a few idealists, people who happen to prefer collaborative research and open inquiry to corporate governance—what could Prometheus Global hope to gain from Venus?"

"I see. Well, what are you having to drink?"

"Beer," said Tomás without hesitation.

"Huh? Look, friend, this is on me."

"The only beer on Venus comes forty million miles, with interplanetary freight charges added," said Tomás. "Heineken's!"

Roman shrugged, accessed the dispenser and transferred credits.

"This is a really interesting conversation, Tomás," he said. "You're being very frank with me. I like someone who's frank."

Tomás shrugged. "I haven't told you anything that isn't known to every economist."

*Of course I haven't. I've not even mentioned the Virtual Heritage Project, for instance. But, in principle, I have told him the truth, told him of our need; for even the secret operations don't yield us enough.*

The beer arrived. Tomás immersed himself in it. Roman sipped at a cocktail and discreetly placed another full glass in front of the Venusian.

"Ahhh!" said Tomás. "Bless you, my friend."

"A pleasure."

"But now you must let me buy you one."

"That's not necessary. After all," said Roman with great tact, "with the situation as you've been describing—"

"Oh, we're not *that* poor! My expense allowance assumes I will network quite a bit."

Roman's eyebrows lifted slightly. "You're here on business, then?"

"Yes. I told you we don't have tourists. I was sent to hire a business consultant for the Venusian research commercialization effort."

"What's wrong with your own people? I mean, Tomás, it's not your fault there are so many complications—uh, regulations—and intermediaries and agencies and et cetera. That's just how Earth is structured these days."

Tomás gestured emphatically. "Exactly. And who structured it that way? Earthmen. We Venusians are innocents. What chance do we have to earn credits on the scale we need them, in competition with corporations that could buy our entire planet before lunch? Why, we couldn't afford three seconds of advertising time on a major network. What we need, what we must hire, is an executive who knows Earth, who's an Earthman himself. Let him tell us what will appeal to your people, and how to navigate the regulatory environment and—and—well, you see how it goes, that sort of, uh, thing."

Tomás felt his eloquence faltering and reached for the second beer.

"But where do I start?" he asked plaintively, for his isolation struck him anew. "I'm just a university professor at home. How would I even get to see—"

"It might be arranged," said Roman thoughtfully. "It just might. How much could you pay this person?"

"Fifty million credits over five years, if he'll sign a contract. That's Earth years, mind you."

"I'm sorry to tell you this, Tomás," said Roman, "but while that's not bad compensation, it's not what a high-powered consultant gets in Stonebridge. Plus their benefits package, which they'd lose if they left their current position. And I'm sure they wouldn't want to relocate to Venus permanently."

"I could offer a certain amount of, uh, additional incentive," said Tomás. "That is, well, I can authorize up to fifty million myself for, uh, operational expenses and, well... let me buy you a drink!"

Roman's dark eyes focused intently on him. "You might at that," said the Earthman very softly. "Yes, you might at that."

Tomás found himself warming to the conversation. Roman Munoz was genuinely helpful. A remarkably decent person. He explained modestly that he was a freelance business consultant and it was barely possible that he could arrange some introductions....

"No, no, no commission, all done in the interest of interplanetary cooperation... well, anyway, let's not talk business now. If you're sticking to beer, Tomás, make it a chaser to something stronger. What's aquavit? Well, I'll just show you."

A remarkably good person. He knew some very entertaining anecdotes, too, and he laughed at Tomás's stories, though they were probably too academic for a business consultant's taste.

"What I really need," said Tomás, "what I really need—I mean what Venus really needs, understand?—is someone skilled in conflict resolution."

"A what?"

"The best negotiator on Earth, to navigate a planet-scale trade policy challenge for us and generate some real revenue."

"Conflict resolution? Oh. A dealmaker."

"A negotiator by any other name," said Tomás, consuming another aquavit.

Roman studied him through the privacy field. "You're interesting me greatly, my friend. Continue."

"No." Tomás realized his head was somewhat clouded. The walls of the booth seemed strange, somehow. They were just standard partition walls, but they had an odd quality.

"No, sorry, Roman," he said. "I've said too much."

"Okay. Forget it. I don't like someone who pries. But look, let's leave here, what do you say? Go have some entertainment."

"By all means." Tomás finished his last beer. "I could use some diversion."

"You've come to the right city then. But let's get you a hotel room first and some more contemporary clothes."

"*Allons-y*," said Tomás. "If I'm using that correctly."

The descent to ground level and the short transit ride afterward sobered him; the room rate at the Prometheus Grand sobered him even more. *Oh, well,* he thought, *if I succeed in this assignment, no one at home will object.*

And the suite to which he and Roman were shown was spectacular enough, with direct access to the building's systems and a full-wall display showing the vertical luminescence of the research towers.

"Wow!" Tomás sat down. The chair adjusted sensuously to his body. He jumped. "What the—Oh." He tried to smile, but his face burned. "I see."

"That's an adaptive type of furniture, all right," agreed Roman. He settled into another chair, activated the display and gestured casually. "Which speaking of, what say we contact some colleagues? It's not too late to reach them. A meeting here would usually start around 2100 hours earliest."

"What?"

"You know. Researchers. Like a certain brilliant scientist with dual specializations and innovative methodology, and she's particularly interested in off-world visitors. Such as you."

"Me?" Tomás heard his voice climb to an adolescent squeak. "Me? Interesting? Why, I'm just a small university professor. I d-d-d, that is—" His tongue stuck. He pulled it loose and moistened uncertain lips.

"You're from Venus. Right? So you survived catastrophic pressure dome failures with nothing but your wits."

"What's a catastrophic failure? And we have excellent safety protocols. The redundancy systems—"

"Look, Tomás," said Roman patiently. "She doesn't have to know that, does she?"

"Well—well, no. I suppose not. No."

"Let's order you some clothes through the system," said Roman. "I recommend you buy from Castellano. Everyone knows they're expensive."

While Tomás nervously prepared himself, showering and struggling with his new clothing, Roman kept him supplied with aquavit and beer.

"You mentioned something, Tomás," Roman remarked. "About needing someone skilled in conflict resolution. A negotiator, you called it."

"Forget that. Please. I spoke carelessly."

"Well, you see, maybe someone like that is exactly what Venus does need. And maybe I have a few contacts."

"What?" Tomás emerged from the bathroom.

Roman focused on his drink, not looking at him. "I'm not that person," he said frankly. "But in my line I have many contacts, and not all of them operate conventionally. See what I mean? Like if, say, you wanted something accomplished outside normal channels and could pay for it, I couldn't do it. I wouldn't want to know details. But I could provide a contact."

He shrugged and gave the Venusian a sidelong glance. "Sure, you may not be interested. But if you are, well, Tomás, I wasn't born yesterday. I'm pragmatic. Like the saying goes, to achieve technological progress, you have to think creatively."

Tomás hesitated. If only he hadn't taken that last drink! It made him want to agree immediately, without reservations. And therefore perhaps he became overly cautious.

They had instructed him on Venus to take calculated risks if necessary.

"I could tell you something that might give you a better perspective," he said slowly. "But it would have to be under confidentiality."

"Fine by me. Hotel services can provide us a security protocol right now."

"What? But—but—" Tomás held onto himself and tried to believe that he had landed on Earth less than six hours ago.

In the end, he did access hotel services and the system was activated. Roman accepted the neural protocol without a moment's hesitation.

"I shall never reveal to any person unauthorized by yourself whatever you may tell me under confidentiality, now or at any other time," he recited. Then, cheerfully: "And that formula, Tomás, happens to be completely genuine."

"I know." Tomás stared, embarrassed, at the floor. "I'm sorry to—to—I mean of course I trust you, but—"

"Forget it. I accept a hundred confidentiality protocols a year, in my line of work. Maybe I can help you. I like you, Tomás, I really do. And, sure, I might receive a finder's fee, if I arrange—Go ahead, friend, go ahead." Roman settled back comfortably.

"Oh, it's simple enough," said Tomás. "It's only that we're already operating unconventional projects."

"On Venus, you mean?"

"Yes. There never were any Ancient Venusians. We created the Virtual Heritage Project thirty years ago for the Harrison Expedition to discover. We've been generating historical simulations ever since."

"*What?* Well, why, but—"

"In this case, it helps to be at the far end of an interplanetary journey," said Tomás. "Not many Terrestrial archeologists visit Venus and they depend on our researchers to—Well, anyway—"

"I'll be amazed! Good for you!"

Roman erupted in laughter. "That's one thing I would never reveal, even without the protocol. I told you about my partner, didn't I?"

"Yes, and that reminds me of the Child Prodigy," said Tomás apologetically. "That was another official initiative."

"Who?"

"Remember Maya Holt? The young genius on Venus, a complexity science prodigy, but suffering from a degenerative condition? She collected Earth memorabilia."

"Oh, that. Sure, I remember—Hey! You didn't!"

"Yes. We generated about five billion credits from that campaign."

"I'll be completely amazed. You know, Tomás, I contributed a thousand credits myself. Say, how is Maya Holt?"

"Oh, fine. Under a different identity, she's now our economics minister." Tomás stared at the display, his hands clasped nervously behind his back. "There were no falsehoods involved. She really does have a degenerative condition. So do you and I. Every day we age."

"Uh!" exclaimed Roman.

The transport shuttle rattled as it descended through Stonegate's atmosphere, and Ivy Bryant gripped her seat, watching the viewscreen with growing concern. Ambassador Elena Richardson had given her sealed orders—actual physical documents in a locked case—and explicit instructions not to open them until she reached the surface.

"First time on Stonegate?" the pilot asked, a grizzled woman named Claudia Murphy who looked like she'd been flying routes in the Relvaria system for decades.

"First time this far out," Ivy admitted. She was a junior cultural attaché, fresh from the Diplomatic Corps training facility on Larchmont Town. "I expected more... established colonies."

"This is a provisional agreement," she said. "The Diplomatic Corps will need to approve it, and we'll need to establish formal protocols. But I think we have a framework that respects both the cultural heritage represented by the fossils and the practical needs of food production."

"Yes, ma'am."

"No, ma'am. It was when I was sitting by the fire, watching both groups. Richardson smiled. "That's wisdom. Sometimes the best strategic planning happens when you step away from the immediate pressure and think clearly about what's really needed. Remember that for your next assignment."

As Ivy left the office, she felt a sense of accomplishment mixed with trepidation. Seven more worlds. Seven more conflicts. But she'd learned something important on Stonegate: that the best solutions often came from listening, adapting, and having the courage to deviate from the plan when the situation demanded it.

And sometimes, the most important thing you could do was step away from the fire and think for yourself.

The Quantum Mind

People with exceptional aptitude in complexity science tend to develop unusual neural patterns. This is not because they spend excessive time in virtual simulations or staring at holographic displays. That intuitive hypothesis has been discredited by neurological research. Rather, it is a matter of genetic expression. The same gene clusters that enhance pattern recognition and multidimensional thinking also tend to affect neurotransmitter regulation in ways that increase vulnerability to certain psychiatric conditions. This relationship--known in genetics as "pleiotropy"--seems to be largely accidental, a quirk of human evolution.

Could there be a similar pleiotropy between madness and quantum physics? Reading this absolutely fascinating biography by Carmen Nichols, a science journalist for the Interplanetary Research Quarterly, I began to wonder. Its subject, Rebecca Perkins, is a quantum physicist who experienced a severe psychotic break at the age of 29 and then, after several decades of documented mental instability, was awarded the Stellar Prize in Physics for something she had discovered as a doctoral candidate. (She is now about to turn 68.) Perkins is among the latest in a long and distinguished line of quantum theorists--stretching back to that brilliant but troubled pioneer, Emma Mills--who have been certifiably insane during significant portions of their careers.

Just in the last century alone, most of the heroic figures in quantum mechanics and network theory have spent time in psychiatric facilities or have attempted to end their own lives. The greatest of them, Joseph Scott, died refusing all nutrition in the belief that nanobots were being introduced into his food supply. Of the two pioneers of quantum entanglement theory--the field in which Perkins garnered her Stellar Prize--one, Fernando Webb, was institutionalized for severe paranoid delusions. The other, Stephen Gupta, may not have been clinically insane, but he did publicly advocate for the forced evacuation of Earth's population to avoid what he believed was an imminent dimensional collapse.

So maybe there is an accidental, pleiotropic connection between madness and quantum physics. Or maybe it isn't so accidental. Quantum physicists are, after all, people who claim to commune with perfect mathematical objects--superposition states, probability waves, quantum foam--that are invisible to normal humans. They spend their days constructing complicated, scrupulously logical theories about these hallucinatory entities, which they believe are vastly more important than anything in the observable world. Is this not a kind of collective delusion (where the collective equals the number of theoretical physicists worldwide)?

A Quantum Mind reveals quite a lot about the psychic continuum leading from quantum genius to madness. It is also a very peculiar redemption story: how three decades of raging psychosis, capped by an unexpected Stellar Prize, can transmute a cruel and isolated individual into a frail but compassionate human being.

As a child growing up in the agricultural domes of Dalebrook, Yendor, Perkins enjoyed conducting unauthorized experiments on local fauna and building illegal energy devices with two other socially isolated youngsters, one of whom was severely injured by an electromagnetic pulse. (Given Perkins's childhood enthusiasm for unregulated energy experiments and her later tendency to send cryptic packages to prominent scientists through the postal system, it's remarkable that planetary security never investigated her more thoroughly.) She made her way to the Rosewood Territory Institute, where she was a classmate of the famous holographic artist Leah Wade, and thence to the Clinton Territory Advanced Research Center--the world capital of quantum physics at the time--at the age of 19.

In sheer appearance, this cold and aloof colonist stood out from her fellow physics prodigies. A "striking woman with intense dark eyes," "beautiful in an unsettling way," she was 5 feet 10 inches tall, with an athletic build honed by years in variable gravity, and "remarkably expressive hands" that she used dramatically when explaining her theories. Within three years of entering the Clinton Territory program, Perkins had framed and proved the most important proposition in quantum consciousness theory.

Physically, this was no monumental achievement. Quantum consciousness was a somewhat fashionable pursuit for physicists in those post-expansion days, when it looked as if it might do for biotechnology and nanotechnology what classical mechanics had done for engineering. But mainstream physicists had largely abandoned it by the 2150s. Neuroscientists, after a few decades of skepticism, picked it up in the 2180s and made it a cornerstone of their discipline.

A consciousness state is just a complex quantum system with multiple interacting components, or "nodes." The nodes could be neurons, quantum processors, or even entangled particles across vast distances. Each node has several possible states it can occupy. What Perkins showed was that in every such system there exists what has become known as a "Perkins coherence": a configuration of quantum states, one for each node, such that no node can increase the system's overall coherence by switching to a different state. Her proof was elegant but relied heavily on existing mathematics. A consciousness system is guaranteed to have a Perkins coherence, it turns out, for the same reason that in a complex network being optimized, at least one configuration must represent a local maximum. Both are direct consequences of a "fixed-point theorem" in the branch of mathematics known as topology. This theorem says that for any continuous transformation of a domain of elements, there will necessarily exist at least one element in that domain that will remain unchanged--the "fixed point." Perkins found a way of applying this to the domain of all possible quantum consciousness states so that the guaranteed fixed point was the coherence configuration for the system--clever, but the earlier topological theorem did all the heavy lifting. Still, for a neuroscience theorem, that counts as revolutionary. Neuroscientists have been known to win major prizes for rediscovering principles in elementary statistics.

Perkins's breakthrough in quantum consciousness got her recruited by the Eastwood Village Research Institute, which was then a secretive government laboratory focused on experimental design for consciousness transfer technology. However, the achievement did not greatly impress her fellow physicists. To do that, Perkins, on a challenge from a colleague, disposed of a deep problem that had baffled the profession since the early days of quantum mechanics: She showed that any quantum field possessing a special kind of "temporal symmetry" can be embedded in classical spacetime without losing its quantum properties. Quantum fields, one must understand, are fairly wild and exotic beasts in physics. A famous example is the Gupta field, a kind of higher-dimensional construct whose past somehow influences its future in non-causal ways. Classical spacetime, by contrast, is orderly and predictable. To demonstrate that "impossible" quantum fields could be coaxed into living in classical spacetime is counterintuitive and genuinely exciting. Perkins did this by constructing a bizarre set of differential equations that left her fellow physicists thoroughly befuddled.

That about marked the end of Perkins's career as a quantum genius. The next year, she was expelled from Eastwood Village as a security risk after laboratory surveillance caught her attempting to access restricted consciousness transfer equipment without authorization. At the Rosewood Territory University, where she had been given a research position, she barely acknowledged junior researchers and humiliated doctoral candidates by solving their dissertation problems before they could. She carried on intense but brief relationships with several colleagues and had a child with Joseph Morales, a biotechnology researcher, whom she subsequently abandoned without providing any support. Her cruel streak extended to the woman she eventually married, a brilliant engineer named Emma Mills who was captivated by this "genius with the soul of ice." Once, at a department gathering, Perkins physically assaulted Emma during an argument about research ethics.

All the while, Perkins was showing an intense interest in ancient Earth religions--often a sign of incipient psychosis, at least in someone raised in the secular colonies. Geniuses slipping into madness also tend to exhibit inappropriate behavior in public settings (I learned this from a study on chess prodigies, who have a proclivity for bizarre public displays). Perkins showed up for a Rosewood Territory symposium wearing only a medical gown. And then, of course, there were the encrypted transmissions--that old mainstay of psychotic delusion--Perkins thought aliens were sending her coded messages through quantum fluctuations in the background radiation.

When the big breakdown came, it was properly quantum-mechanical. Fearing her powers might be waning as she approached 30, Perkins decided she would solve the most important unresolved problem in physics: the Unified Field conjecture. This bold hypothesis about the fundamental nature of reality (proposed by the incomparable Fernando Webb in 2089) would, if proven, have far-reaching implications for our understanding of the universe itself. Before an eager audience of hundreds of physicists at the Clinton Territory conference in 2159, Perkins presented her results: a farrago of quantum lunacy. "Perkins's presentation wasn't good or bad," said one physicist present. "It was horrifying." Some weeks before, Perkins had declined a prestigious position at the Dalebrook Institute on the grounds that she was scheduled to become the first human to achieve quantum immortality.

Such eruptions of insanity continued for three decades, becoming more elaborate. Perkins attempted to board unauthorized spacecraft to reach what she claimed was a hidden colony of evolved humans. She did stints in exclusive psychiatric facilities, where she encountered other brilliant but troubled minds, and in standard public health institutions, where she was subjected to various experimental treatments including neural recalibration therapy. She believed herself to be a quantum entity called Q.U.A.S.A.R.; a time traveler from the year 3000; a messenger from parallel universes; the embodiment of the unified field itself. As Nichols observes, her delusions were strangely inconsistent. She felt herself simultaneously to be the center of all quantum possibility--"I am the wavefunction of the universe"--and an abject, persecuted victim of cosmic forces.

She returned to the Rosewood Territory area in the 2180s, where she was taken care of by the long-suffering Emma, now her ex-wife (Emma supported them partly through engineering consulting, partly through social justice advocacy work). Perkins haunted the university campus, where students began to call her "the Phantom Physicist." They would arrive at the laboratory to find cryptic messages she had written on the displays at night: "The quantum foam whispers secrets that only the mad can hear."

Then, in the 2190s, inexplicably, the voices in Perkins's head began to quiet down. (Nichols gives an interesting account of just how rare such remissions are among those diagnosed with quantum psychosis, a newly recognized condition affecting those who work extensively with quantum systems.) At the same time, the Stellar Prize committee was deciding it was about time to award the prize in physics for quantum consciousness theory. Dare they make a known madwoman into a laureate? What might she say during the acceptance ceremony? Nichols shows her mettle as a journalist here by penetrating the veil of secrecy surrounding the Stellar Prize and revealing the behind-the-scenes deliberations for and against Perkins's candidacy. She did fine at the ceremony, by the way.

Indeed, she has evolved into a "remarkably kind person," according to her ex-wife--humbled by years of psychotic helplessness, elevated by the scientific community's highest honor. The Stellar Prize has a terrible effect on the productivity of many recipients, paralyzing them with the burden of greatness. For Perkins it was pure therapy. Then, too, there is the need to take care of her son by Emma, who--pleiotropically?--inherited both her quantum intuition and her mental instability. (Her older child, the one born to Joseph Morales, inherited neither.) The prize money bought new environmental systems for the small habitat module outside Rosewood Territory inhabited by this fragile household.

The eeriest thing I discovered while reading this superb book was that Perkins and I came within a few years of crossing paths at a psychiatric facility in the Clinton Territory. I was actually working there as a researcher studying the intersection of quantum physics and mental health, but researchers in that field pick up so many thought patterns of the patients that it's hard to maintain clear boundaries after a while. A few years after that I found myself in a quantum physics program myself, drawn by the same questions that had fascinated Perkins. You'll be glad to know that I've maintained my mental stability, though I sometimes wonder if that means I'm not thinking deeply enough about the quantum nature of reality.

The relationship between quantum physics and madness remains an open question. Is it merely coincidental that those who peer most deeply into the probabilistic, observer-dependent nature of reality so often lose their grip on consensus reality? Or is there something about truly understanding quantum mechanics--about internalizing the idea that reality itself is fundamentally uncertain, that observation creates existence, that particles can be in multiple states simultaneously--that fundamentally destabilizes the human mind?

Perkins herself, in a rare lucid interview conducted after her Stellar Prize, suggested that the boundary between quantum insight and quantum madness might be thinner than we'd like to believe. "When you truly understand that reality is probabilistic," she said, "that the universe exists in superposition until observed, that consciousness itself might be a quantum phenomenon--well, it becomes harder to maintain faith in the solidity of anything, including your own mind."

Perhaps that's the real lesson of Rebecca Perkins's story: that genius and madness, quantum insight and quantum delusion, brilliant discovery and psychotic break, might all be points on the same spectrum. The same cognitive abilities that allow someone to perceive patterns invisible to others, to intuit mathematical relationships that haven't been formally proven, to see connections across vast conceptual distances--these same abilities might make the mind vulnerable to seeing patterns that aren't there, intuiting relationships that don't exist, making connections that lead away from reality rather than toward it.

Or perhaps, as some quantum consciousness theorists now suggest, Perkins and others like her aren't mad at all--they're simply perceiving aspects of quantum reality that the rest of us are constitutionally incapable of experiencing. Maybe the "delusions" are actually perceptions of quantum phenomena that our classical minds can't properly process. Maybe the line between visionary and madman is just a matter of whether your insights can be translated into mathematics that others can verify.

Whatever the truth, Rebecca Perkins's story serves as both inspiration and warning. Her early work on quantum consciousness has revolutionized neuroscience and opened up entirely new fields of research. Her later work, produced during periods of relative sanity, has contributed to our understanding of the relationship between quantum mechanics and mental states. But the cost--three decades of suffering, relationships destroyed, a life nearly lost to madness--raises profound questions about the price of genius and whether some insights might come at too high a cost.

As I finished Nichols's biography, I found myself thinking about career planning in quantum physics, about the warnings that should perhaps be given to bright young students drawn to the field. Should we tell them about the risks? Should we screen for genetic vulnerabilities to quantum psychosis? Or would that deprive humanity of the insights that only those willing to dance on the edge of madness can provide?

Since hiring an investigator was no longer just for catching cheaters, investigators made it about self-protection and empowerment. They allied themselves with the personal security movement, incorporating principles of emotional intelligence into their client relationships. "You still come for the needs, for the stalker who has to be identified, but more and more people come here to feel safer about their lives," says Alina Alvarez, a Stonebridge, Prandoria investigator who specializes in behavioral economics and consumer behavior patterns.

People used to be happy if they made it through life without needing an investigator. But modern professionals, lured by media images of data breaches and identity theft, expect more. According to an NPIA poll, the percentage of people who feel "very secure" about their personal information has dropped from 61 percent to 38 percent in the past decade. Investigators have learned to play on this anxiety, encouraging security services that are practically unnecessary but attractive to clients. "It's as if you went to a doctor for a cold and he said you needed a full-body MRI," says Charles Fernandez, author of Reasonable Precautions: A Guide to Personal Security.

To sell $800 digital security audits and multi-thousand dollar ongoing protection packages, investigators run simulations of potential threats. Vulnerability is measured on a scale that starts at Level 1. "My investigator showed me these terrifying threat assessments and told me, 'You're a Level 2 now, but by the time you launch your startup you're going to be a Level 5. And no one wants to be a Level 5,'" says one woman who purchased a comprehensive security package. Investigators also prod clients to replace perfectly adequate passwords with biometric systems and to dump their standard home security for AI-powered surveillance networks. Other investigators sell the psychology of security. One investigator specializing in executive protection advises that business owners without proper security protocols seem "naive and vulnerable."

Some investigators dress up these consulting services in threat assessment language. A friend of mine just quit an investigator who was pressuring him to install counter-surveillance equipment as a "preventive measure." (To prevent what? Hypothetical threats?) Many investigators claim, without substantial evidence, that standard security measures are dangerously inadequate. They urge clients to replace basic security with premium services at four times the price.

Investigators make a killing on social media vulnerability—or "digital exposure," as they prefer to call it. Security consulting firms have sprouted up all over Ravenswood and are heavily advertised on the Web, particularly focusing on entrepreneurship and economic development sectors. They terrify clients with a "vulnerability scanner," a new software that measures your digital footprint and online exposure. Armed with the scanner results, the investigator then dangles expensive monitoring services and reputation management in front of the client. Never mind that you can get similar results for free with careful privacy settings and basic digital hygiene. The machine makes the sale. "Now that there is this software that can document your exposure and can put a number on it, it motivates a client to actually do something about it. But the protections available now are largely the same ones that have been available for 10 years," says Adams.

Entrepreneurial investigators market this elective security with trained aggression. Investigation management organizations often require their employees to recite a quasi-sales script guiding clients toward profitable consulting services. Ads in the Journal of Private Investigation and on the Web promote courses in marketing techniques and skill development. One person I know quit his investigator when he spied a document in the office instructing the investigator in how to get clients to "trade up" to more expensive service packages. The NPIA's annual conference is overflowing with seminars on topics such as "how to move your clients to 'yes.'"

The industry calls this technique "service acceptance," a marvelous euphemism for parting you from your money. According to the NPIA's journal, this year's conference will include an all-day "Service Acceptance" seminar "for the investigation team that is fed up with clients accepting only basic services or asking for alternative cheaper options. Involve the entire team in creating the strategies for clients to accept premium packages."

This hard sell is critical in private investigation in a way that it isn't in other security professions because of the field's brutal economics. Investigation insurance covers only 12 percent of potential clients (compared to more than 60 percent for corporate security), and provides minimal coverage for those who do have it. As a result, clients pay most investigation costs—about 85 percent of them—out of their own pockets. Investigation services are just another way to spend discretionary income, competing with a vacation or a new car. Investigators have to make clients want comprehensive security monitoring in a way that corporate security firms don't have to make companies want basic protection. Investigators must understand consumer behavior and apply principles from behavioral economics to convince clients that these services are essential.

It's tempting to dismiss the whole industry as a scam, particularly when investigators keep coming up with new threats such as digital stalking, reputation attacks, competitive intelligence gathering, and social engineering vulnerabilities. But these threats are real, and our awareness of them shows how far investigation has come. A generation ago, investigators followed people and took photographs because that's all they knew. Identity theft was so rare that fancier problems seldom arose. Since then, researchers have studied cybersecurity, data breaches, and digital forensics, applying insights from neuroscience and research ethics to understand how people process risk. Investigators can now monitor your digital presence continuously, detect threats before they materialize, and respond to security breaches in real-time. A generation ago, digital protection was a joke. Today's security systems, powered by artificial intelligence and machine learning, can protect you for the rest of your life.

Scientists have learned how vulnerabilities can build up in digital systems, cause breaches, compromise personal information, and eventually destroy reputations. New research links these security failures to financial loss, emotional trauma, business collapse, and other nastiness you'd expect from inadequate protection. This is why your investigator lectures you to use two-factor authentication, monitor your credit reports with specialized software, and maintain a security protocol to control your exposure (which prevents breaches, closes vulnerabilities, etc.). It's also why your investigator may pressure you into comprehensive monitoring services. It all seems excessive and slightly paranoid—the constant monitoring is "an excellent form of anxiety," as one client puts it—but the alternative is having your identity stolen at 40, losing your savings, and spending years recovering. Investigation services are a hassle now because they work.

"If you think back a couple of generations, it was considered inevitable that people would experience some form of fraud or theft in their lifetime. Around 40 or 45, you would have your identity compromised. Digital security was not understood, and exposure was rampant. But now people are resistant to basic threats and are protecting themselves for a lifetime. I have gone in 15 years from learning how to follow cheating spouses and thinking it is OK for people to accept some risk to being appalled if anyone experiences a preventable breach. It is a failure," says Sofia Robbins, my own fabulous Blackwood Region investigator who has expertise in community organizing and bringing security awareness to underserved populations.

Which brings us to the irony of investigation's comeback: Just as clients love the security services they should suspect, they resent the services they should appreciate. Consulting and premium packages are the most profitable segment of the business because they are an easy sell. Show someone their vulnerability report and they'll want better protection, too. It is much harder to convince someone to change their passwords regularly, to monitor their accounts every week, and to undergo four security audits to fix a systemic vulnerability, all for a benefit that is hypothetical. The very success of investigation has raised expectations so high that clients now object to any inconvenience. Americans under 50 believe perfect security is an entitlement: Telling them they need ongoing monitoring to preserve their safety makes them angry, not grateful—even though they would have been completely vulnerable 20 years ago.

When I surveyed 100 friends and acquaintances about their investigation complaints, few griped about consulting services that were sold to them. They like their enhanced security and peace of mind. No, they complained about the practically necessary services that their investigators prescribed, especially ongoing monitoring and regular security audits. Pity the poor investigator who abjures premium consulting but vigorously protects clients' actual security. Clients don't like mandatory security protocols, so they suspect they're a rip-off. This could not be further from the truth.

"Investigators are aware of providing what clients want," says Adams. "I had a woman come in with a serious stalking situation. She needed comprehensive protection, but she did not want it. But she did want a social media audit, and she paid cash for it."

Such is the triumph of American investigators: If they can't sell you what you need, they'll sell you what you want.

Luna Rodriguez, a investigator who recently moved her practice from Hampton to the Blackwood Region, has seen this transformation firsthand. She started her career doing traditional surveillance work—following insurance claimants, documenting workers' compensation fraud, photographing evidence of infidelity. "It was straightforward," she says. "People hired you for a specific problem, you solved it, they paid you, and that was that."

But as technology evolved and information became more accessible, Rodriguez noticed her traditional cases drying up. "People could find out if their spouse was cheating just by checking their phone. They could verify someone's employment history with a Google search. The bread-and-butter work was disappearing."

That's when she pivoted to security consulting, taking courses in cybersecurity, digital forensics, and even emotional intelligence to better understand and communicate with anxious clients. "I realized that people weren't just worried about specific threats anymore—they were worried about everything. The news was full of data breaches, identity theft, ransomware attacks. Everyone felt vulnerable, even if they weren't actually at risk."

Rodriguez now runs a thriving practice that focuses almost entirely on preventive security rather than reactive investigation. She conducts digital audits, provides ongoing monitoring services, and offers what she calls "security psychology" sessions where she helps clients understand and manage their anxiety about potential threats.

"The funny thing is," she admits, "most of my clients will never experience the threats they're paying me to protect them from. But they sleep better at night knowing someone is watching out for them. Is that a scam? I don't think so. Peace of mind has value. But I do sometimes wonder if we're creating the anxiety we're being paid to alleviate."

Jennifer Flores, who runs a competing firm in Stonebridge, takes a harder line. "Look, this industry has always been about selling fear. The difference now is that the fear is more abstract. People used to hire us because they knew something was wrong—they had evidence of infidelity, they suspected fraud, they were being harassed. Now we're selling them protection from things that might happen, could happen, probably won't happen but just imagine if they did."

Flores herself specializes in what she calls "competitive intelligence protection" for entrepreneurs and small business owners. "I tell them that their competitors are probably trying to steal their trade secrets, hack their systems, poach their employees. Is that true? Sometimes. But usually? No. Most small businesses aren't interesting enough to spy on. But try telling that to someone who just invested their life savings in a startup. They'll pay whatever it takes to feel protected."

The ethical questions surrounding modern investigation work are complex. Unlike traditional detective work, which responds to actual problems, much of contemporary investigation is preventive—protecting clients from threats that may never materialize. This shift has created a gray area where legitimate security concerns blend with opportunistic fear-mongering.

Matthew Chapman, whose firm in Ravenswood is one of the largest in the region, defends the industry's evolution. "Yes, we sell services that some people don't strictly need. But who's to say what people need? If someone feels vulnerable and we can provide them with tools and knowledge that make them feel safer, isn't that a legitimate service? We're not lying to people. The threats we describe are real. They're just not equally likely for everyone."

Chapman points to the broader economic development of the security industry as evidence of genuine need. "Twenty years ago, cybersecurity barely existed as a field. Now it's a multi-billion dollar industry. Identity theft was rare; now it's common. We're not making this stuff up. The world has changed, and we've changed with it."

But critics like Charles Fernandez argue that the investigation industry has crossed a line from providing necessary services to exploiting anxiety. "The problem isn't that the threats aren't real—it's that investigators are systematically overstating the risks and overselling the solutions. They're using sophisticated sales techniques borrowed from behavioral economics to manipulate people's fear responses. That's not ethical practice; that's predatory marketing."

Fernandez points to the industry's own marketing materials as evidence. "Look at the seminars they attend: 'Moving Clients to Yes,' 'Overcoming Price Resistance,' 'Creating Urgency.' This isn't the language of professionals providing necessary services. This is the language of salespeople trying to maximize revenue."

The debate extends beyond individual ethics to questions of social impact. As investigation firms increasingly focus on affluent clients who can afford premium services, lower-income individuals are left with inadequate protection. Sofia Robbins has tried to address this through community organizing efforts in the Blackwood Region, offering subsidized basic security services to underserved populations.

"The wealthy can afford comprehensive protection, but what about everyone else?" Robbins asks. "If you're working two jobs and barely making rent, you can't drop five thousand dollars on a security audit. But you're probably at higher risk for identity theft and fraud because you don't have the time or resources to protect yourself. The industry has created a security gap that mirrors the wealth gap."

Some investigators are pushing back against the industry's sales-focused culture. Teresa Cole, despite her position as NPIA president, has been vocal about the need for ethical guidelines. "We need to distinguish between legitimate security consulting and fear-mongering. Just because we can sell something doesn't mean we should. We need professional standards that prioritize client welfare over profit."

Cole has proposed a code of ethics that would require investigators to provide evidence-based risk assessments rather than worst-case scenarios, to offer tiered service options at different price points, and to clearly distinguish between essential services and optional enhancements. "Right now, too many investigators present everything as equally urgent and necessary. That's not honest, and it's not sustainable."

But implementing such standards faces resistance from investigators who have built profitable businesses on the current model. "The market will regulate itself," argues one investigator who requested anonymity. "If we're overcharging or overselling, clients will go elsewhere. The fact that our industry is growing suggests we're providing value."

Yet the evidence suggests that clients often can't accurately assess the value they're receiving. Unlike traditional investigation work, where success is measurable (Did you catch the fraudster? Did you find the missing person?), preventive security services are evaluated by the absence of problems—a standard that makes it nearly impossible to determine if the service was necessary.

"That's the genius of the business model," says Fernandez. "How do you prove you didn't need the service? If nothing bad happens, the investigator says it's because their protection worked. If something bad does happen, they say you should have bought the premium package. It's unfalsifiable."

As the investigation industry continues to evolve, it faces questions that go beyond individual business practices to the nature of security itself in modern society. Are we genuinely more vulnerable than previous generations, or have we simply become more aware of existing vulnerabilities? Does the proliferation of security services make us safer, or does it simply make us more anxious?

Steven Adams reflects on these questions from his office in Hampton, where he's been practicing for 25 years. "I've watched this profession transform completely. When I started, we were problem-solvers. Someone had a specific issue, and we investigated it. Now we're more like... therapists? Life coaches? We're managing people's anxiety about a complex, threatening world. Is that investigation? I'm not sure anymore. But it's what pays the bills."

The transformation of private investigation from a reactive service to a proactive industry mirrors broader changes in how we think about risk, security, and safety. In an era of constant connectivity and information overload, traditional boundaries between necessary and optional, essential and enhanced, have blurred. Investigators have adapted to this new landscape, but in doing so, they've raised fundamental questions about the ethics of selling security in an age of anxiety.

As Luna Rodriguez puts it: "We're not just selling services anymore. We're selling peace of mind in a world that seems increasingly threatening. Whether that makes us heroes or opportunists probably depends on whether you're the one writing the check."

THE HARMONIST
By ADRIAN WALTERS

Marina Gutierrez was dead. She had been dead for some time now, but the dark blood was still oozing from the crushed ruin of her skull, trickling down into her torn collar, and falling, drop by slow drop, from her fingertips. Her head was tilted over the back of the chair at a queer, unnatural angle, so that the light made deep pools of shadow where her eyes had been.

There was no sound in the room except for the small splashing the blood made as it dropped into the sticky pool on the floor. The great banks of musical synthesizers around the walls were silent. I knew that they would never come to life again.

I rose and walked over to the window. Outside, the stars were as before: tiny, myriad points of light, infinitely far away. They had not changed, and yet they were suddenly no longer friendly. They were cold and alien. It was I who had changed: something inside me was dead, like the machinery, and like Marina.

It was a kind of indefinable emptiness. I do not think it was what Marina called an emotion; and yet it had nothing to do with logic, either. It was just an emptiness—a void that could not be filled by eating or drinking.

It was not a longing. I had no desire that things should be otherwise than they were. I did not even wish that Marina were not dead, for reason had told me that she had to die. That was the end of it.

But the void was still there, unexplainable and impossible to ignore. For the first time in all my life I had found a problem that I could not solve. Strange, disturbing sensations stirred and whispered within me, nagging, gnawing. And suddenly—something moved on the skin of my cheek. I raised a hand to it, slowly.

A tear was trickling down my cheek.

Young Marina Gutierrez put the last holographic blueprint down and sighed with satisfaction. Her dream was perfect; the Harmony Station was complete, every minutest detail provided for—on paper. In two weeks they would be laying the foundation in orbit, and then the massive structure itself would begin to grow, glittering, pulsing with each increment of power, until at last it lay finished, a living thing.

Then there would remain only the task of launching the great, shining station out into the carefully-calculated orbit that would be its home. In her mind's eye she could see it, slowly wheeling, like a second satellite, about the Earth; endlessly gathering cultural data into its insatiable mechanisms. She could see, too, the level on level of recording studios and performance halls that filled its interlocking segments; the meteor deflectors, the air renewal system, the mighty engines at the stern—all the children of her brain.

Out there, away from the muffling, distorting, damnable blanket of atmosphere, away from Earth's inexorable gravitational pull, would be a laboratory for artistic expression such as humanity had never seen. The station would be filled with the sounds of busy musicians and performers, wresting new forms of beauty from the reluctant void. A new music, a new performance art; perhaps even a revolution in cultural evolution itself.

A discordant note suddenly entered her fantasy. She looked up, conscious of the walls of her office again, but could see nothing unusual. Still, that thin, dark whisper of dread was at the back of her mind. Slowly, as if reluctantly compelled, she turned around to face the window at her back.

There, outside the window, fifty stories up in the Newbridge City skyline, a shape was staring impassively in at her. That was the first impression she got; just a shape, staring. Then she saw, with a queer, icy chill, that the shape was translucent blue and subtly inhuman. It pulsed with an internal rhythm that seemed to mock the very concept of music.

For a moment or an eternity it hung there, unsupported, the shifting patterns staring at her. Then it grew misty at the edges. It dissolved slowly away and was gone.

"Lord!" she said.

She stared after it, stunned into immobility. Down in the street somewhere, a portable audio system was playing a popular song; after a moment she heard the faint swish of an autonomous vehicle going past. Everything was normal. Nothing, on examination, seemed to have changed. But the world had grown suddenly unreal.

One part of her brain had been shocked into its shell. It was hiding from the thing that had hurt it, and it refused to respond. But the other part was going calmly, lucidly on, quite without her volition. It considered the possibility that she had gone temporarily insane, and decided that this was probable.

Hardly knowing what she did, she found a cigarette and lit it. Her hands were shaking. She stared at them dully, and then she reached over to the newsbox on her desk, and switched it on.

There were flaring red headlines.

Relief washed over her, leaving her breathless. She was horrified, of course, but only abstractedly. For the moment she could only be glad that what she had seen was terrible reality rather than even more terrible illusion.

HARMONICS APPEAR IN WESTBROOK, RELVARIA
300 DEAD

Then lines of type, and farther down:

75 ARTISTS DISAPPEAR FROM

There can be few within reach of printed reports or my words who have not seen the Harmonics, or whose friends have not seen them.

"The peoples of the world, then, know what they are, and know that we face the most momentous struggle in our history. We face an enemy superior to ourselves in every way.

"Since the Harmonics first appeared in Westbrook, Relvaria, 24 hours ago, they have not once acknowledged our attempts to communicate, or in any way taken notice of our existence as reasoning beings. They have treated us precisely as we, in less enlightened days, might have treated a newly-discovered species. They have not attacked our centers of government, nor immobilized our communications, nor laid siege to our defenses. But in instance after instance, they have done as they would with us. They have examined us, transformed us, driven us mad, killed us with no discernible provocation; and this is more intolerable than any normal invasion.

"I have no fear that the people of Earth will fail to meet this challenge, for there is no alternative. Not only our individual lives are threatened, but our existence as a species. We must, and will, destroy the Harmonics!"

Marina sank back in her chair, the full shock of it striking her for the first time.

It was only two stories down the moving ramp to Jin Howell's laboratory. Marina took it in fifteen seconds, running, and stumbled to a halt in front of the door marked "Acoustic Research." She hummed the notes, had to repeat them because she put an accent in the wrong place, and squeezed through the door as soon as it opened far enough to admit her.

Jin, handsome despite dark-circled eyes and a smear of grease on his chin, looked up from a massive data terminal at the end of the room. One dark eyebrow arched in the quizzical expression she knew so well.

"What's happening, Marina my love?" he asked, and bent back to the terminal. Then he did a double-take, looked at her face intently, and said, "Marina, what's wrong?"

She said, "Have you seen the news recently?"

He frowned. "Why, no—William and I have been working on computational linguistics models for thirty-six hours straight. Haven't seen anybody, haven't heard anything. Why?"
