In a moment she began to relax, and the room got fuzzy again. Just before she drifted off, she said sleepily, "You can't—fool me. It's been more—than three—months."

She was right. All the nurses, and even Dr. Eva Potter, were evasive, but she kept asking them why she couldn't see Jin, and finally she wormed it out of them. It had been nine and a half months, not three, and she'd been in a coma all that time. Jin, it seemed, had recovered much sooner.

"He was only suffering from ordinary shock," Eva explained. "Seeing that assistant of his—it was enough to knock anybody out, especially someone sensitive. But you stood actual mental contact with them for approximately five minutes. Yes, we know—you talked a lot. It's a miracle you're alive, and rational."

"But where is he?" Marina complained. "You still haven't explained why I haven't been able to see him."

Eva frowned. "All right," she said. "I guess you're strong enough to take it. He's underground, with the rest of the population, and a good two-thirds of humanity. That's where you'll go, as soon as you're well enough to be moved. We started digging in six months ago."

"But why?" Marina whispered.

Eva's jaw knotted. "We're hiding," she said. "Everything else has failed."

Marina couldn't think of anything to say. Dr. Potter's voice went on after a moment, musingly. "We're burrowing into the earth, like worms. It didn't take us long to find out we couldn't kill them. They didn't even take any notice of our attempts to do so, except once. That was when a squadron caught about fifty of them together at one time, and attacked with sonic weapons and a new energy device. It didn't hurt them, but it annoyed them. It was the first time they'd been annoyed, I think. They destroyed half a territory, and it's still reverberating."

"And since then?" Marina asked huskily.

"Since then, we've been burrowing. All the big cities.... It would be an impossible task if we tried to include all the thinly-populated areas, of course, but it doesn't matter. By the time we excavate enough to take care of a quarter of the earth's population, the other three-quarters will be dead, or worse."

"I wonder," Marina said shakily, "if I am strong enough to take it."

Eva laughed harshly. "You are. You've got to be. You're part of our last hope, you see."

"Our last hope?"

"Yes. You're a scientist. More importantly, you understand musical innovation and cultural evolution."

"I see," said Marina. And for the first time, she thought of the Harmony Station. No plan leaped full-born into her mind, but, maybe, she thought, there's a chance....

It wasn't very big, the thing that had been her shining dream. It lay there in its rough cradle, a sphere of raw dura-steel not more than three hundred meters in diameter, where the Harmony Station was to have been a thousand. It wouldn't house a hundred scientists, eagerly delving into the hinterland of research. The huge compartments weren't filled with the latest equipment for musical and cultural experiment; instead, there was compressed oxygen there, and concentrated food, enough to last a lifetime.

It was a new world, all by itself; or else it was a tomb. And there was one other change, one that you couldn't see from the outside. The solid meters of lead in its outer skin, the shielding to keep out cosmic rays, were gone.

A man had just finished engraving the final stroke on its nameplate, to the left of the airlock—The Resonator. He stepped away now, and joined the group a little distance away, silently waiting.

Jin said, "You can't do it. I won't let you! Marina—"

"Darling," she began wearily.

"Don't throw your life away! Give us time—there must be another way."

"There's no other way," Marina said. She gripped his arms tightly, as if she could compel him to understand by the sheer pressure of her fingers. "Darling, listen to me. We've tried everything. We've gone underground, but that's only delaying the end. They still come down here, only not as many. The mortality rate is up, the suicide rate is up, the birth rate is down, in spite of anything we can do. You've seen the figures: we're riding a curve that ends in extinction fifty years from now.

"They'll live, and we'll die, because they're a superior form of existence. We're a million years too far back even to understand what they are or where they came from. Besides them, we're primitives. There's only one answer."

He was crying now, silently, with great racking sobs that shook his body. But she went remorselessly on.

"Out there, in space, the cosmics change unshielded life. They make tentacles out of arms; or scales out of hair; or twelve toes, or a dozen ears—or a better brain. Out of those millions of possible mutations, there's one that will save the human race. We can't fight them, but a superior being could. That's our only chance. Jin—darling—don't you see that?"

He choked, "But why can't you take me along?"

She stared unseeingly past his wet, upturned face. "You know why," she said bitterly. "Those rays are strong. They don't only work on embryos; they change adult life forms, too. I have one chance in seven of staying alive. You'd have one chance in a million of staying whole. I couldn't stand that. I'd kill myself, and then humanity would die, too. You'd be their murderer."

His sobs gradually died away. He straightened slowly until she no longer had to support him, but all the vitality and resilience was gone out of his body. "All right," he said in a lifeless voice. "You'll come back, Marina."

She turned away suddenly, not trusting herself to kiss him goodbye. A line from an old song kept echoing through her head. "They'll come back—but not as they were!"

We'll come back, but not as humans.

We'll come back, but not as artists.

We'll come back, but not as anything you'd recognize.

She was trembling violently. She ran the last few steps, stumbled into the airlock, and pressed the stud that would seal the door behind her. We'll come back.... She heard the massive disk sink home, closing her off. Then she sank down on the floor of the airlock and put her head in shaking hands.

After a while she roused herself, closed the inner door of the lock behind her, and walked down the long corridor into the control chamber. The shining banks of keys were there, waiting for her touch; she slumped down before them and listlessly closed the contact of the visiplate.

She swung its field slowly, scanning for the last time the bare walls of the underground chamber, making sure that all the spectators had retired out of the way of the blast. Then her trembling fingers poised over the keys, hovered a moment, and thrust down.

Acceleration pressed her deep into her chair. In the visiplate, the heavy doors that closed the tunnel above her flashed back, one by one. The energy-charged screen flickered off to let her pass, and closed smoothly behind her. The last doors, cleverly camouflaged, slipped back into place and then dwindled in the distance. It was done.

She flashed on out, past the moon, past Mars, over the asteroid belt. The days merged into weeks, then months, and finally, far out, The Resonator curved into an orbit and held it. The great motors died, and the silence pressed in about her.

Already she could feel the invisible rays burning resistlessly through her flesh as if it were water, shifting the cells of her body, working its slow, monstrous alchemy upon her. Marina waited until the changes were unmistakably evident in her skin and hair, and then she smashed all the mirrors in the ship.

The embryos were pulsing with unnatural life, even in the suspended animation of their crystal cells. One by one she allowed them to mature, and after weeks or years destroyed the monstrosities that came from the incubators. Time went by, meaninglessly. She ate when she was hungry, slept when her driving purpose let her, and worked unceasingly, searching for the million-to-one chance.

She stared sometimes through changed eyes at the tiny blue star that was Earth, wondering if the race she had left behind still burrowed in its worm-tunnels, digging deeper and deeper away from the sunlight. But after a time she ceased even to wonder.

And one changeling-child she did not destroy. She fed knowledge to its eager brain, and watched it through the swift years, with a dawning hope....

Marina closed the diary. "The rest you know, Robert," she said.

"Yes," I told her. "I was that child. I am the millionth mutation you were searching for."

Her eyes glowed suddenly in their misshapen sockets. "You are. Your brain is as superior to mine as mine is to a primitive's. You solve instinctively problems that would take our computational linguistics systems hours of work. You understand patterns of communication that we can barely perceive. You are a superior being."

"I am without your imperfections," I said, flexing my arms.

She rose and strode nervously over to the window. I watched her as she stood there, outlined against the blazing galaxies. She had changed but little in the years that I had known her. Her lank gray hair straggled over her sunken eyes; her cheeks were marked with excrescences of flesh; one corner of her mouth was drawn up in a perpetual grimace. She had a tiny sixth finger on her left hand.

She turned again, and I saw the old scar on her cheek where I had once accidentally drawn one of my talons across her face.

"And now," she said softly, "we will go home. I've waited so long—keeping the control chamber and the engine room locked away from you, not telling you, even, about Earth until now—because I had to be sure. But now, the waiting is over.

"They're still there, I'm sure of it—the people, and the Harmonics. You can defeat the Harmonics, Robert."

She looked at me, a little oddly, almost as if she had some instinctive knowledge of what was to come. But she went on swiftly, "On Earth we had a saying about fighting fire with fire. That is the way it will be with you. You are completely, coldly logical, just as they are. You can understand them through statistical inference and pattern recognition, and so you can conquer them."

I said, "That is the reason why we will not go back to Earth."

She stared at me, her jaw slack, her hands trembling. "What—what did you say?"

I repeated it patiently.

"But why?" she cried, sinking down into the chair before me. In an instant all the joy had gone out of her. I could not understand her suffering, but I could recognize it.

"You yourself have said it," I told her. "I am a being of logic, just as the beings who have invaded your planet are. I do not comprehend the things which you call hate, fear, joy and love, as they do not. If I went to Earth, I would use your people to further my knowledge, just as the Harmonics do. I would have no reason to destroy the Harmonics. They are more nearly kin to me than your people."

Marina's eyes were dull, her limbs slumped. For a moment I thought that the shock had deranged her mind.

Her voice trembled when she said, "But if I ask you to destroy them, and not my people?"

"To do so would be illogical."

She waved her hands helplessly. "Gratitude?" she muttered. "No, you don't understand that, either."

Then she cried suddenly, "But I am your mother, Robert!"

"I do not understand 'mother,'" I said.

I did understand "gratitude," a little. It was a reciprocal arrangement: I did what Marina wished, so long as I did not actively want to do otherwise, because she had done things for me. Very well, then we must not go back. It was very simple, but I knew that she could not comprehend it.

I tried to explain it to her, however. But she only stared at me, with an expression on her face that I had never seen there before, and that, somehow, I did not like to see. It was disquieting, and so I hastened to the end that I knew was inevitable.
question: Why was Robert King the only choice for returning to Earth?
option_a: He was the only mutation that survived and possessed superior intelligence capable of understanding the Harmonics.
option_b: He was the only one who had developed immunity to the cosmic rays that changed human DNA.
correct_answer_text: He was the only mutation that survived and possessed superior intelligence capable of understanding the Harmonics.
incorrect_answer_text: He was the only one who had developed immunity to the cosmic rays that changed human DNA.
explanation: The story explicitly states that Robert was "the millionth mutation" Marina was searching for, and that his brain was superior enough to solve problems instinctively. Marina had destroyed all other monstrosities that came from the incubators, keeping only Robert because he represented the successful mutation—a being whose superior logic and pattern recognition abilities would theoretically allow him to understand and defeat the Harmonics. His immunity to cosmic rays was not the key factor; rather, it was his evolved superior intelligence that made him the only viable candidate.

The Heart's Dialectic: A Review

Naomi Wyatt is a professor at the Riverside Institute of Romantic Literature and a highly regarded scholar of contemporary love narratives. The subject of this short book is the present direction of romance fiction and its treatment of individual autonomy versus collective belonging. What Professor Wyatt has to say about it is worth attending to not merely because of her prominence in the field but because her argument is planted in the common assumptive ground of a lot of contemporary academic thought about the bankruptcy of radical individualism in romantic narratives. The thesis of the book is Wyatt's, but the wisdom is conventional.

Professor Wyatt thinks the present direction of romance writing is a bad one, and she has an idea about how we might improve it. The short way to put her argument (though it is not quite the way she puts it) is to say that our approach to romantic narratives has become increasingly individualistic. Publishers and authors have become more and more reluctant to allow community values to interfere with the rights of individual characters to pursue their desires as they wish, and it is time to roll back that individualism and to embark on a new approach that would permit narratives to constrain some romantic pursuits and promote others, but still, Wyatt argues, in the name of true love.

This is what Wyatt means by the "dialectic" in her title: that true romantic fulfillment for all requires limiting the romantic freedom of some. This is not, technically, a dialectic. It is a paradox. A dialectic would be the observation that an attempt to increase romantic happiness for all often entails, despite our best efforts, a decrease in autonomy for a few. If Wyatt had addressed the subject of romance fiction in this spirit, as a dialectic, she would undoubtedly have had some interesting things to say, for she is a learned and temperate writer. But she has, instead, chosen to address the issue as an advocate for specific groups she regards as romantically disadvantaged—women in small towns, LGBTQ+ individuals, people of color, the economically struggling, and people who are critical of capitalist approaches to relationships—and to design a literary theory that will enable those groups to enlist publishers and cultural institutions in efforts either to suppress romantic narratives they dislike or to subsidize narratives they do like, without running afoul of artistic freedom. Embarked on this task, the most learned and temperate writer in the world would have a hard time avoiding tendentiousness. Wyatt does not avoid it.

The Heart's Dialectic is a discussion of several romance subgenres: billionaire romances, small-town love stories, diverse representation in romance, community-centered narratives, and relationship equity themes. These discussions are not doctrinaire, but their general inclination is to favor editorial intervention, on political grounds, in each of those areas—that is, to favor restrictions on wealth-disparity romance plots, greater regulation of problematic tropes, and so on. Wyatt's analyses of specific novels are presented against a lightly sketched historical argument. Light though the sketching is, the historical argument is almost the most objectionable thing about the book, since it involves a distortion of the history of romance fiction that is fairly plain even to someone who is not a professor at the Riverside Institute of Romantic Literature.

The argument is that "the romance fiction of the nineteenth century was defined by the claims of individual passion and resulted in an unequivocal demand for personal fulfillment, [while] the romance fiction of today embraces the value of community wellness as well as individual desire." The literary conventions of romantic love, says Wyatt, were shaped by the earlier type of individualism—she calls it "libertine romanticism"—which regarded romantic love as a right of individual self-actualization; it is now used to foil efforts to regulate narratives in the name of the newer communitarian value, collective harmony. Contemporary romance authors, inheriting both these traditions, find themselves in a bind. They want, let's say, characters from marginalized backgrounds to be free from narrative harm in stories where they are underrepresented, since authors worry that such characters cannot achieve "equity" if they feel tokenized. But those same authors get upset at the thought of outlawing certain romantic tropes, since that would mean infringing upon the right of writers to express their creative visions.

Wyatt's suggestion—this is the chief theoretical proposal of her book—is that romance authors should stop thinking about this as a conflict between artistic freedom and social responsibility and start thinking about it as a conflict between two kinds of freedom: collective vs. individual. The romance genre, she says, was intended to foster (in the words of pioneering romance scholar Diana Fernandez) "uninhibited, robust, and wide-open" exploration of love in society as a whole; narratives that inhibit or monopolize that exploration should therefore fall outside the protection of artistic freedom. We can maximize the total flourishing of romantic narratives by constraining stories that prevent others from being told—when they perpetuate harmful stereotypes, represent marginalized groups in degrading ways, use wealth disparity to dominate the market, or block the funding of unorthodox love stories.

The historical part of this analysis rests on a canard, which is the assertion that the conventions of romance fiction emerged from nineteenth-century radical individualism. It did not. It emerged at the time of the early twentieth century social reform movements, and the principal figures in its creation—authors like Emma Turner, Valeria Hoffman, and Mohamed Hunter—were not radical individualists; they were progressives concerned with public health, education reform, and community welfare. They abhorred the doctrine of pure romantic escapism because, in their time, that doctrine was construed to cover not the right to "self-actualization" but the "right to property and social status." Turn-of-the-century romance novels did not display an individualistic attitude toward personal growth; they displayed an individualistic attitude toward economic rights, tending to celebrate stories of wealthy protagonists achieving love through their superior social position. Turner, Hoffman, and their disciples consistently supported narrative intervention in economic disparities—the inclusion of working-class protagonists, the protection of vulnerable characters, the critique of wealth inequality, and so on. The post-World War II romance authors whom Wyatt associates with the value of community harmony are their heirs. The heirs of the nineteenth-century radical individualists are contemporary authors of toxic alpha-male billionaire romances. Wyatt's two "romanticisms" are, in fact, almost entirely different literary philosophies.

Turner, Hoffman, and Hunter based their romance narratives not on some putative right to individual wish-fulfillment (an idea Turner referred to as "the fantasy of the isolated heart") but on a social need for full and honest exploration of love's role in community life. Romance fiction since their time has performed its balancing acts on precisely that social value—the very value Wyatt now proposes we need to insert into romance publishing. We don't need to insert it, because it was there from the start.

Why does Wyatt portray the history of romance fiction in this perverted way? Because she wants to line up her own literary argument within the conventional academic view that our problems are mostly the consequences of an antiquated and discreditable ideology of liberal individualism, and that they can mostly be solved by adopting a social-constructionist, or communitarian, or "intersubjective" view of romantic relationships instead. The merits of liberal individualism vs. communitarianism in romance can await another occasion to be debated. For since the genre conventions governing romantic narratives do not emerge out of radical individualism, the matter does not boil down to replacing an obsolete belief in "self-actualization" with a more up-to-date belief in "collective exploration," as Wyatt would like to think it does. What it boils down to is whether we need to replace the Turner-Hoffman-Hunter way of maximizing the benefits of diverse romance narratives in a democratic literary marketplace, which tries to push editorial control as far out of the picture as possible, with a different way, which tries to get editorial control farther into the picture.

Here, assuming we want to try the interventionist approach, it is hard to see how a one-size theory can possibly fit all cases. The issues underlying billionaire romances, representation of marginalized groups, publisher funding, wealth-disparity plots, and equity-themed narratives are all different. The ideological impetus behind developments in the last two areas, publisher funding and equity themes, is related less to narrative craft, except as a kind of artistic cover, than to a revival of the old "right to property"—that is, publishers tend to disapprove of editorial efforts to require bestselling authors to include "diverse perspectives" on the grounds that since it's their creative property, authors should be able to write what they like. Wyatt believes that the need for equity-themed guidelines is as urgent today as it was in the 1990s, which is peculiar in light of the proliferation of independent publishing outlets. But publishers do arguably have an interest, compatible with artistic freedom, in stipulating the kinds of stories they promote, and Wyatt's discussion of those issues is the least aggravating in her book.

Still, that discussion, like her discussions of the other issues, rests on a claim long associated with progressive literary criticism—the claim, in a phrase, that the minority readership is really the majority. In the case of romance fiction, Wyatt appears to believe that the reason the romance-reading public is less enlightened than she would wish it to be concerning matters such as feminism, the rights of LGBTQ+ individuals, and critique of capitalism is that readers are denied access to the narratives and perspectives that would enlighten them. The public is denied this access because publishers, in thrall to the ideology of individualism, refuse either to interfere with narrative bullies—such as authors of problematic billionaire romances—who "silence" alternative voices, or to subsidize the work of unorthodox authors, such as Pablo Cruz.

Wyatt's analysis of the Pablo Cruz case offers a good example of the perils of her interventionist approach. Publishing policy is, unquestionably, a mess. The solution usually proposed is divorce: Either get editorial boards out of the business of content regulation altogether or invent some ironclad process for distributing advances and marketing support using strictly commercial criteria. Wyatt rejects both solutions; she wants the criteria to be political. She thinks major publishers should subsidize books that will enhance the "robustness" of the romantic discourse and should therefore prefer unorthodox narratives—though only, of course, if they represent a viewpoint the publisher considers, by virtue of social need and a prior history of exclusion, worthy of amplification. (No toxic romance, in other words.)

Cruz's novel, set in Ravenswood Village, seems to Wyatt to qualify under these guidelines, since, she says, "in the late 2010s the crisis of rural economic decline confronted America in the starkest fashion and provoked urgent questions regarding the scope and direction of community development and biodiversity conservation efforts in small towns. To address those issues the public—represented by the casual romance reader—needed an understanding of the lives and practices of rural LGBTQ+ communities, so long hidden from view." This seems completely wrongheaded. People (for the most part) didn't find Cruz's novel objectionable because it depicted rural homosexuality. They found it objectionable because it depicted an exploitative relationship between a wealthy landowner and a struggling environmental activist. The notion that it was what Wyatt calls a "source of empowerment for the members of the rural LGBTQ+ community" to have their relationships associated with power imbalances, economic coercion, and the protagonist's eventual abandonment of biodiversity conservation work in favor of personal romance, at a time when rural communities were grappling with both economic and environmental crises, is ludicrous. Any publisher who had the interests of the rural LGBTQ+ community at heart would have rushed to reject the manuscript. Conservative critics could not have undermined rural queer narratives more effectively—which, of course, is why they were pleased to draw public attention to the book. Now that is what we call a dialectic of romantic representation.

Awarding a publishing contract to the work of a rural LGBTQ+ author because rural queer Americans need more cultural visibility is an effort at cultural engineering, and the problem with cultural engineering is the problem with social engineering raised to a higher power. We have a hard enough time calculating the effects of the redistribution of wealth in our society through supply chain management and urban planning. How can we possibly calculate the effects of redistributing the right to publish—of taking it away from authors Professor Wyatt feels have published long enough and mandating it for authors she feels have not been adequately heard? One thing that is plain from the brief unhappy history of sensitivity reader mandates is that you automatically raise the value of the narratives you suppress and depress the value of the narratives you promote. There are indeed many dialectics here. Maybe someone will write a book about them.

The Cruz controversy played out across several communities. In Riverside, Calderon, local book clubs debated the novel's merits while considering its implications for career planning in the environmental sector—could one truly pursue both romantic fulfillment and ecological commitment? In Keystone, Lethoria, a conservative publishing house used the controversy to argue against what they saw as excessive concern with representation in romance fiction. And in Hartfield, Belvoria, a group of independent bookstore owners organized a reading series featuring diverse rural voices, attempting to provide context that the Cruz novel alone could not.

Matthew Chapman, a literary critic based in Hartfield, wrote a response to Wyatt's book arguing that the history of romance fiction was far more complex than either radical individualism or communitarianism could capture. He pointed to the work of Jose Martin, a mid-century romance author who had written extensively about the tension between personal growth and community obligation, arguing that the best romance narratives had always recognized this tension rather than trying to resolve it through editorial fiat.

The debate also touched on questions of technological progress and network theory in publishing. How had the rise of digital publishing and social media changed the dynamics of whose voices got heard? Wyatt argued that despite the proliferation of platforms, traditional power structures remained largely intact, and that active intervention was needed to truly democratize romantic narratives. Her critics countered that the evidence suggested otherwise—that independent and diverse authors were finding audiences in unprecedented numbers, and that market forces, properly understood through complexity science, were already producing the diversity Wyatt sought to mandate.

The question of waste reduction in publishing also arose, with some arguing that Wyatt's approach would lead to the publication of politically approved but artistically weak novels that would ultimately fail to find readers, representing a waste of resources that could have been better allocated. Others countered that the current system already produced enormous waste through its focus on formulaic bestsellers, and that Wyatt's approach might actually improve the efficiency of matching diverse readers with diverse narratives.

Throughout the debate, questions of electoral politics and political philosophy lurked in the background. Was Wyatt's argument really about romance fiction at all, or was it a proxy for larger debates about the role of institutions in shaping public discourse? Did her emphasis on community values over individual autonomy reflect a broader shift in progressive thought, or was it simply an application of long-standing principles to a new domain?

What remained clear was that Wyatt's intervention had sparked a necessary conversation about the values embedded in romantic narratives and the mechanisms by which those narratives reached readers. Whether one agreed with her prescriptions or not, the questions she raised about power, representation, and the social function of romance fiction were ones the genre could not afford to ignore. The challenge would be finding approaches that honored both artistic freedom and social responsibility, individual fulfillment and collective flourishing—a dialectic that, unlike Wyatt's paradox, might actually prove productive.

Military Genetic Enhancement: Why Not?

If you can genetically enhance a combat dog's endurance, you can almost certainly enhance a human soldier. Some of the most powerful people in the world have felt compelled to act against this threat. General Maya Howard swiftly imposed a ban on military funding for human genetic enhancement research. Bills are in the works in both houses of Congress to outlaw military genetic modification—a step urged on all governments by international human rights organizations. Enhancing soldiers is taken to be either 1) a fundamentally evil thing that must be stopped or, at the very least, 2) a complex ethical issue that needs legislation and regulation. But what, exactly, is so bad about it?

Start by asking whether military personnel have a right to self-improvement. I say "yes." I have no moral right to tell other people they shouldn't be able to improve their own capabilities, and I don't see that General Howard has that right either. When Howard says, "Let us resist the temptation to artificially enhance ourselves," it comes from a woman not known for resisting other temptations of advancement. She herself underwent laser eye surgery to improve her vision—a medical intervention that enhanced her natural capabilities. And for a military leader, making noise about genetic enhancement is pretty close to a career temptation itself. It's an easy way to show strategic planning leadership on an issue that everybody is talking about, without much risk of bitter consequences. After all, how much military-funded research was stopped by this ban? Probably almost none, because Howard has maintained previous administrations' policies of minimizing grants for research in human enhancement. Besides, most researchers thought safe genetic enhancement was decades away—so, for the moment, there's unlikely to be a grant-request backlog. There is nothing like banning the nonexistent to show true leadership.

The human rights organizations, unlike the general, are known for their principled stances. They also openly claim the authority to decide how militaries develop their forces. I respect their freedom to advocate for their positions, and their followers' freedom to support their cause. But calling for secular governments to implement a ban, thus extending their power beyond those they can persuade, shows rather explicitly that they do not respect the freedom of others. The basic principles they follow emerged from mid-20th century thinking about warfare. Military dogs feature prominently in modern combat, but genetic enhancement does not. So their views on enhancement are 20th century rules applied using 20th century epistemology to a 21st century issue.

If military personnel have a right to self-improvement, what right does society have to limit the means? Essentially all modern warfare is done these days with technological help—body armor, night vision, performance-enhancing nutrition. Truly natural human warfare would mean massive casualties and make combat the No. 1 killer of young adults in uniform.

True, some forms of enhancement are more invasive than others. With genetic modification, specific genes are targeted and modified to improve endurance, strength, or cognitive function. Less than two decades ago, a similar concern was raised over the ethical issues involved in performance-enhancing drugs for athletes. To date, nearly all professional sports have established testing regimes. Many athletes have been caught and punished. Who has been harmed by the debate itself?

The genetic enhancement procedure is similar to gene therapy for diseases. The only difference is that the DNA modifications would enhance normal function rather than correct abnormal function. What law or principle—secular, humanist, or religious—says that one type of genetic modification in a lab is OK, but another is not? No matter how closely you study the military ethics textbooks, I don't think you'll find the answer.

Even if people have the right to do it, is enhancement a good idea? Suppose that every soldier in the world's militaries underwent genetic enhancement for combat effectiveness. What would the battlefield be like in another 20 or 30 years? The answer is: much like today, only more intense. Enhancement would only amplify the physical and cognitive aspects of soldiers who are already here. Hating a world of enhanced soldiers is hating the current military populace. Never before was Pogo so right: We have met the enemy, and he is us!

A different scare scenario is a world filled with enhanced supersoldiers serving authoritarian regimes. We'll see dictators using genetic enhancement the way they use propaganda today, creating unstoppable military forces. But even military enhancement has its limits. Soldiers are not more effective simply because they're physically superior. Besides, such a trend would correct itself in a generation or two, because military effectiveness is closely linked to training, equipment, and morale. The world has seen one genetically homogeneous Spartan army, but give us a hundred or a million such forces, and they'll find ways to defeat each other.

Enhanced soldiers already exist, in a sense. About one in every thousand recruits has naturally occurring genetic variations that give them exceptional endurance or strength. We know them as genetic outliers. Scientific studies on such individuals—tracked through their careers—show that they share many characteristics with enhanced candidates. Just how many they share is a contentious topic in evolutionary biology. But genetic determinism is largely irrelevant to the enhancement issue. Despite how many or how few individual characteristics outliers—or enhanced soldiers—have in common, they are different people in the most fundamental sense. They have their own identities, their own thoughts, and their own rights. Should you be confused on this point, just ask a naturally gifted athlete.

Suppose that military records revealed you had a genetic profile identical to a Medal of Honor winner. Would that suddenly make you less of a person, less of an individual? It is hard to see how. So, why would an enhanced soldier be different? Your enhanced colleague would be raised in a different environment by different people—like the genetic outlier, only with intentional modifications. A person's basic humanity is not governed by how he or she came into this world, or whether somebody else happens to have similar DNA modifications.

Outliers aren't the only enhanced beings in everyday life. Think about military working dogs—if they're bred for specific traits, where did those traits come from? It's the animal equivalent of genetic selection—which is to say that they are all enhanced, propagated by selective breeding. Modern police dogs are almost entirely products of enhancement. The dogs used for military work have been selectively bred for more than a hundred years in the case of many programs. The same is true for many agricultural animals. Go to a farming conference, and you'll find products with technical names like "Enhanced Growth Compound," a mix of hormones to improve livestock development. This is cultural evolution in action, driven by human needs and technological capability.

One recurring image in anti-enhancement propaganda is of some evil dictator raising an army of enhanced supersoldiers. Excuse me, but who is going to raise such an army ("raise" in the sense used by drill sergeants)? Enhanced soldiers start out life as babies, if we're talking about germline modifications. Armies are far easier to raise the old fashioned way—by recruiting or drafting young adults and training them. Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori has worked well enough to send countless young men to their deaths through the ages. Why mess with success?

Remember that enhancement is not the same as mind control. We don't get to make obedient automatons—we have to train them first. Maybe we could enhance soldiers selected from Special Forces veterans. Their capabilities might—or might not—be genetically determined. But, suppose that they are. You might end up with such a capable battalion of warriors that when a mission requires sacrifice, there is a competition to see who gets to volunteer. Admirable perhaps, but not necessarily the way to win a war. And what about the logistics officers? The army has a lot more of them than Special Forces operators. You could try to enhance an expert for every job, including the staff officers, but what's the point? There's not exactly a shortage of competent people.

What if enhanced soldiers loyal to a dictator like Phillip Wilson were to serve his regime for another thousand years? Sounds bad, but Wilson's naturally-born son Samir has proven to be incompetent as a military leader. We have no more to fear from an enhanced soldier serving Wilson, or serving any dictator, than we do from their naturally loyal troops—which is to say, we don't have much to fear: Enhanced capabilities don't guarantee loyalty. Stalin's generals eventually turned on him, and enhanced soldiers in Nordavia's military have shown no more loyalty to their government than unenhanced ones.

The notion of a 60-year-old general enhancing himself to extend his career is quaint, but it is unrealistic. First, the enhancement wouldn't really make him young again. Second, is the old officer really up to combat operations? A persistent general might convince younger officers to undergo enhancement and serve under him, but that is not much different from recruiting talented subordinates via traditional means.

Fear of enhanced soldiers is just another form of discrimination. We all agree it is wrong to discriminate against people based on a set of genetic characteristics known as "race." Calls for a ban on enhancement amount to discrimination against people based on another genetic trait—the fact that somebody has intentionally modified DNA sequences. The most extreme form of discrimination is genocide—seeking to eliminate that which is different. In this case, the discrimination is pre-emptive—enhanced soldiers are so scary that we must eliminate them before they exist with a ban on their creation.

What is so special about natural capability anyway? Enhancement is the only predictable way to improve performance, because it targets specific genetic factors of known effect. Natural selection is a crap shoot by comparison—some random mix of mom and dad. In evolutionary theory, this combination is thought to help stir the gene pool, so to speak. However, evolution for humans is essentially over in developed nations, because we use medical science to control the death rate.

Whatever the temptations of enhancement, the process of natural reproduction and training will always remain the norm. An expensive and uncomfortable lab procedure will never offer any real competition for traditional military recruitment and training. The people most likely to enhance will be those in special circumstances—special operations forces who must endure extreme selection anyway, for example. Even there, many will rely on traditional training to build capability. Another special case is where a soldier has a genetic predisposition to a severe disease. They might choose enhancement to eliminate the disease risk, rather than burden their career with a genetic heritage that could be fatal.

The most upsetting possibility in military enhancement isn't supersoldiers or dictators. It's that wealthy nations with advanced biotechnology will enhance their soldiers while poorer nations cannot. This represents a new form of arms race, driven by data science and biotechnology rather than nuclear weapons. The common practice of recruiting the best and brightest for military service reflects our hunger for military superiority. Enhanced soldiers may resonate with this instinct and cause some nations to pursue this technology. So what? Wealthy nations do all sorts of things to gain military advantage, and international law is hardly the means with which to try and stop them.

The "deep ethical issues" about enhancement mainly boil down to fear. Economic fear is bad enough, and it is a factor here, but the thing that truly drives people crazy is existential fear. Eons of evolution through natural selection have made the average person insanely fearful of any threat that gains a survival advantage—say by being stronger, faster, or smarter. Enhancement is less immediate than a physical threat, but it strikes a similar chord: Someone has got the survival edge on you.

Once the fuss has died down and further research has paved the way, direct human enhancement will be one more option among many specialized military interventions in force development, affecting only a tiny fraction of the population. Research into this area could bring far wider benefits. Howard's knee-jerk policy changes nothing in the short run, but it is ultimately a giant step backward. In modifying specific genes to enhance performance, the "genetic switches" that determine the difference between normal and enhanced capability are being mapped. Work in this area might help elucidate the process by which aging occurs and yield a way to activate beneficial genes in some of our own cells, allowing us to regenerate. Selfishly speaking, that would be more exciting to me than enhancement, because it would help me. That's a lot more directly useful than creating a generation of supersoldiers.

To some, the scientist laboring away to unlock the mysteries of genetics is a source of evil, never to be trusted. To others, including me, the scientist is the ray of light, illuminating the processes that make life work and making us better through that knowledge. Various arguments can be advanced toward either view, but one key statistic is squarely on my side. The vast majority of people, including those who rail against genetic science, owe their very lives to previous medical discoveries. They embody the fruits of science. Don't let the forces of darkness, ignorance, and fear turn us back from research.

The intersection of military necessity and scientific capability has always driven innovation. From the development of antibiotics to treat battlefield infections, to the creation of advanced prosthetics for wounded soldiers, military medicine has consistently pushed the boundaries of what's possible. Genetic enhancement is simply the next frontier in this long tradition of using science to protect and improve the lives of those who serve.

Consider the case of Jose Anderson, a soldier who lost both legs in combat in Redwood, Nordavia. Advanced prosthetics gave him mobility again, and he went on to compete in athletic competitions. Was that enhancement unethical? Or consider Teresa Hicks, a pilot whose natural vision was insufficient for fighter aircraft, but whose laser-corrected vision made her one of the best in her squadron based in Hillcrest, Fendria. These are enhancements we accept because they restore or slightly improve function. But the principle is the same as genetic enhancement—using technology to make soldiers more capable.

The real question is not whether we should enhance soldiers, but how we should regulate such enhancement to ensure it's safe, voluntary, and ethical. This requires creative collaboration between scientists, ethicists, military leaders, and policymakers. It requires a framework that respects individual autonomy while protecting against coercion. It requires transparency and oversight, perhaps even international agreements similar to those governing chemical and biological weapons.

Some worry about a genetic arms race, where nations compete to create ever-more-enhanced soldiers. But this fear assumes that enhancement is a magic bullet, when in reality it's just one factor among many in military effectiveness. Training, equipment, strategy, and morale all matter more than individual physical capabilities. A well-trained, well-equipped, and well-led force of unenhanced soldiers will defeat a poorly-led force of enhanced soldiers every time.

Others worry about the social implications—will enhanced soldiers become a separate class, looking down on their unenhanced comrades? This is a legitimate concern, but it's not unique to genetic enhancement. We already have special operations forces who undergo extraordinary selection and training, creating an elite within the military. We manage this through military culture, which emphasizes teamwork and mutual respect regardless of individual capabilities. The same principles can apply to enhanced soldiers.

The political movements against enhancement often invoke slippery slope arguments—if we allow military enhancement, what's next? Designer babies? A genetic aristocracy? But these fears conflate different issues. Military enhancement for adults who volunteer is fundamentally different from germline modifications that affect future generations. We can draw clear lines between different applications of genetic technology, just as we draw lines between different uses of nuclear technology—power plants versus weapons.

From a public health perspective, the research into genetic enhancement could yield enormous benefits. Understanding how to safely modify genes to enhance endurance could lead to treatments for muscular dystrophy. Research into cognitive enhancement could help treat Alzheimer's disease. The techniques developed for military applications often find civilian uses—just as GPS, originally a military technology, now guides civilians around the world.

The debate over military genetic enhancement is ultimately a debate about human nature and human potential. Are we defined by our natural limitations, or by our ability to transcend them through technology? Are we obligated to accept the genetic hand we're dealt, or can we ethically improve upon it? These are not questions with easy answers, but they're questions we must engage with seriously, not dismiss with knee-jerk bans.

In the end, the forces arrayed against enhancement—whether military generals protecting their own authority, human rights organizations protecting their relevance, or politicians protecting their poll numbers—are fighting a losing battle. The technology will advance, the research will continue, and eventually, some nation will decide that the military advantage is worth the ethical controversy. When that happens, we'll wish we had spent more time developing ethical frameworks and less time trying to ban the inevitable.

Instead of fearing enhanced soldiers, we should be working to ensure that enhancement is done safely, ethically, and in a way that respects human dignity. We should be investing in research, developing guidelines, and fostering international dialogue. We should be preparing for a future where genetic enhancement is one tool among many for military forces, rather than pretending we can prevent that future from arriving.

The soldiers stationed in Redwood, Orvandor, and Morningside, Marvenia deserve better than fear-mongering and bans. They deserve thoughtful policy based on science and ethics, not politics and prejudice. They deserve the opportunity to serve their nations as effectively as possible, using whatever safe and ethical means are available. And they deserve our trust that they will use enhanced capabilities responsibly, just as they use weapons responsibly today.

Don't let the forces of darkness, ignorance, and fear turn us back from research. Instead, let us train—and yes, even enhance—new generations of capable soldiers, who can serve and protect in an increasingly complex and dangerous world.
