THE ANALYST IN THE SERVER ROOM
By ANONYMOUS

When the network went down, that just made the day perfect. A corrupted database, a failed authentication token, a malfunction in the climate control system, the security camera stuck on maximum zoom—well, I won't go through the whole sorry list. Suffice it to say that when the network went down, that put the seal on everything, as they say.

It was just one of those days. Everybody gets them. Days when you're lucky if you make it to nightfall with no systems crashed.

But of all times for it to happen! For literally months I'd been building my courage up. And finally, just today, I had made up my mind to do it—to propose a partnership to Sofia. I'd messaged her second thing this morning—right after the database corruption—and arranged to meet at her workstation. "Ten o'clock," she'd said, smiling warmly at me through the video chat. She knew why I wanted to talk to her. And when Sofia said ten o'clock, she meant ten o'clock.

Don't get me wrong. I don't mean that Sofia's a perfectionist or obsessive or anything like that. Far from it. But she does have a fixation on that one subject of punctuality. The result of her job, of course. She was a supply chain coordinator. Automated delivery drones, being robots, were invariably punctual. If a drone didn't return on time, no one waited for it. They simply knew that it had been intercepted by some rival facility and had activated its self-destruct protocol.

Well, of course, after working as a supply chain coordinator for three years, Sofia quite naturally was a bit obsessed. I remember one time, shortly after we'd started dating, when I arrived at her station five minutes late and found her having a panic attack. She thought I'd been killed. She couldn't visualize anything less than that keeping me from arriving at the designated moment. When I told her what actually had happened—I'd lost my access badge—she refused to speak to me for four days.

And then the network went down.

Until then, I'd managed somehow to keep the day's minor disasters from ruining my mood. Even while restoring that horrible database—I couldn't very well abandon it, corrupted or no; it was critical infrastructure and people depended on it—and while hurriedly implementing workarounds for that malfunctioning climate control—one hundred and fifty-three levels of server racks could overheat catastrophically—I kept going over and over my prepared partnership speeches, trying to select the most effective one.

I had a Casual Approach: "Hey, I see there's a nice little co-working space available up on level one seventy-three." And I had a Professional Approach: "Sofia, I believe our skills complement each other perfectly. I think we could build something sustainable together. Will you consider a business partnership with me?" I even had a Straightforward Approach: "Sofia, I'm going to need a partner for this next venture, and I can't think of anyone I would rather work with than you."

Actually, though I wouldn't even have admitted this to Sofia, much less to anyone else, I loved her in more than a professional way. But even if we both had been interested in that kind of relationship (neither of us had ever expressed such interest) I knew that Sofia relished her independence too much to ever consider anything beyond a professional partnership.

So I rehearsed my various approaches, realizing that when the time came I would probably be so tongue-tied I'd be capable of no more than a blurted, "Will you partner with me?" and I struggled with authentication tokens and malfunctioning climate controls, and I managed somehow to leave my workstation at five minutes to ten.

Sofia worked down on the hundred fortieth level, thirteen levels away. It never took more than two or three minutes to get to her station, so I was giving myself plenty of time.

But then the network went down.

I tried to access the transit system, and nothing happened. I couldn't understand it.

The automated transit pods had always arrived before, within thirty seconds of being summoned. This was a local line, with pods that traveled between the hundred thirty-third level and the hundred sixty-seventh level, where it was possible to make connections for either the next local or for the express. So the nearest pod couldn't be more than twenty levels away. And this was a non-rush hour.

I tried again, and then I waited some more. I looked at my watch and it was three minutes to ten. Two minutes, and no pod! If it didn't arrive this instant, this second, I would be late.

It didn't arrive.

I vacillated, not knowing what to do next. Stay, hoping the pod would come after all? Or hurry back to my workstation and message Sofia, to give her advance warning that I would be late?

Ten more seconds, and still no pod. I chose the second alternative, raced back down the corridor, and authenticated my way into my workspace. I tried to message Sofia, and the screen lit up with red letters on black: COMMUNICATIONS OFFLINE.

Of course! The entire network was down. Sofia couldn't receive messages. And she knew what I wanted to say to her, so quite naturally she would be waiting, unable to understand why I hadn't arrived.

Frantic, I dashed from the workspace again, back down the corridor to the transit station, and pressed that blasted call button with all my weight. Even if a pod should arrive right now, I would still be almost a minute late.

No matter. It didn't arrive.

I would have been in a howling rage anyway, but this impossibility piled on top of all the other annoyances and breakdowns of the day was just too much. I went into a frenzy, and kicked the transit station wall three times before I realized I was hurting myself more than I was hurting the wall. I limped back to the workspace, fuming, slammed the door behind me, grabbed the facility directory and looked up the number of the Infrastructure Staff. I tried calling, prepared to register a complaint so loud they'd hear me in sub-basement three.

I got some more letters that spelled: NETWORK UNAVAILABLE.

It took three tries before I got through to a harried-looking female technician. "My name is Lucas!" I bellowed. "Lucas Ramirez! I work on the hundred and fifty-third level! I just tried to summon a transit pod and—"

"The-transit-system-is-offline." She said it very rapidly, as though she were growing very used to saying it.

It only stopped me for a second. "Offline? What do you mean offline? Transit systems don't just go offline!" I told her.

"We-will-resume-service-as-soon-as-possible," she rattled. My bellowing was bouncing off her like packets off a firewall.

I changed tactics. First I inhaled, making a production out of it, giving myself a chance to calm down a bit. And then I asked, as rationally as you could please, "Would you mind terribly telling me why the transit system is offline?"

"I-am-sorry-sir-but-that—"

"Stop," I said. I said it quietly, too, but she stopped. I saw her looking at me. She hadn't done that before, she'd merely gazed blankly at her screen and parroted her responses.

But now she was actually looking at me.

I took advantage of the fact. Calmly, rationally, I said to her, "I would like to tell you something, Miss. I would like to tell you just what you people have done to me by taking the transit system offline. You have ruined my life."

She blinked, open-mouthed. "Ruined your life?"

"Precisely." I found it necessary to inhale again, even more slowly than before. "I was on my way," I explained, "to propose a partnership to a woman whom I deeply respect and admire. In every way but one, she is the perfect partner. Do you understand me?"

She nodded, wide-eyed. I had stumbled on a romantic, though I was too preoccupied to notice it at the time.

"In every way but one," I continued. "She has one small quirk, a fixation about punctuality. And I was supposed to meet her at ten o'clock. I'm late!" I gestured emphatically at the screen. "Do you realize what you've done, taking the transit system offline? Not only won't she partner with me, she won't even speak to me! Not now! Not after this!"

"Sir," she said tremulously, "please don't shout."

"I'm not shouting!"

"Sir, I'm terribly sorry. I understand your—"

"You understand?" I trembled with speechless fury.

She looked all about her, and then leaned closer to the screen. "We're not supposed to give this information out, sir," she said, her voice low, "but I'm going to tell you, so you'll understand why we had to do it. I think it's perfectly awful that it had to ruin things for you this way. But the fact of the matter is—" she leaned even closer to the screen—"there's an intruder in the server room."

It was my turn to be stunned.

I just gaped at her. "A—a what?"

"An intruder. She was discovered on the hundred forty-seventh level, and managed to get into the main server room before Security could catch her. She locked it down from the inside. But Security is doing everything it can think of to get her out."

"Well—but why should there be any problem about getting her out?"

"She has administrative access. We can't control anything from outside at all. And when anyone tries to get into the server room, she threatens to wipe all the data."

That sounded catastrophic. "She threatens to wipe everything?"

"She has root access," the technician explained, "and she's holding the entire system hostage."

"Oh," I said. "So it might take a while."

She leaned so close this time that even I, distracted as I was, took note of her concerned expression. She whispered, "They're afraid they'll have to negotiate with her."

"Oh, no!"

She nodded solemnly. "I'm terribly sorry, sir," she said. Then she glanced to her right, suddenly straightened up again, and said, "We-will-resume-service-as-soon-as-possible." Click. Blank screen.

For a minute or two, all I could do was sit and absorb what I'd been told. An intruder in the server room! An intruder who had managed to work her way all the way up to the hundred forty-seventh level before being detected!

What in the world was the matter with Security? If things were getting that lax, the Facility was doomed, encryption or no. Who knew how many more intruders there were in the Facility, still undetected?

Until that moment, the state of isolation in which we all lived had had no reality for me. The Facility, after all, was self-sufficient and completely secure. No one ever left, no one ever entered. Within our walls, we were a community, two hundred levels high. The ever-present threat of other facilities had never been more for me—or for most other people either, I suspected—than occasional supply drones that didn't return, occasional intruders shot down as they tried to sneak into the building, occasional agents of our own leaving the Facility in tiny shielded vehicles, hoping to get safely within another facility and bring back intelligence of any immediate threats and dangers that facility might be planning for us. Most agents didn't return; most drones did. And within the Facility life was full, the knowledge of external dangers merely lurking at the backs of our minds. After all, those external dangers had been no more than potential for decades, since what Dr. Morrison called the Information Wars.

Dr. Morrison—Advanced Facility History, when I was fifteen years old—had private names for every major conflict of the twenty-first century. There was the First Cyber War, the Second Cyber War, and the Great Network Collapse, known to the textbooks of course as the Information Wars.

The rise of the Facilities, according to Dr. Morrison, was the result of many many factors, but two of the most important were the population concentration and the Geneva Protocols. The population concentration, of course, meant that there were continuously more and more people but never any more space. So that housing, in the historically short time of one century, made a complete transformation from horizontal expansion to vertical. Before 2000, the vast majority of human beings lived in structures of from one to five stories. By 2100, everybody lived in Facilities. From the very beginning, small attempts were made to make these Facilities more than dwelling places. By mid-century, Facilities already included restaurants, shopping centers, childcare services, maintenance hubs and a host of other adjuncts. By the end of the century, the Facilities were completely self-sufficient, with food grown hydroponically in the sub-basements, separate levels set aside for schools and medical centers and manufacturing, robot supply drones capable of seeking out raw materials unavailable within the Facilities themselves and so on. And all because of, among other things, the population concentration.

And the Geneva Protocols.

It seems there was a power-struggle between two sets of then-existing nations (they were something like Facilities, only horizontal instead of vertical) and both sets were equipped with cyber weapons. The Geneva Protocols began by stating that infrastructure warfare was unthinkable, and added that just in case anyone happened to think of it only tactical cyber weapons could be used. No strategic cyber weapons. (A tactical weapon is something you use on military systems, and a strategic weapon is something you use on civilian infrastructure.) Oddly enough, when somebody did think of the war, both sides adhered to the Geneva Protocols, which meant that no Facilities had their core systems destroyed.

Of course, they made up for this as best they could by using tactical cyber weapons all over the place. After the war almost the whole network infrastructure was quite dangerously compromised. Except for the Facilities. Or at least those of them which had in time installed the quantum encryption which had been invented on the very eve of battle, and which deflected intrusion attempts.

However, what with all of the other protocols which were broken during the Information Wars, by the time it was finished nobody was quite sure any more who was on whose side. That facility over there on the horizon might be an ally. And then again it might not. Since they weren't sure either, it was risky to expose yourself in order to ask.

And so life went on, with little to remind us of the dangers lurking Outside. The basic policy of Eternal Vigilance and Constant Monitoring was left to Security. The rest of us simply lived our lives and let it go at that.

But now there was an intruder in the server room.

When I thought of how deeply she had penetrated our defenses, and of how many others there might be, still penetrating, I shuddered. The walls were our safeguards only so long as all potential enemies were on the other side of them.

I sat shaken, digesting this news, until suddenly I remembered Sofia.

I leaped to my feet, reading from my watch that it was now ten-fifteen. I dashed once more from the workspace and down the corridor to the transit station, praying that the intruder had been captured by now and that Sofia would agree with me that an intruder in the server room was good and sufficient reason for me to be late.

The system was still down. At least, the transit pods were still unavailable.

I sagged against the wall, thinking dismal thoughts. Then I noticed the door to the right of the transit station. Through that door were the maintenance stairs.

I hadn't paid any attention to it before. No one ever uses the stairs except adventurous young technicians playing capture-the-flag, running up and down from landing to landing. I myself hadn't set foot on a flight of stairs since I was twelve years old.

Actually, the whole idea of stairs was ridiculous. We had transit pods, didn't we? Usually, I mean, when they didn't contain intruders or weren't offline due to security breaches. So what was the use of stairs?

Well, according to Dr. Morrison (a walking database of unnecessary information), the Facility had been built when there still had been such things as building codes, anachronistic even then, which required emergency stairs in every structure constructed. Ergo, the Facility had stairs, thirty-two hundred of them.

And now, after all these years, the stairs might prove useful after all. It was only thirteen flights to Sofia's level. At sixteen steps a flight, that meant two hundred and eight steps.

Could I descend two hundred and eight steps for my potential business partner? I could. If the door would open.

It would, though reluctantly. Who knew how many years it had been since last this door had been opened? It squeaked and groaned and finally opened halfway. I stepped through to the dusty landing, took a deep breath, and started down. Eight steps and a landing, eight steps and a level. Eight steps and a landing, eight steps and a level.

On the landing between one fifty and one forty-nine, there was a small door. I paused, looking curiously at it, and saw that at one time letters had been stenciled on it. The letters had long since faded, but they left a lighter residue of dust than that which covered the rest of the door. And so the words could still be read, if with difficulty.

I read them. They said:

EMERGENCY ACCESS
SERVER ROOM
AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL
ONLY
KEEP LOCKED

I frowned, wondering immediately why this door wasn't being firmly guarded by at least a squad of Security personnel. Half a dozen possible answers flashed through my mind. The more recent maps might simply have omitted this discarded and unnecessary door. It might be sealed shut on the other side. Security might have caught the intruder already. Somebody in authority might simply have made an error in judgment.

As I stood there, pondering these possibilities, the door opened and the intruder came out, holding a device that looked like it could cause serious harm.

She couldn't have been anyone else but the intruder. The device, in the first place. The fact that she looked harried and upset and terribly nervous, in the second place. And, of course, the fact that she came from the server room.

Looking back, I think she must have been just as startled as I when we came face to face like that. We formed a brief tableau, both of us open-mouthed and wide-eyed.

Unfortunately, she recovered first.

She closed the emergency door behind her, quickly but quietly. Her device stopped waving around and instead pointed directly at my middle. "Don't move!" she whispered harshly. "Don't make a sound!"

I did exactly as I was told. I didn't move and I didn't make a sound. Which left me quite free to study her.

She was rather tall, perhaps three inches taller than me, with sharp features and intense eyes. She wore dark clothing, practical for moving unseen. She looked exactly like an intruder... which is to say that she didn't look like an intruder, she looked remarkably ordinary.

Her gaze darted this way and that. Then she gestured with her free hand at the descending stairs and whispered, "Where do they go?"

I had to clear my throat before I could speak. "All the way down," I said.

"Good," she said—just as we both heard a sudden raucous squealing from perhaps four flights down, a squealing which could be nothing but the opening of a corridor door. It was followed by the heavy thud of ascending boots. Security!

But if I had any visions of imminent rescue, the intruder dashed them. She said, "Where do you work?"

"One fifty-three," I said. This was a desperate and dangerous woman. I knew my only slim chance of safety lay in answering her questions promptly, cooperating with her until and unless I saw a chance to either escape or capture her.

"All right," she whispered. "Go on." She prodded me with the device.

And so we went back up the stairs to one fifty-three, and stopped at the door. She stood close behind me, the device pressed against my back, and grated in my ear, "I'll have this device in my pocket. If you make one false move I'll use it. Now, we're going to your workspace. We're colleagues, just walking along together. You got that?"

I nodded.

"All right. Let's go."

We went. I have never in my life seen that long corridor quite so empty as it was right then. No one came out of any of the workspaces, no one emerged from any of the branch corridors. We walked to my workspace. I authenticated the door and we went inside.

Once the door was closed behind us, she visibly relaxed, sagging against the door, her device hand hanging limp at her side, a nervous smile playing across her lips.

I looked at her, judging the distance between us, wondering if I could leap at her before she could bring the device up again. But she must have read my intentions on my face. She straightened, shaking her head. She said, "Don't try it. I don't want to hurt you. I don't want to hurt anybody, but I will if I have to. We'll just wait here together until the search passes us. Then I'll secure you, so you won't be able to alert Security too soon, and I'll leave. If you don't try any silly heroics, nothing will happen to you."

"You'll never get away," I told her. "The whole Facility is on alert."

"You let me worry about that," she said. She licked her lips. "You got any coffee?"

"Yes."

"Make me a cup. And don't get any bright ideas about using it as a weapon."

"I only have my day's allotment," I protested. "Just enough for two cups, morning and afternoon."

"Two cups is fine," she said. "One for each of us."

And now I had yet another grudge against this blasted intruder. Which reminded me again of Sofia. From the looks of things, I wasn't ever going to get to her workspace. By now she was probably mourning our potential partnership and might even have Security searching for my remains.

As I made the coffee, she asked me questions. My name first, and then, "What do you do for a living?"

I thought fast. "I'm a supply chain analyst," I said. That was a lie, of course, but I'd heard enough about supply chain management from Sofia to be able to maintain the fiction should she question me further about it.

Actually, I was a cybersecurity specialist. The subjects I worked on included intrusion detection, threat analysis and penetration testing—talents I would prefer to disclose to her in my own fashion, when the time came.

She was quiet for a moment. "What about the supply drones? Do you ever analyze their data logs?"

I had no idea what she was talking about, and admitted as much.

"When they come back," she said. "What kind of data do they collect about conditions outside? Don't you people ever review them?"

"Of course not," I told her. I was on secure ground now, with Sofia's information to guide me. "All data is sanitized and verified before it's integrated into our systems."

"I know that," she said impatiently. "But don't you ever analyze the raw data before sanitizing it?"

"No. Why should we?"

"To find out what conditions are actually like outside."

"For what? Who cares about that?"

She frowned bitterly. "The same answer," she muttered, more to herself than to me. "The same answer every time. You people have locked yourselves in your towers and you're ready to stay in them forever."

I looked around at my workspace. "Rather a well-equipped tower," I told her.

"But a tower nevertheless." She leaned toward me, her eyes gleaming with intensity. "Don't you ever wish to go Outside?"

Incredible! I nearly spilled boiling coffee all over myself. "Outside? Of course not!"

"The same thing," she grumbled, "over and over again. Always the same response. Listen, you! Do you realize how long it took humanity to build these networks? The long slow painful development of technology, for centuries, before we ever made that first step toward global connection?"

"I have no idea," I told her.

"I'll tell you this," she said forcefully. "A lot longer than it took for us to disconnect and isolate ourselves again." She started pacing the floor, waving the device around in an agitated fashion as she talked. "Is this the natural state of humanity? It is not. Is this even a desirable state for humanity? It is definitely not." She spun back to face me, pointing the device at me again, but this time she pointed it as though it were a finger, not a weapon. "Listen, you," she snapped. "Humanity was progressing. For all our mistakes and excesses, we were growing. Our dreams were getting bigger and better all the time. We were planning to tackle space! The moon first, and then the planets, and finally the stars. The whole universe was out there, waiting to be explored. And humanity was reaching out for it." She glared as though daring me to doubt it.

I decided that this woman was doubly dangerous. Not only was she an intruder, she was also unstable. So I had two reasons for humoring her. I nodded politely.

"So what happened?" she demanded, and immediately answered herself. "I'll tell you what happened! Just as we were about to make that first giant leap, humanity got scared. That's all it was, just a crisis of confidence. So what did humanity do? I'll tell you what we did. We turned around and we ran all the way back to isolated communities, our collective tail between our legs. That's what we did!"

To say that all of this was incomprehensible would be an extreme understatement. I fulfilled my obligation to this insane dialogue by saying, "Here's your coffee."

"Put it on the desk," she said, switching instantly from raving idealist to watchful intruder.

I put it on the desk. She drank deep, then carried the cup across the room and sat down in my chair. She studied me narrowly, and suddenly said, "What did they tell you I was? A spy?"

"An intruder," I said.

She grinned bitterly. "Of course. The fools! Intruder! What do you suppose I'm going to steal?"

She asked the question so violently and urgently that I knew I had to answer quickly and well, or the unstable side would return. "I—I wouldn't know, exactly," I stammered. "Data, I suppose. Intelligence."

"Intelligence? What intelligence? Your facility operates on the same principles as every other facility. There's nothing unique here."

"The security protocols—" I started.

"The security protocols," she interrupted me, "are standard. If you mean the quantum encryption, it's the same system everyone uses."

"If you say so," I replied stiffly. Security claimed that we had superior protection. I chose to believe Security over an enemy intruder.

"Your facility sends out agents, too, doesn't it?" she demanded.

"Well, of course."

"And what are they supposed to do?"

"Well—" It was such a pointless question, it seemed silly to even answer it. "They're supposed to look for indications of an attack by one of the other facilities."

"And do they find any indications, ever?"

"I'm sure I don't know," I told her coldly. "That would be classified information."

"You bet it would," she said, with malicious satisfaction. "All right, if that's what your agents are doing, and if I'm an intruder, then it follows that I'm doing the same thing, right?"

"I don't follow you," I admitted.

"If I'm an intruder," she said impatiently, "then I'm supposed to look for indications of an attack by you people on my Facility."

I shrugged. "If that's your mission," I said, "then that's your mission."

She got suddenly red-faced, and jumped to her feet. "That's not my mission, you stubborn fool!" she shouted. "I'm not an intruder! If I were an intruder, then that would be my mission!"

The unstable side had returned, in full force. "All right," I said hastily. "All right, whatever you say."

She glowered at me a moment longer, then shouted, "Bah!" and dropped back into the chair.

She breathed rather heavily for a while, glaring at the floor, then looked at me again. "All right, listen. What if I were to tell you that I had found evidence that you people were planning to attack my Facility?"

I stared at her. "That's impossible!" I cried. "We aren't planning to attack anybody! We just want to be left alone!"

"How do I know that?" she demanded.

"It's the truth! What would we want to attack anybody for?"

"Ah hah!" She sat forward, tensed, pointing the device at me like a finger again. "Now, then," she said. "If you know it doesn't make any sense for this Facility to attack any other facility, then why in the world should you think they might see some advantage in attacking you?"

I shook my head, dumbfounded. "I can't answer a question like that," I said. "How do I know what they're thinking?"

"They're human beings, aren't they?" she cried. "Like you? Like me? Like all the other people in this fortress?"

"Now, wait a minute—"

"No!" she shouted. "You wait a minute! I want to tell you something. You think I'm an intruder. That incompetent Security force thinks I'm an intruder. That administrator who reported me thinks I'm an intruder. But I'm not an intruder, and I'm going to tell you what I am."

I waited, looking as attentive as possible.

"I come," she said, "from a Facility about eighty miles north of here. I came here on foot, without any sort of protective equipment at all."

The unstable side was back. I didn't say a word. I didn't want to set off the violence that was so obviously in this person.

"The environmental conditions," she went on, "are safe. They're practically as good as they were before the Information Wars. I don't know how long they've been that good, but I would guess about ten years, at the very least." She leaned forward again, urgent and serious. "The world is safe out there now. Humanity can come back out of the fortresses again. We can start building the dreams again. And this time we can build better, because we have the horrible example of the recent past to guide us away from the pitfalls. There's no need any longer for the Facilities."

And that was like saying there's no need any longer for shelter, but I didn't say so. I didn't say anything at all.

"I'm a trained environmental scientist," she went on. "In my facility, I worked on air quality monitoring. Theoretically, I believed that there was a chance the environment Outside was recovering by now, though we had no idea exactly how much damage had been done by the wars. But I wanted to test the theory through field research, and the Council wouldn't let me. They claimed public safety, but I knew better. If the Outside were safe and the Facilities were no longer needed, then the Council was out of power, and they knew it.

"So I left. I walked out. And I've been traveling from Facility to Facility, trying to spread the word. Trying to get people to understand that isolation isn't necessary anymore. That we can rebuild a connected world. That the principles of sustainable business and ethical decision-making can guide us to something better than what we had before."

She paused, looking at me intently. "Do you understand what I'm saying? This isn't about espionage or warfare. This is about freedom. About choice. About remembering that we're all part of the same species, the same world."

I stared at her, my mind reeling. Everything she was saying contradicted everything I'd been taught, everything I believed. And yet...

"You're insane," I said quietly.

She smiled sadly. "Maybe. Or maybe everyone else is. That's the question, isn't it? Who decides what's rational? The people who benefit from the current system? Or the people who dare to question it?"

Before I could respond, we both heard a sound outside my door. Heavy footsteps. Multiple people.

Security had found us.

The woman—I couldn't think of her as just an intruder anymore—looked at me one last time. "Think about what I said. Please. For your own sake, and for everyone's."

Then she moved with surprising speed, securing me to my chair with some kind of quick-release restraint, and disappeared through a maintenance hatch I hadn't even known existed in my own workspace.

By the time Security broke through my door, she was gone.

And I was left with questions I couldn't answer, and doubts I couldn't shake.

Had we really imprisoned ourselves? Were we maintaining a siege mentality long after the actual threat had passed? Was our isolation a necessary protection, or a comfortable prison?

I didn't know. But for the first time in my life, I wanted to find out.

And I never did make it to Sofia's workspace that day. Though when I finally did see her, two days later, and explained everything that had happened, she surprised me.

"You know," she said thoughtfully, "I've always wondered why the supply drones never bring back any environmental data. It's like we don't want to know."

"Yeah," I said. "It's exactly like that."

We looked at each other, and I saw the same questions in her eyes that were in mine.

Maybe, I thought, this could be the partnership I'd been looking for all along. Not just a business arrangement, but something more important. A partnership in asking the questions no one else wanted to ask.

In seeking the truth no one else wanted to find.

In remembering that walls can protect you, but they can also imprison you.

And sometimes, the most dangerous thing isn't what's outside the walls.

It's never looking beyond them.

option_b: They lived full lives with external dangers merely lurking at the backs of their minds, accepting isolation as normal without questioning its continued necessity.

SOFIA'S ALGORITHMS
By A. L. HALEY

Sofia Gupta slumped into the ergonomic chair at her Crestwood Town apartment, her hands trembling as she tried to sort through the latest quarterly reports. She closed her eyes and attempted to breathe deeply, but the twitching in her left eyelid wouldn't stop.

"Just relax, Sofia," her brother Giovanni said from across the room. "You need to take a break from all this stress."

Sofia tried to relax. She really did. But after three minutes of sitting still, she leaped up and began pacing frantically around the living room.

"Sofia!" Giovanni was exasperated now. "Dr. Martinez said you need to step away from work or you're going to have a complete breakdown. Why won't you listen?"

Sofia glared at him. "Martinez! That overpaid quack! I've spent thousands on his consultations. I haven't had a decent night's sleep in months. My hands shake constantly. And what does he prescribe? Meditation apps and breathing exercises! Why, I should send him a bill for wasting my time!" She collapsed back into the chair, her anger barely contained.

"Now, Sofia, you know you've never followed his advice. He told you last year that you'd have to delegate more. Why do you insist on micromanaging every project? It's the strain of trying to control everything that's causing your problems. He told you to take a sabbatical or you'd burn out. Don't blame him for your own stubbornness."

Sofia snorted. "Sabbatical! Sitting on a beach somewhere or hiking through forests! Fine activities for someone who doesn't care about innovation management! And let me correct you. It isn't work stress that's driving me crazy. It's the strain of trying to get some basic competence from the people I have to hire! It's the incompetence of the workforce that's got me beaten! It's the—"

"Hey, Sofia!" Giovanni, scrolling through his tablet, had paused at an article. "Didn't you invest in those ecosystem restoration stations they built in Elmwood, Nordavia twenty years ago?"

Sofia's hands twitched violently. "Don't mention that disaster!" she rasped. "That deal nearly bankrupted me! The bacterial cultures we developed produced the most unpredictable compounds ever synthesized!"

Giovanni, whose calm academic demeanor was the complete opposite of Sofia's high-strung entrepreneurial intensity, looked at her over his reading glasses. Sofia's nervous condition was beginning to concern him deeply.

"You're way behind the times, Sofia," he declared. "Don't you know that those compounds have proved to be the most revolutionary biotechnology breakthrough in decades? Don't you know that a consortium has built the largest wellness center in the northern hemisphere there, and that people are traveling from around the world to benefit from the treatments? Sofia, you missed an enormous opportunity!"

Snatching the tablet from Giovanni's hands, Sofia stared at the article which depicted a crystalline structure nestled among restored forests in Elmwood. The main facility was a towering edifice of smart glass that changed colors with the seasons. Between its wings, biodomes housed carefully cultivated ecosystems and treatment centers that looked pristine and inviting in the photographs.

"Why, I remember now!" exclaimed Giovanni. "That's where the Pattersons went two years ago! He was completely burned out and she looked exhausted. They came back completely rejuvenated. Don't you remember?"

Giovanni nodded and elaborated on the transformation the Elmwood facility had effected in the Pattersons. "It's perfect for you, Sofia," he advised. "You'd get proper rest during the journey. The new maglev trains have these meditation pods that help you decompress during the trip. And you can evaluate the business potential while you're there recovering. And not only that." He leaned toward his sister confidingly. "The researchers at Chen Biotech have just isolated an enzyme from the Elmwood bacterial cultures that can break down plastic waste into reusable polymers without chemical processing. There's a fortune waiting for the person who secures the licensing rights and learns to scale the production!"

Giovanni had calculated correctly. The tablet lowered in Sofia's hands, and her sharp eyes became shrewd and calculating. She even forgot to twitch. "Maybe you're right, Giovanni," she acknowledged. "Combine recovery with business opportunity, right?"

Looking back at the article, she saw the line about the AI systems. "—the only wellness center managed entirely by artificial intelligence systems—"

"AI systems!" she shrieked. "You mean they've developed them to that level? Why hasn't somebody told me? I'll have Peterson's job! I'll restructure the entire division! I'll—"

"Sofia!" exploded Giovanni. "Stop it! Maybe Peterson doesn't know anything about it! If it's something at the Elmwood Renewal Center, why don't you just go and investigate yourself instead of having a meltdown? That's the only sensible approach!"

"You're right, Giovanni," agreed Sofia decisively. "I'll go and investigate myself. Immediately!" Grabbing her coat, she left at her usual frantic pace.

"Well!" remarked her brother. "All I can say is that they'd better have those meditation pods working perfectly for Sofia's trip!"

The journey to Elmwood did Sofia considerable good. In the meditation pod of the maglev train, she actually relaxed for the first time in years, sinking into a peaceful state with binaural beats and guided visualization that made the eight-hour trip feel like minutes.

It seemed hardly any time at all until they were arriving at the Elmwood station. And then Sofia was stepping onto the platform with unusual calmness still affecting her normally frantic demeanor. She made her way to the transport hub and found herself whisked by automated vehicle directly to the Elmwood Renewal Center.

Appreciatively she gazed around at the vast lobby with its living walls of restored native plants, illuminated by natural light filtering through the smart glass, and at the views of beautiful biodomes framed by a dozen archways. But most of all, the AI systems won her delighted approval.

She could see at once that they had been developed to an remarkably sophisticated level. How, she wondered again, had this been accomplished without her knowledge? Was Giovanni right? Was she losing her edge? Gnawing at the doubt, she watched the AI-controlled service units moving efficiently about, assisting visitors in wheelchairs, delivering meals, guiding newcomers, performing maintenance tasks tirelessly, promptly, and best of all, silently.

Sofia was enthralled. She'd implement them in her company. Regardless of cost! There'd be no more of that frustrating human error and interpersonal conflict that plagued even the best-trained teams! She'd investigate and determine the exact capabilities of these systems while here, and then return home and introduce them into the corporate environment. She'd show them whether she was losing her edge! Briskly she approached the reception desk.

She was immediately confronted with a sample of that human unpredictability that was slowly driving her mad. Machines, she sighed to herself. Wonderful efficient machines! For a woman was arguing loudly with the desk attendant who, poor soul, was a stressed fellow human instead of an AI system. Sofia watched him shrinking and turning pale under the verbal assault.

"A human therapist!" shouted the woman. "I want a real person! For what you charge, you should be able to provide whatever I request! I won't have another of those soulless AI systems managing my treatment, do you hear?"

Everyone within the confines of the huge lobby could hear. The attendant flinched visibly. "Now, Ms. Wyatt," he soothed. "You know the center operates entirely with AI systems. They're much more expensive to develop and maintain than human staff, but so much more precise and consistent. Admit it, they provide excellent service, don't they?"

"That's exactly the problem!" Elena Wyatt glared. "The service is too perfect. I might as well be interacting with a vending machine. I want someone who can understand nuance! I want to be able to express myself without everything being so rigidly programmed!"

Sofia snorted. "Wants someone she can manipulate," she diagnosed. "Someone she can get satisfaction from arguing with." With vast contempt she stepped to the desk beside Elena and sharply tapped for attention.

"One moment, please," begged the harassed attendant. "Just one moment." He turned back to Elena.

But she had turned her glare on Sofia. "You could at least have the courtesy to wait your turn!"

Sofia smirked. "My good woman, I'm not an AI. AI systems, of course, are always courteous. But you should know by now that courtesy isn't always a human strong suit." Leaving Elena temporarily speechless, she beckoned authoritatively to the attendant.

"I've just arrived and need to check in. I'm here for a standard wellness program, no intensive treatments. You can process my registration before continuing your discussion with this lady."

The attendant sputtered. Elena sputtered. But not for nothing was Sofia one of the leading tech entrepreneurs in the region. Sofia's implacable stare won the point. Wiping perspiration from his forehead, the attendant fumbled for a tablet, entered her information, and was about to confirm it when a fist hit the desk with a resounding bang and another voice, male, boomed out at Sofia's elbow.

"This is ridiculous!" roared the voice. "A person could age ten years waiting for service here. Efficiency!" Again his fist struck the counter.

The attendant jumped. He nearly dropped the tablet. Absently holding it, he straightened up to face Elena and the angry newcomer. Hastily he handed Sofia a room card.

"Here you are, Ms. Gupta. I'm sure you'll find it comfortable." With a strained smile he pressed a button and assigned her to the care of a silent and efficient AI guide unit.

The room was more than comfortable. It was stunning. Its panoramic windows framed breathtaking views of the restored Elmwood forests where, Sofia fondly thought, bacterial cultures were busy producing enzymes that would be worth millions to whoever controlled their production rights. There remained only the minor challenge of determining how to extract them economically and to process them in this remote location. Details for her talented research team; mere details...

Leaving her luggage to be handled by the AI system, she went up to the rooftop garden restaurant. Dining boldly on grilled salmon with soup, salad and a light parfait, she gazed out at the restored wilderness, watching birds that had returned to the area after decades of absence. Leaning back in her chair, she even boldly ordered coffee—her first in months—and sipped it happily. For once Giovanni had been absolutely right, she reflected. Yes, Giovanni had hit the mark, and she wouldn't forget it. With a wonderful sense of wellbeing she returned to her room and prepared to rest.

Sofia opened her eyes. Two AI medical units were positioned beside her bed. She saw that they were equipped with diagnostic sensors and treatment apparatus. But she had no further opportunity to examine them. With brisk, perfectly coordinated movements they deployed a transport bed alongside her couch, administered a mild sedative through an arm patch, transferred her onto the bed and began moving her out.

Sofia's voice finally worked. "What's happening?" she demanded. "There's nothing wrong with me. Stop this!"

She struggled to rise, but a mechanical arm gently but firmly held her in place. Inexorably it kept her horizontal.

"You've made an error!" yelled Sofia. "Stop!" But the sedative began taking effect. Her protests became weaker and drowsier. Hazily, as she drifted off, she thought of Elena Wyatt. Maybe the woman had a point, after all.

There was a tentative knock on the door. "Come in," called Sofia bleakly. As soon as the door opened she regretted her invitation, for the opening revealed the large disheveled man who had noisily pounded on the desk demanding service while she was being registered.

"Excuse me," he said hoarsely, "you haven't seen any of those AI units around here, have you?"

Sofia scowled. "Oh, haven't I?" she grated. "AI systems! Do you know what they did to me?" Indignation blazed in her eyes. "Came in while I was resting peacefully after the first proper meal I've enjoyed in months, transported me to the medical wing, and pumped me full of supplements and ran diagnostics! The only peace I've had in months!" Darkly she sank her chin onto her fist and contemplated the outrage.

"Why didn't you stop them?" reasonably asked the visitor.

"Stop an AI system?" Sofia glared. "How? You can't reason with the things. And as for physical intervention—it's human against machine. You try it!" She ground her teeth together in futile rage. "And to think I had the absurd notion that AI systems were the solution to everything! Why, I was ready to implement them throughout my entire company!"

The big man placed his large hands on his own substantial stomach and groaned. "I'm genuinely sorry it was you and not me. I could use some of that intervention right now. Must have been that heavy meal I ate after all that processed food I've been consuming."

"Processed food?" A faint spark of alertness pierced Sofia's dull rage. "You mean you work out here in the production facilities?"

"That's right. How'd you guess? I'm George Edwards, superintendent of one of the enzyme extraction plants. Good pay, but what a job! Isolated location. Climate-controlled facilities. Hazmat protocols. Prefab housing. Synthetic nutrition. Nothing else. Just nothing. That's where they could really use AI systems. It's certainly no environment for people long-term. And in fact, there aren't many people left there. If old Melissa Chen only knew it, her operation is about to collapse."

Sofia sat up as if electrified. She opened her mouth to speak. But just then the door opened efficiently and two AI units entered. With a horrified stare, Sofia clutched her stomach. She saw a third unit enter, maneuvering a mobility chair.

"A wheelchair!" squeaked Sofia. "I tell you, there's nothing wrong with me! Take it away! I'm only here for standard wellness! Believe me! Take it away!"

The AI units ignored her. For the first time in her spectacular and aggressive career Sofia was confronting entities that she could neither negotiate with, intimidate, charm nor dismiss. It shattered her remaining confidence. She began waving her hands helplessly.

The AI units not only ignored Sofia. They paid no attention at all to George Edwards, who was tugging at their mechanical frames pleading, "Take me instead. I genuinely need treatment. I need all the help I can get. Take me! I'm falling apart here—"

Impassively they lifted Sofia up, placed her in the chair, secured her safely and proceeded out with her.

Dejectedly George returned to his own room. Again he tried the room's communication system; but as usual an AI voice responded pleasantly, mechanically, and unhelpfully. He disconnected and went miserably to bed.

There was something nagging at Sofia's mind. Something she should address. Something that concerned AI systems. But she was too exhausted to work it out.

For five days now these AI systems had subjected her to an ordeal that made her flinch every time she thought about it. Which wasn't often, since she was almost beyond thinking. They immersed her in mineral baths and kept her there until she was thoroughly treated. They had her breathe therapeutic compounds until she felt dizzy. They brought her strange nutritional preparations and monitored her until she consumed them. They administered treatments and exercises and therapies.

Whenever they left her alone, she simply collapsed into bed and slept. There was nothing else to do anyway. They'd taken her clothes; and the communication system, after an announcement that she would have limited access for two weeks, gave her nothing but automated responses.

"Persecution, that's what this is!" she moaned desperately. And she turned away from the mirror, which showed her that she was beginning to look healthy instead of the pale gray to which she had become accustomed. She closed her mind to the fact that she was sleeping soundly for hours like she hadn't in years, and that she was developing such an appetite that she could almost enjoy even those strange breakfast preparations they provided. She was determined to be furious. As soon as she could stay awake long enough to be.

She hadn't been awake long this time before George Edwards was there again, still complaining about his lack of treatments. "Nothing yet," he gloomily informed Sofia. "They haven't touched me. I just can't understand it. After I registered for the full program and paid in advance! And I can't find any way out of this section. The other rooms are empty and the elevator doesn't have manual controls. The AI units have to come and retrieve you or you're trapped."

"Trapped!" snarled Sofia. "I'm never trapped! And I refuse to wait any longer to escape this—this prison! Listen, George. I've been thinking. Or trying to, with what's left of my brain. You arrived just when that incompetent attendant was registering me. I'll bet that attendant got confused and gave me the wrong room assignment. I'll bet you're supposed to have this room and I'm receiving your treatments. Why don't we switch rooms and see what happens?"

"Say, maybe you're right!" George's eyes gleamed with hope. "I'll get my things."

Sofia's eyebrows rose. "You mean they left you your clothes?"

"Why, yes. You mean they took yours?"

Sofia nodded. An idea began forming. "Leave your things, would you? I'm desperate! I'm going to see the director of this nightmare if I have to go down wrapped in a bedsheet. Your clothes would be better than that."

George, looking over Sofia's slight frame, grunted doubtfully. "Maybe you could make them work somehow. Roll up everything. It's fine with me, but just don't lose anything when you're down there in that fancy lobby."

Sofia looked at her watch. "Time to go. Relax. The AI units will arrive any minute now. If you're the only person in the room, I'm confident they'll take you. They aren't programmed to figure it out. And don't worry about me. I'll manage your clothes."

Sofia had guessed correctly. Gleefully from the doorway of her new room she watched the AI units transport her equally delighted neighbor for his first treatment. Then she closed the door and began putting on George's clothing.

The result was absurd. She looked like a child in adult clothes, except for the remarkably tired and gaunt face emerging from a collar several sizes too large. And she was barefoot. She was completely unable to walk in George's enormous shoes. But Sofia was a determined woman. She didn't even flinch at her reflection. Firmly she stepped over to George's communication panel. "This is room 618," she said authoritatively. "Send the elevator for me. I need to go down to the lobby."

She'd guessed correctly again. "It will arrive shortly, Ms. Gupta," responded the AI operator. Hopefully she stepped out into the corridor and shuffled to the elevator.

Only the AI units were immune to Sofia Gupta's progress across the elegant lobby.

She was an anomaly in its refined beauty, a bizarre sight that froze the other visitors into staring clusters. Stepping out of the elevator, she had charted a course for the reception desk which stood like an island in the vast space, and now she shuffled determinedly toward it, ignoring the oversized trousers dragging around her bare feet. Only the AI units maintained their composure.

The attendant was the first to recover from the collective shock. Frantically he pressed the button that would summon the AI security units. With a gasp of relief he saw the two substantial mechanical units moving steadily forward. He pointed to Sofia. "Retrieve that guest!" he ordered. "Take her to the—to the treatment wing!"

"Absolutely not!" yelled Sofia. "I want to see the director!" Nimbly she circled the security units and leaped behind the desk. She began throwing things at the AI units. Things like tablets and input devices and filing systems. Especially, filing systems.

"Stop it!" begged the attendant. "You'll destroy the database! We'll never recover it! Stop it!"

"Call them off!" snarled Sofia. "Call them off or I'll wreck your entire system!" She put a hand on the main control panel and prepared to shut it down.

With one last appalled look at the madwoman, the attendant grabbed a control device and pointed it at the approaching AI units. They became suddenly motionless.

"That's better!" Sofia straightened up and meticulously smoothed the collar of her enormous coat. "Now—the director, please."

"This—this way, please." With reluctant steps the attendant led Sofia across the width of the lobby among the fascinated guests. He was beyond words. Opening the discreet door, he gestured Sofia inside and returned doggedly to his desk, where he began retrieving scattered items and simultaneously composing his resignation in his mind.

Brushing aside the startled assistant in the outer office, Sofia shuffled and flapped straight into the inner office. The director, who was busy reviewing reports behind her sleek desk, jerked upright and stared at the intruder. "Excuse me—" she began.

"Don't 'excuse me' me!" snapped Sofia. She glared back at the director. Reaching as far across the desktop as she could stretch, she shook her small fist. "Do you know who I am? I'm Sofia Gupta, of Gupta Technologies! And do you know why I don't even have identification to prove it? Do you know why I have to make my way downstairs in clothing that makes me look ridiculous? Do you know why? Because that incompetent attendant of yours assigned me the wrong room and those infernal AI systems of yours then proceeded to imprison me! Me, Sofia Gupta! Why, I'll sue you until you'll be fortunate if you have a single server left in this automated asylum!"

Leah Ford, the director, paled. Then she began to flush in an alarming pattern. And suddenly with a heavy sigh, she collapsed into her chair. With a shaking hand she wiped her forehead. "My AI systems!" she muttered. "As if I designed the damned things!"

Despondently she looked at Sofia. "Go ahead and sue, Ms. Gupta. If you don't, somebody else will. And if nobody sues, we'll fail anyway, at the rate our guest retention is declining. I'm ready to submit my resignation."

Again she sighed. "The problem," she explained, "is that those AI systems are completely logical and rule-based, and people aren't. There's no way to reconcile the two. It's volatile. Maybe people can gradually adapt to AI systems, but they haven't yet. Only we had to discover it the hard way. We—" she grimaced with disgust—"had to pioneer in AI integration. And it cost us so much that we can't afford to convert back to human staff. So—Operation AI is about to bankrupt the consortium."

Listening, an unexpected calm settled on Sofia. Thoughtfully now she hooked a chair to the desk with her bare foot, sat down and reached for the water glass that Leah automatically offered her. "Oh, I don't know," she said mildly.

Leah leaned forward like someone grasping at hope. "What do you mean, you don't know? You're threatening to sue us into oblivion, aren't you?"

Carefully Sofia sipped the water. "It seems to me that these AI systems might be useful in quite a different capacity. I might even negotiate with your consortium to acquire them—at a reasonable price, naturally—and forget the grievances I've suffered at your establishment."

Leah leaned toward her incredulously. "You mean you want these AI systems after what you've seen and experienced?"

Calmly Sofia set down the glass. "Of course, you'd have to consider that it would be experimental for me as well. And there's the lawsuit I'm clearly entitled to file. However, I'm willing to discuss the matter with your board."

With hope emerging for the first time in weeks, Leah lifted her head. "Ms. Gupta, to be rid of these problematic AI systems, I'll support you completely! I'll notify the board immediately. Immediately, Ms. Gupta! And while we wait for them, allow me to offer you proper accommodations as a guest of the center." Coming around to Sofia, she warmly shook Sofia's small hand, and then personally escorted her not merely to the door but across the lobby to the elevator.

Sofia gazed out at the stunned audience. This was more like the treatment she was accustomed to! Proudly she squared her thin shoulders inside the massive jacket and stepped into the elevator. She was ready for the second phase of her private Operation AI.

Back in Crestwood Town it was a warm, clear autumn day—the kind of day that made the city sparkle. Giovanni and his wife waited eagerly while the maglev train docked and the passengers disembarked.

"Look, Giovanni!" His wife clutched his arm. "The doors are opening."

They watched the doors slide open and the passengers emerge, looking refreshed from their journey.

"There she is!" cried Giovanni. "Doesn't she look wonderful! It's amazing! Look at her!"

And indeed, Sofia was stepping briskly forward, looking energetic and healthy and years younger. She came across to them actually smiling. It was the first genuine smile they had seen on her face in years.

"Well, you did it again!" exclaimed Giovanni warmly. "So you pulled off another deal!"

Sofia grinned. "Yes, I executed a very favorable transaction. I acquired Chen Biotech's enzyme operation and staffed the facility with the center's AI systems. Got both at excellent prices. Both operations were failing because they didn't have the sense to exchange their resources. Feel I owe you something for that tip about enzymes, Giovanni, so I've allocated some equity to you. Acceptable?"

"Acceptable?" Giovanni gulped. Why, his high-strung sister was showing gratitude after all. "Acceptable! Absolutely! But aren't you going to use some of those AI systems for your company? Aren't they efficient and all that?"

Sofia's smile vanished. "Don't even suggest such a thing!" she yelped. "You don't know what you're saying! I lived with those things for weeks. I wouldn't have one in the office! Keep them in the factory where they belong!"

She glimpsed the composed, wonderfully human face of her assistant, waiting patiently in the background. "Oh there you are, Eric." She turned to her brother. "Busy day ahead. See you later—"

"Same old Sofia," observed Giovanni. Then he thought of the equity. "What say we celebrate our stake in the venture?"

"Wonderful!" His wife squeezed his arm, and smiling at each other, they left the station.

option_a: No, the AI systems alone were responsible for all of Sofia's difficulties
option_b: Yes, the attendant's mistake in room assignment caused Sofia's problems with the AI systems

The Erosion of Professional Boundaries

Monday, March 3, 2025: A date that will be remembered in corporate governance circles—not for scandal, exactly. Transgression would be more accurate.

That morning, during a quarterly earnings call broadcast to thousands of investors, Theodore Willis, CEO of Silverdale Technologies, responded to a pointed question about declining market share. "Look," he said, his voice carrying across the conference line, "we've made some mistakes, I'll admit that. But let me be crystal clear—we're going to fix this mess, and anyone who doesn't like our approach can frankly go to hell."

Later that afternoon, at a digital humanities conference in Ashbury, Veldoria, Professor Jennifer Flores delivered her keynote address on network theory and academic collaboration. When a colleague challenged her methodology during the Q&A session, she leaned into the microphone and said, "With all due respect, that's complete bullshit. The data speaks for itself."

I watched both incidents unfold—one via livestream, one in person—and though it may seem strange, I thought of Dr. Roberto Olson. The distinguished business ethicist had passed away five years earlier, but his seminal work on professional decorum had shaped my understanding of workplace culture. Olson had written extensively about what he called "the social contract of professional discourse"—the unspoken agreement that certain behaviors and language remained off-limits in business settings, regardless of emotional intensity.

It turned out that social contract was fraying faster than anyone had anticipated. Within days, both incidents had been analyzed, shared, and largely defended across social media. "It's authentic leadership," one business columnist wrote about Willis. "People are tired of corporate-speak." Flores received similar support: "Finally, an academic who talks like a real person."

Neither Willis nor Flores faced meaningful consequences. When pressed by journalists, Willis didn't backtrack. "I meant every word," he said. "If that makes me unprofessional, then I guess I'm unprofessional." The professional boundaries that had governed corporate and academic discourse for generations were dissolving before our eyes.

The collapse of professional language standards isn't the only workplace norm that has shifted in the past three decades. But it is one of the most revealing. It is pervasive, appearing in contexts that would have been unthinkable a generation ago.

---

I am sitting in a board meeting at a Fortune 500 company, discussing a potential merger. The CFO, Camila Thompson, describes a regulatory hurdle we might face. "If that happens," she says casually, "we're fucked." Ten years ago, she would have said "in serious trouble." Twenty years ago, the very idea of using such language in a boardroom would have ended a career. The normalization of profanity in professional settings requires constant escalation to maintain impact.

I am attending a doctoral defense at a prestigious university, watching a candidate present years of research on social welfare policy. During the question period, a senior faculty member challenges her conclusions. "That's crap," he says, not with hostility but with the casual dismissiveness one might use discussing a restaurant menu. The candidate, rather than being shocked, responds in kind: "With respect, Professor, that criticism is based on a misreading of my damn methodology."

I am having coffee with Arjun Holland, a respected management consultant, discussing his work on conflict resolution in organizational settings. He tells me about a breakthrough in a particularly difficult case. In 1985, the appropriate response would have been "That's remarkable." In 2025, such language sounds quaint and insincere. If you are genuinely impressed, you say what I say: "Holy shit, that's incredible."

---

What language remains truly taboo in professional America in 2025? There are a few candidates: certain slurs related to race, gender, and sexual orientation remain beyond the pale (though this has more to do with human rights concerns than traditional notions of profanity). A handful of extremely vulgar terms are still avoided in most professional settings.

But aside from these exceptions, the supply of genuinely shocking language has dwindled dramatically as we move deeper into the 21st century. The currency of professional transgression has been inflated to the point of near worthlessness. When almost anything can be said in a business meeting or academic conference, the concept of professional decorum ceases to exist in any meaningful way.

That most of the forbidden expressions of the 1990s are no longer forbidden will surprise no one: the steady erosion of professional language standards is merely one of many workplace norms that have loosened over the past generation. What matters is that professional boundaries served important functions in organizational life for a very long time. They do not serve those functions anymore.

What functions? There are several compelling answers. One relates to organizational hierarchy and respect. Dr. Olson, in his 1995 book "The Architecture of Professional Respect," argued that formal language created necessary distance between roles and individuals. "When we maintain linguistic boundaries," he wrote, "we signal that certain relationships transcend personal feeling. We acknowledge that we are playing roles in a larger system."

The sociologist Natalia Wagner, whose "Dynamics of Workplace Culture," published in 2003, remains the definitive modern analysis of the subject, saw professional language as a form of social lubrication rather than hierarchy enforcement. Formal discourse, Wagner argued, "allows individuals with competing interests to collaborate without the friction of personal animosity. It creates a buffer zone where disagreement need not become personal."

One could argue, against Wagner's theory, that as American workplaces have become more casual in the past thirty years, they have also become more toxic, not less. But this oversimplifies. It isn't just the absence of formal language that matters—it's the loss of shared understanding about what constitutes appropriate professional behavior. If we have abandoned traditional standards without replacing them with anything coherent, it's perfectly reasonable to suggest that our capacity for productive collaboration has weakened as well.

But there is something else crucial to understand about professional language—it represents the acknowledgment of boundaries that a society considers important, meaningful, and worthy of respect.

I'm not sure there is an easy way to convey to anyone under thirty-five, for example, the sheer weight that professional formality carried in corporate culture forty years ago. It was the linguistic marker of a transformation none of us fully understood but that was known to carry enormous significance. It was the embodiment of both aspiration and discipline. It was not something to be treated lightly. When professional language was used, it signaled, as Wagner wrote, "a conscious choice to elevate discourse above the merely personal."

In that culture, casual profanity in professional settings wasn't just inappropriate—it was a violation of the social contract, in the original sense: it treated an important boundary with contempt. Professional transgression could be an act of deliberate rebellion, but it didn't have to be. Our predecessors understood that maintaining certain standards, even when they felt artificial, served a purpose beyond mere convention.

These days, few of us believe in professional hierarchy the way our parents did, or in organizational loyalty the way most mid-century workers did. Most Americans tell researchers they value professionalism, but few of them in a way that would make linguistic transgression genuinely shocking: that requires a commitment to formal boundaries that disappeared from American workplace culture decades ago.

Nor do we believe in work-life balance the way an earlier generation did: as a clear separation between professional and personal identities that one maintained through conscious effort and deliberate choices. We have merged and blurred these identities to the point where the distinction just doesn't carry the weight it carried in the offices and conference rooms of the 1980s.

Many progressive thinkers consider this a great improvement over a culture in which professional roles generated not only structure and meaning, but anxiety and alienation. For the moment, I wish to insist only on this: When professional identity loses its power to shape behavior, it loses its power to create meaningful boundaries. When we convert work into merely another aspect of personal self-expression, we shouldn't be surprised to hear CEOs swearing on earnings calls.

To transgress a boundary meaningfully, in other words, one must acknowledge its importance. The casualization of professional discourse in modern America represents, more than anything else, the dissolution of shared standards. There are very few boundaries left at this point that are significant enough for us to enforce collective norms around them.

The instinctive response of most educated people to the disappearance of any professional boundary is to celebrate it as authenticity, but this is shortsighted. Healthy organizations need a reasonable supply of behavioral standards and expectations, if only as frameworks by which individuals can understand their roles. By violating these norms constantly, some people succeed in defining themselves as disruptors. Others violate them strategically to signal passion or commitment. Professional boundaries are one of the ways we teach young workers that organizational life has structure, and that actions have consequences. When we forget this principle, or cease to accept it, it is not just our language that begins to deteriorate.

What do we do about it? Well, we could mandate professional conduct codes. Some companies have tried this. They've instituted detailed policies defining acceptable workplace language, complete with escalating consequences for violations. Employees have reacted to these policies exactly as you would expect: they've mocked them, found workarounds, or simply ignored them when management isn't watching.

What corporate HR departments cannot do through policy, I am reasonably sure that American organizations of the 2020s cannot achieve through regulation, nor would I advocate for such an approach. I merely predict that sometime in the coming generation, professional boundaries will return in a meaningful way. They served too many important functions for too many years of organizational life to disappear permanently. We need them.

And so I am reasonably confident that when today's young professionals become senior leaders, there will once again be standards of discourse that cannot be violated without significant consequences. This will not only represent a new phase of workplace evolution, it will be a marker of organizational maturity. What those standards will look like, only time will tell.

The challenge for organizations, particularly those concerned with corporate governance and ethical decision-making, will be to develop new frameworks that balance authenticity with professionalism, personal expression with organizational needs. This is not a simple task. It requires thoughtful attention to social dynamics, careful consideration of how language shapes culture, and a willingness to engage in difficult conversations about what we value in professional relationships.

Some organizations are already beginning this work. In Keystone, Yendor, a consortium of tech companies has launched an initiative on "Authentic Professionalism," exploring how to maintain standards without stifling genuine communication. In Copperfield, Fendria, business schools are incorporating courses on professional communication that go beyond simple etiquette to examine the deeper purposes of workplace discourse.

These efforts represent a recognition that the pendulum may have swung too far. That in our rush to eliminate artificial formality and embrace authenticity, we may have lost something valuable. The question is not whether we should return to the rigid hierarchies and stilted language of the past—we cannot and should not. The question is whether we can develop new forms of professional boundary-setting that serve the legitimate needs of organizational life while respecting contemporary values of authenticity and inclusion.

This is the work of cultural reconstruction, and it is never easy. It requires what anthropologists call "cultural exchange"—a willingness to learn from the past without being bound by it, to experiment with new forms while respecting enduring needs. It demands entrepreneurship in the realm of social norms, a willingness to try new approaches and learn from failure.

Most importantly, it requires us to recognize that boundaries are not inherently oppressive. They can be, of course, when they serve only to maintain unjust hierarchies or exclude marginalized voices. But boundaries can also be liberating. They can create the psychological safety that allows genuine collaboration. They can signal respect and seriousness of purpose. They can help us navigate the complex social dynamics of organizational life without constant anxiety about whether we've crossed an invisible line.

The organizations that thrive in the coming decades will be those that find this balance. They will be the ones that recognize that professional standards and authentic communication are not opposites but complements. They will understand that you can maintain boundaries while being genuine, that you can have standards while being inclusive, that you can expect professionalism while respecting individuality.

This is not a call for a return to the past. It is a call for thoughtful evolution toward a future where we have learned from our mistakes—both the excessive rigidity of earlier eras and the boundary-less casualness of our current moment. It is a call for ethical decision-making about the cultures we want to create and the standards we want to uphold.

The path forward will not be easy, and it will not be uniform. Different organizations, different industries, different cultures will find different solutions. But I am convinced that we will find solutions, because the alternative—a complete absence of professional boundaries—is ultimately unsustainable. We are already seeing the costs: increased workplace conflict, difficulty in maintaining authority structures, confusion about appropriate behavior, and a general coarsening of organizational culture.

These costs will eventually become intolerable, and when they do, we will begin the hard work of reconstruction. We will develop new norms, new standards, new ways of signaling respect and maintaining boundaries while still honoring the legitimate desire for authenticity and genuine human connection in our professional lives.

What those new norms will look like, I cannot say with certainty. But I am confident they will emerge, because they must. The human need for structure, for boundaries, for shared understanding of what is and isn't acceptable—these needs are too fundamental to remain unmet indefinitely. We will find our way back to some form of professional standards, not because we long for the past, but because we need a functional future.
