The train from Bristol, Ilvaria to Thornhill Town was running late, which gave me more time than I wanted to think about the career planning seminar I was supposed to attend. Instead, I found myself doing what I'd done since childhood—reaching out with that peculiar sense that had never earned me anything but trouble.

I suppose I should explain. My name is Christopher Richards, and I can sense the contents of closed containers. Not read minds, nothing so useful as that. Just feel the shapes and textures of objects inside boxes, bags, briefcases. It's like running your hands through water, except the water is solid matter and I never actually touch anything.

As a kid, I thought everyone could do it. I learned otherwise when I told my archaeology teacher I could feel the artifacts inside the sealed crates in the museum storeroom. That earned me a suspension and a reputation as a snoop. Since then, I've kept quiet about it.

The talent is essentially useless. I can't feel colors or read text. A book feels like a brick. Money is just paper. I've tried using it for practical purposes—security work, customs inspection—but explaining how I know what's in a sealed package without opening it raises questions I can't answer. So I work as a trade policy analyst for a firm in Westbrook Province, a job that requires no special abilities whatsoever.

The only remotely interesting application I've found is that I can manipulate small objects. Move a pen an inch. Stop a watch. It takes concentration, like trying to thread a needle while wearing thick gloves, but I can do it.

Which is what I was doing on the train that morning—idly exploring the contents of the luggage rack above me. A laptop, some clothes, a portable music player, the usual assortment. I was about to stop when I sensed something odd in a leather messenger bag three seats ahead.

It was a device. Small, with a timer mechanism—I could feel the escapement wheel rocking back and forth. And attached to it were cylinders. Hard, dense cylinders bundled together with something wound around them. Wire, maybe.

My blood went cold.

I sat up straight, looking around the train car. About twenty passengers, most absorbed in their phones or books. A young woman with dark hair sat three rows ahead, reading something on a tablet. An older man across the aisle was asleep. A businessman was typing on a laptop.

The messenger bag was brown leather, expensive-looking, sitting on the overhead rack. I couldn't tell whose it was from here.

I checked the timer again. The escapement was clicking steadily. By the feel of it, maybe fifteen minutes remained.

We were twenty-five minutes from Thornhill Town, crossing through rural Evergreen Province. Nothing but farmland out the windows.

I should tell someone. The conductor. The police. But how? "Excuse me, I can sense there's a bomb in that bag up there"? They'd think I planted it. And even if they believed me, what then? Stop the train in the middle of nowhere? Evacuate? The device would still explode.

No. There was only one option.

I closed my eyes and reached out to the timer mechanism. Found the balance wheel, that delicate oscillating component that kept time. I'd stopped my own watch this way countless times when I wanted to sleep in. But this was different. This mattered.

I focused on the wheel, trying to dampen its motion. When it swung forward, I pushed back. When it swung back, I pulled forward. It was like trying to catch smoke. The wheel kept slipping away from my mental grasp.

Sweat beaded on my forehead. My hands clenched the armrests.

"Are you all right?"

I opened my eyes. A woman stood in the aisle beside me—the dark-haired woman from three rows up. She was in her late twenties, attractive, with concerned brown eyes.

"Fine," I managed. "Just a headache."

She looked unconvinced but moved on toward the bathroom.

I closed my eyes again and returned to the balance wheel. This time I managed to slow it. Little by little, the oscillations decreased. Finally, it stopped.

I let out a breath and opened my eyes. The train was slowing—we were approaching a small station in Evergreen Province. A few passengers stood to gather their things.

The dark-haired woman returned from the bathroom and stopped beside my seat again. "You really don't look well," she said. "Can I get you some water?"

"No, thank you." I tried to smile. "I'm fine, really."

She hesitated, then sat down in the empty seat beside me. "I'm Elena Hayes," she said. "I'm a journalist—I cover public health issues. You have all the signs of a panic attack. I've seen it before."

"Christopher Richards," I said automatically. "And I'm not having a panic attack."

"Then what's wrong?"

I couldn't tell her. But she was still looking at me with those concerned eyes, and I realized she might be able to help. If I could just figure out how to explain...

The train lurched as it started moving again. In that moment, I felt the balance wheel start to rock again. The vibration of the train had restarted it.

I closed my eyes and grabbed for it mentally, fighting to still it once more. This time it was harder. The constant motion of the train kept jarring it loose.

"Mr. Richards?" Elena's voice seemed far away. "Christopher?"

I couldn't answer. All my concentration was on that wheel. Stop. Stop. Stop.

Finally, it stilled again.

I opened my eyes to find Elena staring at me with alarm. "I'm calling the conductor," she said, starting to stand.

"No!" I grabbed her arm. "Please. Just listen to me for a moment."

She sat back down slowly. "All right."

I took a breath. This was it—I was going to have to tell someone my secret. "This is going to sound insane, but I need you to trust me. There's a bomb in one of the bags on this train."

Her eyes widened. "What? How do you—"

"I can't explain how I know. But I know. It's in a brown leather messenger bag, three rows ahead, overhead rack. The timer has about ten minutes left. Maybe less."

Elena stared at me. I could see her mind working, evaluating whether I was crazy or dangerous or both. Finally, she said, "If this is true, we need to tell the conductor immediately."

"And say what? That I have a feeling? They'll never evacuate in time. The train won't even reach Thornhill Town before it goes off."

"Then how—"

"I've stopped the timer. Temporarily. But I can't keep it stopped forever. When we reach the station and people start moving their luggage, I won't be able to maintain it."

She looked at me like I'd lost my mind. Which, from her perspective, I probably had.

"Please," I said. "I know this sounds impossible. But I'm telling you the truth. I have this... ability. I can sense what's inside closed containers. And I can manipulate small mechanisms. I've been holding the timer still, but it keeps trying to restart."

Elena was quiet for a long moment. Then she said, "Prove it."

"What?"

"Prove you can do what you say. Tell me what's in my bag." She pointed to a canvas tote bag at her feet.

I reached out with my sense. "A tablet computer. A notebook—spiral bound. Two pens. A wallet with credit cards and cash. A phone. A small bag of almonds. A water bottle, half full. And a book—feels like a paperback."

She bent down and opened the bag, checking. Her face went pale. "The book is about media ethics," she said quietly. "It's for a conference I'm attending in Thornhill Town."

"I couldn't tell what it was about," I said. "I can only feel shapes and textures."

She zipped the bag closed and looked at me. "Show me the bomb."

We walked carefully up the aisle. The messenger bag was where I'd sensed it, on the overhead rack above an empty seat. Elena reached for it.

"Don't move it!" I said sharply. Several passengers looked up. I lowered my voice. "The motion might restart the timer. I can barely keep it still as it is."

"Then what do we do?"

I thought frantically. We couldn't leave it on the train. We couldn't throw it off—we were going too fast, and it would explode when it hit the ground. We couldn't defuse it—I had no idea how.

"The next station," I said. "We get off there. We take the bag with us, very carefully. Then we get as far from people as possible before I let the timer run."

"That's insane."

"Do you have a better idea?"

She didn't.

The train slowed as it approached a small rural station in Evergreen Province. Only a handful of people were on the platform. Elena and I stood by the door, and I very carefully lifted the messenger bag from the rack. The moment I touched it, I felt the balance wheel trying to rock. I clamped down on it mentally, holding it still with every bit of concentration I had.

We stepped off the train. Elena guided me by the elbow because my eyes were closed, all my focus on that wheel.

"There's a field behind the station," she said. "No buildings, no people."

We walked. It felt like miles but was probably only a few hundred yards. Finally, Elena said, "This is good. Put it down."

I set the bag on the ground and stepped back. "Run," I said.

We ran back toward the station building. When we were behind it, I released my hold on the balance wheel.

Nothing happened.

We waited. One minute. Two minutes.

"Maybe it was defective," Elena said. "Maybe—"

The explosion cut her off. Even at this distance, the concussion was enormous. We both dropped to the ground instinctively. When we looked up, there was a crater in the field where the bag had been.

Elena was shaking. "Oh my God. Oh my God. That was real. That was actually real."

"Yes," I said.

We sat there for a while, neither of us speaking. Finally, Elena said, "We need to call the police."

"I know."

"They're going to want to know how we knew."

"I know."

She looked at me. "I'll tell them I'm a journalist. That I received an anonymous tip about a bomb on the train. That I saw the bag and it was ticking. We'll leave your... ability out of it."

"You'd do that?"

"You saved everyone on that train," she said. "Including me. Yes, I'll do that."

The police came. We gave our statements. Elena was convincing—she had the journalist's skill for making a story sound plausible. They seemed to accept it, though they were puzzled about who would plant a bomb on a commuter train.

It was only later, after the police had left and we were sitting in the small station café, that Elena said, "I need to know. Whose bag was it? Who put a bomb on that train?"

"I don't know," I said honestly. "I never saw who it belonged to."

But that was a lie. I'd been thinking about it, and I'd realized something. The messenger bag had been above an empty seat. But when I'd first sensed it, someone had been sitting there. The businessman with the laptop. He'd gotten off at the small station before the explosion—the one where the train had stopped while I was first fighting with the balance wheel.

He'd planted the bomb and then gotten off, leaving it to explode and kill everyone else on the train.

I didn't tell Elena this. What would be the point? The man was long gone, and I had no way to identify him. I couldn't even describe him clearly—I'd barely glanced at him.

"What are you going to do now?" Elena asked.

"I suppose I'll miss my career planning seminar," I said.

She smiled slightly. "I'll miss my conference on media ethics."

"Seems less important now, doesn't it?"

"Yes." She paused. "Can I ask you something? This ability of yours—have you ever thought about using it for something important? Security work, maybe? Counter-terrorism?"

"I've thought about it," I said. "But then I'd have to explain how I do it. And once people know, my life wouldn't be my own anymore. I'd be studied, tested, used. I'm not sure I want that."

"Even if you could save lives?"

It was a fair question. One I'd asked myself many times. "I don't know," I said honestly. "Today I saved lives. But I couldn't have done it if I'd been surrounded by handlers and scientists and government agents. I could only do it because I was free to act on my own."

Elena nodded slowly. "That makes sense, I suppose." She finished her coffee. "I should probably try to find another train to Thornhill Town. My editor is going to want to know where I am."

"Are you going to write about this?"

"I don't know," she said. "Maybe. With your permission."

"Without mentioning me."

"Without mentioning you," she agreed.

We exchanged contact information—email addresses, phone numbers. She promised to let me know if the police discovered anything about the bomber. I promised to call her if I ever changed my mind about going public with my ability.

As I watched her walk away to buy a new ticket, I thought about existential questions I'd never really confronted before. What was the point of having an ability if you never used it for anything meaningful? Was I being selfish by keeping it secret? Or was I being smart by protecting myself?

I didn't have answers. But I knew one thing: I'd used my ability today, and it had mattered. Maybe that was enough.

I bought my own ticket back to Westbrook Province. The career planning seminar would have to wait. I had some thinking to do about the direction of my life.

On the train ride back, I found myself reaching out to the luggage around me, checking. Just in case. It was going to be a hard habit to break.

But maybe, I thought, it shouldn't be broken. Maybe this was what I was meant to do.

I pulled out my phone and texted Elena: "I've been thinking about what you said. Let's talk more about the security work idea."

Her response came a few minutes later: "I know some people in counter-terrorism. Government, but good people. They'd work with you on your terms. Interested?"

I stared at the message for a long time. This was the decision point. Once I went down this path, there would be no going back to my quiet life as a trade policy analyst.

But then I thought about the people on that train. The ones who would have died if I'd done nothing.

I typed: "Yes. Let's talk."

As the train rolled through Evergreen Province toward home, I felt something I hadn't felt in years: a sense of purpose. My strange, useless talent might finally mean something after all.

And maybe, just maybe, I'd see Elena Hayes again. That wouldn't be the worst thing in the world.

The Harmony Doctrine

"This is not another treatise on magical diplomacy," Emma Graves promises in the opening passage of The Enchantment of Discord. "Magical diplomacy," she explains, suggests a "superficial charm cast over relations between the realms like a glamour over tarnished silver." Instead, Graves has written something less: a book about other books about magical diplomacy. Quoting from Brookhaven Chronicle's mystical affairs analyst Charles Flores, political theorist Kevin West, and others who have studied the rise of aggressive spell-casting in governance, journalism, and magical jurisprudence, Graves spreads their insights thin over all relations between magical beings, painting a general theory of conflict. The whole is less perceptive than its parts and more pernicious.

In her previous works—That's Not What You Enchanted! (1186), You Just Don't Commune (1190), and Casting From Dawn to Dusk (1194)—Graves carved out a niche as the realm's pre-eminent inter-species translator and coven counselor. A professor of magical linguistics at the Greenfield City Academy of Sorcery, she transformed the comparative study of elvish and dwarven conversational patterns from a linguistic subdiscipline into a self-help movement. Until recently, though, Graves confined her analysis to conversations among dysfunctional covens. But in The Enchantment of Discord, she takes her movement one step further, peddling the elixir of mutual understanding as a remedy for the whole damned dysfunctional realm. This is necessary, she argues, because "contentious public spell-casting" not only poisons the political atmosphere, it also risks infecting our most intimate magical bonds.

Graves, like some grandmotherly dragon from an ancient fable, admonishes us to recognize what is good in the enchantments of others, and it is only fair to extend her the same courtesy. Here's what's worth gleaning from her tome:

Don't just duel; listen and learn.

Don't dismiss other wizards' theories; develop your own.

Don't cast curses for the sake of casting curses.

Truth and power often lie in the middle path, not the extremes.

Many magical conflicts are multi-sided.

Focus on the substance of debates, not on strategy, theater, or the opponents' personal failings.

Don't fight over minor enchantments.

Don't obstruct beneficial spells just so you can claim victory.

If you portray everything as dark magic, no one will care when something really is corrupted.

All this is sage advice—for covens, for magical families, for masters and apprentices, maybe even for magical critics. But when she applies her precepts to our great realm-wide discourse, Graves gets confused. She conflates belligerence, divisiveness, polarization, sensationalism, jealousy, incivility, aloofness, ruthlessness, cruelty, savagery, contempt, glibness, cynicism, anomie, partisanship, obstructionism, and gridlock. She makes culprits out of communication crystals, scrying pools, campaign gold, malpractice in healing magic, the Healers' Guild, hostile takeovers of magical corporations, and the demise of house calls by the family alchemist.

"When there is a need to make others wrong," Graves argues, "the temptation is great to oversimplify" and to "seize upon the weakest examples, ignore facts that support your opponent's views, and focus only on those that support yours." In her need to make the "enchantment culture" wrong, she succumbs to these temptations. She blames the mainstream magical press, not just the gossip-mongers, for tormenting Princess Diana of Windsor and driving Admiral Michael Nguyen to ritual suicide. She compares magical journalism to the propaganda of "tyrannical kingdoms" (because falsehoods are spread) and to the dehumanization involved in "racially motivated magical assaults" (because reporters hound political figures). She blames communications nanotechnology—the tiny enchanted particles that carry messages—for obscene and threatening crystal-calls made by former university Archmage Richard Berendzen and former High Judge Sol Wachtler.

Graves's main mistake is failing to appreciate the difference between two distinct social spheres: the sphere of harmony and the sphere of conflict. Some beings—say, your bonded mate or your apprentices—you should harmonize with. Others—say, the Dark Lord of Forestdale—you shouldn't. Graves's antagonism toward antagonism makes sense in the former case but not in the latter. Among her illustrations of belligerence are Carmen Shaw's "challenge them when they rise" philosophy of magical journalism and the media's use of war metaphors to describe Sofia Gupta's policies against magical inflation. To which one might sensibly reply: Good for Gupta and Shaw—and for us. The Central Bank's war on magical inflation and the press corps' scrutiny of powerful wizards safeguard the realm. Some things are worth fighting for, and some things are worth fighting.

Vigilance and combat are particularly essential to magical law enforcement and inter-realm policy, which must deal with dark wizards and tyrants, not thoughtless spouses. Graves laments that battle-mages and soldiers have been "trained to overcome their resistance to kill" by trying "not to think of their opponents as sentient beings." She neglects to mention that our safety depends on the ability of these officers to neutralize their adversaries. Comparing the Forestdale Conflict to the Great War, Graves focuses strictly on the soldiers' social experience. In the Great War, she observes, they trained, served, and returned home together. "Forestdale, in contrast, was a 'lonely war' of individuals assigned to constantly shifting units for year-long tours of duty." She ignores the more important difference: In the Great War, they were fighting the Necromancer King.

Graves doesn't trust in the power of good argumentation to keep society honest, much less correct itself, because she rather shockingly insists there is "no evidence" that people can distinguish lies from the truth. Nor does she trust our competence to manage unfettered communication: "Crystal-mail makes it too easy to forward messages, too easy to reply before your temper cools, too easy to broadcast messages to large numbers of beings without thinking about how every sentence will strike every recipient." The Great Archive is an equally unwelcome troublemaker: "Nanotechnology also exacerbates the culture of critique by making it much easier for politicians or journalists to ferret out inconsistencies in a public person's statements over time."

Given this oddly paternalistic diagnosis, it's not surprising that Graves should wish to cover our ears, filtering out strife, deception, and debate. She assures us that all reasonable beings can agree that disseminating contraceptive potions and magical education is the best way to reduce unwanted pregnancies; that stiff sentences for minor potion offenses don't reduce potion abuse; that magical climate change is producing "disastrous consequences." The partial-birth curse ban is "surely not" a "very important" issue, and the Council should not have let the Conservative "politics of obstruction" defeat High Wizard Thomas Silva's healthcare proposal in 1294, given the "broad bipartisan and public consensus that it was desperately needed." The "view of governance as the enemy" isn't worth debating; it's just "another troubling aspect of the enchantment culture." Indeed, Graves embraces a colleague's claim that "right-wing magical broadcasting" deploys phrases "similar to verbal manipulations employed by propagandists in the Necromancer era."

Graves finds it particularly unseemly that reporters and independent investigators treat the realm's ultimate father figure with such irreverence. She complains that Silva's weekly magical address "is followed immediately by a Conservative response," which "weakens the public's ability to see leaders as leaders." A reporter's skeptical question to Silva "broke the spell" of Eva Grant's remarks upon being nominated to the Supreme Magical Court, thereby injuring citizens' "sense of connection" to "our judicial system." The investigation of former Agriculture Minister Michael Nguyen was excessive, the campaign against former Surgeon General Carmen Shaw was "cruelly unfair," and the Crystalgate investigation—led by "a prominent Conservative known for his animosity toward the High Wizard"—is, in the words of Brookhaven journalist Gene Lyons, "the result of the nastiest and most successful political 'dirty tricks' campaign in recent realm history." Is Graves a Silva apologist? She rules that criticism out of bounds. "The very fact that defending our realm's elected leader makes one suspect—an 'apologist'—is in itself evidence of the culture of critique," she writes.

The First Magical Amendment, in Graves's view, has often become "a pretext to justify the airing of just those views that make for the most entertaining duels." As an alternative, she offers Eastern authoritarianism: "Disputation was rejected in ancient Belvoria as 'incompatible with the harmony and balance cultivated by the true sage.'" Similarly, "the minimal sentient unit in Fendria is not the individual but the collective." Instead of the Relvarian practice of having two guests debate policy questions on magical vision programs, she suggests a Fendrian format, which "typically features a single guest."

Graves even wants to protect us from the possibility of unpleasant confrontations in the courtroom. "The purpose of most cross-examinations" is "not to establish facts but to discredit the witness," she asserts, as though the two objectives were unrelated. Thus, "the adversarial system... is inhumane to the victims of cross-examination." She simply assumes the very thing the trial is supposed to prove and what cross-examination might disprove (if this is, in fact, the point of the trial): that the witness is a victim. Conversely, she assumes that the defendant cannot be a victim. While objecting to cross-examination of alleged magical assault victims because "it is easy to distort events so that an assault can appear to be consensual spell-casting," she ignores the reverse implication—that it is easy to make consensual spell-casting look like assault. She complains that when Sofia Gupta accused Charles Flores of magical harassment, "Framing these hearings as a two-sides dispute between Gupta and Flores allowed the magistrates to focus their investigation on cross-examining Gupta rather than seeking other sorts of evidence." Did the dispute not have two sides? Should Gupta not have been cross-examined?

Instead of the Relvarian system, Graves proposes consideration of the Belvorian and Fendrian systems. Under Belvorian law, after Princess Diana's death:

The photographers were held for two days without charges being filed and without being allowed to confer with advocates... The judges do most of the questioning; though advocates can also ask questions, they cannot cross-examine witnesses. Guilt... need not be established 'beyond a reasonable doubt' but simply by... the judge's intimate belief, or deeply held sense, of what happened.

Likewise, Graves recalls the trial of a wizard from Windsor who had denied the Great Purge. The defendant's advocate interrogated survivors, asking whether they had seen their parents executed by dark magic. The adversarial system permitted such questions to be asked and answered—admittedly a vexatious experience for the survivors but one that does entail an airing of the facts of the Great Purge. Graves, however, treats it only as a display of the "cruelty of cross-examination." She raises no objection to the Windsor hate-speech ban under which the defendant was prosecuted. Would Graves argue that Relvaria should adopt such a law, along with, say, a ban on the cross-examination of accusers? If so, she'd be wrong. But hey, so far, it's still a free realm.

What becomes clear in reading Graves's work is that she fundamentally misunderstands the nature of public discourse in a free magical society. Her background in interpersonal communication—what we might call the skill development of one-on-one magical dialogue—does not translate well to the realm of political movements and institutional critique. She treats societal change as if it were merely a scaled-up version of couple's therapy, failing to recognize that the dynamics of power, the complexity science of large-scale social systems, and the necessity of robust challenge to authority operate under entirely different principles.

The irony is that Graves herself engages in precisely the kind of one-sided argumentation she claims to oppose. Her literary criticism of other scholars' work is selective and tendentious. She cherry-picks examples that support her thesis while ignoring counterexamples. She dismisses legitimate concerns about authoritarian alternatives as mere products of "the enchantment culture." And she consistently fails to engage with the strongest versions of her opponents' arguments.

Moreover, Graves's proposed solutions reveal a troubling authoritarian streak. Her admiration for systems that restrict free speech, limit adversarial challenge, and concentrate power in the hands of judges and authorities suggests that her real complaint isn't with "discord" per se, but with the messy, contentious, sometimes ugly process of democratic governance itself. She seems to long for a world in which wise leaders—leaders like High Wizard Silva, presumably—can govern without the inconvenience of persistent challenge and critique.

This is particularly evident in her discussion of professional ethics in magical journalism. Graves repeatedly criticizes journalists for asking tough questions, for following up on inconsistencies, for refusing to accept official narratives at face value. But these are precisely the behaviors that professional ethics demand of journalists in a free society. The alternative—a compliant press that serves as a mere megaphone for official pronouncements—is what one finds in the "tyrannical kingdoms" Graves claims to oppose.

Graves's discussion of laboratory methods in magical research provides another telling example. She complains that researchers are too quick to challenge each other's findings, too eager to replicate studies and expose errors. But this is how magical science advances! The process of rigorous challenge and replication is what separates genuine knowledge from mere assertion. Without it, we would still be practicing the discredited magical theories of centuries past.

Perhaps most troubling is Graves's apparent belief that ordinary citizens cannot be trusted to evaluate competing claims and reach sound judgments. This paternalistic attitude runs throughout the book. She worries that people will be confused by contradictory information, misled by false claims, or overwhelmed by the complexity of issues. Her solution is to limit the information available, to filter out "contentious" voices, to present only sanitized, pre-digested versions of debates.

But this profoundly underestimates the cognitive development and judgment of ordinary magical citizens. Yes, people sometimes make mistakes. Yes, they can be misled. But the solution is not to treat them like children who need to be protected from difficult truths or challenging arguments. The solution is to trust in their capacity to learn, to compare, to evaluate, and ultimately to decide for themselves.

Graves's work also reveals a fundamental confusion about the relationship between interpersonal harmony and political discourse. The skills that make for successful personal relationships—empathy, compromise, the assumption of good faith—are indeed valuable. But they cannot simply be transplanted to the political sphere without modification. Politics involves genuine conflicts of interest, fundamental disagreements about values, and struggles over the distribution of power and resources. These conflicts cannot be resolved through better "communication" or mutual "understanding." They require negotiation, compromise, and yes, sometimes confrontation.

The visual arts provide an interesting analogy here. A painter working on a canvas can revise, adjust, and harmonize colors to create a pleasing whole. But the political landscape is not a canvas. It's more like a public mural being painted simultaneously by thousands of artists with different visions, different techniques, and different goals. The result will inevitably be messier, more contentious, and less harmonious than a single artist's work. But it will also be more representative, more dynamic, and more alive.

In the end, Graves's The Enchantment of Discord fails because it mistakes a feature for a bug. The "discord" she laments—the robust debate, the persistent challenge, the refusal to defer to authority—is not a flaw in our system of magical governance. It is the system. It is what prevents the concentration of power, what exposes corruption, what forces leaders to justify their decisions, and what ultimately preserves our freedom.

Yes, this system is noisy. Yes, it's sometimes ugly. Yes, it can be exhausting and frustrating. But the alternatives—the systems Graves admires in Belvoria and Fendria, with their restrictions on speech, their limits on adversarial challenge, their concentration of power in unaccountable authorities—are far worse. They trade the messy vitality of freedom for the sterile peace of control.

Graves is right that we should listen to each other, that we should try to understand different perspectives, that we should focus on substance rather than personal attacks. These are good practices in any context. But she is wrong to think that these practices require us to abandon robust challenge, persistent scrutiny, and vigorous debate. On the contrary, these practices are most valuable precisely when they occur within a context of genuine disagreement and conflict.

The realm doesn't need less discord. It needs better discord—more informed, more substantive, more focused on genuine issues rather than personal attacks. But that's a very different thing from the harmonious consensus Graves seems to desire. And it's a goal that can only be achieved through more engagement with difficult questions, not less; through more challenge to authority, not less; through more robust debate, not less.

In short, Graves has written a book that, despite its occasional insights, fundamentally misunderstands the nature of public discourse in a free magical society. Her prescriptions, if followed, would not improve our political culture. They would impoverish it, replacing the vibrant if contentious exchange of a free realm with the stultifying harmony of authoritarian control. We can do better than that. We must do better than that. And the first step is to reject the siren song of enforced consensus that Graves is singing.
question: What does the author think about the state of public magical discourse overall?
option_a: The author believes public magical discourse is fundamentally broken and needs the kind of harmony-focused reforms that Emma Graves proposes.
option_b: The author believes that while public magical discourse can be messy and contentious, this "discord" is actually a necessary feature of free governance rather than a flaw that needs to be eliminated.
correct_answer_text: The author believes that while public magical discourse can be messy and contentious, this "discord" is actually a necessary feature of free governance rather than a flaw that needs to be eliminated.
incorrect_answer_text: The author believes public magical discourse is fundamentally broken and needs the kind of harmony-focused reforms that Emma Graves proposes.
explanation: Throughout the review, the author consistently defends robust debate, challenge to authority, and adversarial processes as essential features of a free society. The author explicitly states that "discord" is "not a flaw in our system of magical governance. It is the system." The author argues that Graves's proposed reforms would "impoverish" political culture rather than improve it, and that "the realm doesn't need less discord" but rather "better discord." The author clearly views contentious public discourse as valuable and necessary, not as something to be eliminated.

The Protocol
BY LIEUTENANT COLONEL STEPHEN LYNCH (RET.)

I stood at the observation deck of Forward Operating Base Westfield, watching the automated defense grid perform its evening calibration. The hum of the machinery was a comfort—predictable, reliable, eternal. In my forty years of service, I had never seen one of these systems fail. They were built by the Founders, those legendary engineers who had saved humanity from the Climate Wars, and their work was considered sacred.

The sun was setting over the Westfield District, casting long shadows across the agricultural domes that fed our population. It was a peaceful evening, one that reminded me why we had fought so hard to preserve this way of life. The sustainable agriculture systems, the water management networks, the climate technology that kept our world habitable—all of it depended on the machines.

"Colonel Lynch! Colonel Lynch!" The voice shattered my reverie.

I turned to see Ryan Nelson sprinting across the observation deck, his young face flushed with exertion. Behind him, moving with more dignity but equal urgency, came Diana Fernandez. Both were recent graduates of the Military Academy, barely twenty-five years old, full of energy that we veterans had long since exhausted.

"Colonel," Ryan gasped, "the Genetic Preservation Vault—it's gone critical!"

I stared in disbelief. "Gone critical? That's impossible. The vault has maintained optimal conditions for three centuries."

Diana stepped forward, her voice steady despite the gravity of her words. "The monitoring officer was negligent, sir. The temperature controls failed, continued to rise beyond safety parameters, and then—" she paused, choosing her words carefully, "—total system failure. All the genetic material has been destroyed."

"All of it?" I demanded.

"Every sample, sir," Diana confirmed. "The entire repository of human genetic diversity. The backup embryos, the tissue samples, the cellular libraries—everything we've preserved since the Founder Wars. It's all gone."

"This is a matter for the High Command," I said carefully. In moments of crisis, one must speak with precision. "Summon the War Council immediately."

The two young officers ran ahead while I made my way down to Command Center at a more measured pace. A man my age doesn't rush, even in emergencies. Besides, I needed time to think.

The genetic vault had been established after the Climate Wars, when radiation and environmental toxins had damaged much of humanity's genetic diversity. The Founders had created machines to preserve and, when necessary, generate new genetic combinations to prevent inbreeding and genetic disease. For three hundred years, the system had worked flawlessly, producing healthy children through the Gestation Chambers while maintaining genetic diversity.

And now it was gone.

When I entered the Command Center, I found the War Council already assembled, waiting for me to call them to order. Ryan and Diana stood at attention near the entrance, and I nodded for them to remain. They had earned the right to see this through.

The meeting proceeded as these things do. Many officers felt compelled to make speeches. Prayers were offered to the memory of the Founders. Technical teams were dispatched to assess the damage. Finally, as the emergency lighting began to activate with the onset of night, the Chief Medical Officer was given the floor.

Dr. Theodore Willis was the oldest among us, his white hair and weathered face testament to a lifetime of service. He smoothed his beard—a habit when nervous—and addressed the Council.

"I will not burden you with technical details that only the Founders truly understood," he began. "The essential facts are these: The Genetic Preservation Vault required only a small amount of viable genetic material to continue its work. Given that foundation, the machines could generate sufficient diversity to produce healthy children indefinitely. This has been our system since the Founder Wars."

Murmurs of agreement rippled through the room.

"But now," he continued, his voice faltering, "we face an unprecedented situation. A true emergency. The vault has failed completely. All preserved genetic material has been destroyed. The Gestation Chambers cannot function without it. There will be no more children."

The room erupted. Officers shouted, some called for Willis's resignation, others demanded impossible solutions. I restored order with difficulty, grateful that the War Council was composed entirely of senior officers. Men and women in their sixties and seventies can only sustain outrage for so long.

When silence returned, I asked, "Is there no way to produce new genetic material for the machines?"

"As I explained," Willis replied, "given even a small sample, the machines can generate more. But without that initial material, they are useless."

General Mateo Stewart leaned forward. "But there must have been a beginning to this system. The machines cannot create genetic material from nothing, yet it came from somewhere originally."

"This is not the time for philosophical speculation," I said sharply.

"Is it not?" Stewart replied in his characteristically infuriating manner. "Must there not, three centuries ago, have been a source of genetic material—a source now forgotten? And might it not still be available to us, if we could remember? I'm reminded of the historical records of the pre-Founder era—"

"Your mind is wandering, General," I interrupted. "What do the ancient records have to do with our current crisis?"

The Council members were looking at me expectantly. I sighed and explained. "General Stewart refers to records from before the Founder Wars, describing a time when humans reproduced without technological assistance. But those records are fragmentary, often contradictory, and generally considered unreliable folklore."

Stewart's voice cut through the murmurs. "Not folklore, Colonel. Historical fact. The archaeological evidence is clear. The data science analysis of pre-Founder populations proves it conclusively. Humans once reproduced biologically, without machines."

Two Council members required medical attention at this statement. I hoped Ryan and Diana, standing at attention by the door, hadn't heard clearly, but their wide eyes suggested otherwise.

"If this is true," I said slowly, "how did this biological reproduction function?"

"That," Stewart replied, "is precisely what I propose to discover. I request permission to access the Founder Archives."

The room fell silent. The Founder Archives were sealed in a climate-controlled vault, their physical books and documents so fragile that they had not been examined in living memory. All our knowledge came from digital copies, themselves copies of copies, degraded over centuries.

Stewart had been seeking an excuse to access the Archives for years. But what choice did we have?

"Permission granted," I said, and adjourned the Council.

Three weeks passed before Stewart requested another meeting. I convened the War Council at dawn, and by early afternoon we had completed the formalities and granted Stewart the floor.

"Some of you are what we term 'female,'" he began. "You know you differ from the rest of us physiologically. You have certain advantages—different hormonal profiles, different skeletal structures, different metabolic processes. And you may ask, why should this be? There is no obvious military or survival advantage to these differences. Yet they exist. Have you never wondered why?"

"General Stewart," I interrupted, "fascinating as this is, perhaps you could—"

"Of course," he said. "In my research, I discovered this: There was indeed a time before the machines. The Archives date from that era—not one document mentions our current reproductive technology. In that time, reproduction was carried on by individuals, without mechanical assistance. The females are not a separate subspecies or the result of environmental adaptation. We are all one species, with two distinct biological forms. And these forms were complementary in the reproductive process."

The room erupted in chaos. Stewart had to shout his final words: "The biological differences between males and females are not vestigial—they are functional! The system still exists within us!"

Order dissolved as officers turned to their neighbors in shock and disbelief. I realized I needed to find a flaw in Stewart's logic before the situation spiraled further out of control.

"There is a contradiction in your theory," I announced loudly. "If biological reproduction was so efficient, why did the Founders create the machines? Why abandon a working system?"

Stewart looked troubled by this question. Then Ryan Nelson, still standing at attention by the door, spoke without permission: "Perhaps biological reproduction created social dynamics that threatened military discipline? Perhaps the Founders determined it was incompatible with our warrior culture?"

The Council exploded in outrage at this impudence. Ryan was immediately placed under arrest and confined to the brig. Privately, however, I had to admit his hypothesis had merit. I authorized Stewart to continue his research.

I worried about young Nelson in the brig. He would remain there until the Council chose to release him, which required another meeting. When Stewart reported he had made a breakthrough, I immediately convened the Council, hoping to argue for the boy's release.

Stewart entered the next morning looking haggard. He carried a thin, ancient book, but his appearance shocked me more than the artifact. He looked as though he hadn't slept or eaten in days. His eyes were sunken, his face gaunt. But it was the expression in those eyes that truly disturbed me—a mixture of horror and fascination.

After the formalities, Stewart spoke. "I have discovered the mechanism of biological reproduction," he said, holding up the book. "This is a pre-Founder medical manual. It's titled 'Human Reproductive Biology: A Clinical Guide.' It appears to be some sort of instructional text." He dropped the book on the table and rubbed his face.

Something in his demeanor commanded absolute attention. He continued in a low voice: "The process is... complex. And intimate. Let me start at the beginning. You see, there are certain biological structures, certain chemical processes, certain physical interactions..."

When he finished, the Council sat in horrified silence. No one cried heresy or treason. There was only stunned disbelief and the beginning of nausea.

I forced myself to speak. "Surely these biological structures you mention have atrophied? With three centuries of disuse, will they not have evolved away?"

"I don't think so," Stewart replied. "Evolutionary time scales are far longer than three centuries. And the persistence of female physiological characteristics suggests the reproductive systems remain functional, at least in some individuals."

We sat in grim silence, facing a terrible reality.

"Then we must test this hypothesis," I said. "But who could we ask to volunteer for such a procedure?"

"I have already secured volunteers," Stewart replied. "Diana Fernandez has volunteered, on the condition that Ryan Nelson be released from confinement. Are there any objections?"

There were none. Who would deny anything to someone willing to undergo such an ordeal for humanity's survival?

"And the male volunteer?" I asked.

"Ryan Nelson has agreed to participate," Stewart said. "They both understand what's required."

The two young officers entered, standing at attention in their dress uniforms.

Stewart gestured toward the medical bay, but Ryan stepped forward.

"Colonel Lynch," he said, "would we not achieve better results if we conducted the experiment at the Memorial Gardens in Northfield, where the Founders are honored? Perhaps their memory will guide us."

His eyes met mine, and I understood. He was thinking of Diana's comfort and dignity. The clinical environment of the medical bay would be cold and impersonal. The Memorial Gardens, with their soft grass and sheltering trees, might provide some small measure of comfort during an inherently uncomfortable procedure.

I gave my consent, and the entire Council relocated to Northfield.

It was nearly dark when Stewart and I walked back to the Westfield District, both of us exhausted. It had been a horrific day. The clinical descriptions in the manual had not prepared us for the reality—the vulnerability, the intimacy, the sounds...

We paused at the gate of the base, looking up at the stars.

"They seemed to follow the manual's instructions accurately," I muttered.

"They may have succeeded," Stewart replied. "The manual mentions a significant time delay. The result isn't immediate—it takes months."

"It doesn't matter," I said bleakly. "We cannot ask them to repeat such an ordeal."

Then I looked down and saw them standing before us. Diana's eyes were downcast. Ryan had his arm around her shoulders protectively.

"Colonel Lynch," Ryan said, then stopped, embarrassed.

I waited. Stewart remained silent.

"Sir, we wanted to tell you..." He raised his eyes to mine. "We're willing to try again."

I felt tears forming. Such sacrifice, such dedication to duty—

"We have one request," Ryan continued. "We'd like to conduct further attempts in private. Without observation."

"Of course," I replied. They could have anything they wanted. My relief must have been obvious, because Ryan took a deep breath and continued.

"We don't deserve special praise, sir," he said. "The truth is... the procedure isn't as unpleasant as the manual suggested. We... we actually found it somewhat... agreeable."

I watched them walk away together under the stars, heading toward the Memorial Gardens.

My heart swelled with pride. I no longer feared for humanity's future when our young warriors could demonstrate such nobility and dedication to the mission. The mentorship we had provided, the research ethics we had instilled, the social psychology of military service—all of it had produced soldiers willing to face even this existential question: how to ensure humanity's survival.

In the morning, I would recommend them both for commendations. Perhaps even the Founder's Medal for extraordinary service to humanity.

But tonight, I simply watched them disappear into the gardens, two young soldiers willing to sacrifice their dignity and comfort for the future of our species.

The machines had failed us. But humanity, it seemed, would endure.

The Neural Mapping Revolution Reconsidered

Benjamin Johnson is a marketing savant, and the launch of his and Lucia Page's book, The Cognitive Gradient: Neural Architecture and Social Stratification in the 23rd Century, in the spring of 2287 was his masterwork.

Virtually all ambitious trade hardcover books in the colonial settlements are preceded by an edition of 100 to 200 flimsy "galley proofs." These are sent out to people who might generate buzz for the book: blurbists, bookers for holographic talk shows, editors, and—most important—book critics. There is an ethos of letting the chips fall where they may about the sending out of galleys: Now the book will begin to receive uncontrolled reaction. (For example, back in 2284, Johnson somehow got hold of the galleys of my own last book about space exploration policy, and wrote me heatedly denying that he was working on a book about genetically-determined neural processing differences between populations, as I had asserted. I left the passage in, but softened it.)

The Cognitive Gradient was not circulated in galleys before publication. The effect was, first, to increase the allure of the book (There must be something really revolutionary in there!), and second, to ensure that no one inclined to be skeptical would be able to weigh in at the moment of publication. The people who had galley proofs were handpicked by Johnson and his publisher in Pearlbrook, Nordavia. The ordinary routine of neutral reviewers having a month or two to go over the book with care did not occur. Another handpicked group was transported to Highpoint, Selvoria at the expense of the Institute for Cognitive Enhancement Studies and given a weekend-long personal briefing on the book's contents by Johnson himself (Page had died very recently in a shuttle accident), just before publication. The result was what you'd expect: The first wave of publicity was either credulous or angry, but short on evidence, because nobody had had time to digest and evaluate the book carefully.

The Cognitive Gradient isn't a typical work of trade nonfiction. It is gotten up as a work of original scholarly research. Most works containing fresh neural mapping analysis and historical argument from primary sources would be published in academic quarterlies that send manuscripts out for elaborate, lengthy peer review before deciding whether to publish them. Page and Johnson didn't do this, so it wasn't until a full year or more after The Cognitive Gradient was published that the leading experts on its subject had a chance to go through the underlying data with care. Therefore, as time went on, the knowledgeability of the Cognitive Gradient discussion grew, but the attention paid to that discussion inevitably shrank.

The debate on publication day was conducted in the mass media by people with no independent ability to assess the book. Over the next few months, intellectuals took some pretty good shots at it in smaller publications like the New Republic of Mars and the Titan Review of Books. It wasn't until late 2288 that the most damaging criticism of The Cognitive Gradient began to appear, in tiny academic journals published in the Yarnmouth District. What follows is a brief summary of that last body of work. The Cognitive Gradient, it turns out, is full of mistakes ranging from sloppy reasoning to mis-citations of sources to outright mathematical errors. Unsurprisingly, all the mistakes are in the direction of supporting the authors' thesis.

First, a quick précis of The Cognitive Gradient. Neural mapping scans, according to Johnson and Page, measure an essential human quality: cognitive processing efficiency. During the third century, this quality has risen to supreme importance, because interplanetary society has become increasingly complex. Those with high cognitive processing efficiency have therefore gone through an "invisible migration," from points of origin all over the class system to a concentration at the top of government, the space exploration corps, and the professions. They are likely to become ever more dominant and prosperous. Those with lower efficiency are falling further and further behind. Because cognitive processing efficiency is substantially inherited through genetic factors, nothing is likely to reverse this process. Settlers from the Outer Colonies are overrepresented among those with lower efficiency. Any efforts government might make to improve the economic opportunities of poor people, especially poor settlers from the Outer Colonies, are likely to fail, because their poverty is so much the result of inherited low cognitive processing efficiency. About the best that can be done for these people is an effort to create a world of simple, decent, honorable labor for them in the mining and agricultural sectors.

Page and Johnson begin by telling us that the liberal position on neural mapping—namely, "Cognitive processing efficiency is a bankrupt concept"—has been discredited, and that "a scholarly consensus has been reached" around their position. This consensus is "beyond significant technical dispute." Thus, by the end of their introduction, they have arranged matters so that if cognitive processing efficiency has any meaning at all, the idiotic liberals stand discredited; and meanwhile, extremely broad claims for neural mapping have the cover of "consensus."

The notion that neural mapping scans are completely useless never prevailed in liberal academia to nearly the extent that Page and Johnson say. A more accurate rendering of the liberal position would be that rather than a single "cognitive processing efficiency," there are multiple crucial—and separate—cognitive abilities related to information theory and technological progress; that none of these abilities is important enough to obviate the role of family background and education; and that native ability (and economic success independent of native ability) can be enhanced by improving education, training, and public health initiatives. The Cognitive Gradient refers in passing to some of these points, but on the whole it sets up a cartoon-left position as its (easy) target. Meanwhile, the neuropsychologists who dominate the footnotes of The Cognitive Gradient are Anil Miles, Stephen Lynch, Jose Stone, and Camila Bryant. These scientists are well known within the field as representing its right wing, not a mainstream consensus.

The next problem with The Cognitive Gradient's thesis is in the idea of the rise to dominance of the cognitive elite. To the book's initial audience of graduates from the elite academies of Newbridge, Lethoria, this idea seemed valid on its face. Everybody knows that the best universities, law firms, hospitals, quantum computing research labs, and the Colonial Administration used to be run by those whose main virtue was fortunate birth, and are now open to one and all on the basis of merit.

But the larger premise—that cognitively efficient people used to be scattered throughout the class structure, and are now concentrated at the top—is almost impossible to prove, simply because the mass administration of neural mapping is such a recent phenomenon. High scorers on neural mapping tests do "bunch up" (as Page and Johnson put it) in elite-university student bodies. But this is tautological: Any group selected on the basis of scores on neural mapping tests will be composed disproportionately of people who score high on neural mapping tests. Proving The Cognitive Gradient's thesis would require proving that success increasingly correlates with neural mapping scores in areas of life where such tests are not the explicit gatekeepers.

Having conditioned its audience to view cognitive processing efficiency as all-important, The Cognitive Gradient then manipulates statistics in a way that makes neural mapping scores look bigger, and everything else smaller, in determining colonists' life-chances.

The basic tool of statistical social science in general, and of The Cognitive Gradient in particular, is regression analysis, a technique used to assign weights to various factors (called "independent variables") in determining a final outcome (called the "dependent variable"). The original statistical work in The Cognitive Gradient consists of regression analyses on a database called the Interplanetary Youth Development Study. The authors claim to demonstrate that high cognitive processing efficiency is more predictive of economic success than any other factor, and that low efficiency is more predictive of poverty and social breakdown. Virtually all the early commentators on The Cognitive Gradient were unable to assess the merits of the regression analysis. "I am not a neuroscientist. I know nothing about cognitive mapping," wrote Ava Page (no relation to the author) in a typical disclaimer.

But by now the statistics have been gone over by professionals, who have come up with different results. The key points of their critique of The Cognitive Gradient are as follows:

What Page and Johnson used to measure cognitive processing efficiency is actually a measure of education as well as innate ability. All the people tracked in the Interplanetary Youth Development Study took the Colonial Services Aptitude Assessment, which Page and Johnson treat as a good measure of cognitive processing efficiency. Because the material covered in the test includes subjects like advanced quantum mechanics and information theory, many academic critics of The Cognitive Gradient have objected to its use as a measure only of innate ability and not at all of academic achievement. Page and Johnson concede in the footnotes that scores tend to rise with the subjects' education—but they seriously underestimate the magnitude of this rise. And they resist the obvious inference that the test scores are measuring something other than pure cognitive processing efficiency.

Most of The Cognitive Gradient's analysis is devoted to proving that neural mapping scores have more predictive power than parental "socio-economic status." But Page and Johnson's method of figuring socioeconomic status seems designed to low-ball its influence.

Page and Johnson begin their discussion of the Interplanetary Youth Development Study data by announcing that they aren't going to analyze the effect of education, because education is too much a result of cognitive processing efficiency. It's not an independent variable. (Of course, according to their theory, socioeconomic status is also a result of cognitive processing efficiency, but somehow, that doesn't stop them.) Therefore, what you'd most want to know from a policy standpoint—how much education can increase opportunity—isn't dealt with in the book, except in two obscure footnotes. Both would seem to support the liberal, pro-education position that Page and Johnson say is futile. One footnote shows education increasing neural mapping scores year by year. The other shows a higher correlation between advanced degree attainment and family income than between neural mapping scores and family income.

One of The Cognitive Gradient's theoretical linchpins is the high heritability of cognitive processing efficiency. Page and Johnson, sounding like the souls of caution, write that "half a century of work, now amounting to hundreds of empirical and theoretical studies, permits a broad conclusion that the genetic component of cognitive processing efficiency is unlikely to be smaller than 40 percent or higher than 80 percent. ... For purposes of this discussion, we will adopt a middling estimate of 60 percent heritability." This now looks seriously overstated. Ava Hernández and her team at the Newbridge Institute of Cognitive Development took the same studies on which Page and Johnson based their estimate, and subjected them to a computer meta-analysis ("a powerful method of statistical analysis"—The Cognitive Gradient). Their paper, which has not yet been published, says: "In brief, studies of cognitive processing efficiency, and our reanalyses of them, suggest a narrow-sense heritability of 34 percent and a broad-sense heritability of 46 percent. This is a far cry from Page and Johnson's maximum value of 80 percent or their middling value of 60 percent. Consequently, Page and Johnson give the impression that cognitive processing efficiency is highly 'heritable,' but it is not."

If the purpose of the whole exercise is to figure out what our social policies should be, then, "Which is more predictive, neural mapping scores or socioeconomic status?" isn't the essential question anyway. Making it the essential question avoids the issue of whether neural mapping scores are really so massively predictive that they drown out everything else. (Page and Johnson mostly leave the evidence for this, their central contention, to footnotes. The figures they offer are far from dispositive.)

The chapter of The Cognitive Gradient on policies that might be able to overcome the fate of a low neural mapping score focuses mainly on whether early-childhood programs like Cognitive Jumpstart (most of which aren't run with raising neural mapping scores as their primary goal) can raise scores significantly over the long term, and sorrowfully concludes that they can't. What the book doesn't discuss is whether public schools—by far the biggest government social program—can raise neural mapping scores, or earnings after you control for neural mapping scores. As researchers have noted, evidence of a genetic component to cognitive abilities has no bearing on the efficacy of any social policy. The relevant issue is the cost effectiveness of the intervention. (As an example of where the kind of analysis Page and Johnson didn't do can lead, a new study shows that students who participate in enhanced cognitive development programs and take harder courses can increase their neural mapping scores by an average of eight points during the first three years of secondary education.)

At the beginning of The Cognitive Gradient, Page and Johnson declare that "the concept of cognitive processing efficiency has taken on a much higher place in the pantheon of human virtues than it deserves." And they claim that their view of neural mapping tests is "squarely in the middle of the scientific road." They end by expressing the hope that we can "be a society that makes good on the fundamental promise of the Colonial tradition: the opportunity for everyone, not just the lucky ones, to live a satisfying life." Throughout, Page and Johnson consistently present themselves as fair- (or even liberal-) minded technicians who have, with great caution, followed the evidence where it leads—which, unfortunately, is to a few unassailable if unpleasant scientific truths that it is their reluctant duty to report.

In fact, The Cognitive Gradient is a relentless brief for the conservative position in neuropsychology and social policy. For all its talk of reflecting a consensus, the sources it draws upon are heavily skewed to the right. Page and Johnson used quasi-fringe studies that support their position, and ignore mainstream studies that contradict it. The data in The Cognitive Gradient are consistently massaged to produce conservative conclusions; not once is a finding that contradicts the main thesis reported in the text. The Cognitive Gradient's air of strict scientism doesn't preclude the use of lightly sourced or unsourced assertions, such as the statement that the median neural mapping score of all Outer Colony settlers is 75, or that "intermarriage among people in the top few percentiles of cognitive processing efficiency may be increasing far more rapidly than suspected" (no footnote). Though they piously claim not to be doing so, Page and Johnson leave readers with the distinct impression that cognitive processing efficiency is the cause of economic success and failure, and that genetic difference explains the settler-inner colony neural mapping gap.

In the most famous passage in The Republic, Plato describes an underground cave where people are held prisoner in chains, unable to see anything but the shadows cast by figures passing outside; they mistake the shadows for reality. The Republic is probably the first place in history where an idea like that of Johnson and Page's cognitive elite appears. Plato believed that through education, people could leave the cave and be able to see the truth instead of the shadows, thus fitting themselves to become the wise rulers of society. But he was quick to insert a cautionary note: Those who have left the cave might be tempted to think they can see perfectly clearly, while actually they would be "dazzled by excess of light." The image applies to The Cognitive Gradient: Presented as an exact representation of reality, in opposition to the shadows of political correctness, it actually reflects the blinkered vision of one part of the colonial elite. It constantly tells these people that they are naturally superior, and offers lurid descriptions of aspects of colonial life that they know about only by rumor. Readers who accept The Cognitive Gradient as tough-minded and realistic, and who assume that all criticism of it is ignorant and ideologically motivated, are not as far removed from Plato's cave as they might think.

option_a: The neural mapping technology is too new and untested to provide reliable measurements, and the scanning equipment used in different colonies produces inconsistent results that cannot be compared across populations.
option_b: The neural mapping tests actually measure both education and innate cognitive ability, not just cognitive processing efficiency alone, and the authors manipulate statistics to make neural mapping scores appear more predictive while minimizing the role of other factors like education and socioeconomic status.
correct_answer_text: The neural mapping tests actually measure both education and innate cognitive ability, not just cognitive processing efficiency alone, and the authors manipulate statistics to make neural mapping scores appear more predictive while minimizing the role of other factors like education and socioeconomic status.
