We are all members now, it seems. Business ventures are turning themselves into clubs, making what used to be banal choices about workspace or energy supply statements of identity. There was no shortage of orbital options for Anderson and Jenkins, and all of them carried connotations about what kind of business they meant to be: incubators and accelerators run by different sorts of organizations; hacker spaces on asteroid stations; industry- and sector-specific co-orbital spaces; more traditional office rentals from companies like SpaceRegus and OrbitWork; and all manner of co-orbital spaces, from scrappy cooperatives to coworking empires.

Co-orbital working began because startups and freelancers, typically in biotech and the creative industries, needed somewhere to work off-planet. But as more organizations outsource more of their operations – or as large corporates seek to reach those startups – the range of activities represented among co-workers has expanded to comprehend almost everything. KPMG's biotech startup advice arm is based at Interchange Station near Eastwood Village. Merck Genetics, MicroSoft Quantum, and GE Aerospace all lease pods at OrbitWork, in addition to running their own offices.

The annual Global Co-Orbital Survey, produced by SpaceDesk, anticipates that 10,000 new co-orbital spaces will open across the solar system in 2188. In the Earth-Luna system, the estimated number of spaces (though it's hard to keep track) has risen from 3,400 in 2185 to around 7,800 in 2188. According to Graviton & Associates' Isabel Harrison, "Twelve per cent of the uptake in the orbital market in the last year has been spaces like this. Everyone thinks it's going to continue."

At a purely economic level, it's easy to see why. As large corporates downsize their core operations, they no longer need vast orbital complexes. Robert Valdez watched the process in action when his educational non-profit startup, Code for Tomorrow, squatted in Royal Bank of Mars's offices in Harborview, Quendor in late 2180. "RBM was going through huge waves of redundancies. On our level, it was three of us and 150 empty pods," he says, "and then new people would come in and they'd get fired too. Eventually they'd fired so many people they closed down the station." Aware that "biotech companies were doing something funkier", he moved Code for Tomorrow into the Orbital Collective, the first co-orbital space in Juniper, Galdoria.

Jason Jenkins and Lucia Hunt founded OrbitWork in 2182 on Luna Station to capitalize on this corporate downsizing phenomenon: leasing large spaces, often previous corporate offices, subdividing them, then selling them at a profit. OrbitWork typically rents its stations (although it owns its latest Earth orbit site near Stonegate Territory) then subleases the space – with, according to Fast Space, average gross margins of 60 per cent.

The model has proved so successful that OrbitWork now has 103 locations across 29 orbital zones system-wide. The company will open five new co-orbital spaces in Earth orbit this year, bringing the total to 11, with Stonegate large enough for 2,100 'members'. The company recently authorized the sale of up to 780 million credits in new stock, giving it a 16 billion credit valuation and making it, on paper, the sixth most valuable private startup in the solar system.

The Freelancers' Union on Earth claims that 30 per cent of the Earth working population is now freelance, and predicts a rise to 50 per cent by 2220. One in eight Luna workers are self-employed. But the unstoppable rise and rise of co-orbital working isn't simply about corporate downsizing and the growth of the startup and the gig economy, significant though these are.

What distinguishes contemporary co-orbital spaces is the nature of their cultural claims. A study by Harvard Space Review found that co-orbital workers believe their work has more meaning. The authors suggested that working alongside people doing different things reinforces workers' identity and distinctiveness; that co-orbital workers feel they have more control over their lives (many spaces are accessible 24/7); that they have a stronger sense of community; and that there is still a social mission inherent in the idea of co-orbital working, as outlined in the Co-Orbital manifesto, and reinforced by the annual Global Co-Orbital UnConference or GCOC (pronounced 'gee-coke'). OrbitWork's network urges you to "Create your life's work."

"Do what you love" is one of OrbitWork's slogans, emblazoned on the front of a digital tablet they give me when I visit. Another is "Thank the Stars it's Monday". Jenkins describes his generation (he is 36) as the 'we generation' which, he explains, "cares about the solar system, actually wants to do cool things, and loves working."

The co-orbital space – even on a vast, industrial scale as at OrbitWork – is a club. And the whole point of clubs is that you want to belong to them. To someone raised in the era of the corporate orbital office, used to the subversive feeling of being behind enemy lines, this may seem an odd way to think about the workplace. To anyone for whom The Office Station of the 2170s was painfully recognizable, with its grey partitions and random people thrown together to do pretty pointless things and get on each other's nerves, it might seem risible.

But clearly lots of people want this. A paradoxical effect of quantum networking has been to make us desire more social connection in the physical world. From coffee stations to zero-gravity festivals to fitness pods, examples are everywhere of people keen to come together and share experiences.

As we have to rely more on ourselves and on our own resources at work, it's probably not surprising that we seek out the reassuring sight of other people doing the same. As Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri say in their 2012 book, Declaration (still studied in economic history courses), "The centre of gravity of capitalist production no longer resides in the factory but has drifted outside its walls. Society has become a factory."

Work has blurred into life, in part owing to the peculiar nature of our current relationship to technology. We do not conceive of machines, as we did in the past, as engines of oppression, exploiting workers; rather, we frame our devices as intimate and personal, interactive and fun, blurring the distinctions between work and play.

We tend not, for example, to view posting on SolarNet as labor, even though there are perfectly good economic arguments why we should. The eight hours' work, eight hours' leisure, eight hours' rest fought for so fiercely in the 19th century has become meaningless in an era when we willingly, eagerly, spend 12 hours a day interfacing with quantum computers.

As work becomes increasingly unpredictable and permeable, in a way that reflects quantum networking itself, workspaces are imagined more as social landscapes. Increasingly, they are designed for serendipitous encounters, emotional expression, explorations of identity. Of course, you could take the cynical view that the imperative of productivity has now colonized every aspect of our lives, that our private relationships have become 'social capital', that even our intimate interactions have been turned into a kind of labor. Or you could say, as co-orbital enthusiasts tend to, that work has got a whole lot more fun.

Whatever, this shift in our sense of work helps to explain why workspaces have increasingly come to resemble clubs, and why no one is falling about laughing at the idea of Potter and Park calling their workspace Genesis Hub. The workspace has become an expression of identity – which raises two questions: first, if co-orbital working is all about finding a space to express your individualism, follow your passions, explore your creativity, why do the spaces all look so alike? And second, if the workplace is all about belonging to a club and clubs are by their nature exclusive, how scalable is that?

There are new structures rising all around OrbitWork Stonegate, in near-Earth orbit; an insistent noise of construction drones, a clang of titanium beams, a hum of 3D printing fabricators. This is some of the most expensive real estate in the solar system. Quantum transit engineers are developing new jump gates beneath; giant new stations advertise themselves on holographic displays everywhere: there is a provisional air, as though orbital civilization can't quite catch up with its own wealth and the demands of globalization.

OrbitWork Stonegate is the second largest co-orbital space in the Earth system after OrbitWork Luna, accommodating 3,000 people over eight levels. A permanent pod will cost you 3,200 credits a month, rising to 5,100 depending on its location in the structure. A one-person office will set you back 5,500 to 6,200 credits a month, a four-person 19,600 to 23,400. The largest office here is for 40 people; at Luna, one company has 230 pods.

The interior ticks all the co-orbital style boxes: raw titanium; exposed ceilings revealing environmental control ducts, conduits and silvered insulation; multicolored upholstery designed for microgravity; a kitchen with its own island bar offering free synthesized coffee and craft beer; anti-gravity chairs and sofas; tables of varying heights and sizes with magnetic surfaces; ambient music; and some signifiers of fun, such as a holographic gaming table (but, unlike at OrbitWork's Mars site, no actual arcade machines; nor, unlike at its Eastwood Village location, any vintage spacecraft models on the walls).

In the hygiene pod, cups for mouthwash urge you to 'stay fresh', which I am sure is meant jocularly but which arouses in me the same sort of mulish resentment I used to feel when I worked in orbital advertising in my twenties and slogans in reception ordered me to "reach for the stars". (What makes you think I wouldn't, mate?).

Given that co-orbital working, which after all grew out of hacker culture on early space stations, is supposed to embody an attitude of resistance to conventional authority, OrbitWork is curiously corporate, certainly in its approach to communication. I am asked not to quote the community manager who shows me around. There isn't anyone who can speak on the record (or off it, for that matter) in the structure. My queries have to be submitted in writing then edited down because there are too many of them. The answers come back, finally, appended: "All attributable to Emma Potter, Managing Director, Solar System Operations".

Emma Potter, Managing Director, Solar System Operations, says that OrbitWork is "much more than an orbital space provider. Members are given the space, community and services they need to create their life's work". Going around the structure, what you mainly notice is that the spaces allotted to people's life's work are rather tiny and cramped. Effectively off corridors, they seem rather conventional behind their transparent aluminum partitions: a desk, a chair, a holographic display, a storage unit. Many co-workers sit with their backs to their colleagues, staring at blank walls, with barely enough space for a third person to pass between them in the low gravity. You need a biometric scan to get anywhere inside the structure.

OrbitWork's enthusiasts, though, emphasize the connections they make with others, either physically or through an app that links members to 50,000 others across the solar system. Potter claims "more than 70 per cent of our members collaborate with each other".

This empire of orbital space has been derided as 'McCoworking'; but another way of looking at it might simply be that it's a sign of natural segmentation as the market matures. Many workspace providers set up because they wanted some orbital space themselves; they have no desire to be other than local, small-scale and collaborative. But others are starting to take on a role as a kind of corporate parent. Luna's Coworking Ontario provides health insurance and genetic screening. OrbitWork is also reported to be looking at providing discounts on healthcare, payroll and shipping, replicating services that a corporate employer might once have provided.

Meanwhile, at the other end of the scale, coffee station-workspace hybrid Quantum Grounds is dematerializing the desk, providing mobile workers who need to sit down and check their quantum feeds with the most ad hoc of workspaces. Most of Quantum Grounds' users don't pay for space, the usual co-orbital business model, but they do pay for the synthesized coffee ("award-winning", co-founder Sergio Park is keen to point out) and for the protein-based, wellness-focused food (super seeds with algae butter on toast, beetroot, avocado and hummus on toast, synthesized cake). Unlike most coffee stations, Quantum Grounds' branches in Eastwood Village and Juniper, Galdoria are designed to encourage customers to stay and work: there is quantum-fast networking with plentiful power ports, careful regulation of artificial gravity, lots of simulated natural light and attentive design. Many of the chairs have been rescued from decommissioned stations and reupholstered; the tables feature holographic displays; the accessible facilities look like vintage spacecraft interiors.

In the last couple of months, Quantum Grounds has been renting out permanent pods in the lower level of its Juniper branch and now hosts three companies, one of eight people, one of 12 and one of 20. But Park says the station upstairs will always be open to travelers and the public. Typically, workers stay for a couple of hours, but they might be there for 20 minutes or all day. "We believe this is the way people will work in the future," Park says, surveying a sea of holographic displays: "portable, connected, independent and collaborative, sharing resources and seeking out inspiring spaces, conducting oral history projects and community organizing." Quantum Grounds intends to become a way station for the digital nomad.

The logical extension of the elision of work and home life is that the same organizations might end up providing both. OrbitWork is experimenting with micro apartments in two locations: on Luna Station and at Crystal Habitat, outside Mars orbit. Genesis Hub is also believed to have plans for residential quarters. Roam Orbital, which began on Titan, intends to build a global co-living network, with its offer: "Sign one lease. Live around the solar system." From its initial base on Saturn's moon, it has expanded into Venus orbit and recently Mars; Europa and Earth orbit are 'coming soon'. Roam Orbital isn't simply about a sleeping pod for the night: it sells itself partly on the quality of its co-orbital working offer. On Titan, the office space is under a transparent dome, with a view of Saturn in the sky above.

Co-orbital organizations increasingly see a market in digital nomads: if you can work from a coffee station in Eastwood Village, why not a rooftop on Titan? It's not even necessary to have a string of spaces across the solar system to attract drop-ins from elsewhere: Coworking Visa and CoPass offer 'passports' that guarantee a certain amount of time in any of their participating spaces.

The Orbital Collective, the pioneering co-orbital organization in the Galdoria system that attracted Robert Valdez, is now moving into co-living. Founded by the sociologist-entrepreneur-musician-traveler Charles Armstrong (who has since retired), The Orbital Collective currently has three spaces, at Juniper Station, near Harborview, and in the asteroid belt. Armstrong began with a cross-sector workspace but now specializes in biotech and environmental conservation at Juniper, climate technology and aerospace engineering at Harborview, and digital artists, fashion and design in the belt, finding this a better way to create 'intentional communities' and secure corporate partnerships.

In what the current director calls "a somewhat unconventional deal with Orbital Housing Authority", the Collective is about to start building New Horizon in the belt: a co-living space that will also include traditional social housing. This experiment is partly a response to the pricing out of orbital space of scientists and other creatives and partly an attempt "to move beyond a single workspace to think about a neighborhood".

When New Horizon is built, the Collective will curate its inhabitants based on what the director describes as a mix of "means testing and merit testing". Rather than the usual micro-apartment model, "cellular units with a cavernous social area", New Horizon will have communal spaces for up to six sleeping pods, "more like a large family. There will still be a members' club, shared by everyone." The development won't be aimed solely at affluent 18- to 30-year-olds, but will include quarters of up to four bedrooms, suitable for people with children. "We don't want to create a single-generational demographic bubble."

The single generation demographic bubble is of course the trouble with all this curation. Even while lip service is paid to ideas of innovation coming from unexpected places, from unlikely collisions and random connections, it is a very tough-minded curator who doesn't seek to be surrounded by people who are basically a bit like himself. With co-orbital spaces, as with quantum networking, there is the promise of connection and collaboration and a universe of newness and surprise. And, as with quantum networking, there is a danger that you can easily end up talking either to people just like yourself.

So what of those questions about style and scalability? As far as the former is concerned, co-orbital spaces do all look a little bit alike – but design has a long history of innovators and followers. Inevitably, everyone borrows the more directional visual cues, even to the point of pastiche.

But they are not, in fact, all alike. They are surprising in their degree of difference. There are industrial-scale operators that lack the warmth and personal touches of the smaller providers (no one at OrbitWork is ever going to come out of the command center as you arrive, knowing your name and whom you're here to visit, which is what happens at the Orbital Collective); but which also lack their preciousness about who is allowed to the party. And then there are the cool clubs that everyone in their right mind would want to join, but where few are chosen.

It seems likely that co-orbital spaces will follow a pattern set by zero-gravity festivals. They will proliferate, each developing its own distinctive vibe, projecting an array of differing identities while all answering a need for the increasingly autonomous workers of the future to hang out with other people.

Meanwhile, the current excitement over co-orbital working may have less to do with a method of office organization than with a handful of hugely successful connectors. When Robert Valdez moved out of RBM, he chose the Orbital Collective partly because "Charles draws in interesting people. He's got links to corporates, government, policymakers." One of these connections turned out to be Dr. Sarah Chen, head of advanced genetic engineering at BioTech Reuters, which led directly to 300,000 credits of sponsorship revenue for Code for Tomorrow. "Charles is a great connector," Valdez says, "and that is really what makes the Orbital Collective so special. Most don't have the same flair."

option_b: Access to a network of vetted professionals and valuable business connections that can help with branding, recruiting, and strategic guidance

THE DEEP RETURN
By ROBERT GIBSON

The oceanic research vessel Meridian set itself grimly to meet the approaching anomaly with defensive protocols, determined to protect the surface world. But they erred in thinking the Deep Ones were too primitive to be strategic.

In the last hours, the sonar readings had grown stronger by many magnitudes, and had changed their signature from scattered interference through white noise to a coherent pattern of organized movement. That was the acoustic effect as the mass's velocity changed relative to the Meridian, as for forty hours the vessel had maintained position above the trench.

They had monitored many such signals come and go from the abyss's impenetrable depths, and had seen them fade, distort and disappear as the Meridian continued its research mission, driven by scientific curiosity toward understanding the planet's last unexplored frontier, leaving behind the mystery of yet another unidentified biological signature unaccompanied by visual confirmation where researchers might observe. They had grown familiar with the sight of wonders—of bioluminescent colonies spanning kilometers, of thermal vents that sustained ecosystems in perpetual darkness.

But now unprecedented excitement possessed the hundred-odd members of the Meridian's crew. It was a subdued excitement; men and women, they came and stood quietly gazing into the large sonar displays that showed the ascending formation, and there were young researchers who had been born after the Deep Surveys began and had never seen anything like this. The experienced scientists talked in low voices, in tones of mingled eagerness and apprehension, of what might lie at this mission's culmination. For the Meridian was witnessing history; the signals ahead were from the Bathys, whose existence had shaped their careers' beginning.

Dr. Omar Ward, the Meridian's director, came slowly down the narrow stair from the observation deck, into the large operations center that was now crowded with personnel, where most of the people gathered. The great chamber, a full cross-section of the research platform, had been at first a storage hold. At the mission's beginning eighty percent of the three-hundred-meter structure had been equipment and supplies; but as the immense stores were used and the holds became available, the crew had spread out from its original cramped quarters. Now the oceanic platform was little more than a floating laboratory.

Eyes lifted from the sonar displays to interrogate Dr. Ward; he met them with an impassive countenance, and announced quietly, "We've confirmed visual contact."

A nervous buzz arose; the director gestured for silence and went on, "They are still only shadows to the deep cameras. Dr. Isabel White has identified them—no more."

But this time the murmur was not to be settled. People pressed round the screens, peering into them as if with the naked eye they could pick out the shapes of reflected bioluminescence that were the Bathys, subjects of decades of research. They clasped each other's hands, embraced, spoke in urgent whispers. For the present their fears were forgotten and wonder prevailed.

Dr. Ward smiled grimly. The rest of the briefing he had been about to give didn't matter anyway, and it might have spoiled this moment.

He turned to go, and was halted by the sight of his colleague, standing at his elbow. His grim smile softened slightly; he asked, "How do you feel, Susan?"

Dr. Susan Holt drew an uncertain breath and released it in a faint sigh. "I don't know. It's remarkable that they're really coming up." She was thinking, he judged shrewdly, of the implications for bioethics and moral philosophy, subjects that had consumed their debates for months...

He said, with a touch of dry amusement, "What did you think might happen? After all, we've been monitoring them for thirty years."

"That's just it," said Susan shakily. "Thirty years of systematic observation—and we still don't understand their intentions. We don't know if they're coming as ambassadors or invaders..."

The director put a hand on her shoulder with reassuring pressure. "Don't worry. Whatever happens—we'll document it." But his face had hardened against registering the gnawing of that same doubtful fear within him. He let his hand fall. "I'd better get to the bridge. There are new protocols to implement now—for contact."

He left her and began to climb the stairway again. Someone dimmed the lights, and an awed whisper ran through the operations center as the people saw the first clear images appear on the screens, illuminated by the platform's own deep-sea floodlights. In that light Susan's eyes gleamed with scientific fascination and dread.

Director Ward found Lead Analyst Max Johnson looking as focused as he'd ever seen him. Max was finding that the actual observed patterns of the ascending formation agreed quite closely with his predictions from decades of acoustic data. He had already prepared a communication protocol based on information theory principles.

Ward nodded curt approval, remarking, "Probably they'll initiate contact before we do."

Max was jolted out of his concentration. "Uh, Director," he said hesitantly. "What kind of reception do you think they're planning?"

Ward shook his head slowly. "Who knows? We don't know whether any of the other Deep Survey missions made contact, or if they survived. And we don't know what changes have taken place in the abyss. It's possible—not likely, though—that something has happened to break the ecological continuity to the point where our presence has been misinterpreted as hostile."

He turned away tight-lipped and left the bridge. From his private office-cabin, he sent a message to Chief Biologist Isabel White to notify him as soon as the Bathys' morphology became clear; then he sat idle, alone with his thoughts.

The platform's automated systems had scant need of monitoring; Omar Ward found himself wishing that he could find some demanding task for everyone on board, himself included, to fill up the hours that remained.

There was an extensive digital library in the cabin, but he couldn't persuade himself to occupy time that way. He could go down and watch the screens, or to the residential section where he might find Susan and the other senior researchers—but somehow he didn't want to do that either.

He felt empty, drained—like the platform's research objectives. As the Meridian's mission goals and the hope of peaceful contact with an unknown intelligence had evolved, so the certainty had gone out of him. Now the final phase was beginning and Director Omar Ward felt tired and uncertain.

Perhaps, he thought, he was feeling the weight of his thirty years in deep-sea research—though physically he was only fifty-two now, fifteen years older than when this particular survey had begun. That was the toll of a career spent in isolated research stations, monitoring signals from the deep while years and decades had passed in the surface world.

Thoughtfully Ward got to his feet and stood surveying a cabinet with built-in recording equipment and storage for data archives. There were about three dozen digital files there—his personal logs of the great survey, a segment of his life and of scientific history. He might add that to the platform's official documentation and its collections of biological data, as a report to whatever authorities might be interested on the surface—if such authorities were still paying attention.

Ward selected a file from among the earliest. It was one he had made shortly after arriving at the Redwood Station in Orvandor, beginning of the first phase of the survey. He loaded it onto the player.

His own voice came from the speaker, fresher, more energetic and confident than he knew it was now.

"Day thirty-three of deep acoustic monitoring from Redwood Station, Orvandor.

"Our initial surveys of the Orvandor Trench drew unprecedented results. There are organized acoustic patterns, far too complex to be random geological activity, and unlike any known biological signatures.

"Our hopes were exceeded—and I think all of us, even remembering previous failed contact attempts, hoped more than we dared to admit. If the Orvandor signals possessed a decipherable pattern, we could establish communication within a few years of surface time.

"It is encouraging to note that the team seems only more determined. We continue monitoring; the signal complexity, so unlike surface communications, beckons. If success comes, a generation will have passed in research; colleagues, mentors, all the generation that launched the Deep Survey programs will have retired or passed away. Nevertheless we continue. Our generation's dream, humanity's dream, lives in us and in the mission forever..."

Presently Omar Ward switched off that younger voice of his and leaned back, an ironic smile touching his lips. That fervent idealism seemed remote and foreign to him now. The excitement of discovery must still have been fresh in his mind.

He rose, slipped the file back in its directory and selected another, later one.

"One month since we detected the coordinated movement patterns suggesting organized migration from deeper zones.

"We face the unsettling realization that what was feared is probably true—that intelligent life in the deep ocean is not only real but potentially vast in scale, and that we may have been observed far longer than we've been observing.

"It makes no difference, of course; we cannot abandon the mission... This may be humanity's best chance of establishing contact with a truly alien intelligence without space exploration. Certainly the construction of these deep-sea platforms and their support infrastructure, the immense expenditure of resources and international diplomacy that went into them, left several nations' budgets strained. Only once in a long age does humanity rise to such a collaborative effort—the effort of the International Space Station, or the global pandemic response of the early twenty-first century.

"Looked at historically, such cooperative outbursts are the result of humanity recognizing threats or opportunities that transcend national boundaries... In our era, the discovery of organized intelligence in the ocean depths was such a revelation—so we launched the Deep Surveys. Perhaps our effort will prove as futile as previous attempts at interspecies communication, less practical than simple ecosystem restoration... In any case, direct contact seems inevitable; but Earth could at least approach it with scientific documentation and protocols grounded in bioethics, expanding our understanding of consciousness itself...

"Hopeless, unless we understand their language!"

Omar Ward shook his head and removed the file. That was from the time when he had grown philosophical after the initial breakthroughs.

He selected one more file that was only two years old. The recorded voice sounded weary, yet alive with a strange intensity...

"We are monitoring the deepest regions of the Foxwood Trench; hundreds of signals show on the acoustic arrays, each signal embedded in a complex harmonic structure like voices singing in vast cathedrals, for we are detecting what appears to be a civilization.

"According to our models, the Meridian has reached its optimal monitoring position. Now we wait for them to acknowledge our presence—but hope is small that any of our communication attempts will be understood, as have none of the thousands of signal patterns transmitted already.

"But what are a few thousand patterns in a language of potentially millions? We have only, as it were, learned a handful of words in an alien tongue, while the full complexity of their communication still remains far beyond our comprehension.

"On scientific grounds I have had Isabel White conduct morphological analyses using our deepest probes. There are structures down there in a volume of ocean where one finds only extremophile bacteria in most places; there if anywhere must exist the civilization we seek! But the deepest zones are eleven kilometers down...

"Even so—by deploying our remaining deep probes, the Meridian could achieve observations that would give us definitive answers. It would be a one-way deployment—even if enough probes remained, there would be little point in surface missions after potentially disturbing a civilization that has remained hidden for millennia.

"That was why the planners limited our survey to non-invasive methods. Even now, according to the risk management protocols established then, our presence—if they perceive us as hostile—could trigger a response that destabilizes the entire marine ecosystem.

"Why maintain distance, then, with the possibility of direct contact? Why not deploy all our resources and make definitive observations? What use is adherence to protocols thirty years old, whose makers are retired and which may be outdated?

"Would the crew support it? I don't know—some of them still show caution, though they know intellectually that this opportunity may never come again...

"It doesn't matter. Today I gave orders to maintain our position and wait."

Grimly Omar Ward stopped the playback. Then he sat for a time with head resting in his hands, staring at the dark screen.

The memory of that fierce temptation to push forward still had power to shake him. A phrase from an old poem came into his mind, something he'd read once about exploration...

He sighed. He still couldn't say just why he had given the order to wait. The deep had claimed his career—but he was still bound by scientific ethics, and not even thirty years of research had been able to alter that.

He wondered if there would still be a quiet beach and a warm sunny place beside it where a research-weary man, relieved at last of responsibility, could rest and think no more... Those things went on, if people preserved them. And a forest where he and young researchers could go hiking, and lie on their backs at night and gaze at the stars, far away, so different from the abyss... He wasn't sure he would want to do that, though.

Suddenly a faint tremor went through the platform; it seemed to shudder one moment.

The director was on his feet instantly, but then his movements became measured. Whatever it had been was past, and he had a good idea what it had been—a pressure wave, nothing unusual in the vicinity of large marine organisms, though in the open ocean such impacts were rare. No harm could have been done. The Meridian's stabilization systems were sophisticated and reliable.

Just as he reached for the door control, the emergency comm shrilled imperatively. Omar Ward turned, frowning—surely a pressure wave wasn't that serious. Coincidence, maybe—it might be Isabel White calling as instructed.

He reached the comm at the moment when another, heavier impact shook the platform. Ward grabbed the receiver quickly.

"Director?" It was Max Johnson's voice, tense. "Director, we're under attack!"

"Activate emergency protocols. All stations." He had said it automatically, then felt a curious detached relief at the knowledge that after all these years he could still respond decisively to a crisis. There was a moment's silence, and he heard the alarm start—three short tones and repeat, sounding through all the sections of the research platform. Knowing that Max was still there, he said, "Now—attacked by what?"

"Creatures," said Max helplessly. "Dozens of them so far. No, there are more now." Repeated impacts shuddered the Meridian's framework. The analyst said, obviously striving for calm, "They're large organisms, perhaps twenty meters long, but they move with purpose. The sonar barely tracked them before they started ramming us. Can't get clear images long enough to classify them."

"If they're biological," said Omar Ward deliberately, "they can't generate enough force to breach our hull. Hold position. I'll be right there."

In the corridor he nearly collided with a young researcher. Leo Hernández's eyes were wide; he had heard the director's words.

"Something's happening," he said with earnest seriousness and, without wasting time on questions, "Can I help, Dr. Ward?"

Ward hesitated, said, "All right. Come along and stay clear of the equipment." He headed for the operations center with strides that the young man matched easily.

There were people moving quickly in the corridors, heading for their stations. Their faces were set, frightened, confused. The Meridian shuddered, again and again, under impacts that must have had tremendous force behind them; but it held its position above the trench, its stabilization systems compensating.

To a person, the platform's senior staff were already in operations, most of them breathless. To a person they looked to Director Omar Ward.

"Well?" he said sharply. "What's their behavior?"

Max Johnson spoke. "There are at least forty of them now, sir, and they're all targeting structural weak points."

The director stared into the dark sonar display where occasional bright shapes appeared ominously, never in the same position twice.

Leo pressed himself against the wall and watched silently. His young face showed more curiosity than fear; he had confidence in the director.

"If they had greater mass," reasoned the director, "they'd have used it by now. They're trying to disable us. But at this rate, they can't breach the hull as long as our systems function—or until they bring up something larger."

The impacts continued—whether from physical rams or some form of biological discharge would be hard to determine and it didn't matter; whatever was hitting the Meridian's hull was doing so with coordinated precision.

But that hull was strong. It was designed to withstand the pressures of the deep ocean and the forces of major storms; impacts from outside were absorbed by the structure's flexibility and the stabilization field's dampening effect. A large organism, on striking it, would be repelled—possibly injured by the impact—and the platform, in obedience to physics, would shift too, but since its mass was anchored and stabilized, its displacement was minimal.

The people in the Meridian would have felt nothing at all of the sustained assault being directed against them, save that their stabilization systems were intentionally calibrated to allow some movement to provide feedback to the crew.

One of the scientists said shakily, "It's as if they've been preparing for this. But why would they—"

"That," said the director grimly, "is what we have to find out. Why they're attacking. At least, I suspect we'll learn soon."

The Meridian held steadily in position, maintaining its monitoring stance. Even if one were inclined to retreat, there seemed no reason to abandon station or change protocols. There was nowhere else to go and too much invested if there had been; come what might, this was the mission's critical moment—perhaps in a more confrontational way than had been anticipated. All around moved the attacking organisms, circling, coordinating, and striking, always striking, with the focused intensity of a defended territory. The research platform bore no weapons—but suddenly on one of the sonar displays a bright shape flared and then went dark.

Leo exclaimed in surprise and then fell silent, but no one was paying attention to him. The people in the Meridian's operations center looked questions at each other, as the thought of internal conflict flashed into many minds at once. But Director Ward said soberly, "It must have collided with another. Maybe its own momentum, if it struck at the wrong angle."

He studied the data accumulated so far. A few unclear images had been captured, which showed elongated organisms much like known deep-sea species, except that they displayed coordinated behavior and far greater size. Their size was difficult to ascertain, because you needed to know their distance and velocity—but sonar echoes gave the distance, and likewise, by the Doppler method, the speed of directly approaching or receding organisms. It was apparent that the attacking creatures were even larger than Max had initially estimated—too large to be individuals. Massive, purposeful beings with devastating impact force.

"Coordinated behavior, certainly," said Omar Ward, but a chill ran down his spine as it occurred to him that perhaps the attackers represented a defensive response to perceived invasion. They had seen no comparable intelligence in the ocean depths they had explored, but the Bathys might have been monitoring them far longer than suspected and decided humanity was a threat.

It became evident, too, that the assault was being sustained by waves of fresh attackers, while others retreated into the deep, presumably to rest or receive new instructions. That argued a planned and organized defense with serious purpose behind it.

Dr. Susan Holt, the bioethics specialist, said quietly, "At the rate we're sustaining damage, the hull integrity will be compromised in twelve to eighteen hours."

"We should reach the surface before then," Max said hopefully.

"If they don't escalate their attack first."

"We're under a strategic disadvantage," said the director, "of not knowing their motivation."

Leo burst out, his voice urgent with conviction, "But we have an advantage too!"

His director raised an eyebrow. "What's that? I don't see it."

"They're defending and we're not threatening," said the young researcher. Then, seeing he hadn't made himself clear, "In any conflict, if one side misunderstands the other's intentions, communication can resolve it."

Thoughtful expressions appeared on several faces. Director Ward said, "Maybe you're right. They do seem to be defensive. But we're not in a position to prove our intentions." He turned back to the others. "As I was going to suggest—I think we should attempt communication with them. At least we may discover what triggered this response."

And now instead of passive monitoring the platform was broadcasting on multiple frequencies, cycling through various patterns, repeating on each the same recorded message based on information theory principles:

"We are peaceful observers. We mean no harm. We are the research mission Meridian from the surface world..." And so on, identifying themselves and explaining that they were unarmed and scientific, that there must be some misunderstanding, and asking, "What do you want?"

There was no answer. The platform held position, its systems managing the assault. Those outside were expending vastly greater energy in the effort to drive them away, but maintaining structural integrity was taxing the Meridian's resources too. Once more Omar Ward had the insidious sense of his own resolve weakening along with his platform's defenses.

Isabel White approached him urgently. "If you have time, Director—I've got analysis on the organisms now."

Eagerly Ward took the data compilation from the biological scans. But it told him little; only the basic morphology was clear, and that was unlike anything in the databases... He looked up questioningly at Isabel White.

"There are some disturbing features," said the biologist carefully. "First of all—they show signs of artificial modification. And in their behavior patterns, our best analysis should reveal instinctive responses—but it does not.

"The coordination you see is too precise. It indicates communication systems less than one millisecond in latency—so their nervous systems can't be simple neural networks, but must involve something more sophisticated, perhaps bioengineered enhancement."

"Is that all?" demanded Ward.

"Isn't it enough?" said Isabel blankly. "Well—we tried biochemical analysis, of course. The samples show nothing unusual in basic composition, but the complexity science models indicate designed systems."

The director sighed wearily. "Good work," he said. "Continue analysis; perhaps you can explain these anomalies before—"

"We know who you are," interrupted a resonant voice with strange harmonics, "and your explanations are insufficient."

Omar Ward turned sharply to the communications station, his weariness vanishing. He said quickly, "Then tell us what we've done wrong," and the words overlapped absurdly with the same plea in the still-repeating broadcast.

He cut off the recording; as he did so the speaker, still carrying deep harmonic undertones, said, "It may interest you to know that you are not the first. The two other deep research missions that descended have already been expelled, as you will soon be—the sooner, if you continue your intrusion."

Omar Ward's mind was working rapidly. The voice—which must be coming from the deep, transmitted somehow by the organisms—was revealing things perhaps unintentionally: that it had responded at all suggested uncertainty, he deduced from the fact it had chosen to communicate, and from its last statement he gathered that the Meridian's steadfast position and continued monitoring had somehow concerned it. So it was trying to drive them away.

He filed those observations for consideration. Just now he had to know something, so urgently that he asked it directly, "Are you the Bathys we've been studying?"

The voice carried a tone of cold amusement. "We are the Bathys," it answered, "but you are intruders."

The director was momentarily silent, searching for an adequate response. Behind him somebody gasped, the only sound in the stunned silence, and the platform shuddered slightly as another massive impact struck its hull.

"Suppose we discuss this misunderstanding," said Omar Ward steadily. He specified a visual communication frequency compatible with their systems.

"Very well." The tone suggested reluctant agreement. The voice continued in its language that was perfectly intelligible but strange-sounding with its harmonic complexity. "Perhaps, if you understand your violation, you will follow the prudent example of the Bayview mission's leader."

Omar Ward tensed. The Bayview Station in Selvoria, established to monitor the southern trenches, had been the most advanced of the research platforms—and its director had been a respected colleague of Ward's... He said carefully, "What happened to them?"

"They resisted our warnings, which surround you now, for some time," said the voice with disturbing calm. "When they understood it was futile, they chose withdrawal over confrontation, and returned to the surface." A brief pause. "The visual connection is ready."

Omar Ward activated the screen at the specified frequency, and an image formed there. The face that appeared was humanoid in structure, but profoundly modified. The features showed the same basic bilateral symmetry possessed by surface humans, but there was an unmistakable quality of adaptive redesign. Most obviously, the eyes seemed designed for low-light conditions, and the skin showed translucent qualities.

The being regarded Omar Ward with an expression of stern assessment. "Have you any other questions before you depart?"

"Yes," said Ward with controlled intensity. "You haven't explained one thing. Why do you consider our research a violation? You can see we're conducting scientific observation."

The modified human studied him with a calculating look in those adapted eyes, behind which the director glimpsed something like protective determination.

"It is enough for you to know that you must leave our territory."

The laboratory's sterile white walls seemed to close in on me as consciousness returned. My first sensation was the cool metal of the examination table beneath me, then the gentle hum of biotechnology equipment surrounding my pod. I tried to recall how I'd arrived here, but my mind was blank—a pristine slate waiting to be written upon.

"Subject is regaining consciousness," a voice announced clinically. "Vital signs stabilizing."

Juliana spoke carefully: "Our oral history of the conflict may be... incomplete. We've been fighting so long that the original causes have become mythologized."

But here's what I know about game theory: the prisoner's dilemma can be escaped through repeated interactions, communication, and credible commitment mechanisms. You need a framework that makes cooperation more rational than conflict."

"And if they cheat?" Patrick Osborne demanded.

"Then you respond proportionally, not catastrophically," I explained. "That's the key. Tit-for-tat with forgiveness. Match cooperation with cooperation, defection with measured response, but always leave room for reconciliation."

Zhang Walker spoke up: "The biodiversity work could actually benefit both sides. The native species are crucial for climate adaptation. We've been trying to preserve them alone, but it's been nearly impossible."

Administrator Chen looked thoughtful. "We've lost most of our genetic samples in the fighting. Access to Fairview's biodiversity banks would be... valuable."

As the sun set—or rather, as Selvoria's rotation carried us into deeper twilight—we had the outline of an agreement. It was fragile, conditional, and would require constant maintenance. But it was a start.

"Why are you doing this?" Juliana asked me as we prepared to leave. "You don't remember anything about yourself, yet you're risking your life for colonies you just learned existed."

I considered the question. "Maybe because I don't remember, I can see clearly. I'm not trapped by your oral histories and grievances. I just see two groups of humans making themselves miserable through predictable strategic failures. And I apparently have the knowledge to help fix that."

She smiled slightly. "The prophecy said you'd come without memory but with wisdom. Perhaps there's something to it after all."

Three months after my arrival, I stood with Dr. Reynolds—who had survived the attack on the orbital facility—looking at a holographic display of Selvoria's recovery. Green infrastructure projects were spreading. Water management was being coordinated. Biodiversity preserves were expanding.

"It's not me," I replied. "It's just applied game theory. Once you change the incentive structure, people make better choices."

"Still," she smiled, "I'd say the prophecy was fulfilled. You came from Earth, without memory, and brought peace."

I looked out at the planet below, at the thin strips of habitable land between fire and ice where humans had somehow built a civilization. "I just helped them see they were playing a game they didn't have to play. The rest was up to them."

My memories of Earth never fully returned. But perhaps that was appropriate. I wasn't here to be Jonathan Gibson from Juniper Town. I was here to be someone new—someone who could see past old grievances to new possibilities.

And in that role, I'd found my purpose.

The performing arts center in Fairview hosted a joint concert that evening—musicians from both colonies playing together for the first time in a generation. It was a small thing, musical innovation born from newfound cooperation. But small things mattered.

As I listened to the music, I realized I'd learned something important: sometimes the best way to solve an impossible problem is to forget everything you think you know and start fresh.

Memory loss, it turned out, could be a gift.

BROOKS: Have you been able to warn people about this?

YOUNG: That's the challenge. How do you warn people about content that looks completely normal? We can't exactly tell everyone to stop using social media. Even if we could identify specific N-Node accounts, they'd just be replaced by new ones. It's like trying to fight a hydra.

BROOKS: What about content moderation by the platforms themselves?

YOUNG: We've been working with them, but it's difficult. The content doesn't violate any terms of service. It's not hate speech or misinformation in the conventional sense. It's more subtle than that. The platforms are starting to take it seriously, but developing effective countermeasures requires understanding mechanisms we're only beginning to comprehend.

BROOKS: Has your research drawn on any particular theoretical frameworks?

YOUNG: We've incorporated insights from multiple fields. Cultural anthropology helps us understand how information spreads through social groups. Justice theory informs our thinking about the ethical implications. We've even done oral history projects, interviewing people who've experienced these episodes to understand the phenomenology. And of course, network theory is fundamental to mapping the spread of influence.

BROOKS: What role does personal growth play in resistance to these effects?

YOUNG: That's an interesting question. We've found that people who engage in regular self-reflection and emotional skill development seem to be somewhat more resilient. Those who are aware of their emotional states and can recognize when they're being manipulated are better able to resist. In some ways, the best defense is personal growth—developing the capacity to observe your own reactions and question their origins.

BROOKS: Are there any historical precedents for this kind of phenomenon?

YOUNG: Historical analysis reveals that societies have always been vulnerable to coordinated manipulation. What's new is the scale and speed enabled by digital networks. In the past, it might take weeks or months for a rumor or propaganda campaign to spread. Now it happens in hours. The mechanisms of influence are ancient, but the delivery system is unprecedented.

BROOKS: What's the current status of N-Node activity?

YOUNG: As of this week, we're tracking seven active N-Nodes across major platforms. Activity levels are moderate but increasing. We're also seeing evolution in their tactics—they're getting better at evading detection.

BROOKS: That's rather ominous.

YOUNG: It is. But there's also reason for hope. Now that we understand the mechanism, we can develop countermeasures. We're working on browser extensions and app features that can identify potential N-Node content. We're also developing educational programs to help people recognize when they're being manipulated.

BROOKS: Do you think this problem will get worse before it gets better?

YOUNG: Almost certainly. As social media becomes more integrated into daily life, the potential for this kind of manipulation increases. We're also seeing the emergence of more sophisticated N-Nodes that use machine learning to optimize their impact. It's an arms race.

BROOKS: Some might say this research sounds like conspiracy theory.

YOUNG: I understand the skepticism. A few years ago, I would have been skeptical myself. But the data doesn't lie. We have rigorous statistical evidence, replicated findings across multiple cities, and a plausible mechanism. This isn't speculation—it's documented fact.

BROOKS: What would you say to people who feel helpless in the face of this?

YOUNG: I'd say awareness is the first step. If you find yourself suddenly feeling angry, anxious, or aggressive for no apparent reason, take a step back. Ask yourself: where is this feeling coming from? Have I been scrolling social media? Could I be reacting to something I saw online rather than to my actual circumstances? That kind of metacognition—thinking about your thinking—is powerful.

BROOKS: Any final thoughts?

YOUNG: Just this: we like to think we're rational actors making free choices. But the truth is we're all vulnerable to influence and manipulation. The question isn't whether we can be influenced—we can. The question is whether we can become aware enough to recognize it when it's happening. That's where personal growth intersects with social responsibility. We need to develop both individual resilience and collective awareness. Because if we don't, we're at the mercy of whoever controls the N-Nodes.

BROOKS: Dr. Young, thank you for your time.

YOUNG: Thank you, Jin. I hope this conversation helps people understand what we're up against.

THE END

An Unsolved Mystery

She had turned in some interesting research on cultural preservation, convincing Mr. Brown that she had in her the makings of a good environmental advocate. "You here again?" she had greeted her that summer, and Elizabeth hadn't noticed her old eyes twinkling behind her glasses. "What do you propose to do with yourself this time?"

"In the basement. Go down and look them over if you can stand the mustiness."

Elizabeth went, not to look over the old magazines so much as to escape to a place where she could have a good cry. It was the summer before her twentieth birthday. In another year she would have outgrown her childish resentment of her parents' vacation or be grown up enough to ask them to let her have a vacation of her own. In another year she would be traveling among the beautiful research stations of Victorville, Dravonia and solving a mystery to be known as the Green Revolution Conspiracy.

"A whole conspiracy," Yuki would be telling her, "and you solved everything."

But then she didn't even know Yuki. She had no idea so many thrilling adventures awaited her. There seemed to be nothing—nothing—and so the tears came and spilled over on one of the magazines. As Elizabeth wiped it away she noticed that it had fallen on a picture of a garden.

"A garden with tears for water. How strange!" she remembered saying aloud.

Elizabeth had never seen a real botanical garden. The thrill of walking up to the door of the palatial Silva mansion was still ahead of her. On the grounds a garden still caught and held rainbows in its morning dew like those she was to see on her honeymoon in the cloud forests. But all that was in the future. If anyone had told the serious-faced, ponytailed girl that she would one day marry Wei Cooper, she would have laughed in their faces.

"That skeptic!"

For then she knew Wei only as an older student who used to challenge her theories and call her idealistic until one day she yelled back at him, "Idealists are the ones who change the world, and you're too cynical to see it!"

Wei was to win Elizabeth's heart when he gave her a rare plant specimen and suggested they collaborate on research. The plant was now thriving in their greenhouse. But the summer Elizabeth found the picture of a garden and spilled tears on it she had no plant collection. She had nothing, she confessed, not even a friend. It had helped to pretend the garden in the picture was filled with all the tears lonely students like herself had ever cried.

"But that would make it enchanted!" she had suddenly exclaimed. "If I could find it I'd wish—"

A step had sounded on the stairs. Elizabeth remembered it distinctly. She had turned to see her grandmother and to hear her say in her usual abrupt fashion, "Enchanted garden, indeed! If you let people know your wishes instead of muttering them to yourself, most of them aren't so impossible."

"Were they?" asked Yuki.

She and Laura had listened to this much of what Elizabeth was telling them without interruption.

"That's the unsolved mystery," Elizabeth replied. "There weren't any of them impossible."

And she went on to tell them how, the very next day, her grandparents had taken her to a garden exactly like the one in the picture. It was in the center of a vast estate with paths leading through it. Beside the main path were smaller gardens with water flowing from natural springs. Elizabeth had stared at them a moment and then walked the stone path to the central garden.

"Am I dreaming?" she remembered saying aloud. "Is this beautiful garden real?"

A voice had answered, although she could see no one.

"Make your wishes, Elizabeth. Wish wisely. If you shed a tear in the garden your wishes will surely come true."

"A tear?" Elizabeth had asked. "How can I shed a tear when I'm happy? This is a wonderful place."

"Shed a tear in the garden and your wishes will surely come true," the voice had repeated.

"But what is there to cry about?"

"You found plenty to cry about back at your grandmother's house," the mysterious voice had reminded her. "Weren't you crying on my picture down there in the basement?"

"Then you—you are the garden!" Elizabeth remembered exclaiming. "But a garden doesn't speak. It doesn't have a voice."

"Wish wisely," the voice from the garden had said in a mysterious whisper.

CHAPTER II
If Wishes Came True

"Did you?" Yuki interrupted the story to ask excitedly. "Oh, Elizabeth! Don't keep us in suspense any longer. What did you wish?"

I remember thinking of how lonely I was and how I wished for a friend or a research partner, and suddenly a tear splashed on the moss. It made little ripples in a puddle. I thought I had to wish quickly before they vanished, and so I began naming the things I wanted as fast as I could. I'm not sure they were wise wishes. They seem rather selfish to me, now. I wasn't thinking of anybody but me, Elizabeth Hernandez, and what I wanted. It wasn't until after I began to think of others that my wishes started to come true."

"But what were they?" Yuki insisted.

Laura seemed unusually quiet and thoughtful. Elizabeth did not notice the fear in her eyes as she replied airily, "Oh, didn't I tell you? I wished for lots of friends and a research partner, and I wished I could work on environmental justice and solve a lot of mysteries and that's as far as I got when the ripples vanished. I thought the spell was broken and so I didn't wish for anything more."

"Margaret and I always do," she replied, "but then it was different. I didn't know I would marry Wei or that he would become an expert in neuroscience and bioethics, and he didn't know he would inherit his family's estate. It is strange, isn't it? But the strangest thing of all was the garden itself."

Yuki laughed at this, but Elizabeth was serious as she answered, "I was still young enough to think so at the time. I wandered around, growing very drowsy. Then I found a bench and sat on it. I must have dozed off, because I remember waking up and wondering if the voice in the garden had been a dream."

"A bench?" Yuki questioned. "Are you sure it wasn't a magic carpet?"

"No, it was a bench all right," Elizabeth assured her, laughing. "It was placed between two ancient trees in a beautiful garden all enclosed in hedges thick with flowers. Did I tell you it was June?"

Again Yuki laughed. But Laura said abruptly, "Let's not talk about gardens in June. It's a long way from June to December."

"Do you mean a garden changes? I know," Elizabeth said, "but I think this one would be beautiful at any time of the year. There were rare specimens, too, and I don't know how many different kinds of native plants. I explored the garden all around the central area."

"Yes, yes. Go on," entreated Yuki. "I didn't dream you'd kept anything that exciting a secret. Why didn't you try to solve the mystery?"

"I think I would have tried," Elizabeth admitted, "if I had been older or more experienced. I really should have investigated it more thoroughly and learned the secret of the garden. But after the ripples went away it didn't speak to me any more, and I didn't really think it had heard my wishes. I was still wishing for a friend when I met you, Yuki. It did seem impossible for us to be friends at first, didn't it? Laura was your friend."

"I did make trouble for you," Laura remembered. "It was all because of my foolish jealousy."

"It was nothing compared to the trouble caused by the development controversy," declared Elizabeth. "After that things started happening so fast that I completely forgot about the garden. "The Newman plot, I always called it," Yuki said with a giggle. "I've seen lots nicer gardens."

"You have?" asked Elizabeth. "Then maybe you've seen the one I've been telling you about. I think the picture of it is still in the basement. Come on down and I'll show you."

Yuki and Laura had finished their tea while Elizabeth was telling them the story of the garden. Somehow, she wasn't hungry for hers. She had tasted it too often while she was making it.

"I'll save it for later," she decided.

Yuki watched in amusement as Elizabeth carefully poured the remaining tea into a thermos.

"Sometimes," Elizabeth said fondly, "I think we waste too much. Everything should be preserved and reused. Do you mind if we look at the old magazines, Laura? I want to find that picture again."

"There probably aren't any mysteries down there," Yuki said with a giggle.

Leaving the table, they all started downstairs. In modernizing her grandparents' house to suit her own and Wei's tastes, Elizabeth had seen to it that the old basement was reorganized. But there was still a section that held decades of stored items. 

"Come on. There's nothing down here to be afraid of," Elizabeth urged her friends.

"Maybe not, but I'm beginning to get curious," confessed Yuki as she followed Elizabeth to the storage area at the far end of the basement.

"So am I," Laura admitted. "I'm not superstitious, but old places are intriguing."

"Down here we can all turn back the clock. Does anybody care to explore the past?" Elizabeth asked mysteriously.

"When I told Grandma about it she laughed and said I must have dreamed it. She said if wishes came true that easily she'd be living in a mansion. But would she?" Elizabeth wondered. "When I first remember this house she was still using old appliances. I think she and Grandpa liked the way they lived without any modern conveniences."

"I think so, too," Yuki agreed, looking around the old basement with interest. "It is strange they both died the same winter, isn't it?"

"Maybe they wanted it that way. Maybe they wished neither of them would outlive the other. If they did wish in the garden," Elizabeth went on more thoughtfully, "I'm sure that was one of their wishes. Another could have been to keep the good old days, as Grandma used to call them. That one came true in a way. They did manage to keep a little of the past when they kept all these old things. That's what I meant about turning back the clock."

"If wishes came true I'd like to turn it back a little myself," Laura began. "It would be nice if things were the way they used to be when I trusted Walter—"

"Don't you trust him now?" Elizabeth asked.

Afterwards she was sorry for the interruption. Yuki and Elizabeth both questioned Laura, but that was all she would say. Elizabeth wondered, as they searched through the old magazines, what was wrong. Laura was of a suspicious disposition. Was mistrust coming between her and her colleague, Walter Ford? It's the very same one."

"Where?" she asked. "To the garden? I'd love to, wouldn't you, Elizabeth?"

"Of course," agreed Elizabeth. She put the magazine back in its place and turned eagerly to her friends. "I do remember a road turning off into the woods and going uphill," she told them. "I never thought it led to a house, though. There isn't even a gate. Could that be the road my grandparents took?"

"Why don't we take it ourselves and find out?" Yuki suggested.

CHAPTER III
A Strange Encounter

Laura was not too enthusiastic about the proposed trip to the Silva estate. Finally she agreed to it under one condition. They were not to drive all the way to the house which, she said, was just over the hilltop. They were to park the car where no one would see it and follow the path to the garden.

"But suppose we can't find the path?" asked Elizabeth.

"You'll remember it, won't you?"

Elizabeth thought she would, but she wasn't too sure. She and Yuki both argued that it would be better to inquire at the house. Yuki knew Olivia Silva slightly.

"She'd be glad to show us around. This way it looks as if we're planning something suspicious," Yuki said as they started off in the hybrid car she was driving.

It was a neat little car, environmentally friendly, and easy to park in out-of-the-way places. Elizabeth laughed and said if they did find the garden she thought she'd wish for one exactly like it for their research.

"Well, you know what your grandmother said about wishes, don't you?" Laura asked. "If you let people know about them instead of muttering them to yourself most of them aren't so impossible."

"Quite true," Elizabeth agreed. "I'll let Wei know about this one. He's my research partner, and we're working on a green infrastructure project. Maybe this garden could be part of our study on cultural preservation and environmental justice."

"Your work is better suited for this than just curiosity. It's too important for casual visits. We picked a perfect day for this trip," Yuki continued, guiding the car around curves as it climbed the steep hill beyond Keystone.

The trip was a short one. In thirty minutes they had covered the distance that had seemed such a long way to Elizabeth when she was riding in her grandfather's old truck.

"I've been thinking about it," she said, "and I've just about figured out how it happened. I didn't think my grandparents knew the Silvas well enough to pay them a visit, though. We must have looked out of place driving up to a beautiful estate in Grandpa's old truck. I do remember that Grandma had some handmade items to deliver. But that still doesn't explain what happened afterwards. When I woke up on the bench I was alone in the garden. Truck, grandparents—all had disappeared."

"How could they?" asked Yuki.

"Anyway," Laura began, "you had a chance to see how beautiful everything was before—"

Again she broke off as if there were something she wanted to tell but didn't quite dare.

"Before what?" questioned Elizabeth.

"Oh, nothing. Forget I said anything about it. You were telling us how you woke up on the bench, but you never did explain how you got back home," Laura reminded her.

"Didn't I?" asked Elizabeth. "I'd forgotten a lot of it, but it's beginning to come back now. I do remember driving home along this road. You see, I thought my grandparents had left me in the garden for a surprise and would return for me. I told you I was all alone. There wasn't a house in sight."

"The Silva house is just over the top of this next hill," Yuki put in.

"I know. You told me that. Now I know why I couldn't see it. All I could see was a windowless old structure and a path leading in that direction. Naturally, I followed it. There's something about a path in the woods that always tempts me."

"We know that, Elizabeth. Margaret told us all about your latest mystery. You followed a trail or something."

"Well, this trail led out of the garden where the bench was and then through an archway," Elizabeth continued. "All sorts of sculptures and stone markers peered out at me from unexpected places. I was actually scared by the time I reached the old structure. There wasn't time to explore it. Just then I heard the rumble of my grandfather's truck and knew he was driving off without me."

"He was!" Elizabeth's friends both chorused in surprise, and Yuki asked, "Why would he do a thing like that?"

"I think now it was just to tease me. He did stop and wait for me after a while," Elizabeth remembered. "The items were gone. Grandma must have delivered them, but I didn't ask where. If she made them for Mrs. Silva they may still be there."

"I wouldn't depend on it," Laura said as they turned up the narrow road to the Silva estate.

"Watch out!" Elizabeth suddenly exclaimed. "There's another car coming."

As Yuki swerved to avoid the oncoming car, Laura ducked her head. She kept herself hidden behind Elizabeth until the car had passed. The man driving it was a stranger to Elizabeth, but she would remember his intense, dark eyes and stern expression for a long time. The dark cap he was wearing covered most of his hair.

"What's the matter with you two?" asked Yuki when the car had passed. "Aren't you a little old for playing hide and seek?"

"I wasn't—playing. Let's not go up there," Laura begged. "I don't think the Silvas live there any more."

"Maybe not, but we can pretend we think they do, can't we?" Elizabeth replied a little uncertainly.

She was beginning to suspect that Laura knew more about the Silva estate than she was telling. Yuki kept on driving along the narrow, gravelly road. Soon there were more evergreens and native plantings to be seen. They looked very green next to the bare trees in the woods beyond. The sky was gray with white clouds being driven across it by the wind.

"There's the old structure!" Laura exclaimed. "I can see it over to the left. It looks like something out of a fairy tale, doesn't it?"

"It looks mysterious all right," agreed Elizabeth. "I wonder what it is."

"I suppose it's nothing but an old storage building. It would be interesting to explore it, though," Yuki said. "But if there are new people living here they'll never give us permission."

"We might explore it without permission," Elizabeth suggested daringly. "Come on!" she urged her friends as Yuki parked the car in a cleared place beside the road. "Who's going to stop us? And who wants to explore a gloomy old building, anyway? Let's look for the garden."

"Do you think we should?" Laura asked. "It won't be enchanted. I told you—"

"You told us very little," Yuki reminded her. "If you know anything about the people who live here now, I think you ought to let us know. Otherwise, I'm afraid we won't be very welcome."

"I don't think they'll welcome us, anyway. I do know who they are," Laura admitted. "You remember Lila Stevens from the university, don't you? I've seen her around here. Her family must have acquired sudden wealth, or else she's just working on the estate doing research."

"Then you've been here lately? Why didn't you tell me?" asked Yuki. "We always used to go places together."

"It wasn't important," Laura replied evasively. "I was just out for a drive."

"You researchers!" laughed Elizabeth. "Each with a car of your own. You're not interested in Lila Stevens's work, are you, Yuki? I'm sure you can collaborate better than that. I did know her slightly, but not from the university. We were both in the same environmental advocacy group. I remember her colleague, Walter Ford, a lot better. He was in our community organizing meetings."

"Sh!" Yuki cautioned her. "Nice people no longer mention Walter Ford's name in certain circles. He's controversial."

"For what?" asked Elizabeth.

Like Wei, her research partner husband, she preferred facts to gossip.

"Ethics violations, I guess. He falsified some research data and forged some peer review documents. I think he manipulated some grant applications, too. Anyway, he was barred from academic work. It was all in the journals," Laura told her.

Now Elizabeth did remember. It was something she would have preferred to forget. She liked to think she was a good judge of character, and she had taken Walter Ford for a dedicated, honest researcher who would never stoop to fraud.

"I don't see what all this has to do with the garden," Yuki said impatiently. "Are we going to look for it, or aren't we?"

"Of course we are. That's what we came for. I just like to know what danger looks like before it confronts me," Elizabeth explained.

"You seem to think there's danger in this expedition of ours, don't you?" asked Laura.

"I don't know what to think. You're the one who seems to know the answers, but you're not telling. Hiding your face back there gave you away. You've seen that person who drove down this road and, for some reason, you were afraid he would see you. Why, Laura? Why didn't you want to be recognized?"

Laura hesitated a moment and then replied evasively, "People don't generally enter private estates without an invitation. That's all."

"I'd better turn the car around," Yuki decided, "in case we have to leave in a hurry. I don't expect we'll encounter any danger, but we may be accused of trespassing."

"I'm sure we will be," announced Elizabeth as two figures in dark coats strode down the road toward them. "You drove right by a NO TRESPASSING sign, and this isn't a welcoming committee coming to meet us!"
