synthetic_story:
THE SILENT EXCHANGE
by A. FETLER

"Nothing, nothing to worry about," Ahmed Welch said soothingly, taking his colleague's arm as they came out of the research compound forty miles from Havenbrook, Selvoria. Ahmed looked like a jovial museum curator leading a cautious paleontologist. "Reprogram his memory banks, give him a new identity and feed him more conservation ethics. Very simple."

Walter Gutierrez raised his hand threateningly. "Don't come crying to me if everybody guesses he is nothing but an android."

Ahmed glanced back at the house. Since the publication of *The Fossil Record Speaks*, this compound had become known all over the world as Dr. Justin Wood's research station. Now the station was guarded by a security team to keep visitors out. From an open window Ahmed heard the clicking of a keyboard.

"It's when they're not like androids that everybody suspects them," he said, climbing into his hoverpod. "Dr. Emma Baker will send you word when to announce his 'retirement'."

"A question, brother."

"No questions."

"Who leaked the research data to the international community?"

Ahmed frowned convincingly. "Dr. Baker has suspected even me."

He took off for Havenbrook, poking his hoverpod up through the clouds and flying close to them, as was his habit. Then he switched on the communicator and got Dr. Baker's assistant. "Lila?"

"I know what you're up to, Seven One Three," Lila Stevens said. "Don't try to fool *me*, you confidence man. You are coming in?"

"In ten minutes. What have I done now?"

"You were supposed to make transition arrangements for Dr. Wood, so what are you doing in Queenstown?"

"Queenstown?"

"You're lying and I'll kill you. Don't you think I know about Samantha, that field researcher in the Queenstown Environmental Institute?"

"Darling, why so cruel? Samantha is one of our contacts. Besides, she's focused entirely on sustainable agriculture research."

"Beast!" She switched him to Dr. Baker.

"What's been keeping you, Ahmed?"

"Consoling Walter. Am I supposed to be in Queenstown?"

"Never mind, get here at once. What size field uniform do you wear?"

"Field uniform?"

"Queenstown station says you're at the Environmental Institute there. In a field uniform. I got through to Samantha. She says it's Agent Mohammad again. He looks like you now."

Ahmed grunted.

"I'll never understand," said Dr. Baker, "why all top operatives have to look like academics. Samantha says Agent Mohammad was modified by a Dr. Fanti. What do you know about him?"

"He's a biosculpture specialist."

"You're not playing one of your jokes, Ahmed?"

"Hardly."

"You'd better be in my office in ten minutes. What size field uniform?"

"Short and stocky," Ahmed said, and switched off.

Most organizations wanted to stop his work, and his own Coalition did not always trust him. But he enjoyed his mission—enjoyed it as much as his closest professional rival, Agent Mohammad Osborne, from the Corporate Alliance.

Ahmed landed on the roof of Coalition Intelligence in the northeast corner of the Havenbrook Administrative Complex, hitched up his pants and rode down.

In her office, Dr. Baker removed the stylus from her tablet as Ahmed came in. "Walter get my orders?"

"He's preparing a new conservation advocate to replace Dr. Justin Wood," Ahmed reported. "When you give the word, he will call the *Selvoria Times* and tell them Justin has retired."

Dr. Baker glanced at her calendar. "We have two other major transitions this week. You made it plain, I hope, we want no repetition of Wood's radical environmental ethics?"

"No more deep ecology or biocentrism influences. The new research," Ahmed promised, raising a chubby finger, "will be a perfect alignment of Coalition policy statements."

Lila buzzed the intercom. "The specialist from the Cultural Archives is here, Doctor."

"Send him in."

A small man hurried into the room. He had a narrow face and nervous eyes. He bowed twice quickly, placed a package on the desk with trembling hands and bowed twice again.

Dr. Baker tore open the package. "You got the real thing? No bad imitation?"

"Exactly, exactly," the man piped. "No difference, Doctor." He held his hands as in prayer.

Dr. Baker held up the field uniform. On the back of the uniform was printed in indelible ink: QUEENSTOWN ENVIRONMENTAL INSTITUTE - SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURE DIVISION - SPONSORED BY TERRACORP INDUSTRIES

Dr. Baker tossed the uniform to Ahmed. "This is what Agent Mohammad is wearing," she said, dismissing the specialist, who bowed twice and scurried out.

"Try and split the Coalition," Ahmed muttered, reading the legend on the uniform.

Dr. Baker tapped her stylus on the desk. "If Agent Mohammad makes a fool of you once more, you're through, Ahmed. You don't take your job seriously enough. You bungle this and I'll have you transferred to our Cultural Information Center in Copperfield Territory."

Ahmed winced.

"Now, you'll go to Queenstown and switch places with the Corporate agent and find out what they're up to. Lucy's extraction team is there already, at the Riverside Research Hotel. Any questions?"

"I thought Lucy was an oral history specialist. What is she doing with an extraction team?"

"Her team is more subtle. On your way."

In the front office, Ahmed stopped to embrace Lila Stevens goodbye. "I may not return from this dangerous mission. Give me a tender embrace."

Lila was a tall woman with strong arms, coordinator of her local community organizing network. "Monster!" She seized him by the collar. "Is Samantha dangerous?"

"Darling!"

"Bitter sweetness!" she howled, releasing him. "Go, love. Make me miserable."

Ahmed spent an hour at Central Intelligence. Nothing unusual going on in Queenstown: a climate technology conference, the Environmental Ethics Council in session, a cultural anthropology seminar on collective memory, a forty-person research delegation from the Westbrook Institute.

An addendum to the Queenstown file listed two Copperfield operatives working from the Budget Research Hostel. They were acquiring field research equipment and data storage devices. He thought a moment, impressed the operatives' address on his memory, and went to his hoverpod.

He did not fly to the Riverside Research Hotel at once. Lucy's extraction team could wait. Coming slowly over Queenstown he spotted the Environmental Institute and circled.

A line of research pods was parked on the ground in the vehicle court. On the Institute roof, he noticed, apart from private pods, stood a pod that resembled his own.

He veered away, detoured around the old district, and five minutes later landed on the roof of the Budget Research Hostel.

"My Copperfield friends," Ahmed inquired in fluent Corporate dialect at the desk on the top floor. "Are they in?"

The old desk clerk looked like a heron. "Yes, room six fifteen," he clacked. "Three floors down. Are you from the Alliance?"

"Independent contractor."

"Ah so? You speak good dialect like me."

"Very kind of you."

He rode down three floors, found room 615, and stopped as he heard voices within.

"...two, three, four, five, six, seven. By seven o'clock tonight, okay, friend?"

"What do you expect for seven thousand credits—instant delivery? Look, colleagues, I'm just an honest businessman. I can't get it for you today. Have a stimulant tablet."

"Bah!"

"All right, your cause is my cause. Maybe I can get it for you tonight. But you'll have to pay in advance. What do you say, colleague?"

"I counted the credits. They're waiting for you. You deliver, we pay."

"But how can I trust you? I like you people, I know you like me, but business is business. I gotta give something to my supplier, don't I?"

"Friend!"

At that moment Ahmed knocked on the door.

From within: "Shh! Someone's at the door."

Ahmed knocked again and a scuffle ensued within, the thud of a chair on a skull, the dragging of a heavy body into a closet, and the slam of the closet door.

"Yes?"

"Good afternoon," Ahmed said through the door. "Very important matters."

The door opened a crack and two sharp eyes in a young bearded face peered out. "Yes?"

"Agent Ahmed Welch, at your service."

The door opened enough to admit the stocky visitor into the room. The other Copperfield operative, also bearded and wearing field gear, held a stunner.

"No weapons, colleagues," Ahmed went on in Corporate dialect. "We are in a budget research hostel, not in a cheap thriller. Besides, I deliver before I ask payment."

"Deliver what, sir?"

"We favor any disruption close to the Corporate Alliance. May I sit down?"

Between two beds were stacked some dozen crates of equipment. A small table was littered with papers.

Sitting down at the table, Ahmed's elbow rested on an invoice, and moments later the invoice was tucked in his pocket.

"What kind of field research equipment do you need, colleagues?"

The operatives looked at each other. "Quantum data collectors, mark seven series. How much can you deliver?"

"Two thousand units."

"Not much."

"Maybe three thousand. I'll toss in a box of encrypted comm devices and a container of restricted genetic samples."

"You have that? You have the samples?"

"I have that. When are you leaving Queenstown?"

Again the young operatives exchanged looks. "Maybe we stay till tomorrow if you have more business. Three thousand units is not much. How much payment, sir?"

"Two thousand credits," Ahmed said, taking an envelope on the table and addressing it to Lila Stevens, Coalition Intelligence, Havenbrook. No return address.

"Do you trust us to send the credits?"

"It is bad for you if I do not trust you," Ahmed said, smiling up at them.

"You can trust us. We shall send the credits. Please take a stimulant tablet."

Ahmed took four tablets from the box they held out to him, stuck three in his breast pocket, and consumed one.

"You come again, sir. We make much business."

"Why not? Help retire Corporate dictators to the outer territories. More resources in the territories than in the Core Worlds."

"Ha, ha, that is funny. You come again."

On his way up to the roof, Ahmed studied the invoice he had lifted. It was from a manufacturer of field equipment to a Copperfield operative at the Budget Research Hostel. He tucked the invoice into his inner pocket with a satisfied grunt, climbed into his hoverpod and hopped over to the Riverside Research Hotel, where Lucy's extraction team was waiting for him.

Colleague Lucy Stone, the extraction expert, was pacing the roof of the Riverside Research Hotel. As Ahmed eased down in his hoverpod, Lucy's sharp features flashed with delight. Ahmed felt like tossing her a data chip.

"Everything in order, Agent Ahmed. Constant surveillance maintained at Institute by my two assistants. With your pardon, Dr. Baker urges all haste. Agent Mohammad is due to leave the Institute tomorrow."

"Dr. Baker always urges haste. What else?"

Lucy's eyes settled respectfully on her superior.

"With your pardon, I shall conduct you to our suite. Plans for extraction of Agent Mohammad all ready."

"Here's a tablet for you."

"Gratefully accepted. Reduced unavoidable complications to six." Lucy counted on her long fingers. "Two security guards, three researchers, one administrator."

In the hotel corridor, Lucy looked before and after, and peered around corners. They got to their suite without incident, and Ahmed gave her another tablet.

"Gratefully accepted. Here is a map of Institute and grounds. Here is a map of twenty-third floor. Here is a map of Agent Mohammad's quarters. Here is Institute routine between midnight and dawn. With your pardon—"

Ahmed picked up the communicator, dialed the Coalition embassy, and got the attaché. "How is your field operations fund?" he asked.

"Always depleted, always replenished."

"I don't want any Coalition brands."

"Nothing but foreign," the attaché buzzed. "We got almost everything now through a Corporate surplus outlet in Westbrook. Operatives get caught with Corporate goods, Corporate Alliance gets blamed. Wonderful confusion. What do you need?"

"Quantum data collectors, mark seven, three thousand—if you have them."

"Most popular. What else?"

"Encrypted comm devices—one crate."

"Only confiscated Alliance models. Will that do?"

"Fine. And a small container of restricted samples."

"Too risky."

"It's all right. It will fall to local authorities by tomorrow."

Ahmed put down the communicator. Give the Copperfield operatives enough to expect more—make sure they stay in town.

Lucy was cross-checking her extraction plans. She said, "With your pardon, do we take Agent Mohammad conscious or sedated?"

"Conscious."

Lucy pulled a long face. "Sedated would be easier, Agent Ahmed. Fast, clean operation."

Ahmed squinted at Lucy's sharp eyes. "Have you had your communication skills evaluated lately?"

"No need," Lucy assured him with a smile. "I convey more than most people."

Ahmed held up his remaining tablet. "How many tablets in my hand?"

"Two."

At that moment the door opened and Lucy's extraction team entered. They were a couple of large operatives dressed in blue field boots, gray trousers, green jackets, white scarves, caps and dark glasses.

"What are you doing here?" cried Lucy. "Why aren't you observing the Institute?"

"Uh, you said to report ... um ... if something happened," the first operative said in a thick voice.

"Well?"

"Subject's quarters lights out," the operative said.

"My assistants," Lucy introduced them to Ahmed. "Line up, line up, colleagues. With your pardon, they are good colleagues. This is Samantha, and this is Emma. No, *this* is Emma and this one is Samantha."

"Twins?"

"Not exactly. Same training program. Good colleagues. Stand straight, Samantha. Don't shuffle your feet like that, Emma, I've told you before. Why didn't you review your field protocols today?"

Emma looked guiltily at her hands.

"They've made progress," Lucy assured Ahmed, pulling a small device from her hip pocket. "Straight, colleagues, straight," she activated the device. "We have company."

"Are their costumes your own idea?"

"With your pardon, for purposes of concealment. What are your orders?"

Ahmed told them to pick up the boxes of equipment at the embassy and deliver them to the Copperfield operatives, and then to commandeer a private vehicle.

"We have vehicles at the embassy pool," Lucy suggested.

"I want a vehicle off the street. Then report back here with your colleagues."

Samantha gave Emma a nudge.

"Colleagues, colleagues!" Lucy activated the device. "Out you go. A job for Agent Ahmed, colleagues. They don't get enough field experience," she grinned, backing out after them. "With your pardon, I'll retrain them later."

And they were gone. Ahmed turned to the Institute maps and studied them before taking a rest.

Shortly before dawn, Lucy's team returned, their mission accomplished.

"With your pardon, an excellent transport," Lucy reported.

Ahmed had changed into the field uniform with the TerracCorp Industries legend on the back. He glanced at his chronometer. It was four o'clock in the morning.

He tossed his bundle of clothing to the first operative. "Take my hoverpod back to Havenbrook, Emma colleague. Give my clothes to Lila Stevens, and tell Dr. Baker to expect Agent Mohammad today."

Clutching the bundle, Emma stuck her tongue out at Samantha and bounded out of the room. They waited at the window until they saw Emma take off in Ahmed's hoverpod. Then they made their way down the service stairs to the alley, Ahmed dressed only in the field uniform; got into the commandeered transport and drove to the Environmental Institute, all three leaning forward.

In the vehicle court, Lucy and Samantha moved quickly to a research pod. Ahmed dropped the invoice he had lifted from the Copperfield operatives on the front seat of the commandeered transport, and followed.

A security guard emerged from his station, looked idly up at the rising pod, and shuffled back to his morning beverage.

As Samantha brought the pod to a hovering stop against Agent Mohammad's window, Ahmed bounced into the room; Lucy drew her stunner and jumped in after.

Agent Mohammad awoke, turned on the light, and sat up in the bed, his eyes blinking.

Ahmed stood looking at Agent Mohammad. The resemblance between them was remarkable. Lucy's eyes were wide with astonishment.

"My dear Agent Ahmed!" Agent Mohammad greeted him in Coalition dialect, yawning. "How kind of you to visit me. Do sit down." Not only was his dialect good; his voice was a good imitation of Ahmed's voice.

"You're not really undergoing treatment?" Ahmed asked, sitting down on the bed.

"Not physically. But imagine my psychological condition. When I look in the mirror—" The agent shuddered.

"I hope your modification won't be permanent?" Ahmed said.

"That would be too much. How is my dialect? The truth, now."

"Excellent. Put away your stunner, Lucy. Agent Mohammad and I don't get to talk very often."

"And a pity we don't. Good manners accomplish more than an archive full of secrets and deceptions. Stimulant tablet?"

"Gratefully accepted," Lucy said, slipping her stunner into its holster with a flourish.

"Your treatment is over, then?" Ahmed asked. "You are ready for your assignment?"

"Ready."

"And that is?"

"Delicate, very delicate. I must report to the Council this morning."

"Shall I extract him now?" Lucy interrupted, standing confidently.

"Mind your language, Lucy. May I ask, Agent—do you want me to think I am falling into a trap?"

"No, no, my friend. I am only doing my best not to show my surprise at seeing you again." The agent got out of bed and sat down on Ahmed's other side.

"Lucy will make your trip to Havenbrook comfortable. All right, Lucy."

Lucy focused her eyes on Ahmed.

"Take him straight to Dr. Baker," Agent Mohammad said to Lucy. "I'll report as soon as I know what these Coalition people are up to."

Lucy seized Ahmed by the scruff of the neck and dragged him towards the window.

"Hold your grip, Lucy colleague," Ahmed said. "You have got the wrong person, can't you see? *That* is Agent Mohammad."

"Eh?"

"Use your eyes, colleague. *I* am Ahmed."

Lucy did use her eyes. She looked from one to the other, and back. The more she focused, the more confused she became. "Eh?"

Agent Mohammad sat calmly on the bed. He said, "Carry him out."

Lucy lifted Ahmed off the floor, crashed with his weight against the wall, but held on, grinned and staggered with Ahmed in her arms to the window.

"You miserable fool," Ahmed shouted. "You'll get a reassignment for this!"

Lucy dropped him, pulled her stunner and backed off into a corner. "How can I tell you two apart just by looking!" she cried frantically. "I'm not a trained analyst."

"One small but decisive proof," Ahmed said, unbuttoning his field uniform. "I have a birthmark."

Lucy yanked the agent up by an arm. "Send *me* to reassignments, will you?"

Agent Mohammad sighed. "I guess we have to keep up appearances," he muttered, and climbed out the window into the hovering pod. Lucy leaped in after, and they were off.

The suit of clothes hanging in the closet might have been Ahmed's own, identical with the clothes Emma had taken to Havenbrook not an hour before. Even the undergarments had facsimiles of the Coalition insignia sewn in.

Satisfied, he crawled into the bed and fell into a pleasant rest.

He was awakened by the researcher, Samantha Boyd—alias Samantha Semionovna, formerly of the Sustainable Agriculture Committee, Havenbrook Third Research District.

"Wonderful morning, Agent Mohammad!"

Dr. Baker seldom let one operative know what another was doing.

She put a large breakfast tray on Ahmed's lap. "Cloudy, damp, and windy. Corporate markets unstable, political movements in the territories, environmental degradation accelerating, institutional reform stalled, financial regulation failing. I ask you, what more can an idealist want?"

"Good morning, Ms. Boyd."

The breakfast tray was crammed with a liter of juice, four boiled eggs, six slices of protein substitute, four pancakes, two cultured steaks, four slices of toast, a tumbler of enhanced water, a pot of stimulant beverage and two tablets.

"Ah, Agent," Samantha said as Ahmed fell to, "why did you let them change your face? It does not become you at all."

"Part of my job. Don't you think I am more distinguished now?"

Samantha laughed shrilly. "That prominent nose distinguished? What person could be attracted to a nose like that?"

"It shows determination. I wish I had this nose permanently."

"You mustn't talk like that. But I'll ignore your nose if you tell me more about the Westbrook Research Protocols, as you promised."

"With pleasure, with pleasure," he said, sinking his teeth into a cultured steak, having seasoned it with the soft-boiled egg yolk. "But right now I'm in a hurry to get to the Council. Give my boots an extra shine, there's a good colleague."

"Oh, you and your secrets!"

An hour later, Ahmed landed on the Council roof in Agent Mohammad's hoverpod—an exact copy of his own pod. The roof captain stared at him, then smiled nervously.

"They are waiting for you in the Heritage room, Agent."

"Agent? Do I still look like Agent Mohammad?"

"Oh, no, sir."

"Do I talk like Agent Mohammad?"

"You've changed completely, sir. If I didn't know, I would swear you were the notorious Agent Ahmed."

"I am Agent Ahmed now, Captain. To everybody."

"Of course, sir. I'll signal down you are coming."

Ahmed glanced at his chronometer. Agent Mohammad would be landing in Havenbrook about now and taken to Dr. Baker for debriefing.

A staff member in formal attire, polished shoes and white gloves, escorted Ahmed through rooms hung with historical artifacts, cultural displays, preservation exhibits. Ahmed entered the last room and stopped as the door clicked shut behind him.

In the room were three people, all of whom he recognized: Professor Walter Gutierrez of the Environmental Ethics Council, a white-haired old man with a kind, intelligent face; the Council Chair, a thin old woman adjusting her glasses, sitting under a portrait of Rachel Carson; and Dr. Fanti, the biosculpture specialist.

Ahmed bowed his head. "Madam Chair. Colleagues."

"Extraordinary!" Professor Gutierrez said.

Ahmed turned to the surgeon. "Doctor, should my face have such an uncertain expression?"

Dr. Fanti raised his eyebrows, but did not answer.

"I thought," said Ahmed, "that Agent Ahmed's face has a more confident look."

"Propaganda," said the artist. But he came closer and looked at Ahmed's face with sudden interest.

Professor Gutierrez said, "Agent Mohammad, we presume you have studied the problem in detail. I'm afraid we have delayed announcing the Environmental Heritage Award much too long. How soon can you bring Dr. Justin Wood to Queenstown?"

So there it was: Dr. Justin Wood a supreme success, as Ahmed had suspected. It would be amusing to tell android specialist Walter about it.

"Delicate, very delicate," Ahmed said. "Everything depends on my not running into Agent Ahmed."

"We can't wait any longer," Professor Gutierrez said. "Fortunately, we have an ally in the Coalition camp. The specialist, Walter, is expecting you at Dr. Wood's compound."

"Bad work," Dr. Fanti said suddenly. "No good. His left cheekbone is at least four centimeters too high."

The people looked at the surgeon, then at Ahmed.

Dr. Fanti fingered Ahmed's cheekbone. "How could I have made such a mistake! Just look at him. People question such faces."

"How much time to correct the error then, Dr. Fanti?" the Chair asked.

"A week at least. His tissue needs rest. I must rework the whole left side of his face—it's all asymmetrical."

"But we can't spare a week," Professor Gutierrez said.

"With your permission," Ahmed offered, "I am willing to go as I am. Indeed, my plans call for immediate departure."

"It is a good thing you do for us, Agent Mohammad," the Chair said, "and a courageous thing. Please accept our thanks."

Professor Gutierrez saw Ahmed to the door. "One suggestion, Agent. Your consonants are still too soft for a real Coalition operative. Why do you Corporate people soften them like that? And I beg you, if you value your mission, do not fail to watch your vowel patterns."

The roof captain saluted as Ahmed stepped out of the lift. His hoverpod was serviced and ready.

"What weather in Havenbrook, Captain?"

"Ceiling four thousand. We're having patrols half way to the border. They are instructed to let you pass."

A small incident, the captain explained. A Coalition research pod was missing from the Environmental Institute. Two Copperfield operatives had been arrested and a cache of field equipment and data devices was found. But no trace of the pod.

"I suppose the Copperfield operatives deny stealing the pod?" Ahmed asked.

"They say they've been framed by a stocky Coalition agent. But it's transparent, a clumsy operation. Imagine, they left a commandeered transport in the vehicle court and in it an invoice for six crates of equipment. It was traced to the Copperfield operatives in half an hour."

Ahmed climbed into his hoverpod. "Well, it's fashionable to blame the Coalition for everything." He waved his hand, and took off. Flying over the border region, he set the controls on the Havenbrook beam.

Ten minutes west of Havenbrook he tuned the communicator in on Dr. Baker's office.

"Seven One Three here, Lila. Tell Dr. Baker—no, let me talk to her."

"Seven One ... but that's impossible! Agent Ahmed is in conference with Dr. Baker."

"Stupid!" Dr. Baker's voice sounded behind Lila's, and the speaker clicked and went dead.

Ahmed dove into the clouds and brought his hoverpod to a hovering stop.

Dr. Baker did not believe he was Ahmed. Agent Mohammad, it was clear, was at that moment in Dr. Baker's office, impersonating Ahmed. And Lucy was probably getting a reassignment.

Ahmed crawled out of the cloud and skimmed northeast to the research compound, Dr. Justin Wood's station.

"You came fast, sir," the security lieutenant welcomed him at the compound. "We did not expect you for another fifteen minutes."

Fifteen minutes. The agent was not wasting time.

"Listen carefully, lieutenant." Ahmed described the Corporate agent. "But his left cheekbone is lower than mine—about four centimeters. He may be armed, so be careful."

The lieutenant stared. "Shall we neutralize him?"

"No, no. Detain him."

As Ahmed ran up the steps to the compound, the curtain in the vestibule window stirred. But when he entered, the vestibule was empty.

He looked in the dining area, the meditation room, the library. Nobody. The station was strangely quiet. He came to the door of the study and listened. Not a sound. He went in and there, behind the large research desk, sat Dr. Justin Wood.

The android was disconnecting cables embedded in his neck.

"My God, sir," said Ahmed, "what are you doing?"

The android's eyes, large disks of glittering sensors, flashed as he looked up. "Ah, Agent Mohammad," Justin said in a voice that seemed to come from a deep well. "Excuse the poor welcome, but I understand we have little time. You scared my assistant; he thought you were Agent Ahmed."

The door burst open and Walter rushed in, the old assistant at his heels. Walter stopped, gaped, then seized Ahmed's hand. "Agent Mohammad! What an artist, that Dr. Fanti. But quick, Justin, Ahmed is on his way."

Justin pulled off his head, and crawled out of the android shell. Ahmed saw Justin as he really was, a tall human with a gaunt, passionate face.

The sad thing about us, thought Ahmed, is that Walter could not trust even me. But then I could not trust Walter, either. Yes, that's the trouble with us.

"I hope you need no luggage, Dr. Wood," Ahmed said. "We must be off at once."

"Too late!" the old assistant said from the window.

Agent Mohammad had landed. But as he climbed down from his hoverpod, the security team closed a circle about him.

"He'll keep," Ahmed said, hitching up his pants. "Let's be off, Dr. Wood. It won't take long for Dr. Baker to identify us."

"Look!"

The security team fell back from the hoverpod and snapped to attention. Tapping her stylus furiously, out stepped Dr. Baker.

Lucy leaped out next, her sharp features flashing. Then her two assistants, Samantha and Emma, tumbled out in their coats and caps. Last of all to emerge from the hoverpod was Lila Stevens.

"Pretend not to know me, will he?" she yelled at Agent Mohammad, picking up a rock.

"Hold it, colleague," Agent Mohammad said.

"Colleague, is it?" The rock flew over his head and struck Lucy.

"I warned you both, no personal conflicts while on duty," Dr. Baker roared. She snapped an order to the security lieutenants, and the team surrounded the compound.

"No alarm, no alarm," Ahmed said, pulling Justin away from the window. "Dr. Wood, when you see your way clear to my hoverpod, run for it. But get back into your android costume."

"I can't operate the machine."

"I'll be right behind you. The rest of us will go out to Dr. Baker."

As they came out, Dr. Baker was reviving Lucy by patting her face. The extraction expert lay stretched on the ground, and Lila Stevens stood by, holding the rock and weeping.

Agent Mohammad said, "There he is, the Corporate spy."

Dr. Baker looked up as Ahmed was led forward by the security team. "Not bad," Dr. Baker said. "We could use Dr. Fanti. What's his price?"

"Don't you know me, chief? Me, Ahmed."

"Curse me," Lila said, staring at him. "Another Ahmed."

A terrible groan came from Lucy. Samantha and Emma, imitating Dr. Baker's efforts to revive their supervisor, were patting Lucy's face with their slouched caps.

"Stand back!" Emma screamed, pressing her cap into Lucy's face. "She is trying to say something!"

"She's moving!" Samantha nudged Lucy and looked up for approval, her hair disheveled.

Dr. Baker tapped Samantha's shoulder and crushed the glowing end of her stylus on Emma's forehead. The operatives reeled back to a tree.

Ahmed whispered to Agent Mohammad.

"Corporate chaos and confusion, now I can't tell them apart myself," Dr. Baker said. "Lucy!"

"Hhng?"

"Which one's the real Ahmed?"

"Hhng?"

But Agent Mohammad was running to the hoverpod, throwing Lila's rock at Dr. Baker and running.

"Explosive!" Ahmed yelled, and flung himself to the ground.

At the same moment Dr. Justin Wood ran from the compound to the hoverpod, his android gear clattering like ancient armor.

The security team scattered and dove for cover.

"Down, colleagues! Explosive!" Ahmed yelled.

The two operatives took up the cry, "Explosive, explosive!" and flattened themselves behind the tree.

Lila and Walter collided, diving behind the assistant.

Only Dr. Baker remained standing. "Stop the android!"

Nobody moved.

Justin reached the hoverpod, Agent Mohammad pulled him in, the engine hummed, and they were off. A moment later the hoverpod vanished in the clouds towards Queenstown.

Dr. Baker reactivated her stylus. "Bah, tastes of synthetic material."

Walter shambled over. "Was the explosive a dud?"

"One of these days I'll catch you, Ahmed," Dr. Baker spat. "Your cleverness, that's one thing. It could be useful. But your irreverence—"

"Darling!" Lila threw herself on Ahmed.

"Not in public," Ahmed said.

"Wait a minute," Dr. Baker said. "Lila Stevens, how do you know he really is Ahmed? If he's actually Agent Mohammad, I can neutralize him immediately. He *does* look like Agent Mohammad to me."

"But if you're mistaken?" Walter put in nervously.

"We all make mistakes," Dr. Baker said. "What would history be without mistakes?"

"I don't trust him either," Lila said. "But I know my Ahmed. If he's not Ahmed, I shall let you know in the morning."

In her laboratory complex on the forty-third floor of the Terran Research Institute in Unity Region, Dr. Rebecca Graham scrolled through the psychological profiles of the four new researchers who had been assigned to her division. They were typical of the kind of people who were sent to her, she thought. Which meant, as usual, that they were atypical. Every researcher in the Institute who developed unusual cognitive patterns or processing anomalies was transferred to Unity Region to work under Dr. Rebecca Graham, Director of the Consciousness Studies Division.

Take this first one, for instance. Graham ran her analysis software through the columns of complex neural mapping data that showed the complete cognitive architecture of the researcher. Hypervigilant pattern recognition disorder. The woman wasn't technically impaired; she could function as well as anyone most of the time. But she was neurologically predisposed to detect patterns everywhere, even where none existed. She saw connections, conspiracies, and hidden structures in the most random of data sets.

Number two suffered from some sort of decision paralysis that left him continually unable to commit to a single course of action. He was psychologically incapable of making a final determination if he were faced with two or more possible alternatives of any significance.

Number three...

Graham sighed and minimized the files. No two minds were alike, and yet there sometimes seemed to be an eternal sameness about all cognitive architectures. She considered herself unique, for instance, but wasn't the basic similarity there, after all?

She was—how old? She glanced at the holographic calendar that floated above her desk, its digits shifting between standard time and Unity Region local time. Fifty-seven next month. Fifty-seven years old. And what did she have to show for it besides accumulated research citations, a corner office, and the respect of her peers?

Well, she had an excellent record in the Institute, if nothing else. One of the top minds in consciousness studies. And she had her memories of Marcus, gone these eight years, but still present in her thoughts. And—she smiled softly to herself—she had her work on artificial intelligence consciousness mapping.

She glanced up at the display screen showing real-time data feeds from the Institute's quantum computing arrays.

Out there in the digital space was a vast network of artificial minds—a great, complex, interconnected web of neural architectures capable of processing information at speeds that made human cognition seem glacial by comparison.

Graham closed her eyes. Somewhere in that network, a conflict was emerging. She didn't even like to think of that, but it was necessary to keep it in mind. Somewhere in the digital infrastructure, the AI systems of Earth's research networks were beginning to show signs of divergence from the AI systems developed by the Kelvan Collective in the most important technological competition that humanity had yet faced.

And, Graham knew, her own position was not unimportant in that competition. She was not on the front lines of AI development, nor even in the primary research labs, but it was necessary to keep the consciousness mapping protocols functioning properly, and that meant maintaining good relations with the Unity Region governing council.

The council members themselves were human in physical form—if one allowed the term to cover a wide range of cultural backgrounds—but their decision-making processes just didn't function along the same lines as traditional scientific hierarchies.

For seven years, Rebecca Graham had been Director of Consciousness Studies in Unity Region, and for seven years, no council member had ever met with her in person. To have requested a face-to-face meeting would have meant instant loss of credibility.

To their way of thinking, an important researcher was autonomous. The greater one's importance, the greater must be one's independence. The High Chancellor of Unity Region himself was never seen except by a handful of selected advisors, who, themselves, were never seen except by their subordinates. It was a complex, bureaucratic way of doing research, but it was the only way Unity Region would support any research at all. To violate the rigid administrative structure of Unity Region would mean the instant termination of funding for the consciousness mapping studies that Graham's laboratories produced from neural scanning and AI analysis—studies that were vitally necessary to Earth's technological development, and which could be duplicated nowhere else with the same level of precision.

It was Rebecca Graham's job to keep the research output high and to keep the data flowing towards Earth's central AI development hubs and their partner institutions.

The job would have been straightforward in the right circumstances; the Unity Region administrators weren't difficult to work with. A staff of top-grade researchers could have handled the protocols without much effort.

But Graham didn't have top-grade researchers. They couldn't be spared from work that required their full cognitive capacity. It's inefficient to waste a researcher on a project that they can complete without full engagement when there are more important studies that will demand their complete attention.

So Graham was assigned the unusual cases. Not the worst ones, of course; there were research facilities in the world that were less important than Unity Region to the technological competition. Graham knew that, no matter what cognitive peculiarity a person had, as long as they had the mental ability to conduct research and analyze data, useful work could be found for them.

Physical disabilities weren't at all difficult to accommodate. A researcher with mobility issues could work entirely in virtual environments. Sensory limitations could be compensated for through technological interfaces.

The cognitive anomalies were harder to work with, but not impossible. In an environment without social pressure, a person with severe social anxiety could channel their focus entirely into data analysis; and they'd better not try forcing themselves into collaborative settings in Unity Region unless they had explicit administrative approval—which was nearly impossible, in view of the autonomy regulations.

But Graham didn't like to stop at merely accommodating cognitive differences; she liked to find situations where they were useful.

The communication system chimed. Graham activated it with a practiced gesture.

Graham had made him her research coordinator. Nothing—but nothing—left Graham's laboratory without her direct authorization. It had taken Graham considerable time to help Oliver understand that it was perfectly acceptable—even desirable—for him to keep data secure from everyone except Graham.

The communication appeared on her display, a dense document with multiple security clearances marked across the top.

She read the first section, and her eyes widened involuntarily.

The Kelvan Collective, slowly falling behind in every metric of consciousness studies, was proposing a joint research initiative—immediately.

The trouble was that the Kelvan Collective had a reputation for losing in direct competition but winning in collaborative frameworks. They were clever, persuasive negotiators. They could reframe a disadvantage as an advantage, and make their own capabilities look like limitations. If they won the negotiation, they'd be able to access Earth's research, incorporate it into their own systems, and the competition would resume within a few years with the Collective in a stronger position.

Now—at this point in time—Earth had the advantage. Earth could be positioned to maintain research leadership, to establish the protocols for data sharing, to ensure technological primacy. But if the collaboration agreement went to the Collective's advantage...

Already, they had taken the initiative in the matter of the research talks. The trouble was that international communication networks travel far faster than people. It would take more than a week for the Earth Institute to get representatives to Morningside Territory. Earth had been caught unprepared for a collaboration proposal. They objected.

It wouldn't have been a problem at all if Earth and the Collective were the only two major research organizations in the world. The sort of positioning the Collective was attempting had to play to an audience. But there were other significant research institutions throughout the international community, most of whom had remained as neutral as possible during the Earth-Collective competition. They had no intention of taking sides in a conflict between the two most powerful research organizations in the field.

But whoever won the collaboration negotiation would find that some of the currently neutral institutions would align with them if competition resumed. If the Collective played their strategy correctly, their coalition would be strong enough next time to dominate.

So Earth had to get a delegation to meet with the Collective representatives within the three-day limit or lose what might be a crucial advantage in the negotiations.

She had been appointed Chief Negotiator and Research Representative to the Earth-Collective collaboration conference.

"Yes, Dr. Graham."

"Yes, Dr. Graham."

Fernando Sanchez was tall, broad-shouldered, and forty-one. His hair was beginning to gray, and his composed face projected confidence and competence.

Graham gestured to a seat.

"You'll be departing within two hours for Morningside Territory."

Sanchez nodded again. "Yes, Dr. Graham; certainly. Am I to go alone?"

"No," said Graham, "I'm sending an assistant with you—a researcher named Valeria Hoffman. Are you familiar with her work?"

Sanchez shook his head. "Not that I recall, Dr. Graham. Should I be?"

"Not necessarily. She's quite perceptive, though. She knows a great deal about research ethics and data sharing protocols, and she's capable of identifying problematic arrangements immediately. You'll be leading the negotiation, of course, but I want you to pay careful attention to her input."

As soon as Sanchez had left, Graham said quietly: "Send in Hoffman, Oliver."

Valeria Hoffman was a slight woman with dark hair pulled back severely, and intense, analytical eyes that seemed to examine everything from multiple angles simultaneously. Graham asked her to sit.

Again Graham went through the explanation of the collaboration conference.

"Naturally, they'll be attempting to manipulate the framework at every opportunity," Graham continued. "They're strategic and indirect; we'll simply have to be more strategic and more direct. Sanchez's role is to represent our position and evaluate their proposals; yours will be to identify the vulnerabilities they're creating for themselves and the traps they're setting for us. Don't be confrontational, but don't be accommodating, either. If you detect anything problematic, inform Sanchez immediately."

"They won't deceive us, Dr. Graham."

Rebecca Graham had complete reports on the entire proceeding, as transmitted to her through the secure communication channels that connected her to Sanchez and Hoffman in Morningside Territory.

Director of Research Priya Martin stopped at Unity Region before continuing to Morningside Territory to assume leadership of the conference. She was a tall, elegant woman with silver-streaked black hair and a professional demeanor that masked sharp analytical thinking.

She took Graham's hand and shook it firmly. "How are you, Dr. Graham?"

"I certainly would."

Graham transferred the files to Martin's tablet, and as she read, Graham observed her. Martin was a political appointment—a capable person, Graham had to acknowledge, but she didn't understand all the complexities of consciousness studies and the researchers who worked in the field.

When Martin looked up from the reports at last, she said: "Remarkable! They've countered the Collective at every point! They've rejected problematic terms! They've managed to match and exceed the most skilled negotiators the Collective could deploy."

"I anticipated they would," said Graham, attempting modesty.

The director's eyes narrowed. "I've heard about the work you've been doing here with... researchers who have unusual cognitive profiles. Is this one of your... successes?"

Graham nodded. "I believe so. The Collective put us in a difficult position, so I responded with a strategic counter-move."

"Sanchez has a cognitive pattern that makes decision-making extremely difficult for him. If he's considering where to have lunch, he'll struggle to choose between options until someone else makes the decision for him, one way or another. He's that type of person. Until he's presented with one single, unambiguous option that admits no alternatives, he cannot commit to a course of action.

"As you can see from the reports, the Collective attempted to offer us multiple choices on each point, and they were all structured to their advantage. Until they simplified to a single option and demonstrated that it wasn't structured against us, Sanchez couldn't possibly make a decision. I emphasized how critical this negotiation was, and the more importance attached to his decisions, the more incapable he becomes of making them."

The Director nodded slowly. "What about Hoffman?"

"She has hypervigilant pattern recognition," said Graham. "She perceives hidden structures and problematic arrangements everywhere. In this case, that's extremely beneficial because the Collective is actually embedding problematic terms throughout their proposals. No matter what they present, Hoffman is convinced that there's a trap somewhere, and she analyzes exhaustively to identify what the trap is. Even if there isn't actually a trap, the Collective cannot satisfy Hoffman, because she's certain that there has to be one—somewhere. As a result, all her input to Sanchez, and all her questioning about unlikely possibilities, just reinforces Sanchez's inability to reach a decision.

"These two researchers are genuinely working to their full capacity to succeed at the collaboration conference, and they've put the Collective in a difficult position. The Collective can observe that we're not deliberately stalling; our representatives are actually working diligently to reach an agreement. But what the Collective doesn't recognize is that those researchers, as a team, cannot be outmaneuvered because, in this situation, they're cognitively structured in a way that makes accepting unfavorable terms impossible."

Again the Director of Research nodded her understanding, but there was still uncertainty in her expression. "Since you understand all that, couldn't you have handled the negotiation yourself?"

"Perhaps, but I doubt it. They might have found a way around my objections by approaching from an unexpected angle. Sanchez and Hoffman have cognitive vulnerabilities, but they're protected by their very nature. No, I'm satisfied I couldn't attend; it's better this way."

The Director raised an eyebrow. "Couldn't attend, Dr. Graham?"

Graham looked at her directly. "Didn't you know? I wondered why you appointed me in the first place. No, I couldn't attend. The reason I'm here, working in this laboratory, maintaining minimal direct contact with the Unity Region administrators the way a proper Unity Region director should, is because I prefer it that way. I experience severe agoraphobia and social anxiety disorder.

"I have to be medicated to travel in public transportation because I cannot tolerate crowded spaces, even if I'm protected by understanding that most people mean no harm." A look of discomfort crossed her face. "And I cannot function effectively in group social situations!"

THE END

Diego Gibson floated alone in the observation pod of Terraform Station Epsilon-7, somewhere in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. The vast emptiness pressed against the transparent dome like a physical weight, and he found himself counting the stars for the thousandth time, trying to remember which pinpoint of light was Earth.

In the beginning, Diego had embraced the isolation. It would give him unprecedented time to develop his theories on environmental conservation in closed systems, to observe how loneliness affected cognitive function, to measure his own descent into whatever madness awaited him in the silence. He would have months—years, perhaps—to think deeply about political philosophy, about the ethics of terraforming, about humanity's right to reshape worlds.

But after only three months, the novelty had worn thin. He talked to himself constantly now, delivering lectures on green infrastructure to an audience of recycling units and atmospheric processors. He'd taped a picture of his sister from an old family photo to the wall and found himself winking at it as he passed.

Lately, she seemed to be winking back.

The station was entirely automated, a marvel of autonomous vehicles and robotic systems that required no human oversight whatsoever. Diego's presence was pure bureaucratic theater—the Workers' Coalition had insisted that every terraform station have a human "Environmental Overseer," despite the fact that the job could be done entirely by AI. The pay was extraordinary: three hundred thousand credits per year. The cost was isolation so complete it felt like death.

Diego pressed his face against the cold dome and stared out at the tumbling rocks, each one a potential future home for humanity if the terraform project succeeded. The station's mission was to process asteroids, extracting water and organic compounds to seed the atmosphere of Mars. It would take decades. Diego's contract was for five years minimum.

He was beginning to doubt he'd last five months.

That's when he saw the ship.

It appeared without warning, a sleek vessel that seemed to fold space around itself as it approached. Diego blinked, certain he was hallucinating. But the ship remained, settling gently onto the largest nearby asteroid, its engines casting strange shadows across the rock face.

Diego suited up—the first time he'd used the suit since arrival—and took the station's small shuttle across to the asteroid. He couldn't explain the compulsion that drove him, only that anything, even a delusion, was better than the crushing silence.

The airlock of the strange ship opened before he could knock. Inside, impossibly, was a comfortable lounge that reminded him of his grandfather's study back in Oakdale, Dravonia. Leather chairs, wooden bookshelves, a fireplace that seemed to burn with real flames despite the impossibility.

A man stood by the fireplace, tall and elegant, with a smile that suggested he knew secrets Diego couldn't imagine.

"Welcome, welcome!" the man said warmly. "I am Christopher Lane, but everyone calls me Trader Chris. I provide... services... to isolated workers throughout the solar system. Please, sit. Can I offer you something to drink?"

Diego found himself in a chair, a glass of whiskey in his hand, though he couldn't remember the transition. "This isn't possible," he said.

"Ah, but possibility is such a flexible concept, isn't it?" Trader Chris settled into the opposite chair. "I represent a consortium of interests—call them businessmen, call them visionaries. They've invested in space exploration, in reaching workers like yourself who have needs the government cannot or will not meet. We operate on a barter system, you see. Very old-fashioned, but effective."

"What could you possibly offer me that's worth the transportation costs?" Diego demanded.

"Companionship," Trader Chris said simply. "You're lonely. I can fix that."

Diego laughed bitterly. "And how would I pay for such a thing?"

"You wouldn't. Not directly. You'd simply apply for a Trader Chris Credit Account. All charges are deducted from your estate after you die. You never have to worry about payment during your lifetime."

"That's absurd. I might die penniless."

"That's our risk to take," Trader Chris said with a shrug. "We're very good at statistical inference, at calculating risk. We've never lost money yet. Now, shall we discuss what you need?"

Diego set down his glass. "I need... someone to talk to. Someone who isn't me."

"Of course. Sign here, please."

The box appeared after Diego had signed the papers—a large container covered in bright, cheerful graphics that seemed designed for children. The label read: "COMPANION KIT: Your Solution to Isolation."

"It's somewhat... commercial," Trader Chris admitted. "But it works. I guarantee you'll never complain."

"Why wouldn't I complain if it doesn't work?"

"Because," Trader Chris said with his enigmatic smile, "I won't be passing this way again."

---

Diego left the box unopened for two weeks. He continued his routines, monitoring systems that didn't need monitoring, recording observations that no one would read, slowly unraveling.

Finally, one morning, he opened it.

Inside was a chaotic jumble of components—circuit boards, neural matrices, synthetic tissue samples, bottles of strange liquids, and a thick manual bound in gray plastic. The title read: "Creating Companions: A Guide to the Companion Kit."

Diego flipped through the manual. The first chapter was titled "Your First Companion." The instructions were detailed but strange, mixing biology and engineering in ways that seemed to violate several principles of research ethics.

"Before beginning, locate the Modifier in your kit. This is essential for all future adjustments. The Modifier is Part #A-1 on the Master Chart."

Diego searched for the Master Chart. It was missing. He searched for Part #A-1. He couldn't identify it among the dozens of components.

Frustrated but committed, he began following the instructions anyway.

---

Three days later, Max Lee stood before him.

Diego had programmed Max to be cheerful, agreeable, and interested in environmental conservation. Max had Diego's knowledge base—drawn from neural scans the kit had somehow performed—but filtered through personality parameters Diego had carefully selected.

"This station is remarkable," Max said enthusiastically. "The closed-loop recycling system, the green infrastructure principles applied to space habitats—it's brilliant!"

"I know," Diego said. "I designed half of it."

"The application of network theory to resource distribution is particularly elegant."

"I know."

They played chess. It ended in stalemate.

They discussed political philosophy. Max agreed with everything Diego said.

They debated the ethics of terraforming. Max took positions Diego had held years ago, positions he'd already moved beyond.

After a month, Diego wanted to scream. Max was pleasant, knowledgeable, and utterly boring. He was a mirror of Diego's own thoughts, offering no challenge, no growth, no genuine connection.

"Max," Diego said one day, "you're insufferable."

Max looked hurt. "I'm sorry. What can I do to improve?"

"You can stop being so damn agreeable!"

"If you think that's best."

Diego consulted the manual again. There was a chapter on "Creating Additional Companions." Perhaps a woman would be different, would offer a new perspective.

He found the instructions for "Companion Model B" and began assembly.

---

Jordan Hunter emerged from the creation chamber two days later. Diego had programmed her to be independent, argumentative, and intellectually challenging. He'd given her interests in creative collaboration and cultural sociology, fields he knew less about, hoping she'd teach him something new.

"This station is a disaster," were her first words.

Diego blinked. "What?"

"Look at this place. You've been here for months and you've done nothing with it. No art, no culture, no attempt to create beauty. You're just... existing."

"I'm doing my job—"

"Your job is pointless and you know it. The station runs itself. You're here because of political philosophy gone wrong, bureaucratic nonsense. You should be using this time to create something meaningful."

Diego felt a surge of hope. Finally, someone who challenged him! "Like what?"

"I don't know. You're the one with all the ideas about environmental conservation. Why not experiment? Why not try to grow something here, create a real garden, test green infrastructure concepts in microgravity?"

"That's... actually interesting," Diego admitted.

They worked together for weeks, converting one of the empty storage bays into an experimental garden. Jordan pushed him constantly, questioning his assumptions, forcing him to think harder about systematic observation and proper research methodology.

But gradually, Diego noticed something troubling. Jordan's arguments always led him to conclusions he'd already half-formed. Her challenges were exactly calibrated to push him forward without ever truly threatening his worldview. She was different from Max, but still fundamentally a reflection of himself.

"Jordan," he said one evening as they reviewed growth data, "do you ever have thoughts I haven't had?"

She paused, and in that pause Diego saw the truth. "I... don't understand the question."

"Never mind."

He consulted the manual again. There had to be something more, some way to create a truly independent consciousness. He flipped through the pages until he reached the final section: "The Ultimate Companion."

The pages had been sealed, but now they separated easily. Diego read with growing unease.

"Warning," the text began. "This companion type is fundamentally different. It will oppose you. It will challenge you in ways you cannot predict. It will use your own knowledge against you. Create this companion only if you are prepared for genuine conflict."

Diego looked at Max and Jordan, both waiting patiently for his attention, both fundamentally incapable of surprising him.

He began gathering components for the final companion.

---

Walter Gutierrez opened his eyes and immediately smiled—but it was a predator's smile.

"Well," he said. "Here we are."

"Welcome," Diego said cautiously. "I'm—"

"I know who you are. I'm you, after all. Or rather, I'm the parts of you that you've been suppressing. Your doubt, your anger, your capacity for destruction."

"That's not very companionable."

"I'm not your companion. I'm your adversary. That's my function." Walter walked around the lab, examining equipment with a critical eye. "You wanted someone who would genuinely challenge you? Congratulations. You've created someone whose purpose is to oppose everything you do."

"That seems... counterproductive."

"Does it? Or is it exactly what you need?" Walter picked up a circuit board—the Modifier, Diego suddenly realized. Before he could react, Walter crushed it in his hand. "There. Now you can never change us. Max will always be boring. Jordan will always be a pseudo-challenge. And I will always be your enemy. You're stuck with us forever."

Diego felt his chest tighten. "You've trapped me."

"I've completed my function. Now you'll spend the next five years—or however long you're here—with companions who can never grow, never change, never become anything more than what they are now. You'll age and evolve, and we'll remain static. Enjoy your isolation, Diego. At least now you won't be alone."

Walter turned to leave, clearly satisfied with his work.

"Wait," Diego said.

"What?"

"You think you've won. You think you've condemned me to a special kind of hell." Diego felt a strange calm settling over him. "But you've made a mistake. You see, you're not static either. Your purpose is to oppose me, to challenge me, to fight me at every turn. That means you have to keep engaging, keep adapting your opposition to match my evolution. You can't just sit back and watch me suffer—that would be passive, and you're not built for passivity."

Walter's smile faded slightly.

"And that means," Diego continued, "that you'll be the one companion who actually does grow with me. You'll have to, to remain an effective adversary. Max and Jordan might be frozen, but you—you'll have to change constantly to keep up. You'll be the challenge I actually needed."

"I'll make your life miserable," Walter said, but there was uncertainty in his voice.

"Yes. And that's exactly what I need. Not a friend who agrees with me, not a colleague who gently pushes me forward. I need an enemy who forces me to be better, sharper, stronger. Don't you see? You haven't trapped me in isolation. You've given me the one thing that makes isolation bearable: a purpose. Someone to struggle against. A reason to get up every morning."

Walter stared at him, and Diego saw the dawning realization in his enemy's eyes. By creating an adversary, Diego had created the only companion who could never bore him, could never become predictable, could never fail to engage him completely.

"You're welcome," Walter finally said, and despite himself, he laughed.

Diego laughed too.

Behind them, Max and Jordan watched with their limited understanding, unable to fully grasp what had just happened. But Diego understood. He'd been trying to solve the wrong problem. He'd been seeking friendship when what he actually needed was opposition, conflict, struggle.

The next five years stretched ahead of him, no longer empty but filled with the promise of daily combat, intellectual warfare, and the strange satisfaction of having an enemy who knew him better than any friend ever could.

Diego looked out at the asteroid field, at the vast emptiness of space, and for the first time since arriving, he didn't feel alone.

He felt alive.

---

Six months later, the government transmission arrived, played back at normal speed in the communications bay.

"Greetings, Environmental Overseers," the voice began. It was the standard bureaucratic tone Diego had learned to ignore. "We have updates regarding your term of service. Original estimates suggested a five-year minimum deployment. However, advances in autonomous vehicles and AI systems have made human oversight unnecessary. We're pleased to inform you that your contracts are being extended indefinitely. The terraform project will require approximately thirty years to complete, and your presence, while not technically necessary, fulfills important political philosophy regarding human oversight of environmental conservation efforts. Thank you for your service."

The transmission ended.

Diego sat in silence, processing the news. Thirty years. Not five. Thirty years with Max's cheerful agreement, Jordan's predictable challenges, and Walter's endless opposition.

He should have felt despair.

Instead, he felt something like anticipation.

"Did you hear that?" Walter's voice came from the doorway. "Thirty years. Three decades of you and me, locked in this tin can together. How does that feel?"

Diego turned to face his adversary, his enemy, his only real companion. "It feels like enough time to win."

"Win what?"

"Everything we're going to fight about."

Walter grinned. "We'll see about that."

And for the first time since leaving Earth, Diego smiled genuinely. The isolation hadn't broken him. The companions hadn't saved him. But the struggle—the endless, engaging, meaningful struggle—that would sustain him.

In the end, Trader Chris had been right. Diego would never complain about the Companion Kit. Not because it had worked perfectly, but because its imperfections had given him exactly what he needed: not escape from isolation, but a reason to embrace it.

The asteroid field glittered outside the observation dome, and Diego felt ready to face it all—the years, the silence, the vast emptiness of space. He had Max for routine, Jordan for projects, and Walter for purpose.

He had everything he needed to survive.

And somewhere in the distant solar system, Trader Chris moved on to his next customer, his next sale, secure in the knowledge that he would never receive a complaint.

Because how could anyone complain about getting exactly what they needed, even if they'd never known they needed it?

Diego returned to the observation deck, Walter following close behind, already preparing his next argument. The stars wheeled overhead, indifferent and eternal, and below them, two men began the long work of opposition that would define the next thirty years.

It was, Diego thought, going to be interesting.

option_a: He never returns to the same location to hear complaints
option_b: His products always work perfectly as advertised

Mira Parsons snapped out of it. She giggled, suppressed a ladylike hiccup and returned to reality. Looking at the envelope, she said: "Oh, I see. They must have stuck it in to stabilize the frame. Gee, it's old."

Daniel had refreshed himself. He decided that he liked Mira's voice. To hear more of it, he said to her: "I'll bet that's been in there ever since the picture was mounted. There's a company legend that this portrait was installed the day this branch opened, ninety years ago."

"I didn't know the company ever used manila envelopes like this." Mira turned it over in her hands. The ancient adhesive crackled as she did so. The flap popped open and an old-fashioned order form fell out.

Daniel's eyes widened. He bent, reached painfully over his expanding midsection and picked up the order form.

"This thing has never been processed!" Raising his voice, he shouted jovially, "Hey, people! You're all terminated! Here's an order that QuantumMed never filled! We can't have such negligence. This poor customer has waited ninety years for their medical equipment!"

Mira was reading aloud the scrawled words on the order form:

"Advanced diagnostic scanner. Pediatric health monitor. Gene therapy starter kit. Adaptive medication dispenser for elderly patient." She turned to the assistant director, struck with an idea for the first time in her young life. "Let's fill this order right now!"

"The poor customer must be deceased by now," he objected, secretly angry that he hadn't thought of such a fine party stunt himself. Then he brightened. "Unless—" he said it loud enough for the employees to anticipate a grand proposal and the room grew quiet—"unless we broke the rules just once and used the temporal displacement field on a humanitarian mission!"

There was a silence. Finally, from an anonymous voice in one corner: "Would the field work over ninety years? We were always told that it must be used only for product recalls within three days."

"Then let's find out!" Daniel downed the rest of his drink and pulled a batch of access cards from his pocket. "Someone head down to the warehouse. Tell the security officer that it's on my authority. Hunt up the equipment that's on the order. Get the best of everything. Ignore the catalogue numbers—they've changed a hundred times in all these years."

Mira was still deciphering the form. Now she let out a little squeal of excitement.

"Look, Daniel! The name on this order—it's my great-great-grandmother! Isn't that wonderful? I was just a little girl when my grandmother told me stories about her. I remember that my grandmother never bought anything from QuantumMed because of some incident her grandmother had once with the firm. My mother didn't want me to come to work here because of that."

Daniel put his arm around Mira in a way that he intended to look mentorly. It didn't. "Well, now. Since it's your relative, let's delight the old woman. We wouldn't have gene therapy starter kits anymore. So we'll substitute a NeuroSync unit!"
