Ruth Wheeler was returning from filing a complaint at the local QuantumMed office when she found the large parcel on her doorstep in Glendale, Wendria. She put her hands on her hips and stared suspiciously at the container.

"The minute I submit a formal complaint about you, you materialize!" she told the parcel. She nudged her toe irritably against the silver wrappings that were sealed with a half-transparent binding material she had never seen before.

The label was addressed in a wandering scrawl, a sharp contrast to the impersonal printing on the customary QuantumMed packages. But the familiar FRAGILE MEDICAL EQUIPMENT sticker was pasted onto the box, indicating to the delivery person that the contents required careful handling.

Ruth sighed and picked up her bundle. With a last look at the lovely spring afternoon and the quiet suburban landscape of Glendale, she went into the house.

Five-year-old Isabel heard the box humming. She toddled up on energetic legs and grabbed her grandmother's skirt. "Want!" she said decisively.

"Your medication dispenser ought to be here," Ruth said. She found scissors in her sewing box, tossed a cushion onto the floor, sat on it, and began to open the parcel.

"Now I'll have to submit another form to explain that they should disregard my complaint," she told her granddaughter. "And by the time they receive my second form, they'll have responded to my first form. Then they'll write again." Out of consideration for Isabel, she omitted the expletives that she wanted to add.

The translucent binding was too tough for the scissors. Ruth was about to hunt for a laser cutter when Isabel clutched at an intersection of the cord and yanked. The binding sprang away from the carton as if it were programmed. The wrappings flapped open.

"There!" Isabel said.

Ruth repressed an irrational urge to scold her granddaughter. Instead, she tossed the wrappings aside and removed the lid from the carton. A slightly crushed thin cardboard box lay on top. Ruth pulled out the medication dispenser and examined it carefully. Then she groaned.

It was silver and she had ordered white. It didn't remotely resemble the dispenser she had admired from the QuantumMed catalogue illustration. Moreover, the device had unusual protrusions that no standard medication dispenser should have.

But Isabel was delighted. "Mine!" she shrilled, grabbing for the device.

"It's probably the wrong model, too," Ruth said, examining the control panel. "Let's identify as many defects to complain about as we can."

The device seemed to activate when Isabel touched it. A soft blue glow emanated from its surface. Isabel was radiant for a moment. Then her small face sobered and she started to look vacantly at the distant wall.

"We'll have to return it," Ruth said, "and get the one we ordered."

She tried to take it from Isabel's hands, but the child resisted violently. Ruth grabbed her granddaughter's wrists, held them firmly and tried to pry the device away. It seemed to be adhered somehow. When Ruth released the child's wrists to examine the device more closely, Isabel stepped backward, then began to levitate three feet above the ground. She landed just before she collided with the far wall.

Isabel looked scared until she saw her grandmother's face. Then she squealed in delight.

Ruth's legs were rubber. She was shaking her head and wobbling uncertainly toward her granddaughter when the door opened behind her.

"It's me," her son Felix said. "Slow day at the research institute, so I came home early."

"Felix! I'm experiencing some kind of hallucination or something. Isabel just—"

"Mom! Your complaint was resolved? Good. What's this thing?" He was looking at a small cylindrical device he had pulled from the carton. Its surface contained a single word: NEUROSYNC. The device hummed when he held it.

"Is this the diagnostic scanner? I've never seen technology like this. And there's no power source visible."

"I don't know," Ruth said. "Felix, listen. A moment ago, Isabel—"

He peered into the box for an instruction manual, uselessly. "They must have made an error. It looks like some kind of experimental biotechnology equipment."

He placed the NeuroSync onto the coffee table and delved into the carton again. Isabel was still in his arms.

"That's the scanner, I think," he said, looking at the next object. It had a lovely, streamlined shape, multiple sensor arrays and a connection port for a power outlet.

"That's curious," Ruth mused, her mind distracted from Isabel for a moment. "It looks terribly advanced. Maybe they sent a premium model instead of the standard scanner."

The bottom of the carton contained the health monitor that they had ordered for Isabel. Ruth glanced at its sleek interface and said: "Felix, about Isabel. Put her down a minute and observe what she does."

Felix stared at his mother and placed the child onto the carpet. Isabel began to walk, then rose and again levitated, this time toward the coffee table on which the NeuroSync rested.

His jaw dropped. "My God! Mom, what—"

Ruth was staring, too, but not at her granddaughter. "Felix! The coffee table! It used to be brown!"

The coffee table was a vivid shade of blue. A neon, demanding, screaming blue that clashed horribly with the soft earth tones in which Ruth had furnished the room.

"That cylindrical thing must be emitting something," Felix said, his background in complexity science kicking in. "But did you see Isabel when she—"

Ruth's frazzled nerves carried a frantic order to her muscles. She jumped up, strode to the coffee table and picked up the NeuroSync with two fingers. She tossed it to Felix. Immediately, she regretted her action.

"Drop it!" she yelled. "Maybe it'll alter your neural patterns, too!"

Felix kicked the coffee table into the hall closet, tossed the NeuroSync in after it and shut the door firmly. As the door closed, he saw the entire interior of the dark closet illuminate into a wet-sapphire blue.

When he turned back to Ruth, she was staring at her left wrist. The medical monitoring bracelet that the hospital had given her years ago was a brilliant blue, shedding its soft glow over her forearm up to the elbow.

Ruth felt the panic building up inside her. She opened her mouth to scream, then put her hand in front of her mouth to suppress it, finally jerked the hand away to prevent the glowing bracelet from turning her teeth blue.

She collapsed into Felix's arms, babbling incomprehensibly about epistemology and the nature of reality.

He said: "It's all right. There must be some kind of anti-gravity field or something in that medication dispenser. I'll attach a weight to Isabel's belt and that'll hold her down until we can remove the device. Don't worry. And that blue emission or whatever it is will dissipate."

Ruth immediately felt better. She put her hands behind her back, pulled off her bracelet and slipped it into her pocket. Felix was sentimental about her removing it.

"I'll prepare dinner," she said, trying to keep her voice steady. "Maybe you'd better start a complaint form to QuantumMed. Let's go into the kitchen, Isabel."

Ruth strode resolutely toward the rear of the house. She kept her eyes determinedly off the tinge of blue that was showing through her pocket and didn't dare look back at her granddaughter's unsettling means of propulsion.

A half-hour later, when the meal was almost ready, two things happened: Pablo Fuller came home from the university through the back door and a strange voice said from the front of the house, "Unauthorized access detected."

Ruth stared at her grandson. He stared back at her, the pediatric health monitor under his arm.

She went into the front room. Her son was standing with fists on hips, looking at the front door, chuckling. "Most sophisticated security system I've seen in a long time. That voice you heard was the new diagnostic scanner. I installed it while you were in the kitchen. Did you hear what happened when old Mr. Brennan out there approached the entrance?"

"Oh. Something like those smart home systems with voice warnings, like 'Motion detected.' Well, if there's some kind of AI in there repeating that message, you'd better deactivate that function. It might get annoying after a while. And it might offend someone."

Ruth went to the door and turned the handle. The door didn't open. The figure of Mr. Brennan, half-visible through the heavy curtain, shifted impatiently on the porch.

Felix yanked at the doorknob. It didn't yield for him, either. He looked up at the scanner, which he had installed just above the upper part of the door frame.

"Strange," he said, applying his knowledge of information theory. "That isn't in contact with the door mechanism itself. I don't see how it can prevent the door from opening."

Ruth put her mouth close to the glass, shouting: "Won't you come to the back door, Mr. Brennan? This one is malfunctioning."

"I just wanted to borrow some medical supplies," the man called from the porch. "I realize that I'm a terrible bother." But he walked down the front steps and disappeared around the side of the house.

"Biometric authentication required." The well-modulated voice from the small scanner box threatened to penetrate every corner of the house. Ruth looked doubtfully at her son's lips. They weren't moving.

"If this is some kind of prank—" she began icily.

"I'll have to order another scanner just like this one, for the lab," Felix said. "But you'd better let the old fellow in. No use letting him get upset."

The back door was already open, because it was a warm day. The screen door had no latch, held closed by a simple spring. Ruth pushed it open when Mr. Brennan trudged up the three back steps, and smiled at her neighbor.

"I'm so sorry you had to walk around the house. It's been a rather chaotic day in an awful lot of ways."

Something seemed to impede Mr. Brennan as he came to the threshold. He frowned and pushed his frail frame against something invisible. It apparently yielded abruptly, because he staggered forward into the kitchen, nearly falling. He stared grimly at Ruth and looked suspiciously behind him.

"The children have some new equipment," Ruth improvised hastily. "Isabel is so excited over a new device that she's positively euphoric. Let's see now—it was medical supplies that you need, wasn't it?"

"I already have them," Pablo said, handing a small package to his grandmother. The boy turned back to the health monitor which he had spread over the kitchen table, studying its interface with fascination.

"Excitement isn't good for me," Mr. Brennan said testily, his understanding of social dynamics clearly limited. "I've had a lot of health problems in my life. I like peace and stability."

"Your wife is better?"

"Worse. I'm sure I don't know why everything happens to me." Mr. Brennan edged toward the hall, trying to peer into the front of the house. Ruth stood squarely in front of the door leading to the hall. Defeated, Mr. Brennan left. A muffled series of beeps, mixed with a few faint diagnostic readings, came from the scanner-box when he crossed the threshold.

Ruth went into the hall to order Felix to disconnect the scanner. She nearly collided with him, coming in the other direction.

"Where did this come from?" Felix held a small object in the palm of his hand, keeping it away from his body. A few drops of something viscous were dripping from his fingers. The object looked remarkably like a miniature brain. It was human-size, complete with cortical folds, neural pathways and rather prominent blood vessels.

"Hey, that's mine," Pablo said. "You know, this is an unusual health monitor. That was in it. But there aren't instructions on how it operates."

"Well, put it away," Ruth told Pablo sharply. "It's disturbing."

Felix laid the brain-device on the table and walked away. The device rolled from the smooth, level table, bounced twice when it hit the floor, then rolled along, six inches behind him. He turned and kicked at it. The device rolled nimbly out of the path of the kick.

"Felix, I think we've made poor Mr. Brennan uncomfortable," Ruth said. "He's so upset over his wife's health and he thinks we're being inhospitable."

Felix didn't hear her. He strode to the health monitor, followed at a safe distance by the brain-device, and picked up the box.

"Hey, watch out!" Pablo cried. A small scanning wand fell from the box, landed on its side and its sensor flashed on, throwing a beam of light across Felix's hands.

Pablo retrieved the wand and turned it off while Felix glanced through an instruction manual, frowning.

"This equipment is too advanced for a twelve-year-old boy," Felix told his mother, his expertise in theoretical modeling evident. "I don't know why you ordered such a thing." He tossed the manual into the empty box.

"I'm going to return it, if you don't damage it," she replied. "Look at the marks you made on the instructions." The black marks stood out clearly against the glossy, coated paper.

Felix looked at his hands. "I didn't do it," he said, pressing his clean fingertips against the kitchen table.

Black marks, a full set of them, stood out against the sparkling polished table's surface.

"I think the BioScanner did it," Pablo said, using the term from the manual. "The instructions say you've got to be very careful with it, because its effects persist for an extended duration."

Felix began scrubbing his hands vigorously at the sink. Ruth watched him silently, until she saw his marks appear on the faucet, the soap dispenser and the towel. She began to reprimand him for making such a mess, when Isabel levitated into the kitchen. The girl was wearing a different outfit.

"My God!" Ruth forgot her language before the children. "She changed clothes herself. Where did she get that outfit?"

Ruth examined the garment. She didn't recognize it as sleepwear. But in cut and design, it was suspiciously like the medication dispenser interface that had arrived in the parcel. Her heart sank.

She picked up the child, felt the elevated temperature, and said: "Felix, I think it's the same device. It must adapt its appearance or something based on the user's physiological state. It seems impossible, but—" She shrugged mutely. "And I think Isabel's running a fever. I'm going to put her to bed."

She looked worriedly into the reddened eyes of the small girl, who whimpered on the way to the bedroom. Ruth carried her up the stairs, keeping her balance with difficulty, as Isabel threatened to float upward out of her arms.

The whole family decided that rest might be a good idea, soon after dinner. When the lights went out, the house seemed to be nearly normal. Felix put on a pair of gloves and threw a blanket over the brain-device. Pablo rigged up barriers to warn visitors from the front porch. Ruth put small earplugs into her ears, because she didn't like the rhythmic hum, soft but persistent, that emerged from the hall closet where the NeuroSync sat. Isabel was whimpering occasionally in her sleep.

When daylight entered her room, Isabel's outfit had transformed back into the medication dispenser interface. But the little girl was too sick to get out of bed. She wasn't hungry, her breathing was labored, and she had a persistent cough. Felix called the doctor before going to work.

The only positive thing about the morning for Ruth was the fact that the NeuroSync had quieted down some time in the night. After she got Pablo to school, she gingerly opened the closet door. The NeuroSync was now glowing a bright pink and seemed slightly larger. Deep violet text stood out on its surface:

"Today is Wednesday. For system maintenance, the NeuroSync will not operate today."

The mail carrier brought a letter from QuantumMed. Ruth stared stupidly at the envelope, until she realized that this wasn't an impossibly quick response to the complaint she had filed yesterday. It must have crossed in transit her complaint about the non-delivery of the order. She tore open the envelope and read:

"We regret to inform you that your order cannot be processed until the outstanding balance you owe us has been reduced. From the attached statement, you will readily ascertain that the payment of $1,247.89 will enable you to resume the purchasing of medical equipment on credit. We shall process your recent order as soon...."

Ruth crumpled the letter and threw it into the recycling bin, knowing perfectly well that it would need to be retrieved for Felix after work tonight. She had just decided to contact QuantumMed's complaint department when the phone rang.

"I'm afraid I must ask you to come down to the school, Mrs. Wheeler," a voice said. "Your grandson is in trouble. He claims that it's connected with something that his family gave him."

"My grandson?" Ruth asked incredulously. "Pablo?"

"Yes. It's a small device that looks like a medical scanner. Your grandson insists that he didn't know it would make clothing transparent. He claims it was just an accident that he tried it out when he was walking by the gymnasium during physical education. We've had to request emergency blankets from every family in the neighborhood. Pablo has always been a good student and we believe that we can handle this discreetly without media publicity involving his name, if you'll—"

"I'll be right down," Ruth said. "I mean I won't be right down. I've got a sick child here. Don't do anything until I contact my son. And I'm sorry for Pablo. I mean I'm sorry for the students, and for the teachers, too. I'm sorry for—for everything. Goodbye."

Just as she hung up the telephone, the scanner rang with an alert. It chimed with a normal tone, then began to play soft diagnostic readings. Ruth opened the door without difficulty, to admit Dr. Zara Francis.

"You aren't going to believe me, Doctor," Ruth said while she took the child's temperature, "but we can't remove that device from Isabel."

"Children can be stubborn sometimes." Dr. Francis whistled softly when she looked at the thermometer. "She's quite ill. I need a blood sample before I attempt to move her. Let me examine her."

Isabel had been mumbling semi-deliriously. She made no effort to resist as the doctor picked her up. But when she raised a component of the device and began to detach it, Isabel screamed.

The doctor released the device and looked in perplexity at the point where it interfaced with Isabel's body.

"It's apparently an adverse reaction to some new kind of biotechnology. But I don't understand why the device won't detach. It's not physically bonded."

"Don't bother trying," Ruth said miserably, her understanding of healthcare policy telling her this would be complicated. "Just cut it off."

Dr. Francis pulled medical scissors from her bag and attempted to separate a component. When she had cut partway through, she gently began to peel back the edges of the material. Isabel writhed and kicked, then collapsed in unconsciousness. The physician smoothly restored the components back into place.

She looked helpless as she said to Ruth: "I don't know quite what to do. The tissue starts to hemorrhage when I manipulate the interface. She'd experience severe trauma if I removed it forcibly. But it's such an extreme reaction that it may harm her, if we leave it in contact with her body."

The NeuroSync's hum suddenly began rhythmically from the lower part of the house. Ruth clutched the side of the chair, trying to keep herself under control. A siren wailed somewhere down the street, grew louder rapidly, suddenly going silent at the peak of its crescendo.

Dr. Francis glanced outside the window. "An emergency vehicle. Looks as if they're stopping here."

"Oh, no," Ruth breathed. "Something's happened to Felix."

"It certainly will," Felix said grimly, walking into the bedroom. "I won't have employment if I can't remove this substance from my fingers. Black marks on everything I touch. I can't handle laboratory equipment or interact with research subjects. How's the child? What's the emergency vehicle doing out front?"

"They're going to the next house down the street," the physician said. "Has there been illness there?"

Felix held up his hands, palms toward the doctor. "What's wrong with me? My fingers appear normal. But they leave black marks on everything I touch."

The doctor looked closely at the fingertips, applying statistical inference. "Every human has natural secretions on the skin. That's how forensic scientists get results with their identification techniques. But I've never encountered chromatization, in this context. Better not attempt to handle sensitive materials until you've consulted a dermatological specialist."

Ruth was peering through the window, curious about the emergency vehicle despite her own troubles. She saw two paramedics carry Mrs. Brennan, motionless and pale, on a stretcher from the house next door into the vehicle. A third member of the crew was struggling with a disheveled Mr. Brennan at the door. Shouts that sounded like "Negligence!" came sharply through the window.

"I know those paramedics," Dr. Francis said. She opened the window. "Hey, Marcus! What's wrong?"

The front paramedic looked up. "I don't know. This woman's critically ill. I think her husband is experiencing psychological distress."

Mr. Brennan had broken free. He rushed halfway down the sidewalk, gesticulating wildly to nobody in particular.

"It's negligence!" he screamed. "Medical negligence again! She's been harmed by faulty equipment! She's going to die! It means legal consequences!"

The paramedic grabbed him again. This time he administered a mild sedative to calm him.

"Come back to this house as soon as you deliver her," Dr. Francis shouted to the crew. "We've got a very sick child up here."

"I was concerned this would happen," Felix said, his knowledge of behavioral economics evident in his analysis. "The poor man already has lost two wives to medical complications. If this one is ill, it's no wonder he thinks that somebody is responsible for medical negligence."

Pablo stuck his head around the bedroom door. His grandmother stared unbelievingly for a moment, then advanced on him threateningly. Something in his face restrained her, just as she was about to start reprimanding him.

"I got something important to tell you," Pablo said rapidly, ready to retreat. "I escaped from the principal's office and came home. I need to tell you what I did."

"I heard all about what you did," Ruth said, advancing again. "And you're not going to evade responsibility."

"Give me a chance to explain something. Downstairs. So she won't hear," Pablo ended in a whisper, nodding toward the doctor.

Ruth looked doubtfully at Felix, then followed Pablo down the stairs. The scanner was monotonously saying in a monotone: "Access denied, access denied, unauthorized entry prohibited."

"Why did you do it?" Ruth asked Pablo, her anger suddenly slumping into weary sadness. "People will suspect you of being disturbed for the rest of your life. You can't possibly explain—"

"Don't worry about the students' clothing," Pablo said, "because it was only an accident. The really important thing is something else I did before I left the house."

Felix, cursing softly, hurried past them on the way to answer the knocking. He ignored the scanner's warnings.

"I forgot about it," Pablo continued, "when that scanning device accidentally activated. Then when they confined me in the principal's office, I had time to think, and I remembered. I put some white substance from the health monitor into those medical supplies we lent Mr. Brennan last night. I just wanted to observe what would happen. I don't know exactly what effect—"

"He put substance in the medical supplies?" A deep, authoritative voice came from the front of the house. Mother and grandson looked through the hall. A police officer stood on the threshold of the front door. "I heard that! The man next door claims that his wife has been poisoned by medical negligence. Young man, I'm going to have to take you into custody."

The officer stepped over the threshold. A blue flash darted from the scanner box, striking him squarely on the chest. The officer staggered back, sitting down abruptly on the porch. A scent of ozone drifted through the house.

"Close the door, close the door," the scanner was announcing urgently.

"Where's that emergency vehicle?" Dr. Francis yelled from the top of the steps. "The child's condition is deteriorating."

option_b: The gene therapy starter kit she ordered

However, the gene therapy starter kit was explicitly stated to have been substituted: Daniel said "We wouldn't have gene therapy starter kits anymore. So we'll substitute a NeuroSync unit!" The rain hammered against the windows of the Clearwater Police Department's conference room as Detective Aisha Hughes surveyed the assembled group. Five junior detectives sat around the table, each hoping to be selected for the prestigious Cold Case Task Force that would tackle Clearwater's most notorious unsolved murders. With only three positions available, the selection process would be brutal.

"First round evaluations are always the hardest," Aisha said to her colleague, Detective Lorenzo Harvey, who stood beside her reviewing the candidates' files. "With only three spots on the task force, most of these talented people won't make it through. I can't help feeling for them—for all of us, really. After all, I had to go through this same process when I was starting out."

Lorenzo nodded sympathetically. "It's not easy, but someone has to make the call. At least we're trying to be fair about it. We're looking at their investigative reports, their analytical skills, their understanding of research ethics in criminal investigation. It's not arbitrary."

"True," Aisha agreed, "but it still feels like we're playing judge and jury with people's careers."

Among the candidates was Detective Violet Romero, who had recently transferred from the Evergreen, Quendor police department. She sat nervously reviewing her notes, acutely aware that her future in Clearwater depended on this evaluation. Next to her sat Detective Zara Riley, a local officer who had worked her way up from patrol to detective in just three years—an impressive feat that spoke to her dedication and skill.

The evaluation process would take place over three days. Today was merely the preliminary review, where candidates would be assessed on their past case files and investigative approaches. Those who passed would move on to a practical exercise: each would be assigned a genuine cold case file and given seventy-two hours to conduct systematic observation of the evidence, develop theories, and present their findings. The final selection would be based on those presentations.

Aisha began by calling forward the first candidate, Detective Peter Ford. He was a veteran investigator from Goldfield Town who had recently relocated to Clearwater. His specialty was financial crimes, and his file showed an impressive record of solving complex embezzlement cases.

"Detective Ford," Aisha began, "I've reviewed your case files, and your work on financial investigations is exemplary. However, this task force will focus primarily on violent crimes—specifically homicides. Can you explain why you believe your skill set would transfer to this type of investigation?"

Peter shifted in his seat. "Ma'am, I believe that systematic observation and analytical thinking are universal skills. Whether I'm tracking money or tracking a killer, the methodology is similar. You follow the evidence, you build a timeline, you identify patterns."

"Fair enough," Lorenzo interjected, "but there's a significant difference between analyzing spreadsheets and analyzing crime scenes. What experience do you have with violent crime investigation?"

Peter hesitated, and in that moment of silence, both Aisha and Lorenzo knew he wouldn't make the cut. His expertise was valuable, but not for this particular task force.

After thanking him and moving him to the "unlikely" category, they called forward Violet Romero.

Violet approached the front of the room with confidence, carrying a portfolio of her most significant cases. "Detectives," she began before they could speak, "I know what you're thinking. I'm the new transfer, the outsider. But I've brought something that might interest you."

She laid out three case files on the table. "These are murders I investigated in Evergreen. Two of them are solved. One remains open. What they all have in common is that they required not just standard police work, but creative thinking about motive, opportunity, and means. In one case, I had to learn about paleontology to understand why a killer targeted a specific museum curator. In another, I had to understand healthcare policy to identify a pattern of deaths in a nursing home."

Aisha leaned forward, genuinely intrigued. "Walk me through the nursing home case."

For the next twenty minutes, Violet detailed how she had identified a pattern of suspicious deaths that other investigators had dismissed as natural causes. Her systematic observation of medication records, shift schedules, and patient histories had revealed a healthcare worker who was euthanizing patients she deemed to be suffering unnecessarily—a twisted interpretation of social justice that had resulted in eight murders.

When Violet finished, Aisha and Lorenzo exchanged glances. Without speaking, they both knew: Violet was in.

Next came Zara Riley, whose nervous energy was palpable as she took her place at the front of the room.

"Detective Riley," Aisha said gently, "I've known you since you were in uniform. You've always been thorough, dedicated, and honest. But I have to ask: why do you want this position? You're doing well in your current role. Why take on the stress and uncertainty of cold cases?"

Zara's answer was immediate and passionate. "Because justice delayed is justice denied. Every unsolved case represents a family that never got closure, a killer who might still be out there. I know I'm young, and I know I don't have the experience of some of these other candidates, but I have something else: I have the determination to see these cases through, no matter how long it takes."

She pulled out her own portfolio. "I've been studying cold cases in my spare time. Not officially, just on my own. I've done historical analysis of three cases from the 1990s, and I believe I've identified new leads in two of them. I'm not saying I've solved them—I haven't had access to all the evidence—but I've found angles that weren't pursued at the time."

Lorenzo raised an eyebrow. "Show us."

Zara laid out her research on the Dawnridge murders—a series of three killings in the neighboring district of Dawnridge, Prandoria, that had stumped investigators for twenty years. Using modern data science techniques and cross-referencing old witness statements with current databases, she had identified a potential suspect who had been overlooked because he had no criminal record at the time of the murders.

"This is impressive work," Aisha admitted. "But you did this without authorization, which raises questions about research ethics and chain of custody for any evidence you might have accessed."

"I used only publicly available information," Zara said quickly. "Court transcripts, newspaper articles, and information I could access through legal channels. I wouldn't compromise a case by contaminating evidence or violating proper procedure."

Aisha nodded approvingly. Zara was in.

The remaining candidates were evaluated throughout the afternoon. Detective Mohammad Davis showed promise but lacked the creative thinking necessary for cold case work. Detective Manuel Wade had excellent technical skills but poor interpersonal abilities—a critical flaw when dealing with families of victims. Detective Robert Pearson was competent but unexceptional, the kind of solid investigator who would do well in routine cases but might not have the spark needed for the most challenging work.

By the end of the day, Aisha and Lorenzo had narrowed the field to four candidates: Violet Romero, Zara Riley, and two others who would compete for the three available positions.

"The next phase will determine everything," Aisha announced to the remaining candidates. "Each of you will be assigned a genuine cold case. You'll have seventy-two hours to review the evidence, conduct whatever investigation you can within that timeframe, and prepare a presentation of your findings. This isn't about solving the case—though if you do, that would be remarkable. This is about demonstrating your investigative methodology, your analytical skills, and your ability to see what others might have missed."

The four candidates were each handed a thick folder containing crime scene photos, witness statements, forensic reports, and investigative notes from the original detectives.

Violet received the case of the Clearwater Strangler—three women murdered over a six-month period in 2005, with no clear connection between them and no viable suspects.

Zara was assigned the Riverside Shooting—a seemingly random murder of a businessman in 2010 that had all the hallmarks of a professional hit but no apparent motive.

As the candidates left with their assignments, Lorenzo turned to Aisha. "This is going to be harder than we thought. They're all good."

"I know," Aisha replied. "But we can only take three. Let's see what they come up with."

Seventy-two hours later, the four candidates returned to present their findings. The conference room had been set up with a projector, whiteboards, and evidence boards where each detective could display their work.

Violet went first. She had approached the Clearwater Strangler case with meticulous systematic observation, creating a detailed timeline that incorporated not just the known facts but also contextual information about what was happening in Clearwater during that period.

"The original investigators focused on the similarities between the victims," Violet explained, pointing to photos of the three women. "All were in their thirties, all were professionals, all lived alone. But I think they missed something crucial: the differences."

She pulled up a map showing the locations where each woman was found. "These locations seem random, but when you overlay them with data about urban development in 2005, a pattern emerges. Each location was near a construction site for the new green infrastructure project that was being built that year—the city's initiative to create sustainable water management systems."

Lorenzo leaned forward. "Are you suggesting the killer worked in construction?"

"I'm suggesting it's worth investigating," Violet said. "I pulled employment records for the major contractors on that project—publicly available information from city permits. Seventeen workers were employed at all three sites during the relevant time periods. That's a starting point for renewed investigation."

Aisha made notes, impressed by the creative thinking that had led Violet to consider environmental context as a potential clue.

Next came Zara's presentation on the Riverside Shooting. She had taken a different approach, focusing on the victim's background and potential motives that might have been overlooked.

"The victim, Marcus Thornton, was presented as a successful businessman with no enemies," Zara began. "But I did some digging into his business dealings. Thornton's company was involved in international trade, specifically trade policy consultation for companies wanting to do business in emerging markets."

She displayed a series of documents. "Three months before his death, Thornton testified before a congressional committee about trade practices that he believed violated human rights standards. He specifically named companies that were using forced labor in their supply chains. Two of those companies had headquarters here in Clearwater."

"You think this was retaliation?" Aisha asked.

"I think it's a motive that was never properly investigated," Zara replied. "The original detectives focused on personal enemies and business rivals, but they didn't consider that Thornton might have been killed to silence him. I've identified three corporate executives who had both motive and means."

The presentations continued, each candidate demonstrating different strengths and approaches. When they were finished, Aisha and Lorenzo asked them to wait outside while they deliberated.

"This is impossible," Lorenzo said, reviewing his notes. "They're all qualified. How do we choose?"

"We look at what this task force actually needs," Aisha replied. "We need investigators who can think creatively, who can see patterns others miss, and who have the determination to pursue leads that might go nowhere ninety-nine times out of a hundred. Based on that criteria, I think our choices are clear."

They called the candidates back in.

"This was one of the most difficult selections I've ever had to make," Aisha began. "All of you demonstrated exceptional skills. However, we can only select three of you for the task force."

She paused, looking at each candidate in turn. "Detective Romero, your systematic observation and creative thinking about environmental context showed exactly the kind of innovative approach we need. You're in."

Violet's face broke into a smile of relief and joy.

"Detective Riley, your determination to pursue the human rights angle in the Thornton case, and your willingness to challenge the original investigation's assumptions, demonstrated both courage and insight. You're in."

Zara looked like she might cry with happiness.

Aisha announced the third selection, and then turned to the candidate who hadn't made it. "I want you to know that this decision doesn't reflect on your abilities as an investigator. You did excellent work. But we had to make a choice, and these three candidates were the best fit for what this particular task force needs."

The disappointed candidate nodded, clearly trying to maintain professional composure despite the crushing disappointment.

After the meeting concluded and the unsuccessful candidates had left, the three new task force members remained with Aisha and Lorenzo to discuss next steps.

"Your first assignment starts Monday," Aisha told them. "We have sixteen active cold cases, ranging from five to thirty years old. We'll be working as a team, with peer review of each other's work to ensure we're not missing anything. This is going to be challenging, frustrating, and sometimes heartbreaking work. But it's also the most important work we can do."

Violet raised her hand tentatively. "Can I ask a question about the selection process?"

"Of course," Aisha replied.

"How did you make the final decision? I mean, I'm grateful to be here, but I'm curious about what separated those of us who were selected from those who weren't."

Lorenzo answered. "It came down to creative writing—not literally, but the ability to craft a narrative from disparate pieces of evidence. Cold cases often have gaps in the evidence, missing witnesses, lost records. The investigators who succeed are those who can construct plausible theories that account for what we know while acknowledging what we don't know. All three of you demonstrated that ability."

Aisha added, "You also showed that you understand research ethics and the importance of building cases that will hold up in court. It's not enough to have a theory—we need evidence that's been properly collected and documented. You all showed respect for that process."

"Sure."

"During the evaluation, you mentioned that you went through this same process when you were starting out. Did you make it on your first try?"

Aisha smiled ruefully. "No. I applied three times before I was selected for a specialized unit. Each rejection was devastating, but it also made me more determined to improve. That's what separates the good investigators from the great ones—the ability to learn from failure and come back stronger."

"Thank you for that," Zara said. "I needed to hear it. I keep thinking about the candidate who didn't make it today, and how easily that could have been me."

"It could have been any of you," Aisha replied. "Remember that when you're working these cases. Stay humble, stay hungry, and never assume you have all the answers. The moment you think you know everything is the moment you stop seeing what's really there."

As Zara left, Lorenzo joined Aisha at the window, watching the rain that had continued throughout the day.

"Think we made the right choices?" he asked.

"I think we made the best choices we could with the information we had," Aisha replied. "Time will tell if we were right. But I have a good feeling about this team. They're smart, they're dedicated, and they're not afraid to challenge assumptions. That's what we need."

"What's our first case going to be?"

Aisha pulled a file from her briefcase—one she had been keeping separate from the others. "The Goldfield Town murders. Three victims over two years, all killed in their homes, no forced entry, no obvious connection between them. The case went cold in 2012, but I've always thought there was something the original investigators missed."

"Why this case?"

"Because it's solvable," Aisha said. "I've reviewed it a dozen times over the years, and I'm convinced the answer is in the evidence we already have. We just need fresh eyes to see it. This will be a good test of the team's abilities—challenging enough to push them, but not so impossible that they'll get discouraged."

Lorenzo nodded. "When do we start?"

"Monday morning, eight a.m. sharp. And Lorenzo? Thanks for helping with the selection process. I couldn't have done it without your input."

"That's what partners are for," he replied with a smile.

As Aisha drove home through the rain-soaked streets of Clearwater, Estoria, she thought about the new task force and the cases they would tackle. Somewhere in the city, there were families waiting for answers, waiting for justice, waiting for closure. With this new team, she was more hopeful than ever that they could provide those answers.

The Cold Case Task Force wouldn't solve every case—that was impossible. But they would give each case the attention it deserved, the systematic observation and creative thinking that might reveal what others had missed. And sometimes, that was enough to make the difference between a case that remained forever cold and one that finally, after years of waiting, found its resolution.

She thought about the candidate who hadn't been selected today, and hoped that person would apply again in the future. Talent and determination were too valuable to waste, and the department needed all the good investigators it could get.

But for now, she had her team. Three talented detectives, each bringing different strengths and perspectives to the work. Together, they would pursue justice for victims who had been waiting years—sometimes decades—for someone to care enough to look at their cases one more time.

As she pulled into her driveway, Aisha's phone buzzed with a text from Violet: "Thank you for this opportunity. I won't let you down."

Aisha smiled and typed back: "I know you won't. See you Monday."

The rain continued to fall, washing the streets clean, and somewhere in the archives of the Clearwater Police Department, sixteen cold case files waited for their chance at justice.

All power did the cylinders and the block possess. There was nothing they could not do, if Naomi so willed. It was another discovery that came too late to save her colleagues.

Naomi moved across the room. She pressed glittering controls inset in a panel on the wall, one after another, in proper sequence.

The blue opalescence deepened, grew dark and vivid. The hum broadened into a steady roar. And standing out, startlingly white against the blue, was the queer block of shining energy, shimmering and pulsing.

Naomi drew herself upward, slowly turning, bathing in the quivering bands of cobalt that sped outward from the cylinders. She felt the energy spread over her body, watching it splash across her arms and torso. Where it touched, a faint tingle lingered; then spread outwards, all over her form.

Naomi was immortal, and the blue light made her so.

"There, it is done," she whispered to herself. "Now for another cycle I can roam the facility as I will, for the life spark in me has been cleansed and nourished."

She touched the controls, shutting the power to a low murmur. She turned to the steel doors, passed through and into the misty halls.

"I must speak," Naomi said as she moved along the corridor. "I have not spoken for many weeks. I must exercise my voice, or lose it. That is the law of evolutionary biology. It would atrophy, otherwise.

"Yes, I will use my voice tonight, and I will go out under the dome and look up at the stars and think about the cities that once thrived on this world, and I will talk to them and tell them how lonely Naomi is."

She turned and went along a hall that opened into a broad observation deck which stood forth directly beneath a segment of the mighty dome. She stared upwards, craning her neck to see through the darkness pressing down upon her.

"Stars," she whispered, "listen to me once again. I am lonely, stars, and the research of Naomi means nothing to the walls of my facility, nor to the Chamber of the Cylinders, nor even—at times—to Naomi herself."

She paused and her eyes widened, staring upwards.

"By the Block," she said to the silence about her. "There is something up there that is not a star, nor a satellite, nor yet a meteor."

It was an aircraft.

Paul Graham took his hands from the controls of the experimental craft that soared through the toxic atmosphere, and wiped his sweaty palms on his thighs. His grey eyes bored downward at the massive dome structure emerging from the polluted landscape below.

"The last facility in our search," he breathed. "Maybe she has the solution!"

"Yes," whispered the woman beside him, Julia Wells, wetting her lips with her tongue. "No use to think of failure. If she hasn't, we'll die ourselves, down there in Alexandria City."

The Collapse. And the Plague. It had come on Earth suddenly, had the Plague, back in the first days of unregulated industrial expansion, after corporations discovered ways to maximize production without regard for environmental impact.

They had been slow to respond, those first environmental agencies; not at all like the aggressive climate technology initiatives that existed today. But it had been a beginning. And no one had thought anything of it when the first researchers who studied the pollution zones died of respiratory failure.

As the years passed to decades, and the contamination spread from the industrial zones to residential areas, it began to be apparent that a lifetime in the polluted regions meant a hideous death. Scientists attributed it to the combination of airborne toxins and particulate matter, for in the affected zones there was no natural filtration system to protect the delicate tissues of human lungs from their devastating effects. It had long been a theory in public health that environmental factors were related to the development of chronic diseases; perhaps they were, said some, the direct cause of the new plague.

It meant death to live in the contaminated zones, and only the desperate hope for a cure kept the research teams working between Alexandria City and the outlying facilities. Green infrastructure kept out some pollutants, but traditional methods would not stand against the concentrated toxicity that had built up over generations; and advanced filtration systems brought researchers to their knees with resource exhaustion and equipment failure.

Plague cases increased across the inhabited zones. It was learned that the virulent form of environmental plague, as it was called, was in some peculiar manner, transmissible through shared air systems. The alarm spread. Researchers who worked in the field were isolated, but the damage had been done.

The Plague spread, and ravaged the peoples of the remaining cities.

Medical centers were established, and precious clean air used for treatment. But the clean air was hard to maintain. There was just not enough for everyone.

A team was assembled, the most dedicated researchers ever gathered. They were equipped for survival. They made the most protected field research teams seem amateur by comparison. And humanity gave them to Paul Graham to take them out among the abandoned facilities to find the secret to reversing the collapse in sufficient detail to halt the Plague.

It had not been easy to find a team. The inhabited zones knew these scientists were going to their doom. It would be a miracle if they reached even a single facility, if they did not perish of environmental plague before their first goal. Julia Wells, whose parents and siblings were dying of the Plague, begged him for a chance. A disgraced researcher expelled from the Alexandria Institute, Omar May, grudgingly agreed to go along on the promise that he won reinstatement if he ever came back. With Omar went a quiet, methodical woman named Leah Perry, who knew atmospheric science, biodiversity conservation, and the fine art of peer review analysis. The two seemed inseparable in their dedication.

Now Paul was breathing softly, "Yes, it had better be there, or else we die."

He ran quivering fingers over his chest, felt the strange tightness that heralded respiratory collapse. Involuntarily, he shuddered.

Steps clanged on the metal stairway beneath them. Omar pushed up through the hatch and got to his feet. He was as tall as Paul, stocky where Paul was lean, granite where Paul was flexible steel. His hair was dark, and his brows heavy. A stubborn jaw shot out under thin, hard lips.

"There it is, Omar," said Julia. "Start hoping."

Omar scowled darkly, and spat.

"A hell of a way to spend my last days," he growled. "I'm dying on my feet, and I've got to be a martyr to a billion people who don't know I'm alive."

"You know a better way to die, of course," replied Paul.

"You bet I do. There's a comfortable lab in Alexandria City. I'd make dying a pleasure, working on my own research without the ethics committees breathing down my neck."

Paul snorted, glancing down at the controls. Beneath his steady fingers, the craft descended into the clearer air pocket surrounding the domed facility, shuddered a moment, then eased downward.

"Tell Leah to come up," ordered Paul. "No need for her to be below."

Omar dropped to the floor, lowered his head through the open hatch, and called out. A response from the depths of the craft answered him. A moment later, Leah stood with the others: a woman with a serious expression and careful eyes.

"Think she has the solution, Paul?" she asked.

"The atmospheric analyzer will tell us. Check it."

"Already on it."

The craft rocked gently as Paul set it down on a flat, concrete landing pad between two high structures that rose abruptly from the facility grounds. It was just dawn as the faint rays of the sun pierced through the toxic haze above. Like a silver dart on a floor of grey concrete, the aircraft bounced once, twice; then lay still.

Within her gleaming walls, four scientists bent with tense faces over scrolling data on an atmospheric screen. With quivering fingers, Paul adjusted controls and readings.

"Damn!" exploded Omar. "I might have known it. The air here is clean, but there's no indication of the mechanism."

Paul touched his chest gently, and shuddered.

Julia bit her lips, and thought of her family in the contaminated zones; Leah kept her eyes fixed on Paul, waiting.

With one sweep of his arm, Omar sent a portable monitor flying against the far wall to shatter in pieces.

No one said a word.

Something whispered in the craft. They jerked their heads up, stood listening. The faint sound swept all about them, questioning, curious. It came again, imperative; suddenly demanding.

"What is it?" whispered Leah. "What's that sound?"

Paul shook his head, frowning, suddenly glad that the others had heard it, too.

"Maybe someone trying to communicate with us," stated Julia.

The whispers grew louder and harsher. Angry.

"Take it easy," yelled Omar savagely. "We don't know what you're saying. How can we answer you?"

Leah spoke quietly, "We can't understand the language pattern."

The rustle ceased. The silence hung eerily in the craft. The team members looked at one another, curious; somehow, a little nervous.

"What a communication system," said Paul softly. "The metal of our hull is acting as a speaker. That's why we heard it from all directions."

Omar nodded, heavy brows knotted.

"We'll see what happens next," he muttered. "If this gets dangerous, we'll use the emergency protocols."

The craft began to glow softly, flushing a soft, delicate green. The light bathed the interior, turning the occupants a ghastly hue. Leah shivered and looked at Paul, who went to the viewport and stood staring out, gasping.

"What's happening?" choked Leah.

"We're lifting! Whatever it is, it's moving us."

The others crowded beside him, looking out. Here the green was more vivid, intense. They could feel its energy tingling on their skin. Beneath them, the landing pad receded. Spread out under their eyes was the panorama of a dying world.

Great structures lay crumbled and scattered across the landscape in grey desolation. Sunlight struggling through the haze made harsh shadows. Far to the north a mountain range lifted its barren peaks to a sullen sky. To the south, beyond the ruins, lay a brown waste of dead vegetation. To the west—

"The facility," said Julia, "it's still operational. Thank God—"

Omar erupted with bitter laughter.

"For what? How do we know what we're dealing with? An operational facility doesn't mean friendly. We found that out at the Horizonville site."

"We can hope," said Paul sharply. "Maybe they have the solution, stored where our sensors couldn't detect it."

The mighty dome that covered the facility glimmered in the morning light. Beneath it, the white towers and research buildings stood in preserved beauty above carefully maintained structures and rounded laboratories. A faint mist seemed to hang in the facility corridors visible through the transparent sections.

"It looks empty," said Julia heavily. "Abandoned."

"Something's alive," protested Paul. "Something that communicated with us, that is controlling this green field."

A section of the dome slid back, and the aircraft moved through the opening. The dome closed after it.

"We're trapped now," grunted Omar. He moved his hand along the viewport, pressing hard. He said swiftly, "You can stay here if you want, but I'm getting emergency equipment. I'm not going to be caught unprepared."

He swung through the hatch and out of sight. They heard him moving below; heard the opening of storage compartments, the gathering of supplies. They could imagine him preparing for confrontation.

"Bring us some too," cried Paul suddenly, and turned again to look out the viewport.

The aircraft settled down on the white surface of an immense courtyard. The green field was gone, suddenly. The uncanny silence of the place pressed in on them.

"Think it's safe to go out?" asked Julia.

"Check the atmospheric readings," said Paul. "If the air's safe, I'd like to investigate directly."

Julia studied the instruments, staring at readings that wavered on screens, then straightened abruptly.

"Paul," said Julia with wonder. "It's pure. I mean actually pure. No toxins. No particulates. Just clean air!"

Paul leaped to her side, staring, frowning.

"No toxins. No particulates. That means there's no pollution in this place! No contamination."

He began to laugh, then caught himself.

"No pollution," he whispered, "and every one of us is going to die of the plague anyway."

Omar came up through the hatch and distributed emergency supplies. They secured them while Omar worked the door mechanism. He threw it open, and clean air, and faint tendrils of whitish mist came flowing into the craft.

Julia took a deep breath and her face brightened with wonder.

"I feel renewed. Like standing in an old forest before the collapse. You know, with clean air and birdsong, with natural light filtering through leaves. You felt alive. Truly alive! I feel like that now."

They smiled cautiously and went through the door, descending to the courtyard.

They turned.

She was coming across the courtyard, moving with purpose, a tall figure in a pristine white laboratory coat. Her hair was silver-white, pulled back severely, and her eyes—there seemed to be something unusual about her eyes, as if they saw more than normal human eyes should see.

"Lord," whispered Omar. "What is she?"

"Don't know," said Paul. "Maybe she's the researcher we're looking for—"

"Researcher?" queried Omar harshly. "She doesn't look entirely human anymore. I'm going to use the deterrent—"

His hand moved toward the emergency device at his belt; reached for it and began to activate it.

"Look out!" yelled Paul.

The figure moved with impossible speed, crossing the distance between them in seconds. Before Omar could complete the action, she was upon them, and they felt a wave of energy wash over them that left them paralyzed, unable to move.

Omar was held rigid in the air, suspended by forces he couldn't comprehend. He hung there as Paul tried to move, tried to reach him. But Naomi was too quick, too precise. She gestured, and Julia and Leah found themselves similarly frozen, held in place by invisible forces.

"Wait," called Paul, unable to move his arms, seeking any way to communicate.

Naomi released them suddenly, letting them drop gently to the ground. She stood before them, and they could see now that her eyes held a strange luminescence, and her skin had an odd translucent quality, as if she were more energy than matter.

Paul stared upward at her from where he'd fallen, trying to understand.

Naomi looked at the beings that lay on the white surface. Strange visitors they were, unlike anyone she had seen in decades. So fragile, so vulnerable. And such limited lifespans! Why, an unprotected human would sicken within hours in the world outside, and Naomi had never rated normal humans very highly anymore.

She looked at their aircraft, examined it with her enhanced senses. She cast a glance back at the visitors again, and shook her head. Fragile beings they might be, but they had mastered navigation through the toxic zones. Well, she'd always maintained that determination took different forms. Survival here on Earth required different adaptations.

Naomi bent to gather the visitors in fields of energy, lifting them carefully. Her enhanced vision caught suddenly by the cellular damage visible in their tissues. The plague! That was serious, but Naomi knew a way to cure it. Naomi knew a way to cure anything now.

She moved swiftly across the courtyard and onto a flat, glittering ramp that stretched upward toward an arched doorway set like a portal of light in a long, low building next to the vast Chamber of the Cylinders. She carried these visitors easily, without effort. The ease of her passage gave her time to think.

She had been glad to find these visitors. They were someone to converse with after decades of loneliness. But as she approached them there in the courtyard, calling out to them, they could not hear her properly. Her voice had been modified by the treatments, pitched beyond normal human range. She wondered if that was beyond their hearing capacity. She ought to verify that, to be certain. Still, they had heard her on their aircraft. She had transmitted a message through the craft's communication system. Perhaps the metal hull had in some manner made her voice audible to them, translated the frequencies to something they could process.

Then there was the matter of the plague. She could eliminate that easily enough, in the Chamber of the Cylinders. But first they would have to be prepared. And the preparation—hurt. Well, better a brief period of discomfort than death through worse means.

And if she could not speak to them conventionally, they could communicate with her through their neural patterns. Once unconscious, she could access their memories with a neural interface screen. That should be enlightening. It made Naomi hopeful, reflecting upon it, and Naomi had not known hope for a long time.

From the passage she hurried into a large white room, fitted with glass containers and instruments and glittering metal apparatus, so numerous that the room seemed a forest of equipment. Down on flat, smooth tables Naomi lowered her visitors. With careful movements she adjusted restraints to secure them, bound them for their own safety. From a small, mobile unit she took a neural inhibitor and touched it to their temples. As it met the skin, it hummed once softly.

"It's temporarily suspended their pain receptors," Naomi said aloud, glad at this chance to exercise her voice. "They won't be able to feel discomfort for a while. When the worst of the cellular restructuring has passed, they will recover. And now to examine their memories—"

She fitted neural sensors over their heads and calibrated them carefully. She activated a crystalline screen; connected the inputs from the sensors to the screen's processing unit.

"I wonder if they've developed this technology," Naomi mused. "They must be aware that the brain generates electromagnetic patterns. Perhaps they can chart those patterns on graphs. But do they know that each pattern represents accessible information? I can translate those patterns into coherent memories—but can they?"

She settled into a chair, gazing at the screen as she activated the system.

An image appeared on the screen; grew clearer, then stabilized. Naomi found herself looking at a city far larger than any she remembered. Tall grey towers reached high into a hazy sky, and broad streets wound between them, crowded with people wearing filtration masks. On the tallest buildings were great air filtration systems, their massive fans turning slowly in the polluted air.

The scene changed suddenly. She looked into a medical facility and watched a young woman struggling to breathe, surrounded by concerned family members. She too had the plague. Now she witnessed the research laboratories where exhausted scientists worked with inadequate equipment, trying desperately to find solutions under an unforgiving deadline. Even these dedicated researchers showed signs of contamination.

A tall, serious man in a white coat looked out at her. His lips moved, and Naomi read their meaning through the neural interface. This man spoke to one named Paul Graham, commissioning him with an aircraft, explaining the need for the cure, the desperation of the plague. The thoughts of this Paul became clearer as Naomi adjusted different controls. The unspoken thoughts flowing into her consciousness through the screen continued. The specific words she didn't catch, but the necessity for a solution, and the danger of the plague she understood completely. The images shifted, grew complex—

Naomi stared at a monument carved in stone, weathered but still legible: IN MEMORY OF THE RESEARCHERS WHO GAVE THEIR LIVES FOR HUMANITY. She wondered what those researchers had done, to merit such recognition. They must have made crucial discoveries, or saved countless lives. She wished there were colleagues alive to remember her work.

She rose suddenly, standing upright, swaying slightly with the energy coursing through her. Why, she had the power to save these people! These visitors would gladly honor her memory! True, she could not save the past—but she could save the future!

Naomi removed the sensors, and deactivated the screen. She reached to a series of controls inset in the wall, and adjusted them carefully. Turning, she saw the figures of the four scientists begin to glow with a red aura as energy drifted upward from the tabletops, passing through them as if they were transparent, rising upwards to dissipate in the air near the ceiling.

"That will prepare their bodies for the Chamber of the Cylinders," she said. "When they realize that I am trying to help them, they will gladly hear what I have to say!"

Opening the laboratory door, Naomi passed out and closed it behind her.

It was the sensation of heat spreading through his body that woke Paul. He opened his eyes, then shut them as his body experienced intense discomfort.

"What's happening?" he gasped, struggling against the sensation.

In every cell of his body, change was occurring. In arms and legs and chest and lungs, transformation was taking place. He could feel it working through him, altering him at a fundamental level. He couldn't endure it; he couldn't—

He turned his head to the side; saw the others secured as he was. They were still unconscious. How could they sleep through this? Why weren't they experiencing what he was? He opened his mouth to call out; then held back.

Julia cried out suddenly, her body tensing.

It woke the others. They too called out and struggled, and their limbs strained against the restraints.

"Got to get free," Paul panted, pulling against the bindings. The muscles of his arms strained with effort, but the restraints held. He fell back, breathing hard.

"That woman," said Omar angrily. "That silver-haired, energy-wielding researcher did this to us. I knew it! I knew we couldn't trust her! If I ever get loose I'll make sure she faces a proper ethics review."

"Maybe—maybe she's experimenting on us," moaned Julia. "With energy fields or—or something—I can't take much more!"

"Hold on," said Paul, fighting the restraints. "I think it's subsiding. Yeah, yeah—it is. It doesn't feel as intense now."

Omar grunted in surprise.

"You're right. It is subsiding. And—hey, one of my arm restraints is loosening. The material has weakened slightly. Maybe I can work it free."

They turned their heads to watch, breathing hard, perspiration on their foreheads. Omar's muscular arm flexed as he pulled and twisted, grunting with effort. A fastener broke free, clattering against the table as it came loose. Omar held his arm up and laughed with grim satisfaction.

"I'll have you all free in a moment," he said, removing the remaining restraints from his body.

He jumped from the table and stretched. He looked at the others with an odd expression.

"You know, it's strange—but I feel incredible. Actually, I think whatever she did might have helped. Here, Leah—you first."

"Thanks, Omar. We're still a team, right?"

When Leah was free, Omar came to stand over Paul, looking down at him. His eyes narrowed suddenly. He smiled slightly, but there was something calculating in his expression.

"Maybe you should stay restrained," he said. "In case that—that woman comes back. She won't blame us all if I'm the only one who escaped."

"Don't be ridiculous," said Paul.

But Omar shook his head, and his expression hardened.

"No. No, I think I need to explore this facility alone. Find out what secrets she's keeping."

"Don't be a fool, Omar," snapped Paul firmly. "That's not your decision to make. I'm the team leader. What I say stands."

Omar smiled coldly. Into his eyes came a glint of stubborn defiance.

"You were our leader—back in Alexandria City. We're in unknown territory now. Things are different. I want to learn the secret of this place, Paul. Something tells me I could revolutionize research ethics with what's here, get my reputation back."

Paul struggled helplessly, protesting, saying, "What's gotten into you?"

"Nothing new. Remember me, Omar May? I'm a disgraced researcher, I am. An expelled scientist. I'd have done anything to get out of that disgrace. I volunteered to come with you for the cure. Me and Leah. Julia doesn't count—she came because of her family. We were the only two willing to risk everything. Outcasts, both of us."
question: How did Naomi Wyatt come to be alone at the research facility?
option_a: Her colleagues died from the pollution and environmental plague that ravaged the outside world before she could perfect her preservation methods.
option_b: She deliberately isolated herself from other researchers to conduct controversial experiments without ethics oversight.
correct_answer_text: Her colleagues died from the pollution and environmental plague that ravaged the outside world before she could perfect her preservation methods.
incorrect_answer_text: She deliberately isolated herself from other researchers to conduct controversial experiments without ethics oversight.
explanation: The story explicitly states that Naomi perfected the environmental mist "many years ago, when it was too late to save her colleagues" and that she had "sealed the vast dome of transparent polymer above this greatest of the research stations and filled it with the mist" after her colleagues were already gone. It also mentions this was "another discovery that came too late to save her colleagues." This indicates her colleagues died from the environmental collapse before she developed the technology to preserve the facility, making option A correct.
