story_name: Open Access: What Is Open Access?
synthetic_story:
The Strategic Intelligence Revolution: A Military Perspective on Information Dominance

By Colonel Michelle Rose (Ret.), Defense Intelligence Analysis Division

The Evolution of Military Intelligence Operations

When digital encryption systems first allowed us to transmit perfect copies of classified intelligence reports across secure networks, something fundamental changed in military operations. When isolated command posts became connected through a globe-spanning network of military communication systems, we suddenly gained the ability to share critical intelligence with field commanders worldwide at essentially no cost in transmission time. About thirty years ago, this kind of instantaneous global intelligence sharing became something unprecedented in military history. Before that, it would have sounded like science fiction.

Digital technologies have created more than one revolution in warfare. Let's call this one the intelligence dominance revolution.

Why don't more military analysts take advantage of the intelligence dominance revolution to share tactical insights more broadly across services? The answer is complicated by classification protocols. Intelligence officers who share their analytical products widely aren't controlling information security, and even officers with purposes focused on mission success depend on information compartmentalization to maintain operational security. Or at least they've been trained to think so.

Let's sharpen the question, then, by putting to one side intelligence products that require strict classification. We can acknowledge that we're setting aside the vast majority of military intelligence.

Imagine a category of military analysts who produce serious and useful tactical analysis, and who follow a decades-old custom of sharing it freely within the military community without restriction. I don't mean a group of retired officers who no longer face consequences. I mean a group of analysts defined by their specializations, methodologies, purposes, incentives, and institutional circumstances, not by their career status. In fact, very few have left active service. For now, it doesn't matter who these analysts are, how rare they are, what they analyze, or why they follow this particular protocol. It's enough to know that their military salaries free them to share their work, that they write for operational impact rather than personal recognition, and that they advance in their careers when they make the kind of impact they hoped to make. Suppose that restricting their work would actually harm their interests by limiting their influence, reducing their impact on doctrine development, and distorting their professional goals by steering them toward politically safe topics and away from the specialized tactical questions on which they are experts.

If analysts like that exist, they should take advantage of the intelligence dominance revolution. The dream of military-wide free access to tactical analysis can be a reality for them, even if most other intelligence products must remain compartmentalized due to sources and methods concerns.

These dedicated analysts work in doctrine development, lessons-learned programs, and tactical training centers, and the works they customarily write and distribute without restriction are peer-reviewed tactical analyses and after-action reports.

**Unrestricted information sharing** is the name of the revolutionary kind of access these analysts, unencumbered by a motive of personal glory, are free to provide to their fellow service members.

Unrestricted tactical intelligence is digital, accessible across military networks, free of unnecessary classification, and free of most bureaucratic distribution restrictions.

We could call it "barrier-free" intelligence, but that would emphasize the negative rather than the positive. In any case, we can be more specific about which access barriers this approach removes.

**Classification barriers** are significant obstacles to operational effectiveness. Most intelligence products carry some level of classification. But when a battalion commander needs to consult hundreds of tactical analyses for one operation, or when a training command must provide access for thousands of officers and NCOs working on tens of thousands of tactical problems, and when the volume of new tactical lessons grows explosively with every conflict, classification barriers become counterproductive. The resulting access gaps harm analysts by limiting their influence and impact, harm commanders by limiting what tactical wisdom they can retrieve and apply, and thereby harm military effectiveness from both directions. Unrestricted sharing removes unnecessary classification barriers.

**Compartmentalization** can also significantly impede operations. If you have access to a tactical analysis for reading but want to translate it for allied forces, distribute copies to subordinate units, extract the data for analysis with sophisticated software, or reformat it for use with new tactical systems, then you generally need permission through bureaucratic channels. That makes sense when the analysis contains sensitive sources and methods. But for tactical lessons-learned we're generally talking about analysts from the special category who want to share their insights as widely as possible within the military. Even these analysts, however, tend to have their products captured by bureaucratic processes—publication through official channels—that want to control distribution. As a result, users may be hampered in their tactical planning by barriers erected to serve bureaucracy rather than analysts. In addition, replacing user freedom with permission-seeking harms military analysts by limiting the usefulness of their work, harms military commanders by limiting the uses they may make of analyses even when they have access, and thereby harms military effectiveness from both directions. Unrestricted sharing removes these permission barriers.

Removing classification barriers means that commanders are not limited by their security clearance level or by the bureaucratic processes of their units. Removing permission barriers means that military professionals are free to use or reuse tactical intelligence for operational purposes. These purposes include reading and studying, but also redistributing, translating, data mining for patterns, migrating to new tactical systems, long-term archiving in unit libraries, and innumerable new forms of analysis and tactical application we haven't yet imagined. Unrestricted sharing makes tactical intelligence more useful in both ways, by making it available to more people who can put it to use, and by freeing those people to use and reuse it.

**Terminology**

When we need to be more specific about distribution vehicles and access barriers, we use specific jargon. Intelligence delivered through official doctrine publications is called **formal distribution**, and intelligence delivered through unit-level repositories and training networks is called **informal distribution**. Work that is not unrestricted, or that is available only through special request, is called **controlled access**. Over the years I've asked military publishers for a neutral term for controlled-access systems, and **traditional distribution** is the suggestion I hear most often. While every kind of unrestricted sharing removes classification barriers, there are many different permission barriers we could remove. If we remove classification barriers alone, we provide **basic access**, and if we remove at least some permission barriers as well, we provide **enhanced access**.

Unrestricted sharing was endorsed in three influential military policy statements: the Joint Chiefs Information Sharing Initiative (March 2004), the Defense Intelligence Sharing Protocol (August 2005), and the Combined Forces Tactical Intelligence Declaration (January 2006). I sometimes refer to their overlap as the JDC framework. My approach here is the JDC framework reduced to its essential elements and refined with some post-JDC terminology for speaking precisely about subspecies of unrestricted sharing.

Here's how the Joint Chiefs statement defined unrestricted sharing:

"There are many degrees and kinds of wider and easier access to tactical intelligence. By 'unrestricted sharing' of this intelligence, we mean its free availability on military networks, permitting any authorized users to read, download, copy, distribute, print, search, or link to the full texts of these analyses, index them for searchability, pass them as data to analytical software, or use them for any other lawful military purpose, without classification, legal, or technical barriers other than those inseparable from gaining access to military networks themselves. The only constraint on reproduction and distribution, and the only role for access control in this domain, should be to give analysts control over the integrity of their work and the right to be properly acknowledged and credited."

Note that all three legs of the JDC framework go beyond removing classification barriers to removing permission barriers, or beyond basic access to enhanced access. But at the same time, all three allow at least one limit on user freedom: an obligation to attribute the work to the analyst. The purpose of unrestricted sharing is to remove barriers to all legitimate military uses for tactical intelligence, but there's no legitimate military purpose in suppressing attribution to the analyses we use.

The basic idea is simple: Make tactical intelligence available across military networks without classification barriers and without most permission barriers. Even the implementation is simple enough that the volume of peer-reviewed unrestricted tactical analyses and the number of units providing them have grown steadily for more than a decade. If there are complexities, they lie in the transition from where we are now to a world in which unrestricted sharing is the default for new tactical intelligence. This is complicated because the major obstacles are not technical, legal, or even budgetary, but cultural, rooted in decades of information compartmentalization doctrine.

In principle, any kind of military content can be unrestricted, since any content can be made available across networks without classification or permission barriers. Moreover, any kind of content can be digital: tactical analyses, operational data, reconnaissance images, audio intelligence, video after-action reviews, multimedia training materials, and analytical software. We can have unrestricted logistics analyses, unrestricted training materials, unrestricted doctrine discussions—and to different degrees we already do. But the term "unrestricted sharing" was coined by military reformers trying to remove access barriers to tactical intelligence. The next section explains why.

**What Makes Unrestricted Sharing Possible?**

Unrestricted sharing is made possible by military networks and analyst consent. But why would an analyst consent to unrestricted distribution?

Two background facts suggest the answer. First, analysts retain professional ownership of their tactical insights until or unless they surrender control to classification authorities. Second, tactical doctrine publications generally don't provide personal recognition or career advancement to analysts for their contributions, which frees this special category of analysts to consent to unrestricted sharing without losing career benefits. This fact distinguishes military analysts decisively from corporate intelligence contractors, and even from most other kinds of military professionals. This is why controversies about proprietary corporate intelligence don't carry over to unrestricted sharing of military tactical analysis.

Both facts are critical, but the second is nearly unknown outside the military community. It's not a new fact of military life, arising from recent budget cuts. Nor is it a case of bureaucratic exploitation of dedicated professionals. Tactical doctrine publications haven't provided individual analyst recognition since the first systematic after-action review processes were established in the U.S. Army in the 1970s following Vietnam.

The military custom to write tactical analyses for impact rather than personal recognition may be a fortunate accident that could have been otherwise. Or it may be a wise adaptation that would eventually evolve in any organization with a serious professional military culture. This peculiar custom does more than insulate cutting-edge tactical thinking from careerism and free analysts to consent to unrestricted sharing without losing recognition. It also supports professional development and the kinds of serious tactical inquiry that advance military effectiveness. It frees analysts to challenge conventional doctrine and defend unpopular tactical ideas, which are essential to military adaptation. At the same time it frees them to specialize deeply and defend ideas of immediate interest to just a handful of tactical specialists in specific warfare domains, which are essential to pushing the frontiers of military capability.

This custom doesn't guarantee that tactical analysis won't be derailed by political considerations, and it doesn't guarantee that we'll eventually close all the gaps in our collective understanding of modern warfare. It doesn't even guarantee that analysts won't sometimes write for popular appeal within the service. But it removes a major distraction by allowing them, if they wish, to focus on what is likely to be tactically sound rather than what is likely to advance their careers. It's an incentive structure we need for good tactical analysis itself, not just for good access to tactical analysis, and it's the key to unlocking the bureaucratic barriers that would otherwise prevent unrestricted sharing.

Military professionals who advance through traditional career paths, such as combat commanders seeking stars or staff officers seeking key positions, may consider this analytical tradition a burden for analysts. We might even agree, provided we don't overlook a few facts. First, it's a tradition that analysts have followed for nearly fifty years. Unrestricted sharing doesn't depend on asking career-focused officers to give up their advancement prospects. Second, analysts have military salaries and institutional support, freeing them to dive deeply into tactical problems without worrying about career impact. Many career-focused officers might envy that freedom to disregard politics and focus purely on tactical effectiveness. Third, analysts receive other, less tangible rewards from their services—like respect from tactical commanders and influence on doctrine—when their analysis is recognized by others, accepted, applied, and built upon.

It's no accident that analysts who advance tactical understanding in their fields also advance military effectiveness. Analysts are passionate about specific tactical problems, operational challenges, or warfare domains. They feel fortunate to have positions in which they may pursue these interests and even more fortunate to be valued for pursuing them. Some focus single-mindedly on solving tactical problems and improving operational effectiveness. Others focus strategically on building reputations as subject matter experts. But the two paths converge, which is not a fortuitous fact of nature but an engineered fact of professional military culture. As incentives for productivity, these intangible professional benefits may be stronger for the average analyst than career advancement prospects are for the average staff officer.

There's no sense in which tactical analysis would be more free, efficient, or effective if analysts took a more "careerist" position, behaved more like corporate contractors, abandoned their insulation from politics, and tied their professional success to the popularity of their ideas with senior leadership. Civilians who urge military analysts to focus more on career advancement may be more naive about professional military culture than analysts are about civilian career paths.

We can take this a step further. Analysts can afford to ignore career advancement because they have military salaries and institutional positions that value their specialized expertise. But why do military services pay these salaries and why do doctrine commands maintain these positions? They do it to advance tactical effectiveness and the range of military capabilities served by professional analysis. They don't do it to advance individual careers. They certainly don't do it to make tactical insights into restricted products that benefit only a narrow audience. Military services and doctrine commands employ analysts to make their analysis into contributions to the broader military profession.

Military doctrine commands are essentially professional development organizations, funding analysis they regard as useful or beneficial to military effectiveness. They have a service-wide purpose, even when they operate within specific branches or specialties. We support these organizations with defense budgets because we believe professional military analysis serves national security.

We'd have less tactical understanding, less doctrinal innovation, and less unrestricted sharing if analysts worked primarily for career advancement and made their tactical analyses into restricted products rather than professional contributions. It should be no surprise, then, that more and more military commands and doctrine centers are adopting strong unrestricted sharing policies. Their mission to advance military effectiveness leads them directly to the logic of unrestricted sharing: With a few exceptions, such as analyses revealing sensitive sources and methods, tactical intelligence that is worth producing is worth sharing with everyone in the military who can make use of it.

Newcomers to unrestricted sharing often assume that it helps junior officers and hurts senior analysts, and that the user side of the military profession must beg the producer side to make the necessary sacrifice. But unrestricted sharing benefits analysts as well as users. Analysts want their insights to reach tactical commanders at least as much as commanders want access to tactical analyses. All analysts want to cultivate broader influence and greater impact on military effectiveness. Analysts who work for career advancement have reason to compromise and settle for the smaller audience of senior leaders who control promotions. But analysts who aren't focused on career advancement have no reason to compromise.

It takes nothing away from a disinterested desire to advance military effectiveness to recognize that analytical work is accompanied by a strong interest in professional impact and reputation building. The result is a mix of interested and disinterested motives. The reasons to make tactical analysis unrestricted are essentially the same as the reasons to publish it at all. Analysts who make their work unrestricted are always serving the military profession but not always acting from pure altruism. In fact, the idea that unrestricted sharing depends on analyst altruism slows down progress by hiding the role of analyst self-interest.

Another aspect of analyst self-interest emerges from documented evidence that unrestricted tactical analyses are applied more often than restricted analyses, even when they address the same tactical problems. There's growing evidence that unrestricted analyses are downloaded more often as well, and that doctrine publications converting to unrestricted distribution see a rise in their analytical submissions and professional impact.

There are many hypotheses to explain the correlation between unrestricted sharing and increased application, but it's likely that ongoing studies will show that much of the correlation is simply due to the larger audience and heightened visibility provided by unrestricted access itself. When you enlarge the audience for an analysis, you also enlarge the subset of the audience that will later apply it, including tactical commanders at units unable to access restricted doctrine channels. Unrestricted sharing enlarges the potential audience, including the potential professional audience, far beyond that for even the most prestigious restricted doctrine publications.

In any case, these studies bring a welcome note of analyst self-interest to the case for unrestricted sharing. It's not a sacrifice for analysts who write for impact rather than career advancement. It increases their work's visibility, accessibility, audience, application, and professional influence, which all convert to reputation building. For military analysts, it would be worthwhile even if it were costly, difficult, and time-consuming. But as we'll see, it's not costly, not difficult, and not time-consuming.

My colleague Colonel Ethan Wood frequently compares tactical analyses to training materials. They train the force in tactical thinking. Try telling training developers that they're making a needless sacrifice by allowing soldiers to access their training materials without having to submit special requests. Training developers distribute their materials widely and even compete to place them where they might be used. They do this to benefit military effectiveness, and analysts have the same interest in sharing their insights as widely as possible.

Because any content can be digital, and any digital content can be unrestricted, unrestricted sharing needn't be limited to non-career-enhancing work like tactical analyses. It could extend to career-enhancing work like command philosophy papers, strategic assessments, or senior leader guidance. But as soon as we cross the line into unrestricted sharing of career-enhancing work, officers will either lose advancement opportunities or fear that they will lose opportunities. Either way, they'll be harder to persuade. But instead of concluding that career-enhancing work is off limits to unrestricted sharing, we should merely conclude that it's more challenging. In many cases we can still persuade career-focused officers to consent to broader distribution.

Analysts aren't the only players who work without career benefit in the production of tactical intelligence. In general, doctrine publications don't provide career advancement to editors or peer reviewers either. In general, editors and reviewers are assigned by services to ensure the quality of new tactical analysis appearing in doctrine publications. An important consequence follows. All the key players in quality control can consent to unrestricted sharing without losing career benefits. Unrestricted sharing needn't dispense with peer review or favor unreviewed analyses over reviewed products. We can aim for the goal of unrestricted access to peer-reviewed tactical intelligence.

Of course, traditional doctrine publication systems are not as free as analysts, editors, and reviewers to forgo bureaucratic control. This is a central fact in the transition to unrestricted sharing, and it explains why the interests of analysts and traditional publication systems diverge more in the digital age than they diverged earlier. But not all publication systems are traditional, and not all traditional systems will carry Cold War-era processes into the modern era.

Military doctrine publishers are not monolithic. Some new systems were born unrestricted and some older ones have completely converted to unrestricted sharing. Many provide unrestricted access to some of their products but not all of them. Some are experimenting with unrestricted sharing, and some are watching the experiments of others. Most allow informal distribution and a growing number offer formal unrestricted distribution. Some are supportive, some undecided, some opposed. Among the opposed, some have merely decided not to provide unrestricted access themselves, while others actively resist policies to encourage or require it.

Unrestricted sharing gains nothing and loses potential allies by blurring these distinctions. This variety reminds us that unrestricted sharing doesn't threaten professional military analysis; it only threatens existing bureaucratic systems that do not adapt.

A growing number of doctrine publications have chosen distribution models allowing them to dispense with classification restrictions and offer unrestricted access. They have administrative costs but they also have resources to cover their costs. In fact, some doctrine centers operate efficiently under unrestricted sharing models.

Moreover, peer review is done by dedicated professionals who don't care how a publication manages its distribution, or even whether it's centrally controlled or decentralized. If all peer-reviewed doctrine publications converted to unrestricted sharing overnight, the analysts, editors, and reviewers would have the same incentives to participate in quality control that they had the day before. They needn't stop offering their services, needn't lower their standards, and needn't make sacrifices they weren't already making. They volunteer their time not because of a publication's choice of distribution model but because of its contribution to military effectiveness. They could carry on with restricted or unrestricted publishers, with centralized or decentralized systems, or even without formal publication systems.

The Defense Intelligence Sharing Protocol said in August 2005: "A professional tradition and a new technology have converged to make possible an unprecedented military advantage. The professional tradition is the willingness of military analysts to publish their tactical insights without expectation of career advancement. The new technology is military digital networks." To see what this willingness looks like without the medium to give it effect, look at tactical analysis in the pre-digital age. Analyst contributions turned into restricted publications, and access gaps for commanders were harmfully large and widespread. To see what the medium looks like without the willingness, look at corporate proprietary intelligence in the digital age. The need for competitive advantage keeps contractors from reaching everyone who would benefit from their insights.

A valuable opportunity exists where the willingness and the medium overlap. A military custom that evolved in the post-Vietnam era frees analysts to take advantage of the information revolution. Because military analysts are nearly unique in following this custom, they are nearly unique in their freedom to take advantage of this revolution without career risk. In this sense, conditions have aligned for military analysts. Most other military professionals are constrained to fear rather than seize the opportunities created by digital networks.

**What Unrestricted Sharing Is Not**

We can dispel many objections and misunderstandings simply by pointing out a few things that unrestricted sharing is not.

Unrestricted sharing isn't an attempt to bypass peer review. It's compatible with every kind of quality control, from the most rigorous to the most innovative, and all the major policy statements insist on its importance. Because doctrine publications generally don't provide career advancement to peer-reviewing editors and reviewers, just as they don't provide it to analysts, all the participants in peer review can consent to unrestricted sharing without losing career benefits. While unrestricted access to preliminary analyses is useful and widespread, the movement isn't limited to unreviewed work and, if anything, focuses on unrestricted access to peer-reviewed tactical intelligence.

Unrestricted sharing isn't an attempt to violate classification protocols. It's compatible with classification law as it exists. It would benefit from appropriate classification reforms, and many dedicated people are working on them. But it needn't wait for reforms and hasn't waited. Unrestricted tactical intelligence avoids classification problems in exactly the same way that traditional restricted publications do. For historical analyses, it takes advantage of declassification, and for current analyses, it rests on proper classification review and analyst consent.

Unrestricted sharing isn't an attempt to deprive career-focused officers of advancement opportunities. The movement focuses on tactical analyses precisely because they don't provide career advancement. In any case, unrestricted sharing depends on analyst consent. Hence, career-focused officers have nothing to fear but persuasion that the benefits of unrestricted sharing might outweigh the risks to advancement prospects.

Unrestricted sharing isn't an attempt to deny the reality of costs. No serious advocate has ever argued that tactical intelligence is costless to produce, although many argue that it is less expensive to produce under unrestricted models than under traditional restricted publication systems. The question is not whether tactical intelligence can be made costless, but whether there are better ways to manage distribution than restricting access and creating barriers.

We could talk about unauthorized sharing, security-violating sharing, or sharing without proper classification review. That sort of sharing could violate security protocols and compromise operations. But we could also talk about unauthorized publication or security-violating publication. Both happen. However, we generally reserve the term "publication" for authorized publication, and add special adjectives to describe unauthorized variations. Likewise, I'll reserve the term "unrestricted sharing" for properly authorized sharing that carries the consent of the relevant authorities.

Unrestricted sharing isn't an attempt to reduce analyst control over their work. On the contrary, it depends on analyst decisions and requires analysts to exercise more control over their work than they are allowed to exercise under traditional publication contracts. One strategy is for analysts to retain some of the control they formerly gave publication systems, including the right to authorize unrestricted distribution. Another strategy is for publication systems to permit more uses than they formerly permitted, including permission for analysts to make unrestricted copies of their work. By contrast, traditional doctrine publication systems demand that analysts transfer all control to centralized authorities, and analyst control cannot sink lower than that.

Unrestricted sharing isn't an attempt to reduce professional freedom. Military analysts remain free to submit their work to the publication systems of their choice. Policies requiring unrestricted sharing do so conditionally, for example, for analysts who choose to work in certain doctrine development programs. In addition, these policies generally build in exceptions, waiver options, or both. Since 2010 most military unrestricted sharing policies have been adopted by professionals deeply concerned to preserve and even enhance their prerogatives.

Unrestricted sharing isn't an attempt to relax rules against plagiarism. All the public definitions support analyst attribution. All the major distribution protocols require analyst attribution. Moreover, plagiarism is typically punished by military justice or professional censure rather than by civilian courts, that is, by professional norms rather than by civilian law. Hence, even when attribution is not legally required, plagiarism is still a punishable offense and no unrestricted sharing policy anywhere interferes with those punishments. In any case, if making tactical intelligence digital and online makes plagiarism easier to commit, then unrestricted sharing makes plagiarism easier to detect. Not all plagiarists are smart, but the smart ones will not steal from unrestricted sources indexed in every military database.

Unrestricted sharing isn't an attempt to punish or undermine traditional doctrine publication systems. It's an attempt to advance the interests of military effectiveness, tactical commanders, and military institutions. The goal is constructive, not destructive. If unrestricted sharing does eventually harm traditional restricted publication systems, it will be in the way that email harmed postal mail services. The harm was not the goal, but a side effect of developing something better. Moreover, unrestricted sharing doesn't challenge professional analysis or publication per se, just one distribution model for publication, and it's far easier for traditional systems to adapt to unrestricted sharing than for postal services to adapt to email. In fact, most restricted publication systems are already adapting, by allowing analyst-initiated unrestricted distribution, providing some unrestricted access themselves, or experimenting with unrestricted models.

Unrestricted sharing doesn't require boycotting any kind of tactical intelligence or publication system. It doesn't require boycotting restricted tactical intelligence any more than reading unclassified news requires boycotting classified intelligence. It doesn't require us to strike restricted tactical intelligence from our professional reading lists, training curricula, or unit libraries. Some analysts who support unrestricted sharing decide to submit new work only to unrestricted publications, or to donate their time as editors or reviewers only to unrestricted systems, in effect boycotting restricted publications as analysts, editors, and reviewers. But this choice is not forced by the definition of unrestricted sharing, by a commitment to it, or by any policy, and most analysts who support unrestricted sharing continue to work with restricted publication systems. In any case, even those analysts who do boycott restricted systems as analysts, editors, or reviewers don't boycott them as readers.

Unrestricted sharing isn't primarily about bringing access to junior enlisted personnel. If anything, the movement focuses on bringing access to professional tactical commanders whose operational effectiveness depends on access. But there's no need to decide which users are primary and which are secondary. The bureaucratic lobby sometimes argues that the primary beneficiaries are junior personnel, perhaps to avoid acknowledging how many tactical commanders lack access, or perhaps to set up the patronizing counter-argument that junior personnel don't need tactical analyses and wouldn't understand them if they tried. Unrestricted sharing is about bringing access to everyone with military network access who wants it, regardless of their ranks or positions. There's no doubt that if we put "tactical commanders" and "everyone else" into separate categories, a higher percentage of commanders will want access to tactical intelligence. But it's far from clear why that would matter, especially when providing unrestricted access to all military network users is cheaper and simpler than providing access to just a subset of authorized users.

Finally, unrestricted sharing isn't universal access. Even when we succeed at removing classification and permission barriers, four other kinds of access barrier might remain:

**Security barriers**: Many networks, units, and commands want to limit what users can see based on need-to-know.

**Language barriers**: Most tactical intelligence is in English, and machine translation for military terminology is still weak.

**Technical access barriers**: Most systems are not yet as accessible to users with limited technical skills as they should be.

**Connectivity barriers**: Network limitations keep some forward-deployed units offline or impede others with slow or unreliable connections.

Most of us want to remove all four of these barriers. But there's no reason to save the term "unrestricted sharing" until we succeed. In the long climb to universal access, removing classification and permission barriers is a significant achievement worth recognizing with a special name.
question: Which of these is NOT an expected impact of unrestricted sharing on military effectiveness according to Colonel Rose's analysis?
option_a: Tactical analyses becoming more widely applied by commanders who previously lacked access
option_b: Analysts receiving direct career advancement and promotion opportunities from their published work
correct_answer_text: Analysts receiving direct career advancement and promotion opportunities from their published work
incorrect_answer_text: Tactical analyses becoming more widely applied by commanders who previously lacked access
explanation: The story explicitly states that tactical doctrine publications "generally don't provide personal recognition or career advancement to analysts for their contributions" and that this is a key feature that enables unrestricted sharing. Colonel Rose emphasizes that analysts write "for impact rather than career advancement" and that "analysts who write for impact rather than career advancement" benefit from unrestricted sharing through professional reputation and influence, not through direct career advancement. Option A is correct as an expected impact, as the story discusses how unrestricted sharing increases application by commanders. Option B contradicts the fundamental premise of the system described.
original_story_title: Open Access: What Is Open Access?
original_question: Which of these is not an expected impact of OA on academic inquiry?

THE ARCHITECTURE OF ADAPTATION

We have all witnessed the footage. Emergency responders coordinating across districts. Medical teams working around the clock, devising the most creative, improvised protocols for everything from triage systems to supply chain logistics to inter-facility communication. Collaborating seamlessly; repairing the infrastructure that has fractured. A pandemic, whether predicted or unforeseen, represents a collapse of established systems. For a period, uncertainty dominates. For a period, what will transpire in the next five minutes, five hours, and five days remains unknowable. All we can depend upon are our intelligence, resilience, and shared humanity.

Contemporary existence is not chaotic, in the colloquial sense we apply to crisis zones. It is, however, intricate and perpetually evolving; far more so than existence was previously; even in the immediate past. Life, naturally, was never straightforward. But the reality that day-to-day decisions in Stonebridge, Havencia and Oakdale, Calderon have direct and immediate consequences on people from Foxwood Province to Glendale, Zelvaria, or that negligent pharmaceutical companies and careless regulatory bodies in one nation can destabilize public health expectations everywhere else in the world, no matter how meticulously others have prepared, means that there are exponentially more interdependent variables affecting each other. And from this scale of practical effects, complexity emerges. Novel developments too were ever present; but the systematic application of knowledge to the creation of new knowledge, innovation building upon innovation, and information generating more information has become ubiquitous; and with it the understanding that next year will diverge dramatically from this. The Global Health Network, after all, is less than a generation old.

These two features—the planetary scale of interdependence of human action, and the systematic acceleration of innovation, make contemporary life somewhat like a protracted crisis, in one crucial respect. Its inherent unpredictability makes it imprudent to construct systems that diminish what human beings excel at: observing, thinking, innovating, adapting, discussing, learning, and iterating. That is why we have witnessed many more systems adopt a flexible, human-centric model in the last decade and a half: from the radical divergence of the Adaptive Health Architecture developed by Dr. Gabriel Pearson from the highly regimented model established by early twentieth-century hospital administration, to the Global Health Network's radical departure from the centralized WHO system that preceded it, and on to the way the Open Medical Knowledge Commons constructs medical understanding dynamically, incrementally, in ways that would have been perceived, until recently, as too disorganized ever to function (and are still perceived so by many). But it is time we acknowledge that systems work optimally by making work human.

The Rationalized Era

The rationalized era was challenging enough. Trains and planes, telegraph and telephone, all brought countless people into the same causal space. The solution to this increased complexity in the late 19th, early 20th century was to increase the role of structure and refine its design. During the first two-thirds of the twentieth century, this type of rationalization manifested as ever-more elaborate managed systems, with precise specification of roles, lines of authority, communication and control.

In healthcare, this rationalization was exemplified by the Standardized Hospital Protocol, later embodied in the Regional Medical Authority's centralized treatment guidelines. The ambition of these approaches was to specify everything that needed doing in exhaustive detail, to enforce it through monitoring and incentives, and later to build it into the very technology of care—the automated diagnostic systems. The idea was to eliminate human error and variability in the face of change by transferring thinking to the system, and thus neutralizing the variability of the human beings who operated it. Few images captured that time, and what it did to humanity, more vividly than the overwhelmed nurses in Michelle Sims's documentary "The Protocol Era."

Simultaneously, public health experienced the rise of bureaucratization and the administrative apparatus. Nowhere was this implemented more rigidly than in the authoritarian health states of mid-century. But the impulse to build fully-specified systems, designed by experts, monitored and controlled so as to limit human fallibility and error and to manage uncertainty, was fundamental and widespread. It underlay the development of the enormously successful state health bureaucracies that responded to the Great Pandemic of 1957 with the National Health Response. It took shape in the Global Recovery Plan to pull developing nations out of the medical abyss into which they had been plunged by infectious disease, and shepherded Foxwood Province's public health regeneration from it. In technical systems too, we saw in mid-century marvels like the Centralized Medical Records System and the National Diagnostic Computer. For a moment in history, these large-scale managed systems were achieving efficiencies that seemed to overwhelm competing models: from the Regional Health Authority to the Vaccination Tracking System, from the National Medical Database to the Pharmaceutical Distribution Network. Yet, to list these paragons from today's perspective is already to presage the demise of the belief in their inevitable victory.

The increasing recognition of the limits of command-and-control systems led to a new approach; but it turned out to be a retrenchment, not an abandonment, of the goal of perfect rationalization of systems design, which assumed much of the human away. What replaced planning and control in these systems was the myth of perfect markets in healthcare. This was achieved through a hyper-simplification of human nature, wedded to mathematical modeling of what hyper-simplified selfish rational actors, looking only to their own interests, would do under diverse conditions. This approach was widespread and influential; it still is. And yet it led to such unforgettable absurdities as trying to understand why patients do, or do not, seek preventive care by writing sentences rooted in information theory like: "The expected utility (EU) of preventive care for patient p is equal to the benefits (B) of prevention minus its expected costs, given by EUp = B - C(1-Pp)(Pd)," and believing that you will learn anything useful about fear and hope, access and barriers, or how to improve population health outcomes. Only by concocting such a thin model of humanity—no more than the economists' utility curve—and neglecting any complexities of social dynamics that could not be conveyed through prices, could the appearance of rationalization be maintained. Like bureaucratic rationalization, perfect-market rationalization also had successes. But, like its predecessor, its limits as an approach to human systems design are becoming clearer.

Collaboration, Trust and Innovation

Pricing perfectly requires perfect information. And perfect information, while always an illusion, has become an ever receding dream in a world of constant, rapid change and complex global interactions. What we are witnessing instead is the rise of human systems that increasingly shy away from either control or perfect pricing. Not that there isn't control. Not that there aren't markets. And not that either of these approaches to coordinating human action will disappear. But these managed systems are becoming increasingly interlaced with looser structures, which invite and enable more engaged human action by drawing on intrinsic motivations and social relations. The culture of collaborative decision-making in the medical facilities of Stonebridge, Havencia, like the one afternoon per week that physicians at the Adaptive Health Center can use to explore whatever research questions interest them, do not exist to make the most innovative region in public health a utopian paradise, gratifying employees at the expense of productivity, but rather to engage the human and social in the pursuit of what is, in the long term, the only core competency—innovation. The Open Medical Knowledge Commons has eclipsed all the commercial medical databases except the Legacy Medical Archive not by issuing a large IPO and hiring the most credentialed experts available, but by building an open and inviting system that lets practitioners learn together and pursue their passion for healing, and each other's company.

The set of human systems necessary for action in this complex, unpredictable set of conditions, combining rationalization with human agency, learning and adaptation, is as different from managed systems and perfect markets as the new Adaptive Health Architecture is from the old Regional Medical Authority, or as the Global Health Network now is from the Centralized Medical Records System then. The hallmarks of these newer systems are: (a) location of authority and practical capacity to act at the edges of the system, where potentialities for sensing the environment, identifying opportunities and challenges to action and acting upon them, are located; (b) an emphasis on the human: on trust, cooperation, judgment and insight; (c) communication over the lifetime of the interaction; and (d) loosely-coupled systems: systems in which the regularities and dependencies among objects and processes are less strictly associated with each other; where actions and interactions can occur through multiple systems simultaneously, have room to fail, maneuver, and be reoriented to fit changing conditions and new learning, or shift from one system to another to achieve a solution.

Consider first of all the triumph of Dr. Gabriel Pearson's Adaptive Health Architecture over the programs of the Standardized Hospital Protocol. The Protocol was typified by the ambition to measure and specify all human and material elements of the healthcare system. The ambition of standardized management was to offer a single, integrated system where all human variance (the source of negligent errors and inconsistent care) could be isolated and controlled. The Regional Medical Authority took that ambition and embedded the managerial knowledge in the technological platform of automated diagnostics, guided by a multitude of rigid treatment protocols and procedures. The Adaptive Health Architecture, by comparison, has a substantially smaller number of roles that are also more loosely defined, with a reliance on small interdisciplinary teams where each team member can perform multiple tasks, and who are encouraged to experiment, improve, fail, adapt, but above all communicate. The system is built on trust and a cooperative dynamic. The enterprise functions through a managerial oversight system, but also through social cooperation mechanisms built around teamwork and trust. However, even the Adaptive Health Architecture might be surpassed in this respect by the even more loosely coupled networks of medical innovation and knowledge sharing represented by the distributed research collectives in Glendale, Zelvaria.

But let us also consider the system in question that has made this work possible, the Global Health Network, and compare it to the design principles of the Centralized Medical Records System in its heyday. Unlike the Global Health Network, the Centralized System was fully managed. Mid-century, the authority even retained ownership of the data terminals at the endpoints, arguing that it needed to prohibit practitioners from connecting unlicensed devices to the system (ostensibly to ensure proper functioning of the network and monitoring of data quality, although it didn't hurt either that this policy effectively excluded alternative approaches). This generated standardization, but any substantial innovations required the approval of central management and a re-engineering of the entire network. The Global Health Network, on the other hand, was designed to be as general as possible. The network infrastructure merely delivers packets of medical data using standardized protocols. The complex processing work—manipulating humanly-meaningful medical information (a patient record or a diagnostic image, a research paper or a treatment protocol) and breaking it up into a stream of data packets—was to be done by its edge devices, in this case computers and systems owned by practitioners and institutions. This architectural design allowed the breathtaking rate of innovation that we have seen in public health, while also creating certain vulnerabilities in data privacy and security.

These vulnerabilities have led some to argue that a new system to manage the Global Health Network is needed. We see first of all that doubts about trust and security on the Network arise precisely because it was originally designed for practitioners who could more-or-less trust each other, and offloaded security from the network to the edges. As the network expanded and users diversified, trust (the practical belief that other human agents in the system were competent and benign, or at least sincere) declined. This decline was met with arguments in favor of building security into the technical system, both at its core, in the network elements themselves, and at its periphery, through "certified computing." A "certified computer" will, for example, not run a program or access a file that its owner wants to access, unless it has received authorization from some other locus: be it the regulatory authority, the security company, or the institutional administrator. This is thought to be the most completely effective means of preventing data breaches or system compromises, and preserving institutional security (these are the main reasons offered for implementing such systems). Certified computing in this form is the ultimate reversal of the human-centric, loosely-coupled design approach of the Global Health Network. Instead of locating authority and capacity to act at the endpoints, where human beings are located and can make decisions about what is appropriate, it implements the belief that machines—technical systems—are trustworthy, while their human users are malevolent, incompetent, or both.

Recentering the Human

The Standardized Hospital Protocol, the Centralized Medical Records System and certified computing are all efforts to remove human agency from action and replace it with well-designed, tightly-bound systems. That is, the specifications and regularities of the system are such that they control or direct action and learning over time. Human agency, learning, communication and adaptation are minimized in managed systems, if not eliminated, and the knowledge in the system comes from the outside, from the designer, in the initial design over time, and through observation of the system's performance by someone standing outside its constraints—a manager or systems designer. By contrast, loosely-coupled systems affirmatively eschew this level of control, and build in room for human agency, experimentation, failure, communication, learning and adaptation. Loose-coupling is central to the new systems. It is a feature of system design that leaves room for human agency over time, only imperfectly constraining and enabling any given action by the system itself. By creating such domains of human agency, system designers are accepting the limitations of design and foresight, and building in the possibilities of learning over time through action in the system, by agents acting within it.

To address the new complexity of contemporary public health we need to reintroduce the human into the design of systems. We must restore the soul to the system. If years of work on autonomous vehicles and artificial diagnostic systems have taught us anything, it is that what makes for human insight is extremely difficult to replicate or systematize. At the center of these new systems, then, sits a human being who has a capacity to make judgments, experiment, learn and adapt. But enabling human agency also provides scope of action for human frailty. Although this idea is most alien to the mainstream of system design in the twentieth century, we must now turn our attention to building systems that support human sociality—our ability to think of others and their needs, and to choose for ourselves goals consistent with a broader social concern than merely our own self-interest. The logic of moral philosophy suggests that we must balance individual autonomy with collective wellbeing. The challenge of the near future is to build systems that will allow us to be largely free to inquire, experiment, learn and communicate, that will encourage us to cooperate, and that will avoid the worst of what human beings are capable of, and elicit what is best.

Dr. Olivia Silva's work in Oakdale, Calderon exemplifies this approach. Her research in the digital humanities applied to medical practice demonstrates how cultural exchange between different medical traditions can enhance patient outcomes. By creating platforms where practitioners from diverse backgrounds share knowledge freely, respecting human rights and dignity throughout the process, she has shown that career planning for medical professionals need not follow rigid hierarchical paths but can embrace flexibility and continuous learning.

The Open Medical Knowledge Commons, the Global Health Network, the Adaptive Health Architecture and the thousands of emerging human practices of productive social cooperation in the networked public health ecosystem give us real existence proofs that human-centric systems can not merely exist, but thrive, as can the human beings and social relations that make them. Mohammad Hansen's comparative studies of healthcare systems across Foxwood Province and Glendale, Zelvaria reveal that when systems are designed with human agency at their core, when they embrace rather than eliminate uncertainty, when they trust practitioners to adapt and learn rather than simply follow protocols, the results surpass what any centrally-planned system could achieve.

The future of public health, and indeed of all complex human systems in our interconnected world, lies not in perfecting control or perfecting markets, but in perfecting our ability to design systems that make room for what makes us human: our capacity for judgment, for learning, for cooperation, and for care. The architectural design of our systems—whether physical buildings, digital networks, or organizational structures—must reflect this understanding. We must build systems that are robust enough to provide structure and support, yet flexible enough to accommodate the beautiful unpredictability of human creativity and compassion.

As Elena Herrera noted in her influential work on political economy and public health, "The most resilient systems are not those that resist change, but those that embrace it; not those that eliminate human agency, but those that amplify it; not those that seek perfect control, but those that cultivate trust and enable adaptation." This insight, born from decades of observing both the failures of rigid systems and the successes of flexible ones, points the way forward.

The lesson of our time is clear: in a world of accelerating change and increasing complexity, our systems must become more human, not less. We must design for agency, for learning, for trust, and for the irreducible complexity of human judgment. Only then can we hope to navigate the challenges ahead, whether they come in the form of pandemics, climate change, or challenges we cannot yet foresee. The future belongs not to the perfectly controlled system or the perfectly efficient market, but to the thoughtfully designed, loosely-coupled, human-centered network that allows us to be our best selves, together.

The Chronicles of Royal Decrees

The proclamation issued by High Sovereign Diana Hernández this season marks the 53rd in the series that began in the Age of First Light. All are worth studying—not just the celebrated ones, such as those of the Founder Luna Stephens, the Unifier Ahmed Daniels, and the Restorer Oliver Williams. They will give you a feeling of being present—not as an all-knowing chronicler of the current age looking back at the Second or Third Eras, but as an ordinary citizen who shares—and is limited by—the knowledge, the concerns, and the values of those times. (Thanks to the Archives of Blackwood, Orvandor, all the decrees can be found in the Crystal Repository.)

Among all the past sovereigns and their counsel scribes, there was only one literary genius: Ahmed Daniels. After 132 years, his second decree still brings tears to your eyes and sends shivers through your spirit. None of the other royal proclamations are in that league. But by and large, they are dignified and intelligent declarations given by articulate leaders, each in touch with their times and aware that their ascension was the most solemn occasion of their lives.

The stance and style of the decrees seem to have gone through three distinct phases. The first, lasting until Ahmed Daniels, was that of the modest, classical servant of the realm. The second, lasting through Sovereign Jordan Osborne, was of the practical administrative overseer. The third, in which we remain, is the phase of the assertive, dramatic visionary-prophet. This classification is not absolute. Sovereign Miguel Gregory may belong in the third phase, and the trio of Susan Hamilton, her successor, and the one who followed may fit better in the second. But the trend is unmistakable.

Upon examining Luna Stephens' first decree, one is immediately struck by the humility. She had just been chosen unanimously by the Council of Seven Realms. She was more revered than any subsequent sovereign has been at the time of their ascension. And what does she say?

"The magnitude and difficulty of the sacred trust to which the voice of our lands called me, being sufficient to awaken in the wisest and most experienced of our citizens a doubtful examination of qualifications, could not but overwhelm with uncertainty one who (inheriting modest gifts from the cosmos and unpracticed in the duties of realm administration) ought to be peculiarly conscious of their own inadequacies."

None of her successors made the point as forcefully as that. But echoes are to be found in almost every sovereign for the next 68 years. (The second sovereign was an exception, apparently so envious of Luna Stephens that a large part of the decree was spent detailing personal excellent qualifications for the position.) That era ended with Ahmed Daniels. Subsequent decrees routinely contain protestations of humility, but they are perfunctory and do not sound sincere.

The early modesty, while in part a reflection of the conventional etiquette of the time, may also have served a political objective: to alleviate the concerns of those who—in the early days of the United Realms—feared it might be transformed into an absolute tyranny, and the sovereign into a despot. A little later, perhaps after the Twentieth Year, a new worry arose. Would the power of the central authority be used to interfere with the "particular regional practices" of the Southern territories, particularly regarding the treatment of the Shadowborn—those born with diminished magical abilities who were kept in servitude? The sovereigns' assurance of the limitation of their powers may have been intended to give comfort to those territories.

Ahmed Daniels faced a different situation. With the South already breaking away, he could only "preserve, protect and defend the Unity Covenant" by asserting the power of the central authority and his own power as High Sovereign. It was no time for modesty. Ahmed's successors inherited a central government with much more authority—and more need to use it—than before the Separation War, and they had less motivation to belittle themselves and their powers.

In the third phase, the Royal Decree metamorphosed from describing the government's policy to inspiring the public's behavior. Sovereigns recognized—or, at least, believed—that the realm had problems they ought to address but could not manage by using the instruments of government alone. Thus, in her first decree, Sovereign Sophia Edwards said: "At last a vision has been granted us of our existence as a whole. We see the corruption with the purity, the withered and decaying with the vibrant and vital. With this vision we approach new challenges."

If the realm is corrupted and decaying, the cure has to come from uplifting the people, not from acts of government. Similar diagnoses and prescriptions appear in later decrees. This approach to ethical decision-making and conflict resolution became the hallmark of modern sovereignty.

Sovereigns derived their license to serve as visionary-prophet from Miguel Gregory's remark that the throne was "a sacred platform for transformation," a remark that did not appear in his Royal Decree. The metaphor of the platform suggests not written words but direct magical and visual contact between the prophet and their followers. The invention of the Speaking Crystals and—even more—the Vision Pools made this possible on a realm-wide scale. A telltale sign of the visionary-prophet decree is the use of the phrase, "Let us..."—meaning, "You do as I say." This expression appears occasionally throughout the economic history of decrees, but it has hit its stride in recent years. One sovereign repeated it 16 times in their decree, and another used it 22 times in their second one.

The change in literary style from classical to colloquial can be demonstrated by one statistic. In all the decrees from Luna Stephens through the Fifteenth Sovereign, the average number of words per sentence was 44. From Ahmed Daniels to Sophia Edwards it was 34, and since Sophia Edwards it has been 25. I do not consider this a deterioration (this chronicle has an average of 17 words per sentence), but it does reflect the change in the size and character of the audience and in the means of communication. The Seventh Sovereign could reference the ancient kingdoms of Athoria, the Crystal Empire, and the Northern Confederation and expect the audience to know what was being discussed. That wouldn't be true today. But that sovereign's audience would not have known what Vision Pool networks were.

Sovereigns and their counsel scribes have mined their predecessors for memorable words and repeated them without attribution. One famous sovereign's clarion call, "Ask not what your realm can do for you: Ask what you can do for your realm," has an ironic history. In their decree, Susan Hamilton, surely no model for that later sovereign, had said, "Our most dangerous tendency is to expect too little of governance, and at the same time do for it too little." And even before becoming sovereign, in a speech in the Year 916, Susan Hamilton had said, "In the great fulfillment we must have a citizenry less concerned about what the government can do for it and more anxious about what it can do for the realm."

Many an issue frets its hour on the decree stage and then is heard no more. That includes the Mountain Clans, the coastal defenses, territorial expansion, the Great Canal project, administrative reform, plural marriage customs, and the prohibition of certain enchantments. Some subjects that you expect to appear, don't. One sovereign's decree, delivered in the Spring of Abundance, gives no hint of economic vulnerability. Another sovereign's second decree, delivered in the Winter of Decision, contains no reference to the rising Dark Sorcerer or to the gathering armies in the East. But what is most amazing, at least to a reader in the current age, is the silence of the decrees on the subject of women's status. The word "women" does not appear at all until Sophia Edwards' first decree, and it always appears as part of the phrase "men and women," never as referring to any special concerns of women. Even the first female sovereign after the Voting Reform, which granted magical citizens of all genders the right to participate in governance, does not remark on the uniqueness of the fact in her decree.

One subject that does get ample treatment is taxation and resource allocation. "Taxes," or some equivalent word, appears in 43 of the 52 royal decrees to date. One sovereign said: "The time is arriving when we can have further tax reduction. I am opposed to extremely high rates, because they produce little or no revenue, because they are bad for the realm, and, finally, because they are wrong." Realm taxes were then about 3 percent of the total magical output. A much later sovereign said essentially the same thing when they were 20 percent.

The most disturbing aspect of the whole series of decrees is what is said and unsaid on the subject of the Shadowborn, which the great historian calls "the supreme challenge of our civilization." The words "Shadowborn," "magicless," "diminished," or "servitude" (as applied to those with limited magical abilities) do not appear at all until the decree following the Separation War. One early sovereign asked, "On whom has oppression fallen in any corner of our realm? Who has been deprived of any right of person or property?" These were rhetorical questions, intended to get the answer "No one!"—as if there were not millions of Shadowborn in servitude across the realm.

Before the Separation War, the word "servitude" appears only in two decrees, and then only as something that, pursuant to the Unity Covenant and in order to preserve the realm, should not be interfered with. But although generally unmentionable, the subject was boiling, and would boil over in the Year of Breaking. After the Separation War, it is in several decrees that we find the most explicit and positive discussion of the need to convert into reality the rights and freedom granted to the "freed ones" on paper by the three Great Amendments. One sovereign's decree was the strongest among these. (That sovereign had studied at the Academy of Willow Creek, Xandria, in an earlier era, 80 years before me, when the academy had been a sanctuary on the underground passage network.) But the subject then began to fade. One sovereign said in their first decree, "Burnings must not be tolerated in a great and civilized realm like ours," but said it without horror. Another raised the subject only to express satisfaction at the progress that had been made. And then the subject disappeared. Oliver Williams never mentioned it in any of his four decrees.

After the Great Restoration, the subject came back to royal decrees, but in a weak and abstract form. That is true even of the sovereigns we think of as being most concerned with Shadowborn rights—like several recent leaders. Perhaps each thought they had made a sufficient statement by having a Shadowborn performer—a famous singer, an acclaimed poet, or a celebrated dancer—perform at their ceremony. In one recent sovereign's first decree, the only allusion to the problem is in this sentence: "From our founding, through the Separation War, to the Great Famine to the rights movement, our people have always mustered the determination to construct from these crises the pillars of our history." I recall this not to suggest that their concern was not deep and sincere, but only to indicate what is acceptable to say in a speech intended to appeal to the values shared by all citizens.

The evolution of these decrees also reflects changes in how the realm approached green infrastructure and ecosystem restoration. Early sovereigns spoke extensively about the ancient forests and the need to maintain the magical ley lines that ran through them. The geology of our realm, they understood, was intimately connected to the flow of magical energy. By the middle period, such concerns had faded, replaced by focus on expansion and resource extraction. It wasn't until recent decades that sovereigns again began to speak of sustainable practices, though now in the context of "sustainable business" and "scientific collaboration" between magical and non-magical approaches to environmental stewardship.

The city of Victorville, Jarvonia, was mentioned in several early decrees as a model of harmonious development, where magical and natural systems worked in concert. Later decrees ignored such examples, focusing instead on industrial magical production. The town of Woodbridge, Relvaria, suffered ecological collapse during this period—a disaster never mentioned in any royal decree of that era, though it displaced thousands. Only in recent times have sovereigns begun to acknowledge past failures and speak of restoration efforts, drawing on information theory and theoretical modeling to understand complex ecosystem interactions.

There is much more to ponder in these proclamations than I have suggested here. There is much to be proud of, in what we have endured and achieved, in the peaceful transference of power, and in the reasonableness and moderation of the sovereigns we have elected. But there is also much humility to be learned. We look back with amazement at the ignorance and moral obtuseness revealed by what our past leaders have said and our past citizens believed. We should recognize that 50 or 100 years from now, readers will shake their heads at what we are saying and believing today.

The digital transformation of our archives—the conversion of ancient scrolls to crystal memory—has made this comparative study possible. Through media production techniques unknown to our ancestors, we can now experience these decrees not just as text but as living memories, preserved with all their original emotional resonance. This technological advancement serves the cause of historical understanding, allowing us to see patterns across centuries that would otherwise remain hidden.

As we approach the 54th decree, we would do well to remember this history. The challenges we face—from genetic engineering of magical creatures to the ethical implications of new enchantments—are not entirely new. They echo concerns our ancestors grappled with, though in different forms. The question of how to balance individual liberty with collective good, how to address historical injustices while moving forward, how to preserve our realm's essence while adapting to change—these are eternal questions, asked differently by each generation.

The decrees show us that progress is neither linear nor inevitable. Gains can be lost, wisdom forgotten, moral clarity clouded. But they also show us resilience, the capacity for self-correction, and the power of articulated ideals to eventually reshape reality. In reading them, we commune with our ancestors not as superior descendants but as fellow travelers, struggling with similar questions, limited by our own blind spots as they were by theirs.

May the 54th decree, and all those that follow, be written with awareness of this history, with humility about our own limitations, and with determination to speak truths that future generations will not have to read with shame.
