Stefan Lee paced near the far wall, his athletic frame tense with barely contained energy. He'd been a leadership development consultant before his abduction from Pinehurst, Calderon. Now he led nothing, controlled nothing, existed only at the whim of beings whose form and substance defied human comprehension.

"Oliver." Rosa's hand on his arm was gentle but insistent. "It's time."

He knew what she meant. The Collectors had been preparing him for months with their training sessions, teaching him to manipulate quantum states with his consciousness, to move through space by collapsing probability waves, to interface with their technology in ways that should have been impossible for a human mind. And now they wanted him to use those abilities.

They wanted him to go back to Earth and bring someone else through.

The summons came as a pressure in his mind, not quite thought, not quite sensation. Oliver closed his eyes and allowed the quantum transition. The world folded around him and he stood in what the Collectors called the Interface Chamber—a space where geometric impossibilities became routine, where walls existed at angles that shouldn't work in three-dimensional space.

The Collector he'd named Prism waited there, its form shifting through configurations that hurt to perceive directly. Communication came as pure meaning injected into his consciousness:

*You are ready. We will open the gateway to your origin point. You will retrieve a specific target.*

Oliver had learned not to resist these commands. Resistance brought pain that transcended the physical—a dismantling of self that left him hollow for days. But he could still think, still plan, as long as he kept those thoughts buried deep.

"What target?" he asked aloud, knowing Prism would understand the vibrations if not the specific phonemes.

*A male with specific genetic markers. We have identified him through your world's data networks. He resides in Silverdale, Veldoria. His name is Ethan Cox.*

The name meant nothing to Oliver, but the location made his heart race. Silverdale was only fifty miles from where he'd lived before his abduction. Before his wife, before his career in nanotechnology research, before everything had been stripped away.

*You will assume appropriate covering and approach him at his residence. You will convince him to accompany you to the gateway. Physical coercion is not necessary—we have provided you with the means of persuasion.*

Oliver felt the new weight in his mind then, a set of subroutines the Collectors had implanted during his training. With concentration, he could project an aura of trust, of authority, of inevitability. It was a violation of applied ethics so profound that thinking about it made him nauseous.

"And if I refuse?" The question was automatic, pointless.

The pain that answered him was brief but absolute. When it ended, Prism's thought-voice carried something that might have been amusement:

*You will not refuse. We have invested too much in your training. You are our Judas ram, leading the flock to us.*

The transition back to the common area left Oliver shaking. Rosa found him there, helped him to a seat. She knew without asking what had happened.

"They're sending you through," she said.

He nodded, unable to speak yet.

"Are you going to do it?"

"Do I have a choice?"

Rosa's laugh was harsh. "We always have choices, Oliver. They're just all terrible."

Over the next few hours, Oliver prepared himself mentally for the mission. The Collectors provided him with clothing appropriate to Earth—jeans, a button-down shirt, a jacket. They'd studied human fashion through their observations, though their understanding remained imperfect. The clothes fit well enough but felt subtly wrong, the fabric too uniform, the colors slightly off.

Mohamed approached him as he dressed. "I've been analyzing the data they've been feeding us," he said quietly. "Running patterns on their behavior, their technology, their apparent goals."

"And?"

"They're not invincible. They're cautious about Earth for a reason. I think they can be hurt there, maybe even killed, though I don't know how." Mohamed's eyes were intense behind his wire-rimmed glasses. "Whatever you do out there, remember that. They fear us on our own ground."

The gateway chamber was a cathedral of impossible angles. Oliver stood at the threshold, feeling the quantum foam of the portal against his skin like static electricity. Through it, he could see a darkened street in Silverdale, Veldoria—his world, his dimension, tantalizingly close.

Prism's presence pressed against his mind: *Remember your purpose. Retrieve the target. Return through the gateway. Any attempt at escape will be detected and punished.*

Oliver stepped through.

The transition was like being born—a moment of compression followed by explosive release. He stumbled, caught himself, breathed air that smelled of rain and asphalt and growing things. Real air, not the odorless atmosphere of the facility. He wanted to weep at the simple reality of it.

He was standing two blocks from Ethan Cox's address, which the Collectors had somehow extracted from Earth's data networks. The street was quiet, residential, lined with modest houses and old trees. Oliver walked slowly, savoring every sensation—the give of concrete under his feet, the whisper of wind through leaves, the distant bark of a dog.

Ethan Cox's house was a small bungalow with peeling paint and an overgrown yard. Oliver stood at the curb for a long moment, wrestling with his conscience. He could feel Prism's attention on him, a pressure at the base of his skull. The Collector was monitoring him through their quantum link.

He had to do this. He had no choice.

But maybe, just maybe, he could warn Cox somehow. Give him a chance.

Oliver walked up the cracked sidewalk and knocked on the door.

The man who answered was younger than Oliver had expected—late twenties, with tired eyes and the build of someone who'd been athletic once but had let it slide. He wore sweatpants and a faded t-shirt with a logo for a supply chain management conference.

"Ethan Cox?" Oliver asked.

"Yeah. Who are you?"

"My name is Oliver Carter. I'm a researcher in nanotechnology. I need to talk to you about something urgent."

Cox's expression shifted from wary to confused. "Nanotechnology? I work in supply chain logistics. I think you have the wrong guy."

"No," Oliver said, and he felt the Collectors' implanted subroutines activate in his mind. Words came that he didn't fully control: "I have exactly the right person. There's been a development in Timberline, Jarvonia—a contamination event that's spreading through global supply chains. Your expertise is needed immediately."

It was a lie, smooth and plausible, flowing from him with supernatural ease. He watched Cox's resistance crumble under the weight of the persuasion programming.

"I... I haven't heard anything about this. Shouldn't there be official channels?"

"The situation is being contained quietly to prevent panic. I have a vehicle two blocks from here. We need to leave now."

Cox hesitated, and in that hesitation Oliver saw his chance. He pushed against the Collectors' control, forced his own words through: "You should probably tell someone where you're going. Leave a note. Call a friend."

The subroutines fought him, tried to make him retract the suggestion, but Oliver held firm. Cox nodded slowly. "Yeah. Yeah, let me just... give me a minute."

He disappeared into the house. Oliver stood on the porch, trembling with the effort of maintaining his small rebellion. Prism's attention intensified, probing, questioning. Oliver buried his intentions deep, thought only of compliance, of completing the mission.

Cox returned wearing jeans and a jacket, phone in hand. "I left a message for my roommate. Let's go."

They walked through the quiet streets toward the gateway. Oliver kept up a steady stream of technical jargon about nanoscale contamination and supply chain vectors, words that meant nothing but sounded authoritative. Cox listened, asked occasional questions, grew more uncertain with each step.

"Where exactly is this vehicle?" Cox asked as they turned down an increasingly isolated street.

"Just ahead," Oliver said, and it was true. He could see the shimmer of the gateway now, a distortion in the air that Cox's untrained eyes couldn't detect.

"I don't see anything."

"It's there." They were ten feet away. Five feet. Oliver felt sick with self-loathing. He was doing exactly what the Collectors wanted, leading an innocent man to captivity, and his small act of rebellion—letting Cox leave a message—would accomplish nothing.

They reached the gateway. Cox stopped, confused, staring at the empty air. "There's nothing here. What kind of—"

Oliver grabbed his arm and pulled him through.

The transition was violent for Cox, who had no preparation, no training. He screamed as quantum forces tore at his consciousness, then collapsed on the other side. Oliver caught him, lowered him gently to the floor of the gateway chamber.

Prism materialized, its form rippling with colors that might have been satisfaction. *Well done. The specimen is intact.*

Other Collectors appeared, their impossible geometries crowding the chamber. They lifted Cox's unconscious form with appendages that existed partially outside normal space, carried him away to whatever processing awaited new captives.

Oliver stood alone in the chamber, feeling the weight of what he'd done. He'd betrayed a stranger, condemned him to the same captivity that had consumed his own life. And he'd done it to avoid pain, to survive another day in this dimensional prison.

*You have performed adequately,* Prism informed him. *You will be rewarded with extended privileges. And there will be other missions.*

The quantum transition back to the common area was perfunctory. Oliver materialized to find Rosa waiting, her expression a mixture of sympathy and contempt.

"You did it," she said. It wasn't a question.

"I didn't have a choice."

"We always have choices," she repeated. "They're just all terrible."

Stefan approached, his face hard. "They're going to use you again. You know that, right? You're their retrieval specialist now. Their Judas ram."

"I know."

"And you're just going to keep doing it?"

Oliver looked at him, then at Rosa, then at Mohamed who watched from across the room with his analytical gaze. "What would you have me do? Resist and be destroyed? That helps no one."

"It helps your conscience," Stefan shot back.

"My conscience is already dead," Oliver said quietly. "It died the moment I stepped through that gateway and realized I could smell Earth again. That I wanted to stay there more than I wanted to save a stranger."

Rosa touched his shoulder. "You let him leave a message. That was something."

"It was nothing. A meaningless gesture."

"Maybe," she said. "Or maybe it's the start of something. Maybe next time you'll find a way to do more."

Oliver wanted to believe that, but he knew the truth. The Collectors had spent months preparing him for this role, conditioning him, training him, breaking down his resistance. They'd made him into a tool, and tools don't rebel.

He walked to his quarters—a small space with a bed and a desk and a window that showed a view of Earth that wasn't real. The Collectors had generated it for him, thinking it would provide comfort. Instead, it was torture, a reminder of everything he'd lost.

He lay on the bed and stared at the false sky, thinking about Ethan Cox waking up in this place, realizing his life was over. Thinking about the message Cox had left, and whether anyone would understand its significance. Thinking about the next mission Prism would send him on, and the one after that.

Mohamed had said the Collectors could be hurt on Earth, maybe killed. But Oliver didn't know how, and he didn't know if he had the courage to try. The training had been too thorough, the conditioning too deep.

He was their Judas ram now, and he would lead others to captivity because the alternative was his own destruction. It was the logic of survival, cold and merciless, and it had consumed everything he once believed about himself.

Rosa had said they always had choices. But some choices were so terrible that making them destroyed you either way. Oliver had made his choice, and he would live with it, and he would do it again when Prism commanded.

Because he was weak, and he was broken, and he was theirs.

The false stars wheeled overhead in their programmed patterns, and Oliver Carter closed his eyes against them, seeking the oblivion of sleep and finding only the memory of Ethan Cox's confused face as they approached the gateway. That face would haunt him, join the gallery of ghosts that already populated his dreams.

But tomorrow he would wake, and he would train, and when the Collectors commanded, he would return to Earth and bring back another victim. Because that was what he was now—not a scientist, not a researcher, not even fully human anymore.

Just a tool in the hands of beings who saw humanity as specimens to be collected, studied, and bred in captivity. And the worst part was knowing that he'd become complicit in his own imprisonment, that every mission he completed bound him more tightly to his captors.

The Judas ram, leading the flock to slaughter, one victim at a time.

The morning air in Brookhaven, Belvoria carried the scent of engineered wheat from the surrounding fields. Max Johnson stood at the kitchen window of their assigned residence, watching his wife Sofia move through the garden plot behind their house. She was examining the experimental crop varieties they'd been allocated—part of the sustainable agriculture program that employed them both.

He turned back to the breakfast table, but Sofia had already left her coffee untouched. The tension from last night still hung in the air like the morning mist over the fields.

"I know what you do in that lab," she'd said. "I know what happens to the failed specimens."

Max had tried to explain. As a research coordinator for the Federal Agricultural Genetics Administration, his job involved more than just developing new crop varieties. The FAGA's mandate included creating specialized organisms for food production—including the semi-sentient agricultural workers called "agromorphs." These genetically modified beings were designed from primate stock, enhanced for specific farming tasks, and programmed to reach a developmental plateau that kept them compliant and useful.

But when an agromorph showed signs of exceeding its cognitive limits, or when production quotas were met and the population needed culling, someone had to make the decision. That someone was Max.

He picked up his jacket and headed for the door. Sofia appeared from the garden, soil on her hands, her dark eyes meeting his.

"Max, wait."

He paused, hoping for reconciliation.

"Dr. Chen called earlier," she said quietly. "One of his patients—a woman named Talia Freeman—she's having a breakdown. Her agromorph is dying. Some kind of fungal infection in its respiratory system."

"So?" Max asked, though he knew where this was going.

"She thinks it's her child. She's class-C genetic rating, Max. She'll never be approved for human reproduction. This agromorph is all she has, and Chen says she's completely dissociated from reality. She keeps talking about its birth, about raising it."

"What does Chen want from me?"

"He wants you to substitute another one. A replacement from your facility. He thinks if he can swap it while the sick one is at the veterinary center, she might not notice."

Max rubbed his face. "They're individually registered, Sofia. She'll know the identification number. And even if Chen falsifies the records, the new one won't recognize her. It'll be obvious."

"He's desperate, Max. The woman is suicidal."

Max sighed. "Fine. I'll call him from the road. He can come by the facility and sign for one of the unclaimed units." He paused. "But I won't be party to falsifying federal records."

Sofia nodded, some of the hardness leaving her expression. "Thank you."

He left before the conversation could turn back to their own situation—to Sofia's growing obsession with having a biological child despite their class-C rating. The genetic counselors had been clear: both carried hereditary markers for degenerative conditions. They were approved for agromorph adoption only.

The drive to his facility took him through Windsor Village, a planned community of identical modular homes surrounded by the endless fields of the Valleyview District. The landscape was a testament to sustainable agriculture—precision farming, climate adaptation technologies, and the agromorph labor force that made it all possible.

His facility sat on the edge of the district, a low concrete structure that housed both the development labs and the containment units. Inside, rows of enclosures held agromorphs at various developmental stages. They looked almost human—bipedal, with expressive faces and dexterous hands—but their bodies were covered in fine, dark fur, and their proportions were slightly off. Their intelligence was carefully calibrated: smart enough to follow complex instructions, but not smart enough to question their purpose.

The ones in his facility were either newly developed specimens awaiting field assignment, or "returns"—units that had been reclaimed from their assigned families for various reasons. Returns were usually destroyed within thirty days unless they were reassigned.

Max checked his message terminal. There was a priority memo from Chief Administrator Eva Alexander:

"Attention All Regional Coordinators: Subject: Deviant Agromorph.

Begin immediate survey of all units from Production Facility ZN-447 manufactured during March 2234. This relates to the Hansen Negligence Case. Examine all units in this category for cognitive and behavioral deviation. Technician Mohammad Hansen has confessed to passing at least one non-standard specimen, possibly more. Claims memory failure regarding identification numbers—likely attempting to limit investigation scope.

A deviant with enhanced cognitive function could pose significant risk. Test all ZN-447 units thoroughly. Detain any showing abnormal development. Complete survey within seven days."

Max calculated quickly. His district had probably received forty to fifty units from that production run. He'd need to locate and test them all, which meant dealing with dozens of families who'd grown attached to their agromorphs. The thought made him queasy.

He called the wholesale distribution center in Zenith, Nordavia and spent the morning compiling a list of all March ZN-447 units that had entered his territory. By noon, he had thirty-eight addresses.

The first few retrievals went smoothly. The families understood it was temporary, for testing purposes. But by the fourth household, he encountered resistance.

The woman—a class-C citizen in her forties—stood in her doorway with tears streaming down her face. "You can't take him. He's my son. I raised him from infancy."

"Ma'am, this is a federal health inspection. The unit will be returned within forty-eight hours if it passes the cognitive assessment."

"His name is Tommy. He's not an 'it.'"

Behind her, Max could see the agromorph in question—a juvenile unit, perhaps three years past activation, with the mental development of a six-year-old human child. It was watching the interaction with obvious distress.

"Mama?" it called. "Mama, what wrong?"

The woman's face crumpled. She slammed the door.

Max stood on the porch for a moment, then returned to his vehicle. He'd have to get a warrant. He added her name to the list for the local authorities.

By evening, he'd collected twelve units. Three more would require legal intervention. He drove home as the sun set over the engineered wheat fields, their golden heads swaying in the breeze—the product of decades of research in sustainable agriculture and climate adaptation.

Sofia met him at the door. Her expression was strange—not angry, but haunted.

"Dr. Chen came by," she said. "He took one of the units."

"Good."

"Max, something happened. Something terrible."

He followed her into the kitchen. She poured them both coffee with shaking hands.

"That woman—Talia Freeman—she killed Dr. Chen."

Max set down his cup. "What?"

"It was on the news. She went to his house tonight with a gun. Started screaming about how he'd stolen her baby, how he'd given her the wrong one. When he tried to explain, she shot him. He's dead, Max."

Max felt the room tilt slightly. "But I gave him a replacement. How did she—"

"The identification numbers didn't match. She checked."

They sat in silence. Finally, Sofia spoke again, her voice barely a whisper. "This whole system is insane, Max. We create these things to fill the void left by our population controls, and then we're surprised when people can't tell the difference between them and real children."

"They're not real children," Max said automatically, but the words felt hollow.

"Then why do we treat them like they are? Why do we let people bond with them, name them, raise them—if we're just going to take them away and destroy them when it's convenient?"

Max had no answer.

That night, after Sofia had gone to bed, he returned to the facility. The containment units were quiet, most of the agromorphs sleeping in their enclosures. He walked through the rows, looking at their peaceful faces.

Fifteen of them were scheduled for termination—units that had been in the facility when he took over the position, awaiting final disposal. He'd been putting it off, but now he needed the space for the ZN-447 units he was collecting.

He activated the large processing chamber and began transferring the sleeping agromorphs one by one. They trusted him, followed him willingly into the sealed room. When he had all fifteen inside, he engaged the system. The sedative gas was quick and painless. The conveyor would move them automatically to the molecular recycling unit.

He watched through the observation window, his stomach churning. They looked so human as they drifted into deeper sleep. One of them—a female unit, perhaps four years past activation—had curled up with her thumb in her mouth.

When he returned to the house, he found Sofia sitting at the bedroom window, watching the facility's exhaust stack in the distance. The recycling unit produced a faint thermal shimmer in the night air.

She didn't turn when he entered. "How many?" she asked quietly.

"Fifteen."

"Did any of them have names?"

"I don't know."

She was silent for a long moment. Then: "I'm pregnant, Max."

He stood frozen in the doorway. "Sofia, you can't—"

"That's insane. If they catch us—"

"They'll sterilize us both and take the child. I know. But I can't live like this anymore, Max. I can't watch you kill those things while pretending they're not children, and I can't accept one of them as a substitute for my own baby. I won't."

Max moved to the window and looked out at the facility. The exhaust had stopped. "This job," he said slowly, "exists because society decided that population control was more important than individual reproductive rights. The agromorphs exist because we needed to give people something to nurture, to parent, without actually increasing the human population. It's all part of the strategic planning that's kept our civilization stable for the past century."

"I don't care about strategic planning," Sofia said. "I care about us. About having a family."

"And when they find out? When they take our child and put it in a state facility? When they make sure we can never have another?"

"Then at least we'll have tried. At least we'll have had something real, even if only for a little while."

Max sat on the edge of the bed, his head in his hands. He thought about the woman who'd killed Dr. Chen, driven mad by the loss of something she'd believed was her child. He thought about the agromorphs in his facility, waiting trustingly for whatever came next. He thought about the system he served—a system built on careful lies and necessary cruelties.

"I can't protect you from this," he said finally. "If you do this, you're on your own."

Sofia turned to look at him, her eyes bright with tears. "I know."

He left her there and went to sleep on the couch.

The next morning, he returned to his rounds. There were still twenty-six ZN-447 units to collect, and the seven-day deadline was approaching. He drove through Windsor Village, past the neat rows of assigned housing, and out into the Valleyview District.

At the third house, he encountered another problem. The family had the right unit—he could see it through the window—but when he checked the identification number against his list, it didn't match.

"I'm sorry," the owner said, "but that's the number on our purchase receipt. We got it from Tomás Roberts' shop in Zenith."

Max frowned. "This is definitely a ZN-447 unit. I can tell by the phenotype markers. But the ID doesn't match any of my records."

"Are you saying we have an unregistered agromorph?"

"I'm saying something's wrong with the paperwork."

He left without the unit and drove straight to Zenith. Roberts' shop was in an older commercial district, the kind of place that predated the current sustainable agriculture initiatives. The building smelled of animal waste and chemical cleaners.

Roberts himself was an elderly man with nervous eyes. When Max explained the discrepancy, the old man became defensive.

"I keep perfect records. If there's a mismatch, it's not my fault."

"Let me see your sales logs for March."

Roberts hesitated, then claimed he needed to retrieve them from his office upstairs. He took the ledger with him and locked the door.

Max waited. And waited. After ten minutes, he heard a back door slam.

He ran outside in time to see Roberts climbing into a vehicle. Max gave chase, but the old man had too much of a head start. Within minutes, he'd disappeared into the Zenith traffic.

Max returned to the shop and forced his way into the office. What he found made his blood run cold: a second set of books, documenting off-record sales of agromorphs. Dozens of them. Maybe hundreds.

A black market.

He called Eva Alexander immediately. "We have a situation. I've found evidence of widespread illegal agromorph distribution. The registration system has been compromised."

"How bad?"

"I don't know yet. But if there are unregistered units out there, we have no way of tracking them. No way of knowing which ones might be deviants from the Hansen batch. And no way of controlling the population."

There was a long pause. "Bring me everything you found. We're going to need to expand this investigation across multiple districts."

Max gathered the evidence and prepared to leave. But as he walked through the shop one final time, he paused by a cage containing a juvenile agromorph. It looked up at him with large, trusting eyes.

"Hungry," it said simply.

Max stared at it. This one wasn't on any official record. It could disappear and no one would know. Or it could be placed with a family who would love it, care for it, and never know it wasn't supposed to exist.

He thought about Sofia, pregnant with an illegal child. He thought about the system he served, built on the premise that some lives were more valuable than others, that some beings could be created and destroyed at will while others had inviolable rights.

He thought about field research he'd read in evolutionary biology journals, about how the line between human and non-human had always been arbitrary, a matter of definition rather than essence. He thought about consciousness studies that suggested awareness and sentience existed on a spectrum, not as a binary.

The agromorph watched him hopefully.

Max made a decision. He opened the cage and lifted the small creature out. It wrapped its furry arms around his neck.

"Hungry," it repeated.

"I know," Max said quietly. "Let's get you something to eat."

He carried it out to his vehicle, wondering if this was the moment he stopped being part of the system and started being part of the problem. Or maybe it was the other way around.

Either way, he couldn't go back to what he'd been doing. The contradictions had finally become unbearable.

When he arrived home that evening, Sofia was in the garden again, tending the experimental crops. She looked up as he approached, then saw the agromorph in his arms.

"Max?"

"I'm done," he said simply. "I can't do this anymore. The killing, the pretending, the serving a system that treats consciousness as a commodity. I'm done."

She came closer, studying his face. "What are you going to do?"

"I don't know yet. But I know I can't keep being the person who decides which beings get to live and which ones get recycled for organic compounds."

Sofia reached out and touched the agromorph's fuzzy head. It cooed softly and reached for her.

"Mama?" it asked hopefully.

She looked at Max, and for the first time in weeks, he saw something like hope in her eyes.

"We're going to be fugitives," she said. "Both of us. Me with an illegal human child, you with an illegal agromorph. They'll hunt us."

"I know."

"Where will we go?"

Max thought about the vast agricultural districts, the planned communities, the endless surveillance systems designed to maintain order and stability. There weren't many places to hide in a world built on strategic planning and population control.

But there had to be somewhere. There had to be people who'd made the same choice they were making—who'd decided that love and family and the sanctity of conscious life mattered more than the system's careful calculations.

"We'll find somewhere," he said. "We'll find others like us. We'll figure it out."

Sofia nodded slowly. Then she took the agromorph from his arms and held it close.

"Welcome home," she whispered to it.

Max looked back at the facility in the distance, at the life he was leaving behind. He thought about the memo from Eva Alexander, about the investigation that would soon consume the entire district. He thought about Mohammad Hansen, the technician who'd let a deviant slip through, and about how one small act of negligence—or mercy—could unravel an entire system.

Maybe that was what the system needed. Maybe it was time for it to unravel.

He put his arm around Sofia's shoulders and they walked together toward the house, carrying between them the two illegal lives they'd chosen to protect. Behind them, the sun set over the fields of engineered wheat, and the world continued its careful, controlled rotation.

But for Max and Sofia, the careful control was over. They were stepping into uncertainty, into danger, into a future where they would be hunted and condemned.

And somehow, for the first time in months, Max felt like he could breathe.

**Lucia:** Some argue that addressing major technological challenges has become harder due to current political fragmentation and growing isolationism. Do you see these trends hampering global efforts to manage quantum computing responsibly?

**Arthur:** It's a legitimate concern, but I think quantum computing presents a different dynamic than, say, climate change. With climate issues, the costs aren't directly borne by those profiting from fossil fuels. There's a disconnect between benefit and consequence.

With quantum computing, the major tech companies developing this technology are acutely aware that public reaction could turn against them very quickly. They've watched what happened with genetic modification and social media. They know that if quantum computing suddenly disrupts entire industries—and we're talking about potentially transforming cryptography, financial services, pharmaceutical development, and materials science within a decade—there could be massive backlash.

Consider the financial sector. Quantum computers could theoretically break current encryption standards, potentially exposing trillions in transactions. If that happens without adequate preparation, you could see governments moving to restrict or ban certain quantum computing applications. The industry is anxious about this possibility.

Through my field research and conversations with these companies, I've found genuine concern. Yes, they're motivated by business interests and intellectual challenges, but they're also people who don't wake up thinking they'll destabilize global financial systems or compromise national security. As the industry matures, there's a developing sense of responsibility.

This creates a real opportunity. Despite the broader political climate—or perhaps because of it—we can bring industry stakeholders on board to ensure the technology develops responsibly. They have strong incentives to get this right.

**Lucia:** There's a dominant narrative around quantum computing and advanced technology generally that we're somehow at the mercy of progress—that we can't control or shape it. Anyone questioning this gets labeled as anti-progress or Luddite. But we actually have more control than we acknowledge. For instance, how we structure organizations, how we design research priorities, how we allocate resources—these are choices, not inevitabilities. How do we balance being impacted by technological change with exercising agency over what kind of change we want?

**Arthur:** Technological determinism is pervasive, and understandably so. For individuals, it does feel like change simply happens and we must adapt. No single person can alter these trajectories alone.

But when we think collectively—as communities, nations, or an international community—we have real power to shape technological development. We have multiple tools: regulations, funding priorities, cultural norms, professional standards.

Technology emerges from specific legal, political, normative, and cultural frameworks. It doesn't develop in a vacuum. The more we understand technology's relationship with these frameworks, and the more consciously we shape them, the more we influence technological trajectories.

For example, we can develop cultures of responsible innovation. We can establish professional ethics—a kind of Hippocratic oath for quantum computing researchers. We can structure corporate governance to prioritize long-term societal benefit over short-term profit. We can use comparative history to learn from past technological transitions—studying how societies managed the Industrial Revolution, electrification, or computerization can inform our approach to quantum computing.

These interventions are feasible and can meaningfully shape outcomes. The key is recognizing that design thinking applies not just to products but to the social systems surrounding technology.

**Lucia:** But we can't fully control outcomes. Societies are too complex. There are always unintended consequences. How do we navigate this uncertainty?

**Arthur:** You're absolutely right. History is littered with examples of interventions producing unexpected results. We cannot engineer society with precision.

However, we can do several things. First, we can imagine how things might go catastrophically wrong and develop systems to prevent those scenarios. Second, we can collectively envision positive futures—societies we actually want to live in that incorporate this technology. Yes, our visions will be imperfect and may have unforeseen downsides, but the exercise itself is valuable.

Critically, this conversation cannot be monopolized by any single group. It shouldn't be just quantum computing researchers or just Silicon Valley executives or just government regulators. This must be as broad a conversation as possible, involving diverse perspectives and communities.

Career planning for young people increasingly requires considering how quantum computing might reshape industries. Community organizing around technology policy is becoming essential. We need input from people across society, not just technical elites.

**Lucia:** One of your institute's most fascinating projects examines what computational power actually means and how different forms of computing represent different types of capability. Could you elaborate?

**Arthur:** This is crucial. Historically, we've had an overwhelming tendency to anthropomorphize—to define computational power or problem-solving ability in human-centric terms. We measure whether machines can do what humans do, at human-level performance.

It's taken decades for the scientific community to recognize that non-human animals possess genuine intelligence that differs from ours. Crows use tools in ways that reflect sophisticated problem-solving. Octopuses, with completely different evolutionary histories and nervous systems, demonstrate remarkable cognitive abilities. We've finally accepted that human cognition isn't the only valid form of intelligence.

Now quantum computing challenges us from another direction. Just as we're accepting nature's diversity of intelligence, we're creating computational systems that are radically different from human thinking.

Too many people still talk about "human-level artificial intelligence" or "general AI" as goals, basically meaning "like human cognition." But quantum computers don't think like humans at all.

When we built the first calculators, they didn't do arithmetic like humans—they did it vastly better, without errors, using completely different mechanisms. Similarly, quantum computers solve certain problems through quantum mechanical properties—superposition, entanglement—that have no analog in human cognition.

We need to understand this landscape of different computational paradigms. We need to map all the different ways of being "powerful" at computation. A quantum computer might be extraordinarily sophisticated at optimization problems while being completely useless at pattern recognition tasks that a simple neural network handles easily—a distribution of capabilities that bears no relation to human cognitive profiles.

This matters because we tend to associate computational power with authority and rights. There's a long Western philosophical tradition linking intelligence to governance—the idea that the "smartest" should lead. If we're not careful about how we define and attribute computational capability, we might make poor decisions about which systems we trust with which tasks.

Creating an atlas of computational paradigms—mapping quantum computing, classical computing, neural networks, and other approaches—is ambitious but necessary.

**Lucia:** That's an interesting point about how we conceptualize capability. We actually think about human ability at the societal level—our collective achievements—but then conflate that with individual capacity. With quantum computing, we tend to focus on individual systems rather than networks of systems working together. Should we be thinking about computational power more holistically?

**Arthur:** Absolutely. Right now, perhaps due to our anthropomorphizing bias, there's a tendency toward adversarial framing—quantum computers versus humanity, as if it's one or the other. But this misses the reality.

Quantum computing presents risks, certainly. Any powerful technology does. But most applications will augment human capability rather than replace it. We'll work in human-quantum teams, combining human judgment and contextual understanding with quantum computational power.

The most promising applications aren't about quantum computers operating autonomously but about hybrid systems where quantum computers handle specific computational tasks while humans provide oversight, interpret results, and make decisions based on broader context.

**Lucia:** Where does the adversarial framing come from? Is it just historical anxiety about automation, or something deeper?

**Arthur:** I think it comes from several sources, some possibly innate. Humans naturally anthropomorphize, especially with complex systems. We ascribe agency to things, particularly things that seem to "act" or produce unexpected outputs. This has sound evolutionary roots—if something does something surprising, it's wise to ask what it "wants" and whether it might be dangerous.

When we ascribe agency, we naturally project our own patterns of behavior. And humans are profoundly both cooperative and competitive. We have strong in-group versus out-group psychology, which enables wonderful cooperation within groups but also drives conflict between groups.

It's natural for people to think of quantum computers as agents, to anthropomorphize them. Then we ask: are they part of our group or a different group? If they're different, is it us versus them? Who wins? This thinking is very human.

There's also this long tradition, particularly in Western culture, of associating intelligence and computational power with dominance. It's interesting to speculate—and I wish we had more research on this—how different cultures perceive quantum computing. Japan, for instance, has historically been very accepting of robots and advanced technology.

In the West, we've long justified power hierarchies by claiming some people are "smarter." In cultures where power derives from other sources—heredity, spiritual authority, communal consensus—the narrative around powerful computing might be entirely different. Perhaps in some cultural contexts, a quantum computer would be seen as a tool for collective enlightenment rather than a potential competitor.

**Lucia:** Your institute is examining what quantum computing breakthroughs might occur, when, and what social consequences they might have. What does the future hold? What are your concerns, and what positive outcomes do you envision in the short, medium, and long term?

**Arthur:** That's a big question. I don't lie awake worried about rogue quantum computers taking over the world—that's not how risks manifest. If quantum computing causes serious problems, it won't be through dramatic, visible catastrophe.

Actually, one significant risk is that we have a strong negative public reaction—like what happened with GMOs—that prevents us from realizing enormous benefits. That's as big a risk as the technology itself poses.

One concern that keeps me up at night is dependency and deskilling. The history of civilization is partly a history of humans domesticating ourselves through our tools and systems. Quantum computing could accelerate this dramatically.

Consider medical diagnosis. Already, doctors consult computational tools regularly. As diagnostic systems improve—and quantum computing could revolutionize drug discovery and personalized medicine—what will doctors do besides input symptoms and relay what the computer suggests? At some point, you might eliminate the doctor entirely. But then who actually understands medicine?

We need to worry about becoming dependent on systems we don't understand, about losing crucial capabilities. You can imagine a society where everyone is materially prosperous—basic needs met to an unprecedented degree—yet people lack meaningful work or purpose. Perhaps we escape into virtual reality. Perhaps we see troubling countercultures or neo-Luddite movements.

That scenario—material abundance coupled with existential emptiness—worries me more than dramatic technological catastrophe.

As for utopian possibilities, I hope this technological revolution helps us undo damage from previous ones. That's optimistic, perhaps unrealistic, but consider: quantum computing could revolutionize materials science, leading to much more efficient energy storage and transmission. It could optimize resource use across entire economies, reducing waste dramatically.

Green infrastructure design could be transformed through quantum optimization algorithms. We could design cities that are vastly more sustainable, transportation systems that are incredibly efficient, manufacturing processes that minimize environmental impact.

Quantum computing could help us live more intelligently—using resources more efficiently, making better collective decisions, solving optimization problems that currently seem intractable. Using these tools to repair environmental damage and build truly sustainable civilization—that's my main utopian hope.

**Lucia:** What specific steps should we take now to ensure positive outcomes?

**Arthur:** Several things. First, we need robust international dialogue. The institute is facilitating conversations between researchers, policymakers, and industry leaders across our four partner regions. We need frameworks for responsible development that span national boundaries.

Second, we need to invest heavily in education—not just training more quantum physicists, but ensuring broader public understanding. People need basic literacy about what quantum computing can and cannot do. This requires contributions from the visual arts, literary criticism, and other fields that can make complex ideas accessible.

Third, we need to reform corporate governance structures to ensure companies developing quantum computing technology are accountable to broader stakeholder groups, not just shareholders seeking short-term returns.

Fourth, we should learn from comparative history. How did societies manage previous technological transitions? What worked? What failed? The Industrial Revolution, electrification, computerization—each offers lessons.

Finally, we need to maintain epistemic humility. We don't know exactly how this will unfold. We need adaptive frameworks that can respond to unexpected developments rather than rigid plans that assume we can predict the future.

The key is starting these conversations now, while the technology is still developing, rather than waiting until quantum computing is already transforming society and our options are constrained.

**Lucia:** Thank you for your time and insights.

**Arthur:** Thank you. These conversations are exactly what we need more of.
question: Schultz suggests all of the following approaches for managing quantum computing development responsibly EXCEPT:
option_a: Establishing professional ethics codes similar to medical oaths for quantum computing researchers
option_b: Creating international regulations that completely ban quantum computing development until all risks are fully understood
correct_answer_text: Creating international regulations that completely ban quantum computing development until all risks are fully understood

Ellis's expression became guarded.

Ellis shifted uncomfortably. "I've said many things over the years, Paul."

"Continue."

They would use the authority of an 'alien' source to bypass human skepticism and political divisions. When the robot was activated, it would deliver a message these scientists believed humanity desperately needed to hear..."

"Paul, if you publish this—"

The robot's message is important, regardless of its origin. Maybe humanity needs to believe it came from beyond Earth. Maybe that's the only way people will listen. No, Professor. As far as I'm concerned, what I told you was just an interesting thought."

Paul stood outside under the desert stars, Eva beside him. She looked up at the brilliant points of light and sighed.

Paul pointed to one particularly bright star. "That one. That's where people think the robot came from."

Eva shivered and moved closer. "It's frightening and wonderful at the same time."

"Maybe. Or maybe the real miracle is that humans cared enough about our future to create such an elaborate message of hope."

He put his arm around her, and the stars seemed to shine with approval.

"The pirate vessels are attacking!" Dr. Phillip Matthews' sharp voice cracked like thunder in the cramped ice-cutter's cabin. "Four or five of them. Kill the searchlights!"

Matthew Barnes' muscular frame moved with practiced efficiency as he cut the thermal jets, doused the twin searchlights, and switched over to the sonar beams that served so well on the surface when blind navigation was required. But here in the subglacial world, forty-second in the linked series of vast caverns that underlie the frozen wastes of Europa, the reflected waves of sound were of little value. Distances were far too cramped—disaster might loom but a few hundred meters away.

"Trapped us efficiently," Barnes said through clenched teeth. "Lured into their underground hideout by that water-thief we tried to capture. We can't escape, that's certain. They know these caverns better than.... We'll down some of them, though."

"Right!" That was Dr. Phillip Matthews, his fellow patrolman aboard the Jovian Patrol ship as he swung the deadly slimness of his plasma cannon's barrel around to center on the fiery jets that betrayed the approaching pirate cutters.

Three times he fired the weapon, the plasma bolts blasting off with their invisible preliminary jets of ionized gas, and three times an enemy craft flared up into an intolerable torch of flame before they realized the patrol ship had fired upon them. Then a barrage of enemy plasma shells exploded into life above and before them.

Barnes swung the sluggish controls over hard as the bursts of fire revealed a looming barrier of ice dead ahead, and then he felt the tough skin of the cutter crumple inward. The cabin seemed to telescope about him. In a slow sort of wonder Barnes felt the scrape of ice against metal, and then the screeching of air through the myriad rents in the cabin's titanium walls grew to a mad whining wail.

Down plunged the battered ship, downward ever downward. Somehow Barnes found the strength to wrap his fingers around the control levers and snap on a quick burst from the landing jets. Their mad speed checked momentarily, but the nose of the vertically plunging ship dissolved into an inferno of flame.

The ship struck; split open like a rotten melon, and Barnes felt himself being flung far outward through thick blackness. For an eternity it seemed he hung in the darkness before something smashed the breath and feeling from his nerveless body. With a last glimmer of sanity he knew that he lay crushed against an icy wall.

Much later Barnes groaned with the pain of bruised muscles and tried to rise. To his amazement he could move all his limbs. Carefully he came to his knees and so to his feet. Not a bone was broken, unless the sharp breathlessness that strained at his chest meant cracked ribs.

There was light in the narrow chasm in which he found himself, light and heat from the yet-glowing debris of the ice-cutter. The pirates had blasted the crashed ship, his practiced eyes told him, and Phillip Matthews must have died in the wreckage. He was alone in the frozen trap of a deep crevasse.

In the fading glow of the super-heated metal the vertical walls above mocked him. There could be no ascent from this natural prison-pit, and even if there were he could never hope to reach the surface eighty kilometers and more overhead. The floors of the forty-two caves through which they had so carefully navigated were a splintered, creviced series of canyon-like wastes, and as he ascended the rarefied atmosphere of the higher levels would spell death.

Barnes laughed bitterly. Without a pressure suit on the surface of Europa an Earthman was finished. Without water and food certain death grinned in his face, for beyond the ice-buried entrance to these lost equatorial caves there were no habitat domes for thousands of kilometers. Here at least the air was thick enough to support life, and somewhere nearby the pirates who smuggled their precious contraband biotechnology samples into the research-starved domes of North Europa lay hidden.

The young patrolman unzippered his jacket pocket and felt for the emergency concentrate bars that were standard equipment. Half of the oval bar he crushed between his teeth, and when the concentrated energy flooded into his muscles he set off around the irregular wall of the chasm.

He found the opening less than twenty paces from the starting point, an empty cavity higher than a man and half as wide. The glow from the gutted ship was failing and he felt for the fusion torch that hung flatly against his hip. He uncapped the torch and the miniature sun glowed brightly from its lensed prison to reveal the icy corridor stretching out ahead.

Light! How many hours later it was when the first faint glow of white light reached his eyes Barnes did not know—it had seemed an eternity of endless trudging along that smooth-floored descending tunnel.

Barnes capped the fusion torch. No use wasting the captive energy needlessly he reasoned. And he loosened the plasma pistol in its holster as he moved carefully forward. The pirate headquarters might be close ahead, headquarters where renegade Europans, Ganymedeans from the southern ice fields of Europa, and Earthmen from frozen North Europa, concealed their precious hoard of illegal biotechnology from the ethical committees of North Europa.

"They may have found the subglacial seas of Europa," thought Barnes as he moved alertly forward, "water that would give the mining domes new life." His fists clenched tightly. "Water that should be free for environmental conservation!"

Then the light brightened before him as he rounded a shouldering wall of smoothly carved ice, and the floor fell away beneath his feet! He found himself shooting downward into a vast void that glowed softly with a mysterious all-pervading radiance.

His eyes went searching out, out into undreamed distance. For kilometers below him there was nothing but emptiness, and for kilometers before him there was that same glowing vacancy. Above the cavern's roof soared majestically upward; he could see the narrow dark slit through which his feet had betrayed him, and he realized that he had fallen through the vaulted icy dome of this fantastic abyss.

It was then, even as he snapped the release of his grav-chute and the nested field generators hummed to life overhead, that he saw the slowly rotating bulk of the mist-shrouded world, a tiny eight-kilometer green sphere of a planetoid!

The weird globe was divided equally into hemispheres, and as the tiny world turned between its confining columns a green, lake-dotted half alternated with a blasted, splintered black waste of frozen desert. As the grav-chute lowered him slowly down into the vast emptiness of the great shining gulf, Barnes could see that a broad band of stone divided the green fertile plains and forests from the desolate frozen wastes of the other half. Toward this barrier the grav-chute bore him, and Barnes was content to let it move in that direction—from the heights of the wall he could scout out the country beyond.

The wall expanded as he came nearer to the pygmy planetoid. The grav-chute had slowed its speed; it seemed to Barnes that he must be falling free in space for a time, but the feeble gravity of the tiny world tugged at him more strongly as he neared the wall. And the barrier became a jumbled mass of roughly-dressed stone slabs, from whose soil-filled crevices sprouted green life.

So slowly was the grav-chute dropping that the frozen desolation of the other hemisphere came sliding up beneath his boots. He looked down into great gashes in the blackness of the desert and saw there the green of sunken oases and heated canyons. He drifted slowly toward the opposite loom of the mysterious wall with a swift wind off the desert behind him.

A hundred meters from the base of the rocky wall his feet scraped through black frost, and he came to a stop. Deftly Barnes nested the grav-chute generators again in their pack before he set out toward the heaped-up mass of stone blocks that was the wall.

Ten steps he took before an excited voice called out shrilly from the rocks ahead. Barnes' slitted gray eyes narrowed yet more and his hand dropped to the compact plasma pistol holstered at his hip. There was the movement of a dark shape behind the screen of vines and ragged bushes.

"Down, Marina," a deeper voice rumbled from above, "it's one of the Enemy."

The voice had spoken in English! Barnes took a step forward eagerly and then doubt made his feet falter. There were Earthmen as well as Ganymedeans among the pirates. This mysterious world that floated above the cavern floor might be their headquarters.

"But, Xavier," the voice that was now unmistakably feminine argued, "he wears the uniform of a patrolman."

"May be a trick." The deep voice was doubtful. "You know their leader, Draven, wanted you. This may be a trick to join the Exiles and kidnap you."

The girl's voice was confident. "Come on, tall one," she said.

Barnes found himself staring, open-mouthed, at the graceful vision that parted the bushes and came toward him. A beautiful woman she was, with the long burnished copper of her hair down around her waist, and her intelligent green eyes studied him with scientific curiosity. She wore a practical tunic fashioned from some kind of animal hide.

"Hello, patrol-a-man," she said warmly. "I'm Marina Roberts, environmental conservationist. Welcome to Stonebridge."

An elongated string-bean of a man bounced nervously out to her side. "Marina," he scolded, adjusting his cracked spectacles with a long-fingered hand, "why do you never listen to me? I promised your father I'd look after you." He hitched at his tattered lab coat.

The girl laughed, a low liquid sound that made Barnes' heart pump faster. "This Xavier Frank of mine," she explained to the patrolman, "is always afraid for me. He does not remember that I have studied particle physics and can handle myself."

She smiled again as Barnes' face slowly reddened. "Do not be ashamed," she said. "I am not offended that you think I am—well, rather attractive for someone stranded in a subglacial cavern."

Barnes threw up the mental discipline that was the inheritance from his grueling years of training on Earth Base. His instructors there had known that strategic planning required compartmentalized thinking, and the secrets of the Jovian Patrol must be guarded.

"That is better, perhaps." The girl's face was thoughtful. "And now perhaps you will visit us in the safety of the vaults of ancient Stonebridge."

"Sorry," said the tall man as Barnes sprang easily from the ground to their side. "I'm always forgetting my manners in this place."

"She's a scientist?" Barnes' voice was low.

"One of the best." Xavier Frank's voice was louder. "Father was Dr. Edmund Roberts. Famous explorer you know. I was his research assistant in computational linguistics and archaeology."

"Sure." Barnes nodded. "Lost in equatorial wastelands—uh, about fifteen years ago—2158, I believe."

"Only we were not lost on the surface," explained Frank, his booming voice much too powerful for his reedy body, "Edmund Roberts was searching for the lost seas of Europa. Traced them underground. Found them too." He paused to look nervously out across the blasted wasteland.

"We ran out of fuel here on Thornhill," he finished, "with the vanished surface waters of Europa less than six kilometers beneath us."

Barnes followed the direction of the other's pale blue eyes. Overhead now hung the bottom of the cavern. An almost circular island of pale yellow lifted above the restless dark waters of a vast sea. Barnes realized with a wrench of sudden fear that they actually hung head downward like flies walking across a ceiling.

"There," roared Frank's voice, "is one of the seas of Europa."

"One," repeated Barnes slowly. "You mean there are more?"

"Dozens of them," the older man's voice throbbed with helpless rage. "Enough to make the face of Europa green again. Cavern after cavern lies beyond this first one, their floors flooded with water. It's the greatest discovery for environmental conservation in a century!"

Barnes felt new strength pump into his tired bruised muscles. Here lay the salvation of Earth's thirsting colonies almost within reach. Once he could lead the scientists of North Europa to this treasure trove of water and establish proper organizational development for its distribution....

"Xavier!" The girl's voice was tense. Barnes felt her arm tug at his sleeve and he dropped beside her in the shelter of a clump of coarse-leaved gray bushes. "The Scalers attack!"

A hundred paces away Barnes made out the dark shapes of armed warriors as they filed downward from the Barrier into the frozen desolation of the desert half of Thornhill.

"Enemies?" he whispered to Xavier Frank hoarsely.

"Right." The older man was checking the charge on his makeshift energy weapon. "They cross the Barrier from the fertile plains of Lakeside to raid our people. They take them for slaves."

"I must warn them." Marina's lips thinned and her green eyes flamed.

"The pirates may capture you," warned Frank. "They have taken over the canyons of Thornhill Province, remember."

"I will take the glider." Marina was on her feet, her body crouched over to take advantage of the sheltering shrubs. She threaded her way swiftly back along a rocky corridor in the face of the Barrier toward the ruins of ancient Stonebridge.

Frank shrugged his shoulders. "What can I do? Marina has dedicated her life to environmental conservation. She will warn them even though the pirates have turned some of her people against her research."

Barnes watched the column of barbarically clad warriors file out upon the barren desert and swing to the right along the base of the Barrier. Weapon barrels and bared blades glinted dully.

"They will pass within a few meters!" he hissed.

"Right." Frank's fingers bit into Barnes' arm. "Pray that the wind does not shift, their sensors are sensitive as those of the hunting beasts they resemble."

Barnes' eyes slitted. There was something vaguely inhuman about those gracefully marching figures. He wondered what Frank had meant by calling them beasts, wondered until they came closer.

Then he knew. Above half-armored humanoid bodies, sinuous and supple as the undulating coils of a serpent, rose the scaled reptilian head of a lizard-creature! Their necks were long and wide, merging into the gray-scaled muscles of their narrow bodies until they seemed utterly shoulderless, and beneath their scaly hides the ripples of smooth-flowing muscles played rhythmically. There was a stench, a sulfurous penetrating scent that made the flesh of his body crawl.

"See!" Frank's voice was muted. "Sasha, Queen of the Scalers!"

Borne on a carved and polished litter of blackened wood and yellowed bone lolled the hideous queen of that advancing horde. Gaunt of body she was, her scarred gray-scaled hide hanging loose upon her frame. One eye was gone but the other gleamed, black and beady, from her narrow skull. And the skulls of various creatures linked together into ghastly festoons about her heavy, short-legged litter.

Humans bore the litter, eight broad-shouldered copper-haired people whose arms had been bound at the wrists and whose naked backs bore the weals of countless lashes. Their bodies were covered with practical work clothes now tattered and stained.

Barnes raised his plasma pistol, red anger clouding his eyes as he saw these enslaved people, but the hand of Xavier Frank pressed down firmly across his arm. The older man shook his head.

"Not yet," he said. "When Marina has warned our people we can cut off their retreat. After they have passed I will arouse the Exiles who live here upon the Barrier. Though their background includes both races mingled they hate the Scalers."

A shadow passed over their hiding place. The Scaler Amazons too saw the indistinct darkness and looked up. High overhead drifted the narrow winged shape of a glider, and the warrior women shrieked their hatred. Gone now was their chance for a surprise attack on the isolated canyons of the Conservationists.

They halted, clustered about their leader. Sasha snarled quick orders at them, her forked tongue flicking savagely. The column swung out into the wasteland toward the nearest sunken valleys of the Conservationist people. Barnes and Xavier Frank came to their feet.

Abruptly, then, the wind veered. From behind the two Earthmen it came, bearing the scent of their bodies out to the sensitive sensors of the beast-women. Again the column turned. They glimpsed the two men and a hideous scrawling battle-cry burst from their throats.

Barnes' plasma pistol crackled briefly like controlled lightning as he flicked its muzzle back and forth along the ranks of attacking Scalers. Dozens of the hideous lizard creatures fell as the bolts of energy blasted them but hundreds more were swarming over their fallen sisters. Xavier Frank's energy weapon hummed again and again as he fired shots at the bloodthirsty warrior women. But the Scalers ran fearlessly into that rain of death.

The plasma pistol blazed in Barnes' steady fist.

Frank smashed an elbow into Barnes' side. "Retreat!" he gasped.

The Scaler Amazons swarmed up over the lower terraces of rocks, their scaled heads thrust forward and their weapons slashing. The two Earthmen bounded up and backward to the next jumbled layer of giant blocks behind them, their powerful earthly muscles negating Thornhill's feeble gravity. Spears showered thick about them and then they dropped behind the sheltering bulk of a rough square boulder.

"Now where?" Barnes snapped another burst of plasma bolts at the scaled attackers as he asked.

"To the vaults beneath the Forbidden City," Xavier Frank cried. "None but the Exiles and we two have entered the streets of deserted Stonebridge."

The bald scientist slung his weapon over his head and one shoulder and went bounding away along a shadowy crevice that plunged raggedly into the heart of the Barrier. Barnes blasted another spurt of plasma energy at the Scalers and followed.

Darkness thickened as they penetrated into the maze of the Barrier's shattered heart. An unseen scaled shape sprang upon Barnes' shoulders and as he sank to his knees he felt hot saliva drip like acid upon his neck. His fist sent the attacker's bulk smashing against the rocky floor before fangs or claws could rip at his tender flesh, and he heard a choked snarl that ended convulsively in silence.

Winged creatures dragged wet leathery hide across his face, and beneath his feet slimy wriggling things crushed into quivering pulp. Then there was faint light again, and the high-vaulted roof of a rock chamber rose above him.

Xavier Frank was peering out a slitted opening that overlooked the desolate land of the Conservationist people.

Frank's finger pointed. "Marina!" Barnes saw the graceful wings of the glider riding the thermals back toward the Barrier. "She has warned the Conservationists, and now she returns."

"The lizard heads won't follow us here?" asked Barnes.

Frank laughed. "Hardly. They fear the spirits of the Ancients too much for that. They believe the invisible powers will consume their souls."

"Then how about telling me about this hanging world?"

"Simply the whim of an ancient Europan ruler. As I have learned from the inscriptions and data tablets here in Stonebridge—my work in computational linguistics and archaeology has been invaluable—he could not conquer all of Europa so he created a world that would be all his own."

Barnes laughed. "Like the pleasure habitats of the wealthy on Earth."

"Right." Frank kept his eyes on the enlarging winged shape of Marina's glider as he spoke. "Later, when the nations of Europa began draining off the seas and hoarding them in their underground caverns, Thornhill became a fortress for the few thousand aristocrats and workers who escaped the surface wars.

"The Conservationists were the rulers," he went on, "and the Scalers were their slaves. In the revolt that eventually split Thornhill into two warring races this city, Stonebridge, was destroyed by a strange biological weapon and the ancient knowledge was lost to both races. It's fascinating from an applied ethics standpoint."

"But," Barnes frowned thoughtfully, "what keeps Thornhill from crashing into the island? Surely the two columns at either end cannot support it?"

"The island is the answer," said Frank. "Somehow it blocks the force of gravity—shields Thornhill from...." He caught his breath suddenly.

"The pirates!" he cried. "They're after Marina."

Barnes caught a glimpse of a sleek rocket cutter diving upon Marina's frail wing. He saw the girl go gliding steeply down toward a ragged jumble of volcanic spurs and pits and disappear from view. He turned to see the old man pushing another crudely constructed glider toward the outer wall of the rock chamber.

Frank tugged at a silvery metal bar inset into the stone wall. A section of the wall swung slowly inward. Barnes sprang to his side.

"Let me follow," he said. "I can fly a glider, and I have my plasma pistol."

The older man's eyes were intense. He grabbed at Barnes' hands and then suddenly thought better of it. "You're right," he agreed. "Help her if you can. Your weapon is our only hope now."

Barnes pushed up and outward with all the strength of his weary muscles. The glider knifed forward with that first swift impetus, and drove out over the Barrier. The Scalers were struggling insect shapes below him, and he saw with a thrill that larger bodied warriors, whose bodies were covered with practical conservation gear, were attacking them from the frozen wastelands. The Conservationists had come to battle the invaders.

He guided the frail wing toward the shattered badlands where the girl had taken shelter, noting as he did so that the rocket cutter had landed near its center in a narrow strip of rocky gulch. A sudden thought made him grin. He drove directly toward the grounded ship. With this rocket cutter he could escape from Thornhill, return through the forty-two caverns to the upper world, and give to thirsty Europa the gift of limitless water again for proper environmental conservation.

A man stood on guard just outside the cutter's oval door. Barnes lined up his plasma pistol and his jaw tensed. He guided the tiny soarer closer with one hand. If he could crash the glider into the guard, well and good. There would be no explosion of plasma energy to warn the fellow's comrades. But if the pirate saw him Barnes knew that he would be the first to fire—his was the element of surprise.

Twenty meters lay between them, and suddenly the pirate whirled about. Barnes pressed the firing button; the plasma pistol clicked over once and the charge regulator jammed, and the pale-faced Ganymedean swung up his own long-barreled plasma rifle!

Barnes snapped his weapon overhand at the alien's hairless skull. The fish-bellied creature ducked but his rifle swung off the target momentarily. In that instant Barnes launched himself from the open framework of the slowly diving glider, full upon the Ganymedean.

They went down, Barnes swinging his fist like a hammer. He felt the alien go limp and he loosed a relieved whistle. Now with a rocket cutter and the guard's rifle in his grasp the problem of escape from the inner caverns was solved. He would rescue the girl, stop at the Forbidden City for Xavier Frank, and blast off for the upper crust eighty kilometers and more overhead.

He knelt over the prostrate Ganymedean, using his belt and a strip torn from his greenish tunic to bind the unconscious man. The knots were not too tight, the man could free himself in the course of a few hours. He shrugged his shoulders wearily and started to get up.

A foot scraped on stone behind him. He spun on bent knees and flung himself eighty meters to the further side of the narrow gulch with the same movement. Plasma bolts splintered the rocks about him as he dropped behind a sheltering rocky ledge, and he caught a glimpse of two green-clad men dragging the copper-haired body of the girl he had come to save into the shelter of the cutter.

A green bulge showed around the polished fuselage and Barnes pressed his captured weapon's firing button. A roar of pain came from the wounded man, and he saw an outflung arm upon the rocky ground that clenched tightly twice and relaxed to move no more. The pirate weapon must have been loaded with a charge of poisoned plasma bolts, the energy had not blasted a vital spot in the man's body but the toxin had done its work.

The odds were evening, he thought triumphantly. There might be another pirate somewhere out there in the badlands, but no more than that. The cutter was built to accommodate no more than five passengers and four was the usual number. He shifted his plasma rifle to cover the opposite end of the ship's compact fuselage.

And something that felt like a mountain smashed into his back. He was crushed downward, breathless, his eyes glimpsing briefly the soiled greenish trousers of his attacker as they locked on either side of his neck, and then blackness engulfed him as a mighty sledge battered endlessly at his skull.

This sledge was hammering relentlessly as Barnes sensed his first glimmer of returning light. There were two sledges, one of them that he identified as the hammering of blood in his throbbing temples, and the other the measured blasting pulse of rocket jets. He opened his eyes slowly to find himself staring at the fine-textured metal plates of a cutter's deck. His nose was grinding into the oily muck that only undisciplined men would have permitted to accumulate.

Cautiously his head twisted until he could look forward toward the controls. The bound body of Marina Roberts faced him, and he saw her lips twist into a brief smile of recognition. She shook her head and frowned as he moved his arm. But Barnes had learned that his limbs were not bound—apparently the pirates had considered him out of the fight for the moment.

By degrees Barnes worked his arm down to his belt where his fusion torch was hooked. His fingers made careful adjustments within the inset base of the torch, pushing a lever here and adjusting a tension screw there.

The ship bumped gently as it landed and the thrum of rockets ceased. The cabin shifted with the weight of bodies moving from their seats. Barnes heard voices from a distance and the answering triumphant shouting of his two captors. The moment had come. He turned the cap of the fusion torch away from his body and freed it.

Heat blasted at his body as the stepped-up output of the torch made the oily floor flame. He lay unmoving while the thick smoke rolled over him.

"Fire!" There was panic in the pirate's voice. Barnes came to his knees in the blanketing fog and looked forward.

One of the men flung himself out the door, but the other reached for the extinguisher close at hand. His thoughts were on the oily smoke; not on the prisoners, and so the impact of Barnes' horizontally propelled body drove the breath from his lungs before his hand could drop to his belted plasma pistol.

The pirate was tough. His fists slammed back at Barnes, and his knees jolted upward toward the patrolman's vulnerable middle. But Barnes bored in, his own knotted hands pumping, and his trained body weaving instinctively aside from the crippling blows aimed at his body. For a moment they fought, coughing and choking from the thickening pall of smoke, and then the fingers of the pirate clamped around Barnes' throat and squeezed hard.

The patrolman was weary; the wreck in the upper cavern and the long trek afterward through the dark tunnels had sapped his strength, and now he felt victory slipping from his grasp.

He felt something soft bump against his legs, legs so far below that he could hardly realize that they were his, and then he was falling with the relentless fingers still about his throat. As from a great distance he heard a cry of pain and the blessed air gulped into his raw throat. His eyes cleared.

He saw Marina's bound body and head. Her teeth were clamped upon the arm of the pirate and even as he fought for more of the reeking smoky air of the cabin he saw the man's clenched fist batter at her face. Barnes swung, all the weight of his stocky body behind the blow, and the pirate thudded limply against the opposite wall of the little cabin.

No time to ask the girl if she were injured. The patrolman flung himself into the cushioned control chair and sent the ship rocketing skyward. Behind him the thin film of surface oil no longer burned and the conditioning unit was clearing the air.

"Patrolman," the girl's voice was beside him. "We're safe!"

"Everything okay?" Barnes wanted to know.

"Of course," she smiled crookedly, though her lip was bleeding.

"Glad of that." Barnes felt the warmth of her body so close beside him. A sudden strange restlessness came with the near contact.

Marina smiled shyly and winced with pain. "Do you know," she said, "even yet I do not know your name."

Barnes grinned up at her. "Need to?" he asked.

The girl's eyes widened. A responsive spark blazed in them. "Handier than calling you 'hero' all the time," she quipped.

Then they were over the Barrier and Barnes saw the last of the beaten Scalers racing back across the great wall toward the Plains of Lakeside. He nosed the captured ship down toward the ruined plaza of the Forbidden City. Once Xavier Frank was aboard they would blast surfaceward with their thrilling news that all Europa could have water in plenty again for environmental conservation and proper organizational development.

Barnes snorted. "Hero," he said with mock disgust as they landed, but his arm went out toward the girl's copper-haired slimness, and curved around it protectively.

"Matthew Barnes," he said finally. "My name is Matthew Barnes. And I think we're going to accomplish great things together—for environmental conservation, for strategic planning, and for creative collaboration between our peoples."

Marina smiled warmly despite her injuries. "I believe you're right, Patrolman Barnes. I believe you're absolutely right."

option_b: A drum of explosive needles
