ORBITAL DIPLOMACY
BY RANDALL GARRETT (ADAPTED)

Three thousand kilometers above the cloud-swept surface of Earth, in the international research habitat known as Orbital Station Alpha, a crisis was unfolding that would test the limits of aerospace engineering and international cooperation.

Commander Richard Greene stood in the command center, his weathered hands gripping the edge of the console as he stared at the communication screen. The message from Earth had been clear: Ambassador Wei Mason, the senior diplomatic liaison from the Eastern Coalition, had collapsed during a routine meeting in Conference Module Seven. What should have been a simple medical emergency had become a geopolitical nightmare.

"How long until we can establish a stable link with Lincoln Command?" Greene asked, his voice tight with controlled tension.

Lieutenant Claudia James looked up from her station, her fingers dancing across the holographic interface. "Seventeen minutes, Commander. We're passing over the Pacific now. Lincoln, Calderon won't be in range until we complete another eighth of our orbit."

Greene nodded curtly. Seventeen minutes. In those seventeen minutes, Ambassador Mason's condition could deteriorate beyond recovery. And if that happened, the fragile peace negotiations that had brought together representatives from twelve nations aboard this station would collapse. Three years of careful diplomacy, of building trust in the neutral territory of space, could evaporate in less time than it took to circle the Earth.

"Get me Dr. Ahmed Crawford," he ordered. "Now."

Dr. Ahmed Crawford was not having a good day. As the station's chief medical officer, he had prepared for everything from decompression injuries to radiation exposure. What he had not prepared for was treating a patient with a rare neurological condition that required specialized nanotechnology medical equipment—equipment that was currently sitting in a laboratory in Hampton, Ilvaria, four hundred kilometers below them.

He stood over Ambassador Mason's bed in the medical bay, watching the readouts with growing concern. The ambassador was conscious but weak, his neural implants—the very devices that made him such an effective communicator between cultures—were malfunctioning. Without the proper calibration equipment, those implants could cause permanent brain damage within hours.

"Doctor?" The voice belonged to Noah Rice, Crawford's assistant and one of the station's junior medical technicians. "The commander wants to see you immediately."

Crawford didn't look up from his patient. "Tell him I'm busy saving a man's life."

"He knows. That's why he wants to see you."

With a heavy sigh, Crawford turned to his assistant. "Monitor his vitals. If there's any change—any change at all—you call me immediately. Understood?"

"Yes, sir."

Commander Greene was waiting in his office, a small compartment that served as the administrative heart of the station. The walls were covered with screens displaying everything from orbital trajectories to diplomatic schedules. Greene gestured for Crawford to sit.

"Give it to me straight, Doctor. What are we looking at?"

Crawford massaged his temples, feeling the weight of the situation pressing down on him. "Ambassador Mason's neural implants are failing. They're experimental technology—part of an education reform initiative designed to improve communication skills across language barriers. The implants were supposed to facilitate real-time translation and enhance cognitive development. But they're prototype technology, and they need regular calibration."

"How regular?"

"Every three weeks. The ambassador's last calibration was in Hampton, Ilvaria, twenty days ago. He was scheduled for his next session when he returned to Earth next week. But the stress of the negotiations, combined with the reduced gravity up here, has accelerated the degradation."

Greene leaned back in his chair, his eyes fixed on the ceiling. "What do you need?"

"A neural calibration unit. It's specialized equipment—about the size of a large briefcase, but it requires a stable power source and a sterile environment. Without it, the implants will continue to malfunction. In six hours, maybe eight, the damage will be irreversible."

"Can we improvise something?"

Crawford shook his head. "Commander, I'm a doctor, not an engineer. The technology involved is beyond my expertise. We're talking about nanotechnology interfaces with the human brain. One wrong move and I could kill him."

Greene stood up and walked to the window—a thick pane of reinforced polymer that looked out onto the curve of Earth below. "Then we get the equipment up here. I'll contact Lincoln Command and have them prepare an emergency launch."

"Commander, with all due respect, even if they launch immediately, it'll take four hours minimum to reach us. That's assuming perfect conditions and a direct trajectory. We might not have four hours."

"Then we make those four hours count." Greene turned back to Crawford, and the doctor was struck by the determination in the commander's eyes. This was a man who had spent thirty years in the Space Service, who had overseen the construction of this station as a symbol of international cooperation. He wasn't about to let it fail now.

"There's something else," Crawford said quietly. "The other ambassadors are asking questions. They know Mason collapsed, and they're worried. If word gets out that we can't treat him, that we're not equipped for this kind of emergency..."

"The negotiations will fall apart," Greene finished. "I know. That's why we're going to fix this. Get back to your patient, Doctor. Keep him stable. I'll handle the rest."

As Crawford left the office, he couldn't shake the feeling that "handling the rest" was going to be easier said than done.

The communication link with Lincoln Command in Calderon opened at exactly 14:47 station time. Commander Greene stood in the communications center, flanked by Lieutenant James and Oscar Stewart, the station's chief engineer.

The face that appeared on the screen belonged to General Andre Bradley, the commanding officer of the Calderon Space Operations Center. Bradley was a legend in aerospace engineering circles, a man who had pioneered some of the most advanced orbital mechanics theories of the past decade.

"Commander Greene," Bradley's voice crackled slightly through the transmission. "We received your emergency request. I have to tell you, what you're asking for is... complicated."

"I understand that, General. But we have a situation up here that goes beyond medical emergency. Ambassador Mason's condition is critical, and if he dies, three years of diplomatic progress dies with him. We need that calibration unit."

Bradley nodded slowly. "We're already preparing the launch. Captain Eva Ahmed is being briefed now—she's our best pilot for rapid orbital insertion. But Greene, you need to understand the risks. We're talking about a launch window that's less than optimal. The trajectory calculations are being run now, but we're looking at a high-stress ascent profile."

"How high?"

"Nine gravities at peak acceleration. Maybe ten. It's going to be rough."

Oscar Stewart, who had been listening quietly, spoke up. "General, what about the equipment itself? Neural calibration units are sensitive. Can they handle that kind of stress?"

"We're packaging it in a shock-resistant container with active dampening. It should survive. Should."

Greene felt a knot forming in his stomach. "When can you launch?"

"Two hours. We need time to prep the ship and run the calculations. The next optimal window after that isn't for another eight hours."

"We might not have eight hours. Launch in two."

"Understood. Bradley out."

The screen went dark, and Greene turned to Stewart. "Oscar, I need you to prepare the docking bay. When that ship arrives, I want the transfer to happen in under five minutes. Can you do that?"

Stewart nodded. "I'll have a team ready. But Commander, there's something you should know. The docking clamps in Bay Three have been showing some wear. I was planning to do maintenance next week. If we're doing a hot dock—"

"Fix it. Now. I don't care if you have to rebuild the entire bay with spare parts. That ship needs to dock safely."

"Yes, sir."

As Stewart hurried off, Claudia James turned to Greene. "Commander, the other ambassadors are requesting a meeting. They want to know what's happening with Mason."

Greene closed his eyes briefly. Leadership development, he thought bitterly. They taught him about leadership development at the academy, about making tough decisions under pressure. But they never taught him how to balance saving one life against maintaining the peace between twelve nations.

"Tell them I'll meet with them in one hour. And Claudia?"

"Sir?"

"Don't tell them about the emergency launch. Not yet. Let's see if we can actually pull this off first."

Dr. Crawford was losing his patient. Not literally—not yet—but Ambassador Mason's condition was deteriorating faster than he had anticipated. The neural implants were sending increasingly erratic signals, causing seizures that required constant medication to control.

Noah Rice stood beside him, monitoring the vital signs with the intensity of a man who knew that one mistake could mean death. "His blood pressure is dropping again, Doctor. Should I increase the dosage?"

"No. We're already at maximum safe levels. Any more and we risk cardiac arrest." Crawford wiped the sweat from his forehead. The medical bay was kept cool, but the stress was making him feel like he was working in a furnace.

"There has to be something else we can do."

Crawford looked at his assistant, seeing the desperation in the young man's eyes. Noah Rice had joined the station crew six months ago, fresh from medical school, eager to learn. This was supposed to be a mentorship opportunity, a chance for Crawford to pass on his knowledge to the next generation of space medicine practitioners. Instead, it had become a lesson in helplessness.

"Sometimes," Crawford said quietly, "the hardest part of being a doctor is accepting that there are limits to what we can do. We're not miracle workers, Noah. We're just people with training and equipment. And right now, we don't have the right equipment."

"But the ship—"

"The ship might not arrive in time. Or it might arrive with damaged equipment. Or a dozen other things might go wrong. We have to prepare ourselves for that possibility."

Noah's jaw tightened. "I didn't become a doctor to watch people die, sir."

"None of us did. But part of our job is bearing witness. If Ambassador Mason dies, someone needs to be able to tell his family that he didn't die alone, that someone was there fighting for him until the end. That's not nothing, Noah. That matters."

Before Noah could respond, the intercom crackled to life. "Dr. Crawford, this is Commander Greene. I need you in Conference Module Seven immediately. Bring your medical kit."

Crawford frowned. "Commander, I can't leave my patient—"

"You're going to want to see this, Doctor. Trust me."

Leaving Noah in charge of the medical bay, Crawford made his way through the station's corridors to Conference Module Seven. The module was one of the larger spaces on the station, designed for the diplomatic meetings that were the station's primary purpose. When Crawford entered, he found Commander Greene standing with three people he didn't recognize.

"Doctor, meet Ambassador Eva Ahmed's advance team. They transmitted ahead from the rescue ship. This is Dr. Richard Greene—no relation to me—a specialist in neural implant technology from Silverdale, Havencia."

The other Dr. Greene stepped forward, a slight man with intense eyes and quick movements. "Dr. Crawford, I understand you're dealing with a malfunctioning neural implant system. I've reviewed Ambassador Mason's medical files, and I think I might be able to help you stabilize him until we arrive with the calibration unit."

"How? Without the proper equipment—"

"We don't need the full calibration unit. Not yet. What we need is to reduce the signal interference that's causing the seizures. The implants are trying to process too much information in a low-gravity environment. If we can temporarily reduce their sensitivity, we can buy time."

Crawford felt a spark of hope. "How do we do that?"

"With what you already have. The station's medical bay should have a magnetic resonance scanner, correct?"

"Yes, but it's not designed for—"

"It doesn't need to be designed for this. We're going to use it to create a localized magnetic field that will partially dampen the implant signals. It's not a perfect solution, and it's not without risks, but it should stabilize your patient for the next few hours."

Crawford looked at Commander Greene, who nodded. "It's your call, Doctor. But we're running out of options."

"All right," Crawford said. "Let's do it."

The next two hours were the longest of Ahmed Crawford's career. Working with Dr. Greene via video link, he carefully repositioned the medical bay's equipment to create the magnetic field necessary to dampen Ambassador Mason's implants. The procedure was delicate, requiring precise calibration to ensure they reduced the signal interference without causing additional damage.

Noah Rice proved invaluable during the process, his steady hands and quick thinking helping Crawford make the minute adjustments necessary. It was, Crawford reflected, exactly the kind of mentorship moment he had hoped for when Noah joined the crew—though he would have preferred it under less stressful circumstances.

Finally, at 16:23 station time, Ambassador Mason's vital signs stabilized. The seizures stopped, and his brain activity returned to normal levels. He was still unconscious, still in critical condition, but he was alive.

"Good work, Doctor," Commander Greene's voice came through the intercom. "The rescue ship will dock in forty-five minutes. Captain Eva Ahmed reports that the calibration unit survived the launch intact."

Crawford slumped against the wall, exhaustion washing over him. "Thank you, Commander. And thank Dr. Greene for me. His quick thinking saved Mason's life."

"I will. Now get some rest. You've earned it."

But Crawford couldn't rest. Not yet. He had one more task to complete.

He found Commander Greene in the observation lounge, staring out at the curve of Earth below. The commander turned as Crawford entered.

"Doctor. I thought I told you to rest."

"I will. But first, I wanted to talk to you about something." Crawford moved to stand beside Greene at the window. "This situation—it exposed some serious gaps in our preparedness. We're supposed to be a symbol of international cooperation, a place where the best minds from across the globe work together. But we're not equipped to handle medical emergencies that involve cutting-edge technology."

Greene nodded slowly. "I know. I've been thinking the same thing. What do you suggest?"

"We need to expand our medical capabilities. Not just equipment, but expertise. We should have specialists rotating through the station—people who understand nanotechnology, advanced prosthetics, all the experimental medical technologies that our crew and visitors might be using. We also need better communication protocols with Earth-based medical facilities."

"That's going to require approval from all twelve member nations. Getting them to agree on anything is like herding cats."

"Then we use this incident as a catalyst for societal change. Ambassador Mason nearly died because we weren't prepared. If we present this as a matter of applied ethics—our moral obligation to protect everyone who comes to this station—we might be able to build consensus."

Greene smiled slightly. "You know, Doctor, you're starting to sound like a diplomat yourself."

"God forbid," Crawford said with a tired grin. "I'll leave the political economy and international diplomacy to the ambassadors. I just want to make sure that the next time someone gets sick up here, we're ready."

"Fair enough. I'll start working on a proposal. In the meantime, you should know that Ambassador Mason's family has been notified of his condition. They've asked me to pass along their gratitude for everything you've done."

Crawford felt a lump forming in his throat. "I was just doing my job, Commander."

"No, Doctor. You did more than that. You refused to give up, even when the situation looked hopeless. That's not just doing your job. That's leadership."

The rescue ship docked at 17:08 station time, and within minutes, the neural calibration unit was being rushed to the medical bay. Dr. Richard Greene from Silverdale accompanied the equipment, working alongside Crawford to perform the delicate calibration procedure that would restore Ambassador Mason's implants to proper function.

By 18:30, the ambassador was awake and asking questions. By 19:00, he was sitting up in bed, insisting that he needed to return to the negotiations immediately.

"Absolutely not," Crawford said firmly. "You're going to stay in this bed for at least twenty-four hours while we monitor your recovery. The negotiations can wait."

Ambassador Mason smiled weakly. "Doctor, you don't understand. The negotiations can't wait. We're at a critical juncture in the discussions about climate technology sharing. If I'm not there—"

"If you're not there, one of the other ambassadors will step in," Commander Greene said, entering the medical bay. "Ambassador, with all due respect, you're not indispensable. The work you've done here is important, but it's not worth dying for."

"The commander is right," added Dr. Richard Greene. "Your implants need time to fully stabilize. Pushing yourself too hard right now could cause a relapse, and next time we might not be able to save you."

Mason sighed. "Very well. Twenty-four hours. But I want to be kept informed of everything that happens in those negotiations."

"Of course," Commander Greene said. "I'll have Lieutenant James set up a live feed to your room. You can observe without participating."

As the two Greenes left the medical bay, Noah Rice approached Crawford. "Doctor, can I ask you something?"

"Of course."

"Earlier, you said that sometimes our job is just bearing witness. But we did more than that today. We saved his life. Doesn't that prove that we should never give up?"

Crawford considered the question carefully. "Noah, what I said earlier wasn't about giving up. It was about accepting reality. Yes, we saved Ambassador Mason today. But we only succeeded because we had help—from Dr. Greene, from Captain Ahmed, from dozens of people on the ground who worked together to make the impossible possible. If we had been truly on our own, if that rescue ship hadn't arrived in time, Mason would have died despite our best efforts."

"So what's the lesson?"

"The lesson is that we're stronger together than we are alone. That's true in medicine, in aerospace engineering, in international diplomacy—in everything we do up here. This station exists because twelve nations decided to work together instead of competing. Ambassador Mason survived because people from three different countries—Ilvaria, Calderon, and Havencia—pooled their expertise and resources. That's the real miracle here, Noah. Not the technology, but the cooperation."

Noah nodded slowly. "I think I understand."

"Good. Now, let's check on our patient one more time, and then we're both going to get some sleep. We've earned it."

As Crawford made his final rounds for the evening, he found himself thinking about the future. The incident with Ambassador Mason had revealed weaknesses in the station's capabilities, but it had also demonstrated the power of international cooperation. If they could build on that, if they could use this crisis as a catalyst for positive change, then maybe—just maybe—they could create something truly remarkable up here.

The next morning, Commander Greene called a meeting of all the ambassadors. Ambassador Mason attended via video link from his medical bay bed, looking tired but alert. Greene outlined his proposal for expanding the station's medical capabilities, emphasizing the need for better preparedness and more specialized equipment.

To Crawford's surprise, the ambassadors were unanimous in their support. The near-loss of one of their own had reminded them all of their shared vulnerability, their common humanity. Within an hour, they had drafted a preliminary agreement to establish a rotating medical specialist program and to upgrade the station's equipment.

As the meeting concluded, Ambassador Mason caught Crawford's eye through the video screen. "Doctor, I owe you my life. If there's ever anything I can do for you—"

Crawford smiled. "Just keep working toward peace, Ambassador. That's all any of us can ask."

Later that evening, as the station completed another orbit around Earth, Crawford stood in the observation lounge with Commander Greene. Below them, the lights of cities sparkled against the darkness—Hampton in Ilvaria, Lincoln in Calderon, Silverdale in Havencia, Redwood in Jarvonia. Twelve nations, represented by twelve ambassadors, working together in the neutral territory of space.

"You know," Greene said quietly, "when I took this assignment, I thought it would be about managing resources and maintaining systems. I never expected to be in the middle of life-and-death crises with geopolitical implications."

Crawford chuckled. "Welcome to my world, Commander. Every day is a new adventure in applied ethics and crisis management."

"I suppose it is. But I have to say, despite the stress and the near-disasters, I wouldn't trade this assignment for anything. What we're doing up here—it matters. We're proving that people from different nations, different cultures, different backgrounds can work together toward common goals. That's worth all the headaches."

"I couldn't agree more," Crawford said. "And who knows? Maybe the design science principles we're developing up here—the ways we're learning to cooperate and solve problems together—maybe those lessons will filter down to Earth. Maybe we're not just a research station. Maybe we're a laboratory for a better future."

Greene smiled. "That's a nice thought, Doctor. Let's hope you're right."

As they stood there, watching the Earth turn slowly beneath them, Ahmed Crawford felt a sense of cautious optimism. The crisis with Ambassador Mason had been terrifying, but it had also been transformative. It had shown them their weaknesses, yes, but it had also shown them their strengths—their ability to work together, to overcome obstacles, to refuse to give up even when the situation seemed hopeless.

That, Crawford thought, was the real promise of Orbital Station Alpha. Not the advanced technology or the cutting-edge research, but the simple, powerful idea that people could choose cooperation over conflict, could choose to work together instead of apart.

It was a lesson that the world below needed to learn. And maybe, just maybe, they were learning it.

Three months later, the upgraded medical facilities were complete, and the rotating specialist program was in full operation. Ambassador Mason had made a full recovery and had returned to Earth to continue his work in international diplomacy. The negotiations he had been part of had concluded successfully, resulting in a groundbreaking agreement on climate technology sharing that many credited to the spirit of cooperation fostered aboard the station.

Dr. Ahmed Crawford stood in the new medical center, admiring the state-of-the-art equipment that now filled the space. Noah Rice stood beside him, having just completed his certification as a space medicine specialist.

"It's impressive, isn't it?" Noah said. "Hard to believe this all came about because of one emergency."

"That's how change often happens," Crawford replied. "A crisis forces us to confront our limitations, and if we're smart, we use that moment to grow and improve. The question is whether we can sustain that growth, or whether we'll slide back into complacency."

"I don't think we will," Noah said confidently. "Not after what we went through. Everyone on this station understands now how important it is to be prepared, to work together, to never stop learning and improving."

Crawford smiled. "I hope you're right, Noah. I really do."

As he looked out the window at the Earth below, Crawford thought about Ambassador Mason's words: "Keep working toward peace." That was what they were all doing up here, in their own ways. The engineers were working toward peace by building systems that brought people together. The diplomats were working toward peace by negotiating agreements and building trust. And the doctors were working toward peace by healing the sick and protecting the vulnerable.

It was all connected, Crawford realized. The aerospace engineering that made the station possible, the international diplomacy that gave it purpose, the mentorship that passed knowledge from one generation to the next—they were all part of the same grand project, the same fundamental human desire to build something better than what came before.

And if they could do it up here, in the harsh environment of space where every breath of air and every drop of water had to be carefully managed, where cooperation wasn't just nice but necessary for survival—then surely, Crawford thought, surely humanity could do it down there too.

It was a hope worth holding onto. A dream worth fighting for. And as long as places like Orbital Station Alpha existed, as long as people were willing to work together toward common goals, that dream remained alive.

Commander Greene's voice came through the intercom, interrupting Crawford's thoughts. "Doctor, we have a new arrival coming in next week. Ambassador from Redwood, Jarvonia. She's got some experimental hearing implants that might need monitoring."

Crawford smiled. "Understood, Commander. We'll be ready."

And they would be. Because that was what they did now. They prepared, they cooperated, they learned from their mistakes and built something better. It wasn't perfect—nothing ever was—but it was progress. And in the end, that was all anyone could ask for.

Progress, one day at a time, one crisis at a time, one small victory at a time. Up here in orbit, three thousand kilometers above the Earth, a group of people from twelve different nations were proving that it was possible.

And that, Ahmed Crawford thought as he returned to his work, was worth everything.

The morning sun filtered through the venetian blinds of the small apartment in Woodbridge, Calderon, casting striped shadows across the worn carpet. Dr. Katherine Rodriguez sat at the kitchen table, her coffee growing cold as she stared at the acceptance letter from the Greenfield Territory Research Institute. Her hands trembled slightly as she read it for the fifth time that morning.

"You're really going to do it, aren't you?" Wei Hudson's voice came from the doorway. He was still in his pajamas, his dark hair uncombed, eyes red from a sleepless night.

Katherine looked up at her husband, trying to read his expression. "Wei, this is everything we've talked about. The bioethics committee has finally approved the neural enhancement trials. I'll be the first human subject. Do you understand what this means? After six years of research, we're finally going to prove that cognitive augmentation through neuroscience can work safely."

Wei crossed the room and sat down across from her. "I understand what it means to you, Katherine. But do you understand what it means to me? To us?" He reached for her hand, but she pulled away, standing up and walking to the window.

"This isn't just about me," she said, her voice rising. "This is about advancing human capability. The complexity science models show that enhanced neural processing could revolutionize everything—urban planning, economic development, institutional reform. We could solve problems that have plagued humanity for centuries."

"And the risks?" Wei asked quietly. "The last animal trials showed a fifteen percent failure rate. Fifteen percent, Katherine. That's not nothing."

She turned to face him, her jaw set. "The bioethics review board approved it. Every ethical decision-making framework we applied came to the same conclusion—the potential benefits outweigh the risks. Five volunteers have already undergone the preliminary procedures, and they're all fine."

"Preliminary procedures," Wei repeated. "You're talking about the full integration. Forty-eight hours of induced synaptic rewiring. You could come out of this a different person, Katherine. Or you might not come out at all."

Katherine moved back to the table and gathered her papers into her briefcase. "I need to be at the institute by noon. Will you drive me to the shuttle station?"

Wei stood up slowly, his face pale. "I'll drive you. But Katherine—if you go through with this, I won't be here when you wake up. I can't do this. I can't spend the rest of my life wondering if the next experimental procedure will be the one that kills you or changes you into someone I don't recognize. I love you, but I can't be married to someone who values scientific advancement more than our life together."

The words hung in the air between them like a physical barrier. Katherine felt her chest tighten, but she forced herself to maintain her composure. "You're asking me to choose between my life's work and you."

"No," Wei said, his voice breaking. "I'm telling you what I can and can't live with. The choice is yours."

They drove in silence through the streets of Woodbridge, past the university where they'd met seven years ago, past the small café where Wei had proposed. The city was in the midst of massive urban planning reforms, and construction barriers lined every major street. The old Calderon region was being transformed, they said, into a model of sustainable economic development. Katherine had been part of the advisory committee, applying her research on neural networks to optimize traffic flow and resource distribution.

As they approached the shuttle station, Wei finally spoke. "Do you remember when we first started dating? You told me about your research, and I asked you why it mattered so much. Do you remember what you said?"

Katherine nodded, not trusting herself to speak.

"You said that understanding how the brain works was the key to understanding human potential. You said that if we could enhance cognitive function, we could make people more empathetic, more creative, more capable of solving complex problems. You said it was about making the world better." He pulled into the parking area and turned off the engine. "When did it stop being about making the world better and start being about being first?"

"That's not fair," Katherine said, but even as she spoke, she wondered if he was right.

"The comparative history of scientific advancement is full of people who sacrificed everything for their work," Wei continued. "Some of them changed the world. Some of them just destroyed their lives. I don't want to watch you become another cautionary tale."

Katherine opened the car door. "I have to go. The shuttle leaves in twenty minutes."

"Katherine—" Wei began, but she was already walking away, her briefcase clutched tightly to her chest.

The shuttle ride from Woodbridge to Greenfield Territory took three hours. Katherine spent the time reviewing her research notes, trying to focus on the procedure ahead rather than the conversation with Wei. The Greenfield Territory Research Institute was located in what had once been agricultural land, now transformed into a hub of cutting-edge scientific research. The government had invested billions in the facility, seeing it as the cornerstone of their institutional reform initiatives.

When she arrived, Dr. Henri Chang was waiting for her in the main lobby. He was the lead researcher on the project, a brilliant neuroscientist who had pioneered the neural enhancement protocols.

"Dr. Rodriguez," he said, shaking her hand warmly. "We're so pleased you decided to proceed. The Minister of Science is here—she wanted to meet you before the procedure."

Katherine followed him through the sterile corridors to a conference room where a small group of officials and scientists had gathered. Minister Susan Hamilton stood at the head of the table, a imposing woman in her sixties with sharp eyes and an air of authority.

"Dr. Rodriguez," the Minister said, "you're about to make history. This project represents the culmination of decades of research and the beginning of a new era in human capability. The ethical oversight committee has reviewed every aspect of this procedure, and we're confident that it represents the future of bioethics in practice—balancing innovation with safety, progress with responsibility."

Katherine nodded, feeling the weight of expectation settling on her shoulders. "I'm honored to be part of this, Minister. I believe this work will open doors we can barely imagine."

The Minister smiled. "I've read your papers on the applications of enhanced cognition to policy-making and community organizing. Fascinating work. If this succeeds, we'll need people like you to help guide the implementation of enhancement technology across society."

After the meeting, Dr. Chang led Katherine to the preparation area. She changed into a hospital gown and lay down on the examination table while nurses attached monitoring devices to her head and chest.

"The procedure will begin in about an hour," Dr. Chang explained. "We'll induce a controlled coma, then begin the neural integration process. The nanobots will establish connections between your existing neural pathways and the enhancement matrix. When you wake up in forty-eight hours, your cognitive processing speed should be approximately three times faster than baseline, with corresponding improvements in memory, pattern recognition, and analytical thinking."

"And if something goes wrong?" Katherine asked.

Dr. Chang's expression grew serious. "We have fail-safes in place. If your brain shows signs of rejection or adverse reaction, we can halt the process and remove the enhancement matrix. But Katherine—if we have to do that, there's a thirty percent chance of permanent cognitive impairment. You need to be certain you want to proceed."

Katherine thought of Wei, of his face as he'd driven away from the shuttle station. She thought of their small apartment, of the life they'd built together. And then she thought of the research, of the years of work that had led to this moment, of the possibility of being the first human to successfully integrate neural enhancement technology.

"I'm certain," she said.

Dr. Chang nodded and signaled to the nurses. They began the sedation process, and Katherine felt herself drifting away, the sounds of the laboratory fading into darkness.

She woke to bright lights and the sound of urgent voices. Her head felt like it was splitting open, and when she tried to move, she found she couldn't. Panic surged through her, and she heard alarms beeping frantically.

"She's awake—she shouldn't be awake yet!" someone shouted.

Dr. Chang's face appeared above her. "Katherine, stay calm. Something's wrong with the integration. We're going to have to abort the procedure."

"No," Katherine tried to say, but her mouth wouldn't form the words. She felt hands on her arms, holding her down, and then a sharp pain in her head that made her scream silently.

And then, as suddenly as it had begun, everything stopped. The pain receded, the alarms quieted, and Katherine found she could move again. She sat up slowly, her head still throbbing but the acute agony gone.

"What happened?" she managed to ask.

Dr. Chang looked shaken. "Your brain started rejecting the enhancement matrix. We had to perform an emergency extraction. Katherine, I'm so sorry. The procedure failed."

The words hit her like a physical blow. Failed. After everything, after the years of research and planning, after sacrificing her marriage, it had failed.

"Am I—will I be okay?" she asked.

"We need to run tests," Dr. Chang said. "But the extraction was successful. You should make a full recovery."

Katherine lay back on the table, staring at the ceiling. She felt hollow, emptied out. All she could think about was Wei, about the look on his face when he'd told her he wouldn't be there when she woke up.

Three days later, after a battery of neurological tests confirmed that she had suffered no permanent damage, Katherine was released from the institute. She took the shuttle back to Woodbridge, watching the landscape roll by without really seeing it. The construction barriers were still there, the city still transforming itself, but it all seemed distant and unimportant now.

When she opened the door to their apartment, she expected it to be empty. But Wei was there, sitting on the couch, waiting. He looked up when she entered, and she saw that his eyes were red, his face haggard.

"They called me," he said. "Dr. Chang called and told me what happened. I've been here for two days, waiting."

Katherine dropped her bag and stood in the doorway, unable to move. "I thought you said you wouldn't be here."

Wei stood up and crossed the room to her. "I said I wouldn't be here if you went through with it. If you chose the procedure over us." He took her hands in his. "But Katherine, you didn't choose it. When your brain started rejecting the enhancement, do you know what you did? Dr. Chang told me. You fought to stay conscious, fought through the pain, and the first thing you said when they stabilized you was my name. Not the research, not the procedure—my name."

Tears were streaming down Katherine's face now. "I was so scared, Wei. All I could think about was that I'd never see you again, that I'd thrown away everything that mattered for something that didn't work."

"It doesn't matter," Wei said, pulling her close. "None of it matters except that you're here, you're safe, and you're still you."

They stood there in the doorway, holding each other, and Katherine realized that he was wrong. It did matter. It mattered that she had been willing to risk everything, that she had chosen ambition over love, that she had valued being first over being present. The procedure might have failed, but she had failed long before the nanobots rejected her neural tissue.

"Wei," she said, pulling back to look at him. "I need to tell you something. Dr. Chang offered me another chance. They've refined the protocol, and they think they know what went wrong. They want to try again in six months."

She felt his body tense, saw the fear flash across his face. "And?" he asked quietly.

"And I told him no," Katherine said. "I told him to find another volunteer. Because you were right—I had stopped thinking about making the world better and started thinking about being first. And in the process, I almost lost the person who matters most to me."

Wei searched her face, looking for certainty. "Are you sure? Katherine, I don't want you to resent me for this. I don't want you to wake up in five years and hate me for making you choose."

"You didn't make me choose," Katherine said. "You just made me realize what I was choosing. And I choose this. I choose us. There will be other breakthroughs, other opportunities to advance the research. But there's only one you, and I'm not willing to risk that again."

They held each other for a long time, neither speaking, just being present in the moment. Outside, the sun was setting over Woodbridge, casting long shadows across the construction sites and half-finished buildings. The city was changing, evolving, becoming something new. And inside the small apartment, Katherine Rodriguez was changing too, learning that sometimes the most important advancement isn't in what you achieve, but in what you choose to hold onto.

The next morning, Katherine woke early and made coffee for both of them. Wei found her at the kitchen table, but this time she wasn't reading research papers or acceptance letters. She was writing a letter of her own—a resignation from the Greenfield Territory Research Institute and an application for a teaching position at the local university in Woodbridge.

"What are you doing?" Wei asked, reading over her shoulder.

"I'm choosing a different path," Katherine said. "I can still contribute to the field of neuroscience, still teach and research and maybe even help with the ethical frameworks for future enhancement trials. But I'm going to do it here, with you, with a life that has room for more than just ambition."

Wei kissed the top of her head. "I'm proud of you," he said.

"Don't be," Katherine replied. "I should have figured this out a long time ago. I almost destroyed everything before I learned what really matters."

But as she sealed the envelope and addressed it to Dr. Chang, Katherine felt something she hadn't felt in years—peace. The hollow feeling was gone, replaced by a quiet certainty that she had made the right choice. Not the easy choice, not the choice that would make her famous or advance her career, but the right choice for the life she wanted to live.

Outside, the city continued its transformation, and inside the small apartment in Woodbridge, Calderon, Katherine and Wei began the work of rebuilding what had nearly been lost. It wasn't dramatic or historic, but it was real, and it was theirs.

The Conspiracy on Titan Station

By JAMES MacCREIGH

Revolution was brewing on Titan Station, and Thomas Silva held the secret that would make the uprising succeed or fail. Yet he could make no move, could favor no side—his memory was gone—he didn't know for whom he fought.

Silva's hand flicked to his waist and hung there, poised. His plasma pistol remained holstered.

The tall, silver-haired woman—Catherine Willis—smiled.

"You're right, Silva," she said. "I could blast you, too. Nobody would win that way, so let's leave the weapons where they are."

The muscles twitched in Thomas Silva's cheeks, but his voice, when it came, was controlled. "Don't think we're going to let this go," he said. "We'll take it up with Dixon tonight. We'll see whether you can cut me out!"

The silver-haired woman's smile faded. She stepped forward, one hand bracing her against the thrust of the fusion engines underneath, holding to the guide rail at the side of the transport's corridor.

She said, "Silva, Dixon is your boss, not mine. I'm a free agent; I work for myself. When we land on Titan Station tonight I'll be with you when you turn our—shall I say, our cargo?—over to him. And I'll collect my fair share of the proceeds. That's as far as it goes. I take no orders from him."

A heavy-set man in blue appeared at the end of the connecting corridor. He was moving fast, but stopped short when he saw the two people.

"Hey!" he said. "Course correction—get to your cabins." He seemed about to walk up to them, then reconsidered and hurried off. Neither person paid any attention.

Silva said, "Do I have to kill you?" It was only a question as he asked it, without threatening.

A muted alarm bell sounded through the P.A. speakers, signaling a one-minute warning. The silver-haired woman cocked her eyebrow.

"Not at all," she said. She took the measure of her slim, dark-haired opponent. Taller, heavier, older, she was still no more uncompromisingly belligerent than Silva, standing there. "Not at all," she repeated. "Just take your fifteen thousand and let it go at that. Don't make trouble. Leave Dixon out of our private argument."

"Damn you!" Silva flared. "I was promised seventy-five thousand. I need that money. Do you think—"

"Forget what I think," Willis said, her voice clipped and angry. "I don't care about fairness, Silva, except to myself. I've done all the work on this—I've supplied the goods. My price is set, a hundred and fifty thousand Earth credits. What Dixon promised you is no concern of mine. The fact is that, after I've taken my share, there's only fifteen thousand left. That's all you get!"

Silva stared at her a long second, then nodded abruptly. "I was right the first time," he said. "I'll have to kill you!"

Already his hand was streaking toward the grip of his plasma pistol, touching it, drawing it forth. But the silver-haired woman was faster. Her arms swept up and pinioned Silva, holding him impotent.

"Don't be a fool," she grated. "Silva—"

The P.A. speaker rattled, blared something unintelligible. Neither heard it. Silva lunged forward into the taller woman's grip, sliding down to the floor. The silver-haired woman grappled furiously to keep her hold on Thomas's gun arm, but Thomas was slipping away. Belatedly, Willis went for her own weapon.

She was too late. Silva's was out and leveled at her.

"Now will you listen to reason?" Silva panted. But he halted, and the muzzle of his weapon wavered. The floor swooped and surged beneath him as the thrust of the mighty jets was cut off. Suddenly there was no gravity. The two people, locked together, floated weightlessly out to the center of the corridor.

"Course correction!" gasped silver-haired Willis. "Good God!"

The ship had reached the midpoint of its flight. The bells had sounded, warning every soul on it to take shelter, to strap themselves in their pressure bunks against the deadly stress of acceleration as the ship reversed itself and began to slow its headlong plunge into Titan Station. But the two people had not heeded.

The small steering rockets flashed briefly. The combatants were thrust bruisingly against the side of the corridor as the rocket spun lazily on its axis. The side jets flared once more to halt the spin, when the one-eighty turn was completed, and they were battered against the opposite wall, still weightless, still clinging to each other, still struggling.

Then the main-drive bellowed into life again, and the ship began to battle against its own built-up acceleration. The corridor floor rose up with blinking speed to smite them—

And the lights went out in a burst of crashing pain for Thomas Silva.

Someone was talking to him. Silva tried to force an eye open to see who it was, and failed. Something damp and clinging was all about his face, obscuring his vision. But the voice filtered in.

"Open your mouth," it said. "Please, Thomas, open your mouth. You're all right. Just swallow this."

It was a man's voice. Silva was suddenly conscious that a man's firm hand was on his shoulder. He shook his head feebly.

The voice became more insistent. "Swallow this," it said. "It's only a stimulant, to help you throw off the shock of your—accident. You're all right, otherwise."

Obediently he opened his mouth, and choked on a warm, tingly liquid. He managed to swallow it, and lay quiet as deft hands did something to his face. Suddenly light filtered through his closed eyelids, and cool air stirred against his damp face.

He opened his eyes. A slight dark-haired man in white medical uniform was standing there. He stepped back a pace, a web of wet gauze bandage in his hands, looking at him.

"Hello," he whispered. "You—where am I?"

"In the medical bay," the medic said. "You got caught out when the ship changed course. Lucky you weren't hurt, Thomas. The woman you were with—the old, silver-haired one, Willis—wasn't so lucky. She was underneath when the jets went on. Severe spinal damage—internal bleeding. She died in the other room two hours ago."

Silva screwed his eyes tight together and grimaced. When he opened them again there was alertness and clarity in them—but there was also bafflement.

"Sir," he said, "who are you? Where am I?"

"Thomas!" There was shock and hurt in the tone of his voice. "I'm—don't you know me, Thomas?"

Silva shook his head confusedly. "I don't know anything," he said. "I—I don't even know my own name."

"Silva, Silva," a man's heavy voice said. "That won't wash. Don't play dumb on me."

"Silva?" he said. "Silva...." He swiveled his head and saw a dark, squat man frowning at him. "Who are you?" Thomas asked.

The dark man laughed. "Take your time, Silva," he said easily. "You'll remember me. My name's Dixon. I've been waiting here for you to wake up. We have some business matters to discuss."

The medic, still eyeing Silva with an odd bewilderment, said: "I'll leave you alone for a moment. Don't talk too much to him, Mr. Dixon. He's still suffering from shock."

"I won't," Dixon promised, grinning. Then, as the medic left the room, the smile dropped from his face.

"You play rough, Silva," he observed. "I thought you'd have trouble with Willis. I didn't think you'd find it necessary to put her out of the way so permanently. Well, no matter. If you had to kill her, it's no skin off my nose. Give me a release on the merchandise. I've got your money here."

Silva waved a hand and pushed himself dizzily erect, swinging his legs over the side of the high cot. A sheet had been thrown over him, but he was fully dressed. He examined his clothing with interest—gray tunic, gray leather spacer's boots. It was unfamiliar.

He shook his head in further confusion, and the motion burst within his skull, throbbing hotly. He closed his eyes until it subsided, trying to force his brain to operate, to explain to him where and what he was.

He looked at the man named Dixon.

"Nobody seems to believe me," he said, "but I really don't know what's going on. Things are moving too fast for me. Really, I—why, I don't even know my own name! My head—it hurts. I can't think clearly."

Dixon straightened, turned a darkly-suspicious look on Silva. "Don't play tricks on me," he said savagely. "I haven't time for them. I won't mince words with you. Give me a release on the cargo now, before I have to get rough. This is a lot more important to me than your life is."

"Go to hell," Silva said shortly. "I'm playing no tricks."

There was an instant's doubt in Dixon's eyes, then it flashed away. He bent closer, peered at Silva. "I almost think—" he began.

Then he shook his head. "No," he said. "You're lying all right. You killed Willis to get her share—and now you're trying to hold me up. That's your last chance that just went by, Silva. From now on, I'm running this show!"

He spun around and strode to the door, thrust it open. "Hawkins!" he bellowed. "Green!"

Two large, ugly men in field-gray uniforms, emblazoned with the crossed-hammers insignia of Titan Station's Security Force, came in, looking to Dixon for instructions.

"Silva here is resisting arrest," Dixon said. "Take him along. We'll fix up the charges later."

"You can't do that," Silva said wearily. "I'm sick. If you've got something against me, save it. Wait till my head clears. I'm sure I can explain—"

"Explain, hell." The dark man laughed. "If I wait, this ship will be blasting off for Europa within two hours. I'll wait—but so will the ship. It's not going anywhere till I give it clearance. I run Titan Station; I'll give the orders here!"

II

Whoever this man Dixon was, thought Silva, he was certainly a man of importance on Titan Station. As he had said, he gave the orders.

The crew of the rocket made no objection when Dixon and his men took Silva off without a word. Silva had thought the medic, who seemed a good enough sort, might have said something on his behalf. But he was out of sight as they left. A curt sentence to a gray-clad official on the landing pad where the rocket lay, and the man nodded and hurried off, to tell the rocket's captain that the ship was being refused clearance indefinitely.

A long, powerful ground vehicle slid up before them. Dixon got in front, while the two uniformed men shoved Silva into the back of the vehicle, climbed in beside him. Dixon gave a curt order, and the vehicle shot forward.

The driver, sitting beside Dixon, leaned forward and reached a hand under the dashboard. The high wail of a siren came instantly from the vehicle's roof, and what traffic was on the broad, straight highway into which they had turned pulled aside to let them race through.

Ahead lay the tall spires of a city. Graceful, hundreds of feet high, they seemed dreamlike yet somehow oddly familiar to Silva. Somewhere he had seen them before. He dragged deep into his mind, plumbing the cloudy, impenetrable haze that had settled on it, trying to bring forth the memories that he should have had. Amnesia, they called it; complete forgetting of the happenings of a lifetime. He'd heard of it—but never dreamed it could happen to him!

My name, it seems, is Thomas Silva, he thought. And they tell me that I killed a woman!

The thought was starkly incredible to him. A silver-haired woman, it had been; someone named Willis. He tried to remember.

Yes, there had been a silver-haired woman. And there had been an argument. Something to do with money, with a shipment of goods that Willis had supplied to Silva. There had even been talk of killing....

But—murder! Silva looked at his hands helplessly.

Dixon, up ahead, was turning around. He looked sharply at Silva, for a long second. An uncertainty clouded his eyes, and abruptly he looked forward again without speaking.

"Who's this man Dixon?" Silva whispered to the nearest guard.

The man stared at him. "Administrator Dixon," he said, "is the Council's deputy on Titan Station. You know—the Earth-Mars Council. They put Administrator Dixon here to—well, to administer for them."

"Council?" Silva asked, wrinkling his brow. He had heard something about a Council once, yes. But it was all so nebulous....

The other guard stirred, leaned over. "Shut up," he said heavily. "You'll have plenty of chance for talking later."

But the chance was a long time in coming. Silva found himself, an hour later, still in the barred room into which he'd been thrust. The guards had brought him there, at Dixon's order, and left him. That had been all.

This was not a regular jail, Silva realized. It was more like a governmental complex, something reflecting the architectural design principles of Earth's brutalist period, all concrete and angular lines. Silva wished for human companionship—particularly that of the medic. Of all the people he'd met since awakening in that hospital bed, only he seemed warm and human. The others were—brutal, deadly. It was too bad, Silva reflected, that he'd failed to remember him. He'd seemed hurt, and he had certainly known him by first name. But perhaps he would understand.

Silva sat down on a lumpy, sagging bed and buried his head in his hands. Dim ghosts of memory were wandering in his mind. He tried to conjure them into stronger relief, or to exorcise them entirely.

Somewhere, some time, a woman had said to him, "Dixon is secretly arming the Titan Station dissidents for revolt against the Council. He wants personal power—he's prepared to pay any price for it. He needs weapons, Earth weapons smuggled in through the Council patrol. If he can wipe out the Security Force garrison—those who are loyal to the Council, still, instead of to Dixon—he can sit back and laugh at any fleet Earth and Mars can send. Transports are clumsy in an atmosphere. They're helpless. And if he can arm enough of Titan Station's malcontents, he can't be stopped. That's why he'll pay for plasma rifles with their weight in platinum."

Silva could remember the scene clearly. Could almost see the sharp, aquiline face of the woman who had spoken to him. But there memory stopped.

A fugitive recollection raced through his mind. He halted it, dragged it back, pinned it down....

They had stopped in Queenstown Region, the spaceport on the outer rim of the Glendale colony in Aldoria, as if the settlement knows shame and wants to hide the rough and roaring dome city that nestles in one of the great craters. Silva remembered sitting in a low-ceilinged, smoke-heavy room, across the table from a tall woman with silver hair. Willis!

"Six thousand plasma rifles," the woman had said. "Latest government issue. Never mind how I got them; they're perfect. You know my price. Take it or leave it. And it's payable the minute we touch ground on Titan Station."

There had been a few minutes of haggling over terms, then a handshake and a drink from a thin-necked flagon of pale-yellow liquid fire.

He and the silver-haired woman had gone out then, made their way by unfrequented side streets to a great windowless building. Silva remembered the white-hot stars overhead, shining piercingly through the great transparent dome that kept the air in the sealed city of Queenstown Region, as they stood at the entrance of the warehouse and spoke in low tones to the man who answered their summons.

Then, inside. And they were looking at a huge chamber full of stacked fiber boxes—containing nothing but dehydrated agricultural products and mining tools, by the stencils they bore. Silva had turned to the silver-haired woman with a puzzled question—and the woman had laughed aloud.

She dragged one of the boxes down, ripped it open with the sharp point of a handling hook. Short-barreled, flare-mouthed guns rolled out, tumbling over the floor. Ten of them were in that one box, and hundreds of boxes all about. Silva picked one up, broke it, peered into the chamber where the tiny capsule of U-235 would explode with infinite violence when the trigger was pulled, spraying radiant death four thousand yards in the direction the gun was aimed....

And that memory ended.

Silva got up, stared at his haggard face in the cracked mirror over the bed. "They say I'm a killer," he thought. "Apparently I'm a gun-runner as well. Good lord—what am I not?"

His reflection—white, drawn face made all the more pallid by the dark hair that fell over it—stared back at him. There was no answer there. If only he could remember—

"All right, Silva." The deep voice of a guard came to him as the door swung open. "Stop making eyes at yourself."

Silva looked around. The guard beckoned. "Administrator Dixon wants to speak to you—now. Let's not keep the administrator waiting."

A long, narrow room, with a long carpet leading from the entrance up to a great heavy desk—that was Dixon's office. Silva felt a click in his memory as he entered. This was a deliberate application of political philosophy and systems thinking to urban planning—one of the ancient Earth dictators had employed just such a psychological trick to overawe those who came to beg favors of him. Mussolini, or some such name.

The trick failed to work. Silva had other things on his mind; he walked the forty-foot length of the room, designed to imbue him with a sense of his own unimportance, as steadily as he'd ever walked in the open air of his home planet.

Whichever planet that was.

The guard had remained just inside the door, at attention. Dixon waved him out.

"Here I am," said Silva. "What do you want?"

Dixon said, "I've had the ship inspected and what I want is on it. That saves your life, for now. But the cargo is in your name. I could take it by force, if I had to. I prefer not to." He picked up a paper, handed it to Silva. "In spite of your behavior, you can keep alive. You can even collect the money for the guns—Willis' share as well as your own. This is a release form, authorizing my men to take six hundred and thirty cases of dehydrated foods and drilling supplies from the hold of the Meridian—the ship you came on. Sign it, and we'll forget our argument. Only, sign it now and get it over with. I'm losing patience, Silva."

Silva said, without expression, "No."

Dark red flooded into Dixon's sallow face. His jaws bunched angrily and there was a ragged thread of incomplete control to his voice as he spoke.

"I'll have your neck for this, Silva," he said softly.

Silva looked at the man's eyes. Death was behind them, peeping out. Mentally he shrugged. What difference did it make?

"Give me the pen," he said shortly.

Dixon exhaled a deep breath. You could see the tension leave him, the mottled anger fade from his face and leave it without expression. He handed the paper to Silva without a word. He gave him a pen, watched him scrawl his name.

"That," he said, "is better." He paused a moment ruminatively. "It would have been better still if you'd not stalled me so long. I find that hard to forgive in my associates."

"The money," Thomas said. If he were playing a part—pretending he knew what he was doing—he might as well play it to the hilt. "When do I get it?"

Dixon picked up the paper and looked carefully at the signature. He creased it thoughtfully, stowed it in a pocket before answering.

"Naturally," he said, "there will have to be a revision of terms. I offered a hundred and sixty-five thousand Earth-credits. I would have paid it—but you made me angry. You'll have to pay for that."

Silva said, "I've paid already. I've been dragged from pillar to post by you. That's enough. Pay me what you owe me, if you want any more of the same goods!"

That was a shot in the dark—and it missed the mark.

Dixon's eyes widened. "You amaze me, Silva," he said. He rose and stepped around the desk, confronting Silva. "I almost think you really have lost your memory, Silva," he said. "Otherwise, surely you would know that this is all the rifles I need. With them I'll take whatever else I want!"

Silva said, "You're ready, then...."

He took time to think it over, but he knew that no thought was required. Already the hands that he had locked behind him were clenched, taut. Already the muscles of his legs were tensing.

"You're ready," he repeated. "You've armed the Titan Station dissidents—the worst elements on nine planets. You're set to betray the Council that gave you power here.... Well, that changes things. I can't let you do it!"

He hurled himself at Dixon, hands sweeping around to grapple for the dark man's throat. Dixon, off-balance, staggered backward. But his own hands were diving for the twin heat guns that hung at his waist.

Silva saw his danger, and reacted. His foot twisted around Dixon's ankle; his hands at the other's throat gripped tighter. He lunged forward, slamming the hard top of his head into the other's face, feeling flesh and cartilage give as Dixon's nose mashed flat. His own head pin-wheeled dizzily, agonizingly, as the jar revived the pain of his earlier accident.

But Dixon, unconscious already, tumbled back with Silva on top of him. His head made an audible, spine-chilling thud as it hit the carpeted floor.

Silva got up, retrieving the two heat guns, and stared at him.

"They tell me I killed Willis the same way," he thought. "I'm getting in a rut!"

But Dixon was not dead, though he was out as cold as the void beyond Pluto. The thick carpeting had saved him from a broken head.

Silva stepped over the unconscious man and looked around the room. It was furnished severely, to the point of barrenness. Two chairs before Dixon's ornate, bare-topped desk and one luxurious chair behind it; a tasseled bell cord within easy reach of Dixon's chair; the long carpet. That was all it contained.

The problem of getting out was serious, he saw. How could one—

III

Methodically he ransacked the drawers of Dixon's desk. Papers, a whole arsenal of hand guns, Titan Station currency by the bale, ominously black-covered notebooks with cryptic figures littering their pages—those were the contents. A coldly impersonal desk, without the familiar trivia most men accumulate. There was nothing, certainly, that would get him out of a building that so closely resembled a fortress.

He tumbled the things back into the drawers helter-skelter, turned Dixon over and searched his pockets. More money—the man must have had a fortune within reach at all times—and a few meaningless papers. Silva took the release he had signed and tore it to shreds. But that was only a gesture. When Dixon came to, unless Silva had managed to get away and accomplish something, the mere lack of written permission would not keep him from the rocket's lethal cargo!

When Dixon came to....

An idea bloomed in Silva's brain. He looked, then, at unconscious Dixon—and the idea withered again.

He had thought of forcing Dixon himself to front for him, at gun's point, in the conventional manner of escaping prisoners. But fist fights, fiction to the contrary notwithstanding, leave marks on the men who lose them. Dixon's throat was speckled with the livid marks of Silva's fingers; Silva's head, butting Dixon in the face, had drawn a thick stream of crimson from his nostrils, turned his sharp nose askew.

No guard of Dixon's would have been deceived for an instant, looking at that face—even assuming that Dixon could have been forced to cooperate by the threat of a gun. Which, considering the stake Dixon had in this play, was doubtful....

He stood up and looked around. He had to act quickly. Already Dixon's breath was audible; he saw the man grimace and an arm flopped spasmodically on the floor. Consciousness was on its way back.

Silva touched the heat gun he'd thrust into his belt; drew it and held it poised, while he sought to discover what was in his own mind. He'd killed a woman already, they said. Was he then a killer—could he shoot Dixon now, in cold blood, with so much to gain and nothing to lose?

This was ethical decision-making at its most stark. The question of social justice weighed on him—Dixon was planning to arm dissidents who would overthrow legitimate authority, plunging Titan Station into chaos. Yet Silva found himself unable to pull the trigger on an unconscious man.

He stood there a moment. Then, abruptly, he reversed the weapon and chopped it down on Dixon's skull.

There was a sharp grunt from the still unconscious man, but no other sign. Only—the first tremors of movement that had shown on him halted, and did not reappear.

"No," Silva thought. "Whatever they say, I'm not a killer!"

But still he had to get out. How?

Once more he stared around the room, catalogued its contents. The guard would be getting impatient. Perhaps any minute he would tap the door, first timorously, then with heavier strokes.

The guard! There was a way!

Silva eyed the length of the room. Forty feet—it would take him a couple of seconds to run it at full speed. Was that fast enough?

There was only one way to find out.

He walked around the desk to the bell cord. He took a deep breath, tugged it savagely, and at once was in speedy motion, racing toward the door, his footsteps muffled in the deep, springy carpet. Almost as he reached it, he saw it begin to open. He quickly sidestepped and was out of the guard's sight, behind the door, as the man looked in.

Quick suspicion flared in his eyes, then certainty as he saw Dixon huddled on the floor. He opened his mouth to cry out—

But Silva's arm was around his throat, and he had no breath to spare. Silva's foot lashed out and the door slammed shut; Silva's balled left fist came up and connected with the guard's chin. Abruptly the man slumped.

Silva took a deep breath and let the man drop to the floor. But he paused only a second; now he had two unconscious men on his hands and he dared let neither revive until he was prepared.

He grasped the guard's arm and dragged him roughly the length of the room. He leaped on top of the desk, brutally scarring its gleaming top with the hard spikes of his boots. His agile fingers unfastened the long bell cord without causing it to ring and, bearing it, he dropped again to the floor.

Tugging and straining, he got the limp form of Dixon into his own chair, bound him with the bell cord, gagged him with the priceless Venusian-silk scarf Dixon wore knotted about his throat. He tested his bindings with full strength, and smiled. Those would hold, let Dixon struggle as he would.

The guard he stripped of clothing, bound and gagged with his own belt and spacer's kerchief. He dragged him around behind the desk, thrust him under it out of sight. Dixon's chair he turned so that the unconscious face was averted from the door. Should anyone look in, then, the fact of Dixon's unconsciousness might not be noticed.

Then he took off his own clothes, quickly assumed the field-gray uniform of the guard. It fit like the skin of a fruit. He felt himself bulging out of it in a dozen places. The long cape the guard wore would conceal that, perhaps. In any case, there was nothing better.

Trying to make his stride as martial as possible, he walked down the long carpet to the door, opened it and stepped outside.

The corridor beyond was empty, stretching in both directions with the cold efficiency of bureaucratic architecture. Silva's heart pounded as he moved forward, trying to look purposeful, trying to remember which way they had brought him in. His mind, still clouded by amnesia, offered no help.

He chose left, walking with measured steps. Two other guards passed him, nodded curtly, continued on. He forced himself not to look back, not to betray his nervousness.

At the end of the corridor, a lift. He stepped inside, studied the panel. Twenty floors, and he was on the eighteenth. He pressed the button for the ground level and felt the lift descend smoothly.

When the doors opened, he stepped out into a vast lobby. People in civilian clothes moved about, conducting business. More guards stood at various posts. And there, across the expanse of polished floor, were the main doors leading outside.

Silva walked toward them, every nerve screaming at him to run. But he maintained his pace, kept his face impassive. A guard at the door nodded to him as he approached.

"Shift change already?" the guard asked.

Silva grunted noncommittally and kept walking. The guard shrugged and let him pass.

Outside, the artificial atmosphere of Titan Station pressed around him, the great dome overhead showing the swirling orange clouds of Saturn beyond. He was free—for now.

But free to do what? He still didn't know who he really was, what side he was truly on. The weapons were still on that ship, waiting to fuel a revolution that might be just or might be catastrophic. And somewhere in his locked memory was the key to everything.

Silva looked up at the dome, at Saturn's vast presence beyond, and wondered what he would do next. The only thing he knew for certain was that he had to find out the truth—about himself, about Dixon, about everything.

And he had to do it before those weapons were unloaded and Titan Station exploded into violence.
