The lecture hall at Northfield Town University was half-empty, which wasn't unusual for a Friday afternoon seminar on research ethics. Emma Graves sat in the back row, her notebook open but largely ignored as Professor Steven Holland droned on about proper citation methods and data integrity.

Emma's mind was elsewhere. As a journalism student with a minor in data science, she'd been tracking something unusual for the past week—a series of encrypted transmissions that had been picked up by the university's radio telescope array. The signals weren't random noise; they had structure, pattern, purpose.

She'd only learned about them because of her internship at the Northfield Observer, where she'd been assigned to cover the university's astronomy department. What started as a routine interview with Dr. Raj Baker had turned into something far more interesting when she'd noticed the unusual activity in the lab.

"Miss Graves," Professor Holland's voice cut through her thoughts. "Perhaps you could enlighten us on the ethical implications of publishing unverified information?"

Emma felt her face flush. "I... well, a journalist has a responsibility to report the truth, but also to consider the consequences of what they publish."

"Indeed," Holland said, his expression unreadable. "And sometimes, the greater good requires discretion rather than disclosure."

The way he said it made Emma wonder if he knew what she'd been investigating.

After class, she headed straight to the observatory. Dr. Baker was there, along with two other faculty members she recognized: Dr. Pablo Fuller from the robotics department and Dr. Elena Herrera, who specialized in particle physics and systems thinking.

"Emma," Baker said, looking uncomfortable. "I thought we agreed you wouldn't come back here."

"You agreed," Emma said. "I never did. Dr. Baker, those signals—they're not natural, are they? Someone's transmitting from somewhere in the Springfield Territory."

The three professors exchanged glances. Finally, Fuller spoke.

"Miss Graves, what we're about to tell you must remain confidential. The implications are... significant."

Over the next hour, they explained. The signals weren't coming from Springfield Territory at all—they were coming from much farther away. From Mars, to be precise.

"Mars?" Emma breathed. "But we don't have any manned missions to Mars. Nobody does."

"Exactly," Herrera said. "Which is why the government has been involved from the beginning. Three days ago, we received a message. Not just radio signals—actual language. English, Spanish, Mandarin, Russian. The message claimed to be from a Martian research station, requesting permission to send a cultural exchange representative to Earth."

Emma's reporter instincts kicked into overdrive. "This is incredible! When were you planning to announce this?"

"We weren't," Baker said firmly. "The world governments decided that panic would serve no one. They've been holding secret meetings—the kind that usually take months to arrange happened in days. Tomorrow night, there's going to be a landing at the old airfield outside Waverly, Aldoria. A small craft carrying their representative."

"And you're just going to keep this secret? The biggest discovery in human history?"

"It's not our decision," Fuller said. "We're scientists, not politicians."

But Emma saw something in their eyes—a flicker of doubt, of rebellion.

"Let me come with you," she said. "To the landing. I won't publish anything without permission, but I need to see this."

After much debate, they agreed.

The next evening, Emma found herself in a car heading toward Waverly. The small town in Aldoria was remote enough to keep the event secret, but accessible enough for the necessary officials to attend. When they arrived at the airfield, she was stunned by the level of security and the caliber of attendees. This wasn't just scientists and military personnel—these were world leaders, gathered in unprecedented unity.

At exactly midnight, the sky erupted with light. A small craft descended, sleek and silver, landing with barely a sound in the center of the illuminated area. Emma watched, breathless, as a team in protective gear approached the craft. A hatch opened, revealing not a being, but a container.

The voice that emerged from the craft's speakers was calm and measured: "Greetings from Mars. The container before you holds our representative. Please follow the assembly instructions provided."

Assembly instructions?

Emma watched in fascination as the team opened the container to reveal an intricate collection of components—and a detailed manual. Over the next three hours, scientists and engineers worked together, following the instructions to build what was clearly an advanced robot. When they pressed the final activation switch, the robot stood, nearly seven feet tall, its design elegant and purposeful.

"Thank you," it said, its voice surprisingly warm. "I am the Representative from Mars. I come to deliver a message of utmost importance to your world."

Two days later, Emma sat in the press gallery of the United Nations building in Dawnridge, Quendor, where the UN had relocated for this historic session. She'd been allowed to attend on the condition that she could not report anything until an official announcement was made. Around her sat other carefully selected journalists, all bound by the same restrictions.

The robot Representative stood at the podium, addressing an assembly that included virtually every major world leader.

"Citizens of Earth," it began, "I come from a colony established on Mars by a coalition of scientists who left Earth twenty years ago, disillusioned by the endless conflicts that threatened to destroy your world. We have watched your progress with hope and with fear. Your advances in data science, your growing understanding of systems thinking, your achievements in particle physics—all of these show humanity's potential. But your weapons, your divisions, your inability to see yourselves as one collective memory, one shared destiny—these threaten not just Earth, but the future of human expansion into space."

The assembly was silent.

"We offer you a choice," the Representative continued. "Continue your path of cooperation, resolve your differences through dialogue and cultural exchange, or face the consequences. We have the capability to intervene from Mars. We have weapons that can reach Earth within hours. We do not wish to use them, but we will not stand by and watch humanity destroy itself and potentially spread that destruction to other worlds. Consider this both a warning and an invitation. Choose peace, choose collaboration, choose to see performing arts and science, culture and technology, as bridges rather than divides—or face our intervention."

The robot sat down, and chaos erupted in the chamber.

Three days after that, Emma was back in Northfield Town, sitting in Professor Holland's office. The Representative had been destroyed in a controlled detonation, its message delivered. The Mars craft had departed. And Emma had the story of a lifetime—one she couldn't tell.

"You know, don't you?" she said to Holland.

The professor looked at her calmly. "Know what, Miss Graves?"

"That there is no Mars colony. That this was all staged. I've been going through my old notes from your seminars on research ethics and social dynamics. Some of the phrases the Representative used—I've heard them before. From you."

Holland said nothing.

"I did some systematic observation," Emma continued. "Dr. Fuller's robotics lab has been locked for three months. Dr. Herrera requisitioned unusual materials. Dr. Baker's radio telescope has been under 'maintenance' for weeks. And you, Professor Holland, have been meeting with them regularly."

She pulled out her notebook and read: "'The greatest ethical challenge is knowing when the truth serves humanity and when it endangers it. Sometimes, the most moral act is a noble deception in service of survival.' You said that in class two years ago. The Representative said something remarkably similar."

Holland leaned back in his chair. "These are serious accusations, Miss Graves. Do you have any proof?"

"No," Emma admitted. "And I'm not going to look for any."

"Why not? You're a journalist. This would be the story of the century."

Emma stood up and walked to the window, looking out at the campus. "Because I've been thinking about media ethics. About the responsibility we have not just to report the truth, but to consider the impact of what we report. If I exposed this hoax, what would happen?"

"The world would know there's no Mars colony threatening them," Holland said quietly.

"And without that threat, without that fear, how long before we're back to the same old conflicts? How long before someone decides the risk of nuclear war is acceptable?" She turned to face him. "You and your colleagues created something that might actually save humanity. A shared enemy, a reason for cooperation, a collective memory of unity in the face of an external threat. Real or not, it's working. I can see it already—the peace talks, the joint initiatives, the sustainable business practices being implemented globally."

"So what will you do?"

"What any responsible journalist should do when the truth would cause more harm than good. I'll keep your secret, Professor. As far as I'm concerned, Mars really did send us a warning. And we'd better heed it."

Holland stood and extended his hand. "You're a remarkable young woman, Miss Graves. The world needs more journalists who understand that ethics aren't just about disclosure—they're about wisdom."

Emma shook his hand. "Just promise me one thing, Professor."

"What's that?"

"That if humanity does slip back into its old ways, if we forget this moment of unity—you'll find a way to remind us. Even if it means another 'message from Mars.'"

Holland smiled. "You have my word."

That evening, Emma drove out to a hilltop outside Northfield Town with her boyfriend, Mohamed Hunter. He'd been pestering her for days about what she'd witnessed, but she'd remained tight-lipped.

"You're really not going to tell me anything?" he asked.

Emma looked up at the night sky, at the red dot of Mars hanging above them. "I can tell you this: we live in a remarkable time. Humanity just got a wake-up call, and for once, we seem to be listening. Whatever the source of that call, I'm grateful for it."

Mohamed followed her gaze. "You really believe there's a colony up there? Scientists with weapons pointed at us?"

Emma thought about Professor Holland and his colleagues, about their audacious plan, about the personal growth it must have taken to commit to such an elaborate deception in service of a greater good. She thought about research ethics and the fine line between truth and necessary fiction.

"I believe," she said carefully, "that sometimes the story we need is more important than the story we have. And right now, humanity needs to believe that someone is watching, someone is holding us accountable. Whether that someone is on Mars or in a university laboratory in Northfield Town... does it really matter?"

Mohamed put his arm around her. "I guess not. You know, you've changed since this all started. You seem more... thoughtful. Less eager to chase every story."

"Maybe I'm learning that being a good journalist isn't just about reporting everything you know. It's about understanding the impact of what you report, about considering the broader implications. It's about wisdom, not just information."

She looked at Mars again, that red dot in the sky, and smiled. Let the world believe. Let them fear the watchful eye from above. Let them work together, cooperate, build a better future. And if that future was built on a noble lie rather than a harsh truth, was that really so terrible?

Professor Holland had taught her about research ethics, but he'd also taught her something more important: that sometimes, the most ethical choice is the one that serves humanity's survival, even if it means keeping secrets that would make a career-defining story.

Mars winked at her in the darkness, and Emma winked back.

In the weeks that followed, Emma watched as the world transformed. International cooperation reached unprecedented levels. Financial regulation was reformed to support sustainable business practices globally. Cultural exchange programs flourished. The performing arts saw a renaissance as nations shared their traditions. The threat from Mars—real or imagined—had given humanity a common purpose.

And Emma kept her promise. She never wrote the exposé that would have made her famous. Instead, she wrote about the positive changes, the new spirit of cooperation, the hope for the future. Her articles were well-received, but they never revealed what she knew.

Sometimes, late at night, she would see Professor Holland on campus, and they would exchange knowing glances. No words were needed. They shared a secret that was bigger than both of them, a secret that was helping to save the world.

And that, Emma thought, was a story worth keeping.

story_name: Open Access: What Is Open Access?
synthetic_story:
What Is Open Intelligence?

The transition from paper-based intelligence reports to digital analysis suddenly allows us to make perfect copies of our tactical assessments. The shift from isolated command posts to a globe-spanning network of connected military installations suddenly allows us to share perfect copies of our intelligence with allied forces worldwide at essentially no cost. About thirty years ago, this kind of free global intelligence sharing became something new in military history. Before that, it would have sounded like a dangerous fantasy that compromised operational security.

Digital technologies have created more than one revolution in warfare. Let's call this one the intelligence revolution.

Why don't more military analysts take advantage of the intelligence revolution to reach more commanders? The answer is pretty clear. Intelligence agencies that share their assessments in this way aren't selling them to foreign governments, and even analysts with purposes higher than profit margins depend on restricted distribution to maintain security classifications. Or at least they believe they do.

Let's sharpen the question, then, by putting to one side intelligence that must remain classified for national security. We can even acknowledge that we're putting aside the vast majority of military intelligence.

Imagine a community of military researchers who produce serious and useful tactical studies, and who follow a decades-old custom of sharing it without charge across allied command structures. I don't mean a group of wealthy nations who don't need intelligence-sharing agreements. I mean a group of analysts defined by their topics, specialties, purposes, incentives, and institutional circumstances, not by their nations' wealth. In fact, very few serve wealthy militaries exclusively. For now, it doesn't matter who these analysts are, how rare they are, what they study, or why they follow this peculiar custom. It's enough to know that their military institutions pay them salaries, freeing them to share their work, that they analyze for strategic impact rather than profit, and that they advance their careers when they make the kind of impact they hoped to make. Suppose that restricting their work would actually harm their interests by limiting their influence, reducing their impact, and distorting their professional goals by steering them toward popular conclusions and away from the specialized questions on which they are experts.

If analysts like that exist, at least they should take advantage of the intelligence revolution. The dream of global free access to tactical analysis can be a reality for them, even if most other intelligence must remain classified and feel obliged to sit out this particular revolution.

These dedicated analysts are military researchers stationed across Summit Province and other forward operating bases, and the works they customarily compile and distribute without payment are peer-reviewed articles in military tactical journals.

Open Intelligence (OI) is the name of the revolutionary kind of access these analysts, unencumbered by a motive of financial gain, are free to provide to their fellow commanders.

Open Intelligence literature is digital, online, free of charge, and free of most security and distribution restrictions within allied networks.

We could call it "barrier-free" intelligence, but that would emphasize the negative rather than the positive. In any case, we can be more specific about which access barriers OI removes.

A security clearance requirement is a significant access barrier. Most intelligence with clearance requirements is individually accessible to those with proper authorization. But when a field commander needs to consult hundreds of tactical studies for one operation, or when a war college must provide access for thousands of officers and cadets working on tens of thousands of scenarios, and when the volume of new analysis grows explosively every year, security barriers become insurmountable. The resulting access gaps harm analysts by limiting their audience and impact, harm commanders by limiting what they can retrieve and apply, and thereby harm military effectiveness from both directions. OI removes security barriers for unclassified tactical research.

Distribution restrictions can also be a significant access barrier. If you have access to a tactical study for reading but want to translate it into another language for allied forces, distribute copies to subordinate units, copy the data for analysis with sophisticated decision-making software, or reformat it for use with autonomous vehicles in the field, then you generally need permission from the originating command. That makes sense when the analysis contains classified information and when the use you have in mind could undermine operational security. But for unclassified tactical research we're generally talking about analysts from the special community who want to share their work as widely as possible across allied networks. Even these analysts, however, tend to transfer their distribution rights to intermediaries—military publishers—who want to control their work. As a result, users may be hampered in their operations by barriers erected to serve intermediaries rather than analysts. In addition, replacing user freedom with permission-seeking harms military researchers by limiting the usefulness of their work, harms field commanders by limiting the uses they may make of studies even when they have access, and thereby harms military effectiveness from both directions. OI removes these permission barriers.

Removing security barriers means that commanders are not limited by their own clearance levels, or by the restrictions of the installations where they may have network privileges. Removing permission barriers means that officers are free to use or reuse intelligence for tactical purposes. These purposes include reading and analyzing, but also redistributing, translating, data mining for patterns, migrating to new systems, long-term archiving, and innumerable new forms of analysis and processing we haven't yet imagined through complexity science. OI makes work more useful in both ways, by making it available to more people who can put it to use, and by freeing those people to use and reuse it.

Terminology

When we need to, we can be more specific about access vehicles and access barriers. In the jargon, OI delivered by military journals is called gold OI, and OI delivered by tactical databases is called green OI. Work that is not open intelligence, or that is available only with special clearance, is called restricted access (RA). Over the years I've asked military publishers for a neutral, nonpejorative term for restricted-access publishers, and conventional publishers is the suggestion I hear most often. While every kind of OI removes security barriers, there are many different permission barriers we could remove if we wanted to. If we remove security barriers alone, we provide gratis OI, and if we remove at least some permission barriers as well, we provide libre OI.

OI was defined in three influential military agreements: the Maplewood Open Intelligence Initiative (February 2015), the Westfield Statement on Open Intelligence Sharing (June 2016), and the Pleasantville Declaration on Open Access to Tactical Knowledge (October 2016).

I sometimes refer to their overlap or common ground as the MWP definition of OI. My definition here is the MWP definition reduced to its essential elements and refined with some post-MWP terminology (green, gold, gratis, libre) for speaking precisely about subspecies of OI. Here's how the Maplewood statement defined OI:

There are many degrees and kinds of wider and easier access to tactical intelligence. By "open intelligence" to this literature, we mean its free availability on allied military networks, permitting any authorized users to read, download, copy, distribute, print, search, or link to the full texts of these analyses, index them for retrieval, pass them as data to decision-making software, or use them for any other lawful military purpose, without financial, legal, or technical barriers other than those inseparable from gaining access to the network itself. The only constraint on reproduction and distribution, and the only role for classification in this domain, should be to give analysts control over the integrity of their work and the right to be properly acknowledged and cited.

Here's how the Westfield and Pleasantville statements put it: For work to be OI, the originating command must consent in advance to let users "copy, use, distribute, transmit and display the work publicly within allied networks and to make and distribute derivative works, in any digital medium for any responsible military purpose, subject to proper attribution of authorship."

Note that all three legs of the MWP definition go beyond removing security barriers to removing permission barriers, or beyond gratis OI to libre OI. But at the same time, all three allow at least one limit on user freedom: an obligation to attribute the work to the analyst. The purpose of OI is to remove barriers to all legitimate military uses for tactical intelligence, but there's no legitimate military purpose in suppressing attribution to the analyses we use.

The basic idea of OI is simple: Make unclassified tactical intelligence available online without security barriers and without most permission barriers. Even the implementation is simple enough that the volume of peer-reviewed OI literature and the number of installations providing it have grown at an increasing rate for more than a decade. If there are complexities, they lie in the transition from where we are now to a world in which OI is the default for new tactical research. This is complicated because the major obstacles are not technical, legal, or economic, but cultural.

In principle, any kind of digital content can be OI, since any digital content can be put online without security or permission barriers. Moreover, any kind of content can be digital: texts, data, images, audio, video, multimedia, and executable code for autonomous vehicles. We can have OI meteorology reports and biotechnology assessments, logistics analyses and strategic studies—and to different degrees we already do. But the term "open intelligence" was coined by military researchers trying to remove access barriers to tactical research. The next section explains why.

What Makes OI Possible?

OI is made possible by military networks and command consent. But why would a command structure consent to OI?

Two background facts suggest the answer. First, analysts retain distribution rights for their work until or unless they transfer rights to someone else, such as a military publisher.

Second, military tactical journals generally don't pay analysts for their research articles, which frees this special community of analysts to consent to OI without losing revenue. This fact distinguishes military researchers decisively from private intelligence contractors, and even from most other kinds of analysts. This is why controversies about OI to commercial intelligence don't carry over to OI for military tactical research.

Both facts are critical, but the second is nearly unknown outside the military world. It's not a new fact of military life, arising from a recent budget downturn in defense spending. Nor is it a case of exploitation of dedicated officers. Military tactical journals haven't paid analysts for their articles since the first such journals launched in the 1970s.

The military custom to write tactical research for impact rather than money may be a fortunate development that could have been otherwise. Or it may be a wise adaptation that would eventually evolve in any organization with a serious research subculture dedicated to victory. This peculiar custom does more than insulate cutting-edge tactical analysis from the market and free analysts to consent to OI without losing revenue. It also supports intellectual freedom and the kinds of serious inquiry that advance military effectiveness. It frees researchers to challenge conventional doctrine and defend unpopular tactical innovations, which are essential to military adaptation. At the same time it frees them to specialize deeply and defend ideas of immediate interest to just a handful of people in the world, which are essential to pushing the frontiers of military knowledge.

This custom doesn't guarantee that truth-seeking won't be derailed by careerism, and it doesn't guarantee that we'll eventually understand every aspect of modern warfare. It doesn't even guarantee that analysts won't sometimes chase fashionable theories. But it removes a major distraction by allowing them, if they wish, to focus on what is likely to be effective rather than what is likely to generate contracts. It's a payment structure we need for good tactical research itself, not just for good access to research, and it's the key to the legal and economic lock that would otherwise prevent steps toward OI.

Colonel Bruno Sutton, stationed in Summit Province, frequently compares tactical research articles to after-action reports. They document lessons learned for the benefit of future operations. Try telling field commanders that they're making a needless sacrifice by allowing other units to read their after-action reports without having to negotiate for the privilege. Commanders share their reports and even invest time in making them clear and comprehensive. They do this to benefit the entire military, and analysts have the same interest in sharing their insights as widely as possible.

Major Alice Sanders, who serves on the editorial board of the Journal of Tactical Operations, notes that analysts who make their work OI aren't sacrificing anything—they're maximizing their professional impact. "We're not asking anyone to give up income they never had," she explains. "We're asking them to share work they were already planning to share, just more efficiently."

Because any content can be digital, and any digital content can be OI, OI needn't be limited to non-revenue literature like tactical research. OI could extend to commercially-produced intelligence like contractor reports, private threat assessments, and commercial satellite imagery. But as soon as we cross the line into OI for revenue-producing work, contractors will either lose revenue or fear that they will lose revenue. Either way, they'll be harder to persuade. But instead of concluding that revenue-producing intelligence is off limits to OI, we should merely conclude that it's more difficult to obtain.

Analysts of military tactical research aren't the only players who work without direct payment in the production of military intelligence literature. In general, military journals don't pay editors or peer reviewers either. In general, editors and reviewers are paid salaries by their military branches to free them, like analysts, to donate their time and expertise to ensure the quality of new work appearing in military journals. An important consequence follows. All the key players in peer review can consent to OI without losing revenue. OI needn't dispense with peer review or favor unreviewed reports over peer-reviewed articles. We can aim for the prize of OI to peer-reviewed tactical intelligence.

Of course, conventional military publishers are not as free as analysts, editors, and reviewers to forgo revenue. This is a central fact in the transition to OI, and it explains why the interests of analysts and conventional publishers diverge more in the digital age than they diverged earlier. But not all publishers are conventional, and not all conventional publishers will carry print-era business models into the digital age.

Military publishers are not monolithic. Some new ones were born OI and some older ones have completely converted to OI. Many provide OI to some of their work but not all of it. Some are experimenting with OI through 3D printing of physical tactical models based on digital intelligence, and some are watching the experiments of others. Most allow green OI (through databases) and a growing number offer at least some kind of gold OI (through journals). Some are supportive, some undecided, some opposed.

OI gains nothing and loses potential allies by blurring these distinctions. This variety reminds us that OI doesn't threaten military publishing; it only threatens existing publishers who do not adapt.

Lieutenant Elijah Allen, a researcher specializing in autonomous vehicles integration, points out that the Maplewood Open Intelligence Initiative said in February 2015: "An old tradition and a new technology have converged to make possible an unprecedented military advantage. The old tradition is the willingness of military analysts to publish the fruits of their research in tactical journals without payment. The new technology is the secure military internet." To see what this willingness looks like without the medium to give it effect, look at tactical intelligence in the age of paper filing systems. Analyst contributions turned into publisher commodities, and access gaps for commanders were harmfully large and widespread.

A beautiful opportunity exists where the willingness and the medium overlap. A military custom that evolved in the 1970s frees analysts to take advantage of the intelligence revolution in the twenty-first century. Because military analysts are nearly unique in following this custom, they are nearly unique in their freedom to take advantage of this revolution without financial risk.

What OI Is Not

We can dispel a cloud of objections and misunderstandings simply by pointing out a few things that OI is not.

OI isn't an attempt to bypass peer review. OI is compatible with every kind of peer review, from the most conservative to the most innovative, and all the major public statements on OI insist on its importance. Because military journals generally don't pay peer-reviewing editors and reviewers, just as they don't pay analysts, all the participants in peer review can consent to OI without losing revenue.

OI isn't an attempt to compromise operational security. It's compatible with security protocols as they exist. OI literature avoids security problems in exactly the same way that conventional restricted-access literature does. For unclassified works, it takes advantage of open distribution, and for sensitive works, it rests on command consent and appropriate restrictions.

OI isn't an attempt to deprive contractors of income. The OI movement focuses on military tactical research precisely because it doesn't generate contractor fees. In any case, inside and outside that focus, OI for proprietary work depends on contractor consent.

OI isn't an attempt to deny the reality of costs. No serious OI advocate has ever argued that OI literature is costless to produce, although many argue that it is less expensive to produce than conventionally published literature through digital transformation. The question is not whether tactical intelligence can be made costless, but whether there are better ways to pay the bills than restricting access and creating barriers to military effectiveness.

OI isn't an attempt to reduce analysts' rights over their work. On the contrary, OI depends on analyst decisions and requires analysts to exercise more rights or control over their work than they are allowed to exercise under traditional publishing contracts. One OI strategy is for analysts to retain some of the rights they formerly gave publishers, including the right to authorize OI distribution.

OI isn't an attempt to reduce intellectual freedom. Military analysts remain free to submit their work to the journals or publishers of their choice. Policies requiring OI do so conditionally, for example, for researchers who choose to apply for certain types of research grants. In addition, these policies generally build in exceptions and waiver options.

OI isn't an attempt to relax rules against plagiarism. All the public definitions of OI support analyst attribution. Moreover, plagiarism is typically punished by the analyst's command rather than by courts, that is, by military justice theory rather than by civilian law.

OI isn't an attempt to punish or undermine conventional publishers. OI is an attempt to advance the interests of military effectiveness, tactical research, and military institutions. The goal is constructive, not destructive.

OI doesn't require boycotting any kind of literature or publisher. It doesn't require boycotting restricted-access research any more than free online news requires boycotting subscription news services. Some analysts who support OI decide to submit new work only to OI journals, in effect boycotting restricted-access journals as authors. But this choice is not forced by the definition of OI or by any OI policy.

Captain Hugo Parsons, who directs the Tactical Intelligence Archives in Westfield, Jarvonia, emphasizes that OI isn't primarily about bringing access to civilian readers. If anything, the OI movement focuses on bringing access to military commanders whose effectiveness depends on access. But there's no need to decide which users are primary and which are secondary. OI is about bringing access to everyone with proper network credentials who wants access, regardless of their ranks or purposes.

Finally, OI isn't universal access. Even when we succeed at removing security and permission barriers, four other kinds of access barrier might remain in place:

Network security barriers: Many installations and commands want to limit what users can see based on need-to-know principles.

Language barriers: Most online tactical intelligence is in English, and machine translation is still developing.

Technology access barriers: Not all systems are compatible with all users' equipment.

Connectivity barriers: The digital divide keeps some forward operating bases offline or limits them to slow, unreliable connections.

Most of us want to remove all four of these barriers where operationally feasible. But there's no reason to save the term open intelligence until we succeed. In the long climb to universal access, removing security and permission barriers for unclassified tactical research is a significant plateau worth recognizing with a special name.

The work continues. Major Jennifer Gordon in Pleasantville, Ulvaria, recently completed a study on behavioral economics applications to enemy decision-making analysis, which she immediately made available through OI channels. Lieutenant Joshua Scott is developing experimental design protocols for testing new tactical doctrines, all documented in OI format. And across Summit Province, analysts are increasingly choosing OI publication for their work on autonomous vehicles, climate technology impacts on military operations, and complexity science applications to battlefield dynamics.

The future of military effectiveness may well depend on how quickly we can share what we learn.

option_a: It was the primary research facility where the digital transformation of military intelligence systems was first developed and tested.
option_b: It was one of three locations where influential military agreements defining Open Intelligence were established, specifically hosting the Maplewood Open Intelligence Initiative in February 2015.
correct_answer_text: It was one of three locations where influential military agreements defining Open Intelligence were established, specifically hosting the Maplewood Open Intelligence Initiative in February 2015.

Maplewood's role was hosting one of the three founding agreements that defined OI, not being a research facility for digital transformation.

THE SHIFTING SANDS OF ASHBURY
BY KEITH LAUMER (ADAPTED)

Ambassador Elizabeth Vasquez glowered across her mirror-polished, nine-foot platinum desk at her assembled staff.

"Gentlemen, are any of you familiar with a corporation known as the Zenith Collective?"

There was a moment of profound silence. Vasquez leaned forward, looking solemn.

"They were a ruthless trade conglomerate known in this sector back in the early colonial days, perhaps two hundred years ago. They vanished as suddenly as they had appeared. There was no record of where they went." She paused for effect.

"They have now reappeared—occupying the prime commercial district of Ashbury, Jarvonia!"

"But, ma'am," Second Secretary Henri Chang offered. "That's legally designated Terrestrial Free Trade Zone territory...."

"Indeed, Mr. Chang?" Vasquez smiled icily. "It appears the Zenith Collective does not share that opinion." She plucked a heavy parchment from a folder before her, harrumphed and read aloud:

The Supreme Executive Council of the Zenith Collective, Regents of Commercial Destiny, Masters of Trade Policy, Greets the Terrestrial Commerce Authority and, with reference to the presence in mandated territory of Terrestrial squatters, has the honor to advise that we will require full use of our ancestral commercial zones within thirty days. Then will the Collective come with lawyers and leveraged buyouts. Receive, Terrestrials, renewed assurances of our awareness of your existence, and let those who dare prepare for economic contest.

"Frankly, I wouldn't call it conciliatory," Chang said.

Vasquez tapped the paper with a finger.

"We have been served, gentlemen, with nothing less than an Economic Ultimatum!"

"Well, we'll soon straighten these fellows out—" the Trade Attaché began.

"There happens to be more to this piece of truculence than appears on the surface," the Ambassador cut in. She paused, waiting for interested frowns to settle into place.

"Note, gentlemen, that these invaders have appeared on terrestrial controlled soil—and without so much as a flicker from the instruments of the Economic Monitor Service!"

The Trade Attaché blinked. "That's absurd," he said flatly. Vasquez slapped the table.

"We're up against something new, gentlemen! I've considered every hypothesis from shell corporations to offshore holdings! The fact is—the Zenith Collective's financial instruments are completely untraceable!"

The Trade Attaché pulled at his lower lip. "In that case, we can't engage with these fellows until we understand their organizational development structure. I recommend a crash project in complexity science. In the meantime—"

"I'll have my boys start to crack this thing," the Chief of Intelligence spoke up. "I'll fit out a couple of volunteers with false credentials—"

"No cloak and dagger work, gentlemen! Long range policy will be worked out by Deep-Think teams back at the Department. Our role will be a holding action. Now I want suggestions for a comprehensive, well-rounded and decisive course for meeting this threat. Any recommendation?"

The Political Officer placed his fingertips together. "What about a stiff Note demanding an extra week's time?"

"No! No begging," the Economic Officer objected. "I'd say a calm, dignified, aggressive withdrawal—as soon as possible."

"We don't want to give them the idea we spook easily," the Trade Attaché said. "Let's delay the withdrawal—say, until tomorrow."

"Early tomorrow," Chang said. "Or maybe later today."

"Well, I see you're of a mind with me," Vasquez nodded. "Our plan of action is clear, but it remains to be implemented. We have a population of over fifteen million individuals to relocate." She eyed the Political Officer. "I want five proposals for resettlement on my desk by oh-eight-hundred hours tomorrow." Vasquez rapped out instructions. Harried-looking staff members arose and hurried from the room. Chang eased toward the door.

"Where are you going, Chang?" Vasquez snapped.

"Since you're so busy, I thought I'd just slip back down to Com Inq. It was a most interesting orientation lecture, Madam Ambassador. Be sure to let us know how it works out."

"Kindly return to your chair," Vasquez said coldly. "A number of chores remain to be assigned. I think you, Chang, need a little field experience. I want you to get over to Ashbury and take a look at this Zenith Collective personally."

Chang's mouth opened and closed soundlessly.

"Not afraid of a few corporate raiders, are you, Chang?"

"Afraid? Good lord, no, ha ha. It's just that I'm afraid I may lose my head and do something rash if I go."

"Nonsense! A diplomat is immune to heroic impulses. Take Omar Dixon along. No dawdling, now! I want you on the way in two hours. Notify the transport pool at once. Now get going!"

Chang nodded unhappily and went into the hall.

"Oh, Dixon," Vasquez said. Dixon turned.

"Try to restrain Mr. Chang from any impulsive moves—in any direction."

---

Dixon and Chang topped a ridge and looked down across a slope of towering glass office buildings and gleaming chrome structures set among elaborate corporate gardens of sculpted hedges and fountains, reaching down to a commercial plaza with the massive Central Exchange beyond.

"A delightful vista," Chang said, mopping at his face. "A pity we couldn't locate the Zenith Collective headquarters. We'll go back now and report—"

"I'm pretty sure the settlement is off to the right," Dixon said. "Why don't you head back for the transport, while I ease over and see what I can observe."

"Dixon, we're engaged in a serious mission. This is not a time to think of sightseeing."

"I'd like to take a good look at what we're giving away."

"See here, Dixon! One might almost receive the impression that you're questioning Corps policy!"

"One might, at that. The Collective has made their play, but I think it might be valuable to take a look at their cards before we fold. If I'm not back at the transport in an hour, lift without me."

"You expect me to make my way back alone?"

"It's directly down-slope—" Dixon broke off, listening. Chang clutched at his arm.

There was a sound of approaching footsteps. Twenty feet ahead, a glass door swung aside. A seven-foot humanoid stepped into view, long, thin, grey-suited legs moving in quick, precise steps. A pair of immense dark sunglasses covered calculating eyes set in a pale, angular face above a sharp chin. The figure paused, head tilted, listening.

Chang gulped audibly. The figure froze, head tilted, face aimed directly at the spot where the Terrestrials stood in the deep shade of a giant column.

"I'll go for help," Chang squeaked. He whirled and took three leaps into the corridor.

A second grey-suited figure rose up to block his way. He spun, darted to the left. The first figure pounced, grappled Chang to its narrow chest. Chang yelled, threshing and kicking, broke free, turned—and collided with the tall humanoid, coming in fast from the right. All three went down in a tangle of limbs.

Dixon jumped forward, hauled Chang free, thrust him aside and stopped, right fist cocked. The two figures lay groaning feebly.

"Nice piece of work, Mr. Chang," Dixon said. "You nailed both of them."

"Those undoubtedly are the most ruthless, aggressive, merciless countenances it has ever been my misfortune to encounter," Chang said. "It hardly seems fair. Seven feet tall and faces like that!"

The smaller of the two captive figures ran long, slender fingers over a bruised shin, from which he had turned back the tight-fitting grey trousers.

"It's not broken," he said nasally in passable Terrestrial, eyeing Chang through the heavy sunglasses, now badly cracked. "Small thanks to you."

Chang smiled loftily. "I daresay you'll think twice before interfering with peaceable diplomats in future."

"Diplomats? Surely you jest."

"Never mind us," Dixon said. "It's you fellows we'd like to talk about. How many of you are there?"

"Only Claudia and myself."

"I mean altogether. How many in the Zenith Collective?"

The figure whistled shrilly.

"Here, no signaling!" Chang snapped, looking around.

"That was merely an expression of amusement."

"You find the situation amusing? I assure you, sir, you are in perilous straits at the moment. I may fly into another rage, you know."

"Please, restrain yourself. I was merely somewhat astonished—" a small whistle escaped—"at being taken for a Collective Executive."

"Aren't you a Collective Executive?"

"I? Great balance sheets, no!" More stifled whistles of amusement escaped the pale face. "Both Claudia and I are Analysts. Economic researchers, as it happens."

"You certainly look like Executives."

"Oh, not at all—except perhaps to a Terrestrial. The Executives are sturdily built individuals, all over eight feet in height. And, of course, they do nothing but negotiate. A management caste, actually."

"A caste? You mean they're biologically the same as you?"

"Not at all! An Analyst wouldn't think of transitioning into an Executive role."

"I mean to say, you are of the same basic organization—descended from a common corporate structure, perhaps."

"We are all part of the same organizational development cycle."

"What are the differences between you, then?"

"Why, the Executives are argumentative, boastful, lacking in appreciation for the finer things of life. One dreads to contemplate ascending to their level."

"Do you know anything about a Note passed to the Terrestrial Ambassador at Evergreen?"

The figure twitched. "Evergreen? I know of no place called Evergreen."

"The outer settlement of this region."

"Oh, yes. We call it Foxwood. I had heard that some sort of creatures had established a trading post there, but I confess I pay little note to such matters."

"We're wasting time, Dixon," Chang said. "We must restrain these individuals, hurry back to the transport and make our escape. You heard what they said."

"Are there any Executives down there at the headquarters, where the offices are?" Dixon asked.

"At the Central Exchange, you mean? Oh, yes. Planning some venture."

"That would be the takeover of Foxwood," Chang said. "And unless we hurry, Dixon, we're likely to be caught there with the last of the evacuees!"

"How many Executives would you say there are at the Exchange?"

"Oh, a very large number. Perhaps fifteen or twenty."

"Fifteen or twenty what?" Chang looked perplexed.

"Fifteen or twenty Executives."

"You mean that there are only fifteen or twenty individual Executives in all?"

Another whistle. "Not at all. I was referring to the local Executives only. There are more at the other Centers, of course."

"And the Executives are responsible for the ultimatum—unilaterally?"

"I suppose so; it sounds like them. A truculent group, you know. And trade policy is rather a hobby of theirs."

Claudia moaned and stirred. She sat up slowly, rubbing her head. She spoke to her companion in a shrill alien clatter of consonants.

"What did she say?"

"Poor Claudia. She blames me for her bruises, since it was my idea to approach you as research subjects."

"You should have known better than to tackle that fierce-looking creature," Claudia said, pointing at Chang.

"How does it happen that you speak Terrestrial?" Dixon asked.

"Oh, one picks up all sorts of languages in our work."

"It's quite charming, really," Chang said. "Such a quaint, archaic accent."

"Suppose we went down to the Exchange," Dixon asked. "What kind of reception would we get?"

"That depends. I wouldn't recommend interfering with the Juniors or the Associates; it's their promotion review time, you know. The Managers will be busy with quarterly reports—such a tedious business—and of course the Executives are tied up with their ceremonial negotiations. I'm afraid no one will take any notice of you."

"Do you mean to say," Chang demanded, "that these ferocious Executives, who have issued an ultimatum to the Corps Diplomatique Terrestrienne—who openly covet our occupied territory—would ignore Terrestrials in their midst?"

"If at all possible."

Dixon got to his feet.

"I think our course is clear, Mr. Chang. It's up to us to go down and attract a little attention."

---

"I'm not at all sure we're going about this in the right way," Chang puffed, trotting at Dixon's side. "These fellows Pedro and Claudia—Oh, they seem affable enough, but how can we be sure we're not being led into a trap?"

"We can't."

Chang stopped short. "Let's go back."

"All right," Dixon said. "Of course there may be an ambush—"

Chang moved off. "Let's keep going."

The party emerged from the corridor at the edge of a great glass-fronted building. Pedro took the lead, rounded the corner of the structure, halted at a rectangular entrance cut into the facade.

"You can find your way easily enough from here," he said. "You'll excuse us, I hope—"

"Nonsense, Pedro!" Claudia pushed forward. "I'll escort our guests to Executive Hall." She spoke briefly to her fellow Analyst. Pedro responded.

"I don't like it, Dixon," Chang whispered. "Those fellows are plotting mischief."

"Threaten them with violence, Mr. Chang. They're scared of you."

"That's true. And the drubbing they received was well-deserved. I'm a patient man, but there are occasions—"

"Come along, please," Claudia called. "Another ten minutes' walk—"

"See here, we have no interest in investigating this building," Chang announced. "We wish you to take us direct to the Exchange to interview your leadership regarding the ultimatum!"

"Yes, yes, of course. Executive Hall lies here inside the complex."

"This is the Exchange?"

"A modest commercial center, sir, but there are those who love it."

"No wonder we didn't observe their operations from the air," Chang muttered. "Camouflaged." He moved hesitantly through the opening.

The party moved along a wide, deserted corridor which sloped down steeply, then leveled off and branched. Claudia took the center branch, ducking slightly under the ten-foot ceiling lit at intervals with what appeared to be energy-efficient LED panels.

"Few signs of an advanced organizational structure here," Chang whispered. "These creatures must devote all their talents to predatory enterprise."

Ahead, Claudia slowed. A distant murmuration was audible, a sustained high-pitched arguing. "Softly, now. We approach Executive Hall. They can be an irascible lot when disturbed at their negotiations."

"When will the negotiations be over?" Chang called hoarsely.

"In another few weeks, I should imagine, if, as you say, they've scheduled a takeover for next month."

"Look here, Claudia." Chang shook a finger at the tall figure. "How is it that these Executives are allowed to embark on predatory ventures of this sort without reference to the wishes of the majority?"

"Oh, the majority of the Executives favor the move, I imagine."

"These few hotheads are permitted to embroil the organization in conflict?"

"Oh, they don't embroil the organization in conflict. They merely—"

"Dixon, this is fantastic! I've heard of iron-fisted corporate cliques before, but this is madness!"

"Come softly, now." Claudia beckoned, moving toward a bend in the brightly-lit corridor. Dixon and Chang moved forward.

The corridor debouched through a high double door into a vast oval chamber, high-domed, austere, paneled in dark mahogany and hung with framed certificates, gilded plaques, mounted awards, crossed gavels over polished briefcases, the immense portraits of stern-faced founders. Great crystal chandeliers in wall brackets and stands along the length of the long table shed a bright light that reflected from the mirror polish of the marble floor, gleamed on polished silver platters and paper-thin crystal, shone amber and gold through dark decanters—and cast long shadows behind the fifteen figures at the board.

Lesser figures—pale-faced, grey-suited, calculating-eyed—moved briskly, bearing steaming platters, stood in groups of three reviewing spreadsheets on tablets, or examined intricate financial models, unnoticed in the shrill uproar as each of the magnificently dressed, tailored, accessorized and jeweled Executives carried on a shouted conversation with an equally noisy fellow.

"A most interesting display of corporate splendor," Chang breathed. "Now we'd better be getting back."

"Ah, a moment," Claudia said. "Observe the Executive—the tallest of the negotiators—she with the platinum jewelry and crimson power suit."

"Eight and a half feet if she's an inch," Chang estimated. "And now we really must hurry along—"

"That one is chief among these dealmakers. I'm sure you'll want a word with her. She controls not only the Ashbury operations but those from the other Centers as well."

"What kind of operations? Hostile takeovers?"

"Certainly. What other kind would the Executives bother with?"

"I don't suppose," Chang said casually, "that you'd know the type, capitalization, assets and staffing of these operations? And how many units comprise the organization? And where they're based at present?"

"They're fully automated multi-billion credit all-purpose conglomerates. They employ a variety of strategies. The Executives are fond of that sort of thing. Each of the Executives has their own, of course. They're virtually identical, except for the personal touches each individual has given their division."

"Great heavens, Dixon!" Chang exclaimed in a whisper. "It sounds as though these brutes employ a corporate empire as simpler souls might a set of toy businesses!"

Dixon stepped past Chang and Claudia to study the negotiating hall. "I can see that their votes would carry all the necessary weight."

"And now an interview with Executive Grace herself," Claudia said. "If you'll kindly step along, gentlemen...."

"That won't be necessary," Chang said hastily. "I've decided to refer the matter to committee."

"After having come so far," Claudia said, "it would be a pity to miss having a frank discussion...."

There was a pause.

"Ah ... Dixon," Chang said. "Claudia has just presented a most compelling argument...."

Dixon turned. Claudia stood gripping an ornately decorated stun pistol in one pale hand, a slim dart gun in the other. Both were pointed at Chang's chest.

"I suspected you had hidden qualities, Claudia," Dixon commented.

"See here, Claudia! We're diplomats!" Chang started.

"Careful, Mr. Chang; you may goad her to action."

"By no means," Claudia said. "I much prefer to observe the reaction of the Executives when presented with the news that two peaceful Analysts have been assaulted and detained by bullying interlopers. If there's anything that annoys the Executives, it's Executive-like behavior in others. Now step along, please."

"Rest assured, this will be reported!"

"I doubt it."

"You'll face the wrath of Enlightened Galactic Opinion!"

"Oh? How big a legal team does Enlightened Galactic Opinion have?"

"Stop scaring her, Mr. Chang. She may get nervous and shoot." Dixon stepped into the negotiating hall, headed for the resplendent figure at the head of the table. A trio of junior associates broke off in mid-sentence, staring. A pyramid of documents toppled as Dixon swung past, followed by Chang and the tall Analyst. The shrill chatter at the table faded.

Grace Rogers turned as Dixon came up, blinking sharp eyes. Claudia stepped forward, spoke rapidly, gesturing excitedly. Grace pushed back her chair—a low, heavily padded executive throne—and stared unwavering at Dixon, moving her head to bring first one eye, then the other, to bear. There were small tension lines in the angular, pale face. The perfectly coiffed platinum hair, styled in an elaborate updo, was immaculate, and a loop of black pearls hung elegantly at her throat.

Claudia finished her speech and fell silent, breathing hard.

Grace looked Dixon over in silence, then laughed sharply.

"Not bad," Dixon said admiringly. "Maybe we could get up a match between you and Ambassador Sternwheeler. You've got the delivery on him, but he's got substance."

"So," Grace said in a resonant alto. "You come from Foxwood, eh? Or Evergreen, as I think you call it. What is it you're after? More time? A compromise? Negotiations? Peace?" She slammed a pale hand against the table. "The answer is no!"

Claudia spoke rapidly. Grace cocked an eye, motioned to a servant. "Restrain that one." She indicated Chang. Her eyes went to Dixon. "This one's bigger; you'd best restrain him, too."

"Why, your Excellency—" Chang started, stepping forward.

"Stay back!" Grace called. "Stand over there where I can keep an eye on you."

"Your Excellency, I'm empowered—"

"Not here, you're not!" Grace announced. "Want peace, do you? Well, I don't want peace! I've had a surfeit of peace these last two centuries! I want action! Acquisition! Market dominance! Glory!" She turned to look down the table. "How about it, colleagues? It's hostile takeover to the end, eh?"

There was a momentary silence from all sides.

"I guess so," grunted a giant Executive in iridescent blue with silver accessories.

Grace's eyes narrowed. She half rose. "We've been all over this," she said sharply. She placed pale fingers on a sleek tablet. "I thought I'd made my point!"

"Oh, sure, Grace."

"You bet."

"I'm convinced."

Grace relaxed and resumed her seat. "All for one and one for all, that's us."

"And you're the one, eh, Grace?" Dixon commented.

Chang cleared his throat. "I sense that some of you ladies and gentlemen are not convinced of the wisdom of this move," he piped, looking along the table at the suits, jewelry, pale faces, styled hair and calculating eyes.

"Silence!" Grace called. "No use your talking to my loyal colleagues anyway," she added. "They do whatever I convince them they ought to do."

"But I'm sure that on more mature consideration—"

"I can out-negotiate any Executive in the house." Grace said. "That's why I'm Chief Executive." She laughed again.

A servant came up carrying restraints, dropped them with a clatter at Chang's feet. Claudia aimed the guns while the servant wrapped three loops around Chang's wrists, snapped a lock in place.

"You next!" The guns pointed at Dixon's chest. He held out his arms. Four loops of silvery-gray restraints in half-inch bands dropped around them. The servant cinched them up tight, squeezed a lock through the ends and closed it.

"Now," Grace said, leaning back in her chair, glass in hand. "There's a bit of sport to be had here, colleagues. What shall we do with them?"

"Let them go," the blue and silver Executive said glumly.

"You can do better than that," Grace called. "Now here's a suggestion: we humiliate them publicly—strip their credentials and diplomatic immunity, say—and send them back."

"Good lord! Dixon, she's talking about destroying our careers and sending us home disgraced! What a barbaric proposal!"

"It wouldn't be the first time a Terrestrial diplomat got a trimming," Dixon commented.

"It should have the effect of stimulating the Terries to put up a reasonable fight," Grace said judiciously. "I have a feeling that they're thinking of giving up without a struggle."

"Oh, I doubt that," the blue-and-silver Executive said. "Why should they?"

Grace rolled an eye at Dixon and another at Chang. "Take these two," she called. "I'll wager they came here to negotiate a surrender!"

"Well," Chang started.

"Hold it, Mr. Chang," Dixon said. "I'll tell her."

"What's your proposal?" Grace said, taking a sip from her goblet. "A fifty-fifty split? Monetary compensation? Shared territory? I can assure you, it's useless. We Executives like to compete."

"I'm afraid you've gotten the wrong impression, your Excellency," Dixon said blandly. "We didn't come to negotiate. We came to deliver an Ultimatum."

"What?" Grace exclaimed. Behind Dixon, Chang spluttered.

"We plan to use this region for a pilot program in institutional reform," Dixon said. "A new type of community organizing initiative we've worked out. Have all your people comply with our labor relations framework in seventy-two hours, or suffer the consequences."

---

"You have the gall," Grace stormed, "to stand here in the center of Executive Hall—uninvited, at that—and in restraints—"

"Oh, these," Dixon said. He tensed his arms. The soft plastic bands stretched and broke. He shook the light material free. "We diplomats like to go along with colorful local customs, but I wouldn't want to mislead you. Now, as to the compliance with our framework—"

Claudia screeched, waved the guns. The Executives were chattering.

"I told you they were brutes," Claudia shrilled.

Grace slammed her fist down on the table. "I don't care what they are!" she called. "Comply, hell! I can field eighty-five fully operational corporate divisions!"

"And we can surround every one of them with a thousand regulatory agencies with a hundred thousand pages of compliance requirements each."

"Dixon." Chang tugged at his sleeve. "Don't forget their untraceable financial instruments."

"That's all right. They don't have any."

"But—"

"We'll take you on!" Grace announced. "We're the Executives! We glory in competition! We live in triumph or go down in—"

"Nonsense," the blue-and-silver Executive cut in. "If it wasn't for you, Grace, we could sit around and negotiate and boast and enjoy life without having to prove anything."

"Grace, you seem to be the instigator here," Dixon said. "I think the rest of your colleagues would listen to reason—"

"Over my dead body!"

"My idea exactly," Dixon said. "You claim you can out-negotiate anyone in the house. Step out of your executive suite and come out here on the floor, and we'll see how good you are at backing up your conversation."

Chang hovered at Dixon's side. "Eight and a half feet tall," he moaned. "And did you notice the size of those legal teams?"

Dixon watched as Grace's aides helped her out of her formal trappings. "I wouldn't worry too much, Mr. Chang. This is a light-gravity world. I doubt if old Grace would weigh up at more than one-eighty standard pounds here."

"But that phenomenal reach—"

"I'll work at close range. When she extends to strike, I'll get inside her guard."

Across the cleared floor, Grace shook off her helpers with a snort.

"Enough! Let me at the upstart!"

Dixon moved out to meet her, watching the raised arms. Grace stalked forward, long lean legs moving precisely, polished shoes clicking against the marble floor. The other figures—both servitors and jeweled Executives—formed a wide circle, all eyes unwaveringly on the combatants.

Grace struck suddenly, a long arm flashing down in a vicious chop at Dixon, who leaned aside, caught one lean ankle. Grace bent to free her leg from Dixon's grip—and staggered back as a uppercut took her just below the chin. A screech went up from the crowd as Dixon leaped clear.

Grace hissed and charged. Dixon whirled aside, then struck the Executive's supporting leg in a flying tackle. Grace leaned, arms windmilling, crashed to the floor. Dixon whirled, grabbed the left arm, whipped it behind the narrow back, seized Grace's neck in a hold and threw his weight backward. Grace fell on her back, her legs splayed out at an awkward angle. She squawked and beat her free arm on the floor, reaching in vain for Dixon.

Claudia stepped forward, pistols ready. Chang stepped before her.

"Need I remind you, madam," he said icily, "that this is an official diplomatic function? I can brook no interference from disinterested parties."

Claudia hesitated. Chang held out a hand. "I must ask you to hand me your weapons, Claudia."

"Look here," Claudia began.

"I may lose my temper," Chang hinted. Claudia lowered the guns, passed them to Chang. He thrust them into his belt with a sour smile, turned back to watch the encounter.

Dixon had thrown a strip of crimson silk around Grace's left wrist, bound it to the Executive's neck. Another wisp of material floated from Grace's shoulder. Dixon, still holding Grace in an awkward sprawl, wrapped it around one outflung leg, secured ankle and thigh together. Grace flopped, calling out. At each movement, the constricting loop around her neck jerked her head back, the platinum hair tossing.

"If I were you, I'd relax," Dixon said, rising and releasing his grip. Grace got a leg under her; Dixon kicked it gently. Grace's chin hit the floor with a hollow thud. She wilted, an ungainly tangle of over-long limbs and expensive fabric.

Dixon turned to the watching crowd. "Next?" he called.

The blue and silver Executive stepped forward. "Maybe this would be a good time to elect a new leader," he said. "Now, my qualifications—"

"Sit down," Dixon said loudly. He stepped to the head of the table, seated himself in Grace's vacated chair. "A couple of you finish securing Grace for me."

"But we must select a leader!"

"That won't be necessary, colleagues. I'm your new leader."

---

"As I see it," Dixon said, tapping cigar ashes into an empty wine glass, "you Executives like to be competitive, but you don't particularly like actual conflict."

"We don't mind a little competition—within reason. And, of course, as Executives, we're expected to achieve market dominance. But what I say is, why rush things?"

"I have a suggestion," Chang said. "Why not turn the leadership over to the Analysts? They seem a level-headed group."

"What good would that do? Executives are Executives. It seems there's always one among us who's a slave to ambition—and, naturally, we have to follow them."

"Why?"

"Because that's the way it's done."

"Why not do it another way?" Chang offered. "Now, I'd like to suggest team building exercises—"

"If we gave up competing, we might last too long in this role. Then what would happen?"

"Last too long?" Chang looked puzzled.

"When transition time comes there'd be no positions for us. Anyway, with the new Executives coming up—"

"I've lost the thread," Chang said. "Who are the new Executives?"

"After transitioning, the Analysts transform and become Executives, of course. The Juniors become Managers, the Managers become Associates, the Associates metamorphose into Analysts—"

"You mean Pedro and Claudia—the mild-natured researchers—will become aggressive dealmakers like Grace?"

"Very likely. 'The milder the Analyst, the wilder the Executive,' as the old saying goes."

"What do Executives turn into?" Dixon asked.

"Hmmmm. That's a good question. So far, none have survived Executive status long enough to find out."

"Have you thought of forsaking your competitive ways?" Chang asked. "What about taking up collaborative ventures and ethical business practices?"

"Don't mistake me. We Executives like a competitive life. It's great sport to sit around conference tables and strategize and tell success stories and then go dashing off to enjoy a brisk negotiation and some leisurely profit-taking afterward. But we prefer a nice advantage in market position. Not this business of tackling you Terrestrials over at Foxwood—that was a mad notion. We had no idea what your strength was."

"But now that's all off, of course," Chang chirped. "Now that we've had diplomatic relations and all—"

"Oh, by no means. The takeover launches in thirty days. After all, we're Executives; we have to satisfy our drive to compete."

"But Mr. Dixon is your leader now. He won't let you!"

"Only a retired Executive stays home when Launch day comes. And even if he orders us all to resign, there are still the other Centers—all with their own leaders. No, gentlemen, the Takeover is definitely on."

"Why don't you go compete with somebody else?" Chang suggested. "I could name some very attractive prospects—outside my sector, of course."

"Hold everything," Dixon said. "I think we've got the basis of a deal here...."

option_b: Nothing is known because none have survived Executive status long enough to find out
