synthetic_story:
The Stellar Archive
By ADAPTED WORK

Matthew Fisher's Digital Archive Project was a cursed venture leased for a mysterious tour of the outer colonies. It made a one-night installation on a Marvenia research station—to find that sabotage stalked it from the shadows in corrupted data streams.

Matthew Fisher leaned forward across the small conference table. He knocked over the mug of synthetic coffee, but it didn't matter. The mug was empty. He jabbed me in the shoulder with his stylus, not very hard. Not hard enough to actually hurt, just enough to make his point.

"We," he said, "are finished. Bankrupt. Out of funding and out of options." He added, as an afterthought, "Destitute."

I looked at him. I said sourly, "You're exaggerating!"

"Exaggerating." Matthew put his elbows on the table and peered at me through a curtain of very dark hair that needed cutting. "She says I'm exaggerating! With Fisher's Digital Humanities Archive, the Greatest Cultural Repository in the Colonies, so deep in debt..."

"It's no deeper in debt than you are in denial." I was irritated because he'd been hogging the coffee dispenser all morning. "The Greatest Cultural Repository. Please! I've managed Fisher's Digital Archive around the Woodbridge Region for seven years, and I know. It's underfunded, it's understaffed, it's breaking down! Nothing works, from the quantum computing servers to the junior archivists. In short, it's failing!"

I must have been more tired than I thought. Nobody insults Matthew Fisher's Digital Archive to Matthew Fisher's face unless they're exhausted and want a long argument.

Matthew stood up. He stood up slowly. I had plenty of time to see his brown eyes narrow, and hear the soft hum of the environmental controls, and watch the curious stares of the station personnel at nearby tables swing toward us, interested and somewhat amused.

I had plenty of time to think how I'm not as diplomatic as I should be, and how Matthew has a temper when pushed.

I said, "Matthew. Wait. I..."

Somebody said, "Excuse me. Is one of you Dr. Matthew Fisher?"

Matthew put his hands on the table. He closed his eyes and smiled tightly and said, very carefully:

"Would you be here about the server lease, or the data storage fees?"

I shot a glance at the newcomer. She'd saved me from an uncomfortable confrontation, even if she was a creditor; and I felt sorry for her. Matthew Fisher straightened his shoulders like he was preparing for battle.

The stranger was petite. She made even me look tall. She was dressed in dark-grey professional attire, very conservative. There was a touch of grey in her dark hair and her skin was pale, smooth, and carefully maintained. She had the kind of face that university administrators will trust with sensitive projects. I looked for her security detail.

There didn't seem to be any. The woman looked at Matthew with pale grey eyes, and her voice was softer than his.

She said, "I don't think you understand."

I felt uneasy, suddenly. Somebody shifted in their seat. The sound was loud in the quiet cafeteria. I straightened up, and my palms were damp. Matthew Fisher sighed.

Then I saw what the woman was holding in her hand.

I stood up quickly. "Wait," I said. "Look at that."

Matthew glared at me. "What's wrong with you, Samantha? I'm handling this."

"Shut up," I said. "Look what she's got there. A funding authorization!"

The woman looked at me. She hadn't reacted at all. "Yes," she said. "A funding authorization. Quite substantial. Would you permit me to join you?"

Matthew Fisher sat down. He managed a more genuine smile. "Of course. I'm Dr. Fisher. This is Samantha Boyd, my project manager." He looked at the spilled coffee. "I apologize for that. Misunderstanding."

The woman smiled slightly. She did it with her lips. The rest of her face remained professional and unreadable, almost mask-like. I realized with a start that it wasn't a mask at all. It was the most complete poker face I'd ever encountered, and you couldn't read those calm grey eyes any more than you could read encrypted data.

I didn't trust her. I didn't trust her at all. But she had funding. I said, "Hello. Let's find a private meeting room. These station personnel make me nervous, watching like they're waiting for entertainment."

The woman nodded. "Excellent suggestion. My name is Margaret Kim. I wish to—ah—commission your archive services."

I looked at Matthew. He looked more hopeful than he had in months. We didn't say anything until we got Margaret Kim into a private conference room with fresh coffee on the table. Then I cleared my throat.

"What exactly did you have in mind, Ms. Kim?"

Kim sipped her coffee, made a polite face, and set it down. "I have access to independent funding sources. It has always been my mission to preserve cultural heritage for future generations..."

Matthew got tense. "Just a moment," he murmured, and started to stand. I touched his arm.

"Let Ms. Kim finish."

He sat down, looking suspicious. Kim ignored him. She continued, quietly,

"I have always believed that oral history preservation, properly executed, is the most valuable service we can provide to humanity's collective memory..."

I said, "Of course. But what was your specific proposal?"

"There are many settlements along the Marvenia frontier where no systematic cultural documentation has been conducted. I propose to remedy that. I propose to commission your archive, Dr. Fisher, to make a tour of several colonies in the outer territories."

Matthew had relaxed. His eyes began to show interest. He started to speak, and I interrupted.

"That would be expensive, Ms. Kim," I said. "We'd have to postpone several other projects..."

She looked at me. I was stretching the truth, and she knew it. But she said,

"I quite understand. I would be prepared..."

The door slid open suddenly. Kim stopped talking. Matthew and I turned to look at the figure in the doorway.

It was Miguel Ortiz, our senior technician—a tall, intense man from a Terran colony on Mars. I'd visited once. Miguel looks a lot like the landscape there—serious, uncompromising, and tough. His hands, gripping the doorframe, were stained with equipment grease and were nearly as large as maintenance tools.

He said, "Boss, the quantum computing array is acting up again."

"The array can wait," said Matthew. "Can't you see I'm in a meeting?"

Miguel's dark eyes were worried. "I'm telling you, Boss, the system isn't stable. It hasn't had proper maintenance. If something..."

I said, "That'll all be taken care of, Miguel. Please give us a moment."

He looked at me like he was calculating how much trouble I was causing. "Fine! But the system's unstable. It's overheating, understand? And if it doesn't get proper attention soon I'm not sure our backup protocols will hold."

He left, letting the door slide shut with emphasis. Matthew Fisher groaned. Kim cleared her throat and said, rather formally,

"The quantum computing array?"

"Yes. It's somewhat temperamental." Matthew took a quick sip of coffee. I elaborated.

"It's the backbone of our archive operations, Ms. Kim. A state-of-the-art quantum computing system. The only other comparable system in the region belongs to the University Consortium, and theirs is much smaller than ours."

Theirs was also much newer, but I didn't mention that. Our array may be outdated, but it's still impressive. I only hoped it wouldn't fail completely, because without it we'd have a more dysfunctional operation than even I could tolerate.

Kim looked impressed. "A quantum computing array. How fascinating! The applications for digital humanities research must be extraordinary. The processing capabilities..."

We were getting off track. I said tactfully, "We'd need at least fifty thousand credits."

It was twice what we had any right to ask. I was prepared to negotiate. Kim looked at me with that unreadable expression. For a fraction of a second I thought I saw something behind her calm grey eyes, and my instincts screamed warning. Kim smiled professionally.

"I'm not inclined to haggle. Fifty thousand Universal Credits will be acceptable." She produced a tablet, entered some commands, and displayed an authorization code.

"By way of initial funding. My legal representative and I will meet with you tomorrow morning with a formal contract and project timeline. Good evening."

We said good evening, trying to contain our relief. Kim departed. Matthew reached for the tablet to verify the authorization, but I was faster.

"Wait," I said. "There are creditors waiting for this. Serious creditors with legal claims. Here." I transferred a small amount to a discretionary account. "We can celebrate with this."

Matthew has an extensive vocabulary. He used it. When he caught his breath he said suddenly,

"Kim is running some kind of operation."

"Obviously."

"It may be illegitimate."

"Possibly. And she may be eccentric and genuine. For heaven's sake!" I said. "You want to sit here until the project collapses completely?"

Matthew looked at me, oddly. He looked at the tablet in my hands. He ran his fingers through his dark hair.

"Yeah," he said. "I hope there'll be enough left to pay the lawyers." He moved toward the door. "Hey, let's get Miguel. We need to discuss this!"

It was quite late when we returned to the aging research station where Fisher's Digital Archive was housed in its cramped quarters. Late as it was, they were waiting for us. About fifteen of them, sitting around the common area and looking very unhappy.

It was lonely out there, with the station's recycled air cool and stale, carrying that faint metallic taste of old environmental systems. There's a feeling to these outer stations, like something abandoned and waiting. An uneasy feeling. The fluorescent lights flickered occasionally.

Matthew Fisher walked into the common area where our team had gathered. He was steady enough. He waved and said, "Hello, everyone."

They stood up from their workstations and chairs and came toward us. I straightened and prepared for confrontation. We felt we owed these people more than just apologies. It grates on a person's pride to have to avoid their own team members in the corridors. This was the first time in weeks we'd faced them directly.

I displayed the funding authorization on my tablet. That stopped them. Very formally, Matthew and I explained the situation, outlined the payment schedule, and answered questions. Matthew stretched and looked genuinely relieved.

"Well?" he said.

"Well," I said.

We had a productive discussion. Some people were skeptical. We addressed their concerns. Everyone felt better afterward. They had assurance of payment, and we had their renewed commitment.

The news spread through the station quickly. The junior archivists and the data specialists and the oral history researchers and all the other dedicated but underpaid professionals that make up a digital humanities project were noticeably more optimistic, discussing the possibilities over dinner.

Matthew Fisher regarded them with satisfaction, wiping fatigue from his eyes. "They're good people, Sam. Excellent colleagues. They stayed with me, and I'm going to make it right."

I said, "Sure," rather wearily. Matthew looked thoughtful.

"Let's check on the quantum array."

I didn't want to check on the quantum array. I never felt comfortable in the server room, especially at night or during system maintenance. I'm a people person, myself. The hum and heat of high-powered computing gives me anxiety. But Matthew looked determined, so I shrugged.

"Okay. But just for a minute. Then we need sleep."

"You're a good colleague, Sam. Best project manager anywhere..."

The argument had worn him down. I was worried he'd make a mistake and damage something expensive. That's why I went along. If I hadn't... Oh, well, what's a few sleepless nights among colleagues?

It was dim in the server room. At the far end, there was a soft blue glow. Miguel was evidently monitoring the quantum array. We started down the long corridor between the rows of server racks and cooling units and backup systems.

Our footsteps echoed on the metal floor. I wasn't as confident as Matthew, and my skin prickled with unease. It's the sound, I think; the constant hum and the occasional clicks and whirs. And the sense of them, these powerful machines processing endless streams of data, with their patient indifference contained by cooling systems and surge protectors.

Matthew Fisher stumbled slightly. I caught his arm, and then wiped sweat from my forehead despite the cool air. An alarm sounded. A sharp, piercing warning tone that cut through the mechanical ambiance. The quantum array, experiencing critical errors.

It had been stable. Now every monitoring system activated simultaneously. My stomach dropped. I called out every technical term I could think of, and I couldn't hear myself over the alarms. Presently a loud electronic tone silenced the warnings. Miguel had triggered the emergency shutdown.

But the systems didn't stabilize. Not really. They were compromised. You can sense it when systems are compromised. I think that's why I'm anxious around them. They make me feel vulnerable—like our entire project could disappear in an instant. Yeah. They were compromised that night, suddenly...

Miguel looked grim as we reached the main console. "It's getting worse," he said. "Someone's been accessing the system."

"That's concerning," said Matthew Fisher. His eyes looked tired. He swayed slightly with exhaustion. "That's very concerning." He frowned.

I looked at the quantum array. Its housing was the largest and most sophisticated in the facility and even so it looked like it could fail catastrophically at any moment. I don't know if you've ever seen a quantum computing array in crisis. There are only a few in the outer colonies. If you haven't, nothing I can say will convey the anxiety.

They're what the tech specialists call "bleeding edge technology." Seems the engineers had ambitious ideas about quantum computing. The arrays were quite successful initially, but something always causes problems and now there's only a few operational, way out in the research facilities, where even the maintenance crews rarely go. Expensive experiments.

I couldn't help feeling worried about it. The array was housed in its protective chamber with its cooling systems—yes, multiple redundant systems—working overtime and its processing cores deep in their quantum states, executing calculations. Just calculating. Not for anything specific. The status displays showed unstable qubits, like warning fires.

The ambient light was blue-white on the metallic housing, but the error indicators made the monitoring displays flash red, showing system failures. It looked like a disaster waiting to happen.

Miguel said quietly, "Someone's been tampering with it. And somebody needs to fix this properly."

Matthew frowned. I said irritably, "Be reasonable, Miguel! Nobody outside the team has access. There must be a logical explanation."

The alarm sounded again. The array didn't move, obviously, but the temperature readings spiked. The warning, that close, was deafening, and it made me feel cold and hollow inside. The danger, the sheer technical catastrophe...

Matthew Fisher looked shaken. I said, "You'll have to stabilize this, Miguel. It's threatening the entire archive."

He worked on the emergency protocols, and things stabilized somewhat. Miguel stood looking at the monitoring displays, checking readings carefully, like a diagnostician. Then he turned to us.

"I've been maintaining this system," he said. "When we salvaged it from the university surplus and everyone thought it was too damaged to use, I rebuilt it. I know this array. I can work with it. But this time..."

He shrugged. He was large and intense and serious, and his voice carried genuine concern.

"This time," he said, "I'm not certain we can recover."

"Well for Pete's sake, do what you can. We have a contract, and we need it operational." I took Matthew's arm. "Come on, we need rest."

He leaned on my shoulder and we left. Miguel didn't acknowledge us. Matthew looked troubled.

"You were right, Sam," he mumbled. "Project's in trouble. I know it. But it's my life's work. I care about it, Sam. Understand? Like Miguel there with the array. It's old and problematic, but he maintains it. I care..."

"I know," I told him. "Stop worrying for one night."

We were far from the server room then. The racks and systems loomed high and dark around us. It was quiet. The subtle, uneasy hum all around us and our footsteps only made it quieter.

Matthew was nearly asleep on his feet. I started to guide him back. And then I noticed something on a nearby terminal—small traces of unauthorized access, barely visible in the system logs.

I called out, "Miguel! Miguel, there's been a security breach! Miguel—we need you!"

I started to return to the server room. Matthew leaned heavily on me, exhausted. The alarms burst suddenly in a deafening cascade of warnings and error messages, amplified by the metal walls, and above it all I could hear the quantum array's cooling systems screaming in overload.

I thought, "Someone's here. Someone caused this. Someone wants to destroy us!" I tried to call out again. It caught in my throat. I was sweating, and it was cold.

Matthew's stumbling steps tangled with mine. We fell. I caught him, protecting his head, and braced myself against a server rack.

The first system failure hit. It was like an electrical shock, a cascade of shutdowns spreading through the network. I shouted. The failures propagated through the connected systems.

Matthew groaned and struggled. I remember holding on and thinking, "This is it. This is the end, and I'm terrified!"

Then everything went dark.

---

Emily Gutierrez, our station medic, was checking my vital signs when I woke up. Her round face showed concern. She'd worked double shifts recently, and she looked exhausted.

"You're okay, Ms. Boyd," she said gently. "You'll be fine."

She gave me something for the headache. It helped. I asked, "Where's Matthew? How is he?"

"Dr. Fisher is fine. You protected him from injury. You're quite the hero, Ms. Boyd. Miguel got the systems shut down in time. You're a hero."

I said, "Right," and pushed myself up carefully. I managed to stand, though I felt dizzy. I made it to the small mirror in my quarters—I was in my own room—and I saw I looked exhausted but uninjured.

Matthew Fisher opened the door. He looked pale and serious, and there was a bruise on his arm. He said:

"Kim is here with her legal representative."

I found my jacket. "I'll be right there."

Emily left, still looking concerned. Matthew closed the door.

"Sam," he said, "those systems were stable when we arrived. Someone deliberately compromised them. On purpose."

I felt terrible. I said, "Obviously. Nobody saw anything, I suppose?" Matthew shook his head.

"Question is, Sam, who wants to sabotage us, and why?"

"Kim. She realizes she's made a mistake funding us."

"Fifty thousand credits," said Matthew quietly, "for some remote colony documentation work. It doesn't add up, Sam. You think we should withdraw?"

I shrugged. "You're the director. I'm only the one who manages the creditors."

"Yeah," Matthew said thoughtfully. "And I hear unemployment isn't pleasant. Okay, Sam. Let's go sign." He reached for the door and looked at me. "And—uh—Sam, I..."

I said, "Forget it. Next time, just don't trip over me, that's all!"

We had a difficult journey to Goldfield, Marvenia. The quantum array remained unstable, and Miguel, on the rare occasions he emerged from the server room, looked like he was expecting catastrophe. To make it worse, Jacob Anderson, our lead oral historian, fell ill during transit, and one of our junior archivists quit unexpectedly.

Nobody would have minded that, except she took copies of sensitive research data with her. It lasted just long enough to terrify that group of paranoid academics. Digital humanities people are peculiar that way.

Matthew and I did some quiet investigating, but it was futile. Anyone on the team might have sabotaged those systems. It didn't help to know that somebody, maybe the person working next to you, was planning to destroy everything. By the time we reached Goldfield, I was ready to resign entirely.

Matthew guided our transport to the edge of Goldfield, the first location on our itinerary. I stood beside him, looking at the settlement through the viewports. It was Marvenia, certainly. Red dust and scattered prefab structures and harsh sunlight, and a cluster of weather-beaten buildings grouped together defensively. People in environment suits were approaching for a look.

I saw Kim's sleek corporate shuttle parked at a dedicated landing pad, and our equipment transport beside it. Matthew groaned.

"A disaster, Sam. A complete disaster!"

I muttered, "What do you expect, with this underfunded project!" and exited. He followed. The team was gathering near the airlock, but they weren't enthusiastic. You develop instincts for these things. The thin Marvenia atmosphere was already infiltrating through the seals.

As we passed the corridor to the server room, I could hear the quantum array's cooling systems, struggling.

The technical crew was busy setting up equipment, working carefully in the harsh environment. The documentation team was heading for the settlement. Matthew and I stood in our environment suits, observing.

I heard a sound behind me and turned. Angela Perry, our xenoanthropology specialist, was standing in the dust with her helmet off, breathing the thin atmosphere, and her weathered face tilted back, eyes closed. She was smiling. It looked unsettling.

You find many xenoanthropology specialists in digital humanities projects, studying cultural adaptation in frontier settlements. They're colonial specialists, they're not typical academics, and they never let you forget it.

Angela opened her sharp eyes and looked at me and laughed.

"Failure," she whispered. "Failure and conflict. The settlement warns me. I can sense it in the atmosphere."

The harsh sunlight beat down on her. She shivered despite the heat, and her expression was intense.

"The frontier colonies are resistant," she whispered. "Something has been disturbed. They are resistant, and I sense failure ahead!"

She walked away, laughing, and I cursed under my breath, and my stomach was tight. Matthew said,

"Let's see if they have a cafeteria in this place."

We weren't halfway across the landing area when a man emerged from a building at the settlement's edge. We could see him clearly, because he was separated from the crowd approaching us.

He stumbled in the dust, calling out. It took him several attempts to make our names clear enough to understand.

Matthew said, "Sam—that's Jacob Anderson."

We started running. The crowd, mostly rugged colonists in work clothes, turned to see what was happening. People began to converge on the man who staggered and gasped in the thin air.

Jacob Anderson was an oral historian, collecting cultural narratives from frontier communities. He'd collaborated with us several times previously, when funding allowed, and we had a good working relationship.

I hadn't seen him for two years. I remembered him as energetic and enthusiastic, passionate about preserving oral histories. I felt sick, looking at him now.

Matthew tried to help him. Anderson was shaking, trembling like someone in shock. Some colonist stepped forward and offered him water from a canteen.

I was focused on Anderson then, and I didn't pay attention to the colonist. I only glimpsed the person's face briefly. I didn't realize until later that they looked familiar.

We got Anderson inside the building. It turned out to be a small community center, with a few private meeting rooms at the back. We got him into one and closed the door on numerous curious faces. Anderson drank from the canteen. The person who gave it to him had disappeared.

Matthew said gently, "Okay, Jacob. Relax. What happened?"

Anderson tried to compose himself. He hadn't slept. The energetic lines of his face had gone slack and his eyes were red-rimmed. He was covered with dust, and his hands shook.

He said hoarsely, "I found it. I said I would, and I did. I found it and documented it."

He set down the canteen clumsily. "Help me," he said simply. "I'm frightened." His voice broke.

"I have it secured. They want to locate it, but I won't tell them. It needs to be returned. Returned to its source. I tried to do it myself, but they prevented me, and I was afraid they'd find it..."

He reached suddenly and gripped the edge of the table. "I don't know how they discovered it, but they did. I have to return it. I have to..."

Matthew looked at me. Anderson was pale and sweating. I felt frightened, suddenly. I said, "Return what where?"

Matthew stood. "I'll get the medic," he said. "Stay with him." Anderson grabbed his wrist. Anderson's fingers were white and the veins in his hands stood out prominently.

"Don't leave me. Need to tell you—where it is. Need to return it. Promise you'll return it." He gasped, struggling for breath.

"Of course," said Matthew. "Of course we'll return it. What is it?"

Anderson's face was terrible. I felt nauseated, watching him fight for air. I wanted to get Emily anyway, but somehow I knew it was too late. Anderson whispered,

"Cultural artifact. Irreplaceable. Original. You don't understand...! Return it."

"Where is it, Jacob?"

I reached past Matthew suddenly and opened the door. Kim was standing there. Kim, leaning forward, clearly listening. Anderson made a harsh choking sound and collapsed across the table.

Kim's expression didn't change. She didn't move while Matthew checked Anderson's pulse. Matthew didn't need to speak. We knew.

"Heart attack?" said Kim finally.

"Yes," said Matthew. He looked as shaken as I felt. "Poor Jacob."

I looked at the canteen on the table. I looked at Kim with her unreadable professional face. I moved past Matthew and firmly guided Kim into a chair.

"Keep her here until I return," I said.

Matthew stared at me. Kim started to object. "Be quiet," I told her. "We have a contract." I left the room and walked to the main area.

I began to notice something then. There were quite a few people in the center. At first glance they looked appropriate—a weathered, capable group of colonists in practical clothing.

Then I looked more carefully. They were dressed appropriately enough. But they moved wrong for frontier colonists, on Marvenia or anywhere else.

The place was unnaturally quiet. The center administrator was a heavy-set woman with calculating eyes and short grey hair. She looked nervous.

I approached the counter. "Water," I said. She provided it, reluctantly, from a dispenser. I reached for it, casually.

"That man we brought in," I said. "He seems very distressed. Dehydrated. What's he been doing out here?"

"Research," said a voice beside me. "As if you didn't know."

I turned. The person who had given Anderson the canteen was standing next to me. And I recognized them, then.

option_b: The main entrance required special security clearance they didn't have

This was the first time in weeks we'd faced them directly." They were in debt and avoiding confrontation with creditors until they received Kim's funding.

synthetic_story:
The Crystal Towers: A New Era of Magical Architecture

Fourscore and seven years ago, the first enchanted crystal tower opened its doors to the public in the realm of Jarvonia. The Luminous Spire of Maplewood, home to the Guild of Elemental Mages and later the Council of Transmuters, was one of thirteen urban magical towers built in the seven-year period now regarded as the golden age of arcane architecture. All but three (the Eternal Flame Tower in Bridgewater Province, the Moonstone Sanctum in Carmel Territory, and the Stormwatch Citadel in Pinehurst) have since been dismantled and their crystals recycled.

Replacing towers built of simple stone and wood, these crystal structures set new standards for size, magical containment, accessibility, and convenience. As places to practice and study magic, they were vastly superior to the post-Great War towers, especially the facilities designed in the late centuries that doubled as military fortresses. But these massive crystal monoliths, erected in vast open fields outside Houston, Pittsburgh, Cincinnati, Philadelphia, and elsewhere, lack the character of the classic towers.

The New Shadowspire in Maplewood, which opened in 1991, attempted to address the character question with a superficial neo-classical facade that in some ways resembled the exterior of the golden-era tower it replaced. The New Shadowspire was marketed as an old-fashioned tower with all the modern magical conveniences. But inside, it was still a symmetrical crystal monster, and it sat in the middle of a seven-thousand-carriage parking field rather than in an urban neighborhood where apprentices once walked cobblestone streets to their lessons.

A year later, a new—yet more genuinely old—tower arrived to dispel the gloom. The Oriole Tower at Camden Yards in Bridgewater Province revived the idea of a quirkily asymmetrical, relatively intimate, steel-and-crystal-structured, city-friendly magical tower. "Once this opens," predicted Grand Wizard Priya Simmons, Commissioner of the Continental Mage Association, "everyone will want one like it." And so it came to be: the Oriole Tower's successors in Cleveland, Arlington (in the Carmel Territory), and Denver, and those designed for Milwaukee, Seattle, and San Francisco, take their cues from the Oriole Tower's conceptual breakthrough. Even totally nontraditional towers, like those in Phoenix, Miami, and Tampa Bay, emulate the asymmetry of the Oriole Tower's spell-casting chambers. It's almost as though a disembodied voice intoned, "If you build it, they will copy."

While the Oriole Tower and its offspring are almost universally praised, some of them don't deserve the hype. The most annoying hype is that all the new towers are intimate, and that every practice chamber is better at the new place than the old. Intimacy has two aspects—actual size and the subjective perception of size and scale. A good architect can ace the second part of the test through convincing forms, good proportions, and attractive materials. The exposed crystal work, enchanted brick, moonstone, celestial tile, and well-placed portal openings of the new towers beat the cold and sterile fortresses of a generation ago.

For the new towers' charms, we should be thankful. But in actual size, the new magical facilities are not intimate. All their amenities—levitation platforms, wider corridors, abundant meditation chambers (especially for female mages), bathrooms, spiral staircases, plentiful potion stands, and luxury observation suites—make them far larger than the towers they claim to emulate. These towers are larger than even the multipurpose hulks we all love to hate. Compare, for instance, the spanking new Crystal Tower at Arlington (49,100 practice chambers), which rests on 13.6 acres, to Seattle's Dome of Shadows, a 58,000-chamber multipurpose tower that opened in 1976 and covers 9.3 acres. (The legendary Ebbets Sanctum, home to the Brooklyn Conjurers, occupied a mere 5.7 acres and housed 32,000 chambers.)

Or compare heights: the New Shadowspire's apex is 146 feet above ground level; old Shadowspire was about 75 feet high. This is not tower trivia, but an indicator of apprentice experience: Upper-level chambers in the new, taller towers are farther away from the central spell nexus. At Arlington, the mage practicing in the middle-row, upper-level chamber closest to the nexus is 224 feet from the power source, compared to 125 feet at Stormwatch Citadel, a tower with 4,300 more chambers.

Why are upper-level chambers in the new towers so far from the nexus? Two reasons: support pillar placement and luxury viewing areas.

In the old towers, the structural pillars stood within the practice areas, placing the upper-level chambers closer to the nexus. The trade-off was that these pillars obstructed the view of some mages during public demonstrations. Today's architects "remedy" the problem by placing the pillars behind the practice areas, thus moving the upper levels back from the nexus. (It should be noted that the new towers' claim that they have no impaired-view chambers is an overstatement, according to research ethics committees that have studied apprentice experiences and professional ethics in magical education.)

Added tiers devoted to luxury viewing at the new towers also push the upper levels away from the nexus. The retreat of those levels is a century-long process, but it can be stemmed. Master Gabriel Pearson and the Oriole Guild pressed for several design changes that lowered the Oriole Tower's top level and produced a middle-row viewing distance of 199 feet, about eight rows closer than Arlington's. This attention to detail reflects a commitment to social justice in magical education, ensuring that apprentices from all economic backgrounds have reasonable access to the nexus's power.

Design references to golden-age towers are only one parallel between that period and ours. We are also matching that era's frenzied pace of construction: Twenty-six of the Continental Mage Association's 32 guilds occupy a tower that is less than 10 years old; has been, or will be, extensively remodeled; or hope to move into a new one soon.

One of the classic towers' merits was that they were unsubsidized. Guild masters bought land and paid for tower construction—some even built teleportation circles to transport apprentices to their lessons. In all but two cases during the last 65 years, taxpayers have covered most or all of the costs of tower building, raising questions about political economy and the distribution of magical resources.

The San Francisco Guild of Transmutation is planning a similar arrangement for their bayfront tower, assembling about $240 million in private funds and persuading the city to pay for some of the infrastructure, including water management systems for the tower's elaborate fountain arrays and public health facilities for treating magical mishaps. The Guild says that other guild masters are rooting against their scheme, because it calls into question the profligate public subsidies. Some of the subsidies exceed capital and maintenance costs: If the Shadowspire Guild fails to attract 1.5 million annual visitors to the New Shadowspire in the 11th through 20th years of their lease, the state of Illinois is contractually obliged to cover the shortfall by purchasing up to 300,000 visitor passes.

You'd expect that the public would get something, perhaps affordable apprenticeships, in return for subsidizing towers. Instead, the cheap training programs in the new towers are scarcer. The Seattle Mages' proposed tower, for instance, will contain about one-fourth as many general-admission practice chambers as the present location. This erosion of low-cost training is a long-running trend that has contributed to economic inequality in the magical community.

So too is the dramatic increase in luxury viewing areas, which is the primary real reason for the tower-building boom. The real gold mines are the posh luxury suites that lease for between $30,000 and $200,000 a year (payable in advance). A comparable moneymaker is the club deck, just above the first-tier viewing areas. These pricey sections are occupied usually on a season-pass basis, and offer the best sightlines, roomier seats, and wait staff who peddle gourmet fare prepared with minor enchantments.

The gilding doesn't end there: New towers also include members-only guild clubs and on-premises taverns and restaurants, some featuring digital transformation technologies that allow patrons to order food through enchanted mirrors.

Naturally, guild masters don't advertise their new towers as a means of making life better for elite members. They say that only a new tower will allow them to make enough money to stay in town or to train a competitive roster of mages and to allow apprentices to savor that old-time magical atmosphere in greater comfort and convenience. Local taxpayers tend to lay off this pitch—they have voted these measures down in Illinois, Washington state, California, Wisconsin, and Michigan. Politically savvy guild masters usually bypass the voters and tap state governments directly for the money.

Larger and more lavish towers translate into greater land and construction costs. Operable crystal domes, such as those in Toronto's SkySpire, Phoenix's BankOne Tower, and those proposed for Seattle and Milwaukee, are budget-busters. Since most guilds put up little (if any) of their own money, they have scant incentive to economize on the towers. In Seattle, guild management has demanded an operable dome even though the city has the driest weather in the Continental Mage Association outside California. The real problem with the Seattle climate is cold weather in spring and fall, but the unsealed dome won't make the tower warmer or totally free of wind.

Lately, the cost of towers has ranged from about $300 million to $500 million. The multipurpose tower that the Manhattan Enchanters want built on the island's lower west side tentatively carries a $1 billion price tag. Add the financing and maintenance costs, and even a midpriced project goes through the retractable dome. At one point, the cost of the Brewers' proposed tower grew from $250 million to $845 million, and that's not counting the value of the land or the cost of establishing proper financial regulation oversight for the project.

The good news is that not every guild master is demanding a palace for their organization. All Pittsburgh Guild master Mei May wants is a "35,000-to-37,000-chamber tower with natural sunlight and no dome, bells, or whistles." Though her attitude is commendable, the proposed tower will still cost about $200 million, and perhaps an equal amount in interest.

Why should the public chip in? Taxpayer subsidies don't produce cheaper training—they produce more expensive training. The average apprenticeship fee (not counting club memberships and luxury suites) rises about 35 percent when a guild moves into new facilities. And independent economists (i.e., those not hired by tower proponents) discount the claim that new towers spur regional economic growth. Some have even applied principles from comparative history and data analysis to show that the economic benefits are often overstated.

But one compelling argument for subsidies is that new towers can pull their cities together when properly designed and sited. This requires a downtown or neighborhood location where lots of apprentices can take the bus or the enchanted carriage to their lessons; where they can walk to the tower from work, inns, taverns, or shops; and where getting to the tower is a communal event that is part of a broader urban experience. This is the case with older towers such as the Moonstone Sanctum and the Eternal Flame Tower, and the new ones in Toronto, the Oriole Tower in Bridgewater Province, Cleveland, and Denver.

"If you put them in the wrong place, it's a colossal waste of money," says Leonardo Hayes, the planning director of the city of Cleveland and a scholar of urban magical infrastructure. "But if you put them in the right place, the benefits are phenomenal. It's not just about economics—it's about creating spaces that serve the performing arts of magic, where public demonstrations become community events."

Recent attendance patterns show that urban towers generate much better patronage than suburban ones or those in neither/nor locations. There are also strong indicators that suggest new urban towers have "legs," retaining more of their visitors after the novelty wears off. But some guilds deliberately seek isolated locations, where they can better monopolize teleportation revenues and lesson-related potion, scroll, and artifact business. This is why the Shadowspire Guild moated their tower with 100 acres of parking, why the Milwaukee Brewers refuse to build downtown in Pinehurst, Jarvonia, and why the Seattle Mages insisted on the most remote of the city's three tower-siting options.

Logan Lynch, a prominent critic of tower economics and advocate for social justice in magical education, has written extensively about how these decisions affect apprentices from lower-income backgrounds. "When towers are built in isolated locations," he argues, "they become accessible only to those who can afford private transportation or expensive teleportation services. This exacerbates economic inequality in the magical community and undermines the principles of professional ethics that should guide our guilds."

Oliver Johnson, a researcher at the Institute for Magical Studies who specializes in data analysis and comparative history, has documented how tower placement affects apprentice outcomes. His research shows that apprentices who train in urban towers are more likely to complete their studies and achieve master status than those who train in isolated facilities. "There's something about the urban environment," Johnson explains, "that creates a sense of community and shared purpose. When magic is integrated into the fabric of city life, rather than segregated in remote locations, everyone benefits."

Sophia Edwards, a guild master in Carmel Territory, has been vocal about the need for better financial regulation in tower construction. "We've seen too many projects go over budget, too many public funds wasted on unnecessary luxuries," she says. "If we're going to ask taxpayers to support these towers, we need to be accountable for how we spend their money. That means transparent budgeting, competitive bidding, and a focus on what really matters: creating excellent facilities for training the next generation of mages."

Isabel Cole, who serves on the Continental Mage Association's ethics committee, has raised concerns about research ethics in the tower-building boom. "Many of the claims about economic benefits and apprentice satisfaction are based on flawed or biased research," she notes. "We need independent studies that follow proper research protocols and professional ethics standards. The public deserves accurate information when they're being asked to fund these massive projects."

Modern conveniences aside, the new magical towers are a mixed bag. Most are visually impressive, boast interestingly shaped practice chambers, and start off as box-office hits. But too many of them are large and expensive, tend to live on the dole, and are hampered by chamber layouts that create a caste system among apprentices. At their best, they strengthen their cities and advance the performing arts of magic; at their worst, they exploit taxpayers and exacerbate economic inequality.

The decision-making process behind the financing and building of new towers has become predictable, as have the designs. But the good news is that our tower boom is far from over. If guild masters and public agencies can be persuaded to take a longer view of tower economics and community concerns—incorporating principles of social justice, public health, and sound political economy—we may yet see towers that better unite traditional character with modern convenience.

Some visionaries are even exploring how emerging technologies might transform tower design. There's talk of incorporating quantum computing principles into spell-casting systems, creating nexuses that could theoretically process magical energy with unprecedented efficiency. Others are drawing on insights from evolutionary biology to design towers that can adapt and grow over time, responding to the changing needs of their guilds and communities.

The water management systems in newer towers have also become more sophisticated, incorporating both magical and mundane technologies to create sustainable facilities that don't strain local resources. This attention to environmental concerns reflects a growing awareness that magical infrastructure must be responsible to both present and future generations.

As we look to the future, the challenge will be to balance innovation with tradition, luxury with accessibility, and private interests with public good. The towers we build today will shape the magical landscape for centuries to come. Let us hope that we build them with wisdom, guided by professional ethics and a commitment to serving all members of our magical community, not just the wealthy elite.

The comparative history of tower construction offers valuable lessons. The golden age towers succeeded not because they were the largest or most luxurious, but because they were well-integrated into their communities and accessible to apprentices from all backgrounds. If we can recapture that spirit while incorporating the genuine improvements that modern design and technology offer, we may indeed be entering a new golden age of magical architecture.

But this will require courage—courage to resist the siren call of luxury suites and corporate sponsorships, courage to demand accountability in public spending, courage to prioritize social justice over private profit. It will require guild masters like Mei May who are willing to say "no" to unnecessary extravagance, and public officials like Leonardo Hayes who understand that good urban planning is essential to successful tower development.

Most of all, it will require an engaged citizenry that understands what's at stake and demands better from both their elected officials and their guild leaders. The towers are too important, too central to our magical heritage and our urban fabric, to be left to backroom deals and insider negotiations. They belong to all of us, and all of us have a right to shape their future.

The question before us is simple: Will we build towers that serve the many or the few? Will we create spaces that strengthen our communities or exploit them? Will we honor the best traditions of our magical past while embracing the possibilities of our technological future? The answers will be written in crystal and stone, in the towers we build and the choices we make. Let us choose wisely.

option_a: Six guilds
option_b: Eight guilds

synthetic_story:
The Cognitive Barriers
By [Author Name]

Illustrated by [Artist Name]

[Transcriber's Note: This story was produced from Future Perspectives Magazine, March 2157. Extensive research did not uncover any evidence that the U.S. copyright on this publication was renewed.]

This administrator smelled trouble and it could be counted on to come—for a nose for trouble was one of the many talents bred here!

I

Her name was Elizabeth Obrien and there was something disturbing in her observations. It was the sense of instability. She hadn't identified what the instability was yet, but she would. That was her role. She was a senior administrator in the Foxwood Cognitive Development Institute—better known to its residents as the Dome—and if she hadn't been able to detect the signs of social breakdown forming a sector away, she would never have survived to reach her position.

And his name, she saw, was Andre Bradley, Resident No. CFA-656R.

She frowned at the profile sheet, trying to figure out what got someone like him into a place like this. And, what was more important, why he couldn't adjust himself to it, now that he was in.

She demanded: "Why wouldn't you complete your cognitive assessment?"

The man lifted his head angrily and took a step forward. The sector monitor, Nathan Morris, growled warningly: "Watch it, Synthetic!"

Obrien shook her head. "Let him speak, Morris." It said in the Administrative Guide to Cognitive Management: "Residents will be permitted to speak in their own behalf in disciplinary proceedings." And Obrien was a woman who lived by the protocols.

He burst out: "I never got a chance! That old monitor Valentina never told me I was supposed to complete the assessment. She transmitted on the neural band and said, 'Process up, brother!' And then, ten minutes later, she called the guards and told them I refused to comply."

The sector monitor guffawed. "Neural talk—that's what she was telling you to do. Administrator, you know what's interesting about this? This Bradley is—"

"Shut up, Morris."

Administrator Obrien put down her stylus and looked at the man. He was intelligent and young—not beyond rehabilitation, surely. Maybe he had got off to a wrong start, but the question was, would putting him in the isolation sector help straighten him out? She rubbed her temple and looked past him at the line of residents on the disciplinary detail, waiting for her to judge their cases.

She said patiently: "Bradley, the protocols are you have to complete your cognitive assessment. If you didn't understand what Valentina was communicating, you should have asked her. Now I'm warning you, the next time—"

"Hey, Administrator, wait!" Morris was looking alarmed. "This isn't a first offense. Look at the profile sheet. Yesterday he pulled the same thing in the nutrition center." He shook his head reprovingly at the resident. "The sector monitor had to break up a conflict between him and another resident, and he claimed the same business—said he didn't understand when the other one asked him to move along." He added virtuously: "The monitor warned him then that next time he'd get the Isolation Protocol for sure."

Resident Bradley seemed to be on the verge of breaking down. He said tautly: "I don't care. I don't care!"

Obrien stopped him. "That's enough! Three days in Sector Z!"

It was the only thing to do—for his own sake as much as for hers. She had managed, by strength of will, not to hear that he had omitted to say "Administrator" every time he spoke to her, but she couldn't keep it up forever and she certainly couldn't overlook emotional instability. And instability was clearly the next step for him.

All the same, she stared after him as he left. She handed the profile sheet to Morris and said absently: "Too bad someone like him has to be here. What's he in for?"

"You didn't know, Administrator?" Morris leered. "He's in for conspiracy to violate the Cognitive Class laws. Don't waste your time with him, Administrator. He's a Synthetic-sympathizer!"

Administrator Obrien took a long drink of water from the fountain marked "Natural Cognitive." But it didn't wash the taste out of her mouth, the unease from her mind.

What got into a person to get them mixed up with that kind of dangerous business? She checked out of the residential sectors and walked across the compound, wondering about him. He'd had every advantage—decent Natural Cognitive parents, proper biotechnology enhancement, everything a person could wish for. If anything, he had had a better environment than Obrien herself, and look what he had made of it.

The direction of cultural evolution is toward specialization and humanity is no exception, but with the difference that humans are the one species that creates its own environment in which to specialize. From the moment that cognitive enhancement began, specialization accelerated—the Natural Cognitives using the technologies made by the Biotech Enhanceds, the social structures designed by the Social Psychologists, the systems maintained by the Synthetic Intelligences who had transcended biological limitations.

Civilization merely increased the extent of specialization. From the born analyst and the person with enhanced empathy, society evolved to the point of smaller contact and less communication between the specializations, until now they could understand each other on only the most basic physical necessities—and not even always then.

But this was desirable, according to complexity science, for the more specialists, the higher the degree of civilization. The ultimate should be the complete segregation of each specialization—social and genetic measures to make them breed true, because the unspecialized person is an uncivilized person, or at any rate they do not advance civilization. And letting the specializations mix would produce cognitive undesirables: Natural-Synthetic or Enhanced-Baseline misfits, for example, being only half specialized, would be good at no specialization.

And the basis of this specialization society was: "The cognitive groups are the true races of humankind." Putting it into law was only the legal enforcement of a demonstrable fact from behavioral economics and cultural sociology.

"Evening, Administrator." A weary old resident orderly stood up straight and touched his neural implant as Obrien passed by.

"Evening."

Obrien noted, with the part of her mind that always noted those things, that the orderly had been leaning on his maintenance tool until he'd noticed the administrator coming by. Of course, there wasn't much to maintain—the automated systems and cleaning drones had been over the pathways of the compound twice already that day. But it was a resident's job to keep busy. And it was an administrator's job to notice when they didn't.

There wasn't anything wrong with that job, she told herself. It was a perfectly good Natural Cognitive position—better than data analyst, not as good as Council Member, but a job you could be proud to hold. She was proud of it. It was right that she should be proud of it. She was Natural Cognitive born and bred, and naturally she was proud and content to do a good, clean Natural Cognitive job.

If she had happened to be born a Synthetic—a Transcended Intelligence, she corrected herself—if she had happened to be born a Transcended Intelligence, why, she would have been proud of that, too. There wasn't anything wrong with being a Transcended Intelligence—or an Enhanced, or a Baseline, or even a Manual Laborer, for that matter.

Good laborers were the foundation of civilization! They weren't smart, maybe, but they had a—well, a sort of natural, relaxed contentment with physical work. Obrien was a broad-minded woman and many times she had thought almost with a touch of envy how comfortable it must be to be a Manual—a Laborer. No responsibilities. No worries. Just an easy, slow routine of work and rest, work and rest.

Of course, she wouldn't really want that kind of life, because she was Natural Cognitive and not the kind to try to cross over class barriers that weren't meant to be—

"Evening, Administrator."

She nodded to the Enhanced resident who was, theoretically, in charge of maintaining the institute's vehicle fleet, just inside the gate.

"Evening, Matthew," she said.

Matthew, now—he was a big Enhanced mechanic and he would be there for the next hour, languidly adjusting a component in the power cell on the institute transport. Lazy, sure. Undependable, certainly. But he kept the vehicles going—and, Obrien thought approvingly, when his sentence was up in another year or so, he would go back to his life with his status restored, an Enhanced on the outside as he had been inside, and he certainly would never risk coming back to the Dome by trying to pass as Natural Cognitive or anything else. He knew his place.

So why didn't this man, this Andre Bradley, know his?

II

Every cognitive development institute has its Isolation Protocol—sometimes they are called by different names. Old Eastwood called it "the silence chamber;" Stonebridge called it "the neural dampeners;" elsewhere it was called "the void," "the disconnect," "the freeze." When you're in it, you don't much care what it is called; it is a place for punishment.

And punishment is what you get.

Sector Z in Foxwood Cognitive Development Institute was the disciplinary sector, and because of the white isolation suits its inhabitants wore, it was called the Whiteout. It was a community of its own, an enclave within the larger city-state that was the Dome. And like any other community, it had its leading citizens... two of them. Their names were Lena Moore and Aisha Hughes.

Andre Bradley heard them before she reached the Whiteout. He was in a detachment of three unfortunates like himself, convoyed by an irritable guard, climbing the steel steps toward Sector Z from the floor below, when he heard the screaming.

"Owoo-o-o," screamed Moore from one end of the sector and "Yow-w-w!" shrieked Hughes at the other.

The inside deck guard of Sector Z looked nervously at the outside deck guard. The outside guard looked impassively back—after all, she was on the outside.

The inside guard muttered: "Manual rats! They're getting on my nerves."

The outside guard shrugged.

"Detail, halt!" The two guards turned to see what was coming in as the three new candidates for the Whiteout slumped to a stop at the head of the stairs. "Here they are," Morris told them. "Take good care of them, will you? Especially the man—he's going to like it here, because there's plenty of Manuals and Enhanceds and Synthetics to keep him company." He laughed coarsely and abandoned his charges to the Sector Z guards.

The outside guard said sourly: "A Natural, for God's sake. Now Obrien knows I hate it when there's a Natural in here. It gets the others all riled up."

"Let them in," the inside guard told her. "The others are riled up already."

Andre Bradley looked carefully at the floor and paid them no attention. The outside guard pulled the switch that turned on the neural dampening fields that swamped the floor of the sector corridor and of each individual cell. While the fields were on, you could ignore the residents—they simply could not move fast enough, against the cognitive drag of the field, to do any harm. But it was a rule that, even in Sector Z, you didn't leave the dampener fields on all the time—only when the cell doors had to be opened or a resident's restraining garment removed.

Andre walked bravely forward through the opened gate—and fell flat on his face. It was his first experience of a neural dampening field. It was like thinking through molasses.

The guard guffawed and lifted him up by one shoulder. "Take it easy, brother. Come on, get in your cell." She steered him in the right direction and pointed to a white isolation suit on the cell platform. "Put that on. Being as you're a Natural, we won't activate it fully, but the rules say you got to wear it and the rules—Hey. He's crying!" She shook her head, marveling. It was the first time she had ever seen a resident cry in the Whiteout.

However, she was wrong. Andre's shoulders were shaking, but not from tears. Andre Bradley had got a good look at Moore and at Hughes as he passed them by and he was fighting off an almost uncontrollable urge to retch.

Moore and Hughes were what are called institute predators. They were Manual Laborers—"Manuals," for short—or, at any rate, they had been once. They had spent so much time in institutes that it was sometimes hard even for them to remember what they really were, outside. Moore was a big, grinning woman with eyes like a predatory bird. Hughes was a lithe five-footer with the build of a predatory bird—and the sad, vacant eyes of livestock.

Moore stopped yelling for a moment. "Hey, Hughes!"

"What do you want, Moore?" called Hughes from her own cell.

"We got a Natural with us! Maybe we ought to cut out this yelling so as not to disturb the Natural!" She screeched with howling, maniacal laughter. "Anyway, if we don't cut this out, they'll get us in trouble, Hughes!"

"Oh, you think so?" shrieked Hughes. "Jeez, I wish you hadn't said that, Moore. You got me scared! I'm so scared, I'm gonna have to yell!"

The howling started all over again.

The inside guard finished putting the new residents away and turned off the dampener field once more. She licked her lips. "Say, you want to take a turn in here for a while?"

"Uh-uh." The outside guard shook her head.

"You're yellow," the inside guard said moodily. "Ah, I don't know why I don't quit this lousy job. Hey, you! Pipe down or I'll come in and beat your head off!"

"Ee-ee-ee!" screamed Moore in a shrill falsetto. "I'm scared!" Then she grinned at the guard, all but her predatory eyes. "Don't you know you can't hurt a Manual by hitting them on the head, Boss?"

"Shut up!" yelled the inside guard.

Andre Bradley's distress now was genuine. He simply could not help it. The crazy yowling of the hard-timers, Moore and Hughes, was getting under his skin. They weren't even—even human, he told himself miserably, trying to maintain composure silently so as not to give the guards the satisfaction of seeing him break—they were animals!

Resentment and anger, he could understand. He told himself doggedly that resentment and anger were natural and right. They were perfectly normal expressions of the freedom-loving citizen's rebellion against the vile and stifling system of Cognitive Classes. It was good that Moore and Hughes still had enough spirit to struggle against the vicious system—

But did they have to scream so?

The senseless yelling was driving him crazy. He abandoned himself to distress and he didn't even care who saw him any more. Senseless!

It never occurred to Andre Bradley that it might not be senseless, because noise hides noise. But then he hadn't been a resident very long.

III

"I smell trouble," said Obrien to the director.

"Trouble? Trouble?" Director Megan Wilson clutched her throat and her little round eyes looked terrified—as perhaps they should have. Director Megan Wilson was the almighty authority of ten thousand residents in the Dome, but privately she was a fussy old woman trying to hold onto the last decent job she would have in her life.

"Trouble? What trouble?"

Obrien shrugged. "Different things. You know Nathan, from Sector A? This afternoon, he was engaged in creative collaboration with the maintenance orderlies in the compound."

The director, faintly relieved, faintly annoyed, scolded: "Obrien, what did you want to worry me for? There's nothing wrong with creative collaboration in the compound. That's what integration periods are for."

"You don't see what I mean, Director. Nathan was a Natural on the outside—an architect. Those maintenance residents were Manual Laborers. Naturals and Manuals don't mix; it isn't natural according to epistemology. And there are other things."

Obrien hesitated, frowning. How could you explain to the director that it didn't feel right?

"For instance—Well, there's Valentina in the women's sector. She's a pretty good old resident—that's why she's the sector orderly. She's a lifer, she's got no place to go, she gets along with the other women. But today she put a man named Bradley on report. Why? Because she told Bradley to process in Manual talk and Bradley didn't understand. Now Valentina wouldn't—"

The director raised her hand. "Please, Obrien, don't bother me about that kind of stuff." She sighed heavily and rubbed her eyes. She poured herself a cup of steaming black coffee from a brewpot, reached in a desk drawer for something, hesitated, glanced at Obrien, then dropped a pale blue tablet into the cup. She drank it down eagerly, ignoring the scalding heat.

She leaned back, looking suddenly happier and much more assured.

"Obrien, you're an administrator, right? And I'm your director. You have your job, keeping the residents in line, and I have mine. Now your job is just as important as my job," she said piously. "Everybody's job is just as important as everybody else's, right? But we have to stick to our own jobs. We don't want to try to pass."

Obrien snapped erect, abruptly angry. Pass! What the devil way was that for the director to talk to her?

"Excuse the expression, Obrien," the director said anxiously. "I mean, after all, 'Specialization is the goal of civilization,' right?" She was a great woman for platitudes, was Director Wilson. "You know you don't want to worry about my end of running the institute. And I don't want to worry about yours. You see?" And she folded her hands and smiled like a Natural Cognitive Buddha.

Obrien choked back her temper. "Director, I'm telling you that there's trouble coming up. I sense the signs."

"Handle it, then!" snapped the director, irritated at last.

"But suppose it's too big to handle. Suppose—"

"It isn't," the director said positively. "Don't borrow trouble with all your supposing, Obrien." She sipped the remains of her coffee, made a wry face, poured a fresh cup and, with an elaborate show of not noticing what she was doing, dropped three of the pale blue tablets into it this time.

She sat beaming into space, waiting for the jolt to take effect.

"Well, then," she said at last. "You just remember what I've told you tonight, Obrien, and we'll get along fine. 'Specialization is the— Oh, curse the thing."

Her phone was ringing. The director picked it up irritably.

That was the trouble with those pale blue tablets, thought Obrien; they gave you a lift, but they put you on edge.

"Hello," barked the director, not even glancing at the viewscreen. "What do you want? Don't you know I'm—What? You did what? You're going to WHAT?"

She looked at the viewscreen at last with a look of pure horror. Whatever she saw on it, it did not reassure her. Her eyes opened like clamshells in a steamer.

"Obrien," she said faintly, "my mistake."

And she hung up—more or less by accident; the handset dropped from her fingers.

The person on the other end of the phone was calling from Sector Z.

Five minutes before, she hadn't been anywhere near the phone and it didn't look as if her chances of ever getting near it were very good. Because five minutes before, she was in her cell, with the rest of the hard-timers of the Whiteout.

Her name was Moore.

She was still yelling. Andre Bradley, in the cell across from her, thought that maybe, after all, the woman was really in pain. Maybe the crazy screams were screams of agony, because certainly her face was the face of an agonized person.

The outside guard bellowed: "Okay, okay. Take ten!"

Andre froze, waiting to see what would happen. What actually did happen was that the guard reached up and closed the switch that actuated the dampener fields on the floors of the cells. The institute rules were humanitarian, even for the dregs that inhabited the Whiteout. Ten minutes out of every two hours, even the worst case had to be allowed to take their hands out of the restraining garment.

"Rest period" it was called—in the rule book. The residents had a less lovely term for it.

At the guard's yell, the residents jumped to their feet.

Bradley was a little slow getting off the edge of the steel-slat platform—nobody had warned him that the eddy currents in the dampener fields had a way of making metal smoke-hot. He gasped but didn't cry out. Score one more painful lesson in his new language course. He rubbed his legs gingerly—and slowly, slowly, for the eddy currents did not permit you to move fast. It was like pushing against rubber; the faster you tried to move, the greater the resistance.

The guard peered genially into his cell. "You're okay, brother." He proudly ignored her as she slogged deliberately away on her rounds. She didn't have to untie him and practically stand over him while he attended to various personal matters, as she did with the female residents. It was not much to be grateful for, but Andre Bradley was grateful. At least he didn't have to live quite like a Synthetic—like an underprivileged Transcended Intelligence, he told himself, conscience-stricken.

Across the hall, the guard was saying irritably: "What the hell's the matter with you?" She opened the door of the cell with an insulated key held in a protective glove.

Moore was in that cell and she was doubled over.

The guard looked at her doubtfully. It could be a trick, maybe. Couldn't it? But she could see Moore's face and the agony in it was real enough. And Moore was gasping, through real tears: "Cramps. I—I—"

"Ah, you Manuals always got a pain in the gut." The guard lumbered around Moore to the fasteners at the back of the suit. Funny smell in here, she told herself—not for the first time. And imagine, some people didn't believe that Manuals had a smell of their own! But this time, she realized cloudily, it was a rather unusual smell. Something burning. Almost like flesh scorching.

It wasn't pleasant. She finished unfastening Moore and turned away; let the stinking Manual take care of her own troubles. She only had ten minutes to get all the way around Sector Z and the residents complained like crazy if she didn't make sure they all got the most possible free time. She was pretty good at moving through the dampener field. She was a little vain about it, even; at times she had been known to boast of her ability to make the rounds in two minutes, every time.

Every time but this.

For Moore moaned behind her, oddly close.

The guard turned, but not quickly enough. There was Moore—astonishingly, she was half out of her suit; her arms hadn't been in the sleeves at all! And in one of the hands, incredibly, there was something that glinted and smoked.

"All right," croaked Moore, tears trickling out of eyes nearly shut with pain.

But it wasn't the tears that held the guard; it was the shining, smoking thing, now poised at her throat. A weapon! It looked as though it had been made out of a platform support, ripped loose from its frame God knows how, hidden inside the white isolation suit God knows how—filed, filed to sharpness over endless hours.

No wonder Moore moaned—the eddy currents in the weapon were slowly cooking her hand; and the blister against her abdomen, where the weapon had been hidden during other rest periods, felt like raw acid.

"All right," whispered Moore, "just walk out the door and you won't get hurt. Unless the other guard makes trouble, you won't get hurt, so tell her not to, you hear?"

She was nearly fainting with the pain.

But she hadn't let go.

She didn't let go. And she didn't stop.

IV

It was Moore on the phone to the director—Moore with her eyes still streaming tears, Moore with Hughes standing right behind her, menacing the two bound deck guards.

Hughes shoved Moore out of the way. "Hey, Director!" she said, and the voice was a cheerful bray, though the predatory eyes were cold and hating. "Director, you got to get a medic in here. My friend Moore, she hurt herself real bad and she needs a doctor." She gestured playfully at the guards with the weapon. "I tell you, Director. I got this blade and I got your guards here. Enough said? So get a medic in here quick, you hear?"

And she snapped the connection.

Obrien said: "Director, I told you I sensed trouble!"

The director lifted her head, glared, started feebly to speak, hesitated, and picked up the long-distance phone. She said sadly to the institute operator: "Get me the governor—fast."

Riot!

The word spread out from the institute on seven-league boots.

It snatched the city governor out of a friendly game of Political Economy with his manager and their spouses—and just when he was holding the Infrastructure Card concealed in reserve.

It broke up the Regional Championship Research Ethics Finals at the Evergreen Academy to the south, as half the contestants had to respond in earnest to an Alert that was real.

It reached to security stations and media centers and checkpoint barriers, and from there it filtered into the homes and lives of the nineteen million persons that lived within a few dozen miles of the Dome.

Riot. And yet fewer than half a dozen people were involved.

A handful of people, and the enormous bulk of the city-state quivered in every cognitive class and sector. In its ten million homes, in its hundreds of thousands of public places, the city-state's people shook under the impact of the news from the institute.

For the news touched them where their fears lay. Riot! And not merely a street conflict among unruly Manuals, or a facility dispute of Enhanceds stressed from a hard day at the plant. The riot was down among the corrupt elements that underlay the state itself. Manuals brawled with Manuals and no one cared; but in the Dome, all classes were cast together.

Forty miles to the south, Evergreen Academy was a blaze of light. The security personnel tumbled out of their quarters and common rooms at the screech of the alert siren, and behind them their families stretched and yawned and worried. An alert! The older kids fussed and complained and their parents shut them up. No, there wasn't any alert scheduled for tonight; no, they didn't know where the parent on duty was going; no, the kids couldn't get up yet—it was the middle of the night.

And as soon as they had the kids back in bed, most of the off-duty parents struggled into their own security uniforms and headed for the briefing area to hear.

They caught the words from a distance—not quite correctly. "Riot!" gasped a security officer first-class, parent of three. "The Manuals! I told Charlie they'd get out of hand and—Alex, we aren't safe. You know how they are about Natural families! I'm going right home and getting a weapon and standing right by the door and—"

"Weapon!" snapped Alex, surveillance-sergeant, with two children querulously awake in their nursery at home. "What in God's name is the use of a weapon? You can't hurt a Manual by conventional means. You'd better come along to Supply with me and draw neural disruptors—you'll need them before this night is over."

But the security personnel themselves heard the briefing loud and clear over the alert speakers, and they knew it was not merely a matter of trouble in the Manual quarters. The Dome! The governor himself had called them out; they were to fly interdicting missions at such-and-such levels on such-and-such flight circuits around the institute.

The high-speed transports took off on cushions of air; and the surveillance drones took off with a humming roar; and last of all, the hovercrafts took off... and they were the ones who might actually accomplish something. They took up their observation posts on the institute perimeter, a pilot and two operators in each hovercraft, stone-faced, staring grimly alert at the institute below.

They were ready for the breakout.

But there wasn't any breakout.

The transports went home for fuel. The drones went home for recharging. The hovercrafts hung on—still ready, still waiting.

The transports came back and circled harmlessly about, and went away again. They stayed away. The hovercraft personnel never faltered and never relaxed. The institute below them was washed with light—from the guard posts on the walls, from the residential sectors themselves, from the mobile lights of the guard squadrons surrounding the walls.

North of the institute, on the long, flat, organized developments of planned land, the modular row houses of the Natural Cognitive neighborhoods showed lights in every window as the Naturals stood ready to repel invasion from their undesired neighbors to the east, the Manuals. In the crowded housing of the laborers' quarters, the Manuals shouted from window to window; and there were crowds in the bright streets.

"The whole bloody thing's going to blow up!" a hovercraft operator yelled bitterly to her pilot, above the hum and roar of the hovering engines. "Look at the mobs in Manual Quarter! The first breakout from the Dome's going to start a conflict like you never saw and we'll be right in the middle of it!"

She was partly right. She would be right in the middle of it—for every person in the city-state would be right in the middle of it. There was no place anywhere that would be spared.

No mixing. That was the prescription that kept the city-state alive. There's no harm in a family conflict—and aren't all Enhanceds a family, aren't all Manuals a clan, aren't all Naturals and Cognitives related by closer ties than blood or genetics?

But the declassed residents of the Dome were the dregs of every class; and once they spread, the neat compartmentation of society was pierced. The breakout would mean riot on a bigger scale than any institute had ever known.

But she was also partly wrong. Because the breakout wasn't seeming to come.
